Ruth discovers that she is pregnant and secretly considers an abortion because the family cannot afford another child, putting a five-dollar down payment on one. Mama argues against it, and the phrase "the part that's already living" comes up when they discuss it. The new house gives Ruth hope.

**Beneatha's atheism and medical ambitions**
Beneatha declares that God does not exist and that "there is only man and it is he who makes miracles," and Mama slaps her and makes her repeat "In my mother's house there is still God." Beneatha says she became interested in medicine as a child after watching a boy named Rufus get hurt in a sledding accident. After the money is lost she nearly gives up on becoming a doctor.

**George Murchison**
Beneatha's wealthy, assimilated boyfriend, who dismisses her interest in African heritage. Walter tries to talk "investments" with him and mocks his white shoes, which George calls the "college style." Beneatha rejects George for the more idealistic Asagai, and she mocks Walter's business dreams by calling him "Symbol of a Rising Class" and "Titan of the System."

**Tilting at windmills**
The most famous episode: Don Quixote charges a row of windmills, believing they are giants, despite Sancho Panza's protests. His lance catches in a sail and he is thrown, and he blames an enchanter for turning the giants into windmills. It has become the standard giveaway and the source of the phrase "tilting at windmills."

**The Knight of the White Moon (Samson Carrasco)**
The bachelor Samson Carrasco, a neighbor, tries to cure Don Quixote by defeating him in a joust. He fails the first time as the Knight of the Mirrors, then succeeds in Barcelona disguised as the Knight of the White Moon. He makes Quixote promise to return home and give up knight-errantry for a year. Quixote falls ill with a fever, renounces the books of chivalry, and dies as plain Alonso Quixano.

**Sancho Panza**
Don Quixote's plump, practical peasant neighbor, who becomes his squire in exchange for the promise of an island to govern. He rides his donkey Dapple (which the convict Gines de Pasamonte steals at one point) and dubs his master the "Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance."

**Dulcinea del Toboso**
The lady to whom Don Quixote dedicates his deeds. She is really a peasant farm girl, Aldonza Lorenzo, from the village of El Toboso. He attacks merchants from Toledo who refuse to swear to her matchless beauty. In Part Two, Sancho passes off a coarse peasant girl as Dulcinea and convinces Quixote that she has been enchanted.

**Rocinante**
Don Quixote's broken-down old nag, which he names as a proper knight's steed. In the final joust, the Knight of the White Moon's horse is "much swifter than Rocinante."

**The burning of the library**
Alonso Quixano's brain "dries up" from "so little sleeping and so much reading" of chivalric romances. While he sleeps, the priest (the curate) and Master Nicholas the barber, helped by his niece and housekeeper, examine and burn his library, sparing a few books such as Amadis of Gaul. They then wall up the room, and his niece tells him that an enchanter riding a dragon from a cloud carried the books away.

**The blanket tossing and the Balsam of Fierabras**
At an inn he believes is a castle, Don Quixote brews the magical healing Balsam of Fierabras, which makes both him and Sancho violently sick. When Quixote leaves without paying, claiming knights-errant never pay at inns, the guests toss Sancho up and down in a blanket.

**The Helmet of Mambrino**
Don Quixote attacks a traveling barber and seizes his brass shaving basin, believing it to be the enchanted golden Helmet of Mambrino from chivalric legend. He wears the basin on his head.

**Cide Hamete Benengeli**
The fictional Moorish (Arab) historian whose manuscript the narrator claims to have found in Toledo and had translated. The novel is presented as a translation of his work.

**The Duke and Duchess, Barataria, and the 3,300 lashes**
In Part Two, a bored Duke and Duchess who have read Part One play elaborate pranks on the pair. They make Sancho governor of the "island" of Barataria, where he judges cases wisely. A servant dressed as Merlin declares that Sancho must whip himself 3,300 times to disenchant Dulcinea.

**Part Two, the "third sally," and Avellaneda's false sequel**
The novel was published in two parts, in 1605 and 1615. Part Two describes Quixote's third sally and has characters who have read Part One. It was partly written to answer a spurious "Second Part" published by "Avellaneda," which Cervantes mocks in the prologue with the story of a madman who inflates a dog through a hollow reed. At the end, Quixote's will disinherits his niece if she marries a man who reads books of chivalry.

**Marcela and Grisostomo**
The student-shepherd Grisostomo dies for love of the beautiful shepherdess Marcela. At his funeral, the traveler Vivaldo compares the knightly life to a monk's and reads Grisostomo's "Song of Despair." Marcela appears and defends her freedom, arguing that she had no obligation to love him just because he loved her.

**The galley slaves and Master Pedro's puppet show**
Don Quixote frees a chain of galley slaves, who stone him when he orders them to report to Dulcinea. Their leader, Gines de Pasamonte, later reappears as the puppeteer Master Pedro, who has a fortune-telling ape. Quixote suspects the ape of a pact with the Devil and destroys the puppet show, mistaking the puppet Moors for real enemies.

**Cardenio, the wineskins, and "The Man Who Was Recklessly Curious"**
In the Sierra Morena, Quixote meets Cardenio, a ragged man driven mad by love for Luscinda. At the inn, the priest reads aloud the interpolated tale "The Man Who Was Recklessly Curious," in which Anselmo has his friend Lothario test his wife Camilla's fidelity. The reading is interrupted when a sleepwalking Quixote slashes wineskins, thinking he is fighting a giant.

**Literary responses: Borges, Kafka, and Lennox**
Jorge Luis Borges wrote "Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote," about a man who rewrites the novel word for word, and the essay "Partial Magic in the Quixote." Franz Kafka's parable "The Truth about Sancho Panza" calls Quixote Sancho's "demon." Charlotte Lennox's 1752 novel The Female Quixote features Arabella as a female counterpart.

**Okonkwo and Chinua Achebe**
Okonkwo is the proud, hot-tempered Igbo protagonist of Things Fall Apart (1958), the debut novel of Nigerian author Chinua Achebe. A self-made man driven by a fear of failure and weakness, he is the most common giveaway for the novel, which traces his rise and downfall in his village of Umuofia.

**Ikemefuna**
A boy from the neighboring village of Mbaino who is given to Umuofia as compensation for the murder of a Umuofia woman and lives in Okonkwo's household for three years, calling him father. When the Oracle decrees his death, Okonkwo strikes the fatal blow with his machete despite the elder Ezeudu's warning not to take part, because he is afraid of looking weak.

**Amalinze the Cat**
A wrestler nicknamed "the Cat" because his back never touched the ground. Okonkwo first gains fame by throwing him in a wrestling match; his second wife, Ekwefi, later leaves her first husband for Okonkwo after watching him wrestle.

**The Week of Peace**
A sacred week before planting in Umuofia during which no harsh word may be spoken. Okonkwo breaks it by beating his youngest wife, Ojiugo, when she neglects to cook his meal, and he is fined by the priest of the earth goddess Ani.

**Okonkwo's exile (Ezeudu's funeral)**
At the funeral of the elder Ezeudu, Okonkwo's gun accidentally explodes and kills Ezeudu's sixteen-year-old son. This "female" (inadvertent) crime forces Okonkwo and his family into a seven-year exile in Mbanta, his mother's village.

**Nwoye / Isaac**
Okonkwo's eldest son, whom he beats and considers lazy and effeminate. Disturbed by Ikemefuna's death, Nwoye is drawn to the Christian missionaries' hymns and converts, taking the name Isaac; he is later sent to a teachers' training college in Umuru.

**Okonkwo's suicide and "The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger"**
After the clan fails to rise against the colonists, Okonkwo kills a court messenger sent to break up a town meeting, realizing that Umuofia "would not go to war," then hangs himself. Because suicide is an abomination, his clansmen cannot touch the body, and Obierika asks the District Commissioner's men to cut it down. The novel ends with the Commissioner deciding Okonkwo merits "perhaps not a whole chapter but a reasonable paragraph" in his planned book, The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger.

**Unoka**
Okonkwo's father, a lazy, debt-ridden flute player who never had enough cowries and was considered an agbala (a man with no title). He died of a swelling in the stomach and was left to die in the Evil Forest. Okonkwo's whole life is a reaction against his father's weakness.

**Ezinma, Ekwefi, and Chielo**
Ezinma is the only surviving child of Ekwefi, who had lost nine (Ezinma is the tenth) children in infancy, a misfortune blamed on an ogbanje, a spirit child who keeps dying and being reborn; Ezinma's buried iyi-uwa (spirit stone) is dug up to break the cycle. Chielo, priestess of Agbala, the Oracle of the Hills and the Caves, carries Ezinma on her back through nine villages to the oracle's cave at night, while Ekwefi follows. Okonkwo wishes Ezinma had been born a boy.

**Mr. Brown and Reverend James Smith**
Two Christian missionaries. The tolerant Mr. Brown builds a school and a hospital and has friendly debates about religion with the clansman Akunna. His successor, the strict Reverend James Smith, is uncompromising, and his zealous convert Enoch provokes the clan's anger.

**Enoch unmasks an egwugwu**
The fanatical convert Enoch tears the mask off an egwugwu, a masked ancestral spirit, which is a grave sacrilege. In response the egwugwu burn down Mr. Smith's church, and the District Commissioner later jails Okonkwo and other leaders, holding them for a ransom of two hundred bags of cowries.

**Ekwefi and the banana leaves**
Ekwefi, Okonkwo's second wife, cuts leaves from a banana tree to wrap food before a festival. Okonkwo beats her, and when she mutters about "guns that never shot," he fires his gun at her and misses.

**The tortoise and the birds**
Ekwefi tells Ezinma the folktale of Tortoise, who borrows feathers to attend a feast in the sky, renames himself "All of you," and eats the food meant for the birds. The angry birds take back their feathers, and Tortoise falls onto the hard objects in his compound, explaining why his shell is not smooth. Okonkwo also remembers his mother's tale of Mosquito and Ear.

**The "iron horse" and Abame**
The people of Abame kill the first white man they see, riding a bicycle they call an "iron horse," and tie it to their sacred tree. In retaliation, white soldiers massacre the village during market day, a story Obierika brings to Okonkwo during his exile.

**No Longer at Ease and the title's source**
The novel's title comes from W. B. Yeats's poem "The Second Coming." Its sequel, No Longer at Ease, takes its title from T. S. Eliot's "Journey of the Magi" and follows Okonkwo's grandson Obi, an English-educated civil servant who loves the osu (outcast) Clara and takes bribes. Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's short story "The Headstrong Historian" responds to Things Fall Apart by centering the women who stay in its background.

**Snow Country**
Kawabata's most famous novel, set in a remote hot-spring town in Japan's snowy western mountains (the town is identified with Yuzawa). It follows a Tokyo visitor's doomed love affair with a local geisha. It was central to his 1968 Nobel Prize in Literature, the first won by a Japanese writer.

**Shimamura**
The idle, wealthy protagonist of Snow Country. He calls himself an expert on Western ballet and writes about it, even though he has never seen a ballet performed. Over several visits to the hot-spring town, he slowly realizes he cannot truly return Komako's love.

**Komako**
The passionate geisha in Snow Country who has an affair with Shimamura. She taught herself the shamisen by practicing alone and copying music broadcasts. Shimamura notices the shift in their relationship when he starts calling her a "good woman" instead of a "good girl."

**The Master of Go**
Kawabata's semi-fictional novel based on his own newspaper reporting of the 1938 "retirement game" of Go. The match, played on a 19-by-19 board, lasted about six months and pitted the aging master against a younger challenger. It is narrated by the reporter Uragami, Kawabata's stand-in.

**Milky Way and the warehouse fire**
The famous ending of Snow Country. A fire breaks out in a former silkworm-cocoon warehouse, and Yoko falls from the balcony while Komako rushes to carry her out. Shimamura stumbles and feels "the Milky Way flow down inside him with a roar." The novel never makes clear whether Yoko is dead or only unconscious.

**Thousand Cranes**
A novel built around the Japanese tea ceremony, in which the young Kikuji Mitani is drawn into the lives of his late father's mistresses. The title refers to the thousand-crane pattern on the kerchief (furoshiki) carried by Yukiko Inamura, a young woman proposed to Kikuji as a bride.

**Honinbo Shusai and Otake**
The opponents in The Master of Go. Shusai, the aging Meijin (Master), loses his retirement game to the young challenger Otake, a fictionalized version of the real player Minoru Kitani. Shusai dies about a year after the match.

**Sealed move (Black 121)**
The controversial move in The Master of Go. Otake sealed Black 121 at the end of a session, a tactical maneuver that outraged Shusai and seemed to violate the spirit of the game. The game ended with Black 237.

**Mrs. Ota and Kikuji**
In Thousand Cranes, Mrs. Ota, the mistress of Kikuji's late father, begins an affair with Kikuji and later kills herself, possibly with sleeping pills. Kikuji then becomes involved with her daughter Fumiko. Fumiko breaks a white Shino bowl stained with her mother's lipstick and then vanishes.

**The Sound of the Mountain**
A novel about the aging Shingo Ogata, who hears a rumbling from the mountain at night and takes it as an omen of death. He is troubled by his son Shuichi's affair with a war widow and by his own tender feelings for his daughter-in-law Kikuko. The novel ends with a proposal for a family trip to see the autumn maples.

**"The Dancing Girl of Izu"**
An early story about a student on a walking tour of the Izu Peninsula who falls for a young drum-carrying dancer in a troupe of traveling performers. When he sees her run naked from a public bath and wave to him, he realizes she is "a mere child" and laughs with relief.

**Yoko**
The second woman of Snow Country. Shimamura first sees her eye floating in the train window as a reflection, while she tends to the ailing Yukio, the son of Komako's music teacher. Her "beautiful, almost sad" voice haunts Shimamura until she falls in the warehouse fire.

**Palm-of-the-Hand Stories**
Kawabata's collection of very short stories written over his whole career. It includes "The Grasshopper and the Bell Cricket," in which children hunt insects with homemade paper lanterns, and "The Pomegranate," in which Kimiko holds onto the fruit her brother touched before leaving for war. Kawabata also condensed Snow Country into one of these stories.

**Chikako Kurimoto**
A tea ceremony teacher in Thousand Cranes and a former mistress of Kikuji's father. She has a large black birthmark on her breast, an image that haunts Kikuji. She meddles in his life by pushing his marriage to Yukiko Inamura.

**The House of the Sleeping Beauties**
A novella in which Old Eguchi repeatedly visits a secret inn. There, elderly men pay to spend the night beside drugged, naked young women who never wake. The book is a meditation on age, memory, and desire.

**The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle**
Murakami's sprawling 1994–95 novel, the most common title clue for him. It opens with the unemployed Toru Okada searching for his missing cat at the request of his wife Kumiko, who soon disappears as well; the cat is named Noboru Wataya after Kumiko's sinister politician brother.

**Norwegian Wood**
Murakami's 1987 breakthrough bestseller, named after the Beatles song. It opens with Toru Watanabe on a plane landing in Hamburg, where hearing a cover of the song makes him remember his college years in 1960s Tokyo.

**Toru Watanabe, Naoko, and Midori**
The love triangle at the center of Norwegian Wood. The fragile Naoko, whose boyfriend Kizuki (Toru's best friend) killed himself, withdraws to a sanatorium in the mountains where Toru visits her, while the outgoing Midori offers Toru a different life; Naoko eventually commits suicide as well.

**1Q84**
Murakami's longest novel (2009–10), whose title puns on George Orwell's 1984, since the Japanese word for nine ("kyu") sounds like the letter Q. Its two protagonists, Aomame and Tengo, find themselves in an alternate 1984 Tokyo with two moons in the sky, and the book ends with the two of them leaving that world together.

**Janáček's Sinfonietta**
The piece of music playing on the radio of a taxi stuck in traffic at the opening of 1Q84. Aomame then climbs out of the taxi and down an emergency stairway off the expressway, entering the alternate reality.

**Air Chrysalis and the Little People**
Air Chrysalis is a novel within 1Q84, told by the dyslexic teenager Fuka-Eri and rewritten by the math teacher and aspiring writer Tengo. It describes the supernatural "Little People." Fuka-Eri's father is the Leader of the religious cult Sakigake, which grew out of the Takashima commune; Aomame is sent to kill the Leader by the Dowager.

**Kafka on the Shore**
Murakami's 2002 novel whose odd and even chapters follow two storylines. The odd chapters follow a fifteen-year-old runaway who renames himself Kafka after Franz Kafka, has an alter ego called "the boy named Crow," and hides in Miss Saeki's library with the help of Oshima. The even chapters follow Nakata, an elderly, mentally impaired man who can talk to cats.

**Johnnie Walker**
The cat-killer in Kafka on the Shore who takes the form of the whisky-label figure and kills cats to make a flute out of their souls. Nakata kills him, after which fish rain from the sky. Another abstract figure, appearing as Colonel Sanders, helps the truck driver Hoshino find the "entrance stone."

**The Thieving Magpie**
The Rossini overture the narrator listens to while cooking spaghetti at the opening of The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle; he remarks that its length is the perfect time to cook pasta. "The Thieving Magpie" is also the title of the novel's first part, and the opening chapter first appeared as a story in The Elephant Vanishes.

**Lieutenant Mamiya and the well**
In The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle, the veteran Lieutenant Mamiya tells Toru of his service in Manchukuo, of watching a fellow officer skinned alive by "Boris the Manskinner," and of his time at the bottom of a dry well. Toru himself later sits at the bottom of a dry well and comes out with a blue-black mark on his cheek.

**May Kasahara, Malta and Creta Kano, Nutmeg and Cinnamon**
Supporting characters in The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle. May Kasahara is a morbid teenage girl who writes letters to Toru; the clairvoyant sisters Malta and Creta Kano help in the search, with Creta calling herself a "prostitute of the mind"; Nutmeg is drawn to Toru's mark, and her mute son Cinnamon keeps a secret computer archive titled "The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle."

**Trilogy of the Rat and Hear the Wind Sing**
Murakami's early sequence: Hear the Wind Sing (1979), his first novel, in which the narrator spends a summer drinking with his friend "the Rat" at J's Bar and meets a nine-fingered girl; Pinball, 1973, involving a translator's hunt for a three-flipper "Spaceship" pinball machine; and A Wild Sheep Chase. Murakami said he decided to write Hear the Wind Sing while watching Dave Hilton hit a double at a baseball game, and the first novel features the invented writer Derek Hartfield. The first two were republished in English as Wind/Pinball in 2015.

**A Wild Sheep Chase**
The 1982 novel concluding the Trilogy of the Rat proper (Dance Dance Dance is a later sequel). After the narrator publishes a pastoral photograph sent by the Rat, the right-hand man of "the Boss," a dying man with a blood cyst in his brain, forces him to find a sheep with a star-shaped mark on its back. His girlfriend with extraordinary ears leads him to the Dolphin Hotel and the Sheep Professor, and the search ends near the Hokkaido town of Junitaki.

**Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World**
A 1985 novel alternating between two worlds. In "Hard-Boiled Wonderland," a "Calcutec" who uses his brain to encrypt data is threatened by data-stealing "Semiotecs" and dates a very hungry librarian. In "The End of the World," a man reads old dreams from unicorn skulls in a walled town where people lose their minds once their shadows die.

**After Dark, Sputnik Sweetheart, and Killing Commendatore**
Other Murakami novels used as clues. After Dark opens at a Denny's where Mari is reading and involves the beating of a Chinese prostitute at a love hotel. Sputnik Sweetheart is narrated by the schoolteacher "K," whose beloved Sumire disappears on a Greek island. Killing Commendatore follows a painter who searches for the missing girl Mariye. His short stories include "On Seeing the 100% Perfect Girl One Beautiful April Morning."

**Gitanjali ("Song Offerings")**
Tagore's most famous poetry collection, a book of devotional lyrics addressed to God. It was first published in Bengali in 1910, and Tagore's own English prose translation followed in 1912. That English version led to his 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature, which made him the first non-European, and first Asian, laureate. It is the standard giveaway for Tagore.

**"Thou hast made me endless, such is thy pleasure"**
The opening line of the English Gitanjali. The first poem goes on to describe the poet as a "frail vessel" that God empties and fills again with fresh life, and as a "little flute of reed" through which God plays "melodies eternally new."

**"Where the Mind Is Without Fear"**
Poem 35 of Gitanjali, a prayer for a free India. It imagines a place "where the head is held high," "where knowledge is free," "where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls," "where words come out from the depth of truth," "where tireless striving stretches its arms towards perfection," and "where the clear stream of reason has not lost its way." It ends: "Into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake."

**W. B. Yeats's introduction**
The Irish poet William Butler Yeats championed Tagore in the West and wrote the introduction to the 1912 English Gitanjali. In it he praises the poems' simplicity and abundance, quotes an Indian doctor of medicine he spoke with about Tagore, and writes that a single line of Tagore lets us forget "all the troubles of the world."

**"Jana Gana Mana"**
India's national anthem, adapted from a Tagore poem/song. It addresses God as "the ruler of the minds of all people" and the "dispenser of India's destiny," and it ends with the refrain "Victory, victory, victory to thee" ("Jaya he").

**"On the seashore of endless worlds children meet"**
Poem 60 of Gitanjali. Children play on the beach "with shouts and dances," building "their houses with sand" and playing with shells. "The infinite sky is motionless overhead and the restless water is boisterous," and the children "know not how to swim, they know not how to cast nets," while death and storms go unnoticed around them.

**The Post Office**
Tagore's play (Dak Ghar, 1912) about Amal, a sickly boy who is kept indoors on doctor's orders. From his window he talks with passers-by, and a watchman tells him the King has built a new post office across the street. Amal dreams of getting a letter from the King and of becoming a postman. The Royal Physician arrives as he falls into what seems to be his final sleep, and the girl Sudha brings him flowers. André Gide's French translation was read on Paris radio on the eve of the city's fall to the Nazis in 1940.

**The Home and the World**
Tagore's 1916 novel (Ghare Baire), set during the Swadeshi movement, the boycott of British goods after the 1905 partition of Bengal. Bimala is torn between her gentle, liberal husband Nikhil and his charismatic but unscrupulous nationalist friend Sandip.

**Pablo Neruda plagiarism controversy**
Neruda's Poem 16 in Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair is a loose paraphrase of poem 30 of Tagore's collection The Gardener, which begins "You are the evening cloud floating in the sky of my dreams." Neruda was publicly accused of plagiarizing Tagore, and later editions acknowledge the debt.

**"The Golden Boat" ("Sonar Tori")**
The title poem of an 1894 Bengali collection. A farmer stands alone on a small paddy field as the river swells in the rain, and a boat arrives. He asks the boatman "to what foreign land do you sail?" and begs him to "take away my golden paddy." The boat takes the harvest but leaves the farmer behind, and the poem is often read as a symbol of time taking a person's work but not the person.

**"Amar Shonar Bangla"**
A Tagore song meaning "My Golden Bengal," which became the national anthem of Bangladesh. It praises the land's air and skies, which "set my heart in tune." With "Jana Gana Mana," it makes Tagore the author of two national anthems.

**"Ekla Chalo Re" ("Walk Alone")**
A popular patriotic song by Tagore, sung during the Swadeshi movement and loved by Gandhi. Its refrain says that if no one heeds your call, you should walk on alone.

**Kabuliwala**
A Tagore short story about Rahmat, a Pashtun dry-fruit seller from Kabul, and his fatherly friendship with Mini, a five-year-old girl in Calcutta who reminds him of his own daughter back in Afghanistan.

**Red Oleanders**
A symbolic Tagore play (Raktakarabi) set in Yakshapuri, a mining town where workers dig for gold under a tyrannical, unseen king. The heroine Nandini, linked with the red oleander flower, inspires a revolt against the system.

**"Let all my songs gather together into a single current"**
From the final poem of Gitanjali, which begins "In one salutation to thee, my God." The poet asks that his mind be bowed like "a rain-cloud of July hung low with its burden of unshed showers," that his songs flow "to a sea of silence," and that his life return to its "eternal home" like "a flock of homesick cranes."

**"Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird"**
Stevens's poem of thirteen short, haiku-like sections, each giving a different view of a blackbird. It opens "Among twenty snowy mountains, / The only moving thing / Was the eye of the blackbird," and ends "It was evening all afternoon. / It was snowing." It is one of the most frequent giveaways for Stevens.

**"O thin men of Haddam, / Why do you imagine golden birds?"**
A famous section of "Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird," which scolds the people of Haddam, Connecticut, for imagining exotic golden birds instead of seeing the ordinary blackbird. Other sections contrast "the beauty of inflections" with "the beauty of innuendoes," describe icicles filling a window "with barbaric glass," speak of knowing "noble accents / And lucid, inescapable rhythms," and describe a man who rides over Connecticut "in a glass coach" and is frightened by "the shadow of his equipage."

**"The Emperor of Ice-Cream"**
A short poem set at a wake for a dead woman. It opens "Call the roller of big cigars, / The muscular one, and bid him whip / In kitchen cups concupiscent curds," and tells the boys to "bring flowers in last month's newspapers." Its refrain is "The only emperor is the emperor of ice-cream."

**"Let be be finale of seem"**
A line from "The Emperor of Ice-Cream." It asks that appearances give way to reality, in keeping with the poem's acceptance of death and of the pleasures of the present.

**The dresser of deal and the "horny feet"**
The second stanza of "The Emperor of Ice-Cream" asks someone to take a sheet from a cheap pine ("deal") dresser that lacks "the three glass knobs," the sheet on which the dead woman "embroidered fantails once." The sheet is spread to cover her face, but if her "horny feet protrude," that shows "how cold she is, and dumb."

**"Sunday Morning"**
A meditative poem in which a woman stays home from church, enjoying "complacencies of the peignoir, and late / Coffee and oranges in a sunny chair." She thinks about "silent Palestine, / Dominion of the blood and sepulchre," and wonders whether earthly beauty is enough without heaven. It asks "What is divinity if it can come / Only in silent shadows and in dreams?" and answers that "Divinity must live within herself." It ends with "casual flocks of pigeons" that "sink, / Downward to darkness, on extended wings." Harriet Monroe first published a shortened version of it in Poetry magazine.

**"Death is the mother of beauty"**
The repeated central claim of "Sunday Morning," which holds that mortality is what gives earthly things their value. The poem also imagines a "ring of men" who chant "in orgy on a summer morn" to the sun, "not as a god, but as a god might be." Helen Vendler's study of Stevens's longer poems, On Extended Wings, takes its title from the poem's last line.

**Harmonium**
Stevens's first collection (1923). It contains "Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird," "The Emperor of Ice-Cream," "Sunday Morning," "Anecdote of the Jar," "The Snow Man," "Le Monocle de Mon Oncle," "Disillusionment of Ten O'Clock," "Peter Quince at the Clavier," "Domination of Black," and "The Comedian as the Letter C."

**"Anecdote of the Jar"**
A poem in which the speaker places a jar "in Tennessee, / And round it was, upon a hill." The jar makes "the slovenly wilderness" surround that hill. The jar, "gray and bare" and "tall and of a port in air," takes "dominion everywhere" and "did not give of bird or bush, / Like nothing else in Tennessee."

**"The Idea of Order at Key West"**
A poem about a woman singing by the shore who "sang beyond the genius of the sea" and becomes "the single artificer of the world / In which she sang." The speaker asks his companion, the critic Ramon Fernandez, why the lights of the boats in the harbor seemed to arrange the night after she stopped singing. It shows Stevens's idea that the imagination imposes order on reality.

**"The Snow Man"**
A one-sentence poem saying that "one must have a mind of winter" to regard frosted, snow-covered trees without hearing "misery in the sound of the wind." It ends with the listener who, "nothing himself, beholds / Nothing that is not there and the nothing that is."

**"Disillusionment of Ten O'Clock"**
A poem complaining that the houses are "haunted / By white night-gowns," not green or purple ones "with yellow rings." None of the sleepers will "dream of baboons and periwinkles." Only an old, drunken sailor "catches tigers / In red weather."

**"The Comedian as the Letter C"**
Stevens's long poem about Crispin, a poet who sails from Bordeaux to the Yucatan and then to Carolina, abandoning his romantic ideals for local reality. It opens by calling man "the intelligence of his soil" and "the Socrates of snails," and its section "The Idea of a Colony" imagines a colony of poets.

**"The Man with the Blue Guitar" and Notes Toward a Supreme Fiction**
In "The Man with the Blue Guitar," listeners complain that the guitarist "does not play things as they are," and he replies that "things as they are / Are changed upon the blue guitar." He also says "I cannot bring a world quite round, / Although I patch it as I can." Notes Toward a Supreme Fiction is Stevens's long poem setting out his idea of poetry as a "supreme fiction." In "A High-Toned Old Christian Woman," he writes that "Poetry is the supreme fiction, madame."

**Octavio Paz's "Sunstone"**
A 1957 circular poem by Mexico's Nobel laureate Octavio Paz. Its 584 lines match the 584-day cycle of Venus in the Aztec calendar, and it begins and ends with the same lines: "a willow of crystal, a poplar of water." It describes the "turning course of a river that goes curving, advances and retreats, goes roundabout, arriving forever," and contains images like "writing of fire on the slab of jade." Eliot Weinberger translated it into English, and Paz also wrote the poetry collections Eagle or Sun? and Salamander.

**The Labyrinth of Solitude**
Paz's 1950 book of essays on Mexican identity, written while he was a diplomat (he later served as Mexico's ambassador to India). It opens with an essay on the pachucos, young Mexican-Americans in Los Angeles, and discusses the "masks" Mexicans wear. Other chapters include "The Day of the Dead," "The Conquest and Colonialism," and "The Dialectic of Solitude."

**"The Sons of La Malinche"**
The most famous essay in The Labyrinth of Solitude. It analyzes the vulgar verb chingar and the figure of "la Chingada," the violated Mother, which Paz links to La Malinche, Hernán Cortés's indigenous interpreter and mistress. He contrasts this insult with the macho boast "I am your father."

**Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz's "First Dream"**
A long Baroque philosophical poem by the 17th-century nun of New Spain (colonial Mexico) known as the "Tenth Muse." It opens with a "pyramidal, funereal shadow born of the earth" as night falls and the soul tries in sleep to understand the universe. It ends at dawn with "the world illuminated and I awake."

**"You Foolish Men" and "Reply to Sor Filotea"**
In the satirical poem "You Foolish Men" ("Hombres necios"), Sor Juana attacks men who "lay the guilt on women" for faults they cause, asking who is more to blame, she who sins for pay or he who "pays to sin," and mocking men who want a Thais while courting but a Lucretia once they possess her. In her "Reply to Sor Filotea" (Philothea), she defends women's right to education and learning.

**Sor Juana, or The Traps of Faith**
Octavio Paz's 1982 biography and critical study of Sor Juana, which places her life and work in the culture of colonial New Spain.

**The Old Gringo**
A 1985 novel by Carlos Fuentes inspired by the 1913 disappearance in revolutionary Mexico of the American writer Ambrose Bierce. An aging American journalist (the "old gringo") who carries a copy of Don Quixote and wants to die joins Pancho Villa's forces. The American governess Harriet Winslow has an affair with the revolutionary General Tomás Arroyo. Arroyo shoots the gringo, and then Villa has the gringo's body dug up and shot by a firing squad, and has Arroyo executed.

**The Death of Artemio Cruz**
Fuentes's 1962 Latin American Boom novel, told in shifting first, second, and third person. It recounts the memories of Artemio Cruz, a corrupt newspaper tycoon and politician, from his deathbed. He rose from revolutionary soldier to millionaire by betraying his ideals, and he taunts his wife Catalina and daughter Teresa by refusing to say where his will is while a priest gives him last rites. The novel has been compared to Citizen Kane.

**Like Water for Chocolate**
Laura Esquivel's 1989 magical realist novel, divided into twelve monthly chapters that each begin with a recipe. Tita, the youngest daughter, is forbidden to marry her love Pedro, who marries her sister Rosaura instead. Tita's emotions pass into her cooking, so her tears in the wedding cake batter make all the guests sick. At the end, after Pedro dies, Tita eats candles and the ranch burns.

**Pedro Páramo**
Juan Rulfo's 1955 novel. Juan Preciado goes to the town of Comala to find his father, the tyrannical landowner Pedro Páramo, and finds it full of ghosts and whispering voices. Juan himself dies of fright and is buried next to Dorotea. Pedro, heartbroken over the death of Susana San Juan, lets Comala starve, and he is finally killed by his illegitimate son Abundio Martínez.

**Aura**
A short Gothic novella by Fuentes, written in the second person. The young historian Felipe Montero is hired by the ancient widow Consuelo to edit her dead husband's memoirs and falls in love with her green-eyed niece Aura, who turns out to be a magical projection of Consuelo herself.

**The Power and the Glory**
Graham Greene's 1940 novel, set in a Mexican state where the Church is outlawed. A nameless alcoholic "whiskey priest" is on the run from a lieutenant. He is sheltered by Coral Fellows in her family's barn, betrayed by a mestizo, and executed by firing squad, which the English dentist Mr. Tench watches.

**Under the Volcano**
Malcolm Lowry's 1947 novel, set in Quauhnahuac (based on Cuernavaca) on the Day of the Dead, 1938. Geoffrey Firmin, an alcoholic former British consul, is shot and thrown into a ravine, and his estranged wife Yvonne is trampled by a horse frightened by the gunshot.

**The Underdogs**
Mariano Azuela's 1915 novel of the Mexican Revolution. Demetrio Macías, a farmer turned rebel general, leads a band of fighters, and at the end he is found dead, still aiming his rifle.

**Roberto Bolaño's The Savage Detectives and 2666**
Novels by the Chilean writer Bolaño that are set largely in Mexico. In The Savage Detectives, the section "Mexicans Lost in Mexico" is the diary of a young poet who joins the Visceral Realists. In 2666, three literary critics search Mexico for the reclusive German author Benno von Archimboldi.

**One Hundred Years of Solitude**
García Márquez's 1967 masterpiece of magical realism, the defining novel of the Latin American Boom. It follows seven generations of the Buendía family in the fictional Colombian town of Macondo, which first appeared in his 1955 novella Leaf Storm. The Colombian author won the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature and died in April 2014.

**Opening line: the firing squad and ice**
The novel begins: "Many years later, as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendía was to remember that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice." The memory refers to a visit to the gypsies' fair, where Aureliano's father paid to touch a block of ice.

**Colonel Aureliano Buendía**
The founder's son, who leads and loses 32 armed uprisings in the Liberal-Conservative civil wars. He has seventeen illegitimate sons, all named Aureliano, who are later hunted down and shot through the ash crosses on their foreheads. In old age he shuts himself away making little gold fishes, which he melts down and remakes. His child bride was Remedios Moscote.

**Melquíades and his parchments**
The gypsy who brings inventions like magnets, a telescope, and ice to Macondo. He leaves behind parchments written in Sanskrit and in code that predict the family's entire history. They carry the epigraph "The first of the line is tied to a tree and the last is being eaten by the ants."

**The child with a pig's tail**
The family has long feared that incest would produce a child with a pig's tail. That happens at the end, when Aureliano Babilonia and his aunt Amaranta Úrsula have a son with the tail. The mother dies, ants eat the baby, and as Aureliano finally decodes Melquíades's parchments, a whirlwind wipes Macondo off the earth.

**José Arcadio Buendía and Úrsula Iguarán**
The cousins who marry and found Macondo. José Arcadio Buendía becomes obsessed with Melquiades's inventions and eventually goes mad, speaking only Latin, so he is tied to a chestnut tree in the yard until he dies. Úrsula, the practical matriarch, lives for well over a century and holds the family together.

**Other Macondo episodes: the insomnia plague, Pietro Crespi, and Remedios the Beauty**
Rebeca, an orphan who arrives in Macondo and secretly eats earth, brings an insomnia plague that makes the townspeople forget the names of things. The Italian pianola expert Pietro Crespi kills himself after being rejected by Amaranta, having earlier been engaged to Rebeca. The impossibly beautiful Remedios the Beauty rises into heaven while folding sheets.

**Love in the Time of Cholera**
García Márquez's 1985 novel about Florentino Ariza, who waits "fifty-one years, nine months and four days" for his youthful love Fermina Daza. Fermina married the respected Dr. Juvenal Urbino instead, and Urbino dies after falling from a ladder while trying to catch his escaped parrot in a mango tree. As a young man, Florentino ate gardenias and drank cologne to taste of Fermina and became sick, and he later rises in the River Company of the Caribbean.

**Jeremiah de Saint-Amour and the yellow flag**
Love in the Time of Cholera opens with Dr. Urbino examining the body of his chess partner, the photographer Jeremiah de Saint-Amour, who killed himself with gold cyanide fumes. It ends with Florentino and Fermina on a riverboat, the New Fidelity, whose captain raises the yellow cholera flag so they can keep sailing up and down the river together forever. Along the way, Florentino's 17-year-old ward and lover América Vicuña kills herself after he abandons her.

**Chronicle of a Death Foretold**
A 1981 novella in which the narrator reconstructs the murder of Santiago Nasar. On their wedding night, the wealthy Bayardo San Román returns his bride Angela Vicario to her family because she is not a virgin, though she had been advised to fake it, for example by staining the sheets with Mercurochrome. When she names Santiago as the man who deflowered her, her twin brothers Pedro and Pablo Vicario announce all over town that they will kill him. They do it on the day the bishop visits, even though nearly everyone knew, and Cristo Bedoya never manages to warn him. Afterward Angela writes Bayardo letters for years.

**"A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings"**
A short story in which Pelayo and his wife Elisenda, after throwing out the crabs that have flooded their house, find a filthy old man with huge wings, perhaps an angel. They lock him in their chicken coop and charge villagers to see him. Interest fades when a traveling show brings a woman turned into a tarantula for disobeying her parents, and the old man eventually grows new feathers and flies away.

**"The Handsomest Drowned Man in the World"**
A story in which the children of a seaside village find a huge drowned corpse covered in seaweed and jellyfish tentacles. The village women clean him, dress him in a sail, and name him Esteban. His beauty changes them, and they resolve to make their village grand so that ship captains will point to it in his memory.

**No One Writes to the Colonel**
A novella about an aging veteran of the civil war who waits for years for a pension letter that never comes. He and his asthmatic wife are slowly starving, but he refuses to sell the fighting rooster that belonged to their dead son. García Márquez was partly inspired by his own grandfather, also a colonel.

**"The Incredible and Sad Tale of Innocent Eréndira and Her Heartless Grandmother"**
A novella in which fourteen-year-old Eréndira accidentally burns down her grandmother's mansion and is forced into prostitution to repay the debt. Her lover Ulises, whose family smuggles diamonds inside oranges, promises her a new life and eventually stabs the grandmother to death.

**Of Love and Other Demons**
A 1994 novel set in colonial Cartagena. Sierva María, a twelve-year-old girl whose hair has never been cut, is bitten by a rabid dog and locked in a convent to be exorcised. The priest Father Cayetano Delaura falls in love with her and is punished by being sent to work in a leper hospital.

**Frog jumping into an old pond ("Furuike ya")**
This is the most famous haiku, by Matsuo Bashō. It describes an "old pond" (or "ancient pond"), a frog leaping in, and the "sound of water." Donald Keene is among its many translators.

**Matsuo Bashō**
Bashō was a 17th-century Japanese poet and the most celebrated master of haiku. He sought to bring elegance and depth to the form. His pen name comes from a bashō (Japanese banana) plant growing beside his hut.

**5-7-5 structure / seventeen syllables (on or morae)**
A haiku traditionally has seventeen sound units, called on or morae, arranged in three segments of five, seven, and five. In English this is usually rendered as three lines of 5, 7, and 5 syllables.

**Kireji ("cutting word")**
A kireji is a word that creates a pause or break, often dividing two contrasting images or marking a thematic shift. The "ya" in "Furuike ya" is one. Because kireji are hard to translate, English versions sometimes use a dash or ellipsis instead.

**Kigo (seasonal reference)**
A kigo is a word or phrase that places a haiku in a particular season, such as frogs for spring or winter rain for winter. Collections and anthologies are often organized around these season words.

**The Narrow Road to the Deep North (Oku no Hosomichi)**
This is Bashō's most famous travelogue, describing his 1689 journey with his companion Sora. It opens with "The months and days are the travelers of eternity." Early on, Bashō's thatched hut changes owners and becomes a "doll's house." It also contains the parting poem "spring is passing," in which birds cry and fishes' eyes fill with tears.

**The Seashell Game (Kai Ōi)**
This was Bashō's first published collection, from 1672. Its title refers to a children's game of matching seashells. It pairs sixty haiku in a mock poetry contest, with Bashō's commentary judging each pair.

**Kobayashi Issa**
Issa (1763–1828) was a major haiku master whose pen name means "cup of tea." After his daughter died, he wrote the "dewdrop world" poem in The Spring of My Life (Oraga Haru). He also wrote "Don't worry spiders / I keep house / casually" and described his native village as brambles to the touch. He died in a storehouse after his house burned.

**Hokku and renga**
Haiku grew out of renga, a collaborative linked-verse form. Its opening stanza, the hokku, was eventually written as an independent poem. "Hokku" is often accepted as an alternate name for haiku.

**Haibun**
Haibun is a genre that combines prose with haiku. The Narrow Road to the Deep North is the best-known example. Bashō's Saga Diary and Hut of the Phantom Dwelling are also haibun.

**The Monkey's Straw Raincoat (Sarumino)**
This is a celebrated anthology of the Bashō school, organized around the seasons. Its title comes from Bashō's poem about a cold winter shower that makes even a monkey seem to want a little coat of straw.

**R. H. Blyth and Richard Wright**
Reginald Horace Blyth was a scholar who popularized haiku in the English-speaking world, including through a two-volume History of Haiku. His work inspired the American novelist Richard Wright to write about four thousand haiku late in his life.

**Ezra Pound's "In a Station of the Metro"**
This is a famous two-line Imagist poem influenced by haiku: "The apparition of these faces in the crowd; / Petals on a wet, black bough." It is often cited as a key example of haiku's influence on Western poetry.

**Yosa Buson**
Buson was an 18th-century haiku master who was also a painter. He is known for haiga, paintings that accompany haiku. He is often ranked with Bashō and Issa as one of the great classical haiku poets.

**Beat Generation haiku (Kerouac, Ginsberg, Trip Trap)**
Several Beat writers wrote haiku. Trip Trap collects haiku about a cross-country road trip by Jack Kerouac and two companions. Allen Ginsberg wrote an unpublished collection of haiku that opens with him drinking sugarless tea.

**Midnight's Children**
Rushdie's 1981 novel, which won the Booker Prize, written while he was working as an advertising copywriter. It follows the 1,001 "midnight's children" born during the first hour of August 15, 1947, the moment India became independent and was partitioned from Pakistan, each of whom has a magical power. It is the most common title clue and giveaway.

**Saleem Sinai**
The narrator of Midnight's Children, born at the exact stroke of midnight on independence day and raised by a wealthy family in Bombay. His huge, constantly dripping nose gives him telepathy, which he uses to gather the other children into the Midnight's Children's Conference. He later marries Parvati-the-witch, and he loses his telepathy after sinus surgery.

**Mary Pereira and Shiva**
Mary Pereira, a midwife, switches two newborns at birth, so Saleem grows up rich while the real heir is raised as the son of the poor accordion player Wee Willie Winkie. That other child, "Shiva-of-the-knees," has deadly powerful knees and becomes Saleem's rival and the novel's antagonist. Mary later works at the Braganza Pickle Factory and eventually confesses the swap.

**Aadam Aziz and the perforated sheet**
Saleem's grandfather, a doctor, falls in love with his future wife Naseem by examining her one part at a time through a hole in a sheet held up by her family. This opening episode of Midnight's Children is a recurring early clue.

**Other Midnight's Children details**
Saleem's sister becomes a famous singer and is nicknamed the Brass Monkey. Saleem is hit on the head by a silver spittoon, loses his memory, and wanders in the Sundarbans jungle. Indira Gandhi appears as "the Widow," the Englishman William Methwold sells villas to Saleem's family, and one chapter is titled "Snakes and Ladders."

**The Satanic Verses**
Rushdie's 1988 novel, whose title refers to verses supposedly praising three pagan goddesses that were briefly included in revelations and then withdrawn. Dream sequences show a prophet called Mahound in the city of Jahilia, with characters such as the priestess Hind and the satirist Baal. Many Muslims considered it blasphemous, and it led directly to the fatwa against Rushdie.

**Gibreel Farishta and Saladin Chamcha**
The two Indian actors who open The Satanic Verses by falling from a hijacked plane that explodes over the English Channel, and surviving. Gibreel comes to believe he is the archangel Gabriel, while Saladin, a voice actor fired from the children's show The Aliens Show, turns into a horned, goatlike devil. Out of revenge, Saladin uses his talent for voices in obscene phone calls that make Gibreel jealous of his lover, the Everest climber Alleluia "Allie" Cone. Gibreel later kills Allie and then himself.

**Ayesha's pilgrimage to the Arabian Sea**
A dream sequence in The Satanic Verses in which Ayesha, a girl covered in butterflies who claims to receive messages from the archangel Gibreel, leads her villagers on a pilgrimage to Mecca. She convinces them the Arabian Sea will part for them, and they walk into the water and drown.

**The fatwa**
In 1989 Iran's Ayatollah Khomeini issued a fatwa calling for Rushdie's death over The Satanic Verses, forcing him into hiding. The novel's Japanese translator, Hitoshi Igarashi, was stabbed to death in 1991, and Rushdie himself was stabbed in 2022 before giving a public lecture. He describes his years in hiding in the memoir Joseph Anton (2012), titled after the alias he used.

**Haroun and the Sea of Stories**
Rushdie's 1990 children's novel, which opens in "the saddest of cities." Haroun's father Rashid, a storyteller nicknamed "the Shah of Blah," loses his gift of storytelling. They travel to the Valley of K and then to the moon Kahani, where Haroun meets Iff the Water Genie and Butt the Hoopoe and the kingdoms of Gup and Chup are at war.

**The Ground Beneath Her Feet**
A 1999 novel that retells the Orpheus and Eurydice myth through the world of rock music. Ormus Cama, a member of the band VTO, writes the title song for his love, the singer Vina Apsara; U2 later set lyrics from the novel to music as a real song.

**The Moor's Last Sigh**
A 1995 novel narrated by Moraes "Moor" Zogoiby, who ages twice as fast as normal. Its title refers to the legendary sigh of Boabdil, the last Muslim ruler of Granada, as he surrendered the city. Moraes ends up held captive in a Spanish replica of the Alhambra.

**Shame**
A 1983 novel set in a country resembling Pakistan. Omar Khayyam Shakil is raised in the border town of Q by three sisters, Chhunni, Munnee, and Bunny, who all pretend to have given birth to him, and he witnesses the rivalry of Iskandar Harappa and Raza Hyder. Raza's wife Bilquis has a daughter nicknamed Good News.

**Grimus**
Rushdie's first novel (1975). Its protagonist, Flapping Eagle, a Native American, becomes immortal by drinking a magical liquid and wanders for 777 years, 7 months and 7 days before arriving on Calf Island.

**Other later works**
The Golden House (2017) follows Nero Golden, a man from Bombay who moves with his three sons to "the Gardens" in Greenwich Village. Quichotte (2019) is a modern American Don Quixote created inside the novel by the spy writer Sam DuChamp, and the hero imagines a black-and-white son. Shalimar the Clown (2005) involves the American ambassador Maximilian Ophuls and the Kashmiri dancer Boonyi, The Enchantress of Florence (2008) is partly set at the court of Akbar the Great, and the story collection East, West includes "Chekov and Zulu."

**"The Wife of Bath's Tale" and "what women most desire"**
A knight of King Arthur's court rapes a maiden and is sentenced to death. The queen spares him on condition that he discover what women most desire within a year and a day. An ugly old hag gives him the answer, sovereignty (mastery over their husbands), in exchange for his promise to marry her. When he lets her choose whether to be ugly and faithful or beautiful and possibly unfaithful, she becomes both beautiful and true. The tale opens by recalling that in Arthur's day Britain was full of fairies and elves.

**Palamon, Arcite, and Emelye in "The Knight's Tale"**
The first tale, told by the Knight. Theseus marches on Thebes after Creon refuses to let the widows bury their dead, and he imprisons the Theban cousins Palamon and Arcite in a tower. From the tower, both fall in love with Emelye as they watch her gathering flowers in a garden. After release, Arcite returns in disguise as a page named Philostrate. Arcite wins the tournament for her hand but is thrown from his horse and dies, so Palamon marries Emelye. Theseus delivers the philosophical "First Mover" speech near the end.

**The Tabard Inn, Harry Bailly, and the storytelling contest**
The frame story: about thirty pilgrims gather at the Tabard Inn in Southwark. The Host, Harry Bailly, proposes that each tell tales on the road, promising a free supper at the end to whoever tells the best story, and he judges and often interrupts them. Chaucer completed only 24 tales, and the framed structure is often compared to Boccaccio's Decameron.

**The Wife of Bath's Prologue**
Alisoun, the gap-toothed Wife of Bath, boasts of her five husbands and argues for women's authority in marriage. Her fifth husband, the young clerk Jankyn, read to her from a book of wicked wives; she tore pages out of it, and he struck her so hard that she went deaf in one ear. In her tale, she retells Ovid's story of King Midas's ears, making Midas's wife the one who cannot keep the secret and whispers it into a marsh.

**The shrine of Thomas Becket**
The pilgrims are traveling to Canterbury Cathedral to visit the shrine of the "holy blissful martyr" Saint Thomas Becket, the archbishop murdered in 1170, who "helped them when they were sick."

**"When April with his showers sweet..."**
The famous opening of the General Prologue, in Middle English "Whan that Aprill with his shoures soote / The droghte of March hath perced to the roote." It describes April's showers bathing every vein in liquor, the "sweet breath" of Zephyrus, and "small fowls" making melody that sleep all night with open eye, before people long to go on pilgrimages.

**"The Miller's Tale": Nicholas, Alisoun, and the tubs**
A bawdy tale in which the student Nicholas convinces the old carpenter John that a second Noah's flood is coming. John hangs three tubs from the ceiling to float away in, and while he sleeps in his, Nicholas sleeps with John's young wife Alisoun. When John hears the cry for "water," he cuts the rope, crashes to the floor, and breaks his arm.

**Absolon and the hot coulter**
In "The Miller's Tale," the foppish parish clerk Absolon, who also loves Alisoun, is tricked at the window into kissing her backside. He returns with a red-hot coulter (plow blade) from the blacksmith. When Nicholas sticks his rear out the window and farts in his face, Absolon brands him on the buttocks.

**"The Pardoner's Tale" and the three rioters**
Three young revelers in Flanders set out to kill Death. An old man directs them to an oak tree, where they find nearly eight bushels of gold florins. Two stab the third, who had poisoned their wine, so all three die. Afterward the Pardoner tries to sell his fake relics, and the Host retorts that he would like to have the Pardoner's testicles enshrined in a hog's turd.

**"The Nun's Priest's Tale" and Chauntecleer**
A beast fable in which the proud rooster Chauntecleer dreams of danger, which his wife, the hen Pertelote, dismisses. The fox flatters him into closing his eyes and crowing, then seizes him. Chauntecleer tricks the fox into turning to taunt his pursuers, then escapes into a tree. It follows "The Monk's Tale," a string of tragedies that the Knight interrupts.

**"The Franklin's Tale": Dorigen and the rocks of Brittany**
Dorigen, wife of the knight Arveragus, rashly promises the squire Aurelius her love if he removes all the rocks from the coast of Brittany. Aurelius pays a magician-clerk to make them seem to vanish, and her husband tells her she must keep her word. Seeing such generosity, Aurelius releases her from the promise, and the clerk forgives Aurelius's debt.

**"Sir Thopas" and "not worth a turd"**
The pilgrim Chaucer's own deliberately terrible rhyming tale about the knight Sir Thopas, who seeks an elf-queen and meets the three-headed giant Sir Olifaunt. The Host cuts it off, crying "no more of this," and says his rhyming is "not worth a turd." Chaucer then tells the prose "Tale of Melibee."

**The Miller, the Reeve, and "quiting"**
The pilgrims often "quite" (pay back) each other with insulting stories. The Reeve, a carpenter, answers the Miller's tale of a fooled carpenter with a tale about the cheating miller Symkyn. In it, two Cambridge students get revenge by sleeping with his wife and daughter, moving a baby's cradle so the wife climbs into the wrong bed.

**The Friar's and Summoner's Tales**
The Friar and the Summoner trade insulting tales. In the Friar's, a greedy summoner tries to extort an old widow, who damns him to the Devil, and the devil drags him, body and soul, off to hell (she also damns her frying pan). In the Summoner's, a sick man named Thomas tells a greedy friar he has a gift hidden beneath him and farts into the friar's hand.

**"The Merchant's Tale," "The Manciple's Tale," and "The Prioress's Tale"**
In "The Merchant's Tale," the old knight January marries young May, who cheats on him with the squire Damian in a pear tree. In "The Manciple's Tale," the god Phoebus kills his unfaithful wife after his white crow reveals her adultery, then plucks out the crow's feathers and turns it black. In "The Prioress's Tale," a murdered Christian boy keeps singing "Alma redemptoris mater" until a grain is removed from his tongue.

**Edna Pontellier drowns in the Gulf of Mexico**
The protagonist, Edna Pontellier, goes back to Grand Isle at the end of the novel. She takes off her clothes, walks naked into the sea and swims out until she drowns. The ending echoes earlier lines about the "sensuous" touch of the sea that "encloses the body in its warm embrace."

**Mademoiselle Reisz**
Reisz is a disagreeable, isolated older pianist who wears artificial violets in her hair. Her playing moves Edna to tears on Grand Isle, and she calls Edna "the only person worth playing for." She tells Edna that an artist must have a brave soul, and she feels Edna's shoulder blades to see whether her "wings" are growing.

**Robert Lebrun leaves for Mexico**
Robert is the young man who keeps Edna company on Grand Isle, and she falls in love with him. He leaves suddenly for Mexico to escape his feelings for her. After he returns, he leaves her a goodbye note ("Good-by — because I love you"), which leads to her suicide.

**Alcée Arobin**
Arobin is a well-known seducer in New Orleans. Edna has an affair with him while her husband, Léonce, is away on business in New York. She feels guilty about it because her real love is Robert.

**Adèle Ratignolle and the "mother-women"**
Adèle is Edna's friend. She is often pregnant, completely devoted to her family, and stands for the novel's "mother-women," who live entirely for their husbands and children. She and Edna argue about what a mother owes her children: Edna says she would give her life for her children but not her self.

**The parrot shouting "Allez vous-en!"**
The novel opens with a caged parrot at the Grand Isle resort. It shouts "Allez vous-en! Sapristi!" ("Go away!") in French and English and interrupts Léonce while he reads his newspaper. A mockingbird whistles nearby, and the caged bird is often read as a symbol of Edna's confinement.

**Grand Isle**
Grand Isle is a summer resort in the Gulf of Mexico run by Madame Lebrun, Robert's mother. Edna's awakening begins there: she learns to swim and falls for Robert. She returns there at the end to die.

**Dr. Mandelet**
Mandelet is the family doctor. Léonce asks him for help because Edna has stopped obeying him and acting like a dutiful wife. At a dinner party, Edna tells a made-up story about a woman who vanishes into the islands with her lover, and Mandelet takes it as a sign that she is having an affair.

**Victor sings "Ah! Si tu savais!" and the broken wine glass**
Victor is Robert's younger brother. At the lavish birthday dinner Edna gives before moving out of her husband's house, he sings "Ah! Si tu savais!", a song Robert once sang to her. Edna cries "Stop!", sets her glass down so hard that it shatters, and puts her hand over his mouth.

**The "pigeon house"**
This is the small house around the corner where Edna moves on her own while Léonce is away. She pays for it with her own money from painting, a betting win at the races and an inheritance, so it stands for her independence.

**The Farival twins**
The twins are two young girls whose family has committed them to becoming nuns. At the resort they play piano duets, including selections from the opera "Zampa," which the parrot mocks. They also perform on the night Mademoiselle Reisz's playing moves Edna to tears.

**Adèle's childbirth: "Think of the children"**
Edna stays with Adèle while she gives birth, along with Dr. Mandelet, and finds the scene a torture. As Edna leaves, Adèle whispers, "Think of the children, Edna. Oh think of the children! Remember them!"

**A Chopin Impromptu played while Edna reads Robert's letter**
At her apartment in New Orleans, Mademoiselle Reisz plays a Chopin Impromptu. While she plays, Edna reads letters that Robert has sent to Reisz from Mexico, which show that he loves Edna.

**Edna's Kentucky memories**
On the beach with Adèle, Edna remembers walking through a meadow of tall grass at her father's home in Kentucky as a girl; it felt like swimming. She also recalls her teenage crush on a cavalry officer who visited the house, one of several romantic infatuations she had when she was young.

**Swimming "where no woman had swum before"**
After weeks of failing to learn, Edna finally swims on her own one night on Grand Isle. She feels she can reach out "where no woman had swum before," then gets frightened and heads home immediately. Afterward she sits up waiting in a hammock outside her cottage instead of going inside when Léonce tells her to.

**Duino Elegies**
Rilke's masterpiece, a cycle of ten long, philosophical elegies published in 1923. They deal with angels, death, love, and the limits of human existence. The near-universal giveaway is the opening line of the First Elegy: "Who, if I cried out, would hear me among the Angelic Orders?"

**"Beauty is nothing but the beginning of terror" and "Every angel is terrifying"**
Famous lines from the First Elegy, which says that beauty is "nothing but the beginning of terror, which we still are just able to endure," and that "Every angel is terrifying." The Second Elegy opens by repeating the idea ("Every angel is terror") and later calls the angels "Early successes, Creation's favorite ones."

**Gaspara Stampa and the First Elegy**
The First Elegy asks "Have you remembered Gaspara Stampa sufficiently yet?", referring to the Renaissance Venetian poet of unrequited love, and mentions an inscription on a tablet in the church of Santa Maria Formosa. It also describes the "night, when the wind full of space" feeds on our faces, recalls how "you walked under an open window" as "a violin yielded itself to your hearing," notes how strange it is "to no longer inhabit the earth," and ends with the mourning for Linos.

**Duino Castle, Princess Marie von Thurn und Taxis, and Château de Muzot**
Rilke began the Elegies in 1912 at Duino Castle on the Adriatic near Trieste, as the guest of his patron Princess Marie von Thurn und Taxis, to whom they are dedicated. He finished them in February 1922 in a burst of creativity (a "creative storm") at the Château de Muzot in Switzerland.

**The Tenth, Eighth, and Sixth Elegies**
In the Tenth Elegy, a young man is led through the land of Laments by an elder Lament, past the "fountain of joy," and climbs "the mountains of primal pain." It ends by saying that we, who think of happiness as rising, would feel the emotion "that almost dismays us / when a happy thing falls." The Eighth Elegy contrasts animals, which look with all their eyes into "the Open" (the unobstructed world), with humans, whose vision is turned around like "traps" set around freedom. The Sixth Elegy opens by praising the fig tree, which almost wholly omits to flower and goes straight into fruit.

**"Archaic Torso of Apollo"**
Rilke's sonnet about a headless ancient Greek statue of Apollo in the Louvre, the opening poem of the second part of New Poems (1908). It ends with the famous sudden command "You must change your life."

**"We cannot know his legendary head / with eyes like ripening fruit"**
The opening of "Archaic Torso of Apollo." The speaker says the torso is still "suffused with brilliance from inside, like a lamp," so that a smile runs through the hips "to that dark center where procreation flared." The stone glistens "like a wild beast's fur" beneath "the translucent cascade of the shoulders" and would "burst like a star," since "there is no place / that does not see you."

**"The Panther"**
Rilke's famous poem about a caged panther in Paris's Jardin des Plantes. Its gaze is so weary from the passing bars that "It seems to him there are a thousand bars; / and behind the bars, no world." Its padding gait is "like a ritual dance around a center / in which a mighty will stands paralyzed." Sometimes "the curtain of the pupils / lifts, quietly," and an image enters, "plunges into the heart and is gone."

**New Poems, "thing-poems," and Auguste Rodin**
Rilke's New Poems (1907–08) contain his Dinggedichte ("thing-poems"), which describe objects and animals with intense attention. They were inspired by his time working as secretary to the sculptor Auguste Rodin, who urged him to look closely at things. Another example is "The Spanish Dancer," in which a flamenco dancer flares up like a struck match until she is "completely fire," her naked arms whirling like "startled rattlesnakes."

**Sonnets to Orpheus**
A cycle of 55 sonnets that Rilke wrote in a few weeks in February 1922 at Muzot, as a memorial for Wera Ouckama Knoop, a young dancer who died of illness. The first sonnet opens "There rose a tree. Oh pure transcendence! / Oh Orpheus sings!" and calls the lyre-playing god a source of "new beginning, sign, and transformation."

**Lines from the Sonnets to Orpheus**
One sonnet says not to erect a monument, but to "let the rose blossom each year" for Orpheus's sake. Another praises the poet whose "mortal heart presses out / a deathless, inexhaustible wine." One addresses a dog, and the final sonnet urges "Let this darkness be a bell tower."

**Letters to a Young Poet**
Ten letters Rilke wrote between 1903 and 1908 to the young military cadet and aspiring poet Franz Xaver Kappus, published after Rilke's death. He advises Kappus to "go into yourself" and explore "the depths where your life wells forth" to decide whether he truly must write.

**The Book of Hours**
Rilke's early three-part cycle of prayer-like poems addressed to God, inspired by his journeys to Russia. Its parts are "The Book of Monastic Life," "The Book of Pilgrimage," and "The Book of Poverty and Death," and the poems are sometimes published in English as "Love Poems to God."

**The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge**
Rilke's only novel (1910), a fragmentary series of 71 journal-like entries by a young Danish nobleman living in poverty in Paris, who reflects on his childhood, fear, and death.

**Rilke's early life and other poems**
Rilke was born in Prague in 1875, and his mother called him Sophia and dressed him as a girl to make up for the loss of an earlier daughter. His early collections include Life and Songs and Offering to the Lares, which draws on Prague legends such as those of Rabbi Loew. His poem "Autumn Day" ends by saying that whoever is alone now will "wander the avenues, back and forth, restlessly, while the leaves are blowing."

**"The Necklace" (Mathilde Loisel)**
Maupassant's most famous story (1884). Mathilde Loisel, a pretty woman born into the lower middle class "as if by an error of fate," borrows a diamond necklace for a ball and loses it. She and her husband go deeply into debt to buy a replacement, and she spends ten years doing hard labor, such as washing floors, which destroys her beauty.

**Madame Forestier and the paste necklace**
Jeanne Forestier is Mathilde's wealthy school friend, who lends her the necklace. In the story's famous twist ending, Mathilde meets her again years later and confesses, and Madame Forestier reveals that the original was made of paste (fake jewels) and was worth at most 500 francs.

**The Ministry of Education ball**
Mathilde's husband, a lowly clerk, brings home an invitation to a ball held by the Minister of Education (Public Instruction). He gives up the money he had saved for a gun for Sunday hunting trips so she can buy a dress. He is a simple man who is delighted by a plain home-cooked stew, and he dozes in a side room while she dances.

**"Boule de Suif" (Elisabeth Rousset)**
Maupassant's first great story (1880), translated "Ball of Fat" or "Butterball," set during the Franco-Prussian War. The plump prostitute Elisabeth Rousset travels by coach from occupied Rouen toward Le Havre with respectable bourgeois passengers. When a Prussian officer detains them at an inn in the village of Tôtes until she sleeps with him, her companions pressure her into it, then shun her afterward.

**Cornudet and "La Marseillaise"**
Cornudet is the coach's loud democrat. At the end of "Boule de Suif," while the other passengers eat and ignore the weeping Boule de Suif, Cornudet whistles and hums the revolutionary anthem "La Marseillaise" ("Liberty, cherished liberty...") over her sobs.

**The picnic basket**
Early in "Boule de Suif," when the coach is delayed and the passengers grow hungry, Boule de Suif generously shares her large basket of food with them, the same people who later betray her. She is described with fingers "like rows of short sausages" and a noted "embonpoint" (plumpness).

**"Mademoiselle Fifi"**
A story set in a Normandy château occupied by Prussian officers. Mademoiselle Fifi is the mocking nickname of an effeminate, slender-waisted young officer, Wilhelm von Eyrick, who constantly says "fi, fi donc" and amuses himself by wrecking the château, including blowing up a terracotta Venus with a teapot full of gunpowder.

**Rachel and the cheese knife**
In "Mademoiselle Fifi," the Jewish prostitute Rachel, brought in for a party, is enraged when Fifi boasts that France and its women belong to the Prussians. She stabs him in the neck with a small dessert knife used for cheese and escapes, hiding in the church bell tower until the Prussians leave. The village church bell, previously silent in protest, rings for Fifi's funeral.

**"The Horla"**
A story written as the diary of a man who becomes convinced that an invisible being, the Horla, is living in his house and drinking his water and milk at night. To test whether he is drinking in his sleep, he rubs pencil lead on his lips. He finally locks the creature in and burns down his house, forgetting his servants are inside, and concludes he may have to kill himself.

**The Brazilian ship**
At the start of "The Horla," the narrator happily waves at a "superb three-masted" Brazilian ship sailing up the Seine. He later reads that a mind-controlling epidemic has broken out in Brazil and realizes the Horla came on that ship.

**"A Piece of String"**
At the market in Goderville, the Norman peasant Maître Hauchecorne bends down to pick up a piece of string and is seen by his enemy, the harness-maker Malandain. He is accused of stealing a lost pocketbook (wallet), and even after it is returned nobody believes him. He dies still protesting, "A little piece of string."

**"Two Friends"**
A story set during the Siege of Paris. The watchmaker Morissot and his friend Monsieur Sauvage go fishing outside the city, are captured by the Prussians, refuse to reveal the password, and are shot by a firing squad. The Prussian officer then has their fish fried.

**Bel-Ami**
Maupassant's 1885 novel about Georges Duroy, a handsome, unscrupulous former soldier who rises in Parisian journalism and society by seducing and using women. He marries Madeleine, the widow of his friend Forestier, and later divorces her by exposing her adultery.

**Henry James's "Paste"**
Henry James wrote this story as a reversal of "The Necklace." Charlotte gives away a necklace believed to be fake, which turns out to be real; the cousin Arthur Prime claims he broke it, and Mrs. Guy ends up with the valuable piece.

**"Walter Schnaffs' Adventure"**
A comic war story about a fat, peace-loving Prussian soldier with very flat feet who, terrified of combat in Normandy, gorges himself on a meal at the Château de Champignet and happily lets himself be taken prisoner by the French.

**Offred**
The narrator and protagonist of Margaret Atwood's 1985 dystopian novel. She is a Handmaid, a fertile woman forced to bear children for an elite couple; her name means "Of Fred," marking her as the property of her Commander. Her real name is never stated, though readers often infer it to be June.

**Republic of Gilead**
The theocratic, Christian fundamentalist regime that replaces the United States in the novel. It was founded by the Sons of Jacob, who assassinated the President and Congress, froze women's Compucard bank accounts, and stripped women of jobs and property; society is split into castes such as Wives, Handmaids, Marthas, Econowives, Aunts, and Unwomen.

**"Nolite te bastardes carborundorum"**
A mock-Latin phrase meaning roughly "Don't let the bastards grind you down." Offred finds it scratched into the floor of her closet/cupboard, left by the Handmaid who held her post before her and later killed herself; the Commander explains its meaning.

**Scrabble with the Commander**
Offred's Commander, the husband of Serena Joy, secretly summons her to his study at night to play Scrabble, which is forbidden because women are not allowed to read. He also gives her old magazines and hand lotion during these meetings.

**Nick and Serena Joy**
Serena Joy, the Commander's Wife and a former TV gospel singer, arranges for Offred to sleep with the chauffeur Nick so she can become pregnant, since the Commander is likely sterile. Offred begins an affair with Nick, who turns out to be connected to the Mayday resistance and the Eyes (secret police).

**Mayday resistance**
The underground movement fighting Gilead, which runs the "Underground Femaleroad" to smuggle women out. Offred's shopping partner Ofglen is a member, and at the end Nick arranges for Offred to be taken away in a van by men who may be Mayday agents disguised as Eyes.

**Moira and Jezebel's**
Moira is Offred's rebellious lesbian friend from college. She escapes the Red Center by overpowering Aunt Elizabeth and taking her clothes, but is later caught and ends up at Jezebel's, a secret brothel for Commanders, where Offred sees her wearing a bunny costume.

**Professor Pieixoto and the "Historical Notes"**
The novel's epilogue, a transcript of a 2195 academic conference. Professor James Darcy Pieixoto explains that Offred's story was reconstructed from about thirty cassette tapes found in a footlocker in Bangor, Maine; he jokes condescendingly about a female colleague, Professor Maryann Crescent Moon.

**Aunt Lydia and the Red Center**
The Red Center (Rachel and Leah Center) is where Handmaids are indoctrinated. Aunt Lydia, its main instructor, repeats sayings that Offred recalls throughout, such as the idea that the horrors of Gilead will come to seem "ordinary." She is a major character in the 2019 sequel, The Testaments.

**Butter hidden in her shoe**
Handmaids are denied hand cream, so Offred secretly saves a pat of butter from her meal, hides it in her shoe, and rubs it on her skin as lotion, a small act of self-preservation.

**Particicution and Salvaging**
"Salvagings" are public executions in which criminals are hanged, and the bodies are displayed on the Wall (formerly part of Harvard) with bags over their heads. In a "Particicution," Handmaids beat a man accused of raping a pregnant Handmaid to death; Ofglen kicks him in the head to knock him unconscious, revealing he is a fellow Mayday member.

**Ofglen**
Offred's shopping partner, with whom she exchanges greetings like "Blessed be the fruit"/"May the Lord open" and "Under His Eye." She is a member of Mayday and hangs herself when she sees the van from the Eyes coming for her; she is replaced by a new Ofglen.

**Luke and Offred's daughter**
Offred's husband Luke tried to escape with her and their daughter to Canada, killing their cat before leaving; they were caught, and Offred lost them both. She fears seeing Luke's body among those hanging on the Wall.

**Janine (Ofwarren)**
A fellow Handmaid who gives birth to a baby girl, Angela, during a birth ceremony. The baby is later declared a "shredder" (malformed), and Janine breaks down mentally, later appearing dazed and clutching a clump of blond hair after the Particicution.

**"Ceremony" and Genesis 30**
The monthly ritual in which the Commander reads from the Bible, including the Genesis story of Rachel giving her handmaid Bilhah to Jacob, before attempting to impregnate the Handmaid as she lies between the Wife's legs. The novel's epigraphs include Genesis 30, Swift's "A Modest Proposal," and a Sufi proverb: "In the desert there is no sign that says, Thou shalt not eat stones."

**Interpreter of Maladies**
Lahiri's 1999 debut short story collection, which won the 2000 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. It is her most common giveaway, and it contains stories such as "A Temporary Matter," "When Mr. Pirzada Came to Dine," "Sexy," "This Blessed House," and "The Third and Final Continent."

**Mr. Kapasi, Mrs. Das, and Bobby attacked by monkeys**
The title story of Interpreter of Maladies follows Mr. Kapasi, a tour guide who also works as an interpreter for a doctor whose patients speak Gujarati.
