While driving the Indian-American Das family to the Sun Temple at Konarak, he grows infatuated with Mrs. Das, but at the end her son Bobby is swarmed by monkeys after she carelessly drops puffed rice, and Mr. Kapasi rescues him.

**Mrs. Das's secret (Bobby is illegitimate)**
In "Interpreter of Maladies," Mrs. Das confesses to Mr. Kapasi that her son Bobby was fathered by another man during an affair, a secret she has kept for eight years. She hopes he can "interpret" her malady, but he only asks whether what she feels is really pain or guilt, which offends her. The story opens with Mr. and Mrs. Das bickering at a tea stall over who will take their daughter Tina to the toilet.

**"Sexy" (Miranda, Dev, and the Mapparium)**
A story in Interpreter of Maladies in which Miranda has an affair with Dev, a married Bengali man who whispers that she is "sexy" inside the Mapparium, a walk-in stained-glass globe at the Christian Science center in Boston. She breaks off the affair after Rohin, the seven-year-old boy she babysits, defines "sexy" as "loving someone you don't know."

**"A Temporary Matter" (Shoba and Shukumar)**
The opening story of Interpreter of Maladies, about a married couple grieving their stillborn baby. During a series of nightly scheduled power outages, they confess secrets to each other by candlelight; Shukumar admits he cheated on an Oriental Civilization exam and tore a model's photo out of a magazine, and finally reveals that he held their dead son and knows his sex. He had been at an academic conference in Baltimore during the birth.

**The Namesake (Gogol Ganguli)**
Lahiri's first novel (2003), about Gogol Ganguli, the son of Bengali immigrants in Massachusetts, who resents his unusual name and legally changes it to Nikhil. He dates Maxine Ratliff, breaks up with her after his father dies, and later marries his childhood acquaintance Moushumi, who cheats on him with Dimitri Desjardins.

**Ashoke's train accident and "The Overcoat"**
In The Namesake, Gogol's father Ashoke survives a train derailment in India because rescuers notice him clutching (or waving) pages of Nikolai Gogol's short story "The Overcoat." In gratitude he names his son after the Russian author. Ashoke later studies engineering at MIT and dies while working in Cleveland, a departure Gogol misses because he spends the night with his girlfriend.

**"When Mr. Pirzada Came to Dine"**
A story in Interpreter of Maladies narrated by Lilia, a young girl in New England whose family hosts Mr. Pirzada, a professor from Dacca, during the 1971 war that created Bangladesh. Each night she eats a candy he gives her and prays for the safety of his family; after he returns home and writes that they are safe, she throws the candies away.

**The Lowland (Subhash, Udayan, and Gauri)**
Lahiri's 2013 novel, about two brothers in Calcutta. Udayan joins the Naxalite (Maoist) movement and is killed by police, and his brother Subhash, a graduate student in Rhode Island, marries Udayan's pregnant widow Gauri and brings her to America. Subhash has an affair with Holly, whom he meets on the beach with her son Joshua.

**Unaccustomed Earth**
Lahiri's 2008 second story collection, whose title comes from a passage in Nathaniel Hawthorne's "The Custom-House." In the title story, Ruma, living in Seattle, is visited by her widowed father, whose postcard to another woman reveals his new relationship. The collection also contains "Only Goodness," in which Rahul drops out of Cornell, becomes an alcoholic, and ends up working at a laundromat, and "Nobody's Business," in which the graduate student Paul helps his housemate Sang break off her relationship with the deceitful Farouk.

**Hema and Kaushik (death in a tsunami)**
The linked three-story sequence that closes Unaccustomed Earth. Kaushik becomes a war photojournalist and dies in the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami while staying at a resort in Thailand.

**"The Third and Final Continent"**
The final story of Interpreter of Maladies, narrated by a Bengali man who moves from London to Boston and rents a room from Mrs. Croft, a 103-year-old woman on Massachusetts Avenue. She insists he say "Splendid!" about the American flag planted on the moon, and later his wife Mala joins him in America.

**"This Blessed House" (Twinkle and Sanjeev)**
A story in Interpreter of Maladies about a newlywed couple in Connecticut. Twinkle delights in the Christian trinkets left by previous owners, such as a statue of the Virgin Mary and a silver bust of Jesus, while her husband Sanjeev is irritated by them.

**"The Treatment of Bibi Haldar"**
A story in Interpreter of Maladies about a young woman in Calcutta afflicted by a mysterious illness, whose relatives believe marriage will cure her. She is "cured" after she becomes pregnant by an unknown man.

**Writing in Italian ("Teach Yourself Italian," Roman Stories)**
Lahiri moved to Rome and began writing in Italian, explaining the shift in the essay "Teach Yourself Italian" and the book In Other Words. Her later Italian-language works include the novel Whereabouts and the collection Roman Stories, which contains "The Boundary." She teaches at Princeton.

**Death and the King's Horseman**
Soyinka's best-known play (1975), based on a real 1946 incident in the Yoruba city of Oyo, Nigeria. Elesin Oba, the King's Horseman, is supposed to commit ritual suicide after the king's death so he can follow his master into the afterlife. The British District Officer Simon Pilkings arrests him to stop it. Soyinka, the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature (1986), is most often clued through this play.

**Olunde**
Elesin's eldest son, who has been studying medicine in England. He returns for the ritual and tells Jane Pilkings that the British "have no respect for what you do not understand." After his father's suicide is prevented, Olunde kills himself in Elesin's place. When his wrapped body is brought to his chained father, Elesin strangles himself with his chains.

**The "Not-I" bird and the Praise-Singer**
At the start of Death and the King's Horseman, Elesin moves through the market with his Praise-Singer (Olohun-iyo) and drummer and tells the tale of the Not-I bird. In the tale, every creature that Death visits cries "Not I" to escape it, while Elesin boasts that he will not be afraid. The Praise-Singer teases him for enjoying the admiration of the market women.

**Iyaloja and Elesin's bride**
Iyaloja, the "mother" of the market women, lets Elesin marry a beautiful young girl on his final day, even though she is engaged to Iyaloja's own son. Elesin's distraction by this worldly pleasure is part of why he fails to complete the ritual, and Iyaloja later scorns him for his failure.

**The egungun costume and Soyinka's preface**
Simon and Jane Pilkings put on egungun costumes, sacred Yoruba ancestral masquerade robes, for a colonial fancy-dress ball, which horrifies the Nigerian police sergeant Amusa. Soyinka's preface warns against the "reductionist tendency" of reading the play as a simple "clash of cultures" and asks directors to bring out its "threnodic essence," meaning its mourning quality.

**The Lion and the Jewel**
Soyinka's 1959 comedy set in the Yoruba village of Ilujinle. The village beauty Sidi (the "Jewel") is courted by the young, Westernized schoolteacher Lakunle and by the cunning old chief Baroka (the "Lion"). Baroka tricks and seduces her, and at the end Sidi chooses to marry him and join his harem, leaving Lakunle devastated.

**Lakunle**
The comic schoolteacher in The Lion and the Jewel, who wears an old, too-small Western suit and talks in pompous English he learned from a "Shorter Companion Dictionary." He tells Sidi that women are the weaker sex because their brains are smaller, and he refuses to pay her traditional bride price, calling it a savage custom.

**The Stranger's photographs and the "Dance of the Lost Traveller"**
In The Lion and the Jewel, a photographer from Lagos once came to the village and published pictures of Sidi in a magazine, which has made her vain. The villagers act out his arrival in the "Dance of the Lost Traveller": girls play his broken-down motor car, and they mock his motorbike as "the devil's own horse" and his camera as "the one-eyed box." Lakunle is made to play the stranger before being excused to go teach his Primary Four geography class.

**Baroka's stamp machine and "I do not hate progress"**
To seduce Sidi, Baroka shows her a stamp-printing machine and promises to put her picture on postage stamps. He claims he does "not hate progress, only its nature, which makes all roofs and faces look the same." Baroka is first seen having a favorite wife pluck the hairs from his armpits, and his senior wife Sadiku is tricked into thinking he has become impotent.

**Kongi's Harvest**
A 1965 satire of African dictatorship. Kongi, the tyrant of the fictional state of Isma, wants the deposed traditional king Oba Danlola to hand him the ceremonial new yam at the harvest festival so that his power will look legitimate. Danlola's nephew Daodu and his lover Segi plot against Kongi, and at the climax Kongi is presented with the severed head of Segi's father instead of a yam.

**A Dance of the Forests**
A play written for Nigerian independence in 1960. The living hold a Gathering of the Tribes expecting to welcome illustrious ancestors, but the Forest Head and his servant Aroni instead summon a Dead Man and a Dead Woman, who come to "take their case" against the past. The Dead Man turns out to have been a warrior sold into slavery for a flask of rum. The trickster spirit Eshuoro also disrupts the gathering.

**The Trials of Brother Jero**
A comedy about Brother Jeroboam, a fraudulent prophet who preaches on Bar Beach in Lagos. He manipulates his follower Chume and at first forbids him to beat his nagging wife Amope, to whom Jero owes money, then gives him permission. The sequel, Jero's Metamorphosis, sees Jero scheming against rival preachers like Shadrach.

**The Interpreters**
Soyinka's first novel (1965), about a group of young Nigerian intellectuals who have come home after studying abroad and try to make sense of post-independence society. They include the engineer turned sculptor Sekoni, the journalist Sagoe, and the painter Kola. His second novel is Season of Anomy.

**Chronicles from the Land of the Happiest People on Earth**
Soyinka's 2021 satirical novel about Nigerian corruption. The surgeon Dr. Menka discovers a racket that steals human body parts from his hospital for ritual use. His friend Duyole Pitan-Payne, an engineer about to take a United Nations post, is killed by a bomb.

**The Man Died and political imprisonment**
A prison memoir from Soyinka's nearly two years of detention, much of it in solitary confinement, during the Nigerian Civil War for trying to broker peace with Biafra. After his release, he went into exile and edited the magazine Transition. He also adapted Euripides as The Bacchae of Euripides.

**Stephen Kumalo and Absalom**
The protagonist of Alan Paton's 1948 novel is the Reverend Stephen Kumalo, an elderly Zulu Anglican priest (called "umfundisi") from the village of Ndotsheni in Natal. He travels to Johannesburg and searches for his son Absalom, who is arrested, tried, and sentenced to hang for murder.

**Arthur Jarvis**
The white engineer and advocate for racial justice whom Absalom shoots during a botched burglary of his Johannesburg house. His murder is the central event of the novel.

**Theophilus Msimangu and the letter about Gertrude**
The novel's plot begins when Msimangu, a priest at the Mission House in Sophiatown, Johannesburg, writes to Kumalo that his sister Gertrude is "very sick." Msimangu then guides Kumalo through the city, speaks many of the book's most quoted lines, and at the end gives his possessions to Kumalo before entering a religious community.

**Gertrude**
Kumalo's younger sister, who went to Johannesburg and became a liquor seller and prostitute, called a "queen" of bootleggers. Kumalo takes her to stay with him at Mrs. Lithebe's house, but the night before they are to return to Ndotsheni she disappears, leaving behind her red dress and white turban.

**"The Truth About Native Crime"**
The unfinished manuscript Arthur Jarvis was writing when he was killed; it argues that white society is responsible for the conditions that breed crime. His father, James Jarvis, reads it, along with Arthur's other writings, while going through his son's house, and it changes his views.

**Abraham Lincoln and the Gettysburg Address**
Arthur Jarvis admired Lincoln and kept many books about him. After Arthur's death, James Jarvis finds these books in his son's study and reads Lincoln's speeches, including the Gettysburg Address.

**James Jarvis and the milk for Ndotsheni**
Arthur's father, a white landowner whose farm lies above Ndotsheni. When a boy (James's grandson) asks Kumalo for milk, Kumalo answers that there is no milk in the village, so children die; soon afterward Jarvis has cans of milk delivered. He goes on to pay for a dam and hire the agricultural demonstrator Napoleon Letsitsi to restore the valley, and he builds a new church after his wife dies.

**"There is a lovely road that runs from Ixopo into the hills"**
The famous first sentence of the novel. The opening chapter describes the grass-covered, rolling hills around Ixopo and Carisbrooke as "lovely beyond any singing of it," and warns of the land: "Destroy it and man is destroyed."

**"Cry, the beloved country"**
The title phrase comes from a lament "for the unborn child that is the inheritor of our fear," which follows a chapter of white South Africans arguing about native crime, including whether more schooling simply means cleverer criminals. Another often-quoted line, from Msimangu: "The tragedy is not that things are broken. The tragedy is that things are not mended again."

**John Kumalo and Dubula**
Stephen's brother John is a carpenter turned politician with a "great bull voice" but, as Msimangu says, no brain behind it to tell it what to say. After the trial, Stephen falsely hints that John's friends are plotting to betray him, and John throws him out of his shop. Dubula, a more sincere activist, organizes the bus boycott.

**The bus boycott**
A boycott in Johannesburg over higher fares on buses to Alexandra. In support of it, Kumalo and Msimangu walk to Alexandra, and white motorists offer rides to the walkers. Earlier, a young man in the city tricks Kumalo out of some of his money by promising to buy him a bus ticket.

**Mr. Carmichael and the trial ("pro deo")**
The lawyer who takes Absalom's case "pro deo," meaning for free (literally "for God"), at Father Vincent's request. Absalom's accomplices, his cousin Matthew Kumalo (John's son) and Johannes Pafuri, are acquitted, while Absalom is sentenced to death; Carmichael later writes that Absalom will hang.

**Absalom's wedding and his pregnant girlfriend**
Before his execution, Absalom is married in prison by the white priest Father Vincent to the girl who is carrying his child. Kumalo takes her back with him to Ndotsheni.

**Kumalo's vigil on the mountain**
The novel ends with Kumalo praying alone on a mountaintop at dawn, the time of Absalom's execution, as the sun rises over the valley.

**Other clues: Sibeko's daughter, Ezenzeleni, Oppenheimer, and the reformatory**
Before leaving for Johannesburg, Kumalo is asked to look for Sibeko's daughter, who worked for the Smith family. In the city he visits Ezenzeleni, the colony of blind basket weavers, where Msimangu preaches movingly. One chapter discusses the discovery of gold at Odendaalsrust and praises Sir Ernest Oppenheimer, and the white young man at the reformatory where Absalom stayed is based on Paton himself, who ran Diepkloof Reformatory. Paton's author's note says the book was begun in Trondheim and finished in San Francisco during a tour of prisons and reformatories.

**Beloved and Sethe**
Morrison's most famous novel (1987), and the giveaway in nearly every question. Sethe, who escaped slavery, killed her infant daughter (cutting her throat with a handsaw in a woodshed) rather than let slave catchers take her back, and the girl returns years later as a ghost and then as a mysterious young woman named Beloved; the story is loosely based on the escaped slave Margaret Garner.

**124 Bluestone Road**
The house outside Cincinnati where Sethe lives with her daughter Denver, haunted by the baby's ghost. The novel opens "124 was spiteful. Full of a baby's venom," and Sethe's mother-in-law Baby Suggs, a preacher, dies there.

**Paul D and the tobacco tin**
A former slave from Sweet Home who arrives at 124 years later, drives out the ghost, and becomes Sethe's lover. He survived a chain gang in Georgia and escaped by following blossoming trees north, and he keeps his painful memories locked away in a rusted "tobacco tin" where his heart should be; he tells Sethe her love is "too thick."

**Sweet Home and Schoolteacher**
The Kentucky plantation where Sethe, Paul D, Halle (Sethe's husband), and Sixo were enslaved. After the kind Mr. Garner dies, the cruel Schoolteacher takes over, measures the slaves' features, and later has Sixo burned alive; Mrs. Garner had given Sethe a pair of crystal earrings as a wedding gift.

**Denver, Amy Denver, and Mr. Bodwin**
Sethe's surviving daughter, Denver, is named after Amy Denver, the white girl who helped deliver her during Sethe's escape. At the climax, the women of the town gather to exorcise Beloved, and Sethe attacks the white abolitionist Mr. Bodwin with an icepick, mistaking him for Schoolteacher coming to take her children; Stamp Paid, who ferried Sethe across the Ohio River, saved Denver from Sethe's attack.

**Song of Solomon and Milkman Dead**
Morrison's 1977 novel about Macon "Milkman" Dead III, nicknamed by the janitor Freddie because his mother breastfed him until he was too old. He travels south to Shalimar, Virginia, to search for hidden family gold and instead learns that his great-grandfather Solomon flew back to Africa; the novel opens with the insurance agent Robert Smith jumping off the roof of Mercy Hospital, and Milkman is born the next day.

**Guitar Bains and the Seven Days**
Milkman's best friend in Song of Solomon, who joins the Seven Days, a secret society that kills a white person in the same way, and on the same day of the week, as each Black victim of racist violence. Guitar comes to believe Milkman stole the gold, accidentally shoots Pilate, and the novel ends with Milkman leaping toward him.

**Pilate Dead**
Milkman's aunt in Song of Solomon, born without a navel. Her father chose her name blindly from the Bible, as the family names its children (Milkman's sisters are First Corinthians and Magdalene); a green sack hanging in her house that Milkman and Guitar steal, thinking it holds gold, actually contains her father's bones, and her granddaughter Hagar repeatedly tries to kill Milkman.

**The Bluest Eye and Pecola Breedlove**
Morrison's first novel (1970), about Pecola Breedlove, a young Black girl who idolizes Shirley Temple and longs for blue eyes, believing they would make her beautiful. She is raped by her father Cholly, and after her baby dies she goes mad, believing she has the bluest eyes.

**Claudia MacTeer, Dick and Jane, and the marigolds**
The Bluest Eye is narrated mainly by Claudia MacTeer, whose family takes Pecola in for a while, and its section titles come from a run-together "Dick and Jane" primer. Claudia and her sister plant marigold seeds that fail to bloom in 1941, mirroring the death of Pecola's baby.

**Soaphead Church**
A pedophile "spiritualist" in The Bluest Eye whom Pecola asks for blue eyes. He tricks her into feeding poisoned meat to his landlady's old dog, Bob, telling her that if the dog reacts, her wish will be granted.

**Sula, Nel Wright, and Chicken Little**
Sula (1973) follows the friendship of Sula Peace and Nel Wright in the Bottom, a Black neighborhood of Medallion, Ohio. As girls, Sula accidentally swings the boy Chicken Little into a river, where he drowns, and she later returns to town after ten years "accompanied by a plague of robins" and has an affair with Ajax; her one-legged grandmother Eva burns her son Plum to death.

**Shadrack and National Suicide Day**
A shell-shocked World War I veteran in Sula who founds National Suicide Day, held every January 3. Sula visits his shack right after Chicken Little drowns.

**"Recitatif"**
Morrison's only published short story, which opens "My mother danced all night." It follows Twyla and Roberta, who meet at the St. Bonny's orphanage and later end up picketing on opposite sides over school busing, while never revealing which of the two is Black and which is white.

**Later novels (Jazz, A Mercy, Tar Baby, Paradise, Love, Home)**
In Jazz, Joe Trace shoots his young lover Dorcas, and his wife Violet slashes the dead girl's face at her funeral; A Mercy follows Florens, Lina, and Sorrow, who serve the Dutch trader Jacob Vaark and his wife Rebekka in the 1600s; Tar Baby features the romance of the Sorbonne-educated Jadine and Son; Paradise opens with men from the town of Ruby attacking a convent full of women; Love centers on Heed and Christine fighting over Bill Cosey's estate; and Home follows the Korean War veteran Frank Money rescuing his sister Cee. Morrison won the 1993 Nobel Prize in Literature.

**Madame Pace summoned by hanging hats and coats on pegs**
The Father has hats, coats, and mantles hung on racks to recreate the back room of her shop, and Madame Pace ("PAH-chay") magically appears on stage. She owns a dress shop, or "atelier," that secretly operates as a brothel.

**Mixing It Up**
This is the play the acting company is rehearsing when the six characters interrupt. It is Pirandello's own play, also translated as *The Rules of the Game*, so the work pokes fun at its own author.

**The Boy shoots himself and the Child drowns in a fountain**
These deaths form the play's climax. The little girl (the Child) drowns in a garden fountain, and the silent Boy then shoots himself with a revolver, offstage or behind trees.

**"I've lost a whole day over these people!"**
The Manager, also called the Director or Stage Manager, ends the play with this exasperated line. He had agreed to help the characters stage their story and lost his entire day of rehearsal.

**"Demon of Experiment"**
The Father, the most talkative character, claims this force lives inside him. He blames it for his strange, compulsive actions, including his treatment of his family.

**The "vile" pale blue envelope on a mahogany table**
This envelope of money is left in the back room of Madame Pace's shop. The Step-Daughter describes it as the payment from the Father, a client who nearly has sex with her without realizing who she is.

**The Father's near-incestuous encounter with the Step-Daughter**
The Mother works as a seamstress for Madame Pace, who forces the Step-Daughter into prostitution, supposedly to save the Mother's job. The Father unknowingly hires his stepdaughter at the brothel, and this encounter is the central trauma the characters reenact.

**"You represent the shell of the eggs you are beating"**
The Manager says this to the Leading Man, who complains about having to wear a "ridiculous" chef's hat. In *Mixing It Up*, the characters Leo Gala and Philip beat eggs, and the Prompter reads from the script during this exchange.

**Reality vs. "pretence" debate over the Boy's death**
After the revolver shot, the actors argue over whether the Boy is really dead or whether it is "only a pretence." This captures the play's central theme of illusion versus reality.

**Don Abbondio and Sancho Panza "live eternally"**
The Father says these characters, from Manzoni's *The Betrothed* and Cervantes's *Don Quixote*, live forever because they were born in the "fecundating matrix" of fantasy. He argues that fictional characters are more real and permanent than people, whose identities change.

**"Scream as you screamed then!"**
The Step-Daughter commands the Mother to cry out as she did when she discovered the Father with the Step-Daughter at Madame Pace's. This moment is the climax of the brothel reenactment.

**Amalia, the Clerk, and the family's backstory**
The Mother is named Amalia. The Father sent her away to live with his secretary, the Clerk, and forced her to leave behind their son, the Son, when he was two. After the Clerk died, she and her illegitimate children fell into poverty, which led to her seamstress job and the Step-Daughter's prostitution.

**Madame Pace's appearance and the "vulgar trick"**
Madame Pace is a heavily made-up woman in black silk, with a pair of scissors dangling from a silver chain at her waist. She speaks a mangled mix of Spanish and Italian, rendered in English translations as broken English ("laugha atta me"). The actors call her magical summoning a "vulgar trick."

**Masks and the preface's "nimble little maidservant"**
In the stage directions, the characters wear stiff masks expressing their fixed emotions, such as the Mother's mask with wax tears to symbolize sorrow. In his preface, Pirandello credits his "puckish," "nimble little maidservant," Fantasy, with bringing the characters to him.

**Complaints about French comedies**
At the start, the Manager laments that he can't get good French comedies anymore and must stage Pirandello's plays instead. In those plays, an actor complains, "nobody understands anything."

**Tess of the d'Urbervilles**
Hardy's most famous novel (1891), the near-universal giveaway. Tess Durbeyfield, a poor girl whose father learns the family descends from the noble d'Urbervilles, is seduced and raped by Alec, marries Angel Clare, and is finally hanged for murdering Alec. Hardy famously closes it by saying "the President of the Immortals" had "ended his sport with Tess."

**Angel Clare**
The parson's son who falls in love with Tess while she works as a milkmaid at Talbothays Dairy alongside Retty, Izz, and Marian. On their wedding night Tess confesses her past, and Angel abandons her and goes to Brazil; he returns too late, and at the end Tess asks him to marry her younger sister, Liza-Lu.

**Tess stabs Alec and is arrested at Stonehenge**
Tess kills Alec d'Urberville, the man who raped her, at a boarding house called The Herons in the resort town of Sandbourne. She flees with Angel and sleeps on the Stone of Sacrifice at Stonehenge, where she wakes to the police and says "I am ready." A black flag raised over the prison at Wintoncester signals her execution.

**Sorrow**
The name Tess gives the sickly baby born after Alec rapes her. She baptizes the dying infant herself because the vicar will not, and after its death she leaves home to work at Talbothays Dairy.

**The Mayor of Casterbridge and the sale for five guineas**
Hardy's 1886 novel opens at a country fair where a drunken Michael Henchard, after drinking furmity (a porridge) laced with rum, auctions his wife Susan and daughter Elizabeth-Jane to the sailor Newson for five guineas. Ashamed when he wakes, he swears not to drink for twenty-one years, and he later rises to become mayor of Casterbridge.

**Michael Henchard, Donald Farfrae, and Lucetta**
Henchard's rival is the Scottish corn merchant Donald Farfrae, who overtakes his business, marries his former lover Lucetta Le Sueur, and later marries Elizabeth-Jane, who turns out to be Newson's daughter. Lucetta dies after townspeople stage a "skimmity-ride" mocking her past affair, which Jopp exposes by reading her letters aloud. Henchard dies ruined, leaving a will asking "that no man remember me."

**Jude the Obscure**
Hardy's last novel (1895), about the stonemason Jude Fawley, who dreams of becoming a scholar at Christminster. He is tricked into marrying Arabella Donn and loves his cousin Sue Bridehead, who marries the schoolteacher Phillotson before living with Jude. The novel's harsh reception helped push Hardy to give up fiction for poetry.

**Little Father Time and "Done because we are too menny"**
Jude's son by Arabella, raised in Australia and sent to live with Jude and Sue. Told that the family is poor and that Sue is expecting another child, he hangs his half-siblings and then himself, leaving the misspelled note "Done because we are too menny."

**"The Convergence of the Twain"**
Hardy's poem on the 1912 sinking of the Titanic, subtitled "Lines on the loss of the 'Titanic'" and collected in Satires of Circumstance. It begins "In a solitude of the sea / Deep from human vanity," describes a "sea-worm" crawling "grotesque, slimed, dumb, indifferent" and "dim moon-eyed fishes" in the wreck, and says "the Immanent Will that stirs and urges everything" made a "Shape of Ice" grow as the ship grew.

**Far from the Madding Crowd**
An 1874 novel whose title comes from Thomas Gray's "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard." Gabriel Oak is ruined when his dog drives his sheep off a cliff and becomes a shepherd for the farmer Bathsheba Everdene. She sends the farmer William Boldwood a joking valentine that he takes seriously, and she marries the dashing Sergeant Frank Troy, who woos her with a sword exercise and had earlier jilted Fanny Robin after she went to the wrong church. Boldwood shoots Troy, and Bathsheba finally marries Gabriel.

**The Return of the Native**
An 1878 novel set on Egdon Heath that opens with Guy Fawkes Night bonfires. Clym Yeobright gives up his job as a diamond merchant in Paris and becomes a furze-cutter, to the dismay of his wife Eustacia Vye, who longs to escape to Paris and is drawn to Damon Wildeve. Eustacia and Wildeve drown in a weir, and the reddleman Diggory Venn marries Thomasin.

**"The Darkling Thrush"**
A poem dated December 31, 1900, beginning "I leant upon a coppice gate." The bleak landscape is "the Century's corpse outleant," the "ancient pulse of germ and birth" seems shrunken, and "tangled bine-stems" score the sky "like strings of broken lyres." An aged thrush suddenly "fling[s] his soul / Upon the growing gloom," suggesting "some blessed Hope, whereof he knew / And I was unaware."

**Wessex**
The fictional region of southwest England, based largely on Hardy's native Dorset, where most of his novels are set. Hardy revived the old Anglo-Saxon kingdom's name for it, and his major works are often called the Wessex novels.

**Prince and the "blighted star"**
Early in Tess, Tess falls asleep while driving a wagon of beehives to market, and the family's only horse, Prince, is killed in a collision with the mail cart. Just before, she tells her brother that they live on a "blighted" star rather than a sound one.

**A Pair of Blue Eyes**
An 1873 novel in which Elfride Swancourt is courted by the young architect Stephen Smith and later by the critic Henry Knight. A scene in which Knight is left hanging from a cliff, at the end of a serial installment, is often credited with giving rise to the term "cliffhanger."

**"Daddy" and "a man in black with a Meinkampf look"**
Plath's most famous poem, written in 1962 and published in Ariel, is addressed to her father, Otto Plath, a German-born professor and bee expert who died when she was eight. Using Holocaust and Nazi imagery, the speaker casts her father as a Nazi and herself as a Jew. She calls him "a man in black with a Meinkampf look," a "ghastly statue with one gray toe / Big as a Frisco seal," and a teacher who stands "at the blackboard" with "a cleft in your chin instead of your foot."

**"You do not do, you do not do" and "you bastard, I'm through"**
The opening and closing lines of "Daddy." The father is a "black shoe / In which I have lived like a foot / For thirty years." The speaker says "Daddy, I have had to kill you. / You died before I had time," and the poem ends "There's a stake in your fat black heart / And the villagers never liked you... Daddy, daddy, you bastard, I'm through."

**"Every woman adores a Fascist"**
Another line from "Daddy," in which the speaker says she has "always been scared of you, / With your Luftwaffe, your gobbledygoo," and stammers "Ich, ich, ich, ich" when trying to speak German. She rejects the "snows of the Tyrol" and "the clear beer of Vienna" and recalls a Polish town "scraped flat by the roller / Of wars, wars, wars." The father figure merges with "the vampire who said he was you / And drank my blood for a year," widely read as her husband, Ted Hughes.

**"Lady Lazarus" and "I eat men like air"**
A 1962 poem in Ariel in which the speaker, like the biblical Lazarus, keeps returning from death. It opens "I have done it again. / One year in every ten / I manage it," and ends with a threat to "Herr God, Herr Lucifer": "Out of the ash / I rise with my red hair / And I eat men like air."

**"Dying / Is an art, like everything else"**
The most famous lines of "Lady Lazarus," which continue "I do it exceptionally well. / I do it so it feels like hell." The speaker, who is "only thirty" and "like the cat" has "nine times to die," calls this suicide attempt "Number Three. / What a trash / To annihilate each decade." She taunts "Peel off the napkin / O my enemy. / Do I terrify?" and uses Holocaust images such as "a cake of soap, / A wedding ring, / A gold filling."

**Ariel**
Plath's posthumous 1965 collection, edited by Ted Hughes, which contains "Daddy," "Lady Lazarus," "Tulips," and "Morning Song." Its title poem, named for a horse she rode, begins "Stasis in darkness. / Then the substanceless blue" and calls the horse "God's lioness." The speaker unpeels "dead hands, dead stringencies," becomes "the arrow, / The dew that flies," and ends "at one with the drive / Into the red / Eye, the cauldron of morning."

**The Bell Jar and Esther Greenwood**
Plath's only novel (1963), first published under the pseudonym Victoria Lucas about a month before her death. Esther Greenwood, a college student on a summer internship at Ladies' Day magazine in New York, befriends Doreen and pictures her life as a fig tree whose branching choices wither as she fails to pick one. She sinks into depression, receives botched electroshock therapy from Dr. Gordon, attempts suicide, and recovers under Dr. Nolan at a private hospital paid for by the novelist Philomena Guinea.

**Ted Hughes and Plath's 1963 suicide**
Plath married the English poet Ted Hughes in 1956, and his first collection, The Hawk in the Rain, is dedicated to her. They separated in 1962 after his affair, and in February 1963 she killed herself by putting her head in a gas oven in London. Hughes's 1998 collection Birthday Letters, a set of poems addressed to her, includes "The Blue Flannel Suit."

**"Mad Girl's Love Song"**
An early villanelle that repeats "I shut my eyes and all the world drops dead" and the parenthetical refrain "(I think I made you up inside my head.)" The speaker imagines "the stars go waltzing out in blue and red" and wishes "I should have loved a thunderbird instead."

**"The Munich Mannequins"**
A late poem opening "Perfection is terrible, it cannot have children." It describes the "morgue between Paris and Rome," the shop-window mannequins "naked and bald in their furs, / Orange lollies on silver sticks," and ends "The snow has no voice."

**"Tulips"**
A 1961 poem written after Plath was hospitalized for surgery. The speaker wants to be blank and at peace: "I am nobody; I have nothing to do with explosions," having given "my history to the anesthetist and my body to surgeons." The nurses pass "the way gulls pass inland in their white caps," and the vivid red tulips seem to "eat my oxygen" and force her back to life.

**"The Colossus"**
The title poem of Plath's first collection (1960), in which the speaker tries to piece together a huge ruined statue representing her dead father. She calls him "pithy and historical as the Roman Forum" and says "A blue sky out of the Oresteia / Arches above us."

**"The Applicant"**
A satirical poem in which a salesman pitches a wife to a man as if she were a product. She will "bring teacups," "do whatever you tell it," sew, and cook, and the poem ends "Will you marry it, marry it, marry it."

**"Morning Song"**
The poem opening Ariel, about the birth of her daughter, which begins "Love set you going like a fat gold watch." It ends with the baby's "clear vowels" that "rise like balloons."

**"Mirror"**
A poem spoken by a mirror that is "silver and exact" and has "no preconceptions," and that later becomes a lake. A woman bends over it every day, and it ends: "In me she has drowned a young girl, and in me an old woman / Rises toward her day after day, like a terrible fish."

**"The Overcoat"**
Gogol's most famous short story, about Akaky Akakievich, a meek St. Petersburg government copyist. He saves for a new overcoat, which is stolen by robbers on his way home from a party held to celebrate it. He dies after being berated by an official, and his ghost then haunts the city, stealing coats.

**Akaky Akakievich**
The protagonist of "The Overcoat," a lowly clerk who loves copying documents. The story opens by describing "a certain official" in "a certain department." When colleagues mock him, he cries out "I am your brother," which makes a young official ashamed of joining in the teasing.

**Petrovich the tailor**
The one-eyed tailor in "The Overcoat" who refuses to patch Akaky's worn-out coat and instead makes him a new one, using cat fur for the collar because marten is too expensive.

**The "Person of Consequence" (Important Person)**
The pompous high official Akaky turns to for help after his coat is stolen. The official scolds him so harshly that Akaky falls ill and dies. Akaky's ghost later attacks this official and takes his coat, after which the ghost stops appearing.

**"The Nose"**
An absurd story in which Major Kovalyov, a collegiate assessor, wakes up to find his nose missing. The nose appears around St. Petersburg in the gold-braided uniform of a State Councilor, outranking its owner, and is later caught trying to leave for Riga by stagecoach with a forged passport. It eventually reappears on Kovalyov's face.

**Ivan Yakovlevich the barber**
The barber in "The Nose" who finds Kovalyov's nose baked inside a loaf of bread at breakfast. He tries to get rid of it by dropping it into the Neva River from a bridge, which draws a policeman's suspicion. Kovalyov had earlier complained that the barber's hands smelled, prompting the reply, "But why should they stink?"

**Major Kovalyov and Madame Podtochina**
Platon Kuzmich Kovalyov is the vain, rank-obsessed owner of the nose. He suspects that Madame Podtochina, who wanted him to marry her daughter, used witchcraft to take his nose.

**Dead Souls**
Gogol's unfinished novel, the second part of which survives only in fragments. In it, the swindler Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov travels through the provinces buying the legal titles to dead serfs who are still listed on the census rolls, so he can use them as collateral. The surviving text ends mid-sentence during a prince's speech condemning corruption.

**Chichikov's landowners, Captain Kopeikin, and the troika**
In Dead Souls, Chichikov buys dead souls from grotesque landowners such as the miser Plyushkin and the bearish Sobakevich. Townspeople speculate that he may be Napoleon in disguise or the legendary disabled veteran Captain Kopeikin. Part one ends by comparing Russia to a speeding troika (a sled drawn by three horses). In the second part, Chichikov buys an estate from Khlobuyev.

**The Inspector General (The Government Inspector)**
Gogol's satirical comedy in which the corrupt officials of a provincial town mistake the penniless traveler Khlestakov for a government inspector traveling incognito. They shower him with bribes, and he proposes to the mayor's daughter Maria before leaving. A letter he sends to the postmaster mocking the townspeople is opened and read aloud. Other clues include the mayor's order to hang Latin signs above hospital beds and a non-commissioned officer's widow who supposedly "flogged herself."

**"Diary of a Madman"**
A story told through the diary of Poprishchin, a minor clerk who slides into insanity. He reads letters between the dogs Medji and Fidele, worries that the earth will sit on the moon, and finally decides he is the heir to the Spanish throne, signing his name "Ferdinand VIII." It appeared in Gogol's collection Arabesques.

**"Nevsky Prospekt"**
A story contrasting two men who follow women along St. Petersburg's main avenue. The idealistic painter Piskarev follows a beautiful dark-haired woman who turns out to be a prostitute, and after she rejects his attempt to reform her he slits his throat. The shallow Lieutenant Pirogov follows the wife of a German tinsmith, is beaten for it, and soon consoles himself with puff pastries.

**Evenings on a Farm Near Dikanka**
Gogol's first successful collection of Ukrainian folk tales, narrated by the beekeeper Rudy Panko. It includes "St. John's Eve," "A May Night," "Christmas Eve" (in which the blacksmith Vakula rides the devil to St. Petersburg to get the tsaritsa's slippers for the village beauty Oksana), "A Terrible Vengeance" (with Danilo, Katerina, and an evil sorcerer by the Dnieper), and "The Enchanted Spot."

**"St. John's Eve"**
A story in the Dikanka collection in which Petro searches for a fern that blooms only on Kupala Night to find treasure. The witch guarding the treasure makes him behead the child Ivas to get it, and the devil eventually carries Petro off.

**"Viy"**
A horror story from the Mirgorod collection in which the seminary student and philosopher Khoma Brut (Thomas) must read prayers over the corpse of a witch for three nights. On the third night she summons the title demon, the Viy, whose gaze reveals Khoma, and he dies of fright.

**Anna Karenina and Count Vronsky**
Tolstoy's 1878 novel about Anna, the wife of the official Alexei Karenin, who has a disastrous affair with the cavalry officer Count Vronsky. They first meet at a railway station where a worker is killed by a train, and at the end, convinced Vronsky no longer loves her, Anna throws herself under a train.

**"All happy families are alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way"**
The famous opening line of Anna Karenina. The novel begins with the household of Anna's brother Stiva Oblonsky in chaos after his wife Dolly discovers his affair.

**Kitty and Konstantin Levin**
The second main couple of Anna Karenina, whose happy marriage contrasts with Anna and Vronsky's affair. Kitty Shcherbatskaya first rejects Levin because she hopes to marry Vronsky, but she later marries Levin, a landowner who searches for meaning in farm life and faith. Other clues include the French clairvoyant Landau, who advises Karenin not to divorce Anna.

**War and Peace**
Tolstoy's enormous 1869 novel about aristocratic Russian families during the Napoleonic Wars, culminating in Napoleon's 1812 invasion of Russia. It opens in 1805 at a soiree hosted by Anna Pavlovna Scherer, and its epilogue attacks the "Great Man" theory, arguing that history is the sum of countless tiny human actions, like an integral of infinitesimals.

**Pierre Bezukhov and Natasha Rostova**
The central figures of War and Peace. The awkward, illegitimate heir Pierre wounds Dolokhov in a duel, comes to believe he is destined to assassinate Napoleon during the occupation of Moscow, and finally marries Natasha, who earlier broke her engagement to Prince Andrei by trying to elope with the rake Anatole Kuragin.

**Prince Andrei Bolkonsky and the "lofty sky"**
In War and Peace, Andrei lies wounded on the battlefield of Austerlitz and gazes at the infinite "lofty sky," realizing the emptiness of his dreams of glory. He is mortally wounded at the Battle of Borodino in 1812 and later dies.

**Platon Karataev**
The wise, simple peasant whom Pierre meets as a prisoner of the French in War and Peace. He tells the story of a merchant wrongly convicted of murder, and he is shot by the French when he falls behind during the retreat from Moscow.

**The Death of Ivan Ilyich**
An 1886 novella about Ivan Ilyich Golovin, a high-court judge who lives a conventional, careerist life. He hurts his side falling while hanging curtains in his new apartment, and the injury slowly kills him while his wife Praskovya and his colleagues ignore his suffering.

**Gerasim and Ivan Ilyich's final days**
In The Death of Ivan Ilyich, the peasant servant Gerasim is the only person who cares for Ivan honestly, holding his legs up on his shoulders to ease his pain. Ivan wonders "What if my whole life has been wrong?", dreams of being pushed into a black sack, and screams for three days before finding peace as his son kisses his hand; the story opens with colleagues like Peter Ivanovich, who hurries off to play bridge with Schwartz after the funeral.

**The Kreutzer Sonata**
An 1889 novella in which Pozdnyshev, on a train, interrupts a conversation about love and marriage to confess that he killed his wife out of jealousy. She had been playing Beethoven's Kreutzer Sonata with the violinist Trukhachevsky; Tolstoy later added an afterword advocating sexual abstinence.

**"How Much Land Does a Man Need?"**
An 1886 story in which the greedy peasant Pahom is offered by the Bashkirs all the land he can walk around in one day, starting and ending at a spot marked by their chief's fox-fur cap. He overreaches and dies of exhaustion just as he returns, and his servant buries him in a grave six feet long, which answers the title question.

**Sevastopol Sketches**
Three stories based on Tolstoy's service in the Siege of Sevastopol during the Crimean War, set in December 1854, May 1855, and August 1855. The first is written in the second person and tours a military hospital, and the second ends with the declaration that the story's hero is "the truth."

**Resurrection and Hadji Murat**
Resurrection (1899), Tolstoy's last novel, follows Prince Dmitri Nekhlyudov, who as a juror recognizes the defendant Katyusha Maslova as the maid he seduced long ago, and follows her to Siberia after she is wrongly convicted of murder. Hadji Murat, published after his death, follows an Avar commander who defects from the Chechen leader Shamil to the Russians.

**The Cossacks and "Father Sergius"**
In The Cossacks (1863), the Russian officer Olenin falls for the Cossack girl Maryanka, who is engaged to Lukashka and turns Olenin away after Lukashka is wounded by Chechens. In "Father Sergius," a nobleman who becomes a monk cuts off his own finger to resist the temptation of the divorcee Makovkina.

**"What Men Live By" and other later works**
In "What Men Live By," the poor shoemaker Simon takes in Michael, a naked stranger found by a shrine, who is an angel learning the answers to three questions. Tolstoy's other works include the autobiographical trilogy beginning with Childhood, the novella Family Happiness (about Masha and Sergey Mikhaylych), the story "Alyosha the Pot," and The Kingdom of God Is Within You, which sets out his Christian anarchism and nonviolence.

**The Old Man and the Sea**
Hemingway's 1952 novella and his most common giveaway. The aging Cuban fisherman Santiago, who has gone 84 days without catching a fish, hooks a giant marlin in the Gulf Stream and fights it for days, but sharks devour it on the way home, leaving only the skeleton. It won the Pulitzer Prize and helped win Hemingway the 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature.

**Santiago, Manolin, and "the great DiMaggio"**
Details from The Old Man and the Sea. Santiago is called "salao," the worst form of unlucky, so the boy Manolin is forced by his parents to fish on another boat. Santiago idolizes the baseball player Joe DiMaggio, talks to his cramped hand during the struggle, and repeatedly dreams of lions on an African beach.

**A Farewell to Arms**
Hemingway's 1929 World War I novel, drawn from his own service as a Red Cross ambulance driver in Italy. The American ambulance officer Frederic Henry, introduced by his friend the surgeon Rinaldi to the British nurse Catherine Barkley, deserts the Italian army after escaping the battle police during the retreat from Caporetto. He rows with Catherine to Switzerland, where she dies after giving birth to a stillborn son, and the novel ends with him walking back to the hotel in the rain. A frequently mocked priest also befriends Frederic.

**The Sun Also Rises**
Hemingway's 1926 novel about American and British expatriates who travel from Paris to the bullfights at Pamplona. The narrator Jake Barnes, left impotent by a war wound, loves Lady Brett Ashley, who has an affair with the former Princeton boxing champion Robert Cohn and then runs off with the young matador Pedro Romero. Its epigraph quotes Gertrude Stein's line "You are all a lost generation," popularizing the term "Lost Generation"; early on Jake also picks up the prostitute Georgette.

**"Hills Like White Elephants"**
A dialogue-driven short story from the collection Men Without Women, set at a Spanish railway station on the line to Madrid. "The American" tries to persuade his companion Jig to have "an operation," an abortion that is never named, while they drink beer ("dos cervezas") and Anís del Toro brought by a woman behind a bead curtain.

**Nick Adams and In Our Time**
Nick Adams is Hemingway's semi-autobiographical recurring character, appearing in many of the stories in In Our Time (1925), a collection that interleaves stories with short vignettes of war and bullfighting, and in later stories such as "The Killers," "The Battler," and "Fathers and Sons" (in which Nick remembers his youthful encounters with the Ojibwe girl Trudy, sister of Billy).

**"Indian Camp"**
A Nick Adams story in which young Nick goes with his doctor father to an Indian camp, where his father delivers a baby by Caesarean section with a jackknife and no anesthetic. Afterward they discover that the woman's husband, lying in the upper bunk, has cut his own throat with a razor. The story ends with Nick feeling quite sure that he would never die.

**"Big Two-Hearted River"**
The two-part story that closes In Our Time. Nick Adams, back from the war, walks past the burned-out town of Seney, Michigan, camps alone, cooks beans and spaghetti, catches blackened grasshoppers in a jar as bait, and fishes for trout. The war is never mentioned, an example of Hemingway's theory of omission.

**For Whom the Bell Tolls**
Hemingway's 1940 novel set during the Spanish Civil War, drawn from his time reporting on that war. The American Robert Jordan, a Spanish instructor fighting for the Republic, is ordered to blow up a bridge with the help of a guerrilla band led by the unreliable Pablo and his strong wife Pilar. He falls in love with the young Maria; the old man Anselmo is killed when the bridge blows, and the novel ends with the wounded Jordan lying in wait to ambush the enemy.

**"The Short Happy Life of Francis Macomber"**
A safari story in which Francis Macomber shames himself by fleeing a charging lion, after which his wife Margot sleeps with the British hunter Robert Wilson. Macomber regains his courage hunting buffalo, but as a buffalo charges him, Margot fires and shoots him in the back of the head, leaving it ambiguous whether it was an accident.

**"The Snows of Kilimanjaro"**
A story about the writer Harry, who is dying of gangrene in Africa because he did not treat a thorn scratch on his leg with iodine. As vultures and a hyena wait nearby, he remembers his youth, including his time in Paris, and regrets the books he never wrote; at the end his wife Helen is awakened by the hyena and finds him dead.

**"The Killers"**
A Nick Adams story set at Henry's lunch-room, where the hitmen Al and Max, who call people "bright boy," wait to kill the Swedish former boxer Ole Andreson. The counterman George sends Nick to warn Ole, who simply waits in his room for death.

**Death in the Afternoon and the iceberg theory**
Death in the Afternoon (1932) is Hemingway's nonfiction study of Spanish bullfighting, which popularized the phrase "moment of truth" in English. In it he described his "iceberg theory" (theory of omission): the dignity of movement of an iceberg is due to only one-eighth of it being above water, so a writer can omit things he knows and the reader will still feel them.

**"For sale: baby shoes, never worn"**
A six-word story often attributed to Hemingway, supposedly written on a napkin to win a bet, though the attribution is apocryphal. His other famous pieces of writing advice include writing "one true sentence," described in his Paris memoir A Moveable Feast; his works also often explore "nada," the sense of nothingness felt by sleepless men at night.

**To Have and Have Not, Islands in the Stream, and Green Hills of Africa**
Other Hemingway books. To Have and Have Not follows the Key West boat captain and smuggler Harry Morgan, who is hired to smuggle Chinese immigrants. The posthumous Islands in the Stream follows the painter Thomas Hudson on the Bahamian island of Bimini. The nonfiction Green Hills of Africa, about a safari in Tanzania, includes his talk with the Austrian Kandinsky about a "fourth and fifth dimension" of prose and his claim that all modern American literature comes from Huckleberry Finn; he wrote it while living in Key West, in a house now home to polydactyl cats. Another story, "The Gambler, the Nun, and the Radio," centers on Cayetano, recovering from a gunshot wound in a Montana hospital.

**Madame Bovary**
Flaubert's most famous novel (1857), a landmark of realism that led to an obscenity trial when it was published. Emma Bovary, a romantic, bored woman from Normandy, marries the dull country doctor Charles Bovary, has affairs, and falls into ruin. It is the most common giveaway for Flaubert.

**Emma's arsenic suicide and Lheureux**
The scheming merchant and draper Lheureux leads Emma into crushing debt with luxury goods and loans, then calls the debts in. When her former lovers refuse to help her, she swallows arsenic from the pharmacy, claiming she needs it to "kill some rats," and dies an agonizing death. Lheureux also puts the innkeeper Madame Lefrançois's rival out of business.

**Léon Dupuis and Rodolphe Boulanger**
Emma's two lovers. Rodolphe, a wealthy landowner, seduces her and then abandons her when she wants to run away with him. Léon, a law clerk (later a law student) whom she first meets in Yonville, becomes her lover in Rouen, where she meets him by pretending to take weekly piano lessons.

**Charles Bovary and Hippolyte's clubfoot**
Charles is only an officier de santé ("health officer"), not a fully qualified doctor. Pushed by the pharmacist Homais and by Emma, he attempts a fashionable operation on the clubfoot of the stableboy Hippolyte. It fails, gangrene sets in, and the leg must be amputated by a real surgeon, which humiliates Charles and drives Emma toward adultery. His older first wife, Héloïse, died after it was revealed that she had lied about her property.

**Lucia di Lammermoor**
Charles takes Emma to see Donizetti's opera in Rouen, where she meets Léon again and begins her second affair.

**The agricultural fair at Yonville**
A famous scene in which Rodolphe's seductive speech to Emma in the town hall is intercut with officials' speeches outside, including prizes for manure, at the agricultural show. It ironically sets romantic clichés against provincial banality.

**Homais and other Yonville details**
The pompous, self-promoting pharmacist Homais thrives while the Bovarys fall, and at the end of the novel he receives the Cross of the Legion of Honor. When the Bovarys move to Yonville on the coach driven by Hivert, Emma's greyhound Djali runs away.

**"A Simple Heart" (Un cœur simple)**
A story from Three Tales about Félicité, a selfless, uneducated servant who works for decades for Madame Aubain after her lover Théodore marries a rich woman to avoid the draft. She grows devoted to her parrot Loulou, has it stuffed after it dies, and prays to it, and as she dies she sees a giant parrot hovering above her. Early in the story she throws dirt in a bull's eyes to save Madame Aubain and the children.

**Three Tales: "Herodias" and "Saint Julian the Hospitaller"**
The other two stories in Three Tales (1877). "Herodias" retells the beheading of John the Baptist from the court of Herod. "The Legend of Saint Julian the Hospitaller" follows a cruel hunter who slaughters a whole valley of animals until a stag curses him to kill his parents, which he later does by accident before seeking redemption.

**Salammbô**
A historical novel set in Carthage during the Mercenary War that followed the First Punic War; Flaubert traveled to the ruins of Carthage to research it. The mercenary leader Matho, helped by the freed Greek slave Spendius, steals the zaïmph, the sacred veil of the goddess Tanit. Salammbô, the priestess daughter of Hamilcar Barca, recovers it, and the novel ends with Matho's torture and execution and Salammbô's death.

**A Sentimental Education (L'Éducation sentimentale)**
A partly autobiographical novel about Frédéric Moreau, a young man in Paris around the Revolution of 1848 who fails his law exams and is lifelong in love with the older, married Marie Arnoux. He also has affairs with the courtesan Rosanette and with Madame Dambreuse, and his friend Charles Deslauriers marries Louise Roque. Jacques Arnoux is based on the music publisher Maurice Schlesinger.

**"Le mot juste" and authorial impersonality**
Flaubert famously labored for days over sentences in search of "le mot juste," the exactly right word. In a letter to his mistress Louise Colet, he wrote that the author should be "like God in the universe, present everywhere and visible nowhere." He also corresponded with George Sand, whom he called "Master."

**Flaubert's Parrot**
A 1984 novel by Julian Barnes in which the retired doctor Geoffrey Braithwaite tries to work out which of two stuffed parrots was the one Flaubert kept on his desk while writing "A Simple Heart." Mario Vargas Llosa also wrote about Madame Bovary in his essay The Perpetual Orgy and drew on it for his novel The Bad Girl.

**Bouvard and Pécuchet and the Dictionary of Received Ideas**
Flaubert's unfinished final novel follows two Parisian copy-clerks who retire to the countryside near Chavignolles and fail in every field of knowledge they attempt. Flaubert claimed he read some fifteen hundred books to research it. The satirical Dictionary of Received Ideas, a list of bourgeois clichés, was meant to accompany it.

**The Temptation of Saint Anthony**
A dramatic prose work, revised over decades, in which the desert hermit Saint Anthony faces a night of visions and temptations. His former disciple Hilarion leads him through heresies and in the end turns out to be Science, and Anthony recalls his love for the girl Ammonaria.

**Eliza Doolittle**
She is the Cockney flower girl at the centre of the play, and she is trained to speak and behave like a lady. At an embassy reception, Higgins's former pupil Nepommuck, a Hungarian interpreter, wrongly declares that she is a Hungarian princess of "royal blood."

**Henry Higgins and Colonel Pickering's bet**
Henry Higgins is a professor of phonetics who lives on Wimpole Street. Colonel Pickering wrote "Spoken Sanskrit" and studies Indian dialects. The two men bet on whether Higgins can make Eliza speak well enough to pass her off as a duchess. The play is named after the sculptor in Greek myth who fell in love with his own statue, and it was adapted into the musical and film *My Fair Lady*.

**Freddy Eynsford-Hill**
He is a weak but kind young gentleman who bumps into Eliza and her flowers in Covent Garden. He falls for her when he meets her again later. Eliza decides to marry Freddy instead of staying with Higgins.

**Covent Garden opening scene and the Note-Taker**
Act One takes place in the rain under the portico of a church in Covent Garden, London's market district. Higgins, listed as "The Note-Taker," writes down people's speech and guesses where they come from by their accents. Eliza ("The Flower Girl") fears he is a police informer and cries, "I'm a good girl, I am." Other characters in the scene include "The Sarcastic Bystander" and "The Gentleman" (Pickering).

**"Most original moralist" and the Wannafeller Moral Reform World League**
As a joke, Higgins writes to the American millionaire Ezra D. Wannafeller that Eliza's father, Alfred Doolittle, is "the most original moralist" in England. Wannafeller dies and leaves Doolittle money in his will on condition that he gives lectures for the Wannafeller Moral Reform World League. This makes Doolittle unhappily respectable, trapped by "middle-class morality."

**The thrown slippers**
After Eliza's triumph at the embassy party, Higgins ignores her and takes all the credit. When he asks where his slippers are, she throws them at him, calls him a selfish brute, and asks why he didn't leave her in the gutter.

**"Not bloody likely!"**
When Freddy asks Eliza if she is walking across the park, she gives this shocking answer during a visit to Higgins's mother's home. The line caused a sensation in 1914, and "Not Pygmalion likely" became a joking substitute for the swear word.

**"What Happened Afterwards" and Herbert Beerbohm Tree**
Herbert Beerbohm Tree played Higgins in the first London production and suggested that Higgins and Eliza would end up together. Shaw, the author, objected and added a prose epilogue called "What Happened Afterwards." It says Eliza marries Freddy and opens a flower shop with money from Pickering, and that she studies bookkeeping and typewriting to keep it running. It also says that Freddy's sister Clara starts reading the novels of H. G. Wells.

**"The new small talk"**
At Mrs. Higgins's "at-home" (an afternoon reception), Eliza speaks with perfect pronunciation but uses gutter phrases. She claims her aunt was "done in" by relatives and says gin was "mother's milk" to her. Higgins passes this off as "the new small talk," and Freddy's sister Clara is impressed enough to copy it.

**Mrs. Higgins ("Men! Men! Men!")**
She is Henry's sensible mother. She teases him that he never falls in love with anyone under forty-five, and she later shelters Eliza when Eliza runs away from him. Act Three ends with her exasperated cry "Men! Men! Men!" at how thoughtless Higgins and Pickering are.

**Mrs. Pearce, the bath, and the kimono**
Mrs. Pearce is Higgins's housekeeper. She scrubs Eliza in a bath while Eliza screams, and Eliza is so embarrassed by the bathroom mirror that she covers it. Afterwards, Eliza is dressed in a blue Japanese kimono.

**Alfred Doolittle sells his daughter for five pounds**
Eliza's father, a dustman, comes to Higgins's house to get money for his daughter. He takes five pounds and refuses ten. When Pickering asks, "Have you no morals, man?", he replies that he can't afford them.

**The chocolates**
To tempt Eliza into lessons, Higgins pops a chocolate into her mouth to silence her. Because she suspects it is poisoned, he eats half of one to prove it is safe.

**The ring in the fireplace**
During their fight after the embassy party, Eliza gives back a ring Higgins bought her. He angrily throws it into the fireplace, and she later looks for it.

**"Ah-ah-ah-ow-ow-oo!"**
This is Eliza's typical Cockney howl of protest. She "relapses" into it when her father unexpectedly comes in from the balcony near the end of the play, which shows that her new speech is not yet second nature.

**The green light**
The green light at the end of Daisy Buchanan's dock in East Egg, visible across the bay from Jay Gatsby's mansion in West Egg. Gatsby first appears stretching out his arms toward it "in a curious way," trembling. Once he is reunited with Daisy, Nick notes that its "colossal significance" has vanished and Gatsby's "count of enchanted objects had diminished by one." At the end Nick links it to "the orgastic future that year by year recedes before us," and it is usually read as a symbol of Gatsby's unreachable dream.

**The Valley of Ashes and the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg**
A bleak industrial wasteland between West Egg and New York City, watched over by a faded optometrist's billboard showing the huge spectacled eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg. George Wilson's garage is here, and after his wife's death George treats the eyes as the eyes of God. Francis Cugat's famous cover art of floating eyes and a face is often connected to the billboard.

**Myrtle Wilson's death**
Tom Buchanan's mistress Myrtle, the wife of the garage owner George Wilson, runs into the road and is killed by Gatsby's yellow car while Daisy is driving, so that her blood mixes with the ashes. Gatsby takes the blame to protect Daisy. The Greek neighbor Michaelis is the key witness to the accident.

**George Wilson shoots Gatsby in his pool**
After finding an expensive new dog leash that convinces him Myrtle was having an affair, George Wilson is told by Tom that the yellow car belonged to Gatsby. He shoots Gatsby as Gatsby floats in his swimming pool and then kills himself. A gardener finds the body, described as a "laden mattress," and the chapter ends "the holocaust was complete."

**Meyer Wolfsheim**
Gatsby's gangster associate and partner in bootlegging, who wears cufflinks made of human molars and is said to have fixed the 1919 World Series (the Black Sox Scandal). He offers Nick a "gonnegtion," dwells on the memory of the shooting of Rosy Rosenthal, runs the Swastika Holding Company, and refuses to attend Gatsby's funeral. Walter Chase went to jail rather than inform on Gatsby because he feared Wolfsheim.

**Gatsby's parties**
The lavish parties at Gatsby's West Egg mansion, which a "small eyesore" neighbor, Nick, describes as an imitation "Hotel de Ville in Normandy." Five crates of oranges and lemons arrive every Friday, the orchestra plays Vladimir Tostoff's "Jazz History of the World," and after one party two men crash into a ditch when their car loses a wheel. Nick first meets Gatsby at one of these parties.

**Owl Eyes and "a regular Belasco"**
A drunk partygoer with owl-eyed spectacles who is amazed that the books in Gatsby's "Merton College Library" are real, not cardboard, and calls Gatsby "a regular Belasco," after the theatrical producer David Belasco, known for realistic stage sets. He is one of the few people who come to Gatsby's funeral.

**"So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past"**
The novel's famous last line. In the final scene Nick lies on the beach and imagines the "transitory enchanted moment" when Dutch sailors first saw the "fresh, green breast of the new world." The novel opens with Nick recalling his father's advice to remember that not everyone has had his advantages, and its epigraph is attributed to the fictional poet Thomas Parke D'Invilliers.

**James Gatz and Dan Cody**
Gatsby was born James Gatz to poor farmers in North Dakota and briefly attended St. Olaf College in Minnesota. As a teenager he rowed out on Lake Superior to warn the millionaire Dan Cody that his yacht was in danger, and Cody hired him. Gatsby was supposed to inherit Cody's money, but it went to Cody's mistress Ella Kaye. Nick says Gatsby "sprang from his Platonic conception of himself."

**"Old sport," Oxford, and the Montenegro medal**
Gatsby constantly calls people "old sport." To back up his claims of a noble past, he shows Nick a medal from Montenegro inscribed "Nicolas Rex" and a photograph from Oxford. He later admits he attended Oxford for only five months after the war, so he "can't really call [himself] an Oxford man." Rumors at his parties include that he killed a man and that he is related to Kaiser Wilhelm.

**Jordan Baker**
Daisy's friend, a professional golfer who once cheated in a tournament and is habitually dishonest, which Nick finds attractive. She first appears with Daisy lying on a couch in white dresses, holding herself as if balancing something on her chin. When Nick criticizes her careless driving she replies that "it takes two to make an accident." Nghi Vo's novel The Chosen and the Beautiful retells the story from her point of view.

**The shirts scene**
When Gatsby shows Daisy his mansion, he throws piles of his expensive shirts onto the table, and Daisy sobs into them, saying she has never seen such beautiful shirts. Gatsby's resident freeloader Klipspringer plays the piano that day, and later calls Nick about his tennis shoes instead of attending the funeral.

**The Plaza Hotel confrontation**
On a hot afternoon in Manhattan, Tom confronts Gatsby over Daisy and exposes his bootlegging, and Daisy cannot say she never loved Tom. Nick realizes that it is his thirtieth birthday. Tom then sends Daisy home with Gatsby in Gatsby's car, which leads directly to Myrtle's death. Earlier, Daisy had told Gatsby "you always look so cool," revealing her love in front of Tom.

**The party at Myrtle's Manhattan apartment**
Nick gets drunk for the second time in his life at the apartment Tom keeps for Myrtle, along with the McKees and Myrtle's sister Catherine. Catherine repeats the rumor that Gatsby is related to Kaiser Wilhelm and falsely claims that Daisy is Catholic to explain why Tom won't get a divorce. A photo there looks like a hen on a blurred rock. Tom, who hates the word "hulking," breaks Myrtle's nose here when she says Daisy's name.

**Henry C. Gatz and the Hopalong Cassidy schedule**
At Gatsby's poorly attended funeral, his father Henry C. Gatz shows Nick an old copy of Hopalong Cassidy in which the young James Gatz wrote a daily schedule and a list of "General Resolves" for improving himself.

**Heart of Darkness**
Conrad's most famous work, an 1899 novella about a journey up the Congo River in the Belgian-ruled Congo Free State, drawn from Conrad's own 1890 trip there as a steamboat officer. Working for the ivory-trading "Company," the narrator travels from the Outer and Central Stations to the Inner Station to find the agent Kurtz. It was first collected in book form in Youth with "The End of the Tether."

**"The horror! The horror!"**
The dying last words of Mr. Kurtz, the brilliant ivory trader who has gone mad and set himself up as a god among the local people. Back in Europe, Marlow visits Kurtz's grieving fiancée (his "Intended") and lies to her, saying that the last word Kurtz spoke was her name.

**Charles Marlow and the Nellie**
Marlow is Conrad's recurring narrator, who tells the story of Heart of Darkness to fellow passengers aboard the yawl Nellie, anchored on the River Thames. He also narrates Lord Jim, as well as "Youth" and Chance.

**"Exterminate all the brutes!"**
The scrawled postscript at the end of Kurtz's eloquent report for the International Society for the Suppression of Savage Customs. Other Kurtz clues include the severed heads on stakes around his station, his membership in the "party of the unsound method," the Russian "harlequin" who idolizes him, and the manager's boy announcing "Mistah Kurtz—he dead," which T. S. Eliot used as the epigraph to "The Hollow Men."

**The "whited sepulchre" and the knitting women**
Marlow calls the unnamed European city (Brussels) where he is hired by the Company a "whited sepulchre." In the Company office two women sit on straw-bottomed chairs knitting black wool, like guardians of the gates of death. Marlow is hired to replace Fresleven, a Danish captain killed in a quarrel over two black hens. On the steamer Marlow later throws his bloody shoes overboard after his helmsman is speared, and the boat is trapped in a thick white fog.

**Chinua Achebe's "An Image of Africa"**
A 1975 lecture in which the Nigerian novelist Chinua Achebe called Conrad "a thoroughgoing racist" (in the original version, "a bloody racist"). He argued that Heart of Darkness uses Africa as "the other world," "a foil to Europe," and denies its African characters human expression.

**Lord Jim**
A 1900 novel about Jim, a young British first mate who jumps from the steamship Patna, which is carrying Muslim pilgrims to Mecca, when it seems about to sink. The ship stays afloat, and Jim is disgraced at an official inquiry. Captain Brierly, one of the assessors at the inquiry, later commits suicide, and in hospital the ship's chief engineer has delirium-tremens visions of pink toads.

**Patusan, Stein, Jewel, and Dain Waris**
Marlow gets Jim a post through Stein, a butterfly- and beetle-collecting merchant, at the remote trading post of Patusan, where Jim becomes "Tuan Jim" (Lord Jim). He falls in love with Jewel and befriends Dain Waris, son of the chief Doramin. When the pirate Gentleman Brown, helped by the treacherous Cornelius, kills Dain Waris, Jim lets Doramin shoot him. Part of the ending is told from Marlow's visit to Brown's deathbed.

**Nostromo**
A 1904 novel set in the fictional South American republic of Costaguana, centered on the port of Sulaco. The Englishman Charles Gould owns the San Tomé silver mine and backs the Ribiera dictatorship. During a revolution the trusted Italian dockworker Nostromo (Gian' Battista Fidanza) is sent to hide a shipment of silver, and he secretly keeps it.

**Martin Decoud and Holroyd**
In Nostromo the journalist Martin Decoud helps Nostromo carry the silver, is left alone on the Great Isabel island, and kills himself, weighing his body down with silver ingots. Sulaco later secedes as the Occidental Republic. The American financier Holroyd is the novel's emblem of extractive capitalism, and F. Scott Fitzgerald said he would rather have written Nostromo than any other novel.

**The Secret Agent**
A 1907 novel set in London about Adolf Verloc, an agent provocateur who runs a shop selling pornography and is ordered to bomb the Greenwich Observatory. His mentally disabled brother-in-law Stevie trips while carrying the bomb and blows himself up, and Verloc's wife Winnie then kills him. Other characters include the Professor, an anarchist who always carries a bomb strapped to his body, and Chief Inspector Heat.

**"The Secret Sharer"**
A story about a young, new captain anchored in the Gulf of Siam who secretly hides Leggatt, a fugitive mate from the ship Sephora who killed a crewman, and comes to see him as his "double." He tricks the Sephora's captain, then sails dangerously close to the island of Koh-ring so Leggatt can swim ashore, using the white floppy hat he gave Leggatt, floating in the water, to steer.

**Almayer's Folly and Tom Lingard**
Conrad's first novel (1895) follows Kaspar Almayer, a Dutch trader in Borneo who married Captain Tom Lingard's adopted Malay daughter. Their daughter Nina leaves with the Malay prince Dain Maroola, and Almayer is left in his unfinished house (the "folly"), turning to opium. Lingard recurs in An Outcast of the Islands, where he tells Peter Willems "Life is very long," a line Eliot also quotes in "The Hollow Men."

**Critics: Edward Said and Maya Jasanoff**
Edward Said's first book was Joseph Conrad and the Fiction of Autobiography, and his essay "Two Visions in Heart of Darkness" in Culture and Imperialism discusses the novella's imperialism. Maya Jasanoff's The Dawn Watch reads Conrad's life and works in the context of globalization.

**Other works and biography**
Conrad was born Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski in Russian-ruled Poland, worked as a sailor, and only learned English as an adult. His other works include Victory, in which Axel Heyst is pursued by the hostile hotel owner Schomberg and burns himself to death after Lena dies; "Amy Foster," about the castaway Yanko Goorall; The Shadow-Line, in which Captain Giles helps a young man get his first command; and The Rover, about the old pirate Peyrol at Escampobar.

**Kemmerich's boots**
Franz Kemmerich is a schoolmate of the protagonist whose leg is amputated; he dies of gangrene in a field hospital. His fine leather boots pass to Müller. After Müller is killed, the boots pass to the narrator, Paul Bäumer, so they track the deaths of the comrades.

**Gérard Duval**
Gérard Duval is a French soldier and a printer by trade. Paul stabs him during hand-to-hand fighting in a shell-hole and is trapped with him as he slowly dies. Paul repeats "forgive me, comrade" to the corpse and finds photos of Duval's wife and child in his pocketbook.

**Kantorek and the "Iron Youth"**
Kantorek is the patriotic schoolmaster whose speeches pressure Paul's class to enlist. He later sends a letter calling them the "Iron Youth," which makes them smile bitterly. When Kantorek is conscripted, his former student Mittelstaedt mocks his ill-fitting uniform and drills him with the phrase "Inadequate, quite inadequate."

**Stanislaus Katczinsky (Kat)**
Kat is the resourceful 40-year-old former cobbler who mentors Paul and has a "sixth sense" for finding food. He steals and roasts a goose with Paul. Paul carries him to safety after a leg wound, but Kat is killed by a shell splinter during the trip, and Paul loses his will to survive.

**Corporal Himmelstoss**
Himmelstoss is a former postman and the brutal drill corporal who torments the recruits during training, earning the nickname "terror of Klosterberg." Tjaden and others ambush him, throw a bedsheet over his head, and whip him in revenge. He later becomes friendlier, and at the front he carries the mortally wounded Haie Westhus to safety.

**"All quiet on the Western Front" army report**
The title comes from the novel's final page. Paul is killed in October 1918, near the end of the war, on a day so quiet that the army report says only that there is nothing new to report. In German this phrase is "Im Westen nichts Neues."

**Tjaden**
Tjaden is a hungry former locksmith and bed-wetter. Himmelstoss tries to "cure" him by making him share a bunk with another bed-wetter, so that whoever sleeps below is soaked. Tjaden takes the lead in getting revenge on Himmelstoss, including whipping him and later farting at him.

**Swimming to the French women**
Paul, Leer, and Kropp see a poster at a tavern and then defy orders by swimming naked across a canal to spend the night with three French women. Leer is the group's ladies' man and is later killed alongside their commander, Bertinck.

**Detering and the cherry blossoms**
Detering is a peasant soldier who misses his wife and farm. He is distressed by wounded horses screaming on the battlefield and wants them shot. After seeing a blossoming cherry tree that reminds him of home, he carries off some branches and later deserts.

**Paul's leave and his dying mother**
On leave at home, Paul feels a sense of strangeness and alienation and learns that his mother is dying of cancer. Back at a camp guarding Russian prisoners of war, he shares his mother's potato cakes with the starving prisoners.

**Ginger and the rations for 150 men**
The novel opens with the company's cook, Ginger, who has prepared beef and haricot beans for 150 men. Only about 80 survivors returned from the front, so Ginger is pressured into handing the extra rations to the hungry soldiers.

**Kemmerich's watch and mother**
Kemmerich's watch is stolen as he lies dying, prompting the remark "nobody should carry as good a watch as that." On leave, Paul visits Kemmerich's mother and lies that her son was shot through the heart and died instantly. She asks Paul, "Why are you living then, when he is dead?"

**Lewandowski in the hospital**
Lewandowski is a bedridden older patient at the Catholic hospital whose wife visits him. His fellow patients guard the door and look away so the couple can make love. The same hospital section includes Josef Hamacher, who warns that no patient comes back from the "Death Room."

**The Road Back**
This is Remarque's sequel. It follows the soldier Ernst Birkholz and returning characters such as Tjaden as they struggle to readjust to civilian life in Germany after the war.

**Lewis Milestone's 1930 film adaptation**
