This American film helped popularize the novel and won the Academy Award for Best Picture. It ends with Paul reaching out toward a butterfly before being shot by a sniper.

**The Bald Soprano**
Ionesco's first play (1950), which he called an "anti-play," inspired by the empty dialogue of an English-language phrase book. An English couple, the Smiths, receive their friends the Martins, and their conversation decays into clichés and non-sequiturs. It opens with an "English clock" striking seventeen "English strokes," and it ends with the Martins repeating the Smiths' opening lines, showing the play's circularity.

**Rhinoceros and Berenger**
Ionesco's most famous play (1959), an allegory of conformity and the rise of fascism and Nazism in which the inhabitants of a small town turn one by one into rhinoceroses. The everyman Berenger is the only one who resists, and the play ends with his defiant cry, "I'm not capitulating!"

**Daisy, Dudard, Jean, and Mrs. Boeuf**
Characters in Rhinoceros who give in to the transformation. Berenger's friend Jean declares "Humanism is dead" as he turns into a rhinoceros before Berenger's eyes. Mrs. Boeuf leaps down a crushed staircase to join her husband after recognizing him as a rhinoceros, and the office colleagues Botard and Dudard also convert. Berenger's love Daisy is the last to leave him and join the herd.

**The Logician**
A character in Act I of Rhinoceros who delivers absurd syllogisms to the Old Gentleman, for example proving that because all cats die and Socrates died, Socrates must be a cat.

**The Chairs**
A 1952 play in which an Old Man and Old Woman on an island arrange more and more chairs for invisible guests, including an invisible Emperor, who have come to hear the Old Man's message to humanity. Once the Orator arrives to deliver it, the couple shout "Long live the Emperor!" and jump out the windows to their deaths.

**The deaf-mute Orator**
The professional speaker hired to deliver the Old Man's message at the end of The Chairs. After the couple's suicide he turns out to be deaf and mute, can only make guttural sounds, and writes a meaningless string of letters on a blackboard, including a garbled "ANGELFOOD," before leaving the stage to the empty chairs.

**Semiramis and "Then at last we arrived"**
In The Chairs, the Old Woman, whom her 95-year-old husband calls Semiramis, asks him to tell the same story he tells every night, which begins "Then at last we arrived" and concerns a journey to a Paris that he says vanished long ago. She consoles him that if he had wanted, he could have been "head president, head king, or even head doctor."

**The Martins' recognition scene**
In The Bald Soprano, Mr. and Mrs. Martin talk as strangers and slowly realize, through a string of coincidences (the same train, the same street and apartment, a daughter named Alice with one white eye and one red eye), that they must be husband and wife, and they embrace. The maid Mary then reveals that the two children's eyes are on opposite sides, so he is not Donald and she is not Elizabeth.

**Bobby Watson**
In The Bald Soprano, the Smiths discuss the death of Bobby Watson, and it turns out that his wife, and seemingly every member of his family, is also named Bobby Watson, making it impossible to tell who is who.

**The Fire Chief and the bald soprano**
The Fire Chief drops in on the Smiths and Martins looking for a fire to put out. He tells absurd anecdotes, such as one about a calf that ate ground glass and gave birth to a cow, and Mary the maid, who claims to be Sherlock Holmes, recites a poem called "The Fire" in his honor. As he leaves he asks about "the bald soprano," and Mrs. Smith answers that she "always wears her hair in the same style." The title figure never appears.

**The Lesson**
A 1951 one-act play in which a Professor tutors a young Pupil. She can multiply huge numbers only because she has memorized every possible product but cannot subtract; she develops a toothache, and the increasingly violent Professor stabs her with an (often imaginary) knife. The Maid then brings in the next Pupil. The Lesson and The Bald Soprano have run together at the Théâtre de la Huchette in Paris continuously since 1957.

**The Killer**
A play of the Berenger cycle in which Berenger visits a "radiant city" plagued by a murderer who lures victims to a pool by offering to show them "a picture of the colonel" and then drowns them. After the killing of the young woman Dany, Berenger leaves the radiant city and finally confronts the giggling Killer.

**Exit the King**
A 1962 Berenger-cycle play about the dying King Berenger I, who is more than 400 years old and whose kingdom is collapsing around him. His first wife Queen Marguerite insists he accept death, while his second wife Queen Marie begs him to live, and the Doctor also announces his end.

**Jack, or the Submission**
A play in which Jack's family pressures him into marriage. He rejects a bride with two noses and accepts Roberta II, who has three noses, after she proposes that the word "cat" be used for every concept. Its 1951 sequel is The Future Is in Eggs.

**Victims of Duty**
A 1953 play in which a Detective questions Choubert about a man named Mallot and forces him to eat stale bread to "plug the gaps" in his memory.

**Moby-Dick and "Call me Ishmael"**
Melville's masterpiece (1851), an epic novel about a whaling voyage that opens with the famous line "Call me Ishmael." The narrator Ishmael is a wandering sailor who signs on to the whaling ship Pequod out of Nantucket and is the only one to survive its voyage.

**Captain Ahab and the white whale**
Ahab is the Pequod's monomaniacal one-legged captain, who lost his leg to the great white sperm whale Moby Dick and turns the voyage into a hunt for revenge. In the final three-day chase, he hurls his harpoon crying "From hell's heart I stab at thee," and he is dragged under by the line as the whale sinks the ship.

**Queequeg and his coffin**
Queequeg is a tattooed Polynesian harpooner whom Ishmael is forced to share a bed with at a crowded inn, and they become close friends. When Queequeg falls ill, he has a coffin built, which later becomes the ship's life buoy. Ishmael floats on it after the Pequod sinks until he is picked up by the Rachel, a ship searching for its captain's lost son.

**Starbuck, Fedallah, and the Pequod's crew**
Starbuck is the Pequod's sober Quaker first mate, who opposes Ahab's quest, and Stubb and Flask are the other mates. The harpooners are Queequeg, Tashtego, and the giant African Daggoo. Fedallah, a turbaned Parsee (Zoroastrian) whom Ahab secretly brings aboard, makes three prophecies about Ahab's death, including that only hemp can kill him. Before the voyage, the Quaker owners Bildad and Peleg sign Ishmael on, and Bildad's sister Aunt Charity brings Bibles and a copy of Watts.

**The gold doubloon**
Ahab nails a Spanish gold doubloon to the Pequod's mainmast as a reward for the first man to sight Moby Dick. Each crewman reads the coin's symbols differently, and Ahab ends up claiming it himself when he is the first to spot the whale.

**Pip, Father Mapple, and other Moby-Dick episodes**
Pip, the young Black cabin boy, goes mad after jumping overboard from a whaleboat and being left alone at sea. Before the voyage, Father Mapple preaches a sermon on Jonah from a pulpit shaped like a ship's prow. At sea, Tashtego falls into the spermaceti-filled "case" of a whale's head and is rescued, and the one-armed Captain Boomer of the Samuel Enderby cannot understand Ahab's thirst for revenge.

**"Bartleby, the Scrivener: A Story of Wall Street"**
Melville's most famous short story (1853). An unnamed Wall Street lawyer hires Bartleby, a pale copyist who soon answers every request with "I would prefer not to." He stops working entirely and refuses to leave the office, so the lawyer moves his offices away instead.

**Turkey, Nippers, Ginger Nut, and the Tombs**
The narrator's other employees in "Bartleby": the copyists Turkey and Nippers, who are each useful for only half the day, and the office boy Ginger Nut, named for the ginger cakes he fetches (the only food Bartleby seems to eat). Bartleby is taken to the Tombs prison, where he refuses to eat even though the lawyer pays a "grub-man" to feed him, and he dies there. The narrator later hears that Bartleby once worked in a Dead Letter Office, and the story ends "Ah Bartleby! Ah humanity!"

**"Benito Cereno"**
A novella about the American captain Amasa Delano, who boards the struggling Spanish slave ship San Dominick and fails to realize that the enslaved Africans, led by Babo, have revolted and are holding the nervous Spanish captain Benito Cereno hostage. In a tense scene, Babo shaves Cereno with a razor and draws blood. Babo is later executed, and his head, a "hive of subtlety," is set on a pole.

**"Follow your leader" and "what has cast such a shadow upon you?"**
In "Benito Cereno," the ship's figurehead is covered by canvas. When the canvas falls, it reveals the skeleton of the slaveowner Alexandro Aranda with the words "Follow your leader" chalked beneath it. Delano later asks the rescued Cereno, "You are saved; what has cast such a shadow upon you?" (Cereno answers "The negro"), and Ralph Ellison used the exchange as an epigraph for Invisible Man.

**Billy Budd, Sailor**
Melville's last novella, published after his death in 1924. Billy is a handsome, innocent "Handsome Sailor" impressed from the merchant ship Rights-of-Man onto the HMS Bellipotent. The envious master-at-arms John Claggart harasses him through the corporal Squeak and then falsely accuses him of mutiny. Billy, who stutters, cannot speak and strikes Claggart dead. Captain Vere has him hanged ("an angel of God! Yet the angel must hang!"), and Billy's last words are "God bless Captain Vere!" Vere later dies murmuring "Billy Budd."

**The Piazza Tales**
Melville's 1856 story collection containing "Bartleby" and "Benito Cereno." It also includes "The Lightning-Rod Man," in which a salesman fails to scare the narrator into buying a lightning rod during a thunderstorm; "The Bell-Tower," in which the architect Bannadonna is killed by his own automaton (the magistrates are unsettled that Una, one of the figures cast on the bell, looks unlike her sisters); and "The Encantadas," ten sketches of the Galápagos Islands, including the story of the stranded widow Hunilla.

**Typee**
Melville's first novel (1846), subtitled "A Peep at Polynesian Life" and based on his own experience. The narrator Tommo and his friend Toby jump ship from the whaler Dolly and live among the Typee people, rumored cannibals, in a valley of Nuku Hiva in the Marquesas Islands.

**Pierre, Israel Potter, and The Confidence-Man**
In Pierre; or, The Ambiguities, Pierre Glendinning breaks his engagement to Lucy Tartan to protect his illegitimate half-sister Isabel and later kills his cousin Glendinning Stanly. Israel Potter follows a Revolutionary War veteran who meets George III and becomes a spy for Benjamin Franklin. The Confidence-Man follows a shape-shifting swindler who deceives passengers on the Mississippi steamboat Fidèle on April Fools' Day.

**Melville's poetry and other writings**
His Civil War poetry collection Battle-Pieces opens with "The Portent," about the hanging of John Brown, and his late collection Timoleon is named for a poem about the ancient Corinthian statesman Timoleon. His sketch "The Paradise of Bachelors and the Tartarus of Maids" contrasts a London lawyers' dinner with a grim New England paper mill. His earliest work was "Fragments from a Writing Desk," and Hart Crane wrote the poem "At Melville's Tomb."

**The Metamorphosis and Gregor Samsa**
Kafka's most famous work (1915), the near-universal giveaway. The traveling salesman Gregor Samsa wakes one morning to find he has been transformed into a "monstrous vermin," usually pictured as a giant insect. He hides in his room, finds he now prefers rotting scraps to milk and bread, and slowly becomes a burden to his family, who feel relieved and take a tram ride into the country after he dies.

**The apple lodged in Gregor's back**
Gregor's father bombards him with apples from the sideboard, and one becomes lodged in his back. The rotting, infected wound slowly cripples Gregor and contributes to his death.

**Grete and her violin**
Gregor's younger sister first cares for him, bringing him milk and food scraps. Gregor had secretly planned to send her to the conservatory to study violin. When he crawls out to hear her play for the family's three lodgers, they are disgusted, and Grete then tells the family they must get rid of "it."

**The picture of the woman in furs**
A picture Gregor cut out of a magazine and framed, showing a lady in a fur hat and fur boa. When his mother and sister clear out his room, he clings to the picture to keep it from being taken. Some critics link it to Sacher-Masoch's novel Venus in Furs.

**The Trial and Josef K.**
A posthumously published novel (1925) in which the bank official Josef K. is arrested one morning by a mysterious court and never learns his crime. He seeks help from figures such as the court painter Titorelli. At the end, two men lead him to a quarry and stab him in the heart, and his last words are "Like a dog!"

**"Before the Law"**
A parable a priest tells Josef K. in the cathedral in The Trial, which Kafka also published on its own. A man from the country asks a gatekeeper to let him into the Law and is told he may enter later, "but not now." He waits for years, even bribing the gatekeeper, and as he dies he learns the door was meant only for him and is now being shut.

**"In the Penal Colony" and "BE JUST"**
An explorer (or traveler) visiting an island colony is shown an execution machine, made of the Bed, the Designer, and the Harrow, that carves a condemned man's sentence into his body over twelve hours. When the explorer will not support it, the Officer frees the prisoner, sets the machine to inscribe "BE JUST," and lies down in it himself. The machine breaks down and stabs him to death, and his face shows no sign of the promised redemption.

**The old Commandant's grave**
At the end of "In the Penal Colony," the explorer finds the grave of the old Commandant, who designed the machine, under a table in a teahouse used by dockworkers. Its inscription prophesies that he will rise again. The explorer then uses a knotted rope to stop the soldier and the condemned man from following him onto his boat.

**"A Hunger Artist"**
A professional faster displays himself in a cage on straw, but his impresario limits his fasts to forty days. As public interest fades, he joins a circus and is forgotten. Dying, he confesses he fasted only because he never found a food he liked, and he is buried with the straw and replaced by a young panther. Kafka was correcting the proofs of this collection while dying of tuberculosis.

**"The Judgment" and Georg Bendemann**
A 1912 story Kafka wrote in a single night and dedicated to Felice Bauer, to whom he was twice engaged. After Georg writes to a friend in St. Petersburg about his engagement, his father sentences him to "death by drowning." Georg runs to a bridge, cries "Dear parents, I have always loved you," and drops into the river as an "unending stream of traffic" crosses. The German word for traffic (Verkehr) can also mean intercourse.

**Amerika and Karl Rossmann**
An unfinished novel published by Max Brod. Sixteen-year-old Karl Rossmann is sent to America after a maid seduces him and bears his child. In its first chapter, "The Stoker," Karl defends a stoker against the chief engineer Schubal, and Senator Jakob reveals he is Karl's uncle. Later Karl falls in with the tramps Delamarche and Robinson and works as a lift-boy at the Hotel Occidental until the Head Porter fires him.

**The Castle**
An unfinished novel in which the land surveyor K. arrives in a village and tries to gain access to the authorities in the castle above it. He repeatedly tries to reach the official Klamm, becomes engaged to the barmaid Frieda, Klamm's former mistress, and is given a pointless post as school janitor.

**Max Brod**
Kafka's close friend and literary executor. Kafka asked him to burn his unpublished manuscripts, but Brod refused and published The Trial, The Castle, and Amerika after Kafka's death in 1924.

**"A Country Doctor"**
A story in which a doctor must make an urgent night journey in a snowstorm. Two unearthly horses emerge from his pigsty, and the brutish groom who comes with them stays behind with the doctor's servant girl, Rose. The doctor finds his young patient has a horrible wound in his side full of worms.

**"An Imperial Message"**
A short parable in which a dying emperor whispers a message meant for "you alone," his lowly subject. The messenger can never get through the endless crowds, courtyards, and palaces, so the message never arrives, and the subject can only dream of it.

**Dr. Pangloss and "the best of all possible worlds"**
Pangloss is Candide's tutor, and Voltaire uses him to mock the optimism of the philosopher Gottfried Leibniz. He teaches "metaphysico-theologo-cosmolonigology" and keeps saying that "all is for the best in this best of all possible worlds," however much he suffers. He catches syphilis from the maid Paquette, is hanged at an auto-da-fé, and still turns up alive later as a galley slave near Constantinople.

**Cunegonde**
Cunegonde is the daughter of Baron Thunder-ten-Tronckh and the woman Candide loves. She is owned jointly by the Jew Don Issachar and the Grand Inquisitor, and later becomes the mistress of the governor of Buenos Aires. By the end she has become ugly, but Candide marries her anyway.

**Castle Thunder-ten-Tronckh in Westphalia**
The novel opens at this baron's castle in Westphalia, where Candide grows up alongside Cunegonde. He is kicked out after the Baron catches him kissing Cunegonde behind a screen, which starts his travels around the world. Before that, Cunegonde watched Pangloss give "experimental physics" lessons to the chambermaid Paquette in the bushes.

**El Dorado**
El Dorado is a hidden utopia in South America where gold and jewels lie on the ground like pebbles. Its people never pray to God for anything because they have nothing to ask for; they only thank him. Candide rides in a carriage pulled by sheep to meet the king. Candide and Cacambo leave with enormous wealth, and most of it is soon lost.

**"We must cultivate our garden" (Il faut cultiver notre jardin)**
This is the novel's famous last line. Candide says it to Pangloss after he has given up Pangloss's optimism. He and his companions settle on a small farm near Constantinople and decide that steady work, not philosophizing, is what keeps away boredom, vice and poverty.

**Cacambo**
Cacambo is Candide's loyal, resourceful valet, of part-Spanish descent. He travels with Candide to El Dorado and later goes to Buenos Aires to buy back Cunegonde. He also talks the cannibal Oreillons out of eating Candide by proving Candide is not a Jesuit.

**The Old Woman (daughter of Pope Urban X)**
The Old Woman is Cunegonde's servant. She was once the Princess of Palestrina and is the illegitimate daughter of the made-up Pope Urban X. She later became a slave in Morocco, and one of her buttocks was cut off to feed starving soldiers during a siege, so she has only one left. She claims nobody has had a more miserable life than hers. In a note, Voltaire praised his own discretion for inventing a pope rather than naming a real one.

**The 1755 Lisbon earthquake and the auto-da-fé**
Candide and Pangloss arrive in Lisbon just as the real 1755 earthquake strikes. The authorities then hold an auto-da-fé, a public ritual punishing supposed heretics, to prevent more earthquakes: Candide is flogged and Pangloss is hanged. Voltaire uses the disaster to attack the idea that all suffering is for the best.

**Red sheep**
Candide and Cacambo leave El Dorado with about 100 large red sheep loaded with gold and jewels. Almost all of them die on the journey. The Dutch pirate Mynheer Vanderdendur steals two of the last ones, and Candide later recovers only one of them from a sunken ship.

**Jacques the Anabaptist**
Jacques is a kind Dutch Anabaptist who takes Candide in when everyone else refuses to help him. He drowns when their ship sinks near Lisbon. Pangloss stops Candide from trying to save him, arguing that the Bay of Lisbon was made specifically so that Jacques could drown in it.

**Don Issachar and the Grand Inquisitor**
These two men share Cunegonde as their mistress in Lisbon. Candide kills Don Issachar with a sword when Issachar finds them together, and then kills the Grand Inquisitor as well. He then has to run off to South America.

**The two monkeys and the Oreillons**
In South America, Candide shoots two monkeys he sees chasing two women, and then learns the women were the monkeys' lovers. Soon afterward the Oreillons, a cannibal tribe, nearly cook him because they think he is a Jesuit.

**Martin the Manichaean**
Martin is a pessimistic scholar whom Candide picks in Suriname to travel with him to Europe. Candide chose him by holding a contest for the unhappiest man. Martin follows Manichaeism, a belief that evil rules the world, and tells Candide that "all is evil," which makes him Pangloss's opposite. He is often said to be based on the skeptic philosopher Pierre Bayle.

**The Bulgarian army and the 72,000 lashes**
After being expelled from the castle, Candide is tricked into joining the Bulgarian army, Voltaire's satire of Frederick the Great's Prussia. When he goes for a walk he is arrested as a deserter, and he chooses to run a gauntlet of 2,000 soldiers 36 times (72,000 blows) rather than take 12 bullets in the head. After two runs he begs to be shot instead, but the king pardons him.

**Admiral Byng's execution, "to encourage the others"**
On the way to Venice, Candide watches an English admiral being shot. This is based on the real 1757 execution of Admiral John Byng. Candide is told the English kill an admiral now and then "to encourage the others" (pour encourager les autres), and he refuses to set foot in England. In Venice, Candide later dines with six deposed kings and visits the bored art collector Count Pococurante.

**Lu Xun's "Diary of a Madman"**
A 1918 story by Lu Xun, often called the first modern Chinese vernacular story, which borrows its title from Gogol (hence the frequent "it's not Russia" hint). The narrator becomes convinced that everyone around him is a cannibal, reads the words "eat people" between the lines of old history books, and ends with the plea "Save the children..."; it appears in the collection Call to Arms.

**The True Story of Ah Q**
Lu Xun's novella about Ah Q, a ringworm-scarred village laborer who turns every humiliation into a "spiritual victory." He steals turnips from a nunnery and is chased by a black dog, and at the end, sentenced to death, he worries only about drawing a perfect circle as his signature and cannot think of an opera verse to sing on the way to his execution.

**Li Bai's "Quiet Night Thought"**
A famous Tang dynasty poem in which the speaker sees bright moonlight before his bed, mistakes it for frost on the ground, raises his head to look at the moon, and lowers it to think of his hometown. Legend says Li Bai drowned trying to embrace the moon's reflection in a river.

**"Drinking Alone by Moonlight"**
Li Bai's poem in which the speaker, with a cup of wine under the flowering trees, invites the moon and his shadow to make "three" drinkers. He laments that "the moon, alas, is no drinker of wine" and hopes to meet them again on the "Cloudy River of the sky" (the Milky Way); Li Bai was one of the "Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup."

**"The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter"**
Ezra Pound's loose translation (in his 1915 collection Cathay) of a poem by Li Bai. The young wife recalls when her "hair was still cut straight across my forehead" and how "At sixteen, you departed." Li Bai also wrote "The Road to Shu Is Hard."

**Du Fu's "Song of the Wagons"**
An anti-war poem by Du Fu (also translated "Ballad of the Army Carts") that opens with war carts that "rumble and roll" and horses that neigh as conscripts with bows and quivers march off. It mourns that sons are "merely buried amid the grass," and a soldier asks how he could dare to complain.

**Other Du Fu poems ("Jade Flower Palace," the thatched hut)**
In "Jade Flower Palace," Du Fu describes gray rats scurrying over the broken tiles of a ruined palace and ends by noting that "the future slips imperceptibly away." He also wrote about his thatched hut being torn apart by an autumn wind, and he and Li Bai are the two most famous poets of the Tang dynasty.

**Wang Wei's "Deer Park"**
A short Tang poem by Wang Wei (also called "Deer Enclosure") of just twenty characters in Chinese, describing echoing voices in empty mountains and returning light that shines on the green moss. Eliot Weinberger's book Nineteen Ways of Looking at Wang Wei compares many translations of it.

**Liu Cixin's The Three-Body Problem**
A 2008 science-fiction novel, the first in the Remembrance of Earth's Past trilogy, and the first Asian novel to win the Hugo Award (2015). The disillusioned astrophysicist Ye Wenjie contacts the alien civilization of Trisolaris, whose planet alternates between Stable and Chaotic Eras; her Earth-Trisolaris Organization (ETO) aids the aliens, who use proton-sized supercomputers called sophons to sabotage particle accelerators, while scientists in the Frontiers of Science are driven to suicide. The sequel is The Dark Forest.

**Journey to the West and the Monkey King**
One of China's Four Great Classical Novels, about the monk Xuanzang (Tripitaka) traveling to India to fetch Buddhist sutras with his disciples. Sun Wukong, the Monkey King, hatched from a stone egg, is trapped under a mountain by the Buddha for 500 years before the monk frees him; the other disciples are Pigsy (Zhu Bajie), who wields an iron rake, and Sandy (Sha Wujing).

**Water Margin**
A classical novel about 108 outlaws who gather at the Liangshan Marsh to oppose corrupt officials during the Song dynasty. Pearl S. Buck translated it as All Men Are Brothers.

**Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Dream of the Red Chamber**
The other two of the Four Great Classical Novels. Romance of the Three Kingdoms tells of the wars among the states of Wei, Shu, and Wu, including Cao Cao's defeat at the Battle of Red Cliffs; Dream of the Red Chamber follows Jia Baoyu, born with a piece of jade in his mouth, who sees the Twelve Beauties of Jinling in a dream.

**Gao Xingjian's Soul Mountain and Bus Stop**
Gao Xingjian won the 2000 Nobel Prize in Literature. His novel Soul Mountain follows a narrator who travels through rural China after a false lung cancer diagnosis, with chapters narrated by characters called "I," "You," and "She"; his absurdist play Bus Stop shows characters such as Glasses waiting ten years for a bus that never stops.

**Mo Yan's Red Sorghum and The Republic of Wine**
Mo Yan won the 2012 Nobel Prize in Literature. Red Sorghum is a nonlinear novel about a family of sorghum-wine distillers during the Japanese invasion, and The Republic of Wine, about rumors of cannibalism, interweaves stories such as "Meat Boy" and "Cooking Lesson."

**Other modern Chinese works (Rickshaw Boy, Chronicle of a Blood Merchant, The Good Earth)**
In Lao She's Rickshaw Boy, Xiangzi earns the nickname "Camel" after stealing camels to save money for a rickshaw; in Yu Hua's Chronicle of a Blood Merchant, a silk-factory worker repeatedly sells his blood to survive. Pearl S. Buck's The Good Earth is set in China, where the farmer Wang Lung takes two pearls from his wife O-lan to give to his concubine Lotus; Chinese spoken drama began with a 1907 stage adaptation of Uncle Tom's Cabin, Black Slave's Cry to Heaven.

**"Light of my life, fire of my loins"**
The famous opening of Lolita, Humbert's address to Dolores Haze. It continues "Lo-lee-ta: the tip of the tongue taking a trip of three steps down the palate to tap, at three, on the teeth," and notes she was Lo, Dolly, Dolores "on the dotted line," and Lola "in slacks," but Lolita in his arms.

**Humbert Humbert and the "nymphets"**
The novel's narrator, a European-born scholar and French teacher who writes his account from prison. He describes his obsession with "nymphets," girls between nine and fourteen, and calls his book "the only immortality you and I may share, my Lolita." He attributes eerie coincidences, such as the recurring number 342, to a cosmic force he calls "McFate," and laments that he has "only words to play with."

**Clare Quilty**
The playwright and pornographer who is Humbert's rival and shadowy double. He secretly follows Humbert and Lolita across America, takes her from a hospital by posing as her uncle, and brings her to his Duk Duk Ranch, where he wants her to act in his pornographic films and throws her out when she refuses.

**The Enchanted Hunters**
The name of both the hotel where Humbert takes Lolita after picking her up from camp, and where they first have sex (Quilty is also staying there), and the play by Quilty in which Lolita later is cast to star at the Beardsley School.

**Charlotte Haze's death**
Lolita's sentimental, pretentious mother, a widow in Ramsdale whom Humbert marries to stay near her daughter. After she breaks into his locked drawer and reads his diary revealing his desire for Lolita, she runs across the street to mail letters and is struck and killed by a Packard driven by Frederick Beale Jr.

**Annabel Leigh**
Humbert's childhood love, whom he met at his father's Hotel Mirana on the Riviera, a name that echoes Edgar Allan Poe's "Annabel Lee." Their love was never consummated, and she died of typhus in Corfu months later, which Humbert blames for his obsession. He also describes his own "very photogenic mother" dying in a freak accident "(picnic, lightning)" when he was three.

**John Ray Jr.'s foreword**
The novel is framed as a manuscript titled "Lolita, or the Confession of a White Widowed Male," presented by the fictional psychologist John Ray Jr., Ph.D. The foreword reveals that Humbert died in prison before his trial and that "Mrs. Richard F. Schiller" died in childbirth on Christmas Day, 1952.

**Dolly Schiller and Dick**
Years after she escaped, Lolita writes to Humbert asking for money. He finds her pregnant and married to the young, hard-of-hearing Dick Schiller, who knows nothing of her past. She refuses to return with him, and he tearfully gives her $4,000 so they can move to Alaska.

**The murder of Quilty**
Humbert tracks Quilty to his house, Pavor Manor, and shoots him repeatedly in a long, farcical scene in which Quilty pleads, plays the piano, and crawls into bed. Before killing him, Humbert makes him read a poetic "sentence" that parodies T. S. Eliot's "Ash Wednesday," beginning "Because you took advantage of a sinner."

**The red Aztec convertible and Trapp**
During Humbert and Lolita's second road trip, a red Aztec convertible follows them. Humbert nicknames its driver "Detective Trapp," thinking he resembles his Swiss cousin Gustave Trapp; the driver turns out to be Quilty, who leaves taunting false entries in hotel registers.

**Camp Q and Charlie Holmes**
Lolita's summer camp. Humbert collects her there to tell her that her mother is ill (in fact she is dead), and Lolita reveals that she had sex at camp with Charlie Holmes, the camp mistress's son, who is later said to have died in Korea.

**Beardsley School and Headmistress Pratt**
After their first year-long road trip across America, Humbert settles in the college town of Beardsley and enrolls Lolita in the Beardsley School for girls. The headmistress, Mrs. Pratt, urges that Lolita be allowed to take part in the school play, The Enchanted Hunters, where Quilty reconnects with her.

**Valeria**
Humbert's first wife, whom he married in Paris. In a taxi, she tells him she is leaving him for the cab's driver, a Russian ex-colonel named Maximovich. Humbert later wanders with Rita, an alcoholic companion, after Lolita disappears.

**Hourglass Lake and Ramsdale**
In the New England town of Ramsdale, Humbert lodges with Charlotte Haze. While swimming with Charlotte in Hourglass Lake, he considers drowning her but cannot bring himself to do it.

**Reading Lolita in Tehran**
Azar Nafisi's 2003 memoir about the secret class she taught to young women in Tehran after the Islamic Revolution, discussing forbidden Western novels such as Lolita, The Great Gatsby, and the works of Henry James and Jane Austen.

**Mother Courage and Her Children**
Brecht's most famous play (1939), set during the Thirty Years' War. Anna Fierling, nicknamed Mother Courage, pulls a canteen wagon behind the armies and sells supplies to soldiers, profiting from the war that takes all three of her children. It is the most common title clue and the usual giveaway for Brecht.

**Eilif, Swiss Cheese, and Kattrin**
Mother Courage's three children, all of whom die over the course of the play. Early on she foretells that brave Eilif will die for his bravery, honest Swiss Cheese for his honesty (he is shot after hiding the regiment's paybox), and kind Kattrin for her kindness.

**Kattrin beating the drum on the roof**
The climax of Mother Courage. The mute girl Kattrin climbs onto a roof and beats a drum to wake the town of Halle and warn it of an approaching Catholic army, and the soldiers shoot her. Afterward Mother Courage sings a lullaby over her body and keeps pulling the wagon.

**The Threepenny Opera**
Brecht's 1928 "play with music," written with composer Kurt Weill and adapted from John Gay's The Beggar's Opera. Set in London, it follows the criminal Macheath ("Mack the Knife"), who marries Polly Peachum. Her father Jeremiah Peachum, boss of the city's beggars, tries to get Macheath hanged.

**"Mack the Knife" and "Pirate Jenny"**
The two most famous songs from The Threepenny Opera, with Brecht's lyrics. "Mack the Knife" opens the play by comparing Macheath's knife to the "pearly white" teeth of a shark. In "Pirate Jenny," a barmaid dreams of a "Black Freighter" with eight sails and fifty cannons that will destroy the town that mistreats her.

**Tiger Brown**
London's chief of police in The Threepenny Opera and Macheath's old army comrade from the colonial wars. Together they sing the "Cannon Song." Peachum threatens to have Brown fired by sending a crowd of beggars to disrupt Queen Victoria's coronation unless Macheath is arrested.

**Distancing effect (alienation effect, Verfremdungseffekt)**
Brecht's core theatrical idea. Bare sets, songs, placards, and stylized acting keep the audience from identifying emotionally with the characters so that they think critically about what they see. He developed it partly in an essay on Chinese acting and in "A Short Organum for the Theater."

**Epic theater**
The name of Brecht's Marxist dramatic style, which puts political argument ahead of illusion and catharsis. Related terms that appear in clues include gestus (a gesture showing a character's social attitude, such as Mother Courage's "silent scream"), the "Not/But" element, and his didactic "learning-plays" (Lehrstücke).

**The Caucasian Chalk Circle**
Brecht's play inspired by the Chinese drama The Chalk Circle by Li Xingdao. The servant girl Grusha rescues and raises Michael, the baby the Governor's wife abandoned during a revolt, and escapes to the Northern Mountains while the Ironshirts chase her. The rogue judge Azdak places the child in a chalk circle. Grusha refuses to pull him out for fear of hurting him, so Azdak awards her the child.

**The Good Person of Szechwan**
Brecht's parable play, also translated as The Good Woman of Setzuan. Three gods, guided by the water seller Wang, reward the kind prostitute Shen Teh with money that she uses to buy a tobacco shop. To protect herself from freeloaders she disguises herself as her ruthless male cousin Shui Ta. She falls in love with Yang Sun, an unemployed pilot who exploits her.

**Yvette Pottier and the "Song of Fraternization"**
The camp prostitute in Mother Courage. She sings the "Song of Fraternization" about her first love, an enemy cook, and later marries a colonel. Kattrin is fascinated by her red high-heeled boots.

**"Song of the Great Capitulation" and the Chaplain**
In this song from Mother Courage, the title character talks a young soldier out of making an angry complaint. The Chaplain, who chops wood after the war turns against his side, laments that he "studied to be a pastor of souls," and the cook (Lamb) is another camp follower.

**The Resistible Rise of Arturo Ui**
Brecht's 1941 satire of Hitler's rise to power, retold as the story of a Chicago gangster who seizes control of the cauliflower trade by running a protection racket on the Cauliflower Trust.

**Life of Galileo**
Brecht's play about the astronomer. Galileo passes off a telescope as his own invention, presenting it to the Venetian Arsenal (in a red leather casing instead of green), and later recants his beliefs before the Inquisition, which disappoints his student Andrea Sarti. While under house arrest he secretly writes the Discorsi (Discourses), and Andrea smuggles it out of Italy at the end.

**Saint Joan of the Stockyards, Mahagonny, and Baal**
Other Brecht works. In Saint Joan of the Stockyards, Joan Dark of the Black Straw Hats (a Salvation Army-type group) confronts the meatpacking king Pierpont Mauler in Chicago. Rise and Fall of the City of Mahagonny, another collaboration with Weill, features the "Alabama Song" ("show us the way to the next whiskey bar") and the lumberjack Jimmy Mahoney. Baal, his early first play, follows a dissolute poet who seduces women and murders his friend Ekhart.

**Grover's Corners, New Hampshire**
The small, ordinary town where Thornton Wilder's 1938 Pulitzer Prize-winning play takes place, starting in 1901. Professor Willard gives a "scientific account" of it, starting with its geology (he gets onto Devonian rock and fossils) and describing its people as "English brachycephalic blue-eyed stock." The Stage Manager also notes that the cornerstone of the new bank will hold copies of the local Sentinel newspaper, the New York Times, the Bible, the Constitution, and Shakespeare's plays.

**The Stage Manager**
The play's narrator, who speaks directly to the audience, comments on the town, and stops and moves the action through time. He also plays small parts, including Mr. Morgan the druggist and the minister who marries George and Emily. He dismisses the audience at intermission and ends the play with "You get a good rest, too. Good night." Wilder himself played the role on Broadway.

**Emily Webb relives her twelfth birthday**
In Act III, set in the town cemetery, Emily has died giving birth to her second child. Although Mrs. Gibbs and the other dead warn her not to, she goes back to relive one ordinary day, her twelfth birthday, and sees the milkman Howie Newsome and her family again. She finds it unbearable how little the living notice one another, says goodbye to "Mama and Papa," clocks ticking, sunflowers, food and coffee, and returns to the grave.

**"Do any human beings ever realize life while they live it?"**
Emily's question to the Stage Manager after reliving her birthday, adding "every, every minute?" He answers "No. The saints and poets, maybe—they do some." It is the most quoted line of the play.

**George Gibbs**
The doctor's son, Emily's next-door neighbor and future husband, and a star baseball player at school. In Act I he asks Emily, who brags about her speech on the Louisiana Purchase, for algebra hints through the window. In Act II he gives up his plans to attend the State Agricultural School after Emily apologizes for calling him "conceited and stuck-up."

**Ice-cream sodas at Mr. Morgan's drugstore**
The scene, flashed back to in Act II, in which George and Emily realize they love each other. The Stage Manager plays Mr. Morgan and serves them strawberry ice-cream sodas made with imaginary props.

**Simon Stimson**
The alcoholic church organist and choir director, who has "seen a peck of trouble." The gossipy Mrs. Louella Soames and the other choir ladies talk about his drinking. He hangs himself and appears bitterly among the dead in Act III.

**"Blessed Be the Tie That Binds"**
The hymn that Simon Stimson's choir sings in each act, including at George and Emily's wedding and at Emily's funeral.

**No curtain, no scenery**
Wilder's stage directions open the play with "No curtain. No scenery." The stage is nearly bare: the Stage Manager sets out a few tables and chairs for the Gibbs and Webb households, and the actors mime objects such as dishes, newspapers, and the milkman's horse. Actors planted in the audience, such as a "Belligerent Man" and a "Lady in a Box," ask questions about drinking, social injustice, and culture and love of beauty.

**Howie Newsome and Bessie**
The milkman who appears in each morning scene, delivering milk to the Gibbs and Webb houses. He talks to his invisible horse Bessie ("Giddap, Bessie!"), whom the actors mime.

**Joe Crowell**
The newspaper boy who says his knee can tell when it is going to rain. The Stage Manager reveals that Joe will graduate at the top of his class at MIT and then die in France during World War I.

**The wedding of George and Emily**
The focus of Act II, "Love and Marriage." Three baseball players tease George and are sent away, and Handel's "Largo" is played. Both George and Emily panic beforehand (Emily asks "Why can't I stay for a while just like I am?") until their parents reassure them. The Stage Manager says "People are meant to go through life two by two," and Mrs. Soames gushes over the lovely wedding.

**"Daily Life" and "Love and Marriage"**
The titles the Stage Manager gives Acts I and II. He does not name Act III, saying only that the audience can guess what it is about: death and eternity.

**Wally Webb**
Emily's younger brother, whom we learn in Act III died when his appendix burst on a Boy Scout camping trip. He is buried in the town cemetery.

**Mrs. Gibbs**
George's mother, who grows heliotrope and dreams of seeing Paris because "everyone oughta see a country where they don't talk in English." She could have paid for the trip by selling her antique highboy, but never goes. In Act III she is among the dead and advises Emily not to go back.

**The Canterbury Tales**
Chaucer's most famous work, a Middle English frame narrative from the late 1300s. A group of pilgrims riding to the shrine of Thomas Becket at Canterbury hold a storytelling contest, and each tells a tale. It is the most common title clue and the usual giveaway for Chaucer.

**The Wife of Bath's Tale: "what women most desire"**
In this Arthurian story, a knight who has raped a maiden is sentenced to death, but Queen Guinevere spares him on the condition that he find out what women most desire. An old hag gives him the answer, sovereignty or mastery over their husbands, in exchange for his hand in marriage. The Wife of Bath (Alisoun), a five-times-married woman, tells it.

**The Wife of Bath's Prologue**
In this long autobiographical prologue, the Wife recounts her marriages. She tore a page out of her fifth husband Jankyn's book of wicked wives, and he struck her on the ear so hard that she became "somewhat deaf."

**The Miller's Tale**
A bawdy tale told by the drunken Miller. The student "handy" Nicholas persuades the old carpenter John that a second Great Flood is coming, so John sleeps in a tub hung from the roof while Nicholas sleeps with his young wife Alisoun. The suitor Absolon is tricked into kissing Alisoun's "nether eye" (her backside). When Nicholas later farts in his face, Absolon brands him with a hot iron (coulter).

**The Knight's Tale: Palamon, Arcite, and Emily**
The first of the Canterbury Tales, adapted from Boccaccio's Teseida. The imprisoned Theban cousins Palamon and Arcite both fall in love with Emily (Emelye), Theseus's sister-in-law. Arcite wins the tournament for her but is crushed when his horse falls, so Palamon marries her. The story later inspired Shakespeare and Fletcher's The Two Noble Kinsmen.

**The Tabard Inn and the General Prologue**
The Canterbury Tales opens with a General Prologue that begins with "April's sweet showers" ("Whan that Aprill with his shoures soote"). It describes the "sundry folk," about 29 pilgrims, who gather at the Tabard Inn in Southwark. The Host, Harry Bailly, proposes the storytelling contest.

**Troilus and Criseyde**
Chaucer's long poem about two lovers during the Trojan War, adapted from Boccaccio's Il Filostrato and written in rhyme royal. Criseyde, daughter of the seer Calchas, is exchanged as a prisoner to the Greeks. She breaks her promise to return to Troy in ten days and takes Diomede as her lover. It is often cited as the source of the phrase "all good things must come to an end."

**The House of Fame**
A dream poem in which the narrator, a version of Chaucer, wakes in a glass temple of Venus and sees the story of the Aeneid (Dido and Aeneas) engraved on a brass tablet. A golden eagle carries him to the House of Fame and then to a spinning wicker house. It contains the first recorded English use of the word "galaxy."

**The Parlement of Foules**
A dream vision in which Scipio Africanus leads the narrator to a garden where birds gather before the goddess Nature on St. Valentine's Day to choose mates. Three eagles court a female eagle while lower birds such as the duck mock courtly love. It is one of the earliest texts to link Valentine's Day with romance.

**The Pardoner's Tale**
A moral tale in which three rioters set out to kill Death. An old man directs them to an oak tree, where they find a pile of gold coins, and they then murder one another over it, so all three find Death after all.

**Sir Thopas**
Chaucer includes himself as a pilgrim, and his tale "Sir Thopas" is a parody of a chivalric romance in which the knight dreams of an Elf Queen and meets a giant. The Host interrupts it, saying his "dirty rhyming is not worth a turd." Chaucer then tells the prose Tale of Melibee.

**The Book of the Duchess**
Chaucer's early dream poem, an elegy for Blanche of Lancaster, first wife of John of Gaunt. It opens with Ovid's story of Ceyx and Alcyone. A knight in black then tells the dreamer how he lost his "queen" in a game of chess against Fortune.

**The Prioress and her Tale**
The Prioress, Madame Eglantine, swears only "by Saint Loy" and wears a brooch reading "Amor vincit omnia." Her tale tells of a young Christian boy whose throat is cut by Jews but who keeps miraculously singing the hymn "Alma Redemptoris Mater" until a grain is removed from his tongue.

**Other Canterbury tales and pilgrims**
In the Friar's Tale, a summoner tries to extort a frying pan from a poor widow, who curses him to the devil. In the Summoner's Tale, a friar is challenged to divide a fart into twelve equal shares, solved with a cartwheel. In the Squire's Tale, the king Cambuskan receives a flying brass horse and his daughter Canacee gets a ring that lets her speak with a falcon. In the Franklin's Tale, Dorigen promises herself to the squire Aurelius if he can remove the rocks from the coast. The Parson ends the collection with a sermon on the seven deadly sins.

**Treatise on the Astrolabe and the short poems**
Chaucer's prose manual on using the astrolabe, written for his young son Lewis. His short poems include "The Complaint of Chaucer to His Purse," the triple roundel "Merciless Beauty," and "Anelida and Arcite." He translated Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy and was the first poet buried in Westminster Abbey's Poets' Corner.

**Lysistrata (sex strike to end the Peloponnesian War)**
Aristophanes' most famous play (411 BCE), and the most common giveaway for him. The title heroine persuades the women of Athens and Sparta to withhold sex from their husbands until the men make peace and end the Peloponnesian War.

**"Brekekekex koax koax"**
The croaking refrain of the frog chorus in The Frogs, sung as Dionysus rows across the underworld lake Acheron. The frogs' endless chanting irritates Dionysus, and the line is one of the most frequent clues for the playwright.

**The Thinkery (Phrontisterion)**
The school of Socrates in The Clouds. The debt-ridden old farmer Strepsiades enrolls (and later sends his son Pheidippides) there to learn clever arguments for escaping his creditors; at the end, enraged, he burns the Thinkery down.

**Strepsiades and Pheidippides**
The father and son of The Clouds. Strepsiades' debts come from his son's love of horses; after his schooling, Pheidippides beats his father and argues that doing so is morally justified, which drives Strepsiades to burn the school.

**Socrates in a basket**
In The Clouds, Socrates first appears suspended in a basket in the air, claiming he must hang aloft to contemplate the heavens. The play also shows his students measuring how far a flea can jump by dipping its feet in wax and explaining that a gnat buzzes through its rear end.

**Right Logic vs. Wrong Logic**
The two personified arguments (also translated Just and Unjust Argument, or Stronger and Weaker) that debate in The Clouds. Wrong Logic wins, satirizing the sophists who taught people to make the weaker argument defeat the stronger.

**Cloud-cuckoo-land (Nephelokokkygia)**
The city in the sky built by the birds in The Birds. Two Athenians, Pisthetaerus and Euelpides, leave Athens, seek out the Hoopoe (a former man named Tereus), and persuade the birds to build a city between heaven and earth that cuts the gods off from human sacrifices.

**Philocleon and the dog trial (The Wasps)**
In The Wasps, the old man Philocleon is addicted to serving on juries, so his son Bdelycleon locks him in the house and sets up a mock court at home. There a dog resembling Cleon accuses another dog of stealing a Sicilian cheese, with kitchen utensils such as a cheese grater and a pestle as witnesses; the play inspired Racine's comedy Les Plaideurs.

**Cleon**
The Athenian demagogue and war hawk whom Aristophanes repeatedly attacked. Cleon took credit for the victory over Sparta at Sphacteria (Pylos) and prosecuted Aristophanes over his lost play The Babylonians; Aristophanes answered by satirizing him in The Knights and The Wasps, whose names Philocleon ("Cleon-lover") and Bdelycleon ("Cleon-loather") mock him.

**The Knights and the sausage-seller**
In The Knights, a stolen oracle prophesies that the tanner (Paphlagon, a stand-in for Cleon) will be overthrown by a sausage-seller. The sausage-seller, Agoracritus, beats Cleon in a series of contests for the favor of the old man Demos, who personifies the Athenian people.

**Dionysus and Xanthias in the underworld (The Frogs)**
In The Frogs, the bumbling god Dionysus travels to Hades to bring back the tragedian Euripides. He disguises himself as Heracles and repeatedly swaps clothes with his slave Xanthias, makes Xanthias walk around the lake while he takes Charon's boat, and Xanthias gets blamed for Heracles' earlier theft of Cerberus.

**Aeschylus vs. Euripides and the weighing of verses**
The poetry contest that closes The Frogs. Lines from each tragedian are weighed on a scale, and Aeschylus mocks Euripides' prologues by repeatedly ending them with "lost his little oil flask"; Aeschylus is judged the best tragic poet and brought back to life instead of Euripides.

**Reconciliation, the naked handmaid**
A personification who appears in Lysistrata (sometimes translated as Peace). The negotiators for Athens and Sparta are distracted by her naked body and map their territorial demands onto it as the peace treaty is drawn up.

**Lysistrata's wool metaphor and the Commissioner**
In Lysistrata, the heroine tells the Commissioner (Magistrate) that the city should be managed like wool: washed, carded of its parasites, and woven into a cloak for the people. The women dress the Commissioner as a woman and later as a corpse; the play also features the women seizing the Acropolis treasury, old men who try to burn them out and are doused with water, and Myrrhine teasing her husband Kinesias.

**Peace and Trygaeus' dung beetle**
In Peace, the farmer Trygaeus flies to heaven on a giant dung beetle and discovers the gods have left, leaving War in charge, who has buried the goddess Peace in a cave. He rallies the Greeks to free her and marries her attendant Harvest (Opora); the play opens with slaves kneading dung to feed the beetle.

**Edward Rochester and Thornfield Hall**
Rochester is the brooding, sardonic master of Thornfield Hall, where Jane works as a governess, and he becomes the man she loves. They first meet when his horse slips on ice and he sprains his ankle. Later he examines her strange paintings, including one of an icy landscape dominated by a colossal pale head, and abruptly sends her to bed.

**Bertha Mason, the "madwoman in the attic"**
Rochester's insane Creole first wife from Jamaica, secretly kept locked on Thornfield's third floor. She reminds Jane of "the foul German spectre—the Vampyre." She sets Rochester's bed on fire (Jane saves him) and eventually burns down Thornfield Hall, dying in the blaze.

**Grace Poole**
The hard-drinking servant hired to guard Bertha. Rochester and the housekeeper Mrs. Fairfax blame her for the strange laughter, the fire, and other odd events at Thornfield, and Jane believes them until the truth comes out.

**The torn wedding veil and the interrupted wedding**
Two nights before her wedding, Jane wakes to see a ghastly woman try on her veil and tear it in two, and in the morning finds it really torn. At the ceremony, Bertha's brother Richard Mason, the earlier visitor from Jamaica whom Bertha had attacked, reveals that Rochester is already married. Jane flees Thornfield.

**Lowood School and Helen Burns**
Lowood Institution is the harsh charity school where Mrs. Reed sends Jane. There she befriends the patient, deeply religious Helen Burns, whom she first sees reading Samuel Johnson's Rasselas and who is persecuted by Miss Scatcherd, who makes her wear a sign reading "Slattern." Helen dies of consumption in Jane's arms during a typhus epidemic, and years later Jane marks her grave with a stone reading "Resurgam" ("I shall rise again").

**Mr. Brocklehurst and Miss Temple**
Brocklehurst is Lowood's stingy, hypocritical clergyman-manager whose neglect causes the typhus outbreak. He makes Jane stand on a stool and denounces her as a liar after she drops her slate. He had earlier given her a tract called the "Child's Guide" with a story about a naughty liar named Martha. The kind superintendent Maria Temple clears Jane's name after confirming her story with the apothecary Mr. Lloyd.

**The red-room and Gateshead**
As an orphan at Gateshead Hall, Jane is abused by her aunt Mrs. Reed and cousin John Reed, who throws a copy of Bewick's History of British Birds at her. After fighting back, she is locked in the red-room, where her uncle Mr. Reed died, and faints after believing she sees his ghost. As a child she tells Brocklehurst that to avoid hell she "must keep in good health, and not die."

**St. John Rivers**
The cold, ambitious clergyman who, with his sisters Diana and Mary, takes in the starving Jane at Moor House (also called Marsh End). He turns out to be her cousin, makes her learn Hindustani, and proposes so that she will join him as a missionary's wife in India. Jane refuses.

**Jane's inheritance and Rosamond Oliver**
While Jane is at Moor House, St. John tears off a scrap of paper on which she had signed her real name while drawing a portrait of the beautiful Rosamond Oliver. This confirms that she is the heir of her uncle John Eyre, who left her £20,000, which she shares with her newfound cousins.

**Adèle Varens and Mrs. Fairfax**
Adèle is Jane's young French pupil at Thornfield, Rochester's ward and the daughter of his former mistress, the opera dancer Céline Varens. The housekeeper Mrs. Alice Fairfax hired Jane through an advertisement.

**The gypsy fortune-teller and Blanche Ingram**
During a house party at Thornfield, Rochester disguises himself as an old gypsy woman to tell the fortunes of his guests, including the beautiful, snobbish Blanche Ingram, whom everyone expects him to marry, and Jane, who sees through the disguise. Richard Mason arrives from Jamaica the same evening.

**The chestnut tree proposal**
Rochester proposes to Jane in Thornfield's garden beneath a great horse-chestnut tree. That night a bolt of lightning splits the tree in two, foreshadowing disaster.

**"Reader, I married him"**
The famous opening of the final chapter. After hearing Rochester's voice calling her name across the miles, Jane returns to find Thornfield in ruins and Rochester blinded and missing a hand at Ferndean Manor. When he asks if he is hideous, she replies "Very, sir: you always were." They marry, and he regains enough sight in one eye to see their first child. Tracy Chevalier's story anthology Reader, I Married Him is named for the line.

**Wide Sargasso Sea**
Jean Rhys's 1966 prequel novel, which reimagines Bertha Mason as Antoinette Cosway, a Creole heiress in the Caribbean. It includes the burning of the Coulibri estate, an obeah love potion from her nurse Christophine, and Antoinette's dream-like final escape with a candle, remembering "Aunt Cora's patchwork."

**Currer Bell and The Madwoman in the Attic**
Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre (1847), subtitled An Autobiography, under the pseudonym Currer Bell. It opens "There was no possibility of taking a walk that day." Sandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar's 1979 feminist study The Madwoman in the Attic takes its title from Bertha Mason.

**Leaves of Grass**
Whitman's life work, a poetry collection first self-published in 1855 with just twelve untitled poems. He revised and expanded it for the rest of his life, ending with the 1891–92 "deathbed edition." It is the most common giveaway for him and contains nearly all of his famous poems.

**"Song of Myself"**
Whitman's most famous poem, the long free-verse centerpiece of Leaves of Grass, divided into 52 sections. It opens "I celebrate myself, and sing myself" and includes "I loafe and invite my soul." In section 6 a child asks "What is the grass?" and the speaker guesses it is "the beautiful uncut hair of graves"; the poem ends "I stop somewhere waiting for you."

**"I sound my barbaric yawp over the roofs of the world"**
A famous line near the end of "Song of Myself," just after the speaker declares "I too am untranslatable." It sums up Whitman's loud, untamed, distinctly American voice.

**"I am large, I contain multitudes" and "every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you"**
Two signature lines from "Song of Myself." The first answers the charge that the speaker contradicts himself ("Very well then I contradict myself"); the second, from the opening, expresses Whitman's democratic identification with every reader. The poem also states "to die is different from what any one supposed, and luckier."

**"O Captain! My Captain!"**
Whitman's elegy for Abraham Lincoln, unusual in his work for its rhyme and meter. It casts Lincoln as a ship's captain who dies just as "our fearful trip is done"; the speaker sees "the bleeding drops of red" where his Captain lies on the deck "fallen cold and dead," while the shore exults and bells ring.

**"When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd"**
Whitman's longer elegy for Lincoln, built around three symbols: the lilac, the "great star" that "early droop'd in the western sky" (the "powerful western fallen star," Lincoln), and a hermit thrush singing in a swamp. It was first published in Sequel to Drum-Taps, and its speaker mourns "with ever-returning spring." He also wrote the short Lincoln poem "Hush'd Be the Camps To-day."

**"Crossing Brooklyn Ferry"**
A poem set on the ferry over the East River between Manhattan and Brooklyn. It opens "Flood-tide below me! I see you face to face!" and describes sea-gulls "oscillating their bodies." It speaks directly to future "men and women of a generation" who will cross after him, asking what the count of years between them matters, and ends saying the objects "furnish your parts toward the soul."

**"Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking"**
Originally titled "A Child's Reminiscence," this poem describes a boy on the beach of Paumanok (Long Island) who hears a mockingbird mourn its lost mate in italicized songs. The poem ends with the sea whispering the word "death," and its final words are "the sea whisper'd me."

**"I Sing the Body Electric"**
A poem celebrating the human body as inseparable from the soul. It describes a common farmer who is the father of five sons, includes "the armies of those I love engirth me," asks "if the body were not the soul, what is the soul?", and ends "O I say now these are the soul!" Ray Bradbury named a short story collection after it.

**"When I Heard the Learn'd Astronomer"**
A short poem in which the speaker, shown the "proofs, the figures" "ranged in columns" at a lecture, grows "tired and sick." He wanders out into the "mystical moist night-air" and "look'd up in perfect silence at the stars," preferring direct experience to scientific analysis.

**"A Noiseless Patient Spider"**
A short poem comparing a spider that "launch'd forth filament, filament, filament, out of itself" to the speaker's soul, "surrounded, detached, in measureless oceans of space," which seeks connection with the world.

**Drum-Taps and "The Wound Dresser"**
Drum-Taps (1865) is Whitman's collection of Civil War poems, inspired by his work as a volunteer nurse in Washington hospitals. "The Wound Dresser" describes tending the hurt and wounded "with soothing hand," and "Beat! Beat! Drums!" cries "blow! bugles! blow!"

**The "Calamus" poems**
A cluster of poems in Leaves of Grass celebrating "manly love" and comradeship between men. They are the most open expression of Whitman's homosexuality and include "Are You the New Person Drawn Toward Me?", which warns "it may be all maya, illusion."

**Allen Ginsberg's "A Supermarket in California"**
Ginsberg imagines Whitman as a "lonely old grubber, poking among the meats" and "eyeing the grocery boys" in a supermarket. He asks "Where are we going, Walt Whitman?" and "which way does your beard point tonight?"

**Tributes by other poets**
Many poets have written to or about Whitman. Ezra Pound's "A Pact" makes "a truce" with him after detesting him "long enough"; Federico García Lorca's "Ode to Walt Whitman" calls him a "lovely old man" with a "beard full of butterflies"; Rubén Darío wrote a sonnet to him, Pablo Neruda an ode, and Sherman Alexie the poem "Defending Walt Whitman." E. M. Forster took the title A Passage to India from Whitman's poem "Passage to India."

**"Vanished into the Clouds"**
A chapter of The Tale of Genji (Kumogakure) that has a title but no text. Its blankness implies the death of the protagonist, Genji, and it is the single most common clue for the novel. The chapters after it skip ahead to the next generation.

**Lady Murasaki (Murasaki Shikibu)**
The author of The Tale of Genji, a lady-in-waiting at the Japanese imperial court in the early 11th century, during the Heian period. The novel has 54 chapters and is often called the world's first novel. Her pen name comes from the novel's heroine Murasaki.

**Genji, the "Shining Prince"**
The title character, called Hikaru Genji ("the Shining Genji") because of his beauty and talent. He is the son of the Kiritsubo Emperor and a low-ranking consort, the Kiritsubo ("Paulownia Court") lady, who dies when he is three. After a Korean physiognomist warns that disorder would follow if he became emperor, he is made a commoner with the surname Minamoto (Genji).

**Lady Aoi**
Genji's first wife, the daughter of the Minister of the Left and sister of his friend To no Chujo, married to him at the end of Chapter 1. Their marriage is cold. After giving birth to their son Yugiri she is killed by the jealous spirit of Lady Rokujo.

**Lady Fujitsubo**
The Kiritsubo Emperor's consort and Genji's stepmother, chosen because she resembles Genji's dead mother. Genji has an affair with her, and she secretly bears his son, who becomes Emperor Reizei.

**The Uji chapters, Kaoru and Niou**
The final ten chapters, set mainly near the town of Uji after Genji's death. They follow the rivalry between Kaoru, the "fragrant captain," and Niou. Kaoru is legally Genji's son by the Third Princess but actually the son of Kashiwagi, and he has a natural fragrance; he is sometimes called literature's first antihero. Niou is Genji's grandson through his daughter by the Akashi Lady. The two pursue the daughters of the Eighth Prince.

**Exile to Suma and Akashi**
After Genji's affair with Oborozukiyo, the "Lady of the Misty Moon" and a concubine of his half-brother, the Suzaku Emperor, is discovered, he goes into exile at Suma. During a storm he dreams of his dead father and of the "king of the dragon palace." The Akashi Novice then invites him to Akashi along the shore, where Genji fathers a daughter with the Akashi Lady before being recalled to the capital.

**Murasaki (the young girl)**
A ten-year-old girl, Fujitsubo's niece, whom Genji takes from her home and raises to be his ideal wife. She becomes his great love and is often associated with the purple gromwell (murasaki) flower. Her death late in the novel plunges Genji into grief and leads to his withdrawal.

**Lady Rokujo's vengeful spirit and the Battle of the Carriages**
Lady Rokujo is Genji's proud, jealous former mistress. At the Kamo festival her carriage is shoved aside by Aoi's servants in the "Battle (Quarrel) of the Carriages." Afterward her living spirit possesses and kills Aoi, and spirits connected to her plague other women Genji loves.

**"Waves of the Blue Sea" (Seigaiha) dance**
At the autumn maple excursion before the court, Genji performs this dance flawlessly alongside To no Chujo. Next to him, his partner is compared to a mountain shrub beside a blossoming tree.

**Utsusemi, the "Locust/Cicada Shell"**
A married woman who rejects Genji's advances by slipping away and leaving behind a robe. In a poem he compares the robe to a cast-off cicada shell. Many women in the novel are known by such nicknames from poems or traits rather than true names.

**Yugao, the "Lady of the Evening Faces"**
A gentle lover of Genji's who dies mysteriously, apparently killed by a possessing spirit, during a night at an abandoned villa. Her body is secretly taken to the mountains, and Genji falls ill afterward. Her daughter Tamakazura later becomes his adoptive daughter.

**The Broom Tree chapter and the "rainy night" discussion**
In this early chapter, Genji, To no Chujo, and other young men rate types of women on a rainy night. A man from the Ministry of Rites describes a learned woman who wrote in Chinese and smelled of garlic medicine taken for a cold. The chapter's title refers to a poem connected with Utsusemi.

**Suetsumuhana (the "Safflower") and the Lady of the Orange Blossoms**
Suetsumuhana is a shy, impoverished princess whose zither playing attracts Genji but who turns out to have a long red nose, so her nickname puns on the red safflower. Hanachirusato, the "Lady of the Orange Blossoms," is a gentle lover whom Genji keeps under his care.

**Ukifune and "The Mayfly"**
Ukifune, the unacknowledged third daughter of the Eighth Prince, is torn between Kaoru and Niou and tries to drown herself in the Uji River. She is rescued and becomes a nun, which is the novel's final major event.

**Other notable scenes and context**
Genji releases fireflies to reveal his adoptive daughter Tamakazura to a suitor, and he builds a mansion, the Rokujo-in, with quarters for the four seasons to house his main lovers. He wins a picture contest using paintings he made in exile at Suma. Key ideas and context include mono no aware ("the sadness of things"), allusions to Bai Juyi's "Song of Everlasting Sorrow," the 12th-century illustrated Genji scrolls, and English translations by Arthur Waley and Royall Tyler.

**"The Second Coming" and the "rough beast"**
Yeats's most famous poem (1919), an apocalyptic vision written in the aftermath of World War I. It ends by asking "what rough beast, its hour come round at last, / Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?" The speaker sees "a vast image out of Spiritus Mundi," the world's collective soul: a sphinx-like shape "with lion body and the head of a man," whose "twenty centuries of stony sleep / Were vexed to nightmare by a rocking cradle."

**"Turning and turning in the widening gyre"**
The opening of "The Second Coming," which continues "The falcon cannot hear the falconer; / Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold; / Mere anarchy is loosed upon the world." It goes on to say "the ceremony of innocence is drowned" and "The best lack all conviction, while the worst / Are full of passionate intensity." The gyre, a widening spiral, reflects Yeats's cyclical theory of history, which he set out in A Vision.

**"Sailing to Byzantium" and "That is no country for old men"**
A poem from The Tower (1928) in which an aging speaker leaves the sensual world of the young and sails to the holy city of Byzantium. Its first line, "That is no country for old men," supplied the title of Cormac McCarthy's novel No Country for Old Men. The speaker says there is no "singing school but studying / Monuments of its own magnificence."

**"An aged man is but a paltry thing"**
A line from "Sailing to Byzantium," which continues "A tattered coat upon a stick, unless / Soul clap its hands and sing." The speaker asks the "sages standing in God's holy fire / As in the gold mosaic of a wall" to free his heart, "sick with desire / And fastened to a dying animal," and "gather me / Into the artifice of eternity." Once "out of nature," he wants to take "such a form as Grecian goldsmiths make," a golden bird singing to a drowsy emperor.

**"Easter, 1916" and "A terrible beauty is born"**
Yeats's poem on the failed Easter Rising against British rule in Dublin, whose leaders were executed. He recalls passing them with "polite meaningless words" and mocking them "to please a companion / Around the fire at the club," but now "All changed, changed utterly: / A terrible beauty is born." He also warns that "Too long a sacrifice / Can make a stone of the heart."

**"MacDonagh and MacBride / And Connolly and Pearse"**
The executed Easter Rising leaders whom Yeats names at the end of "Easter, 1916," saying "I write it out in a verse" for "wherever green is worn." John MacBride, the estranged husband of Yeats's beloved Maud Gonne, is the "drunken, vainglorious lout" who "had done most bitter wrong" but is still honored.

**"The Lake Isle of Innisfree"**
An early lyric (1890) about an island in Lough Gill, County Sligo, where Yeats spent much of his childhood. It begins "I will arise and go now, and go to Innisfree, / And a small cabin build there, of clay and wattles made." The speaker will have "nine bean-rows" and "live alone in the bee-loud glade," where "peace comes dropping slow," "midnight's all a glimmer," and evening is "full of the linnet's wings."

**"Leda and the Swan"**
A 1923 sonnet about Zeus, in the form of a swan, raping the Spartan queen Leda, which leads to the birth of Helen and the Trojan War. It opens "A sudden blow: the great wings beating still," and the act "engenders there / The broken wall, the burning roof and tower / And Agamemnon dead." It ends by asking "Did she put on his knowledge with his power / Before the indifferent beak could let her drop?"

**"The Circus Animals' Desertion" and "the foul rag and bone shop of the heart"**
A late poem (1939) in which the aging poet "sought a theme and sought for it in vain" and asks "What can I but enumerate old themes?" Reviewing his past work, he finds it rose from "old iron, old bones, old rags." He concludes that now his ladder is gone, "I must lie down where all the ladders start, / In the foul rag and bone shop of the heart."

**"The Wild Swans at Coole"**
A poem set at Coole Park, the estate of Yeats's patron Lady Gregory. It begins "The nineteenth autumn has come upon me / Since I first made my count" of the "nine-and-fifty swans," which "scatter wheeling in great broken rings / Upon their clamorous wings." Unlike the aging poet, the swans paddle "lover by lover" in the "cold / Companionable streams," and "their hearts have not grown old."

**"Among School Children"**
A poem from The Tower in which Yeats, as "a sixty-year-old smiling public man" and senator, visits a convent school. It ends "O body swayed to music, O brightening glance, / How can we know the dancer from the dance?"

**"An Irish Airman Foresees His Death"**
A poem spoken by Major Robert Gregory, Lady Gregory's son, who was killed flying in World War I. He says "I know that I shall meet my fate / Somewhere among the clouds above; / Those that I fight I do not hate, / Those that I guard I do not love," and that he fights out of "a lonely impulse of delight." Yeats also mourned him in "In Memory of Major Robert Gregory."

**Things Fall Apart**
Chinua Achebe took the title of his 1958 novel from "The Second Coming." In it, Okonkwo is exiled to his mother's village after his gun accidentally kills a 16-year-old boy, and his uncle Uchendu teaches him that "Mother is Supreme."

**W. H. Auden's "In Memory of W. B. Yeats"**
Auden's 1939 elegy for Yeats, who died that January. It begins "He disappeared in the dead of winter: / The brooks were frozen, the airports almost deserted," declares "mad Ireland hurt you into poetry" and "poetry makes nothing happen," and includes the lines "Earth, receive an honoured guest: / William Yeats is laid to rest."

**"Tread softly because you tread on my dreams"**
The closing line of "He Wishes for the Cloths of Heaven," often linked to Yeats's unrequited love for Maud Gonne. The poor speaker wishes he had "the heavens' embroidered cloths" to spread under the beloved's feet, but has only his dreams to offer.

**Death in Venice**
Mann's 1912 novella and the most common giveaway for him. The aging, disciplined writer Gustav von Aschenbach, who was given the noble "von" at age 50 for works such as a prose epic on Frederick the Great, travels to the Lido in Venice and becomes obsessed with a beautiful boy, staying on even as a cholera epidemic spreads through the city.

**Tadzio**
The beautiful Polish boy whom Aschenbach watches on the beach and follows through the streets of Venice. Aschenbach never speaks to him; he dies in his beach chair while watching Tadzio wade out into the sea.

**Overripe strawberries and the smell of disinfectant**
Key plot details from Death in Venice. Aschenbach notices the city smells of disinfectant, which officials try to explain away (blaming the sirocco) while hiding the cholera outbreak. He is secretly glad when his luggage is sent to the wrong place, giving him an excuse to return to Venice, and he catches cholera after eating overripe strawberries.

**Red-haired men, the gondolier, and the barber**
Ominous figures in Death in Venice that foreshadow Aschenbach's death: a red-haired stranger at a Munich cemetery, an old fop wearing makeup on the boat, and a red-haired street guitarist. An unlicensed gondolier assures him "I can row you well," and late in the story a barber dyes Aschenbach's hair and paints his face to make him look young.

**The Magic Mountain**
Mann's 1924 novel set at the Berghof, a tuberculosis sanatorium in Davos in the Swiss Alps. The "simple" young engineer Hans Castorp comes to visit for three weeks but stays for seven years, until the outbreak of World War I. Characters include the psychoanalyst Dr. Krokowski and the "good" and "bad" Russian tables in the dining hall.

**Clavdia Chauchat**
The Russian patient at the Berghof whom Hans Castorp falls in love with. He borrows a pencil from her at the Walpurgisnacht carnival party, because her eyes remind him of his schoolboy crush Pribislav Hippe, from whom he once borrowed a pencil; that night he sleeps with her.

**Settembrini and Naphta**
The two intellectuals who argue over Hans Castorp's mind in The Magic Mountain. Lodovico Settembrini is an Italian rationalist humanist (a student of the poet Carducci), and Leo Naphta is a Jewish-born Jesuit who argues for authority and terror. Their debates end in a duel at which Settembrini fires into the air and Naphta shoots himself.

**Joachim Ziemssen**
Hans Castorp's cousin, a soldier who has tuberculosis and is a patient at the Berghof. Castorp's visit to Joachim is what brings him to the sanatorium. Joachim later leaves to rejoin the army in the "flatlands," returns, and dies.

**Buddenbrooks**
Mann's first novel (1901), subtitled "The Decline of a Family," about a family of grain merchants in Lübeck, Mann's hometown. Tony Buddenbrook is forced to marry the swindler Grünlich and later marries the Munich hop merchant Alois Permaneder. Thomas reads Schopenhauer and dies after a botched tooth extraction, his brother Christian ends up in an asylum, and the musical, sickly last heir Hanno dies of typhoid. It was cited when Mann won the 1929 Nobel Prize.

**Doctor Faustus**
Mann's 1947 retelling of the Faust legend. Narrated by Serenus Zeitblom, it tells of the composer Adrian Leverkühn, who deliberately contracts syphilis as a pact with the devil to gain creative genius, renounces love, and invents a twelve-tone method of composition. After Arnold Schoenberg objected, Mann added a note crediting him with the system. Leverkühn's works include Apocalypsis cum figuris and The Lamentation of Doctor Faustus, which he finishes after his beloved young nephew Echo dies. His decline parallels Germany's descent into Nazism.

**Mario and the Magician**
A 1930 novella widely read as an allegory of fascism. At an Italian seaside resort, the hypnotist Cipolla humiliates audience members and makes the waiter Mario kiss him while believing he is his beloved Silvestra. Mario then shoots Cipolla dead.

**Tonio Kröger**
A 1903 novella about an artist torn between art and ordinary life. As a boy, Tonio loves his friend Hans Hansen and the blonde Ingeborg Holm, and is mocked for dancing the ladies' part in dancing class while distracted by her. Years later, at a resort in Aalsgaard, Denmark, he sees a couple resembling Hans and Ingeborg dancing.

**Confessions of Felix Krull, Confidence Man**
Mann's unfinished final comic novel about a charming con man. Felix's father kills himself after his sparkling wine company fails. Felix swaps identities with the Marquis de Venosta, sets off on a world tour, and in Lisbon seduces the wife of Professor Kuckuck.

**Joseph and His Brothers**
Mann's four-volume retelling of the Book of Genesis story of Jacob and Joseph (1933–1943), which he considered his greatest work. The volumes are The Stories of Jacob, Young Joseph, Joseph in Egypt, and Joseph the Provider.

**Tristan**
A 1903 novella set at the sanatorium Einfried. The aesthete writer Detlev Spinell seduces Gabriele Klöterjahn, the sickly wife of the businessman Anton Klöterjahn, by getting her to play Wagner's Tristan und Isolde on the piano, after which her health declines. Mann also wrote Lotte in Weimar (The Beloved Returns), in which Charlotte Kestner meets Goethe again.

**Waiting for Godot**
Beckett's most famous play and a landmark of the Theatre of the Absurd. Two tramps, Vladimir (Didi) and Estragon (Gogo), wait on a country road by a lone tree for a man named Godot, who never arrives. Both acts end with the line "Let's go" followed by the stage direction "They do not move."

**Vladimir and Estragon**
