The two tramps of Waiting for Godot, who pass the time with bickering, routines such as swapping bowler hats, and repeated talk of hanging themselves from the tree. Vladimir discusses why only one of the four Gospels mentions that one of the two thieves crucified with Jesus was saved, and he sings a round about a dog that steals a crust of bread. Estragon dreams of wandering in the Pyrenees and rejects the turnip and radish Vladimir offers him because he wants a carrot.

**Pozzo and Lucky**
The master and slave who pass through Waiting for Godot. Pozzo drives Lucky on a rope, and Lucky dances a dance called "The Net" and kicks Estragon in the shin. In Act II, Pozzo has gone blind and Lucky has gone mute, and the two are often read as reversing or blurring the roles of master and slave.

**Lucky's "Think!" monologue**
When Pozzo orders him to "Think!", Lucky delivers a long, unpunctuated speech of academic gibberish about a "personal God quaquaquaqua." It cites the "public works of Puncher and Wattman" and the "Acacacacademy of Anthropopopometry."

**The tree and the boy**
The only scenery in Waiting for Godot is a bare tree, which sprouts a few leaves in Act II as the only sign that time has passed. At the end of each act, a boy arrives to say that Godot will not come today but surely tomorrow. The boy tends Godot's goats, and he reports that Godot beats his brother, who tends the sheep.

**Susan Sontag's Sarajevo production**
In 1993, during the Siege of Sarajevo, Susan Sontag directed a candlelit production of Waiting for Godot in the besieged city.

**Endgame**
Beckett's one-act play set in a bare room with two small windows in an apparently post-apocalyptic world. Its central characters are the blind Hamm, who cannot stand and sits in a wheelchair, and his servant Clov, who cannot sit. Clov opens the play with "Finished, it's finished, nearly finished," and Hamm repeats "Me to play" like a chess player. At the end, Hamm covers his face with his bloodstained handkerchief.

**Nagg and Nell in the trash cans**
Hamm's legless parents in Endgame live in two ashbins (trash cans) and try but fail to kiss. They lost their legs ("shanks") in a tandem bicycle accident in the Ardennes. Hamm also asks to be wheeled around the walls of the room and put back exactly in its center, and he has a three-legged black toy dog, which Clov hits him with near the end.

**Krapp's Last Tape**
A one-act play in which the old Krapp, on his 69th birthday, eats bananas and listens to a tape recording he made at 39. He savors the word "spool," laughs at his younger self, and finally records one last tape.

**Happy Days**
A play in which Winnie is buried up to her waist in Act I and up to her neck in Act II in a mound of earth. She chatters cheerfully, rummages in her handbag (which holds a revolver), watches an ant and laughs at the word "formication," and remarks on "the way man adapts himself to changing conditions." Her husband Willie mostly stays out of sight and reads aloud from a newspaper.

**Not I**
A short play in which the only lit part of the stage is a woman's disembodied Mouth speaking rapidly about her life ("back in the field"). A silent, hooded Auditor stands nearby.

**The Trilogy: Molloy, Malone Dies, The Unnamable**
Beckett's three postwar novels, which he first wrote in French. In Molloy, the detective Jacques Moran is sent to track down the title wanderer. In Malone Dies, a bedridden man who is unsure whether he is in a hospital or an asylum tells stories about a character called Sapo, later renamed Macmann. In The Unnamable, a disembodied voice thinks about invented figures such as Mahood and Worm.

**Late short plays: Footfalls, Rockaby, A Piece of Monologue**
Footfalls shows May pacing while she speaks with the voice of her (possibly dead) mother. In Rockaby, a woman sits in a rocking chair listening to her own recorded voice. A Piece of Monologue is an old man's brief meditation on birth and death.

**Biography: Irish, Paris, and the Resistance**
Beckett was born in Dublin and studied at Trinity College. He settled in Paris in 1937, worked for the French Resistance during World War II, and later hid in rural France doing farm work. He wrote many of his works in French, and he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1969.

**The Jungle Book**
Kipling's 1894 collection of stories set mostly in the Indian jungle and his most common giveaway. Its central figure is Mowgli, a "man-cub" raised by wolves, alongside the bear Baloo, the panther Bagheera, the python Kaa, and the wolf-pack leader Akela.

**Mowgli and Shere Khan**
Mowgli is the human boy raised by the Seeonee wolf pack in The Jungle Book. His great enemy is the tiger Shere Khan, who wants to kill him; in "Kaa's Hunting," Mowgli is kidnapped by the Bandar-log (monkey people) and rescued by Kaa, Baloo, and Bagheera.

**"Rikki-Tikki-Tavi" and Nag and Nagaina**
A Jungle Book story about a young mongoose adopted by an English family in India. He protects the boy Teddy and his parents from the cobras Nag and Nagaina, killing Nag and then chasing Nagaina into her hole after she bargains for her last egg; the tailorbird Darzee and his wife help him.

**"Gunga Din"**
A poem from Barrack-Room Ballads, told by a British soldier in India in Cockney dialect, about an Indian water-carrier (bhisti) whom the soldiers mock and beat. Gunga Din saves the speaker's life and is shot dead, and the poem ends, "You're a better man than I am, Gunga Din!"

**"Lazarushian-leather" and "squidgy-nosed old idol"**
Mocking descriptions of Gunga Din's skin and appearance used by the speaker, who also says that "for all 'is dirty 'ide, / 'E was white, clear white, inside." Gunga Din carries a goatskin water-bag as his only equipment.

**"The White Man's Burden"**
Kipling's 1899 imperialist poem urging the United States to colonize the Philippines. It opens many stanzas with "Take up the White Man's burden," tells readers to "send forth the best ye breed," and calls the colonized "new-caught, sullen peoples, / Half devil and half child"; it was widely parodied, including by critics who asked about "the brown man's burden."

**"If—"**
A poem of advice addressed to a son (inspired by his son John), first published in Rewards and Fairies after the story "Brother Square-Toes." It opens "If you can keep your head when all about you / Are losing theirs and blaming it on you," calls Triumph and Disaster "two impostors," urges the reader to "fill the unforgiving minute / With sixty seconds' worth of distance run," and ends "you'll be a Man, my son!"

**"Recessional"**
A hymn-like poem written for Queen Victoria's 1897 Diamond Jubilee warning against imperial pride. It addresses the "God of our fathers, known of old, / Lord of our far-flung battle-line," declares that "all our pomp of yesterday / Is one with Nineveh and Tyre," and repeats the refrain "Lest we forget—lest we forget!"

**Kim**
Kipling's 1901 novel about Kimball O'Hara, an orphan of Irish parentage in Lahore known as "Little Friend of all the World." He travels with the Tibetan lama Teshoo Lama, who seeks the River of the Arrow, while being trained as a British spy (by Mr. Lurgan, who teaches him the memory game now called "Kim's Game") in the "Great Game" against Russia, alongside agent Hurree Babu.

**"Mandalay"**
A poem in which a British soldier back in rainy London longs for a Burmese girl he met "by the old Moulmein Pagoda" in Burma. Its refrain is "On the road to Mandalay, / Where the flyin'-fishes play," and the speaker wishes to be shipped "somewheres east of Suez, where the best is like the worst" and "there aren't no Ten Commandments."

**"The Man Who Would Be King"**
A story in which two British adventurers, Daniel Dravot and Peachey Carnehan, tell a journalist narrator that "India is not big enough" and go to remote Kafiristan, where Dravot is worshipped as a god and descendant of Alexander the Great. The scheme collapses when his bride bites him and he bleeds, proving he is human, and he is killed.

**Captains Courageous**
Kipling's 1897 novel about Harvey Cheyne, a spoiled rich American boy who is washed off an ocean liner and rescued by Manuel, a Portuguese fisherman from the Gloucester fishing schooner We're Here. Working on the boat over the season transforms him.

**"Danny Deever"**
A Barrack-Room Ballads poem about the execution of a British soldier by hanging in front of his regiment. It is a dialogue in which Files-on-Parade asks the Colour-Sergeant questions like "What makes you look so white?"

**Just So Stories and other Jungle Book tales**
Just So Stories is a collection of humorous pourquoi (origin) tales; in "How the First Letter Was Written," the girl Taffimai Metallumai sends a picture message to her mother. Other Jungle Book tales include "The White Seal," about Kotick seeking a safe beach for seals away from Novastoshnah, and "Toomai of the Elephants," about a boy and the elephant Kala Nag.

**"The Female of the Species" and other poems**
"The Female of the Species" claims that "the female of the species is more deadly than the male." Kipling also wrote "The Gods of the Copybook Headings" (included in T. S. Eliot's 1941 selection of his verse) and "The Rowers," which helped popularize "Hun" as an insult for Germans.

**"Ode on a Grecian Urn"**
Keats's most famous poem and the most common giveaway for him. The speaker addresses an ancient urn as a "still unravish'd bride of quietness," a "foster-child of silence and slow time," and a "Sylvan historian," and ends with the urn's message: "Beauty is truth, truth beauty, —that is all / Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know."

**Lines from the Grecian Urn**
Other often-quoted lines include "Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard / Are sweeter"; "What leaf-fring'd legend haunts about thy shape?"; "What men or gods are these?"; "Ah, happy, happy boughs! that cannot shed / Your leaves"; and the question "To what green altar, O mysterious priest, / Lead'st thou that heifer lowing at the skies." The urn is also called an "Attic shape."

**"Ode to a Nightingale"**
The 1819 ode that begins "My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains / My sense" and ends "Fled is that music: —Do I wake or sleep?" just after asking "Was it a vision, or a waking dream?" The speaker calls the bird a "light-winged Dryad of the trees" and tells it "Thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird!"

**"Half in love with easeful Death"**
Lines from "Ode to a Nightingale" also used as clues: the speaker wants a "draught of vintage," a "beaker full of the warm South" with "beaded bubbles winking at the brim"; he flies "Not charioted by Bacchus and his pards, / But on the viewless wings of Poesy"; and he notes "tender is the night." The bird's song is the same one heard by Ruth when "she stood in tears amid the alien corn," and the word "forlorn" brings the speaker back to himself, admitting "the fancy cannot cheat so well / As she is fam'd to do, deceiving elf."

**"La Belle Dame sans Merci"**
Keats's ballad, which opens "O what can ail thee, knight-at-arms, / Alone and palely loitering?" The knight, with "anguish moist and fever-dew," tells how he met a lady in the meads, a "faery's child," made her a garland, bracelets, and "fragrant zone," and was taken to her "elfin grot," then dreamed of "pale kings and princes too" warning that she had him "in thrall."

**"Adonais"**
Percy Bysshe Shelley's 1821 elegy for Keats, who died in Rome of tuberculosis at age 25. It opens "I weep for Adonais—he is dead!", asks where Urania was when he died, tells mourners to "Go thou to Rome," blames a hostile reviewer (a "nameless worm," a "noteless blot"), and ends with Keats's soul shining "like a star" from "the abode where the Eternal are."

**Endymion**
Keats's long four-book poem (1818) about the love of the moon goddess Cynthia for the shepherd prince Endymion. It begins "A thing of beauty is a joy for ever," and is dedicated to the memory of Thomas Chatterton. John Gibson Lockhart attacked it in Blackwood's Magazine, telling Keats, who had trained as an apothecary, that it is better to be a starved apothecary than a starved poet.

**"Ode to Psyche"**
The first of the 1819 odes, addressed to the goddess Psyche, who was deified too late to have been worshipped in antiquity. The speaker offers to "be thy choir, and make a moan / Upon the midnight hours" and says "Yes, I will be thy priest, and build a fane / In some untrodden region of my mind," and the poem ends by leaving a window open "To let the warm Love in."

**"Ode on Melancholy" and "Ode on Indolence"**
Two more of the 1819 odes. "Ode on Melancholy" advises the reader to "glut thy sorrow on a morning rose" and, "if thy mistress some rich anger shows, / Emprison her soft hand, and let her rave," and says that "in the very temple of Delight / Veil'd Melancholy has her sovran shrine." In "Ode on Indolence," three figures in "placid sandals, and in white robes" (Love, Ambition, and Poesy) pass by, and the final stanza begins "So, ye three Ghosts, adieu!"

**"To Autumn"**
Keats's 1819 ode to the "Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness, / Close bosom-friend of the maturing sun." It pictures Autumn on a "granary floor" and by a "cider-press," asks "Where are the songs of spring?", and ends with "hedge-crickets" singing and "gathering swallows" twittering in the skies. In a letter to John Hamilton Reynolds, Keats said he had never liked stubble fields so much as on the walk that inspired it.

**"On First Looking into Chapman's Homer"**
Keats's 1816 sonnet about reading George Chapman's translation of Homer. It begins "Much have I travell'd in the realms of gold" and compares the experience to "some watcher of the skies / When a new planet swims into his ken" and to "stout Cortez" staring at the Pacific, "silent, upon a peak in Darien" (the explorer who actually saw it first was Balboa).

**"When I have fears that I may cease to be"**
A sonnet in which Keats fears dying before his pen has "glean'd my teeming brain." He imagines "huge cloudy symbols of a high romance" that he may never "trace / Their shadows, with the magic hand of chance," and ends standing alone "on the shore / Of the wide world" until "love and fame to nothingness do sink."

**"Bright star, would I were stedfast as thou art"**
A sonnet associated with Keats's fiancée Fanny Brawne, in which the speaker wishes to lie on his love's breast, "Awake for ever in a sweet unrest." It gave its name to Jane Campion's 2009 film Bright Star about their romance.

**Hyperion**
Keats's unfinished epic about the overthrow of the Titans by the Olympians, in which the fallen Saturn appears and Hyperion asks whether he too will fall. It breaks off with the word "Celestial" as Apollo, gazing into the eyes of Mnemosyne, is transformed into a god. Keats later recast it as The Fall of Hyperion.

**Keats's letters: "negative capability" and the "vale of Soul-making"**
In an 1817 letter to his brothers, Keats defined "negative capability," the ability to remain in "uncertainties, Mysteries, doubts" without reaching after fact and reason, a quality he said Shakespeare possessed. Other letters compare life to a "Mansion of Many Apartments" and describe the world as "a vale of Soul-making," with the heart as "the Mind's Bible." Late fragments include "This living hand," which would "haunt thy days and chill thy dreaming nights," and the sonnet "On Sitting Down to Read King Lear Once Again," which asks for "new Phoenix wings."

**"The Red Wheelbarrow"**
Williams's most famous poem, a single sentence of 16 words split into four two-line stanzas of four words each: "so much depends / upon // a red wheel / barrow // glazed with rain / water // beside the white / chickens." It first appeared untitled as poem XXII in Spring and All and is a classic example of Imagism's focus on concrete objects.

**"This Is Just to Say"**
A 28-word poem written like a note left for his wife: "I have eaten / the plums / that were in / the icebox // and which / you were probably / saving / for breakfast // Forgive me / they were delicious / so sweet / and so cold." His wife Flossie wrote a joking "Reply" note, and Kenneth Koch parodied it in "Variations on a Theme by William Carlos Williams" ("I chopped down the house that you had been saving to live in next summer").

**Paterson**
Williams's five-book epic about Paterson, New Jersey, a city on the Passaic River, which he imagines as a sleeping giant: Paterson "lies on his right side, head near the thunder / of the waters filling his dreams!" (the Passaic Falls). Book One, "The Delineaments of Giants," contains his credo "Say it, no ideas but in things." Williams worked as a physician in nearby Rutherford, New Jersey, and was on staff at Passaic General Hospital.

**Spring and All**
Williams's 1923 collection mixing poems and prose, which includes "The Red Wheelbarrow," "To Elsie," and "The Rose" (whose petal's edge "cuts without cutting"). Its opening poem begins "By the road to the contagious hospital / under the surge of the blue / mottled clouds" and describes "patches of standing water / the scattering of tall trees." As "Lifeless in appearance, sluggish / dazed spring approaches," plants such as the "wildcarrot leaf" "enter the new world naked, / cold, uncertain of all," and finally "grip down and begin to awaken" with "the stark dignity of / entrance."

**"Danse Russe"**
A poem in which the speaker, while "my wife is sleeping / and the baby and Kathleen / are sleeping" and "the sun is a flame-white disc / in silken mists / above shining trees," dances "naked, grotesquely / before my mirror / waving my shirt round my head," singing "I am lonely." It ends "Who shall say I am not / the happy genius of my household?"

**"Asphodel, That Greeny Flower"**
A long late love poem to his wife Flossie, asking her forgiveness. It opens "Of asphodel, that greeny flower, / like a buttercup / upon its branching stem- / save that it's green and wooden," a flower said to grow in Hades. The speaker says "I come, my sweet, / to sing to you," notes that "All women are not Helen... / but have Helen in their hearts," and observes "It is difficult / to get the news from poems / yet men die miserably every day / for lack / of what is found there." It is written in his "triadic line" (variable foot), stepped tercets indented across the page.

**Pictures from Brueghel and Other Poems**
Williams's final collection (1962), which won the Pulitzer Prize after his death. Its title sequence has poems about paintings by the Flemish painter Pieter Brueghel the Elder, such as The Hunters in the Snow.

**"Landscape with the Fall of Icarus"**
A poem from Pictures from Brueghel about Brueghel's painting, in which a farmer keeps plowing while "unsignificantly / off the coast / there was / a splash quite unnoticed / this was / Icarus drowning."

**"The Dance"**
A poem describing Brueghel's painting The Kermess, in which "the dancers go round, they go round and / around," with "the squeal and the blare and the / tweedle of bagpipes" and peasants "kicking and rolling about." It begins and ends with the same line.

**"The Great Figure"**
A short poem in which the speaker, "Among the rain / and lights," sees "the figure 5 / in gold / on a red / firetruck" rushing "to gong clangs / siren howls / and wheels rumbling / through the dark city." It inspired Charles Demuth's painting I Saw the Figure 5 in Gold.

**"To Elsie"**
A poem from Spring and All that begins "The pure products of America / go crazy." It is about a troubled young woman working as a servant in the Williams household and the rural poverty she came from.

**"The Use of Force"**
A short story drawn from Williams's medical practice. A doctor examining a sick girl, Mathilda, must force open her mouth to check for diphtheria, and he is disturbed by the pleasure he takes in overpowering her resistance.

**White Mule**
Williams's 1937 novel, the first of a trilogy, about the immigrant Joe and Gurlie Stecher and their infant daughter Flossie in New York around 1900. The baby is said to kick like "white mule," a strong moonshine whiskey.

**"Portrait of a Lady"**
A love poem that opens "Your thighs are appletrees / whose blossoms touch the sky." The speaker keeps losing track of his images and asking himself, "Which sky?" and "Agh! what / sort of man was Fragonard?"

**"The Crowd at the Ball Game"**
A poem from Spring and All about a baseball crowd "moved uniformly / by a spirit of uselessness / which delights them." The crowd can turn menacing like a mob.

**The Awakening (Edna Pontellier)**
Chopin's 1899 novel, her most famous work, about Edna Pontellier, a wife and mother in Creole Louisiana who awakens to her own desires and rejects the roles of wife and mother. It was condemned on publication for its frank treatment of female independence and sexuality and is now considered an early feminist classic.

**Drowning in the Gulf of Mexico**
The ending of The Awakening. After Robert Lebrun leaves her with a farewell note ("Good-by—because I love you"), Edna returns to Grand Isle, swims naked out into the Gulf of Mexico, and drowns, thinking of her childhood and of Mademoiselle Reisz as she goes.

**Robert Lebrun and Alcée Arobin**
Edna's two romantic interests in The Awakening. She falls in love with the young Robert Lebrun while vacationing at Grand Isle, but he flees to Mexico and later leaves her again. While he is away, she has an affair with the seducer Alcée Arobin and moves out of her husband Léonce's house into a small "pigeon house."

**"The Story of an Hour" (Louise Mallard)**
Chopin's very short story in which Louise Mallard, who has heart trouble, learns from her sister Josephine that her husband Brently has died in a railroad accident. Alone in her room at an open window, she sees "a long procession of years to come that would belong to her absolutely" and whispers "Free! Body and soul free!"

**"The joy that kills"**
The ending of "The Story of an Hour." Louise descends the stairs "like a goddess of Victory," but Brently Mallard walks in alive, having been far from the accident, and she dies on the spot. The doctors ironically say she died of heart disease, "of the joy that kills."

**"Désirée's Baby" (Armand Aubigny)**
A Chopin story in which Désirée, a foundling adopted by the Valmondes, marries the plantation owner Armand Aubigny, who falls in love with her "as if struck by a pistol shot." When their baby turns out to have visibly African ancestry, Armand coldly rejects her, and she carries the baby off into the bayou and disappears among the reeds and willows.

**The burning of the cradle and the letter from Armand's mother**
The twist ending of "Désirée's Baby." Armand burns Désirée's belongings, including the willow cradle, in a bonfire, and then finds a letter from his own mother thanking God that Armand will never know that "his mother... belongs to the race that is cursed with the brand of slavery." He, not Désirée, had Black ancestry.

**Mademoiselle Reisz and Adèle Ratignolle**
Two contrasting women in The Awakening. The unpleasant, solitary pianist Mademoiselle Reisz, whose playing moves Edna to tears, represents the independent artist and encourages her rebellion. Adèle Ratignolle is the ideal "mother-woman," devoted to her husband and children, who reminds Edna of her duty to her family.

**The parrot ("Allez vous-en!")**
The Awakening opens with a caged parrot at Grand Isle shrieking "Allez vous-en! Allez vous-en! Sapristi!" ("Go away! Go away! For God's sake!") as Léonce Pontellier tries to read his newspaper. The caged bird symbolizes Edna's confinement.

**"The Storm" (Calixta and Alcée)**
A Chopin story in which Calixta's husband Bobinot and their four-year-old son Bibi buy a can of shrimp at the store and wait out a storm there. Meanwhile, her former lover Alcée takes shelter at her house; after lightning strikes a tree, he asks if she remembers their time at Assumption, and they make love. The story ends, "So the storm passed and every one was happy." It was not published in Chopin's lifetime.

**"A Pair of Silk Stockings" (Mrs. Sommers)**
A Chopin story in which the poor mother Mrs. Sommers unexpectedly gets fifteen dollars, plans to spend it on her children, but instead buys herself silk stockings, gloves, magazines, a fine lunch, and a theater ticket. On the cable car home she wishes it would "go on and on with her forever," as a "man with keen eyes" studies her.

**Grand Isle**
The Louisiana resort island where the first part of The Awakening takes place. There Edna learns to swim, falls for Robert Lebrun, and meets characters such as the lady in black and the twins in blue. She returns there to drown herself at the end.

**At Fault**
Chopin's first novel (1890), about the widowed Louisiana landowner Thérèse Lafirme. She loves David Hosmer but persuades him to remarry his alcoholic ex-wife Fanny because she believes divorce is wrong.

**Bayou Folk and "Lilacs"**
Bayou Folk (1894) is a collection of Chopin's Louisiana local-color stories, including "Désirée's Baby." Her story "Lilacs" concerns Adrienne, a Parisian singer who yearly visits a convent and drops lilacs at its portico; when she is finally barred from it, the flowers are swept away.

**Katherine O'Flaherty (Creole Louisiana local color)**
Kate Chopin was born Katherine O'Flaherty in St. Louis and lived in Louisiana after marrying Oscar Chopin. Her fiction depicts Creole and Cajun society in New Orleans, Grand Isle, and the Natchitoches area.

**Tom Robinson's trial for the rape of Mayella Ewell**
The novel centers on this trial. Tom Robinson, a Black man, is falsely accused of raping Mayella Ewell, a poor white woman. Her father Bob Ewell backs the accusation, and an all-white jury convicts Tom even though the evidence shows he is innocent. After the trial Bob Ewell spits in Atticus's face, and Tom is later shot 17 times while trying to escape from prison.

**Atticus Finch, lawyer in Maycomb, Alabama**
Atticus is the widowed lawyer who defends Tom Robinson. He is the father of the narrator, Jean Louise "Scout" Finch, and her older brother Jem. The book is set in the 1930s in the fictional town of Maycomb, Alabama. An earlier draft of the novel was published in 2015 as *Go Set a Watchman*.

**Boo Radley**
Arthur "Boo" Radley is the Finches' reclusive neighbor. Town rumor says he once stabbed his father with a pair of scissors. Scout, Jem and their summer friend Dill are obsessed with him and try to lure him out, for example by trying to leave a note on his windowsill with a fishing pole. At the end he turns out to be the children's quiet protector.

**Scout's ham costume and Bob Ewell's attack after the Halloween pageant**
At a school Halloween pageant about Maycomb County, Scout plays a ham. She misses her cue to come on stage, and on the walk home the costume keeps her from running when Bob Ewell attacks her and Jem in revenge for the trial. Jem's arm is broken, which explains the crooked arm mentioned in the novel's first line. Boo Radley kills Ewell and carries Jem home. Earlier that night, classmate Cecil Jacobs jumps out and scares the children on their way to the pageant.

**Mrs. Dubose and her camellias**
Mrs. Dubose is a cranky, racist old woman who lives near the Finches. After she insults Atticus, Jem cuts the tops off her camellia bushes. As punishment he has to read to her every afternoon until she dies. Atticus later explains that she was fighting her morphine addiction, and he calls her the bravest person he knew.

**"One-Shot Finch" and the rabid dog Tim Johnson**
A neighbor's dog, Tim Johnson, goes mad with rabies and wanders down the street. The maid Calpurnia warns the neighbors. Sheriff Heck Tate hands his rifle to Atticus, who kills the dog with one shot. Miss Maudie then tells the surprised children that their father was once known as "One-Shot Finch," the best shot in the county.

**The lynch mob at the jail and Mr. Cunningham**
The night before the trial, Atticus guards Tom at the Maycomb jail, and a mob led by Mr. Cunningham comes for Tom. Scout, Jem and Dill have sneaked out to watch. Scout innocently chats with Mr. Cunningham about his entailment, his son Walter, and how he paid Atticus for legal work with hickory nuts and firewood. Embarrassed, he breaks up the mob.

**Tom Robinson's useless left arm and the chiffarobe**
Tom's left arm was crippled in a cotton gin accident when he was a boy. Mayella's bruises are on the right side of her face, which means a left-handed person hit her, and Atticus shows that Bob Ewell is left-handed. Tom says Mayella asked him to bust up an old chiffarobe (a wardrobe-dresser) and then tried to kiss him. The prosecutor mocks him by asking if he is good at "busting up chiffarobes" with one hand.

**Gifts in the tree knothole**
Scout and Jem find small gifts in the knothole of an oak tree by the Radley house. They include chewing gum, Indian-head pennies, twine, soap carvings of the two children, a spelling medal and a pocket watch. The children realize the gifts come from Boo, but his brother Nathan fills the hole with cement.

**Dolphus Raymond's Coca-Cola in a paper sack**
Dolphus Raymond is a wealthy white man who lives with a Black woman and has mixed-race children. He drinks Coca-Cola out of a paper sack so the town thinks he is a drunk, which gives people an excuse for how he lives. During the trial he gives the upset Dill a sip.

**Walter Cunningham and the molasses**
On Scout's first day of school, she tries to explain the poor Cunningham family to her new teacher, Miss Caroline Fisher, and gets her hand slapped with a ruler. Later, when Walter Cunningham comes home with the Finches for dinner, he pours molasses all over his food. Scout makes a rude comment, and Calpurnia scolds her for being bad-mannered to a guest.

**Miss Maudie's house fire and the blanket**
One winter night, the house of the Finches' neighbor Miss Maudie Atkinson burns down. While Scout stands outside watching, someone puts a blanket around her shoulders without her noticing. The family later realizes it was Boo Radley.

**Heck Tate's cover-up and "a sin to kill a mockingbird"**
After Bob Ewell's body is found with a knife in his ribs, Sheriff Heck Tate insists that Ewell "fell on his knife" so that the shy Boo will not be put in the public eye. Scout agrees, saying that exposing Boo would be like shooting a mockingbird. This connects to the title: Atticus calls killing mockingbirds a sin, and Miss Maudie explains that they "don't do one thing but sing their hearts out."

**Calpurnia and First Purchase church**
Calpurnia, the Finches' Black cook, takes Scout and Jem to her church, First Purchase African M.E. Church. It got its name because freed slaves paid for it with their first earnings. Since few members can read, Calpurnia's son Zeebo, the town garbage collector, leads the hymns by reading out each line first.

**The "colored" balcony and Reverend Sykes**
At the crowded trial, Reverend Sykes of First Purchase saves seats for Scout, Jem and Dill in the courthouse's segregated "colored" balcony. They watch Atticus's defense of Tom from there. Calpurnia later finds them there, which upsets her.

**Tartuffe**
Molière's most famous play (1664), about a falsely pious religious hypocrite and "impostor" who worms his way into the household of the wealthy, gullible Orgon. It is the near-universal giveaway for Molière, and it was banned for years after protests from religious authorities.

**Orgon hides under a table while Elmire is seduced**
The most famous scene of Tartuffe. Orgon's wife Elmire persuades her skeptical husband to hide under a cloth-covered table so he can witness Tartuffe making advances on her, finally proving the man's hypocrisy.

**Louis XIV's intervention and Tartuffe's arrest**
Tartuffe ends with a deus ex machina: after Tartuffe has gained the deed to Orgon's house and a strongbox of incriminating letters belonging to Orgon's friend, an officer sent by King Louis XIV, Molière's patron, arrests Tartuffe and restores the family's property.

**Damis, Mariane, Valère, and Madame Pernelle**
Members of Orgon's family in Tartuffe. Damis, Orgon's son, reports Tartuffe's attempted seduction but is disbelieved, banished, and disinherited in Tartuffe's favor. Orgon tries to marry his daughter Mariane to Tartuffe, though she loves Valère, whom she marries at the end. Orgon's mother Madame Pernelle is as fooled by Tartuffe as he is, while Orgon's brother-in-law Cléante serves as the voice of reason.

**Monsieur Loyal and Panulphe**
Monsieur Loyal is the bailiff who arrives to evict Orgon's family, and he is mocked for his ironic name. Panulphe was the title character's name in the revised 1667 version of Tartuffe (titled The Impostor), which was also banned, with threats of excommunication for anyone who saw or read it.

**The Misanthrope**
Molière's 1666 comedy about Alceste, a brutally honest man who despises the flattery and hypocrisy of society. His reasonable friend Philinte argues for tact, and the play is often called Molière's masterpiece.

**Oronte's sonnet**
In The Misanthrope, the fop Oronte asks Alceste's opinion of a sonnet he has written. Alceste mocks it as terrible, and Oronte sues him over the insult, bringing Alceste before a tribunal.

**Célimène**
The witty, flirtatious young widow loved by Alceste in The Misanthrope. She is courted by several suitors, including Oronte, Acaste, and Clitandre, and is exposed when her letters mocking each of them are read aloud. When she refuses to follow Alceste into isolation, he leaves society to live as a hermit.

**The Imaginary Invalid and Molière's death**
Molière's final play (1673) is about the hypochondriac Argan. Molière collapsed while playing Argan during its fourth performance and died a few hours later, an often-cited irony.

**Argan, Toinette, and Thomas Diafoirus**
In The Imaginary Invalid, Argan wants his daughter Angélique to marry the foolish doctor-to-be Thomas Diafoirus so he can get free medical care, though she loves Cléante. The maid Toinette disguises herself as a doctor (advising Argan to cut off an arm and poke out an eye) and has Argan pretend to be dead, revealing that his second wife Béline only wants his money while Angélique truly loves him. The play ends with Argan himself becoming a doctor in a ceremony in mock Latin.

**The School for Wives**
Molière's 1662 comedy in which the middle-aged Arnolphe raises his ward Agnès in ignorance (she asks if babies come from the ear) so that she will be an obedient wife. His plans fail when she falls for the young Horace and marries him. Molière defended the play in The Critique of The School for Wives, and William Wycherley drew on it for The Country Wife.

**The Bourgeois Gentleman**
Molière's 1670 comedy-ballet about Monsieur Jourdain, the social-climbing son of a cloth merchant who hires tutors in music, dancing, fencing, and philosophy. He is famously delighted to learn he has been speaking prose all his life, and he is tricked into a fake Turkish ceremony while his daughter Lucile marries Cléonte, who is disguised as the son of the Sultan of Turkey.

**The Miser**
Molière's 1668 comedy about the stingy Harpagon. His son Cléante competes with him for Mariane, and Cléante's valet La Flèche steals a box of money Harpagon has buried in his garden. The play ends when Anselme reveals that he is Don Thomas d'Alburcy and the long-lost father of Mariane and Valère, who survived a shipwreck.

**The Doctor in Spite of Himself and Sganarelle**
In this 1666 farce, Martine gets revenge on her drunken woodcutter husband Sganarelle by telling a rich man's servants that he is a brilliant doctor who will only admit it if beaten. Sganarelle is a recurring Molière character who also appears as Don Juan's servant in Molière's Dom Juan.

**The Affected Young Ladies and Amphitryon**
The Affected Young Ladies (Les Précieuses ridicules) satirizes the pretentious cousins Magdelon and Cathos, daughter and niece of Gorgibus, who reject their suitors, including La Grange. Molière's adaptation of Plautus's Amphitryon gave French the word "sosie" (look-alike), from the servant Sosie.

**"Harlem" ("What happens to a dream deferred?")**
Hughes's short 1951 poem, also called "Dream Deferred," from the collection Montage of a Dream Deferred. It asks whether a deferred dream will "dry up / like a raisin in the sun," "fester like a sore," "stink like rotten meat," or "crust and sugar over— / like a syrupy sweet," suggests "maybe it just sags / like a heavy load," and ends with the italicized question "Or does it explode?"

**A Raisin in the Sun**
Lorraine Hansberry's 1959 play takes its title from the line "like a raisin in the sun" in "Harlem," and the poem serves as its epigraph. It is a common way to link Hughes to other authors.

**"The Weary Blues"**
The title poem of Hughes's first collection (1926). The speaker hears a Black musician playing a "drowsy syncopated tune" "down on Lenox Avenue the other night" "by the pale dull pallor of an old gas light," swaying "on his rickety stool" with "ebony hands on each ivory key," his foot going "thump, thump, thump." The poem ends as "the stars went out and so did the moon" and the singer "slept like a rock or a man that's dead."

**"The Negro Speaks of Rivers"**
Hughes's early poem, written as a teenager, in which the speaker says, "I've known rivers ancient as the world and older than the flow of human blood in human veins." He "bathed in the Euphrates when dawns were young," built his hut near the Congo, which "lulled me to sleep," raised the pyramids above the Nile, and heard the singing of the Mississippi, seeing "its muddy bosom turn all golden in the sunset." Its refrain is "My soul has grown deep like the rivers."

**"I, Too"**
A poem in which the speaker declares, "I, too, sing America. / I am the darker brother. / They send me to eat in the kitchen / When company comes." He predicts that "tomorrow, / I'll be at the table," and that "they'll see how beautiful I am / And be ashamed," ending, "I, too, am America." It responds to Walt Whitman's "I Hear America Singing."

**"Theme for English B"**
A poem framed as an assignment from a college instructor who tells the class, "Go home and write a page tonight. / And let that page come out of you." The speaker, the only Black student in his class, writes that he likes "to eat, sleep, drink, and be in love," "to work, read, learn, and understand life," and wants "a pipe for a Christmas present, / or records—Bessie, bop, or Bach." He tells the white instructor, "As I learn from you, / I guess you learn from me."

**"Mother to Son"**
A dramatic monologue in which a mother tells her son, "Life for me ain't been no crystal stair." Her staircase has had "tacks in it, / And splinters, / And boards torn up, / And places with no carpet on the floor," but she has kept "climbin' on," and she urges him not to turn back.

**Montage of a Dream Deferred and "Dream Boogie"**
Hughes's 1951 book-length poem sequence about Harlem, structured like bebop jazz, which contains "Harlem." It opens with "Dream Boogie," which begins "Good morning, daddy! / Ain't you heard / The boogie-woogie rumble / Of a dream deferred?" and is interrupted by an italic voice asking, "You think / It's a happy beat?"

**"Let America Be America Again"**
A 1935 poem in which the speaker longs for America to "be the dream it used to be," while a parenthetical voice interjects, "America never was America to me." The speaker identifies himself as the poor white, the Negro, the Native American, and the immigrant, saying "I am the man who sailed those early seas," and answers the question of who he is with phrases like "the worker sold to the machine." It ends with the call to "make America again!"

**"Dreams" ("Hold fast to dreams")**
A short poem urging the reader to "hold fast to dreams," for "if dreams die / Life is a broken-winged bird / That cannot fly," and "when dreams go / Life is a barren field / Frozen with snow." Dreams are one of Hughes's central themes, also appearing in "As I Grew Older," which begins "It was a long time ago. / I have almost forgotten my dream" and describes a wall rising "between me and my dream."

**"Ballad of the Landlord"**
A poem in which a tenant complains to his landlord about a leaking roof and broken steps and refuses to pay rent. When he threatens the landlord, the landlord shouts "Police! Police! / Come and get this man! / He's trying to ruin the government / And overturn the land!" and the tenant is jailed, ending in newspaper-style headlines.

**Lenox Avenue and the Harlem Renaissance**
Hughes was a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance, the 1920s flowering of African American art centered in Harlem, New York. His poetry draws on blues and jazz rhythms and is often set on Harlem's Lenox Avenue.

**The Big Sea ("Beyond Sandy Hook")**
Hughes's 1940 autobiography. Its opening chapter, "Beyond Sandy Hook," describes him throwing his books into the sea as he sailed to Africa as a ship's crewman. He also recounts being "discovered" by the poet Vachel Lindsay after leaving poems by Lindsay's plate while working as a busboy at a Washington, D.C., hotel.

**Fine Clothes to the Jew and other poems ("Life Is Fine," "Tired," "Note on Commercial Theatre")**
Fine Clothes to the Jew (1927) is Hughes's second poetry collection, which draws on the blues. In "Life Is Fine," a man fails to drown himself and later "took the elevator / Sixteen floors above the ground" but doesn't jump, concluding "Life is fine! / Fine as wine!" "Tired" imagines taking "a knife / And cut[ting] the world in two," and "Note on Commercial Theatre" complains that white artists have taken Black culture, putting it "in Macbeth and Carmen Jones" and "everything but what's about me." Other clued poems include "Freedom" ("I cannot live on tomorrow's bread"), "One-Way Ticket," "Harlem Night Club," and "April Rain Song."

**Mule Bone (with Zora Neale Hurston)**
A 1930 comic play that Hughes co-wrote with Zora Neale Hurston, based on her folktale "The Bone of Contention." A dispute over its authorship ended their friendship, and the play was not staged until 1991.

**Grendel**
The man-eating monster, a "God-cursed" descendant of Cain, who is enraged by the singing and feasting in Hrothgar's hall and raids it for twelve years, killing many warriors. Beowulf fights him barehanded, with the grip of thirty men in each hand, and tears off his arm. Grendel flees to die in his lair, and the arm is hung up in the hall as a trophy.

**Heorot and King Hrothgar**
Heorot is the great mead-hall built by Hrothgar, king of the Danes. Beowulf, a Geatish warrior and the son of Ecgtheow, sails to Denmark to rid it of Grendel, partly to repay Hrothgar for once settling a feud his father started by killing Heatholaf of the Wulfings.

**Wiglaf and the dragon**
In the poem's third fight, fifty years later, Beowulf has become king of the Geats. A thief steals a jeweled cup from a dragon's hoard in a barrow, and the enraged dragon burns Geatland. When Beowulf fights it, all his men flee except the young Wiglaf, who helps him kill the dragon. The dying Beowulf gives Wiglaf his golden collar and armor and names him his successor.

**Grendel's mother and the mere**
The "monstrous hell-bride" who attacks Heorot to avenge her son, carrying off Hrothgar's trusted counselor Aeschere and beheading him. Beowulf dives into her haunted lake, where fire burns on the water at night, and fights her in an underwater cave. When his borrowed sword fails, he kills her with a giant sword "from the days of the giants" found in her lair. Its blade melts in her blood, leaving only the hilt, which is engraved with the story of the flood that destroyed the race of giants.

**Hrunting and Unferth**
Unferth, a Danish warrior at Hrothgar's court said to have killed his own brothers, first taunts Beowulf at a feast. He later lends Beowulf his famous sword Hrunting for the fight with Grendel's mother, but the "unbeatable" blade fails to wound her. Some scholars suspect Unferth gave Beowulf a useless weapon on purpose.

**The swimming contest with Breca**
At the welcoming feast, Unferth mocks Beowulf for losing a seven-day swimming match at sea against his boyhood friend Breca. Beowulf replies that sea monsters dragged him under, that he killed them, and that he washed ashore in the land of the Finns.

**"Hwæt!"**
The poem's famously hard-to-translate first word, an exclamation calling for attention, usually rendered "Listen!" or "Lo!" Seamus Heaney's acclaimed 1999 translation renders it "So.", J.R.R. Tolkien's translation uses "Lo!", and Maria Dahvana Headley's 2020 feminist translation opens with "Bro!"

**"Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics"**
J.R.R. Tolkien's influential 1936 lecture, which argued that critics should read Beowulf as a work of art rather than mainly as a historical document. Tolkien defended the monsters as central to the poem and described its theme as man at war with a hostile world and his inevitable overthrow in Time.

**Beowulf's funeral**
After his death, the Geats burn Beowulf on a pyre while a Geatish woman sings a lament, and "Heaven swallowed the smoke." They spend ten days building a barrow on a headland, visible to sailors, and bury the dragon's treasure with him. The poem ends by praising him as "kindest to his people and keenest to win fame."

**Shield Sheafson's ship burial**
The poem opens with the founder of the Danish royal line, Shield Sheafson (Scyld Scefing), a foundling who became a great king. At his death he is set adrift on a ship laden with treasure. The narrator remarks, "Behavior that's admired is the path to power among people everywhere."

**Queen Wealhtheow**
Hrothgar's queen, who welcomes Beowulf and passes the mead cup among the warriors at the feasts in Heorot. She is often discussed as a "peace-weaver," the Anglo-Saxon role of a noblewoman who binds peoples together through marriage and courtesy.

**The Finnsburg episode**
A story sung by Hrothgar's poet at the feast celebrating Grendel's death. Hildeburh, a Danish princess married to the Frisian king Finn, loses her brother Hnaef and her son, who fought on opposite sides, and has their bodies burned on the same pyre. The Danes under Hengest later take revenge by killing Finn.

**John Gardner's Grendel**
A 1971 novel that retells the story from the monster's point of view, with Grendel as a lonely, philosophical narrator. Grendel is fascinated by the Shaper, Hrothgar's court poet, whose songs glorify the Danes' bloody history.

**Queen Modthryth**
A queen mentioned in a digression as a foil to Hygd, the gracious young wife of the Geatish king Hygelac. Modthryth had any man who dared look at her put to death for "fancied insults," but became a gracious queen after marrying King Offa.

**The Nowell Codex**
The single surviving manuscript of Beowulf, written around the year 1000 and now catalogued as Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv in the British Library. It was damaged in a 1731 fire. Scholars debate how far the Christian elements in the poem were added to an older pagan story.

**Catch-22 paradox and Doc Daneeka**
The title rule, explained to Yossarian by the flight surgeon Doc Daneeka: a pilot who is crazy can be grounded, but he has to ask, and anyone who asks to stop flying combat missions is showing a rational concern for his own safety and so is sane. Yossarian lets out a "respectful whistle" at its "absolute simplicity," and later the catch is described as a law that nobody is allowed to read. The phrase has entered English as a name for any no-win situation built on circular logic.

**Milo Minderbinder and M&M Enterprises**
Milo is the squadron's mess officer, who turns his job into a huge black-market syndicate called M&M Enterprises. He adds an ampersand and a second "M" to make his one-man company look like a partnership, and he insists that "everybody has a share." He later becomes the Vice-Shah of Oran, Imam of Damascus, and Caliph of Baghdad, and he is court-martialed after he takes a German contract to bomb his own squadron's base on Pianosa.

**Eggs bought for seven cents and sold for five**
Milo's most famous scheme. He buys eggs in Malta for seven cents each and sells them to the mess halls for five cents each, yet still makes a profit through a circular series of sales between his own syndicate and the military.

**Chocolate-covered Egyptian cotton**
After M&M Enterprises buys up the world's entire supply of Egyptian cotton and cannot sell it, Milo dips the cotton in chocolate and tries to serve it to the men in the mess hall as candy (a joke on "cotton candy").

**Major Major Major Major**
An officer whose father named him Major Major Major as a joke, and whom an IBM machine "with a sense of humor" then promotes to the rank of major. He is said to look like Henry Fonda. A shy man, he jumps out of his office window to avoid talking to people and only sees visitors when he is not there. He is beaten up while wearing a disguise during a basketball game.

**Snowden ("I'm cold")**
A young gunner hit by flak during a mission over Avignon. Yossarian treats an obvious wound in his thigh, then finds that his guts are spilling out under his flak suit, and Snowden keeps saying "I'm cold" while Yossarian answers "There, there." From this Yossarian concludes that "the spirit gone, man is garbage." He also asks, "Where are the Snowdens of yesteryear?" (a play on Villon's "Where are the snows of yesteryear?").

**Yossarian naked in a tree**
After Snowden's death, Yossarian refuses to wear clothes because Snowden's blood had soaked his uniform. He sits naked in a tree during Snowden's funeral and later receives a medal while naked in formation.

**"Washington Irving" and the chaplain**
While in the hospital, Yossarian censors enlisted men's letters at random and signs some of them "Washington Irving" (or "Irving Washington"). C.I.D. (Criminal Investigation Division) men come to investigate, and the suspicion falls on Chaplain Tappman, an Anabaptist, who is then interrogated. The novel's opening line, "It was love at first sight," describes Yossarian's first meeting with the chaplain, and Yossarian is in the hospital with a "pain in his liver that fell just short of being jaundice."

**Nately's whore**
The Roman prostitute who is loved by the young, idealistic pilot Nately. When Nately is killed, she blames Yossarian and keeps trying to kill him. In the chapter titled "Catch-22," she stabs him with a bone-handled kitchen knife just after he accepts Colonels Cathcart and Korn's deal.

**Colonel Cathcart and the rising mission count**
The group commander, who keeps raising the number of missions his men must fly before they can be sent home, hoping it will get him promoted to general and get his picture in The Saturday Evening Post. Near the end he and Colonel Korn offer Yossarian an "odious" deal: he can go home if he agrees to praise them.

**Orr and the escape to Sweden**
Yossarian's tent-mate, a tinkerer who stuffs crab apples or horse chestnuts in his cheeks and says crab apples are better because of their shape. He keeps crash-landing his plane in the sea, which turns out to be practice. At the end of the novel Yossarian learns that Orr has rowed to neutral Sweden, and Yossarian deserts to follow him.

**Kid Sampson and McWatt**
McWatt, a cheerful pilot who likes to buzz the beach with his plane, flies too low and his propeller cuts Kid Sampson in half. Overcome with guilt, McWatt then flies his plane into a mountain and kills himself.

**Doc Daneeka declared dead**
Doc Daneeka has his name put on McWatt's flight log to collect flight pay without flying, so he is officially listed as dead when McWatt crashes. His wife receives a form letter about the death of "your husband, son, father or brother," collects the insurance and pension money, and moves to Lansing, Michigan, while the living doctor is ignored by everyone.

**Pianosa and the Great Big Siege of Bologna**
The novel is set at an American bomber base on the small Mediterranean island of Pianosa, off Italy. Before a feared raid on Bologna, Yossarian secretly moves the string on the map that marks the front line so that the city seems to have been captured, which gets the mission called off for a while.

**Hungry Joe and Chief White Halfoat**
Hungry Joe is a pilot who claims to have been a Life magazine photographer and keeps trying to photograph naked women; he has screaming nightmares whenever he is not flying missions. Chief White Halfoat, a Native American who shares a tent with Doc Daneeka, says his family was a "human divining rod" because oil companies kept finding oil wherever they settled and forcing them to move, and he predicts he will die of pneumonia.

**Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984) and Winston Smith**
Orwell's 1949 dystopian novel (Orwell was the pen name of Eric Arthur Blair). It is set in Oceania, ruled by the Party under the ideology Ingsoc (English Socialism) and the all-seeing Big Brother. Winston Smith rewrites history at the Ministry of Truth (Minitrue). He begins an illicit affair with Julia, who outwardly belongs to the Junior Anti-Sex League. The Party's slogans are "War is Peace, Freedom is Slavery, Ignorance is Strength."

**Newspeak and Syme**
The Party's artificial language, built to make dissent unthinkable by shrinking vocabulary. Its words include "doublethink," "thoughtcrime" (crimethink), "unperson," "doubleplusgood," "Miniplenty," and "thinkpol" (Thought Police). The lexicographer Syme works on the eleventh edition of the Newspeak dictionary and is "vaporized" for understanding things too clearly.

**Room 101, O'Brien, and "Do it to Julia!"**
O'Brien, an Inner Party member who pretends to belong to the resistance, betrays Winston and tortures him in the Ministry of Love. Mr. Charrington, the junk-shop owner who rents Winston and Julia a room, turns out to be a Thought Police agent. In Room 101, faced with a cage of rats strapped to his face, Winston breaks and screams, "Do it to Julia!" In prison he meets the poet Ampleforth, jailed for leaving the word "God" in a Kipling poem because there are only twelve rhymes for "rod."

**Emmanuel Goldstein, "the Book," and the Two Minutes Hate**
Goldstein is the Party's arch-enemy, who may not exist, and he is the target of the daily Two Minutes Hate. He is the supposed author of "the Book," The Theory and Practice of Oligarchical Collectivism. The Book describes the endless war among Oceania, Eurasia, and Eastasia over a disputed quadrilateral with corners at Tangier, Brazzaville, Darwin, and Hong Kong.

**Animal Farm: Napoleon and Snowball**
Orwell's 1945 allegorical novella of the Russian Revolution. Inspired by old Major and the song "Beasts of England," the animals of Manor Farm overthrow the farmer Mr. Jones. The pig Napoleon (Stalin) drives out his rival Snowball (Trotsky) and becomes a tyrant. The farm's Hoof and Horn flag is later replaced with a plain green flag.

**Boxer**
The loyal, hardworking cart horse of Animal Farm, whose mottoes are "I will work harder" and "Napoleon is always right." When he collapses, the pigs claim to send him to a veterinarian, but he is actually sold to the knacker (glue maker), and Napoleon uses the money to buy whisky for the pigs.

**"All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others"**
The pigs gradually rewrite the Seven Commandments to justify their privileges, for example forbidding drinking alcohol only "to excess" and sleeping in beds only "with sheets." Finally only this single maxim remains. The novella ends with a card game in which Napoleon and Mr. Pilkington both play an ace of spades, and the animals can no longer tell pigs from men.

**Moses, Mr. Frederick, and Mr. Pilkington**
Moses the tame raven tells the animals about Sugarcandy Mountain, an animal heaven where it is Sunday seven days a week. Animal Farm lies between two neighboring farms: Foxwood, owned by Mr. Pilkington, and Pinchfield, owned by Mr. Frederick, who attacks the farm and blows up the windmill with dynamite.

**"Politics and the English Language"**
Orwell's 1946 essay arguing that vague, bloated prose hides political truth and serves authoritarian regimes. It attacks "dying metaphors," "verbal false limbs," "pretentious diction," and "meaningless words," and it ends with six rules, such as "Never use a long word where a short one will do." It parodies Ecclesiastes ("the race is not to the swift") as "objective considerations of contemporary phenomena compel the conclusion that success or failure in competitive activities exhibits no tendency to be commensurate with innate capacity." It also compares insincerity to a cuttlefish spurting out ink.

**"Shooting an Elephant"**
An essay drawn from Orwell's years as a colonial police officer in Burma. In Moulmein, an elephant in "must" (a frenzied state) kills a coolie. Although the danger has passed, the narrator shoots it in front of a large Burmese crowd "solely to avoid looking a fool." He reflects that "when the white man turns tyrant it is his own freedom that he destroys."

**Other essays**
"A Hanging" describes a condemned Burmese prisoner stepping around a puddle on the way to the gallows. "Why I Write" lists four great motives, including "sheer egoism" and "aesthetic enthusiasm." "Inside the Whale" reviews Henry Miller's Tropic of Cancer through the story of Jonah and attacks W. H. Auden's phrase "the necessary murder." Others include "Decline of the English Murder" (the Cleft Chin Murder versus Jack the Ripper), "The Lion and the Unicorn," an essay calling Kipling a "good bad poet," and his "As I Please" columns for the Tribune.

**Homage to Catalonia and The Road to Wigan Pier**
Homage to Catalonia (1938) recounts Orwell's service in the POUM militia during the Spanish Civil War, alongside commander Georges Kopp, and his disillusionment with the Stalinist communists. The Road to Wigan Pier (1937) is a two-part book: a study of the poverty of the working class in northern England (including the Brooker family's lodging house) and an essay on why socialism was not more popular.

**Burmese Days**
Orwell's first novel, published first in the United States in 1934, about the timber merchant John Flory in colonial Burma. It opens with the corrupt magistrate U Po Kyin plotting to ruin the reputation of Flory's friend Dr. Veraswami.

**Keep the Aspidistra Flying and A Clergyman's Daughter**
In Keep the Aspidistra Flying (1936), the poet Gordon Comstock "declares war" on money and quits his copywriting job at the New Albion advertising agency. He struggles with his unfinished poem London Pleasures, gets help from the publisher Ravelston, and finally settles down and buys an aspidistra, the symbol of middle-class respectability. In A Clergyman's Daughter (1935), Dorothy Hare loses her memory, sleeps rough in Trafalgar Square, and becomes a schoolteacher.

**"You who hear the sound, in scattered rhymes" / Il Canzoniere**
This line opens Petrarch's collection of 366 Italian vernacular poems, mostly sonnets. Its Latin title is *Rerum vulgarium fragmenta*, and it is also known as *Rime sparse* ("scattered rhymes") or *Il Canzoniere* ("The Songbook"). It became the model for European love poetry for centuries.

**Laura, met on Good Friday in Avignon**
Laura is the woman to whom Petrarch addressed most of the Canzoniere. He first saw her on Good Friday, April 6, 1327, at the church of Sainte-Claire in Avignon. She was already married and never returned his love. She is often identified as Laura de Noves, wife of Count Hugues de Sade.

**Petrarchan sonnet (octave + sestet)**
This fourteen-line form is named for Petrarch. It divides into an eight-line octave, usually rhymed ABBAABBA, which poses a problem or emotion. A six-line sestet follows, turning or resolving it, after a shift called the *volta*. It is also called the Italian sonnet, in contrast to the Shakespearean sonnet with its final couplet.

**Africa (epic on Scipio Africanus)**
Petrarch's unfinished Latin epic in hexameters covers the Second Punic War. It centers on Scipio Africanus's defeat of Hannibal at the Battle of Zama. It opens with "Scipio's Dream" and includes episodes such as Syphax's palace, the death of Sophonisba, and the dying lament of Hannibal's brother Mago. Petrarch was crowned poet laureate partly on the strength of this work.

**"The Ascent of Mont Ventoux"**
This letter, collected in the *Epistolae Familiares*, describes Petrarch's climb of a mountain in Provence with his brother Gherardo, ignoring an old shepherd's warnings. At the summit he opens Augustine's *Confessions* at random and rebukes himself for "admiring earthly things," since "nothing is wonderful but the soul." He claims to be the first person since antiquity to climb a mountain just for the view. The letter is addressed to Dionigi da Borgo San Sepolcro, later Bishop of Monopoli.

**Triumphs (Trionfi)**
This allegorical vernacular poem presents a dream vision of six successive triumphal processions, in which each figure conquers the one before. The order is Love, Chastity, Death, Fame, Time, and Eternity. The vision begins in Valchiusa (Vaucluse), where the sleeping poet sees Love pass in a chariot. Chastity, led by Laura with virtuous women such as Lucretia and Penelope, binds Love to a column. In the Triumph of Death, Death plucks a golden hair from Laura's head.

**Secretum (My Secret Book)**
This Latin dialogue between Petrarch and Saint Augustine is witnessed by the silent personification Lady Truth. Augustine criticizes Petrarch's love for Laura and his pursuit of fame. He says that accidie (spiritual listlessness) binds Petrarch's will in "adamantine chains." The work was not meant for publication during Petrarch's lifetime.

**On Illustrious Men (De viris illustribus)**
This is Petrarch's unfinished Latin collection of biographies, modeled on Plutarch's *Parallel Lives*. It profiles mainly Roman heroes, along with biblical and mythical figures such as Romulus and Hercules. Many of the same figures appear in *Africa*.

**"The world's delight is a brief dream"**
This line closes the opening sonnet of the Canzoniere. In that poem Petrarch recalls "those sighs on which I fed my heart" during his "first youthful error." He admits he has become "an old tale" among the people, so that "shame is the fruit of my vanities." He also hopes to find "pity, and forgiveness" for all the ways he talks and weeps.

**"The sun's ray was darkened in pity for its Maker"**
This line comes from Canzoniere Sonnet 3, which recounts falling in love with Laura on Good Friday. The sun dimmed in mourning for Christ's crucifixion. On that day Love found the poet "weaponless" and captured him through Laura's "lovely eyes."

**Letter to Posterity**
This autobiographical letter by Petrarch concludes his late letter collection, the *Seniles*. Petrarch's letter collections (*Familiares* and *Seniles*) were inspired by his 1345 discovery of Cicero's letters to Atticus in Verona. He dedicated the *Familiares* to his friend "Socrates" (Ludwig van Kempen).

**Thomas Wyatt and the Earl of Surrey translations**
These Tudor poets brought the Petrarchan sonnet to England. Wyatt's "Whoso List to Hunt" adapts Petrarch's sonnet of a white deer whose collar reads "Noli me tangere" ("touch me not"). Surrey translated a line as "Love that doth reign and live within my thought."

**"In Life" and "In Death" / Prayer to the Virgin**
The Canzoniere is divided into two parts: poems written during Laura's life and poems after her death in the plague of 1348. The collection ends with a canzone, "Prayer to the Virgin." In it Petrarch asks to "die in peaceful harbor" and to let his "vanishing, at least, be virtuous."

**"Golden hair scattered in the breeze"**
This image comes from the sonnet "Erano i capei d'oro a l'aura sparsi." In it Laura's gold hair is twined by the wind "in a thousand sweet knots." The phrase "l'aura" ("the breeze") is a pun on Laura's name, a wordplay Petrarch uses throughout the collection.

**Coronation Oration**
Petrarch delivered this speech on Rome's Capitoline Hill in 1341, when he was crowned poet laureate. It was the first such coronation since antiquity. Petrarch is also credited with coining the concept of the "Dark Ages" for the period after Rome's fall.

**Willy Loman's suicide by car crash for life insurance**
Willy Loman, an aging, failing traveling salesman, deliberately crashes his car offstage so his family can collect a $20,000 life insurance policy. He hopes the money will let his son Biff succeed. Earlier he tells his neighbor Charley that he is "worth more dead than alive."

**"The Woman" in Boston and the silk stockings**
In a flashback, teenage Biff goes to Willy's Boston hotel and finds him with a mistress known only as "The Woman." Willy had given her new silk stockings while his wife Linda mends her old ones, and he grows angry whenever he sees Linda mending. Willy pleads "She's nothing to me... I was lonely," but Biff is shattered, calls him a fake, and loses his faith in his father.

**Biff steals Bill Oliver's fountain pen**
Biff waits all day to ask his former employer Bill Oliver for a business loan, but Oliver barely remembers him. Biff impulsively steals Oliver's fountain pen and runs "down eleven flights with a pen in [his] hand." The theft fits Biff's lifelong habit of stealing, including a football from his high school and a carton of basketballs from Oliver.

**Biff flunks math and burns his "University of Virginia" sneakers**
Biff was a star high school football player who had printed "University of Virginia" on his sneakers. After he failed math and then discovered Willy's affair in Boston, he burned the sneakers in the furnace. He never retook the class or went to college, which ended his football future.

**Uncle Ben: "the jungle is dark but full of diamonds"**
Ben is Willy's dead older brother, who appears in Willy's hallucinations. Ben boasts, "When I was seventeen I walked into the jungle, and when I was twenty-one I walked out. And by God I was rich!" He set out for Alaska but ended up in Africa and made a fortune in diamonds, and Willy forever regrets refusing Ben's offer of work in Alaska. Flute music accompanies Willy's memories of his family.

**Howard Wagner, the wire recorder, and "a man is not a piece of fruit"**
Howard is Willy's young boss and the son of Frank Wagner, the man who first hired Willy. When Willy asks for a non-traveling job in New York, Howard is busy showing off a recording of his son reciting state capitals ("The capital of Ohio is Cincinnati..."), and he then fires Willy. Willy protests, "You can't eat the orange and throw the peel away—a man is not a piece of fruit!" He also invokes Dave Singleman, an old salesman who sold from his hotel room and died "the death of a salesman."

**Frank's Chop House and the waiter Stanley**
Willy meets his sons Biff and Happy at this restaurant. Biff struggles to admit that Oliver turned him down, while Happy keeps covering up the bad news. Happy picks up two women, Miss Forsythe and Letta, and the sons abandon Willy, who is left babbling in the restroom. The waiter Stanley finds him there.

**Bernard and the Supreme Court**
Bernard is Charley's studious son, who once tried to help Biff with his math and was mocked by Willy as "liked, but not well liked." He grows up to become a successful lawyer about to argue a case before the Supreme Court, which makes Willy envious. Bernard tells Willy about Biff burning his sneakers.

**The "Florida idea" sporting-goods plan**
Happy proposes that he and Biff sell sporting goods together under the Loman Brothers name. This plan is why Biff seeks the loan from Bill Oliver. The idea briefly revives Willy's hopes before it collapses.

**Planting seeds at night: "I don't have a thing in the ground"**
At the Chop House, Willy suddenly asks Stanley where he can buy seeds, lamenting that nothing is planted. Late that night he plants them by flashlight in his yard while talking to Ben. The garden can't grow because high-rise apartments now block the sunlight where elm trees once stood.

**The Requiem and Linda's "We're free"**
The play's short final scene is the "Requiem," held at Willy's funeral. Biff says Willy "had the wrong dreams," and Charley defends him: "A salesman is got to dream, boy. It comes with the territory." Linda sobs that she made the last mortgage payment that day, repeating "We're free."

**Charley, the neighbor**
Charley plays cards with Willy and secretly lends him money, including money for his insurance premium. He offers Willy a job, which Willy proudly refuses. Willy scorns Charley because he can't put up a ceiling, saying "A man who can't handle tools is not a man... You're disgusting."

**"Well liked"**
Willy's core belief is that success comes from being "well liked" and having personal charm. He tells his sons that Bernard is "liked, but not well liked." Charley mocks this belief by pointing out that J.P. Morgan wasn't successful because he was well liked.

**The rubber hose in the cellar**
Linda finds a short rubber hose hidden in the cellar, attached near the gas heater, which shows that Willy has been planning suicide. Biff later confronts Willy by throwing the hose in front of him. In the same confrontation Biff reveals he spent three months in jail for stealing a suit in Kansas City.

**"Attention must be paid"**
Linda says this line to her sons, insisting that Willy deserves respect despite his flaws: "He's not the finest character that ever lived. But he's a human being... So attention must be paid." It is one of the play's most famous lines.

**Abigail**
Abigail is Barabas's daughter in *The Jew of Malta*. She first pretends to convert so she can enter a nunnery and recover her father's hidden gold. Later she genuinely converts to Christianity after her father engineers her suitors' deaths, and Barabas poisons her in revenge.

**Barabas dies in a boiling cauldron**
Barabas, the Jewish merchant who is the title character of *The Jew of Malta*, schemes against both the Christians and the Turks. In the end he falls through a trapdoor into the boiling cauldron he had prepared for the Turkish commander Calymath. The play begins after Malta's governor Ferneze seizes Barabas's wealth to pay tribute to the invading Turks.

**Machiavel's prologue ("there is no sin but ignorance")**
*The Jew of Malta* opens with the ghost of Machiavelli ("Machiavel") as a caricatured prologue speaker. He complains that "some speak openly against my books" and declares "I count religion but a childish toy" and "there is no sin but ignorance." He also asks, "What right had Caesar to the empire? Might first made kings."

**Tamburlaine, Zenocrate, and Cosroe**
In *Tamburlaine the Great*, a Scythian shepherd rises to conquer the Persian Empire. He helps Cosroe overthrow his brother, the weak king Mycetes, then betrays Cosroe and takes the crown himself. Tamburlaine woos and marries the Egyptian princess Zenocrate, and later he conquers Babylon.

**"Come live with me and be my love"**
This is the famous opening line of Marlowe's pastoral poem "The Passionate Shepherd to His Love." In it, the shepherd promises his beloved gifts such as "a gown made of the finest wool" and "silver dishes for thy meat." Sir Walter Raleigh wrote an answer to it, "The Nymph's Reply to the Shepherd," and C. Day-Lewis later wrote a modern parody.

**Mephistopheles and the contract**
In *Doctor Faustus*, the scholar Faustus summons the devil Mephistopheles, who serves Lucifer. Faustus signs a contract in his own blood, trading his soul for 24 years of magical power. When the clock strikes twelve at the end, devils drag him to hell, and he pleads "I'll burn my books!"

**"Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?"**
Faustus speaks this line when Mephistopheles conjures the shade of Helen of Troy. He continues with "Sweet Helen, make me immortal with a kiss." It is one of the most quoted lines in English drama.

**Ithamore and Bellamira**
Ithamore is the Turkish slave Barabas buys and uses as his accomplice in murder. The courtesan Bellamira and her pimp Pilia-Borza seduce Ithamore and get him to blackmail his master. Barabas then poisons all three, but they betray him before they die.

**Bajazeth in a cage**
In *Tamburlaine the Great*, Tamburlaine defeats the Ottoman Sultan Bajazeth and locks him and his wife Zabina in a cage. He also uses Bajazeth as a footstool. In despair, the couple kill themselves by "braining" themselves against the bars of the cage.

**Poisoned rice for the nuns**
After Abigail converts and joins the convent, Barabas sends poisoned rice porridge to the nunnery. The poison kills all the nuns, including his daughter.

**Lodowick and Mathias**
Lodowick, the governor's son, and Mathias are rival suitors for Abigail in *The Jew of Malta*. Barabas forges a letter so that each believes the other has challenged him to a duel. The two kill each other in the fight.

**Hero and Leander**
This is Marlowe's unfinished narrative poem about Leander of Abydos, who swims across the Hellespont each night to reach his beloved Hero, a priestess at Sestos. George Chapman completed the poem after Marlowe's death.

**Tamburlaine burns the Qur'an**
In *Tamburlaine the Great, Part 2*, the conqueror burns a copy of the Qur'an after taking Babylon and defies Muhammad. Shortly afterward he falls fatally ill. The scene is often read as punishment for his overreaching pride.

**"Homo fuge"**
In *Doctor Faustus*, the Latin words "Homo, fuge" ("O man, fly!") appear on Faustus's arm as he signs his contract in blood. It is a warning he ignores.

**Valdes and Cornelius**
These are the two magicians and scholars in *Doctor Faustus* who introduce Faustus to necromancy. They help him begin conjuring, which leads to his summoning of Mephistopheles.

**"Because I could not stop for Death"**
Dickinson's most famous poem and the most common giveaway. Death "kindly stopped for me," and the speaker rides in a carriage that "held but just Ourselves - / And Immortality," passing a school, "Fields of Gazing Grain," and the "Setting Sun - / Or rather - He passed us," before pausing at "a House that seemed / A Swelling of the Ground" (her grave); it ends with the realization that "the Horses' Heads / Were toward Eternity."

**"I heard a Fly buzz - when I died"**
A poem narrated by a speaker at the moment of her death. There is "Stillness in the Room" like the "Stillness in the Air - / Between the Heaves of Storm," she has "Signed away / What portion of me be / Assignable," and then a fly with a "Blue - uncertain - stumbling Buzz" comes between her and the light until "I could not see to see."

**"'Hope' is the thing with feathers"**
A poem describing hope as a little bird "That perches in the soul - / And sings the tune without the words - / And never stops - at all." The speaker has "heard it in the chillest land - / And on the strangest Sea," yet it "never, in Extremity, / It asked a crumb - of Me."

**"I felt a Funeral, in my Brain"**
A poem describing a mental breakdown as a funeral inside the speaker's head. "Mourners to and fro" keep treading, "A Service, like a Drum - / Kept beating - beating - till I thought / My Mind was going numb," mourners in "Boots of Lead" creak across her soul, and finally "a Plank in Reason, broke." In a related poem, Dickinson wrote that "The Brain - is wider than the Sky."

**"I'm Nobody! Who are you?"**
A short poem in which the speaker happily declares herself a "Nobody" and asks if the reader is one too. She remarks "How dreary - to be - Somebody!", comparing public fame to being a frog that tells its name all day "To an admiring Bog."

**"Wild Nights - Wild Nights!"**
A short, famously sensual love poem. The speaker says that "Futile - the Winds - / To a Heart in port - / Done with the Compass - / Done with the Chart!", imagines "Rowing in Eden," and longs, "Might I but moor - tonight - / In Thee!"

**"Success is counted sweetest"**
One of the few poems published in Dickinson's lifetime, arguing that "Success is counted sweetest / By those who ne'er succeed" and that "To comprehend a nectar / Requires sorest need." It ends with a dying soldier of the defeated side hearing the "distant strains of triumph" of the "purple Host" that won.

**Thomas Wentworth Higginson**
The writer and editor who became Dickinson's longtime correspondent and literary mentor. She first wrote to him in 1862 after reading his Atlantic article "Letter to a Young Contributor," asking whether her "Verse is alive"; he recorded her saying that she knew something was poetry if she felt "physically as if the top of my head were taken off," and he co-edited her poems after her death.

**The "Master" letters and "My Life had stood - a Loaded Gun"**
Three draft letters addressed to an unidentified "Master," found after her death and possibly never sent. "Master" also appears in the poem "My Life had stood - a Loaded Gun," in which the speaker's gun belongs to a mysterious "Owner" and which ends "For I have but the power to kill, / Without - the power to die."

**"Safe in their Alabaster Chambers"**
A poem about the dead lying in their tombs, "Untouched by Morning - / And untouched by Noon," as "the meek members of the Resurrection." Dickinson revised its second stanza several times, in one version writing that "Diadems - drop - and Doges - surrender - / Soundless as dots - on a Disc of Snow."

**"Much Madness is divinest Sense"**
A poem arguing that the majority decides what counts as sanity. If you "Assent - and you are sane," but "Demur - you're straightway dangerous - / And handled with a Chain."

**"A narrow Fellow in the Grass"**
A poem about encountering a snake, which parts the grass "as with a Comb." The speaker has felt friendly toward many creatures, but never met this fellow "Without a tighter breathing / And Zero at the Bone."

**"I taste a liquor never brewed"**
A poem in which the speaker becomes drunk on nature itself, drinking "From Tankards scooped in Pearl" a liquor "Not all the Frankfort Berries / Yield such an Alcohol!" She calls herself an "Inebriate of air" and a "Debauchee of Dew."

**The "Belle of Amherst," her dashes, and Susan Gilbert**
Dickinson lived reclusively in Amherst, Massachusetts, and is known for her heavy use of dashes, slant rhyme, and capitalized nouns; William Luce's one-woman play The Belle of Amherst is about her. Her closest correspondent was her sister-in-law Susan Gilbert Dickinson, and their letters are collected in Open Me Carefully.

**Other frequently cited poems**
Other clue poems include "Tell all the truth but tell it slant," which warns that "The Truth must dazzle gradually / Or every man be blind"; "There's a certain Slant of light," which "oppresses, like the Heft / Of Cathedral Tunes"; "The Soul selects her own Society," whose speaker is "Unmoved" by chariots and an emperor kneeling at her mat; "I like to see it lap the Miles," about a train; "I'm wife - I've finished that," which includes "I'm Czar"; and "Arcturus is his other name," which mocks a scientist who "Computes the stamens" of a flower and "has her in a class!"

**A Doll's House (Nora and Torvald Helmer)**
Ibsen's most famous play (1879), about Nora Helmer, who realizes her husband Torvald has treated her like a doll, as her father did before him. It ends with Nora leaving her husband and children and the famous offstage slam of the front door. Lucas Hnath's 2017 Broadway play A Doll's House, Part 2 imagines Nora's return.

**Krogstad and the forged signature**
Years before the play, Nora secretly borrowed money to take the seriously ill Torvald to Italy, forging her dying father's signature on the loan.
