Nils Krogstad, a disgraced employee at Torvald's bank, blackmails her with the forgery when Torvald plans to fire him. Nora's friend Christine Linde, Krogstad's former sweetheart, persuades him to relent.

**The tarantella, the macaroons, and the "little skylark"**
Torvald patronizingly calls Nora his "little skylark" and "squirrel" and scolds her for secretly eating macaroons. To keep him from opening Krogstad's revealing letter in the mailbox, she wildly rehearses the tarantella. The dying family friend Dr. Rank confesses his love for her.

**"The most wonderful thing of all"**
The ending of A Doll's House. When Torvald insists her most sacred duties are to her husband and children, Nora answers that she has "duties to myself," and she realizes she has been living with a "strange man" for eight years; this is their first serious conversation. She says that only "the most wonderful thing of all" could reunite them, and after she leaves, Torvald repeats the phrase with a flash of hope.

**Hedda Gabler**
Ibsen's 1890 play about Hedda, the daughter of General Gabler, who is bored in her marriage to the dull scholar Jørgen (George) Tesman. Seeking control over someone's fate, she manipulates those around her and finally shoots herself offstage with one of her father's pistols, after wildly playing the piano.

**Eilert Løvborg and the burned manuscript**
Tesman's brilliant rival and Hedda's former admirer, who has written a groundbreaking manuscript with the help of Thea Elvsted. When he loses it while drunk, Hedda secretly burns it, calling it his and Thea's "child," and gives him a pistol, urging him to die "beautifully," imagining him with "vine leaves in his hair." He instead dies sordidly when the pistol goes off in his breast pocket.

**Judge Brack**
The scheming family friend in Hedda Gabler who wants to be "the one cock in the basket" in the Tesman household. He recognizes the pistol from Løvborg's death and uses it to blackmail Hedda, who kills herself rather than be in his power. The play ends with his stunned line, "People don't do such things!"

**An Enemy of the People (Dr. Stockmann)**
An 1882 play in which Dr. Thomas Stockmann discovers that his town's new public baths, the source of its prosperity, are contaminated by waste. When he tries to reveal this, the town turns on him and declares him an "enemy of the people."

**The People's Messenger**
The newspaper in An Enemy of the People. Its editor Hovstad and the printer Aslaksen first promise to print Stockmann's article about the baths but back out after Stockmann's brother Peter, the mayor, warns that the cost of repairs would fall on the taxpayers and ruin the town's economy.

**Ghosts**
An 1881 play in which Mrs. Helene Alving learns that her son Oswald has inherited syphilis from his dissolute late father, Captain Alving, whose memory haunts the family. It ends with Oswald, losing his mind, repeating "the sun, the sun" as his mother screams, undecided whether to give him a lethal dose of morphine.

**The Wild Duck**
An 1884 play in which the idealist Gregers Werle insists on revealing truths to the family of Hjalmar Ekdal, destroying the "life-lie" that, according to Dr. Relling, makes life bearable. The teenage Hedvig, who is losing her eyesight, is persuaded to sacrifice the wounded wild duck kept in the attic where Old Ekdal hunts rabbits, but instead shoots herself. Gregers ends by saying his destiny is "to be the thirteenth at table."

**When We Dead Awaken**
Ibsen's last play (1899), about the aging sculptor Arnold Rubek and his former model Irene, who posed for his masterpiece "Resurrection" and now considers herself dead. The play ends when the two climb a mountain and are buried in an avalanche.

**Peer Gynt**
An 1867 verse drama about the boastful, wandering Norwegian Peer Gynt, who adventures among trolls and around the world. At the end the Button Molder comes to melt his soul down, warning they will meet at "the final crossroads," and Peer is redeemed in the arms of the faithful Solveig. Edvard Grieg's incidental music includes "In the Hall of the Mountain King" and "Solveig's Song."

**The Master Builder**
An 1892 play about the architect Halvard Solness, who fears being replaced by younger people. The young Hilde Wangel arrives claiming he promised her a "kingdom" ten years earlier, and she urges him to climb the tower of his new house to hang a wreath, from which he falls to his death.

**Rosmersholm**
An 1886 play in which Johannes Rosmer's first wife Beata drowned herself in the mill-race, driven to suicide partly by Rebecca West, who loves Rosmer. In the end Rosmer and Rebecca jump into the mill-race together.

**Mrs. Dalloway**
Woolf's 1925 stream-of-consciousness novel set over a single June day in London after World War I. The society hostess Clarissa Dalloway goes to buy flowers on Bond Street and prepares for the party she gives that evening, where she learns of the suicide of a young man she never met. Clarissa has a "perpetual sense" of being "out, out, far out to sea and alone," and was first explored in the short story "Mrs. Dalloway in Bond Street."

**Septimus Warren Smith**
The shell-shocked World War I veteran who is Clarissa's double in Mrs. Dalloway. He hallucinates his dead friend and officer Evans in Regent's Park and kills himself by jumping out of the window of his lodgings as the doctor Holmes comes to take him away. Clarissa hears of his death at her party and reflects on it.

**Sally Seton and Peter Walsh**
Figures from Clarissa's youth at Bourton. Clarissa remembers kissing the bold Sally Seton as "the most exquisite moment of her whole life." Peter Walsh, whom she refused to marry in favor of Richard Dalloway, returns from India and visits her on the day of the party. Other details: Clarissa's daughter Elizabeth is drawn to the religious tutor Doris Kilman, whom Clarissa dislikes, and early in the novel a car backfires on Bond Street while an airplane skywrites letters that people read as "toffee." Michael Cunningham's novel The Hours (1998) reworks Mrs. Dalloway and features Woolf herself.

**To the Lighthouse**
Woolf's 1927 novel set at the Ramsay family's summer house on the Isle of Skye in Scotland. In the first section, "The Window," young James Ramsay wants to sail to the lighthouse, but his father, the philosopher Mr. Ramsay, insists the weather will not allow it. In the final section, "The Lighthouse," years later, Mr. Ramsay finally sails there with James and Cam, who have resolved not to speak to him.

**Lily Briscoe and Charles Tansley**
Lily Briscoe is the unmarried painter staying with the Ramsays who tries to paint Mrs. Ramsay, representing her as a purple triangle, and finally completes the painting at the end of the novel. The awkward young philosopher Charles Tansley, a guest of Mr. Ramsay, keeps repeating "Women can't paint, women can't write," which haunts Lily.

**"Time Passes"**
The short middle section of To the Lighthouse, covering about ten years during which the empty house decays. Major events appear only in square brackets: Mrs. Ramsay dies suddenly, her daughter Prue dies from complications of childbirth, and her son Andrew is killed by a shell in World War I.

**A Room of One's Own**
Woolf's 1929 feminist essay, based on lectures she gave at Cambridge women's colleges, arguing that "a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction," specifically five hundred pounds a year. It imagines Judith Shakespeare, William's equally gifted sister, whose talent is crushed by society and who kills herself.

**"Chloe liked Olivia" and other scenes from A Room of One's Own**
The narrator praises the sentence "Chloe liked Olivia" from an imagined novel by Mary Carmichael, because it shows a relationship between two women. At the fictional "Oxbridge," a beadle orders her off the grass and back onto the gravel path, sending the "little fish" of her thought into hiding, and she is turned away from the library because she is a woman; she also laughs while wondering whether men hummed Tennyson at luncheon parties before the war.

**Orlando**
Woolf's 1928 mock-biography of a young Elizabethan nobleman who lives for over 300 years, until 1928, and wakes up a woman while serving as ambassador to Constantinople. Orlando lives with a band of Romani, almost causes a sailor to fall from the rigging by showing her ankle (and cries "Praise God that I'm a woman!"), skates on the frozen Thames during the Great Frost, and works for centuries on the poem "The Oak Tree."

**Vita Sackville-West and the Hogarth Press**
Woolf's lover, the writer Vita Sackville-West, inspired Orlando. Woolf and her husband Leonard Woolf founded the Hogarth Press, which published Woolf's own books and had commercial success with Sackville-West's novels such as Seducers in Ecuador and The Edwardians. Woolf was a central figure of the Bloomsbury Group.

**The Waves**
Woolf's 1931 experimental novel, which she called a "playpoem," made up of soliloquies by six friends, including Bernard, Neville, and Rhoda, interspersed with italic descriptions of the sun moving over the sea. The seventh friend, Percival, never speaks; his death in India from a fall from his horse is related by the others, and Bernard compares the friends to a six-sided flower.

**Flush**
Woolf's 1933 mock-biography of Elizabeth Barrett Browning's cocker spaniel, Flush. The jealous dog bites Elizabeth's suitor Robert Browning at her home on Wimpole Street before accompanying the couple to Italy.

**Jacob's Room**
Woolf's 1922 novel, the first of her experimental novels, published by the Hogarth Press. It portrays the young man Jacob Flanders only through the impressions of others, such as the women Clara Durrant and Florinda, and ends after his death in World War I with his mother holding up his empty shoes.

**"The Death of the Moth," "How Should One Read a Book?", and Freshwater**
In the essay "The Death of the Moth," Woolf watches a moth's struggle against death at a windowpane. In "How Should One Read a Book?" she advises readers to give the writer "the benefit of every doubt" at first, and later to "judge with the utmost severity." Her comic play Freshwater satirizes her great-aunt, the photographer Julia Margaret Cameron, and the Tennyson circle on the Isle of Wight.

**Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?**
Edward Albee's 1962 play, whose title puns on Woolf's name and the song "Who's Afraid of the Big Bad Wolf?" The history professor George and his wife Martha torment their young guests, the biology professor Nick and his wife Honey, through a night of drinking, and George finally "kills" the couple's imaginary son.

**A Modest Proposal**
Swift's 1729 satirical pamphlet that "proposes" solving Irish poverty and famine by having poor Irish parents sell their one-year-old children as food for the rich. It is the most common giveaway for Swift and mocks the heartless economic thinking of English landlords and policymakers.

**"A young healthy child... is, at a year old, a most delicious, nourishing, and wholesome food"**
The deadpan central claim of A Modest Proposal. The narrator suggests children can be stewed, roasted, baked, or boiled, or served in "a fricassee, or a ragout," and calculates that 120,000 children could be sold each year.

**Gulliver's Travels**
Swift's 1726 satirical novel in four voyages, narrated by the ship's surgeon Lemuel Gulliver. He visits Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Laputa (along with Balnibarbi, Glubbdubdrib, Luggnagg, and Japan), and finally the land of the Houyhnhnms. Gulliver first sails as a surgeon on the Antelope, and his second voyage is on the Adventure.

**Lilliput and Blefuscu**
The first voyage of Gulliver's Travels. Gulliver is shipwrecked and wakes up tied to the beach by the six-inch-tall Lilliputians. Lilliput is at war with the neighboring island of Blefuscu, and Gulliver helps by wading across and stealing the Blefuscudian fleet, though he later flees to Blefuscu.

**Big-Endians and Little-Endians**
The factions in Gulliver's Travels whose conflict centers on whether a boiled egg should be broken at the big end or the little end. The pointless dispute satirizes the religious conflicts between Catholics and Protestants in Europe.

**Houyhnhnms and Yahoos**
The final voyage of Gulliver's Travels takes him to a land ruled by the Houyhnhnms, rational talking horses, who keep the filthy, brutish, human-like Yahoos as domesticated animals. Gulliver comes to believe the Houyhnhnms are more civilized than humans and is reluctant to return to human society.

**A Tale of a Tub (Peter, Martin, and Jack)**
Swift's first major work (1704), a religious satire in which a father leaves coats to his three sons with a will forbidding any changes. Peter represents the Roman Catholic Church, Martin represents Lutherans and Anglicans (after Martin Luther), and Jack represents Calvinists and Dissenters (after John Calvin). The work was attacked by William Wotton.

**"Shoulder-knots" and the "Digression on Madness"**
Episodes in A Tale of a Tub. The brothers, wanting to follow fashion, justify adding shoulder-knots to their coats by picking the individual letters of the word out of their father's will. The book also includes digressions, such as the "Digression Concerning Madness," and describes the Aeolists, who believe wind is the essence of all things.

**The Battle of the Books (the spider and the bee)**
A satire published with A Tale of a Tub depicting a battle between ancient and modern authors in St. James's Library, part of the "Ancients versus Moderns" debate. It contains an allegory in which a self-spinning spider represents the Moderns and a bee gathering from nature represents the Ancients, and it ends with an episode about the modern scholars Bentley and Wotton.

**Psalmanazar the Formosan**
A Modest Proposal cites George Psalmanazar, a famous impostor who claimed to be a native of Formosa (Taiwan). Swift's narrator reports Psalmanazar's tale that in Formosa the bodies of executed young people were sold as delicacies, including a girl crucified for trying to poison the Emperor.

**"Lessen the number of Papists"**
One of the "advantages" listed in A Modest Proposal: since Catholics have the most children, eating Irish babies would reduce the number of "Papists," whom the narrator calls the nation's "most dangerous enemies." Other advantages include making the children's skin into "admirable gloves for ladies, and summer boots for fine gentlemen."

**Isaac Bickerstaff and John Partridge**
Under the pseudonym Isaac Bickerstaff, Swift mocked the astrologer and almanac-maker John Partridge in 1708 by "predicting" his death and then publishing an account of that death, insisting Partridge was dead despite his protests.

**Laputa (the flying island and the flappers)**
The third voyage of Gulliver's Travels includes Laputa, a flying island of absent-minded intellectuals so lost in thought that servants called "flappers" must strike their ears and mouths with bladders to get their attention. Their houses are badly built, with no right angles, because of their impractical geometry.

**Brobdingnag**
The second voyage of Gulliver's Travels, a land of giants in which Gulliver is tiny. The King of Brobdingnag, after hearing Gulliver describe England, calls humans "the most pernicious race of little odious vermin."

**Stella (Esther Johnson) and Journal to Stella**
While Swift served as secretary to Sir William Temple, he tutored the young Esther Johnson, whom he called "Stella." He wrote her the letters collected as Journal to Stella and many poems, and it is rumored they were secretly married. He was also Dean of St. Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin.

**The Drapier's Letters**
Writing as "M. B. Drapier," Swift published pamphlets in the 1720s protesting William Wood's patent to mint copper coins ("Wood's halfpence") for Ireland, a campaign that made him an Irish patriotic hero.

**Other poems and essays ("The Lady's Dressing Room," "A Meditation upon a Broomstick")**
In "The Lady's Dressing Room," the speaker sneaks into Celia's dressing room and is disgusted by the filth he finds, concluding that "such gaudy tulips raised from dung." "A Meditation upon a Broomstick" calls man a "topsy-turvy creature," and "An Argument Against Abolishing Christianity" ironically defends nominal Christianity. Swift also wrote "we have just enough religion to make us hate, but not enough to make us love one another" and that a true genius is known because "the dunces are all in confederacy against him."

**"The Library of Babel"**
Borges's most frequently clued story, from Ficciones. The universe is a seemingly infinite library of identical hexagonal galleries whose shelves hold every possible 410-page book made from 25 symbols (22 letters, the period, the comma, and the space). Almost all the books are gibberish. The narrator ends by guessing that the library is "unlimited and periodic," saying his "solitude is gladdened by this elegant hope."

**The Purifiers, the Crimson Hexagon, and the "Vindications"**
Details of the librarians' society in "The Library of Babel." Pilgrims hunt for "Vindications," books that would justify each person's life. Fanatical "Purifiers" destroy millions of books they think useless, and others seek the Crimson Hexagon and the "Man of the Book," a librarian said to have read the catalog of all catalogs. The story has an epigraph from Robert Burton's The Anatomy of Melancholy, and a footnote suggests the whole library could fit in a single volume with infinitely thin pages.

**"The Garden of Forking Paths," Yu Tsun, and Stephen Albert**
A World War I spy story. Dr. Yu Tsun, a Chinese professor spying for Germany in England, is pursued by Captain Richard Madden. To tell Berlin that a new British artillery park is in the French town of Albert, on the Ancre, he looks up the sinologist Stephen Albert in the phone book and murders him, knowing the newspapers will print the victim's name.

**Ts'ui Pen's labyrinth and the forbidden word "time"**
Before his death, Stephen Albert reveals that Yu Tsun's ancestor Ts'ui Pen, who retired to write a book and build a labyrinth, made them one and the same. His chaotic novel is a labyrinth in time in which every possible outcome happens at once. Albert asks, "In a riddle whose answer is chess, what is the only prohibited word?" Just as "chess" is forbidden there, the word "time" never appears in Ts'ui Pen's book, because time is its subject.

**"The Aleph" and Carlos Argentino Daneri**
The title story of a 1949 collection. After the death of his beloved Beatriz Viterbo, the narrator "Borges" keeps visiting her house and her cousin, the pompous poet Carlos Argentino Daneri. In Daneri's cellar is the Aleph, "a small iridescent sphere of almost unbearable brilliance" that contains every point in the universe seen from every angle. It is named for the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

**Ficciones**
Borges's most famous collection (1944). It combines The Garden of Forking Paths (1941) with a second part, Artifices, and includes "Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius," "Pierre Menard," "The Library of Babel," "Death and the Compass," "Funes the Memorious," "The South," "The Secret Miracle," and "Three Versions of Judas," in which the theologian Nils Runeberg argues that God became incarnate as Judas. Many of these stories also appear in the English selection Labyrinths.

**"Death and the Compass," Erik Lönnrot, and Red Scharlach**
A metaphysical detective story. The detective Erik Lönnrot investigates a series of murders that begins with a rabbi, beside whose typewriter is left the message "The first letter of the Name has been uttered." Lönnrot decides the killings follow the four letters of the Tetragrammaton, but the pattern is a trap set by the criminal Red Scharlach, who lures him to the villa of Triste-le-Roy and kills him. Lönnrot holds that "reality may avoid the obligation to be interesting, but... hypotheses may not."

**"Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote"**
A story written as a mock critical essay about a fictional French Symbolist writer. Menard sets out not to copy but to compose fragments of Cervantes's Don Quixote word for word in the 20th century. The narrator argues that Menard's identical text is far richer than the original.

**"Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius"**
A story that begins when Adolfo Bioy Casares quotes a heresiarch of Uqbar: "mirrors and copulation are abominable, for they multiply the number of men." The narrator and Bioy find an article on Uqbar in only one copy of the Anglo-American Cyclopaedia, and later an encyclopedia of Tlön, an imaginary idealist world whose languages lack nouns. It turns out to be the invention of a secret society, and objects from Tlön start to appear in the real world.

**"The South" and Juan Dahlmann**
The librarian Juan Dahlmann, excited about his newly acquired copy of the Thousand and One Nights, gashes his head, nearly dies of septicemia, and then travels south to recover on his family's ranch. At a country store a drunken young tough challenges him, an old gaucho tosses him a dagger, and Dahlmann walks out onto the plain for a knife fight he is sure to lose. The ending may be his dream of a heroic death in the hospital.

**"The Lottery in Babylon"**
A narrator who has been both "proconsul" and "slave" describes how Babylon's lottery, run by the secretive Company, grew from a simple game of chance into a system in which chance governs every part of life. Losers who once had to pay fines chose jail instead, and the drawings came to hand out punishments as well as rewards.

**"The Circular Ruins"**
A story with an epigraph from Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass. A wizard comes to a ruined circular temple to dream a son into reality, building him detail by detail starting with his heart. When a fire engulfs the temple, the wizard walks into it unburned and realizes that someone else was dreaming him too.

**"The Book of Sand"**
The title story of a 1975 collection. A retired librarian trades a black-letter Wycliffe Bible for a book with infinitely many pages, labeled "Holy Writ" on its spine, from a Scottish Presbyterian Bible seller. Terrified by it, he hides it behind volumes of the Thousand and One Nights and finally loses it among the shelves of the National Library. The same collection includes "The Other," in which an old Borges meets his younger self.

**"The Zahir"**
A story from The Aleph in which the narrator "Borges" receives a twenty-centavo coin as change after a wake. The coin is the Zahir, an object that becomes impossible to forget once seen, and his obsession with it slowly crowds out everything else.

**"A Survey of the Works of Herbert Quain"**
A mock obituary and review of a fictional writer. Quain's detective novel The God of the Labyrinth deliberately offers a false solution, and his novel April March is told backward in branching chapters that combine into several different novels.

**Hester Prynne and the letter "A"**
The protagonist, a young woman in Puritan Boston who bears a child out of wedlock and is sentenced to wear a scarlet "A" for adultery on her breast. She embroiders the letter herself in fine cloth with gold thread, and she later supports herself through needlework. This is the most common giveaway.

**Arthur Dimmesdale and the mark on his chest**
The eloquent young minister who is secretly Pearl's father. Wracked by guilt for seven years, he keeps his hand over his heart and wastes away. After delivering the Election Day Sermon, he climbs the scaffold with Hester and Pearl, confesses, reveals a letter-like mark on his chest, and dies in Hester's arms.

**The meteor seen from the scaffold**
In the novel's midnight scaffold scene, Dimmesdale stands on the pillory platform and is joined by Hester and Pearl, and the three hold hands. A meteor traces a huge letter "A" across the sky, and Roger Chillingworth is seen watching them. Pearl asks Dimmesdale to stand with them at noon the next day, but he refuses.

**Roger Chillingworth, "the Leech"**
Hester's much older husband, a scholar with uneven, deformed shoulders who arrives in Boston under an assumed name and sees Hester on the scaffold. He was held captive by Native Americans and learned herbal medicine from them. Posing as Dimmesdale's physician, called "the leech" in chapter titles, he torments the minister. Gossip links him to the Overbury poisoning affair in England. When Dimmesdale confesses, he cries, "Thou hast escaped me!"

**Pearl**
Hester's "elfish" daughter with Dimmesdale. She pelts the scarlet letter with wildflowers, sees it magnified to gigantic proportions in a suit of armor at the governor's mansion, and tells Governor Bellingham that she was plucked from a rosebush rather than made by God. After Chillingworth dies, she inherits his fortune and settles in Europe.

**The Custom House and Jonathan Pue**
The long introductory sketch in which the narrator, a surveyor at the Salem Custom House who resents his lazy co-workers, finds the faded scarlet letter and a manuscript by the earlier Surveyor Jonathan Pue wrapped in faded red tape. It also recalls an old general who once exclaimed "I'll try, Sir!" The manuscript supposedly provides the story of Hester Prynne.

**"On a field, sable, the letter A, gules"**
The novel's last line describes the heraldic inscription on the single tombstone shared by Hester and Dimmesdale: a red ("gules") letter A on a black ("sable") background.

**The forest scene and the brook**
Hester and Dimmesdale meet in the forest and plan to flee to Europe, and Hester throws off the letter and lets down her hair. Pearl refuses to cross the brook until her mother puts the letter back on, and she washes Dimmesdale's kiss off her forehead in the brook. Earlier on the walk, Pearl tells Hester, "The sunshine does not love you. It runs away and hides itself."

**The prison door and the wild rosebush**
The first chapter notes that the founders of any new colony first set aside ground for a cemetery and a prison. A wild rosebush grows beside the prison door, and it is said to have sprung up under the footsteps of the "sainted Ann Hutchinson."

**Mistress Hibbins and the Black Man**
Governor Bellingham's sister, a suspected witch who invites Hester to a midnight meeting with the "Black Man" (the Devil) in the forest. Hester replies that, had her daughter been taken from her, she would gladly have signed her name in the Black Man's book with her own blood.

**Governor Bellingham's mansion and the embroidered gloves**
Hester brings a pair of embroidered gloves to Governor Bellingham's stucco mansion, described as fitter for Aladdin's palace. The authorities, including the Reverend John Wilson, are considering taking Pearl from her, and Dimmesdale persuades them to let Hester keep her daughter.

**The Election Sermon**
The great sermon Dimmesdale delivers on Election Day, the high point of his career, just before he publicly confesses on the scaffold and dies.

**Master Brackett and the prison interview**
The jailer Master Brackett brings Chillingworth, posing as a physician, into Hester's cell to calm her and her baby. Hester asks, "Hast thou enticed me into a bond that will prove the ruin of my soul?", and he answers, "Not thy soul... No, not thine!" He swears her to keep his identity secret.

**"Unaccustomed earth"**
A line from "The Custom-House" in which the narrator says his children "shall strike their roots into unaccustomed earth." Jhumpa Lahiri took the title of her 2008 story collection Unaccustomed Earth from it.

**Middlemarch**
Eliot's most famous novel (1871–72), subtitled "A Study of Provincial Life" and set in a fictional Midlands town around 1830. Its idealistic heroine is Dorothea Brooke. It ends by praising those who "lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs." Early on, Dorothea and her sister Celia divide their dead mother's jewels, and Dorothea takes only an emerald ring and bracelet.

**Edward Casaubon and The Key to All Mythologies**
Casaubon is the dry, aging clergyman-scholar whom Dorothea marries, hoping to help with his great work. He never finishes The Key to All Mythologies, an outdated attempt to trace all myths to a single source, and he rejects her help. Before he dies, he adds a clause to his will that takes away her inheritance if she marries his young cousin Will Ladislaw. She gives up the fortune and marries Will anyway.

**Tertius Lydgate and Rosamond Vincy**
Lydgate is an ambitious young doctor in Middlemarch whose career is ruined by debt and by his marriage to the pretty, selfish Rosamond Vincy. The kind vicar Camden Farebrother is among those who try to help him.

**Nicholas Bulstrode and John Raffles**
Bulstrode is Middlemarch's hypocritical, Evangelical banker who lends money to Lydgate. The drunken John Raffles blackmails him over his past: Bulstrode made his fortune in a pawnbroking business that dealt in stolen goods, and he hid the fact that the rightful heir to that money (Will Ladislaw's mother) was alive. When Raffles dies in Bulstrode's care, the resulting scandal also stains Lydgate. Another subplot involves the miser Peter Featherstone, who dies before he can have one of his two wills burned, so his fortune goes to his illegitimate son Joshua Rigg.

**Silas Marner**
Eliot's 1861 short novel about the "weaver of Raveloe," a lonely linen weaver. He was driven out of Lantern Yard, his religious community, after his friend William Dane framed him for theft by planting his pocketknife where a dying deacon's money had been stolen. The congregation drew lots to decide his guilt, and Dane then married Silas's fiancée Sarah.

**Dunstan Cass and Silas's gold**
Dunstan "Dunsey" Cass, the squire's wastrel son, kills his brother's horse Wildfire while out riding, then steals Silas's hoarded gold and disappears. The peddler Jem Rodney is suspected at first. Years later, Dunstan's skeleton is found in a drained stone pit, still clutching the gold.

**Eppie, Molly Farren, and Godfrey Cass**
Molly Farren, the opium-addicted secret wife of Godfrey Cass, dies in the snow on New Year's Eve on her way to the Red House to expose the marriage. Her golden-haired toddler Eppie wanders into Silas's cottage, and he adopts and raises her, finding happiness again. Godfrey marries Nancy Lammeter, and when he later claims Eppie as his daughter, she chooses to stay with Silas.

**Adam Bede**
Eliot's first novel (1859), set in the village of Hayslope and named for an upright carpenter. Adam loves the pretty, vain Hetty Sorrel, who is seduced by the young squire Arthur Donnithorne. In the end Adam marries the Methodist preacher Dinah Morris, completing the book's "love rectangle."

**Hetty Sorrel's trial**
In Adam Bede, Hetty leaves town pregnant, gives birth, and abandons the baby in a field, where it dies of exposure. She is tried and sentenced to death for child murder, but Arthur arrives with a reprieve that reduces her sentence to transportation.

**The Mill on the Floss**
Eliot's 1860 novel about the siblings Tom and Maggie Tulliver of Dorlcote Mill on the river Floss. Their father loses the mill to the lawyer Wakem and writes a curse against him in the family Bible. The siblings, estranged for years, reconcile just before both drown in a flood at the end.

**Maggie Tulliver, Philip Wakem, and Stephen Guest**
Maggie is the passionate, intelligent heroine of The Mill on the Floss. As a child she lets Tom's rabbits die by forgetting to feed them, and as a teenager she turns to renunciation after reading Thomas à Kempis's The Imitation of Christ. She has a secret friendship with the hunchbacked Philip Wakem, the lawyer's son, and is disgraced after drifting downriver toward Mudport with Stephen Guest, her cousin Lucy's suitor.

**Daniel Deronda**
Eliot's last novel (1876). Daniel, raised by the wealthy Sir Hugo Mallinger, first sees Gwendolen Harleth losing at roulette and redeems the turquoise necklace she has pawned. He becomes her moral guide during her miserable marriage to Grandcourt.

**Mirah Lapidoth and Mordecai**
In Daniel Deronda, Daniel saves the Jewish singer Mirah from drowning herself in the Thames. He learns that his mother was Jewish, becomes the disciple of Mirah's visionary brother Mordecai, marries Mirah, and leaves for "the East" to work toward a Jewish homeland, a proto-Zionist ending.

**Scenes of Clerical Life**
Eliot's first fiction (1858), a collection of three stories: "The Sad Fortunes of the Reverend Amos Barton," in which Amos neglects his wife Milly for the Countess Czerlaski; "Mr. Gilfil's Love Story," in which Gilfil finds Caterina "Tina" Sarti with a knife and fears she has killed Captain Wybrow; and "Janet's Repentance."

**Mary Ann Evans, translator and critic**
George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans. Her first published work was a translation of David Strauss's Life of Jesus, and she also translated Feuerbach's The Essence of Christianity. She edited the Westminster Review and wrote essays such as "Silly Novels by Lady Novelists." Her other works include Felix Holt, the Radical, in which an election riot leads Felix to accidentally kill a constable as Harold Transom runs for office in Treby Magna; Romola, set in Savonarola's Florence and featuring the deceitful Tito Melema; and the verse drama The Spanish Gypsy.

**Conch shell**
A large seashell that Ralph and Piggy find on the beach soon after the plane crash. Ralph blows it to call the first assembly, and whoever holds it may speak at meetings, so it symbolizes order and democracy. When it is first found, Piggy recalls a similar shell on a friend's garden wall and how his auntie said it "mooed like a cow."

**The pig's head on a stick (the "Lord of the Flies")**
Jack's hunters mount a sow's head on a stake sharpened at both ends as an offering to "the beast." Simon hallucinates that it speaks to him, calling him "an ignorant, silly little boy" and saying "You knew, didn't you? I'm part of you," "I'm the reason why it's no go," and "We are going to have fun on this island!" Simon then faints in a seizure. Ralph later smashes the white skull, which ends up grinning on the ground "six feet across."

**Dead parachutist mistaken for "the beast"**
An airman killed in an unseen air battle lands on the mountain, and his flapping parachute makes him look like a giant ape. The twins Sam and Eric see him first, and the boys abandon their smoke-signal fire out of fear. Simon later climbs the mountain, discovers the truth, and frees the body, which the wind carries out to sea.

**Piggy's glasses**
Piggy's spectacles focus sunlight and are the only way the boys can start fires. Jack's tribe raids Ralph's group and steals them, and Piggy is killed while trying to get them back.

**Roger's boulder kills Piggy**
At Castle Rock, the sadistic Roger releases a boulder that strikes Piggy, the fat, asthmatic boy, throws him onto the rocks below, and shatters the conch at the same moment. This marks the final collapse of order on the island.

**Jack Merridew and the choir**
Jack leads a group of choirboys who become the "hunters." He claims he should be chief because he is head boy of the choir and can sing C sharp, but loses the vote to Ralph. He objects to being called by his first name, "a kid's name," paints his face, and eventually forms a rival savage tribe.

**Simon's death: "Kill the beast! Cut his throat! Spill his blood!"**
Simon is a gentle, mystical boy often read as a Christ figure. He staggers out of the forest during a stormy feast and ritual dance to tell everyone that the beast is only a dead man, but the chanting boys mistake him for the beast and kill him. Ralph, Piggy, and Samneric take part in the dance. Earlier, a version of the chant ending "Kill the pig. Cut her throat. Bash her in" was used while the boys circled another boy in a mock hunt.

**The naval officer and "the end of innocence"**
At the end of the novel, Jack's tribe sets the island ablaze while hunting Ralph, and the smoke draws a British naval officer. He wears a white-topped cap with "a crown, an anchor, gold foliage" and compares the scene to R. M. Ballantyne's *The Coral Island*, the Victorian adventure novel that inspired Golding. Ralph then weeps "for the end of innocence, the darkness of man's heart, and the fall through the air of the true, wise friend called Piggy."

**Littlun with the mulberry-colored birthmark**
A small, unnamed boy with a mulberry-colored birthmark on his face is the first to voice fear of a "snake-thing" or "beastie." He disappears when the boys' first signal fire burns out of control and razes part of the island, and he is presumed dead.

**Percival Wemys Madison**
One of the youngest "littluns." He clings to reciting his name and address ("The Vicarage, Harcourt St. Anthony") as a link to civilization. By the end, when the naval officer arrives, he can no longer remember them, showing how far the boys have regressed.

**Sandcastles destroyed by Roger and Maurice**
In an early scene, the older boys Roger and Maurice kick over the sandcastles of the littluns, including Percival and Johnny. Maurice gets sand in Percival's eye and makes him cry. Roger then throws stones near another littlun but deliberately misses, still restrained by the "taboo of the old life."

**Simon's body and the glowing fish**
After Simon is killed, the tide carries his corpse out to sea. Golding describes it surrounded by phosphorescent creatures, fish with "fiery eyes," with his shoulder like "sculpted marble." It is one of the novel's most lyrical passages.

**"Sucks to your ass-mar"**
An insult mocking Piggy's asthma ("ass-mar" is Piggy's own pronunciation). Ralph first says it, and it captures the casual cruelty Piggy suffers throughout the book.

**Castle Rock**
A fortress-like rocky outcrop at one end of the island. Jack's tribe makes it their stronghold, and it is where Piggy is killed. Stephen King borrowed the name for his fictional Maine town.

**Samneric tortured**
The inseparable twins Sam and Eric, so linked that the boys merge their names into "Samneric," are captured and tortured by Jack's tribe, with Roger leading the torment. They are forced to join the savages and eventually reveal Ralph's hiding place.

**"The Gift of the Magi"**
O. Henry's most famous short story and the near-universal giveaway for him. A poor young married couple, Jim and Della Young, each secretly sacrifice their most prized possession to buy the other a Christmas present, and the gifts end up useless, a classic example of his ironic twist endings.

**Della sells her hair; Jim sells his watch**
The central irony of "The Gift of the Magi." Della sells her long hair to buy Jim a platinum fob chain for his gold watch, while Jim sells that watch to buy Della a set of expensive tortoiseshell combs she can no longer use.

**"One dollar and eighty-seven cents"**
The opening of "The Gift of the Magi," in which Della cries because she has only $1.87 saved to buy Jim a Christmas gift. She later looks at herself in a pier-glass (a tall mirror) before deciding to sell her hair.

**Madame Sofronie**
The owner of the hair-goods shop where Della sells her hair for twenty dollars in "The Gift of the Magi."

**"The Ransom of Red Chief"**
A comic story in which two small-time crooks, Bill Driscoll and Sam Howard, kidnap the son of Ebenezer Dorset, a prominent man in a small town, expecting a big ransom. The boy turns out to be such a terror that the plan backfires completely.

**Ebenezer Dorset and the $250**
The father of the kidnapped boy (Johnny Dorset) in "The Ransom of Red Chief." The kidnappers first demand $2,000, but Dorset counters that they must pay him $250 to take his son back, and they gladly do.

**Old Hank and Snake-eye**
The names Johnny Dorset, who calls himself "Red Chief," gives his kidnappers while playing Indian. He threatens to scalp Bill ("Old Hank") and burn Sam ("Snake-eye") at the stake, and he is first seen throwing rocks at a kitten.

**"The Cop and the Anthem" and Soapy**
A story in The Four Million about Soapy, a homeless man in New York who tries to get arrested so he can spend the winter in jail on Blackwell's Island. All his attempts fail (he is even mistaken for a Yale student celebrating, and keeps an umbrella he thinks he stole), but after hearing church organ music he resolves to reform, and he is then arrested for loitering.

**"The Last Leaf"**
A story set in Greenwich Village in which the young artist Johnsy, sick with pneumonia, believes she will die when the last ivy leaf outside her window falls. The old painter Behrman secretly paints a lifelike leaf on the wall during a storm, saving her, but he dies of pneumonia himself; the leaf was his "masterpiece."

**"A Retrieved Reformation" and Jimmy Valentine**
A story (collected in Roads of Destiny) about the reformed safecracker Jimmy Valentine, who goes straight after falling in love with banker's daughter Annabel Adams. When a child is locked in a bank vault he uses his tools to open it, and detective Ben Price, who came to arrest him, pretends not to recognize him.

**The Four Million**
O. Henry's 1906 collection, titled after the population of New York City at the time (a reply to the idea that only "the Four Hundred" elite people mattered). It contains "The Gift of the Magi," "The Cop and the Anthem," and "The Furnished Room."

**Cabbages and Kings**
O. Henry's only novel, a set of linked stories set in the fictional Central American "banana republic" of Anchuria (a term he coined in it). Its title comes from Lewis Carroll's poem "The Walrus and the Carpenter."

**William Sydney Porter**
O. Henry's real name. He wrote many stories after serving prison time for embezzlement, and the pen name is said to come possibly from a prison guard or a French pharmacist; he is famous for stories with surprise twist endings.

**"The Clarion Call"**
A story in which detective Barney Woods discovers that his old friend Johnny Kernan murdered a man named Norcross, but hesitates to arrest him because he owes Kernan $1,000. He finally pays the debt with a newspaper reward and makes the arrest.

**"A Municipal Report"**
A story set in Nashville in which the narrator discovers that the cab driver Uncle Caesar killed the brutal Major Caswell to protect the poor writer Azalea Adair. The narrator throws away the coat button that would incriminate Caesar into the river.

**Other stories: "The Duplicity of Hargraves" and "The Cactus"**
In "The Duplicity of Hargraves," an actor studies the mannerisms of the Southern gentleman Major Talbot for a play and secretly gives him $300 while disguised as "Uncle Mose." In "The Cactus," a woman accepts a marriage proposal by sending her suitor a cactus whose Spanish name means "come and take me," which he fails to understand.

**Trapped under a mountain for 500 years**
After losing his bet with the Buddha, the Monkey King Sun Wukong is pinned under the Five Elements Mountain for five centuries. He is freed only when the monk Xuanzang (Tang Sanzang) passes by, and in return he must protect the monk on the pilgrimage to India.

**Ruyi Jingu Bang (the size-changing staff)**
This is Sun Wukong's magic iron staff, which can grow or shrink at will. It began as an iron pillar used to measure the depth of the sea, kept in the undersea palace of the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea, Ao Guang. The pillar glowed when its rightful owner arrived, and it weighs 13,500 jin. Sun Wukong can shrink it to the size of a needle and keep it behind his ear.

**Zhu Bajie ("Pigsy") and his nine-toothed iron rake**
Zhu Bajie is a gluttonous, lustful pig-man who carries a nine-toothed rake and is often called "the idiot." He was once Marshal Tianpeng, commander of Heaven's river navy, but was banished for flirting with the Moon Goddess and reborn with a pig's form. He lived in the Cloud Pathway Cave and tried to marry a village elder's daughter at Gao Village until his huge appetite gave him away. At the end of the novel he becomes the "Cleanser of the Altars," so he can eat leftover offerings.

**Sha Wujing ("Sandy") and the smashed crystal goblet**
Sha Wujing was once the Curtain-Lifting General in Heaven. He was beaten 800 times with a rod and exiled after he accidentally broke the Queen Mother's crystal goblet (a vase in some versions) at the Peach Banquet. As a monstrous sand demon wearing a necklace of skulls, he terrorized travelers at a river crossing until he joined the pilgrims.

**Urinating on the Buddha's fingers (the palm wager)**
Sun Wukong bets the Buddha that he can leap out of his palm. He somersaults to what he thinks is the edge of the universe, sees five huge pillars, and writes his name on one and urinates on it. The pillars turn out to be the Buddha's fingers. Sun Wukong has also mastered 72 transformations, while Pigsy knows 36.

**Tang Sanzang / Xuanzang, the "Golden Cicada"**
The monk at the center of the pilgrimage, also called Tripitaka or Tang Seng, is based on the real 7th-century monk Xuanzang. He is the reincarnation of the Buddha's disciple Golden Cicada, so demons keep attacking him because eating his flesh is said to grant immortality. An early episode tells how his mother pretends to donate 100 pairs of shoes so she can meet her son. He had proven who he was with a letter written in blood.

**Peaches of immortality, "Protector of the Horses," and "Great Sage Equal to Heaven"**
To calm Sun Wukong down, Heaven gives him the lowly job of Protector (Keeper) of the Horses. Insulted, he rebels and calls himself the "Great Sage Equal to Heaven," which angers the Jade Emperor. He then eats the peaches of immortality and disrupts the Queen Mother's Peach Banquet, and that rampage leads to his punishment by the Buddha.

**Book of Life and Death**
When Sun Wukong's soul is dragged to the underworld, he crosses his own name, and the names of his monkey followers, out of the register that records lifespans. This makes him immortal.

**Vulture Peak scriptures and the 81 tribulations**
The pilgrims must survive 81 trials, including a lair of spider spirits. At the end they receive the Buddhist scriptures from the Buddha at Vulture Peak. In the final trial the scriptures fall into a river and get soaked.

**Golden headband and the tightening spell**
The bodhisattva Guanyin arranges the pilgrimage and its disciples. She has Sun Wukong tricked into wearing a golden headband. Whenever Xuanzang chants a spell, the band tightens and gives the Monkey King a crushing headache, which is how the monk controls him.

**Born from a stone egg / Water Curtain Cave**
Sun Wukong hatches from a stone egg on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. He becomes king of the monkeys after jumping through a waterfall and finding the Water Curtain Cave behind it, which becomes the monkeys' home.

**"Fiery eyes and golden gaze"**
Laozi tries to destroy Sun Wukong by sealing him in his Eight Trigrams Furnace for 49 days. He survives, and the smoke leaves him with fiery eyes that can see through disguises. He uses them, for example, to recognize the shape-shifting White Bone Spirit, who disguises herself as a young girl and old people.

**Kingdom of Women and the pregnancy river**
On the way west, Xuanzang and Pigsy drink from a river whose water makes anyone who drinks it pregnant. This happens near the Kingdom of Women, a land with no men whose queen wants to marry the monk.

**Arthur Waley's *Monkey***
Arthur Waley's famous abridged English translation of the novel is simply titled *Monkey*, and it popularized the names "Sandy" and "Pigsy." Gerald Vizenor's novel *Griever* is a modern adaptation of the story.

**Wu Cheng'en and the Four Great Classical Novels**
This 100-chapter novel from the Ming dynasty is usually credited to Wu Cheng'en. It is one of China's Four Great Classical Novels, along with *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, *Water Margin*, and *Dream of the Red Chamber*.

**Blood Wedding**
Lorca's most frequently clued play (1933), the first of his Rural Trilogy. The Mother, whose husband and son were killed by the Félix family, sees her son the Groom marry the Bride. The Bride was once the lover of Leonardo Félix, now married to her cousin, and at the wedding she runs off with Leonardo on horseback. The Groom chases them into the forest, where Leonardo and the Groom kill each other with knives.

**The Moon and Death as a Beggar Woman**
Symbolic characters in the forest scene of Blood Wedding's last act, which opens with three woodcutters. The Moon, played as a young woodcutter with a white face, longs for blood and promises to light the lovers' way. Death appears as a Beggar Woman and orders the Moon to give light so that "the knives will know the road."

**"Lament for Ignacio Sánchez Mejías" and "at five in the afternoon"**
Lorca's famous 1935 elegy for his friend, the bullfighter Ignacio Sánchez Mejías, who died in 1934 after being gored. Its first section, "The Goring and the Death," repeats "at five in the afternoon" as a refrain after almost every line, including "A boy brought the white sheet" and "a basket of lime already prepared." The poem is also known in English as "Lament for the Death of a Bullfighter."

**"I will not see it!"**
The refrain of "The Spilled Blood," the second section of the "Lament," in which the speaker refuses to look at his friend's blood on the sand (also translated "I don't want to see it!"). The elegy continues with "The Laid-Out Body" and "Absent Soul," which tells the dead man "you have died forever." It ends "I sing of his elegance with words that groan, / and I remember a sad breeze through the olive trees."

**The House of Bernarda Alba**
Lorca's last play (1936), with an all-female cast and the third play of the Rural Trilogy. After her second husband's funeral, the tyrannical widow Bernarda imposes an eight-year mourning period and locks her five unmarried daughters inside the house. Her servant La Poncia warns her of the trouble brewing among them.

**Adela and Pepe el Romano**
The central conflict of The House of Bernarda Alba. Pepe el Romano is engaged to Angustias, the oldest and wealthiest daughter, but secretly meets the youngest, Adela, who defiantly wears a green dress. Bernarda fires her gun at Pepe, her daughter Martirio falsely says he is dead, and Adela hangs herself. Bernarda insists Adela died a virgin, orders that no one weep, and demands "Silence!"

**"Romance Sonámbulo" and "Green, how I want you green"**
Lorca's most famous lyric, the "Sleepwalking Ballad" from Gypsy Ballads. It opens "Green, how I want you green. / Green wind. Green branches. / The ship out on the sea / and the horse on the mountain," while a gypsy girl with green flesh, green hair, and "eyes of cold silver" dreams on her balcony.

**"I want to trade my horse for her house"**
Lines from "Romance Sonámbulo," spoken by a wounded young smuggler who asks an older friend to trade "my horse for her house, my saddle for her mirror, my knife for her blanket." The two friends climb toward the high balconies, but the girl is already dead, her body held "up above the water" of a cistern by "an icicle of moon."

**Gypsy Ballads (Romancero gitano)**
Lorca's popular 1928 collection of eighteen ballads (romances) about the Roma of Andalusia, which includes "Romance Sonámbulo." In "Ballad of the Moon, Moon," the moon comes to the forge and shows her breasts to a gypsy boy before carrying him away. Another ballad describes the arrest of Antoñito el Camborio, "brown as a green moon," carrying a willow rod on the road to Seville.

**The Rural Trilogy**
The name for Lorca's three tragedies of rural Andalusian life, Blood Wedding, Yerma, and The House of Bernarda Alba. They focus on frustrated passion, honor, and the restrictions placed on women, and are his best-known plays.

**Yerma**
The second play of the Rural Trilogy (1934). Its title character, whose name means "barren," longs for a child, but her husband Juan does not want one. She is drawn to the shepherd Víctor, is watched by her two sisters-in-law, visits the conjurer Dolores for a fertility ritual, and is gossiped about by washerwomen at a stream. At the end she strangles Juan and cries "I have killed my son!", since she can now never have a child.

**Poet in New York**
A surreal collection written during Lorca's 1929–1930 stay in New York, while he studied at Columbia, and published after his death. It reacts to the city's alienation, racism, and the 1929 stock market crash, and includes "Ode to Walt Whitman."

**"City That Does Not Sleep"**
A poem from Poet in New York (subtitled "Brooklyn Bridge Nocturne") that opens "In the sky there is nobody asleep. Nobody, nobody." It warns that "living iguanas will come and bite the men who do not dream" and declares "Life is not a dream. Careful! Careful! Careful!"

**Lorca's execution in 1936**
In August 1936, at the start of the Spanish Civil War, Lorca was arrested in Granada and shot by Nationalist forces, and his body was never found. A leading member of the Generation of '27, he became a symbol of the war's victims. Allen Ginsberg's "A Supermarket in California" asks "what were you doing down by the watermelons?" of him, and the Irish biographer Ian Gibson investigated his death.

**"Gacela of the Dark Death"**
A poem from Lorca's late collection The Tamarit Divan, modeled on Arabic and Persian ghazals. Its speaker says "I want to sleep the sleep of the apples, / far from the tumult of cemeteries."

**I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings**
Angelou's 1969 autobiography, the first of seven, and the most common giveaway for her. Its title comes from the last stanza of Paul Laurence Dunbar's poem "Sympathy." It covers her childhood as Marguerite Johnson, and she wrote it partly in response to a challenge from James Baldwin.

**Stamps, Arkansas**
The segregated town where young Marguerite and her brother Bailey are sent by train with wrist tags reading "To Whom It May Concern." They live with their grandmother "Momma" (Annie Henderson), who runs the William Johnson General Merchandise Store with the disabled Uncle Willie. At Marguerite's eighth-grade graduation there, the white speaker Mr. Donleavy gives a condescending, racist speech.

**Mr. Freeman**
Her mother's boyfriend in St. Louis, who rapes Marguerite when she is eight. After she testifies at his trial, he is found beaten to death, apparently by her uncles. Believing her words killed him, she stops speaking for about five years.

**Mrs. Bertha Flowers**
The refined Black woman in Stamps who helps Marguerite out of her silence. She reads aloud the opening of A Tale of Two Cities ("It was the best of times...") and encourages her to read poetry aloud.

**Streetcar conductor in San Francisco**
After moving to San Francisco to live with her mother, Vivian Baxter, the teenage Marguerite becomes the city's first Black streetcar conductor, after persisting through the hiring process and making things up on her application. Caged Bird ends with the birth of her son, Guy.

**Bailey**
Marguerite's beloved older brother, who protects and comforts her. He comforts her when she cries after forgetting her lines while reciting a poem at church on Easter Sunday. He develops a stutter after they move to St. Louis.

**"On the Pulse of Morning"**
The poem Angelou recited at Bill Clinton's first inauguration in 1993. It begins "A Rock, A River, A Tree / Hosts to species long since departed," and the Rock tells the reader "You may stand upon me, / But do not hide your face." The River invites the people to "my riverside, / If you will study war no more," the Tree says "I am that Tree planted by the River," and the poem ends "Good morning."

**"Still I Rise"**
A defiant 1978 poem: "You may write me down in history / With your bitter, twisted lies, / You may trod me in the very dirt / But still, like dust, I'll rise." It asks "Does my sassiness upset you?", "Does my haughtiness offend you?", and "Does my sexiness upset you?" It describes the speaker walking "like I've got oil wells / Pumping in my living room" and rising "Just like moons and like suns, / With the certainty of tides," and says "I am the dream and the hope of the slave."

**"Caged Bird"**
Angelou's poem contrasting a free bird, which "leaps / on the back of the wind / and floats downstream" and "thinks of another breeze," with a caged bird that "stands on the grave of dreams" and sings "with a fearful trill" of freedom, a tune "heard on the distant hill."

**Gather Together in My Name**
Angelou's second autobiography (1974). As a young single mother of her son Guy (then called Clyde), she is rejected by the Army because she attended the California Labor School, which was thought to be communist. She falls for the gambler L. D. Tolbrook, who leads her into prostitution.

**All God's Children Need Traveling Shoes**
Angelou's 1986 autobiography about living in Accra, Ghana, where she befriends the playwright Efua Sutherland and a young man named Kojo reminds her of her son. It follows The Heart of a Woman, which covers her civil rights activism and her time in New York and Africa.

**Mrs. Viola Cullinan**
The white woman Marguerite works for as a maid in Caged Bird. When Mrs. Cullinan insists on calling her "Mary" instead of her real name, Marguerite deliberately breaks her prized china.

**Dolores and the drive from Mexico**
An episode from Caged Bird. While visiting her father in California, Marguerite drives him back from Mexico when he is drunk, despite never having driven before. His girlfriend Dolores then cuts her with scissors, and Marguerite runs away and lives for a time in a junkyard of abandoned cars.

**Just Give Me a Cool Drink of Water 'fore I Diiie**
Angelou's first poetry collection (1971), nominated for the Pulitzer Prize. Its first section is "Where Love Is a Scream of Anguish," and it opens with "They Went Home" (about men who "liked my smile, my wit, my hips"). It also includes "Riot: 60's" ("a hundred Watts, / Detroit, Newark and New York") and "The Thirteens." Angelou also wrote the screenplay Georgia, Georgia, the first by a Black woman to be produced, and acted as the White Queen in Jean Genet's The Blacks.

**"Phenomenal Woman"**
A poem celebrating a confident woman's self-assurance and attractiveness that has nothing to do with conventional beauty. The men around her "swarm around me, / A hive of honey bees," and each stanza ends with the refrain "Phenomenal woman, / That's me."

**Firs left locked in the house as axes chop the trees**
The play ends with Firs, the old footman, forgotten inside the boarded-up house. Everyone thought he had been sent to the hospital. He lies down on a couch, apparently to die, while offstage axes are heard cutting down the cherry trees.

**Lopakhin buys Madame Ranevskaya's estate at auction**
Yermolai Lopakhin is a rich merchant whose father and grandfather were serfs on the estate. He buys Lyubov Ranevskaya's family property at a debt auction in Act III and boasts about it while she weeps. He had urged her to cut down the orchard and build summer cottages (dachas) to rent out, and she refused. After buying it, he goes ahead with the plan.

**Peter Trofimov, the "eternal student"**
Trofimov is a shabby idealist called the "eternal" or "perpetual student" because he never finishes university and has been expelled twice. He used to tutor Ranevskaya's son. Anya, Ranevskaya's daughter, loves him, and he argues with Ranevskaya about the orchard and the past.

**The drowning of Grisha**
Ranevskaya's seven-year-old son Grisha drowned in the river. Afterward she fled to Paris for five years. When she comes home and sees Trofimov, his former tutor, she breaks down crying.

**Gayev's speech to the hundred-year-old bookcase**
Leonid Gayev, Ranevskaya's sentimental brother, gives an emotional ode to a family bookcase (sometimes translated as "cupboard") after learning it is a hundred years old. The speech shows his useless, rambling nostalgia.

**Gayev's imaginary billiards and candies**
Gayev keeps calling out billiards shots ("Cannon off the red!") in the middle of conversations. He also sucks on candies and jokes that he ate up his fortune in sweets. When his family tells him to stop talking, he says "I'll be quiet."

**Charlotta's magic tricks and ventriloquism**
Charlotta Ivanovna is Anya's governess and a child of circus performers who doesn't know who her parents were. At the Act III party she does card tricks, such as finding the eight of spades in Pishchik's pocket. She also makes people appear from under a shawl and shows off her ventriloquism.

**Yepikhodov, "Twenty-Two Misfortunes"**
Semyon Yepikhodov is the estate's clumsy clerk, with squeaky boots and bad luck that earn him the nickname "Twenty-Two Misfortunes" (or "Calamities"). He plays a guitar while insisting it's a mandolin, and he is in love with the maid Dunyasha. At the party, Varya scolds him after he breaks a billiard cue.

**Ranevskaya's telegrams from her lover in Paris**
Ranevskaya keeps getting telegrams from the man she loved in Paris, who robbed and abandoned her but is now sick and begging her to come back. At first she tears them up without reading them, but by the end of the play she returns to him.

**Varya and Lopakhin's proposal that never happens**
Varya is Ranevskaya's adopted daughter, and everyone expects Lopakhin to marry her. In Act IV they are left alone so he can propose, but he never does. Varya leaves to work as a housekeeper on another estate.

**Pishchik and the white clay**
Simeonov-Pishchik is a landowner who is always in debt and always borrowing money. In the last act he happily pays back what he owes after Englishmen find white clay on his land and lease it.

**The gold coin given to a tramp**
In Act II, a drunken passerby asks for 30 kopecks. Ranevskaya has no silver, so she gives him a gold coin, and Varya scolds her for it. The scene shows how carelessly she spends money while the family is going broke.

**The Act III party and Trofimov's fall down the stairs**
Ranevskaya throws a party on the day of the auction. Barons and generals once came to such balls, but now only the stationmaster and the post-office clerk show up. During the party she argues with Trofimov, he storms out, and he falls down the stairs.

**"Above love" and "All Russia is our orchard"**
In their argument, Trofimov says that he and Anya are "above love," and Ranevskaya tells him he must be "beneath love." Elsewhere he tells Anya that "all Russia is our orchard" and that the earth is "so wide, so beautiful."

**"My little cucumber"**
The servant Yasha calls the maid Dunyasha his "little cucumber" (sometimes translated "little pickle") when he kisses her, and she drops and breaks a saucer.

**"Paul Revere's Ride"**
Longfellow's most famous poem, which begins "Listen, my children, and you shall hear / Of the midnight ride of Paul Revere" and is set "on the eighteenth of April, in Seventy-five." The silversmith Revere waits for a signal from the belfry of the Old North Church, rides to spread the "cry of alarm / To every Middlesex village and farm," and delivers a "midnight message" that "the people will waken and listen to hear." It was published in Tales of a Wayside Inn and is the near-universal giveaway.

**"One if by land, and two if by sea"**
The line describing the lantern signal hung in the Old North Church tower in "Paul Revere's Ride"; two lanterns mean the British are crossing by water. The poem takes liberties with history: the real Revere was captured near Lexington and never reached "the bridge in Concord town."

**The Song of Hiawatha**
Longfellow's 1855 epic about an Ojibwe hero, set "By the shores of Gitche Gumee, / By the shining Big-Sea-Water" (Lake Superior). It is written in trochaic tetrameter, a meter Longfellow borrowed from the Finnish epic Kalevala, and has sections such as "The Four Winds" and "The White Man's Foot."

**Minnehaha**
Hiawatha's beloved and wife, the "Laughing Water," whose wooing and marriage are a central plotline of The Song of Hiawatha. She dies of fever and hunger during a terrible winter famine, one of the poem's most famous episodes.

**Nokomis, Wenonah, and Mudjekeewis**
Hiawatha's family in The Song of Hiawatha. His grandmother Nokomis fell to earth from the full moon; her daughter Wenonah was seduced by Mudjekeewis, the West Wind, and gave birth to Hiawatha. Hiawatha later fights his father Mudjekeewis, and also kills the magician Pearl-Feather after passing the Kenabeek serpents. The section on the winds also tells how Shawondasee, the South Wind, fell in love with a dandelion he mistook for a golden-haired maiden.

**Evangeline, A Tale of Acadie**
Longfellow's 1847 narrative poem in dactylic hexameter, which opens "This is the forest primeval. The murmuring pines and the hemlocks." It follows an Acadian girl from the village of Grand-Pré whose people are expelled from Nova Scotia by the British in 1755.

**Gabriel Lajeunesse**
Evangeline's fiancé, separated from her during the expulsion of the Acadians. Evangeline searches for him across America for years and finally finds him, old and dying in an almshouse during an epidemic, in Philadelphia, where she works as a Sister of Mercy.

**"The Wreck of the Hesperus"**
A ballad in which a skipper ignores warnings (including a "golden ring" around the moon) and sails into a winter storm. He ties his young daughter to the mast to keep her from being swept away, but the schooner, named for the evening star, is wrecked "on the reef of Norman's Woe" and she is found dead, still lashed to the mast. In the poem she thinks "of Christ, who stilled the wave, / On the Lake of Galilee."

**"The Cross of Snow"**
A sonnet mourning Longfellow's second wife, Frances "Fanny" Appleton, who died in 1861 after her dress caught fire; Longfellow was burned trying to save her and grew his famous beard to hide the scars. It describes "a soul more white / Never through martyrdom of fire was led / To its repose" and ends with "the cross I wear upon my breast," comparing his grief to a cross of snow on a mountain that stays "changeless" through the seasons. It was found among his papers after his death.

**"The Village Blacksmith"**
A poem that opens "Under a spreading chestnut-tree / The village smithy stands." The blacksmith has "large and sinewy hands," hair "crisp, and black, and long," and goes on "toiling,—rejoicing,—sorrowing" through life, serving as a model of honest labor.

**"The Children's Hour"**
A domestic poem in which the speaker hears "the patter of little feet" as his three daughters, "Grave Alice, and laughing Allegra, / And Edith with golden hair," ambush him in his study. He calls them "blue-eyed banditti" and says he will keep them forever "in the dungeon / In the round-tower of my heart."

**The Courtship of Miles Standish**
A narrative poem set in early Plymouth Colony. The shy Puritan captain Miles Standish sends his friend John Alden to propose to Priscilla Mullins for him, and she replies, "Why don't you speak for yourself, John?" Alden and Priscilla eventually marry.

**Tales of a Wayside Inn**
A collection framed like The Canterbury Tales, beginning "One Autumn night, in Sudbury town," in which a group of travelers at an inn tell stories. It includes "Paul Revere's Ride" (the Landlord's Tale), "The Saga of King Olaf" about a Viking king, and the source of the phrase "ships that pass in the night."

**"A Psalm of Life"**
An inspirational poem that rejects the idea that "Life is but an empty dream," declaring "Life is real! Life is earnest! / And the grave is not its goal." It urges readers to leave "footprints on the sands of time."

**"The Skeleton in Armor" and "Excelsior"**
Two other short poems used as clues. "The Skeleton in Armor" was inspired by a skeleton found in Massachusetts believed to be a Viking's; the Viking ghost tells how he eloped with a "blue-eyed maid," fled to America, cried "Skoal!", and killed himself after she died. In "Excelsior," a youth climbs the Alps carrying a "banner with the strange device" and is found frozen to death, still grasping it. Longfellow also made the first American translation of Dante's Divine Comedy.

**Sabina's bowler hat**
Sabina is a Czech painter and Tomas's mistress. She wears a black bowler hat, often with nothing else on, during sex with Tomas and later with Franz. The hat belonged to her grandfather, and when her father died it was the only thing she wanted to inherit. Tereza also photographs her wearing it.

**"War on kitsch"**
Sabina declares war on kitsch, which the novel defines as an aesthetic ideal that denies the existence of shit and hides everything ugly about human life. She especially hates the "totalitarian kitsch" of Communist May Day parades. The novel's discussion of kitsch begins with Stalin's son Yakov, who died by throwing himself against an electric fence in a POW camp, and with the question of whether God has intestines.

**Tomas's Oedipus article**
Tomas, a gifted Prague surgeon, writes a letter to a newspaper comparing the Czech Communists to Oedipus. Oedipus blinded himself when he learned what he had done unknowingly, so Tomas argues that Communists who say they "didn't know" should still take responsibility. After the Soviet invasion, the Chief Surgeon and the authorities pressure him to sign a statement retracting it, and he refuses more than once.

**Tomas becomes a window washer**
Because he refuses to retract the article, Tomas can no longer work as a surgeon. He first works as a country doctor and then becomes a window washer in Prague. The job gives him more chances to seduce women.

**Karenin**
Karenin is Tomas and Tereza's dog. She is female but has a male name, taken from Anna Karenina's husband in Tolstoy's novel. On the collective farm she befriends a pig named Mefisto. She dies of a cancerous tumor on her leg after Tomas puts her down with an injection, and the novel's final part is called "Karenin's Smile."

**"Es muss sein!"**
This German phrase means "It must be!" It comes from the last movement of Beethoven's final string quartet (Op. 135), where it answers the question "Muss es sein?" ("Must it be?"). Tomas uses it to stand for necessity and fate. He says it to his boss in Zurich when he quits his job to follow Tereza back to occupied Prague, and he wonders whether his love for Tereza is his own "es muss sein."

**Franz and the Grand March in Cambodia**
Franz is a married Swiss professor in Geneva who becomes Sabina's lover. Longing to be part of the "Grand March" of history, he joins a protest march of Western intellectuals and celebrities to the Cambodian border, where they are turned back. An American actress bursts into tears during the march after being insulted. Soon afterward Franz is beaten by muggers in Bangkok and dies from his injuries.

**"A return after long wanderings"**
Franz's wife, Marie-Claude, has this inscription put on his gravestone. She takes charge of his body and treats his affair with a young student as a midlife crisis, imagining that he came back to her begging for forgiveness. The novel mocks her as the "Platonic ideal of a woman," and she declares that "Stendhal is a night author!"

**"He wanted the Kingdom of God on Earth"**
Simon, Tomas's estranged son from an earlier marriage, has this epitaph put on his father's grave. Simon is religious, and he is also the one who writes to Sabina to tell her that Tomas and Tereza have died.

**Death of Tomas and Tereza in a truck accident**
After moving to a collective farm in the countryside, Tomas and Tereza are killed when the brakes of their truck fail and they are crushed underneath it. The novel reveals their deaths early, through Simon's letter to Sabina, who then moves to California.

**Eternal return and "Einmal ist keinmal"**
The novel opens with Nietzsche's idea of eternal return, the idea that everything recurs endlessly, which would give life "weight." It contrasts this with Parmenides's division of the world into opposites, including lightness and heaviness, and asks whether heaviness is truly deplorable and lightness splendid. The German saying "Einmal ist keinmal" ("What happens once might as well not have happened at all") sums up the lightness of a life lived only once. Italo Calvino praises this quality of the novel in "Lightness," the first of his Six Memos for the Next Millennium.

**Tereza's photography**
Tereza first works as a waitress in a provincial town, where six coincidences ("fortuities") bring her and Tomas together, including Beethoven playing in the restaurant. In Prague, Sabina helps her move from the darkroom to working as a photographer. Tereza photographs the Soviet invasion of 1968, and she later worries that the police used her photos to identify protesters.

**"Dictionary of Misunderstood Words"**
This section of the novel defines words such as "woman," "music," and "cemetery." Each word means something different to Sabina and Franz, which shows why the two lovers cannot understand each other. It contains the line "if you're looking for infinity, just close your eyes."

**"He gave birth to two rolls and a bee"**
This is the inscription on Karenin's grave. It refers to Tereza's dream in which Karenin gives birth to two rolls (bread) and a bee.

**Tomas's "erotic friendships"**
Tomas is a compulsive womanizer who has slept with around two hundred women. He keeps his mistresses as "erotic friends" and claims his affairs do not change his love for his wife, Tereza. The novel calls him an "epic" rather than "lyrical" womanizer, and he searches each woman for the "one-millionth part" that makes her unique, which he believes appears only in bed.

**Rosa the Beautiful**
Rosa del Valle, famous for her green hair, dies in the novel's first chapter. She drinks poisoned brandy meant for her father, the Liberal Party Senate candidate Severo del Valle. She had been engaged to Esteban Trueba.

**Clara del Valle**
Rosa's clairvoyant younger sister, who foresaw Rosa's death and blames herself for predicting it. She falls silent for nine years afterward, then breaks her silence to announce she will marry Esteban Trueba, Rosa's former fiancé. She holds Friday sessions with the spiritualist Mora sisters around a three-legged table, against her father's wishes.

**Esteban Trueba**
The novel's patriarch and one of its narrators. He works in a mine to earn enough money to marry Rosa, then marries Clara after Rosa dies. He is violent and conservative, rapes peasant women including Pancha García, and dies in his granddaughter Alba's arms after writing his memoir.

**"Barrabás came to us by sea"**
The novel's opening line, describing the arrival of the huge dog Barrabás. Clara receives him after her Uncle Marcos dies. Barrabás is stabbed in the back and dies at Clara's engagement party; Esteban later has him made into a rug, and Clara faints on seeing it.

**Pedro Tercero García**
The son of the Tres Marías foreman, a revolutionary songwriter, Blanca Trueba's lover, and the father of Alba. When Esteban finds him with Blanca, he cuts off three of Pedro's fingers with an axe, and Pedro flees on horseback. Pedro and Blanca later escape the coup to Canada, where his songs about chickens and foxes are popular. Esteban later receives three fingers in the mail.

**Tres Marías**
The rural hacienda (estate) that Esteban rebuilds into a "model hacienda." It is the setting of his abuses of the peasants and of Blanca and Pedro Tercero's childhood romance. Its old man Pedro García rids the estate of an ant infestation and heals Esteban's broken bones after an earthquake.

**Count Jean de Satigny**
A French count who wants to start a chinchilla farm. He reveals Blanca's affair with Pedro Tercero, and Blanca is then forced to marry him. She leaves him after finding his pornographic photographs of their Indian servants.

**Alba Trueba**
Blanca's daughter and Esteban's granddaughter. She narrates the frame story, writing the family history while awaiting the birth of a child conceived by rape in a military prison. She joins student protests with Ana Díaz and is the lover of the revolutionary Miguel, who witnessed her birth from a closet. She is the last of four generations of women whose names mean "white" or "light": Nívea, Clara, Blanca, Alba.

**Tránsito Soto**
A prostitute whom Esteban meets at the Red Lantern brothel and lends money to. Years later, as a well-connected madam, she repays him by securing Alba's release from prison after the military coup.

**"Those who have always won will win again"**
The Conservative Party campaign slogan Esteban Trueba uses when he runs for the Senate. It contrasts with the earlier Liberal candidacy of Severo del Valle, which ends after the poisoning that kills Rosa.

**Clara's knocked-out teeth**
When Esteban learns of Blanca's affair, Clara defends her, and he strikes Clara, knocking out her front teeth. Clara never speaks to him again and moves out with Blanca.

**Nívea del Valle's head in a hatbox**
Clara's mother Nívea, a suffragette and mother of fifteen children, is decapitated in a car crash. Clara finds the head and keeps it in a hatbox under her bed, then goes into labor with the twins Jaime and Nicolás.

**Nicolás and the Institute of Union with Nothingness**
After returning from India, Clara's son Nicolás founds this spiritual institute and persuades his young niece Alba to shave her head. When he chants naked in front of the gates of Congress, Esteban has a heart attack. His brother Jaime, a doctor, performs an abortion for Nicolás's lover Amanda.

**Férula Trueba**
Esteban's devoted sister, whom he throws out of the house after finding her in bed with Clara. She curses him, saying his body and soul will shrivel and he will die like a dog.

**Uncle Marcos**
Clara's eccentric uncle, who courts his cousin by giving her a parrot with a foul vocabulary and vanishes in a homemade flying machine. After he dies, Clara inherits the dog Barrabás.

**Pride and Prejudice**
Austen's most famous novel (1813), which begins "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife." It follows the five Bennet sisters, whose estate is entailed away from the female line, as their mother tries to marry them off.

**Elizabeth Bennet and Fitzwilliam Darcy**
The quick-witted second Bennet daughter and the proud, wealthy owner of the Derbyshire estate Pemberley. Elizabeth rejects Darcy's insulting first proposal, but his letter afterward explains his past conduct, including Wickham's attempt to elope with his young sister Georgiana. While visiting Elizabeth's newly married friend Charlotte, Darcy remarks that "the far and the near must be relative." Elizabeth later accepts his second proposal.

**George Wickham and Lydia Bennet**
Wickham is a charming but dishonest militia officer who once tried to elope with Georgiana Darcy to get her fortune. He runs off with the reckless youngest Bennet sister, Lydia, which threatens the whole family's reputation. Darcy secretly pays Wickham's debts and bribes him to marry Lydia.

**Jane Bennet, Mr. Bingley, and Netherfield**
The gentle eldest Bennet sister, Jane, is courted by the amiable Charles Bingley, Darcy's friend, who rents Netherfield Park. Elizabeth walks three miles through the mud to nurse Jane when she falls ill there. At the Netherfield ball, Elizabeth endures two "dances of mortification" with Mr. Collins. Jane and Bingley are eventually engaged.

**Mr. Collins and Lady Catherine de Bourgh**
William Collins is the pompous clergyman cousin who will inherit the Bennets' estate. He reads Fordyce's Sermons aloud to the girls and endlessly praises his patroness, Darcy's aunt Lady Catherine de Bourgh.
