At his fortified cottage in Walworth he cares for his deaf father, "the Aged P" (Aged Parent). A small cannon called the Stinger is fired there every night at nine o'clock to please the old man.

**Miss Havisham's fire**
Miss Havisham's wedding dress catches fire when she stands too close to the hearth after begging Pip's forgiveness. Pip burns his hands rescuing her. She later dies of her injuries.

**Mr. Pumblechook**
Joe's pompous, greedy uncle, described with "a mouth like a fish" and "dull staring eyes." He takes Pip to Satis House for the first time. He constantly brags that he was the founder of Pip's fortunes. At a Christmas dinner he drinks brandy that Pip has diluted with tar-water.

**Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair**
Neruda's breakthrough 1924 collection, published when he was 19. It contains twenty numbered love poems followed by one final despairing poem, and it is by far the most common title clue and giveaway for him.

**"In you everything sank!"**
The refrain of "The Song of Despair," the closing poem of Twenty Love Poems. The speaker addresses a lost lover, calling her a "pit of debris" into which all his hopes fell.

**"Tonight I can write the saddest lines"**
The opening of Poem 20, the last of the twenty love poems, which comes just before "The Song of Despair." As examples of sad lines, the speaker offers "The night is starry" and "the night wind revolves in the sky and sings." The poem includes "She loved me, sometimes I loved her too" and "Love is so short, forgetting is so long," and it ends hoping this will be "the last pain that she makes me suffer."

**"It is the hour of departure"**
The other refrain of "The Song of Despair," which opens "The memory of you emerges from the night around me." The speaker, "deserted like the wharves at dawn," recalls the lover as a "cemetery of kisses" and says "There were thirst and hunger, and you were the fruit. / There were grief and the ruins, and you were the miracle."

**"Body of a Woman"**
Poem 1 of Twenty Love Poems, which begins "Body of a woman, white hills, white thighs, / you look like a world, lying in surrender." The speaker says he was "alone like a tunnel" and "forged you like a weapon" to survive, and his "rough peasant's body" digs into hers.

**Elemental Odes**
Neruda's 1950s collections of odes in short, plain lines that celebrate everyday things. Subjects include the onion, which can "make us cry without hurting us"; tomatoes, which "invade the kitchen" in summer; conger chowder; artichokes; socks; and a large tuna in the market.

**"Ode to My Socks"**
An elemental ode about a pair of woolen socks knitted for him by Maru Mori. He compares his feet in them to "two fish," "two long sharks," "two immense blackbirds," and "two cannons," and ends by saying that "beauty is twice beauty / and what is good is doubly good" when it comes to two wool socks in winter.

**"White Bee"**
A poem from Twenty Love Poems that begins "White bee, you buzz in my soul, drunk with honey" and repeats the refrain "Ah you who are silent!" The speaker calls himself "the one without hope, the word without echoes" and tells the beloved, "In my barren land you are the final rose."

**Canto General and "The Heights of Macchu Picchu"**
Neruda's 1950 epic history of the Americas, which includes sections such as "The Conquistadors," "The Liberators," and "America, I Do Not Invoke Your Name in Vain." He wrote much of it in hiding after the Chilean government persecuted him as a Communist, before fleeing over the Andes in 1949. Its most famous section, "The Heights of Macchu Picchu," begins by moving "from air to air, like an empty net" and ends with "Arise to birth with me, my brother," asking the dead workers to "speak through my words and my blood."

**"Ode to the Artichoke"**
An elemental ode that pictures the "tender-hearted" artichoke as a soldier "dressed as a warrior" in armor among the frail vegetables of the garden. At the end, María buys it at the market along with shoes, a white cabbage, and a bottle of vinegar, and cooks and eats it leaf by leaf.

**"Every Day You Play"**
Poem 14 of Twenty Love Poems, which opens "Every day you play with the light of the universe." The speaker offers to bring "rustic baskets of kisses" and closes with "I want to do with you what spring does with the cherry trees."

**"United Fruit Company"**
A political poem from Canto General attacking the American fruit company. It begins with a trumpet sounding and Jehovah parceling out the world to "Coca-Cola Inc., Anaconda, Ford Motors," while United Fruit takes the "central coast" of the Americas, the "Banana Republics." It mocks the dictators it props up as flies, accusing the company of having "abolished free will."

**"A Dog Has Died"**
A late poem that begins with the speaker burying his dead dog in the garden "next to a rusted old machine," adding that "some day I'll join him right there." Though he has "never believed in any promised heaven in the sky," he believes "in a heaven I'll never enter."

**"Walking Around"**
A poem from Neruda's surrealist collection Residence on Earth, opening "It so happens I am sick of being a man." The speaker fantasizes that it would be marvelous "to terrify a law clerk with a cut lily, / or kill a nun with a blow on the ear."

**"Ah Vastness of Pines"**
Poem 3 of Twenty Love Poems, which opens "Ah vastness of pines, murmur of waves breaking." The speaker tells the beloved, "In you the rivers sing and my soul flees in them as you desire."

**Battle Royal**
In the first chapter, the narrator and other Black teenagers are forced to watch a "magnificent blonde" with an American flag tattooed on her stomach dance. They are then blindfolded and made to box each other for the entertainment of the town's white leaders. Afterward the boys scramble for coins on an electrified rug. The narrator then gives his graduation speech and slips by saying "social equality" instead of "social responsibility." He is rewarded with a briefcase and a scholarship to a Black college.

**Ras the Exhorter (Ras the Destroyer)**
Ras is a West Indian Black nationalist street speaker in Harlem who attacks the Brotherhood for working with white people. Near the end he becomes "Ras the Destroyer," riding a horse with a spear and shield during a Harlem race riot. The narrator throws Ras's own spear at him and it goes through his jaw.

**Dr. Bledsoe**
Bledsoe is the president of the narrator's college and appears to bow to white people while holding power for himself. He expels the narrator after the Mr. Norton disaster. He sends him to New York with sealed "letters of recommendation" that secretly tell employers to keep the boy "running." The narrator later dreams of a document that says the same thing.

**Mr. Norton and the Golden Day**
Norton is a rich white trustee of the college who sees the narrator as his "fate." While driving him, the narrator takes Norton to Jim Trueblood's cabin. When Norton faints, the narrator brings him to the Golden Day, a run-down bar and brothel full of mentally ill Black veterans. Norton is hurt there during a fight.

**Jim Trueblood**
Trueblood is a Black sharecropper who got his own daughter, Matty Lou, pregnant; his wife Kate was pregnant at the same time. He tells Norton about a dream in which a naked white woman tries to keep him "out of the clock," which he had just before sleeping with his daughter. Showing Norton this man is the main reason the narrator is expelled.

**The Brotherhood and Brother Jack**
The Brotherhood is a communist-style political group in Harlem led by Brother Jack. Jack recruits the narrator as a speaker. At his first rally the narrator speaks about the "dispossessed," and members criticize the speech for not being "scientific." In one meeting, Jack's glass eye falls into a glass of water, which shows he cannot really see clearly. The narrator later dreams that Jack castrates him.

**Liberty Paints and Lucius Brockway**
The narrator gets a factory job at Liberty Paints. Its famous "Optic White" paint is made by mixing in ten drops of black liquid, a symbol of race in America. In the boiler room he works for Lucius Brockway, an old Black worker who loses his dentures in a fight because he thinks the narrator is a union man after his job. Brockway sets off a boiler explosion that injures the narrator.

**Electroshock therapy at the factory hospital**
After the explosion, doctors give the narrator electroshock treatment inside a machine, a scene often read as a kind of rebirth. When they show him a card asking "What is your name?", he cannot remember his own name or his mother's. He thinks of folk characters like Buckeye the Rabbit (Brer Rabbit).

**1,369 light bulbs and Monopolated Light and Power**
In the prologue, the narrator lives hidden in a forgotten cellar of a whites-only building. He has wired 1,369 light bulbs and powers them with electricity stolen from Monopolated Light and Power. He ends up there after falling into an open manhole while running from men who want to know what is in his briefcase.

**Tod Clifton and the Sambo dolls**
Tod Clifton is a handsome young Brotherhood leader in Harlem who leaves the group, "plunging outside history." The narrator finds him on the street selling dancing paper Sambo dolls, a racist caricature. A police officer shoots Clifton dead. The narrator's speech at his funeral leads to his break with the Brotherhood.

**Rinehart**
Rinehart is never seen in the novel. He is a gambler, numbers runner, pimp, and reverend all at once. When the narrator puts on dark glasses and a wide hat, people keep mistaking him for Rinehart. This shows him how easily identity can change.

**Sybil**
Sybil is the drunk white wife of a Brotherhood member. The narrator seduces her to get information, choosing her over Jack's mistress Emma. Sybil fantasizes about being raped by a Black man. The narrator writes "Sybil, you were raped by Santa Claus. Surprise" on her stomach in lipstick.

**Mary Rambo**
Mary is a kind older Black woman in Harlem who takes in the narrator after the paint factory injury. She lets him stay without paying rent. He later lies to her about where he got the money to pay her back.

**Opening and closing lines**
The prologue opens: "I am an invisible man," and he says he is not a spook or a "Hollywood-movie ectoplasm." He is "of flesh and bone, fiber and liquids—and I might even be said to possess a mind." He is invisible "simply because people refuse to see me." The novel ends: "Who knows but that, on the lower frequencies, I speak for you?"

**Louis Armstrong's "(What Did I Do to Be So) Black and Blue"**
In the prologue, the narrator smokes marijuana and listens to this Armstrong recording, and his sense of time shifts. He sinks into imagined levels of the past and talks with an old slave woman who both loved and poisoned her master. He says he wants five record players all playing the song at once.

**"The Tyger"**
Blake's most famous poem and the giveaway in nearly every question. It opens "Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night" and asks "What immortal hand or eye / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?", wondering what "hammer," "chain," "furnace," and "anvil" could have made the beast; when "the stars threw down their spears / And water'd heaven with their tears," the speaker asks, "Did he smile his work to see? / Did he who made the Lamb make thee?"

**Songs of Innocence and of Experience**
Blake's 1794 combined collection of illustrated poems, showing "the two contrary states of the human soul." Many poems in the gentle Songs of Innocence (1789) have darker counterparts in Songs of Experience, as "The Lamb" is paired with "The Tyger"; Blake engraved, printed, and hand-colored the books himself.

**"The Lamb"**
The Songs of Innocence counterpart to "The Tyger," in which a child asks the lamb "Little Lamb who made thee / Dost thou know who made thee?" The creator gave the lamb "clothing of delight, / Softest clothing wooly bright" and a tender voice "Making all the vales rejoice," and the child answers that the maker is Christ, who "calls himself a Lamb," ending "Little Lamb God bless thee."

**"The Chimney Sweeper" (Songs of Innocence)**
A poem that begins "When my mother died I was very young," spoken by a boy sold into chimney sweeping before he "could scarcely cry 'weep!'" His friend Tom Dacre cries when his curly hair is shaved, then dreams of sweeps "lock'd up in coffins of black" whom an angel frees to run "down a green plain"; the poem ends with the sadly ironic line "So if all do their duty, they need not fear harm."

**"The Chimney Sweeper" (Songs of Experience)**
The bitter companion poem, which opens with "A little black thing among the snow, / Crying 'weep, 'weep, in notes of woe!" The child says his parents, because he was "happy upon the heath," "clothed me in the clothes of death" and have gone to church to praise "God & his Priest & King / Who make up a heaven of our misery."

**"London"**
A Songs of Experience poem in which the speaker wanders "thro' each charter'd street" and sees in every face "Marks of weakness, marks of woe," hearing "the mind-forg'd manacles." The chimney-sweeper's cry appalls "every blackning Church," "the hapless Soldiers sigh / Runs in blood down Palace walls," and "the youthful Harlots curse" blights "the Marriage hearse."

**"A Poison Tree"**
A Songs of Experience poem that begins "I was angry with my friend: / I told my wrath, my wrath did end. / I was angry with my foe: / I told it not, my wrath did grow." The speaker waters his anger with tears and suns it "with smiles, / And with soft deceitful wiles" until it bears "an apple bright," and in the morning he sees his foe "outstretch'd beneath the tree."

**"And did those feet in ancient time" ("Jerusalem")**
The short poem in the preface to Blake's epic Milton, asking whether Christ once walked in England and whether Jerusalem was built "Among these dark Satanic Mills." The speaker demands "Bring me my Bow of burning gold: / Bring me my Arrows of desire" and "my Chariot of fire"; set to music by Hubert Parry, it is now the hymn "Jerusalem."

**Milton: A Poem**
One of Blake's prophetic books, in which the spirit of the poet John Milton returns from eternity to correct his errors. Milton falls like a comet and enters the narrator's left foot, and his female counterpart Ololon, who appears as "a Virgin of twelve years," descends to find him.

**The Marriage of Heaven and Hell**
A satirical prose-and-verse work responding to the mystic Emanuel Swedenborg. It claims Milton "was a true Poet and of the Devil's party without knowing it," and its "Proverbs of Hell" include "The road of excess leads to the palace of wisdom," "Exuberance is Beauty," and "Drive your cart and your plow over the bones of the dead" (the source of Olga Tokarczuk's novel title); its line "If the doors of perception were cleansed" gave Aldous Huxley the title The Doors of Perception.

**"The Sick Rose"**
A short, enigmatic Songs of Experience poem beginning "O Rose thou art sick." An "invisible worm, / That flies in the night" finds the rose's bed of "crimson joy," and "his dark secret love / Does thy life destroy."

**The Four Zoas, Albion, Urizen, and Los**
Blake's private mythology, developed in his prophetic books such as Vala, or The Four Zoas. The primeval man Albion falls and splits into four Zoas: Urizen (reason), Luvah (passion), Tharmas (the senses), and Urthona, whose fallen form is Los, the blacksmith-like figure of imagination.

**Other prophetic books (America, Visions of the Daughters of Albion, Europe)**
In America a Prophecy, the fiery rebel Orc embodies the American Revolution, and in Visions of the Daughters of Albion, Oothoon is called "the soft soul of America." Blake's famous image The Ancient of Days, the frontispiece to Europe a Prophecy, shows the bearded Urizen reaching down with a compass to measure the world.

**"Earth's Answer"**
The second poem of Songs of Experience, replying to its "Introduction," which calls on Earth to wake. Earth "rais'd up her head / From the darkness dread & drear" and pleads, "Break this heavy chain, / That does freeze my bones around."

**Other Songs (The Clod and the Pebble, Infant Joy and Infant Sorrow, Lyca)**
In "The Clod and the Pebble," the clay clod describes a selfless love that "seeketh not itself to please" and builds "a Heaven in Hells despair," while the pebble praises a selfish love that "builds a Hell in Heavens despite." "Infant Joy" presents a two-day-old baby named Joy, while in "Infant Sorrow" a "bound and weary" baby "thought best / To sulk upon my mothers breast"; other clue poems include "The Little Girl Lost" and "The Little Girl Found" (about Lyca), "Holy Thursday," "The Fly" ("Am not I / A fly like thee?"), and "A Divine Image" ("Cruelty has a Human Heart / And Jealousy a Human Face").

**"The Legend of Sleepy Hollow"**
Irving's most famous story, set in a Dutch settlement near Tarrytown, New York. The superstitious schoolmaster Ichabod Crane courts the heiress Katrina Van Tassel, then vanishes after being chased by the Headless Horseman one night.

**Ichabod Crane, Brom Bones, and Katrina Van Tassel**
Ichabod Crane is the lanky Connecticut schoolmaster in "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow." His rival for the wealthy Katrina Van Tassel is the strong local prankster Brom Bones (Abraham Van Brunt), who marries Katrina after Ichabod disappears and seems to know more about the incident than he admits.

**The Headless Horseman and the smashed pumpkin**
The ghost of a Hessian soldier whose head was shot off by a cannonball in the Revolutionary War, said to ride at night searching for it. After he throws his "head" at Ichabod, only Ichabod's hat and a shattered pumpkin are found the next morning, implying Brom Bones played the Horseman.

**"Rip Van Winkle"**
A story about a lazy, good-natured Dutch villager in the Catskill (Kaatskill) Mountains who escapes his nagging wife and falls asleep for twenty years. He wakes to find the American Revolution has happened, and in confusion he declares himself a loyal subject of King George III at an election, nearly causing a riot.

**Henry Hudson's crew playing ninepins**
While wandering with his dog Wolf, Rip meets strange, silent men in old Dutch clothing playing ninepins in a mountain hollow, revealed to be the ghosts of Henry (Hendrick) Hudson's crew; the rumbling of their game is said to be the thunder of the Catskills. Rip drinks their liquor and falls into his twenty-year sleep.

**The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon**
Irving's 1819–1820 collection, published under the pen name Geoffrey Crayon, containing both "Rip Van Winkle" and "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow." It made him the first American writer to gain wide fame in Europe.

**Diedrich Knickerbocker**
Irving's fictional Dutch historian persona, the narrator of his satirical 1809 A History of New York, which first made him famous; both Sleepy Hollow and Rip Van Winkle are claimed to come from his papers. That History describes the Dutch governor Wouter Van Twiller as "exactly five feet six inches in height, and six feet five inches in circumference." Irving also wrote early pieces as Jonathan Oldstyle.

**"The Devil and Tom Walker"**
A Faust-like story from Tales of a Traveller in which the miserly Tom Walker, after kicking a skull with a tomahawk lodged in it in a swamp, meets the Devil ("Old Scratch"), who has marked trees with the names of the colony's great men. He sells his soul for Captain Kidd's treasure and becomes a usurer, but is carried off by the Devil when he leaves his Bible at home.

**Tom Walker's wife**
Tom's greedy wife goes into the swamp to bargain with Old Scratch herself, taking the household silver in her apron. She never returns, and Tom finds only her apron containing a heart and liver hanging in a tree.

**Tales of the Alhambra**
A collection of sketches and Moorish legends Irving wrote while staying in the Alhambra palace in Granada, Spain. It includes "Legend of the Arabian Astrologer," about King Aben Habuz and a magic weathervane warrior, as well as pieces like "Mementos of Boabdil" and "The Court of Lions"; Irving's guide was Mateo Ximenes.

**Gunpowder and Major André's tree**
Gunpowder is the old plow horse Ichabod borrows to ride to the Van Tassel party; it stubbornly refuses to cross the bridge as the Horseman approaches. On his way home Ichabod passes the giant tulip tree linked to the captured British spy Major John André.

**Dame Van Winkle and Nicholas Vedder**
On waking, Rip learns that his shrewish wife has died after she "broke a blood-vessel in a fit of passion" at a New England peddler. Nicholas Vedder was the village innkeeper whose opinions could be read from how he puffed his pipe, and the inn's portrait of King George has been repainted as George Washington.

**Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus**
Irving's 1828 romanticized biography of Columbus, written while in Spain. It helped spread the myth that educated medieval Europeans believed the Earth was flat. Irving later served as U.S. Minister to Spain and also wrote A Chronicle of the Conquest of Granada.

**Bracebridge Hall and Christmas**
Irving's Christmas sketches about the English country estate Bracebridge Hall (in The Sketch Book and the follow-up book Bracebridge Hall) helped shape the modern American celebration of Christmas.

**Other tales: "The Adventure of the German Student" and "Kidd the Pirate"**
In "The Adventure of the German Student," Gottfried Wolfgang spends the night in Paris with a woman who turns out to be a guillotine victim. In "Kidd the Pirate," the discovery of an old Spanish pistol while fishing leads to stories about Captain Kidd's buried treasure.

**Ulysses and Leopold Bloom**
Joyce's 1922 modernist masterpiece, which follows the Jewish advertising canvasser Leopold Bloom as he wanders Dublin on a single day, June 16, 1904 (now celebrated as "Bloomsday"). Its 18 episodes, grouped into three parts, parallel Homer's Odyssey, and it makes heavy use of stream of consciousness.

**Molly Bloom's soliloquy, "yes I said yes I will Yes"**
The final episode of Ulysses, "Penelope," is a nearly unpunctuated stream-of-consciousness monologue by Bloom's wife Molly. In bed, she muses about her affair that afternoon with Hugh "Blazes" Boylan and remembers accepting Leopold's proposal, ending with "yes I said yes I will Yes."

**"The Dead" and Gabriel Conroy**
The final and longest story in Dubliners. At a party, the tenor Bartell D'Arcy sings "The Lass of Aughrim," which reminds Gabriel Conroy's wife Gretta of Michael Furey, a boy who loved her and died young ("I think he died for me"). Gabriel has an epiphany as he watches the snow "faintly falling... upon all the living and the dead," including Furey's grave.

**The Morkan sisters' party**
The setting of "The Dead": the annual Christmas-season dance held by Gabriel's aunts Kate and Julia Morkan and their niece Mary Jane. There, the nationalist Molly Ivors teases Gabriel as a "West Briton" for writing reviews for a pro-British newspaper, and Gabriel worries whether to quote Robert Browning in his after-dinner speech.

**Stephen Dedalus and Buck Mulligan**
Joyce's alter ego, the hero of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man and a central figure in Ulysses. Ulysses opens with "Stately, plump Buck Mulligan" shaving atop the Martello tower where Stephen lives. In "Nestor," Stephen teaches a history class on Pyrrhus attended by the ugly student Cyril Sargent. He tells Mr. Deasy that God is "a shout in the street" and that "history is a nightmare from which I am trying to awake."

**Other episodes of Ulysses: "Ithaca," "Circe," "Nausicaa"**
"Ithaca" is written as a question-and-answer catechism describing Bloom and Stephen's return to Bloom's home at 7 Eccles Street. "Circe" is written as a play set in Dublin's red-light district: Bloom hallucinates turning into a woman dominated by "Bello" (the brothel-keeper Bella Cohen), rescues Stephen, and sees the ghost of his dead son Rudy. In the controversial "Nausicaa," Bloom watches Gerty MacDowell on the beach. Another episode is "Lotus-Eaters."

**Father Arnall's hell sermon**
In A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, Stephen goes on a religious retreat where Father Arnall preaches terrifying sermons on death, judgment, and the torments of Hell. Overcome with guilt over his visits to prostitutes, Stephen confesses and briefly becomes fervently devout, before ultimately rejecting the Church to become an artist.

**"Araby"**
A Dubliners story in which a boy on North Richmond Street becomes infatuated with Mangan's sister and promises to bring her a gift from the Araby bazaar. His uncle comes home late and gives him a florin, and he arrives as the bazaar is closing. He sees himself as "a creature driven and derided by vanity," and his eyes burn "with anguish and anger."

**Opening and childhood of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man**
Joyce's 1916 semi-autobiographical novel opens with a baby-talk story: "Once upon a time... there was a moocow coming down along the road and this moocow... met a nicens little boy named baby tuckoo." At Clongowes Wood College, the bully Wells shoulders Stephen into a cesspool (the "square ditch"). At Christmas dinner, Dante Riordan and Mr. Casey argue bitterly over the fall of Charles Stewart Parnell.

**Stephen Hero, the villanelle, and Emma**
Stephen Hero was Joyce's earlier draft of Portrait, published posthumously. In Portrait, Stephen writes a villanelle for his beloved Emma that repeats "Are you not weary of ardent ways?" Earlier, rumors spread that some Clongowes boys ran away because they stole altar wine from the sacristy or were caught "smugging."

**Finnegans Wake and "riverrun"**
Joyce's final, dreamlike novel (1939), written in a punning language drawing on dozens of languages. It begins mid-sentence with "riverrun, past Eve and Adam's... by a commodius vicus of recirculation back to Howth Castle and Environs." The book's unfinished last sentence loops back to this opening.

**HCE, ALP, and "Three quarks for Muster Mark"**
Finnegans Wake centers on the Dublin publican H. C. Earwicker (Humphrey Chimpden Earwicker, whose initials recur as "Here Comes Everybody" and "Howth Castle and Environs") and his wife Anna Livia Plurabelle (ALP), who is also the River Liffey. The line "Three quarks for Muster Mark" gave physicist Murray Gell-Mann the name "quark."

**"A Painful Case" and "Ivy Day in the Committee Room"**
In "A Painful Case," the solitary James Duffy breaks off a friendship with Mrs. Emily Sinico and later reads in the newspaper that she has died. In "Ivy Day in the Committee Room," canvassers for the mayoral candidate Richard Tierney gather on the anniversary of Parnell's death, and Joe Hynes is accused of spying for Colgan.

**Other stories in Dubliners**
The 15-story collection (1914) opens with "The Sisters," in which a boy deals with the death of the priest Father Flynn. In "An Encounter," a strange old man says boys who talk to girls should be whipped. In "A Little Cloud," Little Chandler is shaken by his successful friend Ignatius Gallaher. In "Clay," the laundress Maria sings the same verse of "I Dreamt that I Dwelt" twice after a Halloween game. Other stories include "Eveline" and "After the Race," in which Jimmy Doyle tries to fit in with Charles Segouin and his friends.

**Chamber Music**
Joyce's first book, a 1907 collection of 36 love poems. One of his poems was included in Ezra Pound's anthology Des Imagistes.

**If on a winter's night a traveler**
Calvino's 1979 metafictional novel, which opens "You are about to begin reading Italo Calvino's new novel." The odd-numbered chapters are told in the second person and follow "You, the Reader," who keeps finding that the book he has started is defective or unfinished. The even-numbered chapters are the opening chapters of ten different novels, each of which breaks off at a moment of suspense.

**Ludmilla**
The "Other Reader," a woman the Reader meets in a bookstore when he goes to exchange his defective copy of the book. They chase the missing novels together, and the book ends with the Reader and Ludmilla married, reading in bed side by side.

**Ermes Marana**
A fraudulent translator and literary forger who founds the Organization of Apocryphal Power. He deliberately splices together and falsifies manuscripts, which is why the Reader can never finish any book. He is driven by jealousy of Ludmilla, who was once his lover, and the Reader follows his trail to the revolution-torn country of Ataguitania. One novel he "translates" is Looks Down in the Gathering Shadow, credited to the fictional Bertrand Vandervelde.

**Professor Uzzi-Tuzii and Cimmeria**
Uzzi-Tuzii is a university professor and the last remaining expert in the literature of Cimmeria, a fictional and now vanished country. He identifies one of the interrupted novels as the Cimmerian Outside the town of Malbork. In the novel Cimmeria was absorbed by its neighbor Cimbria, and rival scholars argue over which country a text belongs to.

**Silas Flannery**
A blocked Irish thriller writer in If on a winter's night a traveler, whose diary forms one chapter. He watches a woman (Ludmilla) reading through a telescope, thinks about copying out Crime and Punishment word for word, is visited by UFO enthusiasts, and is told that a computer could finish his novel In a network of lines that enlace.

**Invisible Cities**
Calvino's 1972 book, framed as conversations between the Venetian traveler Marco Polo and the Mongol emperor Kublai Khan. Polo describes 55 imaginary cities, all named after women, and arranges them in categories such as "thin cities," "hidden cities," "continuous cities," "cities and memory," and "cities and the dead." The two men at first communicate through gestures and objects, without a common language.

**Individual Invisible Cities and "something about Venice"**
Polo admits that "every time I describe a city I am saying something about Venice." Frequently clued cities include Diomira (with sixty silver domes), Octavia (a spider-web city strung across a chasm), Theodora (where exterminated creatures return), Melania (whose people keep playing stock dramatic roles), and Argia (filled with earth instead of air). The book also contains the line "it is not the voice that commands the story: it is the ear."

**Cosmicomics and Qfwfq**
A 1965 collection of whimsical stories, each starting from a scientific fact about the universe. Most are narrated by Qfwfq, an ageless being who has existed since the beginning of the universe and taken many forms. He returns in the follow-up collection t zero. Other stories include "At Daybreak" (in which Granny Bb'b recalls when matter was uniformly scattered), "Without Colors" (in which the narrator's love Ayl flees when colors appear), and "The Aquatic Uncle" (about a fish relative who refuses to leave the sea for land).

**"The Distance of the Moon"**
The first story of Cosmicomics. When the Moon was very close to the Earth, people rowed out to the Zinc Cliffs and used ladders to climb up and gather "Moon-milk," a kind of cheese. Qfwfq loves Mrs. Vhd Vhd, but she loves his deaf cousin, who is the best at the task. She ends up stranded on the Moon as it moves away from the Earth.

**"All at One Point"**
A Cosmicomics story set when all matter in the universe was packed into a single point. Mrs. Ph(i)Nk₀ generously cries that she would love to make them all some noodles, and that wish to make room for kneading pasta sets off the Big Bang.

**The Baron in the Trees**
Part of Calvino's Our Ancestors trilogy. In 1767, twelve-year-old Cosimo Piovasco di Rondò refuses to eat a dish of snails cooked by his sister Battista and climbs into the trees, vowing never to come down. He spends the rest of his life there, has a love affair with Viola, and finally vanishes by grabbing the rope of a passing hot-air balloon, so no body is ever found. The story is narrated by his brother Biagio.

**The Cloven Viscount**
The first novel of Our Ancestors. Viscount Medardo of Terralba is split in half by a cannonball during a war against the Turks. The two halves return separately as a cruel "Bad 'Un" and a sickeningly virtuous "Good 'Un," who duel over the peasant girl Pamela and are finally sewn back together.

**The Nonexistent Knight**
The third novel of Our Ancestors, about Agilulf, a paladin of Charlemagne who is an empty suit of white armor held together only by willpower and devotion to rules. He saves the maiden Sofronia, and his squire Gurduloo is his opposite, a man with a body but no sense of self.

**The Path to the Nest of Spiders**
Calvino's 1947 debut novel, about the Italian partisan resistance in World War II. The orphan Pin, whose sister is a prostitute called "the Dark Girl of Long Alley," steals a pistol from a German sailor who is one of her customers and hides it at a secret place where spiders nest. Jailed, he meets the young Communist partisan Red Wolf, then joins the ragtag band of the commander Dritto, who betrays the unit by sleeping with the cook's wife. At the end Pin befriends the partisan known as Cousin.

**Mr. Palomar**
Calvino's last novel (1983), made up of short meditations by Mr. Palomar as he tries to observe the world precisely. Famous scenes include his watching a gecko on the glass of his terrace from below so that its insides are visible, his trying to "read" a single wave, and his trips to the zoo, where he watches an albino gorilla.

**Inspector Javert drowns himself in the Seine**
Javert is the police inspector who hunts Jean Valjean for decades. After Valjean spares his life at the barricades and Javert later lets Valjean go, Javert cannot reconcile mercy with his rigid belief in the law, so he throws himself into the Seine River.

**Bishop Myriel's silver candlesticks**
Bishop Myriel, called "Monseigneur Bienvenu," shelters Valjean, who then steals his silverware. When police bring Valjean back, Myriel says the silver was a gift and adds two silver candlesticks, which sets Valjean on the path to redemption. Myriel had earlier given his mansion to be used as a hospital.

**Friends of the ABC**
This is a student revolutionary group led by Enjolras, and Marius and the elderly Mabeauf are among those who join them. Its members build barricades during the June Rebellion of 1832, which breaks out after General Lamarque's death. Almost all of them are killed, but Marius survives.

**Fantine sells her hair and front teeth**
Fantine is abandoned by her lover Félix Tholomyès and leaves her daughter Cosette with the Thénardiers. She is fired from her factory job, sells her hair and front teeth to keep paying them, and becomes a prostitute. She dies of shock when Javert reveals that Monsieur Madeleine is Valjean, and Valjean promises to look after Cosette.

**Gavroche shot while collecting cartridges**
Gavroche is the Thénardiers' son and a Paris street boy. During the barricade fighting, he is shot dead while collecting ammunition from fallen soldiers. Earlier, he shelters two little boys inside a giant plaster elephant statue without knowing they are his own brothers.

**Éponine saves Marius**
Éponine is the Thénardiers' daughter and loves Marius. Disguised as a boy, she lures him to the barricades, then blocks a shot aimed at him and is the first to die at the barricades. Earlier, she proves she can write by writing "The cops are here" on a sheet of paper.

**Petit Gervais's coin**
Soon after leaving the bishop, Valjean steps on a coin dropped by Petit Gervais, a Savoyard boy, and refuses to give it back. The boy runs away, and Valjean immediately regrets the theft. Years later he throws the coin into a fireplace.

**Patron-Minette and the Gorbeau House ambush**
Patron-Minette is a gang of four criminals: Montparnasse, Babet, Gueulemer, and Claquesous. Thénardier recruits them to rob Valjean at the Gorbeau House, where the Thénardiers live under the false name Jondrette. The Thénardiers have their daughter Azelma punch a window and cut her hand to draw sympathy, and Javert captures the gang during the ambush.

**Monsieur Madeleine**
This is the alias Valjean uses in Montreuil-sur-Mer. There, he grows rich from a new method of making jet beads and becomes mayor. While deciding whether to confess, his hair turns white. He then reveals his true identity in court to free Champmathieu, an apple thief who has been mistaken for him.

**Nineteen years in prison for stealing a loaf of bread**
Valjean steals bread to feed his sister's starving children and spends 19 years as a convict, partly because his escape attempts lengthen his sentence. After his release, inns turn him away because his yellow passport marks him as an ex-convict.

**Carrying Marius through the Paris sewers**
After the barricades fall, Valjean carries the unconscious Marius through the sewers of Paris. Thénardier takes 30 francs to unlock the sewer gate for him. Later, Thénardier unknowingly reveals to Marius that it was Valjean who saved him.

**Thénardier at Waterloo**
The novel includes long digressions, including one on the Battle of Waterloo. While robbing corpses after the battle, Thénardier accidentally saves Colonel Georges Pontmercy, Marius's father. Thénardier later mistreats the young Cosette at his inn, and at the end of the novel Marius pays him to move to America with Azelma, where he becomes a slave trader.

**Fauchelevent and the cart**
As Monsieur Madeleine, Valjean lifts a heavy cart to save Fauchelevent from being crushed. Fauchelevent later becomes a gardener at a Paris convent and repays the favor by sheltering Valjean and Cosette there. To leave the convent and come back in openly, Valjean is carried out in a coffin.

**Rescue of a sailor in a ship's rigging**
After being sent back to prison, Valjean saves a sailor caught in a ship's rigging at Toulon. He then falls into the sea and lets everyone believe he has drowned, which lets him escape and rescue Cosette from the Thénardiers.

**"One Day More" and "I Dreamed a Dream"**
These songs come from the musical adaptation by Claude-Michel Schönberg and Alain Boublil. "One Day More" closes Act One. Fantine sings "I Dreamed a Dream," young Cosette sings "Castle on a Cloud," and the students sing "Red and Black." In "Confrontation," Valjean faces Javert.

**"Lines Composed a Few Miles Above Tintern Abbey"**
Wordsworth's meditative poem from 1798 about returning to the ruined abbey on the River Wye in Wales. It opens "Five years have past; five summers, with the length / Of five long winters!" The speaker "repose[s] / Here, under this dark sycamore," looks at "steep and lofty cliffs" and "hedge-rows," and imagines "some Hermit's cave." It ends by addressing his "dear, dear Sister," Dorothy.

**"I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud"**
Wordsworth's most famous lyric, often called "Daffodils." The speaker, wandering like a cloud that "floats on high o'er vales and hills," comes upon "a host, of golden daffodils," "Continuous as the stars that shine / And twinkle on the milky way," "tossing their heads in sprightly dance." He says "A poet could not but be gay, / In such a jocund company," and later the flowers "flash upon that inward eye / Which is the bliss of solitude," so that his heart "dances with the daffodils."

**Lyrical Ballads**
The 1798 collection Wordsworth published with Samuel Taylor Coleridge, often seen as the start of English Romanticism. Tintern Abbey closes the first edition; the 1800 edition added Wordsworth's famous Preface on poetry written in "the real language of men."

**Lucy poems**
A group of short lyrics about a mysterious girl named Lucy who has died, possibly inspired by Dorothy. They include "She dwelt among the untrodden ways," "Strange fits of passion have I known," "I travelled among unknown men," and "A slumber did my spirit seal," in which she "seemed a thing that could not feel / The touch of earthly years" and is now "Rolled round in earth's diurnal course."

**"The World Is Too Much With Us"**
A sonnet attacking materialism: "Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers; / Little we see in Nature that is ours; / We have given our hearts away, a sordid boon!" Because we are "out of tune" with nature, the speaker would "rather be / A Pagan suckled in a creed outworn," so he could feel less forlorn and see Proteus or "hear old Triton blow his wreathèd horn."

**"Ode: Intimations of Immortality from Recollections of Early Childhood"**
An 11-stanza ode about losing the visionary perception of childhood. Famous lines include "Whither is fled the visionary gleam? / Where is it now, the glory and the dream?", "Our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting," and "nothing can bring back the hour / Of splendour in the grass, of glory in the flower."

**Dorothy Wordsworth**
William's sister and close companion, whose Grasmere Journal describes the daffodils "tossing and reeling and dancing" that inspired "I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud." She is the "dear, dear Sister" of Tintern Abbey, and in "The Sparrow's Nest" William says of her, "She gave me eyes, she gave me ears; / And humble cares, and delicate fears."

**"London, 1802"**
A sonnet opening "Milton! thou shouldst be living at this hour: / England hath need of thee," lamenting the moral decline of England. G. K. Chesterton parodied it in a sonnet to Stilton cheese.

**"Composed upon Westminster Bridge"**
A sonnet about London at dawn that begins "Earth has not anything to show more fair." It ends with the city at rest: "Ne'er saw I, never felt, a calm so deep!" and "all that mighty heart is lying still!"

**The Prelude**
Wordsworth's long autobiographical poem in blank verse, subtitled "Growth of a Poet's Mind." Begun in 1798–99 and published after his death in 1850, it was meant as an introduction to a never-finished philosophical epic called The Recluse.

**The Excursion**
A long poem published in 1814 as the only completed part of The Recluse. It features characters called the Wanderer, the Solitary, and the Pastor. William Blake reportedly claimed that reading a passage from it gave him a bowel complaint that nearly killed him.

**"The Solitary Reaper"**
A poem about a "solitary Highland Lass" singing as she reaps grain. The speaker says "No Nightingale did ever chaunt / More welcome notes," and ends "The music in my heart I bore, / Long after it was heard no more."

**"Michael"**
A pastoral narrative poem from Lyrical Ballads about an old shepherd who risks losing his land and sends his son Luke to the city to earn money. Before Luke leaves, they lay the cornerstone of a sheepfold together; Luke falls into bad ways and never returns, and the sheepfold is left unfinished.

**"Resolution and Independence"**
A poem in which a despondent speaker meets an old leech-gatherer whose endurance restores him. It contains the lines "We Poets in our youth begin in gladness; / But thereof come in the end despondency and madness."

**"Ode to Duty"**
A poem addressing duty as "Stern Daughter of the Voice of God," containing the line "My hopes no more must change their name." Other clue poems include the sonnet "It is a beauteous evening, calm and free" and "Extempore Effusion upon the Death of James Hogg" ("How fast has brother followed brother, / From sunshine to the sunless land!").

**Black Death frame story (the brigata fleeing Florence)**
The frame narrative is set during the 1348 plague. A group called the "brigata," seven young women and three young men, meets at the Basilica of Santa Maria Novella and leaves Florence for countryside villas with gardens and fountains. There they tell ten stories a day for ten days, 100 tales in all, which gives the book its Greek-derived title meaning "ten days."

**Patient Griselda (Gualtieri, Marquis of Saluzzo)**
This is the final story of the collection (Day 10, Story 10), told by Dioneo. The nobleman Gualtieri marries the peasant Griselda and tests her obedience. He takes away their son and daughter, claims to have had them killed, and secretly sends them to Bologna. He then pretends to divorce her and sends her home, and later pretends to marry a twelve-year-old girl, who is actually their daughter. Griselda's unwavering patience is finally rewarded when he reveals the ruse.

**Dioneo**
Dioneo is the most mischievous member of the brigata and is often seen as a stand-in for Boccaccio himself. He is the only storyteller allowed to ignore the day's assigned theme, and he always tells the last tale of each day, including many of the bawdiest and wittiest stories and the closing Griselda tale.

**The Parable of the Three Rings (Melchizedek and Saladin)**
In this tale (Day 1, Story 3), told by Filomena, the sultan Saladin needs money and tries to trap the wealthy Jewish moneylender Melchizedek by asking which religion is true: Judaism, Christianity, or Islam. Melchizedek answers with a parable about a father who owns one precious ring. Unable to choose among his three sons, he has two identical copies made, so no one can tell which ring is the original. The parable inspired Gotthold Ephraim Lessing's Enlightenment play "Nathan the Wise."

**Federigo's falcon**
In a tale told by Fiammetta (Day 5, Story 9), the impoverished nobleman Federigo degli Alberighi has spent his fortune courting Monna Giovanna. When she unexpectedly visits him, he has nothing else to serve her, so he cooks his prized falcon, his last possession. She had actually come to ask for the falcon for her sick son. The son dies, and she later marries Federigo, moved by his generosity.

**Lisabetta's pot of basil**
In this tale told by Filomena (Day 4, Story 5), Lisabetta (Isabella) of Messina loves Lorenzo, but her three brothers secretly murder him. Guided by a dream, she digs up his body and cuts off his head. She buries the head in a pot of basil, which she waters with her tears. John Keats adapted the story as the poem "Isabella, or the Pot of Basil."

**Ser Ciappelletto (Cepparello)**
The book's first story, told by Panfilo, concerns Ser Cepparello of Prato, called Ciappelletto, a thoroughly wicked notary. While dying in Burgundy, he makes a completely false deathbed confession to a friar, even claiming to be a virgin. After his death he is venerated as a saint.

**Fiammetta, Pampinea, Filostrato, Panfilo, and Filomena**
These are major members of the brigata. The women are Pampinea, Fiammetta, Filomena, Emilia, Lauretta, Neifile, and Elissa, and the men are Panfilo, Filostrato, and Dioneo. Fiammetta is traditionally associated with Boccaccio's muse. Pampinea proposes fleeing the city, and Filostrato's name means "overcome by love."

**Kings and queens of the day**
Each day one member of the brigata is crowned king or queen and sets the theme for that day's stories. For example, Filostrato decrees that Day 4's tales concern loves with unhappy endings. Days 1 and 9 have no set theme. Boccaccio also interrupts the work with an authorial defense of his writing in the introduction to Day 4.

**Bridge of Geese**
In this tale (Day 9, Story 9), Giosefo goes to King Solomon for advice on handling his unruly, disobedient wife and is told to "go to the Bridge of Geese." There he sees a muleteer beating a stubborn mule across the bridge. Giosefo then applies the same violent tactic to his wife, who becomes obedient.

**Marguerite de Navarre's Heptameron**
The Decameron's format and title inspired the French queen Marguerite de Navarre's story collection "The Heptameron." It also uses a frame story of travelers telling tales, but she planned 100 stories and completed only 72 before her death.

**Peronella and the barrel**
In this tale (Day 7, Story 2), set in Naples, Peronella's husband returns home unexpectedly, so she hides her lover in a large barrel. She claims the man inside is a buyer inspecting the barrel. While the husband climbs in to scrape it clean, she and her lover resume their affair.

**Prince Galehaut (Principe Galeotto)**
This is the work's alternate title or subtitle. It refers to Galehaut, the go-between who brought together Lancelot and Guinevere in Arthurian romance. The name also echoes Dante's Francesca in "Inferno" Canto 5, who calls the book that led to her adultery a "Galeotto."

**Chaucer's "Clerk's Tale"**
In Geoffrey Chaucer's "Canterbury Tales," the Clerk tells the story of patient Griselda. Chaucer drew it from Boccaccio's final tale, largely through Petrarch's Latin translation of that story.

**Frate Alberto as the Archangel Gabriel**
In this tale (Day 4, Story 2), the hypocritical friar Alberto convinces a vain Venetian woman, Madonna Lisetta, that the Archangel Gabriel is in love with her. He then visits her bed disguised as the angel. When he is finally discovered, he escapes by leaping out her window into the canal.

**Pygmalion**
Shaw's most famous play (1913), named after the Greek myth of the sculptor whose statue comes to life. The phonetics professor Henry Higgins bets Colonel Pickering that he can teach the Cockney flower girl Eliza Doolittle to speak so well that she could pass for a duchess. It opens outside Covent Garden, where Higgins, at first called "the note-taker," is copying down Eliza's speech and she fears he is a police informer. It was later adapted as the musical My Fair Lady.

**"Walk! Not bloody likely!"**
Eliza's shocking exit line in Act III of Pygmalion, when Freddy offers to walk her across the park after Mrs. Higgins's at-home. During the same visit she describes how her gin-loving aunt was "done in," and Freddy's sister Clara calls it "the new small talk," which she finds "delightful and quite innocent." Shaw's friend Mrs. Patrick Campbell spoke the line in the first London production, scandalizing audiences.

**Freddy Eynsford-Hill and "What Happened Afterwards"**
Freddy is the poor young gentleman who bumps into Eliza at Covent Garden, making her drop her flowers, and later falls in love with her. Annoyed by actor-manager Herbert Beerbohm Tree's attempts to give the play a romantic ending with Higgins, Shaw added a prose sequel, "What Happened Afterwards," explaining that Eliza marries Freddy and they open a flower shop.

**Eliza's rebellion and Alfred Doolittle**
At the end of Pygmalion, after her triumph, the neglected Eliza throws Higgins's slippers at him and tries to claw his face, and later returns his ring, which he throws into the fireplace. Her father, the dustman Alfred Doolittle, is made wealthy and miserable after Higgins jokingly calls him "the most original moralist in England" in a letter to an American millionaire, who leaves him a yearly grant to lecture for a moral reform society. The housekeeper Mrs. Pearce tells Higgins to stop swearing, and Higgins's former pupil Nepommuck appears at the ambassador's reception.

**Man and Superman**
Shaw's 1903 comedy of ideas about the "Life Force." The revolutionary John (Jack) Tanner, author of "The Revolutionist's Handbook" (published with the play), flees to Spain to escape the determined Ann Whitefield, who represents the Life Force; in the Sierra Nevada he is captured by the brigand leader Mendoza, a Jewish anarchist, but Ann finally wins him.

**"Don Juan in Hell"**
The long dream sequence in Act III of Man and Superman, often performed separately or cut from the play. Tanner becomes Don Juan, Ann becomes Doña Ana (who chooses to be twenty-seven years old in the afterlife), Roebuck Ramsden becomes the statue of the Commander, and Mendoza becomes the Devil, with whom Don Juan debates philosophy.

**Arms and the Man**
Shaw's 1894 comedy set during the Serbo-Bulgarian War of 1885, whose title comes from the first line of Virgil's Aeneid ("Arms and the man I sing"). The Swiss mercenary Captain Bluntschli, who carries chocolates instead of ammunition, climbs into Raina Petkoff's bedroom window and is nicknamed the "chocolate-cream soldier"; Raina ends up engaged to him instead of the pompous hero Sergius. The servant Louka tells Nicola, who dreams of opening a shop in Sofia, "You have the soul of a servant," and he replies that is "the secret of success in service."

**Major Barbara**
Shaw's 1905 play in which Barbara Undershaft, a major in the Salvation Army, is disillusioned when the Army accepts donations from her father Andrew Undershaft, a munitions maker who calls poverty the worst of crimes, and from a whisky distiller. Undershaft, separated from his wife Lady Britomart, leaves his business to the foundling Greek scholar Adolphus Cusins, Barbara's fiancé, who translates Euripides with Barbara's name substituted for "loveliness." The bully Bill Walker hits the Salvation Army girl Jenny Hill on the mouth and later tries to make amends.

**Candida**
One of Shaw's "Plays Pleasant." Candida, wife of the Christian Socialist clergyman James Morell, must choose between him and the young poet Eugene Marchbanks, who loves her; she chooses her husband as "the weaker of the two." The play ends with the stage direction that the couple embrace but "they do not know the secret in the poet's heart."

**Mrs. Warren's Profession**
One of Shaw's "Plays Unpleasant," long banned by British censors. The educated Vivie Warren learns that her mother's fortune came from running a chain of brothels, a business in which Sir George Crofts is a partner; Praed is a friend of Mrs. Warren. Vivie rejects both her mother and her suitor Frank Gardner and ends the play working at Honoria Fraser's chambers.

**Heartbreak House**
Shaw's 1919 play, subtitled "A Fantasia in the Russian Manner on English Themes" (a nod to Chekhov). It is set at the house of the eccentric old inventor Captain Shotover, whose daughters are Hesione Hushabye and Lady Utterword; the play ends with an air raid in which bombs explode the dynamite Shotover has stored.

**Saint Joan**
Shaw's 1923 play about Joan of Arc, who has the Dauphin crowned Charles VII at Reims before she is tried and burned. The English chaplain de Stogumber is a fanatical supporter of her execution, and in the Epilogue, set 25 years after her death, Joan appears to Charles in a dream.

**Back to Methuselah**
Shaw's cycle of five plays on Creative Evolution. The first part, "In the Beginning," shows Adam and Eve in Eden realizing their own mortality after finding a fawn that has broken its neck, and the final part, "As Far as Thought Can Reach," is set in the year 31,920 AD.

**Caesar and Cleopatra, The Doctor's Dilemma, and other plays**
Caesar and Cleopatra has an "Alternative to the Prologue" in which the Egyptian guard captain Belzanor is warned of Caesar's invasion. In The Doctor's Dilemma, Sir Colenso Ridgeon must decide whether to save the talented but immoral painter Louis Dubedat with his new tuberculosis cure, and the play opens with his assistant Redpenny. Captain Brassbound's Conversion features Lady Cicely and Sir Howard, and You Never Can Tell, another "Play Pleasant," features the twins Philip and Dolly Clandon; Shaw also wrote The Devil's Disciple.

**The Fabian Society and The Perfect Wagnerite**
The Dublin-born Shaw began as a critic and was a leading member of the socialist Fabian Society. His book The Perfect Wagnerite interprets Wagner's Ring cycle as a socialist allegory about capitalism. He won the 1925 Nobel Prize in Literature.

**Mr. Collins and Charlotte Lucas**
Mr. William Collins is a pompous, obsequious clergyman and Mr. Bennet's cousin. Because the estate of Longbourn is entailed to male heirs, he will inherit it. He first proposes to Elizabeth Bennet, who refuses him. Within days he becomes engaged to her practical friend Charlotte Lucas, who marries him for security.

**Lydia's elopement with George Wickham**
Lydia, the youngest and most flirtatious Bennet sister, runs off with the charming but dishonest militia officer George Wickham while visiting Brighton. The scandal threatens the whole family's reputation. Mr. Darcy secretly tracks the couple down, pays Wickham's debts, and bribes him into marrying her. Wickham grew up alongside Darcy as the son of the elder Mr. Darcy's steward.

**Lady Catherine de Bourgh**
Lady Catherine is Mr. Darcy's domineering, snobbish aunt. She lives at the estate of Rosings in Kent and is Mr. Collins's patron, whom he flatters endlessly. Late in the novel she visits Longbourn and demands that Elizabeth promise never to accept Darcy. Elizabeth refuses to make that promise.

**"It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife."**
This is the famous ironic opening sentence of the novel, published in 1813. It introduces the arrival of the wealthy Mr. Bingley and the marriage-obsessed world of the Bennet family, especially Mrs. Bennet.

**Charles Bingley, Jane Bennet, and Netherfield Park**
The novel begins when the wealthy, good-natured Charles Bingley rents Netherfield Park, near the village of Meryton and the Bennets' home at Longbourn. He falls for Jane, the eldest and gentlest Bennet sister. They are separated for a time, but he eventually proposes and marries her.

**"Tolerable, but not handsome enough to tempt me"**
At the opening assembly ball in Meryton, Elizabeth overhears Darcy say this about her. Just before, he had told Bingley that Bingley was "dancing with the only handsome girl in the room," meaning Jane. The insult forms Elizabeth's poor first impression of Darcy, the "prejudice" of the title.

**Pemberley and Mrs. Reynolds**
Pemberley is Darcy's grand estate in Derbyshire. Elizabeth tours it with her aunt and uncle, the Gardiners. There the housekeeper, Mrs. Reynolds, praises Darcy's kindness and shows them a portrait of him, which helps change Elizabeth's opinion of him. Elizabeth later jokes that her love for him dates from first seeing Pemberley's grounds.

**Jane's ride in the rain and Elizabeth's muddy walk**
Mrs. Bennet sends Jane to Netherfield on horseback rather than by carriage, hoping rain will force her to stay overnight near Bingley. Jane catches a fever and is stuck there. Elizabeth then walks about three miles across muddy fields to nurse her. The Bingley sisters sneer that her petticoat is "six inches deep in mud."

**The Gardiners**
Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner are Mrs. Bennet's brother and his wife. They are sensible, kind relatives who live in London, and Jane stays with them for a time. They take Elizabeth on the tour of Derbyshire where she visits Pemberley. Mrs. Gardiner earlier warns Elizabeth against getting involved with Wickham.

**Georgiana Darcy and Mrs. Younge**
Georgiana is Darcy's shy younger sister, who is skilled at the piano. Before the novel begins, Wickham tried to elope with her to get her fortune, helped by her companion Mrs. Younge. Darcy reveals this history to Elizabeth in his letter. Caroline Bingley flatters Georgiana in hopes of winning Darcy.

**Darcy's first proposal, "In vain I have struggled. It will not do."**
Darcy's first proposal to Elizabeth at Hunsford in Kent begins with these words, but he insults her family while proposing, and she angrily rejects him. He then gives her a letter explaining his conduct toward Wickham and why he separated Bingley from Jane. After reading it, Elizabeth realizes her own prejudice and exclaims, "Till this moment I never knew myself."

**Caroline Bingley**
Caroline is Bingley's snobbish sister, who lives with him at Netherfield along with her sister Louisa Hurst. She wants Darcy for herself. She mocks Darcy for admiring Elizabeth's "fine eyes," belittles Elizabeth's looks (including calling her teeth merely "tolerable"), and helps persuade Bingley to leave Jane.

**Fordyce's Sermons**
Mr. Collins reads aloud to the Bennet girls from this book of sermons on female conduct. Lydia interrupts him with gossip about the militia officers, offending him. He gives up and plays backgammon with Mr. Bennet instead.

**Mary Bennet's singing at the Netherfield ball**
Mary is the bookish, pedantic middle Bennet sister. At the Netherfield ball she insists on singing and playing the piano despite her weak voice, which mortifies Elizabeth. Her performance is one of several embarrassing family displays that evening.

**"From this day you must be a stranger to one of your parents"**
Mr. Bennet says this dryly to Elizabeth after she refuses Mr. Collins. He explains that her mother will never see her again if she does not marry Collins, and he will never see her again if she does.

**The Importance of Being Earnest**
Wilde's most famous comedy (1895), a farce built on the pun between "earnest" and the name Ernest. Jack Worthing calls himself "Ernest" in London, and his friend Algernon Moncrieff also poses as "Ernest" to woo Jack's ward, Cecily Cardew. Both Cecily and Gwendolen Fairfax insist they can only love a man named Ernest, so both men arrange to be christened by Dr. Chasuble.

**Bunburying**
In The Importance of Being Earnest, Algernon invents a permanently sick friend named Bunbury as an excuse to escape social obligations, such as dinners with his aunt Lady Bracknell. The play opens with his servant Lane preparing cucumber sandwiches for Lady Bracknell's visit, and Algernon eats them all.

**The handbag at Victoria Station**
The revelation in The Importance of Being Earnest that Jack was found as a baby in a handbag in the cloakroom at Victoria Station, where the absent-minded governess Miss Prism had left him by mistake. Lady Bracknell remarks that losing one parent may be a misfortune but "to lose both looks like carelessness," and objects to a man whose origin was a "Terminus." Jack turns out to be Algernon's older brother, and his real name is in fact Ernest.

**Lady Windermere's Fan**
Wilde's 1892 comedy. Lady Margaret Windermere finds payments to the scandalous Mrs. Erlynne in her husband's bank book and suspects an affair, because of his daily visits to her in Curzon Street. She threatens to strike Mrs. Erlynne with her fan, then runs off to Lord Darlington's rooms, where she leaves the fan behind. Mrs. Erlynne, secretly her mother, saves her reputation by claiming the fan is hers, and at the end Mrs. Erlynne is set to marry Lord Augustus Lorton.

**"We are all in the gutter, but some of us are looking at the stars"**
A line spoken by Lord Darlington in Lady Windermere's Fan. The same play gives Lord Darlington the definition of a cynic as "a man who knows the price of everything and the value of nothing," in reply to Cecil Graham, and has Dumby say that there are only two tragedies in the world, "not getting what one wants, and getting it."

**"The Ballad of Reading Gaol"**
A long poem Wilde wrote after his release from prison and published in 1898 under his prison number, "C.3.3." Its famous refrain is "Yet each man kills the thing he loves," followed by "The coward does it with a kiss, / The brave man with a sword!" It describes a condemned man who "looked / So wistfully at the day."

**Charles Thomas Wooldridge**
The real Royal Horse Guards trooper, hanged at Reading Gaol in 1896 for murdering his wife, to whom "The Ballad of Reading Gaol" is dedicated. The poem opens "He did not wear his scarlet coat, / For blood and wine are red."

**The Picture of Dorian Gray**
Wilde's only novel (1890/1891). The painter Basil Hallward paints a portrait of the beautiful young Dorian, who falls under the influence of the cynical Lord Henry Wotton and wishes that the picture would age instead of him. The portrait grows old and ugly with each of his sins while he stays young. Dorian murders Basil, and when he finally stabs the painting, he is found dead and withered beside a restored portrait.

**Sibyl Vane**
In Dorian Gray, a young actress who plays Shakespeare's heroines and calls Dorian "Prince Charming." After falling in love, she gives a wooden performance, and Dorian cruelly rejects her, so she kills herself. Her brother James Vane, a sailor, later hunts Dorian for revenge.

**Preface to The Picture of Dorian Gray**
A list of aphorisms defending aestheticism, ending "All art is quite useless." It also says that the nineteenth century's dislike of Realism is "the rage of Caliban seeing his own face in a glass," and that there is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book.

**De Profundis**
A long letter Wilde wrote in Reading Gaol to his lover Lord Alfred "Bosie" Douglas. Its title is the Latin opening of Psalm 130 ("Out of the depths"), and it contains the line "Suffering is one very long moment." In it Wilde reproaches Douglas and reflects on his own downfall.

**Lord Alfred Douglas and the trials**
Wilde's relationship with Douglas led Douglas's father, the Marquess of Queensberry, to plan to disrupt the premiere of Earnest with a bouquet of rotten vegetables and to accuse Wilde of homosexuality. Wilde's failed libel suit against Queensberry led to his conviction for "gross indecency." Douglas's poem "Two Loves" coined the phrase "the love that dare not speak its name," and A. E. Housman's "Oh who is that young sinner" was inspired by Wilde's imprisonment.

**Salome**
A one-act tragedy Wilde wrote in French, about the princess who performs the Dance of the Seven Veils for Herod and demands the head of John the Baptist (Jokanaan). It opens with a Page warning the young Syrian not to keep looking at Salome. Herod orders her killed after she kisses the severed head. The Lord Chamberlain banned it from the English stage for showing biblical characters; the English translation, credited to Douglas, was illustrated by Aubrey Beardsley; and Richard Strauss turned it into an opera.

**An Ideal Husband**
Wilde's 1895 play, premiered at the Haymarket Theatre. Sir Robert Chiltern made his fortune by selling a Cabinet secret about Suez Canal shares to Baron Arnheim. Mrs. Cheveley blackmails him into supporting a fraudulent Argentine canal scheme, and Lord Goring foils her with a diamond brooch she once stole. Lady Chiltern learns to forgive her husband for not being perfect.

**Fairy tales: "The Happy Prince" and "The Nightingale and the Rose"**
In "The Happy Prince," a jeweled statue asks a swallow to strip away his rubies, sapphires, and gold leaf for the poor, and the swallow stays with him into winter and dies. In "The Nightingale and the Rose," a nightingale presses her breast against a thorn and sings all night to stain a white rose red for a student. Other tales include "The Birthday of the Infanta," in which a dwarf dies of a broken heart and the Infanta demands that playmates have no hearts, and "The Remarkable Rocket," about a conceited firework that cries and fails to go off.

**"The horror! The horror!"**
The famous last words of Kurtz, whispered as he dies aboard Marlow's steamer heading back down the Congo River. This is the most common giveaway.

**"Exterminate all the brutes!"**
The scrawled postscript at the end of Kurtz's eloquent seventeen-page report for the International Society for the Suppression of Savage Customs. The report is full of high-minded talk of civilizing Africans, and the postscript reveals what lies beneath it. Marlow later hands the report over with the postscript torn off.

**Mr. Kurtz**
The Company's most successful ivory trader, a "universal genius" (painter, musician, writer) who runs the remote Inner Station. He has made himself a god among the local people and has fallen into savagery. Marlow is sent to retrieve him, and Kurtz dies on the voyage back.

**Charles Marlow**
The narrator of the inner story, a seaman who as a child loved the "blank spaces" on maps and was "charmed" by the snake-like river on a map of Africa. With help from his aunt, he gets a job with the Company as captain of a river steamboat. Conrad also used Marlow as the narrator of Lord Jim.

**The Nellie and the Thames frame story**
The novella opens on the Nellie, a "cruising yawl" anchored in the Thames, where Marlow, sitting "in the pose of a meditating Buddha," tells his story to friends. He imagines Roman soldiers arriving in Britain at "the very end of the world" and says, "this also has been one of the dark places of the earth." It ends when the Director of Companies says, "We have lost the first of the ebb," and the narrator sees a black bank of clouds over the river.

**The Intended**
Kurtz's fiancee in Brussels, whom Marlow visits at the end. When she asks for Kurtz's last words, Marlow lies and says they were her name, rather than "The horror! The horror!"

**The Russian "Harlequin"**
A young Russian trader in a patchwork suit of many colors who worships Kurtz and repeats that Kurtz has "enlarged my mind." His copy of An Inquiry into Some Points of Seamanship by Tower, Towson contains notes in Russian that Marlow mistakes for code. He leaves a note on a woodpile: "Hurry up. Approach cautiously."

**The "whited sepulchre," the knitting women, and the doctor**
Marlow calls the Company's European city (Brussels) a "whited sepulchre," borrowing Jesus's image of hypocrisy from Matthew. In the Company's office, two women knit black wool like Fates guarding the door of Darkness. A company doctor measures Marlow's skull, notes that "the changes take place inside," and warns him to avoid exposure to the sun.

**Fresleven and the two black hens**
Marlow's predecessor, a Danish captain described as "the gentlest, quietest creature." He was killed in a quarrel over two black hens after beating a village chief, and his death creates the vacancy that Marlow fills.

**Kurtz's painting of a blindfolded woman with a torch**
At the Central Station, Marlow sees a small oil sketch by Kurtz of a draped, blindfolded woman carrying a lighted torch against a dark background. It is in the room of the brickmaker, a scheming agent whom Marlow calls a "papier-mache Mephistopheles."

**The Central Station and the rivets**
At the Central Station, Marlow finds his steamboat sunk and waits months for rivets to repair it, while the Manager seems to want Kurtz to fail. On the way there, at the Outer Station, he meets the immaculately dressed Chief Accountant, who complains that a dying agent's groans distract him from his books, and he sees a chain gang of starving workers. The Eldorado Exploring Expedition passes through, and all that is later heard of it is that "all the donkeys were dead."

**The attack on the steamer and the helmsman's death**
Near the Inner Station, natives attack the steamer at Kurtz's order. The African helmsman is killed by a spear, and Marlow throws his own blood-filled shoes overboard, then the helmsman's body. A fat "pilgrim" in pink pyjamas takes the wheel. Earlier, Marlow is amazed that the starving cannibal crew, whose rotten hippo meat was thrown overboard, do not attack the whites.

**The heads on stakes and Kurtz's mistress**
Kurtz's hut at the Inner Station is surrounded by posts topped with the shrunken heads of "rebels." A tall, magnificent African woman, apparently Kurtz's mistress, appears on the shore with her hair done up in the shape of a helmet and stands defiantly as the steamer leaves.

**Chinua Achebe's "An Image of Africa"**
Achebe's 1975 lecture, which famously called Conrad "a bloody racist" (later revised to "a thoroughgoing racist"). It argues that the novella portrays Africa as "the other world" and denies Africans human expression.

**"Mistah Kurtz—he dead," The Hollow Men, and Apocalypse Now**
The manager's servant announces Kurtz's death contemptuously with the line "Mistah Kurtz—he dead," which T. S. Eliot used as the epigraph of "The Hollow Men." Francis Ford Coppola adapted the story as the Vietnam War film Apocalypse Now (1979), with Martin Sheen as Captain Willard and Marlon Brando as Colonel Kurtz.

**Suicide under a train**
Anna, convinced that her lover Vronsky has lost interest in her, throws herself under a freight train at a railway station near the end of the novel. This is the near-universal giveaway for the novel and its title character.

**Count Alexei Vronsky**
The dashing cavalry officer with whom Anna has her affair. He first courts Kitty Shcherbatskaya, then abandons her for Anna; the two eventually live together abroad and in the country, but Anna's jealousy and isolation drive them apart.

**"Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way."**
The famous opening line of the novel, often translated as "All happy families resemble one another." It gave rise to the "Anna Karenina principle," the idea that success requires avoiding every one of many possible failures.

**Stiva Oblonsky and Dolly**
The novel opens with the household of Stepan "Stiva" Oblonsky, Anna's brother, in chaos because his wife Dolly has discovered his affair with the family's French governess. Anna travels to Moscow to persuade Dolly to forgive him, and Dolly later serves as a go-between for the novel's two main storylines.

**Konstantin Levin and Kitty**
Levin, a landowner who lives in the countryside, proposes to Kitty Shcherbatskaya and is rejected because she hopes to marry Vronsky. After Vronsky abandons her, Kitty accepts Levin's second proposal, and their happy marriage is the novel's counterpoint to Anna's doomed affair. Levin is widely seen as a stand-in for Tolstoy himself.

**Frou-Frou and the horse race**
During an officers' steeplechase, Vronsky races his mare Frou-Frou against Makhotin's horse Gladiator. He makes a careless movement in the saddle at a jump, the horse breaks her back and has to be shot, and Anna's open distress at the accident reveals the affair. On the ride home she confesses it to her husband.

**Alexei Karenin**
Anna's cold, rigid husband, a high-ranking St. Petersburg government official. He refuses to grant her a divorce, keeps custody of their son, and is humiliated when his political rival Stremov receives the post he wanted.

**Landau, the French clairvoyant**
A French psychic, also called Count Bezzubov, who gives advice while apparently asleep. On the recommendation of Countess Lidia Ivanovna, Karenin consults him, and Landau's sleeping pronouncements convince Karenin to refuse Anna's request for a divorce.

**"Vengeance is mine; I will repay"**
The novel's epigraph, taken from Paul's Epistle to the Romans. It suggests that judgment of Anna belongs to God rather than to society.

**The railway worker's death (the "evil omen")**
When Anna arrives by train in Moscow and first meets Vronsky, a railway watchman is crushed to death by a train, which Anna calls an evil omen. Her own suicide under a train at the end of the novel mirrors this scene.

**Anna's near-death in childbirth and Vronsky's suicide attempt**
Anna nearly dies of fever after giving birth to Vronsky's daughter, Annie. Karenin forgives both of them at her bedside, and Vronsky, humiliated by that forgiveness, shoots himself in the chest but survives. Anna and Vronsky then leave for Italy.

**Seryozha's birthday visit**
Anna's son by Karenin, Seryozha, has been told that his mother is dead. She secretly visits him on his ninth birthday. Her love for him is one reason she hesitates over a divorce.

**Levin mowing with the peasants**
Levin takes comfort in physical work by mowing grass with a scythe alongside his peasants, a famous pastoral scene that reflects Tolstoy's idealization of rural labor. Related clues include Levin refusing to shake hands with a merchant after Stiva sells a forest too cheaply, and peasants telling him "as God wills."

**The chalk-letter proposal**
Levin and Kitty become engaged by writing only the first letters of the words of each sentence in chalk on a card table, and each understands the other perfectly.

**Varenka, Madame Stahl, and the mushroom-picking scene**
At a German spa, Kitty befriends the pious Varenka but becomes disillusioned when she learns that Madame Stahl, an invalid who seems saintly, stays in bed only to hide her short legs. Later Levin's half-brother Sergei Koznyshev means to propose to Varenka while they are picking mushrooms but fails to, partly out of loyalty to his late love Marie.

**The Temple of the Golden Pavilion**
Mishima's 1956 novel, based on the real 1950 burning of Kinkaku-ji in Kyoto. The narrator Mizoguchi, an ugly, stuttering acolyte trained at the temple under its superior, Father Dosen, becomes obsessed with the temple's beauty and comes to feel he must destroy it. Near the end of the war he wishes "let the darkness of my heart equal the darkness of the night." After setting the fire, he throws away the arsenic and knife he brought to kill himself, smokes a cigarette, and decides that he wants to live.

**"When you meet the Buddha, kill the Buddha"**
A Zen saying from the Rinzai Roku (the recorded sayings of the master Linji) that Mizoguchi remembers just before he sets fire to the Golden Pavilion. He takes it as permission to destroy what he worships.

**Kashiwagi**
Mizoguchi's cynical, clubfooted friend at Otani University, who boasts that he uses his deformity to seduce women by making them pity him. Kashiwagi and Mizoguchi discuss the Zen koan "Nansen kills a kitten," which Father Dosen tells the acolytes from The Gateless Gate, a collection of koans; in the koan, Joshu responds by putting his sandals on his head.

**Confessions of a Mask**
Mishima's semi-autobiographical 1949 novel about Kochan, a young man who hides his homosexuality behind a "mask" of normality. It opens with Kochan claiming to remember the moment of his own birth, which disturbs the adults around him. As a schoolboy he is drawn to the physique of the older classmate Omi.

**Joan of Arc and Saint Sebastian**
Two images from Kochan's childhood in Confessions of a Mask. He is disgusted when his nurse tells him that a picture of a handsome knight he loves actually shows Joan of Arc, a woman. Later, Guido Reni's painting of the martyred Saint Sebastian gives him his first sexual arousal, feeding his obsession with beautiful young men dying.

**Sonoko**
The sister of Kochan's friend Kusano in Confessions of a Mask, whose piano playing captivated him. He tries to fall in love with her but cannot feel desire for her. In the final scene, while he is with her, he is entranced by a shirtless young tough with a peony tattoo on his chest.

**The Sea of Fertility**
Mishima's final tetralogy, named after a lunar mare: Spring Snow, Runaway Horses, The Temple of Dawn, and The Decay of the Angel. It follows Shigekuni Honda, who goes from law student to judge to old man while trying to protect a series of reincarnations of his friend Kiyoaki Matsugae, an effort that ultimately ruins him.

**Spring Snow and Kiyoaki Matsugae**
The first Sea of Fertility novel, set among the aristocracy around 1912. Kiyoaki, a student at the Peers School, has a doomed love affair with Satoko Ayakura after she is engaged to an imperial prince. He dies young after giving Honda his dream diary and saying they will meet again "beneath the falls." Two Siamese princes at the school leave after one loses his emerald ring.

**Three moles and the reincarnations**
Honda recognizes Kiyoaki's reincarnations by a cluster of three moles on the left side of the body. The reincarnations are Isao Iinuma, a young kendo fanatic in Runaway Horses who plots to assassinate capitalist businessmen; the Thai princess Ying Chan in The Temple of Dawn; and the orphan Toru Yasunaga, whom the elderly Honda adopts in The Decay of the Angel.

**Seppuku in 1970**
On November 25, 1970, after delivering the final Sea of Fertility manuscript, Mishima and members of his private militia, the Tatenokai, took over a Self-Defense Forces headquarters in Tokyo and called for a coup to restore the emperor's power. When the soldiers jeered him, he committed ritual suicide by seppuku. His real name was Kimitake Hiraoka.

**The Sailor Who Fell from Grace with the Sea**
A 1963 novel about 13-year-old Noboru, who spies through a peephole on his widowed mother Fusako and her lover, the sailor Ryuji Tsukazaki.
