Pedro Lascurain served as president for less than an hour so the transfer of power to General Victoriano Huerta would look legal.

**Zimmermann Telegram**
A 1917 secret message from German foreign minister Arthur Zimmermann, decoded by British naval intelligence in Room 40, proposing a German-Mexican alliance against the U.S. in World War I. It promised Mexico the return of territory like Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona; President Carranza rejected it and kept Mexico neutral.

**Tampico Affair and the occupation of Veracruz**
In 1914, U.S. sailors were briefly arrested in Tampico, and Mexico's refusal to give a 21-gun salute as an apology led the U.S. to occupy the port of Veracruz. The occupation also aimed to stop the German ship SS Ypiranga from delivering arms to Huerta. The ABC Powers (Argentina, Brazil, and Chile) then mediated at the Niagara Falls peace conference.

**Punitive Expedition**
The 1916–1917 U.S. military campaign led by General John J. Pershing into northern Mexico to capture Pancho Villa after Villa raided Columbus, New Mexico. President Venustiano Carranza opposed the incursion, and Villa was never caught.

**Assassination of Leon Trotsky**
The exiled Soviet revolutionary lived in Mexico City, where he survived an attack led by the muralist David Alfaro Siqueiros in 1940. Later that year he was killed with an ice axe by NKVD agent Ramon Mercader, in a plot code-named Operation Duck. His bodyguard Robert Sheldon Harte died after the earlier raid.

**Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) and el dedazo**
The party that ruled Mexico without interruption from 1929 to 2000, emerging out of the Maximato period dominated by Plutarco Elias Calles. Under "el dedazo" ("the big finger"), the outgoing president personally chose his successor. Its rule ended with the 2000 election victory of the National Action Party (PAN) candidate Vicente Fox.

**Battle of Puebla and the French intervention**
After President Benito Juarez suspended foreign debt payments for two years following the Reform War, France invaded. Mexican forces defeated General Charles de Lorencez at Puebla on May 5, 1862, now celebrated as Cinco de Mayo. Napoleon III then installed the Austrian Maximilian I as emperor, who was executed by firing squad at the Hill of the Bells in 1867, a scene painted by Edouard Manet.

**Pastry War**
An 1838–1839 conflict in which France blockaded and attacked Mexico over unpaid damages to French citizens, including a French pastry cook whose shop in Mexico City had been looted. Santa Anna lost a leg fighting the French at Veracruz.

**Tlatelolco Massacre**
On October 2, 1968, government forces, including the Olympia Battalion, opened fire on student protesters in the Plaza of the Three Cultures in Mexico City, killing many. It happened days before Mexico City hosted the 1968 Summer Olympics, under President Gustavo Diaz Ordaz.

**Lazaro Cardenas and oil nationalization**
In 1938, President Cardenas invoked Article 27 of the 1917 Constitution to nationalize foreign oil companies, creating Pemex and prompting an international boycott. In the same year, Mexico was the only country to formally protest the Anschluss to the League of Nations.

**Aztecs and Tenochtitlan**
The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was built on an island in Lake Texcoco and was centered on the Templo Mayor; Mexico City now stands on its ruins. The Aztecs farmed on chinampas, artificial "floating gardens," and fought ritual "Flower Wars" to capture prisoners for sacrifice. Hernan Cortes conquered the city in 1521.

**Olmec colossal heads**
The Olmec, Mesoamerica's earliest major civilization, lived on Mexico's Gulf Coast and carved giant basalt heads, thought to depict rulers. They are also known for jaguar figures.

**Porfirio Diaz and the cientificos**
Diaz ruled Mexico for most of 1876–1911, a period called the Porfiriato, guided by technocratic advisors called the cientificos, such as finance minister Jose Limantour. His 1908 interview with journalist James Creelman, in which he said Mexico was ready for democracy, helped inspire the opposition that set off the Revolution.

**Santa Anna and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo**
Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna dominated Mexican politics in the mid-1800s and lost Texas in 1836. The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the Mexican-American War and gave California and much of the Southwest to the United States.

**Bracero program and Operation Wetback**
The bracero program (1942–1964) brought Mexican laborers to work temporarily on U.S. farms. The 1954 U.S. deportation campaign known as Operation Wetback sent many Mexican workers back to Mexico.

**Risorgimento (Italian unification)**
The 19th-century movement that unified the states of the Italian peninsula into the Kingdom of Italy. It was led politically by the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia, whose king Victor Emmanuel II became the first king of Italy in 1861, and it was completed when Rome became the capital in 1871.

**Giuseppe Garibaldi and the Expedition of the Thousand**
Garibaldi, a nationalist general who had earlier fought in the Uruguayan Civil War, led about a thousand volunteer "Redshirts" from Genoa in 1860. They conquered Sicily and Naples from the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, winning at Calatafimi and ending with the Siege of Gaeta, and then handed these lands to Victor Emmanuel II. Garibaldi was later shot in the foot at the Battle of Aspromonte in 1862.

**Count Cavour and the Plombieres Agreement**
Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, the prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia, made a secret 1858 deal with Napoleon III at Plombieres for French help against Austria in exchange for Nice and Savoy. After the French victories at Magenta and Solferino, Napoleon III made a separate peace at Villafranca, and Cavour resigned in protest.

**Carbonari**
A secret revolutionary society, whose name means "charcoal burners," that worked for Italian independence and constitutional government in the early 19th century. It forced King Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies to accept a constitution in 1820 and was condemned by Pope Pius VII. Giuseppe Mazzini was a member before founding the Young Italy movement.

**Aldo Moro and the Years of Lead**
The "Years of Lead" (late 1960s to the 1980s) were a period of left-wing and far-right terrorism in Italy, including the bombings of Milan's Piazza Fontana and Brescia's Piazza della Loggia. In 1978 the far-left Red Brigades kidnapped and killed former Christian Democrat prime minister Aldo Moro, while Pope Paul VI offered himself in exchange for Moro.

**Historic Compromise**
The 1970s arrangement in which the Italian Communist Party, under Enrico Berlinguer, agreed to cooperate with and support the Christian Democrats. Aldo Moro was a key backer of the arrangement.

**Benito Mussolini and the March on Rome**
Mussolini, founder of Italian Fascism, came to power in 1922 after his Blackshirts marched on Rome. After being deposed in 1943, he was freed by Otto Skorzeny's glider raid at Gran Sasso; in 1945 partisans shot him near Lake Como and hung his body upside down at a Milan gas station alongside his mistress Clara Petacci.

**Italian Campaign of World War II (Monte Cassino and Anzio)**
The Allies invaded Sicily in Operation Husky (1943), deceived by Operation Mincemeat, in which a corpse (Glyndwr Michael) was dressed as an officer carrying false plans. They then landed at Salerno and at Anzio (Operation Shingle, led by John P. Lucas). German defenses under Albert Kesselring included the Gustav Line, and the Allies bombed the Benedictine abbey of Monte Cassino.

**Battle of Adwa and the Ethiopian wars**
Italy's 1889 Treaty of Wuchale with Ethiopia was disputed over its translation, leading to Italy's crushing defeat by Menelik II at Adwa in 1896. Mussolini invaded Ethiopia in 1935, and Emperor Haile Selassie appealed to the League of Nations, while the secret Hoare-Laval Pact tried to end the war by giving Italy much of Ethiopia.

**Orsini's bombs**
In 1858, Italian nationalist Felice Orsini threw mercury fulminate bombs at Napoleon III's carriage outside the Paris opera house on the rue Le Peletier. The attack failed but pushed Napoleon III toward supporting Italian unification, and the bombs had been made in Britain, which helped bring down Palmerston's first ministry.

**Sicily and Syracuse (Sicilian Expedition)**
Sicily, the island off the toe of Italy, was part of Greek "Magna Graecia." Athens's disastrous Sicilian Expedition (415–413 BC) under Nicias was defeated at Syracuse, and Archimedes died when the Romans under Marcellus took Syracuse in 212 BC. The 1282 War of the Sicilian Vespers drove out Charles of Anjou.

**Lateran Treaty and the Roman Question**
After Italian troops took Rome in 1870, Pope Pius IX declared himself a "prisoner in the Vatican," starting the "Roman Question." It was settled by the 1929 Lateran Treaty, in which Mussolini's government recognized Vatican City as an independent state.

**Gabriele D'Annunzio and Fiume**
The nationalist poet D'Annunzio led a force that occupied the city of Fiume (now Rijeka, Croatia) in 1919, angry that the Allies had not honored the 1915 Treaty of London's territorial promises to Italy. His style of rule influenced Mussolini's Fascism.

**Ostrogoths, Lombards, and Charlemagne**
After Odoacer deposed the last Western Roman emperor, Theodoric the Great's Ostrogoths killed him and ruled Italy from Ravenna, where Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy while imprisoned. Byzantine exarchs later governed Ravenna, the Lombard kingdom's last king was Desiderius, and Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor at St. Peter's in 800.

**Silvio Berlusconi and Rubygate**
Berlusconi, a media tycoon who served as prime minister several times, was charged in the "Rubygate" scandal for paying for sex with an underage nightclub dancer, linked to his "bunga bunga" parties.

**Janissaries and the devshirme**
The Janissaries were the elite infantry corps that guarded the sultan and formed the core of the Ottoman army. They were recruited through the devshirme ("collection," sometimes called the "blood tax"), in which Christian boys, mostly from the Balkans, were taken from their families, converted to Islam, and trained for military or civil service.

**Suleiman the Magnificent**
The sultan who ruled from 1520 to 1566, under whom the empire reached its peak. Known in Turkish as "the Lawgiver" (Kanuni) for his legal codes blending sultanic law with sharia, he won at Mohács, took Belgrade, Rhodes, and Baghdad, besieged Vienna in 1529, and married Roxelana (Hürrem Sultan).

**Mehmed II and the fall of Constantinople (1453)**
Mehmed II, "the Conqueror," captured Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire. He made the city (later Istanbul) his capital and converted the Hagia Sophia into a mosque, adding minarets to the former Orthodox cathedral.

**Auspicious Incident (1826)**
Sultan Mahmud II's forcible destruction of the Janissary corps after they revolted against his military reforms. Thousands of Janissaries were killed, many executed in Thessaloniki's "Blood Tower," clearing the way for a modern, European-style army.

**Tanzimat and the Edict of Gülhane**
The Tanzimat ("reorganization") was a period of Westernizing, centralizing reforms from 1839 to 1876. It began with the 1839 Edict of Gülhane (the "Noble Edict of the Rose Chamber"), which guaranteed subjects' lives and property, abolished tax farming, and reformed taxation and conscription; later reforms reorganized the millet system.

**Sieges of Vienna (1529 and 1683)**
Suleiman's 1529 siege of Vienna marked the limit of Ottoman expansion into Central Europe. The 1683 siege under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa was broken at the Battle of Kahlenberg by the Holy League led by Polish king Jan III Sobieski, whose Winged Hussars made one of history's largest cavalry charges; legends say the croissant (kipferl) and Vienna's coffeehouses came from this victory.

**Battle of Mohács (1526)**
Suleiman's crushing victory over King Louis II of Hungary and Bohemia, who died fleeing the battle. It ended the Jagiellonian line in Hungary and led to Hungary being partitioned between the Ottomans and the Habsburgs.

**"Sick Man of Europe"**
A nickname for the declining Ottoman Empire in the 19th and early 20th centuries, tied to the "Eastern Question" of what would happen to its territories. The empire joined the Central Powers in World War I, defended Gallipoli against the Allies, and was dissolved after the war.

**Battle of Lepanto (1571)**
A naval battle in which the Holy League fleet, commanded by Don John of Austria, destroyed much of the Ottoman navy in the Gulf of Patras. It checked Ottoman naval power in the Mediterranean, though the fleet was quickly rebuilt.

**Hayreddin Barbarossa**
The Ottoman admiral and corsair who commanded Suleiman's navy. In an alliance with Francis I of France, he helped the French besiege Nice in 1543.

**Topkapi Palace, the harem, and the valide sultan**
Topkapi in Istanbul was the sultans' palace and seat of government. Its imperial harem was overseen by the Chief Black Eunuch, and the valide sultan (the sultan's mother) held great power, especially during the "Sultanate of Women" that began around Suleiman's marriage to Roxelana and lasted about a century.

**Fratricide and the kafes**
To prevent succession wars, new sultans often had their brothers killed; Mehmed III had his 19 brothers strangled with silk cords in 1595. This was later replaced by the kafes ("cage"), where princes were confined in the palace, which is blamed for rulers like Ibrahim "the Mad."

**Osman I and his dream**
Osman I founded the dynasty and gave the empire its name in Anatolia around 1300. Legend says he dreamt of a giant tree growing from his navel and spreading over the world, foretelling the empire. New sultans were girded with the Sword of Osman at their accession.

**Young Turks and the Committee of Union and Progress**
The reformist Young Turk movement, organized as the Committee of Union and Progress (CUP), took power after 1908 and dominated the government during the Balkan Wars and World War I. It carried out genocides of Armenians, Assyrians (the Sayfo), and Greeks.

**Treaty of Karlowitz (1699)**
The treaty ending the Great Turkish War that followed the failed 1683 siege of Vienna. The Ottomans gave up most of Hungary to the Habsburgs and the Morea (Peloponnese) to Venice, the first major loss of territory in Europe.

**Treaty of Sèvres and the end of the empire**
The 1920 treaty that carved up the empire after World War I. It was rejected by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk's nationalists, who won the Turkish War of Independence, abolished the sultanate in 1922 (ending the reign of the last sultan, Mehmed VI), and founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923.

**"Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!"**
The most famous line of Reagan's 1987 speech at the Brandenburg Gate in West Berlin, delivered with West German chancellor Helmut Kohl present. Reagan also urged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev to "open this gate," and the line is a near-universal giveaway for him.

**Attempted assassination by John Hinckley Jr.**
In March 1981, barely two months into Reagan's presidency, John Hinckley Jr. shot him outside the Washington Hilton hotel in an effort to impress actress Jodie Foster. Reagan joked to his wife Nancy, "Honey, I forgot to duck," Secret Service agent Jerry Parr pushed him into the limousine, and Secretary of State Alexander Haig wrongly claimed "I am in control here" at the White House.

**James Brady and the Brady Bill**
Reagan's press secretary James Brady was left permanently disabled by a gunshot wound to the head in the Hinckley shooting. The 1993 Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act, signed by Bill Clinton, was named for him and created a federal background-check system for gun purchases (NICS). Part of the law was struck down in Printz v. United States (1997) as a violation of the Tenth Amendment.

**Iran-Contra affair**
A scandal in Reagan's second term in which administration officials secretly sold arms to Iran and used the profits to fund the Contra rebels fighting Nicaragua's Sandinista government. This violated the Boland Amendment, which banned such aid, and was investigated by the Tower Commission, which criticized Reagan's detached management style.

**"A Time for Choosing"**
Reagan's 1964 televised speech supporting Republican presidential candidate Barry Goldwater, also called the "Rendezvous with Destiny" speech. It ends by borrowing FDR's line "You and I have a rendezvous with destiny," raised large sums for Goldwater, and launched Reagan's political career.

**Challenger disaster speech**
Reagan's 1986 address after the space shuttle Challenger exploded shortly after launch, killing its seven crew members. Quoting the poem "High Flight," he said they had "slipped the surly bonds of earth to touch the face of God," and compared them to the explorer Francis Drake, who "lived by the sea, died by the sea, and was buried at sea."

**Governor of California and Berkeley**
Reagan defeated incumbent Pat Brown in 1966 to become governor of California after promising to "clean up the mess at Berkeley," and won reelection in 1970 over Jesse "Big Daddy" Unruh. In 1969 he sent the Highway Patrol and National Guard against the People's Park protests in Berkeley, where one bystander was killed. As governor he also signed the first no-fault divorce law in the US and a 1967 law liberalizing abortion that he later regretted.

**Mulford Act**
A 1967 California law signed by Governor Reagan that banned carrying loaded firearms in public. It was aimed at the armed patrols the Black Panther Party used to monitor police.

**Air traffic controllers' strike (PATCO)**
In 1981 Reagan fired more than 11,000 striking members of the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization (PATCO) who ignored his order to return to work. The move was a major blow to organized labor in the United States.

**Election of 1980 and "There you go again"**
Reagan defeated incumbent Jimmy Carter amid the Iran Hostage Crisis and a weak economy, with John B. Anderson running as an independent. In a debate he deflected Carter's attacks with "There you go again" and asked voters, "Are you better off than you were four years ago?" Iran released the American hostages minutes after Reagan was inaugurated.

**Reaganomics and "voodoo economics"**
Reagan's economic program of tax cuts, deregulation, and reduced domestic spending, based on supply-side economics. George H.W. Bush, his 1980 primary rival and later vice president and successor, derided it as "voodoo economics."

**Strategic Defense Initiative ("Star Wars")**
Reagan's 1983 proposal for a missile defense system, partly based in space, that would shoot down Soviet nuclear missiles. Critics nicknamed it "Star Wars," and it was a sticking point at the 1986 Reykjavik Summit with Gorbachev.

**Election of 1984 and "Morning in America"**
Reagan won reelection in a landslide over Walter Mondale, helped by the "It's morning again in America" ad celebrating the economic recovery. In a debate he joked that he would not "exploit, for political purposes, my opponent's youth and inexperience," defusing concerns about his own age.

**INF Treaty and the Reykjavik Summit**
Reagan and Gorbachev's 1986 summit in Reykjavik, Iceland, nearly reached a deal to eliminate nuclear weapons but collapsed over SDI. Their 1987 Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty eliminated an entire class of nuclear missiles.

**Invasion of Grenada (Operation Urgent Fury) and the bombing of Libya**
In 1983 Reagan ordered the invasion of Grenada after a coup in which Prime Minister Maurice Bishop was killed. In 1986 he ordered air strikes on Libya (Operation El Dorado Canyon) after a terrorist bombing of a West Berlin discotheque, following earlier clashes with Libya in the Gulf of Sidra.

**Harold Holt and "All the way with LBJ"**
Holt was a Liberal prime minister who succeeded Robert Menzies in 1966 and backed the U.S. war in Vietnam, declaring that Australia would go "all the way with LBJ." In December 1967 he disappeared while swimming at Cheviot Beach in Victoria, and his body was never found.

**Robert Menzies and "The Forgotten People"**
Australia's longest-serving prime minister, who founded the modern Liberal Party and governed 1939–1941 and 1949–1966. His 1942 radio speech "The Forgotten People" praised the middle class as the backbone of the nation; his government handled the defection of Soviet spy Vladimir Petrov in 1954 and sent troops to the Malayan Emergency and Vietnam.

**Stolen Generations and Kevin Rudd's apology**
The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, many of mixed descent, who were removed from their families by government policy and placed with white families or institutions, mostly from the late 19th century to the 1970s. The 1997 Bringing Them Home report documented the removals, National Sorry Day commemorates them, and Prime Minister Kevin Rudd issued a formal national apology in 2008 after John Howard had refused to.

**Rum Rebellion and William Bligh**
In 1808 officers of the New South Wales Corps led by George Johnston, encouraged by the wool pioneer John Macarthur, overthrew Governor William Bligh, who had earlier lost his ship in the Mutiny on the Bounty. The coup, named for the Corps' control of the rum trade, led Britain to appoint Lachlan Macquarie as governor.

**The Dismissal (1975)**
The constitutional crisis in which Governor-General Sir John Kerr removed Labor Prime Minister Gough Whitlam and appointed Liberal leader Malcolm Fraser as caretaker. It followed the Loans Affair, in which minister Rex Connor tried to raise overseas loans through the broker Tirath Khemlani, and the Senate's blocking of the budget; Whitlam is the only prime minister to be dismissed.

**Ned Kelly and the bushrangers**
Bushrangers were outlaws, often escaped convicts, who lived in the Australian bush. The most famous, Ned Kelly, killed three policemen at Stringybark Creek with his gang, including his brother Dan, and was captured in 1880 at Glenrowan wearing homemade iron armor before being hanged; Peter Carey's novel True History of the Kelly Gang fictionalizes his life.

**First Fleet, Arthur Phillip, and Botany Bay**
James Cook landed at Botany Bay on HMS Endeavour in 1770 and claimed eastern Australia for Britain. In 1788 Captain Arthur Phillip led the First Fleet of convict ships, settling at Port Jackson (Sydney) to found the penal colony of New South Wales.

**Eureka Stockade**
A 1854 rebellion by gold miners at Ballarat during the Victorian gold rush, protesting expensive mining licenses and lack of voting rights. Troops stormed the miners' stockade, but the revolt led to reforms and is seen as a founding moment of Australian democracy.

**White Australia policy**
The set of policies restricting non-European, especially Asian, immigration, formalized by the Immigration Restriction Act of 1901. It grew out of anti-Chinese violence during the gold rushes, such as the Buckland and Lambing Flat riots, and was dismantled in stages from the late 1940s to the 1970s.

**ANZAC and Gallipoli**
The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps fought in the failed 1915 Gallipoli campaign against the Ottoman Empire in World War I. The landing is commemorated each year on ANZAC Day, April 25.

**John Curtin and the bombing of Darwin**
John Curtin was the Labor prime minister during most of World War II, when Japanese aircraft bombed Darwin in February 1942 and Japan fought Australians in the Territory of New Guinea. His successor Ben Chifley, who led postwar reconstruction, gave the "light on the hill" speech describing Labor's ideals.

**Mabo decision and terra nullius**
The 1992 High Court ruling in Mabo v. Queensland recognized native title for Indigenous Australians and rejected the doctrine of terra nullius, the claim that the land had belonged to no one before British settlement. Later that year Prime Minister Paul Keating acknowledged past injustices against Aboriginal people in his Redfern Speech.

**Black War in Van Diemen's Land**
The violent conflict between British settlers and Aboriginal Tasmanians (Palawa) in Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania) in the 1820s and early 1830s. Governor George Arthur organized the "Black Line," a sweep by settlers to drive Aboriginal people from the settled districts, and George Augustus Robinson led "Friendly Missions" that relocated survivors.

**Burke and Wills expedition**
The 1860–1861 expedition sponsored by the Royal Society of Victoria to cross Australia from Melbourne to the Gulf of Carpentaria. Robert O'Hara Burke and William Wills reached the gulf but died on the return trip near Cooper Creek, where a "Dig Tree" marked buried supplies; John King was the only member of the final party to survive.

**Pacific Solution and the Tampa affair**
In 2001 the Norwegian freighter MV Tampa rescued 433 mostly Hazara asylum seekers, and John Howard's government refused to let them land in Australia. This led to the "Pacific Solution," under which asylum seekers were sent to offshore detention on Nauru and other places.

**"Starving Time"**
The catastrophic winter of 1609–1610, when Jamestown's population fell from roughly 500 to about 60 amid famine, disease, and a Powhatan siege. Colonists ate horses, rats, and shoe leather, and there is evidence of cannibalism; survivors included Temperance Flowerdew.

**John Rolfe and tobacco**
Rolfe introduced a sweeter strain of tobacco, grown from seeds obtained from the Spanish Caribbean, around 1612. Tobacco became the colony's cash crop and made Virginia economically viable.

**John Smith and Pocahontas**
Smith was an early leader of Jamestown who, according to his own later account, was captured by the Powhatans and saved from execution by Pocahontas, daughter of Chief Powhatan. He imposed the rule "he that will not work shall not eat" before returning to England in 1609 after a gunpowder injury.

**Bacon's Rebellion (1676)**
An uprising led by Nathaniel Bacon against Governor William Berkeley, who had refused to authorize a militia commission to fight Native Americans. It began after a dispute with the Doeg people over Thomas Mathews's plantation, saw attacks on Native groups including the Pamunkey, and ended with Bacon's forces burning Jamestown before Bacon died of dysentery.

**Opechancanough and the 1622 massacre**
The brother and eventual successor of Chief Powhatan, who once captured John Smith on a hunting trip. He led the 1622 surprise attack that killed about a third of the colonists, including at Martin's Hundred, and a later 1644 attack; he was shot in the back by a guard while a prisoner and was succeeded by Necotowance.

**Lord De La Warr**
Thomas West, Baron De La Warr, the colony's governor, arrived with relief ships and supplies in June 1610 just as the starving survivors were abandoning the settlement. His arrival saved Jamestown and launched the First Anglo-Powhatan War.

**Sea Venture and the Third Supply**
The flagship of the 1609 Third Supply mission, which was wrecked on Bermuda in a hurricane. The loss of its supplies and leaders worsened the Starving Time, and the wreck is thought to have inspired Shakespeare's The Tempest.

**Susan Constant, Godspeed, and Discovery**
The three ships, commanded by Christopher Newport, that brought the first colonists to Jamestown in 1607. Newport later returned with supply missions.

**Triangular fort**
The original James Fort, built in 1607 as a triangle of wooden palisade walls with bulwarks at each corner. It is the source of clues calling Jamestown a "triangle-shaped colony."

**Werowocomoco and the Powhatan Confederacy**
Werowocomoco was the capital of Chief Powhatan, across the York River area from Jamestown, and a hub for trading English copper and beads for food. Pocahontas, also called Matoaka, came from there and later took the name Rebecca when she married John Rolfe.

**House of Burgesses**
The first elected legislative assembly in English America, which first met at Jamestown in 1619 under Governor George Yeardley. That same year, enslaved Africans, including a woman named Angela, arrived at Point Comfort.

**Edward Maria Wingfield and Bartholomew Gosnold**
Wingfield was the first president of the colony's council and chose the settlement's site, but he was deposed in 1607 amid accusations including atheism. Gosnold, a key organizer of the expedition, died at Jamestown that same year.

**Thomas Dale and the "Lawes Divine, Morall and Martiall"**
Dale, a deputy governor, imposed this harsh martial-law code around 1611 to restore discipline. He also founded the upriver settlement of Henricus to grow food.

**Chanco's warning to Richard Pace**
Chanco, a Powhatan boy living with colonist Richard Pace, warned him of the planned 1622 attack. Pace alerted Jamestown in time to save it, though outlying settlements like Martin's Hundred were devastated.

**George Percy**
A colonist who led Jamestown during the Starving Time and wrote an account of its horrors. He also recorded a 1610 raid in which his soldiers killed the children of a Paspahegh chief by throwing them into the water and shooting them.

**Hulagu Khan's sack of Baghdad (1258)**
The Mongol siege and sack of Baghdad led by Hulagu Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan, after Caliph al-Musta'sim refused to surrender. Huge numbers of people were killed and the Abbasid Caliphate ended, and the event is often used to mark the end of the Islamic Golden Age.

**House of Wisdom**
Baghdad's great library and research institution (Bayt al-Hikma), linked to Harun al-Rashid and expanded by his son al-Ma'mun. Scholars there translated Greek, Persian, and Indian texts into Arabic, and it was destroyed in the 1258 Mongol sack, though the scholar Nasir al-Din al-Tusi saved some books and later built the Maragheh observatory.

**Tigris ran black with ink**
A legend that the Mongols threw so many books from the House of Wisdom and Baghdad's other libraries into the Tigris River that its waters turned black with ink. It is the most common giveaway image for the 1258 sack.

**Al-Musta'sim trampled in a carpet**
The last Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, killed by the Mongols after the city fell. Because the Mongols had a taboo against spilling royal blood, he was rolled up in a carpet and trampled to death by horses.

**Al-Mansur and the "Round City"**
The second Abbasid caliph, al-Mansur, founded Baghdad on the Tigris in 762 as his new capital, which he called Madinat al-Salam, the "City of Peace." Its original core was a perfectly circular walled city with gates such as the Khorasan and Kufa gates.

**Translation Movement**
The large-scale effort, centered in Abbasid Baghdad and especially encouraged by al-Ma'mun, to translate Greek philosophy, science, and medicine into Arabic. It preserved many ancient works that later reached medieval Europe.

**Al-Khwarizmi**
A mathematician who worked at the House of Wisdom and whose book on "al-jabr" gave the field of algebra its name. The word "algorithm" also comes from the Latin form of his name.

**Banu Musa and the Book of Ingenious Devices**
The Banu Musa ("Sons of Moses") were three brothers in 9th-century Baghdad who wrote the Book of Ingenious Devices. It describes automatic machines such as self-trimming and self-refilling lamps, trick fountains, a mechanical "drinking" animal, and an early gas mask.

**Barmakid family**
A powerful family of viziers to the early Abbasid caliphs, descended from Buddhist administrators of the Nava Vihara monastery near Balkh. Khalid ibn Barmak served al-Mansur, Yahya ibn Khalid helped Harun al-Rashid take power, and the family is credited with founding Baghdad's first paper mill and backing translation work.

**Harun al-Rashid**
The Abbasid caliph whose reign marked the height of Baghdad's Golden Age. He sent gifts to Charlemagne, including a water clock from which mechanical horsemen emerged on the hour and an elephant named Abul-Abbas.

**Palace of the Golden Gate**
Al-Mansur's palace at the center of the Round City, crowned by a great green dome. A figure of a horseman with a lance stood on top and was said to point toward the direction of the caliph's enemies.

**Doquz Khatun**
Hulagu Khan's wife, a Nestorian Christian princess of the Kerait tribe. Because of her influence, Baghdad's Christians were spared during the massacre that followed the 1258 sack.

**Mihna**
An inquisition started by al-Ma'mun that forced scholars to accept the Mu'tazilite teaching that the Quran was created, not eternal. The jurist Ahmad ibn Hanbal was imprisoned and punished for refusing, and Caliph al-Mutawakkil later ended it.

**Battle of the Zab, Samarra, and later dynasties**
The Abbasids' 750 victory over the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, at the Battle of the Zab led to their new capital at Baghdad. Caliph al-Mu'tasim briefly moved the capital to Samarra because of his Turkish ghulam (slave-soldier) guards, and the Buyids and then the Seljuk Tughril Beg (in 1055) later took power in Baghdad.

**Firdos Square and the Green Zone**
In modern Baghdad, the 2003 toppling of a statue of Saddam Hussein in Firdos Square during the U.S.-led invasion was broadcast live around the world. The fortified Green Zone, around Saddam's former Republican Palace, became the seat of the post-invasion government, and the city also has the Victory Arch's crossed swords and the bookselling Mutanabbi Street.

**Expedition of the Thousand**
Garibaldi's 1860 campaign in which about a thousand volunteers sailed from near Genoa, landed at Marsala in Sicily, and overthrew the Bourbon Kingdom of the Two Sicilies under King Francis II. It is his most famous achievement and the central event of the Italian unification (Risorgimento).

**Redshirts**
The name for Garibaldi's volunteer soldiers, who wore distinctive red shirts. The tradition began in Montevideo, Uruguay, where his Italian Legion was supplied with red shirts originally intended for slaughterhouse workers.

**"Hero of the Two Worlds"**
Garibaldi's nickname, earned because he fought for liberal causes in both South America and Europe. His years in South America made him famous before his campaigns in Italy.

**Uruguayan Civil War and the Colorados**
In the 1840s Garibaldi led the Italian Legion and the Uruguayan navy for the Colorado faction of Fructuoso Rivera, helping defend Montevideo against the Blancos of Manuel Oribe and their ally, Argentina's Juan Manuel de Rosas. He won the Battle of Sant'Antonio near Salto against a much larger force.

**Ragamuffin War and Anita Garibaldi**
The Ragamuffin War (Farroupilha Revolution) was a rebellion of the Brazilian province of Rio Grande do Sul, in which Garibaldi fought for the rebels and helped capture Laguna, where the Juliana Republic was proclaimed. There he met his wife Anita (Ana Ribeiro da Silva), who fought beside him and died in 1849 while fleeing Austrian and French forces after the fall of the Roman Republic.

**Victor Emmanuel II and the meeting at Teano**
In October 1860, Garibaldi met King Victor Emmanuel II of Piedmont-Sardinia at Teano and handed over his conquests in southern Italy, putting aside his republican beliefs for the sake of unification. Victor Emmanuel became the first king of unified Italy in 1861.

**Hunters of the Alps**
A volunteer unit (Cacciatori delle Alpi) Garibaldi led against Austria in the 1859 Second Italian War of Independence, operating in the mountains while the allied French and Piedmontese won battles such as Magenta. The name was later revived for an elite Italian Army unit.

**Battle of Volturno**
The decisive 1860 battle of the Expedition of the Thousand, fought along the Volturno River near Capua and Caserta. Garibaldi defeated the Neapolitan army, ending the Bourbon Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

**Battles of Calatafimi and Milazzo**
Early victories of the Expedition of the Thousand in Sicily. At Calatafimi, Garibaldi's outnumbered men won with an uphill bayonet charge; at Milazzo they secured Sicily before crossing the Strait of Messina to the mainland.

**Count Cavour**
Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia and the main architect of Italian unification. He distrusted Garibaldi's radicalism but used his conquests to unify Italy under Victor Emmanuel II; Cavour, Mazzini, and Garibaldi are called the "brain," "heart," and "sword" of the Risorgimento.

**Battle of Bezzecca and "Obbedisco"**
In the 1866 war with Austria, Garibaldi's volunteers won the Battle of Bezzecca while advancing into Trentino. When ordered to withdraw, he replied with a one-word telegram, "Obbedisco" ("I obey").

**Army of the Vosges**
A volunteer army Garibaldi led in support of France during the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871. He was afterward elected to the French National Assembly but soon resigned.

**Aspromonte and Mentana**
Failed attempts by Garibaldi to capture Rome, which was still under the pope. At Aspromonte in 1862 he was wounded and captured by Italian royal troops, having told his men not to fire on them, and at Mentana in 1867 he was defeated by French and papal forces.

**Giuseppe Mazzini**
The republican nationalist and founder of the Young Italy movement who inspired Garibaldi and publicized his exploits. Garibaldi was also involved with the Carbonari revolutionary societies in his early career.

**Declining Lincoln's offer**
At the start of the American Civil War, Abraham Lincoln's government offered Garibaldi a command in the Union army. He declined, partly because he wanted supreme command and an immediate commitment to abolish slavery.

**My Lai Massacre**
The March 1968 killing of hundreds of unarmed Vietnamese civilians by U.S. soldiers of Charlie Company in the hamlet of My Lai (codenamed "Pinkville"), in the Son Tinh district. Villagers were herded into ditches and shot. Lieutenant William Calley was the only soldier convicted. Helicopter pilot Hugh Thompson tried to stop the killing, Ronald Ridenhour's letters prompted an investigation, and journalist Seymour Hersh exposed the story. Army photographer Ronald Haeberle's photo of the bodies became the antiwar poster "And babies."

**Tet Offensive**
A massive surprise attack by the Viet Cong and North Vietnamese Army launched in January 1968 during a truce for Tet, the Lunar New Year. Attackers struck cities across South Vietnam, briefly breached the U.S. embassy compound in Saigon, and fought a long urban battle in Hue. Although it was a military defeat for the communists, it shattered American public confidence in the war and in General William Westmoreland, the U.S. commander, who was replaced by Creighton Abrams.

**Siege of Khe Sanh**
A siege of U.S. Marines and allied forces at a mountain combat base in northwestern South Vietnam from January to April 1968, around the time of the Tet Offensive. Some historians believe it was meant partly to distract U.S. attention from the coming attacks on the cities.

**Gulf of Tonkin incident**
In August 1964 the destroyer USS Maddox reported attacks by North Vietnamese patrol boats in the Gulf of Tonkin; a second reported attack probably never happened. Congress responded with the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, which gave President Lyndon Johnson broad power to escalate U.S. military involvement in Vietnam.

**Agent Orange and Operation Ranch Hand**
Agent Orange was a dioxin-contaminated herbicide that Operation Ranch Hand sprayed from C-123 aircraft to strip jungle cover and destroy crops, including along supply trails. Manufacturers included Monsanto and Dow Chemical, and Ranch Hand crews used the parody motto "Only you can prevent a forest." It caused lasting health problems in Vietnam and among veterans. Napalm, an incendiary jelly, was also widely used.

**Kent State shootings**
On May 4, 1970, Ohio National Guardsmen fired on students protesting Richard Nixon's invasion of Cambodia at Kent State University, killing four. A famous photo shows 14-year-old runaway Mary Ann Vecchio kneeling and screaming over the body of a slain student.

**Strategic Hamlet Program**
A program begun in 1962 by South Vietnam's government, with U.S. support, to move rural peasants into fortified villages and cut them off from communist guerrillas. It was modeled on British resettlement camps from the Malayan Emergency. It was resented and largely failed.

**Tinker v. Des Moines**
A 1969 Supreme Court case in which the Court ruled that Iowa students who wore black armbands to school to protest the Vietnam War were exercising protected free speech. In the Court's words, students do not "shed their constitutional rights... at the schoolhouse gate."

**Fall of Saigon and Operation Frequent Wind**
On April 30, 1975, North Vietnamese forces captured Saigon, the South Vietnamese capital (later renamed Ho Chi Minh City), ending the war after Le Duan's Spring Offensive. South Vietnam's last president, Duong Van Minh, surrendered. Irving Berlin's "White Christmas" played on Armed Forces Radio as the signal to begin Operation Frequent Wind, the helicopter evacuation of Americans and Vietnamese. A famous photo shows people climbing a ladder to a helicopter on a Saigon rooftop. Vietnam now celebrates April 30 as a national holiday.

**Thich Quang Duc and Ngo Dinh Diem**
In 1963 the Buddhist monk Thich Quang Duc burned himself to death in a Saigon street to protest persecution of Buddhists by South Vietnam's Catholic president Ngo Dinh Diem. Malcolm Browne's photograph of the burning monk, with his car's hood open behind him, became world famous. The Buddhist crisis prompted U.S. fact-finding missions (Krulak–Mendenhall, then McNamara–Taylor), and Diem was overthrown and killed in a coup in November 1963.

**Pentagon Papers**
A secret Defense Department history of U.S. decision-making in Vietnam, leaked in 1971 by military analyst Daniel Ellsberg to The New York Times and The Washington Post. Senator Mike Gravel read portions into the record, and the 2017 film The Post depicts their publication.

**Ho Chi Minh Trail**
A network of roads and paths through Laos and Cambodia that North Vietnam used to supply Viet Cong guerrillas in the South. It was built and run by a North Vietnamese unit called Group 559. The U.S. bombed it, sprayed it with herbicides, and laid an "electronic fence" of sensors along it, which enemy soldiers reportedly fooled with buckets of urine.

**Operation Rolling Thunder**
A long U.S. aerial bombing campaign against North Vietnam from 1965 to 1968. It was restricted in its targets and meant to pressure Hanoi gradually and choke off supplies to the South.

**Antiwar protests and the draft**
Opposition to the war took many forms, including burning draft cards, fleeing to Canada to "dodge" the draft, the 1967 March on the Pentagon (where Abbie Hoffman tried to "levitate" the building and Norman Mailer was arrested), and the Catonsville Nine, led by the priests Daniel and Philip Berrigan, who burned draft files. Boxer Muhammad Ali refused induction. Nixon appealed to the "silent majority" against protesters, and pro-war construction workers attacked protesters in the 1970 Hard Hat Riot.

**Paris Peace Accords**
The 1973 agreement that ended direct U.S. military involvement in Vietnam. Henry Kissinger and North Vietnam's Le Duc Tho were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for negotiating it, and Le Duc Tho declined his share. Earlier, in 1968, Anna Chennault allegedly worked to stall peace talks on behalf of Richard Nixon's presidential campaign.

**Partitions of Poland**
Three partitions in 1772, 1793, and 1795, in which Russia, Prussia, and Austria divided up the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth until it vanished from the map. The first came after the Bar Confederation's failed revolt, Catherine the Great's Russia was the leading power behind them, and Poland did not regain independence until 1918.

**Sejm and the liberum veto**
The Sejm is the Polish parliament. Under the old Commonwealth, the liberum veto let any single deputy cancel a session and all of its legislation, which paralyzed the government and let foreign powers bribe deputies to block reform.

**Constitution of May 3, 1791**
A reform constitution passed by the Great Sejm under King Stanisław II August that abolished the liberum veto. Conservative nobles formed the Targowica Confederation and asked Russia to overturn it, which led to the Second Partition.

**Invasion of Poland (September 1, 1939)**
Nazi Germany's invasion that started World War II in Europe, followed by a Soviet invasion from the east on September 17. It was justified by the Gleiwitz incident, a staged attack on a German radio station by SS men in Polish uniforms (Operation Canned Goods), and the invasion was followed by the Western "Phoney War."

**Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact**
The August 1939 non-aggression pact between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union, whose secret protocol split Poland between them. Germany invaded nine days after it was signed.

**Solidarity and Lech Wałęsa**
Solidarity was the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc, founded in 1980 at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk and led by electrician Lech Wałęsa. Banned under General Wojciech Jaruzelski's 1981 martial law, it negotiated the 1989 Round Table Talks, won the following election using posters of Gary Cooper from High Noon, and Wałęsa became president.

**Union of Lublin and Jogaila-Jadwiga marriage**
The 1386 marriage of Queen Jadwiga of Poland to Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania created a personal union and the Jagiellonian dynasty. The 1569 Union of Lublin, under the last Jagiellonian king Sigismund II Augustus, turned it into the single Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

**Golden Liberty and the szlachta**
The szlachta were Poland's very large noble class, about a tenth of the population, who claimed descent from the ancient Sarmatians. Their "Golden Liberty" system, based on laws like Nihil Novi (1505), gave them an elective monarchy, the liberum veto, and the right to legal revolt (rokosz).

**Henrician Articles**
Terms that every elected Polish king had to swear to, named for Henry of Valois (later Henry III of France), the first king chosen by free election in 1573. Each king also signed a personal agreement called the pacta conventa.

**The Deluge**
The devastating mid-1600s Swedish invasion under Charles X Gustav during the Second Northern War, which came after the Khmelnytsky Uprising of the Cossacks. It killed around a third of Poland's population and cost the Commonwealth Livonia.

**John III Sobieski and the Winged Hussars**
King John III Sobieski led the relief army, spearheaded by Poland's famous Winged Hussars (heavy cavalry who wore wings on their backs), that broke the Ottoman Siege of Vienna in 1683. Legend says the first bagel was made to honor him.

**Warsaw Ghetto Uprising and Nazi camps**
In 1943, Jewish fighters of the ŻOB revolted in the Warsaw Ghetto, the largest Jewish ghetto in occupied Europe, until SS general Jürgen Stroop crushed them and deported the survivors to Treblinka. Major Nazi death camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau stood in occupied Poland, and the separate 1944 Warsaw Uprising saw the Wola massacre.

**Piast dynasty**
Poland's first ruling dynasty, which included Bolesław the Brave and Casimir the Great. Henry the Pious, a Piast duke, died fighting the Mongols at the 1241 Battle of Legnica; the Jagiellonians came after the Piasts.

**Tadeusz Kościuszko**
A Polish military engineer who helped the Americans win the Battle of Saratoga in the Revolutionary War. He led the 1794 Kościuszko Uprising against Russia, whose defeat (including the Massacre of Praga) led to the Third Partition.

**Battle of Klushino and Augustus the Strong**
At Klushino in 1610, Polish forces crushed a Russian-Swedish army during the Time of Troubles and went on to occupy Moscow until Minin and Pozharsky drove them out. Later, Augustus the Strong, Elector of Saxony, became Catholic to win the Polish throne and fought Sweden alongside Peter the Great in the Great Northern War.

**Masada**
A mountaintop fortress near the Dead Sea where the Sicarii, an extreme faction of the Zealots, held out at the end of the First Jewish-Roman War. When the Roman general Lucius Flavius Silva broke through around 73–74 CE, the roughly 960 defenders reportedly committed mass suicide rather than be captured, as chronicled by Josephus.

**Bar Kokhba Revolt**
The last major Jewish revolt against Rome (132–136 CE), led by Simon bar Kokhba, whose name means "Son of the Star." It was sparked partly by Hadrian's refounding of Jerusalem as the Roman colony Aelia Capitolina and ended with the fall of the fortress of Betar to forces under Julius Severus; letters from the revolt were found in the Cave of Letters, and its defeat is mourned on Tisha B'Av.

**Destruction of the Second Temple (70 CE)**
During the Great Jewish Revolt, which began in 66 CE, the future emperor Titus besieged Jerusalem and destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE. Afterward Vespasian imposed the Fiscus Judaicus, a tax on Jews redirected to the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus in Rome.

**Josephus**
Flavius Josephus was a Jewish commander turned Roman-allied historian who wrote The Jewish War, Antiquities of the Jews (containing the disputed Testimonium Flavianum passage about Jesus), and the polemic Against Apion. The "Josephus problem" in mathematics comes from a story of him surviving a suicide pact in which every third man in a circle was killed.

**Pogroms and the Pale of Settlement**
Pogroms were organized massacres of Jews, especially in the Russian Empire, where most Jews were confined to the Pale of Settlement and lived in small towns called shtetls. Notable pogroms struck Kishinev in 1903, stirred up by the newspaper Bessarabets, and Odessa in 1905, with the Black Hundreds often taking part; Alexander III's 1882 May Laws further restricted Jewish life.

**Blood libel**
The false accusation that Jews murdered Christians, especially children, to use their blood in rituals such as baking Passover matzah. An early English case followed the 1144 death of William of Norwich, publicized by Thomas of Monmouth; the legend of the Golem of Prague describes a clay guardian protecting Jews from such charges.

**Alhambra Decree and the Sephardim**
The 1492 edict of Ferdinand and Isabella that expelled Jews from Spain. The expelled Sephardic Jews, who spoke Ladino, largely resettled in the Ottoman Empire under Bayezid II (notably in Thessaloniki) and elsewhere; those who stayed and converted were called conversos, or marranos if suspected of practicing Judaism in secret.

**Kitos War**
A Jewish uprising in the Roman diaspora (115–117 CE) in places such as Cyrene, Egypt, and Cyprus, led in part by Lukuas, whose followers damaged Alexandria. It was crushed by the general Lusius Quietus, whose name the war bears.

**Doctors' Plot and "rootless cosmopolitans"**
In Stalin's final years, a Soviet anti-Jewish campaign derided Jews as "rootless cosmopolitans." In the 1953 Doctors' Plot, mostly Jewish Kremlin physicians were falsely accused of plotting to murder Soviet leaders; earlier, on the 1952 Night of the Murdered Poets, thirteen Soviet Jews were executed in Lubyanka prison.

**Dreyfus Affair and "J'Accuse...!"**
Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish French army captain, was wrongly convicted of treason in 1894. Émile Zola's open letter "J'Accuse...!" in the newspaper L'Aurore attacked the government's cover-up; Georges Picquart uncovered the real culprit, and Dreyfus was pardoned by President Émile Loubet in 1899.

**Maccabean Revolt and the Hasmoneans**
A revolt against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV, begun by the priest Mattathias and led by his son Judah Maccabee, which created the independent Hasmonean dynasty and is commemorated at Hanukkah. Later, a feud between the Hasmonean brothers Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II gave Pompey an opening to take Jerusalem in 63 BC.

**Black Death well-poisoning accusations**
During the plague of the mid-1300s, Jews were falsely blamed for poisoning wells and massacred across Western Europe. Many fled east to Poland, where Casimir the Great offered protection, helping to make Poland a center of Ashkenazi Jewry.

**The Holocaust and Jewish resistance**
The Nazi genocide of about six million Jews, coordinated at the 1942 Wannsee Conference, with deportation logistics run by Adolf Eichmann, who was later captured by Mossad and tried in Israel. The 1943 Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, led by Mordecai Anielewicz, resisted deportations to Treblinka, and rescuers such as Oskar Schindler, Raoul Wallenberg, and Chiune Sugihara are honored as "Righteous Among the Nations."

**Jews in American history**
Ulysses S. Grant's General Order No. 11 (1862) expelled Jews from his military district during the Civil War. The 1915 lynching of Leo Frank in Georgia followed the founding of the Anti-Defamation League, Jewish refugees on the MS St. Louis were turned away in 1939, and the 1991 Crown Heights riot in Brooklyn began after a car in a Hasidic Rebbe's motorcade killed a Black child.

**Expulsion from and readmission to England**
Edward I expelled the Jews from England in 1290 with the Edict of Expulsion. In 1655 Oliver Cromwell called the Whitehall Conference after the Dutch rabbi Menasseh ben Israel petitioned for readmission, and Jews were informally allowed to resettle in England.

**Gold Rush and Sutter's Mill**
In January 1848, the carpenter James Marshall found gold at Sutter's Mill on the American River, a sawmill he was building for John Sutter. The discovery set off the Gold Rush, which drew about 300,000 "forty-niners" (also called "argonauts") to California and quickly grew towns like San Francisco. President James Polk confirmed the discovery to Congress in December 1848. This is by far the most common clue for the state.

**Samuel Brannan**
A Mormon newspaper publisher (of the California Star) and merchant who first publicized the gold discovery. He famously ran through the streets of San Francisco waving a bottle of gold dust and shouting about gold on the American River, then made a fortune selling supplies to miners.

**Levi Strauss and blue jeans**
A German-Jewish immigrant who moved to San Francisco during the Gold Rush to sell dry goods. With tailor Jacob Davis, he later patented copper-riveted denim work pants, the first blue jeans, which became popular with miners and laborers.

**New Helvetia (Sutter's Fort)**
The colony that the Swiss immigrant John Sutter founded near present-day Sacramento in 1839. His workers abandoned it for the gold fields, and the Gold Rush ruined him financially.

**Bear Flag Revolt**
A June 1846 uprising in which American settlers, led by men such as William B. Ide, seized the Mexican town of Sonoma and declared the short-lived "California Republic." Their flag, with a grizzly bear and a star, became the basis of today's state flag.

**John C. Frémont and the conquest of California**
An explorer and army officer, nicknamed "the Pathfinder," who mapped much of California, including the San Joaquin Valley, in the 1840s. During the Mexican-American War he led the California Battalion, while Commodore Robert Stockton and General Stephen W. Kearny fought battles such as San Pasqual. He was also blamed for massacres of Native Americans, such as the 1846 Sacramento River massacre.

**Harvey Milk, Dan White, and the "Twinkie defense"**
Harvey Milk, called the "Mayor of Castro Street," was one of the first openly gay elected officials in the U.S. when he joined San Francisco's Board of Supervisors in 1977. In 1978 the former supervisor Dan White assassinated Milk and Mayor George Moscone. White's light manslaughter sentence, after a defense that critics mocked as the "Twinkie defense," set off the White Night Riots of 1979.

**Black Panther Party**
A Black Power organization founded in Oakland in 1966 by Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale, with members like Eldridge Cleaver. It released a Ten-Point Program, carried out armed patrols to monitor police, and ran community efforts such as the Free Breakfast for Children Program.

**Watts Riots**
Six days of rioting in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles in August 1965. They began after the police officer Lee Minikus stopped Marquette Frye for drunk driving. The state's McCone Commission report blamed the riots on unemployment, poor schools, and bad police relations. Frustration over Proposition 14, which overturned the Rumford Fair Housing Act, also contributed.

**Free Speech Movement and Mario Savio**
A 1964–1965 student protest movement at the University of California, Berkeley, against limits on political activity on campus. Its leader Mario Savio gave the "bodies upon the gears" speech, criticizing the university bureaucracy under UC president Clark Kerr.

**Japanese American internment, Korematsu, and Earl Warren**
After Executive Order 9066 in 1942, Japanese Americans on the West Coast were forced into camps such as Manzanar in California. Fred Korematsu was arrested in San Leandro for resisting removal, leading to the Supreme Court case Korematsu v. United States (1944). Earl Warren, then the state's attorney general and later its governor and Chief Justice of the U.S., supported the internment and later regretted it.

**Haight-Ashbury and the Summer of Love**
A San Francisco district that became the center of the 1960s hippie counterculture. It drew thousands of young people during the 1967 "Summer of Love," which followed the "Human Be-In" gathering in Golden Gate Park.

**Donner Party**
A group of pioneers bound for California who were trapped by snow in the Sierra Nevada in the winter of 1846–1847. Some survivors resorted to cannibalism.

**"Battle of Los Angeles" and the Bombardment of Ellwood**
In February 1942, the Japanese submarine I-17 shelled an oil facility at Ellwood near Santa Barbara, the first attack on the U.S. mainland in World War II. Days later, false reports of enemy aircraft (possibly a weather balloon) led to a massive anti-aircraft barrage over Los Angeles, known as the "Battle of Los Angeles."

**Bridge Gulch Massacre and the Modoc War**
Two episodes of violence against Native Americans in the state. In the 1852 Bridge Gulch Massacre, around 150 Wintu people were killed in Trinity County during the Gold Rush. In the Modoc War of 1872–1873, the Modoc leader "Captain Jack" held out against the U.S. Army in the lava beds of northeastern California.

**Battle of Thermopylae (480 BCE)**
The famous last stand in which King Leonidas I and 300 Spartans, along with Thespians and other Greek allies, held the narrow coastal pass called the "Hot Gates" against the Persian army of Xerxes I, including his Immortals. After the Persians were shown a way around the pass, the Spartans fought to the death; only a couple of Spartans, such as Aristodemus, who had been sent away with an eye infection, survived.

**Agoge**
Sparta's harsh state education and military training system, which boys entered at about age seven, living in barracks. Trainees were given a single red cloak a year, deliberately underfed and expected to steal food without being caught; the story of a boy who let a hidden stolen fox maul him rather than confess illustrates this. Only the firstborn heirs of the two royal houses were exempt.

**Lycurgus and the Great Rhetra**
The legendary lawgiver credited with Sparta's constitution, the Great Rhetra, which he reportedly received from the Oracle of Delphi. He is said to have created the agoge, the gerousia and the communal mess halls, and to have banned gold and silver coins in favor of iron bars. Plutarch pairs him with Rome's King Numa Pompilius in the Parallel Lives.

**Helots**
The enslaved population, mostly conquered Messenians and Laconians, who farmed Spartan land so that citizens could devote themselves to war. They vastly outnumbered the citizens, which made revolt a constant fear. Free non-citizens living around Sparta were called perioikoi.

**Dual kingship (Agiads and Eurypontids)**
Sparta was always ruled by two kings at once, one from the Agiad house and one from the Eurypontid house, which traced their descent from the legendary twins Eurysthenes and Procles. The kings mainly served as military leaders and priests.

**Gerousia**
Sparta's council of elders: 28 men over the age of 60 plus the two kings, for 30 members. Members were reportedly elected by acclamation, with the candidate who received the loudest shouts from the assembly (the Apella) winning, and the council prepared proposals for the assembly to debate.

**Krypteia**
The "secret service" in which young Spartans who had completed the agoge were sent into the countryside armed with knives to spy on and kill helots, especially any who were out at night or seemed dangerous. It kept the helot population terrorized.

**Ephialtes of Trachis**
The local Greek who betrayed the defenders at Thermopylae by showing the Persians a mountain path around the pass. His name became a byword for traitor in Greek.

**"Molon labe"**
"Come and take them," Leonidas's reported reply when Xerxes demanded that the Spartans lay down their weapons at Thermopylae. It is one of the most famous examples of a terse "laconic" saying.

**Gorgo**
The wife of Leonidas and daughter of King Cleomenes I. Herodotus says that as a child she warned her father against being bribed, and that she later realized a blank wax tablet sent by the exiled king Demaratus held a hidden message under the wax warning of Xerxes' invasion.

**Battle of Leuctra (371 BCE)**
The battle in which Thebes, led by Epaminondas and Pelopidas with the elite Sacred Band, crushed the Spartan army and killed King Cleombrotus I. Epaminondas massed his troops on an unusually deep left wing to strike the Spartan right ("cutting off the snake's head"), and the defeat ended Spartan supremacy in Greece.

**Peloponnesian War, Lysander and Aegospotami**
Sparta led the Peloponnesian League to victory over Athens and its Delian League in the 27-year war (431–404 BCE). Its admiral Lysander destroyed the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami in 405 BCE and then installed the Thirty Tyrants in Athens. Earlier in the war, Spartans trapped on the island of Sphacteria surrendered, and the Spartan general Gylippus helped Syracuse defeat Athens' Sicilian Expedition.

**Ephors**
The five magistrates elected each year who supervised the kings, the agoge and daily government. They could overrule the kings in some matters; for example, the ephor Sthenelaidas pushed for war with Athens despite King Archidamus II urging caution.

**Syssitia**
The communal mess halls where Spartan men ate together. Each citizen had to contribute a fixed share of food from his allotted land (kleros), and failing to pay could cost him his full citizenship.

**Carneia festival and Marathon**
The Carneia was a festival of Apollo during which the Spartans would not march to war. Because of this religious restriction, they waited for the full moon and arrived too late for the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE; the same festival was one reason only a small force was sent to Thermopylae.

**Zheng He's treasure voyages**
Seven large naval expeditions (1405–1433) across the Indian Ocean led by the Muslim eunuch admiral Zheng He, sponsored mainly by the Yongle Emperor. They reached Southeast Asia, India, the Persian Gulf (Strait of Hormuz), and the Swahili Coast of East Africa, using enormous "treasure ships" (junks), and are one of the most common clues for the Ming.

**Forbidden City**
The vast imperial palace complex in Beijing, built under the Yongle Emperor after he moved the capital there from Nanjing. It remained the seat of Chinese emperors through the following Qing dynasty.

**Battle of Lake Poyang**
A huge 1363 naval battle on China's largest freshwater lake in which Zhu Yuanzhang defeated his rival Chen Youliang, leader of a rival "Han" regime, partly by using fire ships. The victory cleared his path to founding the Ming.

**Hongwu Emperor (Zhu Yuanzhang)**
The founder of the Ming, a former peasant and Buddhist monk who rose as a commander in the Red Turban Rebellion and proclaimed the dynasty in 1368, driving out the Mongol Yuan. He ruled harshly, purged officials after the alleged plot of chancellor Hu Weiyong, abolished the chancellorship, and imposed the haijin sea bans.

**Tumu Crisis**
A 1449 disaster in which the Zhengtong Emperor (temple name Yingzong), urged on by his eunuch Wang Zhen, personally led an army against the Oirat Mongols under Esen Taishi and was captured at Tumu Fortress. It is one of the most frequent mid-question clues for the dynasty.

**Yongle Emperor**
The third Ming emperor, whose reign name means "perpetual happiness." He took the throne from his nephew, the Jianwen Emperor, in the Jingnan Campaign, moved the capital to Beijing, built the Forbidden City and the Porcelain Tower of Nanjing, and sponsored Zheng He's voyages.

**Red Turban Rebellion**
A mid-14th-century uprising against the Mongol Yuan dynasty, tied to millenarian White Lotus Buddhist movements. Zhu Yuanzhang rose to power as a Red Turban commander, and the Ming emerged from it.

**Ming porcelain (blue-and-white vases)**
The dynasty is famous for its blue-and-white porcelain, made especially at the kilns of Jingdezhen, with notable advances in the Xuande era. "Ming vases" are the standard giveaway in questions on the dynasty.

**Li Zicheng and the Chongzhen Emperor's suicide**
In 1644 the rebel leader Li Zicheng, the "Dashing King," captured Beijing and declared a short-lived Shun dynasty. The last Ming emperor, Chongzhen, hanged himself from a tree on Jingshan (Coal Hill) behind the Forbidden City.

**Wu Sangui and Shanhai Pass**
A Ming general who opened the Shanhai Pass of the Great Wall to the Manchus in 1644 so they could help him defeat Li Zicheng. The Manchus then took Beijing and founded the Qing dynasty, ending the Ming.

**Giraffe presented as a qilin**
During the Yongle reign, a giraffe brought back from East Africa (Malindi) by the treasure fleet was presented at court as a qilin, a mythical auspicious beast, and taken as a sign of the emperor's Mandate of Heaven.

**Embroidered Uniform Guard (Jinyiwei)**
A secret police force set up by the Hongwu Emperor to spy on and punish officials. Together with the eunuch-run Eastern Depot, it is a recurring clue for Ming court repression.

**Matteo Ricci**
An Italian Jesuit missionary who reached China in the late 16th century and was eventually allowed to live in Beijing under the Wanli Emperor. He introduced European science and maps and founded what became the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception in Beijing.

**Gavin Menzies' 1421**
A widely discredited pseudohistory book, "1421: The Year China Discovered the World," arguing that a Ming treasure fleet sailed around the globe. Menzies, a former British submarine officer, focused on the sixth of Zheng He's voyages.

**Wei Zhongxian**
A powerful eunuch of the late Ming who controlled the court under the Tianqi Emperor, commanded the secret police, and violently persecuted the Donglin faction of reformist Confucian scholars.

**Nurhaci and the Seven Grievances**
The Jurchen (Manchu) leader who unified the Jurchen tribes and in 1618 issued the Seven Grievances, a list of complaints against the Ming that served as a declaration of war. His successors founded the Qing, which replaced the Ming.

**Nicolae Ceaușescu and Elena**
The Communist dictator of Romania from 1965 to 1989, who ruled from Bucharest. During the 1989 Romanian Revolution, he and his wife Elena were tried by a hasty military tribunal and executed by firing squad on Christmas Day; the footage was shown on television. The near-universal giveaway for Romania.

**Securitate**
Communist Romania's secret police, founded in 1948 under Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej and greatly expanded under Ceaușescu. Its former deputy chief Ion Mihai Pacepa defected and wrote the memoir Red Horizons. It was rumored to give dissidents cancer with radiation (the "Radu gun"), and it was replaced after 1989 by the SRI (Romanian Intelligence Service).

**Decree 770**
Ceaușescu's 1966 decree that banned most abortions and restricted contraception in order to boost the birth rate. Women with many children were honored as "heroine mothers." The policy led to a surge of unwanted children placed in notoriously overcrowded orphanages.

**July Theses**
A 1971 speech by Ceaușescu, given after a visit to China and North Korea, that launched a "mini cultural revolution." It reimposed strict ideological control over culture and built up a personality cult in imitation of Kim Il-sung's regime.

**Timișoara and László Tőkés**
The 1989 revolution began in the western city of Timișoara when the authorities tried to evict László Tőkés, an ethnic Hungarian Reformed pastor who had criticized the regime, including its "systematization" policy. Protests in his defense were bloodily repressed, and Ceaușescu's final public speech in Bucharest was drowned out by crowds chanting "Timișoara."

**Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej and the Grivița strike**
Romania's first Communist leader (1947–1965), who as a young railway worker helped lead the 1933 Grivița railroad strike and was sentenced to twelve years of hard labor. He led the Party's "prison faction" and purged the Moscow faction of Ana Pauker, a Communist leader who became the world's first female foreign minister. Forced labor under his regime was used to dig the Danube–Black Sea Canal.

**Iron Guard**
Romania's interwar fascist, antisemitic movement, also called the Legion of the Archangel Michael, whose death squads included the Nicadori. Under Horia Sima it shared power with Ion Antonescu in the "National Legionary State" (1940–1941) before Antonescu crushed it during the Legionnaires' Rebellion of January 1941.

**Ion Antonescu**
The pro-Nazi military dictator, styled Conducător ("Leader"), who ruled Romania for most of World War II after forcing King Carol II to abdicate in 1940. He joined Operation Barbarossa to retake Bessarabia, which had been ceded to the Soviet Union. He was overthrown in King Michael I's coup of August 1944, which switched Romania to the Allied side.

**Ploiești and Operation Tidal Wave**
Ploiești was the center of Romania's oil industry and one of the Axis's most important fuel sources. In Operation Tidal Wave (1943), US bombers made a costly low-level raid on its refineries.

**Systematization and the Palace of the People**
Ceaușescu's urban-planning program, inspired by North Korea, which demolished historic neighborhoods and villages to build uniform apartment blocks and huge "hunger circus" food halls. Its centerpiece was the enormous Palace of the People (House of the People) in Bucharest.

**Petru Groza and the abdication of King Michael I**
Petru Groza headed the Soviet-backed government installed in 1945, which crushed the democratic opposition led by Iuliu Maniu of the National Peasant Party. In 1947 King Michael I, the last king of Romania's Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen dynasty, was forced to abdicate, and Romania became a People's Republic.

**Carol II and Magda Lupescu**
The interwar king whose relationship with his mistress Magda Lupescu scandalized the country. He returned to take the throne in 1930, feuded with the National Peasant Party, set up a royal dictatorship with the Străjeria youth organization, and relied on a weak line of fortifications nicknamed the "Imaginot Line." He was forced to abdicate in 1940.

**National Salvation Front**
The organization, led by former Communists such as Ion Iliescu, that took power after Ceaușescu fell in 1989. Its rule prompted the Golaniad protests in Bucharest's University Square and the violent Mineriads, in which miners were brought to the capital to attack protesters.

**World War I and Greater Romania**
Romania entered World War I on the Allied side in 1916 after two years of neutrality, was quickly defeated, and left the war with the Armistice of Focșani. Queen Marie lobbied at the Paris Peace Conference, and Romania gained Transylvania, Bukovina, and Bessarabia, roughly doubling its territory. In 1919 its army occupied Budapest, ending Béla Kun's Hungarian Soviet Republic.

**Dacia, Wallachia, and Vlad the Impaler**
In antiquity the region was Dacia, whose king Decebalus was defeated by the Roman emperor Trajan at Sarmizegetusa. Its medieval principalities, Wallachia, Moldavia, and Transylvania, were home to Vlad III the Impaler, Stephen the Great, and John Hunyadi, and were briefly united by Michael the Brave in 1600. Romania won full independence from the Ottomans after the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878, under Carol I.

**Emancipation Proclamation**
Lincoln had been waiting for a Union victory so that emancipation would not look like an act of desperation, and Antietam gave him one. Five days after the battle, on September 22, 1862, he issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, which declared that slaves in areas still in rebellion on January 1, 1863, would be free.

**Bloodiest single day in American history**
The battle was fought on September 17, 1862, near Sharpsburg, Maryland, along Antietam Creek, and the two sides suffered about 23,000 combined casualties. Confederates called it the Battle of Sharpsburg. It was tactically a draw but a strategic Union victory, because it ended Robert E. Lee's first invasion of the North.

**Special Order 191 (the "Lost Order")**
A copy of Lee's campaign orders, found wrapped around three cigars in a field near Frederick, Maryland, by Union soldiers including Corporal Barton W. Mitchell a few days before the battle. It showed that Lee had divided his army, but George McClellan moved too slowly to take full advantage of it.

**Bloody Lane (the Sunken Road)**
A worn-down farm road at the center of the Confederate line that Confederates under D.H. Hill used as a ready-made trench. Union divisions including William French's suffered terrible losses attacking it before finally breaking through, earning it the name "Bloody Lane."

**Burnside's Bridge**
The stone Rohrbach Bridge over Antietam Creek on the southern end of the field. Ambrose Burnside's IX Corps made repeated costly assaults against a small Confederate force before capturing it in the afternoon. McClellan urged Burnside on with the message "tell him if it costs 10,000 men he must go now."

**A.P. Hill's arrival from Harpers Ferry**
Confederate General A.P. Hill's division, which had stayed behind to complete the capture of the Union garrison at Harpers Ferry, marched to the battlefield late in the day. Its counterattack drove Burnside's troops back toward the creek and saved Lee's army from destruction.

**George B. McClellan's failure to pursue**
The Union commander, who believed reports (fed by detective Allan Pinkerton) that he was badly outnumbered, held large reserves out of the fight and let Lee retreat across the Potomac River into Virginia at Boteler's Ford. Lincoln removed him from command in November 1862, ending his military career.

**Miller's Cornfield**
The site of the battle's opening fighting at dawn, where Joseph Hooker's I Corps attacked south down the Hagerstown Turnpike. Control of the cornfield changed hands repeatedly, and the infantry in it was devastated by artillery fire.

**Dunker Church**
A small whitewashed church belonging to a German Baptist sect known as the Dunkers, which was the objective of the morning Union attacks. Union troops under George Sears Greene briefly held the plateau around it but were forced to withdraw.

**Joseph Mansfield and the XII Corps**
Union General Joseph Mansfield was mortally wounded leading the XII Corps into the morning fighting. Alpheus Williams took command of the corps after him.

**Alexander Gardner's photographs and "The Dead of Antietam"**
Photographer Alexander Gardner took pictures of corpses on the field days after the battle, among the first photographs of battlefield dead in American history. Mathew Brady exhibited them in New York in October 1862 under the title "The Dead of Antietam," shocking the public.

**Maryland Campaign**
Lee's 1862 invasion of Maryland, the first major Confederate offensive into the North, launched after his victory at Second Bull Run. It included the capture of Harpers Ferry and ended with the retreat after Antietam.

**West Woods and Hagerstown Turnpike**
The road running north–south along the battlefield's northern sector, which served as the axis of the morning Union attacks. Union troops pushing through the nearby West Woods suffered heavy losses in a Confederate counterattack.

**"Iron Lady"**
Thatcher's famous nickname, coined in 1976 by the Soviet army newspaper Red Star to mock her strong anti-communist stance. She embraced the label, and it appears as the giveaway in nearly every question about her.

**Falklands War**
The 1982 war in which Thatcher sent British forces to retake the Falkland Islands after they were invaded by Argentina's military junta under Leopoldo Galtieri. Britain's victory, including fighting at Goose Green and Mount Harriet and the recapture of South Georgia (after which she told the public to "rejoice"), greatly boosted her popularity.

**Sinking of the General Belgrano**
The Argentine cruiser General Belgrano was sunk by the British submarine HMS Conqueror on Thatcher's orders during the Falklands War, killing over 300 sailors. The decision was controversial because the ship was outside the exclusion zone; schoolteacher Diana Gould confronted Thatcher about it on live television in 1983. The British destroyer HMS Sheffield was sunk by an Argentine Exocet missile in the same war.

**Brighton hotel bombing**
A 1984 assassination attempt in which Provisional IRA member Patrick Magee planted a bomb in the Grand Hotel in Brighton during the Conservative Party conference. Thatcher survived, but five people were killed.

**Miners' strike and Arthur Scargill**
The 1984–1985 strike by the National Union of Mineworkers, led by Arthur Scargill, against the closure of state-run coal mines. Thatcher's government defeated the strike, a major blow to British trade unions; it included the violent clash between police and pickets at the Battle of Orgreave.

**Community Charge (poll tax)**
A flat-rate local tax charged per adult that replaced the property-based "rates" system. It was deeply unpopular, sparking the 1990 Poll Tax Riots in London, and contributed directly to Thatcher's downfall and resignation in 1990.

**"Milk Snatcher"**
A nickname Thatcher earned as Education Secretary under Edward Heath in the early 1970s, when she ended free milk for schoolchildren over age seven as a cost-cutting measure. Critics chanted "Thatcher, Thatcher, milk snatcher."

**Winter of Discontent**
The wave of widespread strikes in the winter of 1978–1979 under Labour Prime Minister James Callaghan. Public anger over the strikes helped Thatcher's Conservatives win the 1979 general election, beginning 18 years of Conservative rule.

**John Major**
Thatcher's Conservative successor as prime minister, who took over after she resigned in 1990 following a leadership challenge by Michael Heseltine.

**Privatization and the "Big Bang"**
Thatcher's economic policy (Thatcherism) sold off state-owned companies such as British Petroleum, British Airways, Jaguar, and the water utilities of England and Wales. The 1986 "Big Bang" suddenly deregulated the London Stock Exchange, opening it to foreign-owned firms.

**Ronald Reagan**
The U.S. president who was Thatcher's closest international ally during the 1980s. The two shared free-market economic views and a strong anti-Soviet stance during the Cold War.

**Westland affair and Michael Heseltine**
