Alfred was the youngest son of King Æthelwulf of Wessex. He became king in 871 after three elder brothers had ruled in turn, the last being Æthelred I. He was succeeded by his son Edward the Elder, who as a commander had defeated a Viking army at Farnham in 893.

**"Rule, Britannia!"**
The patriotic song first appeared in Alfred, a 1740 masque about the king with music by Thomas Arne and a text by James Thomson and David Mallet. The masque itself is now largely forgotten.

**Adams-Onís Treaty**
The 1819 treaty, negotiated by Secretary of State John Quincy Adams and Spanish minister Luis de Onís under President James Monroe, in which Spain ceded Florida to the United States. In return, the U.S. took on up to $5 million in claims and gave up its claims to Spanish Texas. It is the most common clue for Florida.

**Seminole Wars and Osceola**
Three wars (1817–1818, 1835–1842, and 1855–1858) between the U.S. and the Seminole people, who resisted removal to Indian Territory. Osceola was the most famous Seminole leader of the Second Seminole War. Many Seminoles retreated into the Everglades, where they lived in thatched-roof "chickee" houses.

**St. Augustine**
Founded in 1565 by the Spanish admiral Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, it is the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded settlement in the continental United States.

**Dade Massacre**
The December 1835 ambush that began the Second Seminole War. Seminole warriors under leaders such as Micanopy wiped out a column of about 110 U.S. soldiers led by Major Francis Dade, who were marching to Fort King; only three soldiers survived. On the same day, Osceola killed the Indian agent Wiley Thompson.

**Treaty of Payne's Landing**
An 1832 treaty that required the Seminoles to give up their Florida lands and move west of the Mississippi. Many Seminoles rejected it, and according to legend Osceola stabbed a treaty document with his knife. The dispute led to the Second Seminole War.

**Andrew Jackson's invasion and the First Seminole War**
In 1818 Andrew Jackson invaded Spanish Florida, captured Pensacola, and executed two British subjects, Alexander Arbuthnot and Robert Ambrister, for helping the Seminoles. The invasion showed Spain could not defend Florida and pushed it to sell the territory.

**Negro Fort**
A fort on the Apalachicola River held by formerly enslaved people and Native American allies. On Jackson's orders, U.S. forces destroyed it in 1816 when a cannonball hit its powder magazine, killing most of those inside. The attack helped lead to the First Seminole War.

**Treaty of Moultrie Creek**
An 1823 treaty that forced the Seminoles to move onto a reservation in central Florida. James Gadsden helped negotiate it, and it was later replaced by the Treaty of Payne's Landing.

**Thomas Jesup's capture of Osceola**
In 1837 General Thomas Jesup had Osceola seized near St. Augustine while Osceola was meeting under a white flag of truce. Osceola died in prison at Fort Moultrie, South Carolina, in 1838, and the betrayal caused public outrage.

**2000 presidential election recount**
George W. Bush won Florida, and with it the presidency, by just 537 votes over Al Gore; Bush's brother Jeb was Florida's governor at the time. The dispute involved "hanging chads," Palm Beach County's confusing "butterfly ballot" (which may have given extra votes to Pat Buchanan), Secretary of State Katherine Harris, and the "Brooks Brothers riot" that stopped the Miami-Dade recount. The Supreme Court ended the recount in Bush v. Gore.

**Juan Ponce de León and the Fountain of Youth**
The Spanish explorer who named Florida in 1513 and, according to legend, searched for a Fountain of Youth. He died in 1521 after being wounded by a Calusa arrow while trying to start a colony.

**Narváez expedition and Cabeza de Vaca**
Pánfilo de Narváez led a disastrous 1528 expedition to colonize Florida that clashed with the Apalachee. Only four men survived, including Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca and the enslaved Moroccan Estevanico. Cabeza de Vaca wrote about their shipwreck on an island he called Malhado ("Misfortune") and their years of wandering across the Gulf Coast and the Southwest.

**Fort Caroline**
A French Huguenot colony founded in 1564 on the St. Johns River. Pedro Menéndez de Avilés destroyed it in 1565 and killed most of its settlers, securing Spanish control of Florida.

**Miami and Cuban immigration**
Miami's Little Havana became the center of the Cuban exile community after Fidel Castro took power in 1959, and many exiles there took part in the CIA's Bay of Pigs invasion. Later waves included the 1965–1973 "Freedom Flights," the 1980 Mariel Boatlift, and the 1994 balsero rafter crisis. In 2000 the Elián González case ended when Attorney General Janet Reno had federal agents remove the boy from his relatives' Miami home to return him to his father.

**Rosewood massacre**
In January 1923 a white mob destroyed Rosewood, a predominantly Black town in Florida, after a white woman in a nearby town claimed a Black man had assaulted her. At least six Black residents were killed and the town was abandoned.

**Josip Broz Tito**
The Communist leader of Yugoslavia from the end of World War II until his death in 1980. He commanded the Partisans during the war, built an independent socialist state, and promoted the slogan "Brotherhood and Unity" to hold together Yugoslavia's many ethnic groups. He is buried in the House of Flowers mausoleum in Belgrade.

**Non-Aligned Movement**
A bloc of countries that refused to side with either the US or the USSR in the Cold War. Yugoslavia was its only European founding member, joining India (Nehru), Egypt (Nasser) and Indonesia (Sukarno). The movement held its first summit in Belgrade in 1961, and Tito became its first secretary-general.

**Tito–Stalin split and expulsion from the Cominform**
In 1948 Tito refused to submit to Stalin's control, and Yugoslavia was expelled from the Cominform, the Soviet-led organization of Communist parties. Tito is said to have written to Stalin: "Stop sending people to kill me... If you don't stop sending killers, I'll send one to Moscow."

**Informbiro period and Goli Otok**
The period of hostility with the Soviet bloc after the 1948 split, lasting until about 1955, named after the Yugoslav term for the Cominform. Suspected pro-Soviet dissidents were sent to the brutal labor camp on the island of Goli Otok in the Adriatic.

**Partisans and Chetniks**
The two main resistance movements in Axis-occupied Yugoslavia during World War II. Tito's Communist Partisans fought both the Axis and the royalist, Serbian-nationalist Chetniks led by Draža Mihailović. At the 1943 Tehran Conference the Allies shifted their support from the Chetniks to the Partisans.

**Ustaše**
The Croatian fascist movement that ran the Nazi puppet Independent State of Croatia during World War II and carried out mass murders of Serbs, Jews and Roma. Many Ustaše and other collaborators who fled to Austria in 1945 were killed after being sent back in the Bleiburg repatriations. Archbishop Aloysius Stepinac was later convicted of collaboration in a heavily criticized show trial.

**Slobodan Milošević and the breakup of Yugoslavia**
The Serbian nationalist leader who rose to power in the late 1980s, including with a 1989 speech on the 600th anniversary of the Battle of Kosovo. He presided over the violent breakup of the country in the 1990s (the Yugoslav Wars) and was toppled in the 2000 "Bulldozer Revolution." He died in The Hague in 2006 while on trial for war crimes and genocide before the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY).

**Operation Allied Force and the Chinese embassy bombing**
NATO's 1999 bombing campaign against Yugoslavia during the Kosovo War, launched after the Rambouillet talks failed. A US strike accidentally hit the Chinese embassy in Belgrade, killing three journalists and sparking protests in China; CIA director George Tenet testified that the intended target was an arms depot.

**Corfu Declaration and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes**
The 1917 agreement between Serbia's government-in-exile and the Yugoslav Committee that led to a joint South Slavic kingdom in 1918. Its original name was the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes; it was renamed the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1929.

**Alexander I and the January 6th Dictatorship**
The first Yugoslav king, who abolished the constitution and imposed royal dictatorship on January 6, 1929. He was assassinated in Marseille in 1934 by Vlado Chernozemski of the Macedonian revolutionary group IMRO, working with the Ustaše.

**Peter II**
Alexander I's son, who became king at age 11 in 1934 under the regency of Prince Paul. Paul joined the Axis in 1941, a coup then put Peter on the throne, and Germany invaded soon after. Peter's government-in-exile reached the Treaty of Vis with Tito, but Peter was formally deposed in November 1945 when the monarchy was abolished.

**Workers' self-management**
The distinctive Yugoslav model of socialism, in which workers' councils, rather than central state planners, ran enterprises, and local government was organized in communes (opštine). Yugoslavia was also home to the humanist Marxist "Praxis School" of philosophers.

**Ten-Day War**
The brief 1991 conflict in which Slovenia won its independence from the Yugoslav People's Army. It was the first of the Yugoslav Wars and was partly provoked by the JBTZ trial of Slovene journalists who had criticized the army.

**Bosnian War, Srebrenica and the Dayton Accords**
The 1992–95 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina included the siege of Sarajevo and the 1995 Srebrenica massacre of about 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys by Bosnian Serb forces. The Dayton Accords ended the war and contain Bosnia's current constitution.

**Kosovo War**
The 1998–99 conflict between Milošević's forces and the ethnic Albanian Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) in the province of Kosovo, whose capital is Pristina. It ended with NATO intervention and the Kumanovo Agreement.

**Paris Commune (1871)**
A radical socialist government that seized Paris from March to May 1871 after France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War, opposing Adolphe Thiers's national government at Versailles. It began when Thiers sent troops to remove the National Guard's cannons from the Butte of Montmartre; the soldiers mutinied and Generals Lecomte and Thomas were killed. The Commune banned night work in bakeries, flew a plain red flag, and deeply influenced Karl Marx.

**"Bloody Week" (Semaine sanglante)**
The final week of May 1871, when Marshal Patrice de MacMahon's regular army retook Paris street by street and killed thousands of Communards. During the fighting the Tuileries Palace and Hôtel de Ville were burned, with female arsonists called pétroleuses blamed, and captured Communards were shot at the Communards' Wall (Mur des Fédérés) in Père Lachaise Cemetery.

**Louise Michel**
A schoolteacher and anarchist known as the "Red Virgin of Montmartre," who fought for the Commune and wrote a memoir and poems such as "The Red Carnation." She was deported to New Caledonia in the South Pacific, where thousands of Communards were exiled and where she worked among the Kanak people.

**Auguste Blanqui, Jarosław Dąbrowski, and Archbishop Darboy**
The Commune elected the revolutionary Louis-Auguste Blanqui as a leader while he was imprisoned by Thiers, and offered to exchange hostages, including Archbishop Georges Darboy of Paris, for him. Polish exile Jarosław Dąbrowski commanded its military, and Darboy was shot by the Communards during the Bloody Week.

**Vendôme Column**
A column in the Place Vendôme topped by a statue of Napoleon I, built from melted cannons captured at Austerlitz. The Commune pulled it down in May 1871 as a symbol of imperialism, and participants who posed for a photograph with the fallen statue were later tracked down.

**Baron Haussmann's renovation**
Under Napoleon III, prefect Georges-Eugène Haussmann demolished crowded medieval neighborhoods in the 1850s–60s and built wide boulevards, parks inspired by London, and uniform apartment blocks. The wider streets were meant partly to make revolutionary barricades harder to build.

**Storming of the Bastille**
On July 14, 1789, Parisian crowds stormed the Bastille fortress-prison, freeing just seven prisoners and beginning the French Revolution; the date is now France's national holiday. The July Column in the Place de la Bastille instead commemorates the July Revolution of 1830.

**St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre (1572)**
The slaughter of thousands of Huguenots (French Protestants) that began in Paris days after the wedding of the Protestant Henry of Navarre to Margaret of Valois. It was likely ordered by Catherine de' Medici, and the Huguenot leader Admiral Gaspard de Coligny was among the first killed.

**"Paris is well worth a mass"**
A remark attributed to Henry IV (Henry of Navarre), who converted from Protestantism to Catholicism in 1593 after failing to besiege the Catholic League–held city. He entered Paris in 1594. Earlier, the 1588 Day of the Barricades was a Catholic League uprising backed by the Council of Sixteen and the Spanish ambassador Bernardino de Mendoza.

**Treaties of Paris**
Many major treaties were signed in Paris: the 1763 treaty ending the Seven Years' War (Britain gained Canada, France regained Martinique), the 1783 treaty ending the American Revolution (signed by Franklin, Adams, and Jay with Britain's David Hartley), the 1856 treaty ending the Crimean War and demilitarizing the Black Sea, the 1898 treaty ending the Spanish-American War (U.S. gained Guam and Puerto Rico), and the 1951 treaty creating the European Coal and Steel Community.

**July Revolution (1830) and the Revolution of 1848**
The "Three Glorious Days" of July 1830, sparked by Charles X's repressive Four Ordinances, overthrew the last Bourbon king and installed the "citizen king" Louis-Philippe. Louis-Philippe survived Giuseppe Fieschi's 1835 "infernal machine," a 25-barrel gun fired from a window, but was overthrown in February 1848 after he suppressed the reformist Banquet Campaign.

**Siege of Paris (1870–1871)**
After Napoleon III was captured at Sedan, Prussian forces besieged Paris. Léon Gambetta escaped by hot-air balloon to organize resistance, and starving Parisians ate zoo animals, including the elephants Castor and Pollux.

**Taxis of the Marne**
In September 1914, Paris's military governor Joseph Gallieni requisitioned about 600 Paris taxicabs to rush reinforcements to the front during the First Battle of the Marne, which halted the German advance on the city.

**May 1968**
A student uprising that began at Nanterre and the Sorbonne and grew into a general strike, briefly causing Charles de Gaulle to leave Paris. Afterward the University of Paris was split into thirteen separate universities.

**Landmarks: Notre-Dame, Sainte-Chapelle, and the Arc de Triomphe**
Notre-Dame Cathedral was begun under Bishop Maurice de Sully and was badly damaged by fire in 2019. Louis IX built Sainte-Chapelle to house relics such as the Crown of Thorns bought from Baldwin II. Montmartre is named for the martyrdom of Saint Denis, who supposedly walked away carrying his own head, and the Arc de Triomphe bears François Rude's sculpture Departure of the Volunteers (La Marseillaise).

**"Cross of Gold" speech**
Bryan's 1896 speech at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago attacking the gold standard and championing free silver. It won him the presidential nomination and is the most famous giveaway for him.

**"You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold"**
The closing line of the Cross of Gold speech, preceded by "You shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns." Earlier in the speech he declared "we have petitioned, and our petitions have been scorned" and warned that if farms were destroyed "the grass will grow in the streets of every city in the country."

**Free silver and 16 to 1**
Bryan's central cause was bimetallism, the unlimited coinage of silver at a ratio of 16 ounces of silver to 1 ounce of gold. The inflationary policy appealed to indebted farmers in the West and South; cartoons showed him carrying a bag labeled "16 to 1."

**Scopes Trial and Clarence Darrow**
In 1925 Bryan helped prosecute John Scopes for teaching evolution in violation of Tennessee's Butler Act. Defense attorney Clarence Darrow famously called Bryan to the stand as a Bible expert, questioning him about Adam and Eve and the date of the Great Flood. Bryan won the case but died five days later.

**Resignation over the Lusitania**
Bryan was Woodrow Wilson's first Secretary of State, but he resigned in 1915 because he felt Wilson's strong protest notes to Germany after the sinking of the RMS Lusitania endangered U.S. neutrality. He was replaced by Robert Lansing.

**1896 election and William McKinley**
Bryan lost the 1896 election (and again in 1900) to Republican William McKinley, whose manager Mark Hanna ran a well-funded "front porch campaign" from McKinley's home in Canton, Ohio. At 36, Bryan was the youngest major-party presidential nominee ever.

**Three-time Democratic nominee**
Bryan was the Democratic presidential nominee in 1896, 1900, and 1908, losing each time; his 1908 loss was to William Howard Taft. His running mates included Arthur Sewall (1896) and John Kern (1908).

**Populist fusion and Thomas Watson**
In 1896 the Populist Party also nominated Bryan, but chose Georgia's Thomas Watson as his running mate instead of the Democrats' Arthur Sewall. Gold-standard Bourbon Democrats bolted to form the National Democratic Party, nominating John Palmer.

**The Commoner and "The Great Commoner"**
After his 1896 loss Bryan founded and published a newspaper called The Commoner, which pushed reforms such as railroad regulation. "The Great Commoner" and "The Boy Orator of the Platte" were his nicknames.

**"The Prince of Peace" and the Chautauqua circuit**
Bryan was a hugely popular lecturer on the Chautauqua circuit, where his speeches included "The Prince of Peace," which grounded morality in religion and criticized evolution, and "The Value of an Ideal."

**"Cooling-off" treaties**
As Secretary of State, Bryan negotiated arbitration treaties with about 30 nations requiring disputes to be referred to an international commission before any war. He gave signatories paperweights shaped like plowshares made from melted-down swords.

**Bryan–Chamorro Treaty**
A 1914 treaty with Nicaragua, negotiated with Emiliano Chamorro, that gave the United States exclusive rights to build a canal through Nicaragua and to lease bases there.

**"Shall the People Rule?"**
Bryan's slogan in the 1908 campaign against Taft, during which he also advocated citizenship for Puerto Ricans. Opponents quipped that "you can vote for Bryan anytime" given how often he ran.

**Anti-imperialism and the Philippines**
Although he supported the Spanish-American War, Bryan opposed annexing the Philippines and made imperialism a theme of his 1900 campaign, including a speech warning against the "flag of an empire."

**1896 convention: Altgeld and Richard Bland**
At the 1896 Chicago convention, Illinois governor John Peter Altgeld helped swing delegates to Bryan, who overtook front-runner Richard "Silver Dick" Bland on the fifth ballot to win the nomination.

**Charge of the Light Brigade**
A disastrous British cavalry attack at the Battle of Balaclava on October 25, 1854. A vague order from the commander Lord Raglan, passed on by Captain Nolan and the Earl of Lucan, sent the Earl of Cardigan's Light Brigade of about 600 men straight down the North Valley into massed Russian artillery, and the brigade suffered heavy losses. Alfred, Lord Tennyson's poem "The Charge of the Light Brigade" ("Half a league, half a league, / Half a league onward... Into the valley of Death / Rode the six hundred") made it famous.

**Florence Nightingale, the "Lady with the Lamp"**
A British nurse who led a team of nurses to the army hospital at the Selimiye Barracks in Scutari, across the Bosporus from Constantinople. She greatly improved sanitation and earned her nickname by making night rounds of the wards. She used her "rose" or "coxcomb" diagrams, a kind of polar area chart, to show that disease killed far more soldiers than battle wounds.

**Siege of Sevastopol**
The central campaign of the war, an allied siege of Russia's main Black Sea naval base from October 1854 to September 1855, lasting about eleven months. It ended when French troops stormed the key Malakoff Redoubt, after which the Russians blew up their fortifications and scuttled their fleet before abandoning the city.

**"Thin Red Line"**
At Balaclava, Sir Colin Campbell's 93rd (Sutherland) Highlanders, in their red coats, formed a line only two men deep and drove off a Russian cavalry attack on the British base. The journalist William Howard Russell described them as a "thin red streak," and the phrase became "the thin red line."

**Battle of Balaclava**
The October 1854 battle in which Russian forces tried to cut the British off from their supply port at Balaclava during the siege of Sevastopol. It featured three famous actions: the Thin Red Line, the successful Charge of the Heavy Brigade, and the disastrous Charge of the Light Brigade.

**Battles of the Alma and Inkerman**
The Alma (September 1854) was the first major battle on the Crimean Peninsula. British and French troops under Lord Raglan and Marshal Armand de Saint-Arnaud forced Prince Menshikov's Russians from the heights above the river, including the area near Telegraph Hill. Inkerman (November 1854) was a confused battle in thick fog, sometimes called "the soldiers' battle," with fierce fighting around the "Sandbag Battery." Menshikov's attempt to break the siege of Sevastopol failed.

**Mary Seacole and the "British Hotel"**
A Jamaican-born nurse and businesswoman who, after being turned down for Nightingale's nursing corps, paid her own way to the Crimea. Near Balaclava she set up the "British Hotel," where she sold food and supplies to officers and treated sick and wounded soldiers with herbal remedies.

**Roger Fenton's "The Valley of the Shadow of Death"**
Fenton, one of the first war photographers, documented the conflict with the backing of the publisher Thomas Agnew & Sons. His best-known image shows a desolate road covered with cannonballs, and its title quotes Psalm 23. A second version with no cannonballs on the road has raised long debate over whether the scene was staged. Combined with William Howard Russell's reports for The Times, this made the Crimean War one of the first wars covered by modern media.

**Lord Raglan**
The British commander-in-chief, a veteran of Wellington's staff who had lost an arm at Waterloo. His ambiguous order at Balaclava led to the Charge of the Light Brigade, and he was widely blamed for the army's supply failures in the first winter. He died of illness during the siege in 1855.

**Battle of Sinop (Sinope)**
In November 1853, a Russian fleet under Admiral Pavel Nakhimov destroyed an Ottoman squadron in the harbor of Sinop on the Black Sea, using explosive shells. Only the steamer Taif escaped. It was the last major naval battle involving sailing ships, and the British and French public's outrage at the "massacre" helped bring both countries into the war in 1854.

**Causes: Holy Land sites, the Danubian Principalities, and the Straits**
The war grew out of a dispute between France, which protected Catholics, and Russia, which protected Orthodox Christians, over control of holy sites in Palestine. France sent the warship Charlemagne to the Dardanelles in apparent violation of the 1841 London Straits Convention, and Tsar Nicholas I then demanded to be recognized as protector of the Ottoman Empire's Orthodox subjects and occupied Moldavia and Wallachia. During the Danube campaign that followed, the Russians besieged Silistra.

**Treaty of Paris (1856)**
The peace that ended the war in Russia's defeat. It neutralized the Black Sea, banning warships and naval arsenals there, guaranteed the Ottoman Empire's territory, and placed the Danubian Principalities under the joint protection of the great powers. A separate convention demilitarized the Åland Islands.

**Siege of Kars**
The last major action of the war, in the Caucasus in 1855. The British officer William Fenwick Williams led the Ottoman garrison of Kars through a months-long Russian siege. Omar Pasha's relief expedition arrived too late, and the starving town surrendered in November 1855.

**Baltic and Pacific campaigns**
The war spread beyond the Black Sea. In the Baltic, a British fleet under Charles Napier joined the French in capturing and destroying the Russian fortress of Bomarsund in the Åland Islands, and British ships shelled Russian positions on the island of Gogland. In the far north, an allied squadron bombarded the White Sea coast, and in the Pacific an allied attack on Petropavlovsk on Kamchatka was driven back.

**Battle of Kinburn and other "firsts"**
At Kinburn in 1855, French armored floating batteries bombarded Russian forts, one of the first combat uses of ironclad warships. The war also saw early use of the telegraph and railways in war, Nikolay Pirogov's advances in field surgery and anesthesia, Alexis Soyer's field stove, Isambard Kingdom Brunel's prefabricated hospital at Renkioi, and the creation of the Victoria Cross. Piedmont-Sardinia also sent about 15,000 troops under Alfonso La Marmora to join the allies.

**First Battle of Panipat (1526)**
The battle that founded the Mughal Empire, in which Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, the last sultan of the Delhi Sultanate's Lodi dynasty. Babur's small army used field cannons and matchlocks, plus a line of carts tied together, to break Lodi's much larger force and frighten his war elephants.

**Taj Mahal**
The white marble mausoleum in Agra built by the emperor Shah Jahan for his beloved wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth in 1631. Its chief architect is usually named as Ustad Ahmad Lahori, and it is the most common giveaway for the empire.

**Akbar the Great**
The third Mughal emperor (r. 1556–1605), under whom the empire reached its height. He was illiterate but highly cultured, was guided early on by the regent Bairam Khan, abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims, and pursued a policy of religious tolerance.

**Din-i Ilahi**
The syncretic "Divine Faith" created by Akbar, blending elements of Islam, Hinduism, Zoroastrianism, Jainism and Christianity. It forbade animal slaughter and promoted abstinence and devotion to God, but had few followers outside Akbar's court.

**Jizya tax**
The tax on non-Muslims under Islamic rule. Akbar abolished it, and Aurangzeb, who called himself Alamgir ("Conqueror of the World"), reinstated it in 1679 as part of his stricter, less tolerant Islamic policies.

**Babur**
The founder of the empire, a descendant of Timur (Tamerlane) and Genghis Khan who was driven out of his homeland in the Ferghana Valley. His memoir, the Baburnama, was written in Chagatai Turkic and later translated into Persian; he also defeated the Rajput Rana Sanga at the Battle of Khanwa (1527).

**Shah Jahan**
The fifth Mughal emperor, famous for his architecture: the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort in Delhi, and the jeweled Peacock Throne. He was deposed and imprisoned by his son Aurangzeb.

**Aurangzeb and the Battle of Samugarh**
Aurangzeb won the 1658 war of succession against his brother Dara Shikoh at Samugarh, imprisoned his father Shah Jahan, and later executed Dara. He extended the empire to its largest size but exhausted it in long wars in the Deccan, and the Fatawa-e-Alamgiri law code was compiled under him.

**Fatehpur Sikri**
The red sandstone capital that Akbar built near Agra and soon abandoned. It held a palace associated with the queen Jodha Bai and the Ibadat Khana, or "House of Worship," where Akbar hosted debates among Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuit missionaries.

**Nine Jewels (Navaratnas)**
The nine celebrated courtiers of Akbar, including the witty advisor Birbal, the court historian Abul Fazl (author of the Akbarnama) and the musician Tansen. Abul Fazl drew on the memoirs of Babur's daughter Gulbadan Begum.

**Nader Shah, the Koh-i-Noor and the Peacock Throne**
The Afsharid ruler of Persia defeated the Mughals at the Battle of Karnal (1739) and sacked Delhi, carrying off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond. The raid showed how weak the empire had become after Aurangzeb.

**Sher Shah Suri and the Sur Empire**
The Afghan ruler who defeated Babur's son Humayun at the battles of Chausa and Kannauj, interrupting Mughal rule (1540–1555). Humayun took refuge with the Safavid shah Tahmasp I in Persia before reconquering India.

**Second Battle of Panipat (1556)**
The battle in which the young Akbar's regent Bairam Khan defeated Hemu, a Hindu general who had served the Suri dynasty. Hemu was struck in the eye by an arrow and captured, which secured Mughal rule.

**Marathas and Shivaji**
The Hindu Maratha state founded by Shivaji fought the Mughals in the Deccan, including the War of Twenty-Seven Years (1681–1707) against Aurangzeb. The conflict drained the empire and helped cause its decline.

**Mansabdar system**
The Mughal ranking system for military and civil officers, with ranks expressed as the number of cavalry each mansabdar had to supply (roughly 10 to 5,000 or more). Officers were often paid through jagirs, which were assignments of land revenue.

**Bahadur Shah II and the Sepoy Mutiny (1857)**
The last Mughal emperor, a powerless figurehead by then, who was named leader of the Indian Rebellion of 1857. After it failed, the British exiled him to Rangoon in Burma (Myanmar), ending the dynasty.

**Sukarno and Suharto**
Indonesia's first two presidents and the most common giveaways. Sukarno led the independence struggle against the Dutch and ruled from 1945 until he was pushed aside in 1966–67 by General Suharto, who ruled as an authoritarian until 1998 and reportedly embezzled as much as $15–35 billion.

**30 September Movement (1965)**
A failed coup attempt in which six army generals were kidnapped and killed in Jakarta. Suharto crushed it, blamed the communist PKI, and used it to sideline Sukarno; the event was later commemorated by a violent propaganda film broadcast every September 30.

**PKI and the 1965–66 mass killings**
The Communist Party of Indonesia, once one of the largest communist parties in the world. After the 30 September Movement, the army and allied militias killed roughly half a million or more suspected communists, an episode Vincent Bevins linked to later CIA-backed anti-leftist violence in his book The Jakarta Method.

**"Guided Democracy"**
Sukarno's authoritarian system, in place from 1957/59 to 1966, which replaced parliamentary democracy with rule balanced between the army, nationalists, religious groups, and the PKI. It caused a rift with his vice president Mohammad Hatta, who resigned in 1956.

**"New Order" (Orde Baru)**
Suharto's anti-communist, military-backed regime (1966–1998), which replaced Guided Democracy. Suharto was given emergency powers by the Supersemar order of March 11, 1966, and his economic policy was shaped by U.S.-trained technocrats nicknamed the "Berkeley Mafia."

**Bandung Conference (1955)**
A meeting of 29 Asian and African nations hosted by Sukarno in Bandung, attended by leaders like Zhou Enlai and Jawaharlal Nehru. It is considered the forerunner of the Non-Aligned Movement; Sukarno later tried to organize a "Conference of the New Emerging Forces."

**East Timor invasion and the Santa Cruz massacre**
Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony of East Timor in 1975 (Operation Seroja, "Lotus") to crush the FRETILIN independence movement and occupied it until 1999; it became independent in 2002. In the 1991 Santa Cruz massacre in Dili, troops shot pro-independence mourners in a cemetery, an event filmed by Max Stahl and witnessed by journalist Amy Goodman, who was beaten by soldiers.

**Batavia and the Dutch East India Company (VOC)**
The VOC founded Batavia (modern Jakarta) as its Asian headquarters in 1619 to control the spice trade; the colony was later called the Dutch East Indies. Colonial policies included the 1830 Culture System (forced cultivation of export crops on a share of village land) and the early-1900s "Ethical Policy" aimed at native welfare.

**Pancasila**
Indonesia's state ideology of "five principles" (belief in God, humanitarianism, national unity, democracy, and social justice), first articulated by Sukarno in 1945 and heavily enforced under Suharto. It is symbolized by the mythical bird Garuda on the national emblem, which carries the motto "Bhinneka Tunggal Ika" ("Unity in Diversity").

**Mohammad Hatta and the independence war**
Hatta and Sukarno proclaimed independence on August 17, 1945, just after the Japanese occupation ended. The Dutch tried to retake the colony in "police actions" such as Operation Product, the Linggadjati and Renville agreements set temporary terms, and the U.S. threatened Marshall Plan aid after the Dutch seized the revolutionary capital Yogyakarta; the Netherlands recognized independence in 1949.

**Majapahit Empire, Gajah Mada, and Hayam Wuruk**
A Hindu-Buddhist empire based on Java, founded by Raden Wijaya after the Singhasari kingdom's era and the defeat of a Mongol expedition in 1293. It peaked in the 14th century under King Hayam Wuruk and his prime minister Gajah Mada, who swore the Sumpah Palapa oath to abstain from spices until he unified the archipelago.

**Borobudur**
The world's largest Buddhist temple, in central Java, built by the Sailendra dynasty in the 8th–9th centuries. Its three levels represent the realms of desire (Kamadhatu), form (Rupadhatu), and formlessness (Arupadhatu).

**Konfrontasi and "To hell with your aid!"**
Sukarno's 1963–66 undeclared conflict opposing the formation of Malaysia, fought largely on Borneo against British Commonwealth forces. During this period Sukarno told the U.S. "To hell with your aid!" and withdrew Indonesia from the United Nations in 1965.

**Benedict Anderson's "Cornell Paper"**
A 1966 analysis by Cornell scholars Benedict Anderson and Ruth McVey that challenged the army's official account blaming the PKI for the 30 September Movement. Anderson was banned from entering Indonesia until 1999 as a result.

**Largest Muslim population and Aceh**
Indonesia has the world's largest Muslim population, with Islam spreading after the decline of the Srivijaya empire. Aceh, on the northern tip of Sumatra, observes sharia law; Javanese Islam is divided between pious santri and syncretic abangan, and the reformist Muhammadiyah is a major organization.

**Whiskey Ring scandal and Orville Babcock**
A conspiracy of distillers, distributors, and Treasury officials, centered in St. Louis, who bribed officials so they could keep federal excise taxes on whiskey. Treasury Secretary Benjamin Bristow exposed it in 1875. Grant's personal secretary, Orville Babcock, was indicted but acquitted after Grant testified for him. This is the most common scandal clue for Grant's presidency.

**Crédit Mobilier scandal**
A construction company created by Union Pacific Railroad insiders, including Thomas Durant, to overcharge the government for building the transcontinental railroad. Congressman Oakes Ames handed out discounted shares to members of Congress to head off investigations. The New York Sun exposed the scheme in 1872 using letters leaked by Henry McComb. It tarnished Vice President Schuyler Colfax, who was dropped from the 1872 ticket, and touched James Garfield.

**Black Friday (1869) and Jay Gould and James Fisk**
Financiers Jay Gould and James Fisk tried to corner the gold market, using Grant's brother-in-law Abel Corbin to get inside information and influence over Grant. When Grant ordered the Treasury to sell gold on September 24, 1869, gold prices collapsed and caused a financial panic.

**Benjamin Bristow**
Grant's reform-minded Secretary of the Treasury, who broke the Whiskey Ring and pushed for the prosecution of Orville Babcock.

**Appomattox Court House**
The Virginia village where Robert E. Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to Grant on April 9, 1865, effectively ending the Civil War. Grant later campaigned as the "Hero of Appomattox."

**Schuyler Colfax**
Grant's first-term vice president, who was implicated in the Crédit Mobilier scandal for accepting shares from Oakes Ames. He was replaced on the 1872 ticket by Henry Wilson.

**Treaty of Washington and the Alabama Claims**
A treaty of 1871 negotiated under Secretary of State Hamilton Fish. It sent U.S. claims against Britain over damage done by Confederate raiders built in Britain, such as the CSS Alabama, to arbitration, and Britain paid $15.5 million. It also settled Atlantic fishing rights and, through later arbitration, the San Juan Islands boundary dispute.

**Attempted annexation of Santo Domingo**
Grant tried to annex Santo Domingo (the Dominican Republic). Orville Babcock helped negotiate the treaty, but the Senate rejected it in 1870 after opposition led by Charles Sumner and Carl Schurz.

**"Unconditional Surrender" Grant and Fort Donelson**
In February 1862 Grant captured Fort Donelson in Tennessee after telling the Confederate commander that "no terms except an unconditional and immediate surrender can be accepted." This earned him the nickname "Unconditional Surrender" Grant, a play on his initials.

**William Belknap and the trading post kickbacks**
Grant's Secretary of War, who took kickbacks from the sutler (licensed trader) at Fort Sill in Indian Territory. In 1876 the House impeached him even though he had just resigned, making him the first Cabinet secretary ever impeached.

**Panic of 1873**
A severe financial crisis set off by the collapse of the Jay Cooke & Company bank, which had over-invested in railroads. It began a long economic depression during Grant's second term.

**Force Acts (Enforcement Acts)**
Laws of 1870–1871 that let Grant use federal power, including troops and the suspension of habeas corpus, against the Ku Klux Klan to protect African Americans' voting rights during Reconstruction.

**Election of 1872 and Horace Greeley**
Grant won re-election over Horace Greeley, the New York Tribune editor nominated by the Liberal Republicans (and backed by the Democrats). Greeley died shortly after the election, before the electoral votes were cast.

**Coinage Act of 1873 and Specie Resumption Act**
The Coinage Act of 1873, called the "Crime of '73" by its critics, ended the coinage of silver dollars and moved the U.S. toward a gold standard. Grant vetoed the 1874 Inflation Bill, which would have added paper money, and then signed the 1875 Specie Resumption Act to make greenbacks redeemable in gold. These deflationary policies helped spur the Greenback Party.

**Battle of Monterrey and the Mexican-American War**
As a young lieutenant in the Mexican-American War, Grant volunteered to carry a message for ammunition through the streets of Monterrey. He rode hanging off the side of his horse to avoid enemy fire.

**Funeral Oration**
Pericles' famous speech, recorded by Thucydides, honoring Athenians who died in the first year of the Peloponnesian War (431 BC). It praises Athenian democracy and culture, opens with the wish that the reputation of many brave men not depend on the eloquence of one speaker, and contains the line "famous men have the whole earth as their memorial." It is often credited as a source of the idea of "equal justice under law."

**Death in the Plague of Athens**
An epidemic struck Athens in 430 BC, made worse by crowding refugees inside the city walls. Pericles died of it in 429 BC, as did his legitimate sons Paralus and Xanthippus.

**Ostracism of Cimon**
Cimon, the pro-Spartan leader of Athens' conservatives, was Pericles' main rival. Pericles had earlier joined in prosecuting him for allegedly taking bribes from Alexander I of Macedon, and Cimon was ostracized in 461 BC after Sparta humiliatingly rejected the Athenian troops he led to help suppress a helot revolt (the Third Messenian War).

**Aspasia**
Pericles' partner, a highly educated woman from Miletus who was not an Athenian citizen. Her house drew intellectuals such as Socrates, comic poets attacked her, and Pericles reportedly wept in court to secure her acquittal on charges of impiety. Their son, also named Pericles, was later granted citizenship.

**Phidias and the Parthenon**
Pericles' building program on the Acropolis, funded partly by Delian League money, produced the Parthenon, overseen by his friend, the sculptor Phidias, who also made its huge gold-and-ivory statue of Athena. Pericles' opponents attacked him through his associates, and Phidias was prosecuted and imprisoned.

**Xanthippus and the Battle of Mycale**
Pericles' father, Xanthippus, was ostracized but recalled during the Persian Wars and commanded the Athenian fleet at the Battle of Mycale (479 BC), a major Greek victory over Persia.

**Megarian Decree**
Economic sanctions Pericles backed around 432 BC, barring the city of Megara from the harbors and markets of the Athenian empire, reportedly after an Athenian herald was killed. It was one of the main causes of the Peloponnesian War.

**Moving the Delian League treasury**
In 454 BC the treasury of the Delian League, an anti-Persian alliance, was moved from the island of Delos to Athens. This turned the league into an Athenian empire whose tribute funded Pericles' building projects.

**Long Walls and the "island" strategy**
Walls linking Athens to its port of Piraeus. At the start of the Peloponnesian War, Pericles told rural Athenians to shelter behind them, avoiding land battles with Sparta and relying on the navy, effectively treating Athens like an island.

**Golden Age of Athens**
The period of Athenian cultural and political dominance in the mid-5th century BC, often called the Age of Pericles. Thucydides called him the "first citizen" of Athens, and he was elected strategos (general) year after year.

**Samian War and other revolts**
Pericles led the siege of Samos (440–439 BC); his enemies claimed he attacked it to please Aspasia, a native of Miletus, which was Samos' rival. He also crushed a revolt in Euboea (446 BC), reportedly bribing the Spartan king Pleistoanax to withdraw so he could focus on it.

**Elpinice's rebuke**
Elpinice, the sister of Cimon, criticized Pericles for making war on fellow Greeks rather than on Persia. According to Plutarch, he replied with a line from Archilochus: "As an old woman you should not anoint yourself with oils."

**Elongated head and the "lion" dream**
Pericles' head was unusually long, so he was usually portrayed wearing a helmet, and comic poets mocked him as "squill-head" (schinocephalos). Before his birth, his mother Agariste reportedly dreamed she would give birth to a lion.

**Citizenship law and jury pay**
Pericles' 451 BC law limited Athenian citizenship to people with two Athenian parents, which later complicated the status of his son by Aspasia. He also introduced pay for jurors and other public service, and payments to let poorer citizens attend the theater are traditionally linked to his era.

**Patron of Aeschylus and Anaxagoras**
As a young man, Pericles served as choregos (producer) for Aeschylus' The Persians in 472 BC. He was a friend of the philosopher Anaxagoras, who was prosecuted for impiety and retired to Lampsacus.

**Carnation Revolution (1974)**
The largely bloodless military coup of April 25, 1974, carried out by the Armed Forces Movement, that overthrew the Estado Novo dictatorship of Marcelo Caetano. The radio broadcast of Portugal's Eurovision entry "And After the Farewell" and of the banned song "Grândola, Vila Morena" served as signals to begin. It ended the colonial wars, and Lisbon's 25th of April Bridge (formerly named for Salazar) commemorates it.

**António Salazar and the Estado Novo**
Salazar ruled Portugal as dictator from 1932 to 1968 under the authoritarian, Catholic, corporatist Estado Novo ("New State"), which signed the Concordat of 1940 with the Vatican. Its secret police, the PIDE, ran the Tarrafal prison camp in Cape Verde and murdered opposition leader Humberto Delgado. Salazar was succeeded by Marcelo Caetano.

**Vasco da Gama**
The explorer who made the first sea voyage from Europe to India (1497–1499), rounding the Cape of Good Hope and reaching Calicut, where the ruler (the Zamorin) was unimpressed by his cheap gifts. He erected a stone pillar called a padrão near Malindi, and on his second voyage in 1502 he burned the pilgrim ship Miri with its passengers aboard.

**Prince Henry the Navigator**
A son of King John I of the Aviz dynasty who sponsored early Portuguese exploration of the African coast and helped begin the Age of Discovery. He is linked to a navigation school at Sagres and the development of the caravel, sent Gil Eanes past Cape Bojador, urged the capture of Ceuta, and led a failed attack on Tangier that left his brother Ferdinand a captive.

**Treaty of Tordesillas (1494)**
The agreement between Spain and Portugal, following papal bulls of Alexander VI, that divided newly discovered lands along a north–south line in the Atlantic. Portugal received the lands to the east of the line, which gave it Africa, the route to Asia, and later Brazil.

**Portuguese Colonial War in Angola and Mozambique**
Portugal fought independence movements in its African colonies from 1961 to 1974. In Angola the rebels included the MPLA and Jonas Savimbi's Ovimbundu-based UNITA; in Mozambique, FRELIMO was led by anthropologist Eduardo Mondlane and later Samora Machel, and Portugal's Operation Gordian Knot failed to crush it. The colonies, along with Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde, became independent after the Carnation Revolution.

**Caravel**
A small, fast, maneuverable sailing ship with lateen sails developed by the Portuguese in the 15th century. It allowed sailors to travel far down the African coast and sail against the wind, making Portuguese exploration possible.

**Goa and Operation Vijay (1961)**
Goa, on India's west coast, was captured by Afonso de Albuquerque in 1510 from the Adil Shahi dynasty and became the capital of Portuguese India. In 1961 India seized Goa, Daman, and Diu in Operation Vijay.

**1755 Lisbon earthquake and the Marquis of Pombal**
A massive earthquake, followed by a tsunami and fires, that destroyed Lisbon in 1755. The Marquis of Pombal, chief minister of King Joseph I, rebuilt the city on a planned grid, while the shaken king refused to live in buildings and moved to a tent complex at Ajuda.

**Pedro Álvares Cabral and Brazil**
Cabral reached Brazil in 1500 while sailing to India and is considered its European discoverer. The colony was named for brazilwood, a tree that produced red dye, and became Portugal's largest possession.

**Bartolomeu Dias**
The explorer who rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488, passing what became known as the Cape of Good Hope. His voyage proved there was a sea route to the Indian Ocean, which Vasco da Gama followed.

**Conquest of Ceuta (1415)**
Portugal's capture of the North African port of Ceuta from the Marinid dynasty under John I is usually counted as the start of the Portuguese Empire.

**The Pink Map, pluricontinentalism, and Lusotropicalism**
The Pink Map was Portugal's 1880s claim to a band of land linking Angola and Mozambique across Africa, which Britain blocked. In the 20th century the Estado Novo defended its empire with pluricontinentalism (the idea that the colonies were part of one Portugal on several continents) and Lusotropicalism (the claim that Portugal was an unusually benevolent colonizer).

**King Sebastian and the Iberian Union**
King Sebastian disappeared at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir in Morocco in 1578, and legends that the "hidden king" would return became known as Sebastianism. His death ended the Aviz line, Philip II of Spain took the throne in 1580, and the 1640 Restoration War restored independence under the House of Braganza.

**Ferdinand Magellan**
A Portuguese-born explorer who led the first expedition to circumnavigate the globe, sailing for Spain. He was killed by Lapu-Lapu's forces at the Battle of Mactan in the Philippines in 1521.

**Easter Rising**
A 1916 armed rebellion in Dublin against British rule, launched on Easter Monday when rebels seized the General Post Office and Patrick Pearse read the Proclamation of the Irish Republic. The British crushed it within a week and executed sixteen leaders, including Pearse and James Connolly, which turned public opinion toward independence. Éamon de Valera, who commanded at Boland's Mill, was spared partly because he was born in America.

**Great Famine (Potato Famine)**
The famine of 1845-1852, caused by the potato blight Phytophthora infestans, in which about a million people died and millions emigrated on overcrowded "coffin ships," with 1847 remembered as "Black '47." Robert Peel repealed the Corn Laws in response, but Lord John Russell's government and official Charles Trevelyan held to laissez-faire policies; the "Gregory Clause" denied relief to anyone holding over a quarter acre, and people who converted to Protestantism for food were called "soupers."

**Michael Collins and Éamon de Valera**
The two leading figures of Irish independence. Collins ran the IRA's intelligence war and signed the 1921 Anglo-Irish Treaty, while de Valera opposed the treaty, and their sides fought the Irish Civil War of 1922-1923, in which Collins was killed. De Valera later founded Fianna Fáil and became Taoiseach and president.

**Charles Stewart Parnell**
The 19th-century leader of the Irish Home Rule movement and president of the Land League. Forged letters by journalist Richard Pigott falsely tied him to the Phoenix Park Murders, and he is remembered each year on Ivy Day, the anniversary of his death.

**Sinn Féin, Fianna Fáil, and Fine Gael**
Sinn Féin is the nationalist party founded by Arthur Griffith. Ireland's two main modern parties came out of its treaty split: Fianna Fáil, founded by the anti-treaty de Valera, and Fine Gael, from the pro-treaty side. The head of government is called the Taoiseach, and the parliament is the Dáil.

**Black and Tans**
British auxiliary police, mostly World War I veterans and named for their mixed uniforms, sent to Ireland during the 1919-1921 War of Independence against the IRA. They became notorious for reprisals against civilians, and many Anglo-Irish "Big Houses" were burned during that war.

**Home Rule**
The movement for a self-governing Irish parliament within the United Kingdom, started by Isaac Butt and led by Parnell. Prime Minister William Gladstone backed Home Rule bills in 1886 and 1893, but both failed.

**Phoenix Park Murders**
The 1882 stabbing of Chief Secretary for Ireland Lord Frederick Cavendish and Under-Secretary Thomas Burke in Dublin's Phoenix Park by the Invincibles, a radical nationalist group. Parnell was falsely accused of approving of the killings.

**Land League and the "Three Fs"**
The Irish National Land League, founded by Michael Davitt in 1879, led the "Land War" for tenant farmers' rights. Its goals were the "Three Fs": fair rent, fixity of tenure, and free sale.

**Roger Casement**
An Irish nationalist and former British diplomat who tried to bring German rifles to the Easter Rising on a ship disguised as the Norwegian SS Aud. He was executed for treason; he was said to be "hanged on a comma" because the conviction depended on how a comma in an old treason law was read, and the "Black Diaries" were used to discredit him.

**Bloody Sunday (1920) and the Cairo Gang**
On November 21, 1920, Michael Collins's assassination unit, "the Squad" or "Twelve Apostles," killed British intelligence agents known as the "Cairo Gang." Later that day, British forces opened fire on a crowd at a Gaelic football match at Croke Park. Collins had earlier organized protests while held at the Frongoch internment camp after the Easter Rising.

**The Troubles and the Good Friday Agreement**
The roughly thirty-year conflict in Northern Ireland between mostly Catholic nationalists, including the Provisional IRA, and mostly Protestant unionists such as Ian Paisley's Democratic Unionist Party, which was ended by the 1998 Good Friday Agreement. IRA attacks included the 1984 Brighton hotel bombing, which nearly killed Margaret Thatcher.

**Bobby Sands and the Maze hunger strike**
The "blanket" and "dirty" protests by IRA prisoners at the Maze Prison against the loss of Special Category (political prisoner) status grew into the 1981 hunger strike led by Bobby Sands. Sands was elected to the British Parliament during the strike and died weeks later.

**Bloody Sunday (1972)**
A massacre in the Bogside area of Derry, Northern Ireland, in which soldiers of the British Parachute Regiment shot 26 unarmed civil-rights marchers, killing 14. It boosted support for the Provisional IRA, and the later Saville Inquiry found the killings unjustified.

**Cromwellian conquest and the plantations**
Oliver Cromwell's brutal 1649 conquest of Ireland, after which rebel land was seized under the Adventurers' Act and given to New Model Army veterans. Together with earlier English plantations in Munster and Ulster and the later anti-Catholic Penal Laws, it built the dominance of the Protestant Ascendancy.

**Coronation by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day, 800**
In Rome on December 25, 800, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne "Emperor of the Romans," and he is usually counted as the first Holy Roman Emperor. Charlemagne had earlier restored Leo after the pope was attacked and accused of crimes by enemies in Rome, and the papacy backed him partly because the Byzantine throne was held by a woman, Empress Irene.

**Einhard and the Vita Karoli Magni**
Einhard was a courtier and scholar who wrote the Life of Charlemagne (Vita Karoli Magni), the main biography of the emperor, and later served his son Louis the Pious. A legend says Einhard eloped with one of Charlemagne's daughters. A later, more anecdotal biography was written by the monk Notker the Stammerer.

**Massacre of Verden and the Saxon Wars**
Charlemagne spent about thirty years conquering and Christianizing the pagan Saxons. In 782 he had about 4,500 Saxon prisoners beheaded at Verden (the "Bloody Verdict of Verden"), and he destroyed the Saxons' sacred pillar or tree, the Irminsul. The Saxon leader Widukind finally submitted and was baptized.

**Alcuin of York and the Carolingian Renaissance**
Alcuin was an English scholar who ran Charlemagne's palace school and led a revival of learning named for Charlemagne's dynasty. Other scholars included Theodulf of Orléans and Paul the Deacon, author of the History of the Lombards. Alcuin retired as abbot of St. Martin at Tours, and Charlemagne's letter De litteris colendis urged monasteries to promote literacy.

**Aachen and the Palatine Chapel**
Charlemagne's capital and favorite residence, in modern western Germany. Its octagonal Palatine Chapel, an early example of a westwork entrance, is the core of today's Aachen Cathedral, where Charlemagne was buried.

**Battle of Roncevaux Pass (778) and The Song of Roland**
After a failed campaign against Zaragoza in Spain, joined by the Muslim governor Sulayman al-Arabi, Charlemagne's rear guard was ambushed by Basques in a pass through the Pyrenees. The death of the commander Roland there became the subject of the Old French epic The Song of Roland, which turns the attackers into Saracens.

**Desiderius and the conquest of the Lombards**
Charlemagne married the daughter of the Lombard king Desiderius, then divorced her and married Hildegard. He besieged Desiderius at Pavia in 773–774, took the title King of the Lombards, and confirmed the Donation of Pepin, his father's grant of land to the papacy.

**Pepin the Short and Charles Martel**
Charlemagne was the son of Pepin the Short, who deposed the last Merovingian king, Childeric III, with the pope's approval and founded the Carolingian dynasty. His grandfather was Charles Martel, "the Hammer," the Mayor of the Palace who defeated a Muslim army at the Battle of Tours in 732.

**Treaty of Verdun (843)**
The treaty in which Charlemagne's grandsons Lothair I, Louis the German, and Charles the Bald divided his empire into three kingdoms after the death of his son Louis the Pious. The division roughly anticipates later France and Germany.

**Carolingian minuscule**
A clear, standardized handwriting script developed by scholars under Charlemagne, associated with Alcuin, to make texts like the Vulgate Bible easier to read and copy. It is the ancestor of modern lowercase letters.

**Missi dominici**
"Envoys of the lord," royal agents sent out in pairs, usually one cleric and one noble, to inspect the provinces, enforce Charlemagne's capitularies (decrees), and check on local counts.

**Harun al-Rashid's elephant, Abul-Abbas**
The Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid sent Charlemagne gifts including an elephant named Abul-Abbas and an elaborate water clock, part of diplomatic contacts between the two rulers.

**Spanish March**
A buffer zone of territory south of the Pyrenees that Charlemagne created to protect his empire from the Umayyad emirate of Córdoba in Spain.

**Monetary reform**
Charlemagne replaced the old gold-based coinage with a silver standard based on the pound, shilling, and penny (denier). Offa of Mercia adopted a similar silver penny in England, and the system lasted in Britain until decimalization.

**Capitulary for the Jews and other capitularies**
Capitularies were Charlemagne's written decrees. The Capitulary for the Jews is attributed to him and restricted Jewish moneylending, while the Capitulare de villis regulated the management of his royal estates.

**Code of Hammurabi**
A collection of 282 laws issued by Hammurabi, the most famous king of Babylon's First (Amorite) Dynasty, in the 18th century BC. It is known for "if... then" laws and harsh retaliatory punishments summed up as "an eye for an eye." The best-known copy is a black basalt stele, topped by a relief of Hammurabi before the sun god Shamash, that the Elamites carried off to Susa. It was found there in 1901 and is now in the Louvre. The code divides society into awilum (free men), mushkenum (dependents), and wardum (slaves).

**Hanging Gardens of Babylon**
One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: terraced gardens that, according to legend, Nebuchadnezzar II built for his wife Amytis, who missed the green hills of her native Media. Ancient accounts describe machinery lifting water up the terraces, but archaeologists have found no clear evidence of them, and some scholars think they are fictional or were actually in Nineveh.

**Nebuchadnezzar II and the Battle of Carchemish**
The greatest king of the Neo-Babylonian (Chaldean) Empire, who reigned c. 605–562 BC and was the son of Nabopolassar. As crown prince, in 605 BC he led the Babylonian forces that defeated Pharaoh Necho II of Egypt and the remnants of the Assyrian army at Carchemish. He rebuilt Babylon on a grand scale, making it among the largest cities in the world.

**Babylonian Captivity**
The exile of the people of Judah to Babylon after Nebuchadnezzar II's campaigns against Jerusalem. In 587/586 BC his forces sacked Jerusalem and destroyed the First Temple (Solomon's Temple). The exile ended after Cyrus the Great conquered Babylon in 539 BC and let the Jews return home.

**Ishtar Gate and the Processional Way**
A monumental city gate built under Nebuchadnezzar II, covered in blue glazed bricks with reliefs of aurochs (bulls) and dragon-like mushussu, the beast of Marduk. It opened onto the Processional Way, which was lined with reliefs of lions. The German archaeologist Robert Koldewey excavated it in the early 20th century, and it was reconstructed in Berlin's Pergamon Museum.

**Sennacherib's destruction of Babylon**
In 689 BC the Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib razed Babylon in revenge for rebellions, including one in which his son, the city's appointed ruler, was handed over to the Elamites and killed. He carried off the statue of Marduk and reportedly dumped rubble into the Arahtu canal. He was later murdered by his own sons, and his son and successor Esarhaddon rebuilt the city.

**Cyrus the Great, the Battle of Opis, and Nabonidus**
In 539 BC Cyrus the Great of Persia defeated the Babylonian army at Opis, taking the Median Wall north of the city, and then captured Babylon itself. According to Herodotus, his forces got in by diverting the Euphrates so that they could wade along the riverbed. This ended the reign of Nabonidus, the last king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, whose son Belshazzar governed the city.

**Cyrus Cylinder**
A clay cylinder inscribed in Akkadian cuneiform and discovered in Babylon in 1879. It describes Cyrus's conquest of the city, his restoration of temples, and the return of deported peoples, and it has sometimes been called the earliest declaration of human rights.

**Kassite dynasty**
After the Hittite king Mursili I sacked Babylon around 1595 BC, ending Hammurabi's dynasty, the Kassites took over and ruled for about four centuries. This was the city's longest-ruling dynasty, and they called the land Karduniash. Kassite rule was ended by Elamite attacks, including a sack by Shutruk-Nakhunte, who carried plunder off to Susa.

**Marduk, the Esagila, and the Etemenanki**
Marduk was Babylon's patron god. His main temple was the Esagila, and next to it stood the Etemenanki, a huge ziggurat ("temple of the foundation of heaven and earth") that is often linked to the biblical Tower of Babel. Each New Year, Marduk's statue was carried in procession to the Akitu House outside the city for the Akitu festival.

**Nabopolassar and the Chaldean dynasty**
Nabopolassar, a Chaldean, made Babylon independent of Assyria in 626 BC and founded the Neo-Babylonian Empire. Allied with the Medes, he helped destroy the Assyrian Empire, including the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC. His son was Nebuchadnezzar II.

**Amorite (First) Dynasty**
Babylon's First Dynasty, of Amorite origin, made the city a major power. Under Hammurabi it conquered rivals such as Larsa (ruled by Rim-Sin) and Mari, and Hammurabi's letters to his official Sin-iddinam in Larsa survive. His son Samsu-iluna faced revolts, including one led by a later Rim-Sin, that weakened the kingdom.

**Belshazzar's Feast**
In the Book of Daniel, a disembodied hand writes "Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin" on the wall during a feast held by Belshazzar, foretelling Babylon's fall. Rembrandt painted the scene and wrote the Hebrew inscription in an unusual arrangement, reportedly on the advice of his friend, the rabbi Menasseh ben Israel.

**Shamash-shum-ukin's revolt**
Shamash-shum-ukin, an Assyrian prince installed as king of Babylon, rebelled against his brother, the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, from 652 to 648 BC. The revolt failed after a siege of Babylon.

**Semiramis and the walls of Babylon**
The Greek historian Diodorus Siculus credited the legendary queen Semiramis with building Babylon's great walls and described a failed invasion of India by her against King Stabrobates. Babylon was famed for its moat and double walls, and the Median Wall was built north of the city as an outer defense.

**Battle of New Orleans**
Jackson's famous victory on January 8, 1815, over a British army under Edward Pakenham, aided by Jean Lafitte's pirates. It was fought after the Treaty of Ghent ending the War of 1812 had already been signed, and it made Jackson a national hero.

**"Old Hickory"**
Jackson's nickname, earned for his toughness as a commander. It appears as the giveaway in nearly every question about him.

**Bank War and Nicholas Biddle**
Jackson's fight against the Second Bank of the United States, headed by Nicholas Biddle. Jackson vetoed the bill rechartering the bank in 1832 and then moved federal deposits out of it into state "pet banks," which effectively killed it.

**"Corrupt Bargain"**
Jackson's name for the deal that decided the 1824 election. Jackson won the most electoral and popular votes but no majority, so the House chose John Quincy Adams, who then made Henry Clay Secretary of State. Jackson charged that Clay had traded his support for the job.

**Arbuthnot and Ambrister affair**
During the First Seminole War (1818), Jackson invaded Spanish Florida and executed two British subjects, Alexander Arbuthnot and Robert Ambrister, for aiding the Seminoles and Creeks. The executions caused a diplomatic outcry and calls in Congress to censure him, but John Quincy Adams defended him, and the invasion helped lead to the Adams-Onís Treaty.

**Indian Removal Act and the Trail of Tears**
Jackson signed the 1830 Indian Removal Act, which led to the forced relocation of southeastern tribes west of the Mississippi. The Cherokee were removed under the Treaty of New Echota (1835), signed by a minority faction led by John Ridge and Elias Boudinot over Principal Chief John Ross's opposition, and thousands died on the Trail of Tears.

**Petticoat Affair (Peggy Eaton Affair)**
A social scandal in which Washington society wives, led by Floride Calhoun (wife of Vice President John C. Calhoun), shunned Peggy Eaton, wife of Secretary of War John Eaton. Jackson defended her, and the feud led to the resignation of most of his cabinet in 1831, including Secretary of State Martin Van Buren.

**Kitchen Cabinet**
The informal circle of advisors, including Martin Van Buren and the editor Amos Kendall, whom Jackson relied on more than his official cabinet. Its influence grew after the Eaton Affair and the purge of Calhoun's allies from the cabinet.

**Nullification Crisis and the Force Bill**
In 1832 South Carolina, inspired by Calhoun's theories, passed an Ordinance of Nullification declaring the federal tariffs of 1828 (the "Tariff of Abominations") and 1832 void within the state. Jackson got Congress to pass the 1833 Force Bill authorizing military action to enforce federal law, while a compromise tariff defused the crisis.

**Battle of Horseshoe Bend**
Jackson's decisive 1814 victory over the Red Stick Creeks that ended the Creek War. Red Stick leader William Weatherford (Red Eagle) then surrendered to him, and the Treaty of Fort Jackson forced the Creeks to cede about 23 million acres.

**Specie Circular**
Jackson's 1836 executive order requiring that public land be paid for in gold or silver (specie) rather than paper money. Together with the collapse of the Bank of the United States and the pet-bank system, it helped cause the Panic of 1837, which hit his successor Martin Van Buren.

**Richard Lawrence assassination attempt**
In 1835 Richard Lawrence, a mentally ill house painter, tried to shoot Jackson outside the Capitol, but both of his pistols misfired. Jackson beat him with his cane. It was the first attempt to assassinate a U.S. president.

**Rachel Donelson Jackson**
Jackson's wife, whom he married before her divorce from her first husband was legally final. This led to bigamy and adultery charges in the vicious 1828 campaign. She died shortly after the election and before his inauguration, and attacks on her honor led to Jackson's duels, including one in which he killed Charles Dickinson.

**Maysville Road veto**
Jackson's 1830 veto of a bill to fund a road from Maysville to Lexington, Kentucky. He argued that federal money should not pay for internal improvements lying entirely within one state, a blow to Henry Clay's American System.

**Roger Taney**
A Jackson ally who, as Treasury Secretary, carried out the removal of federal deposits from the Second Bank of the United States. Jackson later appointed him Chief Justice of the Supreme Court to succeed John Marshall.

**Election of 1828 and the Coffin Handbills**
Jackson beat John Quincy Adams in the bitter 1828 rematch, becoming the first Democratic president. Adams's supporters circulated the "Coffin Handbills," which showed coffins for militiamen Jackson had executed. His raucous first inauguration in 1829, when crowds trashed the White House, was mocked as the start of the "reign of King Mob."

**Hannibal Barca**
Carthage's most famous general. In the Second Punic War (218–201 BC) he led an army with war elephants from Spain over the Alps into Italy. He won major victories at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene, and Cannae, but he never took Rome itself and was finally recalled to defend Africa.

**Battle of Cannae**
Hannibal's greatest victory, in 216 BC. His troops were arranged in a crescent that gave way in the center, then his flanks and cavalry closed around the Roman army under the consuls Varro and Paullus. This "double envelopment" destroyed one of the largest armies Rome had ever fielded, and it is still studied as the model encirclement battle.

**"Carthago delenda est" ("Carthage must be destroyed")**
The phrase the Roman senator Cato the Elder was said to add to the end of his speeches in the years before the Third Punic War (149–146 BC). He had become alarmed by Carthage's economic recovery, and he pushed Rome toward a final war to eliminate the city.

**Battle of Zama**
The final battle of the Second Punic War, fought in North Africa in 202 BC. Scipio Africanus, aided by the Numidian cavalry of King Masinissa, defeated Hannibal. Scipio's troops used trumpets and horns to panic Hannibal's war elephants and opened lanes in their lines to let the animals pass harmlessly through.

**Scipio Aemilianus and the destruction of Carthage (146 BC)**
Scipio Aemilianus, the adoptive grandson of Scipio Africanus, captured and razed Carthage after a long siege at the end of the Third Punic War, in the same year that Rome destroyed Corinth. The historian Polybius, his friend, was present. The story that the Romans sowed the ground with salt is a later legend. The war began after Carthage broke its treaty by fighting back against Masinissa's Numidian raids, and Rome then demanded that Carthage hand over its weapons and abandon the city.

**Lake Trasimene and the Fabian strategy**
In 217 BC Hannibal ambushed the consul Gaius Flaminius's army along the shore of Lake Trasimene and destroyed it. Rome then appointed Quintus Fabius Maximus "Cunctator" (the Delayer) as dictator. He avoided pitched battles and wore Hannibal down through attrition, an approach now called the Fabian strategy. Earlier, Hannibal had also won at the Trebia River in 218 BC.

**Dido (Elissa) and the oxhide founding legend**
According to legend, Carthage was founded by Queen Dido, also called Elissa, who fled Tyre in Phoenicia. The local king Iarbas offered her as much land as an oxhide could cover, so she cut the hide into thin strips and used them to surround the hill that became the Byrsa citadel. In Virgil's Aeneid, Dido's tragic affair with Aeneas and her curse on his descendants foreshadow the wars between Carthage and Rome.

**Phoenician origin and the name "New City"**
Carthage was a Phoenician colony from Tyre in modern Tunisia, possibly founded as a stop on the route to Gadir (Cádiz) in Spain. Its name, Qart-hadasht, means "New City" in Phoenician, and its people spoke Punic. The name "Punic Wars" comes from the Latin word for Phoenician.

**Mercenary War (Truceless War) and the Battle of the Saw**
A brutal war from 241 to 237 BC between Carthage and its unpaid mercenaries after the First Punic War. Hamilcar Barca trapped a rebel army under Autaritus in a canyon or pass called "the Saw," where the starving soldiers reportedly turned to cannibalism before being massacred. Rome took advantage of the chaos to seize Sardinia and Corsica.

**First Punic War, the corvus, and the Aegates Islands**
The first war with Rome (264–241 BC) began over Sicily after the Mamertines of Messana asked Rome for help. Rome made up for Carthage's naval superiority with the corvus, a boarding bridge with a spike, and first used it to win at Mylae in 260 BC. Carthage won with help from the Spartan mercenary Xanthippus, who defeated Regulus in Africa, but it lost the war after the naval Battle of the Aegates Islands in 241 BC.

**The Barcid family, Spain, and Saguntum**
After the First Punic War, Hamilcar Barca built a Carthaginian empire in Spain and, according to legend, made his young son Hannibal swear eternal hatred of Rome over a sacrificial fire. Hamilcar's family founded New Carthage (Cartagena), and tradition links Barcelona to the Barcid name. Hannibal's siege of Saguntum, a city allied with Rome, in 219 BC was the trigger for the Second Punic War, and Rome considered it a breach of the Ebro Treaty.

**Battle of the Metaurus River**
In 207 BC Hannibal's brother Hasdrubal crossed the Alps with reinforcements but was defeated and killed by the Roman consuls Gaius Claudius Nero and Marcus Livius Salinator. Nero had Hasdrubal's head thrown into Hannibal's camp. This defeat ended Hannibal's hopes of winning in Italy.

**Suffetes and the Tribunal of 104**
Carthage was a republic led by two annually elected chief magistrates called suffetes, who did not command the army, together with a council of elders and a popular assembly. A court called the Tribunal (Council) of One Hundred and Four held generals and officials accountable. Aristotle praised Carthage's constitution and compared this body to the Spartan ephors.

**Magonid dynasty, the Sicilian Wars, and Hanno the Navigator**
The Magonids, descendants of Mago I, dominated Carthage in the 500s and 400s BC and led its long wars against the Greek cities of Sicily. The Magonid Hamilcar was defeated and killed by Gelon of Syracuse and Theron of Akragas at the Battle of Himera in 480 BC, and legend says he threw himself into a sacrificial fire. Later Sicilian opponents of Carthage included Dionysius I of Syracuse, Agathocles, who was defeated at the Himera River in 311 BC and then invaded Africa, and Pyrrhus of Epirus. In the same era, Hanno the Navigator sailed down Africa's Atlantic coast, perhaps as far as Gabon, and described the voyage in a Periplus said to be copied from an inscription in the temple of Ba'al Hammon. Himilco explored the Atlantic coast of Europe.

**Great Cothon and the Tophet of Salammbo**
The Great Cothon was Carthage's artificial harbor, with a rectangular outer basin for merchant ships and a circular inner basin with sheds for the war fleet. The Tophet of Salammbo is a sacred precinct full of urns with the burned remains of infants and animals, and many scholars think it was a site of child sacrifice to Ba'al Hammon and Tanit.

**Ninety-Five Theses (1517)**
Luther's list of propositions attacking the sale of indulgences. According to tradition, he nailed it to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg, and it is usually treated as the start of the Protestant Reformation. One thesis asks why the pope, whose wealth exceeds that of the richest Crassus, does not build St. Peter's Basilica with his own money instead of the money of poor believers.

**Diet of Worms and "Here I stand, I can do no other"**
The 1521 imperial assembly before Emperor Charles V where Luther was ordered to recant his writings. He sorted his books into categories (works of faith that even his enemies accepted, attacks on the papacy and its abuses, and attacks on individual opponents) and refused to retract any of them. He reportedly ended with "Here I stand, I can do no other," although that line may be apocryphal. The resulting Edict of Worms declared him an outlaw.

**Johann Tetzel and indulgences**
Tetzel was the Dominican friar whose aggressive preaching of indulgences near Wittenberg provoked Luther; he is linked to the jingle "As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs." The campaign raised money for rebuilding St. Peter's Basilica and to pay off the debts of Archbishop Albert (Albrecht) of Mainz.

**Exsurge Domine and Pope Leo X**
The 1520 papal bull issued by Leo X that condemned 41 of Luther's propositions and gave him 60 days to recant. It opens by asking God to "arise" and "judge your own cause" against a "wild boar from the forest" ravaging the Lord's vineyard. Luther publicly burned it, and he was formally excommunicated by the follow-up bull Decet Romanum Pontificem in 1521.

**Marburg Colloquy (1529)**
A meeting arranged by Philip of Hesse to unite the German and Swiss Protestants, where Luther debated Ulrich Zwingli over the Eucharist. Luther insisted that Christ's body and blood are really present in the bread and wine, while Zwingli held that they are symbolic, and the two sides failed to agree.

**German Peasants' War and Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of Peasants**
The 1524–1525 uprising, partly inspired by Luther's ideas and associated with the radical preacher Thomas Müntzer. Luther turned against the rebels and urged the princes to crush them, calling them "filthy swine" and "mad dogs" in his pamphlet Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of Peasants.

**On the Jews and Their Lies**
Luther's 1543 antisemitic treatise urging authorities to burn synagogues, destroy Jewish homes and forbid rabbis to teach. It contrasts sharply with his earlier, friendlier 1523 work That Jesus Christ Was Born a Jew, which called the Jews blood relatives of Christ.

**Wartburg Castle and the German Bible**
After the Diet of Worms, Luther was "kidnapped" for his own protection and hidden for about a year in Wartburg Castle near Eisenach. There he translated the New Testament into German (published 1522), the start of his full German Bible.

**Frederick the Wise**
Frederick III, Elector of Saxony, was Luther's protector. He secured Luther safe conduct to the Diet of Worms and arranged his hiding at the Wartburg.

**Katharina von Bora**
A former Cistercian nun who escaped her convent and married Luther in 1525. She managed their household and finances in Wittenberg, and she called her husband "Sir Doctor" ("Herr Doktor").

**"A Mighty Fortress Is Our God"**
Luther's most famous hymn ("Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott"), based on Psalm 46. Its lyrics include "The Spirit and the gifts are ours through Him who with us sideth."

**Vow to St. Anne in a thunderstorm**
In 1505, while studying law, Luther was caught in a violent thunderstorm and cried out "Help, St. Anne! I will become a monk!" He then left law school and entered the Augustinian monastery at Erfurt.

**Cardinal Cajetan**
Thomas Cajetan was the papal legate who questioned Luther at Augsburg in 1518 and demanded that he recant. Luther refused and slipped out of the city.

**Philip Melanchthon and the Loci Communes**
Melanchthon was Luther's closest colleague at Wittenberg. His Loci Communes (1521) was the first systematic presentation of Lutheran theology, built around justification by faith alone, and he later wrote the Augsburg Confession.

**Small and Large Catechisms and the Schmalkald Articles**
Luther wrote his Small and Large Catechisms in 1529 to teach the basics of the faith to ordinary people and to pastors. He drafted the Schmalkald Articles in 1537 as a summary of Lutheran doctrine for the Schmalkaldic League of Protestant princes.

**Potemkin villages**
Grigory Potemkin, Catherine's favorite, lover, and governor of the newly won southern lands, supposedly built fake, prosperous-looking village facades along the Dnieper River to impress her during her 1787 tour of Crimea. The story is probably exaggerated, but "Potemkin village" now means any sham display meant to hide a bad reality.

**Pugachev's Rebellion**
