The largest peasant and Cossack revolt of Catherine's reign (1773–1775), led by the Cossack Yemelyan Pugachev, who claimed to be her deposed husband Peter III and promised to abolish serfdom. Her forces, including Alexander Suvorov and Peter Panin, crushed it, and Pugachev was executed.

**Coup against Peter III**
Catherine took the throne in a 1762 palace coup against her unpopular husband, Emperor Peter III, who was killed days later in custody. Her lover Grigory Orlov and his brothers led the coup with the Imperial Guards.

**Partitions of Poland and Stanisław Poniatowski**
Catherine placed her former lover Stanisław August Poniatowski on the Polish throne in 1764, which provoked the anti-Russian Bar Confederation. Russia then joined Prussia's Frederick the Great and Austria's Maria Theresa in the First Partition (1772), and Russia and Prussia (with Austria in the third) carried out the Second (1793) and Third (1795) Partitions, which wiped Poland off the map.

**Nakaz (Great Instruction)**
Catherine's 1767 Instruction to the Legislative Commission she called to draft a new law code to replace the old Muscovite code. It borrowed heavily, sometimes word for word, from Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws and Cesare Beccaria's On Crimes and Punishments. Catherine said of Montesquieu that "his book was my breviary," and Diderot wrote a critique of it.

**Grigory Orlov**
A Guards officer and Catherine's lover who helped organize the 1762 coup and was a leading favorite in the early years of her reign. His brother Alexei Orlov commanded the Russian fleet in the Mediterranean, where he backed the Greek "Orlov Revolt." The famous Orlov Diamond is named for Grigory.

**Enlightened despot and her correspondence with Voltaire and Diderot**
Catherine is a textbook "enlightened despot," a ruler who embraced Enlightenment ideas while keeping absolute power. She corresponded with Voltaire, who called her the "Star of the North," and was a patron of Denis Diderot, buying his library and inviting him to St. Petersburg.

**Battle of Chesma and the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca**
In the Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774, a Russian fleet, with the help of the Scottish officer Samuel Greig and his fireships, destroyed the Ottoman navy at Chesma (1770). General Pyotr Rumyantsev then won the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca (1774), which gave Russia Black Sea access and made the Crimean Khanate independent of the Ottomans.

**Annexation of Crimea and the Treaty of Jassy**
Catherine annexed the Crimean Khanate in 1783. After a second Russo-Turkish War, the Treaty of Jassy (1792) made the Ottomans recognize the annexation, gave Russia the Yedisan region, and set the border at the Dniester River, where Odessa was soon founded.

**Hermitage Museum**
Catherine's vast private art collection, housed in buildings attached to the Winter Palace in St. Petersburg, became the State Hermitage Museum, one of the world's largest art museums.

**League of Armed Neutrality**
An alliance of neutral powers that Catherine formed in 1780, during the American Revolutionary War, to protect neutral shipping from searches and seizures by the British navy.

**Pale of Settlement**
A region in Russia's western borderlands, created by Catherine's 1791 decree, to which Jews were largely restricted. It lasted until the end of the Russian Empire.

**Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst**
Catherine's birth name. She was born in 1729 to a minor German princely family and grew up in Stettin in Prussia. She came to Russia to marry the future Peter III, converted to Orthodoxy, took the name Yekaterina Alekseyevna, and became Russia's longest-reigning female ruler (1762–1796).

**Thomas Dimsdale and smallpox inoculation**
In 1768 Catherine had the English doctor Thomas Dimsdale inoculate her against smallpox, along with her son, to calm public fears and encourage inoculation across Russia.

**Nikita Panin and the Northern Accord**
Catherine's foreign-policy advisor Nikita Panin pushed the "Northern Accord," a planned alliance of Russia, Prussia, Poland, and Sweden to counter France and Austria. It failed, and Panin was eventually replaced by Ivan Osterman. In the same years, Catherine's threat to intervene helped end the War of the Bavarian Succession with the 1779 Treaty of Teschen.

**Battle of Navarino**
The decisive 1827 naval battle of the Greek War of Independence, fought off the southwestern Peloponnese. An allied British, French, and Russian fleet under British admiral Edward Codrington destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet of Ibrahim Pasha, effectively securing Greek independence; Codrington was later criticized by the British Admiralty for provoking the engagement.

**Otto of Bavaria (Otto I)**
A Bavarian prince of the Wittelsbach dynasty who became the first king of modern Greece, installed by the Great Powers through the London Protocol and London Conference of 1832. He ruled from Athens (the capital was moved there from Nafplio), was forced to grant a constitution after the September 3rd Revolution of 1843, and was eventually deposed and exiled to Bavaria with his wife Amalia.

**Alexander Ypsilantis and the Filiki Eteria ("Society of Friends")**
The Filiki Eteria was a secret society that launched the Greek War of Independence in 1821. Its leader, Alexander Ypsilantis, was a Phanariote Greek and former Russian cavalry officer whose expedition into the Danubian Principalities was crushed at the Battle of Dragashani, after which he was imprisoned in Austria.

**Lord Byron and Missolonghi**
The English Romantic poet Lord Byron was a famous Philhellene who joined the Greek independence cause and died at Missolonghi in 1824. Missolonghi was later besieged and taken by Ibrahim Pasha, the son of Muhammad Ali of Egypt.

**Ibrahim Pasha**
The son of Muhammad Ali of Egypt, he led Egyptian forces on behalf of the Ottoman Sultan during the Greek War of Independence. He besieged Missolonghi and ravaged the Peloponnese, but his fleet was destroyed at Navarino.

**Regime of the Colonels**
The right-wing military junta that ruled Greece from 1967 to 1974 after a coup led by Georgios Papadopoulos. It was opposed by the student uprising at the Athens Polytechnic (National Technical University), which gave the name to the terrorist group Revolutionary Organization 17 November, and by the 1973 mutiny of the destroyer Velos during a NATO exercise; it collapsed after backing a coup against Archbishop Makarios III in Cyprus in pursuit of enosis.

**Greek Civil War and the Truman Doctrine**
A 1946 to 1949 civil war in which the communist Democratic Army of Greece (DSE) fought the royalist, US-backed government army. US support to Greece (and Turkey) under the 1947 Truman Doctrine was a key early Cold War policy; the war also saw children placed in "child towns" and refugee camps named for Queen Frederica.

**Massacre at Chios (Eugene Delacroix)**
An 1824 painting by the French Romantic artist Eugene Delacroix depicting the 1822 Ottoman slaughter and enslavement of Greek inhabitants of the island of Chios. It became a major symbol of the Greek cause in Western Europe.

**Greek debt crisis, PASOK, and SYRIZA**
After the government elected in 2009 revealed that its budget deficit was far higher than reported, Greece fell into a severe debt crisis requiring multiple EU bailout packages and raising fears of a "Grexit" from the Eurozone. Prime Minister George Papandreou of PASOK resigned, and in the January 2015 elections the leftist SYRIZA party won power under Alexis Tsipras, governing in coalition with the nationalist ANEL.

**Persian Wars (Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, Plataea)**
The early 5th-century BC conflicts in which Greek city-states such as Athens and Sparta repelled invasions by the Achaemenid Persian kings Darius I and Xerxes. Key battles include Marathon (490 BC), Thermopylae and Artemisium, the naval victory at Salamis led by Themistocles, and Plataea, where the Persian commander Mardonius was killed.

**Organization X and the December Events (Dekemvriana)**
Organization X was a right-wing royalist paramilitary group that fought the communist-led resistance movement EAM-ELAS. Their clash, along with British forces, in Athens in December 1944 is known as the December Events, a prelude to the Greek Civil War.

**Klephts and armatoloi**
Klephts were Greek mountain bandits who resisted Ottoman rule, while armatoloi were Christian militias employed by the Ottomans to keep order. Both groups became important fighters in the Greek War of Independence.

**Operation Mercury and the Metaxas Regime**
Greece under the "4th of August" dictatorship of Ioannis Metaxas resisted an Italian invasion in 1940 before being conquered by Germany in 1941. Operation Mercury was the German airborne invasion of Crete, the first major invasion conducted primarily by paratroopers, beginning with landings at Maleme airfield; Greece was then subjected to a "triple occupation" by Germany, Italy, and Bulgaria.

**Elgin Marbles and the Parthenon**
Marble sculptures removed from the Parthenon on the Acropolis of Athens by Lord Elgin's agents between 1801 and 1812 and later sold to the British Museum. The Parthenon had earlier been badly damaged in 1687 when a Venetian bombardment ignited Ottoman gunpowder stored inside it.

**Mycenaeans and Linear B**
The Bronze Age civilization of mainland Greece known for Cyclopean masonry, the Lion Gate at Mycenae, and the Linear B script, an early form of Greek. The Mycenaeans supplanted the Minoan civilization centered at Knossos on Crete, and their collapse led to the Greek Dark Ages, which ended with the Geometric period.

**Sicilian Expedition**
The disastrous Athenian campaign of 415–413 BC during the Peloponnesian War, aimed at capturing Syracuse, Sicily's leading Greek city. It ended with the near-total destruction of the Athenian force and is the single most common clue for the island.

**Alcibiades and the mutilation of the Hermai**
Alcibiades was the chief planner and champion of the Sicilian Expedition. Just before the fleet sailed, the herms (Hermai) statues across Athens were vandalized and the blame fell partly on him; he was recalled from Sicily to stand trial and instead defected to Sparta.

**Nicias and the lunar eclipse**
Nicias opposed the expedition but was made one of its commanders. When a lunar eclipse occurred in 413 BC as the Athenians prepared to withdraw, he insisted on waiting 27 days on the advice of seers, letting the Syracusans trap the army. He was executed after the surrender.

**Gylippus and Lamachus**
Gylippus was the Spartan general sent to organize the defense of Syracuse, turning the tide against Athens. Lamachus was the third, aggressive Athenian commander, killed during the fighting around the Syracusan siege walls.

**Archimedes' heat ray and claw**
The inventor Archimedes of Syracuse defended his city against the Roman siege under Marcus Claudius Marcellus (214–212 BC) during the Second Punic War. Legend credits him with a heat ray of mirrors that set ships on fire, and he built the "Claw of Archimedes," a crane-like device that lifted enemy ships out of the water.

**"Do not disturb my circles"**
Archimedes' legendary last words to the Roman soldier who killed him while he was drawing geometric figures in the sand, after Syracuse fell to Marcellus during a festival to Artemis.

**Sicilian Vespers**
A 1282 revolt that began at the hour of Vespers on Easter Monday outside a church in Palermo, in which Sicilians massacred the French officials of Charles of Anjou. Peter III of Aragon then claimed the island, setting off the War of the Sicilian Vespers. Rioters supposedly identified Frenchmen by asking them to pronounce the Sicilian word for "chickpeas" (ciciri).

**Peace of Caltabellotta**
The 1302 treaty that ended the War of the Sicilian Vespers, leaving Sicily under an Aragonese prince (Frederick III) while the Angevins kept Naples. The earlier Treaty of Anagni (1295) had attempted to settle the same dispute.

**Mamertines and the First Punic War**
The Mamertines were Campanian mercenaries, originally hired by Agathocles of Syracuse, who seized the city of Messana. Threatened by Hiero II of Syracuse, they appealed to Rome, sparking the First Punic War (264–241 BC), most of which was fought on Sicily; Rome gained the island at the war's end.

**Robert Guiscard and the Norman conquest**
Robert Guiscard ("the Cunning" or "the Fox") and his brother Roger I (Roger Bosso), sons of Tancred of Hauteville, conquered Muslim Sicily in the 11th century, winning battles like Misilmeri. Anna Komnene described Robert, who fought her father Alexios at Dyrrhachium and was the father of Bohemond, as "in mind most cunning."

**Roger II and the Tabula Rogeriana**
Roger II founded the Norman Kingdom of Sicily in 1130. He commissioned the Arab geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi to produce the Tabula Rogeriana (1154), a world map oriented with south at the top. His son William I ("the Bad") fought his chancellor Maio of Bari.

**Expedition of the Thousand**
Giuseppe Garibaldi's 1860 campaign in which about a thousand volunteer "Redshirts" landed at Marsala, won battles like Calatafimi and Milazzo, and overthrew the Bourbon Kingdom of the Two Sicilies (Sicily plus Naples) under Francis II, a key step in Italian unification.

**Operation Husky**
The Allied invasion of Sicily in July 1943 during World War II, approved at the Trident Conference. It was preceded by the British deception Operation Mincemeat, and its launch helped push Hitler to call off the Kursk offensive; it opened the way to the invasion of mainland Italy.

**Battle of Himera**
The 480 BC battle in which Gelon of Syracuse and Theron of Akragas (Agrigentum) defeated a large Carthaginian invasion of Sicily, traditionally said to have happened on the same day as the Battle of Salamis.

**Syracusan tyrants and Phalaris**
Syracuse was ruled by tyrants including Gelon, Hiero I and II, and Dionysius I and II; the historian Philistus wrote about the Dionysii, whose court hosted Plato and the poet Philoxenus. Phalaris, tyrant of Acragas, was said to roast victims in a hollow brazen bull and was supposedly burned in it himself.

**Aghlabid conquest and Emirate of Sicily**
In 827 the Aghlabids of Ifriqiya invaded Sicily, aided by a rebellion against Byzantine emperor Michael II; the fall of Taormina in 902 completed the Muslim conquest. The Fatimids later replaced the Aghlabids, and the island became the Emirate of Sicily until the Norman conquest.

**Sextus Pompey and the Servile Wars**
Sextus Pompey, son of Pompey the Great, used Sicily as a base to blockade Italy until his defeat in 36 BC. Earlier, Sicily was the site of the First and Second Servile Wars, large slave revolts against Rome in the late 2nd century BC.

**Fort Sumter**
The Union fort in Charleston Harbor where the Civil War began in April 1861. Confederate General P.G.T. Beauregard bombarded Major Robert Anderson's garrison, which surrendered on April 13 and evacuated on April 14. Earlier, in January 1861, batteries including Fort Moultrie had driven off the supply ship Star of the West, and Governor Francis W. Pickens had demanded the fort's surrender.

**First state to secede**
South Carolina seceded from the Union in December 1860, shortly after Abraham Lincoln's election. It was the first of the states that went on to form the Confederacy.

**Denmark Vesey**
A free Black carpenter in Charleston who bought his freedom with lottery winnings he won in 1799. He planned a large slave uprising for July 14, 1822 (Bastille Day), but the plot was betrayed and he was executed. In response, white Charlestonians tightened slave laws and founded the military college known as The Citadel.

**Preston Brooks caning Charles Sumner**
In 1856 South Carolina congressman Preston Brooks beat Massachusetts senator Charles Sumner unconscious with a cane on the Senate floor. The attack came days after Sumner's "Crime Against Kansas" speech, which insulted Brooks's relative, South Carolina senator Andrew Butler.

**John C. Calhoun and the Nullification Crisis**
Calhoun, a South Carolina politician and vice president, secretly wrote the South Carolina Exposition and Protest (1828), arguing that a state could nullify federal laws such as the "Tariff of Abominations." South Carolina's 1832 nullification of the tariffs set off a crisis with President Andrew Jackson. The "forty bales" theory, which held that tariffs took forty of every hundred bales of cotton from Southern producers, was used to blame the state's economic troubles on the tariff.

**Stono Rebellion**
The largest slave revolt in Britain's mainland North American colonies. It broke out in 1739 near the Stono River and was led by an enslaved man named Jemmy (also called Cato), whose mostly Kongolese followers marched toward Spanish Florida shouting "Liberty!"

**Charleston**
South Carolina's largest city and major port, long a center of the slave trade. The International African American Museum opened at the former slave-landing site of Gadsden's Wharf in 2023. In 2015, after a white supremacist killed nine Black worshippers at Charleston's Emanuel AME Church, Governor Nikki Haley had the Confederate battle flag removed from the statehouse grounds.

**Revolutionary War battles: Charleston, Camden, and Cowpens**
In 1776 William Moultrie defended Charleston from a palmetto-log fort on Sullivan's Island, later named Fort Moultrie. American General Benjamin Lincoln surrendered Charleston to Henry Clinton in 1780, Horatio Gates suffered a disastrous defeat at Camden that same year, and in 1781 Daniel Morgan crushed Banastre Tarleton at Cowpens. Other sites include Ninety Six and Eutaw Springs.

**Francis Marion, the "Swamp Fox"**
A South Carolina militia officer who waged guerrilla warfare against the British after the fall of Charleston, striking from the state's swamps and then disappearing.

**Eliza Lucas Pinckney and indigo**
In the 1740s Eliza Lucas (later Pinckney) developed indigo, the plant source of a blue dye, into a profitable cash crop. Along with rice, it made the Lowcountry plantation economy rich, and by the antebellum period South Carolina had a Black majority.

**Gullah and the Sea Islands**
Gullah is a creole language and culture of descendants of enslaved Africans, many brought from rice-growing regions of West Africa, in the Sea Islands and coastal Lowcountry of South Carolina and Georgia. It preserves African words, names, and foods such as benne (sesame) wafers.

**"Pitchfork Ben" Tillman**
Benjamin Tillman, a white supremacist governor and senator of South Carolina in the late 1800s and early 1900s. He threatened to stick a pitchfork into President Grover Cleveland and openly defended lynching.

**Strom Thurmond and the Dixiecrats**
A longtime segregationist senator from South Carolina who ran for president in 1948 as the candidate of the States' Rights Democratic ("Dixiecrat") Party. After his death it was revealed that he had fathered a daughter, Essie Mae Washington-Williams, with a Black teenager who worked for his family.

**James Henry Hammond and the "mudsill" speech**
A South Carolina politician who, in an 1858 Senate speech, argued that every society needs a "mudsill" class to do menial work, a role filled in the South by slaves. As a congressman in the 1830s he pushed for the gag rule that blocked consideration of antislavery petitions. Also from South Carolina were the abolitionist Grimké sisters and the Civil War diarist Mary Chesnut.

**Reconstruction: Port Royal, Robert Smalls, and the KKK Act**
During the Civil War, freed people farmed abandoned plantations in the Sea Islands in the Port Royal Experiment, and Robert Smalls escaped slavery by sailing the Confederate ship Planter out of Charleston Harbor and later served in Congress. In 1871 President Grant suspended habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties under the Ku Klux Klan Act, and Attorney General Amos Akerman led prosecutions of Klansmen. In 1876 Wade Hampton's armed "Red Shirts" helped end Reconstruction in the state.

**Six wives**
Henry VIII married six times: Catherine of Aragon, Anne Boleyn, Jane Seymour, Anne of Cleves, Catherine Howard, and Catherine Parr. Their fates are remembered by the rhyme "divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived"; Jane Seymour bore his only legitimate son, Edward VI, and his daughters became Mary I and Elizabeth I.

**Catherine of Aragon and the "King's Great Matter"**
Henry's first wife, a Spanish princess and widow of his older brother Arthur, did not give him a surviving son. His attempt to annul the marriage, called the "King's Great Matter," was blocked by Pope Clement VII, who was under the influence of Catherine's nephew, Emperor Charles V. The impasse led to England's break with Rome.

**Act of Supremacy (1534)**
The parliamentary act declaring Henry the Supreme Head of the Church of England, which completed the break from the Roman Catholic Church and founded the Anglican Church. Refusing to accept the break and the oaths that came with it was treated as treason.

**Dissolution of the Monasteries**
From 1536 to 1541, Henry and his chief minister Thomas Cromwell closed England's monasteries, convents, and friaries and seized their land and wealth for the Crown. According to one story, his dying words were "Monks! Monks! Monks!"

**Field of the Cloth of Gold**
A lavish 1520 summit near Calais between Henry and King Francis I of France, organized by Cardinal Thomas Wolsey. Both kings tried to outdo each other with displays of wealth, but the meeting produced little lasting alliance.

**Pilgrimage of Grace**
A 1536 popular uprising, centered in Yorkshire and following an earlier rising in Lincolnshire, that protested the dissolution of the monasteries and demanded the removal of ministers like Thomas Cromwell. Its leader, the lawyer Robert Aske, was executed by hanging in chains at Clifford's Tower in York in 1537.

**Thomas Cromwell**
Henry's chief minister in the 1530s, who engineered the Reformation legislation and the dissolution of the monasteries. He arranged Henry's marriage to Anne of Cleves, and after the king was displeased with her, Cromwell was attainted and beheaded in 1540.

**Defense of the Seven Sacraments**
A 1521 treatise attributed to Henry that attacked Martin Luther and defended Catholic doctrine. In reward, Pope Leo X granted him the title "Defender of the Faith," which English monarchs still use.

**Thomas More**
The humanist author of Utopia who served as Henry's Lord Chancellor. He refused to accept Henry's supremacy over the Church and the annulment, and he was beheaded for treason in 1535 after testimony by Solicitor General Richard Rich; Bishop John Fisher was executed for the same reason that year.

**Cardinal Thomas Wolsey**
Henry's powerful Lord Chancellor and chief minister early in his reign, who organized the Field of the Cloth of Gold. His failure to win the annulment from the pope led to his fall in 1529, and he died in 1530 while being brought to face treason charges.

**Anne Boleyn**
Henry's second wife and the mother of Elizabeth I, for whom he broke with Rome. She was beheaded in 1536 on charges of adultery and treason, partly based on the testimony of the musician Mark Smeaton; Thomas Wyatt's poem "Whoso List to Hunt" is thought to be about her.

**Anne of Cleves ("Flanders Mare")**
Henry's fourth wife, a German princess chosen for a Protestant alliance. Henry found her unattractive in person, reportedly calling her a "Flanders Mare"; the marriage was quickly annulled, and Cromwell, who had arranged it, was executed.

**Thomas Cranmer**
The Archbishop of Canterbury who annulled Henry's marriage to Catherine of Aragon in 1533 and led the early English Reformation. He later wrote the Book of Common Prayer, published under Henry's son Edward VI.

**Battle of the Spurs and Battle of Flodden**
In 1513 Henry, allied with Emperor Maximilian I, routed a French force at the Battle of the Spurs, named for the haste of the French retreat, and captured Tournai. That same year, while Henry was in France, the Earl of Surrey defeated and killed the invading King James IV of Scotland at Flodden.

**Executions of the reign**
Henry's reign saw many executions, including two queens, Anne Boleyn and Catherine Howard, as well as ministers and critics. Early on he executed his father's unpopular tax collectors Sir Richard Empson and Edmund Dudley, and he later executed Elizabeth Barton, the "Holy Maid of Kent," who had prophesied against his remarriage.

**Suez Canal and the Suez Crisis (1956)**
The canal designed by Ferdinand de Lesseps and opened in 1869, which links the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea and greatly shortened the voyage from Europe to India. In 1956 Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalized it to pay for the Aswan High Dam, and Britain, France and Israel, which had secretly coordinated their plan in the Protocol of Sèvres, invaded in an Anglo-French operation code-named Musketeer. U.S. and Soviet pressure forced them to withdraw, and a UN Emergency Force was then stationed in the Sinai.

**Gamal Abdel Nasser**
The leader of the Free Officers Movement, whose 1952 coup overthrew King Farouk; Farouk's infant son Fuad II was briefly king before the monarchy was abolished in 1953. As president, Nasser championed pan-Arab nationalism and Arab socialism and merged Egypt with Syria in the United Arab Republic (1958–1961).

**Anwar Sadat and the Camp David Accords**
Nasser's successor, who signed the 1978 Camp David Accords with Israeli prime minister Menachem Begin under the mediation of U.S. president Jimmy Carter. He was assassinated by Islamist soldiers during a 1981 Cairo military parade marking the anniversary of the 1973 crossing of the Suez Canal, an attack that also wounded his successor Hosni Mubarak.

**Operation Badr and the Yom Kippur War (1973)**
Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack on Israel on the Jewish holy day of Yom Kippur. In Operation Badr, Egyptian forces crossed the Suez Canal and used high-pressure water cannons to breach the sand ramparts of Israel's Bar-Lev Line, which earned Sadat the title "Hero of the Crossing." The fighting included the Battle of the Chinese Farm.

**Six-Day War and the Sinai Peninsula**
In 1967 Egypt closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping, and Israel struck first, defeating Egypt, Syria and Jordan and capturing the entire Sinai Peninsula. Egypt regained the Sinai after the 1979 peace treaty that followed the Camp David Accords.

**Aswan High Dam and Lake Nasser**
The huge Nile dam built under Nasser with Soviet help after the U.S. and Britain withdrew their offer to fund it. Its reservoir, Lake Nasser, flooded ancient sites, so temples such as Abu Simbel were moved to higher ground.

**Pharaoh: crowns, crook and flail, and the Narmer Palette**
Pharaohs wore the white crown of Upper Egypt (hedjet), the red crown of Lower Egypt (deshret), or the two combined in the double crown (pschent), along with a false beard, the uraeus cobra and the crook and flail. The Narmer Palette shows King Narmer, possibly the same person as the legendary Menes, who is credited with unifying Egypt and founding Memphis, smiting an enemy with a mace; its other side shows two serpopards with intertwined necks.

**Hatshepsut**
The female pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty who ruled with, and then above, her stepson Thutmose III, and was depicted with a false beard. She sent a famous trading expedition to the land of Punt for frankincense and myrrh. After her death her name and images were erased from many monuments, and she was buried in tomb KV20 in the Valley of the Kings.

**Cleopatra VII and the Ptolemaic dynasty**
The Ptolemaic dynasty was founded by Ptolemy I, a general of Alexander the Great, after Alexander's conquest of Egypt. Its last ruler, Cleopatra VII, reportedly had herself smuggled to Julius Caesar rolled in a carpet; she allied with Mark Antony and killed herself after their defeat at Actium in 31 BCE. Octavian then had her son Caesarion executed and made Egypt a Roman province.

**Library of Alexandria and the Pharos lighthouse**
Alexander's city of Alexandria, whose street plan was said to have been marked out with barley flour, became the Ptolemies' capital. Its great library was catalogued in Callimachus's Pinakes and was partly burned during Julius Caesar's war in Alexandria. The Lighthouse of Alexandria on the island of Pharos, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, was later destroyed by earthquakes.

**Napoleon's Egyptian campaign (1798–1801)**
Napoleon invaded Egypt and defeated the Mamluks at the Battle of the Pyramids, where he reportedly told his troops that "forty centuries look down upon you." Horatio Nelson destroyed the French fleet at the Battle of the Nile (Aboukir Bay), and the scholars (savants) who came with the expedition produced the Description de l'Égypte. French soldiers found the Rosetta Stone, a trilingual stele that later helped decipher hieroglyphics.

**Muhammad Ali Pasha**
The Ottoman Albanian officer who became ruler of Egypt in 1805 and broke the power of the Mamluks by massacring their leaders in 1811. He modernized the army and economy, built the Mahmudiyah Canal for year-round irrigation, and promoted cotton growing. His dynasty ruled Egypt until King Farouk was overthrown in 1952.

**British Egypt, Saad Zaghlul and the 1919 Revolution**
Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 and made it a protectorate in 1914; resentment grew after the 1906 Denshawai incident, in which villagers were harshly punished after a clash with British officers. The British exile of the nationalist leader Saad Zaghlul sparked the 1919 Revolution, and his Wafd Party led the push for independence, which Britain partly granted in 1922.

**Hosni Mubarak and Tahrir Square (2011)**
Sadat's successor, who ruled Egypt for about 30 years. Huge Arab Spring protests centered on Cairo's Tahrir Square forced him to resign in 2011, and Abdel Fattah el-Sisi later took power after a 2013 coup.

**Manetho, the Kingdoms and the Intermediate Periods**
Manetho was a priest of the Ptolemaic era who wrote a history that divided Egypt's rulers into the dynasties still used today; his list includes the possibly legendary queen Nitocris. Historians group these dynasties into the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms, separated by periods of disunity called Intermediate Periods. During the First Intermediate Period, the governors (nomarchs) of Egypt's 42 provinces, or nomes, gained power at the pharaohs' expense.

**New Deal**
FDR's program of relief, recovery, and reform (the "three R's") to fight the Great Depression. It created many "alphabet agencies," including the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), Works Progress Administration (WPA), Public Works Administration (PWA), and Securities and Exchange Commission, whose first head was Joseph Kennedy. It also included Social Security and the Wagner Act, which guaranteed collective bargaining and created the National Labor Relations Board.

**Court-packing plan**
FDR's 1937 Judiciary Reorganization Bill, proposing to add up to six Supreme Court justices, one for each justice over age 70 who did not retire. It responded to rulings striking down New Deal laws, but it failed in Congress after the death of its Senate champion Joseph Robinson and the retirement of Willis Van Devanter.

**"Switch in time that saved nine"**
Justice Owen Roberts's 1937 shift to vote with the Court's liberal "Three Musketeers," upholding New Deal-era laws and defusing the court-packing fight. The Court's conservative bloc that had blocked FDR, including James McReynolds and Willis Van Devanter, was known as the "Four Horsemen."

**Fireside chats**
FDR's informal radio addresses to the nation. The first, in March 1933, explained the national bank holiday and was addressed to "the overwhelming majority of you who use banks"; the term was coined by broadcaster Robert Trout.

**"The only thing we have to fear is fear itself"**
The most famous line of FDR's first inaugural address in March 1933, delivered at the depth of the Great Depression as he promised bold action.

**"A date which will live in infamy"**
The opening of FDR's address to Congress on December 8, 1941, the day after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, asking for a declaration of war. It also declared "we will gain the inevitable triumph, so help us God."

**Arsenal of Democracy and Lend-Lease**
In a December 1940 fireside chat FDR declared that the U.S. "must be the great arsenal of democracy," supplying Britain against the Axis. He justified the Lend-Lease program with the analogy of lending a garden hose to a neighbor whose house is on fire.

**Four Freedoms speech**
FDR's January 1941 State of the Union address naming four universal freedoms: freedom of speech, freedom of worship, freedom from want, and freedom from fear. Norman Rockwell illustrated them in a famous series of four paintings.

**Executive Order 9066 and Korematsu v. United States**
FDR's 1942 order authorizing the removal and internment of Japanese Americans from the West Coast. The Supreme Court upheld it in Korematsu v. United States (1944), with Justices Frank Murphy, Robert Jackson, and Owen Roberts dissenting.

**Schechter Poultry v. United States ("Sick Chicken Case")**
The 1935 Supreme Court decision, sometimes called "Black Monday" for the New Deal, that struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act and ended the National Recovery Administration, whose symbol was a blue eagle and which was led by Hugh Johnson.

**Brain Trust and Frances Perkins**
FDR's circle of advisers included Rexford Tugwell, who promoted planned "greenbelt towns" and later governed Puerto Rico, and Harry Hopkins, who ran relief programs such as the WPA. Labor Secretary Frances Perkins was the first woman to serve in a U.S. Cabinet.

**James Cox's running mate and early career**
FDR served as Woodrow Wilson's Assistant Secretary of the Navy and was the Democratic vice-presidential nominee with James Cox in 1920. After contracting polio in 1921, he returned to politics, nominating Al Smith as "the Happy Warrior" and succeeding him as Governor of New York in 1929.

**Business Plot**
An alleged 1933 conspiracy by wealthy businessmen, including bond salesman Gerald MacGuire, to overthrow FDR and install a fascist-style government. Marine general Smedley Butler exposed it to the McCormack–Dickstein Committee, with reporter Paul Comly French corroborating his testimony.

**Giuseppe Zangara's assassination attempt**
In February 1933, before FDR's inauguration, Giuseppe Zangara fired at him in Miami and mortally wounded Chicago mayor Anton Cermak, who reportedly told FDR "I'm glad it was me instead of you."

**Four terms and the New Deal coalition**
FDR was the only president elected more than twice, winning four elections and dying in his fourth term in 1945; his vice presidents included John Nance Garner and Henry Wallace, previously his Secretary of Agriculture. His alliance of workers, minorities, intellectuals, and white Southerners formed the New Deal coalition of the Fifth Party System.

**Reconquista**
The roughly 700-year process (c. 718–1492) by which Christian kingdoms of northern Iberia retook the peninsula from Muslim rule. It is the single most common topic in Spain questions, running from the founding of Asturias to the fall of Granada.

**Battle of Covadonga and Pelagius**
Around 718–722, the Visigothic noble Pelagius (Pelayo) defeated an Umayyad force at Covadonga, preserving the Christian Kingdom of Asturias. It is traditionally considered the start of the Reconquista and followed the 711 invasion led by Tariq ibn Ziyad that toppled the Visigothic Kingdom.

**Fall of Granada (1492) and Boabdil**
Granada, ruled by the Nasrid dynasty from the Alhambra palace, was the last Muslim state in Iberia. Its last emir, Boabdil (Muhammad XII), surrendered to Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492; legend says he wept at the mountain pass called "The Moor's Last Sigh" as he left, and he was briefly given lands in the Alpujarras before departing for Morocco.

**El Cid**
Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, an 11th-century Castilian knight who fought for both Christian and Muslim rulers and conquered and ruled Valencia. He became Spain's national hero; legend says his horse was named Babieca ("stupid") and that his corpse was strapped onto his horse to rally the defenders of Valencia.

**Ferdinand and Isabella (the Catholic Monarchs)**
Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile married in 1469, uniting the two crowns into what became modern Spain (their motto was "Tanto monta, monta tanto"). They completed the Reconquista, established the Spanish Inquisition under Tomás de Torquemada, and were the parents of Joanna the Mad and Catherine of Aragon, first wife of Henry VIII.

**Alhambra Decree**
The 1492 edict issued by Ferdinand and Isabella that expelled from Spain all Jews who refused to convert to Christianity. It was issued in the same year as the fall of Granada and Columbus's first voyage.

**Christopher Columbus and the Capitulations of Santa Fe**
Ferdinand and Isabella sponsored Columbus's 1492 voyage across the Atlantic, setting its terms in the Capitulations of Santa Fe. This launched the Spanish colonial empire in the Americas, including the viceroyalty of New Spain (Mexico).

**Taifa kingdoms, the Almoravids and the Almohads**
After the Caliphate of Córdoba collapsed in civil war in the early 11th century, al-Andalus split into small Muslim states called taifas. The North African Almoravid and later Almohad dynasties crossed into Iberia and took over the taifas; the Almohad caliph Muhammad al-Nasir was crushed by a Christian coalition at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.

**Abd al-Rahman I and the Emirate of Córdoba**
An Umayyad prince who fled the Abbasid Revolution and founded the independent Emirate of Córdoba in 756, keeping the Umayyad dynasty alive in al-Andalus, the Arabic name for Muslim Iberia. Earlier, an Umayyad army that crossed from Iberia into Gaul was halted at the Battle of Tours (732).

**Charles V (Charles I of Spain)**
The Habsburg son of Joanna the Mad who ruled Spain and the Holy Roman Empire. He put down the Comuneros revolt, captured Francis I of France at the Battle of Pavia (1525), oversaw the Sack of Rome (1527), sponsored Magellan's circumnavigation, and called the Diet of Worms before abdicating in 1555–56 and retiring to a monastery.

**Philip II and the Spanish Armada**
Charles V's son, who married Mary I of England and later gained the Portuguese throne in the Iberian Union. He sent the Duke of Alba, who set up the "Council of Blood," to crush the Dutch Revolt led by William the Silent, and in 1588 launched an Armada against England that was defeated at Gravelines (Francis Drake had earlier raided Cádiz).

**Hispania and Saguntum**
The Roman name for the Iberian Peninsula. Hannibal's siege of Saguntum began the Second Punic War, Scipio Africanus won the region at the Battle of Ilipa, and Augustus later divided it into Baetica, Tarraconensis and Lusitania. The emperor Trajan was born there.

**Ferdinand VII, the Constitution of 1812 and the Carlist Wars**
Ferdinand VII was forced to abdicate during Napoleon's Peninsular War, while the Cortes of Cádiz wrote the liberal Constitution of 1812. A French army, the "Hundred Thousand Sons of Saint Louis," ended the Trienio Liberal in 1823. When his daughter Isabella II succeeded him in 1833, his brother Don Carlos's supporters launched the Carlist Wars.

**Spanish–American War and the USS Maine**
Spain was blamed for the 1898 explosion of the USS Maine in Havana Harbor, which helped spark war with the United States. In the resulting Treaty of Paris, Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines.

**Francisco Franco and the Spanish Civil War**
Franco's Nationalists defeated the Republicans in the Spanish Civil War (1936–39), and he ruled as dictator, backed by the Falange party, until his death in 1975. King Juan Carlos I then oversaw Spain's transition to democracy.

**October Crisis**
In 1970 the Quebec separatist group FLQ (Front de libération du Québec) kidnapped British diplomat James Cross and Quebec Deputy Premier Pierre Laporte, whom they killed. Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau invoked the War Measures Act, and when asked how far he would go he replied "Just watch me."

**Pacific Scandal**
The 1873 scandal in which Canada's first prime minister, John A. Macdonald, was revealed to have taken election money from railway tycoon Hugh Allan, who sought the contract to build the transcontinental railway. A stolen telegram exposed the deal, Macdonald resigned, and the Liberals took power for the first time.

**Louis Riel and the Métis rebellions**
Riel led the Métis, a people of mixed Indigenous and European descent, in the 1869–1870 Red River Rebellion, during which his provisional government executed the Ontario loyalist Thomas Scott; the Wolseley expedition was sent to restore order. He returned to lead the 1885 North-West Rebellion with Gabriel Dumont, who won at Duck Lake, and was hanged under Macdonald's government.

**Conscription Crises**
Robert Borden's introduction of conscription in 1917 during World War I bitterly divided English and French Canada, leading to the 1918 Easter riots in Quebec City; Henri Bourassa was a leading French-Canadian opponent. William Lyon Mackenzie King faced a second Conscription Crisis in 1944.

**Battle of the Plains of Abraham**
The 1759 battle outside Quebec City in which British general James Wolfe defeated the French under the Marquis de Montcalm; both commanders were killed. It led to the British conquest of New France.

**New France and the King's Daughters**
The French colony along the St. Lawrence, whose capital Quebec City was founded by Samuel de Champlain in 1608. Intendant Jean Talon helped bring about 800 young women, the King's Daughters (Filles du Roi), to boost the population; the colony also featured the seigneurial land system and fur-trading coureurs des bois.

**Quebec sovereignty and the Quiet Revolution**
Quebec underwent rapid secularization and modernization in the 1960s Quiet Revolution under Premier Jean Lesage, following the conservative "Great Darkness" of Maurice Duplessis. Separatism grew, Charles de Gaulle proclaimed "Vive le Québec libre!" at Expo 67, and independence referendums failed in 1980 and narrowly in 1995 under Prime Minister Jean Chrétien.

**William Lyon Mackenzie King**
Canada's longest-serving prime minister, who led the country through World War II and secretly sought advice from spirits, including those of his dead dogs, all named Pat. In the 1926 King–Byng affair, Governor General Julian Byng refused his request to dissolve Parliament and invited Arthur Meighen to form a government, causing a constitutional crisis.

**Juno Beach and the Dieppe Raid**
In World War II, Canadian troops, including the Queen's Own Rifles, landed at Juno Beach on D-Day in 1944; most of the ground forces in the disastrous 1942 Dieppe Raid were also Canadian. The Netherlands sent Canada tulips after the war in thanks for liberating the country and sheltering its royal family.

**If Day**
A staged mock Nazi invasion and occupation of Winnipeg in February 1942, organized to promote the sale of Victory Bonds for Canada's war effort.

**Battle of Vimy Ridge**
An April 1917 World War I battle in France in which all four divisions of the Canadian Corps fought together for the first time and captured the ridge, an event often seen as a birth of Canadian national identity.

**Halifax Explosion**
On December 6, 1917, the French munitions ship SS Mont-Blanc collided with another vessel in the harbor of Halifax, Nova Scotia, and exploded, killing about 2,000 people in one of the largest man-made explosions before the atomic bomb.

**Rebellions of 1837 and the Family Compact**
William Lyon Mackenzie led a rebellion in Upper Canada (now Ontario) against the Family Compact, a conservative elite associated with John Robinson; during it the American steamship Caroline, supplying the rebels, was set ablaze. The rebellions led to reforms that paved the way for Confederation in 1867.

**Fenian Raids and United Empire Loyalists**
United Empire Loyalists who backed Britain fled to Canada after the American Revolution, settling largely in Upper Canada. Canada was later targeted by the Fenian Raids (1866–1871), invasions by Irish-American nationalists hoping to pressure Britain over Irish independence.

**Lester Pearson and Brian Mulroney**
Lester Pearson won the 1957 Nobel Peace Prize for resolving the Suez Crisis with a UN peacekeeping force, later became prime minister, and saw his proposed flag mocked as the "Pearson Pennant." Brian Mulroney won the 1984 election after telling John Turner "You had an option, sir" over patronage appointments, and his term was marred by the failure of the Meech Lake Accord on Quebec's constitutional status.

**Quiet Revolution**
A period of rapid secularization and modernization in Quebec during the 1960s, launched when Jean Lesage's Liberal Party won the 1960 provincial election. The provincial government took over education, health care, and welfare from the Catholic Church (creating, for example, the CEGEP college system), and it built up Quebecois nationalism. It is the single most common clue for Quebec.

**October Crisis and the FLQ**
In October 1970 the Front de libération du Québec (FLQ), a militant separatist group, kidnapped British trade commissioner James Cross (taken by its Liberation Cell) and Quebec Deputy Premier and labor minister Pierre Laporte (taken by its Chenier Cell while he was playing football on his front lawn). Laporte was murdered, and members of the Chenier Cell such as Paul Rose were later convicted. The FLQ had earlier carried out bombings, including the February 1969 bombing of the Montreal Stock Exchange.

**War Measures Act and "Just watch me"**
Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau invoked the War Measures Act during the October Crisis, the only time it was used in peacetime. This suspended civil liberties and sent troops into Quebec. Asked by a reporter how far he would go, Trudeau answered "Just watch me."

**1995 referendum and "money and the ethnic vote"**
Quebec held two referendums on sovereignty, in 1980 and 1995, both pushed by the separatist Parti Québécois. The 1995 vote failed by roughly one percentage point, and Premier Jacques Parizeau blamed the loss on "money and the ethnic vote." In response, the federal government passed the Clarity Act in 2000, which set conditions for any future secession referendum.

**Meech Lake Accord**
A 1987 set of constitutional amendments negotiated by Prime Minister Brian Mulroney to win Quebec's acceptance of the Constitution Act of 1982. Quebec Premier Robert Bourassa demanded that Quebec be recognized as a "distinct society." The accord collapsed in 1990 after Elijah Harper, an Indigenous member of Manitoba's legislature, held up an eagle feather and blocked its ratification there. The later Charlottetown Accord (1992) also failed.

**Great Darkness and Maurice Duplessis**
The "Grande Noirceur," the name for the conservative, Church-allied, and often corrupt rule of Premier Maurice Duplessis and his Union Nationale party (1936–1939 and 1944–1959). It featured the anti-communist Padlock Law, and critics such as the journal Cité Libre and Frère Untel (who attacked Quebec's education system) opposed it. The Quiet Revolution began soon after Duplessis's death.

**Asbestos Strike**
A 1949 strike by miners in the town of Asbestos, Quebec, which Duplessis's government tried to crush. It is seen as a forerunner of the Quiet Revolution, and the young Pierre Trudeau gained prominence by editing a book of essays about it.

**Pierre Trudeau**
The Liberal prime minister of Canada, born in Montreal, who handled the October Crisis and opposed Quebec separatism. He is also known for claiming he had only said "fuddle duddle" when accused of mouthing a curse in Parliament. He is often given as a Quebec-born leader along with Jean Chrétien.

**René Lévesque, the Parti Québécois, and Bill 101**
René Lévesque nationalized hydroelectric companies into Hydro-Québec as a minister under Lesage, then founded the separatist Parti Québécois and became premier in 1976. His government passed Bill 101, the Charter of the French Language, which made French the province's only official language, and it held the 1980 sovereignty referendum.

**Bloc Québécois**
A federal political party founded in 1991 by Lucien Bouchard after the failure of the Meech Lake Accord. It represents Quebec sovereigntists in Canada's Parliament, and Bouchard was a leader of the "Yes" side in the 1995 referendum.

**"Vive le Québec libre!"**
"Long live free Quebec!", the line French President Charles de Gaulle shouted from a balcony in Montreal during his 1967 visit for Expo 67, the World's Fair held in Montreal. It angered the Canadian government, and Prime Minister Lester Pearson replied that Canadians "do not need to be liberated."

**Battle of the Plains of Abraham**
A 1759 battle outside Quebec City during the French and Indian War (Seven Years' War), in which the British under James Wolfe defeated the French under the Marquis de Montcalm. Both commanders were mortally wounded, and the battle led to British control of New France. The French won a later victory nearby at the Battle of Sainte-Foy in 1760, but could not retake the city.

**Quebec Act**
A 1774 British law that let Catholics in Quebec worship freely and extended the province's borders south to the Ohio River. American colonists counted it among the Intolerable Acts, and the Declaration of Independence denounced it as setting "an example and fit instrument for introducing the same absolute rule into these Colonies."

**Kitchen Accord and the Constitution Act of 1982**
During November 1981 talks to patriate Canada's constitution, federal and provincial officials struck a deal overnight in a hotel kitchen while Quebec's René Lévesque was absent. Quebec never endorsed the resulting Constitution Act of 1982, which set the stage for the Meech Lake and Charlottetown attempts.

**New France, Samuel de Champlain, and the King's Daughters**
Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec City in 1608 around a fortified post called l'Habitation on the St. Lawrence River, and it became the capital of New France. Intendant Jean Talon brought over the "King's Daughters" (Filles du roi), young women sent to boost the colony's population. The colony was also known for its seigneurial land system and for the coureurs des bois, fur traders who dealt with Native Americans.

**Fidel Castro**
The revolutionary who overthrew Fulgencio Batista in 1959 and ruled Cuba from Havana as a Communist leader for nearly five decades, surviving numerous American assassination attempts. He handed power to his brother Raúl Castro, provisionally in 2006 and formally in 2008. The most common giveaway for Cuba.

**USS Maine and the Spanish-American War**
The American battleship that exploded in Havana Harbor in February 1898, killing most of its crew. The American press blamed Spain, and the explosion helped trigger the Spanish-American War, which ended Spanish rule in Cuba.

**Theodore Roosevelt's Rough Riders and San Juan Hill**
The Rough Riders, a volunteer cavalry regiment commanded by Leonard Wood with Theodore Roosevelt as second-in-command (later its colonel), famously charged up Kettle Hill and San Juan Hill near Santiago de Cuba in July 1898. Other clues from this campaign include the Battle of Las Guásimas, the overweight commanding general William Shafter, and the "embalmed beef" scandal over spoiled army rations bought under Secretary of War Russell Alger.

**Moncada Barracks and "History Will Absolve Me"**
On July 26, 1953, Fidel Castro led a failed attack on the Moncada Barracks in Santiago de Cuba. At his trial he gave a defense speech ending with "History will absolve me," and the attack's date gave its name to his 26th of July Movement.

**Fulgencio Batista**
The army strongman who rose to power after the 1933 Sergeants' Revolt, served as elected president from 1940 to 1944, and seized power again in a 1952 coup. His corrupt, U.S.-backed dictatorship was tied to American mobsters like Meyer Lansky, and he fled Cuba when Castro's revolution triumphed on January 1, 1959. In 1946, Mafia leaders including Lucky Luciano and Lansky had held a major meeting in Havana, the Havana Conference.

**Bay of Pigs Invasion**
The failed April 1961 invasion of Cuba at Playa Girón by Brigade 2506, a force of CIA-trained Cuban exiles, under the codename Operation Zapata. Castro's forces quickly defeated it, embarrassing President Kennedy, who reportedly vowed to "splinter the CIA into a thousand pieces."

**Cuban Missile Crisis**
The October 1962 standoff after the U.S. discovered Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba. Kennedy managed it through the ExComm (Executive Committee of the National Security Council) and imposed a naval "quarantine" (blockade); Secretary of State Dean Rusk remarked "We're eyeball to eyeball, and I think the other fellow just blinked." The crisis ended when the Soviets withdrew their missiles, in exchange for a U.S. pledge not to invade Cuba and the quiet removal of American Jupiter missiles from Turkey and Italy. Soviet officer Vasili Arkhipov is credited with refusing to launch a nuclear torpedo from the submarine B-59.

**Che Guevara and the Cuban Revolution**
Ernesto "Che" Guevara, an Argentine doctor, joined Castro's 26th of July Movement in Mexico, where they trained under the Spanish Civil War veteran Alberto Bayo. In 1956 the rebels sailed to Cuba on the yacht Granma, waged guerrilla war from the Sierra Maestra mountains, defeated Batista's Operation Verano offensive, and took power in 1959.

**Valeriano "Butcher" Weyler**
The Spanish general who, from 1896, forced Cuban civilians into fortified camps (reconcentrados) to cut off support for the independence rebels; the camps are often cited as the origin of the term "concentration camp." Reports of the camps' horrific conditions inflamed American opinion against Spain.

**Teller and Platt Amendments**
The Teller Amendment (1898) promised that the U.S. would not annex Cuba after defeating Spain. The Platt Amendment (1901), which Cuba was forced to write into its constitution, replaced it and gave the U.S. the right to intervene in Cuba and to lease a naval base at Guantánamo Bay. It was invoked for the U.S. intervention of 1906 after President Tomás Estrada Palma resigned.

**Ostend Manifesto**
An 1854 document drafted by American diplomats James Buchanan, Pierre Soulé, and John Mason in Ostend, Belgium, at the direction of Secretary of State William Marcy. It argued the U.S. should buy Cuba from Spain, or seize it if Spain refused, and its publication embarrassed the Franklin Pierce administration.

**Yellow journalism and "You furnish the pictures and I'll furnish the war"**
The newspaper publishers William Randolph Hearst and Joseph Pulitzer sensationalized events in Cuba to sell papers and stir up war fever. Hearst allegedly told the illustrator Frederic Remington, who wanted to come home from Cuba, "You furnish the pictures and I'll furnish the war."

**Mariel boatlift and Cuban exiles**
In 1980, after Cubans stormed the Peruvian embassy in Havana seeking asylum, Castro allowed mass emigration from the port of Mariel, and about 125,000 Cubans reached Florida. Related clues include the "wet foot, dry foot" policy (which let Cubans who reached U.S. soil stay), the 2000 custody battle over the boy Elián González, and Miami's Little Havana.

**Ten Years' War and the independence struggle**
Cuba's first major war for independence from Spain (1868–1878), launched when the planter Carlos Manuel de Céspedes freed his slaves and issued the "Grito de Yara" (Manifesto of October 10). It was followed by the Little War and the 1895 war led by José Martí and Antonio Maceo, the "Bronze Titan." During the Ten Years' War, Spain's capture of the blockade-runner Virginius and execution of its crew created a crisis that Secretary of State Hamilton Fish resolved peacefully.

**Special Period**
The severe economic crisis of the 1990s after the collapse of the Soviet Union ended the subsidies and sugar trade Cuba depended on. Unrest during it included the 1994 "Maleconazo" protests along Havana's Malecón seawall, and later dissent includes the Ladies in White, founded after the 2003 "Black Spring" crackdown, and the protest song "Patria y Vida."

**Hungarian Revolution of 1956 and Imre Nagy**
A nationwide uprising against the Soviet-backed communist government that began in Budapest in October 1956. Student demonstrators trying to broadcast their demands at the Magyar Radio building were shot by the ÁVH secret police; protesters toppled a giant Stalin statue, leaving only its boots, and freed Cardinal Mindszenty. Reformist prime minister Imre Nagy announced Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact, but Soviet tanks crushed the revolution and Nagy was later executed.

**János Kádár and "Goulash Communism"**
Kádár was installed by the Soviets after the 1956 revolution and ruled Hungary until 1988. After harsh early repression, his "Goulash Communism" allowed limited market reforms and consumer goods, which made Hungary known as the "happiest barracks" in the Eastern Bloc.

**Lajos Kossuth and the Revolution of 1848**
Kossuth led Hungary's 1848 revolution and war of independence against the Austrian Habsburgs, which produced the April (March) Laws and the Twelve Points of reform. The young emperor Franz Joseph I called in Tsar Nicholas I of Russia, whose army helped crush the revolt; Artúr Görgei surrendered in 1849, and Kossuth went into exile and toured the United States in 1851.

**Ausgleich of 1867 and the Dual Monarchy**
The "Compromise" that turned the Austrian Empire into Austria-Hungary, a dual monarchy in which Hungary had its own government and parliament but shared a monarch (Franz Joseph I), army, and foreign policy with Austria. The Dual Monarchy dissolved at the end of World War I in 1918.

**Battle of Mohács (1526)**
A crushing defeat of the Hungarian army by Suleiman the Magnificent's Ottoman forces. Commander Pál Tomori was killed and the young King Louis II drowned while fleeing in his armor, and Hungary was afterward divided among the Ottomans, the Habsburgs, and the principality of Transylvania.

**Saint Stephen and the Árpád dynasty**
Stephen I, of the Árpád dynasty descended from the Magyar chieftain Árpád, was crowned Hungary's first king in 1000 with a crown sent by Pope Sylvester II, and he Christianized the country. His father, Grand Prince Géza, had converted earlier. Stephen's preserved right hand, the Holy Dexter, is a relic, and the Holy Crown named for him has a distinctive bent cross.

**Matthias Corvinus and the Black Army**
The Renaissance king of Hungary (reigned 1458–1490) and son of the general John Hunyadi, who had fought the Ottomans and escaped the disastrous Crusade of Varna in 1444. Matthias built the Black Army, one of Europe's first standing mercenary armies, captured Vienna, and collected the Bibliotheca Corviniana, one of Europe's largest libraries; his name comes from the raven on his coat of arms.

**Miklós Horthy and Operation Panzerfaust**
Admiral Horthy was Hungary's regent from 1920 to 1944 and allied it with Nazi Germany in World War II. When he tried to make a separate peace in 1944, German commando Otto Skorzeny kidnapped Horthy's son (reportedly rolled up in a carpet) in Operation Panzerfaust, forcing Horthy to hand power to Ferenc Szálasi of the fascist Arrow Cross Party, which persecuted and murdered Budapest's Jews.

**Raoul Wallenberg**
A Swedish diplomat in Budapest in 1944–1945 who, working with Swiss diplomat Carl Lutz and others, issued protective passports and set up safe houses that saved thousands of Hungarian Jews. He was arrested by the Soviets during the siege of Budapest and disappeared in Soviet custody.

**"Blood in the Water" match**
A violent water polo semifinal at the 1956 Melbourne Olympics, played weeks after the Soviet invasion, in which Hungary beat the Soviet Union 4–0. It became famous after Hungarian player Ervin Zádor left the pool bleeding from a punch.

**Treaty of Trianon (1920)**
The post-World War I peace treaty between the Allies and Hungary that took away about two-thirds of the old Kingdom of Hungary's territory, leaving millions of ethnic Hungarians in neighboring states. Resentment over Trianon shaped interwar Hungarian politics.

**Mátyás Rákosi and "salami tactics"**
The Stalinist leader who took over Hungary after World War II, coining "salami tactics" for eliminating rival parties such as the Smallholders slice by slice. His regime relied on the ÁVH secret police and imprisoned Cardinal József Mindszenty.

**Martyrs of Arad**
Thirteen Hungarian rebel generals executed at Arad in October 1849 after the failed revolution, on the orders of the Austrian general Julius Haynau, called the "Hangman of Arad." According to legend, Austrians clinked beer glasses to celebrate, so Hungarians vowed not to clink beer mugs for 150 years.

**Béla Kun and the Red and White Terrors**
After the 1918 Aster Revolution ended Habsburg rule, Béla Kun set up the short-lived Hungarian Soviet Republic in 1919, whose violence was called the Red Terror. It was overthrown, and forces associated with Miklós Horthy carried out a retaliatory White Terror.

**Battle of Lechfeld (955)**
The battle in which the German king Otto I (later Otto the Great) decisively defeated the Magyar raiders near Augsburg. It ended decades of Magyar raids into Western Europe and pushed the Magyars to settle and Christianize.

**Mansa Musa's hajj**
Mansa Musa I, Mali's most famous ruler, made a pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 with a huge caravan of attendants and camels carrying gold. He gave away and spent so much gold, especially in Cairo, that its value fell in Egypt for years. Legend says he built a mosque every Friday along the way, and this hajj is the giveaway in almost every Mali question.

**Sundiata Keita**
The Mandinka founder of the Mali Empire in the 13th century. According to oral tradition he was the son of the hunchbacked Sogolon and was born unable to walk, but he overcame this, returned from exile, and united the Mandinka against the Sosso. He set his capital at Niani, and the empire grew out of the small Mandinka state of Kangaba.

**Battle of Kirina and Sumanguru**
The battle (c. 1235) in which Sundiata defeated Sumanguru (Soumaoro) Kanté, the sorcerer-king of the Sosso. Legend says Sundiata destroyed Sumanguru's magic by hitting him with an arrow tipped with the spur of a white rooster. The victory founded the empire.

**Sankore University and Timbuktu**
Timbuktu, a trading city on the Niger River, became Mali's great center of Islamic learning. Its Sankore mosque, built of mud brick, grew into the madrasa known as the University of Sankore, traditionally credited to Mansa Musa. The later scholar Ahmad Baba was associated with it.

**Gbara (Great Assembly)**
Mali's deliberative assembly, which checked the power of the mansa (emperor). It included representatives of the leading clans and groups, among them the military "Carriers of Quivers" and the Dyula merchants.

**Kouroukan Fouga**
The founding charter or "constitution" of the Mali Empire, traditionally proclaimed by Sundiata after the Battle of Kirina at Kangaba. It contained forty-four edicts, organized society into clans and castes, and set up the Gbara.

**"Carriers of Quivers"**
The sixteen noble clans responsible for Mali's military forces, said to descend from Sundiata's companions. They were drawn from the free horon class and formed a voting bloc in the Gbara.

**Griots and the Epic of Sundiata**
Griots are hereditary Mandinka storytellers, musicians, and keepers of oral history. They preserved the Epic of Sundiata, the oral epic that tells of Sundiata's childhood, exile, and victory over Sumanguru.

**Al-Sahili and the Djinguereber Mosque**
Abu Ishaq al-Sahili was an Andalusian poet and architect who returned with Mansa Musa from his hajj. He is credited with designing the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu and a royal audience chamber that the historian Ibn Khaldun praised as an "admirable monument." Islamist militants damaged Timbuktu's shrines in 2012.

**Twelve Doors**
The name for the core possessions and allied territories that made up the Mali Empire, including lands such as Siby and the Kaniaga region taken from the Sosso.

**Mansa (title)**
The title of Mali's emperors, roughly meaning "king of kings." Holders included the founder Sundiata, Mansa Musa, and Sakura, a former slave who seized the throne in the late 13th century.

**Atlantic expeditions of Abu Bakr II**
The Arab writer al-Umari records Mansa Musa's account that his predecessor sent a fleet of ships to explore the Atlantic, none of which returned except one whose captain reported a river with a powerful current. The ruler then set out with an even larger fleet and never came back, and Musa took the throne.

**Catalan Atlas**
A 1375 map from Majorca that shows Mansa Musa enthroned in West Africa, wearing a crown and holding a gold nugget and a scepter. It reflects how famous Mali's wealth had become in Europe.

**Ibn Battuta and Taghaza**
The Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta visited Mali in 1352–1353 under Mansa Suleyman and described its court and its salt-mining town of Taghaza, a key source of the salt traded for gold across the Sahara.

**Decline and the Songhai Empire**
Mali weakened in the 15th century as Gao rebelled, Tuareg raiders took Timbuktu, and Bamana and other groups attacked. The Songhai Empire, centered at Gao, replaced it as the dominant power of West Africa.

**Treaty of Waitangi**
The 1840 treaty signed by British representative William Hobson and more than 500 Maori chiefs (rangatira), which made New Zealand a British colony with Hobson as its first governor. Its English and Maori versions differ, most notably in how the word "sovereignty" was translated, and the dispute over its terms fueled later conflicts and land claims.

**Musket Wars**
A series of early 19th-century wars among Maori tribes (iwi), made far deadlier by European firearms. The Ngapuhi chief Hongi Hika acquired muskets and launched raids as far as Lake Rotorua and the Bay of Plenty. Maori adapted their hillforts into "gunfighter" pa to cope with the new weapons.

**Flagstaff War and Hone Heke**
An 1845–1846 conflict begun when the Ngapuhi chief Hone Heke, Hongi Hika's nephew, repeatedly cut down the British flagstaff at Kororareka (Russell). The flagstaff had been a gift from Heke to British Resident James Busby, who helped draft the Treaty of Waitangi. The war featured sieges of fortified pa.

**Maori**
The Polynesian indigenous people of New Zealand, who call the country Aotearoa. Their ancestors arrived by canoe, according to legend led by Kupe the Navigator, bringing the kumara (sweet potato). They built hillforts called pa, perform the haka war dance (made famous by the All Blacks rugby team), and call white settlers "Pakeha."

**First women's suffrage (1893)**
In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country in the world to give all women the right to vote in national elections.

**Rogernomics and Ruthanasia**
Rogernomics was the free-market program of deregulation and restructuring pushed by Finance Minister Roger Douglas in David Lange's Fourth Labour Government from 1984. Its harsher continuation under National Party finance minister Ruth Richardson in the early 1990s was nicknamed "Ruthanasia."

**Robert Muldoon and the "Schnapps Election"**
Muldoon was a National Party prime minister (1975–1984) who promoted large state-funded industrial projects under the "Think Big" strategy. After losing a vote over nuclear policy, he called the snap 1984 election on live television while visibly drunk, and he lost it to David Lange.

**Sinking of the Rainbow Warrior**
In 1985 agents of the French intelligence service DGSE bombed the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland harbor, in an attack code-named Operation Satanic, to stop its protests against French nuclear testing in Polynesia. Photographer Fernando Pereira was killed. The attack strengthened New Zealand's anti-nuclear stance under David Lange.

**1981 Springbok Tour**
Muldoon allowed South Africa's apartheid-era national rugby team, the Springboks, to tour New Zealand, which critics said broke the Gleneagles Agreement against sporting contact with South Africa. Massive protests followed, including clashes on Molesworth Street and a light plane dropping flour bombs on the field during a match.

**New Zealand Wars (Maori Wars or Land Wars)**
A series of 19th-century wars between British colonial forces and Maori over land and sovereignty. They include the Hutt Valley campaign under Governor George Grey, the Waikato War against the Maori King Movement, the Battle of Gate Pa, where Maori defeated General Duncan Cameron, and later guerrilla campaigns led by Te Kooti and Titokowaru.

**Boyd Massacre**
In 1809, after Te Ara, the son of a Maori chief, was flogged aboard the ship Boyd, Maori at Whangaroa Harbour killed and ate most of the crew and passengers. The event discouraged European contact with Maori for years afterward.

**Abel Tasman**
The Dutch explorer who in 1642 became the first European to see New Zealand and encounter the Maori. James Cook later mapped the islands, and Cook Strait between the North and South Islands is named for him.

**ANZAC and Gallipoli**
The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps was formed in World War I and suffered heavy casualties in the 1915 Gallipoli campaign against the Ottoman Empire.

**New Zealand Company and Edward Gibbon Wakefield**
A colonization company founded on the plans of Edward Gibbon Wakefield, who had earlier promoted settlement in South Australia. It sent the ship Tory to New Zealand in 1839 to buy land, and its settlers founded Wellington. A land dispute involving its settlers led to the 1843 Wairau Affray with Te Rauparaha's Ngati Toa.

**Moriori massacre in the Chatham Islands**
In 1835 Maori groups displaced during the Musket Wars invaded the Chatham Islands and killed or enslaved many of the peaceful Moriori people living there.

**Nika Riots**
A massive 532 CE uprising in Constantinople that began in the Hippodrome, where rioters chanted "Nika!" ("Conquer!"). It destroyed much of the city, including the original Hagia Sophia, and was crushed when Justinian's generals trapped and massacred tens of thousands of rioters in the Hippodrome.

**Blues and Greens**
The two rival chariot-racing factions (demes) of Constantinople, also called the Veneti and Prasini. They usually feuded with each other, but they united against Justinian in the Nika Riots after he refused to pardon two condemned murderers, one from each faction. Justinian had generally favored the Blues.

**Belisarius**
Justinian's most famous general. He helped crush the Nika Riots, beat the Sassanid Persians at Dara, conquered the Vandal kingdom in North Africa at Ad Decimum and Tricamarum, and fought the Ostrogoths in Italy, taking Naples (by entering through a disused aqueduct), Rome, and Ravenna.

**Theodora**
Justinian's wife and empress, a former actress and reputed courtesan. During the Nika Riots she persuaded him not to flee by declaring that "royalty (purple) is a good burial shroud," and she is credited with influencing laws that protected women and actresses.

**Hagia Sophia**
The great domed church in Constantinople that Justinian rebuilt after the original burned in the Nika Riots, completed in 537. On seeing it he supposedly said "Solomon, I have outdone thee," and the poet Paul the Silentiary wrote a poem describing it.

**Procopius's Secret History**
A scathing, long-hidden history by Procopius, the court historian who traveled with Belisarius and also wrote the official History of the Wars. It describes Justinian as a demon whose head could vanish and reappear, accuses him of killing "a myriad myriads of myriads" (a trillion) people, and attacks Theodora's past.

**Corpus Juris Civilis**
Justinian's codification of Roman law, also called the Justinian Code. It has four parts: the Codex (imperial laws), the Digest (or Pandects, jurists' opinions), the Institutes (a textbook), and the Novels ("new constitutions," later laws). It was preceded by the "Fifty Decisions," which settled conflicting legal opinions, and its rediscovery in medieval Italy helped found the University of Bologna's legal studies.

**Tribonian**
The jurist and quaestor who led the commissions that compiled the Corpus Juris Civilis. Justinian removed him from office during the Nika Riots to calm the crowds, but he later returned to his post.

**Hypatius**
A nephew of the former emperor Anastasius whom the rioters crowned emperor in the Hippodrome during the Nika Riots. After the revolt was crushed, Justinian had him executed.

**Eternal Peace with Khosrau I**
The "Perpetual" or "Eternal Peace" of 532, which ended the Iberian War with the Sassanid Persians. Justinian paid Khosrau I 11,000 pounds of gold, which freed him to reconquer the West, but the peace broke down about eight years later, leading to further wars such as the Lazic War in Georgia.

**Gelimer and the Vandalic War**
Gelimer was the last king of the Vandals in North Africa. Belisarius beat him at Ad Decimum and Tricamarum in 533, bringing the Vandal kingdom around Carthage back under Roman rule.

**Gothic War (Vitiges and Totila)**
Justinian's long war to retake Italy from the Ostrogoths. Belisarius fought and captured King Vitiges, and the eunuch general Narses later defeated and killed King Totila at the Battle of Taginae in 552.

**John the Cappadocian**
Justinian's praetorian prefect and unpopular finance and tax official, whose harsh taxes helped spark the Nika Riots. He also took part in the legal commissions, and Peter Barsymes was another of Justinian's finance officials.

**Narses and Mundus**
Two more of Justinian's generals. Mundus helped Belisarius massacre the rioters in the Hippodrome, and the eunuch Narses helped end the Nika Riots by bribing the Blues and later won the conquest of Italy.

**Three Chapters Controversy**
Justinian's condemnation of writings by Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret, and Ibas of Edessa, meant to win back Monophysites. When Pope Vigilius resisted, Justinian had him seized and brought to Constantinople.

**Plague of Justinian**
An outbreak of bubonic plague, first recorded at Pelusium in Egypt in 541. It killed huge numbers across the empire, including in Constantinople, and Procopius described it.

**San Vitale mosaic**
A famous mosaic in the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna, Italy, showing Justinian with a halo, crown, and purple robe among his officials. A matching mosaic of Theodora and her attendants faces it.

**Tulip mania**
A speculative craze in the Dutch Republic during the 1630s, when the price of tulip bulbs soared and then collapsed suddenly in 1637. It is often called the first recorded economic bubble, and Charles Mackay famously described it as a "national delusion" in his 1841 book Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds.

**Dutch East India Company (VOC)**
The Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie, chartered in 1602 and often called the first publicly traded company and the richest company in history. It was run by a board called the Heeren XVII ("Lords Seventeen") and based in Amsterdam, and it was rivaled by the English East India Company in the Asian spice trade. Under Jan Pieterszoon Coen it conquered the Banda Islands to monopolize nutmeg, and in the 1623 Amboyna Massacre its agents tortured (including by waterboarding) and executed English traders. It also funded Abel Tasman's voyages.

**Dejima and rangaku**
Dejima was a small, fan-shaped artificial island in Nagasaki Bay where Dutch traders were confined during Japan's Tokugawa (Edo) period. During the sakoku isolation policy, the Dutch were the only Europeans allowed to trade with Japan. "Rangaku," or "Dutch learning," was the Western science and technology Japanese scholars learned through Dutch books brought in this way.

**Batavia and the Dutch East Indies**
Batavia, founded by the VOC in 1619 on the site of Jayakarta, was the capital of the Dutch East Indies and was renamed Jakarta. The Dutch ruled what is now Indonesia for centuries, and they expanded control through the Padri and Aceh Wars in Sumatra. After Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta declared Indonesian independence in 1945, the Dutch fought back with "police actions" such as Operation Product, imposed the Van Mook Line and the Renville Agreement, and captured the Republican capital of Yogyakarta. U.S. threats to cut Marshall Plan aid helped force the Dutch to recognize Indonesia in 1949.

**Max Havelaar and the Cultivation System**
Max Havelaar (1860) is a novel by Eduard Douwes Dekker, a former colonial official in the Indies who wrote under the pen name Multatuli ("I have suffered much"). It exposed abuses of the Cultivation System, which forced Javanese farmers to grow export crops such as coffee for the Dutch government. Criticism of the system led to the more paternalistic "Ethical Policy," adopted in 1901.

**Eighty Years' War and the Sea Beggars**
The Dutch revolt against Spanish Habsburg rule (1568–1648). The Duke of Alba's harsh "Council of Blood" (Council of Troubles) inflamed the revolt, the Sea Beggars (Watergeuzen) were Dutch rebel privateers who fought the Spanish at sea, and Spain besieged and captured the city of Breda. The northern provinces declared independence from Philip II in the 1581 Act of Abjuration, and Spain formally recognized the Dutch Republic in the Peace of Münster in 1648.

**Rampjaar (Disaster Year)**
1672, the year France, England, and two German bishoprics all attacked the Dutch Republic. The Dutch held off the French by flooding land along the Dutch Water Line. Grand Pensionary Johan de Witt and his brother Cornelis were lynched by an Orangist mob in The Hague, which reportedly mutilated and ate parts of their bodies, and William III was made stadtholder.

**William III and the Glorious Revolution**
The Dutch stadtholder William III of Orange was invited by the "Immortal Seven" English nobles to take the throne from his father-in-law James II. He landed at Brixham in 1688, accepted the English Bill of Rights, ruled jointly with Mary II, and defeated James at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690. He thus ruled both England and the Netherlands.

**Anglo-Dutch Wars and the Raid on the Medway**
A series of four naval wars between England and the Netherlands in the 17th and 18th centuries over trade and maritime dominance. In the 1667 Raid on the Medway, during the Second Anglo-Dutch War, the Dutch fleet sailed up the Thames and Medway, burned English ships, and towed away the flagship Royal Charles. The Treaty of Breda that ended that war let England keep New Amsterdam while the Dutch kept Suriname and the spice island of Run.

**New Amsterdam and Peter Stuyvesant**
The Dutch colony of New Netherland was centered on New Amsterdam on Manhattan, which became New York City after the English seized it in 1664. Peter Stuyvesant was its last director-general, and the colony granted large estates to landlords called patroons. Other Dutch colonies included Suriname and the Guiana settlements of Essequibo and Demerara, whose capital Stabroek became Georgetown under the British.

**Stadtholders and the House of Orange**
