Stadtholders were the leading executives of the provinces of the Dutch Republic, and the office was usually held by princes of the House of Orange-Nassau. William the Silent, who led the revolt against Spain, was assassinated in 1584 by Balthasar Gérard, the first head of state killed with a handgun. Descendants of the House of Orange have ruled the Kingdom of the Netherlands as monarchs since 1815.

**Dutch disease**
An economic term, coined in 1977, for the decline of a country's manufacturing sector after a natural resource boom strengthens its currency. It is named for the Netherlands after its large natural gas discovery near Groningen in 1959. A separate period of 18th-century Dutch economic stagnation is called the "Periwig Era."

**Polders and windmills**
Polders are low-lying tracts of land reclaimed from the sea or lakes and protected by dikes. The Dutch drained them with windmills, which became national icons.

**Hugo Grotius and Mare Liberum**
The Dutch jurist Hugo Grotius wrote Mare Liberum ("The Free Sea," 1609), arguing that the oceans were open to all nations. This opposed the Portuguese "Mare Clausum" (closed sea) claim to exclusive trade routes and supported Dutch commerce in the East Indies.

**Modern Dutch politics: Theo van Gogh, Pim Fortuyn, and Geert Wilders**
Filmmaker Theo van Gogh was murdered in 2004 by Mohammed Bouyeri after making the film Submission with Somali-born critic of Islam Ayaan Hirsi Ali. Right-wing politician Pim Fortuyn was assassinated in 2002, and Geert Wilders leads the anti-immigration Party for Freedom (PVV). The Netherlands was also the first country to legalize same-sex marriage and among the first to legalize euthanasia.

**Ayatollah Khomeini and the 1979 Islamic Revolution**
Ruhollah Khomeini, an exiled Shia cleric, returned in 1979 after mass protests toppled the Shah and became the first Supreme Leader of the new Islamic Republic. He famously called the United States the "Great Satan."

**Mohammad Reza Pahlavi (the Shah)**
The last Shah of Iran, ruling from 1941 until he fled the country in 1979. His admission to the U.S. for cancer treatment in October 1979 triggered the seizure of the American embassy.

**Iran hostage crisis (444 days)**
In November 1979, Islamist students stormed the U.S. embassy in Tehran and took 66 Americans hostage; 52 of them were held for 444 days until January 1981. The crisis helped Jimmy Carter lose the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan.

**Operation Ajax and Mohammad Mosaddegh**
Mosaddegh, the elected prime minister, nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company in 1951, sparking the Abadan Crisis with Britain. A 1953 coup run by the CIA (organized by Kermit Roosevelt Jr.) and British intelligence overthrew him and strengthened the Shah's rule.

**White Revolution**
A program of reforms launched by the Shah in 1963, including land reform, women's suffrage, and a Literacy Corps in which conscripts did their military service by teaching villagers to read. Clerical opposition to it led to the June 1963 uprising (the 15 Khordad movement) led by Khomeini, who compared the Shah to the Umayyad caliph Yazid I.

**SAVAK**
The Shah's feared secret police, founded in 1957 with American and Israeli help, which persecuted opponents such as the communist Tudeh Party. Protesters blamed SAVAK for the 1978 Cinema Rex fire in Abadan, which killed hundreds.

**Operation Eagle Claw**
The failed U.S. military mission of April 1980 to rescue the embassy hostages. It was aborted in the desert, and eight American servicemen died when a helicopter collided with a transport plane.

**Iran–Iraq War (1980–1988)**
Saddam Hussein's Iraq invaded Iran in 1980, partly to contain the Shia revolution. The eight-year war featured Iraqi poison gas attacks and ended in a stalemate that restored the borders set by the 1975 Algiers Agreement.

**Qajar and Pahlavi dynasties**
The Qajar dynasty ruled Persia from 1789 until 1925. Reza Khan, a commander of the Persian Cossack Brigade, seized power and crowned himself Reza Shah Pahlavi, founding the Pahlavi dynasty.

**2,500-year celebration at Persepolis**
In 1971 the Shah held a lavish party at a tent city near Persepolis to mark 2,500 years of the Persian monarchy since Cyrus the Great. Its extravagance became a symbol of the regime's distance from ordinary Iranians.

**Stuxnet and the nuclear deal**
Stuxnet was a computer worm, widely attributed to the U.S. and Israel, that destroyed roughly 1,000 uranium-enrichment centrifuges around 2010. The 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) limited Iran's nuclear program in exchange for lifting sanctions, helping President Hassan Rouhani win re-election in 2017.

**2009 election and the Green Movement**
Mahmoud Ahmadinejad's disputed re-election over reformist Mir-Hossein Mousavi triggered mass protests in Tehran known as the Green Movement (sometimes called the Green Revolution). The government, backed by Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, suppressed them.

**Ali Khamenei**
Khomeini's successor as Supreme Leader since 1989. His right arm was paralyzed by a 1981 bomb attack while he was a cleric and politician.

**"Canadian Caper"**
The rescue of six American diplomats who escaped the embassy seizure and hid with Canadian ambassador Ken Taylor. CIA officer Tony Mendez smuggled them out in 1980 posing as a film crew, a story later dramatized in the movie Argo.

**Iran Air Flight 655**
A civilian airliner shot down in 1988 by the U.S. Navy cruiser USS Vincennes over the Persian Gulf, killing all 290 people aboard. The ship was inside Iranian territorial waters at the time.

**Duel with Aaron Burr**
On July 11, 1804, sitting Vice President Aaron Burr fatally shot Hamilton in a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey. They fought there because New York had outlawed dueling, near the spot where Hamilton's son Philip had been killed in a duel in 1801. Hamilton's own shot struck a tree above Burr, and seconds such as Burr's William P. Van Ness later gave conflicting accounts of what happened.

**First Secretary of the Treasury**
Hamilton served as the first US Treasury Secretary under George Washington (1789–1795). In that role he also founded the US Mint and the Revenue Cutter Service, the forerunner of the Coast Guard. He appears on the ten-dollar bill and is the subject of Lin-Manuel Miranda's musical Hamilton.

**The Federalist Papers and "Publius"**
A series of 85 essays (1787–1788) urging New York to ratify the Constitution, written under the shared pseudonym "Publius" by Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay. Hamilton wrote 51 of them, the most of the three authors.

**Report on Public Credit and assumption of state debts**
Hamilton's 1790 First Report on Public Credit proposed that the federal government take on ("assume") the states' Revolutionary War debts and repay federal securities at full face value ("funding at par"), backed by a sinking fund. He later issued further reports on public credit.

**First Bank of the United States**
A national bank created in 1791 at Hamilton's urging. Jefferson argued it was unconstitutional, while Hamilton defended it on the basis of the Constitution's implied powers, and it was a founding issue in the split between Federalists and Democratic-Republicans.

**Report on Manufactures**
Hamilton's 1791 report urging the government to encourage American industry through protective tariffs and "pecuniary bounties" (subsidies). It became a foundation of the "American School" of economics. He also inspired the Society for Establishing Useful Manufactures, which developed Paterson, New Jersey, as an industrial center.

**Maria Reynolds affair**
Hamilton had an affair with Maria Reynolds, whose husband James Reynolds then blackmailed him. When the payments surfaced and an investigation involving James Monroe seemed to suggest financial corruption, Hamilton published a pamphlet in 1797 admitting the affair. The scandal damaged his reputation and nearly led to a duel with Monroe.

**Federalist No. 78 ("neither FORCE nor WILL")**
Hamilton's essay "The Judiciary Department," which calls the courts the "least dangerous," or weakest, of the three branches, citing Montesquieu. He argued the judiciary has "neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment," and the essay also defends judicial review.

**Federalist No. 70 ("Energy in the Executive")**
Hamilton's essay arguing for a single executive rather than a council, because a unitary executive provides "decision, activity, secrecy, and dispatch." It cites the instability caused by ancient Rome's two consuls.

**Whiskey tax and the Whiskey Rebellion**
To raise revenue to pay the assumed debts, Hamilton proposed an excise tax on whiskey. Western Pennsylvania farmers revolted against it in the 1794 Whiskey Rebellion, which Washington and Hamilton suppressed with militia.

**Compromise of 1790**
At a dinner with Thomas Jefferson and James Madison, Hamilton won Southern support for assuming state debts in exchange for placing the national capital on the Potomac River, the future Washington, D.C.

**Election of 1800 and Jefferson as the "lesser evil"**
When Jefferson and Burr tied in the Electoral College, Hamilton urged Federalists in the House to support Jefferson, whom he considered less dangerous than Burr. That year he also damaged his own party by publishing a letter attacking John Adams. His continuing opposition to Burr, including in the 1804 New York governor's race that Burr lost to Morgan Lewis, led to the duel.

**Early life and pre-war writings**
Hamilton was born in the British West Indies on Nevis and grew up on St. Croix, where his vivid letter describing a hurricane in Christiansted led locals to pay for his education in New York. As a student at King's College, he defended the Patriot cause against the Loyalist bishop Samuel Seabury in "A Full Vindication" and "The Farmer Refuted," and he once helped the Loyalist college president Myles Cooper escape an angry mob.

**Revolutionary War service and Yorktown**
Hamilton commanded a New York artillery company and then served for years as aide-de-camp to George Washington. At the 1781 Siege of Yorktown he led the night assault that captured Redoubt No. 10.

**Annapolis Convention and the Constitutional Convention**
At the 1786 Annapolis Convention, which he attended for New York with Egbert Benson, Hamilton drafted the report calling for a convention to revise the Articles of Confederation. When his fellow New York delegates Robert Yates and John Lansing left the 1787 Constitutional Convention, he became the only New Yorker to sign the Constitution.

**Pacificus and Camillus essays**
Hamilton wrote as "Pacificus" in 1793 to defend Washington's Neutrality Proclamation in a pamphlet debate with Madison ("Helvidius"). He wrote as "Camillus" to defend the unpopular Jay Treaty with Britain, and he also helped draft Washington's Farewell Address.

**Ides of March assassination**
Caesar was stabbed to death in a meeting of the Senate on March 15, 44 BC, by a conspiracy led by Marcus Junius Brutus and Gaius Cassius Longinus. Tillius Cimber distracted him by pleading for his exiled brother, and Servilius Casca struck the first blow. His wife Calpurnia reportedly dreamed of his death the night before and begged him not to go. Tradition (popularized by Shakespeare) says he spoke "Et tu, Brute?" to Brutus, whom gossip claimed might be his own son. The assassins were defeated by the Second Triumvirate at Philippi in 42 BC, in the Liberators' Civil War.

**Crossing the Rubicon and "alea iacta est"**
In January 49 BC Caesar led his army across the Rubicon, the river marking the border of his province, into Italy. This was an act of treason that started a civil war against Pompey and the Senate's Optimates. He reportedly said "alea iacta est" ("the die is cast"), and his senior legate Titus Labienus defected to Pompey's side.

**Battle of Pharsalus and the death of Pompey**
Caesar's decisive 48 BC victory in Greece over Pompey the Great, which came after Caesar had been forced to retreat at the Battle of Dyrrhachium. Pompey fled to Egypt, where courtiers of the boy-king Ptolemy XIII murdered him. When Pompey's severed head was presented to Caesar, he reportedly wept in disgust and had his rival's remains properly buried.

**First Triumvirate and the Luca Conference**
An informal political alliance formed around 60 BC between Caesar, Pompey, and Marcus Licinius Crassus. At the Luca (Lucca) Conference in 56 BC the three renewed the pact: Pompey and Crassus would run for consul, and in return Caesar's governorship in Gaul was extended by five years. The alliance broke down after Crassus died at Carrhae and Caesar's daughter Julia died.

**Commentaries on the Gallic War (De Bello Gallico)**
Caesar's third-person account of his conquest of Gaul (58–50 BC), which famously opens "All Gaul is divided into three parts." It describes the Gauls, Germans, and Druids, including human sacrifices in which victims were burned inside giant wicker figures. He also wrote the Commentaries on the Civil War, whose third book ends with events in Egypt, as well as lost works such as the Anticato (an attack on Cato the Younger) and the grammatical treatise De Analogia.

**Battle of Alesia and Vercingetorix**
The 52 BC siege that effectively completed Caesar's conquest of Gaul. Caesar trapped the Arverni chieftain Vercingetorix in the hilltop town of Alesia, building one ring of fortifications facing inward to besiege the town and another facing outward to hold off a huge Gallic relief army. Vercingetorix surrendered and was later paraded in Caesar's triumph and executed.

**Capture by pirates**
As a young man Caesar was kidnapped by Cilician pirates. Insulted that they asked a ransom of only 20 talents, he insisted it be raised to 50 and promised them he would crucify them. After the ransom was paid, he raised a fleet, captured them, and had them crucified.

**Cleopatra and the Alexandrian War**
After following Pompey to Egypt, Caesar sided with Cleopatra VII in her dynastic struggle with her brother Ptolemy XIII. He held out in the Siege of Alexandria and defeated Ptolemy at the Battle of the Nile in 47 BC. Cleopatra bore him a son, Caesarion. Displaying Cleopatra's captured sister Arsinoe IV in his triumph backfired, as Roman crowds sympathized with her.

**Pompeia and the Bona Dea scandal**
In 62 BC, while Caesar was Pontifex Maximus, the politician Publius Clodius Pulcher disguised himself as a woman to sneak into the women-only Bona Dea festival held at Caesar's house, allegedly to meet Caesar's wife Pompeia. Caesar divorced her, reportedly saying that "Caesar's wife must be above suspicion."

**Cornelia and Sulla's proscriptions**
Caesar's wife Cornelia was the daughter of Cinna, an enemy of the dictator Sulla, and Caesar had earlier been betrothed to the wealthy Cossutia. When Sulla ordered Caesar to divorce Cornelia he refused and had to go into hiding, until relatives and allies including Mamercus Aemilius Lepidus and Aurelius Cotta won him a pardon. He later gave funeral orations for Cornelia and for his aunt Julia (widow of Marius), claiming that the Julian family was descended from the goddess Venus.

**"Queen of Bithynia"**
A mocking nickname that came from Caesar's long stay at the court of King Nicomedes IV of Bithynia during his youth, which led to persistent rumors of a sexual relationship between them.

**Dictatorship and reforms**
After the civil war Caesar held the office of dictator repeatedly, finally being named "dictator perpetuo" (dictator in perpetuity) in 44 BC. He took the titles "Father of the Fatherland" and Prefect of Morals and enlarged the Senate to about 900 members. He also introduced the Julian calendar.

**Julia, daughter of Caesar**
Caesar's only legitimate child. She married Pompey to cement the First Triumvirate, and her death in childbirth in 54 BC weakened the bond between the two men. Caesar's great-nephew and adopted son Octavian (later Augustus) went on to form the Second Triumvirate.

**Invasions of Britain**
Caesar led expeditions across the English Channel to Britain in 55 and 54 BC. In the second he defeated the British leader Cassivellaunus and imposed tribute, but he never permanently conquered the island.

**"Veni, vidi, vici"**
"I came, I saw, I conquered," Caesar's message to the Senate after his swift victory over Pharnaces II of Pontus at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC.

**Hiroshima and Nagasaki atomic bombings**
Truman, who became president when Franklin D. Roosevelt died in April 1945, authorized dropping atomic bombs on these two Japanese cities in August 1945. Japan surrendered days later, ending World War II; this is the most common giveaway for him.

**"Dewey Defeats Truman" (Chicago Tribune headline)**
In the 1948 election, the Chicago Daily Tribune printed this headline before the results were in, expecting Republican Thomas Dewey to win. A famous photograph shows a grinning Truman holding up the mistaken paper after his upset victory.

**Taft-Hartley Act and the "Do-Nothing Congress"**
A 1947 law sponsored by Robert Taft and Fred Hartley that restricted the power of labor unions after a wave of postwar strikes. Congress overrode Truman's veto, and he campaigned in 1948 against the Republican-controlled "Do-Nothing Congress."

**Firing of Douglas MacArthur**
During the Korean War, Truman relieved General MacArthur of command in 1951 for publicly contradicting presidential policy, such as by pushing to bomb mainland China and use Nationalist Chinese troops from Taiwan. MacArthur was replaced by Matthew Ridgway and gave a farewell speech to Congress ending "old soldiers never die; they just fade away."

**Tom Pendergast machine**
The Kansas City Democratic political machine run by boss Tom Pendergast (the "Goat" faction) launched Truman's career by backing him for county judge in Jackson County, Missouri. Pendergast's support also helped Truman reach the U.S. Senate in 1934.

**Blair House assassination attempt**
In 1950, while the White House was being renovated and Truman lived at Blair House, Puerto Rican nationalists Oscar Collazo and Griselio Torresola tried to kill him. Torresola was killed by White House police officer Leslie Coffelt, who was mortally wounded; the attack followed the Nationalist uprising in Puerto Rico that included the Jayuya Uprising.

**Truman Doctrine**
Truman's 1947 policy of supporting free peoples resisting communist subversion, beginning with aid to Greece and Turkey. It put into practice George Kennan's strategy of containment and is a cornerstone of early Cold War foreign policy.

**Executive Order 9981**
Truman's 1948 order that desegregated the U.S. armed forces. He also created the President's Committee on Civil Rights, whose report "To Secure These Rights" called for measures such as federal anti-lynching law.

**Fair Deal**
Truman's domestic program, extending FDR's New Deal, which proposed national health insurance, civil rights legislation, and expanded social programs. Its successes included the Housing Act of 1949, which funded slum clearance and roughly 800,000 public housing units.

**1948 election and the Dixiecrats**
Truman won a surprise victory over Thomas Dewey despite a split in his party: Southern delegates led by Strom Thurmond walked out of the Democratic convention to form the States' Rights ("Dixiecrat") Party, while Henry Wallace ran on the Progressive ticket. Truman used a cross-country whistle-stop train tour, giving hundreds of speeches from a rail car, and called a special "Turnip Day" session of Congress.

**"The buck stops here"**
The motto on a sign that sat on Truman's Oval Office desk, expressing that the president bears final responsibility for decisions. The reverse side read "I'm from Missouri."

**Truman Committee**
As a senator during World War II, Truman chaired a special committee that investigated waste, fraud, and profiteering in defense production, reportedly saving billions of dollars. The work made him nationally prominent and led to his selection as FDR's running mate in 1944.

**Marshall Plan and Point Four Program**
Under Truman, Secretary of State George Marshall's European Recovery Program poured aid into rebuilding Western Europe to resist communism. The Point Four Program, announced in his 1949 inaugural address, offered technical assistance to developing countries.

**Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer**
The 1952 Supreme Court case that struck down Truman's seizure of the nation's steel mills, which he ordered to avert a strike during the Korean War. The Court held that he lacked the constitutional or statutory authority for the seizure.

**Potsdam Conference, Berlin Airlift, and NSC-68**
Truman met Stalin and Churchill (later Attlee) at Potsdam in 1945 to settle postwar Germany, including reparations. He responded to the Soviet blockade of Berlin with the 1948–49 airlift, and his administration's policy paper NSC-68 called for a major military buildup against the Soviet Union.

**Battle of Chalons (Battle of the Catalaunian Plains)**
The 451 battle in Gaul where Attila's invasion was stopped by a coalition of the Roman general Flavius Aetius and the Visigothic king Theodoric I, who was killed in the fighting. It is often called Attila's only major defeat; according to legend, he prepared a funeral pyre of horse saddles in case the battle was lost.

**Honoria and her ring**
Honoria, sister of the Western Roman Emperor Valentinian III, sent Attila her ring to ask for help escaping an arranged marriage to a Roman senator. Attila treated it as a marriage proposal, demanded half of the Western Roman Empire as her dowry, and used the refusal as a pretext to invade Gaul and later Italy.

**Pope Leo I**
In 452 Pope Leo I (Leo the Great) met Attila in northern Italy and persuaded him to withdraw rather than march on Rome. Accounts credit Leo's eloquence or divine intervention, while historians suggest a bribe, famine, and disease in the Hunnic army also played a role.

**"Scourge of God" (Flagellum Dei)**
The epithet Christian chroniclers gave Attila, portraying him as a divine punishment sent against the Roman world. It is the standard giveaway nickname for him.

**Bleda**
Attila's older brother and co-ruler of the Huns after they inherited the throne together. Bleda died around 445, probably murdered by Attila (Jordanes says during a hunt), leaving Attila as sole ruler; Bleda was also known for keeping a Moorish dwarf named Zerco at his court.

**Nosebleed death and Ildico**
Attila died in 453 on the night of his wedding to a young bride named Ildico, reportedly choking on a severe nosebleed after a drunken feast. Some later accounts suggested Ildico murdered him.

**Flavius Aetius and Theodoric I**
Aetius was the Western Roman magister militum (supreme military commander), often called "the last of the Romans," who organized the coalition against Attila. Theodoric I was the Visigothic king who joined him and died at the Catalaunian Plains.

**Priscus of Panium**
The Eastern Roman historian and diplomat who visited Attila's court in 449 on an embassy and wrote the main surviving eyewitness account of him. Priscus described a lavish feast at which Attila himself ate simply from a wooden plate, and the Huns' mourning, in which warriors cut their hair and gashed their faces after his death.

**Rugila and the inheritance of power**
Attila's uncle Rugila (also called Rua or Roas), who ruled the Huns before him, supposedly struck dead by lightning around 434. Attila and Bleda, sons of Mundzuk, then inherited the throne jointly.

**Battle of Nedao and Ellac**
The 454 battle after Attila's death in which a coalition of subject peoples led by Ardaric, king of the Gepids (and a former adviser of Attila), defeated the Huns. Attila's eldest son Ellac was killed, and the Hunnic Empire collapsed.

**Sword of Mars**
According to Priscus, a shepherd found an ancient sword after following a wounded cow and brought it to Attila, who proclaimed it the sword of Mars, the war god. He took it as a sign that he was destined to rule the world.

**Treaty of Margus and tribute from Constantinople**
A treaty Attila and Bleda concluded with the Eastern Roman Empire around 435, doubling the Romans' annual gold tribute to the Huns to 700 pounds and requiring the return of Hunnic fugitives. When payments lapsed the Huns sacked Margus and Singidunum, and later raids near Constantinople forced Theodosius II to triple the tribute; the next emperor, Marcian, stopped paying.

**Battle of the Utus**
A 447 battle in the Balkans where Attila defeated the Eastern Roman general Arnegisclus, who died in the fighting. Attila then ravaged the Balkans as far south as Thermopylae.

**Etzel in the Nibelungenlied**
Attila appears as King Etzel in the medieval German epic the Nibelungenlied, where Kriemhild marries him and her brothers the Burgundians are slaughtered at his court. He likewise appears as Atli in Norse legend.

**Saint Genevieve and Paris**
According to legend, the prayers of Saint Genevieve, later the patron saint of Paris, spared the city from Attila's army during his 451 invasion of Gaul.

**Vercingetorix and the Siege of Alesia**
In 52 BCE Julius Caesar besieged the Gallic chieftain Vercingetorix, leader of the Arverni, at Alesia. Caesar built two concentric rings of walls, one facing inward to trap the defenders (circumvallation) and one facing outward to hold off a Gallic relief army (contravallation), and Vercingetorix surrendered. It completed the Roman conquest of Gaul, the region that became most of modern France.

**Caesar's Commentaries on the Gallic War**
Caesar's account of his campaigns in Gaul (58–50 BCE), which famously opens by saying "all Gaul is divided into three parts," inhabited by the Belgae, Aquitani, and Celts. It begins with the migration of the Helvetii and covers wars against tribes like the Suebi of Ariovistus; the final book was written by Aulus Hirtius.

**Dien Bien Phu and the First Indochina War**
The 1954 battle in which Vo Nguyen Giap's Viet Minh besieged and defeated a French garrison in a remote valley of northern Vietnam. The French had dropped paratroopers there in Operation Castor and built strongpoints with women's names like Beatrice and Gabrielle under Colonel Christian de Castries; artillery commander Charles Piroth killed himself with a grenade. The defeat led to the Geneva Accords, France's withdrawal from Indochina (which included Tonkin and Cochinchina), and the partition of Vietnam at the 17th parallel.

**Vichy France and Philippe Pétain**
The collaborationist regime set up in the spa town of Vichy after France fell to Germany in 1940, led by Marshal Philippe Pétain, the "Lion of Verdun" from World War I, with Pierre Laval as prime minister. Its motto was "Work, Family, Fatherland"; it used the Milice to fight the maquis Resistance and helped carry out the 1942 Vel' d'Hiv Roundup of Jews, who were sent through the Drancy camp.

**Charles de Gaulle**
The general who led Free France, calling for resistance in his radio "Appeal of 18 June" 1940 from London. He later founded the Fifth Republic (1958), the current French government. He caused controversy by declaring "Long live free Quebec" in Montreal in 1967, and during the May 1968 unrest he secretly flew to Baden-Baden, Germany.

**Battle of France (1940)**
The German invasion that ended the eight-month "Phony War." German armor went through the Ardennes Forest, bypassing the fortified Maginot Line, and defeated France in about six weeks despite Maxime Weygand's attempted counterattack. France signed the Second Armistice at Compiègne, and Hitler posed in front of the Eiffel Tower.

**New France**
France's North American empire, centered on the St. Lawrence River, where Jacques Cartier explored and Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec City in 1608. Intendant Jean Talon brought over about 800 "King's Daughters" (filles du roi) to boost the population, fur traders called coureurs des bois ("runners of the woods") traded with Native peoples, and land was held under the seigneurial system. Voltaire dismissed it as "a few acres of snow."

**Plains of Abraham (1759)**
The battle outside Quebec City in which British general James Wolfe defeated the Marquis de Montcalm during the Seven Years' War (French and Indian War); both commanders were mortally wounded. France lost New France to Britain, and Britain had earlier expelled the French-speaking Acadians in the Great Expulsion.

**Clovis I and the Franks**
Clovis I united the Frankish tribes, converted to Christianity, and founded the Merovingian dynasty around 500 CE; the Salic law code from his reign barred women from inheriting land. Pepin the Short later founded the Carolingian dynasty, made the Donation of Pepin that created the Papal States, and fathered Charlemagne.

**Henry IV of France**
The first Bourbon king, formerly Henry III of Navarre, a Protestant who married Margaret of Valois days before the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre. He won the War of the Three Henrys, converted to Catholicism (supposedly saying "Paris is well worth a mass"), promised "a chicken in every pot," and was stabbed to death by François Ravaillac in 1610 while his carriage was stuck in Paris traffic.

**May 1968**
A wave of student protests in France that turned into a nationwide general strike. It was ended in part by the Grenelle Accords, which raised wages, and it badly shook de Gaulle's government.

**French decolonization in Africa**
France fought a brutal war in Algeria (dramatized in Gillo Pontecorvo's film The Battle of Algiers), using Algerian Muslim auxiliaries called harkis; the 1962 Évian Accords granted Algerian independence despite terrorism by the OAS, which tried to stop it. Senegal, home to the "Door of No Return" on Gorée Island and the separatist Casamance region, was led after independence by the poet Léopold Senghor.

**Rainbow Warrior and the French Pacific**
In 1985 French agents bombed the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in New Zealand as it prepared to protest French nuclear tests at Mururoa Atoll, killing photographer Fernando Pereira. France's Pacific territories include New Caledonia (capital Nouméa), a major nickel producer that rejected independence in referendums in 2018, 2020, and 2021, and French Polynesia, whose island of Tahiti was home to painter Paul Gauguin.

**Bourbon Restoration and the July Revolution**
After Napoleon's exile (and his brief return in the Hundred Days, which interrupted the Congress of Vienna), the Bourbon monarchy was restored. The ultraroyalist Charles X invaded Algeria in 1830 after its ruler Hussein Dey struck a French consul with a fly-whisk, but his repressive Four Ordinances sparked the "Three Glorious Days" of the July Revolution, which overthrew him.

**French intervention in Mexico**
France fought Mexico in the 1838 "Pastry War" over debts, including a French pastry chef's claim. After Benito Juárez suspended foreign debt payments, Napoleon III invaded and installed Maximilian I as emperor; the French defeat at Puebla in 1862 is celebrated as Cinco de Mayo, and Maximilian's 1867 execution was painted by Édouard Manet.

**François Mitterrand**
The Socialist president of France from 1981 to 1995, who commissioned the "Grands Projets" of Paris monuments such as the Louvre Pyramid. He had to share power in two "cohabitations" with right-wing prime ministers, the first with Jacques Chirac, who later succeeded him as president.

**Treaty of Ghent**
The treaty signed in December 1814 in Ghent (in modern Belgium) that ended the war between the United States and Britain, largely restoring prewar conditions. News traveled slowly, so the Battle of New Orleans was fought weeks after it was signed.

**Battle of New Orleans**
Andrew Jackson's decisive January 1815 victory over a British army under Edward Pakenham, who was killed in the attack. Jackson's men defended a line along the Rodriguez Canal at Chalmette with help from Jean Lafitte's pirates and Choctaw warriors. Because it came after the Treaty of Ghent, the battle had no effect on the peace terms but made Jackson a national hero.

**Burning of Washington and the Battle of Bladensburg**
In August 1814, British regulars under Robert Ross routed American militia under William Winder at Bladensburg, Maryland, a defeat often called the most humiliating in American history; President Madison was nearly captured. The British then burned the White House and Capitol, Dolley Madison fled after saving a portrait of George Washington, and a freak storm and tornado the next day helped put out the fires.

**Oliver Hazard Perry and the Battle of Lake Erie**
Perry's 1813 victory over Robert Barclay's British squadron near Put-in-Bay gave the U.S. control of Lake Erie and allowed Detroit to be retaken. After his flagship, the Lawrence, was wrecked, Perry transferred to the USS Niagara and won, then reported, "We have met the enemy and they are ours." He had earlier floated his ships over a sandbar to get out of Presque Isle.

**Fort McHenry and "The Star-Spangled Banner"**
In September 1814, a British fleet bombarded Fort McHenry while trying to force its way into Baltimore harbor. Francis Scott Key watched the bombardment and wrote the poem that, set to the tune of "To Anacreon in Heaven," became the U.S. national anthem.

**Tecumseh and the Battle of the Thames**
The Shawnee leader Tecumseh built a Native confederacy and allied with Britain; the related conflict, including William Henry Harrison's burning of Prophetstown, is sometimes called Tecumseh's War. Tecumseh besieged Fort Meigs and was killed at the 1813 Battle of the Thames, where Richard Mentor Johnson claimed to have shot him (inspiring the slogan "Rumpsey dumpsey, Colonel Johnson killed Tecumseh").

**Battle of Lundy's Lane**
The bloodiest battle of the war, fought in July 1814 near Niagara Falls during an American invasion of Canada. Future general Winfield Scott, later the victor at Veracruz in the Mexican-American War, was badly wounded there. It was a costly, roughly drawn fight that ended American advances on the Niagara front.

**USS Constitution ("Old Ironsides")**
The American frigate that earned its nickname in 1812 when British cannonballs seemed to bounce off its oak hull during its victory over HMS Guerriere. It later destroyed HMS Java off Brazil. Along with the capture of HMS Macedonian, these single-ship victories boosted American morale.

**Battle of Queenston Heights and Isaac Brock**
An October 1812 American invasion of Upper Canada across the Niagara River, led by Stephen Van Rensselaer, which failed at Queenston Heights. The British commander Sir Isaac Brock, who had earlier forced William Hull to surrender Detroit, was killed in the battle.

**Laura Secord and the Battle of Beaver Dams**
Laura Secord, a Canadian woman, walked about 20 miles to warn the British officer James FitzGibbon of an American force marching from Fort George. Thanks to her warning, British and Native forces won the 1813 Battle of Beaver Dams, and she became a Canadian heroine.

**Impressment, War Hawks, and Macon's Bill No. 2**
The British practice of impressment (forcing sailors, including Americans, into the Royal Navy), dramatized by the 1807 Chesapeake–Leopard affair, together with Britain's trade-restricting Orders in Council, caused the war. Macon's Bill No. 2 (1810) manipulated trade policy in ways that helped draw the U.S. toward war, and western congressmen who pushed for war were called "War Hawks."

**"Don't give up the ship"**
The dying command of Captain James Lawrence in his 1813 defeat aboard the USS Chesapeake. Perry had the phrase sewn onto the battle flag he flew at the Battle of Lake Erie.

**Battle of Plattsburgh (Lake Champlain)**
A September 1814 American naval victory in which Thomas Macdonough captured the British flagship Confiance, turning back a British invasion from Canada. His anchored-line tactics, reminiscent of Nelson's at the Nile, earned it the nickname "the False Nile."

**River Raisin Massacre**
After the January 1813 Battle of Frenchtown in Michigan Territory, Native allies of the British killed wounded American prisoners. "Remember the River Raisin!" became a rallying cry for Kentucky troops for the rest of the war.

**Hartford Convention and the "Blue Lights"**
New England Federalists opposed the war, and at the Hartford Convention (1814–1815) some discussed secession; the meeting's timing, just as the war ended, destroyed the Federalist Party. Federalists were also mocked as "Blue Lights" for allegedly signaling British ships with lanterns. The war's end ushered in the "Era of Good Feelings."

**Berlin Wall and "Tear down this wall!"**
The heavily guarded barrier that divided East and West Berlin from August 1961 until November 9, 1989. In a 1987 speech at the Brandenburg Gate, Ronald Reagan challenged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!" East Germany officially called it the "Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart."

**Berlin Airlift (Operation Vittles)**
When the Soviets blockaded all land routes into West Berlin in 1948–1949, the U.S. and Britain supplied the city by air. The operation was organized under U.S. military governor Lucius D. Clay, and planes landed at Tempelhof, Gatow, and Tegel airports.

**Checkpoint Charlie and the 1961 tank standoff**
The best-known crossing point between East and West Berlin, named for the letter C in the NATO phonetic alphabet (after Alpha and Bravo). In October 1961, East German guards stopped U.S. diplomat Allan Lightner from entering East Berlin to see an opera. Lucius Clay responded by sending American tanks, and U.S. and Soviet tanks faced each other at the checkpoint for about 16 hours.

**Gail Halvorsen, the "Candy Bomber"**
An American Berlin Airlift pilot who dropped candy attached to small handkerchief parachutes to Berlin's children. He was nicknamed "Uncle Wiggly Wings" because he wiggled his plane's wings so children could recognize him. His effort grew into "Operation Little Vittles," and the planes were called "raisin bombers."

**Peter Fechter and the "death strip"**
An 18-year-old East German bricklayer who was shot while trying to cross the Wall in August 1962. He bled to death in the "death strip," the guarded no-man's-land behind the Wall, while journalists and onlookers watched helplessly. Ida Siekmann, who jumped from a window on Bernauer Straße in 1961, is considered the first person to die at the Wall.

**Walter Ulbricht and Operation Rose**
The East German leader who ordered the Wall built in August 1961 to stop the mass exodus of East Germans to the West. "Operation Rose" was the secret code name for the overnight sealing of the border.

**Yevgeny Khaldei's flag photograph over the Reichstag**
The Soviet photographer Khaldei staged the iconic photo "Raising a Flag over the Reichstag" in May 1945, at the end of the Battle of Berlin. He edited the photo to remove an extra wristwatch on one soldier's arm, which suggested looting.

**Battle of Berlin and Hitler's bunker**
The final major battle of World War II in Europe in April and May 1945, preceded by the Battle of the Seelow Heights and the Battle of Halbe. The German plan to defend the city was code-named Operation Clausewitz. Hitler spent his last months in the Führerbunker and killed himself there on April 30, 1945. On May 2, Polish soldiers raised their flag on the Victory Column in the Tiergarten.

**"My God, Help Me to Survive This Deadly Love"**
A mural by the Russian artist Dmitri Vrubel on the East Side Gallery, a surviving stretch of the Wall. It reproduces a 1979 photograph of Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev and East German leader Erich Honecker sharing a "socialist fraternal kiss." Keith Haring also painted a long mural of interlocking figures on the Wall.

**Reichstag fire and the Reichstag Fire Decree**
In February 1933, Berlin's parliament building, the Reichstag, was set on fire. The Dutch communist bricklayer Marinus van der Lubbe was blamed, and the Nazis used the fire to justify the Reichstag Fire Decree, which suspended civil liberties. In 1995 the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped the building in fabric.

**1936 Summer Olympics and Jesse Owens**
Berlin hosted the 1936 "Nazi Olympics," the first Games with a torch relay and the first to be televised. They were filmed by Leni Riefenstahl in Olympia. The African American sprinter Jesse Owens won four gold medals there, undercutting Nazi racial propaganda.

**Fall of the Wall and Günter Schabowski's press conference**
On November 9, 1989, East German spokesman Günter Schabowski mistakenly announced that new travel rules took effect "immediately, without delay." Crowds rushed the border crossings that night and the Wall opened, which led to German reunification on October 3, 1990.

**JFK's "Ich bin ein Berliner" speech**
John F. Kennedy's 1963 speech in West Berlin expressing solidarity with the city. A popular myth claims his phrase meant "I am a jelly doughnut," but it was correct German. Kennedy had privately remarked that the Wall was "a hell of a lot better than a war."

**Berlin Conference and Congress of Berlin**
Two major diplomatic meetings held in the city. The 1878 Congress of Berlin revised the Treaty of San Stefano after the Russo-Turkish War and recognized the independence of Serbia, Montenegro, and Romania. The 1884–1885 Berlin Conference, hosted by Bismarck, set the rules for European colonization of Africa and helped set off the "Scramble for Africa."

**Ghost stations, Tunnel 57, and escape attempts**
The Wall cut through Berlin's transit network, so some U-Bahn and S-Bahn stations in East Berlin became closed "ghost stations" where West Berlin trains passed without stopping. Escapees tried many methods, including Tunnel 57, which let 57 people flee in 1964.

**Emancipation of the serfs (1861)**
Alexander II's Emancipation Reform freed Russia's serfs, peasants legally bound to the land and their landlords. Freed peasants stayed organized in village communes called mirs (obshchinas) and owed redemption payments for their land until these were abolished in 1907. Exiled writer Alexander Herzen's newspaper The Bell reported on the reform in advance, and new local councils called zemstvos were created to run local affairs.

**Assassination of Alexander II by the People's Will (1881)**
The "Tsar Liberator" was killed by bombs thrown at his carriage in St. Petersburg by the revolutionary group People's Will (Narodnaya Volya), which grew out of the Narodnik populist movement. The Church of the Savior on Spilled Blood stands on the spot; his reign also saw the 1863 January Uprising in Poland and gains of Kars and Batum from the Ottomans in 1878.

**Nicholas II and the execution of the Romanovs**
The last tsar, who abdicated in the February Revolution of 1917. In 1918 the Bolsheviks shot him and his family in Yekaterinburg; some bullets bounced off jewels sewn into the daughters' clothing, which fed myths that Anastasia survived, and Anna Anderson was the most famous of the women who claimed to be her.

**Empress Alexandra and Rasputin**
Nicholas II's wife, a German-born princess, was deeply unpopular for her belief in strict autocracy and her reliance on the mystic Grigori Rasputin, who she believed could ease the hemophilia of her son Alexei.

**Revolution of 1905 and the October Manifesto**
It began on Bloody Sunday (January 1905), when troops fired on a peaceful workers' march led by the priest Father Georgy Gapon. Nicholas II responded with the October Manifesto, which created an elected Duma, followed by the 1906 Fundamental (Basic) Laws. Sergei Witte, architect of Russia's industrialization, became the first prime minister, and the reactionary Black Hundreds carried out violence in the tsar's name.

**Revolutions of 1917**
The February Revolution forced Nicholas II's abdication and ended the Romanov dynasty, leaving a Provisional Government later led by Alexander Kerensky. The October Revolution then overthrew Kerensky and brought Lenin's Bolsheviks to power.

**Peter the Great**
The modernizing tsar who toured Western Europe in the Grand Embassy, created the merit-based Table of Ranks, defeated Charles XII of Sweden at Poltava (1709) in the Great Northern War, and built St. Petersburg on the Baltic. He crushed a streltsy revolt meant to restore his half-sister Sophia, and he put aside his conservative first wife Eudoxia Lopukhina, later taking Anna Mons as a mistress.

**Catherine the Great**
The German-born empress (ruled 1762–1796) who wrote the Nakaz ("Instruction") for a new law code and annexed Crimea. Her favorite Grigory Potemkin supposedly built fake "Potemkin villages" to impress her on a tour of Crimea, and her reign saw Pugachev's Rebellion and Russia's role in starting the First Partition of Poland.

**Empress Elizabeth**
Peter the Great's daughter (ruled 1741–1762), who never carried out a single execution during her reign. Hostile to Prussia, she fought Frederick the Great in the Seven Years' War, and her death prompted the "Miracle of the House of Brandenburg," when her successor Peter III made peace and saved Prussia.

**Ivan III and Ivan IV ("the Terrible")**
Ivan III ("the Great") threw off Mongol overlordship and rebuilt the Moscow Kremlin. Ivan IV (Grozny) created the streltsy musketeers and the oprichnina, a terror apparatus run by the oprichniki, and in 1581 killed his own son with a staff in a fit of rage, which helped end the Rurikid dynasty.

**Time of Troubles**
The chaos from 1598 to 1613 after the Rurikid line died out. It included the elected tsar Boris Godunov, three "False Dmitry" pretenders, and a Polish occupation of Moscow after the Battle of Klushino. Kuzma Minin and Dmitry Pozharsky led the force that drove out the Poles, and the Romanov dynasty began in 1613.

**Alexander Nevsky and Alexander I**
Alexander Nevsky, a Prince of Novgorod, defeated the Teutonic Knights in the 1242 Battle on the Ice while cooperating with the Mongol Golden Horde, and was canonized in 1547. Tsar Alexander I took power after his father Paul I was murdered, signed the Treaty of Tilsit with Napoleon on a raft in the Neman River in 1807, and employed the reformer Mikhail Speransky.

**Siberia and the Trans-Siberian Railway**
Russia's conquest of Siberia began when the Cossack Yermak defeated Kuchum Khan of the Siberian Khanate in the 1580s. Indigenous peoples paid the yasak tribute in furs, and Siberia became a place of exile and forced labor (katorga). The Trans-Siberian Railway, ending at Vladivostok and routed around Lake Baikal, tied the empire together.

**Bering, the Alaska colony, and the Alaska Purchase**
Peter the Great sponsored Danish-born explorer Vitus Bering's first expedition, and a later expedition (from 1733) included naturalist Georg Steller, namesake of Steller's jay. Russia set up fur-trading colonies in Alaska but sold the territory to the U.S. in 1867 in a deal negotiated by Eduard de Stoeckl and mocked as "Seward's Folly."

**Prehistoric Russia: Denisova Cave, Sintashta, and Beringia**
The Denisovans, an extinct group of archaic humans, are named for a cave in Siberia's Altai Mountains. The Sintashta culture built the earliest known chariots, the Yamnaya culture is linked to the Proto-Indo-Europeans in Marija Gimbutas's Kurgan hypothesis, and the Beringia land bridge let humans migrate from Siberia to the Americas.

**Enrico Dandolo and the Fourth Crusade**
Enrico Dandolo was the elderly, blind doge (in his eighties or nineties) who agreed to transport the Fourth Crusade. When the crusaders could not pay, he had them sack the Christian city of Zara on the Dalmatian coast, for which Pope Innocent III excommunicated the army, and then diverted the crusade to sack Constantinople in 1204.

**Doge**
The title of Venice's elected chief magistrate for about a thousand years. Notable doges include Enrico Dandolo, Francesco Foscari, and Ludovico Manin, the last doge; the doge's powers were limited by an oath called the promissione ducale and by councils such as the Great Council (Maggior Consiglio).

**Marriage of the Sea and the Bucentaur**
An annual ceremony held on Ascension Day in which the doge sailed out on the ceremonial state barge, the Bucentaur, and threw a gold ring into the Adriatic Sea. It symbolized Venice's "marriage" to, and dominion over, the sea.

**League of Cambrai**
An alliance formed in 1508 by Pope Julius II with France, Aragon, and the Holy Roman Emperor to curb Venetian expansion on the Italian mainland. Venice was badly defeated at the Battle of Agnadello in 1509 but survived when the league broke apart.

**Council of Ten**
A powerful secret governing council created after the failed 1310 conspiracy of Bajamonte Tiepolo. It ran Venice's security and secret service, read anonymous denunciations dropped into lion's-mouth letterboxes, and forced the long-reigning doge Francesco Foscari to abdicate in 1457.

**Saint Mark and his relics**
Venice's patron saint, whose body was smuggled out of Alexandria by Venetian merchants in 828, supposedly hidden under pork so Muslim inspectors would not search it. He replaced Saint Theodore as patron, his symbol the winged lion became Venice's emblem, and his relics lie in St. Mark's Basilica on St. Mark's Square.

**Rivalry with Genoa and the War of Chioggia**
Venice's chief maritime and trading rival was Genoa, which it fought in a series of wars, including the War of Saint Sabas (with a Venetian victory at Acre in 1258). In the War of Chioggia (1378–1381), Venice under Vettor Pisani defeated a Genoese fleet led by the Doria family in a battle that saw early use of shipboard gunpowder weapons.

**Marco Polo and Il Milione**
The Venetian merchant who traveled to Kublai Khan's China in the late 13th century. He dictated his travels, known as Il Milione, to Rustichello da Pisa while a prisoner of the Genoese during a war between the two republics.

**Horses of Saint Mark**
Four bronze horse sculptures looted from the Hippodrome of Constantinople during the 1204 sack and installed on the façade of St. Mark's Basilica. They are a symbol of Venice's share of the Fourth Crusade's plunder.

**"Most Serene Republic" and the Stato da Mar**
Venice's official name was the Most Serene Republic (La Serenissima). Its overseas maritime empire, the Stato da Mar, included Dalmatian coastal territories, Corfu (bought from King Ladislaus of Naples), Crete (called the Kingdom of Candia, lost to the Ottomans after a 24-year siege), Cyprus, and for a time the Morea.

**Treaty of Campo Formio and Ludovico Manin**
In 1797 Napoleon's French army ended the Venetian Republic; the last doge, Ludovico Manin, abdicated. In the Treaty of Campo Formio that year, France handed Venice to Austria.

**Battle of Lepanto and Marcantonio Bragadin**
Venice supplied much of the fleet of the Holy League that defeated the Ottoman navy at Lepanto in 1571. Earlier that year the Ottomans had taken Venetian Cyprus; the commander of Famagusta, Marcantonio Bragadin, had his ears cut off and was flayed alive after surrendering, becoming a Venetian martyr.

**The Arsenal**
Venice's huge state shipyard, the Arsenale, which mass-produced galleys and other warships in an assembly-line fashion. It was the backbone of Venetian naval power.

**The Ghetto**
In 1516 Venice confined its Jewish population to an area on the site of an old foundry (getto), which is commonly cited as the origin of the word "ghetto."

**Aldine Press**
The printing house founded by Aldus Manutius in Venice around 1494. It introduced italic type and small, portable octavo editions of classical texts, a forerunner of the modern pocket book.

**Free French Forces**
After France fell to Germany in 1940, de Gaulle fled to London and led the Free French, the exiled forces that kept fighting the Axis. He opposed the collaborationist Vichy regime of his former mentor and commander Marshal Philippe Pétain, and he is most often identified as the leader of Free France during World War II.

**Appeal of 18 June**
De Gaulle's 1940 radio speech from the BBC in London urging the French to keep resisting Nazi Germany rather than accept the armistice. It asked rhetorically, "Must hope disappear? Is defeat final?" and answered "No!", and it is considered the founding moment of the French Resistance.

**Évian Accords**
The 1962 agreements between the French government and Algeria's National Liberation Front (FLN) that ended the Algerian War with a ceasefire and led to Algerian independence. They were approved by referendum and enraged French settlers and hardline officers.

**OAS assassination attempts**
The Organisation armée secrète (OAS), a far-right paramilitary group of French Algeria loyalists co-founded by General Raoul Salan, tried repeatedly to kill de Gaulle for abandoning Algeria. In the 1962 Petit-Clamart ambush organized by Jean Bastien-Thiry, de Gaulle survived and remarked that the attackers "shoot like pigs." The novel The Day of the Jackal fictionalizes a plot against him.

**May 1968**
A wave of student protests, including the occupation of the Sorbonne, combined with massive wildcat general strikes that nearly toppled de Gaulle's government. Slogans included "Under the paving stones, the beach!", and de Gaulle answered with "Reform yes, chaos [chienlit] no"; at the height of the crisis he secretly flew to Baden-Baden in West Germany to consult General Jacques Massu.

**"Vive le Québec libre!"**
De Gaulle shouted "Long live free Quebec!" from a balcony in Montreal during his 1967 visit for Expo 67, seeming to endorse Quebec separatism. Canadian Prime Minister Lester Pearson rebuked him, saying that "Canadians do not need to be liberated," and de Gaulle cut his trip short.

**Fifth Republic**
De Gaulle returned to power in 1958 during the Algerian crisis, replacing Pierre Pflimlin as prime minister after a military revolt in Algiers and the planned coup "Operation Resurrection," which began with the seizure of Corsica. He oversaw a new constitution with a strong presidency and became the first President of the Fifth Republic, succeeding René Coty.

**Empty Chair Crisis**
In 1965 de Gaulle withdrew French representatives from the European Economic Community's Council of Ministers. He was protesting Commission President Walter Hallstein's proposals on financing the Common Agricultural Policy and the move toward majority voting; the crisis ended with the 1966 Luxembourg Compromise, which preserved a national veto.

**Georges Pompidou and the Grenelle agreements**
Pompidou was de Gaulle's prime minister during May 1968; he negotiated the Grenelle agreements with unions, raising the minimum wage by about 35%, and persuaded de Gaulle to dissolve the National Assembly and call elections. Pompidou succeeded de Gaulle as president in 1969.

**1969 referendum and resignation**
De Gaulle staked his presidency on a 1969 referendum to create regional councils and reform the Senate. When voters rejected it, he resigned immediately.

**Gerboise Bleue (Blue Jerboa)**
France's first nuclear weapons test, carried out in the Algerian Sahara in 1960. De Gaulle hailed it by saying France was "stronger and prouder," reflecting his pursuit of an independent nuclear deterrent, the force de frappe.

**Brazzaville Conference**
A 1944 meeting de Gaulle's Free French held in Brazzaville in French Equatorial Africa to discuss the future of the French colonies, which had served as a base for Free France. It promised reforms but rejected independence.

**Military writings**
Before WWII, de Gaulle wrote The Enemy's House Divided, analyzing Germany's leadership in World War I, partly drawing on his time as a prisoner of war. In Toward a Professional Army (translated as The Army of the Future) he criticized reliance on static defenses like the Maginot Line and advocated a mechanized, professional army.

**Foreign policy of "national independence"**
De Gaulle sought French independence from the superpowers, withdrawing France from NATO's integrated military command in 1966. He reconciled with West Germany through the 1963 Élysée Treaty signed with Konrad Adenauer, and in Poland he recognized the Oder-Neisse border.

**Dirigisme and the RPF**
De Gaulle's government practiced dirigisme, state direction of the economy, during France's postwar boom known as the Trente Glorieuses ("Thirty Glorious Years"). After resigning as head of the provisional government in 1946, he founded the political party Rally of the French People (RPF) in 1947.

**An Lushan Rebellion**
A huge revolt from 755 to 763 led by An Lushan, a general of Sogdian and Turkic descent who commanded several frontier armies. He declared his own Yan dynasty, took Luoyang and later the capital Chang'an, and forced Emperor Xuanzong to flee to Sichuan. The rebellion is also called the An–Shi Rebellion after An and his successor Shi Siming. It ended the Tang golden age and left the dynasty permanently weakened.

**Wu Zetian**
A former consort of Emperor Taizong who became Emperor Gaozong's empress and ruled through him. In 690 she took the throne herself as the only woman in Chinese history to rule as emperor in her own name, proclaiming a "Zhou" dynasty (often called the Second or Wu Zhou) that briefly interrupted the Tang until 705. She used secret police and informers, crushed a revolt by Tang princes, favored Luoyang as her capital, and created the "Scholars of the Northern Gate" as an advisory group that bypassed the regular bureaucracy.

**Yang Guifei**
The favorite consort of Emperor Xuanzong and the last of China's "Four Beauties." She embodied the Tang ideal of plump beauty and was said to "put flowers to shame." Her favor toward An Lushan, who became her adopted son, and the power of her cousin Yang Guozhong helped provoke the rebellion. While fleeing, Xuanzong's guards forced him to have her put to death at Mawei, a story told in Bai Juyi's poem "Song of Everlasting Regret."

**Emperor Xuanzong**
The Tang emperor who ruled from 712 to 756. His early Kaiyuan era was the dynasty's cultural and political height, and he gained power by defeating his aunt, the Taiping Princess, who was forced to commit suicide. His later neglect of government, his devotion to Yang Guifei, and the An Lushan Rebellion ended his reign, and he abdicated in favor of his son.

**Emperor Taizong (Li Shimin) and the Xuanwu Gate Incident**
In 626, Li Shimin ambushed and killed his brothers, the crown prince Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji, at the Xuanwu Gate north of the palace in Chang'an. His father then abdicated in his favor. His Zhenguan era is seen as a model of good government. He defeated the Eastern Turks and took the title "Heavenly Khagan," and according to legend he swallowed locusts during a plague, asking that the punishment fall on him rather than his people.

**Li Yuan (Emperor Gaozu) and the Sui–Song sequence**
Li Yuan, a Sui general, founded the Tang in 618 after the collapse of the Sui dynasty and deposed the puppet Sui emperor Gong. The Tang lasted until 907 and was followed by the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period and then the Song. Every Tang emperor belonged to the Li family.

**Li Bai and Du Fu**
The two greatest poets of the Tang golden age, which is often considered the high point of Chinese poetry. Li Bai (also called Li Po) was a free-spirited Daoist-leaning poet famous for poems about wine and the moon. Du Fu (Tu Fu), the "Poet-Sage," wrote about the suffering caused by the An Lushan Rebellion. Bai Juyi and Wang Wei are other major Tang poets.

**Battle of Talas**
A battle fought in 751 in Central Asia between a Tang army under the Korean-born general Gao Xianzhi and the Abbasid Caliphate. The Tang lost, which ended their expansion into Central Asia. According to tradition, Chinese prisoners taken there brought papermaking to the Islamic world, starting with Samarkand.

**Jiedushi**
Regional military governors placed on the Tang frontiers. After the An Lushan Rebellion, which An himself launched as a jiedushi, they became semi-independent warlords whose territories were called fanzhen. Emperor Xianzong tried to bring them back under control. The jiedushi Zhu Wen deposed the last Tang emperor in 907 and founded the Later Liang, opening the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.

**Chang'an**
The Tang capital, at the site of modern Xi'an. It was probably the largest city in the world at the time, with a carefully planned grid and a cosmopolitan population at the eastern end of the Silk Road. Japan copied its layout for the capitals Nara and Heian-kyō (Kyoto). Chang'an was sacked during the An Lushan Rebellion and briefly occupied by Tibetan forces under King Trisong Detsen in 763.

**Xuanzang's journey to India**
During Taizong's Zhenguan era, the Buddhist monk Xuanzang traveled to India to collect Buddhist scriptures, returned to Chang'an in 645, and translated them. He described his travels in the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, and his journey was later fictionalized in the Ming novel Journey to the West.

**Alliance with Silla and the conquest of Goguryeo**
The Tang allied with the Korean kingdom of Silla to destroy Baekje (including a victory at the Battle of Baekgang in 663 over Baekje and its Japanese allies) and Goguryeo, which fell in 668 after resisting under the general Yeon Gaesomun. The Tang then set up the Protectorate General to Pacify the East. Silla later pushed out the Tang and unified most of Korea, ending the Three Kingdoms period.

**Equal-field system**
A land system inherited from earlier dynasties under which the state assigned farmland to households according to the number of adults. The Tang were the last dynasty to use it. It broke down in the 700s and was replaced in 780 by the Two-Tax system.

**Huang Chao Rebellion**
A massive uprising from 875 to 884 led by the salt smuggler Huang Chao, who had failed the civil service exam. He captured Chang'an and declared a Qi dynasty. The eunuch-led Shence ("Divine Strategy") Army could not stop him, and although the revolt was put down, it destroyed what remained of Tang central authority.

**Huichang persecution of Buddhism**
The "Great Anti-Buddhist Persecution" of the 840s under Emperor Wuzong, a devoted Daoist. Thousands of monasteries were closed, monks and nuns were forced back into lay life, and temple wealth was seized to fund the state. Other foreign religions, such as Nestorian Christianity, which the missionary Alopen had brought to Tang China in 635, were also suppressed.

**Francisco Solano López**
The dictator-president of Paraguay who started and led his country through the war (1864–1870). His aggressive policy brought Paraguay into conflict with all three of its neighbors, and he is often portrayed as megalomaniacal or possibly insane.

**Battle of Cerro Corá**
The final engagement of the war, fought on March 1, 1870 in northeastern Paraguay, where Brazilian troops caught and killed Solano López. Its occurrence effectively ended the war; a soldier nicknamed "Chico Diabo" ("Devil Frank") lanced López, who reportedly cried "I die with my country!" Alfredo Stroessner later funded a film about the battle.

**Invasion of Mato Grosso**
The Paraguayan invasion of the Brazilian province of Mato Grosso in late 1864, led by Vicente Barrios, which opened the war. It was preceded by Paraguay's seizure of the Brazilian steamer Marquês de Olinda on the Paraguay River.

**Duke of Caxias**
Luís Alves de Lima e Silva, Brazil's most celebrated general, who took command of allied forces, retrained the army (including setting up a health corps against cholera), captured the fortress of Humaitá, and led the decisive campaigns that followed.

**Battle of Riachuelo**
The decisive naval battle of the war, fought on the Paraná River in June 1865. Brazilian admiral Francisco Barroso destroyed the Paraguayan fleet by ramming enemy ships; Paraguayan commander Pedro Ignacio Meza was mortally wounded.

**Massive Paraguayan population loss**
Paraguay suffered catastrophic casualties, often estimated at 60–70 percent of its total population and up to 90 percent of its adult men, making this the deadliest war in Latin American history and possibly the highest national mortality rate of any modern war.

**Blancos and Colorados in Uruguay**
The war grew out of Uruguay's civil conflict between the Blanco and Colorado parties. Brazil backed the Colorado Venancio Flores in overthrowing the Blanco president Atanasio Aguirre (after Bernardo Berro's earlier presidency), and López, an ally of the Blancos, responded by going to war.

**Siege of Humaitá**
Humaitá was the great Paraguayan river fortress guarding the Paraguay River. Allied ironclads forced their way past it in 1868 and it fell later that year, a turning point of the war; the allies had earlier suffered a bloody defeat at nearby Curupayty.

**Rutherford B. Hayes arbitration**
After the war, U.S. President Rutherford B. Hayes arbitrated the dispute between Paraguay and Argentina over the Chaco land between the Verde and Pilcomayo Rivers, ruling for Paraguay in 1878. In gratitude, Paraguay named its Presidente Hayes Department after him.

**Bartolomé Mitre**
The president of Argentina who served as commander-in-chief of the allied armies for much of the war's early phase, before overall command passed to the Duke of Caxias. He had earlier refused López permission to send troops across Argentine territory.

**Battle of Acosta Ñu**
An August 16, 1869 battle in which Brazilian troops under the Count of Eu (Gaston d'Orléans, husband of Brazil's Princess Isabel) slaughtered a Paraguayan force largely made of children, some wearing fake beards to look older. Paraguay commemorates the date as its Children's Day.

**Deed of December (Dezembrada)**
A string of allied victories in December 1868, including Itororó, Avay, and Lomas Valentinas, won by Caxias after he built a road through the swampy Chaco to outflank Paraguayan defenses and approach Asunción.

**Eliza Lynch and Las Residentas**
Eliza Lynch was the Irish-born mistress and de facto first lady of Solano López; she survived Cerro Corá, where their son was killed. "Las Residentas" were Paraguayan women who supported and followed the army during the war.

**Invasion of Corrientes and Urquiza**
Paraguay invaded the Argentine province of Corrientes in 1865, hoping to win support from the Argentine caudillo Justo José de Urquiza. The move brought Argentina into the alliance, and allied forces defeated a Paraguayan column at Yatay.

**Battle of Tuyutí**
The May 1866 battle in southern Paraguay, the largest battle of the war and one of the largest ever fought in South America, in which the allies repulsed a massive Paraguayan attack.

**López executing his mother**
Late in the war, the increasingly paranoid López turned on his own family, having his elderly mother flogged and condemned after she revealed that he had been born out of wedlock, along with executing many other suspected conspirators.

**Atahualpa and Francisco Pizarro**
Atahualpa was the last true Sapa Inca (emperor), captured by the Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro in 1532 and executed in 1533. Pizarro's conquest of the empire, centered in modern-day Peru, is the most common giveaway in questions about the Incas.

**Quipu**
Knotted strings, sometimes called "talking knots," that the Incas used for record-keeping, accounting, and relaying information, since they had no conventional written language. The color, position, and type of knots encoded numbers and other data.

**Battle of Cajamarca and the thrown Bible**
The 1532 encounter in which Pizarro's small force ambushed Atahualpa's retinue and captured him. According to Spanish accounts, the friar Vicente de Valverde handed Atahualpa a Bible (or breviary), and Atahualpa threw it to the ground, which the Spanish used as a pretext for the attack.

**Room full of gold (ransom)**
While held captive, Atahualpa offered to fill a room with gold, and two rooms with silver, in exchange for his release. The ransom was paid, but the Spanish executed him anyway in 1533.

**Huascar and the Inca Civil War**
Huascar was Atahualpa's half-brother, and the two fought a war of succession after the death of their father Huayna Capac. Atahualpa's generals, such as Quisquis (Quizquiz) and Atoc (Atoc won at Chillopampa), defeated Huascar's forces, and Atahualpa had Huascar executed. The war weakened the empire just as Pizarro arrived.

**Chasqui**
Relay runners who carried messages and quipus along the Inca road system, chewing coca leaves for stamina. By passing messages from runner to runner between waystations, they could cover around 200 miles in a single day.

**Qhapaq Ñan, tambos, and rope bridges**
The Qhapaq Ñan was the vast Inca royal road network that crossed the Andes and was used by chasquis and llama caravans. Along it stood tambos (waystations) and qullqas (storehouses), and it crossed gorges on suspension bridges woven from ichu grass, which local peasants were required to rebuild regularly.

**Machu Picchu**
A mountaintop royal estate in Peru, probably built for the emperor Pachacuti and abandoned after the Spanish conquest. It was brought to international attention in 1911 by the American explorer Hiram Bingham, and it contains structures like the Temple of the Sun and the Room of the Three Windows.

**Pachacuti**
The ninth Sapa Inca, who transformed the Kingdom of Cusco into an empire in the 15th century after defeating the invading Chancas. He began the rapid expansion of the state, reorganized its administration into the four suyu, and is credited with building Machu Picchu.

**Tawantinsuyu and the four suyu**
The Incas' name for their empire, meaning roughly "the four parts together" in Quechua. It was divided into four provinces called suyu, led by governors called apos and further subdivided into more than 80 administrative units called wamani.

**Cusco (Cuzco)**
The Inca capital in the Peruvian Andes, regarded as the center of the universe and said to have been laid out in the shape of a puma. It held the Coricancha ("House of the Sun"), the most sacred temple, and was divided into upper and lower halves called hanan and hurin. It was defended by the fortress of Sacsayhuaman, built of finely fitted mortarless stone such as the famous "twelve-angled stone."

**Mit'a**
A compulsory labor tax owed to the state, under which subjects worked in rotation on public projects, farming, military service, and building roads and terraces. The Spanish later adapted the system, most notoriously for forced labor in the silver mines of Potosí.

**Manco Capac**
The legendary founder of the Inca dynasty and of Cusco. In myth, he emerged near Lake Titicaca and founded the city where his golden staff sank into the ground.

**Tupac Amaru and Vilcabamba**
After the conquest, Manco Inca led a rebellion and set up a Neo-Inca State in the remote jungle region of Vilcabamba. Its last ruler, Tupac Amaru, was captured by the Spanish and executed in 1572, ending the line of Inca rulers.

**Vertical archipelago**
A term coined by the anthropologist John Victor Murra for the Andean practice of controlling farmland at many different altitudes, letting a community grow a wide range of crops. It was supported by terrace farms (andenes), like those in the Sacred Valley and at the circular site of Moray, and by local clans called ayllus that exchanged labor through reciprocity (ayni).

**Rough Riders and San Juan Hill**
Roosevelt resigned as Assistant Secretary of the Navy to help raise the 1st U.S. Volunteer Cavalry, nicknamed the Rough Riders, during the 1898 Spanish-American War. He led them in the famous charge up Kettle Hill and San Juan Hill near Santiago, Cuba, which made him a national hero.

**Bull Moose Party (1912 election)**
After breaking with his successor William Howard Taft, Roosevelt ran for a third term in 1912 as the candidate of the Progressive Party, nicknamed the "Bull Moose" Party. He finished second, ahead of Taft, and remains the only third-party candidate to do so, but the split Republican vote let Woodrow Wilson win.

**Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine**
Roosevelt's 1904 addition to the Monroe Doctrine claimed that the U.S. could act as an "international police power" in the Western Hemisphere, intervening in Latin American nations to keep European powers out. It followed the 1902–1903 Venezuela crisis, in which Britain and Germany blockaded and bombarded Venezuela to collect debts.

**Great White Fleet**
A fleet of U.S. Navy battleships with white-painted hulls that Roosevelt sent on a voyage around the world from 1907 to 1909 to show off American naval power.

**Square Deal**
Roosevelt's domestic program, based on the "three C's": conservation of natural resources, control of corporations, and consumer protection. He was known as a "trust-buster" for suing large monopolies under the Sherman Antitrust Act.

**Elkins Act and Hepburn Act**
Railroad regulation laws passed under Roosevelt. The 1903 Elkins Act fined railroads for giving rebates to favored shippers, and the 1906 Hepburn Act gave the Interstate Commerce Commission (ICC) the power to set maximum railroad rates.

**Treaty of Portsmouth and the Nobel Peace Prize**
Roosevelt mediated the 1905 Treaty of Portsmouth, signed in New Hampshire, which ended the Russo-Japanese War. This earned him the 1906 Nobel Peace Prize, the first won by an American.

**Shot by John Schrank in Milwaukee**
On October 14, 1912, while campaigning, Roosevelt was shot by the saloonkeeper John Schrank. The folded copy of his speech and his glasses case in his breast pocket slowed the bullet. He went on to give his roughly 90-minute speech, opening with "I don't know whether you fully understand that I have just been shot" and declaring that "it takes more than that to kill a Bull Moose."

**"Speak softly and carry a big stick"**
A West African proverb that Roosevelt quoted to sum up his "Big Stick" foreign policy: negotiate peacefully while backing diplomacy with the threat of military force.

**Panama Canal and Panamanian independence**
When Colombia refused to ratify a treaty for a canal, Roosevelt sent U.S. naval forces to support Panama's 1903 independence movement. The new Panamanian government quickly signed the Hay–Bunau-Varilla Treaty, which gave the U.S. control of the Canal Zone, and canal construction began.

**Pure Food and Drug Act and Meat Inspection Act**
Two consumer protection laws Roosevelt signed in 1906, partly in response to the horrors of the meatpacking industry exposed in Upton Sinclair's The Jungle.

**Gentlemen's Agreement and Taft-Katsura Agreement**
In the informal 1907 Gentlemen's Agreement, Japan agreed to stop issuing passports to laborers emigrating to the U.S., and San Francisco ended the segregation of Japanese students. The 1905 Taft–Katsura Agreement was a secret understanding in which the U.S. accepted Japanese control of Korea in exchange for Japan accepting U.S. control of the Philippines.

**Conservation, Gifford Pinchot, and the Forest Service**
Roosevelt, a dedicated naturalist, created the U.S. Forest Service in 1905 with Gifford Pinchot as its first chief. He protected huge areas of land as national forests, parks, monuments, and wildlife refuges.

**The Naval War of 1812 and The Winning of the West**
Roosevelt was also a prolific historian. He published The Naval War of 1812 in 1882 and The Winning of the West, a four-volume history of American westward expansion. He also gave the speech "The Strenuous Life," which attacked the "doctrine of ignoble ease."

**Brownsville Affair and Booker T. Washington**
In 1906, after a shooting in Brownsville, Texas, was blamed on Black soldiers of the 25th Infantry, Roosevelt dishonorably discharged 167 of them despite little evidence. Earlier, in 1901, he had caused controversy by inviting Booker T. Washington to dine at the White House.

**Battle of the Zab and Marwan II**
The decisive 750 battle near the Great Zab River in Iraq where Abbasid forces defeated Marwan II, the last Umayyad caliph in Damascus. It brought the Abbasids to power, with Abu al-Abbas as-Saffah as their first caliph.

**Successor to the Umayyads**
The Abbasids replaced the Umayyad Caliphate in 750 as the third major Islamic caliphate. They were named after al-Abbas, an uncle of the Prophet Muhammad. One surviving Umayyad, Abd al-Rahman I, escaped to Spain and founded the Emirate of Córdoba.

**Hulagu Khan and the 1258 Sack of Baghdad**
The Mongol commander Hulagu Khan destroyed Baghdad in 1258. According to legend, so many books were thrown into the Tigris that the river ran black with ink. The last Baghdad caliph, al-Musta'sim, was rolled in a carpet and trampled to death by horses, because the Mongols avoided spilling royal blood.

**House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma)**
The great library and translation center in Baghdad, associated with Harun al-Rashid and especially his son al-Ma'mun. It led the Graeco-Arabic translation movement, which put Greek, Persian and Sanskrit works into Arabic, and it was destroyed in the 1258 Mongol sack.

**Harun al-Rashid**
The fifth Abbasid caliph (r. 786–809), whose reign is considered the dynasty's peak. He is a character in the One Thousand and One Nights, and according to Charlemagne's biographer Einhard he sent Charlemagne an elephant named Abul-Abbas and a water clock.

**Battle of Talas River**
The 751 battle in Central Asia where Abbasid forces, helped by Karluk Turks who defected and by Tibetan allies, defeated a Tang Chinese army under Gao Xianzhi. It ended Tang expansion westward, and legend says that Chinese prisoners brought papermaking to Samarkand, from where it spread west.

**Abu Muslim and the Black Standard**
The Persian general who led the Abbasid Revolution from Khorasan, starting at Merv, under black banners. Despite his key role, he was murdered on the orders of the second caliph, al-Mansur, in 755.

**The Barmakids**
A Persian family from Balkh, originally administrators of a Buddhist monastery there, who served as powerful viziers to the early Abbasids. Yahya the Barmakid ran much of Harun al-Rashid's government before Harun abruptly purged the family in 803.

**Baghdad and al-Mansur**
The second caliph, al-Mansur, founded Baghdad in 762 as the "City of Peace" (Madinat al-Salam), a round city on the Tigris, after facing revolts such as that of the Rawandiyya. It was the Abbasid capital and a center of world learning.

**Zanj Rebellion**
A huge revolt (869–883) of African slaves forced to labor in the salt marshes near Basra, led by Ali ibn Muhammad. It was eventually crushed by the caliph's brother and regent al-Muwaffaq.

**Anarchy at Samarra**
A chaotic period (861–870) that began with the murder of the caliph al-Mutawakkil by his Turkish guards. Four caliphs followed one another in about nine years while the Turkish military controlled the government from the new capital, Samarra.

**Mamluks and Turkish slave soldiers**
Al-Ma'mun and his brother al-Mu'tasim began using enslaved Turkish soldiers (mamluks or ghilman) as the core of the army. These soldiers later came to dominate the caliphs.

**Buyids and Seljuks**
The Shi'ite Persian Buyids took Baghdad in 945 and ruled the caliphs as figureheads for about a century. The Seljuk Turks replaced them in 1055. Other states broke away from Abbasid control, including the Tulunids, Saffarids, Samanids, Ghaznavids, Aghlabids and Idrisids.

**Fourth Fitna**
The civil war (811–813) between Harun al-Rashid's sons al-Amin and al-Ma'mun. Al-Ma'mun's general Tahir ibn Husayn defeated al-Amin's army at the Battle of Rayy, and al-Ma'mun took Baghdad.

**Islamic Golden Age scholars**
