Vivaldi's best-known sacred choral work (RV 589). It was revived in 1939 during a Vivaldi Week organized by the composer Alfredo Casella in Siena, part of the 20th-century rediscovery of his music.

**Turin manuscripts and the Ryom catalog**
Much of Vivaldi's music was forgotten after his death until large collections of his manuscripts were rediscovered and acquired by the National Library in Turin in the late 1920s. His works are now numbered in Peter Ryom's catalog (Ryom-Verzeichnis, "RV" numbers). A set of sonatas published as his "Op. 13," Il pastor fido, was later shown to be by Nicolas Chédeville.

**Operas, including Orlando furioso**
Vivaldi wrote dozens of operas, including several based on Ludovico Ariosto's epic Orlando Furioso, such as Orlando furioso and Orlando finto pazzo. Others include Tito Manlio, written for the wedding of the governor of Mantua, and L'oracolo in Messenia, a pasticcio on a libretto by Apostolo Zeno.

**Frida Kahlo**
Mexico's most famous painter, known for her many self-portraits that emphasize her unibrow and often include pet monkeys. Major works include The Broken Column (her spine shown as a cracked Ionic column, her body studded with nails, painted in response to a bus accident), The Two Fridas (two versions of herself joined by an artery between their exposed hearts), Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird, Henry Ford Hospital, and What the Water Gave Me. Her family home, the Blue House (Casa Azul) in Coyoacán, is now a museum.

**Diego Rivera's Man at the Crossroads**
A mural Rivera painted in 1933 for Rockefeller Center in New York. Nelson Rockefeller objected to its portrait of Vladimir Lenin and had it destroyed when Rivera refused to remove the portrait. Rivera repainted it in Mexico City's Palacio de Bellas Artes as Man, Controller of the Universe, which shows a worker gripping machinery controls. Rivera, Kahlo's husband, also painted the Detroit Industry Murals.

**The Suicide of Dorothy Hale**
Kahlo's 1938 painting commissioned by Clare Boothe Luce as a memorial to the former showgirl and socialite Dorothy Hale. Instead of a flattering portrait, Kahlo showed Hale falling from the Hampshire House building in New York and lying dead and bloody on the ground. A blood-red inscription at the bottom describes the event.

**José Clemente Orozco's The Epic of American Civilization**
Orozco's fresco cycle in Dartmouth College's Baker Library. Its panels include "Gods of the Modern World," in which a skeleton in academic dress gives birth to a skeleton baby on a pile of books, and "Modern Human Sacrifice." Orozco also painted the Guadalajara mural of the independence hero Miguel Hidalgo with his fist raised and a torch in hand.

**David Alfaro Siqueiros's The March of Humanity**
A huge mural titled The March of Humanity on Earth and Towards the Cosmos, which covers the Polyforum Cultural Siqueiros in Mexico City. Siqueiros, Orozco, and Rivera are the "big three" of the Mexican muralist movement.

**Leonora Carrington and Remedios Varo**
Two European-born Surrealist women who settled in Mexico during World War II. Carrington's earlier Self-Portrait (Inn of the Dawn Horse), painted during her relationship with Max Ernst, shows her with a hyena and a rocking horse, and her bronze How Doth the Little Crocodile shows crocodiles riding in a crocodile-shaped boat. Varo's Alchemy, or the Useless Science shows a woman whose checkered cloak merges with the checkered floor.

**Diego Rivera's Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in Alameda Park**
A Rivera mural crowded with figures from Mexican history strolling through Mexico City's Alameda park. At its center is La Calavera Catrina, an elegant female skeleton in a white dress and feathered hat, wearing a feathered-serpent boa, with Frida Kahlo standing nearby holding a yin-yang symbol.

**Mariachi**
The folk ensemble that developed in the state of Jalisco. It typically includes violins, trumpets, a guitar, a vihuela (a small, high-pitched guitar), and a guitarrón (a large bass guitar), and it plays songs such as "La Cucaracha," "Cielito Lindo," and rancheras. Other regional styles include son jarocho, played on the eight-string jarana and danced on a wooden platform called a tarima, and norteño music, which uses the twelve-string bajo sexto.

**Aaron Copland's El Salón México**
A 1936 orchestral piece that Copland wrote after visiting Mexico, named for a popular Mexico City dance hall. It weaves together several Mexican folk melodies.

**Carlos Chávez's Sinfonía India**
Chávez's Symphony No. 2, which uses indigenous melodies and calls for native percussion such as rattles made of butterfly cocoons and strings of deer hooves. Chávez was Mexico's leading 20th-century composer and a friend of Aaron Copland.

**Silvestre Revueltas, Juventino Rosas, Julián Carrillo, and Conlon Nancarrow**
Other composers connected to Mexico. Revueltas wrote the orchestral piece Sensemayá, Rosas wrote the 19th-century waltz Over the Waves (Sobre las olas), and Carrillo developed a microtonal system called "Sonido 13" ("the thirteenth sound"). The American-born Conlon Nancarrow emigrated to Mexico City and wrote his Studies for Player Piano there.

**Roma and the "Three Amigos" directors**
Alfonso Cuarón's 2018 film Roma follows Cleo, an indigenous housekeeper in Mexico City played by Yalitza Aparicio, and it won the Academy Award for Best International (Foreign Language) Film. Cuarón, Alejandro G. Iñárritu (Birdman, which was shot to look like one continuous take, had a mostly drum score by Antonio Sánchez, and was filmed by the Mexican cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki), and Guillermo del Toro (Pan's Labyrinth) are called the "Three Amigos."

**Coco and the Day of the Dead**
Pixar's 2017 film set in Mexico during the Day of the Dead, in which the boy Miguel sings "Remember Me" to his great-grandmother Coco. Disney drew backlash for trying to trademark "Día de los Muertos" during production. The holiday is known for decorated sugar skulls.

**Chichen Itza and the Olmec colossal heads**
Chichen Itza is a Maya city in Yucatán with a step pyramid nicknamed El Castillo ("the castle") and reclining stone figures called chacmools. The Olmecs, an earlier civilization of the Gulf Coast, carved giant basalt heads.

**Teotihuacan, Monte Albán, and Tula**
Teotihuacan, near Mexico City, has the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon connected by the Avenue of the Dead and exemplifies the slope-and-panel (talud-tablero) building style. Monte Albán in Oaxaca was the Zapotec capital, known for its carved "Danzantes" (dancers) reliefs. Tula (Tollan) was the capital of the Toltecs.

**The Broken Column**
Kahlo's 1944 self-portrait in which her nude torso is split open to reveal a cracked Ionic column in place of her spine. Her body is held together by a steel orthopedic corset with white bands and studded with nails, and tears run down her face. It reflects the lifelong pain from the 1925 accident in which the bus she was riding collided with a streetcar and she was impaled by a metal handrail. She began painting while recovering from that accident.

**The Two Fridas**
A 1939 double self-portrait painted around her divorce from Diego Rivera. Two seated Fridas, one in a white European-style dress and one in traditional Tehuana dress, hold hands, and their exposed hearts are linked by a single artery. One holds a small portrait of Diego, while the other uses surgical forceps to clamp a severed vein that drips blood onto her dress.

**Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird**
A 1940 self-portrait in which a necklace of thorns digs into her bleeding neck and a dead hummingbird, a Mexican love charm, hangs from it like a pendant. A black monkey sits on one shoulder and a black cat on the other.

**What the Water Gave Me**
A 1938 painting seen from Kahlo's point of view as she lies in a bathtub, with only her feet visible above the water. Floating in the water are images from her life, including a skyscraper (the Empire State Building) erupting from a volcano, a seashell with bullet holes, an empty dress, a dead bird, a skeleton, and two nude women.

**The Suicide of Dorothy Hale**
A 1938 painting commissioned by Clare Boothe Luce as a memorial to Dorothy Hale, a former Ziegfeld showgirl and socialite who jumped from the Hampshire House building in New York on October 21, 1938. Kahlo showed her falling through clouds and then lying bloody at the building's base. Luce was horrified and had the sculptor Isamu Noguchi paint out part of the inscription.

**Henry Ford Hospital**
A 1932 painting made in Detroit after Kahlo's miscarriage. She lies naked and bleeding on a hospital bed in a barren landscape with the Ford factory skyline behind her. She holds red ribbons, like umbilical cords, that connect to floating objects, including a male fetus, a snail, an orchid, a pelvis, an orthopedic model, and a machine.

**The Wounded Deer**
A 1946 painting that puts Kahlo's own head, with antlers, on the body of a young stag pierced by nine arrows in a forest. The word "carma" (karma) is written in the lower left corner.

**Diego Rivera**
The Mexican muralist whom Kahlo married in 1929, divorced in 1939, and remarried in 1940. She painted their double portrait Frida and Diego Rivera, and Rivera included her, holding a yin-yang symbol, in his mural Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in Alameda Park.

**Unibrow and self-portraits with pet monkeys**
Kahlo emphasized her joined eyebrows and faint mustache in her many self-portraits. She often painted herself with pets such as her spider monkey Fulang-Chang, which are often read as substitutes for the children she could not have, and these works stress her Mexican and mestiza identity.

**Viva la Vida**
One of Kahlo's last paintings (1954), a still life of whole and sliced watermelons. She inscribed "Viva la Vida" ("Long live life") on one of the red slices.

**Self-Portrait Dedicated to Leon Trotsky**
A 1937 self-portrait, also called Between the Curtains, in which Kahlo stands between drawn curtains holding a letter dedicating the painting to the exiled Soviet revolutionary Leon Trotsky "with all my love." Trotsky lived in her home in Mexico and had a brief affair with her.

**La Casa Azul (The Blue House)**
Kahlo's family home in Coyoacán, Mexico City, where she was born and died. It is now the Frida Kahlo Museum.

**The Wounded Table**
A large, lost 1940 painting that parodies Leonardo's Last Supper. Kahlo sits at a table with human legs that drips blood, between figures including a Judas effigy and a skeleton, with a pet fawn and a red theatrical curtain.

**Roots**
A 1943 painting in which Kahlo, in an orange dress, reclines on barren, cracked earth while green vines with leaves grow out of her open chest and spread across the ground.

**Self-Portrait on the Borderline Between Mexico and the United States**
A 1932 painting in which Kahlo stands on the border. On the Mexican side are a pre-Columbian temple, the sun and moon, and native plants and idols, and on the American side are Ford factory smokestacks, skyscrapers, and machines, with the American flag in the smoke.

**Aida**
Verdi's 1871 opera set in ancient Egypt, which premiered in Cairo. The Egyptian commander Radamès loves Aida, an enslaved Ethiopian princess whose father, King Amonasro, is at war with Egypt. The Egyptian princess Amneris is her rival. Radamès receives the sacred arms at the Temple of Vulcan, and the opera features a grand "Triumphal March." At the end, Radamès is condemned as a traitor and entombed beneath the temple, where Aida joins him to die.

**La traviata**
Verdi's 1853 opera based on Alexandre Dumas fils's The Lady of the Camellias. The courtesan Violetta Valéry falls in love with Alfredo Germont. Alfredo's father, Giorgio Germont, persuades her to leave him, and she pretends to love Baron Douphol. At a gambling party, Alfredo throws his winnings at her feet, and in the last act Violetta dies of tuberculosis in his arms.

**Rigoletto**
Verdi's 1851 opera about the hunchbacked court jester of the womanizing Duke of Mantua. A courtier's curse falls on Rigoletto, who hires the assassin Sparafucile to kill the Duke. Instead, his daughter Gilda sacrifices herself, and Rigoletto finds her body in a sack and cries "La maledizione!" ("The curse!").

**"La donna è mobile"**
The Duke of Mantua's famous aria in Rigoletto, whose title means "woman is fickle." When Rigoletto hears the Duke singing it in the distance, he realizes the body in the sack is not the Duke's.

**"Va, pensiero" (Chorus of the Hebrew Slaves)**
The chorus from Nabucco (1842), Verdi's first major success, in which the exiled Hebrews in Babylon long for their homeland, asking their thoughts to fly "on golden wings." Nabucco is about the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar, who later prays to the Hebrew God. The chorus became an anthem of Italian nationalism.

**Il trovatore and the "Anvil Chorus"**
Il trovatore ("The Troubadour," 1853) is set in 15th-century Spain, where the Count di Luna pursues the troubadour Manrico, his rival for Leonora. In the "Anvil Chorus," Roma workers strike anvils at dawn. The Roma woman Azucena sings "Stride la vampa" about her mother being burned at the stake. Leonora takes poison from her ring rather than give herself to di Luna, and Manrico turns out to be di Luna's own brother.

**"Libiamo ne' lieti calici"**
The drinking song (brindisi) sung by Alfredo and Violetta at the party in Act I of La traviata. The same act ends with Violetta's showpiece aria "Sempre libera," during which Alfredo's voice is heard singing of love in the distance. In the last act, the reunited lovers sing "Gran Dio! Morir sì giovine" ("Great God! To die so young").

**Un ballo in maschera (A Masked Ball)**
An opera about the assassination of King Gustav III of Sweden at a masked ball. Censors forced Verdi to move the setting to colonial Boston, where the king becomes Governor Riccardo. The fortune-teller Ulrica predicts that Riccardo will be killed by the next man who shakes his hand, who turns out to be his friend Renato.

**La forza del destino (The Force of Destiny)**
An opera based on the Spanish play Don Álvaro, o la fuerza del sino. Leonora, daughter of the Marquis of Calatrava, loves Don Álvaro, who accidentally kills her father when his thrown pistol goes off. Its overture opens with three unison E's in the brass.

**Otello**
Verdi's late opera based on Shakespeare's Othello, with a libretto by Arrigo Boito. It opens in a storm with Otello's entrance aria "Esultate!", in which he celebrates the defeat of "the Muslim's pride." In Act IV, Desdemona sings the "Willow Song," repeating "Salce," before her "Ave Maria."

**Requiem**
Verdi's Messa da Requiem (1874), written in memory of the novelist Alessandro Manzoni. Its Dies irae alternates loud G minor orchestral chords with offbeat bass drum strokes, and its Tuba mirum features trumpet fanfares, including offstage trumpets.

**Don Carlos**
A grand opera based on Friedrich Schiller's play about Don Carlos, the son of King Philip II of Spain. It ends with a figure who seems to be the ghost of Carlos's grandfather, Emperor Charles V, pulling Carlos into the cloister of a monastery.

**"Caro nome"**
Gilda's aria in Rigoletto, in which she dreams of her disguised lover, actually the Duke. It is accompanied by two flutes and is a coloratura showpiece for the soprano.

**"Ritorna vincitor!"**
Aida's aria ("Return victorious!"), in which she is torn between her love for Radamès, who is leading Egypt's army, and her loyalty to her father and her Ethiopian homeland.

**Peer Gynt**
Grieg's incidental music (1875–76) for Henrik Ibsen's verse play about the boastful, wandering Norwegian Peer Gynt. Grieg later arranged parts of it into two orchestral suites, and it is the most common giveaway for him.

**"In the Hall of the Mountain King"**
The famous closing number of Peer Gynt Suite No. 1, set in the hall of the Troll King in the Dovre mountains (Dovrefjell). Cellos and basses play a quiet, tiptoeing B minor theme pizzicato, with bassoons, representing Peer sneaking through the hall. The theme repeats again and again, getting louder and faster, until the trolls chase him in a frenzied prestissimo ending.

**"Morning Mood"**
The opening piece of Peer Gynt Suite No. 1, which depicts a sunrise. In the play, it is actually set in the Moroccan desert. The flute and oboe trade a gentle pentatonic melody in 6/8 time (beginning B, G-sharp, F-sharp, E, F-sharp, G-sharp) that builds to a full orchestral sunrise.

**"The Death of Åse" and "Anitra's Dance"**
The other two pieces of Peer Gynt Suite No. 1. "The Death of Åse" is a mournful piece for strings depicting the death of Peer's mother, and "Anitra's Dance" is a light, exotic mazurka-like dance by the Bedouin chief's daughter who tries to seduce Peer.

**"Solveig's Song," "Ingrid's Lament," and "Arabian Dance"**
Pieces from Peer Gynt Suite No. 2. "Solveig's Song" is sung by the faithful woman who waits her whole life for Peer to return, "Ingrid's Lament" is the bride Peer abducts and abandons, and the "Arabian Dance" comes from Peer's adventures in North Africa.

**Piano Concerto in A minor**
Grieg's only completed concerto (1868), modeled on Robert Schumann's Piano Concerto in the same key, and the two are often recorded together. It opens with a crescendoing timpani roll, after which the soloist plunges down the keyboard in a flourish of falling seconds and thirds. Its finale is based on the halling, a lively Norwegian folk dance.

**Lyric Pieces**
Grieg's collection of 66 short piano pieces published in ten books between 1867 and 1901. They are character pieces in a song-like, often folk-influenced style, and include "To Spring," "Butterfly," "Bell Ringing" (in which the left hand repeats ringing open fifths), and pieces based on the halling dance.

**"Arietta" and "Remembrances"**
The first and last of the Lyric Pieces. The gentle opening "Arietta" (Op. 12, No. 1) has a melody beginning with repeated Gs, and Grieg reused that melody as a nostalgic waltz in "Remembrances" (Op. 71, No. 7), which closes the entire collection decades later.

**"Wedding Day at Troldhaugen"**
A festive Lyric Piece written for Grieg's 25th wedding anniversary with his wife, the singer Nina Hagerup. Troldhaugen was their villa near Grieg's hometown of Bergen. It begins with alternating D–A chords between the hands in a long-short-short-long rhythm.

**"March of the Dwarfs" ("March of the Trolls")**
A Lyric Piece (Op. 54, No. 3) that opens with quickly repeated staccato D and A notes and a descending chromatic line representing the small marching creatures.

**Holberg Suite (From Holberg's Time)**
A neoclassical suite "in olden style," written in 1884 for the 200th anniversary of the birth of Ludvig Holberg, the Danish-Norwegian playwright of Jeppe on the Hill. It was originally for piano and later arranged for string orchestra. It imitates a Baroque dance suite with a Prelude, Sarabande, Gavotte, an Air marked "Andante religioso" (often compared to Bach's Air on the G String), and a closing Rigaudon.

**Lyric Suite**
An orchestral suite drawn from the fifth book of the Lyric Pieces (Op. 54), including "Shepherd Boy," "Norwegian Rustic March," "Nocturne," and "March of the Dwarfs." The conductor Anton Seidl first orchestrated four of the pieces, and Grieg then revised the arrangement.

**Slåtter and Percy Grainger**
Slåtter (Op. 72) are Grieg's piano transcriptions of Norwegian peasant fiddle dances. He said that his devoted champion, the Australian pianist Percy Grainger, was the only one who played them with the right feeling. Grieg also used folk melodies collected by Ludvig Lindeman, for example in his Symphonic Dances.

**Haugtussa**
Grieg's only song cycle, setting poems by Arne Garborg about a young girl in the Norwegian mountains who can see supernatural beings. It is written for voice (usually mezzo-soprano or soprano) and piano.

**Funeral March for Rikard Nordraak**
A funeral march Grieg wrote for his friend Rikard Nordraak, a young nationalist composer who died at age 23 and who composed the music to Norway's national anthem, "Ja, vi elsker."

**Impression, Sunrise and Louis Leroy**
The movement took its name from Claude Monet's 1872 painting Impression, Sunrise, a hazy, sketch-like view of an orange sun rising over the harbor of Le Havre, Monet's hometown, with small fishing boats in the foreground. The critic Louis Leroy mocked it in a satirical review of the artists' first group exhibition in 1874, calling them "Impressionists" and claiming a preliminary drawing for a wallpaper pattern was more finished than the painting.

**Claude Monet's Water Lilies and Giverny**
Monet, the movement's leading figure, spent his last decades painting the water garden at his home in Giverny, including its Japanese footbridge, in a series of roughly 250 Water Lilies paintings, some of them huge mural-like canvases. His later works became more yellowish and abstract as his cataracts worsened.

**Monet's series paintings**
Monet painted the same subject repeatedly under changing light, weather, and seasons to capture fleeting effects. His series include the Haystacks (grainstacks), Rouen Cathedral, Poplars (he paid to delay the felling of the trees so he could finish), and the Houses of Parliament in London.

**Luncheon of the Boating Party**
Pierre-Auguste Renoir's 1881 painting of his friends eating and drinking on a balcony at the Maison Fournaise restaurant on the Seine, under an orange-and-white striped awning. At left, his future wife, the seamstress Aline Charigot, plays with a small dog, while the painter Gustave Caillebotte sits at right in a white sleeveless shirt beside empty wine glasses.

**The Child's Bath**
Mary Cassatt's 1893 painting, influenced by Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock prints, showing a mother in a striped dress holding a child on her lap and washing its feet in a basin of water. Cassatt, an American who worked in Paris, specialized in intimate scenes of mothers and children.

**Little Girl in a Blue Armchair**
Mary Cassatt's 1878 painting of a bored young girl sprawled in one of several blue armchairs, with a small dog sleeping on another chair. Edgar Degas, Cassatt's friend and mentor, reportedly helped work on the background.

**Other Mary Cassatt works**
Cassatt painted her sister Lydia in an opera box with a mirror reflecting the auditorium in Lydia in a Loge, Wearing a Pearl Necklace, and her mother Katherine reading a newspaper in Reading "Le Figaro." She also painted The Coiffure (a woman putting up her hair, inspired by Japanese prints), The Boating Party, and the early Spanish Dancer Wearing a Lace Mantilla.

**Berthe Morisot and The Cradle**
Berthe Morisot, one of the movement's "three grandes dames," painted The Cradle (1872), in which her sister Edma watches over her sleeping baby through a gauzy white curtain draped over the cradle. Morisot also painted Woman and Child on a Balcony and was depicted by Édouard Manet, whose brother she later married, in The Balcony.

**Woman with a Parasol**
Monet's 1875 painting of his wife Camille Doncieux and their son on a breezy hillside, with Camille half-turned toward the viewer and silhouetted against a bright blue sky. Camille was a frequent model for Monet.

**American Impressionism and The Ten**
Impressionism spread to the United States through artists like Mary Cassatt and the group "Ten American Painters," which included William Merritt Chase and Childe Hassam. Hassam, nicknamed "Muley," signed his works with a crescent and painted New York scenes, including American flags hanging along Fifth Avenue in the rain in The Avenue in the Rain. John Singer Sargent blended Impressionism with realism in Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose, showing two girls lighting paper lanterns among flowers.

**Edgar Degas**
A founding member of the group exhibitions who disliked the name "Impressionist" and preferred to be called a realist. His works include L'Absinthe (a downcast woman staring at her drink beside a pipe-smoking man), The Bellelli Family, A Cotton Office in New Orleans, and many paintings of ballet dancers.

**Alfred Sisley**
A British-born painter in France, often called the "forgotten Impressionist," who devoted himself almost entirely to plein air landscapes. His works include Molesey Weir, Morning, The Bridge at Hampton Court (often with boaters), and views of the Thames.

**En plein air painting and visible brushwork**
Impressionists often painted outdoors ("en plein air") to capture changing natural light, using quick, visible, sketch-like brushstrokes, bright colors, and avoiding black paint. Other examples include Monet's snowscape The Magpie, showing a magpie perched on a wooden gate.

**Other Renoir works**
Renoir painted The Swing, in which a girl in a white dress with blue bows stands on a swing in dappled sunlight, Two Sisters (On the Terrace) at the Maison Fournaise, and Girls at the Piano. His work is the target of the satirical online group "Renoir Sucks at Painting," whose members pose in protest in front of his works.

**Heidelberg School and Marie Bracquemond**
The Heidelberg School was an Australian offshoot of Impressionism, including artists like Arthur Streeton and Jane Sutherland. Marie Bracquemond, the third of the "grandes dames," was discouraged from painting by her husband Félix Bracquemond, whose discovery of Hokusai prints used as packing material helped spark the French craze for Japonisme.

**Futurism and Unique Forms of Continuity in Space**
An Italian avant-garde movement launched by F. T. Marinetti's 1909 manifesto, which praised speed, machines, and violence, called war "the world's only hygiene," and declared that "a roaring automobile... is more beautiful than the Victory of Samothrace." Umberto Boccioni's armless bronze striding figure, Unique Forms of Continuity in Space, is its icon, and he also painted the States of Mind series and sculpted Development of a Bottle in Space. Other Futurists include Giacomo Balla, who painted Street Light and Girl Running on a Balcony, and Gino Severini, who painted Armored Train in Action.

**Antonio Vivaldi and The Four Seasons**
A Venetian Baroque composer who taught at the Ospedale della Pietà, an orphanage for girls. The Four Seasons is a set of four violin concertos in his collection The Contest Between Harmony and Invention, each with an accompanying sonnet. "Spring" includes a viola imitating a barking dog, and "Summer" ends with a violent storm. He also wrote the oratorio Juditha triumphans and concertos nicknamed "The Storm at Sea" and "Pleasure."

**Bicycle Thieves and Italian Neorealism**
Neorealism was a movement of the 1940s and 1950s that made films about the poor and working class in postwar Italy, often shot on location with non-professional actors. In Vittorio De Sica's Bicycle Thieves, a poor man hired to hang posters of Rita Hayworth has his bicycle stolen and searches Rome for it with his son, Bruno. Roberto Rossellini's Rome, Open City, set under Nazi occupation, includes the famous scene of Pina, the fiancée of a Resistance member, running after a truck with her arm outstretched.

**Federico Fellini's La Dolce Vita and 8½**
La Dolce Vita ("The Sweet Life") opens with a helicopter carrying a statue of Christ over Rome. Its most famous scene shows the actress Sylvia (Anita Ekberg) wading into the Trevi Fountain and calling to the gossip journalist Marcello. 8½ opens with a director trapped in a smoke-filled car in a traffic jam who climbs out and floats into the sky. The film follows that director as he struggles with creative block while trying to make his next film.

**Niccolò Paganini**
A legendary Italian violin virtuoso whose 24 Caprices for solo violin include ones nicknamed "The Hunt," "The Trill," and "The Devil's Laughter." He asked Hector Berlioz for a viola piece, which became the symphony Harold in Italy, based on Byron's Childe Harold's Pilgrimage. Paganini then refused to play it because the solo viola part had too many rests.

**Ottorino Respighi's Roman trilogy**
Respighi wrote three tone poems about Rome: Fountains of Rome, Pines of Rome, and Roman Festivals. Pines of Rome ends with "The Pines of the Appian Way," in which offstage buccine, usually played by flugelhorns, depict a Roman army. He also arranged old lute music in Ancient Airs and Dances.

**Maurizio Cattelan**
A provocative contemporary Italian artist. His Comedian is a real banana duct-taped to a wall, America is a working solid-gold toilet installed at the Guggenheim, and L.O.V.E. is a giant marble hand raising its middle finger outside the Milan stock exchange.

**Giorgio de Chirico**
The founder of Metaphysical painting, whose eerie, empty piazzas influenced Surrealism. The Song of Love sets a classical statue's head beside a red rubber glove and a green ball, and The Mystery and Melancholy of a Street shows a girl rolling a hoop down a deserted street.

**Titian and Venetian painting**
Venice was a major Renaissance painting center. Titian painted the Venus of Urbino, in which a nude goddess reclines with a dog at her feet while maids dig through a chest behind her. He also painted Bacchus and Ariadne, Sacred and Profane Love, and the off-center Pesaro Madonna, and the Pastoral Concert once credited to Giorgione is now often given to him. Tintoretto, another Venetian, painted The Miracle of the Slave and a diagonal Last Supper.

**Gian Lorenzo Bernini's Ecstasy of Saint Teresa**
A Baroque marble sculpture in Rome. An angel holding a spear stands over the swooning Saint Teresa of Ávila, while gilded bronze rays of light fall behind them.

**Sergio Leone, Pier Paolo Pasolini, and giallo**
Sergio Leone directed "spaghetti westerns" such as The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, whose climax uses Ennio Morricone's "The Ecstasy of Gold." Pasolini adapted the Marquis de Sade in Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom, which is divided into sections such as the "Circle of Manias" and "Circle of Blood," and he was murdered in 1975, shortly before it was released. Giallo, a genre of lurid murder-mystery thrillers, is named for the Italian word for "yellow." Michelangelo Antonioni, another Italian director, made Blow-Up, about a photographer who thinks he has photographed a murder in a park.

**Gioachino Rossini and Giacomo Puccini**
Two leading Italian opera composers. Rossini wrote The Thieving Magpie, in which the servant Ninetta is accused of stealing a silver spoon that a magpie actually took, and William Tell, whose overture ends with a famous galloping "cavalry charge." Puccini's Tosca, set in Rome, features the villainous police chief Baron Scarpia and the painter Cavaradossi.

**Palestrina and Italian musical terminology**
Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina composed the Pope Marcellus Mass in a clear polyphonic style that let the words be understood. Opera and the concerto both began in Italy, and Italian became the standard language for musical terms and tempo markings. The "Neapolitan" chord, a major chord on the lowered second scale degree, is named for Naples. Other key Italian composers include Arcangelo Corelli, whose Christmas Concerto ends with a pastorale, Domenico Scarlatti, who wrote 555 keyboard sonatas including the "Cat Fugue," and Luigi Boccherini, who wrote a famous Minuet and Night Music of the Streets of Madrid.

**Renzo Piano and the Uffizi**
Renzo Piano, with Gianfranco Franchini and Richard Rogers, designed the "inside-out" Centre Pompidou in Paris, with color-coded pipes and escalators on its outside. Piano also designed the California Academy of Sciences, with its green roof of grassy mounds. In Florence, Giorgio Vasari designed the Uffizi as offices for city magistrates, along with the hidden Vasari Corridor that connects it across the river to the Pitti Palace.

**Ballet in Italy**
Ballet began in Italian Renaissance courts in the 1400s and 1500s before spreading to France. The Italian ballet master Enrico Cecchetti created a strict training method of set daily exercises, and the Italian ballerina Carlotta Grisi danced the title role at the premiere of Giselle. The top ranks for female dancers, prima ballerina and prima ballerina assoluta, are Italian phrases, and Prokofiev's ballet Romeo and Juliet is set in Italy.

**Odette and Odile**
The ballet's two lead female roles, traditionally danced by the same ballerina. Odette is the princess cursed to be a swan by day and a woman only at night, costumed in white; Odile is the sorcerer's daughter disguised as her look-alike and costumed in black. The ballet's acts are often divided into "white acts" (the lakeside scenes) and "black acts" (the ball).

**Von Rothbart**
The evil sorcerer (sometimes called Baron von Rothbart or a "bird-sorcerer") who places the swan curse on Odette. He sometimes appears in the form of an owl, and at the Act III ball he presents his daughter Odile, disguised as Odette, to trick the prince.

**Prince Siegfried**
The male protagonist, who is told on his 21st birthday that he must choose a bride. He receives a crossbow as a birthday present, goes hunting, finds Odette at the lake, and falls in love with her, but at the ball he is tricked into swearing his love to Odile instead.

**32 fouettés**
The famous series of thirty-two consecutive whipping turns (fouettés en tournant) performed by Odile in the coda of the Act III "Black Swan" pas de deux. The feat was introduced by the Italian ballerina Pierina Legnani, who starred in the 1895 revival.

**Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov**
The choreographers of the 1895 St. Petersburg revival at the Mariinsky Theatre, the basis of nearly all modern productions. Ivanov choreographed the lakeside "white" acts, including the dances of the swans, while Petipa handled the court scenes.

**Riccardo Drigo**
The Italian conductor and composer who revised and rearranged Tchaikovsky's score for the 1895 revival, after Tchaikovsky's death in 1893. Among other changes, he reordered numbers, such as moving music from one act to another.

**Benno and Wolfgang**
Siegfried's companions in Act I. Benno (sometimes Benno von Sommerstern) is his best friend who goes hunting with him, and Wolfgang is his tutor, who gets drunk at the birthday celebration. Some productions cut Benno or replace him with a jester.

**Dance of the Little Swans**
A famous Act II dance (the "Danse des petits cygnes") choreographed by Lev Ivanov, in which four dancers with interlocked arms perform sixteen pas de chat in unison. It is meant to evoke young swans huddling together, and in some versions the dancers break apart and fall at the end.

**Act III national dances**
At the ball where Siegfried must choose a bride, guests perform a set of character dances, including a Hungarian dance (csárdás), a Spanish dance, a Neapolitan dance, and a mazurka. Siegfried dances disinterestedly with his prospective brides before Odile arrives.

**Oboe "Scene" theme**
The ballet's famous leitmotif, a melancholy B minor oboe melody (F-sharp, B, C-sharp, D, E, F-sharp) played over string tremolos and harp. It closes Act I and opens Act II, and is often heard in concert as the "Scene" from Swan Lake.

**Lovers' death in the lake**
In the common ending, Siegfried and Odette throw themselves into the lake together, and their sacrifice breaks Rothbart's curse; some versions show them ascending into heaven. In the original libretto, the lake itself was formed from tears shed over Odette.

**Matthew Bourne**
The British choreographer whose 1995 reinterpretation replaced the female corps of swans with a cast of bare-chested male dancers. It became the longest-running ballet on Broadway and in London's West End.

**Julius Reisinger**
The choreographer of the original 1877 production at Moscow's Bolshoi Theatre, which was not a great success. The original lead was Pelageya Karpakova, and Anna Sobeshchanskaya later had an extra dance inserted for her by Ludwig Minkus.

**Dance of the Goblets**
A festive polonaise-style drinking dance that ends the celebrations of Act I. Afterward, Siegfried and his companions set off on the hunt that leads him to the lake.

**Undina, The Voyevoda, and Sylvia**
Tchaikovsky reused music from his abandoned operas Undina and The Voyevoda in this score, his first ballet (Op. 20). After hearing Léo Delibes's ballet Sylvia, he reportedly felt his own ballet paled in comparison.

**The Thinker**
Rodin's most famous sculpture: a muscular nude man seated on a rock, leaning forward with his chin resting on his fist (often described as his right elbow resting on his left knee). It was created for the top of The Gates of Hell, where it originally represented Dante (titled The Poet) contemplating his poem, and it was later enlarged as an independent work.

**The Gates of Hell**
A monumental bronze portal inspired by Dante's Inferno, commissioned in 1880 for a planned Museum of Decorative Arts in Paris that was never built. Rodin worked on it for decades and never fully finished it. Its roughly 180 figures served as the source for many of his independent sculptures, including The Thinker, The Kiss, and Ugolino.

**The Kiss**
A marble sculpture of the nude lovers Paolo and Francesca da Rimini from Dante's Inferno, embracing as they begin their adulterous kiss; Paolo holds a book in one hand, recalling that they fell in love while reading about Lancelot. It was first conceived for The Gates of Hell, but Rodin removed it because its happy mood did not fit the work.

**The Burghers of Calais**
A bronze group of six leading citizens of Calais who, during the Hundred Years' War siege of 1347, offered their lives to England's Edward III to save their city. They are shown barefoot with nooses around their necks; Eustache de Saint-Pierre is the bearded elder and Jean d'Aire holds the city's key. Rodin set the figures at ground level rather than on a heroic pedestal.

**Camille Claudel**
A sculptor who was Rodin's student, assistant, and lover. After their breakup she became convinced Rodin was stealing her ideas, destroyed many of her own works, and spent her last thirty years in an asylum. Her sculpture The Mature Age is read as Rodin choosing his longtime companion Rose Beuret over her, and Rodin's marble Thought shows Claudel's head, in a bonnet, emerging from a rough block.

**Ugolino and His Sons**
A group from The Gates of Hell showing Count Ugolino, whom Dante places in hell, crouching on all fours over his dying sons and grandsons. In the Inferno, the archbishop Ruggieri had them locked in a tower to starve, and Ugolino is implied to have eaten his children's bodies.

**The Three Shades**
Three identical male nudes standing with bowed heads and their left arms reaching toward a common point, placed on top of The Gates of Hell above The Thinker. They are the shades of the damned, and are often linked to the inscription Dante sees over the gate of hell, "Abandon all hope, ye who enter here."

**The Age of Bronze**
A life-size nude of a young man raising one hand to his head, partly influenced by Michelangelo's Dying Slave. It was so lifelike that critics accused Rodin of casting it directly from a living model, a scandal that shaped his later work.

**Saint John the Baptist Preaching and The Walking Man**
Partly to answer the Age of Bronze accusations, Rodin made his striding Saint John the Baptist Preaching larger than life. The Walking Man is a related, deliberately unfinished figure with no head or arms, standing with both feet on the ground in mid-stride.

**Monument to Balzac**
A statue of the novelist Honoré de Balzac, commissioned by the Société des Gens de Lettres, showing him wrapped in a huge, shapeless dressing gown with a massive neck and head. Critics mocked it, comparing it to a sack of coal, and the commissioning society rejected it in 1898. Edward Steichen photographed the plaster by moonlight, including The Silhouette, 4 A.M.

**Man with the Broken Nose**
An early mask of a handyman called Bibi with a battered face. The back of the clay head froze and broke off in Rodin's cold studio, leaving only a mask, and the Paris Salon rejected it in 1864. It reflects Rodin's interest in fragments and unfinished forms.

**I Am Beautiful**
A group from The Gates of Hell in which a standing man lifts a crouching woman in the air, like Atlas supporting the heavens. Its base is inscribed with lines from Baudelaire's poem "La Beauté," beginning "I am beautiful, O mortals, like a dream of stone."

**Rose Beuret**
Rodin's lifelong companion and the mother of his son. She modeled for early works such as Mignon and the Young Woman in a Flowered Hat. Rodin finally married her in January 1917; she died weeks later, and Rodin died later that year.

**Cleveland Thinker and Philadelphia Rodin Museum**
In 1970 a bomb, attributed to the radical Weather Underground, badly damaged the cast of The Thinker outside the Cleveland Museum of Art, which still displays it unrepaired. The Rodin Museum in Philadelphia was founded by the theater magnate Jules Mastbaum.

**Rainer Maria Rilke and Hanako**
The poet Rilke worked for a time as Rodin's secretary and wrote a monograph on him; their friendship is the subject of Rachel Corbett's book You Must Change Your Life. Rodin also made dozens of studies of the face of the Japanese actress Hanako, a former geisha.

**Les Demoiselles d'Avignon**
Picasso's 1907 painting of five nude prostitutes in a brothel on the Carrer d'Avinyó in Barcelona. Their angular faces were inspired by African masks and Iberian sculpture. A squatting woman with her back to the viewer and a basket of fruit at the bottom are common clues. The painting is seen as the forerunner of Cubism, and Picasso long referred to it as "my brothel."

**Guernica**
Picasso's huge 1937 black-and-white mural protesting the bombing of the Basque town of Guernica by the German Luftwaffe during the Spanish Civil War. It features a screaming horse, a bull, a mother wailing over her dead child, a jagged lightbulb shaped like an eye, and a severed arm holding a broken sword with a flower growing beside it.

**African masks / primitivism**
Picasso's "African period" (around 1907–1909) drew on African masks and sculpture he saw at the ethnographic museum at the Trocadéro in Paris. This primitivist influence is most evident in the faces of Les Demoiselles d'Avignon.

**Cubism and Georges Braque**
Picasso co-founded Cubism with the French painter Georges Braque, who was impressed and challenged by Les Demoiselles d'Avignon. Cubism breaks objects into geometric facets and shows several viewpoints at once. It developed from an "analytic" phase into a "synthetic" phase that used flatter shapes and collage.

**Blue Period and The Old Guitarist**
From about 1901 to 1904, Picasso painted melancholy scenes of poverty and despair in mostly blue tones. The Old Guitarist, showing an emaciated, blind man with his head bowed over his guitar, is its most famous work. The Tragedy, showing a dejected family on a beach, is another example.

**Carles Casagemas**
Picasso's close friend, who shot himself in 1901 after a failed love affair. Picasso painted The Death of Casagemas (with a candle glowing in vivid colors), and the suicide is often said to have triggered the Blue Period. Casagemas's features also appear on the artist figure in La Vie.

**La Vie**
A 1903 Blue Period painting in which a man with Casagemas's features, holding a nude woman leaning on his shoulder, faces a woman in a blue robe who cradles an infant.

**Rose Period and Family of Saltimbanques**
From about 1904 to 1906, Picasso used warmer pink and orange tones and painted circus performers, harlequins, and acrobats. Major works include Family of Saltimbanques and Acrobat and Young Harlequin.

**Three Musicians**
A 1921 Synthetic Cubist painting showing a harlequin with a guitar, a Pierrot, and a monk playing instruments. Picasso painted two versions of it.

**Boy with a Pipe**
A 1905 Rose Period painting of a Parisian boy wearing a garland of flowers and holding a pipe, posed in front of a wall decorated with floral shapes. It later sold for over $100 million at auction.

**Parade**
A 1917 ballet for Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, with music by Erik Satie and a scenario by Jean Cocteau. Picasso designed its drop curtain and its Cubist costumes, including skyscraper-like "Managers." He met his first wife, the dancer Olga Khokhlova, while working on it.

**The Weeping Woman**
A 1937 series of paintings related to Guernica, showing Picasso's lover, the photographer Dora Maar, crying in fractured, brightly colored forms. Some versions show glassy, crystal-like tears on her cheek.

**Dove of Peace**
Picasso's lithograph of a dove was chosen as the emblem of the 1949 World Peace Congress in Paris. He drew many later doves, some holding olive branches, which became international peace symbols.

**Portrait of Gertrude Stein**
Picasso's 1905–1906 portrait of the American writer and art collector Gertrude Stein, shown seated and brooding. He famously struggled with the face and finished it with a mask-like look influenced by Iberian sculpture.

**Don Quixote sketch**
A 1955 ink sketch showing the gaunt Don Quixote on his spindly horse Rocinante, holding a lance and shield, with Sancho Panza and windmills in the background.

**Moonlight Sonata**
Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 14 in C-sharp minor (Op. 27, No. 2), subtitled "quasi una fantasia." Its slow first movement (Adagio sostenuto) is built on soft, repeated triplet arpeggios and is marked "senza sordino," which means the damper pedal is held down throughout. The critic Ludwig Rellstab compared the movement to moonlight reflecting on Lake Lucerne, which gave the piece its nickname. Its third movement is a stormy Presto agitato of rising C-sharp minor arpeggios. Liszt called the middle movement "a flower between two abysses."

**32 piano sonatas**
Beethoven's set of 32 piano sonatas is a cornerstone of the repertoire, and Artur Schnabel made the first complete recording of it. Nicknamed sonatas include the "Pathétique," "Moonlight," "Waldstein" (No. 21, dedicated to Count Waldstein), "Appassionata," and "Les Adieux" (No. 26). The "Les Adieux" sonata has three movements, "The Farewell," "The Absence," and "The Return," and the syllables "Le-be-wohl" are written over its first three chords.

**"Ode to Joy"**
Friedrich Schiller's poem, which Beethoven set in the choral finale of his Ninth Symphony. The text praises a "spark of divinity" and "daughter of Elysium" and celebrates universal brotherhood. The bass soloist first enters with the recitative "O friends, not these tones!" In 1989, Leonard Bernstein conducted the symphony to celebrate the fall of the Berlin Wall, changing the word "Freude" (joy) to "Freiheit" (freedom).

**Symphony No. 9 ("Choral")**
Beethoven's final symphony, in D minor, which he wrote while almost completely deaf. It unusually puts the scherzo second and adds four vocal soloists and a chorus in the finale, which also includes a "Turkish march." His earlier Choral Fantasy anticipated its finale. Wagner chose it to celebrate the laying of the Bayreuth Festspielhaus foundation stone in 1872.

**1824 premiere of the Ninth Symphony**
The symphony premiered in 1824 at Vienna's Kärntnertor Theater, with Michael Umlauf as the actual conductor. The deaf Beethoven stood beating time and had to be turned around to see the audience applauding. The soloists included Henriette Sontag and Caroline Unger, and the concert also included the Consecration of the House Overture.

**Symphony No. 5**
Beethoven's C minor symphony (Op. 67). It opens with the "short-short-short-long" motif that is often described as "fate knocking at the door." The scherzo leads without a pause (attacca) into a triumphant C major finale, which adds piccolo, contrabassoon, and three trombones and ends with a long run of C major chords.

**Eroica Symphony**
Beethoven's Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major. It opens with two forte E-flat chords, includes a C minor funeral march as its second movement, and is often called the start of musical Romanticism. Beethoven scratched out its dedication to Napoleon after Napoleon crowned himself emperor, and replaced it with "composed to celebrate the memory of a great man." The finale's variations use the same contredanse theme as his Eroica Variations, Op. 35.

**Pathétique Sonata**
Piano Sonata No. 8 in C minor, dedicated to Prince Karl Lichnowsky. Its first movement alternates a slow Grave introduction with a fast Allegro di molto e con brio, and its Adagio cantabile second movement has a famous A-flat major theme. Elgar said the opening of "Nimrod" was a "hint" of this Adagio. C minor is often called Beethoven's most dramatic key.

**Für Elise**
Beethoven's Bagatelle No. 25 in A minor, dedicated to an unidentified "Elise." It begins with the right hand alternating E and D-sharp, and it is one of the most popular pieces for piano students.

**Hammerklavier Sonata**
Piano Sonata No. 29 in B-flat major, which opens with fortissimo B-flat major chords. It ends with a huge three-voice fugue whose subject begins with a leaping tenth. It was long considered unplayable until Franz Liszt performed it in public.

**Piano Sonata No. 32 and its "Arietta"**
Beethoven's final piano sonata, in C minor, has only two movements and is dedicated to Archduke Rudolf. Its second movement, the "Arietta," is a set of variations in time signatures such as 9/16 and 12/32, and its syncopated rhythms led the pianist Jeremy Denk to call it "proto-jazz."

**Pastoral Symphony**
Beethoven's Symphony No. 6, a programmatic work depicting country life. Its second movement, "Scene by the Brook," ends with woodwinds imitating a nightingale, a quail, and a cuckoo. A fourth-movement "Thunderstorm," the only movement that uses timpani, interrupts the "Merry Gathering of Country Folk."

**String quartets**
Beethoven's quartets include the three "Razumovsky" quartets, the "Harp" and "Serioso" quartets, and six late quartets. The late quartets include the seven-movement C-sharp minor quartet, Op. 131, and the A minor quartet, Op. 132, whose slow movement in the Lydian mode is the "Heiliger Dankgesang." The Grosse Fuge was originally the finale of the Op. 130 quartet.

**Heiligenstadt Testament**
A letter Beethoven wrote in 1802 to his brothers, in which he despairs over his growing deafness but resolves to keep living for the sake of his art. It is often linked to the beginning of his heroic "middle period," including the Eroica.

**An die ferne Geliebte**
"To the Distant Beloved," a set of six songs often considered the first true song cycle. The songs are played without a break, and the cycle ends by returning to the melody of the first song. Beethoven's other vocal works include the song "Adelaide" and his only opera, Fidelio, which features the "Prisoners' Chorus."

**The Course of Empire**
Cole's five-painting series (1833–1836) depicting the rise and fall of an imaginary civilization in the same valley, commissioned by New York merchant Luman Reed. The paintings are The Savage State (hunters in a wilderness), The Arcadian or Pastoral State, The Consummation of Empire, Destruction, and Desolation. A distinctive rocky crag topped by a boulder appears in the background of every painting to identify the setting.

**The Oxbow**
Cole's most famous painting (1836), formally View from Mount Holyoke, Northampton, Massachusetts, after a Thunderstorm. The left side shows dark storm clouds over untamed wilderness and shattered trees, while the right side shows sunlit cultivated farmland along the dramatic oxbow-shaped bend of the Connecticut River, contrasting wilderness and civilization.

**Hudson River School**
The mid-19th-century movement of American Romantic landscape painters, named for the Hudson River Valley of New York, of which Cole is considered the founder. Other members included Asher Durand, Frederic Edwin Church (Cole's student), and Albert Bierstadt.

**Destruction**
The fourth painting of The Course of Empire, showing invaders sacking the classical city amid a storm. A bridge collapses under a fleeing crowd, and a headless statue posed like the ancient Borghese Gladiator lunges forward holding a chipped shield; Cole's signature appears on its pedestal.

**Desolation**
The final painting of The Course of Empire, showing the moonlit ruins of the abandoned city reclaimed by nature, with no humans present. A single ivy-covered column, topped by a bird's nest, dominates the foreground.

**"Noah" in Hebrew and the self-portrait in The Oxbow**
Logging scars on the distant hillside of The Oxbow appear to spell "Noah" (נח) in Hebrew letters, which read upside down (as from heaven) resemble "Shaddai," meaning "the Almighty." Cole also included a tiny self-portrait of himself at his easel among the rocks and shrubbery at the bottom of the painting, looking out at the viewer.

**The Voyage of Life**
Cole's four-painting allegorical series (1840, Childhood, Youth, Manhood, Old Age) following a voyager in a boat down the river of life, accompanied by a guardian angel. In Childhood an infant emerges from a cave in a golden boat; in Youth a young man steers toward a castle in the clouds; in Old Age an old man looks toward heaven as light breaks through. The series was popularized by engravings by James Smillie.

**Kindred Spirits**
An 1849 painting by Asher Durand made as a tribute after Cole's death, showing Cole and the poet William Cullen Bryant standing together on a rock ledge overlooking a gorge in the Catskills. It was sold by the New York Public Library to Alice Walton and is now at the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art.

**The Titan's Goblet**
An 1833 fantasy painting of a colossal stone goblet standing in a landscape, its rim covered with vegetation and small buildings, while tiny sailboats float on the water inside it.

**The Architect's Dream**
An 1840 painting in which a man (the architect) reclines on a column atop giant books, gazing at an imaginary panorama of architecture from different eras, including an Egyptian pyramid, a Greek temple, and a Gothic cathedral.

**"Essay on American Scenery"**
Cole's 1836 essay praising the American wilderness as a source of the sublime and lamenting its destruction by development. It ends by warning that through "ignorance and folly" we are shutting ourselves out of "the walls of Eden."

**Expulsion from the Garden of Eden**
An 1828 painting in which Adam and Eve leave the radiant Garden of Eden through a rocky gate into a dark, hostile world, with a volcano erupting in the background.

**The Departure and The Return**
A pair of 1837 paintings depicting a medieval lord and his knights riding out from a castle in the morning light, then returning wounded and defeated at sunset.

**L'Allegro and Il Penseroso**
A pair of 1845 paintings inspired by John Milton's companion poems, contrasting a cheerful pastoral landscape with a melancholy, contemplative one near Lake Nemi in Italy, in which a woman kneels before an outdoor shrine of the Virgin and Child.

**Scene from The Last of the Mohicans**
Cole painted several scenes from James Fenimore Cooper's novel, including one showing a circular gathering of figures on top of a mountain plateau surrounded by vast wilderness. He also painted Daniel Boone sitting at the door of his cabin with a staff and a dog.

**Grant Wood**
The Iowa-born American Regionalist painter who created American Gothic in 1930. Other Wood paintings that come up include Woman with Plants, a portrait of his mother.

**Man holding a pitchfork**
The painting's male figure, a bespectacled, balding farmer in a black coat, collarless shirt, and denim overalls, grips a three-pronged pitchfork (hay fork) in his right hand and stares directly at the viewer.

**Dibble House in Eldon, Iowa**
The small white house in the background is based on a real house in Eldon, Iowa, which Wood saw in 1930. It is now a tourist site known as the American Gothic House.

**Gothic arched window**
The title comes from the pointed-arch window in the house's upper gable. It is in the Carpenter Gothic style, a 19th-century American version of Gothic Revival architecture built in wood. The window has a patterned curtain.

**Nan Wood Graham (artist's sister)**
Wood's sister Nan modeled for the woman. She insisted that the figures were a farmer and his daughter, not husband and wife, and Wood also described them that way. The woman looks off to the side rather than at the viewer.

**Dr. Byron McKeeby (artist's dentist)**
Wood's 62-year-old dentist from Cedar Rapids, Iowa, who modeled for the farmer. Wood's signature appears on the man's overalls at the bottom of the painting.

**Colonial print apron and cameo brooch**
The woman wears a brown apron with a colonial-style print trimmed in rickrack, over a dark dress fastened with a cameo brooch. The cameo has been interpreted as showing Persephone.

**Repeated pitchfork motif**
The three-pronged shape of the pitchfork is echoed in the stitching of the man's overalls and shirt, the vertical lines of the Gothic window, the boards of the house, and the leaves of the plants behind the woman.

**Gordon Parks's American Gothic, Washington, D.C.**
A famous 1942 photograph by Gordon Parks that parodies the painting. It shows Ella Watson, an African-American government cleaning woman, standing in front of an American flag holding a mop and a broom, as a critique of racism.

**Potted plants on the porch**
Two potted plants appear on the porch behind the woman's shoulder, beneath a window with green blinds. They are a mother-in-law's tongue (snake plant) and a beefsteak begonia, and they also appear in Wood's Woman with Plants.

**Red barn and church steeple**
In the background, a red barn stands on the right side of the painting, while a church steeple rises above rounded, ball-like treetops.

**Art Institute of Chicago prize**
The painting won a bronze medal and a $300 prize in the Art Institute of Chicago's 1930 exhibition, after which the museum bought it. It is still there today. One judge reportedly dismissed it as a "comic valentine."

**Satire controversy**
Iowans initially took offense at the painting; one farm wife said Wood should have his "head bashed in." Gertrude Stein said "we should fear Grant Wood" for his "devastating satire," but Wood denied that he meant to mock his subjects. During the Depression the painting came to be read as a celebration of steadfast American pioneer values.

**Guy Davenport's "The Geography of the Imagination"**
In this essay, the writer Guy Davenport traces the cultural origins of every detail in the painting, such as the gingham curtains, the mail-order clothing, and the eyeglasses. He also reads the pair as echoes of Pluto and Proserpina.

**Kelly Grovier and Pluto**
The art critic Kelly Grovier argued that the painting alludes to the newly discovered planet Pluto (1930), noting the brooch, a cropped weathervane, and a small globe, and he identified the woman with Proserpina.

**The School of Athens**
Raphael's most famous fresco (c. 1509–1511), depicting the great thinkers of antiquity gathered beneath a grand barrel-vaulted classical arch. At the center, Plato (modeled on Leonardo da Vinci, holding the Timaeus) points upward toward the realm of Forms, while Aristotle (holding the Nicomachean Ethics) gestures forward and down toward the earth. Statues of Apollo and Athena (Minerva) stand in niches in the background.

**Figures in The School of Athens**
Euclid bends to draw a circle with a compass as students watch, Pythagoras writes in a book, and Diogenes of Sinope sprawls on the steps in a blue robe. A brooding Heraclitus, leaning on a marble block and writing, was added as a portrait of Michelangelo. At the right edge, Ptolemy and Zoroaster hold a terrestrial and celestial globe next to Raphael's own self-portrait.

**Stanza della Segnatura**
One of four rooms in the Vatican's Apostolic Palace, now called the Raphael Rooms (Stanze di Raffaello), that Pope Julius II commissioned Raphael to decorate. Its four walls depict Philosophy (The School of Athens), Theology (La Disputa), Poetry (The Parnassus), and Law (The Cardinal Virtues, in which Fortitude pets a lion, Temperance holds reins, and two-faced Prudence looks in a mirror).

**La Disputa**
The Disputation of the Holy Sacrament, the fresco facing The School of Athens in the Stanza della Segnatura. It is divided into a heavenly level, with Christ enthroned between Mary and John the Baptist, saints, and prophets on clouds, and an earthly level where theologians debate around an altar holding a monstrance with the Eucharist, symbolizing the doctrine of transubstantiation.

**Madonna of the Goldfinch**
A painting (c. 1505–1506) in which the young John the Baptist hands a goldfinch, a symbol of Christ's Passion, to the infant Jesus as the Virgin Mary looks up from a book. It shattered into about seventeen pieces when its owner's house collapsed in 1547 and was later restored. Raphael painted many other Madonnas, including the Madonna of the Meadow (Madonna del Prato) and La Belle Jardinière.

**Sistine Madonna**
An altarpiece (c. 1512) for the church of San Sisto in Piacenza, now in Dresden, showing the Virgin and Child standing barefoot on clouds between Pope Sixtus II and Saint Barbara. Two bored-looking cherubs leaning their arms on the ledge at the bottom have become one of the most reproduced images in art.

**The Parnassus**
A fresco in the Stanza della Segnatura showing Apollo playing a lira da braccio on Mount Parnassus, surrounded by the nine Muses and famous poets including Homer, Dante, and Sappho. Raphael based the face of the blind Homer on the head of Laocoön from the ancient sculpture Laocoön and His Sons, rediscovered in 1506.

**Perugino and The Marriage of the Virgin**
Raphael trained under Pietro Perugino, whose influence shows in his early works. His Marriage of the Virgin (Lo Sposalizio, 1504) closely resembles Perugino's version, with a domed temple in the background and a rejected suitor breaking his rod over his knee in the foreground. His first documented work was the Baronci Altarpiece, and the Oddi Altarpiece shows St. Thomas receiving Mary's girdle.

**Mond Crucifixion**
An early altarpiece (c. 1502–1503), heavily influenced by Perugino, showing Christ on the cross beneath an "INRI" sign, with two angels catching his blood in chalices, flanked by the sun and moon. It is now in the National Gallery, London.

**The Transfiguration**
Raphael's final painting, left unfinished at his death in 1520 and completed by his workshop. Its upper half shows Christ floating in glory on Mount Tabor, while the lower half shows the apostles failing to heal a possessed boy.

**The Triumph of Galatea**
A fresco (c. 1514) in the Villa Farnesina in Rome, commissioned by banker Agostino Chigi. The sea nymph Galatea in a red cloak rides a seashell chariot pulled by two dolphins, surrounded by Tritons, nereids, and cupids shooting arrows.

**Other Raphael Rooms frescoes**
Raphael and his workshop decorated the other Vatican stanze with The Expulsion of Heliodorus from the Temple (a heavenly horseman tramples a man stealing temple treasure), The Mass at Bolsena, and The Fire in the Borgo, in which Pope Leo IV extinguishes a fire and a man carries his father on his back like Aeneas with Anchises. After his death, his student Giulio Romano led the decoration of the Hall of Constantine.

**Portraits of Popes Julius II and Leo X**
Raphael's Portrait of Pope Julius II shows the aging pope seated pensively against a green background, holding a handkerchief. His Portrait of Leo X with Two Cardinals shows the pope in a red velvet cap holding a magnifying glass beside an illuminated book and a silver bell, flanked by two cardinals in red.

**Portrait of Baldassare Castiglione**
A portrait of Raphael's friend, the author of The Book of the Courtier, dressed in a dark fur-trimmed outfit. Castiglione's term "sprezzatura" (effortless grace) is often applied to Raphael's style, contrasted with Michelangelo's "terribilità."

**Raphael Cartoons and La Fornarina**
Raphael designed full-size drawings ("cartoons") for ten tapestries depicting the lives of Saints Peter and Paul for the Sistine Chapel, including The Miraculous Draught of Fishes; seven survive. La Fornarina depicts his supposed lover, a baker's daughter, holding her bare breast, and she may also be the model for La Donna Velata (The Veiled Woman). The Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood founded by William Holman Hunt, John Everett Millais, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti rejected the academic art they believed descended from Raphael.

**Hungarian Rhapsodies**
Liszt's set of 19 virtuosic piano pieces based on Roma ("Gypsy") music and verbunkos dance tunes from his native Hungary. Many alternate a slow, brooding lassan section with a fast, wild friska, use the "Gypsy" scale, and imitate the cimbalom, a hammered dulcimer. No. 2 is the most famous, and No. 15 is based on the "Rákóczi March."

**Transcendental Etudes**
A set of 12 extremely difficult piano studies, grown out of a set of studies Liszt wrote at age fifteen, and dedicated to his teacher Carl Czerny. They include No. 4, "Mazeppa," which depicts a Cossack tied to a galloping horse (Liszt also wrote a symphonic poem of the same name), and No. 5, "Feux follets" ("Will-o'-the-wisps").

**Mephisto Waltzes**
Four waltzes inspired by Nikolaus Lenau's version of Faust, not Goethe's. The first, "The Dance in the Village Inn," opens with stacked fifths in 3/8 time that imitate Mephistopheles tuning a violin he has grabbed from a fiddler, before he plays wild music while Faust dances. The late "Bagatelle without Tonality" was labeled as a fourth Mephisto Waltz.

**"La Campanella"**
The third of Liszt's six Grandes études de Paganini, based on the rondo of Paganini's Violin Concerto No. 2. The right hand jumps rapidly between the melody and a high, repeated D-sharp that represents the little bell of the title.

**Lisztomania**
The term Heinrich Heine used for the frenzied fan hysteria, especially among women, at Liszt's concerts in the 1840s. Liszt is also credited with inventing the modern solo recital, playing from memory with the piano turned sideways to the audience.

**Symphonic poem and Les Préludes**
Liszt coined the term "symphonic poem" for a one-movement orchestral work that tells a story or illustrates a program, and he wrote 13 of them, including Prometheus, Orpheus, and Mazeppa. The most famous, Les Préludes, takes its title from an ode by Alphonse de Lamartine and grows out of a short three-note motif.

**Years of Pilgrimage (Années de pèlerinage)**
Three piano suites inspired by Liszt's travels. "First Year: Switzerland" includes "William Tell's Chapel" and "Au bord d'une source" ("Beside a Spring"). "Second Year: Italy" includes the Petrarch Sonnets, "Il penseroso" (after a Michelangelo statue), and the Dante Sonata, with the supplement "Venice and Naples" (Gondoliera, Canzone, Tarantella). "Third Year" includes the threnodies "To the Cypresses of the Villa d'Este."

**Dante Sonata**
"Après une lecture du Dante: Fantasia quasi sonata," a one-movement piece in Years of Pilgrimage whose title comes from a Victor Hugo poem. It opens with octaves on A and E-flat, separated by the dissonant tritone, to depict the gates of Hell.

**Liebesträume**
"Dreams of Love," three piano nocturnes based on poems by Ludwig Uhland and Ferdinand Freiligrath. The third, in A-flat, sets Freiligrath's "O lieb, so lang du lieben kannst" ("Love as long as you can"), and its sections are separated by difficult cadenzas.

**Totentanz**
"Dance of Death," a piece for piano and orchestra made of variations on the medieval "Dies irae" chant, the same melody Berlioz used in the Symphonie fantastique. It opens with harsh, percussive piano writing and is full of glissandi.

**Faust Symphony**
Liszt's three-movement symphony based on Goethe's Faust, with one movement each for Faust, Gretchen, and Mephistopheles. His Dante Symphony is a similar program symphony based on the Divine Comedy.

**Piano Sonata in B minor**
Liszt's massive one-movement sonata, which develops a few themes throughout the whole piece. He dedicated it to Robert Schumann.

**Don Sanche**
Liszt's only opera, written when he was a teenager. In it, the magician Alidor, lord of the Castle of Love, tests Princess Elzire's love for Don Sanche. The manuscript was lost for decades.

**Weimar and the New German School**
As music director at Weimar, Liszt led the progressive "New German School" against the conservatives (Brahms's camp) in the War of the Romantics. He conducted the 1850 premiere of Wagner's Lohengrin, and Wagner later married Liszt's daughter Cosima.

**Transcriptions, paraphrases, and the Hexameron**
Liszt made piano transcriptions of all nine Beethoven symphonies and opera "paraphrases," such as one on the Rigoletto quartet. He also wrote the introduction to the collaborative Hexameron variations on the "March of the Puritans," which is tied to his famous piano "duel" with Sigismond Thalberg at Princess Belgiojoso's salon.

**Fountain**
Duchamp's most famous readymade (1917): a store-bought porcelain urinal turned on its side or upside down and signed "R. Mutt 1917." The pseudonym refers to J. L. Mott Iron Works, the sanitary-supply company whose showroom the urinal was bought from. It was rejected by the Society of Independent Artists in New York. Alfred Stieglitz photographed it in front of Marsden Hartley's painting The Warriors for the Dada journal The Blind Man.

**Readymades**
Duchamp's term for ordinary manufactured objects that he selected, sometimes altered slightly, and presented as art. He wanted to challenge "retinal" art, which appeals only to the eye, in favor of art of ideas, and the readymades are considered forerunners of Conceptual art. Altered examples are called "assisted readymades."

**L.H.O.O.Q.**
A 1919 readymade in which Duchamp drew a mustache and goatee in pencil on a cheap postcard reproduction of Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa. Read aloud in French, the letters sound like "Elle a chaud au cul," a crude pun roughly meaning "she has a hot ass" ("she has hot pants").

**Rrose Sélavy**
Duchamp's female alter ego, whose name puns on "Éros, c'est la vie" ("Eros, that's life"). Man Ray photographed Duchamp dressed as Rrose in a fur-trimmed coat and hat, and Duchamp signed several works with her name.

**Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2**
Duchamp's 1912 painting showing a figure broken into overlapping, cone- and cylinder-like forms in successive positions to suggest motion, influenced by Cubism and chronophotography. It caused a scandal at the 1913 Armory Show in New York, where critic Julian Street mocked it as "an explosion in a shingle factory."

**The Large Glass (The Bride Stripped Bare by Her Bachelors, Even)**
A large work made of oil, lead foil, wire, and dust between two glass panels, worked on from 1915 to 1923 and left "definitively unfinished." The upper panel is the Bride's domain, and the lower "Bachelor Machine" contains nine "Malic Molds," a water mill, and a chocolate grinder. It cracked in transit after an exhibition, and Duchamp accepted the cracks as part of the work. His notes for it were published in The Green Box.

**Étant donnés**
Duchamp's last major work (1946–1966), secretly assembled after he had supposedly quit art for chess, and now in the Philadelphia Museum of Art. Its full title is Given: 1. The Waterfall, 2. The Illuminating Gas. Through two peepholes in an old wooden door, the viewer sees a nude woman lying spread-eagled on twigs and grass and holding up a gas lamp, in front of a landscape with a waterfall.

**Why Not Sneeze, Rose Sélavy?**
A 1921 assisted readymade: a small birdcage filled with 152 white marble cubes that look like sugar cubes, along with a thermometer and a cuttlebone. The title refers to his alter ego.

**In Advance of the Broken Arm**
A 1915 readymade consisting of an ordinary snow shovel hung from the ceiling with its title painted on the handle. It was Duchamp's first readymade made in America, and it is sometimes called Prelude to a Broken Arm.

**Chess and Reunion**
Duchamp became a serious chess player, playing for France in Chess Olympiads, and was said to have given up art for chess around 1923. At the 1968 performance Reunion, he played chess with John Cage on a board wired to produce sounds as pieces moved. A famous 1963 photograph from his retrospective in Pasadena shows him playing chess with the nude Eve Babitz.

**50 cc of Paris Air**
A 1919 readymade: a glass pharmacy ampoule that Duchamp had emptied, sealed with Paris air inside, and brought to New York as a gift for the collector Walter Arensberg.

**Bicycle Wheel**
A 1913 readymade, generally considered Duchamp's first: a bicycle wheel mounted upside down by its fork on a painted wooden kitchen stool, so that it can be spun.

**Bottle Rack**
A 1914 readymade consisting of a galvanized iron rack with spikes for drying wine bottles. Duchamp bought it in Paris and later forgot what inscription he had planned to put on it.

**3 Standard Stoppages**
A 1913–1914 work in which Duchamp dropped three one-meter threads from a height of one meter onto canvas, fixed them where they fell, and cut wooden rulers matching their curves. It parodies the standard meter and refers to chance and to ideas from Henri Poincaré.

**Anémic Cinéma**
A 1926 short film made by Duchamp with Man Ray and Marc Allégret, alternating spinning spiral "Rotoreliefs" with discs bearing punning phrases signed by Rrose Sélavy. Duchamp also appears playing chess with Man Ray in René Clair's Dada film Entr'acte.

**Arnolfini Portrait (Arnolfini Wedding)**
Van Eyck's 1434 double portrait of the Italian merchant Giovanni Arnolfini, in a dark cloak and a large black hat, holding the hand of his wife, who wears a green dress and only appears to be pregnant. Famous details include oranges on the windowsill, a brass chandelier with a single lit candle, a small dog, and discarded wooden pattens (clogs). Erwin Panofsky famously argued that the painting served as a visual marriage certificate.

**Convex mirror and "Johannes de eyck fuit hic 1434"**
On the back wall of the Arnolfini Portrait hangs a convex mirror that reflects the backs of the couple and two figures in the doorway, one possibly the artist himself. Its frame holds tiny roundels of scenes from the Passion of Christ. Above it, van Eyck wrote in elaborate script "Jan van Eyck was here 1434."

**Ghent Altarpiece**
A huge polyptych of twelve panels, painted on both sides, in St. Bavo's Cathedral in Ghent. It was begun by Jan's brother Hubert and completed by Jan in 1432 for the patron Joos Vijd and his wife Elisabeth Borluut.

**Adoration of the Mystic Lamb**
The central lower panel of the Ghent Altarpiece. The Lamb of God stands on an altar, bleeding from its chest into a chalice, while angels kneel around it. Crowds representing Old and New Testament figures, saints, and martyrs gather on all sides, and below it the Fountain of Life feeds a small stream.

**God the Father, singing angels, and Adam and Eve**
The upper register of the open Ghent Altarpiece. It shows an enthroned figure in a jeweled red robe and a papal triple crown, usually read as God the Father or Christ, flanked by Mary, John the Baptist, singing angels, and an angel playing an organ. Nude figures of Adam and Eve stand in niches at the far ends, with small scenes of Cain killing Abel above them.

**Exterior of the Ghent Altarpiece**
When the altarpiece is closed, it shows the donors Joos Vijd and Elisabeth Borluut kneeling before grisaille (gray, stone-like) imitation statues of St. John the Baptist and St. John the Evangelist. Above them is an Annunciation in which Mary's reply, "Ecce ancilla Domini," is painted upside down, so that it can be read from heaven.

**"Just Judges" panel and the Monuments Men**
The Ghent Altarpiece is often called the most stolen artwork in history. Its lower-left "Just Judges" panel was stolen in 1934 and has never been recovered. The Nazis seized the altarpiece during World War II, and the Monuments Men recovered it from the Altaussee salt mine in Austria and returned it to Ghent.

**"Als ich can" ("As I can")**
Van Eyck's personal motto, a modest pun on his own name ("ich"/"Eyck"). He inscribed it on the frames of several paintings, sometimes in Greek letters, including the Man in a Red Turban and the portrait of his wife Margaret.

**Madonna of Chancellor Rolin**
A painting showing Nicolas Rolin, chancellor of the Duchy of Burgundy, kneeling in prayer before the Virgin Mary. An angel holds a crown over her head, and the infant Christ blesses Rolin while holding a crystal globe topped with a cross. Behind the loggia, peacocks walk along a balcony overlooking a detailed river city and landscape.

**Virgin and Child with Canon van der Paele**
A 1436 painting in which St. George lifts his helmet to present the elderly canon Joris van der Paele, in a white surplice and holding a book and spectacles, to the Virgin and Child. St. Donatian stands on the other side.

**Man in a Red Turban**
A 1433 portrait, widely believed to be a self-portrait, of a man wearing an elaborately folded red chaperon, a headdress often mistaken for a turban. Its frame carries the motto "Als ich can."

**Portrait of Margaret van Eyck**
A 1439 portrait of the artist's wife, wearing a red dress and a horned headdress. Its frame is inscribed with his motto and a note that her husband Jan completed the painting.

**New York Diptych (Crucifixion and Last Judgment)**
A pair of tall panels attributed to van Eyck and his workshop, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. In the Last Judgment panel, the archangel Michael stands on the back of a huge, bat-winged skeleton representing Death, which spreads over the damned in Hell.

**Lucca Madonna**
A painting of the Virgin nursing the Christ Child on a canopied throne decorated with four small lions, in a richly detailed interior. It is named after a former owner, the Duke of Lucca.

**Myth of inventing oil painting**
The Renaissance biographer Giorgio Vasari wrongly credited van Eyck with inventing oil paint. Van Eyck did not invent it, but his mastery of thin, layered oil glazes produced unprecedented detail and luminosity and made him the leading figure of Early Netherlandish painting.

**Rhapsody in Blue**
Gershwin's most famous work (1924), a fusion of classical music and jazz for solo piano and jazz band, commissioned by bandleader Paul Whiteman, who called it a "jazz concerto." Gershwin was the soloist at the premiere and improvised parts of the piano part, and he said the piece came to him on a train ride to Boston.

**Opening clarinet trill and glissando**
Rhapsody in Blue opens with a low clarinet trill followed by a wailing upward glissando. Gershwin wrote a 17-note rising scale, but Whiteman's clarinetist Ross Gorman played it as a smooth slide during rehearsals, and Gershwin kept it; clarinetists gradually open the tone holes to bend the pitch.

**"An Experiment in Modern Music"**
The title of Paul Whiteman's 1924 concert at New York's Aeolian Hall, where Rhapsody in Blue premiered as the second-to-last piece on the program.

**An American in Paris and its taxi horns**
Gershwin's 1928 tone poem (later used as a ballet in a 1951 film) depicting an American tourist wandering the streets of Paris. Gershwin brought back real French taxi horns to depict the bustling traffic, and a bluesy trumpet solo represents the visitor's "spasm of homesickness."

**Porgy and Bess and Catfish Row**
