Gershwin's "folk opera" (1935), with lyrics by DuBose Heyward and Ira Gershwin, set among the African American residents of Catfish Row in Charleston, South Carolina. The disabled beggar Porgy tries to protect Bess from her violent lover Crown and the drug dealer Sportin' Life.

**"Summertime"**
The lullaby that opens Porgy and Bess, sung by Clara to her baby (and later reprised by Bess). Its famous opening lines say "the livin' is easy, / Fish are jumpin', and the cotton is high," and its blues-inflected melody draws on the minor pentatonic scale.

**"It Ain't Necessarily So"**
A song in Porgy and Bess in which the cynical drug dealer Sportin' Life mocks the Bible, casting doubt on stories such as David and Goliath and Jonah and the whale.

**"My Man's Gone Now"**
Serena's lament in Porgy and Bess after her husband Robbins is killed by Crown with a cotton hook during a craps game; Catfish Row residents place money in a saucer to pay for his burial.

**"I Got Rhythm" and "rhythm changes"**
A song from the 1930 musical Girl Crazy, with lyrics by Ira Gershwin and the refrain "Who could ask for anything more?" Its 32-bar chord progression, called "rhythm changes," became a basis for countless jazz tunes, including Dizzy Gillespie's "Salt Peanuts" and Charlie Parker's "Anthropology."

**Ira Gershwin**
George's older brother and chief lyricist, who wrote the words for songs such as "I Got Rhythm," "Embraceable You," "Fascinating Rhythm," and "Let's Call the Whole Thing Off," and co-wrote the lyrics for Porgy and Bess.

**Concerto in F**
Gershwin's only piano concerto (1925), commissioned by conductor Walter Damrosch. Its first movement opens with timpani strokes and a cymbal crash and uses the rhythm of the Charleston, its slow second movement features a muted trumpet solo, and the finale has ragtime elements.

**Cuban Overture**
An orchestral piece (1932), originally titled Rumba, inspired by a trip to Havana. Gershwin asks for Cuban percussion (claves, guiro, maracas, and bongos) to be placed right in front of the conductor, and the piece quotes the song "Échale Salsita."

**Ferde Grofé**
The arranger in Paul Whiteman's band who orchestrated Rhapsody in Blue, first for jazz band and later for full symphony orchestra.

**Nadia Boulanger**
The famous French composition teacher who supposedly refused to teach Gershwin, saying she could teach him nothing and that studying with her would only spoil his natural style.

**"Swanee" and early works (Blue Monday)**
"Swanee," with lyrics by Irving Caesar, became Gershwin's first big hit when Al Jolson recorded it; Gershwin had begun as a song plugger in Tin Pan Alley. His early one-act opera Blue Monday (later renamed 135th Street) is a Harlem tale often compared to Pagliacci, and Gershwin also wrote Three Preludes for piano, one of them the "Blue Lullaby."

**Bronze David**
Donatello's most famous work and the first freestanding male nude sculpture since antiquity, probably made for the Medici. The effeminate, boyish David stands in contrapposto with his left hand on his hip, wearing only a laurel- or flower-trimmed hat and boots, leaning on Goliath's sword with his foot on the giant's severed head. A wing from Goliath's helmet creeps up David's leg.

**Gattamelata**
Donatello's bronze equestrian statue of the Venetian mercenary (condottiero) Erasmo da Narni, nicknamed Gattamelata ("Honeyed Cat"), in the Piazza del Santo outside the Basilica of St. Anthony in Padua. Inspired by the ancient statue of Marcus Aurelius, it is the earliest surviving Renaissance equestrian bronze; the horse rests a hoof on a small orb, and the pedestal has two fake doors suggesting the gates of the underworld.

**Zuccone (Habakkuk)**
Donatello's marble statue of the prophet Habakkuk for the bell tower (Campanile) of Florence Cathedral, nicknamed "Zuccone" ("pumpkin head") because of its bald head. According to Vasari, Donatello considered it his favorite work and shouted "Speak, damn you, speak!" at it because it looked so lifelike. He also made other prophets for the Campanile, such as the "Bearded" and "Beardless" prophets.

**Penitent Magdalene**
A painted poplar-wood statue made for the Florence Baptistery, showing Mary Magdalene in her old age as a gaunt, wrinkled hermit clothed in ragged hair, with her hands pressed together in prayer. Its extreme realism may draw on icons of the emaciated hermit Mary of Egypt, and Vasari praised it highly.

**Stiacciato (schiacciato)**
An extremely shallow relief technique pioneered by Donatello, in which tiny variations in depth create the illusion of deep space, much like a drawing in stone. Its earliest surviving example is the relief St. George Freeing the Princess (St. George and the Dragon) below his St. George statue.

**St. Mark (Orsanmichele)**
Donatello's marble statue made for the linen weavers' guild's niche at Orsanmichele, the Florentine guild church. It stands in classical contrapposto, and its proportions were deliberately distorted to look correct when viewed from below in the raised niche; legend says the guild first objected to its appearance at street level.

**St. George (Orsanmichele)**
Donatello's marble statue of the warrior saint for the armorers' guild niche at Orsanmichele, now in the Bargello museum. Its base holds the stiacciato relief of St. George slaying the dragon and freeing the princess.

**Feast of Herod**
A gilded bronze relief Donatello made for the baptismal font of the Siena Cathedral Baptistery. It shows Salome's dance and the presentation of John the Baptist's head, using linear perspective and shallow relief to create deep architectural space.

**Judith and Holofernes**
Donatello's late bronze statue of the biblical heroine Judith raising a sword to behead the drunken Assyrian general Holofernes. It was cast in several separate pieces and designed to be viewed from multiple angles, and Michelangelo's David later replaced it at the Palazzo Vecchio.

**Amor-Atys**
A small bronze in the Bargello of a laughing, winged child with a faun's tail, raising his arms in the air and wearing open leggings that expose his buttocks and genitals. Its identity is unclear, combining traits of Cupid, Atys, and Mercury, such as winged sandals.

**Tomb of Antipope John XXIII**
A wall tomb in the Florence Baptistery for Baldassare Cossa, the deposed Antipope John XXIII, designed by Donatello together with his partner Michelozzo. It includes the Cossa coat of arms and allegorical figures of three Virtues.

**St. John the Evangelist**
A seated marble statue made for the facade of Florence Cathedral. Its lower body is elongated so that the figure appears correctly proportioned when seen from below, which some viewers read as a proto-Mannerist distortion.

**Chellini Madonna (Virgin and Child with Four Angels)**
A small bronze roundel that Donatello gave to his doctor, Giovanni Chellini. Its back is hollowed out as a mold so that copies could be made by pouring in molten glass.

**Bust of Niccolò da Uzzano**
A realistic painted terracotta portrait bust of the Florentine statesman Niccolò da Uzzano, attributed to Donatello and one of the earliest Renaissance portrait busts.

**"Donatello among the wild beasts"**
At the 1905 Salon d'Automne, critic Louis Vauxcelles saw a classical-style sculpture surrounded by brightly colored paintings by Matisse and his circle and quipped "Donatello chez les fauves" ("Donatello among the wild beasts"), giving Fauvism its name.

**Louis Armstrong ("Satchmo")**
An enormously influential New Orleans jazz trumpeter and singer, mentored by King Oliver. With his Hot Five and Hot Seven bands he recorded "Potato Head Blues" and "Heebie Jeebies," a track that helped popularize scat singing. He is also famous for singing "What a Wonderful World" ("I see trees of green, red roses too") and "Hello, Dolly!"

**Miles Davis and Kind of Blue**
A trumpeter and bandleader whose 1959 album Kind of Blue is a landmark of modal jazz. It opens with "So What," whose famous "So What chord" stacks three fourths with a major third on top, and it also includes "Freddie Freeloader," "All Blues," and "Flamenco Sketches." Davis also released Birth of the Cool and Someday My Prince Will Come.

**Dizzy Gillespie's bent trumpet**
The bebop trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie played a trumpet with its bell bent upward and was known for his hugely puffed-out cheeks. He wrote "A Night in Tunisia" and "Salt Peanuts," and with the Cuban percussionist Chano Pozo he co-wrote "Manteca," a founding tune of Afro-Cuban jazz.

**Wynton Marsalis and Blood on the Fields**
A trumpeter who is artistic director of Jazz at Lincoln Center. His oratorio about slavery, Blood on the Fields, opens with "Calling the Indians Out" and in 1997 became the first jazz composition to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music. Early in his career he played in Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers.

**"West End Blues"**
A 1928 recording by Louis Armstrong and his Hot Five that opens with a famous solo trumpet cadenza. The cadenza, which climbs to a high note, is considered one of the greatest moments in early jazz.

**Also sprach Zarathustra**
Richard Strauss's tone poem, which opens with trumpets playing the rising "nature" motif C–G–high C over a low pedal note. The opening is famous from the sunrise scene in Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey.

**Brandenburg Concerto No. 2**
A concerto by J. S. Bach whose solo group (concertino) is trumpet, recorder, oboe, and violin. Its very high trumpet part was written for the valveless natural trumpet in the clarino register. Today it is often played on the small "piccolo" trumpet, which Maurice André popularized for Baroque works.

**Trumpet Voluntary**
The popular name for Jeremiah Clarke's Prince of Denmark's March, a stately Baroque piece often played at weddings.

**Mahler's Symphony No. 5**
This symphony opens with a solo trumpet call built on repeated C-sharps. The call launches a funeral march in C-sharp minor.

**Haydn and Hummel concertos for Anton Weidinger**
Anton Weidinger, a Viennese trumpeter, developed the keyed trumpet, which could play the full chromatic scale for the first time. Haydn wrote his Trumpet Concerto in E-flat for him, and Johann Nepomuk Hummel wrote his Trumpet Concerto in E major for him.

**Pictures at an Exhibition "Promenade"**
In Maurice Ravel's orchestration of Mussorgsky's piano suite, a solo trumpet plays the opening "Promenade" theme. The melody begins G–F–B-flat and switches between 5/4 and 6/4 time.

**Fanfare for the Common Man**
Aaron Copland's work for brass and percussion. After a percussion introduction, three trumpets play the opening melody, which rises through F, B-flat, and F.

**"The Trumpet Shall Sound"**
A bass aria from Part III of Handel's Messiah, accompanied by a prominent solo trumpet. Its text is "The trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised."

**The Pines of Rome**
Ottorino Respighi's tone poem. In "Pines Near a Catacomb," an offstage trumpet plays a solo. The finale, "Pines of the Appian Way," brings in buccine (ancient Roman horns, usually played by modern brass instruments) to depict a victorious Roman army.

**Arban's method and "The Carnival of Venice"**
Jean-Baptiste Arban wrote the standard teaching method for trumpet and cornet, often called the trumpet "Bible." He also wrote famously difficult virtuoso variations on the folk tune "The Carnival of Venice."

**"Jack the Dripper" / drip and action painting**
Pollock's nickname, which comes from his technique of laying canvases on the floor and dripping, pouring, and flinging paint onto them while moving around the work. The critic Harold Rosenberg's term "action painting" is closely tied to this method, which made Pollock the best-known Abstract Expressionist.

**Lavender Mist (Number 1, 1950)**
One of Pollock's best-known drip paintings, a dense tangle of pinks, blacks, whites, and silvery tones that reads as purplish from a distance. Pollock's own handprints appear in the upper right corner as a kind of signature.

**Full Fathom Five**
A 1947 drip painting named after a line from Ariel's song in Shakespeare's The Tempest ("Full fathom five thy father lies"). Pollock embedded nails, tacks, buttons, keys, coins, and cigarette butts into its thick layers of paint.

**Lee Krasner**
Pollock's wife and a significant Abstract Expressionist painter in her own right. She introduced him to influential figures in the art world, and they lived and worked together at a studio in Springs, East Hampton, on Long Island.

**Blue Poles (Number 11, 1952)**
A large painting crossed by eight diagonal blue "poles" laid over a dense drip background. Its 1973 purchase by the National Gallery of Australia for about $1.3 million was a national political controversy.

**Hans Namuth**
The photographer whose 1950 photographs and films of Pollock at work in his studio made the physical act of drip painting famous and helped build the Pollock legend.

**Thomas Hart Benton**
The American Regionalist painter who taught Pollock at the Art Students League. Pollock's early work, especially Going West, shows Benton's swirling, rhythmic style.

**Going West**
An early Pollock painting of a covered wagon train pulled by mules under a moonlit sky, done in the style of Thomas Hart Benton. A bridge in Cody, Wyoming, Pollock's birthplace, may have inspired it.

**Carl Jung / anima and animus**
Pollock underwent Jungian psychotherapy in the late 1930s, and Jungian ideas about archetypes and the male and female principles (animus and anima) shaped his early, symbol-heavy paintings such as Male and Female and Guardians of the Secret.

**The She-Wolf**
A 1943 painting showing the outline of a wolf, inspired by the Roman myth of the she-wolf who suckled Romulus and Remus. It was one of the first Pollock paintings bought by the Museum of Modern Art.

**The Moon-Woman Cuts the Circle**
An early painting influenced by Native American art and myth. It shows a figure in a feathered headdress holding a knife, and diamond shapes appear to spill from the cut circle.

**Mural (for Peggy Guggenheim)**
A huge, roughly twenty-foot-wide 1943 canvas commissioned by Peggy Guggenheim for the entrance hall of her New York townhouse. Pollock described it as a stampede of every animal in the American West, and its swirling black rhythms point toward his later all-over style.

**Autumn Rhythm (Number 30)**
A large 1950 drip painting of black, white, and brown skeins of paint, held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. It is a classic example of Pollock's "all-over" compositions, which have no single focal point.

**Mural on Indian Red Ground**
A 1950 Pollock painting owned by the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art, one of the most valuable works in Iran's collection. It became the subject of news in 2012 when it was held by Iranian customs on its return from an exhibition in Japan.

**No. 5, 1948**
A drip painting of brown and yellow tangles over a gray-brown ground. It sold privately in 2006 for about $140 million, at the time the highest price ever paid for a painting.

**Fallingwater**
Wright's most famous building, a weekend house (1935–1939) for Pittsburgh department-store owner Edgar J. Kaufmann at Mill Run in southwestern Pennsylvania. Its reinforced-concrete terraces are cantilevered directly over a waterfall on the stream Bear Run, so the water seems to flow beneath the house.

**Cantilevers over Bear Run (and "Rising Mildew")**
Fallingwater's dramatic cantilevered floors and balconies sagged over time; supervisor Robert Mosher had secretly doubled the steel reinforcement, angering Wright, and a 2002 restoration added post-tensioned steel cables. Persistent leaks and dampness earned the house the nickname "Rising Mildew." A natural boulder also emerges from the floor at the living room hearth.

**Prairie School and the Robie House**
Wright led the Prairie School, a style of low, horizontal homes with broad overhanging roofs and open interiors meant to echo the flat Midwestern landscape. Its masterpiece is the Frederick C. Robie House (1909) in Chicago's Hyde Park on the University of Chicago campus, whose long thin Roman bricks stress horizontal lines.

**Usonian homes (the Jacobs House)**
"Usonian" was Wright's term for small, affordable single-story homes for middle-class Americans. The first was the L-shaped Herbert Jacobs House in Madison, Wisconsin, built after Jacobs challenged him to design a house for $5,000; Wright coined the word "carport" for these homes. Other Usonian homes include the Rosenbaum House in Alabama and Kentuck Knob in Pennsylvania.

**Taliesin and Taliesin West**
Wright's home-studios, named after the Welsh bard Taliesin: the original Taliesin in Spring Green, Wisconsin, and Taliesin West, a winter home built of "desert masonry" in Scottsdale, Arizona. In 1914 servant Julian Carlton set the Wisconsin Taliesin on fire and murdered Wright's mistress Mamah Borthwick, her two children, and four others.

**Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum**
Wright's museum on Fifth Avenue in New York City, completed in 1959, originally for "non-objective" (abstract) painting. Its white exterior has been called an "inverted ziggurat," and inside a continuous spiral ramp winds up around a central skylit atrium.

**Imperial Hotel, Tokyo**
Wright's hotel in a "Maya Revival" style, built on a shallow, floating foundation. It survived the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake largely intact; it was demolished in 1968, but its lobby and entrance with a reflecting pool were rebuilt at the Meiji Mura museum near Nagoya.

**Johnson Wax Headquarters**
Wright's administration building for S. C. Johnson in Racine, Wisconsin. Its "Great Workroom" is filled with slender, tapered white "dendriform" or "lily pad" columns topped by wide circular discs, with light entering through glass tubing; Wright later added a Research Tower built around a "taproot" core.

**Mamah Borthwick**
The wife of a client, with whom Wright had an affair that led him to leave his wife and Oak Park and build Taliesin. She was murdered in the 1914 Taliesin fire, which the press sensationalized because the newspapers had called the house a "love castle."

**Unity Temple and Oak Park, Illinois**
Wright's early career was centered in the Chicago suburb of Oak Park, where he built his own home and studio (with a barrel-vaulted playroom) for himself and his first wife, Catherine Tobin. His Unity Temple there (1908), for a Unitarian Universalist congregation, is an early landmark of exposed poured reinforced concrete and bears the inscription "For the worship of God and the service of man."

**The Illinois (mile-high skyscraper)**
A never-built skyscraper Wright proposed for Chicago in 1956. It would have stood one mile high and was to use atomic-powered elevators.

**Price Tower**
Wright's only realized skyscraper, completed in 1956 in Bartlesville, Oklahoma, for the H. C. Price Company. Its interiors included geometric furniture designed by Wright.

**Kentuck Knob**
A Usonian house near Fallingwater built for the Hagan family, made of sandstone and red cypress, with a copper roof pierced by hexagonal skylights. Wright's signature is on a Cherokee red tile on its exterior.

**Broadacre City and The Disappearing City**
Broadacre City was Wright's decentralized, car-centered vision of suburban planning in which each family would have an acre of land, laid out in his 1932 book The Disappearing City. In it he argued that the gasoline service station was the beginning of decentralization.

**Organic architecture and the Wasmuth Portfolio**
Wright's guiding philosophy was "organic architecture," the idea that a building should be in harmony with its site and its inhabitants. The Wasmuth Portfolio, a 1910 German publication of his drawings, spread his work to Europe and influenced modernist architects there.

**Picasso's Blue Period**
The phase of Pablo Picasso's career (roughly 1901–1904) when he painted in somber, monochromatic blues and blue-greens. He depicted poverty-stricken, melancholy subjects such as beggars, the blind, and outcasts, and it is usually contrasted with his warmer, later "Rose Period."

**The Old Guitarist**
Picasso's most famous Blue Period painting (1903–1904), showing a gaunt, blind, bowed street musician hunched over a brown guitar, the only warm color in the picture. It hangs in the Art Institute of Chicago.

**Carles Casagemas**
Picasso's close friend, whose suicide in 1901 Picasso said prompted him to start painting in blue. Picasso painted The Death of Casagemas and Casagemas in His Coffin, and Casagemas appears as the male figure in the Blue Period painting La Vie, in which pairs of figures clutch each other in despair. The Tragedy, showing a dejected couple and child on a beach, is another work from the period.

**Ultramarine and lapis lazuli**
The most prized blue pigment of medieval and Renaissance painting, ground from the semiprecious stone lapis lazuli, mined in Afghanistan; its name means "beyond the sea." It was so expensive that it was usually reserved for the robes of the Virgin Mary. Vermeer used it for the headscarf in Girl with a Pearl Earring, and Michelangelo reportedly left The Entombment unfinished while awaiting the costly pigment.

**Prussian blue**
The first modern synthetic pigment, discovered in Berlin in the early 1700s. Imported to Japan, it transformed ukiyo-e woodblock prints, most famously Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa. A related iron compound produced the cyanotype "blueprints" long used for technical and architectural drawings.

**Yves Klein and International Klein Blue**
The French artist Yves Klein patented a deep ultramarine pigment called International Klein Blue (IKB) and used it for his series of single-color "Monochrome" paintings, such as IKB 191. He also used it in his Anthropometries, in which nude models covered in the blue paint pressed their bodies against canvas.

**Der Blaue Reiter**
"The Blue Rider," a German Expressionist group founded in Munich in 1911 by Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc. It was named after a Kandinsky painting of a rider, and Marc, who associated blue with spirituality and masculinity, painted The Tower of Blue Horses.

**Kind of Blue**
Miles Davis's 1959 album, the best-selling jazz album of all time and a landmark of modal jazz. It features John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley on saxophones, Bill Evans on piano (Wynton Kelly plays on "Freddie Freeloader"), and Jimmy Cobb on drums, and it opens with "So What."

**Rhapsody in Blue**
George Gershwin's 1924 jazz-influenced piece for piano and jazz band, commissioned by bandleader Paul Whiteman for the concert "An Experiment in Modern Music." It was orchestrated by Ferde Grofé and opens with a famous rising clarinet glissando, improvised by Whiteman's clarinetist Ross Gorman. Gershwin said the piece was inspired by the rhythms of a train ride to Boston.

**Blue notes**
Notes sung or played slightly flat of standard pitch, especially the third, fifth, and seventh scale degrees. They are characteristic of the blues, the genre that originated among Black musicians in the American South, and of jazz.

**"Blue Rondo à la Turk"**
A Dave Brubeck Quartet hit from the 1959 album Time Out. Its main theme is in 9/8, grouped 2+2+2+3, a rhythm Brubeck adapted from the "aksak" asymmetrical meters he heard Turkish street musicians play.

**The Blue Boy**
Thomas Gainsborough's portrait (c. 1770) of a young man in a shimmering blue satin costume, traditionally identified as Jonathan Buttall. It is often seen as a homage to Anthony van Dyck, and it hangs at the Huntington Library in California.

**"The Blue Danube"**
Johann Strauss II's waltz "By the Beautiful Blue Danube" (1866), the most famous work by the "Waltz King." It was later used in Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey.

**Blue Mosque**
The Sultan Ahmed Mosque in Istanbul, built in the early 1600s for Sultan Ahmed I. It has six minarets and is nicknamed for the blue İznik tiles that cover its interior.

**Wilton Diptych and woad**
In the late-14th-century Wilton Diptych, the right-hand panel shows the Virgin Mary and a crowd of angels dressed almost entirely in ultramarine blue. Woad was the plant-based blue dye used in medieval Europe, including for the blues of the Unicorn Tapestries.

**Jackson Pollock and the drip technique**
The best-known Abstract Expressionist, nicknamed "Jack the Dripper." He laid unstretched canvases on the floor and dripped, poured, and flung paint onto them from above. In his mature period he often titled works only with numbers. He struggled with alcoholism and died in a car crash in 1956.

**Lavender Mist and Autumn Rhythm**
Two of Pollock's most famous 1950 drip paintings. Lavender Mist (also called Number 1, 1950) is a dense web of pale, pinkish skeins of paint. Autumn Rhythm (Number 30) is a huge mural-sized canvas of black, white, and brown loops.

**Lee Krasner**
An Abstract Expressionist painter and Jackson Pollock's wife, who introduced him to the critic Clement Greenberg. Her own works include the "Little Image" series of small, dense, glyph-like marks, which has been linked to Hebrew calligraphy.

**Hans Namuth**
The photographer who, in 1950, photographed and filmed Pollock dripping paint onto canvases laid on the floor. His images made Pollock's process famous and shaped the idea of "action painting."

**Willem de Kooning's Woman series**
De Kooning was a Dutch-born leader of the movement and husband of the painter Elaine de Kooning (born Elaine Fried). His violent, gestural paintings Woman I through Woman VI, including the long-labored Woman I, partly drew on ancient Mesopotamian idols. Related works include Woman and Bicycle and his later sculpture Seated Woman on a Bench.

**Clement Greenberg and Harold Rosenberg**
The two critics who championed the movement. Greenberg wrote in the Partisan Review and promoted Pollock and later color field painting. Rosenberg coined the term "action painting" for the gestural branch of the movement, which includes Franz Kline's large black-and-white canvases such as Mahoning.

**Helen Frankenthaler's Mountains and Sea**
A 1952 painting inspired by the Nova Scotia landscape, in which Frankenthaler poured oil paint thinned with turpentine onto unprimed canvas so that it soaked in. This "soak-stain" technique was a key step toward color field painting.

**Rothko Chapel**
A nondenominational chapel in Houston, Texas, whose walls hold fourteen of Mark Rothko's dark, nearly black canvases. Rothko is the chief painter of the color field branch of Abstract Expressionism, known for soft-edged rectangles of color.

**Seagram murals**
A series of dark maroon and black murals Rothko painted for the Four Seasons restaurant in New York's Seagram Building. He said he wanted the images to ruin the appetites of the wealthy diners. He withdrew from the commission instead of finishing it, and the paintings went to museums, including the Tate in London.

**The Irascibles**
The eighteen artists who signed a 1950 open letter protesting the Metropolitan Museum of Art's exhibition "American Painting Today," which they saw as hostile to modern art. Fifteen of them posed for a famous 1951 photograph in Life magazine, in which Hedda Sterne was the only woman.

**Joan Mitchell**
A second-generation Abstract Expressionist known for energetic, landscape-inspired brushwork. Her painting Hemlock, with its green and white strokes, was inspired by Wallace Stevens's poem "Domination of Black," and her City Landscape is dominated by pinks and whites.

**Arshile Gorky's The Liver Is the Cock's Comb**
A 1944 painting by the Armenian-born Gorky, who bridged Surrealism and Abstract Expressionism and was praised by Clement Greenberg. His work was shaped by his memories of the Armenian Genocide, during which his mother died.

**Hans Hofmann and the name "Abstract Expressionism"**
Hofmann was a German-born painter whose teaching influenced many members of the movement, including Lee Krasner and Joan Mitchell. The critic Robert Coates of The New Yorker applied the term "abstract expressionism" in a 1946 review of Hofmann's work.

**Pollock's Mural for Peggy Guggenheim**
A roughly six-meter-wide 1943 canvas that the collector Peggy Guggenheim commissioned for her New York townhouse. The critic Robert Hughes called it the first painting to fully realize the goals of Abstract Expressionism.

**Full Fathom Five**
A 1947 Pollock drip painting titled after a song in Shakespeare's The Tempest. It has nails, buttons, keys, coins, and cigarette butts embedded in its thick paint.

**"Der Hölle Rache kocht in meinem Herzen" ("Hell's vengeance boils in my heart")**
The Queen of the Night's Act 2 rage aria, one of the most famous coloratura showpieces in opera. It climbs repeatedly to a high F6 and contains staccato runs and the cry "Hört, Rachegötter" ("Hear, gods of vengeance"), with "hört" repeated over orchestral chords. In it the Queen gives her daughter Pamina a dagger, orders her to kill Sarastro, and threatens to disown her ("so bist du meine Tochter nimmermehr").

**Queen of the Night**
The opera's coloratura soprano antagonist and Pamina's mother. She appears to be good at first but is revealed as a vengeful villain who opposes Sarastro. At the end, she, her Three Ladies, and Monostatos are cast down into eternal night.

**Tamino and the magic flute**
The prince and tenor hero who opens the opera fleeing a giant serpent and faints. He is sent to rescue Pamina and receives the title enchanted flute, which can change people's hearts and calm wild animals. Its playing protects him and Pamina through their final trials.

**Papageno and "Der Vogelfänger bin ich ja" ("I am the birdcatcher")**
The comic birdcatcher, dressed in feathers, who trades birds to the Queen of the Night's attendants for food and drink. He introduces himself with this folk-like aria and goes with Tamino on his quest. He fails Sarastro's trials comically and longs only for a wife.

**Padlock on Papageno's mouth**
Papageno falsely claims that he strangled the serpent that chased Tamino. The Three Ladies, the Queen's attendants who actually killed it, punish the lie by padlocking his mouth shut.

**Sarastro**
The bass high priest of Isis and Osiris, who holds Pamina in his temple to protect her from her mother. He sings the prayer "O Isis und Osiris" and the aria "In diesen heil'gen Hallen" ("In these sacred halls"), and he sets the trials Tamino must pass to win Pamina.

**"Dies Bildnis ist bezaubernd schön" ("This image is enchantingly lovely")**
Tamino's Act 1 aria, which he sings after the Three Ladies show him a portrait of Pamina, and he falls in love with her at once.

**"O zittre nicht, mein lieber Sohn" ("Oh, tremble not, my dear son")**
The Queen of the Night's first aria, which begins with a recitative. She tells Tamino that Pamina has been abducted and promises him her hand if he rescues her. The flute is given to Tamino right afterward.

**Trials of silence, fire, and water**
The initiation ordeals Sarastro's brotherhood sets for Tamino. Tamino stays silent even when the Three Ladies tempt him and when Pamina is heartbroken by his silence. Then he and Pamina pass together through chambers of fire and water while he plays the flute. Earlier, priests turn Tamino away ("Zurück!") from the temples of Reason and Nature before he reaches the Temple of Wisdom.

**"Pa-pa-pa" duet and Papagena**
The "stutter duet" in which Papageno and his bride Papagena excitedly stammer each other's names when they are finally united. Papagena first appears as an old woman who claims to be eighteen, and she becomes young once Papageno pledges himself to her.

**Magic bells and "Ein Mädchen oder Weibchen"**
Papageno is given a set of magic silver bells (a glockenspiel, which Mozart's score called a "stromento d'acciaio" and which is often played on a celesta today). In the aria "Ein Mädchen oder Weibchen" ("A maiden or a little wife"), he sings of his wish for a wife while the glockenspiel accompanies him.

**Three Boys and Papageno's suicide attempt**
Three child-spirits guide Tamino and stop the despairing Papageno from hanging himself, singing "Halt ein, o Papageno, und sei klug! Man lebt nur einmal" ("Stop, be wise, you only live once"). They tell him to ring his bells, which summons Papagena. They also stop Pamina from killing herself.

**Monostatos**
Sarastro's Moorish servant and overseer of his slaves, who tries to force himself on Pamina and later joins the Queen of the Night in an attack on the temple. He is cast into eternal night with her at the end.

**Emanuel Schikaneder and Singspiel**
The Freemason impresario who wrote the libretto and created the role of Papageno at the 1791 Vienna premiere, a few months before Mozart's death. The work (K. 620) is a German-language Singspiel, with spoken dialogue between musical numbers, and is full of Masonic symbolism.

**Overture's three E-flat chords**
The overture opens with three solemn chords in E-flat major, often linked to a Masonic three-fold knock, which return later in the overture. A fugal Allegro follows, and its theme resembles a piano sonata by Muzio Clementi.

**Bach's Six Cello Suites**
J.S. Bach's six suites for unaccompanied cello (BWV 1007–1012). Each has six movements, beginning with a prelude and ending with a gigue; the first opens with a famous Prelude of flowing arpeggiated G major chords. The fifth requires the A string to be tuned down to G, and the sixth was written for an instrument with an extra fifth (E) string.

**Yo-Yo Ma**
A Chinese-American cellist born in Paris, a former child prodigy and one of the most famous classical musicians alive, with 19 Grammy Awards. He founded the Silk Road Ensemble, played the solos in the film score for Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, performed John Williams's "Air and Simple Gifts" at Barack Obama's 2009 inauguration, and has recorded the Bach suites several times.

**Pablo Casals**
A Catalan cellist who rediscovered the Bach Cello Suites and made the first complete recording of them (1936–1939). Exiled from Franco's Spain, he often played his arrangement of the Catalan folk song "El Cant dels Ocells" ("The Song of the Birds") as an encore; he also formed a famous piano trio with Alfred Cortot and Jacques Thibaud and wrote the oratorio El Pessebre (The Manger).

**Elgar's Cello Concerto in E minor and Jacqueline du Pré**
Edward Elgar's 1919 concerto, his last major work, became the signature piece of the British cellist Jacqueline du Pré, whose 1965 recording made it famous. Du Pré, who was married to pianist and conductor Daniel Barenboim, had to stop performing at 28 because of multiple sclerosis.

**"The Swan" from The Carnival of the Animals**
The thirteenth and second-to-last movement of Camille Saint-Saëns's Carnival of the Animals, in which the cello plays a slow, graceful melody over rippling accompaniment from two pianos. It is a popular encore piece for cellists.

**Dvořák's Cello Concerto in B minor**
Antonín Dvořák's last concerto (1895), written in New York after he heard Victor Herbert's Second Cello Concerto. It was dedicated to his friend, the cellist Hanuš Wihan, but premiered in London by Leo Stern; its slow second movement begins with soft woodwind chords.

**Mstislav Rostropovich and Shostakovich's cello concertos**
Rostropovich was a great Soviet cellist who premiered both of Dmitri Shostakovich's cello concertos. The First, in E-flat major, opens with the cello playing a four-note motto (G, F-flat, C-flat, B-flat). On the day the Warsaw Pact invaded Czechoslovakia in 1968, Rostropovich played Dvořák's concerto at the Proms in London.

**Saint-Saëns's Cello Concerto No. 1 and Tchaikovsky's Rococo Variations**
Saint-Saëns's Cello Concerto No. 1 in A minor is unusual because its sections are played as one continuous movement. Tchaikovsky's Variations on a Rococo Theme is a set of variations for cello and orchestra in an elegant 18th-century style.

**Haydn and Boccherini's cello concertos**
Joseph Haydn's early Cello Concerto in C major was lost until it was rediscovered in Prague in 1961 by Oldřich Pulkert. Luigi Boccherini, an Italian cello virtuoso, wrote a Cello Concerto in B-flat that is best known in a heavily Romanticized arrangement by Friedrich Grützmacher, as well as the string quintet Night Music of the Streets of Madrid and a famous Minuet.

**Bloch's Schelomo and Bruch's Kol Nidrei**
Two works for cello and orchestra inspired by Jewish music. Ernest Bloch's Schelomo is a "Hebrew rhapsody" in which the cello represents King Solomon, and Max Bruch's Kol Nidrei uses the melody of a prayer chanted on Yom Kippur, with the cello imitating a cantor.

**David Popper**
A 19th-century Bohemian cello virtuoso who wrote the Opus 73 etudes known as the High School of Cello Playing. He also wrote short showpieces for cello such as Spinnlied ("Spinning Song") and Elfentanz ("Dance of the Elves").

**Richard Strauss's Don Quixote**
A tone poem in the form of variations, subtitled "Fantastic Variations on a Theme of Knightly Character," in which a solo cello represents the title knight. A solo viola represents his squire Sancho Panza.

**Villa-Lobos's Bachianas Brasileiras No. 5**
One of nine works by Brazilian composer Heitor Villa-Lobos that blend Bach's style with Brazilian music. The fifth is scored for soprano and an orchestra of eight cellos and includes a famous wordless "Aria."

**The cello in ensembles and orchestral music**
The cello is the lowest instrument in a string quartet and pairs with a harpsichord or organ in Baroque basso continuo groups; its music is written mainly in bass and tenor clef. Five solo cellos open Rossini's William Tell Overture, and the cellos and basses play recitative-like passages in the finale of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony.

**2Cellos and Sheku Kanneh-Mason**
2Cellos is a Croatian duo of Luka Šulić and Stjepan Hauser famous for YouTube covers of pop songs and film music. Sheku Kanneh-Mason, a young British cellist, performed at the 2018 wedding of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle.

**Boléro**
Ravel's most famous orchestral work (1928), a one-movement piece named for a Spanish dance in 3/4 time. Over a two-bar snare drum ostinato repeated 169 times, two melodies are passed around the orchestra, beginning with the flute and including a sopranino saxophone, in one long crescendo without any development, until a sudden modulation near the end.

**Ida Rubinstein**
The dancer who commissioned Boléro as a ballet. She originally asked Ravel to orchestrate pieces from Isaac Albéniz's piano suite Iberia, but rights problems led him to write an original piece instead; Ravel imagined it set outside a factory, while the first staging showed a woman dancing on a table in a Spanish tavern.

**Gaspard de la nuit**
Ravel's 1908 three-movement piano suite based on prose poems by Aloysius Bertrand. "Ondine" depicts a water nymph trying to seduce a mortal, "Le Gibet" depicts a hanged man on a gallows, with a repeated B-flat octave like a tolling bell, and "Scarbo" depicts a mischievous goblin.

**"Scarbo" and Balakirev's Islamey**
The final movement of Gaspard de la nuit, depicting a goblin darting about at night. Ravel deliberately wrote it to be more difficult than Mily Balakirev's Islamey, then considered the hardest piano piece, and it is among the most difficult works in the piano repertoire.

**Orchestration of Pictures at an Exhibition**
Ravel's 1922 orchestration of Modest Mussorgsky's piano suite inspired by Viktor Hartmann's artworks is by far its most popular version. It opens with a solo trumpet "Promenade," gives "The Old Castle" to an alto saxophone, and uses a high tuba solo for the ox cart in "Bydło."

**Miroirs and Les Apaches**
Miroirs (1905) is a five-movement piano suite, each movement dedicated to a member of Les Apaches ("the hooligans"), an informal group of artists including Ravel and pianist Ricardo Viñes who supported Debussy's opera Pelléas et Mélisande. Its movements include "Noctuelles" ("Night Moths"), "Oiseaux tristes" ("Sad Birds"), "Une barque sur l'océan" ("A Boat on the Ocean"), and the Spanish-flavored "Alborada del gracioso."

**Le Tombeau de Couperin**
A six-movement piano suite (1917) in the style of Baroque French keyboard music, honoring François Couperin. Each movement, including a Forlane, a Rigaudon, and a closing Toccata, is dedicated to a friend of Ravel's killed in World War I.

**Daphnis et Chloé**
Ravel's ballet for Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, choreographed by Michel Fokine and based on the ancient Greek romance by Longus set on the island of Lesbos. It opens with young people bringing offerings to an altar of three nymphs; its famous later sections include the "Lever du jour" ("Sunrise"), a pantomime in which the lovers act out the story of Pan and Syrinx, and a closing bacchanalian "Danse générale."

**Pavane pour une infante défunte (Pavane for a Dead Princess)**
A slow piano piece (1899), later orchestrated with an opening horn solo, dedicated to the Princesse de Polignac. Ravel said it evokes a pavane that a little princess, as painted by Diego Velázquez, might have danced at the Spanish court.

**Piano Concerto for the Left Hand and Piano Concerto in G**
Ravel wrote his D major Concerto for the Left Hand for Paul Wittgenstein, who lost his right arm in World War I. The jazz-influenced Concerto in G, dedicated to Marguerite Long, opens with a whip crack, and Ravel said he wrote its Adagio assai "one bar at a time."

**Tzigane**
A Romani-inspired "concert rhapsody" (1924) for violin and piano (or orchestra), written for Hungarian violinist Jelly d'Arányi. It opens with a long unaccompanied violin cadenza, and Ravel originally called for a piano with a luthéal attachment, which imitates a cimbalom.

**String Quartet in F major**
Ravel's only string quartet (1903), modeled on Debussy's G minor quartet, whose "Assez vif" marking Ravel reused for his pizzicato-heavy A minor second movement. Its finale is in 5/8 time.

**Ma mère l'Oye (Mother Goose)**
A suite for piano four hands (later a ballet) written for the children of Ravel's friends the Godebskis. Its movements depict fairy tales, including "Pavane of Sleeping Beauty," "Little Tom Thumb," and "The Fairy Garden."

**La Valse**
Ravel's "choreographic poem" (1920) for orchestra, a tribute to the Viennese waltz that grows increasingly distorted and ends in a violent, frenzied collapse; it was originally intended as a ballet for Diaghilev but is mostly performed in concert.

**Rapsodie espagnole**
A Spanish-inspired orchestral suite (1908) drawing on the malagueña and habanera. Its opening "Prélude à la nuit" repeats a descending four-note F-E-D-C-sharp motif. Ravel's Spanish interest also shows in Boléro and "Alborada del gracioso."

**"Pathétique" Symphony (Symphony No. 6 in B minor)**
Tchaikovsky's last symphony, premiered in 1893 just nine days before his death, possibly by suicide. It opens with a low bassoon melody in E minor, has a first-movement bassoon passage marked with six p's (pppppp), and ends unusually with a slow "Adagio lamentoso" finale whose melody alternates between the first and second violins.

**"Limping waltz" in 5/4 time**
The second movement (Allegro con grazia) of the Pathétique Symphony is a waltz written in 5/4 instead of the usual 3/4, giving it a lopsided, "limping" feel. It is the single most common clue in Tchaikovsky questions.

**1812 Overture**
Tchaikovsky's 1880 orchestral work commemorating Russia's defeat of Napoleon's invasion, including the Battle of Borodino. "La Marseillaise" represents the French army and is drowned out by the Russian anthem "God Save the Tsar," and the score calls for church bells and real cannon fire.

**Symphony No. 4 in F minor and the "Fate" motif**
This symphony opens with a powerful brass fanfare on A-flat representing Fate, inspired by Beethoven, which returns in the finale. Its second movement is an "Andantino in modo di canzona" with a melancholy oboe melody, its scherzo has the strings play pizzicato throughout, and its finale quotes the folk song "In the Field Stood a Birch Tree." It was dedicated to his patron Nadezhda von Meck.

**Piano Concerto No. 1 in B-flat minor**
Opens with a fortissimo French horn fanfare and crashing D-flat major piano chords. It was originally meant for Nikolai Rubinstein, who harshly criticized it before later reconsidering, and Van Cliburn's 1958 performance of it won the first International Tchaikovsky Competition in Moscow.

**Swan Lake**
Ballet in which the sorcerer von Rothbart turns Odette into a swan by day, and Prince Siegfried is tricked into pledging his love to Rothbart's daughter Odile, the "Black Swan," who is disguised as Odette. Lev Ivanov choreographed its "Dance of the Little Swans," in which four dancers move with their hands linked.

**The Nutcracker**
Christmas ballet in which Clara (or Marie) helps the Nutcracker defeat the Mouse King and travels to the Land of Sweets. It features the celesta in the "Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy," the "Waltz of the Flowers," and national dances such as the Spanish chocolate dance and the Russian Trepak, with its squatting prisiadka kicks.

**The Sleeping Beauty**
Ballet (Op. 66) in which Princess Aurora pricks her finger on a spindle given by the wicked fairy Carabosse and falls into a cursed sleep until Prince Désiré awakens her. It features the difficult "Rose Adagio," in which four suitors bring Aurora roses, and its waltz was adapted as "Once Upon a Dream" in Disney's Sleeping Beauty.

**Eugene Onegin**
Tchaikovsky's opera based on Pushkin's verse novel about the daughters of Madame Larina. Tatyana pours out her love for Onegin in the "Letter Scene," the Frenchman Triquet sings couplets in her honor, and the poet Lensky is killed by Onegin in a duel. Tchaikovsky's other operas include The Queen of Spades, also from Pushkin, and Iolanta.

**Romeo and Juliet Overture-Fantasy**
Tchaikovsky's tone poem on Shakespeare's play, written at the urging of Mily Balakirev, who also convinced him to revise it. Its sweeping "love theme" is one of the most famous melodies in classical music.

**Symphony No. 5 in E minor**
Opens with a melancholy motto theme in the low clarinets (long G, two short Gs, long A) that recurs throughout and returns triumphantly in major at the start of the finale. Its second movement contains a famous D major horn solo in 12/8 time.

**Capriccio Italien**
An orchestral fantasy inspired by Tchaikovsky's 1880 stay in Rome. It opens with a trumpet fanfare imitating the bugle call he heard every day from a cavalry barracks near his hotel.

**Serenade for Strings and Mozartiana**
Both works honor Tchaikovsky's love of Mozart. The C major Serenade for Strings opens with a "Pezzo in forma di sonatina" and includes a waltz and an élégie, while his fourth orchestral suite, Mozartiana, orchestrates Mozart pieces including Liszt's transcription of Ave verum corpus and the Variations on a Theme by Gluck.

**Piano Trio in A minor**
A two-movement trio "dedicated to the memory of a great artist," Nikolai Rubinstein, who died in 1881. The opening "Pezzo elegiaco" is followed by a long set of variations that ends by returning to the funereal opening theme.

**"Little Russian" Symphony (Symphony No. 2)**
Tchaikovsky's second symphony, nicknamed for its use of Ukrainian folk songs, including "Down by Mother Volga" in a solo horn and "The Crane" in its finale. His other named symphonies include No. 1 "Winter Dreams," No. 3 "Polish," and the Manfred Symphony, based on Lord Byron's poem.

**Also sprach Zarathustra (Thus Spoke Zarathustra)**
Strauss's 1896 tone poem, subtitled "freely after Nietzsche" and based on Friedrich Nietzsche's philosophical novel. It is by far his most common giveaway, made famous by its use at the opening of Stanley Kubrick's film 2001: A Space Odyssey, which also used Johann Strauss II's Blue Danube (a different, unrelated composer). Its sections include "Of Science and Learning," "The Grave-Song," and "The Song of the Night Wanderer," which ends unresolved with the keys B major (humanity) and C major (nature or the universe) set against each other.

**"Sunrise" and the C–G–C "nature" motif**
The opening of Zarathustra: over a low organ and contrabassoon pedal, trumpets play the rising notes C–G–C, called the "nature" or "world riddle" motif, followed by a full orchestral chord and pounding timpani. It represents the sun rising.

**Salome**
Strauss's 1905 one-act opera based on Oscar Wilde's play, considered shocking and blasphemous at its premiere. Salome, stepdaughter of King Herod, demands the head of the prophet Jochanaan (John the Baptist). Before this, Herod slips in the blood of the guard captain Narraboth, who has killed himself, and imagines he hears the beating of wings.

**Dance of the Seven Veils and the kiss of the severed head**
In Salome, the title character performs the seductive Dance of the Seven Veils for Herod in return for Jochanaan's head. In the final scene she kisses the severed head while the orchestra plays a famously dissonant chord, sometimes called "the most sickening chord in all opera." Horrified, Herod orders his soldiers to crush her to death under their shields.

**Der Rosenkavalier (The Knight of the Rose)**
Strauss's 1911 comic opera with a libretto by Hugo von Hofmannsthal, set in 18th-century Vienna. The young Count Octavian, a trouser role sung by a mezzo-soprano, is sent to present a ceremonial silver rose to Sophie von Faninal for her engagement, but the two fall in love at first sight.

**Baron Ochs and "Mariandel"**
The crude, boorish Baron Ochs is Sophie's intended husband in Der Rosenkavalier. Octavian disguises himself as a chambermaid named "Mariandel," whom Ochs tries to seduce, and with the help of the Italian intriguers Valzacchi and Annina sets a trap that humiliates Ochs and ruins his marriage plans. The opera ends with the young Black page Mohammed running onstage to fetch a dropped handkerchief.

**The Marschallin and the trio "Hab mir's gelobt"**
The Marschallin, an aging princess and Octavian's older lover, gracefully gives him up to Sophie and resolves to love even "his love for another." Her final-act trio "Hab mir's gelobt" is sung by three female voices because Octavian is a trouser role, and it is followed by the Octavian–Sophie duet "Ist ein Traum." Georg Solti conducted the trio at Strauss's funeral. In an earlier monologue she admits that she sometimes stops all the clocks at night.

**Elektra**
Strauss's 1909 opera, his first with librettist Hofmannsthal, based on Sophocles' tragedy about Agamemnon's daughter seeking revenge for her father's murder. In her monologue "Allein! Weh, ganz allein," Elektra sings her father's name to the opening Agamemnon motif. The "Elektra chord," E major and C-sharp (D-flat) major triads played at the same time, expresses her violent emotions.

**Till Eulenspiegel's Merry Pranks**
An 1895 tone poem about the German folk trickster Till Eulenspiegel. A rollicking French horn theme and a shrill D clarinet represent Till. At the end he is tried and led to the gallows, and his death is shown by a squawking high clarinet.

**Ein Heldenleben (A Hero's Life)**
A semi-autobiographical 1898 tone poem that opens with rising E-flat major triads representing the hero. Its sections include "The Hero's Adversaries" (critics, depicted by grumbling woodwinds and tubas playing a motif in parallel fifths), "The Hero's Companion" (a violin solo portraying his wife), "The Hero's Battlefield," and "The Hero's Works of Peace," which quotes Strauss's own earlier works.

**An Alpine Symphony**
A 1915 tone poem in 22 continuous sections that is called a symphony even though it is not one in the traditional sense. It portrays a day climbing a mountain, inspired by a climb Strauss made as a boy, with sections like "Entry into the Forest," "Wandering by the Brook," "On the Summit," "Thunderstorm," and "Descent." It uses a wind machine, a thunder machine, offstage brass for a hunting party, and a heckelphone, whose low written notes led to the invention of the lupophon.

**Four Last Songs**
Strauss's final major work, for soprano and orchestra, written in 1948 when he was in his 80s and published after his death by his friend Ernst Roth. Three songs set poems by Hermann Hesse ("Spring," "September," and "When Falling Asleep"). The fourth, "Im Abendrot" ("At Sunset"), sets Joseph von Eichendorff and depicts an old couple at sunset, with two trilling flutes as larks, and ends "Is this perhaps death?" Strauss wanted Kirsten Flagstad to give the premiere.

**Metamorphosen**
A 1945 elegy for 23 solo strings, written near the end of World War II as German cities and opera houses were being destroyed. Near the end, the cellos and basses quote the funeral march from Beethoven's Eroica Symphony, and Strauss wrote "IN MEMORIAM!" in the score at that point.

**Symphonia Domestica (Domestic Symphony)**
An autobiographical 1903 tone poem depicting a day in Strauss's household with his wife and baby son, including bathing the baby. A glockenspiel strikes seven to show the hour. In a love scene, an oboe solo is interrupted by the sound of the baby crying.

**Death and Transfiguration (Tod und Verklärung)**
An 1889 tone poem portraying the last moments of a dying artist, his memories, and his soul's transfiguration after death. It is often grouped with his other early tone poems Don Juan and Don Quixote, the latter featuring a large solo cello as the knight and bleating sheep imitated by flutter-tongued brass.

**Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini**
Rachmaninoff's 1934 work for piano and orchestra, a set of 24 variations on the theme of Niccolo Paganini's 24th Caprice in A minor for solo violin. It was written at his Swiss villa near Lucerne, quotes the "Dies irae" chant, and is the most common giveaway for him.

**18th variation (Andante cantabile, D-flat major)**
The famous lyrical variation of the Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini. Rachmaninoff inverts Paganini's A minor theme (turns it upside down), slows it, and sets it in D-flat major, producing one of his best-loved melodies.

**Piano Concerto No. 2 in C minor**
His 1900-01 concerto, which opens with the soloist playing eight bars of crescendoing, bell-like chords alternating with a low F before the strings take up the main theme. Its slow second movement begins with piano arpeggios before a flute and then a clarinet present the melody. He dedicated it to Nikolai Dahl, the hypnotherapist who helped him recover from years of depression.

**Prelude in C-sharp minor ("The Bells of Moscow")**
His Op. 3 No. 2, part of the Morceaux de fantaisie, which opens with three fortissimo notes, A, G-sharp, C-sharp, imitating church bells. Its climactic middle section is written on four staves. It became so popular that Rachmaninoff grew to hate being asked to play it.

**Piano Concerto No. 3 in D minor**
A famously difficult concerto whose Allegro ma non tanto first movement begins with quiet strings before the piano plays a simple D minor theme in octaves. It has two cadenzas, and the heavier, chordal one is printed as the "ossia." Rachmaninoff joked that it was written "for elephants," Vladimir Horowitz was renowned for playing it, and Yunchan Lim won the 2022 Van Cliburn Competition with it.

**The Isle of the Dead**
A symphonic poem inspired by Arnold Bocklin's painting of a rowboat carrying a shrouded figure to a rocky island of cypresses. A rocking ostinato in 5/8 time represents the oars of Charon, the ferryman of the dead, and the piece quotes the "Dies irae."

**Symphonic Dances**
His last completed work (1940), in three movements originally titled "Noon," "Twilight," and "Midnight." The first, "Non allegro," movement contains his only use of the alto saxophone and quotes the theme of his failed First Symphony. The finale sets the "Dies irae" against a chant from his All-Night Vigil.

**"Dies irae"**
The medieval Latin chant for the dead ("Day of Wrath") that Rachmaninoff quoted obsessively. It appears in his First Symphony, The Isle of the Dead, the Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini, and the Symphonic Dances.

**Symphony No. 2 in E minor**
His successful 1907 symphony. Its slow third movement, the Adagio, opens with a long, famous clarinet solo, and the violins introduce a yearning motif (G-sharp, A, F-sharp).

**Symphony No. 1 and its disastrous premiere**
His D minor First Symphony, which quotes the "Dies irae," was premiered in 1897 under the conductor Alexander Glazunov, who was reportedly drunk. The premiere was a fiasco, and Rachmaninoff fell into a depression that kept him from composing for several years, until his treatment by Nikolai Dahl.

**Vocalise**
A wordless song for a voice singing on a single vowel, published as the last of his Fourteen Songs, Op. 34. It is often arranged for instruments.

**All-Night Vigil**
His 1915 unaccompanied choral setting of the Russian Orthodox vigil service, also called the Vespers. He asked that its fifth movement, a setting of the "Nunc dimittis," be sung at his funeral, and he quoted the Vigil in his Symphonic Dances.

**Enormous hands and Vladimir Horowitz**
Rachmaninoff was one of the greatest pianists of his time, and his huge hands could span about a thirteenth, which is why his piano writing has such wide chords. Vladimir Horowitz idolized him, met him soon after arriving in the US in 1928, and became a close friend.

**Etudes-Tableaux**
His two sets of "study-pictures" for piano, Opp. 33 and 39. Some were given descriptive titles such as "The Sea and the Seagulls" and "A Scene at the Fair," and several were orchestrated by Ottorino Respighi.

**Variations on a Theme of Corelli**
His 1931 solo piano work, based on the "La Folia" theme that Arcangelo Corelli used in a violin sonata. He also wrote Variations on a Theme of Chopin, the Trio elegiaque, and the one-act opera The Miserly Knight.

**Girl with a Pearl Earring**
Vermeer's most famous work (c. 1665), nicknamed the "Mona Lisa of the North" and held in the Mauritshuis in The Hague. It is a tronie (a study of a face or character type, not a commissioned portrait) of a girl in a blue-and-yellow turban who turns over her shoulder toward the viewer against a dark background, showing a large pearl earring. The blue was made from ultramarine (crushed lapis lazuli), and the painting inspired Tracy Chevalier's 1999 novel, in which a Protestant maid named Griet models for the painting.

**The Milkmaid**
Vermeer's painting (c. 1658, Rijksmuseum) of a sturdy kitchen maid in a yellow bodice and blue apron pouring milk from a jug into a bowl beside a basket of bread. A foot warmer sits on the floor behind her in front of Delft tiles, one of which shows Cupid.

**View of Delft**
Vermeer's cityscape (c. 1660–1661, Mauritshuis) of his hometown seen from across the Schie River, with small figures on the near shore, boats in the harbor, and dark clouds casting shadows. Sunlight hits the bell-less tower of the Nieuwe Kerk (New Church), and he mixed sand into the paint for texture. Marcel Proust's character Bergotte dies looking at its "little patch of yellow wall."

**The Art of Painting**
Also called The Allegory of Painting (Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna). An artist seen from behind paints a model posing as Clio, the muse of history, who holds a trumpet and a book and wears a laurel wreath. Behind them hang a large map of the Seventeen Provinces of the Netherlands and a chandelier topped with a double-headed Habsburg eagle.

**The Astronomer and The Geographer**
A pair of paintings of scholars, probably modeled by the same man, possibly Vermeer's fellow Delft citizen Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, the pioneer of microscopy, who later served as executor of Vermeer's estate. In The Astronomer, a man in a robe reaches toward a celestial globe beside a book by Adriaan Metius. In The Geographer, a long-haired man holding dividers looks up from a map toward a window. The two canvases were cut from the same bolt of cloth.

**The Concert**
Vermeer's painting of two women, one at a harpsichord and one singing, with a lutenist seen from behind; a copy of Dirck van Baburen's The Procuress hangs on the wall. It was stolen from Boston's Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in the 1990 heist and has never been recovered; it is often called the most valuable stolen painting in the world.

**The Allegory of Faith**
A late Vermeer allegory (Metropolitan Museum of Art) of a woman personifying the Catholic faith. She rests her hand on her chest and her foot on a terrestrial globe, gazes up at a glass sphere hanging from the ceiling, and sits in front of a painting of the Crucifixion. Vermeer had converted to Catholicism when he married.

**Window on the left**
A hallmark of Vermeer's quiet domestic interiors: light usually falls into the room from a window on the left side of the picture. Examples include The Geographer, The Milkmaid, and Woman Holding a Balance, while A Lady Writing a Letter is a notable exception.

**Camera obscura**
An optical device that projects an image through a lens or pinhole, which many scholars think Vermeer used to help achieve his precise light effects and soft, blurred highlights. The inventor Tim Jenison argued, in the documentary Tim's Vermeer, that Vermeer used a lens with a "comparator mirror."

**The Love Letter**
A Vermeer painting (Rijksmuseum) viewed through a doorway from a dim hallway with slippers and a broom on the floor, as if intruding on the room. A seated woman holding a cittern (a lute-like instrument) receives a letter from her maid.

**The Music Lesson**
Also called A Lady at the Virginals with a Gentleman (Royal Collection, UK). A young woman stands with her back to the viewer at a virginal (a small keyboard instrument) while a man watches; a viola da gamba lies on a black-and-white tiled floor, and an Oriental rug covers a table in the foreground.

**Woman Holding a Balance**
Vermeer's painting (National Gallery of Art, Washington) of a woman in blue weighing on an empty scale while standing in front of a painting of the Last Judgment. It is often read as a meditation on worldly versus spiritual judgment.

**Théophile Thoré-Bürger**
The French critic who rediscovered Vermeer in the 19th century, after he had largely been forgotten. Writing as "William Bürger," he published influential articles in the Gazette des Beaux-Arts in 1866, attributed many works to Vermeer that had been credited to others, and called him the "Sphinx of Delft."

**Han van Meegeren**
A Dutch forger of the 1930s–40s who painted fake Vermeers, most famously The Supper at Emmaus, which was modeled partly on Caravaggio's painting of the same subject. After selling a forgery to Hermann Göring he was charged with treason, and he proved his innocence by showing he had painted the works himself.

**The Ghost of Vermeer of Delft Which Can Be Used as a Table**
Salvador Dalí's 1934 painting of a dark, Vermeer-like figure kneeling with an extremely long leg that serves as a tabletop. Vermeer's early works include The Procuress, a brothel scene in which the man on the left looking at the viewer may be a self-portrait.

**"Unfinished" Symphony (Symphony No. 8 in B minor, D. 759)**
Schubert's most famous symphony, begun in 1822 and left with only two complete movements, though a third-movement scherzo survives in sketches. Its 3/4 first movement opens with a dark, quiet melody in the cellos and basses (B, C-sharp, D, B) before an oboe and clarinet theme enters, and its second movement is an Andante con moto in E major. It was not premiered until 1865, decades after his death.

**"Erlkönig" ("The Erlking")**
Schubert's setting of Goethe's ballad about a father riding through the night with his sick son, who is lured and finally killed by the supernatural Erlking. The piano's relentless octave triplets depict the galloping horse, and a single singer portrays four characters: narrator, father, son, and Erlking.

**Trout Quintet (Piano Quintet in A major)**
A chamber work for the unusual ensemble of piano, violin, viola, cello, and double bass, so it has only one violin. Its fourth movement is a set of variations on Schubert's song "Die Forelle" ("The Trout"), whose rising piano sextuplets depict the fish leaping in the stream.

**Winterreise**
Schubert's song cycle setting 24 poems by Wilhelm Müller about a rejected lover's bleak winter journey. It opens with "Gute Nacht," includes "Der Lindenbaum" (The Linden Tree), "Die Wetterfahne" (a creaking weathervane), "Die Post" (a posthorn call), and "Irrlicht" (Will-o'-the-Wisp), and ends with "Der Leiermann" (The Hurdy-Gurdy Man), whose left hand repeats a drone-like open fifth.

**Die schöne Müllerin**
Schubert's earlier song cycle on Wilhelm Müller poems about a journeyman miller who falls in love with a miller's daughter. It opens with "Das Wandern," uses a constant repeated F-sharp in "Die liebe Farbe" to show his obsession with the color green, and ends with the brook singing a lullaby after he drowns himself in it.

**Rosamunde entr'acte**
Schubert wrote incidental music for Helmina von Chézy's play Rosamunde, Princess of Cyprus. Its B minor entr'acte is often theorized to be the intended finale of the Unfinished Symphony, and a Rosamunde theme also appears in his String Quartet No. 13 in A minor, the "Rosamunde" Quartet.

**Death and the Maiden**
A lied setting Matthias Claudius's poem in which Death comforts a frightened girl. Schubert used it as the theme for variations in the slow movement of his String Quartet No. 14 in D minor (D. 810), written in 1824 after his syphilis diagnosis; the quartet is known for sudden dynamic contrasts and ends with a tarantella.

**"Great" C major Symphony (Symphony No. 9)**
Schubert's longest symphony, called "Great" to distinguish it from his "Little" Sixth Symphony in the same key. It opens with two unison horns playing a motto theme, uses a three-key exposition (C major, E minor, G major), and was premiered posthumously by Felix Mendelssohn after Robert Schumann, who praised its "heavenly length," discovered the manuscript.

**"Gretchen am Spinnrade" ("Gretchen at the Spinning Wheel")**
An early lied setting a scene from Goethe's Faust, in which Gretchen sings "My peace is gone, my heart is heavy" while longing for Faust. The piano's whirling figures depict the spinning wheel and a foot treadle, and the motion stops abruptly when she recalls his kiss ("sein Kuss!").

**"Ave Maria" ("Ellens dritter Gesang")**
"Ellen's Third Song," part of Schubert's Op. 52 settings of Sir Walter Scott's The Lady of the Lake, in which Ellen prays to the Virgin Mary. Because it begins with the words of the Latin prayer, it is now known as Schubert's "Ave Maria."

**Wanderer Fantasy**
Schubert's virtuosic C major Fantasy for solo piano, based on his song "Der Wanderer." It was so difficult that Schubert himself could not play it, reportedly saying "the devil may play it," and Liszt later transcribed it for piano and orchestra.

**Piano Sonata in B-flat major (D. 960)**
Schubert's last piano sonata, written in the final months of his life in 1828. Early in its first movement, an ominous low trill on G-flat interrupts the serene theme and foreshadows a striking modulation away from B-flat major.

**String Quintet in C major**
Schubert's only string quintet, written in 1828, which adds a second cello to the standard string quartet. It is one of his final masterpieces.

**"Tragic" Symphony (Symphony No. 4 in C minor)**
An early Schubert symphony that he himself nicknamed "Tragic." It is often clued alongside his "Little" C major Sixth Symphony.

**Schubertiades and Johann Michael Vogl**
Schubertiades were informal Viennese gatherings devoted to Schubert's music, famously depicted by his friend Moritz von Schwind. The baritone Johann Michael Vogl championed his songs during his lifetime, and the 20th-century baritone Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau became the most famous interpreter of his more than 600 lieder.

**The Rite of Spring (Le Sacre du printemps)**
Stravinsky's most famous ballet, subtitled "Pictures from Pagan Russia," written for Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes with choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky. Its savage rhythms, dissonance, and provocative choreography sparked a near-riot at its 1913 Paris premiere. It is divided into two parts, "The Adoration of the Earth" and "The Sacrifice."

**Opening high bassoon solo**
The Rite of Spring begins with a solo bassoon playing in an unusually high register, starting on a long C followed by B, G, E, B, and a long A. The melody is based on a Lithuanian folk song, and Stravinsky likened the introduction's woodwinds to a swarm of spring pipes.

**"Sacrificial Dance" and the Chosen One**
The finale of The Rite of Spring, in which a young girl chosen in the "Glorification of the Chosen One" dances herself to death to appease the god of spring. Its meter changes almost every measure. Other Part II sections include "Mystic Circles of the Young Girls" and "Evocation of the Ancestors."

**"Augurs of Spring" polychord**
In the Rite's "Augurs of Spring," the strings pound out a harsh repeated chord combining an F-flat major triad with an E-flat dominant seventh, with irregular accents mirrored by the stomping dancers. Part I also includes the "Procession of the Sage" (Wise Elder) and "The Kiss of the Earth."

**The Firebird and Koschei's egg**
Stravinsky's first ballet for Diaghilev (1910), based on Russian folklore. Prince Ivan enters the garden of the sorcerer Koschei (Kashchei) the Immortal, captures the magical Firebird, and with her help destroys Koschei by smashing the egg that holds his soul.

**"Infernal Dance"**
The violent dance in The Firebird, introduced by a timpani stroke, in which the Firebird bewitches Koschei and his monsters into dancing until they collapse from exhaustion.

**Berceuse and 7/4 Finale**
After the "Infernal Dance," the Firebird lulls the monsters to sleep with a Berceuse (lullaby) featuring a famous bassoon solo over harp and strings. The ballet's finale grows from a quiet horn melody into a grand ending that switches from 3/2 to 7/4 time.

**Thirteen princesses and the golden apples**
In The Firebird, thirteen princesses held captive by Koschei, led by the Tsarevna, play a game with golden apples and dance a khorovod (Russian round dance) before Ivan falls in love with one of them.

**Petrushka chord**
A bitonal chord superimposing C major and F-sharp major triads, a tritone apart, first introduced by two clarinets. It represents the title puppet whenever he appears in Petrushka and is one of the most famous chords in 20th-century music.

**Petrushka**
Stravinsky's 1911 ballet about a straw puppet who comes to life at the Shrovetide Fair in St. Petersburg. Petrushka loves the Ballerina but is trapped in his cell and finally killed by the Moor; one fair scene includes the "Wet-Nurses' Dance."

**Symphony of Psalms**
A 1930 neoclassical choral symphony written for the 50th anniversary of the Boston Symphony Orchestra. It sets three biblical psalms (including "Expectans expectavi Dominum" from Psalm 40), omits violins, violas, and clarinets, and opens with a distinctively voiced E minor chord.

**Pulcinella**
A 1920 ballet based on music attributed to Pergolesi (some actually by other 18th-century composers), often seen as the start of Stravinsky's neoclassical period. He later arranged parts of it as the Suite italienne; other neoclassical works include the Dumbarton Oaks Concerto, written for Robert and Mildred Bliss's 30th wedding anniversary, and the ballet Orpheus.

**Agon**
A plotless ballet for twelve dancers choreographed by George Balanchine, marking Stravinsky's move toward serialism. It includes a sarabande, galliard, and branles inspired by a 17th-century French court dance manual, and completes his "Greek trilogy" with Apollon musagète and Orpheus.

**The Rake's Progress**
Stravinsky's English-language opera based on William Hogarth's series of paintings and engravings, with a libretto by W. H. Auden and Chester Kallman. It follows Tom Rakewell, who abandons his beloved Anne Trulove and is led to ruin by the devilish Nick Shadow.

**Violin Concerto and the "passport chord"**
Stravinsky's Violin Concerto in D, written with violinist Samuel Dushkin, begins every movement with a triple-stop chord spanning more than two octaves. Stravinsky sketched it on a napkin; Dushkin first thought it unplayable, then found it possible, and Stravinsky called it the "passport" to the concerto.

**The Birth of Venus**
Botticelli's most famous painting (c. 1485, Uffizi, Florence), in tempera on canvas. The nude goddess Venus stands in a modest pose on a giant scallop shell, covering herself with her long red-gold hair, while the wind god Zephyrus, embracing Chloris, blows her to shore amid falling roses. On the right, a Hora (a goddess of the seasons) rushes to cover her with a flowered cloak.

**Primavera**
Botticelli's allegory of spring (c. 1480, Uffizi), set in a dark orange grove. Venus stands in the center beneath a blindfolded Cupid, with the Three Graces dancing at the left, and at the right the blue-skinned Zephyrus seizes the nymph Chloris, who turns into Flora, the flower-strewn goddess of spring. The painting draws on Ovid's Fasti and the poetry of Poliziano.

**Zephyrus and Chloris**
The west wind and the nymph he pursued, who appear in both of Botticelli's great mythological paintings. In Primavera, the ghostly Zephyrus grabs Chloris, who is transformed into Flora; in The Birth of Venus, the two fly together, blowing Venus toward the shore.

**Mercury and his caduceus**
At the far left of Primavera, the messenger god Mercury, in a red cloak with a sword at his side, raises his caduceus (snake-entwined staff) to push away wispy clouds or reach toward the oranges. He is often seen as representing the month of May.

**Three Graces**
The trio of dancing goddesses at the left of Primavera, who hold hands in a circle and wear translucent white gowns. Cupid aims a flaming arrow at one of them from above.

**The Mystical Nativity**
Botticelli's late nativity (c. 1500, National Gallery, London), his only signed and dated work. A Greek inscription at the top refers to the Book of Revelation and the troubles of the time. Above the thatched stable, twelve angels in white, red, and green (the colors of faith, hope, and charity) dance in a circle holding olive branches, while in the foreground angels embrace men as small demons flee.

**Venus and Mars**
Botticelli's painting (c. 1485, National Gallery, London) of the goddess Venus, awake and alert, watching her lover Mars sleep. Mischievous baby satyrs play with Mars's lance and armor, one wears his helmet, and another blows a conch shell in his ear. Wasps buzz near Mars's head, possibly a pun on the Vespucci family name.

**Madonna of the Magnificat**
A Botticelli tondo (circular painting) in the Uffizi showing the Virgin Mary writing the Magnificat, her hymn of praise, in a book, as two angels hold a delicate golden crown over her head. The infant Christ guides her hand, and the Madonna may have been modeled on Lucrezia Tornabuoni.

**Madonna of the Pomegranate**
Another Botticelli tondo in the Uffizi, in which Mary holds the Christ Child, who holds a pomegranate, a symbol of the Passion and resurrection. Six angels surround them, and golden rays shine down from above.

**Sistine Chapel frescoes**
In 1481–1482, years before Michelangelo painted the ceiling, Botticelli was among the Florentine painters called to Rome to fresco the chapel's walls. His scenes include The Youth of Moses (Trials of Moses), The Temptations of Christ, and The Punishment of Korah.

**Girolamo Savonarola**
The Dominican friar whose apocalyptic preaching dominated Florence in the 1490s and led to the "Bonfire of the Vanities." Botticelli is said to have fallen under his influence, and his late works, like The Mystical Nativity, take on a more somber, religious tone.

**Adoration of the Magi**
Botticelli's painting (c. 1475, Uffizi) in which members of the Medici family, his chief patrons, appear as the three Magi and their attendants. Botticelli included a self-portrait at the far right, looking out at the viewer.

**Pallas and the Centaur**
A Botticelli painting (Uffizi) in which the goddess Pallas Athena, holding a large halberd (a battle-axe on a pole), grips the hair of a sheepish centaur. It is often read as wisdom or reason taming passion.

**The Calumny of Apelles**
A late Botticelli allegory (c. 1494, Uffizi) recreating a lost painting by the ancient Greek painter Apelles, as described by Lucian. A judge with donkey ears is advised by Ignorance and Suspicion, who pull at his ears and hair, while Calumny drags a victim by the hair before him, and the nude figure of Truth points up to heaven.

**Fra Filippo Lippi**
The Florentine painter who was Botticelli's teacher; his graceful, linear style shaped Botticelli's early Madonnas. Botticelli's other works include the fresco Saint Augustine in His Study, which shows the saint surrounded by books and an armillary sphere.

**Peter Grimes**
Britten's breakthrough 1945 opera, based on George Crabbe's poem The Borough. The title fisherman is suspected of murder after his apprentices die at sea. When his new apprentice John falls to his death, the hostile townspeople hunt him, and at the end he takes his boat out and sinks it, drowning himself. In his last mad scene, an offstage foghorn (played by a tuba) and a chorus calling "Grimes!" accompany him.

**Four Sea Interludes**
An orchestral suite drawn from the interludes of Peter Grimes: "Dawn," "Sunday Morning" (in which horns imitate church bells), "Moonlight," and "Storm." It is often performed together with the opera's Passacaglia.

**"Now the Great Bear and Pleiades"**
Peter Grimes's visionary aria, sung after he storms into the Boar tavern during a storm. Afterward, Ned Keene calms the uneasy crowd by starting the round "Old Joe has gone fishing." Grimes's earlier aria "What harbour shelters peace?" comes just before the "Storm" interlude.

**Ellen Orford and the "Embroidery Aria"**
Ellen is the widowed schoolmistress who loves Grimes and tries to help him. In Act III, after Captain Balstrode shows her the drowned apprentice's jersey, she sings the "Embroidery Aria," recognizing the anchor she had stitched on it. The opera's prologue ends with an unaccompanied duet between her and Grimes in which they start in different keys and then converge.

**The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra**
Britten's 1946 piece introducing children to the orchestra, written for the educational film Instruments of the Orchestra; Eric Crozier wrote its narration. It states a Rondeau theme from Henry Purcell's incidental music to Aphra Behn's play Abdelazer, follows it with 13 variations that each feature a different instrument or section, and ends with a fugue, opened by the piccolo, that Britten called "a race between the instruments." It is dedicated to the children of John and Jean Maud.

**War Requiem**
A large 1962 choral work written for the consecration of the new Coventry Cathedral, rebuilt after its destruction in World War II. It sets the Latin Requiem Mass alongside antiwar poems by Wilfred Owen. It uses a separate boys' choir accompanied by a portative organ, and a recurring C–F-sharp tritone serves as a motif.

**Wilfred Owen**
The English World War I poet whose poems Britten set in the War Requiem. "Anthem for Doomed Youth" ("What passing bells for these who die as cattle?") appears in the first movement, and "Strange Meeting" appears in the final Libera me.

**Peter Pears**
The English tenor who was Britten's lifelong partner.
