Britten wrote most of his major tenor roles for him, including Peter Grimes, Albert Herring, Captain Vere in Billy Budd, and Aschenbach in Death in Venice. Pears also premiered song cycles such as the Seven Sonnets of Michelangelo and the Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings.

**Albert Herring**
Britten's 1947 comic chamber opera based on Guy de Maupassant's story "Le Rosier de Madame Husson." Lady Billows has the virtuous grocer's boy Albert crowned "King of the May" because no girl is pure enough to be May Queen. Sid and Nancy spike his lemonade with rum, so the Tristan chord sounds whenever he hiccups, and he disappears that night on a wild spree.

**Variations on a Theme of Frank Bridge**
A 1937 string orchestra work based on a theme from his teacher Frank Bridge's Three Idylls for string quartet. Each variation portrays a trait of Bridge, in movements such as "Aria Italiana" and "Bourrée classique."

**Paul Bunyan**
Britten's operetta about the giant American lumberjack, with a libretto by W. H. Auden. It was written while he lived in the United States and premiered in 1941. Its characters include the cook Hot Biscuit Slim.

**Billy Budd**
Britten's 1951 opera based on Herman Melville's novella, with a libretto by E. M. Forster and Eric Crozier. The innocent sailor Billy strikes and kills the evil master-at-arms John Claggart and is hanged, a story told in flashback by Captain Vere.

**Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings**
A 1943 song cycle written for Peter Pears and the horn player Dennis Brain. It sets English poems and begins and ends with a Prologue and Epilogue for solo natural horn.

**Curlew River**
The first of Britten's three "church parables," with a libretto by William Plomer. Based on the Japanese Noh play Sumidagawa, it premiered at Orford Church and begins with monks processing in to the plainchant hymn "Te lucis ante terminum." The flute is associated with the Madwoman and the horn with the Ferryman.

**The Rape of Lucretia**
A 1946 chamber opera about the Roman noblewoman Lucretia, who is raped by Tarquinius and then kills herself. A Male Chorus and a Female Chorus stand outside the action and comment on it from a Christian viewpoint.

**Two violins, a viola, and a cello**
The standard instrumentation of a string quartet, which nearly every question gives as the giveaway. Like a symphony, a string quartet usually has four movements.

**Joseph Haydn, "Father of the String Quartet"**
Haydn wrote 68 string quartets and established the genre's classic form, which earned him the title "father" of both the string quartet and the symphony.

**Haydn's "Emperor" Quartet**
Op. 76 No. 3, from a set of six quartets dedicated to Count Joseph Erdődy. Its second movement is a set of variations on Haydn's anthem "Gott erhalte Franz den Kaiser" ("God Save Emperor Francis"). That melody later became the tune of the German national anthem, "Das Lied der Deutschen" ("Deutschland über alles"). The Op. 76 set also includes the "Sunrise" Quartet (No. 4) and the "Largo" Quartet (No. 5), named for its long Largo cantabile e mesto in F-sharp major.

**Schubert's "Death and the Maiden"**
Schubert's String Quartet No. 14 in D minor. Its second movement is a set of variations on his earlier lied "Der Tod und das Mädchen," a setting of a poem by Matthias Claudius, and its finale is a tarantella. Schubert has 15 numbered quartets, including No. 13 in A minor, the "Rosamunde," which takes a melody from his incidental music to the play Rosamunde.

**Beethoven's "Razumovsky" Quartets**
The three quartets of Beethoven's Op. 59, commissioned by Count Andreas Razumovsky, the Russian ambassador in Vienna. Each one includes a Russian theme. Beethoven's other named quartets include the "Harp" (Op. 74) and the "Serioso" (Op. 95).

**Grosse Fuge**
Beethoven's massive, dissonant double fugue, Op. 133. It was originally the finale of his String Quartet No. 13 (Op. 130), but his publisher had him write a new finale, and the fugue was published separately.

**Dvořák's "American" Quartet**
Antonín Dvořák's String Quartet No. 12 in F major. He wrote it in 1893 while staying in the Czech community of Spillville, Iowa. It opens with a pentatonic theme often linked to American spirituals and folk music.

**Smetana's "From My Life"**
Bedřich Smetana's autobiographical String Quartet No. 1 in E minor. Its movements depict his youth (including a polka), his love for his wife, and finally his deafness, represented by a sustained high E in the first violin that imitates the ringing in his ears.

**Haydn's "The Joke"**
Haydn's String Quartet Op. 33 No. 2 in E-flat major, from the set of six "Russian" Quartets. It gets its nickname from the rondo finale, which keeps stopping with long pauses before the theme returns, so the audience cannot tell when the piece has ended.

**Mozart's "Dissonance" Quartet**
Mozart's String Quartet No. 19 in C major, K. 465, named for the unusually dissonant slow introduction at its opening. It is the last of the six quartets Mozart dedicated to Haydn.

**Janáček's "Intimate Letters" and "Kreutzer Sonata"**
Leoš Janáček's String Quartet No. 2, "Intimate Letters," was inspired by his decade-long, unrequited passion for the much younger Kamila Stösslová. His String Quartet No. 1 was inspired by Tolstoy's novella The Kreutzer Sonata.

**Bartók's quartets and the "Bartók pizzicato"**
Béla Bartók wrote six string quartets. His Fourth uses the "snap" or "Bartók pizzicato," in which a string is plucked so hard that it slaps against the fingerboard.

**Shostakovich's String Quartet No. 8**
Shostakovich wrote this C minor quartet in about three days in Dresden in 1960, while he was working on the film score Five Days, Five Nights. Dedicated "to the victims of fascism and war," it is built on his musical signature, the D-S-C-H motif.

**Berg's Lyric Suite**
Alban Berg's six-movement work for string quartet, dedicated to the composer Alexander von Zemlinsky. It is now known to encode Berg's secret love affair with Hanna Fuchs-Robettin.

**Barber's Adagio for Strings**
Samuel Barber arranged the slow second movement of his String Quartet, Op. 11, for string orchestra as the famous Adagio for Strings.

**The Swing**
Jean-Honoré Fragonard's 1767 painting, the definitive Rococo image. A woman in a pink dress and straw hat swings in a garden and kicks off her slipper, while a young man hiding in the bushes below looks up her skirt. An older man pushes the swing from behind. The patron's original request was for a bishop to push the swing, but in the finished painting the figure is usually read as a cuckolded husband.

**Cupid statue with finger to lips**
In The Swing, a statue of Cupid on the left puts his finger to his lips, urging silence and secrecy about the flirtation taking place below.

**The Embarkation for Cythera**
Antoine Watteau's 1717 painting of elegant couples beside a golden boat with cherubs (putti) flying overhead and a rose-covered statue of Venus on the right. Cythera is the island sacred to Aphrodite (Venus), and scholars debate whether the couples are arriving or leaving.

**Fête galante**
A genre of painting invented by Watteau, showing aristocrats in fancy dress enjoying amorous outdoor leisure in idyllic parkland. The French Academy created the category to admit Watteau with The Embarkation for Cythera.

**Jean-Antoine Watteau**
The French painter who launched Rococo painting. Besides the Embarkation, he painted Pierrot (formerly called Gilles), a life-size image of the commedia dell'arte clown standing in white in front of other stock characters.

**Jean-Honoré Fragonard**
A student of François Boucher and the last great Rococo painter. His works include The Swing, The Stolen Kiss (a youth secretly kissing a young woman holding a striped shawl), and The Progress of Love series.

**François Boucher**
A leading Rococo painter and favorite of Madame de Pompadour. He painted The Toilette of Venus, in which a nude Venus holds a dove while cherubs attend her (one reaches for a pearl necklace), and Diana Leaving Her Bath, also called Diana After the Hunt. He also decorated parts of the Hôtel de Soubise in Paris and helped popularize chinoiserie.

**Blonde Odalisque / Diderot**
Boucher painted Marie-Louise O'Murphy, a teenage mistress of Louis XV, lying nude on her stomach. The critic Denis Diderot attacked Boucher's erotic subjects, and he accused him of "prostituting his own wife" by using her as the model for a similar odalisque.

**Madame de Pompadour**
The influential mistress of Louis XV, who was a major patron of Rococo art and helped popularize the style. Boucher painted several portraits of her, and he painted The Toilette of Venus for her château at Bellevue.

**Jupiter and Callisto**
Boucher painted several versions of the myth in which Jupiter disguises himself as the goddess Diana to seduce the nymph Callisto, with putti flying around them.

**The Progress of Love**
A series by Fragonard commissioned for Madame du Barry, who rejected it. Its panels include The Pursuit, The Meeting, The Lover Crowned, and Love Letters, in which two lovers read letters with a dog at their feet. The series is now at the Frick Collection in New York.

**Clodion**
Claude Michel, known as Clodion, was the leading Rococo sculptor. He made small, playful terracotta works with bacchanalian themes, such as Nymph and Satyr Carousing and the reliefs The Intoxication of Wine and Faun Family.

**Giovanni Battista Tiepolo**
The great Venetian Rococo fresco painter. He decorated the Würzburg Residence in Germany and painted The Apotheosis of Spain on the ceiling of the Royal Palace of Madrid.

**Thomas Chippendale**
An English cabinetmaker whose furniture designs, published in The Gentleman and Cabinet-Maker's Director, mixed Rococo, Gothic, and Chinese motifs and helped popularize the style in England.

**Pilgrimage Church of Wies**
A Bavarian church designed by Dominikus Zimmermann, considered a masterpiece of Rococo architecture for its white-and-gold interior full of light and ornate stucco.

**Olympia**
Manet's 1863 painting, exhibited in 1865, of a nude prostitute reclining on a white bed and staring coldly at the viewer. She wears only a black ribbon choker, an orchid in her hair, a bracelet, and one slipper. A Black servant brings her a bouquet of flowers from an admirer, and a black cat arches its back at the far right. It reworks Titian's Venus of Urbino and caused a huge scandal at the Salon.

**The Luncheon on the Grass (Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe)**
A painting of a nude woman picnicking in a wood with two fully dressed men, looking out at the viewer, while a second, oddly oversized woman bathes in a stream behind them. A basket of fruit and her discarded clothes lie in the foreground. Originally titled The Bath, it was based on Marcantonio Raimondi's engraving after Raphael's Judgment of Paris and on Titian's (formerly Giorgione's) Pastoral Concert.

**A Bar at the Folies-Bergère**
Manet's last major painting (1882), showing a tired-looking barmaid in a black dress behind a marble counter of liquor bottles and a glass bowl of oranges at a Paris music hall. The mirror behind her reflects the crowd and a mustached man in a top hat who seems to be talking to her, at an angle that is physically impossible. The green-booted feet of a trapeze performer appear in the upper left corner.

**The Execution of Emperor Maximilian**
A series of paintings and a lithograph showing the 1867 execution by firing squad of Maximilian, the Austrian archduke installed as emperor of Mexico by Napoleon III. The composition draws on Goya's The Third of May, 1808. One version was cut into pieces, later gathered and reassembled by Edgar Degas, and is now in London's National Gallery.

**Victorine Meurent**
Manet's favorite model, who posed for the nude in The Luncheon on the Grass, for Olympia, for Mademoiselle V... in the Costume of an Espada, and for the woman in The Railway. She later became a painter herself.

**Salon des Refusés (1863)**
The "Salon of the Rejected," an exhibition ordered by Napoleon III for works turned down by the official Paris Salon of 1863. The Luncheon on the Grass caused the biggest scandal there, making Manet a hero to the young painters who became the Impressionists.

**Music in the Tuileries**
An early painting of a fashionable crowd in top hats and bonnets gathered for an outdoor concert in the Tuileries Gardens in Paris. It includes portraits of Manet's friends, such as Baudelaire, Théophile Gautier, and Jacques Offenbach, along with Manet himself, and two women in yellow dresses and blue bonnets sit at the left.

**The Balcony**
A painting of figures on a balcony framed by green shutters and a green iron railing: the painter Berthe Morisot seated in white, the violinist Fanny Claus standing, and a man behind them. It is loosely based on Goya's Majas on a Balcony.

**Berthe Morisot**
The Impressionist painter who was Manet's frequent model and, after marrying his brother Eugène, his sister-in-law. Manet painted her in The Balcony and in Berthe Morisot with a Bouquet of Violets, where she wears a black mourning dress with violets at her neckline.

**The Railway (Gare Saint-Lazare)**
A painting of a woman in dark blue, modeled by Victorine Meurent, seated with a book and a puppy and looking at the viewer. Beside her a little girl in blue and white grips an iron fence and gazes at the cloud of steam rising from the railway tracks below.

**Émile Zola**
The novelist defended Manet in print, predicting that future generations would go into ecstasies over his pictures. Manet thanked him with a portrait of Zola seated at his desk, with a Japanese print and screen, a reproduction of Olympia, and a Velázquez print in the background.

**The Fifer**
A painting of a boy in a military uniform with bright red trousers playing a fife against a flat, empty gray background, influenced by Velázquez. It was rejected by the 1866 Salon.

**Spanish-themed paintings**
Manet was deeply influenced by Spanish art, especially Velázquez and Goya. His Spanish subjects include The Spanish Singer, a guitarist in a white headscarf; Mademoiselle V... in the Costume of an Espada, showing Victorine Meurent as a bullfighter; Young Man in the Costume of a Majo; Spanish Ballet; and The Dead Toreador, a bullfighter lying dead with one hand on his chest near his pink cape.

**The Races at Longchamp**
A painting of horses at the Longchamp racecourse in Paris charging straight toward the viewer, past a crowd of spectators. It is an unusual head-on view of motion for its time.

**"Jupiter" Symphony (Symphony No. 41 in C major)**
Mozart's 41st and final symphony, nicknamed after the Roman king of the gods. Its finale opens with the whole-note theme "C, D, F, E" and ends in a famous five-voice fugato that combines all of the movement's themes at once.

**"Great" and "Little" G minor symphonies**
Symphony No. 40 ("Great" G minor) and Symphony No. 25 ("Little" G minor) are Mozart's only two minor-key symphonies. No. 40, his penultimate symphony, opens with a bar of accompaniment from divided violas before the violins' sighing "E-flat, D, D" figure, and Mozart later revised it to add two clarinet parts.

**Requiem in D minor (K. 626)**
Mozart's final composition, a mass for the dead secretly commissioned by Count Franz von Walsegg. Mozart died in 1791 having written only the first eight or so bars of the "Lacrimosa," and his pupil Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it, writing the Sanctus and Agnus Dei; the final "Lux aeterna" reuses the music of the opening two sections.

**"Tuba mirum"**
A section of the Requiem's sequence in which a solo trombone outlines a descending B-flat major triad that the bass soloist then imitates. Other Requiem clues include the opening bassoon and basset horn theme modeled on Handel's Funeral Anthem for Queen Caroline, the Kyrie double fugue quoting Handel's "And with his stripes we are healed," and the sighing 12/8 Larghetto "Lacrimosa" that follows the "Confutatis."

**The Magic Flute (Die Zauberflöte)**
Mozart's 1791 German-language singspiel. The Queen of the Night sings the coloratura aria "Der Hölle Rache," with its repeated high F6 notes, ordering her daughter Pamina to murder the sorcerer Sarastro.

**"Rondo alla Turca" (Piano Sonata No. 11 in A major, K. 331)**
The A minor finale of this sonata imitates the percussion-heavy music of Turkish Janissary bands. The sonata unusually skips sonata form in its first movement, which is a set of variations on a 6/8 siciliana-like theme marked "Andante grazioso"; Max Reger wrote "Variations and Fugue" on that theme.

**Sonata facile (Piano Sonata No. 16 in C major, K. 545)**
A simple piano sonata that Mozart labeled "for beginners," also called "semplice." It begins with an ascending C major triad melody over a rocking Alberti bass and is a staple for piano students.

**Clarinet Concerto in A major (K. 622)**
One of Mozart's last works, written for clarinetist Anton Stadler and originally intended for the lower-ranged basset clarinet. Mozart also featured the clarinet alongside viola and piano in the "Kegelstatt" Trio, named for a bowling alley where skittles are played.

**Horn concertos for Joseph Leutgeb**
Mozart wrote four horn concertos for his friend Leutgeb, a skilled natural horn player. The manuscripts are written in multicolored ink and include joking, mocking comments aimed at the soloist.

**Eine kleine Nachtmusik (Serenade No. 13 in G major, K. 525)**
A serenade for strings whose title translates to "A Little Night Music." It opens with a rising arpeggiated figure known as a Mannheim rocket.

**Così fan tutte**
An opera in which Ferrando and Guglielmo, egged on by the cynical Don Alfonso, bet on whether their fiancées Fiordiligi and Dorabella will stay faithful, and test them by returning in disguise. It includes the trio "Soave sia il vento," wishing the departing men gentle winds, and Ferrando's aria "Un'aura amorosa."

**"Jeunehomme" and "Coronation" piano concertos**
Two of Mozart's 27 piano concertos. The "Jeunehomme" (No. 9, E-flat major) was long thought to be for an unnamed young woman but was actually written for Victoire Jenamy, and its rondo finale is interrupted by a slow minuet; the "Coronation" (No. 26) was played around Leopold II's 1790 coronation and has a left-hand piano part Mozart left largely unwritten.

**Don Giovanni and The Marriage of Figaro**
Two Mozart operas with libretti by Lorenzo Da Ponte. In Don Giovanni, the unrepentant title seducer is dragged to hell by the statue of the Commendatore, and Don Ottavio swears vengeance in "Il mio tesoro"; in Figaro, the title servant marries Susanna after thwarting Count Almaviva, and sings "Non più andrai."

**Gran Partita (Serenade No. 10, K. 361)**
A seven-movement serenade scored for twelve wind instruments and double bass. It is one of several prominent Mozart wind works, alongside his B-flat major bassoon concerto, C major oboe concerto, and the Concerto for Flute and Harp commissioned by the Duke of Guînes.

**Child prodigy from Salzburg**
Mozart was born in Salzburg and toured Europe as a child with his father Leopold and his older sister Nannerl, whose playing he emulated when learning keyboard. He wrote his first symphony at about eight years old.

**"What a Wonderful World"**
Armstrong's 1967 recording of the optimistic ballad by Bob Thiele and George David Weiss, sung in his signature gravelly voice. It opens "I see trees of green, red roses too" and later describes "skies of blue and clouds of white," "friends shaking hands, saying how do you do" who are "really saying I love you," and hearing "babies cry." It is the most common giveaway for him.

**"Heebie Jeebies"**
A 1926 Hot Five recording of a Boyd Atkins song, often credited with popularizing (and sometimes said to "invent") scat singing, the improvised singing of wordless syllables. According to legend, Armstrong dropped his lyric sheet during the recording session and began scatting to cover the gap, although scat singing actually predates the recording.

**Hot Five and Hot Seven**
The studio bands Armstrong led for Okeh Records in Chicago from 1925 to 1928, whose recordings shifted jazz from collective ensemble improvisation toward virtuosic individual solos. Members included clarinetist Johnny Dodds and Armstrong's second wife, pianist Lil Hardin, with whom he wrote songs like "My Heart"; Earl Hines later replaced her on piano. Critic Gunther Schuller called Armstrong "the first great soloist" in jazz.

**"West End Blues"**
A King Oliver composition that Armstrong recorded in 1928 with a band including Earl Hines, Fred Robinson, and Jimmy Strong. It opens with a famous unaccompanied virtuoso trumpet cadenza, includes a wordless scat chorus traded with clarinet, and features a long-held high note near the end; it is often called one of the greatest jazz recordings.

**King Oliver**
Joe "King" Oliver, Armstrong's mentor from New Orleans, brought him to Chicago in 1922 to play second cornet in King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band. Armstrong later recorded Oliver's compositions "West End Blues" and "Weather Bird." In 1924 he left to join Fletcher Henderson's orchestra in New York.

**"Hello, Dolly!"**
Armstrong's 1964 cover of the title song of Jerry Herman's Broadway musical, in which he inserted his own name ("This is Louis, Dolly") and sang that Dolly will never go away again and "it's so nice to have you back where you belong." It reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, displacing the Beatles and making him the oldest artist to top the chart at the time; it also titled his album Hello, Dolly!

**"Potato Head Blues"**
A 1927 Hot Seven recording famous for Armstrong's dramatic stop-time trumpet solo, in which the band plays only short chords on the first beats while he improvises in between. It also features a long clarinet solo by Johnny Dodds.

**"Weather Bird"**
A 1928 duet recording of a King Oliver composition with pianist Earl "Fatha" Hines, regarded as a landmark of jazz improvisation for its intricate interplay between trumpet and piano. Armstrong had earlier recorded it with Oliver's band. He and Hines later recorded a famous live "Honeysuckle Rose" in Pasadena in 1951.

**Ella Fitzgerald collaborations**
Armstrong recorded a series of albums with Ella Fitzgerald for Verve in the 1950s, including Ella and Louis and a 1959 album of songs from George Gershwin's opera Porgy and Bess. Their notable duets include "Summertime" and "They Can't Take That Away from Me."

**"Satchmo," New Orleans, and "When the Saints Go Marching In"**
Armstrong was born in New Orleans and nicknamed "Satchmo" (from "Satchel Mouth") and "Pops." His popular recording of the spiritual "When the Saints Go Marching In" strengthened that song's association with New Orleans jazz.

**"Mack the Knife"**
Armstrong's hit 1955 jazz version of "The Ballad of Mack the Knife" from Kurt Weill and Bertolt Brecht's The Threepenny Opera helped make it a jazz standard. Ella Fitzgerald's 1960 live recording in Berlin name-checks both Armstrong and Bobby Darin, who also had a hit with the song.

**The Real Ambassadors**
A 1962 jazz musical created by Dave and Iola Brubeck, inspired by Armstrong's role as a State Department "jazz ambassador" touring the world. Armstrong starred on the recording, singing the civil rights-themed lines "They say I look like God / Could God be black?"

**Hoagy Carmichael songs**
Armstrong had successful re-workings of Hoagy Carmichael's "Stardust," in which he added the improvised words "Oh, memory" before an instrumental break, and "Lazy River."

**The All Stars**
The small band Armstrong led from 1947 onward, after the big-band era, which included trombonists Jack Teagarden and Trummy Young. He performed hits such as "Hello, Dolly!" and "What a Wonderful World" in this later phase of his career.

**French songs and other recordings**
Armstrong recorded popular versions of Édith Piaf's "La Vie en Rose" (arranged with Sy Oliver) and "C'est si bon," which he heard at the 1948 Nice Jazz Festival. Other recordings include "(I'll Be Glad When You're Dead) You Rascal You," "Gone Fishin'" with Bing Crosby, a 1954 album of W. C. Handy songs, and an initially unbilled appearance on Jimmie Rodgers's "Blue Yodel No. 9."

**Moonlight Sonata**
Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 14 in C-sharp minor, subtitled "quasi una fantasia." Its first movement, an Adagio sostenuto, repeats soft G-sharp–C-sharp–E triplets and is played "senza sordino," with the sustain pedal held down. The critic Ludwig Rellstab compared it to moonlight on Lake Lucerne. Liszt called the D-flat major second movement "a flower between two abysses," and the Presto agitato finale races through C-sharp minor arpeggios. Chopin's Fantaisie-Impromptu is often said to echo it.

**Beethoven's 32 piano sonatas**
The "New Testament" of the piano repertoire. Nicknamed sonatas include the "Pathétique," "Waldstein," "Appassionata," "Les Adieux" (with "Lebewohl" written over its opening chords), and the huge "Hammerklavier," which Liszt premiered in public. The last, No. 32 in C minor, ends with a syncopated "Arietta" that Jeremy Denk called "proto-jazz." Artur Schnabel made the first complete recording.

**Mozart's piano sonatas and "Rondo alla turca"**
Mozart wrote 18 piano sonatas. No. 11 in A major ends with the "Rondo alla turca," which imitates Turkish Janissary bands with a "B–A–G-sharp–A–C" theme. The easy C major "Sonata facile" ("for beginners") opens over an Alberti bass, and the A minor sonata K. 310 was written around the time his mother died.

**Mozart's piano concertos and "Twinkle" variations**
Mozart wrote 27 piano concertos (counting early arrangements), including the E-flat concerto K. 271, which Alfred Einstein called Mozart's "Eroica." His twelve variations on "Ah vous dirai-je, Maman," the tune of "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star," were also written for piano.

**Thelonious Monk**
The bebop pianist called the "genius of modern music." He composed "'Round Midnight" and "Straight, No Chaser" and is known for saying the piano "ain't got no wrong notes."

**Dave Brubeck and "Take Five"**
The Dave Brubeck Quartet's album Time Out used unusual time signatures, as in "Take Five" (in 5/4, written by saxophonist Paul Desmond) and "Blue Rondo à la Turk." Brubeck's Jazz Impressions of Japan includes a track in which the piano imitates a koto.

**Herbie Hancock**
A jazz pianist and keyboardist who wrote "Watermelon Man" (re-recorded on his jazz-funk album Head Hunters) and "Cantaloupe Island" (from Empyrean Isles).

**Chick Corea, Keith Jarrett, and other jazz pianists**
Chick Corea founded the fusion band Return to Forever, recorded Light as a Feather, and wrote the standard "Spain." Keith Jarrett's improvised Köln Concert is a best-selling solo piano album. Other jazz pianists include Bill Evans, composer of "Waltz for Debby," and Joe Zawinul, who co-founded Weather Report with Wayne Shorter and wrote "Birdland."

**Frédéric Chopin and the "Minute Waltz"**
The Polish composer and pianist who wrote almost entirely for solo piano. His Waltz in D-flat major, the "Minute Waltz," was supposedly inspired by a little dog chasing its own tail.

**Famous piano concertos and competitions**
Nikolai Rubinstein at first harshly criticized Tchaikovsky's Piano Concerto No. 1, which later became a favorite. Rachmaninoff's Second Piano Concerto opens with bell-like chords, and his famously difficult Third, in D minor, has an optional harder "ossia" cadenza and was premiered in New York; Yunchan Lim played it to win the 2022 Van Cliburn Competition. Ravel's G major concerto opens with a whip crack, and his Concerto for the Left Hand was written for Paul Wittgenstein, who lost his right arm in World War I. Van Cliburn and Martha Argerich are famous winners of major piano competitions.

**Spanish piano music**
Isaac Albéniz's suite Iberia opens with "Evocación," and Alicia de Larrocha made a celebrated complete recording of it. Enrique Granados's Goyescas includes "The Maiden and the Nightingale," which reportedly inspired "Bésame Mucho." Manuel de Falla's Nights in the Gardens of Spain, for piano and orchestra, begins "In the Generalife" and was premiered by Ricardo Viñes.

**John Cage: prepared piano and 4′33″**
Cage invented the "prepared piano," in which screws, bolts, and rubber are placed between the strings, and used it in his Sonatas and Interludes, inspired by the Indian rasas. His 4′33″, conceived after a visit to an anechoic chamber, has three movements all marked "tacet," so the pianist sits silently at the instrument.

**Erik Satie**
A French composer of hypnotic piano pieces, including the three Gymnopédies and the Gnossiennes. He answered critics who called his music formless with Three Pieces in the Shape of a Pear, for piano four hands.

**Debussy's "Clair de lune" and the sustain pedal**
The third movement of Debussy's Suite bergamasque, which relies on the right-foot sustain (damper) pedal to blur its harmonies. Debussy's other piano works include the Preludes (such as "The Girl with the Flaxen Hair") and Children's Corner.

**Etudes**
Piano studies that teach technique. Famous sets include Liszt's 12 Transcendental Etudes (with "Mazeppa" and "Feux follets") and his Paganini Etudes (with "La Campanella"). Others are Bartók's 153 progressively harder Mikrokosmos pieces, which end with "Six Dances in Bulgarian Rhythm," Ligeti's etudes such as "The Devil's Staircase," and Conlon Nancarrow's Studies for Player Piano.

**Villa Savoye**
Le Corbusier's most famous house (completed 1931) in Poissy, outside Paris, and the classic demonstration of his Five Points. It is a white box raised on thin pilotis, with ribbon windows, a roof garden, and an interior ramp that creates an "architectural promenade" up to the rooftop solarium. The ground floor's curve was set by the turning radius of a car, and the house later suffered from leaks and heating problems.

**Five Points of Architecture**
Le Corbusier's principles for modern buildings: pilotis (supports that lift the building off the ground), a free plan, a free facade, horizontal ribbon windows, and a roof garden. All of them are made possible by a reinforced concrete frame that frees walls from bearing loads, an idea he first set out in his Dom-Ino House design for mass-produced housing.

**Towards a New Architecture**
Le Corbusier's 1923 manifesto (Vers une architecture), compiled from essays in his magazine L'Esprit Nouveau. It declares that "a house is a machine for living in," and in sections like "Eyes Which Do Not See" it holds up ocean liners, airplanes, and cars as models of functional design. It also praises the Parthenon for its pure, unornamented form.

**Chandigarh**
The planned capital city of Punjab, India, which Le Corbusier designed in the 1950s after Partition left Lahore in Pakistan. He built on earlier plans by Albert Mayer and Maciej Nowicki and drew on his Radiant City ideas, organizing the city into sectors and a hierarchy of roads (V1–V7). Its Capitol Complex includes the Palace of Assembly, the Secretariat, and the High Court (Palace of Justice).

**Open Hand Monument**
A huge sheet-metal sculpture of an open hand in Chandigarh's Capitol Complex. It turns in the wind like a weathervane and is shaped somewhat like a dove. The open hand was a recurring Le Corbusier motif symbolizing peace and reconciliation, "open to give and open to receive."

**Notre-Dame du Haut**
The pilgrimage chapel at Ronchamp, France (1955), one of Le Corbusier's most expressive late works. It has thick, curving white walls pierced by irregular, randomly sized windows of colored glass, topped by a dark, upturned, boat-like concrete roof, and a pilgrim shelter stands nearby.

**Modulor**
Le Corbusier's system of architectural proportions, developed during World War II. It is based on the golden ratio and the height of a six-foot man with his arm raised, and its emblem is a stylized human figure. He used it to proportion buildings such as the Unité d'habitation.

**Contemporary City, Plan Voisin, and Radiant City**
Le Corbusier's utopian urban plans. The Contemporary City (1922) proposed housing three million people in sixty-story cruciform "Cartesian skyscrapers" set in parkland. The Plan Voisin (1925) would have bulldozed much of central Paris to build such towers, and the later Radiant City (Ville Radieuse) refined these ideas.

**Unité d'habitation**
Le Corbusier's postwar housing block in Marseille (1952), a vertical "city" of apartments with internal shopping streets and a rooftop terrace, raised on massive pilotis. It was built of béton brut (raw concrete), the term from which "Brutalism" derives, and was repeated in several other European cities.

**Purism and Amédée Ozenfant**
Le Corbusier was also a painter. With Amédée Ozenfant he founded Purism, a movement that sought to strip Cubism of decoration and return to clean, machine-like forms, and the two wrote its manifesto Après le cubisme (After Cubism, 1918). They also edited the journal L'Esprit Nouveau, and he later designed the white-box L'Esprit Nouveau Pavilion for the 1925 Paris exposition.

**United Nations Headquarters**
The UN complex in New York City, designed by a team that included Le Corbusier and the Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer. Its centerpiece is the 39-story slab of the Secretariat Building. Earlier, his entry for the League of Nations headquarters competition in Geneva was famously rejected on a technicality.

**Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts**
The building at Harvard University (1963), Le Corbusier's only building in the United States. It is built of raw concrete, with a ramp running through the middle of the building.

**Sainte Marie de La Tourette**
A Dominican monastery near Lyon, France, designed by Le Corbusier with Iannis Xenakis, the Greek composer who was then working in his studio. Xenakis designed its rhythmically spaced glass facade panels.

**Furniture: LC4 chaise longue and Grand Confort**
Le Corbusier designed tubular-steel furniture with Charlotte Perriand and Pierre Jeanneret. The LC4 chaise longue is a reclining chair he called a "relaxing machine," and the Grand Confort is a cube-shaped leather armchair.

**National Museum of Western Art and Curutchet House**
Two of Le Corbusier's buildings outside Europe and India. The National Museum of Western Art (1959) in Tokyo is a late work, and the Curutchet House (1949–1953) in La Plata, Argentina, was built for the surgeon Pedro Curutchet and was his only house in the Americas.

**Gateway Arch**
Saarinen's most famous work, a 630-foot (192-meter) stainless-steel arch in St. Louis on the west bank of the Mississippi River, completed in 1965 after his death. Shaped as an inverted weighted catenary curve with an equilateral-triangle cross-section, it is the tallest monument in the United States. It commemorates westward expansion and the Lewis and Clark expedition as the centerpiece of the Jefferson National Expansion Memorial (now Gateway Arch National Park), and it frames the Old Courthouse.

**TWA Flight Center**
Saarinen's terminal at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York (completed 1962), whose sweeping thin-shell concrete roof resembles a bird or airplane in flight with outstretched wings. The roof is made of wing-shaped shells supported on four Y-shaped piers, and the flowing interior is often likened to a landing strip.

**Kresge Auditorium**
A thin-shell concrete auditorium at MIT (1955) whose copper-clad roof is shaped as one-eighth of a sphere, touching the ground at only three equidistant points. The shell is enclosed by glass curtain walls, and inside Saarinen used floating acoustic "clouds."

**Ingalls Rink**
Yale University's hockey arena (1958), nicknamed "the Yale Whale" for its doubly curved form resembling a whale. A central reinforced-concrete arch, or spine, supports a timber roof hung on cables. A 1970 bombing during a rock concert there cracked the interior arch.

**Dulles International Airport main terminal**
Saarinen's terminal outside Washington, D.C. (1962), whose hammock-like catenary-curved concrete roof is suspended between rows of tall, outward-leaning columns, giving an airfoil-like profile. Passengers were originally carried between the terminal and planes in "mobile lounges."

**MIT Chapel**
A small, windowless brick cylinder chapel at MIT, built next to Kresge Auditorium (the two together are sometimes called the Kresge Chapel and Auditorium). Light enters from an oculus above the marble altar, where it glitters on Harry Bertoia's metal screen sculpture, and through slits at the base reflecting off a surrounding moat. Theodore Roszak designed the aluminum spire and bell tower.

**Tulip Chair**
Saarinen's 1950s pedestal chair, produced by Knoll, with a molded seat on a single slender stem, designed to eliminate the "slum of legs" under tables; it typically has a white frame and red or other colored cushion. It was famously used on the bridge of the USS Enterprise in the original Star Trek.

**Miller House**
A modernist house and garden in Columbus, Indiana, designed for industrialist J. Irwin Miller. It features sixteen free-standing columns supporting a grid of skylights, glass walls, a cylindrical fireplace, and a famous sunken "conversation pit."

**Bell Labs Holmdel Complex**
A massive research facility in Holmdel, New Jersey, for Bell Laboratories, whose mirrored-glass curtain walls made it, as it was called, the "biggest mirror ever." It was used as the setting for the Lumon offices in the TV series Severance.

**CBS Building ("Black Rock")**
Saarinen's only skyscraper, the CBS headquarters in Manhattan, completed in 1965 after his death, nicknamed "Black Rock" for its dark granite piers and tinted windows. Its interiors were designed by Florence Knoll.

**Corporate headquarters**
Saarinen designed several major corporate campuses, including the General Motors Technical Center in Warren, Michigan, the Deere & Company (John Deere) headquarters in Moline, Illinois, and IBM's Thomas J. Watson Research Center in Yorktown Heights, New York, where Jeopardy! filmed episodes featuring the IBM Watson computer.

**North Christian Church**
A hexagonal church in Columbus, Indiana, also commissioned through J. Irwin Miller, topped by a tall central spire rising from a low roof. It was completed in 1964, after Saarinen's death.

**Morse and Ezra Stiles Colleges**
Two residential colleges at Yale University designed by Saarinen, built of rubble masonry with irregular, village-like forms intended to evoke an Italian hill town.

**Womb Chair and Grasshopper Chair**
Other Saarinen furniture produced by Knoll, the company of family friends Hans and Florence Knoll; the Grasshopper chair has angled armrests resembling the insect. Earlier, with Charles Eames, Saarinen won a 1940 Museum of Modern Art competition with molded plywood chair designs.

**Eliel Saarinen**
Eero's father, a Finnish architect who emigrated to the United States and was president of the Cranbrook Academy of Art in Michigan. Father and son collaborated on works such as Kleinhans Music Hall in Buffalo, New York; quizbowl questions specify Eero to avoid confusion with Eliel.

**Andy Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans and Marilyn Monroe silkscreens**
Warhol, the most famous Pop artist, painted 32 canvases of Campbell's soup cans (1962), one for each flavor then sold, and used the commercial silkscreen process to mass-produce images of celebrities like Marilyn Monroe (including the fading Marilyn Diptych) and Jacqueline Kennedy. These are the most common giveaways for the movement.

**Roy Lichtenstein and Ben-Day dots**
Lichtenstein imitated the look of cheap comic-book printing by painting Ben-Day dots, the small colored dots used to create shading in mechanical printing. His enlarged comic-panel paintings, complete with speech balloons and thick outlines, made the technique a hallmark of Pop art.

**Drowning Girl ("I'd rather sink -- than call Brad for help!")**
A 1963 Lichtenstein painting adapted from a romance comic, showing a tearful blue-haired woman surrounded by stylized waves. Her thought balloon reads "I don't care! I'd rather sink -- than call Brad for help!"

**Whaam!**
Lichtenstein's 1963 two-panel painting adapted from a war comic, in which a fighter plane fires a missile that blows up an enemy plane. The explosion is labeled with a huge onomatopoeic "WHAAM!" rendered in comic lettering.

**Just what is it that makes today's homes so different, so appealing?**
A 1956 collage by British artist Richard Hamilton, made for the "This Is Tomorrow" exhibition. It shows a muscular bodybuilder holding a giant Tootsie Pop lollipop labeled "POP" and a nude woman wearing a lampshade on her head in a modern living room; the lollipop is often credited as a source of the movement's name.

**The Independent Group and "This Is Tomorrow"**
The Independent Group was a circle of British artists and critics in London in the 1950s, including Richard Hamilton and Eduardo Paolozzi, who studied mass culture and are considered the forerunners of Pop art. Their contributions to the 1956 "This Is Tomorrow" exhibition at the Whitechapel Gallery helped launch British Pop.

**Eduardo Paolozzi's I Was a Rich Man's Plaything**
A 1947 collage by the Scottish artist Paolozzi, made from magazine clippings including a pin-up girl and a gun firing a puff of smoke labeled "POP!" It is often called the first work of Pop art.

**Robert Rauschenberg's "combines" (Monogram, Canyon)**
Rauschenberg's combines merged painting and sculpture by attaching found objects to canvases. Monogram features a stuffed Angora goat with a car tire around its middle, and Canyon includes a stuffed bald eagle.

**Erased de Kooning Drawing**
A 1953 work for which Rauschenberg obtained a drawing from Abstract Expressionist Willem de Kooning and spent weeks erasing it, then exhibited the nearly blank sheet as his own art. It questioned ideas of authorship and the dominance of Abstract Expressionism.

**Claes Oldenburg's soft sculptures and giant objects**
Oldenburg made oversized and soft versions of ordinary things, such as a soft fan and soft light switches. With his wife Coosje van Bruggen he built huge public sculptures like Spoonbridge and Cherry, a giant spoon holding a cherry in the Minneapolis Sculpture Garden; his Lipstick (Ascending) on Caterpillar Tracks stands at Yale University.

**David Hockney's A Bigger Splash**
A 1967 painting by the British artist Hockney, made in California, showing a burst of water rising from a swimming pool beneath a yellow diving board. The person who has just jumped in is never seen.

**Jasper Johns's Flag**
Johns painted the American flag in encaustic (pigment mixed with hot wax) over a collage of newspaper scraps in 1954–55. His flags, maps, and targets used familiar, flat images and made him a key bridge between Abstract Expressionism and Pop art.

**The Factory and Warhol's films and Oxidation Paintings**
The Factory was Warhol's New York studio, where assistants helped mass-produce his silkscreens and where he shot films like Empire (an eight-hour shot of the Empire State Building) and the Western spoof Lonesome Cowboys. His Oxidation Paintings were made by urinating on canvases coated with copper paint.

**Warhol's Death and Disaster series**
A series of silkscreens from the early 1960s based on newspaper photos of car crashes, electric chairs, suicides, and poisonings, including tuna cans linked to botulism deaths ("Tunafish Disaster"). The repetition of the images comments on how mass media numbs viewers to tragedy.

**Lichtenstein's other works (Look Mickey, Oh, Jeff, Artist's Studio)**
Look Mickey (1961), his first comic-style painting, shows Donald Duck hooking his own coat with a fishing line while Mickey Mouse covers his mouth laughing. Oh, Jeff...I Love You, Too...But... shows a blonde woman clutching a telephone, and his Portrait of Madame Cézanne turned a diagram of a Cézanne painting into art.

**Manuel de Falla**
Spain's leading 20th-century composer and the most common music clue for the country. His ballet El amor brujo ("Love, the Magician") follows the Roma woman Candela, who tries to drive off her dead husband's ghost, and contains the "Ritual Fire Dance" and the "Song of the Will-o'-the-Wisp." His ballet The Three-Cornered Hat, about a magistrate who tries to seduce a miller's wife, includes a fandango and a final jota. He also wrote Nights in the Gardens of Spain for piano and orchestra, whose first movement is "In the Generalife."

**Sagrada Família**
Antoni Gaudí's huge, still-unfinished basilica in Barcelona, begun in 1882–1883 and scheduled for completion around 2026, the centenary of his death. Its Nativity Facade has columns resting on the backs of turtles, and its starker Passion Facade was sculpted by Josep Maria Subirachs. The design calls for 18 spires, with four on each of the main facades.

**Park Güell**
A Barcelona park designed by Gaudí. Its entrance stairway features "El Drac," a colorful mosaic salamander (or dragon), and the plaza above rests on 86 Doric columns and is edged by a long, wavy mosaic bench shaped like a sea serpent.

**Casa Milà and Casa Batlló**
Two Gaudí houses in Barcelona, both examples of Catalan Modernisme. Casa Milà is nicknamed "La Pedrera" ("The Stone Quarry") for its rippling stone facade; Josep Maria Jujol worked on it. Casa Batlló, the "House of Bones," has bone-like balconies and columns and a roof arched like a dragon's back with a turret representing Saint George's lance. It stands on the "Block of Discord."

**Symphonie espagnole**
Édouard Lalo's five-movement work for violin and orchestra, written for the Spanish violinist Pablo de Sarasate. Sarasate also wrote the virtuoso showpiece Zigeunerweisen ("Gypsy Airs"), and Camille Saint-Saëns wrote his Introduction and Rondo Capriccioso for him.

**Capriccio espagnol**
Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov's orchestral piece based on Spanish folk melodies. It has two "Alborada" movements built on the same theme and ends with a Fandango of the Asturias.

**España**
Emmanuel Chabrier's orchestral rhapsody, which opens with pizzicato C's in the strings. Chabrier jokingly described it as "a piece in F and nothing more." Related clue: Maurice Ravel's Spanish-inspired works include the Rapsodie espagnole, whose first movement repeats a descending F–E–D–C-sharp theme, Alborada del gracioso from his piano suite Miroirs, and Boléro, with its snare drum ostinato.

**Isaac Albéniz**
A Spanish composer and pianist best known for Iberia, a piano suite in four books that opens with "Evocación" and includes "El Puerto." His piece "Asturias" is a staple for classical guitar and uses flamenco-style rhythms.

**Alhambra**
The palace complex of the Nasrid dynasty in Granada. It contains the Court of the Lions, whose fountain basin rests on 12 stone lions; the Court of the Myrtles, with a long reflecting pool in front of the Comares Tower; the Hall of the Ambassadors, with a vaulted ceiling of muqarnas; and the nearby Generalife gardens. Another key Moorish building is the Great Mosque of Córdoba, known for its red-and-white striped double arches, gold-mosaic mihrab, and Court of the Oranges.

**Guggenheim Bilbao**
Frank Gehry's 1997 museum on the Nervión River in Bilbao, covered in curving titanium sheets. Jeff Koons's giant flower sculpture Puppy stands outside it. The "Bilbao effect" refers to how a showy piece of architecture can revive a declining city.

**Salvador Dalí**
A Spanish Surrealist known for The Persistence of Memory, with its melting clocks and a pocket watch covered in ants. He also made the Lobster Telephone, Soft Construction with Boiled Beans (a premonition of the Spanish Civil War), and Metamorphosis of Narcissus, in which a hand holds an egg with a flower sprouting from it. His wife Gala was his frequent model.

**Joan Miró**
A Catalan Surrealist. The Farm, bought by Ernest Hemingway, shows a newspaper titled "L'Intransigeant" cut off to "L'INTR." Harlequin's Carnival includes a "ladder of escape," a ladder also appears in Dog Barking at the Moon, and an oversized ear grows from a tree in The Tilled Field. His public sculpture in Chicago shows a female figure with a fork projecting from her head.

**Diego Velázquez and the Prado**
Velázquez was the court painter of Philip IV. His most famous work is Las Meninas, in which maids of honor attend the Infanta Margarita. He also painted the Rokeby Venus and the Portrait of Pope Innocent X. Madrid's Prado Museum, whose building was originally planned as a natural history museum, holds Las Meninas along with Bosch's The Garden of Earthly Delights.

**Francisco Goya**
A Spanish painter and printmaker who made The Third of May 1808, the Disasters of War prints, and the aquatint The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters, in which a man slumps on a desk as bats and owls swarm behind him. His late "Black Paintings" include Saturn Devouring His Son.

**Operas set in Spain**
Bizet's Carmen is set in Seville, where Carmen sings the Habanera "Love is a rebellious bird" and is stabbed by Don José after turning to the bullfighter Escamillo. Rossini's The Barber of Seville (with "Largo al factotum"), Mozart's The Marriage of Figaro (which opens with the duet "Cinque, dieci, venti"), and Mozart's Don Giovanni (whose hero is dragged to hell by the Commendatore's statue) are also set in or near Seville.

**The Death of Marat**
David's 1793 painting of the murdered radical journalist Jean-Paul Marat, editor of The Friend of the People. Marat slumps in his bathtub (he bathed to soothe a chronic skin disease) wearing a turban-like head cloth, holding a quill in his drooping right arm and a letter in his left hand. A bloody knife lies on the floor, and a wooden crate serves as his desk. It is often called a secular "Pietà of the Revolution."

**Charlotte Corday**
The Girondin sympathizer who stabbed Marat in his bath in 1793. In David's painting, Marat holds her letter, which reads "My great unhappiness gives me a right to your kindness," the excuse she used to get in to see him.

**The Oath of the Horatii**
David's 1784 Neoclassical masterpiece, based on a legend told by Livy. Three Roman brothers, the Horatii, stretch out their arms in a salute and swear to fight to the death for Rome as their father holds up three swords. On the right, their mother, sisters, and children weep, since one sister is engaged to one of the enemy Curiatii. The scene is framed by three arches on columns.

**The Death of Socrates**
A 1787 painting of the Athenian philosopher about to drink hemlock in prison. Socrates points upward with one hand as he reaches for the cup with the other. The grieving disciple handing him the cup covers his eyes, Crito grips Socrates's leg, Plato sits dejected at the foot of the bed, and in the background men climb a staircase.

**The Lictors Bring to Brutus the Bodies of His Sons**
A 1789 painting of Lucius Junius Brutus, founder of the Roman Republic, who ordered the execution of his sons for plotting to restore the monarchy. Brutus broods in shadow beneath a statue of Roma (inscribed "DEA ROMA") while lictors carry in the bodies on the left. On the right, his anguished wife, in orange, clutches their daughters, one of whom faints, and a servant covers her face with a shawl.

**The Intervention of the Sabine Women**
A painting David began while imprisoned after the fall of Robespierre. Hersilia, in white with outstretched arms, throws herself between her husband Romulus and her father Titus Tatius to stop the battle between the Romans and Sabines, as other women hold up their babies. David described his aim as a return to "pure Greek" style.

**Napoleon Crossing the Alps**
David's heroic equestrian portrait of Napoleon in a billowing red-orange cloak on a rearing horse, pointing upward as he leads his army through the Great St. Bernard Pass. Rocks in the foreground are carved with the names Bonaparte, Hannibal, and Karolus Magnus (Charlemagne), and soldiers drag cannons in the background. David also painted Napoleon in His Study at the Tuileries.

**The Coronation of Napoleon**
David's huge painting of Napoleon's 1804 coronation at Notre-Dame Cathedral. Instead of showing Napoleon crowning himself, as originally planned, it shows him crowning the kneeling Joséphine as Pope Pius VII looks on.

**Portrait of Madame Récamier**
A portrait of the Parisian socialite Juliette Récamier in a simple white Empire-waist dress and black headband, reclining on an antique-style sofa and glancing over her shoulder.

**Mars Being Disarmed by Venus and the Three Graces**
David's last major painting, made in exile in Brussels. Venus offers Mars a crown of flowers, a Cupid unties his sandal, and the Graces take his weapons and offer him wine.

**Jacobin politics and The Tennis Court Oath**
David was a Jacobin and an ally of Robespierre, served in the National Convention (including a brief term as its president), and voted for the execution of Louis XVI. His unfinished Tennis Court Oath depicts the 1789 pledge of the Third Estate deputies. After Robespierre's fall he was imprisoned, and he later became Napoleon's official painter.

**Portrait of Antoine Lavoisier and His Wife**
David's 1788 double portrait of the chemist Antoine Lavoisier seated at a table of scientific instruments with his wife Marie-Anne, who leans on his shoulder. Marie-Anne had studied painting with David.

**Leonidas at Thermopylae**
A late painting of the Spartan king Leonidas before his last stand against the Persians. On the left, a soldier carves a farewell message into the rock of the mountain pass.

**Belisarius Begging for Alms**
An early David painting of the blind Byzantine general Belisarius, fallen from favor and reduced to begging, being recognized by a soldier who once served under him.

**Kind of Blue**
Davis's 1959 masterpiece and the best-selling jazz album of all time, which pioneered modal jazz (improvising over scales rather than fast chord changes). It was recorded by a sextet including saxophonists John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley and pianist Bill Evans, and it has five tracks.

**"So What"**
The opening track of Kind of Blue. Its AABA form spends sixteen bars in D Dorian, eight bars in E-flat Dorian, then eight more in D Dorian, while the bass states the melody and the horns answer with a two-chord "So What" figure.

**"Freddie Freeloader"**
A twelve-bar blues on Kind of Blue, named after a Philadelphia hanger-on and notable as the only track featuring Wynton Kelly on piano instead of Bill Evans.

**"Flamenco Sketches" and "Blue in Green"**
Two other Kind of Blue tracks. "Blue in Green" is a short, melancholy ballad, and "Flamenco Sketches" closes the album by moving through a series of five modes; reissues include an alternate take of it.

**Sketches of Spain**
A 1960 album arranged by Gil Evans and inspired by Spanish music. Besides its version of Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez, it includes "Will o' the Wisp" from Manuel de Falla's ballet El amor brujo and Evans's pieces "The Pan Piper," "Saeta," and "Solea."

**Concierto de Aranjuez**
A guitar concerto by Spanish composer Joaquín Rodrigo. Davis and Gil Evans adapted its famous Adagio, whose melody is first played by the English horn, as the opening of Sketches of Spain.

**Gil Evans**
The arranger who was Davis's most important collaborator. He contributed arrangements to Birth of the Cool and later created the orchestral albums Miles Ahead, Porgy and Bess (arrangements from Gershwin's opera), Sketches of Spain, and Quiet Nights with him.

**Birth of the Cool**
A compilation of 1949–50 recordings by Davis's nonet, with arrangements by Gil Evans, Gerry Mulligan, and John Lewis. Tracks like "Boplicity," "Move," "Moon Dreams," and "Darn That Dream" launched cool jazz, which grew into West Coast jazz.

**Bitches Brew**
Davis's 1970 double album, a landmark of jazz-rock fusion featuring electric instruments. It includes Joe Zawinul's "Pharaoh's Dance," Wayne Shorter's "Sanctuary," and a track named for guitarist John McLaughlin, and it was heavily assembled from tape edits.

**Teo Macero**
Davis's longtime Columbia producer. On In a Silent Way and Bitches Brew he used tape loops and splicing inspired by musique concrète to build finished tracks such as "Pharaoh's Dance" out of hours of studio jamming.

**In a Silent Way**
The 1969 album that began Davis's "electric period," featuring guitarist John McLaughlin, keyboardists Joe Zawinul, Herbie Hancock, and Chick Corea, and saxophonist Wayne Shorter. Side A is the long track "Shhh/Peaceful," and Davis continued in this vein with albums like Jack Johnson.

**Second Great Quintet**
Davis's mid-1960s post-bop band with saxophonist Wayne Shorter, pianist Herbie Hancock, bassist Ron Carter, and drummer Tony Williams. Its albums include E.S.P., Sorcerer, and Miles Smiles, which features Shorter's "Footprints."

**Nefertiti**
A 1968 Second Great Quintet album that contains no compositions by Davis himself. Its title track by Wayne Shorter has the horns repeat the melody while the rhythm section improvises, and it also includes Shorter's "Pinocchio."

**First Great Quintet**
Davis's 1950s quintet with John Coltrane, pianist Red Garland, bassist Paul Chambers, and drummer Philly Joe Jones. Two marathon 1956 sessions for Prestige produced four albums (Cookin', Relaxin', Workin', and Steamin'), and members' drug problems contributed to its breakup.

**Ascenseur pour l'échafaud (Elevator to the Gallows)**
Louis Malle's 1958 French film, for which Davis improvised the soundtrack with a small group while watching the film projected.

**The Scream**
Munch's most famous work, which exists in several painted, pastel, and lithograph versions. A bald, skull-like figure on a bridge or boardwalk clutches its face under a swirling blood-red and orange sky above the Oslo fjord, while two dark figures walk away in the background. Munch said it came from a moment at sunset when the "air turned to blood" and he sensed an infinite scream passing through nature, hence the original German title The Scream of Nature.

**The Frieze of Life**
Munch's large, loosely defined cycle of paintings on the themes of love, anxiety, and death. It includes The Scream, Vampire, Madonna, Ashes, The Dance of Life, Death in the Sickroom, and Anxiety.

**Vampire (Love and Pain)**
A painting first exhibited as Love and Pain, showing a red-haired woman bending over a dark-haired man and pressing her mouth to his neck while a dark shadow surrounds them. Its common title came from the writer Stanisław Przybyszewski, who read it as a broken man with a vampire biting his neck.

**Death in the Sickroom**
A painting of the death of Munch's sister Sophie, who died of tuberculosis at 15. Black-clad family members stand apart, each grieving alone; one man prays against the back wall and his sister Laura sits bowed in the foreground, while Sophie is hidden in a wicker chair.

**The Sick Child**
A painting, repeated in several versions, of Munch's dying sister Sophie propped on a large pillow in a green-toned bed, while a grieving woman bows her head and holds her hand. Munch scraped and reworked the paint heavily, and he considered it a breakthrough in his art.

**Madonna**
A series of paintings and lithographs of a bare-chested woman with flowing dark hair, eyes half-closed, and a red halo, seen as if from a lover's point of view. The lithograph version has a border of swimming sperm and a small fetus-like figure in one corner. A painted version was stolen from the Munch Museum along with The Scream in 2004 and recovered in 2006.

**Thefts of The Scream**
On February 12, 1994, the opening day of the Lillehammer Winter Olympics, thieves stole a version of The Scream from Oslo's National Gallery and left a note reading "Thanks for the poor security." It was recovered months later. Another version was stolen with Madonna from the Munch Museum in 2004.

**Krakatoa, Ekeberg, and "could only have been painted by a madman"**
One theory holds that The Scream's red sky reflects vivid sunsets caused by the 1883 eruption of Krakatoa. The view is from Ekeberg hill above Oslo, near a slaughterhouse and the asylum where Munch's sister Laura was a patient. One version bears the faint pencil inscription "Could only have been painted by a madman," written by Munch himself.

**Puberty**
A painting of a nude adolescent girl sitting on the edge of a white bed, staring at the viewer with her arms crossed over her lap, while a large, ominous dark shadow rises on the wall behind her.

**Ashes**
A Frieze of Life painting set at the edge of a forest near a stone-filled stream. A woman in a white dress stands facing the viewer clutching her disheveled red hair, while a man in black crouches in the corner and hides his face, a scene of the aftermath of a love affair.

**Self-portraits (with Burning Cigarette, Between the Clock and the Bed, with Skeleton Arm)**
Munch produced many self-portraits, including Self-Portrait with Burning Cigarette (1895), a lithograph of his pale face against black with a skeletal arm along the bottom, a Self-Portrait with the Spanish Flu, and the late Self-Portrait: Between the Clock and the Bed, showing the aged artist standing between a grandfather clock and a bed.

**The Death of Marat**
Munch's version of the murder of the French revolutionary, showing a nude Charlotte Corday standing upright facing the viewer beside a man's body on bloodstained sheets. It is often read as a reference to the 1902 quarrel with his lover Tulla Larsen in which Munch was shot in the hand.

**The Dance of Life**
A Frieze of Life painting of couples dancing on a shore under a moon whose reflection forms a pillar of light on the water. At the center a man dances with a woman in red, flanked by a young woman in white and an older woman in black, representing stages of a woman's life (a theme also seen in Woman in Three Stages).

**Anxiety**
A Frieze of Life painting set on the same railing and fjord as The Scream, under a similar red sky. A crowd of pale, staring, top-hatted figures moves toward the viewer.

**The Girls on the Bridge**
A painting, made in many versions, of a group of girls leaning on the railing of a bridge or pier that cuts across the canvas on a strong diagonal. Behind them are a white villa and a large dark tree reflected in the water.

**"Clair de lune"**
The third movement of Debussy's Suite bergamasque and his most famous piece, named after Paul Verlaine's poem about moonlight, which itself evokes Watteau's fêtes galantes. It is in D-flat major and 9/8 time, marked "Andante très expressif," and opens softly with an F–A-flat third echoed an octave higher, with its key hovering ambiguously between B-flat minor and D-flat major. It was originally titled "Promenade sentimentale" and was used in the fountain scene of the 2001 film Ocean's Eleven.

**Suite bergamasque**
Debussy's four-movement piano suite: Prélude, Menuet, "Clair de lune," and a closing "Passepied" in F-sharp minor. The title echoes Verlaine's poem "Clair de lune," which mentions "bergamasques," Renaissance-style dances.

**Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun**
Debussy's orchestral tone poem (Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune), based on Stéphane Mallarmé's poem about a faun, a goat-man, who daydreams about chasing nymphs. It opens with a famous solo flute line that slides chromatically down from C-sharp to G, evoking the faun's panpipes. Vaslav Nijinsky choreographed a scandalous ballet to it, and Leonard Bernstein discussed it as a turning point in his Norton Lectures.

**Children's Corner**
A piano suite dedicated to Debussy's young daughter Claude-Emma ("Chouchou"). It opens with "Doctor Gradus ad Parnassum," which parodies dull piano exercises, and also includes "Jimbo's Lullaby" and "The Little Shepherd."

**"Golliwogg's Cakewalk"**
The ragtime-flavored final movement of Children's Corner, depicting a dancing blackface rag doll. Its middle section mockingly quotes the opening of Wagner's Tristan und Isolde, including the Tristan chord, which is repeatedly cut off by cheeky chords marked "with great emotion."

**"The Sunken Cathedral"**
"La cathédrale engloutie," a piano prelude based on the Breton legend of the cathedral of the drowned city of Ys, which rises from the sea at dawn. It opens with rising parallel fifths on a pentatonic scale, marked "emerging little by little from the fog," to evoke distant bells. It climaxes with massive parallel chords, an example of "planing," over a low C, marked "sonorous but without harshness."

**Preludes**
Debussy's 24 piano preludes in two books of 12. He printed each one's descriptive title in parentheses at the end rather than the beginning. They include "Voiles" (meaning either "Veils" or "Sails," built on the whole-tone scale), "The Girl with the Flaxen Hair," "What the West Wind Saw," "The Dancers of Delphi," "Puck's Dance," "Homage to S. Pickwick Esq.," which quotes "God Save the King," and "Fireworks," which quotes "La Marseillaise."

**"The Girl with the Flaxen Hair"**
"La fille aux cheveux de lin," the eighth prelude in Book I. It is a gentle, simple melody inspired by a poem by Leconte de Lisle.

**La mer**
"The Sea," Debussy's set of three "symphonic sketches" for orchestra: "From Dawn to Noon on the Sea," "Play of the Waves," and "Dialogue of the Wind and the Sea."

**Estampes and gamelan**
"Prints," a three-movement piano suite. Its first movement, "Pagodes," imitates Javanese gamelan music, which Debussy heard at the 1889 Paris Exposition, using pentatonic scales. Its last movement, "Jardins sous la pluie" ("Gardens in the Rain"), depicts a rainstorm and quotes the French folk songs "Nous n'irons plus au bois" and "Dodo, l'enfant do."

**Nocturnes**
An orchestral triptych inspired partly by James McNeill Whistler's paintings: "Nuages" ("Clouds"), "Fêtes" ("Festivals"), and "Sirènes" ("Sirens"). Like Holst in "Neptune," Debussy used a wordless women's chorus in "Sirènes."

**Pelléas et Mélisande**
Debussy's only completed opera, based on Maurice Maeterlinck's Symbolist play. Prince Golaud marries the mysterious Mélisande, who falls in love with his half-brother Pelléas.

**Paul Verlaine**
The Symbolist poet whose work inspired many Debussy pieces, including "Clair de lune" and Suite bergamasque and the song cycles Fêtes galantes.

**L'isle joyeuse**
"The Joyful Island," a dazzling piano piece inspired by Watteau's painting of the voyage to Cythera, the island of love. It opens with a trill on C-sharp and D-sharp, followed by a whole-tone passage marked "quasi una cadenza."

**Syrinx**
A short piece for solo flute that depicts the god Pan's panpipes. It is often played from offstage, and the flutist Marcel Moyse added breath marks to the published edition.

**Phillies cigar advertisement ("Only 5¢")**
A sign running along the top of the diner advertises five-cent Phillies cigars. It is the most frequently cited visual detail of the painting and a near-giveaway clue.

**Edward Hopper**
The American realist painter who created Nighthawks in 1942. His works, including Automat, Chop Suey, and Early Sunday Morning, typically depict isolation and loneliness in modern American life.

**Yellow knobless door / no visible entrance**
At the back of the diner is a yellow (or golden) door with no doorknob, and the diner's glass-walled interior has no apparent exit or entrance to the street. This feature heightens the sense that the figures are trapped or isolated.

**Woman in a red dress (modeled on Jo Hopper)**
The only woman in the painting is a red-haired figure in a red dress or blouse, seated next to a man at the counter. Hopper's wife, the painter Josephine "Jo" Nivison Hopper, served as the model for her.

**Gottfried Helnwein's Boulevard of Broken Dreams**
A famous 1984 parody by the Austrian artist Gottfried Helnwein that replaces the diner's figures with Hollywood icons: Humphrey Bogart, Marilyn Monroe, James Dean, and Elvis Presley (with Elvis as the attendant).

**Banksy parody**
Banksy's version of Nighthawks shows a shirtless soccer hooligan in Union Jack (Union Flag) boxer shorts pointing at a diner window he has smashed with a white plastic chair, with overturned chairs scattered outside.

**Two silver coffee urns**
Two metal coffee canisters, carafes, or urns sit on the counter at the back of the diner, right next to the yellow door. They are a common mid-question clue.

**Man in white behind the counter**
A soda jerk or waiter in a white uniform and white cap stoops or bends down behind the triangular counter, as if fetching something, while serving the three patrons.

**Three patrons (two men in fedoras)**
The diner's customers are a couple (a man in a dark suit and fedora sitting next to the woman in red) and a second man in a fedora sitting alone with his back to the viewer. None of them seem to acknowledge one another.

**Title from the man's "beak"**
According to Jo Hopper's notes, the title refers to the beak-like nose of the man sitting next to the woman, who holds a cigarette. The name "Nighthawks" evokes people who stay awake late at night.

**"The loneliness of a large city"**
Hopper said that "unconsciously, probably, I was painting the loneliness of a large city." Nighthawks is widely viewed as the defining image of urban alienation.

**Greenwich Avenue / Mulry Square**
Hopper said the painting was suggested by a restaurant on Greenwich Avenue in Greenwich Village, New York, where two streets meet. Writer Jeremiah Moss speculated that the setting was the triangular lot at Mulry Square.

**Empty storefront with a cash register**
Across the street, a dark, vacant shop window on the left side shows a cash register. The building above it has a row of windows with half-drawn shades, and it resembles the row of buildings in Hopper's Early Sunday Morning.

**Painted after Pearl Harbor (1942)**
Hopper began the painting right after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 and finished it in 1942. Its gloom is often linked to the wartime mood in America.

**Art Institute of Chicago**
Nighthawks has been held by the Art Institute of Chicago since the museum bought it in 1942, the year it was painted.

**"Flight of the Bumblebee"**
Rimsky-Korsakov's most famous single piece, an orchestral interlude from his opera The Tale of Tsar Saltan. Frantic, nonstop runs of chromatic sixteenth notes in the violins and flute depict Prince Gvidon, who has been turned into a bumblebee, buzzing off to sting his wicked aunts.

**Scheherazade**
A four-movement 1888 symphonic suite inspired by The Thousand and One Nights (Arabian Nights), in which Scheherazade tells stories night after night to delay her execution by the Sultan. It is famous for its brilliant, colorful orchestration.

**"The Sea and Sinbad's Ship"**
The first movement of Scheherazade. It opens with the stern, heavy Sultan theme in the low brass and strings, and the music then evokes the rolling sea. Rimsky-Korsakov later withdrew the programmatic movement titles because he did not want listeners tied to a specific story.

**Scheherazade's solo violin theme and the Sultan's theme**
Scheherazade herself is represented by a sinuous, high, triplet-filled solo violin melody, accompanied by harp chords, which recurs throughout the suite. The Sultan's opposing theme opens with the descending notes E, D, C, B-flat in unison.

**"The Kalendar Prince," "The Young Prince and the Young Princess," and "Festival at Baghdad"**
The other three movements of Scheherazade. "The Kalendar Prince" features a solo bassoon narrating the tale of a wandering dervish prince. The lyrical third movement depicts a pair of young lovers, and the finale combines a festival at Baghdad with the shipwreck of Sinbad's vessel.

**The Tale of Tsar Saltan**
An opera based on a Pushkin fairy tale. Tsar Saltan's wife and infant son Gvidon are cast out to sea in a barrel by her jealous sisters, and Gvidon, helped by a magical Swan-Princess, is changed into insects to visit his father, which gives rise to "Flight of the Bumblebee."

**Capriccio Espagnol**
An 1887 orchestral showpiece based on Spanish folk melodies. Its five movements include an "Alborada" (morning song) that appears as both the first and third movements, with a "Variazioni" between them, and it ends with a "Fandango asturiano," a dance from Asturias.

**Russian Easter Festival Overture**
An 1888 concert overture based on chants from the Obikhod, the collection of Russian Orthodox liturgical melodies. It opens with a slow introduction in 5/2 time, with solo cello passages that evoke the chant, and it builds to a depiction of joyous Easter celebrations.

**The Snow Maiden (Snegurochka)**
An opera based on a play by Alexander Ostrovsky. Snegurochka, daughter of Spring and Frost, lives among the Berendeys; when she finally feels love for Mizgir she melts in the sun. It contains the popular "Dance of the Tumblers."

**The Golden Cockerel (Le Coq d'Or)**
Rimsky-Korsakov's last opera, a satire based on Pushkin. An Astrologer gives King Dodon a golden cockerel that warns of danger. Dodon's sons Gvidon and Afron kill each other in battle, Dodon is seduced by the Queen of Shemakha, who sings the "Hymn to the Sun," and the cockerel finally kills Dodon when he refuses the Astrologer's reward.

**Sadko**
A Russian bylina (folk epic) that Rimsky-Korsakov treated first in the Op. 5 "musical tableau" Sadko and later in an opera that reuses its themes. In the opera the minstrel Sadko wins a fortune by catching golden fish and visits the realm of the Sea King, whose daughter Volkhova loves him. It includes the songs of the Varangian, Indian, and Venetian guests, the "Song of India" being the best known.

**Mlada and Night on Mount Triglav**
Mlada is an opera-ballet on a pagan Slavic subject in which the murdered princess Mlada, a silent role, returns as a spirit. Rimsky-Korsakov later arranged music from its mountain scene into the orchestral piece Night on Mount Triglav.

**Antar**
A work first published as Rimsky-Korsakov's Symphony No. 2 and based on the tale of the Arab poet-hero Antar. Rimsky-Korsakov later insisted it was not a symphony and renamed it a symphonic suite.

**The Mighty Five and Fantasy on Serbian Themes**
Rimsky-Korsakov belonged to the "Mighty Handful" (Mighty Five) of Russian nationalist composers, with Balakirev, Cui, Borodin, and Mussorgsky. The critic Vladimir Stasov coined the phrase "mighty handful" in a review of an 1867 concert that included Rimsky-Korsakov's Fantasy on Serbian Themes. Rimsky-Korsakov had also served as a naval officer before turning fully to music.

**Editing Mussorgsky and Principles of Orchestration**
After Mussorgsky's death, Rimsky-Korsakov edited and reorchestrated his works, including Boris Godunov and Night on Bald Mountain, for publication. His treatise Principles of Orchestration was completed after his death by his son-in-law Maximilian Steinberg. His many students included Igor Stravinsky.

**Campbell's Soup Cans**
Warhol's 1962 series of 32 canvases, each showing a can of a different Campbell's soup variety, such as "Tomato," "Split Pea," "Beef Noodle," "Pepper Pot," "Clam Chowder," "Consomme," and "Beef Broth." The paintings were traced from projected images, and each has a hand-stamped fleur-de-lis band along the bottom. They were first shown at Irving Blum's Ferus Gallery in Los Angeles, lined up on a shelf like a grocery aisle. Muriel Latow was paid $50 for suggesting he paint "something people see every day." This is the near-universal giveaway for Warhol.

**The Factory**
Warhol's New York City studio, where assistants mass-produced his silkscreens on an assembly line. During the "Silver Era," Billy Name covered it in aluminum foil and silver paint, and it became famous for its red couch and its crowd of "Superstars" like Edie Sedgwick.

**Silkscreen printing**
The printmaking method Warhol used for most of his famous work. Ink is pushed through a fine mesh screen onto the canvas, which let him reproduce photographs over and over, often in loud, artificial colors.

**Marilyn Diptych**
A 1962 silkscreen painting made in the year Marilyn Monroe died. It repeats her face 50 times, with the left half in bright colors (yellow hair, purple face) and the right half in fading black and white. Most of his Marilyn images came from a publicity still for the 1953 film Niagara. Related works include Gold Marilyn Monroe and the Shot Marilyns, which Dorothy Podber shot with a revolver at the Factory.

**Valerie Solanas**
The radical feminist author of the SCUM Manifesto. She shot and nearly killed Warhol at the Factory in 1968. Before the shooting, she had given him a play script that he lost.

**Death and Disaster series**
Warhol's silkscreen series based on newspaper photos of tragedies. It includes car-crash images such as Silver Car Crash (Double Disaster), Five Deaths on Orange, Green Disaster Ten Times, and Red Car Crash, plus 129 Die in Jet!, poisoned tuna cans, suicides, and electric chairs.

**Exploding Plastic Inevitable**
A series of 1966–67 multimedia events Warhol put on. They combined film projections, pioneering light shows, and live performances by the Velvet Underground, the rock band he managed.

**The Velvet Underground & Nico album cover**
Warhol designed the cover of the band's 1967 debut album. It shows a yellow banana sticker that could be peeled back to reveal a pink banana underneath.

**Mao, Elvis, and Jackie silkscreens**
Warhol's silkscreen portraits of celebrities and political figures. These include many images of Mao Zedong (including a Mao wallpaper), Elvis Presley, and Jacqueline Kennedy, whose series shows her before and after her husband's assassination.

**Eight Elvises**
A 1963 silkscreen that repeats an overlapping image of Elvis Presley in cowboy costume, taken from a publicity still for the western Flaming Star, aiming a gun at the viewer.

**Empire and Sleep**
Two of Warhol's minimalist long-take films. Empire is about eight hours of slow-motion footage of the Empire State Building at night, and Sleep shows the poet John Giorno sleeping for more than five hours.

**Chelsea Girls**
A 1966 film Warhol made with Paul Morrissey. It is shown as two films projected side by side and follows residents of New York's Chelsea Hotel, with Nico among the cast. Other Warhol films include Poor Little Rich Girl (starring Edie Sedgwick), Vinyl, Lonesome Cowboys, and Batman Dracula.

**Screen Tests**
Short, silent film portraits, each about three minutes long, of visitors to the Factory. The sitters were told to stay still and not blink while the camera rolled.

**Oxidation paintings**
A series in which Warhol and others urinated on canvases coated with copper paint, so that the paint oxidized into colorful patterns. One is a portrait of Jean-Michel Basquiat.

**Thirteen Most Wanted Men**
A mural Warhol made for the New York State Pavilion at the 1964 World's Fair, made from 22 police mugshots of wanted criminals. Officials had it painted over before the fair opened.

**Madama Butterfly**
Puccini's opera set in Nagasaki, based on a John Luther Long short story (via David Belasco's play). U.S. Navy Lieutenant B. F. Pinkerton marries and abandons the young geisha Cio-Cio-San, who finally kills herself with her father's sword after learning he has an American wife. A motif from "The Star-Spangled Banner" accompanies Pinkerton.

**Tosca and Baron Scarpia**
Puccini's opera set in Rome in 1800. The singer Floria Tosca stabs the corrupt police chief Baron Scarpia after he promises to free her lover in exchange for her body; at the end she leaps to her death from the Castel Sant'Angelo. Scarpia joins the Te Deum at the end of Act I.
