**La bohème (Rodolfo and Mimì)**
Puccini's opera about starving artists in Paris's Latin Quarter, based on Henri Murger's loosely plotted Scènes de la vie de bohème. The poet Rodolfo falls in love with the seamstress Mimì, who dies of tuberculosis (consumption) at the end, prompting Rodolfo's cries of her name. Jonathan Larson adapted it into the 1996 rock musical Rent.

**Mario Cavaradossi and "E lucevan le stelle"**
Cavaradossi is Tosca's lover, a painter. "E lucevan le stelle" ("And the stars were shining"), introduced by a melancholy B minor clarinet solo, is the tenor aria he sings while writing a farewell letter to Tosca as he awaits execution; the firing squad that was supposed to be using blanks actually kills him.

**Turandot and "Nessun dorma"**
Puccini's unfinished final opera, set in Peking (Beijing), about a cold Chinese princess who beheads suitors who fail to answer her three riddles. The "unknown prince" Calaf solves them and sings "Nessun dorma" ("None shall sleep"), ending with the triumphant cry "Vincerò!" ("I will win!"), wagering that she will not learn his name by dawn.

**"Un bel dì" ("One fine day")**
Cio-Cio-San's aria in Madama Butterfly, in which she imagines seeing a ship appear on the horizon carrying Pinkerton home to her.

**"Recondita armonia"**
Cavaradossi's Act I aria in Tosca. While painting a portrait of Mary Magdalene modeled on the blonde Marchesa Attavanti, he contrasts the model's beauty with that of the dark-haired Tosca, whom he loves.

**"Vissi d'arte" ("I lived for art")**
Tosca's Act II aria, sung after Scarpia demands that she sleep with him to save Cavaradossi. She asks God why she is being punished after a life of art, love, and piety (she even gave jewels for the Madonna's mantle).

**Gianni Schicchi and "O mio babbino caro"**
Puccini's one-act comic opera, the last part of his trilogy Il trittico (with Il tabarro and Suor Angelica). Relatives scheme to change the will of the dead Buoso Donati, who left his fortune to a monastery, and Lauretta sings "O mio babbino caro" ("Oh my dear papa"), threatening to throw herself into the Arno unless her father lets her marry Rinuccio.

**Ping, Pang, and Pong**
The three ministers in Turandot, who try to dissuade Calaf from striking the gong to enter the riddle contest and wistfully dream of their country homes, such as a house in Honan with a little blue lake.

**Liù and "Tu che di gel sei cinta"**
Liù is the slave girl in Turandot who secretly loves Calaf. In "Tu che di gel sei cinta" ("You who are girdled with ice") she tells Turandot that she too will come to love him, then kills herself rather than reveal his name; Calaf earlier sings "Non piangere, Liù" ("Do not cry, Liù").

**Franco Alfano and Toscanini**
Puccini died in 1924 before finishing Turandot, and Franco Alfano completed its final scene. At the 1926 premiere, conductor Arturo Toscanini stopped after Liù's death, telling the audience that this was where the maestro had laid down his pen.

**"Che gelida manina" and the lost key**
In Act I of La bohème, Mimì's candle goes out and she drops her key; Rodolfo and she search for it in the dark, and he takes her hand and sings "Che gelida manina" ("What a cold little hand"). Mimì later sings "Donde lieta uscì" when they part.

**Musetta's Waltz ("Quando m'en vo")**
The flirtatious waltz sung by Musetta in Act II of La bohème at the Café Momus to win back her former lover, the painter Marcello.

**Manon Lescaut and other operas**
Puccini's first big success, Manon Lescaut (1893), adapts Abbé Prévost's novel, also set by Massenet; it ends with Manon singing "Sola, perduta, abbandonata" as she dies in Des Grieux's arms in the Louisiana desert. His other operas include his debut Le Villi, La fanciulla del West (The Girl of the Golden West, in which Minnie loves the bandit Dick Johnson, actually Ramerrez), and La rondine.

**Twelve-tone technique**
The method of composition Schoenberg developed in the early 1920s. All twelve notes of the chromatic scale are arranged in a fixed order called a tone row, and in its strictest form no note is repeated before the others have sounded. The row and its transformations (inversion, retrograde, and transposition) then generate the whole piece. It is the foundation of serialism.

**Pierrot Lunaire**
Schoenberg's 1912 setting of 21 poems by Albert Giraud (in German translation) about Pierrot, a moonstruck commedia dell'arte clown. A soprano performs it in Sprechstimme, accompanied by a small ensemble of flute, clarinet, violin, cello, and piano. It opens with "Mondestrunken" ("Moondrunk"), and in later songs Pierrot longs for his home of Bergamo.

**Verklärte Nacht (Transfigured Night)**
Schoenberg's 1899 string sextet in D minor, based on a poem by Richard Dehmel. While walking through a moonlit forest, a woman confesses to her lover that she is pregnant by another man, and he forgives her. A concert society rejected it at first because it contains an "inverted ninth" chord that was not allowed by the rules of the time. Anthony Tudor later used it for his ballet Pillar of Fire.

**Sprechstimme**
A half-sung, half-spoken vocal style in which the performer touches the written pitches but then slides away from them as in speech. Schoenberg used it in Pierrot Lunaire and for the narrator in Gurre-Lieder, and his student Alban Berg used it in the operas Wozzeck and Lulu.

**A Survivor from Warsaw**
A short 1947 cantata for narrator, male chorus, and orchestra. The narrator, who says he "cannot remember everything," describes Jews being rounded up in the Warsaw ghetto while a German sergeant shouts at them to count off faster. It ends with the male chorus singing the Jewish prayer Shema Yisrael, which includes Deuteronomy 6:7.

**Second Viennese School**
The group of composers in Vienna led by Schoenberg, including his students Alban Berg and Anton Webern. They pioneered atonality and twelve-tone music. Alexander von Zemlinsky, Schoenberg's own teacher and later his brother-in-law, conducted the premiere of Erwartung.

**Five Pieces for Orchestra and the "Farben" chord**
A 1909 orchestral set whose movements include "Farben" ("Colors," also called "Summer Morning by a Lake"), "Peripetie," and "Das obligate Rezitativ." "Farben" slowly shifts one soft chord (C–G-sharp–B–E–A) among different instruments. This is the best-known example of Klangfarbenmelodie ("tone-color melody"), in which the changing instrumental color acts like a melody.

**Gurre-Lieder**
A huge late-Romantic cantata for soloists, choruses, and orchestra on poems by Jens Peter Jacobsen. It tells of King Waldemar's love for Tove, her murder, and his grief. In the "Song of the Wood Dove" a dove reports Tove's death, and later the cursed Waldemar leads a wild hunt of his dead vassals. A narrator speaks part of it in a style close to Sprechstimme.

**Chamber Symphony No. 1**
Schoenberg's Opus 9, a single-movement work in E major for 15 solo instruments. Its themes are built from stacked fourths. It was on the program of the riotous 1913 "Skandalkonzert."

**Skandalkonzert**
A 1913 Vienna concert conducted by Schoenberg that included his Chamber Symphony and music by Webern, Berg, Zemlinsky, and Mahler. Riots broke out during Berg's Altenberg Lieder and the concert had to be stopped.

**Moses und Aron**
Schoenberg's unfinished twelve-tone opera about Moses, who can only speak, and his brother Aaron, who sings. Fearing the number 13, Schoenberg dropped a letter from "Aaron" so that the title would not have thirteen letters. All of the opera is built from a single tone row.

**Erwartung**
Schoenberg's one-act atonal "monodrama" for a single soprano, who plays a woman searching a dark forest at night and finding her lover's dead body. It is often paired on a double bill with Bartók's Duke Bluebeard's Castle.

**Society for Private Musical Performances**
An organization Schoenberg founded in Vienna in 1918 to give carefully rehearsed performances of new music, with critics excluded. It performed reduced chamber arrangements of large works, including those of his friend Gustav Mahler.

**The Book of the Hanging Gardens**
Schoenberg's atonal song cycle for voice and piano setting poems by Stefan George, among the first works to abandon tonality completely.

**Jacob's Ladder**
An oratorio that Schoenberg left unfinished at his death in 1951, along with Moses und Aron and the Modern Psalms. It builds much of its material from six-note groups (hexachords) and is an important step toward his twelve-tone method.

**Seagram Building**
Mies's 38-story bronze-and-glass skyscraper at 375 Park Avenue in Manhattan (1958), designed with Philip Johnson, who did interiors including the Four Seasons Restaurant. Non-structural bronze I-beams on the exterior express the hidden steel frame, the tower sits back behind an open plaza, and the window blinds were limited to three positions (open, half, closed) to keep the facade uniform.

**Farnsworth House**
Mies's glass-walled weekend retreat (1951) in Plano, Illinois, outside Chicago, built for the physician Edith Farnsworth. It is a white-painted steel frame raised about five feet on stilts above a floodplain, with floor-to-ceiling glass walls hung with curtains. The only enclosed area is a central "core" holding the kitchen, bathrooms, and fireplace.

**"Less is more"**
The minimalist maxim most associated with Mies, summing up his reduced, unornamented style. He is also linked to the saying "God is in the details."

**Last director of the Bauhaus**
Mies led the influential German design school from 1930 until he closed it in 1933 under Nazi pressure. He later emigrated to the United States, where he became a leading figure of the International Style.

**Barcelona Pavilion and Barcelona chair**
The German Pavilion that Mies designed for the 1929 International Exposition in Barcelona: a flowing open plan of freestanding walls of marble, onyx, and glass under a flat roof on slender chrome columns. A Georg Kolbe statue titled Alba (Dawn) stands in a small reflecting pool. For it, Mies and Lilly Reich designed the Barcelona chair, a leather-cushioned seat on an X-shaped steel frame, and a matching table.

**Villa Tugendhat**
The house Mies designed (1930) in Brno, Czechoslovakia, for Fritz and Grete Tugendhat. Its main living space has a translucent onyx wall, and its huge windows facing the garden could be lowered into the floor. Mies and Lilly Reich designed the cantilevered Brno chair and the Tugendhat chair for it.

**Lake Shore Drive Apartments**
Mies's pair of steel-and-glass apartment towers at 860–880 Lake Shore Drive in Chicago (1951), overlooking Lake Michigan and exemplifying his "skin and bones" architecture. Their exterior I-beam mullions are non-structural, which made them controversial as decoration on a supposedly honest steel frame.

**S. R. Crown Hall**
The home of the architecture school at the Illinois Institute of Technology (1956), where Mies headed the architecture department and taught. It is a single huge open room with glass walls, its roof hung from exposed steel girders above, and it was built on the site of the demolished Mecca Flats apartment building.

**Lilly Reich**
The German designer who was Mies's longtime collaborator in the 1920s and 1930s. She co-designed furniture and interiors for the Barcelona Pavilion and the Villa Tugendhat, including the Barcelona and Brno chairs.

**Chicago Federal Center**
Mies's complex of dark steel-and-glass federal buildings in downtown Chicago. Its plaza features Alexander Calder's bright red sculpture Flamingo, whose color contrasts with the black buildings.

**Neue Nationalgalerie**
The New National Gallery in Berlin's Kulturforum (1968), Mies's last major work, nicknamed a "temple of light and glass." A glass hall sits beneath a vast steel roof supported by only eight columns, and the artist Jenny Holzer later installed an LED text work on its ceiling.

**Lafayette Park**
A residential development in Detroit with townhouses and high-rise apartments, containing the largest collection of Mies-designed buildings anywhere.

**Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library**
The central public library of Washington, D.C., Mies's only library. It was completed in 1972, a few years after his death in 1969, and was recently renovated to bring in more natural light.

**Weissenhof Estate and the Deutscher Werkbund**
Mies, as a leader of the Deutscher Werkbund, directed the 1927 Weissenhof Estate exhibition in Stuttgart. It was a model housing development featuring buildings by leading modernists, including Le Corbusier and Walter Gropius.

**The Starry Night**
Van Gogh's most famous painting, made in 1889 from the view out of his window at the asylum in Saint-Rémy, a former monastery. Swirling stars and a crescent moon fill the night sky above a village with a tall church spire, and a dark, flame-like cypress tree rises on the left. His Olive Trees paintings are sometimes treated as companion pieces to it.

**The Potato Eaters**
His dark 1885 masterpiece of peasant life, painted in the Dutch village of Nuenen. Five peasants share a meal of potatoes by the light of a single hanging oil lamp. A woman pours coffee or chicory, a man holds out a cup, and a girl stands with her back to the viewer.

**The Night Café**
An 1888 painting of an all-night café in Arles with clashing colors: a poisonous green ceiling, blood-red walls, and an acid-yellow floor. A man in a white coat stands beside the green billiard table in the center while a few drunks slump at the tables. A clock reads just after midnight. Van Gogh said he used red and green to express "the terrible passions of humanity."

**Self-portrait with Bandaged Ear**
In December 1888, after a violent quarrel with Paul Gauguin, Van Gogh cut off part of his ear and gave it to a woman at a brothel in Arles. He then painted self-portraits showing the bandage, one with a Japanese print in the background, wearing a fur-trimmed cap. He painted many other self-portraits, including Self-Portrait as a Painter on the Road to Tarascon and one with a straw hat painted on the back of an earlier Nuenen work.

**Bedroom in Arles**
His painting of his own narrow bedroom in the Yellow House, with a large yellow wooden bed, a red blanket, chairs, and pictures on the walls. He painted three versions, two of them while at Saint-Rémy, and one is in the Musée d'Orsay.

**Sunflowers**
His famous series of still lifes of sunflowers in vases, painted mainly in Arles in 1888–89 to decorate the Yellow House for Gauguin's visit.

**Arles and the Yellow House**
Van Gogh moved to Arles in southern France in 1888 and rented the Yellow House, hoping to start an artists' colony. Paul Gauguin joined him there for about two months before the ear incident. His Arles works include The Yellow House, The Red Vineyard, portraits of Madame Ginoux as L'Arlésienne, and Starry Night Over the Rhône.

**Portrait of Dr. Gachet**
Van Gogh painted two versions of Dr. Paul Gachet, the physician who cared for him in his final months at Auvers-sur-Oise. The red-haired, melancholy doctor in a blue coat rests his head on his fist at a red table that holds a sprig of foxglove, the plant from which the heart drug digitalis is made.

**Wheatfield with Crows**
A painting from July 1890 showing a yellow wheat field under a stormy dark-blue sky, with black crows and three paths. It is often called his last painting, although scholars such as Jan Hulsker have disputed this. Van Gogh died of a gunshot wound in Auvers-sur-Oise that month, and his other late works there include Daubigny's Garden, The Church at Auvers, and The White House at Night.

**Joseph Roulin**
The postman in Arles who befriended Van Gogh. Van Gogh painted him several times in his blue uniform with a large forked beard, and also painted Roulin's children. Roulin's wife, Augustine, is the subject of La Berceuse ("The Lullaby"), in which she holds a rope for rocking a cradle in front of flowered wallpaper.

**Theo van Gogh**
Vincent's younger brother, an art dealer in Paris, who supported him financially throughout his life. Vincent's hundreds of letters to Theo are a major source on his life and ideas.

**Japonisme and Portrait of Père Tanguy**
Van Gogh collected Japanese woodblock prints and copied works by Hiroshige and others, as in The Courtesan. His Portrait of Père Tanguy, the Paris paint seller, shows Tanguy in front of a wall of Japanese prints, including cherry blossoms and Mount Fuji.

**Skull of a Skeleton with Burning Cigarette**
A darkly humorous early painting from Van Gogh's time at the art academy in Antwerp in 1886. It shows a skeleton's skull with a lit cigarette between its teeth and may mock the academy's traditional training.

**Café Terrace at Night**
His 1888 painting of a gas-lit, bright yellow café terrace on a cobblestone street in Arles under a deep blue sky full of stars.

**Dreams**
Akira Kurosawa's 1990 film in which Martin Scorsese plays Van Gogh. In the episode "Crows," a young art student enters Van Gogh's paintings and wanders through their landscapes.

**Carnaval**
Schumann's piano suite of 21 short pieces depicting a masked ball before Lent. Its movements portray real and imaginary figures, including "Florestan," "Eusebius," "Chiarina" (his future wife Clara), "Chopin," and "Paganini," and it quotes his earlier piano work Papillons. It ends with the "March of the League of David against the Philistines."

**Scenes from Childhood (Kinderszenen)**
A suite of short, simple piano pieces about childhood. It opens with "Of Foreign Lands and Peoples" and includes "Blind Man's Bluff," "Knight of the Hobbyhorse," and "The Poet Speaks." Vladimir Horowitz famously played a piece from it at his 1986 Moscow recital.

**"Träumerei" ("Dreaming")**
The famous dreamy seventh piece of Scenes from Childhood, in F major. Its melody rises gently over soft chords, and it is one of the most familiar piano pieces of the Romantic era.

**"Rhenish" Symphony (Symphony No. 3)**
A five-movement symphony in E-flat major inspired by a trip Schumann and Clara took to the Rhine region. Its first and last movements are marked "Lebhaft" ("lively"). Its solemn fourth movement, marked "Feierlich," opens with trombones and horns playing a chorale in E-flat minor. That movement depicts the ceremony at Cologne Cathedral where the archbishop was elevated to cardinal.

**"Spring" Symphony (Symphony No. 1)**
Schumann's B-flat major first symphony, premiered in 1841 with Felix Mendelssohn conducting. It was inspired by a spring poem by Adolf Böttger that ends "O turn, o turn, and change your course." Its movements were originally given titles such as "Evening" and "Merry Playmates," and its finale, "In Full Bloom," borrows a melody from Kreisleriana.

**Clara Wieck**
A celebrated piano virtuoso who married Schumann in 1840 over the objections of her father, Friedrich Wieck, who had been Schumann's piano teacher. She premiered and championed many of his works, including the Piano Concerto, and is portrayed in the "Chiarina" movement of Carnaval.

**Florestan and Eusebius**
Two imaginary characters Schumann used to stand for the two sides of his personality: the passionate, impulsive Florestan and the dreamy, introspective Eusebius. They have their own movements in Carnaval and sign the pieces of the Davidsbündlertänze. They also appear in his music criticism, where his review of Chopin's early work includes the line "Hats off, gentlemen, a genius!"

**A-S-C-H motif**
A musical code used throughout Carnaval. The letters spell Asch, the Bohemian hometown of his then-fiancée Ernestine von Fricken, and are played as the notes A–E-flat–C–B or A-flat–C–B (in German note names, Es = E-flat, As = A-flat, H = B). The letters also appear in his own name, SCHumAnn. The note groups are printed in Carnaval as "Sphinxes," which are usually left out in performance.

**Dichterliebe ("A Poet's Love")**
A cycle of 16 songs setting poems by Heinrich Heine, written in 1840, his "Year of Song." It opens with "Im wunderschönen Monat Mai" ("In the lovely month of May") and includes "Ich grolle nicht" ("I bear no grudge, though my heart is breaking"). It ends with the speaker burying his old, bad songs in a huge coffin. That same year he also wrote two Liederkreis cycles, one of them on nine Heine poems.

**Album for the Young**
A collection of easy piano pieces written in 1848 for his daughters. It includes "The Happy Farmer," "The Wild Horseman," and "Knecht Ruprecht."

**Kreisleriana**
A piano cycle named for Johannes Kreisler, the moody, antisocial musician created by E. T. A. Hoffmann. Schumann dedicated it to Chopin, who reportedly liked only the title page.

**Rhine suicide attempt and asylum**
In 1854, suffering from severe mental illness, Schumann tried to drown himself by jumping into the Rhine. He was then placed in an asylum at Endenich, where he died in 1856. His Ghost Variations, his last piano work, date from just before the attempt.

**Piano Concerto in A minor**
Schumann's only piano concerto, which, like Grieg's, is in A minor. It began as a one-movement "Phantasie" for Clara. Its first movement is marked "Allegro affettuoso," and its middle "Intermezzo: Andantino grazioso" features the cellos and leads directly into the finale.

**League of David (Davidsbündler)**
An imaginary society Schumann created to fight the "Philistines" of shallow musical taste. It gives its name to his 18-piece Davidsbündlertänze and to the finale of Carnaval, which quotes the traditional "Grandfather's Dance." He spread its ideas through the New Journal for Music (Neue Zeitschrift für Musik), which he co-founded with Friedrich Wieck and others.

**"The Two Grenadiers"**
A Schumann song setting a Heine poem about two of Napoleon's soldiers returning from Russia. It quotes "La Marseillaise" at its climax.

**Bombing of a Basque town (1937)**
Guernica is Pablo Picasso's response to the April 1937 bombing of the Basque town of Guernica during the Spanish Civil War. The attack was carried out by the German Luftwaffe's Condor Legion, with Italian support, on behalf of Franco's Nationalists, on a market day.

**Broken sword and flower**
At the bottom of the painting lies a dismembered soldier whose severed arm still grips a broken sword, with a small flower growing beside it as a faint symbol of hope. His open hand bears a stigmata-like mark.

**Light bulb shaped like an eye**
At the top center, a bare, jagged light bulb inside an eye-shaped burst of light hangs over the scene. It is often read as an evil eye or as a pun on the Spanish "bombilla" (light bulb) and "bomba" (bomb).

**Screaming horse with a dagger tongue**
At the center, a horse speared through its side screams in agony. Its tongue, like those of several figures, is shaped like a knife or dagger, and some see a hidden skull in its body. The hatched marks on its body resemble newsprint.

**Bull with a smoking tail**
On the left, a bull with its tail curling into smoke or fire looms over the scene. Picasso's friends and critics, such as Juan Larrea, debated whether the bull or the horse represented Spain, the people, or fascism.

**Mother with a dead child**
At the far left, beneath the bull, a mother throws her head back and wails while holding her dead child. The image is often compared to a pietà.

**"KILL LIES ALL"**
In 1974, while the painting was on loan to the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the art dealer Tony Shafrazi spray-painted these words on it in red, in protest against the Vietnam War and the pardon of William Calley over the My Lai massacre.

**Woman holding a lamp**
On the right, a ghostly woman leans in through a window and holds out a lamp or candle on an elongated arm, next to the eye-shaped bulb.

**Grisaille (black, white, and gray)**
The huge mural-sized canvas (about 11 by 25.6 feet) is painted entirely in black, white, and gray, evoking newspaper photographs of the atrocity. It reuses imagery, such as the bull and the candle-bearing woman, from Picasso's 1935 etching Minotauromachia, and its monochrome style was later echoed in his painting The Charnel House.

**1937 Paris International Exposition**
Picasso painted Guernica for the Spanish Republic's pavilion at the 1937 Paris World's Fair, designed by Josep Lluís Sert. There it was displayed beside Alexander Calder's Mercury Fountain, and it was accompanied by Paul Éluard's poem "Victory of Guernica."

**Dora Maar**
Picasso's lover, a photographer, who found the large studio on the Rue des Grands-Augustins where he painted it and photographed the work's stages of creation. She was also the model for his related Weeping Woman series.

**UN tapestry and Colin Powell**
Nelson Rockefeller commissioned a tapestry copy, woven by Jacqueline de la Baume Dürrbach, which hung outside the UN Security Council. It was covered with a blue curtain during Colin Powell's 2003 press appearance making the case for war in Iraq. In 2021, the Rockefeller family temporarily took it back.

**Dove on a shelf**
In the upper left, behind the bull, a bird (usually read as a dove) spreads its wings and cries out on a shelf or table, almost hidden in the dark background.

**Man in flames at the right**
At the far right, a figure with arms raised in terror screams from a burning building with a small open window. Some critics compare the raised arms to the shapes of airplanes.

**Return to Spain (1981)**
Picasso asked that the painting not go to Spain until democracy was restored, so it stayed at MoMA for decades. It was returned in 1981 after Franco's death and now hangs in the Museo Reina Sofía in Madrid.

**Venus of Urbino**
Titian's most famous painting (1538), showing a nude woman reclining on a white bed and gazing at the viewer while holding a small bouquet of flowers. A small dog, often read as a symbol of fidelity, sleeps curled at her feet, and in the background two maids rummage through a cassone (marriage chest). It was the main model for Manet's Olympia.

**Bacchus and Ariadne**
A painting for the Duke of Ferrara in which the wine god Bacchus leaps from his chariot, drawn by two cheetahs, toward Ariadne, who has been abandoned by Theseus, whose ship sails away in the distance. Bacchus's revelers include a man wrestling with snakes and a satyr child dragging a calf's head. A ring of eight stars in the upper left represents the crown Bacchus will turn into a constellation for her.

**Sacred and Profane Love**
An allegorical painting showing two similar-looking women seated at either end of a stone fountain carved like a sarcophagus: one richly clothed as a bride in white, the other nude. Cupid reaches into the water between them, and the side of the fountain shows a relief of a flogging. The figures have been read as two forms of Venus, and one theory identifies them as Polia and Venus.

**Giorgione**
The Venetian painter, Titian's teacher and early collaborator, who shaped his rich use of color. Titian completed Giorgione's Sleeping Venus, painting its landscape, and that work was the model for the Venus of Urbino. The Pastoral Concert was long attributed to Giorgione but is now often given to Titian.

**Pesaro Madonna**
An altarpiece in Venice's Frari church, painted for Jacopo Pesaro. It is daringly asymmetrical: the Madonna and Child sit off-center to the right, while a large red banner bearing the papal and Pesaro coats of arms balances the left side. An armored soldier leads in a turbaned Turkish prisoner, and the Christ Child turns toward Saint Francis.

**Poesie for Philip II**
Titian's name ("poesie," poems) for a series of mythological paintings, drawn largely from Ovid, that he made for King Philip II of Spain and regarded as the painted equivalent of poetry. The series includes Danaë, Venus and Adonis, Diana and Actaeon, Diana and Callisto, Perseus and Andromeda, and The Rape of Europa. The poesie were reunited in a 2021 exhibition that ended at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, which owns The Rape of Europa.

**Diana and Actaeon / The Death of Actaeon**
In Diana and Actaeon, the hunter Actaeon pushes aside a red curtain and stumbles on the goddess Diana and her nymphs bathing at a stone fountain, while a stag's skull foreshadows his fate. In the later Death of Actaeon, Diana shoots her bow as Actaeon, now with a stag's head, is torn apart by his own hounds.

**The Rape of Europa**
One of the poesie, showing Jupiter disguised as a white bull carrying the princess Europa out to sea as she clings to one of his horns. It is held by the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston.

**Danaë**
A series of paintings, made in several versions, of the mythical princess Danaë reclining as Jupiter visits her as a shower of gold. Some versions include Cupid, and others an old nursemaid trying to catch the coins.

**Allegory of Prudence**
A late painting showing three human heads, an old man, a middle-aged man, and a youth, often identified as Titian, his son Orazio, and a young relative. Below them are the heads of a wolf, a lion, and a dog, representing past, present, and future, and the work carries a Latin inscription about prudence.

**Assumption of the Virgin (Frari)**
Titian's huge altarpiece for the high altar of the Frari church in Venice. The Virgin, in a red dress, rises on a cloud borne by cherubs into a brilliant golden glow where God the Father waits, while the apostles below gesture upward in amazement.

**The Flaying of Marsyas**
One of Titian's last works, showing the satyr Marsyas hanging upside down from a tree, his panpipes hanging nearby, as Apollo flays him for daring to challenge the god to a musical contest. A small dog laps up his blood beneath him.

**Equestrian Portrait of Charles V (Battle of Mühlberg)**
A portrait of Holy Roman Emperor Charles V in armor on a rearing black horse, painted in Augsburg to commemorate his 1547 victory over Protestant forces at Mühlberg. It helped found the tradition of the royal equestrian portrait; the writer Pietro Aretino had helped connect Titian with Charles V.

**Pastoral Concert**
A painting of two clothed young men, one a lute player in red, sitting in a landscape with two nude women, one of whom pours water from a glass jug into a stone well. Once attributed to Giorgione and now often to Titian, it inspired Manet's Luncheon on the Grass.

**Man with a Blue Sleeve**
An early portrait of a man seen from the right side, dominated by a huge, quilted, blue-gray sleeve that juts out toward the viewer over a stone ledge. It was once thought to show the poet Ludovico Ariosto and may be a self-portrait of Titian.

**"Degenerate Art" exhibition (Entartete Kunst)**
A 1937 exhibition in Munich organized by the Nazi regime to ridicule modern art. Expressionist, Dada, and New Objectivity works were hung chaotically with mocking captions such as "The ideal: cretin and whore." The Nazis also looted thousands of artworks and stored them in salt mines such as Altaussee.

**Der Blaue Reiter (The Blue Rider)**
An Expressionist group founded in Munich in 1911 by the Russian-born Wassily Kandinsky, author of Concerning the Spiritual in Art, and Franz Marc. The group took its name from a Kandinsky painting. Marc painted brightly colored animals in works like The Yellow Cow, Fighting Forms, and The Fate of the Animals, in which fire rains down on a blue deer.

**Die Brücke (The Bridge) and Ernst Ludwig Kirchner**
An Expressionist group founded in Dresden in 1905, co-founded by Ernst Ludwig Kirchner. Kirchner's Street, Berlin shows two prostitutes in fur-collared coats among men in black suits and belongs to his Street Scenes cycle. His Self-Portrait as a Soldier shows him with a severed hand. After the Nazis labeled him degenerate, he killed himself in 1938. Emil Nolde, another Brücke member, painted Dance Around the Golden Calf.

**Bauhaus and Walter Gropius**
An influential school of art, design, and architecture founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919. Gropius had earlier co-designed the glass-walled Fagus Factory with Adolf Meyer. Bauhaus teachers included Josef Albers (later famous for Homage to the Square at Yale), Paul Klee (author of the Pedagogical Sketchbook), and Hannes Meyer, who designed the ADGB Trade Union School with Hans Wittwer.

**Ludwig Mies van der Rohe**
The German architect and last director of the Bauhaus, who coined the maxim "less is more." He designed the Barcelona Pavilion, the Tugendhat House in Brno, the glass-walled Farnsworth House on stilts beside the Fox River near Plano, Illinois, and the Seagram Building in New York with Philip Johnson.

**Caspar David Friedrich**
The leading German Romantic painter, known for solitary figures seen from behind (Rückenfiguren) contemplating nature. His works include Wanderer Above the Sea of Fog, The Sea of Ice (The Polar Sea) with a ship crushed in jagged ice, The Stages of Life with five ships, and the Cross in the Mountains (Tetschen Altar).

**New Objectivity (Neue Sachlichkeit)**
A movement of the 1920s Weimar Republic that rejected Expressionism in favor of harsh, satirical realism. George Grosz mocked the establishment in The Pillars of Society, which shows a man with a newspaper and a teacup on his head, and Republican Automatons, which shows faceless robot-like figures holding a German flag. Otto Dix painted the Metropolis triptych of a jazz club and crippled war veterans.

**Max Beckmann**
A German painter associated with New Objectivity and Expressionism, known for the triptych Departure, which includes a woman with a crystal ball, and for The Night (1918–1919), a nightmarish scene of torture and hanging in a cramped room.

**Max Ernst**
A German-born Dada and Surrealist artist who invented frottage (rubbing over textured surfaces) and grattage (scraping paint across a canvas). His paintings include Celebes, which shows a mechanical elephant beside a headless nude torso, Two Children Are Threatened by a Nightingale, and Ubu Imperator. He was briefly married to Peggy Guggenheim.

**Albrecht Dürer and Albrecht Altdorfer**
Leading German Renaissance artists. Dürer's engraving Melencolia I shows a brooding winged figure beside an irregular polyhedron and a magic square. Altdorfer's The Battle of Alexander at Issus shows a vast battle beneath a floating tablet and a swirling sky.

**German Expressionist cinema**
Films of the Weimar era with distorted sets and stark shadows, including The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari and Nosferatu (1922). Nosferatu was an unauthorized Dracula adaptation by Prana Film featuring Count Orlok, and Bram Stoker's widow sued over it. Fritz Lang directed Metropolis, a science fiction dystopia, and M, in which a child murderer is identified by his whistling of "In the Hall of the Mountain King."

**Leni Riefenstahl**
A Nazi-era filmmaker who directed Triumph of the Will, a propaganda film of the 1934 Nuremberg rally that shows Hitler laying a wreath at a World War I memorial. She also directed Olympia, about the 1936 Berlin Olympics, which opens with athletes imitating Myron's Discobolus and uses innovative tracking shots.

**Gerhard Richter**
A contemporary German painter known for blurred "photo-paintings" based on photographs, such as Uncle Rudi, which shows his uncle in a Wehrmacht uniform. He also made the grid painting 4900 Colours and abstract paintings inspired by John Cage.

**Reichstag and Berlin's Museum Island**
In 1995, Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped Berlin's Reichstag parliament building in fabric, and Norman Foster later added its glass dome. Berlin's Museum Island includes the Pergamon Museum, which houses a reconstruction of the Pergamon Altar.

**German photography**
August Sander documented types of Germans, such as a pastry chef and a bricklayer, in People of the 20th Century. Andreas Gursky makes huge, flat, horizontal photographs such as Rhein II and 99 Cent. The performance artist Joseph Beuys, known for working with felt, spent several days sharing a room with a coyote in I Like America and America Likes Me.

**"Surprise" Symphony (No. 94 in G major)**
Haydn's most famous symphony, one of his London symphonies. Its Andante second movement opens with a soft theme on C-C-E-E-G-G-E, which is followed by a sudden fortissimo G major chord, supposedly meant to wake dozing listeners; in German it is called the "Paukenschlag" ("drumstroke") symphony. Haydn later quoted the theme in his oratorio The Seasons, where a plowman whistles it.

**"Farewell" Symphony (No. 45 in F-sharp minor)**
A Sturm und Drang symphony in the unusual key of F-sharp minor. In the finale the musicians stop playing one by one, snuff out the candles on their stands, and leave, until only two muted violins remain; it was a hint to Prince Nikolaus Esterházy that his musicians wanted to leave his summer palace at Eszterháza and go home to their families.

**"Father of the Symphony" and "Father of the String Quartet"**
Haydn's standard nicknames. He wrote 104 numbered symphonies (often counted as 106 with two unnumbered ones) and dozens of string quartets, works for two violins, viola, and cello, and he did more than anyone else to establish both genres in the Classical era.

**"Emperor" Quartet and "Gott erhalte Franz den Kaiser"**
Haydn wrote the anthem "Gott erhalte Franz den Kaiser" ("God Save Emperor Francis," lyrics by Lorenz Leopold Haschka) for Francis II and then used it as the theme of variations in the second movement of his "Emperor" Quartet. The melody, opening G-A-B-A-C-B, was later set to August Heinrich Hoffmann von Fallersleben's words as the "Deutschlandlied," the German national anthem.

**The Creation**
Haydn's oratorio (1798) based on the Book of Genesis and Milton's Paradise Lost. It opens with "The Representation of Chaos"; when the chorus sings "and there was light," it bursts into a fortissimo C major chord. The archangels Raphael, Uriel, and Gabriel narrate the six days of creation, Part I ends with the chorus "The Heavens Are Telling the Glory of God," and Adam and Eve appear as bass and soprano in Part III.

**Esterházy family**
The Hungarian princely family that employed Haydn as court musician (and later Kapellmeister) for decades, especially Prince Nikolaus "the Magnificent" at the palace of Eszterháza. He wrote his late masses, such as the "Nelson" Mass, for the Esterházys.

**London Symphonies**
Haydn's final twelve symphonies (Nos. 93–104), written for impresario Johann Peter Salomon during two visits to London in the 1790s. They include the "Surprise," "Miracle," "Military," "Clock," "Drumroll" (No. 103, which opens with a timpani roll), and "London" symphonies.

**"The Joke" Quartet (Op. 33 No. 2)**
A string quartet in E-flat major whose finale repeatedly fakes its ending with pauses, so the audience cannot tell when it has actually finished. It belongs to the six Op. 33 "Russian" quartets, dedicated to Grand Duke Paul of Russia, which inspired Mozart's six quartets dedicated to Haydn (including the "Hunt" and "Dissonance").

**Op. 76 "Erdődy" Quartets ("Fifths," "Emperor," "Sunrise")**
A set of six string quartets dedicated to Count Joseph Erdődy. The "Fifths" quartet opens with falling perfect fifths and contains a canonic "Witches' Minuet"; the set also includes the "Emperor" and the "Sunrise," named for its rising opening melody.

**"Miracle" Symphony**
The nickname of Symphony No. 96, from the story that a chandelier fell during its London premiere but injured no one because the audience had crowded toward the stage. The incident is now believed to have actually occurred at the premiere of Symphony No. 102.

**Masses (Nelson Mass, Mass in Time of War, Harmoniemesse)**
Haydn's late masses for the Esterházys include the "Nelson" Mass (Missa in Angustiis, "Mass for Troubled Times," originally scored without woodwinds), the "Mass in Time of War" (Paukenmesse, named for the timpani in its Agnus Dei), and his last major work, the B-flat major "Harmoniemesse," named for its large wind section.

**The Seven Last Words of Christ**
An orchestral work by Haydn of slow meditations on Christ's last words on the cross, ending with a fast "Earthquake" movement. Haydn also arranged it for string quartet and as an oratorio.

**Trumpet Concerto in E-flat major**
Haydn's concerto (1796) written for Anton Weidinger's newly invented keyed trumpet, which could play chromatic melodies in the low register. Johann Nepomuk Hummel also wrote a concerto for the same instrument.

**Other symphony nicknames ("Hornsignal," "Bear," "Philosopher," "Military," "Clock")**
No. 31 "Hornsignal" uses four horns, No. 82 "Bear" (a Paris symphony) has a droning, bagpipe-like finale, and No. 22 "Philosopher" uses two English horns instead of oboes. The "Military" (No. 100) imitates Turkish janissary music with percussion, and the "Clock" (No. 101) has a ticking accompaniment in its slow movement.

**Hoboken catalog**
The standard catalog of Haydn's works compiled by Dutch musicologist Anthony van Hoboken, so his works are identified with "Hob." numbers.

**Nighthawks**
Hopper's most famous painting (1942), showing three customers and a white-uniformed server inside a brightly lit corner diner late at night, seen through a huge curved window from a dark, empty street. No door into the diner is visible, which adds to the sense of isolation. Details often clued include the man in a fedora beside a red-haired woman in a red dress, a man seen from behind, and two large metal coffee urns at the end of the counter. It is said to have been inspired by a Greenwich Village diner near Mulry Square.

**Advertisement for Phillies cigars**
A sign reading "Phillies" with "Only 5¢" sits atop the diner in Nighthawks. It is the most common late giveaway clue for both the painting and Hopper.

**Automat**
A 1927 painting of a lone woman in a yellow hat and green coat sitting at a table in an automat (a coin-operated cafeteria), staring into her coffee cup at night. She has removed only one glove, a bowl of fruit sits in the window behind her, and the dark window reflects two long rows of ceiling lights. His wife Jo was the model.

**Josephine "Jo" Nivison Hopper**
Hopper's wife, a painter herself, who modeled for nearly all the women in his paintings after their 1924 marriage, including those in Automat, Chop Suey, and New York Movie. She also kept detailed record books of his work.

**Chop Suey**
A 1929 painting of two women in hats facing each other across a table in a Chinese restaurant, with a small red teapot between them. Through the window, part of a red sign with the letters "SUEY" can be seen. The two women look almost like twins, since Jo modeled for both.

**New York Movie**
A 1939 painting of a nearly empty movie theater. On the right, a blonde usher in a blue uniform leans against the wall beneath a lamp near red curtains and a staircase, lost in thought, while a few patrons on the left watch the film. Jo posed for the usher.

**Early Sunday Morning**
A 1930 painting of an empty street of red-brick storefronts on Seventh Avenue in New York, lit by low morning sun. A barber pole and a fire hydrant in the foreground cast long shadows across the sidewalk.

**House by the Railroad**
A 1925 painting of a lone Victorian mansion with a mansard roof, whose lower part is cut off by railroad tracks in the foreground. It inspired the Bates house in Alfred Hitchcock's Psycho and the farmhouse in Terrence Malick's Days of Heaven.

**Rooms by the Sea**
A 1951 painting of an open doorway in Hopper's Cape Cod studio at South Truro that opens directly onto the ocean, with sunlight falling on the bare wall and part of a red chair visible in the next room. Hopper called the view "The Jumping Off Place."

**Office at Night**
A 1940 painting of a man in a suit reading at a desk while a curvy secretary in a blue dress stands by a filing cabinet looking at him. Its view looks down into the office from above, inspired by glimpses into buildings from New York's elevated trains.

**Gas**
A 1940 painting of an attendant in a vest working at one of three red gas pumps beside a road at dusk, with dark woods behind. A sign showing the Mobil flying horse, Pegasus, hangs over the station.

**Arthayer R. Sanborn and Gail Levin**
Sanborn, a Baptist minister, claimed to have been given thousands of Hopper sketches and other works from the Hopper home in Nyack, New York. Gail Levin, who compiled Hopper's catalogue raisonné, argues that many of these works were taken improperly.

**Parodies of Nighthawks**
Gottfried Helnwein's Boulevard of Broken Dreams replaces the diner's customers with Humphrey Bogart, Marilyn Monroe, James Dean, and Elvis Presley (as the server). Banksy also parodied the painting, adding a man in Union Jack boxer shorts standing outside beside overturned plastic chairs.

**Cape Cod paintings**
Hopper spent his summers in Truro on Cape Cod, the setting of many works. Cape Cod Evening shows a couple outside their white house while a dog stands alert in tall grass, and Cape Cod Morning shows a woman in an orange or pink dress leaning out of a bay window to look outside.

**Two Comedians**
Hopper's final painting (1966), showing two figures in white Pierrot costumes bowing at the edge of a stage. It is read as Hopper and Jo taking their final bow.

**The Burial of the Count of Orgaz**
El Greco's most famous painting (1586–88), made for the church of Santo Tomé in Toledo and the near-universal giveaway. It illustrates a local legend that at the 14th-century funeral of the nobleman Don Gonzalo Ruiz, lord of Orgaz, Saints Stephen and Augustine miraculously came down from heaven to lay his armored body in the tomb.

**Saints Stephen and Augustine and the earthly and heavenly halves**
In the Burial, the two saints in gold vestments lower the Count's body in the lower, earthly half, in front of a horizontal row of black-clad Toledo noblemen. In the upper, heavenly half, the clouds part as an angel in yellow carries the Count's soul (shown as a wispy, infant-like form) toward a deesis of Christ flanked by the Virgin Mary and John the Baptist, with St. Peter holding his keys among the saints.

**Jorge Manuel's handkerchief and Andrés Núñez**
In the Burial's lower left, a boy holding a torch and pointing to the saints is El Greco's son Jorge Manuel. A handkerchief in his pocket carries the painter's Greek signature and the year 1578, Jorge Manuel's birth year. Andrés Núñez, the parish priest who commissioned the painting, is shown reading at the right.

**The Opening of the Fifth Seal (The Vision of Saint John)**
A late, unfinished painting now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, illustrating the Book of Revelation. St. John in shimmering blue robes raises his arms to the sky at left, while writhing nude souls of martyrs behind him receive white robes of salvation, with yellow and green draperies. It was called Profane Love until 1908.

**Influence on Les Demoiselles d'Avignon**
The Opening of the Fifth Seal was owned by the Spanish painter Ignacio Zuloaga, who bought it cheaply after a failed restoration had damaged it and part of the canvas had been lost. Pablo Picasso studied it in Zuloaga's studio while painting Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, and its group of nudes may have inspired that painting's composition.

**View of Toledo**
One of the earliest pure landscapes in Western art (now at the Met), showing El Greco's adopted city of Toledo on a green hill above the Tagus River under dark, stormy, swirling clouds. The Castle of San Servando appears on the right.

**The Disrobing of Christ (El Expolio)**
A painting for the sacristy of Toledo Cathedral in which Christ, in a brilliant red robe, gazes upward as a man in green grabs the robe to strip it from him. Men in the crowd point at him, an armored soldier stands nearby, and in the lower corner a bent-over carpenter drills holes in the cross.

**The Three Marys dispute**
The Toledo Cathedral officials objected to the Disrobing of Christ because the Three Marys in the lower left were shown in the same scene as the crowd, which did not match the Gospels, and because figures' heads were placed above Christ's. This led to a lawsuit over his fee, and El Greco accepted a reduced payment instead of removing the Marys.

**Laocoön**
El Greco's only surviving mythological painting, now in the National Gallery of Art in Washington. The Trojan priest Laocoön and his sons wrestle with serpents sent by the gods in front of a view of Toledo, while mysterious nude figures, often identified as gods such as Apollo and Artemis (one figure appears to have two faces), watch at the right.

**Domenikos Theotokopoulos and his Cretan origin**
El Greco ("The Greek") was born Domenikos Theotokopoulos on Crete, then ruled by Venice, and trained as an icon painter in the Byzantine tradition. He worked in Venice, where he was influenced by Titian, and in Rome (where he painted the portrait of the half-armored Vincenzo Anastagi), before settling in Toledo, Spain. He signed his paintings in Greek letters.

**Mannerism, elongated figures, and the "El Greco fallacy"**
El Greco is a Mannerist known for long, flame-like, distorted figures, unnatural colors, and dramatic gray or stormy backgrounds. A popular theory said his elongated figures came from astigmatism. The psychologist Irvin Rock and others called this the "El Greco fallacy," since an artist with distorted vision would also see the canvas distorted and so would paint normally proportioned figures.

**Modena Triptych**
A small, early portable altarpiece from El Greco's Cretan or Venetian period, combining Byzantine and Western styles. Its scenes include the Adoration of the Shepherds, the Baptism of Christ, an Allegory of the Christian Knight in which Christ steps over a skeleton and crowns a kneeling knight, and a view of Mount Sinai with pilgrims traveling to St. Catherine's Monastery.

**The Dormition of the Virgin**
An icon from El Greco's early Cretan period, kept in a church on the Greek island of Syros where it is still venerated. Its signature was discovered in 1983, which confirmed his Cretan training in Orthodox icon painting.

**View and Plan of Toledo**
A late painting showing the city of Toledo from a different angle than View of Toledo. It includes a map of the city held by a young man and shows the Tavera Hospital floating on a cloud in the foreground.

**The Agony in the Garden**
A painting showing Christ praying on the Mount of Olives while an angel in yellow floats above him, his sleeping apostles lie in a cocoon-like cloud below, and Judas leads soldiers toward him in the distance.

**The Persistence of Memory**
Dalí's most famous painting (1931), showing soft, melting pocket watches draped over a tree branch, a table edge, and a distorted, fleshy self-portrait face with long eyelashes lying on the ground. An orange pocket watch in the lower left is covered in crawling ants, and the background shows the rocky Catalonian coast near Port Lligat and Cap de Creus; Dalí said the soft watches were inspired by Camembert cheese melting in the sun, not by Einstein's theory of relativity.

**The Disintegration of the Persistence of Memory**
A 1950s reworking of Dalí's most famous painting, made after the atomic bomb sparked his interest in nuclear physics. The original landscape breaks apart into a grid of floating bricks or blocks, the tree splits into segments, and a fish floats above the scene.

**Metamorphosis of Narcissus**
A 1937 painting made with Dalí's "paranoiac-critical method" of creating double images. The mythical Narcissus kneels gazing into a pool, and beside him is his double: a stone hand holding a cracked egg from which a narcissus flower sprouts.

**Gala Dalí**
Dalí's wife and muse, who appears in many of his paintings, including The Madonna of Port Lligat, Galatea of the Spheres, Leda Atomica, Dream Caused by the Flight of a Bee, and The Hallucinogenic Toreador. Dalí also painted himself from behind painting Gala, who faces her own mirror image.

**Un Chien Andalou (An Andalusian Dog)**
A 1929 Surrealist short film Dalí made with director Luis Buñuel, built on dream logic. It opens with a shot of a razor appearing to slice a woman's eye, inspired by a dream of the moon being sliced by a cloud, and includes a man dragging pianos filled with dead donkeys and priests, one of whom is played by Dalí.

**Dream Caused by the Flight of a Bee Around a Pomegranate a Second Before Awakening**
A 1944 painting of a nude Gala floating asleep above a rock as two tigers leap at her from the mouth of a fish emerging from a pomegranate, while a bayonet is about to touch her arm. A spindly-legged elephant walks in the background, and Dalí said the painting expressed Freud's discovery of a dream with a long narrative caused by an instant event.

**The Temptation of Saint Anthony**
A 1946 painting in which a nude Saint Anthony kneels in the desert, holding up a cross against a rearing white horse and a procession of elephants on impossibly long, spindly legs carrying temptations on their backs.

**Swans Reflecting Elephants**
A double-image painting in which three swans and the bare trees behind them are reflected in a lake so that their reflections form elephants.

**Nuclear mysticism**
Dalí's post-World War II phase, inspired by the bombing of Hiroshima and atomic physics; in his "Anti-Matter Manifesto" he declared "My father today is Werner Heisenberg." Works include Galatea of the Spheres (Gala's face built from floating spheres, referencing Pygmalion's statue), Leda Atomica (a nude Gala as Leda on a pedestal with a suspended swan), and The Sacrament of the Last Supper.

**The Madonna of Port Lligat**
A painting in which Gala appears as the Virgin Mary with a rectangular hole cut through her torso, where the Christ Child floats. A seashell and an egg hang suspended above her head.

**Crucifixion (Corpus Hypercubus)**
A 1954 painting of Christ crucified on the unfolded net of a four-dimensional hypercube, watched from below by Gala. Ayn Rand called it her favorite painting.

**The Hallucinogenic Toreador**
A large late painting in which repeated images of the Venus de Milo form the face of a bullfighter, with a bullring and a small portrait of Gala included. Dalí also made a sculpture, Venus de Milo with Drawers.

**Soft Construction with Boiled Beans (Premonition of Civil War)**
A 1936 painting of a monstrous, self-tearing figure of body parts balanced on a box and stump, with boiled beans scattered on the ground, foreshadowing the Spanish Civil War. Dalí also painted The Burning Giraffe at the start of that war.

**Lobster Telephone and Mae West Lips Sofa**
Two famous Surrealist objects by Dalí: a telephone with a lobster as its handset and a nonfunctional sofa shaped like the red lips of actress Mae West. His Theatre-Museum in Figueres displays such objects along with portraits of Gala.

**Spellbound and Destino**
Dalí designed the dream sequence for Alfred Hitchcock's 1945 film Spellbound, featuring curtains covered in eyes and a warped wheel. He also collaborated with Walt Disney on Destino, a short about Chronos and Dahlia that was only completed in 2003.

**Finlandia**
Sibelius's most famous work, an 1899 patriotic tone poem that became a symbol of Finnish resistance to Russian rule. It begins with turbulent, ominous brass and builds to rousing music before a serene closing "Finlandia Hymn." It is not Finland's national anthem, but it is often treated as a second one.

**Press Celebrations and Russian censorship**
Finlandia began as the last of a series of tableaux in Sibelius's music for the 1899 Press Celebrations, an event protesting Russian censorship of the Finnish press. To get it past the censors, it was performed under disguised titles such as "Impromptu" and "A Scandinavian Choral March."

**Finlandia Hymn**
The calm, hymnlike melody near the end of Finlandia, first stated by woodwinds and often sung by a choir. It was later published as a separate choral piece with Finnish words, and in English it is sung as the hymn "Be Still, My Soul."

**The Swan of Tuonela**
A tone poem in which a solo English horn (cor anglais) represents a sacred swan gliding on the black river around Tuonela, the land of the dead in Finnish mythology, over muted, shimmering strings. It is the second piece of the Lemminkäinen Suite and the most common non-Finlandia clue.

**Lemminkäinen Suite (Four Legends)**
A set of four tone poems based on the adventures of the hero Lemminkäinen in the Kalevala: "Lemminkäinen and the Maidens of the Island," "The Swan of Tuonela," "Lemminkäinen in Tuonela," and "Lemminkäinen's Return." Lemminkäinen is killed while trying to hunt the swan.

**Kalevala**
The Finnish national epic, compiled by Elias Lönnrot from folk poetry. It inspired many Sibelius works, including the Lemminkäinen Suite, Kullervo, and the unfinished Wagner-inspired opera The Building of the Boat.

**Violin Concerto in D minor**
Sibelius's only concerto (Op. 47). It opens with the soloist playing a long G, A, and low D over muted, shimmering violins, and its first movement has a large cadenza in place of a development section. Donald Francis Tovey called its finale "a polonaise for polar bears."

**Symphony No. 7**
Sibelius's last symphony, a single continuous movement in C major. It premiered as a "Fantasia sinfonica," and it features a prominent trombone theme often called "Aino," after his wife.

**Valse triste**
A brooding "Sad Waltz" from Sibelius's incidental music to Kuolema ("Death"), a play by his brother-in-law Arvid Järnefelt. In the scene, a dying woman dances with a figure she thinks is her dead husband, who turns out to be Death.

**Kullervo**
An early five-movement symphonic work for soloists, male chorus, and orchestra based on the tragic Kalevala hero Kullervo. It follows his youth, his unknowing seduction of his sister, his going to war, and his death, and parts of it are written in 5/4 time.

**Symphony No. 5**
A symphony in E-flat major that Sibelius revised several times, including by fusing the first two movements into one. The finale's broad "swan hymn" horn theme was inspired by the sight of 16 swans flying overhead, and the work ends with six widely separated full-orchestra chords.

**Symphony No. 2**
Sibelius's most often performed symphony, in D major, partly written in Rapallo, Italy. It is often heard as a nationalist statement. Its second movement was inspired by an image of Death meeting Don Juan, and its triumphant finale theme begins D–E–F-sharp.

**Eighth Symphony and the "Silence of Järvenpää"**
Sibelius composed almost nothing in roughly the last 30 years of his life at his home, Ainola, in Järvenpää. He worked for years on an Eighth Symphony, which Serge Koussevitzky hoped to premiere, but he is believed to have burned it in the 1940s.

**Karelia Suite**
Orchestral music drawn from Sibelius's music for historical tableaux about Karelia, a region of southeastern Finland. Its movements include an Intermezzo, a "Ballade" with an English horn solo depicting a minstrel singing for Karl Knutsson at Viipuri Castle, and an "Alla marcia."

**Tapiola**
Sibelius's last major tone poem (1926), depicting the dark Finnish forest of Tapio, the forest god of the Kalevala. It is built from a single brooding theme.

**Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun**
Claude Debussy's 1894 symphonic poem, inspired by a poem by Stéphane Mallarmé and often seen as the start of modern music. It opens with a famous unaccompanied flute solo that slides chromatically down from C-sharp to G (a tritone) and back up. Georges Barrère played the solo at the premiere.

**The Magic Flute**
Mozart's 1791 Singspiel (Die Zauberflöte), with a libretto by the Freemason Emanuel Schikaneder. Prince Tamino receives the enchanted flute from the Three Ladies, and its music protects him and Pamina during the trials of fire and water. The bird-catcher Papageno gets magic bells, and the Queen of the Night orders her daughter Pamina to kill the priest Sarastro in the coloratura aria "Der Hölle Rache."

**Boléro**
Maurice Ravel's 1928 orchestral piece, commissioned as a ballet by the dancer Ida Rubinstein. It is built on a snare-drum ostinato that runs through the whole work, and the flute is the first instrument to play the repeating melody, entering over the snare drum.

**Syrinx**
Debussy's short 1913 piece for unaccompanied flute, a cornerstone of the solo repertoire. It is named after the nymph who was turned into reeds that the god Pan made into his pan pipes, and it was the first important solo piece written for the modern Boehm flute.

**"Morning Mood"**
The opening movement of Edvard Grieg's Peer Gynt Suite No. 1. The flute plays a serene pastoral melody in E major (B, G-sharp, F-sharp, E, F-sharp, G-sharp), which the oboe then answers.

**Peter and the Wolf**
Sergei Prokofiev's 1936 children's piece for narrator and orchestra, in which each character is represented by an instrument. The flute plays the chirping bird, who argues with the duck (the oboe). The flute is also often used elsewhere to imitate birdsong.

**Density 21.5**
Edgard Varèse's 1936 piece for solo flute, written for Georges Barrère's new platinum flute. Its title refers to the density of platinum, about 21.5 grams per cubic centimeter.

**Theobald Boehm**
The 19th-century German flutist and inventor who designed the modern flute's key mechanism, the Boehm system. It uses ring keys, interlinked rods, and acoustically placed tone holes, and it was later adapted to the clarinet and oboe.

**Cécile Chaminade's Concertino**
The French composer's Concertino in D major, Op. 107 (1902), commissioned by the Paris Conservatoire as an exam piece for flute students. It is a standard part of the flute repertoire.

**Frederick the Great and Johann Quantz**
King Frederick II of Prussia was an accomplished flutist. His teacher Johann Joachim Quantz wrote a famous treatise on playing the transverse flute. J.S. Bach dedicated The Musical Offering to Frederick, and its trio sonata is scored for flute, violin, and continuo.

**Badinerie**
The fast, virtuosic final movement of J.S. Bach's Orchestral Suite No. 2 in B minor, in which the flute plays the lead melody. Bach also gave the flute a prominent role in Brandenburg Concerto No. 5.

**Mozart's flute concertos**
Mozart wrote Flute Concertos No. 1 in G major and No. 2 in D major, as well as the Concerto for Flute and Harp in C major, his only work featuring the harp. In letters to his father he complained that he disliked writing for the flute.

**Paul Taffanel**
The 19th-century French flutist and teacher who founded the French flute school, known for its light, flexible tone. He compiled the 17 Daily Exercises (with his student Philippe Gaubert), and his students included Georges Barrère.

**James Galway and Jean-Pierre Rampal**
Two of the most famous modern flute soloists. Galway is a Northern Irish virtuoso nicknamed "The Man with the Golden Flute," and Rampal was a French flutist known for playing a gold flute and for reviving Baroque flute music.

**Poulenc's Flute Sonata**
Francis Poulenc's Sonata for Flute and Piano, FP 164 (1957), one of the most frequently performed 20th-century flute works. Its first movement is marked Allegro malinconico. Other repertoire staples include Gabriel Fauré's Fantaisie and Olivier Messiaen's Le merle noir ("The Blackbird").

**Symphony of a Thousand**
Mahler's Symphony No. 8 in E-flat major, nicknamed for the huge forces it needs: an enlarged orchestra, organ, several choirs, and eight soloists, as at its 1910 Munich premiere. Part I sets the 9th-century Latin hymn "Veni, Creator Spiritus" ("Come, Creator Spirit") and opens with an E-flat organ chord, with the chorus later singing "Accende lumen sensibus." Part II sets the final scene of Goethe's Faust, with roles such as Pater Ecstaticus, Pater Profundus, and Doctor Marianus (tenor). It ends with the "Chorus Mysticus" praising the "Eternal Feminine."

**Resurrection Symphony**
Mahler's Symphony No. 2 in C minor. Its first movement began as a symphonic poem called Totenfeier ("Funeral Rites"), and its second movement is a gentle Ländler. Its finale sets Friedrich Klopstock's hymn "Die Auferstehung" ("The Resurrection"), which begins "Rise again, yes, rise again." Mahler wanted real church bells for the finale.

**"Urlicht"**
"Primal Light," the fourth movement of the Second Symphony. In it an alto sings "O Röschen rot!" ("O little red rose!") and hopes that God will give her "a little light" to lead her to eternal blissful life. Like several Mahler movements, it is a song taken from Des Knaben Wunderhorn.

**Symphony No. 5 and its trumpet solo**
Mahler's Fifth Symphony opens with a solo trumpet playing a "short-short-short-long" fanfare on C-sharp, which begins a funeral march (Trauermarsch). The symphony has five movements and is often said to begin his middle period. Its stormy second movement in A minor builds to a D major brass chorale, and its scherzo features a prominent obbligato horn.

**Adagietto**
The fourth movement of the Fifth Symphony, in F major and scored for strings and harp alone. It is widely read as a love letter to Mahler's wife Alma, and Leonard Bernstein loved conducting it. It also became famous through the film Death in Venice.

**Tragic Symphony and the "hammer blows of fate"**
Mahler's Symphony No. 6 in A minor. It opens with a march, contrasts an A major chord with an A minor chord over a timpani rhythm, and includes a soaring "Alma theme" for his wife as well as offstage cowbells. Its finale originally had three huge hammer blows, which Alma linked to three disasters in his life, including his forced resignation from the Vienna Court Opera. Mahler later removed the third blow. He also swapped the order of the scherzo and the Andante between editions.

**Titan Symphony and "Frère Jacques"**
Mahler's Symphony No. 1 in D major, named after a novel by Jean Paul. It opens with a quiet A drone spread across seven octaves, quotes his own song "Ging heut' morgen übers Feld" ("I went over the field this morning"), and its third movement turns the round "Frère Jacques" into a minor-key funeral march.

**Des Knaben Wunderhorn**
"The Youth's Magic Horn," a collection of German folk poems that Mahler set as songs. Material from these songs runs through his first four "Wunderhorn" symphonies, including "Urlicht" and St. Anthony of Padua's sermon to the fishes, which became the scherzo of the Second Symphony.

**"Death shriek"**
Mahler's name for the huge dissonant climax of the Second Symphony's scherzo. That movement is based on his Wunderhorn song about St. Anthony of Padua preaching to the fish, and it opens with pairs of soft timpani strokes on G and C.

**Das Lied von der Erde**
"The Song of the Earth," a song-symphony for tenor and alto (or baritone) based on ancient Chinese poems by Li Bai (Li Po) and others in German translation. It opens with "The Drinking Song of Earth's Misery," whose refrain is "Dark is life, is death," and it ends with the voice fading on "ewig... ewig" ("forever... forever"). Mahler did not give it a number, supposedly to avoid the "curse of the ninth."

**Symphony No. 3**
Mahler's longest symphony, at about 100 minutes and in six movements. It opens with eight horns in unison, and its scherzo includes a long offstage posthorn solo, usually played today on a flugelhorn.

**Symphony No. 4**
Mahler's lightest symphony. It opens with sleigh bells and flutes, and its second movement uses a solo violin tuned a whole step higher to depict Death playing the fiddle. Its third movement is marked "Ruhevoll" ("peacefully"), and its finale sets the Wunderhorn song "Das himmlische Leben" ("The Heavenly Life"), a child's vision of heaven sung by a soprano.

**Symphony No. 10 and Deryck Cooke**
Mahler's unfinished last symphony. He fully orchestrated only the opening Adagio, and its five movements include a central "Purgatorio" between two scherzos. The musicologist Deryck Cooke made the standard performing version.

**Kindertotenlieder**
"Songs on the Death of Children," Mahler's song cycle on poems by Friedrich Rückert. A few years after he wrote it, his own elder daughter died.

**Alma Mahler**
Alma Schindler, Mahler's wife, whom he married in 1902. She is linked to the Adagietto of the Fifth Symphony and the "Alma theme" of the Sixth, and her accounts shaped how people interpret many of his works.

**Migrant Mother**
Lange's most famous photograph (1936), taken at a pea pickers' camp in Nipomo, California. It shows Florence Owens Thompson, a worn-looking mother, gazing anxiously into the distance with her hand raised to her face while two of her children turn their faces away and lean on her shoulders, and a baby rests in her lap. It became the defining image of the Great Depression.

**Florence Owens Thompson**
The subject of Migrant Mother, a 32-year-old migrant farmworker who was identified only decades later. Lange took a short series of photos of her and her children in about ten minutes, moving closer with each shot.

**"Destitute Pea Pickers" and "Human Erosion in California"**
Alternate titles for Migrant Mother. Lange's original caption began "Destitute pea pickers in California," and the image was also published as "Human Erosion in California"; it was later retouched to remove Thompson's thumb from the lower right corner of the frame.

**White Angel Breadline**
A 1933 photograph taken at a San Francisco soup kitchen run by a woman nicknamed the "White Angel." An unshaven man in a battered hat, his eyes hidden by its brim, leans on a wooden railing with his hands clasped around an empty tin cup, turned away from the crowd of men behind him. It was one of the first photos that brought Lange attention as a documentary photographer.

**Farm Security Administration (FSA)**
A New Deal agency that hired photographers including Lange, Walker Evans, and Arthur Rothstein to document rural poverty and migrant workers during the Great Depression and Dust Bowl. Lange took Migrant Mother while working for its photography program.

**Manzanar and Japanese American internment**
In 1942 the War Relocation Authority (WRA) hired Lange to document the forced removal of Japanese Americans under Executive Order 9066, including at the Manzanar camp in California. Her images were so sympathetic that the government impounded many of them, and they were not widely published until decades later.

**Children reciting the Pledge of Allegiance**
A 1942 Lange photo of schoolchildren, including Japanese American students, at Raphael Weill Elementary School in San Francisco standing with their hands on their hearts saying the Pledge of Allegiance shortly before the internment. It is sometimes titled One Nation Indivisible.

**"I Am an American" sign**
A 1942 Lange photograph of a grocery store in Oakland, owned by a Japanese American, with a large banner reading "I AM AN AMERICAN" hung after the attack on Pearl Harbor. The store was later closed when its owner was sent to an internment camp.

**Members of the Mochida Family Awaiting Evacuation**
A 1942 internment photograph showing a Japanese American family in Hayward, California, standing with their luggage, each wearing identification tags as they wait to be taken away. It is one of her best-known WRA images.

**An American Exodus and Paul Taylor**
A 1939 book combining Lange's Dust Bowl and migrant photographs with text by her husband, the economist Paul Schuster Taylor. It includes The Road West, a photo of U.S. Highway 54 stretching across New Mexico.

**Ditched, Stalled, and Stranded**
A 1935 photograph of a worried migrant couple sitting in their broken-down car in California's San Joaquin Valley. Lange cropped it tightly to emphasize the man's anxious expression.

**Death of a Valley and Pirkle Jones**
A photo essay made with photographer Pirkle Jones documenting the town of Monticello in California's Berryessa Valley before it was flooded by the Monticello Dam to create Lake Berryessa. It was published as an issue of Aperture magazine in 1960.

**Freedom of Religion: The Three Denominations**
A 1938 photograph of three small churches (Catholic, Lutheran, and Baptist) standing in a diagonal row on the plains near Winner, South Dakota.

**Public Defender**
A 1957 close-up portrait of an Oakland public defender, emphasizing his furrowed forehead and intense eyes. It reflects Lange's later interest in individuals and social institutions.

**Arnold Genthe, The Family of Man, and other career clues**
Lange learned photography in New York, including under Arnold Genthe, before opening a portrait studio in San Francisco. She later helped Edward Steichen organize the 1955 MoMA exhibition The Family of Man and photographed rural Ireland with her son Daniel Dixon for Life magazine; her assistant Rondal Partridge took a famous photo of her perched on top of a car with her camera.

**Opening glissando of Rhapsody in Blue**
George Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue (1924), commissioned by Paul Whiteman for the concert "An Experiment in Modern Music," opens with a low clarinet trill followed by a famous two-octave upward glissando. Gershwin wrote a 17-note scale, but Whiteman's clarinetist Ross Gorman played it as a wailing slide, and the effect became standard.

**Mozart's Clarinet Concerto in A major and Anton Stadler**
Mozart's last concerto (K. 622, 1791), a fast-slow-fast work written for his friend, the virtuoso Anton Stadler. It was originally written for the basset clarinet, a version of the instrument with extra low notes, and Mozart also wrote his Clarinet Quintet in A major (with string quartet) for Stadler.

**Benny Goodman, "King of Swing"**
The swing-era bandleader and clarinetist whose 1938 Carnegie Hall concert, the first jazz concert there, was released as the double album The Famous 1938 Carnegie Hall Jazz Concert. He also commissioned classical works, including Aaron Copland's Clarinet Concerto and Béla Bartók's Contrasts.

**"Sing, Sing, Sing" and Gene Krupa**
A Louis Prima song that became the signature number of Benny Goodman's band. Drummer Gene Krupa's extended tom-tom solo opens it, and it closed the 1938 Carnegie Hall concert.

**Artie Shaw, "Begin the Beguine," and the Gramercy Five**
Goodman's great rival clarinetist and bandleader, whose big-band version of Cole Porter's "Begin the Beguine" was a huge hit. He also led a small "band within a band" called the Gramercy Five, an idea pioneered by Goodman's small groups, and wrote his own clarinet concerto.

**Aaron Copland's Clarinet Concerto**
Copland's concerto (for clarinet, strings, harp, and piano) commissioned by and dedicated to Benny Goodman. Its two movements, a slow lyrical one and a jazz-inspired fast one, are linked by a solo cadenza; Jerome Robbins choreographed the ballet The Pied Piper to it.

**Chalumeau register and "crossing the break"**
The chalumeau is the clarinet's Baroque predecessor and gives its name to the instrument's lowest register. Johann Christoph Denner is credited with inventing the clarinet by adding a register key to the chalumeau; that key raises notes by a twelfth into the "clarion" register, and moving between these registers is called "crossing the break." The weak notes just below the break are the "throat tones," and the highest register is the altissimo.

**Carl Maria von Weber and Heinrich Baermann**
Weber wrote two clarinet concertos and an E-flat major Concertino for the virtuoso Heinrich Baermann. The soloist in the Second Concerto enters with a dramatic three-octave leap downward, and the First Concerto is in F minor.

**Brahms and Richard Mühlfeld**
Late in his career, Brahms was inspired by the playing of clarinetist Richard Mühlfeld to write four chamber works for him: the Clarinet Trio, the B minor Clarinet Quintet, and two Clarinet Sonatas.

**"Abyss of the Birds" (Quartet for the End of Time)**
The third movement of Olivier Messiaen's Quartet for the End of Time (1941, composed in a POW camp), an extremely slow unaccompanied clarinet solo. The clarinet is the only wind instrument in the quartet, and in the first movement, "Crystal Liturgy," it imitates a blackbird.

**Single reed, B-flat and A clarinets**
The clarinet is a woodwind played with a single reed attached to a mouthpiece, traditionally with a black body made of grenadilla wood. The standard soprano clarinet is pitched in B-flat or A (the bass clarinet is also in B-flat), and it is held similarly to the double-reed oboe.

**Stravinsky's Ebony Concerto and Three Pieces**
Stravinsky wrote the jazz-influenced Ebony Concerto for clarinetist and bandleader Woody Herman and his band, the Herd. He also wrote Three Pieces for Solo Clarinet as a thank-you to his patron Werner Reinhart.

**Debussy's Première rhapsodie**
A piece for clarinet and piano (later orchestrated) that Debussy wrote as a test piece for the Paris Conservatoire's clarinet competition. He also wrote a Petite pièce for the instrument.

**Mozart's Kegelstatt Trio**
Mozart's trio for clarinet, viola, and piano; its nickname means "skittle alley," from the legend that Mozart composed it while playing skittles (bowling).

**Other orchestral and chamber solos**
The clarinet represents the cat in Prokofiev's Peter and the Wolf and plays a long solo opening the slow third movement of Rachmaninoff's Second Symphony. Francis Poulenc's Clarinet Sonata (1962) was his last completed work, and Bartók's Contrasts is a trio for clarinet, violin, and piano.

**Carmen (Georges Bizet)**
The most famous French opera, about a Gypsy cigarette-factory worker in Seville. Carmen sings the "Habanera," calling love a "rebellious bird" ("L'amour est un oiseau rebelle"), dances a seguidilla after her arrest by Lieutenant Zuniga, seduces the soldier Don José, and is stabbed by him after she turns to the toreador Escamillo.

**The Pearl Fishers and other French operas**
Bizet's The Pearl Fishers contains the "friendship duet" "Au fond du temple saint," in which Nadir and Zurga recall seeing a woman in a temple. Other famous French opera excerpts include the "Flower Duet" sung by Lakmé and her servant by a river in Léo Delibes's Lakmé, and the violin "Méditation" from Jules Massenet's Thaïs.

**War of the Buffoons (Querelle des Bouffons)**
A 1750s Parisian pamphlet war between supporters of France's serious operatic "musical tragedy" (tragédie lyrique) and supporters of Italian comic opera buffa, sparked by performances of Pergolesi's La serva padrona. Jean-Philippe Rameau came under fire as the leading representative of the French style.

**Jean-Baptiste Lully**
The Italian-born court composer to Louis XIV who dominated French Baroque music and pioneered the comédie-ballet with Molière and choreographer Pierre Beauchamp. He is credited with the "French overture" (a slow section with dotted rhythms followed by a fast fugal section), and he died of gangrene after striking his foot with the long staff he used to beat time.

**Jean-Philippe Rameau**
A French Baroque composer and theorist whose 1722 Treatise on Harmony controversially grounded harmony in mathematical and acoustic principles. His operas include the tragédie lyrique Hippolyte et Aricie and the opéra-ballet Les Indes galantes, whose exotic acts include one set among Peruvian Incas and the "Dance of the Peace Pipe."

**François Couperin**
A French Baroque harpsichordist nicknamed "le Grand," who wrote the treatise The Art of Playing the Harpsichord (L'art de toucher le clavecin) and the harpsichord piece "Les Barricades mystérieuses," written in the arpeggiated French "broken style" (style brisé). Maurice Ravel honored him with the six-movement suite Le Tombeau de Couperin.

**Boléro (Maurice Ravel)**
