God floods the earth, sparing only Noah's family and the animals on the ark. A dove returning with an olive branch signals that the waters have receded, and God sends a rainbow as a sign of his covenant never to destroy the earth by flood again.

**Jacob's ladder**
Jacob's dream at Bethel of a ladder (or stairway) reaching from earth to heaven, with angels going up and down it, during which God renews the covenant made with Abraham.

**Abraham's covenant and the birth of Isaac**
God makes a covenant with Abram, renames him Abraham, and promises his descendants the land "from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates." His elderly wife Sarah, renamed from Sarai, miraculously gives birth to Isaac.

**Hagar and Ishmael**
Because Sarah could not conceive, she gave her Egyptian maid Hagar to Abraham, and Hagar bore Ishmael. After Isaac's birth, Hagar and Ishmael are cast out into the wilderness. Ishmael is regarded as an ancestor of the Arabs.

**Sodom and Gomorrah and Lot's wife**
Abraham bargains with God, who agrees to spare Sodom if even ten righteous men can be found there, but they cannot. Two angels rescue Lot's family, and Lot's wife is turned into a pillar of salt for looking back at the destruction. Lot's daughters later bear his sons Moab and Ben-Ammi, ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites.

**Joseph and Potiphar**
Jacob's favorite son, sold into slavery in Egypt by his jealous brothers and bought by Potiphar. In prison he interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker, then interprets Pharaoh's dreams to predict seven years of plenty and seven of famine, rising to power under the Egyptian name Zaphnath-Paaneah. Genesis ends with Joseph forgiving his brothers and dying at age 110.

**Jacob, Laban, Rachel, and Leah**
Jacob works fourteen years for his uncle Laban to marry Laban's two daughters, Leah and Rachel. He also has children by their maids Bilhah and Zilpah, producing the twelve sons who become the tribes of Israel (including Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Dan). Jacob multiplies his own share of Laban's flocks by setting peeled branches of poplar and other trees before the animals.

**Jacob wrestling with the angel**
Jacob wrestles all night with a mysterious divine being, who cannot defeat him and touches the hollow of his thigh, dislocating his hip. Jacob is then renamed Israel.

**The curse of Ham**
After the flood, Noah plants a vineyard and gets drunk. His son Ham sees his nakedness, while his other sons Shem and Japheth cover him, so Noah curses Ham's son Canaan.

**Wife-sister stories with Abimelech of Gerar**
Twice in Genesis a patriarch passes his wife off as his sister to protect himself: Abraham with Sarah before Abimelech, king of Gerar, and later Isaac with Rebekah. Abraham and Abimelech later swear a treaty at Beersheba.

**Melchizedek**
The priest-king of Salem, "priest of the most high God," who blesses Abram with bread and wine after Abram rescues his nephew Lot from a coalition of kings that included the king of Shinar.

**Ali ibn Abi Talib as Muhammad's rightful successor**
The defining belief of Shia Islam is that Ali, the Prophet Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, should have succeeded him as leader of the Muslim community. Sunnis instead accepted Abu Bakr as the first caliph. The name "Shia" comes from "Shi'at Ali," meaning "the party of Ali."

**Twelvers (Ithna Ashari)**
The largest Shia branch, making up the large majority of Shia Muslims and named for its belief in a line of twelve divinely guided Imams beginning with Ali. Twelver Shiism is the state religion of Iran, and Twelvers are also the majority in Iraq.

**Imamate of the Ahl al-Bayt**
Shia Muslims hold that leadership of the community belongs to the Imams, descendants of the Prophet's household (Ahl al-Bayt, "People of the House") through Ali and Fatima. Twelvers regard these Imams as infallible.

**Seveners (Ismailis) and the Fatimid Caliphate**
The Ismailis, or Seveners, split from other Shia over the succession to the sixth Imam, following his son Ismail. An Ismaili dynasty founded the Fatimid Caliphate (909–1171), which ruled North Africa and Egypt and founded Cairo.

**Zaydis (Fivers)**
A Shia branch, centered in Yemen, that follows Zayd ibn Ali as the fifth Imam. Unlike Twelvers, Zaydis do not regard the Imams as infallible and are doctrinally closer to Sunni Islam.

**Occultation and the Mahdi**
Twelvers believe the twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, did not die but went into Occultation (ghayba), a hidden state from which he will return at the end of time as the Mahdi. In Islamic eschatology, the Mahdi aids Jesus (Isa) in defeating the false messiah, ad-Dajjal.

**Ja'fari jurisprudence**
The school of Islamic law followed by Twelver Shia, named for the sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sadiq. Shia doctrine divides religion into Usul al-Din (the "roots," or fundamental beliefs) and Furu al-Din (the "branches," or required practices).

**Hadith of the Cloak**
A tradition in which Muhammad gathered Ali, Fatima, Hasan, and Husayn under his cloak, and a Quranic verse was revealed declaring that God wished to purify the People of the House. Shia Muslims cite it as proof of the special status of the Prophet's family.

**"Ali is the wali of God"**
Many Shia add a phrase to the declaration of faith and the call to prayer affirming that Ali is the wali (friend, guardian, or custodian) of God.

**Mawlid on 17 Rabi' al-Awwal**
Shia Muslims celebrate Mawlid, the Prophet Muhammad's birthday, on the 17th of the month Rabi' al-Awwal, while most Sunnis celebrate it on the 12th.

**Bada'**
A Shia doctrine that God may change a decree in response to human actions or circumstances. Shia scholars distinguish this from any change in God's knowledge.

**Alawites**
A Shia-derived sect (also spelled Alavis), concentrated in Syria and heavily represented among that country's ruling elite under the Assad family.

**Sawm and Ramadan**
Sawm is the Islamic fast and the fourth of the Five Pillars of Islam. During Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, adult Muslims abstain from food, drink, and sexual relations from dawn to sunset; the Qur'an (Al-Baqara 2:183) says fasting "is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you" so that believers may gain piety (taqwa).

**Suhoor and iftar**
The two meals framing each day of the Ramadan fast. Suhoor is eaten before dawn and the fajr prayer, and iftar breaks the fast at sunset, traditionally beginning with dates and water or milk, following the example of Muhammad.

**Eid al-Fitr**
The "Festival of Breaking the Fast," celebrated on the first day of Shawwal when the new moon marks the end of Ramadan. Fasting is forbidden on this day, which is marked by prayers, sweets, and charity.

**Yom Kippur**
The Jewish Day of Atonement, the tenth day of the High Holy Days, on which Jews fast for about 25 hours while praying for repentance. It is the only fast commanded in the Torah (Leviticus 23:26-32) and the only fast that takes place even on Shabbat.

**Tisha B'Av**
The ninth of the Hebrew month of Av, considered the saddest day of the Jewish calendar, observed with a full fast. It mourns the destruction of the First and Second Temples in Jerusalem, among other disasters.

**Sallekhana (Santhara)**
The Jain practice of gradually fasting to death at the end of one's life, undertaken when a person has no remaining responsibilities, as a way to shed karma. The Mauryan emperor Chandragupta Maurya is said to have died this way; it was briefly banned by an Indian court in 2015 before the Supreme Court stayed the ban. Jains also practice lesser fasts, especially during the festival of Paryushana.

**Lent**
The forty-day Christian season of penance before Easter, beginning on Ash Wednesday, which commemorates Jesus fasting for forty days in the desert while being tempted by Satan. Catholics are required to fast and abstain from meat on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and many give up a luxury for the season.

**Baha'i Nineteen-Day Fast**
Baha'is fast from sunrise to sunset during the 19-day month of Ala, the last month of the Baha'i calendar, which immediately precedes the new year festival of Naw-Ruz at the spring equinox.

**Karva Chauth**
A one-day Hindu festival, observed mainly in northern India, on which married women fast from sunrise until moonrise to pray for the safety and long life of their husbands.

**Ta'anit and minor Jewish fasts**
Ta'anit is the Hebrew term for a fast. Besides Yom Kippur and Tisha B'Av, Jews observe minor fasts such as the Fast of Gedaliah (mourning the assassination of the governor Gedaliah), Asara B'Tevet, the Seventeenth of Tammuz, the Fast of Esther the day before Purim, and the Fast of the Firstborn on the day before Passover.

**Fidya and kaffara**
Compensations in Islam for fasts missed during Ramadan. Fidya is paid by those who cannot fast at all, such as the chronically ill or elderly, while kaffara is the penalty for deliberately breaking a Ramadan fast, such as by intercourse, requiring 60 consecutive days of fasting or feeding 60 poor people.

**The Buddha and Sujata**
Before his enlightenment, Siddhartha Gautama practiced extreme fasting until he nearly died, an episode depicted in famous emaciated "Fasting Buddha" sculptures from Gandhara. He abandoned extreme asceticism for the Middle Way after accepting a bowl of milk-rice from a village woman named Sujata.

**Voluntary fasts in Islam and the "shield" hadith**
A hadith narrated by Abu Hurayrah and collected by al-Bukhari calls fasting a "shield" against sin and hellfire. Muslims are encouraged to fast voluntarily on days such as Ashura and the Day of Arafah, and for six days in Shawwal, the month after Ramadan.

**Black fast**
An especially strict form of fasting, abstaining from all food (and in some forms all drink) for a period, practiced by some Pentecostals and historically in Christian penitential traditions. A related practice is the "Daniel fast," limited to vegetables and pulses, modeled on the Book of Daniel.

**Mormon fast Sunday**
Members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints fast on the first Sunday of each month and donate the money they would have spent on those meals as a "fast offering" to help the poor.

**Yakub (Dr. Yakub)**
The central figure of Nation of Islam mythology: a "big-headed" Black scientist who, on the island of Patmos, used selective breeding ("grafting") to create the white race, described as a race of devils. This story appears in nearly every question about the group.

**Malcolm X**
The Nation of Islam's most famous minister, who led Temple No. 7 in Harlem and became its national spokesman. He broke with the group in 1964, converted to Sunni Islam, and was assassinated in 1965 by members of the Nation. His life is told in The Autobiography of Malcolm X, ghostwritten by Alex Haley, in which he describes teaching himself in prison by copying the dictionary.

**Wallace D. Fard (W. Fard Muhammad)**
The founder of the Nation of Islam, a door-to-door silk peddler who started the movement in Detroit in 1930. Followers regard him as the Messiah and God in person (Allah incarnate); he mysteriously disappeared in 1934.

**Elijah Muhammad**
The Nation's leader from 1934 until his death in 1975, who built it into a national movement. He wrote "Message to the Blackman in America," and he renamed the boxer Cassius Clay as Muhammad Ali.

**Louis Farrakhan**
The current leader of the Nation of Islam. He rebuilt the organization in 1978 after Warith Deen Mohammed moved the original group toward Sunni Islam, revived The Final Call newspaper, and organized the 1995 Million Man March in Washington.

**Mother Plane (Mother Wheel)**
A giant wheel-shaped spacecraft that Nation of Islam teaching identifies with the "wheel" seen in the Book of Ezekiel. It is said to have been built in Japan of Nippon steel at a cost of fifteen billion dollars, and to carry bombs that were used to raise the Earth's mountains.

**The Final Call**
The Nation of Islam's official newspaper, revived by Louis Farrakhan in 1979. It takes its name from an early publication of Elijah Muhammad.

**Rejection of "slave names"**
Members give up their surnames as names imposed by slaveowners. They often take the letter "X" to represent their unknown African name (as in Malcolm X) or receive Muslim names.

**Temple No. 7**
The Nation of Islam's mosque in Harlem, New York, led by Malcolm X. Clarence 13X, a member there, broke away in 1964 to found the Five Percenters.

**Five Percenters (85-10-5 teaching)**
The teaching that 85% of people are ignorant masses, 10% are rich "slave-makers" who deceive them, and 5% are "poor righteous teachers" who know the truth. The Five-Percent Nation, founded by Clarence 13X, takes its name from this doctrine.

**Tribe of Shabazz**
In Nation of Islam teaching, the original Black tribe from which humanity descends. According to the group, they settled in Africa and declined after the creation of the white race.

**Savior's Day**
The Nation's main annual holiday, held on February 26 to celebrate the birth of founder Wallace Fard Muhammad.

**Warith Deen Mohammed**
Elijah Muhammad's son, who took over in 1975 and moved most of the movement toward orthodox Sunni Islam, renaming it the World Community of Al-Islam in the West (later the American Muslim Mission). Farrakhan's 1978 schism re-established the Nation of Islam with its original teachings.

**Bean pies**
A dessert made from navy beans that members sell to raise money. It reflects Elijah Muhammad's dietary teachings.

**The Hate That Hate Produced**
A 1959 television documentary by Mike Wallace and Louis Lomax that first brought the Nation of Islam and Malcolm X to national attention.

**Temple Mount (Mount Moriah) and the Binding of Isaac**
The hill in Jerusalem's Old City traditionally identified with Mount Moriah, where Abraham nearly sacrificed his son Isaac before an angel stopped him and a ram appeared as a substitute (Genesis 22). In Islamic tradition the son is usually identified as Ishmael. Both Jewish Temples were built here, and today it holds the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa Mosque.

**Western Wall (Wailing Wall or Kotel)**
A surviving retaining wall built during King Herod's expansion of the Second Temple complex, and the holiest place where Jews may pray today. Visitors push written prayers into its crevices; these notes are collected twice a year, including before Rosh Hashanah, and buried on the Mount of Olives. A tunnel runs along its hidden sections, and the area called Robinson's Arch has been set aside for egalitarian and women's prayer.

**Dome of the Rock and the Foundation Stone**
A golden-domed Islamic shrine on the Temple Mount, built in the late 7th century under the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik. It covers the Foundation Stone, a rock that Jewish tradition places at the site of the Holy of Holies and from which the world was created. Beneath the rock is a cave called the Well of Souls.

**Al-Aqsa Mosque and the Night Journey**
Al-Aqsa, "the farthest mosque," stands on the Temple Mount and is the third-holiest site in Islam after Mecca and Medina. In the Isra and Mi'raj (Night Journey), Muhammad rode the winged steed Buraq from Mecca to this "farthest mosque" in one night and then ascended to Heaven. Worshippers perform ablutions (wudu) at a nearby fountain called al-Kas ("the Cup").

**First qibla**
The qibla is the direction Muslims face during prayer. Before it was changed to face the Kaaba in Mecca, early Muslims prayed toward Jerusalem, which Muslims also call al-Quds ("the Holy").

**First Temple (Solomon's Temple)**
The Temple built by King Solomon on Mount Moriah to house the Ark of the Covenant in its innermost room, the Holy of Holies. His father David was forbidden to build it because he was a man of war who had shed blood, and King Hiram of Tyre supplied wood for it. It was destroyed by the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II in 587/586 BCE, ending the Kingdom of Judah.

**Second Temple and its destruction by Titus**
Built after the Babylonian exile under Zerubbabel and greatly expanded by Herod the Great, it was destroyed by the Roman general Titus in 70 CE during the First Jewish-Roman War. The Arch of Titus in Rome commemorates this sack of Jerusalem and depicts Romans carrying off the Temple menorah.

**"Next Year in Jerusalem"**
In Hebrew, "L'shanah haba'ah b'Yerushalayim," a phrase expressing the hope of return to Jerusalem. It is traditionally said or sung at the end of the Passover seder and at the end of the Ne'ilah service that closes Yom Kippur.

**Tisha B'Av**
The Ninth of Av, a Jewish fast day that mourns the destruction of both the First and Second Temples in Jerusalem, as well as other tragedies in Jewish history.

**Church of the Holy Sepulchre and Calvary**
Jesus was crucified on the hill of Calvary (Golgotha) outside the city walls after being sentenced by Pontius Pilate and mocked as "King of the Jews." The Church of the Holy Sepulchre is traditionally believed to contain both the crucifixion site and his tomb. Jerusalem also contains the Cenacle, the traditional "Upper Room" of the Last Supper remembered on Maundy Thursday.

**Cleansing of the Temple**
In the Gospels, Jesus enters Jerusalem on Palm Sunday, then makes a whip of cords, overturns the tables of the money changers in the Temple, and calls it a "house of prayer." He also weeps over the city and prophesies that its enemies will leave "not one stone upon another."

**Threshing floor of Araunah**
In 2 Samuel 24, after a plague sent as punishment for his census, King David bought the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite on Mount Moriah and built an altar there. This site later became the location of Solomon's Temple.

**Hanukkah and Judas Maccabeus**
After the Maccabean revolt against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV, Judas Maccabeus recaptured and cleansed the Temple in Jerusalem. Hanukkah celebrates its rededication and the miracle of a single jug of oil that kept the menorah lit for eight days.

**"Jerusalem of Gold"**
In Hebrew, "Yerushalayim Shel Zahav," a famous 1967 Israeli song by Naomi Shemer. Its title comes from a Talmudic story in which Rabbi Akiva gives his wife a piece of jewelry called a "Jerusalem of gold," and the lyrics call the singer a "lyre for all your songs."

**Peter and John at the Temple and Paul's arrest**
In Acts 3, Peter and John say "silver and gold have I none" before healing a man lame from birth at the Temple's Beautiful Gate. In Acts 21, Paul is seized in the Temple and arrested in Jerusalem after paying the expenses for four men completing a vow, which included having their heads shaved.

**Angra Mainyu (Ahriman)**
The "Destructive Spirit," the evil adversary of Ahura Mazda in Zoroastrianism and the cause of all suffering, death, and grief. The cosmic struggle between the two, which good is destined to win, is the central theme of the religion.

**"Wise Lord"**
The literal meaning of Ahura Mazda's name, the supreme creator god of Zoroastrianism. In later Middle Persian he is called Ohrmazd or Ormazd, and Greek writers called him Oromasdes.

**Amesha Spentas**
The "Bounteous Immortals," six divine beings or "divine sparks" that emanate from Ahura Mazda and help him in his work, each tied to an aspect of creation. They include Vohu Manah ("Good Mind"), Asha ("Truth"), and Spenta Armaiti ("Devotion"), and Ahura Mazda is sometimes counted as their leader or as a seventh.

**Avesta**
The sacred scripture of Zoroastrianism, written in the Avestan language, which sings the praises of Ahura Mazda. Its oldest part is the Gathas, hymns attributed to the prophet Zoroaster (Zarathustra) himself; it also includes the Vendidad, a code against evil spirits, and commentaries called the Zend.

**Zurvan**
The god of infinite time in Zurvanism, a later variant of Zoroastrianism. In this tradition, Ahura Mazda and Angra Mainyu are twin sons of Zurvan rather than Ahura Mazda being the uncreated creator.

**Faravahar (winged disc)**
The ancient symbol of a winged disc with a human figure, carved on Achaemenid monuments such as those at Persepolis. It has traditionally been associated with Ahura Mazda and is today the best-known symbol of Zoroastrianism.

**Atar and Azhi Dahaka**
Atar, the divine personification of fire, is described as the son of Ahura Mazda. He fought the three-headed dragon Azhi Dahaka, a monstrous servant of evil.

**Ahuras versus daevas**
Zoroastrianism contrasts the ahuras ("lords"), headed by Ahura Mazda, with the daevas, who are demonized as false gods and evil spirits. In the Indian Vedic tradition the roles are reversed: the devas are gods and the asuras are demonic.

**Sraosha**
The divinity of "obedience" or "hearing" who serves as Ahura Mazda's messenger and guardian of prayer. He is said to live in a house with a thousand pillars and must be present at every ritual.

**Spenta Mainyu**
The "Bounteous" or "Holy Spirit," the creative force of goodness through which Ahura Mazda acts and which opposes Angra Mainyu. In later tradition it is often identified with Ahura Mazda himself.

**Achaemenid empty chariot**
Achaemenid Persian armies, as described by Herodotus for Xerxes's invasion of Greece, brought along a sacred empty chariot drawn by white horses, reserved for the supreme god. Achaemenid kings such as Darius I credited their rule to Ahura Mazda in their inscriptions.

**Fire temples**
The Zoroastrian places of worship, where a sacred fire, a symbol of Ahura Mazda's truth and purity, is kept burning perpetually. Zoroastrians pray facing a source of light or fire.

**Afrinagan**
A Zoroastrian liturgy of blessing and thanksgiving in which offerings such as wine, fruit, and flowers are presented. It is performed in honor of Ahura Mazda and the righteous dead.

**Ashi and Armaiti**
In the Avesta, the goddess Ashi, who brings reward and fortune, is described as the daughter of Ahura Mazda and Spenta Armaiti. Comparisons with Vedic religion are also used to link Ahura Mazda with Indo-European sky-father gods.

**Four Questions ("Mah Nishtanah")**
A set of questions traditionally asked by the youngest child at the seder, beginning "Mah nishtanah ha-laylah ha-zeh?" ("Why is this night different from all other nights?"). The questions ask why only matzah and bitter herbs are eaten, why food is dipped twice, and why everyone reclines, and the rest of the seder answers them by telling the Exodus story. This is the most common clue for the holiday.

**Matzah**
Flat, unleavened bread eaten throughout Passover. It recalls that the Israelites fled Egypt so quickly that their dough had no time to rise, and it is also called the "bread of affliction."

**Seder**
The ritual feast held on the first night of Passover (and on the second night outside Israel), whose name means "order." It follows 15 set steps, including Urchatz (a hand-washing without a blessing), Yachatz (breaking the middle matzah), and Rachtzah (a hand-washing with a blessing before eating matzah), and includes the Hallel psalms (Psalms 113–118). It traditionally ends with the declaration "Next year in Jerusalem!"

**Haggadah**
The text read at the seder, which tells the story of the Exodus and gives the order of rituals, prayers, and songs. It includes the passage of the Four Sons (wise, wicked, simple, and one who does not know how to ask). The free Maxwell House Haggadah, first given out by the coffee company in the 1930s, became one of the most widely used editions in America, and feminist versions such as The Women's Haggadah by E. M. Broner and Naomi Nimrod have also appeared.

**Chametz**
Leavened grain products, which Jews may not eat or own during Passover. Before the holiday, households clean thoroughly and search for chametz (bedikat chametz), then nullify it by declaration (bittul), burn it (biur), or sell it to a non-Jew (mechirah).

**"Dayenu"**
A joyful seder song whose title means "it would have been enough for us." Its 15 stanzas list God's gifts to the Israelites, such as freeing them from Egypt, splitting the sea, and giving the Torah, saying after each one that it alone would have been enough.

**"Chad Gadya"**
An Aramaic song sung at the end of the seder, meaning "one little goat," about a goat that a father bought for two zuzim. In a chain, the goat is eaten by a cat, the cat is bitten by a dog, and so on through a stick, fire, water, an ox, a slaughterer, and the Angel of Death, until God smites the Angel of Death. It is often read as an allegory of the nations that conquered and oppressed Israel.

**Afikoman**
Half of the middle matzah, broken off during the Yachatz step and hidden. Children search for it (or "steal" it) and often bargain for a reward to return it, since it must be eaten as the final food of the meal.

**Ten drops of wine for the Ten Plagues**
As each of the Ten Plagues of Egypt is recited, participants remove a drop of wine from their cup, often with a little finger, and place it on their plate. This shows that joy is lessened by the suffering of the Egyptians, and the drops are also spilled for the abbreviations Rabbi Judah made of the plagues ("D'tzach, Adash, B'achav").

**Cup of Elijah and the four cups of wine**
Each adult drinks four cups of wine during the seder. A fifth cup is poured for the prophet Elijah, who is expected to announce the coming of the Messiah, and the front door is opened to welcome him.

**Maror and charoset**
Maror is a bitter herb, often horseradish, eaten to recall the bitterness of slavery. Charoset is a sweet paste of chopped apples, nuts, and wine that represents the mortar the Israelites used to build for Pharaoh. They are eaten together between pieces of matzah in "Hillel's sandwich" (korech).

**Seder plate**
The ceremonial plate that holds the symbolic foods of the seder: maror, charoset, karpas (a green vegetable dipped in salt water), the zeroa (a roasted lamb shank bone recalling the Passover sacrifice), and the beitzah (a roasted egg); the shank bone and egg are displayed but not eaten. A newer custom, popularized by Susannah Heschel, adds an orange to symbolize the inclusion of women and LGBT people in Jewish life.

**15th of Nisan and the Angel of Death**
Passover begins on the 15th of the Hebrew month of Nisan and lasts seven days in Israel and eight days elsewhere. Its name comes from the Tenth Plague, when the Angel of Death "passed over" the Israelite homes marked with lamb's blood and killed only Egypt's firstborn. The original Passover lamb sacrifice (korban Pesach) is still performed today only by the Samaritans on Mount Gerizim.

**Counting of the Omer**
A count of 49 days (seven weeks) that begins on the second day of Passover and leads up to the holiday of Shavuot on the 50th day. Much of it is observed as a period of partial mourning.

**Kitniyot**
Legumes, rice, corn, and similar foods, which Ashkenazi Jews traditionally avoid during Passover but Sephardic Jews eat. North African (Maghrebi) Jews also mark the end of the holiday with the Mimouna celebration, where they eat a thin pancake called mufleta.

**Zazen**
"Seated meditation," the central practice of Zen Buddhism. The 13th-century Japanese monk Dogen, founder of the Soto school, championed shikantaza ("just sitting"), a form of zazen with no object of focus. Practitioners often bow with palms pressed together (gassho) before sitting on a round cushion called a zafu.

**Vipassana**
"Insight" meditation, which grew out of the Theravada tradition and centers on directly observing the three marks of existence: impermanence, suffering, and non-self. Its method is taught in the Satipatthana Sutta (the Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness), and S. N. Goenka developed ten-day vipassana courses that were famously given to prisoners at Delhi's Tihar Jail.

**Buddha under the Bodhi tree**
Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment while meditating under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya, India. According to legend, his first experience of meditation came as a child, while he sat in the shade of a rose-apple (jambu) tree.

**Dhyana (jhana)**
The Sanskrit (and Pali) term for states of deep meditative absorption, which gave its name to Chan and Zen Buddhism. Buddhist texts describe four jhanas followed by four formless attainments (samapattis), and achieving samadhi (concentration) through dhyana is "right concentration," the final step of the Noble Eightfold Path.

**Koans**
Paradoxical riddles or stories, such as "What is the sound of one hand clapping?", that Zen teachers give students to contemplate during meditation. They are meant to break down ordinary logical thinking and trigger sudden insight, and they are especially used in the Rinzai school.

**Mantras and "Om"**
Sacred syllables or phrases that are repeated during meditation to focus the mind, with "Om" the best-known example. Repetition of mantras (japa) is often counted on a string of prayer beads called a japa mala.

**Pure Land nianfo**
The central practice of Pure Land Buddhism is nianfo (nembutsu in Japanese), mindful recitation of the name of Amitabha Buddha. In Japan it takes the form of chanting "Namu Amida Butsu" in the hope of rebirth in Amitabha's Pure Land.

**Anapanasati and sati**
Anapanasati is "mindfulness of breathing," the practice of focusing attention on the in-breath and out-breath, which the Buddha himself taught. Sati, or "mindfulness," is the attentive awareness of the present moment that such meditation cultivates.

**Visuddhimagga and kasinas**
The "Path of Purification," a 5th-century Theravada manual by Buddhaghosa that lists forty subjects of meditation (kammatthana) as a path to dhyana. They include ten kasinas, devices such as colored discs or elements like earth and fire used as focus objects, and ten kinds of "foulness," the stages of a decaying corpse, such as worm-infested or hacked apart.

**Samatha**
"Calm abiding," the form of Buddhist meditation focused on calming and concentrating the mind, often by fixing it on a single object. It is traditionally paired with vipassana, so that concentration supports insight.

**Bodhidharma**
The semi-legendary Indian monk who, according to tradition, brought Chan (Zen) Buddhism to China in the 5th or 6th century. He is said to have meditated facing a cave wall near the Shaolin Monastery for nine years, which made him the model for seated Zen meditation.

**Loving-kindness (metta) and the brahmaviharas**
Metta, or loving-kindness, meditation cultivates goodwill toward oneself and all beings, and the American teacher Sharon Salzberg helped popularize it in the West. It is one of the four brahmaviharas ("divine abodes"), along with compassion, empathetic joy, and equanimity.

**Five hindrances**
The five mental states that Buddhism says block meditation: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and worry, and doubt. Overcoming them is needed to enter the jhanas.

**Phowa**
A Tibetan Buddhist meditation practice for the moment of death, in which one's consciousness is transferred out through the crown of the head to a pure land or a higher rebirth.

**Lotus position and the dhyana mudra**
The lotus position (padmasana) is the cross-legged sitting posture, with each foot resting on the opposite thigh, in which the Buddha is often shown meditating. In the dhyana mudra, the hands rest in the lap with the right hand on the left and the thumbs touching, symbolizing meditation.

**Sukkah (booths)**
The temporary hut that gives Sukkot its English names, the "Festival of Booths" or "Feast of Tabernacles." Observant Jews eat, and often sleep, in the sukkah throughout the holiday. It is traditionally built with at least three walls.

**Four Species**
The four plants held and waved together on Sukkot: the etrog (citron), the lulav (a palm frond), hadassim (myrtle branches), and aravot (willow branches). The palm, myrtle, and willow are bound together into a bundle that is also called the lulav.

**Etrog and lulav**
The two best-known items among the Four Species. The etrog is a lemon-like citron fruit, and the lulav is a closed date-palm frond bound together with the myrtle and willow. Worshippers hold them together during blessings and prayers.

**Na'anuim (shaking the Four Species)**
The ritual waving of the Four Species in six directions: the four directions of the compass, then up and down. It symbolizes God's presence everywhere.

**Ushpizin**
Aramaic for "guests"; the seven "exalted guests" ceremonially invited into the sukkah, one on each night of the festival. They are traditionally Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Joseph, and David.

**S'chach**
The roof covering of the sukkah, made of cut plant material such as palm leaves, branches, or bamboo. It must give more shade than sun, yet be sparse enough to see the stars through it.

**Wandering in the desert**
Sukkot began as a harvest festival (the "Feast of Ingathering") and was reinterpreted to commemorate the Israelites' forty years of wandering in the wilderness after the Exodus, when they lived in temporary shelters. Some traditions say the sukkah also recalls the protective "Clouds of Glory," sometimes represented by white sheets.

**15th of Tishrei**
The start date of Sukkot in the Hebrew calendar, five days after Yom Kippur. It is one of the three pilgrimage festivals, when Jews traditionally went up to the Temple in Jerusalem.

**Hoshana Rabbah**
"The Great Supplication," the seventh day of Sukkot. Worshippers circle the synagogue seven times reciting the hoshanot prayers (whose refrain is "Hosha na," "save us") and beat willow branches on the ground.

**Shemini Atzeret**
The "Eighth Day of Assembly," the holiday immediately following Sukkot. On it the Geshem prayer for rain is first recited. In many communities it is combined with or followed by Simchat Torah.

**Hakhel**
A biblical ceremony held on Sukkot once every seven years, after the sabbatical year. The king publicly read from the Torah (Deuteronomy) to the assembled people at the Temple.

**Samaritan pilgrimage to Mount Gerizim**
The Samaritans celebrate Sukkot as one of their three annual pilgrimage festivals to their holy mountain, Mount Gerizim. Because it falls in the autumn, it is the last of these pilgrimages in the calendar year.

**Joseph Smith**
The founder and first prophet of Mormonism, who organized the Church of Christ (later the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints) in New York in 1830. He claimed to have translated the Book of Mormon from ancient records, and he is the most common giveaway in questions on the religion.

**Golden plates and the angel Moroni**
Smith said the angel Moroni led him to a set of golden plates buried in a hill (Cumorah) near Palmyra in upstate New York. The plates were engraved in a language called "reformed Egyptian." A gold statue of Moroni blowing a trumpet tops many LDS temples and serves as a symbol of the faith.

**Book of Mormon: Lehi, Nephites, and Lamanites**
The central scripture of the faith. It tells how the prophet Lehi and his family fled Jerusalem around 600 BCE, guided by a compass-like "ball of curious workmanship" called the Liahona, and sailed to the Americas in a ship built at a place called Bountiful. His descendants split into the warring Nephites and Lamanites, and the book is named after Mormon, a Nephite prophet who abridged the records before the Nephites were wiped out in the final battle at Cumorah.

**Brigham Young and Utah**
The second president of the church, who led the Mormon pioneers west to the Salt Lake Valley in 1847 after Smith's death. Members called the territory they settled Deseret, and the church is headquartered in Salt Lake City, home of the famous Tabernacle Choir. Later leaders included John Taylor and Wilford Woodruff.

**Celestial, Terrestrial, and Telestial Kingdoms**
The three "kingdoms of glory" in the Mormon Plan of Salvation, into which nearly all people will be sorted after death. The highest, the Celestial Kingdom, can lead to exaltation, in which the faithful become like God, a belief summarized as "as man is, God once was; as God is, man may become." Only the "sons of perdition" are cast into Outer Darkness, separated from God forever.

**Melchizedek and Aaronic priesthoods**
The two orders of the LDS priesthood, open to worthy male members. Boys enter the lesser Aaronic priesthood at age 12, holding the offices of deacon, teacher, and priest. The higher Melchizedek priesthood includes elders, high priests, and Seventies, and the church is led by the First Presidency and the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, who are sustained as "prophets, seers, and revelators."

**Word of Wisdom**
The church's health code, revealed to Smith in 1833 and found in the Doctrine and Covenants. It forbids alcohol, tobacco, and "hot drinks," interpreted as coffee and tea, and following it is required to enter a temple.

**Pearl of Great Price and Doctrine and Covenants**
Along with the Bible and the Book of Mormon, these make up the LDS "standard works." The Doctrine and Covenants collects Smith's revelations. The Pearl of Great Price includes the Book of Abraham, which describes Kolob as the star nearest God's throne, and the thirteen Articles of Faith, which come from Smith's letter to the newspaper editor John Wentworth.

**Three Witnesses and Eight Witnesses**
Two groups of Smith's early followers who signed testimonies, printed in the Book of Mormon, stating that they had seen the golden plates. The Three Witnesses claimed that an angel showed them the plates.

**Urim and Thummim and seer stones**
Smith said he translated the golden plates with the help of the Urim and Thummim, a pair of seer stones he said were buried with the plates, and with other seer stones. The name comes from the objects used for divination by Israelite priests in the Hebrew Bible.

**Death of Joseph Smith at Carthage**
In 1844, Joseph Smith and his brother Hyrum were killed by a mob that stormed the jail in Carthage, Illinois, where they were being held. The succession crisis that followed was won by Brigham Young, though splinter groups such as the Strangites formed.

**Missouri Executive Order 44 and Nauvoo**
In 1838, Missouri governor Lilburn Boggs issued Executive Order 44, the "Extermination Order," which ordered Mormons to be driven from the state or killed. The Mormons then settled in Nauvoo, Illinois, which became their headquarters until their move west.

**Temple endowment, garments, and sealing**
Sacred temple ceremonies closed to outsiders. In the endowment, members make covenants and receive temple garments, sacred undergarments worn for life, and in sealing, couples and families are bound together for eternity. Members can also perform these ordinances by proxy for the dead, which is why the church runs the genealogy website FamilySearch and stores records in the Granite Mountain vault in Utah.

**Missions**
Young members, especially men, are expected to serve full-time proselytizing missions of about two years, typically between the ages of 18 and 25. Missionaries jokingly call the halfway point "hump day" and the final day "trunk day."

**End of polygamy**
Plural marriage was practiced openly by early Mormons in Utah, and federal laws such as the Poland Act and the Edmunds Act were used to prosecute church leaders. President Wilford Woodruff issued the 1890 Manifesto ending official approval of new plural marriages, and Utah became a state in 1896 with a constitutional ban on polygamy.

**Bodhi tree**
The fig tree at Bodh Gaya in northeastern India under which Siddhartha meditated until he attained enlightenment and became the Buddha ("awakened one"). Accounts say he then spent seven weeks (49 days) in its vicinity; during one of those weeks a storm arose and the serpent king Mucalinda coiled around him and spread his hoods over him as shelter.

**Four Sights**
On trips outside the palace where he had been shielded from all suffering, Prince Siddhartha saw an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and finally a wandering ascetic (holy man). The first three revealed the reality of suffering, and the fourth inspired him to renounce his royal life to seek a way out of it.

**Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path**
The core of the Buddha's teaching: life is marked by suffering (dukkha), suffering arises from craving, suffering can end (nirvana), and the way to end it is the Noble Eightfold Path. The path consists of right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and concentration.

**Deer Park at Sarnath**
The park near Benares (Varanasi) where the Buddha gave his first sermon after his enlightenment to five former ascetic companions, an event called "setting in motion the wheel of the Dharma." In it he taught the Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Path, and the Middle Way.

**Queen Maya's white elephant dream**
The night the Buddha was conceived, his mother, Queen Maha Maya, dreamed that a white elephant with six tusks entered her right side. This was interpreted as a sign that she would bear a great being.

**Mara and the earth-touching mudra**
As Siddhartha sat beneath the Bodhi tree, the demon Mara attacked him with armies and sent his daughters to tempt him. When Mara challenged his right to the seat of enlightenment, Siddhartha touched the ground with his right hand and the earth bore witness for him; this bhumisparsha ("earth-touching") mudra is the most common gesture in Buddha images.

**Middle Way**
The Buddha's teaching that the path to liberation lies between the extremes of luxurious indulgence, which he knew as a prince, and harsh self-mortification, which he practiced for six years as an ascetic. He realized this after nearly starving himself to death.

**Siddhartha Gautama, prince of the Shakyas**
The Buddha's birth name. He was a Kshatriya prince of the Shakya clan, hence the title Shakyamuni ("sage of the Shakyas"), born at Lumbini and raised in Kapilavastu by his father, King Suddhodana. The seer Asita predicted he would become either a universal monarch or a great spiritual teacher, so his father kept him confined within the palace.

**The Great Departure: Rahula, Kanthaka, and Channa**
When his son was born, Siddhartha named him Rahula ("fetter"), seeing the child as a new bond tying him to worldly life. He soon left his wife Yashodhara and son at night, riding his horse Kanthaka with his charioteer Channa, to become a wandering ascetic.

**Cunda's last meal and Sujata's milk-rice**
Just before his enlightenment, the young woman Sujata offered the starving Siddhartha a bowl of milk-rice (rice pudding), which ended his period of extreme fasting. Decades later, his final meal came from the blacksmith Cunda (Kunda), either spoiled pork or mushrooms; it made him gravely ill, and he soon died and entered parinirvana at Kushinagar.

**Flower Sermon**
A story in which the Buddha, instead of speaking, silently held up a flower, and only his disciple Mahakashyapa understood and smiled. It is regarded as the origin of Zen (Chan) Buddhism's tradition of wordless, mind-to-mind transmission.

**Bamiyan Buddhas and other famous statues**
Two giant Buddhas carved into a cliff in Afghanistan's Bamiyan valley, the larger about 180 feet tall, were dynamited by the Taliban in 2001. Other famous examples include the bronze Daibutsu ("Great Buddha") at Todai-ji in Nara, Japan; the rock-cut statues of China's Yungang Grottoes and the Mogao Caves ("Caves of the Thousand Buddhas"); a Buddha head enclosed in tree roots at Wat Mahathat (the Temple of the Great Relic) in Ayutthaya, Thailand; and a monolithic statue in Hussain Sagar lake in Hyderabad.

**Gandharan art, relics, and stupas**
The gold Bimaran casket, a reliquary from Gandhara in Afghanistan, shows the Buddha in a Greco-Roman influenced style and is among the earliest images of him. Legend says the Buddha showed the shape of a stupa (relic mound) by turning his alms bowl upside down; the Temple of the Tooth in Kandy, Sri Lanka, houses his tooth relic, and symbols of his footprints are often marked with wheels.

**Parable of the poisoned arrow and the 84th problem**
The Buddha compared someone who demands answers to metaphysical questions before practicing to a man shot by a poisoned arrow who will not let the surgeon remove it until he learns who shot it. In another story, he told a farmer that everyone has 83 problems he cannot fix, but he can help with the 84th: the wish to have no problems.

**Angulimala**
A brigand who killed people and wore their fingers as a garland, supposedly to collect a thousand fingers as a fee demanded by his teacher. The Buddha calmly confronted and converted him, and Angulimala became a monk; the Buddha similarly tamed the demon Alavaka.

**Yoga Sutras of Patanjali**
The foundational text of classical yoga: a collection of 196 short aphorisms (sutras) attributed to the sage Patanjali, compiled roughly 2,000 years ago. It defines yoga as the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind and lays out the "eight limbs" of practice.

**Eight limbs (ashtanga)**
Patanjali's eightfold path. It begins with the yamas (ethical restraints) and niyamas (observances), moves through asana (posture), pranayama (breath control), pratyahara (withdrawal of the senses), dharana (concentration), and dhyana (meditation), and culminates in samadhi, a state of absorbed meditative union.

**Bhakti, karma, and jnana yoga**
The three classical paths to moksha (liberation), set out in the Bhagavad Gita. Bhakti yoga is the path of loving devotion to a personal deity (central to Vaishnavism and Shaivism), karma yoga is the path of selfless action, and jnana yoga is the path of knowledge or wisdom.

**Hatha yoga and asanas**
The physical branch of yoga, built on asanas (bodily postures) such as Cobra, Camel, and Downward Dog, together with breathing techniques. It is the basis of most yoga practiced as exercise in the West.

**Swami Vivekananda and Raja Yoga**
The Indian monk who introduced yoga and Vedanta to the West, most famously at the 1893 Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago. His 1896 book Raja Yoga translated and commented on Patanjali's Yoga Sutras. "Raja" ("royal") yoga has become a common name for Patanjali's meditative system.

**Pranayama**
Regulated breathing exercises, one of the eight limbs, meant to control and extend prana, the vital life force that flows through the body.

**Surya Namaskar (Sun Salutation)**
A flowing sequence of asanas performed as a single routine. It is a staple of modern exercise-oriented yoga, though it is not part of the ancient tradition.

**Samkhya, purusha, and prakriti**
The Yoga school is one of the six orthodox darshanas (schools) of Hindu philosophy and draws on the closely related Samkhya school's dualism. Its goal is to free purusha (pure witness-consciousness) from its entanglement with prakriti (matter or nature).

**Kundalini**
A coiled serpent energy believed to rest at the base of the spine, regarded as a form of the goddess Shakti. Kundalini and laya yoga aim to awaken it, using techniques such as mula bandha (the "root lock," a contraction of the pelvic floor), so that it rises through the body's chakras.

**Tirumalai Krishnamacharya and vinyasa**
The 20th-century Indian teacher often called the father of modern yoga, who revived hatha yoga. He developed vinyasa, a style that links asanas through breath-coordinated movement, and trained influential teachers such as B.K.S. Iyengar and K. Pattabhi Jois.

**Yogacara**
A school of Mahayana Buddhist philosophy founded by the half-brothers Asanga and Vasubandhu, whose name means "practice of yoga." It taught that reality is "consciousness-only" and was the main rival of Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka school.

**"Union" and the word "yoke"**
"Yoga" comes from the Sanskrit root yuj, "to join" or "to yoke," and is often interpreted as union with the divine or the universal self. It shares an Indo-European root with the English "yoke," the wooden bar that harnesses oxen.

**Katha Upanishad**
One of the earliest texts to describe yoga. In it, the god of death Yama teaches the boy Nachiketa that yoga, the steady control of the senses, is the path to realizing the atman (the true self).

**Ra Ma Institute and Guru Jagat**
A Kundalini yoga school founded by the teacher Guru Jagat, which drew controversy and accusations of cult-like behavior.

**Qingming Festival (Tomb-Sweeping Day)**
A Chinese spring festival held about two weeks after the spring equinox (usually April 4–6). Families visit the graves of their ancestors to clean and sweep them, leave food and flowers, and make offerings, which makes it the most common holiday clue for ancestors.

**Filial piety**
The Confucian virtue of respect and devotion toward one's parents and elders (xiao in Chinese). It extends beyond death, so veneration of deceased forebears is one of its central expressions, and questions often end with it as a giveaway.

**Burning fake money ("hell money")**
In Chinese ceremonies, families burn imitation paper banknotes, also called joss paper or spirit money, as offerings. The burned money is believed to pass to the dead for their use in the afterlife, and it is commonly burned during Qingming.

**Green mugwort dumplings**
Green dumplings colored and flavored with Chinese mugwort (often called qingtuan) that are traditionally eaten around the Qingming Festival, the holiday dedicated to honoring the dead of one's family.

**Ancestral tablets (shinwi)**
Dedicated wooden tablets bearing the names of deceased family members, kept at household shrines or in lineage halls in Chinese and Korean tradition. Shinwi is the Korean term for these spirit tablets, which serve as the focus of offerings.

**Jesa**
A Korean ritual of memorial offerings to deceased forebears, typically performed on death anniversaries and major holidays. Food is arranged on a table before the spirit tablets, and family members bow to honor the dead.

**Shi (ritual personator)**
In ancient Chinese religious practice, especially during the Zhou dynasty, a living person called a shi (often a grandson of the deceased) acted as a medium who impersonated the dead during sacrificial rites, receiving food and drink on their behalf.

**Ex illa die**
A 1715 papal bull issued by Pope Clement XI. Its provisions prohibited Chinese Catholic converts from taking part in rites honoring their deceased forebears and Confucius, in an attempt to settle the Chinese Rites Controversy.

**Chinese Rites Controversy**
A dispute within the Catholic Church in the 17th and 18th centuries over whether Chinese converts could keep performing traditional rites for their dead relatives and for Confucius. Jesuit missionaries argued the rites were civil rather than religious, but the papacy eventually banned them.

**Non-divine status**
Questions stress that the figures being honored are not gods but deceased human family members. Their veneration centers on maintaining a relationship with the dead rather than on worshipping deities.

**Home shrines and family altars**
Household altars where tablets for deceased relatives are kept and where incense, food, and prayers are offered regularly. They are a central part of everyday veneration in Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese, and Japanese homes.

**Visiting family graves**
Paying respects at the tombs of deceased relatives, cleaning the gravesite, and leaving offerings. It is one of the most basic ways of honoring forebears and is the main activity of Tomb-Sweeping Day.

**Joshu's "Mu"**
The most famous koan, the first case of The Gateless Gate. When a monk asked the Chinese master Joshu (Zhaozhou) whether a dog has Buddha-nature, Joshu answered "mu," meaning "no" or "nothing." Contemplating "mu" is a classic first koan for Zen students.

**The Gateless Gate**
A 13th-century Chinese collection of 48 koans (Mumonkan, or Wumenguan) compiled with commentary by the monk Wumen Huikai. It opens with Joshu's "Mu" and is one of the two standard koan collections.

**The Blue Cliff Record**
A 12th-century Chinese collection of 100 koans (Hekiganroku, or Biyan Lu) with verses and commentary, compiled by Yuanwu Keqin from earlier verses by Xuedou. Along with The Gateless Gate it is the most cited koan collection.

**"What is the sound of one hand clapping?"**
Perhaps the best-known koan in the West, created by the Japanese Rinzai master Hakuin Ekaku. It is meant to break the student's reliance on ordinary logical, dualistic thinking.

**"If you meet the Buddha, kill him"**
A saying attributed to the Chinese master Linji (Rinzai), founder of the Linji school. It warns students not to cling to any concept or image of the Buddha, even as an object of reverence, on the road to enlightenment.

**Baizhang's wild fox and the slap**
In a koan in The Gateless Gate, Baizhang frees an old man who had been reborn as a fox for 500 lifetimes because of a wrong answer about karma, then gives the dead fox a monk's funeral rites. Afterward his student Huangbo slaps Baizhang in the face.

**Rinzai school and zazen**
Koans are most closely associated with the Rinzai school of Zen, whose practitioners contemplate them during zazen (seated meditation) and discuss them with a teacher. The Soto school emphasizes "just sitting" instead.

**Original face before your parents were born**
A koan asking the student to show their "original face" from before their father and mother were born. It points to one's true nature beyond the self and individual existence.

**Breaking dualistic thinking**
Koans are short, paradoxical stories, questions, or statements designed to be unanswerable by rational thought. By exhausting logic they aim to overcome dualist thinking and trigger sudden insight, or satori.

**Gong'an**
The original Chinese term for koans, literally meaning "public case," referring to the records of a magistrate's court decisions. "Koan" is the Japanese reading.

**The twelve caveats**
An appendix to The Gateless Gate lists twelve "caveats" or warnings for practitioners. The first likens following rules and keeping regulations to binding oneself without a rope.

**Holi**
A Hindu spring festival famous for participants throwing brightly colored powders and water balloons at one another. Bonfires lit on its eve (Holika Dahan) commemorate the boy Prahlada, a devotee of Vishnu, who survived unharmed when the demoness Holika, who was supposed to be immune to fire, sat with him in her lap in a fire and was burned herself. Drinks made from bhang (cannabis) are traditionally consumed during Holi.

**Diwali**
The Hindu "festival of lights," a five-day festival in which people light diyas (oil lamps) and lanterns. It commemorates Rama's return to Ayodhya after his fourteen-year exile in the forest and his defeat of the demon king Ravana. Gambling is considered auspicious during Diwali because of a story in which the goddess Parvati won a game of dice against Shiva.

**Kumbh Mela**
A massive Hindu pilgrimage held in a 12-year cycle, in which millions of pilgrims ritually bathe in sacred rivers. It rotates among four sites: Prayagraj (Allahabad) on the Ganges, Haridwar, Nashik on the Godavari, and Ujjain on the Shipra.

**Smarta tradition**
A Hindu tradition associated with the 8th-century philosopher Adi Shankara, which treats several deities as equal manifestations of the one Brahman. Its followers worship five deities, including the sun god Surya, a deity dating back to the Vedic period.

**Shaivism, Vaishnavism, and Shaktism**
The major denominations of Hinduism, centered respectively on Shiva, Vishnu and his avatars, and the Great Goddess (Mahadevi or Devi). The gods Brahma (the creator), Vishnu (the preserver), and Shiva (the destroyer) make up the Trimurti.

**Vedas, Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita, and Mahabharata**
Key Hindu scriptures. The Vedas are the oldest texts, the Upanishads are philosophical treatises about Brahman and the self, and the Sanskrit epic Mahabharata contains the Bhagavad Gita, a dialogue between Krishna and the warrior Arjuna.

**Laws of Manu**
The Manusmriti, an ancient Hindu law book that lays out social and religious duties, including the varnas (castes) and the shraddha rites performed for deceased ancestors. Members of the upper three varnas are called "twice-born" because of an initiation ceremony.

**Raksha Bandhan and rakhis**
A Hindu festival in which sisters tie protective threads or bracelets called rakhis around their brothers' wrists. In return, brothers promise to protect their sisters.

**Hindu temples (mandirs)**
Hindu temples are designed on square grids according to sacred architecture, with a 64-square grid among the most favored. South Indian temples have towering, sculpture-covered gateways called gopurams, the Konark Sun Temple features erotic sculptures, and Angkor Wat in Cambodia was originally built as a Hindu temple to Vishnu. The Swaminarayan Akshardham in Robbinsville, New Jersey claims to be one of the largest Hindu temples in the world.

**Rath Yatra and Jagannath**
A festival in Puri in which huge chariots carrying the deity Jagannath, a form of Krishna/Vishnu, and his siblings are pulled through the streets. Exaggerated claims that devotees threw themselves under the wheels gave English the word "juggernaut." The ISKCON (Hare Krishna) movement spread the festival worldwide.

**Hare Krishna movement (ISKCON)**
The International Society for Krishna Consciousness, founded in New York City in 1966 by A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada. It is a Western-friendly branch of Vaishnavism known for chanting the sixteen-word Maha Mantra ("Hare Krishna, Hare Rama") and for its Food for Life charity.

**Four goals of life (purusharthas)**
The four aims of human life in Hinduism: dharma (duty and righteousness), artha (wealth and power), kama (pleasure), and moksha (liberation).

**Samsara, karma, and moksha**
Hindus believe in samsara, the cycle of rebirth, in which a person's karma (the moral consequences of actions) determines their next life, so someone with bad karma may be reborn as an animal. Moksha is liberation from this cycle.

**Samkhya and Yoga**
Two of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy. Samkhya, founded by the sage Kapila, holds a dualistic view of reality in which both prakriti (matter) and purusha (consciousness) are real, while Yoga uses physical postures called asanas and meditation.

**Four yugas**
Hinduism describes cosmic time as cycles of four ages, or yugas, which become progressively worse. The current age is the Kali Yuga, the dark or iron age.

**Golden plates and the angel Moroni**
Smith said the angel Moroni led him to a set of golden plates buried in the Hill Cumorah near Manchester, New York. He translated them as the Book of Mormon, published in 1830, and the plates appear in nearly every question about him.

**Urim and Thummim (seer stones)**
Seer stones that Smith said he used to translate the golden plates; the name is borrowed from the priestly objects in the Hebrew Bible. In 2015 the LDS Church released the first photographs of a seer stone attributed to him.

**Reformed Egyptian**
The script in which, according to Smith, the golden plates were written. He presented the Book of Mormon as a translation of this otherwise unknown language.

**Three Witnesses**
Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer, and Martin Harris, who testified that an angel showed them the golden plates. Their statement is printed in most editions of the Book of Mormon. Cowdery was also Smith's main scribe, and the two said John the Baptist appeared to them and baptized them.

**Death at Carthage Jail**
In June 1844, while held in jail in Carthage, Illinois, Smith and his brother Hyrum were shot and killed by an armed mob. Hostility toward him had grown in nearby Nauvoo, including over his destruction of a critical newspaper and rumors of polygamy.

**Nauvoo, Illinois**
The city Smith's followers built on the Mississippi River after they were expelled from Missouri in 1838–1839. It became the center of the movement and the place where Smith publicly denied charges of polygamy.

**Word of Wisdom**
A revelation by Smith, part of the Doctrine and Covenants, that warns against alcohol ("strong drinks"), tobacco, and "hot drinks" (understood as coffee and tea). It is the basis of Latter-day Saint dietary rules.

**Lost 116 pages**
Martin Harris borrowed and lost the first 116 manuscript pages of Smith's translation, known as the Book of Lehi. Smith said God punished him and did not have him retranslate that section, replacing it with a different account from the small plates of Nephi.

**Doctrine and Covenants and Pearl of Great Price**
Two Latter-day Saint scriptures alongside the Bible and Book of Mormon. Doctrine and Covenants collects Smith's revelations, including instructions on baptism for the dead, while the Pearl of Great Price contains his translation of part of Matthew and his Articles of Faith, the second of which rejects inherited original sin.

**First Vision (Sacred Grove)**
Smith's account of seeing God the Father and Jesus Christ while praying in a grove of trees near his home in upstate New York around 1820. He described it in sources including the 1842 Wentworth Letter.

**Jackson County, Missouri (Zion)**
Smith declared Jackson County, Missouri, to be the site of Zion, the New Jerusalem, and visited it with Oliver Cowdery and others. The Latter-day Saints were later driven out of the county and then out of Missouri.

**King Follett discourse**
A sermon Smith gave in 1844 at the funeral of church member King Follett. It taught exaltation, the controversial idea that God was once a man and that humans can become gods.

**Endowment, Quorum of the Twelve, and Council of Fifty**
Smith created the endowment, a temple ceremony that reenacts the Fall of Adam and Eve and whose oaths resemble Masonic ones. He also organized the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and the secret Council of Fifty.

**James Strang**
One of several men who claimed to succeed Smith after his death. Strang led his followers to Beaver Island in Lake Michigan and was crowned "King of the Kingdom of God," while most Latter-day Saints followed Brigham Young to Utah.

**Salamander Letter**
A forged letter attributed to Martin Harris, created by Mark Hofmann in the 1980s. In its version of the story of the golden plates, a white salamander that turned into a spirit took the place of the angel Moroni. Hofmann later killed two people with bombs to avoid exposure and was convicted of murder.

**Institutes of the Christian Religion**
Calvin's masterwork of systematic Protestant theology, first published in 1536 and expanded many times until its final 1559 edition. Its four books begin with "The Knowledge of God the Creator" and "The Knowledge of God the Redeemer," and it is by far the most common title clue for him.

**Geneva**
The Swiss city where Calvin led the Reformation and tried to build a godly society governed by biblical principles, often described as a theocracy. He organized its church, enforced strict moral discipline through the Consistory, and founded the Geneva Academy.

**Michael Servetus**
A Spanish physician and theologian who denied the doctrine of the Trinity. Calvin denounced him, and he was burned at the stake for heresy in Geneva in 1553, an execution that has long been held against Calvin.

**Predestination**
The doctrine, central to Calvinism, that God has eternally chosen who will be saved and who will not, independent of human merit. Calvin taught "double predestination," in which God elects some to salvation and others to damnation.

**Martin Bucer and Strasbourg**
Martin Bucer, the leading reformer of Strasbourg, invited Calvin and other religious exiles to the city in 1538 after Calvin was expelled from Geneva. Calvin pastored a congregation of French refugees there, and the experience shaped the church reforms he later carried out in Geneva.

**Five Points of Calvinism (TULIP)**
The summary of Calvinist doctrine: Total depravity, Unconditional election, Limited atonement, Irresistible grace, and Perseverance of the saints. The points were formulated after Calvin's death, at the Synod of Dort (1618–1619), in response to the Remonstrants.

**Theodore Beza**
Calvin's student and successor as leader of the Genevan church. Among his works is the satirical Passavantius, an attack on the French Catholic official Pierre Lizet.

**John Knox and Presbyterianism**
The Scottish reformer John Knox, while exiled from Scotland, studied with Calvin in Geneva and brought his ideas home. Knox founded the Presbyterian Church of Scotland, a major branch of the Reformed tradition based on Calvin's teaching.

**Huldrych Zwingli and the Eucharist**
Calvin largely agreed with the Zurich reformer Zwingli in rejecting a physical presence of Christ in the Eucharist, though Calvin taught a real spiritual presence. In 1549 he reached a common position with Zwingli's successor Heinrich Bullinger in the Consensus Tigurinus (Zurich Agreement).

**Jacobus Arminius and the Remonstrants**
The Dutch theologian Arminius and his followers, the Remonstrants, rejected Calvinist predestination in favor of conditional election and human free will. Their challenge led to the Synod of Dort, which condemned them and affirmed the Five Points.

**Exile from Geneva**
Calvin's strict reforms were poorly received at first, and in 1538 the city council expelled him and his colleague Guillaume Farel. Calvin was invited back in 1541 and remained in Geneva until his death in 1564.

**Psychopannychia**
Calvin's first theological work, which argues against "soul sleep," the belief that the soul sleeps or is unconscious between death and the final resurrection.

**Born 1509 in Noyon**
Calvin (originally Jehan Cauvin) was born in 1509 in Noyon, France, to a middle-class family. He studied the humanities and law before his conversion to Protestantism forced him to flee France.

**Response to Questions and Objections of a Certain Jew**
A treatise by Calvin answering a Jewish critic's arguments against Christianity. Calvin also taught that those who "obey the commands by faith working through love" belong to the New Covenant.

**Salat (salah or namaz)**
The ritual prayer of Islam and the second of the Five Pillars. Muslims must perform it five times a day: Fajr (dawn, two rak'ahs before sunrise), Dhuhr (midday), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (sunset), and Isha (night). On Fridays, the Dhuhr prayer is replaced by the congregational Jumu'ah prayer led by an imam.

**Wudu and ghusl**
Ritual purification required before salat. Wudu is the partial ablution of washing the face, arms, head, and feet, while ghusl is the full-body ablution required after major impurity.

**Adhan and the muezzin**
The adhan is the Islamic call to prayer, traditionally given from a mosque's minaret by a muezzin and today often broadcast by loudspeaker. Before the dawn prayer it adds the line "prayer is better than sleep," and it includes the phrase "hayya 'ala al-falah" ("come to success"). The first muezzin was Bilal, a freed Abyssinian slave.

**Qibla and the mihrab**
Salat must be performed facing the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca. In a mosque, the qibla is marked by the mihrab, a niche in the wall, and worshippers often pray on prayer mats.

**Rak'ah, ruku, and sujud**
Each salat is made up of a set number of units called rak'ahs, each a cycle of standing, bowing (ruku), prostration (sujud), and sitting. The prayer begins with the intention (niyyah) and the takbir ("Allahu akbar," "God is the greatest"), which is also said between movements. The Fatiha, the first surah of the Quran, is recited in each rak'ah, and the prayer ends with the taslim, a greeting of peace said while turning to the right and left.

**Reduction from fifty to five prayers**
During Muhammad's Night Journey and Ascension to Heaven, God first commanded fifty daily prayers. On the advice of Moses, Muhammad returned repeatedly to ask for a reduction until the number was lowered to five.

**Sujud al-sahw**
The "prostration of forgetfulness," two extra prostrations performed to make up for mistakes during salat, such as adding or leaving out a required act.

**Special forms of salat: qasr, witr, tahajjud, and janazah**
Qasr is a shortened form of the prayer allowed while traveling. Witr ("odd") is an optional night prayer with an odd number of rak'ahs that often includes the supplication called qunut, and tahajjud is an optional prayer performed after rising from sleep at night. Other forms include the funeral prayer (salat al-janazah) and a special eclipse prayer, which Muhammad performed during the eclipse that coincided with the death of his son Ibrahim.

**The Lord's Prayer ("Our Father")**
The prayer Jesus taught his disciples when they asked him how to pray, found in Matthew's Sermon on the Mount and in Luke. It begins "Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name" and includes the petition "give us this day our daily bread." Christians differ on whether to say "debts," "sins," or "trespasses," and Catholics omit the closing doxology, "for thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory." Christian prayers usually end with "Amen," meaning "truly" or "so be it."

**Hail Mary and the rosary**
The Hail Mary is a Catholic prayer addressed to Mary as "full of grace." It draws on Elizabeth's greeting in Luke, "Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!" Catholics pray it repeatedly on the beads of the rosary, with the Lord's Prayer said between each decade.

**Amidah**
The central prayer of Jewish worship, also called the Shemoneh Esreh, which today contains nineteen blessings. Its name means "standing," since it is said standing with the feet together, and worshippers traditionally take three steps back and then three steps forward before beginning it.

**Shacharit, Mincha, and Ma'ariv**
The three daily Jewish prayer services (tefillot): Shacharit in the morning, Mincha in the afternoon, and Ma'ariv (or Arvit) in the evening. They are read from a prayer book called a siddur, such as the popular Koren Sacks edition. Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel said that when he marched with Martin Luther King Jr. at Selma, he felt his "legs were praying."

**Tefillin, tallit, minyan, and Kaddish**
Jewish men traditionally pray wearing tefillin (phylacteries), small leather boxes with scripture strapped to the head and arm, and a fringed prayer shawl called a tallit. Certain prayers, including the Kaddish, which mourners recite, require a minyan, a quorum of ten adults. Other major Jewish prayers include the Shema ("Hear, O Israel") and the Kol Nidre, recited on Yom Kippur eve to annul vows.

**"Pray without ceasing" and The Way of a Pilgrim**
A command from Paul's First Letter to the Thessalonians. In the 19th-century Russian text The Way of a Pilgrim, the narrator hears this verse and wanders across Russia trying to learn how to pray constantly, eventually learning the Jesus Prayer.

**Jesus's teachings on prayer**
In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells his followers not to pray on street corners like hypocrites but in their rooms in secret, and not to use long repetitive prayers as pagans do. His parables on prayer include the Pharisee who proudly compares himself to a tax collector, and the persistent widow who wears down an unjust judge. In the Garden of Gethsemane he prayed while his disciples slept, then asked, "Could you not watch with me one hour?"

**Haman**
The book's villain, an Agagite (a descendant of the Amalekite king Agag) who serves as the Persian king's chief minister. Angered that Mordecai will not bow to him, he plots to exterminate all the Jews of the empire, but he is ruined when the king finds him "falling on the couch" where Esther lay while begging her for mercy, and he is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.

**Vashti**
The first queen of King Ahasuerus, who refuses his command to appear at a drunken banquet wearing the "crown royal" to display her beauty (in rabbinic tradition, wearing only the crown). She is deposed, the king sends out a decree that "every man should bear rule in his own house," and a search for a new queen begins, with the candidates given a year of beauty treatments with myrrh and perfumes under the eunuch Hegai.

**Mordecai**
Esther's cousin, often described as her uncle, who raised her after her parents died. He refuses to bow to Haman, uncovers a plot against the king, urges Esther to intervene for her people, and is ultimately made the king's chief minister in Haman's place.

**Ahasuerus**
The Persian king who makes Esther his queen, usually identified with Xerxes I. He grants Haman permission to destroy the Jews, but later lets Mordecai issue a counter-edict allowing the Jews to defend themselves.

**Bigthan and Teresh**
Two of the king's eunuch guards who plot to assassinate Ahasuerus. Mordecai uncovers the plot, they are hanged, and the deed is recorded in the royal chronicles; when the sleepless king later has the chronicles read to him, he orders Haman to publicly honor Mordecai.

**No mention of God**
Esther is one of only two books of the Hebrew Bible, along with the Song of Songs, that never explicitly mentions God. The Greek version of Esther includes added passages with prayers that mention God.

**Purim and the casting of lots**
The joyous Jewish holiday that celebrates the deliverance of the Jews from Haman's plot, and the occasion on which the Book of Esther is read aloud. Its name comes from pur, the "lot" Haman cast to choose the date of the massacre, the 13th of the month Adar.

**Fifty-cubit gallows**
The gallows (or impaling pole), about 75 feet high, that Haman builds on the advice of his wife Zeresh in order to hang Mordecai. Haman himself is hanged on it instead.

**Esther approaches the king unsummoned**
After fasting for three days, Esther risks death by going to the king without being called, but he extends his golden scepter and promises her any request "even to the half of the kingdom." At banquets she prefaces her requests with "if it please the king" and reveals that she is Jewish and that Haman plans to destroy her people.

**"For such a time as this"**
Mordecai's words to Esther when she hesitates to approach the king: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" The phrase is often quoted as a call to action.

**Hadassah**
Esther's Hebrew name, meaning "myrtle." "Esther" is her Persian name.

**Graggers (groggers)**
Noisemakers that Jews shake, along with booing and stamping, to drown out Haman's name every time it is read aloud from the Megillah on Purim.

**Shushan (Susa)**
The Persian capital where the story is set. Shushan Purim, celebrated a day later in walled cities such as Jerusalem, is named for it.

**Megillah**
The Hebrew name for the scroll of Esther (Megillat Esther), the best known of the five "megillot" (scrolls) of the Hebrew Bible. The rare cantillation marks yerach ben yomo and qarnei farah appear together on a single word in it.

**Babylonian deity names**
Some scholars note that the names Mordecai and Esther resemble those of the Babylonian gods Marduk and Ishtar. Combined with the book's lack of reference to God, this has led some to read it as an allegory or as adapted from older Mesopotamian material.

**Chariot of fire**
Elijah's most famous giveaway. Instead of dying, he was taken up into heaven in a whirlwind by a chariot and horses of fire, as his disciple Elisha watched (2 Kings 2).

**Contest on Mount Carmel against the prophets of Baal**
Elijah challenged 450 prophets of Baal (along with 400 prophets of Asherah) to see whose god would send fire to burn a sacrificed bull. Baal's prophets failed, while Elijah had his altar doused with water before God sent fire from heaven to consume it; the false prophets were then slaughtered.

**Elisha and the mantle**
Elijah's successor was Elisha, the son of Shaphat. Elijah threw his mantle (cloak) over Elisha to call him, and Elisha later picked it up after Elijah's ascension, the origin of the phrase "taking up the mantle." Elisha asked for and received a "double portion" of Elijah's spirit.

**Ahab and Jezebel**
Elijah's chief enemies were King Ahab of Israel and his wife Queen Jezebel, who promoted the worship of Baal. After Jezebel arranged the death of Naboth so Ahab could seize his vineyard, Elijah prophesied that dogs would lick Ahab's blood and eat Jezebel.

**The drought and the ravens at the Cherith**
Elijah announced to Ahab a drought sent as punishment for Baal worship, which lasted over three years. During it, he hid by the brook Cherith (Kerith), where ravens brought him bread and meat each morning and evening.

**The widow of Zarephath**
During the drought, Elijah stayed with a widow in Zarephath whose jar of flour and jug of oil miraculously never ran out. When her son died, Elijah prayed over him and restored him to life.

**Elijah's chair at the brit milah**
At Jewish circumcision ceremonies (brit milah), an empty chair is set aside for Elijah, who is regarded as the protector of children and the "angel of the covenant."

**Elijah's cup at Passover**
At the Passover seder, Jews pour an extra cup of wine for Elijah and open the door for him, since he is expected to return and announce the coming of the Messiah.

**"Still, small voice" on Mount Horeb**
Fleeing Jezebel after Carmel, Elijah traveled forty days to a cave on Mount Horeb (Mount Sinai), complaining that he alone remained faithful to God. God was not in the wind, earthquake, or fire, but revealed himself in a "still, small voice" or gentle whisper, and commanded him to anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha.

**The juniper (broom) tree**
After fleeing Jezebel's wrath, Elijah sat under a juniper (broom) tree in the wilderness and prayed to die. An angel touched him and showed him bread baked on hot coals and water to strengthen him for the journey to Horeb.

**Return prophesied in Malachi**
The final book of the Christian Old Testament ends with God promising to send Elijah before the "great and terrible day of the Lord," to turn the hearts of fathers to their children and children to their fathers. This is the basis for the belief that he will herald the Messiah.

**"Eliyahu HaNavi" and Havdalah**
A hymn calling for Elijah the Prophet ("Eliyahu HaNavi") to return soon with the Messiah is traditionally sung at the conclusion of Havdalah, the ceremony marking the end of Shabbat.

**The Transfiguration and John the Baptist**
In the New Testament, Elijah (Elias) appears with Moses alongside Jesus at the Transfiguration. Jesus identifies John the Baptist with the Elijah who was to come.

**Ahaziah and the fire on the soldiers**
When Ahab's son King Ahaziah sent captains with fifty soldiers each to seize Elijah, Elijah called down fire from heaven that consumed two of the companies. He also prophesied Ahaziah's death for consulting the god Baal-zebub.

**Elijah the Tishbite**
Elijah is described as coming from Tishbe in Gilead, so he is often called "the Tishbite." He is known as Elias in Greek and Latin traditions and as Ilyas in Islam.

**Wu wei**
The central Daoist ideal of "effortless action," "non-action," or "action through inaction": acting in harmony with the natural flow of the Dao instead of forcing outcomes. Chapter 37 of the Daodejing says the Dao "does nothing, yet nothing is left undone," and the economist François Quesnay is said to have rendered the idea as "laissez-faire."

**Zhuangzi's butterfly dream**
The most famous passage of the Zhuangzi, a foundational Daoist text named after its 4th-century BCE author. Zhuangzi dreams he is a butterfly, then wakes and cannot tell whether he is a man who dreamed of being a butterfly or a butterfly now dreaming that it is a man.

**Laozi**
