The legendary founder of Daoism, whose name means "Old Master." Tradition says he was an archivist at the Zhou royal court who grew tired of society and left China riding a water buffalo (ox), writing down the Daodejing at the request of a border guard before he disappeared.

**Daodejing (Tao Te Ching)**
The central Daoist text, attributed to Laozi and usually translated as "The Book of the Way and Its Virtue." Its 81 short chapters begin "The Dao that can be told is not the eternal Dao; the name that can be named is not the eternal name," and it praises the "mysterious female," the gate from which Heaven and Earth emerge. The saying "A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step" also comes from it.

**Yin and yang**
The two complementary opposing forces, such as dark and light or feminine and masculine, whose interplay makes up the universe. They are shown in the taijitu (the yin-yang symbol), which is sometimes surrounded by the eight trigrams of the I Ching ("Book of Changes"), a divination classic that Daoism draws on.

**Three Treasures**
The three virtues of compassion, moderation (frugality), and humility, laid out in chapter 67 of the Daodejing. In internal alchemy, the term also refers to jing (essence), qi (vital energy), and shen (spirit).

**The Vinegar Tasters**
A traditional allegorical painting in which Confucius, the Buddha, and Laozi taste vinegar. Confucius looks sour and the Buddha bitter, while Laozi smiles, showing Daoism's positive acceptance of life as it is.

**Pu (the uncarved block) and ziran**
Pu, the uncarved block of wood, is a Daoist symbol of simplicity and of human nature before society shapes it. It is connected to ziran, "naturalness" or "self-so," the spontaneous way things happen by themselves.

**Other Zhuangzi stories**
The Zhuangzi includes a debate with the logician Huizi about whether one can know the happiness of fish, and Zhuangzi drumming on a tub and singing after his wife's death because death is like the changing of the seasons. It also tells of Cook Ding, whose butchering is so skillful that his knife stays sharp for nineteen years, and of Hundun (Chaos), who dies when two emperors drill the seven openings of the human face into him.

**Jade Emperor**
The supreme ruler of Heaven in popular Daoism, who presides over a celestial bureaucracy. Legend says he chose the twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac through a race.

**Three Pure Ones**
The highest deities of religious Daoism, usually shown as elderly men: the Jade Pure One, the Supreme Pure One, and the Grand Pure One (a deified Laozi). One is said to have divided time into epochs, and they are often depicted holding objects such as a fan or a fly whisk.

**Celestial Masters and the Five Pecks of Rice**
The Way of the Celestial Masters, the first organized Daoist religious movement, was founded in the 2nd century CE by Zhang Daoling and was called the Five Pecks of Rice (Wudoumi) movement after its membership dues. Its descendant, Zhengyi Daoism, is one of the two main modern schools; the other is the monastic Quanzhen school, centered at the White Cloud Abbey in Beijing, whose master Qiu Chuji met Genghis Khan.

**Hell Bank Notes and joss paper**
Paper offerings, often printed with the image of the Jade Emperor, that are burned so that they reach ancestors and spirits in the afterlife. They are a modern form of sacrifice in Chinese religion.

**Eight Immortals**
A group of legendary Daoist figures who achieved immortality, often shown together in Chinese art. They include He Xiangu, the only woman among them, who is said to have become immortal by eating powdered mica.

**Pangu**
The giant of Chinese creation myth who hatched from a cosmic egg and separated Heaven and Earth, pushing them apart for 18,000 years. When he died, his body became the features of the world.

**Baptism of Jesus by John the Baptist in the Jordan River**
John the Baptist, son of Elizabeth and a relative of Jesus, baptized Jesus in the Jordan River. As Jesus came up from the water, the Holy Spirit descended on him "like a dove," and a voice from heaven said, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." The event is the First Luminous Mystery of the Rosary and is celebrated at Theophany (Epiphany) in Eastern churches; John said that Jesus would baptize "with the Holy Spirit."

**Great Commission and the Trinitarian formula**
In Matthew 28:19, the risen Jesus commands his disciples to "make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." Most churches therefore require this Trinitarian formula for a valid baptism, though some "Oneness" churches baptize in the name of Jesus only.

**Baptism for the dead (Mormons)**
Members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints perform proxy baptisms in temples on behalf of the deceased, citing 1 Corinthians 15:29 ("Else what shall they do which are baptized for the dead?"). The practice caused controversy when it was performed for Holocaust victims such as Anne Frank, and early church writers attributed a similar vicarious baptism to the Marcionites.

**Anabaptists and believer's baptism**
Radical Reformation groups such as the Mennonites, Amish, and Hutterites rejected infant baptism as meaningless, because infants cannot understand or profess faith. They "re-baptized" adults, earning the name Anabaptists. Believer's baptism (credobaptism) for people who have reached the "age of accountability," often by full immersion, is also practiced by Baptist churches such as the Southern Baptist Convention, the largest Protestant denomination in the U.S.

**Baptism of blood and baptism of desire**
Catholic doctrine holds that people who die before being baptized with water can still receive its grace. Baptism of blood, defended by Cyprian of Carthage, applies to unbaptized martyrs who die for the faith, and baptism of desire applies to those who sincerely wished for it; the Good Thief, Dismas, is often cited as an example. The Jesuit Leonard Feeney's denial of these forms, insisting that only water baptism saves, was condemned, and his view is called Feeneyism.

**Aspersion, affusion, and immersion**
The three methods of baptism: aspersion is sprinkling water on the person, affusion is pouring water over the head, and immersion is dipping the whole body. Eastern Orthodox churches baptize even infants by triple immersion, once for each person of the Trinity, and water is held in a baptismal font.

**Infant baptism (christening) and original sin**
Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, and many other churches baptize infants, a rite often called christening because the child is also named. Baptism is the first sacrament of initiation in Catholicism and is believed to wash away original sin; in an emergency, any person can validly baptize.

**Ulrich Zwingli's symbolic view**
The Swiss Reformer Huldrych Zwingli argued that baptism is a symbolic sign of belonging to the covenant community rather than a means of grace. He still defended infant baptism, and his followers broke with him over it to form the first Anabaptist movement. By contrast, John Calvin described baptism as being "engrafted into Christ."

**Mandaeans and yardna**
The Mandaeans, a Gnostic religion of Iraq and Iran that honors John the Baptist, perform baptism (masbuta) repeatedly as a purification ritual in flowing "living" water. They call such water yardna, a word derived from the Jordan River.

**Renouncing Satan, "his works and pomps"**
In the baptismal vows, the candidate or the godparents answer "I do renounce" when asked to reject Satan, "all his works," and "all his pomps." Catholics renew these baptismal promises, for example at the Easter Vigil.

**Elcesaites and rabies**
The Elcesaites (Elkasaites), an early Jewish-Christian sect, reportedly practiced repeated baptisms, including as a cure for people bitten by rabid dogs.

**Tevilah and the mikvah**
Christian baptism is often traced to tevilah, the Jewish rite of full immersion for purification in a ritual bath called a mikvah, which is also used in conversion to Judaism. Comparable initiation rites in other faiths include the Sikh Amrit Sanchar and the Zoroastrian Navjote, at which initiates receive the sudreh (sacred shirt) and kusti (sacred cord).

**Catechumens and the baptismal font**
Catechumens are people receiving religious instruction to prepare for baptism. Baptism takes place at a font, sometimes in a separate building called a baptistery; in medieval Italy, rural churches called pievi had their own fonts, so people did not have to travel to the cathedral.

**"Born of water and the Spirit"**
In John 3:5, Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one "can enter into the kingdom of God" unless born of water and the Spirit, a key text for the necessity of baptism. Methodists teach that baptism brings a person into the covenant of grace.

**Noah's Flood and circumcision as types**
In 1 Peter 3, baptism is compared to the Flood, through which eight people were saved in Noah's Ark. Colossians 2 links baptism to circumcision, so it is often called its New Testament counterpart, and Ephesians 4 speaks of "one Lord, one faith, one baptism."

**Zamzam**
The sacred well in Mecca that miraculously sprang up when an angel (Gabriel) struck the ground with his heel or wing to save Hagar (Hajar) and her infant son Ishmael. Pilgrims drink its water, and in 930 CE the Qarmatians desecrated it by throwing corpses into it when they sacked Mecca.

**Safa and Marwa**
The two hills in Mecca between which Hagar ran seven times searching for water for Ishmael. Pilgrims re-enact her search by walking between them seven times during the Hajj and Umrah, a rite called the sa'i.

**Wudu and ghusl**
Wudu is the Islamic ritual washing of the face, hands, arms, head, and feet with water before salat (prayer). Ghusl is the full-body ablution required after major impurities such as sexual intercourse, menstruation, or childbirth.

**Tayammum**
The Islamic dry ablution performed with clean sand, earth, or dust when water is unavailable or unsafe to use. It serves the same purpose as wudu.

**Baptism**
The Christian sacrament of initiation in which water is used to wash away sin, performed by full immersion, by affusion (pouring), or by aspersion (sprinkling). A baptism that includes naming an infant is often called a christening, and the Holy Spirit is often compared to the "water of life."

**Holy water**
Water blessed by a priest, often with exorcised salt added in the form of a cross, and used to bless people, homes, and cars. Congregants dip their fingers in it from a stoup or font when entering a church to make the sign of the cross, and it is sprinkled with an aspergillum, which replaced the earlier hyssop branch.

**Mikveh**
The Jewish ritual bath used for purification, for example by women after menstruation or childbirth and by converts. Water is also used in taharah, the ritual washing of a body before burial, and in netilat yadayim, the ritual washing of the hands before eating bread.

**Wedding at Cana**
The Gospel of John's account of Jesus's first miracle, in which he turned water into wine at a wedding feast after telling his mother, "My hour has not yet come." Jesus also famously walked on water during a storm on the Sea of Galilee, where Peter at first thought he was a ghost.

**Ganges River and the Kumbh Mela**
The Ganges (Ganga) is Hinduism's holiest river, personified as the goddess Ganga, and bathing in it is believed to wash away sins. The Kumbh Mela is a massive pilgrimage festival at which millions of Hindus bathe in sacred rivers such as the Ganges, and devotees at Varanasi bathe from the steps called ghats.

**Every living thing created from water**
A teaching of the Quran, found in Surah 21, verse 30 and Surah 24, verse 45, that God made every living creature from water. The second verse goes on to distinguish creatures that crawl on their bellies from those that walk on two or four legs.

**Water as the best charity**
A hadith in which Muhammad, asked by Sa'd ibn Ubadah what the best form of charity was, answered "water," after which Sa'd dug a well. Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh) also classifies water into mutlaq (pure, unmixed) and mudaf (mixed) types for purification purposes.

**Misogi and harae**
Shinto purification rituals. Misogi is purification by washing the body in water, often under a waterfall or in the sea, while harae is the broader rite of purification that can use water and salt to remove impurity.

**Moses striking the rock**
The episode in which Moses brought forth water for the thirsty Israelites by striking a rock with his staff. In the Book of Numbers, he was punished by being barred from the Promised Land for striking the rock twice instead of speaking to it as God commanded.

**Epiphany (Theophany) and Timkat**
Eastern Christian feasts commemorating Jesus's baptism in the Jordan, marked by the Great Blessing of the Waters, as opposed to the "lesser" blessing that can be held at other times. In Ethiopia's Timkat festival, a tabot (a replica of the tablets of the Ark of the Covenant) is carried in procession to a body of water; in the Byzantine Divine Liturgy, heated water called zeon is added to the communion wine.

**Tashlikh, geshem, and Miriam's cup**
Jewish water traditions. In tashlikh, performed around Rosh Hashanah, bread crumbs symbolizing sins are cast into flowing water; the prayer for rain (geshem) is recited on Shemini Atzeret; and in a modern Passover custom, a cup of water is set out for Miriam alongside Elijah's cup of wine.

**Cave of Hira and the command to "Recite!"**
Around 610, while Muhammad was meditating in a cave on Mount Hira near Mecca, the angel Jibril (Gabriel) appeared and commanded him to "Recite" (or "Read," iqra). Muhammad, traditionally held to be illiterate, replied that he could not read, and the angel delivered the first revelation (Surah 96): "Recite in the name of thy Lord who created, created man from a clot." The night of this first revelation is commemorated as Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, and the revelations he received over about 23 years became the Quran's 114 surahs.

**The Hijra to Yathrib (Medina)**
In 622, persecuted by Mecca's leaders, Muhammad and Abu Bakr fled from Mecca to the city of Yathrib, soon renamed Medina ("the city [of the Prophet]"). His cousin Ali slept in his bed under his green cloak to fool would-be assassins, and the mosque at Quba was founded on the way. This migration marks year one of the Islamic calendar, and an earlier "first Hijra" sent some Muslims to shelter with the Christian king of Aksum. In Medina he drew up a charter, the Constitution of Medina, that gave protections to the Jewish tribes, who were among the People of the Book.

**Night Journey on the Buraq (Isra and Mi'raj)**
In one night Muhammad rode al-Buraq, a winged, horse-like steed often shown with a human face, from Mecca to the "farthest mosque" (al-Masjid al-Aqsa, the Bayt al-Muqaddas) in Jerusalem. From there he ascended through the seven heavens (the Mi'raj), meeting earlier prophets such as Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. When offered a choice of milk, wine, and water, he chose milk, which was praised as choosing the natural path (fitra).

**Moses bargaining down the daily prayers**
During the Mi'raj, God commanded fifty daily prayers. On his way down, Moses repeatedly urged Muhammad to go back and ask for a reduction, until the number was lowered to the five daily prayers (salat) Muslims observe today.

**Lote Tree of the Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha)**
The great lote tree marking the end of the seventh heaven, beyond which even the angels, including Jibril, cannot pass. Muhammad alone went past it during the Mi'raj into the divine presence.

**Khadija and Aisha**
Khadija, a wealthy Quraysh merchant widow who had employed him, was Muhammad's first wife and the first to believe in his revelation, comforting him after the experience at Hira. Her death and that of his uncle Abu Talib in 619 made it the "Year of Sorrow." Aisha, daughter of Abu Bakr, was his favorite later wife; she was once falsely accused of adultery and was cleared by a Quranic revelation.

**Hadith and Sunnah**
Hadith (plural ahadith) are the collected reports of Muhammad's sayings and actions, passed down through chains of narrators and compiled long after his death. Together they record the Sunnah, his normative example, which is the second source of Islamic law after the Quran.

**Orphan of the Quraysh raised by Abu Talib**
Muhammad was born into the Banu Hashim clan of Mecca's ruling Quraysh tribe. His father died before his birth and his mother when he was six, so he was raised first by his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and then by his uncle Abu Talib, after being nursed by the Bedouin foster mother Halimah. In stories from his childhood, angels cleansed his heart in a golden basin, and the Christian monk Bahira recognized him as a future prophet when he was about twelve, during a caravan journey to Syria.

**Year of the Elephant**
Muhammad's birth (traditionally c. 570) fell in the year the Abyssinian ruler of Yemen, Abraha, marched on Mecca with an army including an elephant. According to Surah al-Fil, the army was destroyed by birds pelting it with stones. His birthday is celebrated as Mawlid.

**Seal of the Prophets**
Muhammad's title (Khatam an-Nabiyyin), marking him as the final prophet in Islam. A hadith illustrates this with a parable of a beautiful house missing one brick, with Muhammad as that final brick.

**Satanic Verses: Lat, Uzza, and Manat**
A controversial tradition holds that Muhammad once recited verses praising the three pre-Islamic Meccan goddesses al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Manat as "exalted cranes" whose intercession could be sought, words later said to have been put on his tongue by Satan and withdrawn. Mainstream Islam rejects the story and stresses his strict rejection of these idols.

**Battles of Badr and the Trench; conquest of Mecca**
At Badr (624) the badly outnumbered Muslims of Medina, including the Ansar ("Helpers") who had welcomed the Prophet, defeated the Meccan Quraysh after a series of caravan raids. At the Battle of the Trench (627), Medina was defended by a ditch, a tactic credited to Salman the Persian. In 630 Muhammad conquered Mecca and destroyed the idols in the Kaaba, including that of Hubal.

**Treaty of Hudaybiyyah and the Pledge of the Tree**
In 628, when Muslims were turned away from making pilgrimage to Mecca, they swore the Pledge of Ridwan (the "Pledge under the Tree") to fight to the death after a rumor that the envoy Uthman, Muhammad's son-in-law, had been killed. Muhammad then negotiated the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, a truce with the Quraysh; its violation by allies of the Quraysh led to his march on Mecca.

**Placing the Black Stone**
When the Kaaba was being rebuilt before his prophethood, the Meccan clans quarreled over who would set the Black Stone back in place. Muhammad, known as al-Amin ("the trustworthy"), placed it on a cloth and had a leader of each clan lift a corner, and then set it in place himself.

**Fatima, Ali, and Ghadir Khumm**
Muhammad's youngest and favorite daughter Fatima, the child of Khadija, married his cousin Ali, and their sons Hasan and Husayn became the second and third Shia imams. Shia Muslims hold that Muhammad named Ali his successor at the pond of Ghadir Khumm, which is the root of the Sunni–Shia split. Sunnis forbid visual depictions of the Prophet.

**Tawaf around the Kaaba**
The ritual of walking seven times counterclockwise around the Kaaba, the black cube-shaped shrine in the Masjid al-Haram (Great Mosque) of Mecca. Men traditionally walk the first three circuits at a brisk pace and the last four more slowly; versions include the arrival tawaf (al-Qudum), the obligatory tawaf al-Ifadah, and the farewell tawaf (al-Wida).

**Stoning of the Devil (Jamarat)**
The ritual in Mina in which pilgrims throw seven pebbles at each of three pillars (now walls), called the jamarat, representing Satan, who in tradition tempted Abraham to disobey God. Pilgrims cross the multi-level Jamarat Bridge to reach them, and Mina was the site of a deadly crowd crush in 2015.

**Ihram**
The state of ritual purity a pilgrim enters before the hajj or umrah, upon crossing a boundary point called a miqat. Men wear two unhemmed, unstitched white sheets, and pilgrims in ihram must avoid acts such as hunting, sexual relations, cutting hair, and vanity.

**Sa'i between Safa and Marwah**
The ritual of walking or running seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah, now enclosed indoors within the Great Mosque. It commemorates Hagar (Hajar), the wife of Abraham, searching desperately for water for her infant son Ishmael.

**Zamzam Well**
The sacred well in Mecca that, according to tradition, God caused to spring up to save Hagar and Ishmael from thirst. Pilgrims drink its water during the hajj.

**Umrah**
The "lesser pilgrimage" to Mecca, which shares rituals such as ihram, tawaf, sa'i, and hair-cutting but is not obligatory and can be performed at any time of year. In the most common form of hajj, called Tamattu', pilgrims perform an umrah and then the hajj.

**Mount Arafat**
A hill and plain outside Mecca, also called the Mount of Mercy, where Muhammad delivered his Farewell Sermon. Standing in prayer there on the Day of Arafah (the 9th of Dhu al-Hijjah) is the central and essential rite of the hajj.

**Black Stone**
A sacred stone set into the eastern corner of the Kaaba, which pilgrims try to kiss or touch, or point toward, as they begin each circuit of the tawaf.

**Eid al-Adha and the animal sacrifice**
The "Feast of the Sacrifice," held at the end of the hajj on the 10th of Dhu al-Hijjah, commemorating Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son, identified in Islamic tradition with Ishmael. Pilgrims slaughter a sheep, goat, or other animal (one camel can count for seven people), and the meat is traditionally divided into thirds for family, friends, and the poor.

**Halq and taqsir**
The shaving (halq) or trimming (taqsir) of the hair, which marks a pilgrim's exit from the state of ihram. Men typically shave their heads, while women cut off only a small lock or the tips of their hair.

**Fifth Pillar of Islam**
The hajj is the fifth of the Five Pillars of Islam, required once in a lifetime of every adult Muslim who is physically and financially able. It takes place from the 8th to the 12th or 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah, the last month of the Islamic lunar calendar.

**Muzdalifah**
An open area between Arafat and Mina where pilgrims spend the night after the Day of Arafah, combining the sunset and night prayers. Pilgrims collect the pebbles there that they later throw at the jamarat.

**Talbiyah ("Labbayk")**
The prayer pilgrims chant repeatedly after entering ihram, beginning "Labbayk Allahumma labbayk," meaning "Here I am, O God, here I am," which declares their readiness to answer God's call.

**Kiswah**
The black silk cloth, embroidered with Qur'anic verses in gold, that drapes the Kaaba. It is replaced each year during the hajj season.

**Richard Francis Burton**
The British explorer who in 1853 disguised himself as a Muslim pilgrim to perform the hajj and enter Mecca, which was forbidden to non-Muslims. He described the journey in his book about his pilgrimage to Medina and Mecca.

**Havdalah and the braided candle**
The ceremony that ends Shabbat on Saturday night, traditionally once three stars are visible in the sky. Blessings are said over a cup of wine, fragrant spices, and a multi-wicked braided candle, which is then extinguished by dipping it in the wine. Its name means "separation," marking the division between the holy day and the ordinary week.

**39 melachot**
The thirty-nine categories of creative work forbidden on Shabbat, derived from the tasks used to build the Tabernacle. They include plowing, sowing, baking, weaving, kindling or extinguishing a fire, and writing two or more letters. A Jew who keeps all of Shabbat's laws is called "shomer Shabbat."

**"Lekhah Dodi"**
A 16th-century song by the Kabbalist Shlomo Halevi Alkabetz, sung at the Friday evening service, that personifies Shabbat as a bride (and queen) to be welcomed. It contains the words "shamor" ("keep") and "zachor" ("remember"), reflecting the two versions of the Sabbath commandment in Exodus and Deuteronomy. During its final verse the congregation rises and turns to face the door to greet the arriving Sabbath.

**Challah and lechem mishneh**
Two loaves of braided, egg-enriched challah bread are blessed at Shabbat meals. The pair, called lechem mishneh ("double bread"), recalls the double portion of manna that fell on Fridays in the wilderness so the Israelites would not have to gather it on the Sabbath.

**Candle lighting and Kiddush**
Shabbat begins at sundown on Friday with the lighting of (usually two) candles and the Kiddush, a blessing of sanctification recited over wine. The Friday-night Kiddush includes the opening verses of Genesis 2, which describe God resting on the seventh day.

**Kabbalat Shabbat**
"Receiving the Sabbath," the Friday evening service welcoming the holy day, developed by 16th-century Kabbalists in Safed. It consists mainly of a group of psalms followed by "Lekhah Dodi."

**"Shalom Aleichem"**
A song sung at home on Friday night before the first of Shabbat's meals, welcoming the ministering angels of peace who, according to the Talmud, accompany a person home from synagogue on the Sabbath eve.

**Fourth Commandment**
In the Jewish numbering of the Ten Commandments, the fourth commands Jews to "remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy" (Exodus 20) or "observe" it (Deuteronomy 5). The commandment grounds the day of rest in God's resting on the seventh day of creation.

**Seventh day of creation**
In Genesis 2, God finishes creating the world in six days and rests on the seventh, blessing and sanctifying it. Shabbat is therefore the first holy day mentioned in the Hebrew Bible, observed by God himself.

**Shabbos goy**
A non-Jew who performs tasks forbidden to observant Jews on Shabbat, such as turning lights on and off, extinguishing candles, or lighting an oven fire.

**Seudah shlishit**
The "third meal," eaten late on Saturday afternoon; Shabbat is marked by three festive meals in all. As the day nears its end, wistful songs are often sung at this meal.

**Zemirot and "Eshet Chayil"**
Zemirot are hymns sung around the Shabbat table. "Eshet Chayil" ("A Woman of Valor"), from Proverbs 31, is traditionally sung on Friday night in praise of the wife of the household.

**"V'shamru"**
A prayer drawn from Exodus 31:16–17 ("The children of Israel shall keep the Sabbath"), recited in the Shabbat evening service and again in the Kiddush of Shabbat day.

**Hamin (cholent)**
A slow-cooked stew (called hamin by Sephardim and cholent by Ashkenazim) prepared before sundown on Friday so it can cook overnight and be eaten hot on Saturday without violating the ban on cooking.

**Eruv**
A symbolic boundary, often a wire strung around a neighborhood, that turns a public area into a single private domain. Inside it, Jews may carry objects on Shabbat, which would otherwise be forbidden outside the home.

**Iblis refuses to bow**
In the Quran, God commanded the angels to bow down (prostrate) before Adam, and all obeyed except Iblis, who said he was better because he was made of smokeless fire while Adam was made of clay. For this pride Iblis was cast out of heaven and became Satan (Shaitan).

**Eve (Hawwa)**
Adam's wife, called Hawwa or Hawa in Islam. In Genesis, God creates her from one of Adam's ribs while he sleeps, after Adam has named the animals and found no suitable partner among them.

**Lilith**
In Jewish folklore, Adam's first wife, who refused to be subordinate to him and left Eden; some traditions say she joined or coupled with the demon Samael. She is often portrayed as a demon who threatens newborn children.

**Tree of Knowledge and the expulsion from Eden**
God forbade Adam and Eve to eat the fruit of the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil, but the serpent (Iblis or Shaitan in the Quran) tempted them and they ate it. As a result they were expelled from the Garden of Eden (Jannah, or Paradise, in Islam).

**"Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return"**
Part of God's curse on Adam in Genesis 3, along with the sentence that he will eat bread "in the sweat of thy face [brow]." Adam was formed from dust or clay (in the Quran by God's command "Be"), and his name is linked to the Hebrew adamah, "ground," and in Arabic tradition to a word for "skin" or the surface of the earth.

**Sixty cubits tall**
According to a hadith narrated by Abu Huraira, Muhammad said that God created Adam sixty cubits tall. The same tradition says that everyone who enters Paradise will have Adam's form and height.

**Forty years given to David (Dawud)**
In a hadith, Adam was shown his descendants and, seeing that David (Dawud) had a short life, gave him forty years from his own 1,000-year lifespan. When the angel of death came, Adam forgot or denied the gift, which is said to be why his descendants deny, forget, and make mistakes.

**First prophet of Islam (Safiullah)**
In Islam, Adam is regarded as the first prophet, bearing the honorific Safiullah, "the Chosen of God." Muslims consider him the first in the line of prophets that ends with Muhammad.

**Taught the names of all things**
In the Quran (Surah 2), God taught Adam the names of all things and then asked the angels to name them, which they could not do, showing Adam's superiority. In Genesis, Adam similarly gives names to all the animals.

**Cain and Abel**
Adam and Eve's first two sons. Cain murdered his brother Abel out of jealousy over God's acceptance of Abel's offering, and the Quran draws a lesson from the story that killing one person is like killing all of humanity.

**Seth**
Adam's third son (Sheth in Islamic tradition), born after Abel's murder as a replacement for him. In Islamic tradition, Adam named him his successor.

**Twin children**
Islamic tradition holds that Eve bore Adam many sets of twins (sometimes said to be 120 pairs), with each son marrying the twin sister of another son. In Shia tradition, Adam's first child was a single daughter named Anaq.

**Romans 5 and original sin**
In Romans 5, Paul calls Adam "a type of the one who was to come," presenting Christ as a new Adam whose obedience undoes Adam's disobedience. The fall of Adam and Eve is the basis of the Christian doctrine of original sin, developed especially by Augustine.

**Mount Arafat**
According to some Islamic traditions, Adam and Eve were separated after being sent down from Paradise and were finally reunited at Mount Arafat near Mecca, a central site of the Hajj.

**Sri Pada (Adam's Peak)**
A mountain in Sri Lanka with a large footprint-shaped rock at its summit. Muslims attribute the footprint to Adam, who is said to have first set foot on earth there, while Buddhists attribute it to the Buddha and Hindus to Shiva.

**Dalai Lama and Tenzin Gyatso**
The Dalai Lama is the spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism and, historically, the ruler of Tibet. The current, 14th Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso, fled into exile in India in 1959 after China crushed a Tibetan uprising, and he leads the Tibetan community from Dharamsala.

**Red Hat and Yellow Hat sects**
The two broad divisions of Tibetan Buddhism. The "Red Hat" schools are the older Nyingma, Sakya, and Kagyu, while the "Yellow Hat" school is the Gelug (Gelugpa), which stresses monastic discipline and celibacy and is led by the Dalai Lama.

**Sand mandalas**
Intricate circular diagrams of the cosmos that Tibetan monks build grain by grain out of colored sand over days or weeks. After they are finished, they are ritually swept away to show the impermanence of all things.

**Bardo Thodol (Tibetan Book of the Dead)**
A Nyingma funerary text read aloud to the dying and the dead, often called the Tibetan Book of the Dead to contrast it with the Egyptian one. It guides the consciousness through the bardos, the intermediate states between death and rebirth.

**Bon**
The indigenous religion of Tibet, which existed before Buddhism arrived and has animistic and shamanistic roots. It survives as a separate tradition alongside Tibetan Buddhism and shares many practices with it, such as prayer flags and the Dzogchen ("Great Perfection") teachings.

**Padmasambhava (Guru Rinpoche)**
The 8th-century Indian tantric master who, according to tradition, brought Vajrayana Buddhism to Tibet, subdued the local demons, and helped found Samye, Tibet's first Buddhist monastery. The Nyingma school regards him as its founder, and he is said to have hidden treasure texts (termas) to be rediscovered later by treasure-finders called tertons.

**Vajrayana (tantric) Buddhism**
The "Diamond Vehicle," the esoteric form of Mahayana Buddhism practiced in Tibet. It uses mantras, mandalas, visualization practices such as deity yoga, and rituals passed from teacher to student to speed the path to enlightenment.

**Reincarnation and selection of the Dalai Lama**
The Dalai Lama is believed to be reborn after death, and a search is made for a child born around that time. Tenzin Gyatso was identified at about two years old when he recognized objects that had belonged to the 13th Dalai Lama. The Qing dynasty introduced a golden urn lottery to choose among candidates.

**Panchen Lama**
The second-highest lama of the Gelug school, traditionally involved in identifying the reincarnation of the Dalai Lama and vice versa. The current Panchen Lama is disputed, since the boy chosen by the Dalai Lama in 1995 disappeared into Chinese custody and China installed its own candidate.

**Potala Palace**
The huge palace in Lhasa that was the winter residence of the Dalai Lamas until 1959. It is divided into the White Palace, which held living quarters and offices, and the Red Palace, which holds chapels and the stupa tombs of past Dalai Lamas.

**Chinese occupation of 1950**
The Chinese People's Liberation Army invaded Tibet in 1950 and took control of it. A failed uprising in 1959 forced the Dalai Lama into exile, and today the region is governed as the Tibet Autonomous Region (Xizang) of China.

**Kangling**
A ritual trumpet made from a human thighbone (femur), used in Tibetan tantric rituals such as chod, in which the practitioner cuts through attachment to the self and the body.

**Lhamo La-tso and Palden Lhamo**
Lhamo La-tso is an oval "oracle lake" where senior lamas go to receive visions that help locate the next Dalai Lama. It is guarded by Palden Lhamo, a fierce protector goddess depicted with blue skin and flaming hair.

**Kalachakra and Tara**
The Kalachakra ("Wheel of Time") is a tantric teaching and initiation about cosmic time and the body, important to all Tibetan schools and frequently given by the Dalai Lama. Tara is a female bodhisattva and mother figure who is among the most widely worshiped deities in Tibet.

**Shambhala and the Rime movement**
Shambhala is a mythical hidden kingdom linked to the Kalachakra teachings, thought to have inspired the fictional paradise of Shangri-La. The Rime movement was a 19th-century nonsectarian movement that encouraged the Tibetan schools to share and preserve one another's teachings.

**Tenzin Gyatso**
The religious name of the 14th and current Dalai Lama, born Lhamo Thondup in 1935 in the village of Taktser in Amdo. His full religious name is Jetsun Jamphel Ngawang Lobsang Yeshe Tenzin Gyatso, and he is the most common identifying clue for the title.

**Lhamo Latso**
A sacred lake in Tibet, southeast of Lhasa, visited by senior Gelug monks and regents who seek visions there that guide the search for the next Dalai Lama. In the search for the 14th, the regent saw letters and a house with unusual gutters, which led searchers to Taktser. Tradition holds that several Dalai Lamas died after visiting the lake.

**Potala Palace**
The great palace in Lhasa that was the Dalai Lamas' winter residence and seat of government. The 5th ("Great Fifth") Dalai Lama began building it in the 17th century, naming it after Mount Potalaka, the mythical dwelling of Chenrezig.

**Dharamsala and the 1959 exile**
After the failed 1959 Tibetan uprising against Chinese rule, the 14th Dalai Lama fled Lhasa to India, with help from the CIA. He set up the Tibetan government-in-exile in Dharamsala and proposed the "Middle Way Approach," which seeks genuine autonomy for Tibet within China rather than full independence.

**Golden Urn**
A method of choosing reincarnations by drawing lots from a golden urn, introduced by the Qing Qianlong Emperor in 1793 to curb corruption in the selection process. It was used in choosing some of the 10th through 12th Dalai Lamas, and the urn was kept at the Jokhang Temple in Lhasa.

**Avalokiteshvara (Chenrezig)**
The bodhisattva of compassion, called Chenrezig in Tibetan. Each Dalai Lama is believed to be a manifestation of Avalokiteshvara and a tulku, the reincarnation of his predecessor.

**Recognition of the predecessor's belongings**
The final test in identifying a new Dalai Lama is whether the child recognizes items that belonged to the previous one. In 1939 the two-year-old Lhamo Thondup correctly picked out the 13th Dalai Lama's possessions, such as a walking stick and a drum, a scene shown in the film Kundun.

**Gelug (Yellow Hat) school**
The school of Tibetan Buddhism founded by Tsongkhapa, which the Dalai Lamas lead. Its senior monks carry out the search for each new Dalai Lama.

**Altan Khan**
The Mongol ruler who in 1578 gave the title "Dalai Lama" to Sonam Gyatso, who became the 3rd Dalai Lama. "Dalai" is the Mongolian word for "ocean," a translation of "Gyatso," and the title was applied after death to two earlier lamas. The 4th Dalai Lama, Yonten Gyatso, was Altan Khan's great-grandson.

**Gendun Drup**
The first Dalai Lama (recognized as such after his death), a disciple of Tsongkhapa who founded Tashilhunpo Monastery, which later became the seat of the Panchen Lama.

**Dorje Shugden**
A controversial protector spirit, said to have been opposed with ritual by the 5th Dalai Lama. The 14th Dalai Lama discouraged the spirit's worship and rejected The Yellow Book, a text promoting it, which caused conflict with the New Kadampa Tradition, a group that venerates Shugden.

**Thubten Gyatso and the turning head**
Thubten Gyatso was the 13th Dalai Lama, who died in 1933. His embalmed body's head was reported to have turned toward the northeast, which pointed searchers toward Amdo, where the 14th was found. Baron Carl Gustaf Mannerheim gave him a pistol during a Russian expedition in 1908.

**Nechung Oracle**
The state oracle of Tibet, a medium who goes into trance and is consulted by the Dalai Lama and the Tibetan government on important matters, including the search for a new Dalai Lama. The 5th Dalai Lama made it an official institution.

**Kundun**
A 1997 Martin Scorsese film about the early life of the 14th Dalai Lama, from his discovery as a child to his flight into exile in 1959.

**Mind and Life Institute and The Art of Happiness**
The 14th Dalai Lama's dialogues with lawyer R. Adam Engle and neuroscientist Francisco Varela led to the founding of the Mind and Life Institute, which brings science together with contemplative practice. The Art of Happiness is a bestselling book based on psychiatrist Howard Cutler's conversations with him.

**Zhuangzi's butterfly dream**
The most famous passage of the Zhuangzi, the second great Taoist classic, named after its author. Zhuangzi dreams he is a butterfly and on waking cannot tell whether he is a man who dreamed of being a butterfly or a butterfly now dreaming it is a man. The story illustrates the fluidity of identity and the "transformation of things."

**Wu wei**
The central Taoist ideal of "effortless action," "non-action," or "action through inaction": acting in harmony with the natural flow of things rather than forcing outcomes. Chapter 37 of the Tao Te Ching says the Tao "does nothing, yet nothing is left undone."

**Laozi and the Tao Te Ching**
Laozi ("Old Master"), the legendary founder of Taoism, is credited with the Tao Te Ching ("Book of the Way and its Virtue"), an 81-chapter text of short aphoristic verses. Legend says he was an archivist at the Zhou royal court who left China riding a water buffalo (or ox) and wrote the text at the request of a gatekeeper at the western border pass.

**"The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao"**
The opening of the Tao Te Ching, which continues "the name that can be named is not the eternal name." It establishes that the Tao ("the Way"), the source and pattern of all things, cannot be captured in words. The text also calls the Tao the "mysterious female" whose gateway is the root of heaven and earth, and it is the source of the saying "a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step."

**Yin and yang**
The two complementary opposing forces of the cosmos, with yin associated with darkness and the feminine and yang with light and the masculine. They are symbolized by the taijitu (the "supreme ultimate" diagram), often surrounded by the eight trigrams (bagua) of the I Ching, the "Book of Changes," which Taoism shares with Confucianism.

**Three Treasures**
The Tao Te Ching names three virtues, compassion, moderation (frugality), and humility, as the Three Treasures (sanbao or Three Jewels). In Taoist internal alchemy (neidan), the term also refers to the bodily energies jing (essence), qi (vital energy), and shen (spirit), which practitioners cultivate in seeking longevity and immortality.

**The Vinegar Tasters**
A traditional allegorical painting showing Confucius, the Buddha, and Laozi tasting vinegar. Confucius looks sour and the Buddha bitter, but Laozi smiles, representing Taoism's view that life, accepted in its natural state, is sweet.

**Pu (the uncarved block) and ziran**
Pu, the uncarved block of wood, is a Taoist image of simplicity and the natural state before human shaping. It is closely tied to ziran, "naturalness" or "self-so," the idea that things are spontaneously what they are and happen by themselves.

**Hundun (Wonton)**
A Zhuangzi parable in which Hundun ("Chaos"), emperor of the center, lacks the seven openings that humans have for seeing, hearing, eating, and breathing. His friends, the emperors Shu and Hu, bore one hole a day to repay his kindness, and on the seventh day he dies, a warning against imposing artificial order on nature.

**The happiness of fish**
A Zhuangzi dialogue in which Zhuangzi says the fish in a river are happy, and the logician Huizi asks how he can know. Zhuangzi answers that he knew it by standing there by the river. Other Zhuangzi stories include Cook Ding, a butcher so skilled his knife stays sharp for nineteen years, and Zhuangzi drumming on a tub and singing after his wife's death because death is just another natural change, like the seasons.

**Jade Emperor and the Three Pure Ones**
The Three Pure Ones are the highest deities of religious Taoism, and Laozi in deified form is counted among them. The Jade Emperor is the ruler of heaven in popular Chinese and Taoist belief; legend says he chose the animals of the Chinese zodiac.

**Celestial Masters and the Five Pecks of Rice**
The Way of the Celestial Masters, founded by Zhang Daoling in the 2nd century CE, is the first organized Taoist religious movement. It was also called the Five Pecks of Rice movement after its membership dues, and it continues today as the Zhengyi school, which performs the multi-day jiao renewal ritual. The other major modern school is Quanzhen ("Complete Perfection"), centered at the White Cloud Temple in Beijing; its master Qiu Chuji famously visited Genghis Khan.

**Eight Immortals**
A group of legendary figures in Taoism who achieved immortality, including He Xiangu, the only woman among them, said to have eaten powdered mica. They are popular subjects of Chinese art and folklore. Sun Bu'er, who disfigured her face with boiling oil to travel safely, is one of the Seven Perfected of the Quanzhen school.

**Hell Bank Notes (joss paper)**
Paper "money," sometimes printed with the Jade Emperor, burned as offerings so that deceased ancestors can use it in the afterlife. It is a modern form of sacrifice in Chinese folk and Taoist practice.

**Pangu**
In Chinese creation myth associated with Taoism, Pangu is a giant who hatches from a cosmic egg and separates heaven and earth, holding them apart for 18,000 years. When he dies, his body becomes the features of the world.

**Kaaba**
The cube-shaped shrine at the center of Mecca's Great Mosque and the most sacred site in Islam. It is draped in the kiswah, a black cloth embroidered in gold, and its interior is cleaned with rosewater twice a year. Muslims believe Abraham and Ishmael built it.

**Hajj and tawaf**
The hajj, the annual pilgrimage to Mecca during the month of Dhu al-Hijjah, is the fifth Pillar of Islam, required once in a lifetime of every Muslim who is able to make it. Its central rite is tawaf, walking seven times counterclockwise around the Kaaba, with men taking the first three circuits at a quicker pace. During hajj, Mecca's population of about two million roughly doubles.

**Black Stone**
A sacred stone set in a silver frame in the eastern corner of the Kaaba, which pilgrims try to kiss, touch, or point to during tawaf. Tradition says it was originally white and turned black from the sins of those who touched it. The Qarmatians stole it in 930 and returned it in 952.

**Well of Zamzam**
A sacred well near the Kaaba that, according to tradition, God made spring up to save Hagar (Hajar) and her infant son Ishmael from dying of thirst in the desert. Pilgrims drink its water during the hajj.

**Sa'i between Safa and Marwah**
The hajj and umrah rite of walking or running seven times between the two small hills of Safa and Marwah, now enclosed within the Great Mosque. It re-enacts Hagar's frantic search for water for Ishmael.

**Stoning of the Devil**
A hajj ritual at Mina, outside Mecca, in which pilgrims throw seven pebbles at each of three pillars (now walls) that represent Satan tempting Abraham. The Jamarat Bridge was built to manage the dangerous crowds at this rite. Afterward, pilgrims sacrifice an animal for Eid al-Adha, with the meat going to the poor, and men shave their heads (halq) while women trim their hair (taqsir).

**Ihram**
The state of ritual purity pilgrims enter at boundary stations (miqat) before hajj or umrah. Men wear two unstitched, unhemmed white sheets, and pilgrims must avoid acts such as hunting, cutting their hair, and vanity. They recite the Talbiyah prayer, "Here I am, O God, here I am."

**Hijrah**
Muhammad's emigration in 622 from Mecca to Yathrib, which was renamed Medina, to escape persecution by the Quraysh. Ali slept in Muhammad's bed to deceive the assassins while Muhammad escaped with Abu Bakr. The event marks year one of the Islamic lunar calendar (AH).

**Qibla**
The direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, which Muslims face during their five daily prayers. In a mosque it is shown by the mihrab, a niche in the qibla wall.

**Quraysh and Hubal**
The Quraysh were the tribe that controlled Mecca and its shrine in Muhammad's time, and they at first opposed him. Before Islam, the Kaaba housed some 360 idols, chief among them Hubal, whose idol was used for divination with arrows. Muhammad cleared the idols after conquering Mecca with about ten thousand men in 630.

**Masjid al-Haram**
The Great Mosque of Mecca, which surrounds the Kaaba and is the largest mosque in the world. Non-Muslims are forbidden to enter Mecca.

**Maqam Ibrahim**
The "Station of Abraham," a stone near the Kaaba kept in a gold-colored case. It bears footprints said to have been left by Abraham as he stood on it while building the Kaaba.

**Mount Arafat**
A hill and plain outside Mecca where pilgrims stand in prayerful vigil on the ninth of Dhu al-Hijjah, the climax of the hajj. It commemorates Muhammad's Farewell Sermon, delivered on the Mount of Mercy (Jabal al-Rahmah). Pilgrims then spend the night at Muzdalifah.

**Umrah**
The "lesser pilgrimage" to Mecca, which shares rites such as ihram, tawaf, and sa'i with the hajj. Unlike hajj, it can be performed at any time of year and is not obligatory.

**Birthplace of Muhammad and the Cave of Hira**
Muhammad was born in Mecca in the "Year of the Elephant," named for a failed attack on the city by the Abyssinian ruler Abraha, whose army included an elephant. In the Cave of Hira, on a mountain just outside the city, he received his first revelation. His wife Khadijah and uncle Abu Talib died in Mecca in the "Year of Sorrow."

**Wedding at Cana**
In John 2, Jesus turns water into wine at a wedding feast in Cana, his first miracle and the first of the "seven signs" in John's Gospel. When his mother Mary tells him the wine has run out, he answers, "Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come." Servants then fill six stone jars with water, and the head waiter (steward) tells the bridegroom that, unlike others, he has kept the best wine for last.

**Borei pri hagafen**
The Hebrew blessing over wine, "Blessed are you, Lord our God, King of the universe, who creates the fruit of the vine." "Fruit of the vine" is the standard Jewish term for wine, and grape juice may be used in its place.

**Kiddush**
The prayer of sanctification recited over a cup of wine at the start of Shabbat and festival meals. On Shabbat, blessings are made over the candles, the wine, and the two challah loaves (with the HaMotzi blessing), and the challah is traditionally covered while the blessing over the wine is said.

**Four cups at the Passover Seder**
Everyone at the Passover Seder drinks four cups of wine, each of which is blessed with borei pri hagafen. Rabbinic tradition links the cups to God's four promises of redemption in Exodus, and one midrash links them to the four kingdoms that oppressed Israel: the Chaldeans (Babylonians), Medes, Greeks, and Romans.

**Drops for the Ten Plagues**
During the Seder, participants spill or dip out a drop of wine for each of the ten plagues on Egypt, lessening their own cup of joy to remember the suffering of the Egyptians.

**Last Supper and the Eucharist**
At the Last Supper, Jesus passes a cup of wine to his disciples and says, "This is my blood of the covenant" (Matthew 26), just before they leave for the Mount of Olives. In the Eucharist (Communion), sacramental wine is consumed along with the bread or host as the blood of Christ, and doctrines such as transubstantiation and sacramental union describe how the two are joined.

**Purim drinking**
The Talmud says Jews should drink wine on Purim until they can no longer tell the difference between "cursed be Haman" and "blessed be Mordecai," the villain and hero of the Book of Esther.

**Drunkenness of Noah**
After leaving the Ark, Noah plants a vineyard, drinks its wine, and lies drunk and naked in his tent (Genesis 9). His son Ham sees him, while Shem and Japheth walk in backward and cover him with a cloth, and Noah then curses Ham's son Canaan.

**Lot and his daughters**
After the destruction of Sodom, Lot's two daughters get him drunk on wine on two nights and sleep with him (Genesis 19). They give birth to Moab and Ben-Ammi, the ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites.

**"Wine that cheers the hearts of men"**
A phrase from Psalm 104 praising God's gifts. Because wine brings joy, Jewish law holds that drinking it fulfills the mitzvah of rejoicing on festival days.

**Mevushal wine and Manischewitz**
Mevushal ("cooked") wine has been heated so that it stays kosher even if a non-Jew or a non-observant Jew handles or pours it. Manischewitz is the best-known American brand of sweet kosher wine.

**Cup of Elijah**
A cup of wine poured at the Passover Seder for the prophet Elijah, who is expected to herald the Messiah. The door is opened during the Seder so that Elijah may enter and drink from it.

**Havdalah, brit milah, and Tu Bishvat**
In Havdalah, the ceremony that ends Shabbat, the braided candle is put out in wine. A drop of wine is given to the baby at a brit milah (bris), the circumcision ceremony. At the Tu Bishvat Seder, red and white wine are mixed in four cups.

**Prohibitions on wine**
The Nazirite vow requires abstaining from wine and all grape products. God warns Aaron and his sons not to drink wine before entering the Tabernacle, Proverbs 20:1 says "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is a brawler," and the Quran's Surah al-Ma'idah forbids intoxicants.

**Sour wine at the Crucifixion**
As Jesus is dying on the cross, a bystander offers him sour wine (vinegar) on a sponge on a reed, while others say, "Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to save him."

**Coat of many colors**
The richly ornamented coat that Jacob gave to Joseph, his favorite son, in Genesis 37. It made his brothers jealous, and they later dipped it in goat's blood to convince Jacob that Joseph had been killed by a wild animal.

**Potiphar's wife**
As a slave in Egypt, Joseph served Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, whose wife (traditionally named Zuleika or Zulaikha) tried to seduce him. When he refused, she falsely accused him of trying to rape her, and he was thrown into prison.

**Pharaoh's dreams of fat and lean cows**
Joseph interpreted Pharaoh's dreams, in which seven thin cows ate seven fat cows and seven thin ears of grain swallowed seven full ones. He explained that they meant seven years of plenty would be followed by seven years of famine, and he advised storing grain during the good years.

**Grand vizier of Egypt**
As a reward for interpreting Pharaoh's dreams, Joseph was made the second most powerful man in Egypt, in charge of preparing for the famine. Pharaoh gave him the Egyptian name Zaphnath-Paaneah and the wife Asenath.

**Sold into slavery by his brothers**
Joseph's jealous brothers threw him into a pit (well) and sold him to traders, who took him to Egypt as a slave. Reuben, the eldest, tried to save him, and Judah suggested selling him instead of killing him.

**Cupbearer and baker**
While in prison, Joseph interpreted the dreams of two of Pharaoh's officials. He correctly predicted that the cupbearer would be restored to his post and the baker executed, and the cupbearer later remembered him when Pharaoh needed a dream interpreter.

**Silver cup in Benjamin's sack**
When his brothers came to Egypt to buy grain during the famine, Joseph, who they did not recognize, had his silver cup hidden in the sack of his youngest brother Benjamin and then accused Benjamin of theft. This tested whether the brothers had changed before Joseph revealed who he was and brought the family to Egypt.

**Dream of the sheaves**
In his youth, Joseph dreamed that his sheaf of grain stood upright while his brothers' sheaves bowed down to it. In a second dream, the sun, moon, and eleven stars bowed to him, which angered his brothers even more.

**Manasseh and Ephraim**
Joseph's two sons by Asenath. When the aged and nearly blind Jacob blessed them, he crossed his hands to put his right hand on the younger Ephraim, giving him the greater blessing. Both became founders of tribes of Israel.

**Rachel, Jacob, and Laban**
Joseph was the first son of Rachel, Jacob's beloved wife. Jacob worked fourteen years for Rachel's father Laban to marry her and her sister Leah, and Rachel later died giving birth to Joseph's younger brother Benjamin.

**Burial at Shechem**
Before dying, Joseph made the Israelites swear to carry his bones out of Egypt. During the Exodus, Moses took his remains, and they were buried at Shechem in the land of Canaan.

**Joseph, husband of Mary**
In the New Testament, Joseph is the carpenter husband of Mary and the earthly father of Jesus. The genealogies in Matthew and Luke disagree on whether his father was Jacob or Heli.

**Joseph's dreams in Matthew**
When Joseph learned Mary was pregnant, he planned to divorce her quietly until an angel told him in a dream not to be afraid to take her as his wife. In a later dream, an angel told him to "flee to Egypt" with Mary and the infant Jesus to escape Herod, and after Herod's death he settled the family in Nazareth.

**Feasts of Saint Joseph**
The Catholic Church celebrates Saint Joseph's main feast on March 19. In 1955, Pope Pius XII created the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker on May 1 as a Christian alternative to the socialist May Day.

**Transubstantiation**
The Catholic doctrine that during the Eucharist the substance of the bread and wine truly becomes the body and blood of Christ, while their "accidents" (appearance, taste) remain, using Aristotelian categories. The Eastern Orthodox use the related Greek term "metousiosis."

**Last Supper**
The final meal Jesus shared with his apostles on the night he was betrayed, which the Eucharist commemorates and re-enacts. At it, he blessed bread and wine, called them his body and blood, and commanded "Do this in remembrance of me." It is commemorated on Holy (Maundy) Thursday.

**Real Presence**
The belief that Christ is truly, not just symbolically, present in the Eucharistic bread and wine. Catholics explain it through transubstantiation; Lutherans hold a "sacramental union" in which Christ is present "in, with, and under" the bread and wine (sometimes called consubstantiation); many other Protestants see the rite as a symbolic memorial.

**Marburg Colloquy**
A 1529 meeting where Martin Luther and Ulrich (Huldrych) Zwingli tried to unite the Protestant movement. They agreed on most points but split over the Eucharist: Luther insisted on the Real Presence, while Zwingli saw the rite as symbolic.

**Fourth Lateran Council**
The 1215 church council under Pope Innocent III that formally used and defined the term "transubstantiation." The Council of Trent reaffirmed the doctrine in the 16th century against Protestant objections.

**Anaphora (Eucharistic Prayer)**
The central consecration prayer of the Eucharist, especially in Eastern churches. It includes the anamnesis (a remembrance of Christ's saving acts) and the epiclesis (calling the Holy Spirit down on the gifts); common Orthodox versions are attributed to St. John Chrysostom and St. Basil.

**Words of Institution**
The words of Jesus repeated by the priest over the bread and wine, such as "This is my body" (Latin "Hoc est enim corpus meum") and "This is my blood" and "Do this in memory of me." They are drawn from 1 Corinthians 11:23–25 and the Gospels (e.g., Matthew 26 and Mark 14).

**Holy Qurbana**
The name for the Eucharist in Syriac Christian traditions, meaning "offering" or "sacrifice." It is associated with the ancient Liturgy of St. James.

**Bread (host, prosphora)**
The element representing Christ's body. Catholics use unleavened wafers (hosts); the Orthodox use leavened prosphora stamped with a seal (sphragis) bearing letters for "Jesus Christ conquers." Catholics sing the Agnus Dei during the Fraction Rite, when the host is broken.

**Melchizedek**
The priest-king of Salem who brings out bread and wine and blesses Abraham in Genesis 14. Church Fathers such as Clement of Alexandria, and later Thomas Aquinas, saw this offering as a prefiguration of the Eucharist.

**Agape feasts (love feasts)**
Communal meals held by early Christians, at which the Eucharist was originally celebrated. The two were later separated, and figures such as St. Augustine criticized holding the rite at such feasts.

**Foot washing**
A practice that precedes communion among groups such as Mennonites and Seventh-day Adventists, imitating Jesus washing the disciples' feet at the Last Supper. Adventists hold communion quarterly as an "open" rite available to non-members.

**Quam Singulari and First Communion**
A 1910 decree of Pope Pius X that allowed children to receive communion once they reach the "age of reason," around seven. Catholic children usually make their first confession (Reconciliation) first, and girls often wear white dresses resembling wedding gowns for First Communion.

**Monstrance and Eucharistic adoration**
A monstrance is an ornate vessel, often sunburst-shaped, used to display the consecrated host. Catholics use it for adoration of the Blessed Sacrament, which hymns like "Ave verum corpus" honor.

**Mustum, intinction, and the Didache**
Mustum is barely fermented grape juice permitted in place of wine; many Protestants use plain grape juice. Intinction is dipping the bread into the wine before receiving it. The Didache, an early Christian text, gives Eucharistic prayers in which the cup comes before the bread.

**Ash Wednesday**
The first day of Lent in Western Christianity. A priest marks worshippers' foreheads with a cross of ashes, traditionally made by burning palms from the previous year's Palm Sunday, while saying "Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return" (from Genesis 3:19) or "Repent, and believe in the Gospel."

**Forty days in the desert**
Lent's roughly forty days commemorate the forty days Jesus spent fasting in the wilderness after his baptism, where he was tempted by Satan. In one temptation, Jesus refuses the devil's challenge to turn stones into bread, replying that "man shall not live by bread alone."

**Clean Monday and Great Lent**
In Eastern Orthodox churches the season is called "Great Lent" and begins on Clean Monday, the Monday seven weeks before Easter. In Greece, the day is marked by eating lagana flatbread and meatless foods like shellfish and by flying kites.

**Giving something up**
Many Christians, especially Catholics, give up a luxury such as chocolate, coffee, or meat during Lent as an act of penance and self-discipline, alongside prayer, fasting, and almsgiving.

**Mardi Gras (Fat Tuesday)**
The day before Ash Wednesday, the climax of the Carnival season of feasting and celebration before the Lenten fast. It is also known as Shrove Tuesday.

**Abstaining from meat on Fridays**
Catholics are required to abstain from meat on Ash Wednesday and on all Fridays of Lent, which is why fish dishes are popular during the season.

**Good Friday and Holy Week**
Lent leads into Holy Week, which commemorates Jesus's entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday, the Last Supper, and his crucifixion on Good Friday. In Catholic practice, Lent proper ends before the Mass of the Lord's Supper on the evening of Holy Thursday, and Easter follows.

**Maundy Thursday**
The Thursday of Holy Week, commemorating the Last Supper and Jesus washing his disciples' feet. Many churches hold foot-washing ceremonies, and the British monarch traditionally distributes specially minted "Maundy money" in red and white leather purses.

**Omission of the Gloria and Alleluia**
As a sign of penance, the Catholic Mass leaves out the joyful "Gloria in excelsis Deo" and the "Alleluia" on Lent's Sundays and weekdays, and the Te Deum is dropped from the Office of Readings. The Alleluia returns at Easter.

**Purple vestments**
Catholic priests wear violet or purple vestments during Lent to signify penance, sacrifice, and preparation.

**Passiontide and veiled statues**
The last two weeks of Lent, beginning on the fifth Sunday, are called Passiontide. Traditionally, crosses, statues, and images in churches are covered with purple cloth during this time.

**Quadragesima**
The Latin name for Lent, meaning "fortieth," referring to its forty-day length. The six Sundays within Lent are not counted among the forty fasting days.

**Ambrosian Rite in Milan**
The Archdiocese of Milan follows its own Ambrosian Rite, in which Lent begins on the Sunday after the Roman Ash Wednesday rather than on Ash Wednesday itself.

**Funken bonfires and Śledzik**
Regional customs at the start of Lent. In parts of southern Germany, Austria, and Switzerland, Funken bonfires are lit on the first weekend of Lent. In Poland, Śledzik ("herring day") marks the end of Carnival with herring and vodka before the fast.

**Paschalis Sollemnitatis**
A 1988 Vatican document on preparing and celebrating the Easter feasts. Its first chapter concerns the observance of Lent.

**Haman**
The villain of the Book of Esther, chief minister (vizier) to the Persian king and called "the Agagite" (linked by tradition to the Amalekites). Angered that Mordecai will not bow to him, he plots to massacre all the Jews of the empire, but he is hanged on the very gallows he built for Mordecai.

**Mordecai**
Esther's cousin and guardian (often called her uncle), who raised her after her parents died. He refuses to bow to Haman, urges Esther to go to the king, and is ultimately honored and promoted to Haman's position.

**Purim**
The Jewish holiday celebrating the events of the Book of Esther, held on the 14th of Adar (the 15th in walled cities like Shushan). Its name comes from "pur," the lots Haman cast to choose the date of the massacre, and the book is read aloud during the festival.

**Megillah (Megillat Esther)**
"Scroll," the name for the Book of Esther as it is read from a handwritten scroll on Purim. It is one of the Five Megillot in the Writings section of the Hebrew Bible.

**Vashti**
The first queen of King Ahasuerus. She refuses his command to appear at his drunken banquet "with the crown royal" to show off her beauty, so she is deposed and banished, and a decree is sent out that "every man should bear rule in his own house." Esther is chosen to replace her.

**Ahasuerus (Xerxes)**
The Persian king of the story, usually identified with Xerxes I. He rules from the capital Shushan (Susa), marries Esther, lets Haman's decree go out, and later lets Mordecai issue a counter-decree allowing the Jews to defend themselves.

**God is never mentioned**
The Book of Esther, like the Song of Songs, never explicitly mentions God. This unusual feature is a frequent clue, along with theories that names like Esther and Mordecai echo the Babylonian deities Ishtar and Marduk.

**Bigthan and Teresh**
Two royal eunuchs (doorkeepers) who plot to assassinate King Ahasuerus. Mordecai overhears them and reports the plot through Esther; they are hanged, and Mordecai's deed is later read to the sleepless king, leading to his public honoring.

**Gallows of fifty cubits**
The gallows (or stake) about 75 feet high that Haman builds for Mordecai on the advice of his wife Zeresh. After Esther reveals the plot, Haman himself is hanged on it.

**Casting lots for the 13th of Adar**
Haman casts lots (pur) to pick the date of the massacre, which falls on the 13th of Adar. On that day the Jews instead defend themselves and defeat their enemies, and Purim celebrates the following day.

**Hadassah**
Esther's Hebrew name, meaning "myrtle." The American Jewish women's volunteer organization Hadassah is named after it.

**"For such a time as this" / "If I perish, I perish"**
Two famous quotes from Esther's decision to approach the king uninvited, which could be punished by death. Mordecai tells her she may have come to royal position "for such a time as this," and Esther, after a three-day fast, answers "if I perish, I perish."

**Esther's banquets and Haman on the couch**
Esther invites the king and Haman to banquets, where she reveals she is Jewish and exposes Haman's plot. When Haman throws himself on the couch where Esther is reclining to plead for his life, the king takes it as an assault on the queen and orders him executed.

**Graggers**
Noisemakers (also spelled groggers) that Jews shake, along with booing and stamping, to drown out Haman's name every time it is read from the Megillah on Purim.

**Hegai and the harem at Susa**
Hegai is the eunuch in charge of the king's women at Shushan. The young women chosen as candidates for queen undergo twelve months of beauty treatments (six months with oil of myrrh and six with perfumes) before going in to the king.

**Four Sights**
While Prince Siddhartha Gautama was growing up, his father, King Suddhodana, kept him sheltered in the palace. On trips outside it, Siddhartha saw an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic (monk). Shaken by the reality of suffering, he made the "Great Renunciation," leaving his wife Yasodhara and newborn son Rahula (whose name means "fetter") and riding off on his horse Kanthaka, which is said to have died of a broken heart afterward.

**Bodhi tree**
The sacred fig tree at Bodh Gaya under which Siddhartha meditated until he attained enlightenment and became the Buddha ("Awakened One"). Tradition says he then spent seven weeks (49 days) meditating nearby, during which the serpent king Mucalinda coiled around him and spread his hoods to shelter him from a storm.

**Deer Park at Sarnath (First Sermon)**
The Buddha's first sermon after enlightenment, delivered near Benares (Varanasi) to the five ascetics who had been his companions, including Kondanna (Kaundinya) and Assaji. Called "Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dharma," it laid out the Four Noble Truths and the Middle Way, and the five ascetics became his first disciples and the first arhats.

**Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path**
The core of the Buddha's teaching: life involves suffering (dukkha); suffering arises from craving; suffering can end; and the way to end it is the Eightfold Path (right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and concentration). Following it leads to nirvana and release from samsara, the cycle of rebirth.

**Middle Way**
The Buddha's teaching that the path to liberation avoids both indulgence in sensual pleasure and extreme self-denial. He arrived at it after years of severe asceticism nearly starved him to death.

**Queen Maya's dream of the white elephant**
Before Siddhartha was conceived, his mother, Queen Maya, dreamed that a white elephant with six tusks entered her right side. He was born in the Lumbini grove in present-day Nepal, and Theravada Buddhists celebrate his birth, enlightenment, and death on the holiday of Vesak.

**Flower Sermon**
A wordless teaching in which the Buddha simply held up a white flower before his assembled disciples at Vulture Peak. Only Mahakashyapa understood and smiled, and this mind-to-mind transmission is regarded as the origin of Zen Buddhism.

**Mara and the earth-touching mudra**
Before his enlightenment, the demon Mara attacked Siddhartha with armies and tempted him with his daughters. When Mara challenged his right to enlightenment, Siddhartha touched the ground and called the Earth to witness. This earth-touching gesture (bhumisparsha mudra) is one of the most common poses in Buddha statues.

**Fire Sermon**
A sermon that begins "All is burning," in which the Buddha teaches that the senses, the mind, and their objects are aflame with greed, hatred, and delusion. By growing disenchanted with them, a disciple achieves liberation.

**Parable of the poisoned arrow**
The Buddha's explanation for refusing to answer metaphysical questions (the "unanswered questions"). A man shot with a poisoned arrow who refuses treatment until he knows who shot it, and what the bow and arrow were made of, will die before learning the answers. Likewise, speculation distracts from ending suffering.

**Angulimala**
A notorious bandit who killed travelers and wore their fingers as a necklace, having been told by his teacher to collect a thousand fingers. The Buddha stopped him before he could kill his own mother, and Angulimala converted and became a monk.

**Last meal from Cunda**
The Buddha's final meal was given by Cunda, a blacksmith. It was a dish called sukara-maddava, interpreted as either pork or a food enjoyed by pigs, such as mushrooms. He fell ill afterward and passed into parinirvana (final nirvana) at Kushinagar.

**Anatta (Anattalakkhana Sutta)**
The Buddha's second discourse, given to the same five ascetics, teaching that form, feeling, perception, and the other aggregates are "not-self" (anatta). On hearing it, the five became arhats.

**Bamiyan Buddhas and other statues**
Two giant Buddha statues carved into a cliff in Afghanistan's Bamiyan valley were destroyed by the Taliban in 2001. Other famous images include the Daibutsu (Great Buddha) at Todai-ji in Nara, Japan, a stone Buddha head entwined in tree roots at Wat Mahathat in Ayutthaya, Thailand, and a statue standing in Hussain Sagar lake in Hyderabad. In the Chinese painting The Vinegar Tasters, the Buddha wears a bitter expression, Confucius a sour one, and Laozi a smile.

**Thirty-two marks of a great man**
Physical signs said to distinguish a Buddha, such as forty even teeth, a lion-like body, and wheels imprinted on the soles of the feet. At Siddhartha's birth, seers predicted he would become either a universal monarch or a world-saving spiritual teacher.

**Swallowed by a great fish (whale)**
The giveaway clue for Jonah: after being thrown overboard, he is swallowed by a "great fish," popularly called a whale, and spends three days and three nights inside it before it spits him onto dry land.

**Nineveh**
The Assyrian capital that God orders Jonah to preach against. When Jonah finally goes there and announces that the city will be destroyed in forty days, the people and their king repent, and God spares the city.

**Fleeing to Tarshish from Joppa**
Instead of going to Nineveh, Jonah runs away from God by boarding a ship at the port of Joppa (modern Jaffa) bound for Tarshish, a distant city in the opposite direction.

**The gourd and the worm**
While Jonah waits outside Nineveh to see whether it will be destroyed, God makes a plant (often translated "gourd" or "vine") grow to shade him, then sends a worm to make it wither. When Jonah is angry about the plant, God rebukes him for caring about a plant but not about the city. St. Jerome's Vulgate translated the plant as "ivy."

**The storm, casting lots, and being thrown overboard**
God sends a great storm against Jonah's ship. While Jonah sleeps below deck, the sailors cast lots to find out who caused it, and the lot falls on Jonah. He admits his guilt and tells them to throw him overboard, and the sea becomes calm.

**"The sign of Jonah"**
In the Gospels of Matthew (12:39) and Luke (11), when people demand a miraculous sign, Jesus says none will be given "but the sign of the prophet Jonas." In Matthew he compares Jonah's three days in the fish to his own three days in the earth before the resurrection, and he says that "a greater than Jonas is here."

**Son of Amittai**
Jonah's identifying patronym. 2 Kings 14:25 mentions "Jonah, the son of Amittai, the prophet" as having foretold King Jeroboam II's restoration of Israel's borders.

**"Cannot discern between their right hand and their left"**
God's final words in the Book of Jonah describe Nineveh's more than 120,000 people as unable to tell their right hand from their left, which God gives as a reason to have pity on them.

**Jonah's prayer from the belly of Sheol**
Chapter 2 of the book is a psalm Jonah prays inside the fish, beginning "I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the Lord, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell [Sheol] cried I." It includes the line "the earth with her bars was about me for ever."

**The king's sackcloth and fast**
After hearing Jonah's warning, the king of Nineveh removes his royal robe, covers himself in sackcloth, sits in ashes, and decrees a fast and repentance for everyone, even the animals.

**"It is better for me to die than to live"**
Jonah's complaint to God, spoken after God spares Nineveh and again after the plant withers. It reflects his anger that God showed mercy to Israel's enemies.

**Read on Yom Kippur**
The Book of Jonah is read in synagogues during the afternoon service of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, because of its themes of repentance and God's mercy.

**Dag and dagah**
The Hebrew text calls the fish a masculine "dag gadol" ("great fish") but in chapter 2 uses the feminine "dagah." Some interpreters, including a rabbinic tradition, explain the switch by saying Jonah was moved from one fish to another.

**Elijah and the widow's son**
According to rabbinic tradition, Jonah was the son of the widow of Zarephath whom the prophet Elijah raised from the dead.

**Yunus in Islam and Addas**
Jonah, called Yunus, is a prophet in the Quran, where a surah is named after him. According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad won over Addas, a Christian servant from Nineveh he met at Ta'if, by speaking of "my brother Yunus" from Addas's hometown.

**Holika and Prahlada**
The central legend of Holi. The demoness Holika, who was protected against fire, tried to kill her nephew Prahlada by sitting with him on a burning pyre on the orders of her brother. Because of Prahlada's devotion to Vishnu, he survived unharmed while Holika burned to death, and the festival is named after her.

**Holika Dahan bonfires**
On the night before the main day of Holi, people light large bonfires that represent Holika's pyre. They celebrate the triumph of good over evil and Prahlada's protection.

**Hiranyakashipu and Narasimha**
Hiranyakashipu was the demon king, Prahlada's father and Holika's brother, who hated his son's worship of Vishnu. He had a boon that made him nearly impossible to kill, including immunity to both thrown and handheld weapons (astra and shastra), so Vishnu took the form of Narasimha, a half-man, half-lion, and killed him with his claws.

**Gulal and abir**
The brightly colored powders that people throw at and smear on one another on Holi, which is why it is called the "Festival of Colors." Couples often paint each other's faces with gulal.

**Lathmar Holi**
A celebration in Barsana, the hometown of Radha in Uttar Pradesh, in which women playfully beat men with long bamboo sticks called lathis while the men protect themselves with shields. It is held in the days leading up to the main Holi celebration.

**Bhang and thandai**
Bhang is an edible preparation of cannabis traditionally consumed on Holi for its euphoric effects. It is often mixed into thandai, a cold, spiced milk drink. Bhang is also associated with Maha Shivaratri, which falls earlier in the year.

**Radha and Krishna**
Holi celebrates the love between Krishna and Radha. In legend, Krishna playfully colored the faces of Radha and the gopis (cowherd girls), who threw colors back at him. Celebrations are especially elaborate in Mathura and Vrindavan, where Krishna grew up, and can last for about 16 days.

**Phalguna Purnima**
The main Holi celebration falls on the full moon (Purnima) of the Hindu month of Phalguna, usually in March. It marks the end of winter and the arrival of spring.

**Kama and Rati**
In one origin legend, Shiva burned the love god Kamadeva to ashes with his third eye for disturbing his meditation. Kama's wife Rati then performed a 40-day penance, after which Shiva restored Kama to life, and some people make offerings to Kamadeva on Holi.

**Putana**
A demoness sent to kill the infant Krishna by nursing him with poisoned breast milk. Krishna sucked the life out of her instead, and in some regions her death is one of the legends associated with Holi.

**Pichkaris and natural colors**
Revelers fill water guns (pichkaris) and water balloons with colored water. Traditional colors were made from natural plant sources such as neem, kumkum, haldi (turmeric), and bilva.

**Human pyramids and the pot of butter**
In some celebrations, men form human pyramids to reach and break a pot of butter or curd hung high above the street. This imitates the young Krishna's habit of stealing butter, and the custom is more famously associated with the summer festival of Janmashtami.

**Rangapanchami**
A festival held five days after Holi, mainly in Maharashtra and central India, in which people throw colors again. It is especially popular in rural communities.

**Phagwah**
