In the Story of Sanjan (Qissa-i Sanjan), their ancestors are said to have convinced the local ruler Jadi Rana to accept them by stirring sugar into a full glass of milk, showing that they would sweeten the community without overflowing it.

**Frashokereti and the Saoshyant**
Frashokereti is the "final renovation" of the world at the end of time, when evil is destroyed and the dead are resurrected. It is brought about by the Saoshyant, a savior who will be born from a virgin who bathes in Lake Kansava, where Zarathustra's seed is preserved. During it, everyone must pass through a river of molten metal, which feels like warm milk to the righteous but burns the wicked.

**Navjote, sedreh, and kushti**
The Navjote is the initiation ceremony in which a Zoroastrian child formally enters the faith. The child receives a sedreh, a white cotton undershirt, and a kushti, a sacred girdle woven from 72 white woolen threads that represent the 72 chapters of the Yasna, and must wear both for life.

**Amesha Spentas**
The six "Bounteous Immortals" or "Divine Sparks," divine beings or aspects of Ahura Mazda that each represent a virtue. They are Vohu Manah (Good Mind or Good Purpose), Asha Vahishta (Best Righteousness), Khshathra Vairya (Desirable Dominion), Spenta Armaiti (Holy Devotion), Haurvatat (Wholeness), and Ameretat (Immortality). Zarathustra's prophetic calling began with a vision of Vohu Manah.

**Zurvanism and Mazdakism**
Zurvanism was a heretical branch of Zoroastrianism that made Zurvan, the god of infinite time and space, the first principle and father of both Ahura Mazda and Angra Mainyu. Mazdakism was a later reform movement led by Mazdak in Sasanian Persia, who preached a proto-socialist sharing of property and was accused by his enemies of promoting free love.

**Zarathustra (Zoroaster)**
The ancient Iranian prophet who founded the religion and composed the Gathas; his dates are uncertain and estimates range widely. Friedrich Nietzsche used him as the mouthpiece for his ideas, including the Übermensch, in Thus Spoke Zarathustra.

**Gayomart and Gavaevodata**
In the Zoroastrian creation story, told in the Middle Persian text Bundahishn, Gayomart was the first human and Gavaevodata was the primordial ox, from whose body the animals came. Both were killed by Angra Mainyu, and the first human couple, Mashya and Mashyana, grew from Gayomart's seed.

**Denkard**
A large encyclopedic Middle Persian work compiled in the 9th and 10th centuries that summarizes Zoroastrian beliefs, customs, and history, including traditions about how the 21 books (nasks) of the Avesta were preserved.

**Battle of Jericho**
Joshua's most famous victory and the usual giveaway. Following God's instructions, the Israelites marched around the walled city once a day for six days with seven priests blowing trumpets (shofars) and carrying the Ark of the Covenant; on the seventh day they circled it seven times, gave a great shout, and the walls collapsed.

**Successor of Moses**
Joshua, son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim, was Moses's assistant and was appointed to lead the Israelites after Moses died. He led the conquest of Canaan, the Promised Land, and the Book of Joshua tells his story.

**Rahab**
A prostitute (harlot) in Jericho who hid the two spies Joshua sent from Shittim, concealing them under stalks of flax on her roof. In return, she and her family were spared when the city fell; she marked her house by hanging a scarlet cord from her window.

**Sun and moon standing still at Gibeon**
During a battle against an alliance of five Amorite kings attacking the Gibeonites, Joshua asked God to make the sun stand still over Gibeon and the moon over the Valley of Aijalon so that the Israelites could finish the fight in daylight. The book claims there was never a day like it, when God heeded the voice of a man.

**Caleb and the twelve spies**
Moses sent twelve men, one from each tribe, to scout Canaan. Only Joshua and Caleb gave a favorable report urging the Israelites to enter; the people nearly stoned them, and God declared that these two would be the only adults of their generation to enter the Promised Land.

**Achan**
An Israelite who took forbidden plunder from Jericho (a Babylonian garment, silver, and a wedge of gold) that was meant to be devoted to God. His sin caused the Israelites' first defeat at Ai; he was identified by casting lots, and Joshua had him and his family stoned in the Valley of Achor.

**Ai**
A city whose first attack failed because of Achan's theft. In the second attempt, Joshua held out his javelin toward the city and used a feigned retreat to lure the defenders of Ai and Bethel out, while a hidden ambush force entered and burned the city.

**Gibeonites' deception**
The Hivite inhabitants of Gibeon, fearing destruction, disguised themselves as travelers from a distant land with worn-out sandals, patched wineskins, and moldy bread. They tricked Joshua into making a peace treaty, and afterward he made them woodcutters and water carriers for the Israelites.

**Battle of Rephidim against the Amalekites**
Joshua's first appearance (Exodus 17), when Moses had him lead the Israelite fighters against the Amalekites. The Israelites prevailed as long as Moses held up his hands on a nearby hill, so Aaron and Hur supported his arms until sunset.

**Crossing the Jordan and the twelve stones**
When priests carrying the Ark of the Covenant stepped into the Jordan River, its waters stopped flowing so the Israelites could cross on dry ground. Twelve stones, one per tribe, were taken from the riverbed as a memorial at Gilgal, and Joshua also set up twelve stones in the middle of the river where the priests had stood.

**Waters of Merom and Hazor**
Joshua defeated a northern coalition led by Jabin, king of Hazor, at the Waters of Merom, then captured and burned Hazor. This completed his conquests, and the book lists 31 kings that he defeated.

**Circumcision at Gibeath Haaraloth**
After crossing the Jordan, Joshua circumcised the generation of Israelite men born in the wilderness, using flint knives, at a place called the "hill of foreskins." It took place at Gilgal before the campaign against Jericho.

**Five kings in the cave at Makkedah**
After the battle at Gibeon, the five Amorite kings hid in a cave at Makkedah. Joshua had the cave sealed with large stones until the battle was over, then brought the kings out, executed them, and hung their bodies on trees.

**Hoshea and Timnath-serah**
Joshua's original name was Hoshea, which Moses changed to Joshua ("Yahweh is salvation"); the name is the same as "Jesus" in Greek. He received the town of Timnath-serah in Ephraim as his inheritance, oversaw the division of the land among the tribes (including the half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan), and was buried there.

**Yusha ibn Nun and Khidr**
In Islamic tradition, Joshua (Yusha) is identified as the young servant who traveled with Moses in the Quran's Surah 18 in search of the wise figure Khidr. They carried a fish that came back to life and slipped into the sea at the meeting place of the two seas, and the servant forgot to tell Moses until later.

**Tashlikh (tashlich)**
An afternoon ritual, usually on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, in which observers throw bread crumbs or pebbles into a river, stream, or other body of water to symbolically cast away their sins. It is based on Micah 7:19 ("You will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea") and is the single most common clue for the holiday.

**Shofar**
A ram's horn blown during Rosh Hashanah services, traditionally 100 times each morning (it is not blown when the holiday falls on Shabbat). The blasts include the tekiah (one long blast), shevarim (three broken blasts), and teruah (rapid staccato blasts), and they are meant as a call to spiritual awakening and repentance.

**Apples dipped in honey**
The signature food of Rosh Hashanah, eaten in hopes of a "sweet new year." Other symbolic foods include pomegranates (sometimes said to have 613 seeds, matching the 613 commandments) and carrot tzimmes; some avoid nuts because the gematria of the Hebrew word for nut (egoz) equals that of the word for sin (chet).

**First of Tishrei**
Rosh Hashanah falls on the first (and second) day of the month of Tishrei, the start of the civil year in the Hebrew calendar. It is the first of the High Holy Days and comes nine days before Yom Kippur on the tenth of Tishrei.

**Days of Awe (Yamim Nora'im) / Ten Days of Repentance**
The ten-day penitential period that begins on Rosh Hashanah and ends on Yom Kippur, devoted to teshuvah (return or repentance). The Avinu Malkeinu ("Our Father, Our King") prayer is recited throughout this period.

**Book of Life (Sefer Hachaim)**
According to tradition, God opens the Book of Life on Rosh Hashanah and inscribes each person's fate for the coming year, but the judgment is not sealed until Yom Kippur. This gives rise to the holiday greeting wishing someone to be "inscribed and sealed" for a good year.

**Yom Teruah**
The biblical name of the holiday ("Day of Shouting" or "Day of Blasting"), referring to the sounding of the shofar commanded in the Book of Numbers. Other alternate names are Yom HaZikaron ("Day of Remembrance") and Yom HaDin ("Day of Judgment").

**Jewish New Year**
Rosh Hashanah literally means "head of the year." It commemorates the creation of the world, and observers greet each other with "Shana tova" ("a good year"). Questions about New Year's celebrations in general often mention it alongside Nowruz and Chinese New Year.

**Selichot**
Penitential prayers recited in the days leading up to Rosh Hashanah (during the preceding month of Elul for Sephardim, and starting the Saturday night before the holiday for Ashkenazim). They ask God for forgiveness ahead of the season of judgment.

**Machzor**
The special prayer book used on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur in place of the everyday siddur. It contains the extended holiday liturgy, including a lengthened repetition of the Amidah prayer.

**Piyyutim and Unetanneh Tokef**
Piyyutim are liturgical poems added to the High Holy Day services. The most famous is Unetanneh Tokef, which describes God judging all creatures and deciding "who shall live and who shall die" in the coming year.

**Binding of Isaac (Akedah)**
The Torah readings for Rosh Hashanah are the birth of Isaac (Genesis 21) on the first day and the Akedah, Abraham's near-sacrifice of Isaac (Genesis 22), on the second day. The ram caught in the thicket in that story is linked to the use of a ram's horn as the shofar.

**Uman pilgrimage**
Breslov Hasidim travel each year to Uman, Ukraine, to spend Rosh Hashanah at the grave of their founder, Rabbi Nachman of Breslov. Tens of thousands of pilgrims make the journey.

**Fast of Gedaliah**
A minor fast day observed on the third of Tishrei, the day after Rosh Hashanah ends. It mourns the assassination of Gedaliah, the Jewish governor of Judah after the Babylonian conquest.

**Shana tova cards**
Greeting cards sent for the new year, popularly called "tovas." The Israeli artist Haggai is known for the images and light verses he created for them.

**Menorah (hanukkiah) and the shamash**
Hanukkah is celebrated by lighting a special nine-branched menorah, called a hanukkiah, over eight nights. The ninth candle, the shamash ("helper" or "servant"), is used to light the other eight, with one more candle added each night.

**Dreidel and "Nes gadol hayah sham"**
A four-sided spinning top used in a traditional Hanukkah gambling game, often played for coins or chocolate coins called gelt. Its four Hebrew letters, nun, gimel, hey, and shin, stand for "Nes gadol hayah sham," "A great miracle happened there." In Israel, the shin is replaced by a pe for "po," meaning "here."

**Miracle of the oil**
According to the Talmud, when the Maccabees rededicated the Second Temple, they found only enough pure oil to light the Temple menorah for one day, but it miraculously burned for eight days. This is why Hanukkah lasts eight days and is called the Festival of Lights. "Hanukkah" itself means "dedication."

**Maccabees and Antiochus IV**
Hanukkah commemorates the Maccabean Revolt (167–160 BCE), in which Jewish rebels led by Judah Maccabee defeated the Seleucid Greek king Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Antiochus had outlawed Jewish practice and desecrated the Temple in Jerusalem, which the rebels recaptured and rededicated.

**Ma'oz Tzur**
"Rock of Ages," the best-known Hanukkah hymn, sung after the candles are lit. It recounts God's deliverances of the Jewish people from Egypt, Babylon, Haman, and the Greeks, and one stanza laments that "deliverance has too long been delayed."

**Latkes and sufganiyot**
Foods fried in oil are eaten on Hanukkah to recall the miracle of the oil. Latkes are fried potato pancakes, and sufganiyot are jelly-filled doughnuts popular in Israel.

**25th of Kislev**
The Hebrew calendar date on which Hanukkah begins, usually falling in late November or December. It marks the date on which the Maccabees rededicated the Temple.

**Hillel and Shammai's debate**
The Talmud records a dispute between these two schools of rabbis over the order of lighting the candles. The House of Shammai said to light eight candles on the first night and one fewer each night, while the House of Hillel said to start with one and add one each night; Hillel's practice is followed today.

**Judith and Holofernes**
Some Jews eat cheese and other dairy foods on Hanukkah to honor Judith, the heroine of the Book of Judith. She fed salty cheese and wine to Holofernes, the general of the Assyrian army, and beheaded him once he fell asleep, saving her town.

**Al HaNissim**
"For the Miracles," a prayer added during Hanukkah to the hoda'ah (thanksgiving) section of the Amidah and to the grace after meals. It thanks God for the miracles and victories of the Maccabees.

**Mi Yimalel**
"Who Can Retell?", a popular Hanukkah song asking who can recount the mighty deeds of Israel and praising the heroes who saved the Jewish people.

**Zot Hanukkah**
"This is Hanukkah," the name given to the eighth and last day of the holiday. It is named after a phrase in the Torah reading for that day about the dedication of the altar.

**Psalm 91**
Some Jews have a custom of reciting Psalm 91, a psalm of divine protection, seven times after lighting the Hanukkah candles.

**Yad**
The small pointer, usually shaped like a rod ending in a hand with an extended index finger ("yad" means "hand"), used to follow the text while reading from a Torah scroll. It is used because the parchment should not be touched by bare hands, both to protect the scroll and to avoid making it impure.

**Simchat Torah**
The joyous holiday ("Rejoicing in the Torah") in the month of Tishrei that comes right after Sukkot, coinciding with or following Shemini Atzeret, the "eighth day of assembly." Torah scrolls are taken out of the Ark and carried in circuits while congregants sing and dance, sometimes in the street, as the annual cycle of readings ends and starts again.

**Aron kodesh (Torah Ark)**
The cabinet or chest in a synagogue in which the Torah scrolls are kept, usually on the wall facing Jerusalem. It is covered by a decorated curtain called the parochet, and the scrolls inside are often adorned with crowns.

**613 commandments (mitzvot)**
The traditional number of commandments contained in the Torah. The last of them, the 613th, commands every Jew to write (or have written) a Torah scroll.

**Sofer**
The trained scribe who handwrites a Torah scroll in a special script (ktav stam) with decorative crowns (tagin) on certain letters, using ink on parchment made of gevil or klaf. A scroll has 304,805 letters with no vowels, often 42 lines per column, and can take over a year to write; a sheet with errors must be replaced and a new one sewn in.

**Bar mitzvah**
The coming-of-age ceremony at which a Jewish boy, at age 13, is called up to read from the Torah for the first time. Girls do the same at a bat mitzvah in many communities.

**Parashot (weekly portions)**
The 54 sections into which the Torah is divided, one (or sometimes two) of which is read at synagogue each week so that the whole Torah is completed every year. The first portion, Bereshit ("In the Beginning"), covers the creation of the world.

**Bimah and aliyah**
The bimah is the raised platform in the synagogue on which the Torah scroll is laid and read. An aliyah ("going up," the same word used for immigrating to Israel) is the honor of being called to the bimah to recite the blessings over a Torah reading, which begin "Barchu et Adonai ha-mevorach," with the gabbai directing who is called; the final aliyah is called maftir.

**Cantillation (trope)**
The system of musical marks that indicate how each word of the Torah is to be chanted, including signs such as the etnachta, pazer, and the rare shalshelet, which appears only four times. Because the scroll itself has no vowels or trope marks, readers prepare with a printed guide called a tikkun.

**Hagbah and gelilah**
The rituals after a Torah reading in which the open scroll is lifted up to show the congregation (hagbah) and then rolled up and dressed in its cover (gelilah). During hagbah some congregants point toward the scroll with their little finger or the fringes of their prayer shawl.

**Tefillin and mezuzah**
Ritual objects containing small handwritten parchments with passages from the Torah, such as the Shema. Tefillin are small black leather boxes worn on the arm and head during weekday morning prayer, and a mezuzah is a case attached to a doorpost.

**Oral Torah**
The body of interpretation believed to have been given to Moses alongside the Written Torah and passed down orally until it was written down in the Mishnah and the Gemara, which together form the Talmud. It is rejected by the Karaites and was rejected by the ancient Sadducees, who accepted only the Written Torah.

**Five Books of Moses**
The Torah's contents: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, also called the Pentateuch and forming the first part of the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh). Tradition holds that Moses wrote them, with Joshua writing the final lines describing Moses's death, and that Ezra the Scribe later restored and compiled the text.

**Documentary Hypothesis**
The scholarly theory that the Torah was assembled from several earlier independent sources, usually labeled J, E, D, and P, rather than written by a single author. It is a common modern-scholarship clue for the Torah.

**Rumi and the Mevlevi Order**
Jalal al-Din Rumi, the 13th-century Persian poet who lived in Konya, Anatolia, is the most famous Sufi. The Mevlevi order, named for his title "Mevlana" ("our master"), was founded by his followers, and his long mystical poem, the Masnavi, is a central Sufi text.

**Whirling dervishes**
Members of the Mevlevi order who perform a spinning dance as a form of worship. "Dervish" refers to a Sufi initiate who has embraced a life of spiritual poverty.

**Dhikr**
"Remembrance" of God, the central Sufi devotional practice: rhythmic, repeated recitation of God's names or short religious phrases, done alone or in groups.

**Sema (sama)**
"Listening," a Sufi ceremony of music, poetry, and sometimes dance used as communal dhikr. The Mevlevi sema features the whirling dance, and a large annual pilgrimage to Konya commemorates Rumi's death with sema performances.

**Tariqas**
Sufi orders or "paths," each led by a master (shaykh) and passing down its teachings through a chain of masters and disciples. Examples include the Mevlevi, Chishti, Naqshbandi, Qadiri, and Mouride orders.

**Wool garments (suf)**
The name "Sufi" is traditionally derived from suf, the Arabic word for wool, after the coarse woolen robes worn by early ascetic mystics.

**Fana**
"Annihilation" of the self in God, the goal of the Sufi path, in which the ego is extinguished. It is often paired with baqa ("subsistence"), a state of living on in God after the self is annihilated.

**Chishti order and Fatehpur Sikri**
The Chishti order is prominent in South Asia. Its saint Salim Chishti is buried in a dargah (shrine tomb) at the Mughal city of Fatehpur Sikri, which the emperor Akbar built in his honor and which is a major pilgrimage site.

**Mourides and the Grand Magal**
The Mouride brotherhood is a Sufi order in Senegal founded by Amadou Bamba. Its Grand Magal is an annual pilgrimage to the holy city of Touba.

**Rabia al-Adawiyya**
An 8th-century woman mystic of Basra who stressed pure love of God. She is known for a prayer asking God to burn her in Hell if she worshipped him from fear of Hell, and to bar her from Paradise if she worshipped him in hope of Paradise.

**Al-Ghazali**
A medieval Persian theologian of the Ash'ari school who turned to Sufism after a spiritual crisis. His Revival of the Religious Sciences helped bring Sufism into mainstream Sunni Islam.

**Ibn Arabi**
A 12th–13th-century Andalusian mystic, called "the Greatest Master," who was among the most influential Sufi thinkers. He wrote extensively on mystical love and union with God.

**Walayah and walis**
Walayah is the "saintly" power or closeness to God held by Sufi saints, called walis ("friends of God"). Sufis see it as a reflection of the light of prophecy.

**Al-fuqara ("the poor")**
Sufis call themselves "the poor," following the saying attributed to Muhammad that "poverty is my pride." The Arabic word faqir (poor man) is the source of the English word "fakir."

**Marifa**
Direct, experiential knowledge of God, contrasted with book learning. Sufis seek it as one of the highest goals of the spiritual path.

**Stoning of Stephen**
Stephen, one of seven deacons chosen to serve the Jerusalem community, is tried before the Sanhedrin. After declaring that he sees the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God, he is stoned to death, becoming the first Christian martyr (Acts 7). A young man named Saul watches and approves of the execution.

**Conversion of Saul on the road to Damascus**
Saul, a persecutor of Christians, is struck blind by a light from heaven on the road to Damascus and hears Jesus ask, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" (Acts 9). A disciple named Ananias restores his sight and baptizes him. Saul, also called Paul, becomes the great missionary apostle whose journeys fill the second half of the book.

**Dedication to Theophilus and Lukan authorship**
Like the Gospel of Luke, Acts opens with a dedication to a man named Theophilus, and both books are traditionally attributed to Luke the Evangelist. Acts is the fifth book of the New Testament, following the four Gospels.

**Pentecost and tongues of fire**
In Acts 2, the Holy Spirit descends on the apostles with a sound like a rushing wind and tongues of fire resting on each of them. They begin speaking in other languages and are understood by a crowd from many nations, and Peter preaches a sermon that converts about three thousand people.

**Matthias chosen by lot**
In Acts 1, the apostles cast lots to choose Matthias as the replacement for Judas Iscariot. Acts describes Judas falling headlong and bursting open, so that all his intestines spilled out.

**Paul at the Areopagus and the "unknown god"**
In Athens, Paul preaches on the Areopagus (Mars Hill), telling the Athenians that the god they honor at an altar "to an unknown god" is the true God (Acts 17). Dionysius the Areopagite is among those who believe.

**Philip, Simon Magus, and the Ethiopian eunuch**
Philip the Evangelist, another of the seven deacons, converts the Samaritan sorcerer Simon Magus, who then tries to buy the power of the Holy Spirit from Peter. The attempt gave the word "simony" its name. Philip is then sent to the road to Gaza, where he baptizes an Ethiopian eunuch, the treasurer of Queen Candace.

**Ananias and Sapphira**
A married couple in the early Jerusalem church who sell land but secretly keep part of the money while claiming to give all of it to the apostles. When Peter confronts them about the lie, each falls dead (Acts 5).

**Shipwreck on Malta and journey to Rome**
The book ends with Paul being taken to Rome as a prisoner to appeal to Caesar. His ship wrecks on Malta, where he survives a viper bite and heals the father of Publius, the island's chief official, of fever and dysentery.

**Peter's vision and Cornelius**
Peter, staying at Joppa, sees a vision of a sheet full of unclean animals and hears a voice say, "Rise, Peter; kill and eat" (Acts 10). Meanwhile an angel tells the Roman centurion Cornelius to send for Peter, and Cornelius and his household become the first Gentile converts baptized by Peter.

**Paul and Barnabas called Zeus and Hermes**
After Paul heals a lame man in Lystra, the crowd takes Paul and Barnabas for the gods Hermes and Zeus and tries to sacrifice to them, and the two tear their clothes in protest (Acts 14). They had been set apart for missionary work by the church at Antioch.

**Earthquake at the Philippi prison**
Paul and Silas, jailed in Philippi, are freed when an earthquake opens the prison doors, but they stay so the jailer will not be punished. The grateful jailer and his household convert (Acts 16).

**Ascension of Jesus**
Acts opens with Jesus ascending into heaven forty days after his resurrection, after promising the disciples that they will receive the Holy Spirit.

**Peter's release from prison and Tabitha**
An angel frees Peter from Herod's prison in Acts 12. Earlier, Peter heals the paralyzed Aeneas and raises the disciple Tabitha (Dorcas) from the dead at Joppa (Acts 9).

**Eutychus, Gamaliel, and Priscilla and Aquila**
Eutychus is a young man in Troas who falls asleep during Paul's long sermon, falls from a third-story window, and is restored to life by Paul. Gamaliel is a Pharisee who advises the Sanhedrin to leave the apostles alone, since a movement from God cannot be stopped. Priscilla and Aquila are tentmakers who host and work with Paul.

**Diyas**
Small clay oil lamps lit in rows in homes, temples, and streets during Diwali, which is why it is called the "festival of lights." The holiday's other name, Deepavali, means "row of lamps." The lamps symbolize the victory of light over darkness and good over evil, and they are said to light the way home for Rama and to welcome Lakshmi.

**Rangoli**
Colorful decorative patterns drawn on floors and doorsteps, often in circular or radial designs, using colored powder, chalk, rice, sand, or flower petals. They are made to welcome guests and the goddess Lakshmi into the home, and some households also draw small footprints in rice flour and vermilion to represent her entering.

**Lakshmi and Lakshmi Puja**
Lakshmi is the Hindu goddess of wealth and prosperity, and Diwali celebrates her birth from the churning of the Ocean of Milk. The Lakshmi Puja, the main worship of the festival, takes place on the third and central day, when families clean their homes and light lamps so she will visit, offer her sweets, and often worship Ganesha as well. People also make major purchases, such as new clothes, in her honor.

**Rama and Sita's return to Ayodhya**
The most common story behind Diwali comes from the epic Ramayana: the prince Rama returned to his kingdom of Ayodhya with his wife Sita (and his brother Lakshmana) after 14 years of exile and his victory over the demon king Ravana. The people of Ayodhya lit lamps to welcome them home, a custom Diwali's diyas recall.

**Bhai Duj**
The fifth and final day of Diwali, which celebrates the bond between brothers and sisters; it is also called Bhaubeej, Bhai Tika, or Yama Dvitiya. Brothers visit their sisters' homes, where sisters pray for their well-being and feed them, and brothers give gifts in return. It is linked to the stories of the death god Yama visiting his sister Yamuna and of Krishna visiting his sister Subhadra.

**Narakasura and Naraka Chaturdashi**
The second day of Diwali, Naraka Chaturdashi (also called Choti Diwali), celebrates the slaying of the demon Narakasura, usually credited to Krishna, which freed the many people he held captive. In southern India, it is marked by an early-morning ritual oil bath, often with sesame oil.

**Bandi Chhor Divas**
The Sikh holiday celebrated at the same time as Diwali, meaning "Day of Liberation." It commemorates the release of the sixth Sikh Guru, Hargobind, from imprisonment in Gwalior Fort by the Mughal emperor Jahangir. The Guru insisted that 52 imprisoned princes be freed with him, and he returned to Amritsar on Diwali.

**Mahavira's nirvana**
Jains celebrate Diwali as the anniversary of Mahavira, the 24th tirthankara, attaining final liberation (moksha or nirvana) on the new moon night of Kartik. The following day begins the Jain new year.

**Dhanteras**
The first day of Diwali, when people traditionally buy new utensils, metal goods, and gold as a sign of good fortune. It honors Dhanvantari, the god of medicine and Ayurveda, who emerged from the Ocean of Milk carrying the nectar of immortality. A legend also tells how the wife of King Hima's son saved him from death by keeping him awake with lamps and treasures, so that Yama, coming as a snake, was dazzled and left.

**Annakut and Padwa**
The fourth day of Diwali, which marks the start of the Hindu month of Kartik and the new year in many regions. Annakut ("mountain of food") or Govardhan Puja recalls Krishna lifting Govardhan Hill, and devotees offer mounds of food and sometimes build small hills of cow dung decorated with flowers. Padwa celebrates the bond between husband and wife, and husbands give gifts to their wives.

**Tihar**
The Nepali version of Diwali, a five-day festival celebrated by Hindus and Buddhists. Each day honors a different being: Kukur Tihar, the second day, honors dogs with garlands and food, and garlands of globe amaranth flowers are used in rituals such as Bhai Tika. Among the Newar people, the festival also includes Swanti.

**Kali Puja**
In West Bengal and other parts of eastern India, people worship the fierce goddess Kali on the Diwali new moon night instead of, or alongside, Lakshmi.

**Month of Kartik and the merchants' new year**
Diwali's main day falls on the new moon (amavasya), the darkest night, in the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, usually in October or November. Many Hindu merchants and business owners, especially Gujaratis and Marwaris, begin their new financial year at Diwali and open new account books.

**Mithai**
Sweets, such as barfi, ladoo, and sandesh, that are offered to Lakshmi in puja and exchanged as gifts with family and friends. Eating and sharing large amounts of sweets is one of the most characteristic customs of the festival.

**Firecrackers**
Fireworks and firecrackers are set off widely during Diwali, which causes severe air and noise pollution in Indian cities. In 2015, the Supreme Court of India declined to impose a complete ban on firecrackers during the festival, although later rulings restricted their use.

**Lingam**
Shiva's most common symbol of worship, an aniconic, often cylindrical stone, usually set in a base called the yoni, and widely interpreted as phallic. It represents Shiva's creative energy and formless nature, and it stands in the inner sanctum of most Shiva temples.

**Nataraja**
"Lord of Dance," Shiva's form as the cosmic dancer who performs the tandava, the dance that destroys and re-creates the universe. In the famous Chola bronzes he dances inside a ring of fire, holding a drum and a flame, while trampling the dwarf Apasmara, who embodies ignorance.

**Destroyer in the Trimurti**
Shiva is the member of the Hindu trinity (Trimurti) responsible for destruction, alongside Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver. His destruction clears the way for renewal, and his devotees, the Shaivas, worship him as the supreme god.

**Mount Kailash**
The Himalayan peak in Tibet where Shiva lives with his wife Parvati and their children. It is a major pilgrimage site, and devotees walk around its base.

**Rudra**
The fierce Vedic storm god of the Rig Veda, feared and asked to be pacified, who is the main predecessor of the later Shiva. "Shiva," meaning "auspicious," began as an epithet for Rudra.

**Ganesha and Kartikeya**
Shiva's sons with Parvati. Ganesha is the elephant-headed remover of obstacles, and Kartikeya (also called Skanda or Murugan) is the god of war.

**Halahala poison and the blue throat**
During the churning of the ocean of milk, a deadly poison called halahala emerged that threatened to destroy the world. Shiva drank it and held it in his throat (Parvati stopped it from going further), which turned his throat blue and earned him the name Nilakantha ("blue-throated").

**Sati and Parvati**
Shiva's wives. Sati burned herself to death after her father Daksha insulted Shiva, and she was reborn as Parvati, who won Shiva through intense austerities.

**The Ganges in his hair**
When the river Ganga descended from heaven to earth, Shiva caught her in his matted locks to soften the impact of her fall so it would not shatter the earth. He then released her in gentle streams.

**Trident (trishula) and the third eye**
Shiva carries a trident and has a third eye on his forehead, whose fiery gaze burned Kama, the god of love, to ashes. His epithet Tryambaka means "three-eyed."

**Nandi**
The sacred white bull who is Shiva's mount and gatekeeper. A statue of Nandi usually sits facing the inner sanctum of Shiva temples, gazing at the lingam.

**Twelve Jyotirlingas**
Twelve major Shiva shrines in India, said to mark places where Shiva appeared as an endless pillar of light (fire). In the related myth, Brahma and Vishnu searched in vain for the top and bottom of the pillar.

**Pashupatastra and Arjuna**
In the Mahabharata, Shiva, disguised as a Kirata (a mountain hunter), quarreled with Arjuna over a boar they had both shot and then fought him. Pleased by Arjuna's courage, Shiva revealed himself and granted him the mighty Pashupatastra weapon.

**Maha Mrityunjaya Mantra**
A Rig Vedic mantra ("Tryambakam yajamahe...") addressed to Shiva as the three-eyed one, praying for liberation from death. It is one of the most widely chanted Hindu mantras.

**Nayanars, Amarnath, and Ravana**
The Nayanars were 63 Tamil Shaiva poet-saints whose lives are told in the Periya Puranam, written by Sekkizhar. The Amarnath cave in Kashmir holds an ice stalagmite worshipped as a natural lingam, and the demon king Ravana is famed as a great devotee of Shiva. In abhisheka worship, a pot with a small hole is hung above the lingam to drip milk or water onto it.

**Binding of Isaac on Mount Moriah (the Akedah)**
God tests Abraham by commanding him to sacrifice his son Isaac on Mount Moriah; Abraham binds the boy on an altar, but an angel stops him and a ram caught in a thicket is offered instead. God then promises to multiply his descendants "as the stars in the heavens and as the sand on the shores of the sea." Jewish tradition calls this the Akedah ("binding"), and Abraham answers God's call with "Hineini" ("Here I am").

**Eid al-Adha and Qurbani**
The Islamic "Festival of the Sacrifice" commemorates Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son, whom Muslims usually identify as Ishmael (Isma'il) rather than Isaac. Muslims perform Qurbani, the slaughter of an animal, in his honor, and pilgrims on Hajj perform the Stoning of the Devil at three pillars, recalling Ibrahim driving away Shaitan when he tempted him to disobey God.

**Builder of the Kaaba**
In Islamic tradition, Ibrahim and his son Ishmael built (or rebuilt) the Kaaba in Mecca, the cube-shaped shrine Muslims face in prayer, and the angel Jibreel brought him the Black Stone set in its corner. The Maqam Ibrahim, a stone near the Kaaba kept in a gilded enclosure, is believed to bear his footprints, and he is credited with establishing the rites of Hajj.

**Hagar (Hajar) and Ishmael; Safa and Marwa; Zamzam**
Abraham fathered his firstborn Ishmael with Hagar, the Egyptian handmaid of his wife Sarah, and later sent mother and son away at Sarah's insistence after Isaac's birth. In Islamic tradition Hajar ran seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa seeking water until God made the Zamzam well spring up near the crying infant; Hajj pilgrims re-enact her run, and Ishmael became the ancestor of the Arabs and of Muhammad.

**Thrown into Nimrod's fire**
In the Quran and Jewish midrash, the tyrant king Nimrod (Namrud) has Ibrahim thrown (in some versions catapulted) into a great fire for rejecting idols. God commands the fire to be "cool" and "peaceful" for him, and in some tellings it burns only his chains, so he walks out unharmed.

**"Make the sun rise from the West"**
In Surah al-Baqarah, Ibrahim debates Nimrod about God's power. When Nimrod claims he too can give life and death, Ibrahim says that God brings the sun from the East and challenges the king to make it rise from the West, leaving him dumbfounded. In later legend, Nimrod is then destroyed by an army of gnats.

**Smashing his father's idols (Azar / Terah)**
The Quran names his father Azar; Genesis names him Terah, an idol maker or idol seller in Ur. In a famous midrash, the young Abraham smashes every idol in the shop except the largest, hangs his axe on it, and says the big idol did it, exposing that idols are powerless. This rejection of idolatry earns him the Islamic epithet hanif (a pure monotheist before Islam, opposed to the pagan Jahiliyyah) and the title Khalilullah, "Friend of God."

**Bargaining for Sodom: ten righteous men**
In Genesis 18, Abraham pleads with God to spare Sodom and Gomorrah, haggling the number of righteous people needed down from fifty to ten. Ten cannot be found, so the cities are destroyed, though his nephew Lot and Lot's daughters escape.

**Claiming his wife was his sister**
Twice Abraham passes off his wife Sarah as his sister to protect himself: first before the Pharaoh of Egypt, and later before Abimelech, king of Gerar, who takes her into his house. Abimelech returns her after a divine warning and gives Abraham a thousand pieces of silver; Abraham later swears an oath with Abimelech at Beersheba and plants a tamarisk tree there.

**Battle of the Vale of Siddim and Melchizedek**
When King Chedorlaomer and his allies capture Lot, Abraham leads 318 trained men to rescue him. Afterward Melchizedek, priest-king of Salem, brings out bread and wine and blesses him, and Abraham gives him a tenth of the spoils; Hebrews 7 uses this tithe to argue that Christ's priesthood "after the order of Melchisedec" is superior to the Levitical priesthood.

**Cave of Machpelah (Cave of the Patriarchs)**
Abraham buys this cave in Hebron from Ephron the Hittite to bury Sarah, and he is later buried there himself. It becomes the tomb of the patriarchs and matriarchs, and after Sarah's death Abraham fathers more children, including Midian, with Keturah.

**Three visitors and Sarah's laughter**
At the oaks of Mamre, Abraham hosts three strangers, later revealed as angels, and serves them a meal of meat and dairy. They announce that the elderly Sarah, about ninety, will bear a son; she laughs, and the boy is named Isaac (Yitzhak, "he laughs"). Christians often read this scene as a foreshadowing of the Trinity, and in the Quranic version the guests refuse to eat.

**Covenant: from Abram to Abraham**
God calls Abram out of his homeland to Canaan in the Torah portion "Lech Lecha" ("Go forth"), and he builds an altar at Shechem where the land is promised to his offspring. In the covenant of Genesis 17, his name changes from Abram to Abraham ("father of many nations"), Sarai becomes Sarah, and Abraham circumcises himself at age 99.

**Four birds on four hills**
In Surah al-Baqarah, when Ibrahim asks God to show him how He raises the dead, God tells him to cut up four birds and place their pieces on separate hills. When Ibrahim calls them, the birds come back to life and fly to him.

**Faith "counted to him as righteousness"**
Genesis 15:6, which says Abraham "believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness," is quoted three times in the New Testament, notably in Romans 4, where Paul notes that Abraham saw his own body "as good as dead" yet trusted God's promise of an heir. Hebrews 11 praises him for leaving home "not knowing where he was going," and in John 8 Jesus tells the Pharisees, "Before Abraham was, I am."

**Golden calf**
While Moses was on Mount Sinai receiving the Law, his brother Aaron made a golden calf idol for the impatient Israelites to worship. On returning, Moses smashed the two stone tablets in anger, burned the calf, ground it to powder, mixed it with water, and made the people drink it.

**Burning bush**
On Mount Horeb, while tending his father-in-law's flocks in Midian, Moses encountered God speaking from a bush that burned without being consumed. God revealed his name as "I AM THAT I AM" (associated with Yahweh) and gave Moses signs, turning his staff into a snake and making his hand leprous, "white as snow," and then healing it, before sending him back to Egypt.

**Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai**
Moses ascended Mount Sinai to receive the Ten Commandments on two stone tablets, establishing God's covenant with Israel. When he came down, his face shone so brightly with God's glory that he wore a veil.

**Parting of the Red Sea**
During the Exodus, Moses stretched out his staff to divide the sea so the Israelites could cross on dry land, then stretched out his hand again to bring the waters down and drown Pharaoh's pursuing army. Afterward his sister, the prophetess Miriam, led the women in song: "the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea."

**Zipporah and Jethro**
In Midian, Moses defended the seven daughters of the priest Jethro (also called Reuel) from shepherds at a well, and he married one of them, Zipporah. In a strange episode, God sought to kill Moses until Zipporah circumcised their son with a flint and called Moses a "bridegroom of blood."

**Basket in the Nile**
To save him from Pharaoh's decree that Hebrew baby boys be killed, Moses's mother Jochebed placed him in a basket (ark) of reeds among the bulrushes of the Nile. He was found by Pharaoh's daughter (called Batyah in Jewish tradition), who raised him in the royal court, while his sister Miriam arranged for Jochebed to nurse him.

**Striking the rock**
Moses brought forth water for the thirsty Israelites by striking a rock with his staff, first at Rephidim. On a later occasion at Meribah, he struck the rock instead of speaking to it as God commanded, and for this disobedience he was forbidden to enter the Promised Land of Canaan.

**Bronze serpent (Nehushtan)**
When the Israelites were plagued by "fiery serpents," Moses mounted a bronze serpent on a pole, and those who looked at it were healed of their snakebites. In John 3:14, speaking to Nicodemus, Jesus compares his own coming crucifixion ("lifted up") to this act.

**Mount Nebo**
The mountain from which Moses viewed the Promised Land across the Jordan before dying at the age of 120; Deuteronomy says that "his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated." Leadership of the Israelites then passed to Joshua.

**Killing the Egyptian overseer**
As a young man, Moses saw an Egyptian taskmaster beating a Hebrew slave and killed him. When the deed became known, he fled Egypt to Midian.

**Hot coal test**
In a Jewish legend, Pharaoh tested whether the infant Moses was a threat by offering him gold (or a jewel) and a hot coal. An angel guided his hand to the coal, which he put in his mouth, burning his tongue, which is said to explain his later speech impediment.

**Battle against the Amalekites**
At Rephidim, the Israelites prevailed against the Amalekites as long as Moses held up his hands with his staff. When he grew tired, Aaron and Hur held his arms aloft until sunset, giving Joshua the victory.

**Ten Plagues and Passover**
Moses and Aaron confronted Pharaoh, and God sent ten plagues upon Egypt, culminating in the death of the Egyptian firstborn. The Jewish holiday of Passover commemorates this final plague, in which the Israelites were "passed over," and the Exodus that followed.

**Khidr**
In the Qur'an's Surah al-Kahf and related hadith, Moses (Musa) learns that he is not the most knowledgeable of men and travels with the mysterious sage Khidr. Khidr performs puzzling acts, such as repairing a wall in an inhospitable town, whose divine wisdom Moses fails to understand.

**Waters of Marah**
Soon after the Exodus, the Israelites found the water at Marah too bitter to drink. Moses threw a tree (a piece of wood) that God showed him into the water, making it sweet.

**Loa (lwa)**
The spirits of Vodou, who act as intermediaries between humans and the distant creator god and are often blended with Catholic saints. Practitioners serve them with offerings, music, and dance, and the lwa respond by possessing worshippers. Examples include Papa Legba, Baron Samedi, Damballah, and the Erzulie spirits, such as Erzulie Freda and Erzulie Dantor, who are regarded as protectors of gay men and lesbians respectively.

**Papa Legba**
The lwa of the crossroads and the gatekeeper between the human and spirit worlds, who must be invoked first at every ceremony before any other spirit can come through. He is depicted as an old man with a cane, a pipe, and a straw hat, and his veve includes his cane.

**Baron Samedi**
The lwa of death and the dead, and leader of the Ghede family of spirits. He is shown as a skeletal figure in a top hat and black tuxedo, smoking a cigar and with cotton stuffed in his nostrils like a corpse prepared for burial. His wife is Maman Brigitte.

**Bondye**
The supreme creator god of Vodou, whose name comes from the French "Bon Dieu" ("good God"). Bondye is distant and does not intervene directly in human affairs, so worship is directed instead to the lwa who serve him.

**Houngans and mambos**
The male and female priests of Vodou, respectively, who lead ceremonies, heal, and call down the lwa. Their symbol of office is the asson, a sacred calabash rattle, so becoming a priest is called "taking the asson."

**Damballah and Ayida-Weddo**
Damballah is the great serpent sky father, a creator spirit associated with peace and purity. In Vodou myth, he formed the stars and planets with his 7,000 coils and shed his skin to make the waters of the earth. His wife is the rainbow serpent Ayida-Weddo.

**Gros bon ange and ti bon ange**
The two parts of the soul in Vodou belief: the gros bon ange ("big good angel") is the general life force shared by all humans, while the ti bon ange ("little good angel") is the individual personality and conscience of each person. The ti bon ange can leave the body, which is believed to make it vulnerable to sorcery.

**"Mounting the horse"**
The term for spirit possession, the central experience of Vodou ritual. A possessed worshipper is called the chwal ("horse") who is "ridden" by the lwa, and possession usually takes place during drumming and dancing around the poto mitan, the center pole of the temple's peristyle that serves as the pathway for the spirits.

**Rada, Petro, and Ghede**
The main "nations" or families into which the lwa are grouped. The Rada spirits, such as Damballah, are "cool," peaceful, and linked to Dahomey in West Africa, while the Petro spirits are "hot," fierce, and associated with Haiti itself. The Ghede are the spirits of the dead, led by Baron Samedi.

**Kanzo initiation**
The initiation ceremony through which a person enters the Vodou priesthood, starting as a hounsi kanzo and possibly later becoming a houngan or mambo. It includes seclusion, ritual baths, the crushing of leaves, and white clothing and straw hats, and the initiate is dedicated to a personal protective lwa called the met tet ("master of the head").

**Hounfour**
The Vodou temple, whose name is often said to mean "abode of the spirits." It contains altars to the lwa and an open area for ceremonies, the peristyle, with its central pole.

**Veve**
Symbolic geometric designs, usually drawn on the ground in cornmeal or other powder, that are used to summon a specific lwa during a ceremony. Each lwa has its own veve, such as the cane in Papa Legba's.

**Marie Laveau**
The 19th-century "Voodoo Queen" of New Orleans, the most famous practitioner of Louisiana Voodoo. She was a devout Catholic who encouraged her followers to attend Mass, and she is said to have kept a snake named Zombi. Visitors draw X marks on her tomb in St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 hoping she will grant their wishes.

**Bokor and zombies**
A bokor is a sorcerer who works with both good and harmful magic, in contrast to houngans and mambos, and is believed to be able to turn people into zombies. In The Serpent and the Rainbow, ethnobotanist Wade Davis argued that bokors used powders containing tetrodotoxin, a poison from pufferfish, to create zombies.

**Marasa**
The sacred twins of Vodou, considered the first children of Bondye and the first humans. They represent innocence and abundance and are honored in ceremonies alongside the lwa.

**Baha'u'llah**
The founder of the Baha'i Faith, born Mirza Husayn-Ali in Persia in 1817; his title means "Glory of God." A follower of the Bab, he was exiled from Persia and spent his final decades as a prisoner of the Ottomans, including many years in the prison city of Acre (Akka), where he died in 1892.

**Universal House of Justice in Haifa, Israel**
The supreme governing body of the Baha'i Faith, an elected institution located at the Baha'i World Centre on Mount Carmel in Haifa. National and local Spiritual Assemblies around the world are subordinate to it, and it has issued statements such as the letter "The Promise of World Peace" addressed to the peoples of the world.

**Book of Certitude (Kitab-i-Iqan)**
Baha'u'llah's chief doctrinal work, which explains progressive revelation: God has sent a series of messengers whose religions are stages of one unfolding faith, a doctrine sometimes called the unity of all religions. It includes the "Tablet of the True Seeker" passage describing how a seeker must become detached from everything but truth, and Shoghi Effendi translated it into English.

**The Seven Valleys**
A mystical, allegorical work by Baha'u'llah, written in answer to questions from Sufis, describing the soul's journey toward God through seven stages, such as Search and Love. The final valley is that "of True Poverty and Absolute Nothingness."

**Shoghi Effendi, the Guardian**
The grandson of Abdu'l-Baha and the first and only Guardian of the Baha'i Faith, who led it from 1921 until his death in 1957. He translated major texts into English, wrote the history "God Passes By," and launched the Ten Year Crusade.

**19 months of 19 days and the 19-day fast**
The Baha'i (Badi') calendar has 19 months of 19 days each, plus four or five intercalary days called Ayyam-i-Ha ("Days of Ha"), a time for gift-giving, hospitality and charity. They come just before the final month, 'Ala, during which Baha'is keep a 19-day sunrise-to-sunset fast.

**Manifestations of God**
The Baha'i term for the great messengers through whom God progressively reveals Himself, including Abraham, Krishna, Zoroaster, Buddha, Moses, Jesus, Muhammad, the Bab, and Baha'u'llah. Questions often list several of these figures as a giveaway.

**The Bab and Babism**
Siyyid Ali-Muhammad, "the Bab" ("the Gate"), founded the predecessor religion Babism in Persia in 1844, with eighteen early disciples called the Letters of the Living, and foretold "He whom God shall make manifest." At his 1850 execution by firing squad, the first volley famously failed to kill him and he briefly disappeared before he was shot again. His Declaration is commemorated on the evening of May 22–23.

**Ten Year Crusade and the Hands of the Cause**
A global teaching campaign from 1953 to 1963, launched by Shoghi Effendi, that greatly spread the faith worldwide. The Hands of the Cause of God are distinguished believers appointed to protect and spread the faith, including Martha Root, and they guided the faith after Shoghi Effendi's death until the Universal House of Justice was first elected in 1963.

**Garden of Ridvan**
The garden outside Baghdad where, in 1863, Baha'u'llah declared that he was the one foretold by the Bab. It is commemorated by the twelve-day Festival of Ridvan (April 21 to May 2), whose first, ninth, and twelfth days are holy days.

**Kitab-i-Aqdas**
The "Most Holy Book," Baha'u'llah's book of laws, written in Acre, which sets out practices such as obligatory prayer, the fast, and the calendar. It is often called the central or main text of the faith.

**Epistle to the Son of the Wolf**
Baha'u'llah's last major work, addressed to a hostile Muslim cleric, Aqa Najafi, the son of the cleric he called "the Wolf." It recalls the execution of the Nahri brothers, honored as the "King of Martyrs" and "Beloved of Martyrs" (the "twin shining lights"), whose deaths Baha'u'llah had also condemned in the Lawh-i-Burhan (Tablet of the Proof).

**Nine-pointed star, Lotus Temple, and Wilmette**
The nine-pointed star is the common symbol of the faith (nine stands for completeness), and another symbol is the "Ringstone" emblem. Baha'i Houses of Worship are nine-sided, notably the lotus-shaped Lotus Temple in New Delhi and the House of Worship in Wilmette, Illinois.

**Abdu'l-Baha**
Baha'u'llah's eldest son and successor, the second leader of the faith, who wrote "The Secret of Divine Civilization," the Tablets of the Divine Plan, and the Tablet to The Hague. His Will and Testament appointed Shoghi Effendi as Guardian and set up the faith's administrative order, including the institutions covered by the "Lesser Covenant" on succession.

**Gleanings and The Hidden Words**
"Gleanings from the Writings of Baha'u'llah" is a widely read anthology compiled by Shoghi Effendi from Baha'u'llah's huge body of writings; one passage compares religions to branches of one tree. The Hidden Words is a short book of ethical and mystical aphorisms by Baha'u'llah.

**114 suras and ayat**
The Quran is divided into 114 chapters called suras (surahs), each made up of verses called ayat (singular ayah). Apart from the first sura, they are arranged roughly from longest to shortest.

**Hafiz**
The title for a person who has memorized the entire Quran (feminine hafiza). Memorizing it is considered a great honor, and a hafiz can recite the whole text without looking at it.

**Tajweed**
The set of rules for correctly pronouncing and reciting the Quran, covering things like heavy and light letters, elongation, and pauses. A qari is a skilled reciter who performs the text in this melodic, embellished style.

**Al-Fatiha ("The Opening")**
The first sura, a seven-verse prayer also nicknamed "the Key" and recited in every unit of the daily prayer (salah). It praises God as "Lord (Sustainer) of all the worlds" and "Master of the Day of Judgment."

**Al-Baqara ("The Cow")**
The second and longest sura, revealed mostly in Medina after the Hijra. It is named for the story of a cow the Israelites were ordered to sacrifice to identify a murderer. It includes laws on fasting during Ramadan, the condemnation of alcohol and gambling, and the Quran's longest verse, about recording debts and transactions.

**Ayat al-Kursi (Throne Verse)**
Verse 255 of Al-Baqara, one of the most memorized and recited passages in Islam. It describes God's eternal power and says His Throne (Kursi) "extends over the heavens and the earth."

**Basmala and Sura 9**
"Bismillah ir-Rahman ir-Rahim" ("In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful") opens every sura except the ninth, At-Tawba ("Repentance"). Sura 9 begins instead with a declaration of dissociation from polytheists who broke treaties and contains the "Sword Verse."

**Gabriel, the Cave of Hira, and "Recite!"**
Muslims believe the Quran was revealed to Muhammad by the angel Gabriel (Jibril) over about 23 years. The first revelation came in the Cave of Hira on the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), with the command "Recite!" (or "Read!"), which opens Sura 96, Al-Alaq ("The Clot").

**Uthman's standardization**
The third caliph, Uthman, had an official standard text of the Quran compiled from earlier oral and written sources and ordered variant copies destroyed. Many early manuscripts are written in the angular Kufic script.

**Juz' and manazil**
Divisions of the Quran used for regular reading: 30 roughly equal juz' let a reader finish it in a month (often during Ramadan), and 7 manazil let a reader finish it in a week.

**Al-Kahf ("The Cave")**
Sura 18, which tells of pious youths who sleep in a cave for 300 years "and nine more" (the Sleepers of Ephesus story). It also tells of Moses travelling with a mysterious servant of God (traditionally Khidr) who punctures a boat, and of Dhul-Qarnayn, who journeys to the farthest East and West.

**Hadith and tafsir**
The hadith are separate reports of Muhammad's sayings and actions; together with the Quran they form the basis of Sharia law. Tafsir is Quranic commentary; a famous modern example is Sayyid Qutb's 30-volume "In the Shade of the Quran."

**Naskh (abrogation)**
The doctrine that some Quranic verses were superseded by later revelations. Scholars use it to resolve apparent contradictions between rulings in the text.

**Mu'tazila and the createdness of the Quran**
The rationalist Mu'tazila school argued that the Quran was created by God in time. Mainstream Sunni theology holds that the Quran is God's eternal, uncreated word.

**An-Nas and Al-Falaq**
The last two suras, protective prayers often recited for the sick or against evil. Al-Falaq ("The Daybreak") is the 113th, and the final sura, An-Nas ("Mankind"), begins "I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind" and asks protection from the whispering of Satan.

**Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah**
The sixth Fatimid caliph of Egypt, who mysteriously disappeared in 1021. The Druze regard him as a manifestation of God on earth and believe he went into occultation rather than dying, and he appears in nearly every question on the faith.

**Hamza ibn Ali**
A Persian Ismaili missionary who founded the Druze movement in the early 11th century by proclaiming the divinity of al-Hakim. He also disappeared, and many of the faith's founding letters are attributed to him.

**Epistles of Wisdom (Rasa'il al-Hikma)**
The sacred scripture of the Druze, a collection of letters attributed to Hamza ibn Ali, al-Hakim, and other early leaders. Access to the full text is restricted to initiated members.

**Five-colored star**
The Druze symbol, a five-pointed star whose five colors (green, red, yellow, blue, and white) stand for five cosmic principles, including the Universal Intellect, the Universal Soul, and the Word. It is often shown on the Druze flag.

**Juhhal and uqqal**
The two classes of Druze believers. Most members are juhhal ("the ignorant" or uninitiated), who are not allowed to read the sacred texts, while a small group of uqqal ("the wise" or initiated) has full access to the teachings and rituals.

**Ban on conversion and intermarriage**
The Druze faith is closed: no one may convert into or out of it, and members are expected to marry only other Druze. The community has accepted no converts since the early 11th century.

**Muwahhidun ("Unitarians")**
The name the Druze use for themselves, meaning "people of unity" or "monotheists." It reflects their central doctrine of the absolute oneness of God (tawhid).

**Offshoot of Ismaili Shia Islam**
The Druze faith grew out of the Ismaili branch of Shia Islam under the Fatimid dynasty but developed into a separate, syncretic religion. Its followers live mainly in Lebanon, Syria, and Israel.

**Sultan al-Atrash**
A Druze leader from the Jabal al-Druze region of Syria who led the Great Syrian Revolt against French rule beginning in 1925. His forces occupied the town of Suwayda early in the uprising.

**Kamal Jumblatt**
A prominent Lebanese Druze politician and founder of the Progressive Socialist Party. He was assassinated in 1977, an act widely attributed to the Syrian government of Hafez al-Assad, and was succeeded by his son Walid Jumblatt.

**Israel Defense Forces service**
Druze citizens of Israel are subject to military conscription, making them the only large non-Jewish community widely represented in the Israel Defense Forces.

**1860 Mount Lebanon massacres**
During the 1860 civil conflict in Mount Lebanon, Druze fighters massacred Maronite Christians in towns including Deir al-Qamar and Zahle. The violence prompted a French intervention and a new administrative system for Mount Lebanon.

**Tomb of Jethro**
The Druze revere Jethro (Nabi Shu'ayb), the father-in-law of Moses, as a prophet. His traditional tomb near Hittin in northern Israel is the site of an annual Druze pilgrimage.

**Taqiyya**
The practice of concealing or denying one's faith to avoid persecution. Druze are permitted to use it, which helps explain the secrecy of the religion.

**Partnership with the Maronites**
In the Ottoman period, Druze lords of Mount Lebanon cooperated with their Maronite Christian neighbors, including in developing the region's silk production.

**Haile Selassie**
The Ethiopian emperor (crowned 1930, born Ras Tafari Makonnen, from whom the religion takes its name) whom Rastafarians venerate as the returned messiah, the second coming of Christ, or an incarnation of God. He is symbolized by the Lion of Judah, though some Rastas regard him only as a prophet.

**Ital (I-tal) diet**
The Rastafarian dietary code, whose name derives from the word "vital." It favors natural, unprocessed, mostly vegetarian food, avoiding chemicals, preservatives, and often added salt; many followers also avoid alcohol, shellfish, and pork.

**Holy Piby**
A 1920s text by the Anguillan preacher Robert Athlyi Rogers, often called the "Black Man's Bible," which begins with books named for Athlyi. It declares Ethiopians to be God's chosen people and names Marcus Garvey, Robert Lincoln Poston, and Henrietta Vinton Davis as apostles, making it a major influence on Rastafari.

**Mansions**
The term for the different branches or orders of Rastafari. The main ones are the Nyabinghi Order, the Bobo Ashanti, and the Twelve Tribes of Israel, the last founded by Vernon Carrington ("Prophet Gad"), who urged members to read a chapter of the Bible each day.

**Bobo Ashanti (Bobo Shanti)**
A strict mansion founded by Prince Emmanuel Charles Edwards, whom members revere as a divine figure. Members wear long robes and tight turbans, women are called empresses or queens, and followers carry brooms as a symbol of cleanliness.

**Nyabinghi**
The oldest Rastafarian mansion, named for a legendary East African queen, and also the name of its ceremonial gatherings and chanting music. Nyabinghi drumming uses a three-drum set (the akete) consisting of the bass or "thunder" drum, the funde, and the high-pitched repeater.

**Jah**
The Rastafarian name for God, taken from the shortened form of Yahweh in the Bible. Because Rastas believe Jah dwells in every person, they use "I and I" instead of "we" and replace word beginnings with "I" (as in "I-tal"), part of the Iyaric dialect, which also features words like "overstanding" and "downpression."

**Ganja and "reasonings"**
Cannabis, called ganja or "the herb," is used as a sacrament in Rastafari. It is smoked, often from a pipe called a chalice, during "reasonings," informal communal gatherings for prayer and discussion with Jah.

**Dreadlocks**
The matted locks of hair worn by many Rastas as a sign of their covenant with God, justified by biblical passages such as the Nazirite vow. Non-believers who do not wear them are sometimes called "baldheads."

**Leonard Howell and The Promised Key**
Howell is often considered the first Rasta preacher. He wrote The Promised Key under the pseudonym G. G. Maragh, a tract that describes King Alpha and Queen Omega and contains the line "Gross beauty is the Queen in hell"; he also founded Pinnacle, the first self-sustaining Rasta commune, where ganja was grown, and was jailed for sedition for proclaiming loyalty to Haile Selassie over the British king.

**Livity**
The Rastafarian idea of righteous, natural living in harmony with Jah, along with the life force that such living sustains. The ital diet, dreadlocks, and avoiding corrupting substances all serve to increase one's livity.

**Grounation Day**
A Rastafarian holy day held on April 21 to commemorate Haile Selassie's 1966 visit to Jamaica. Rastafarian gatherings in general are also called "groundations" or "groundings."

**Babylon and Zion**
Babylon is the Rastafarian name for the oppressive, materialistic Western world and its power structures, which cause "downpression." Zion is the promised homeland in Africa, identified with Ethiopia (sometimes specifically Lalibela or Mount Zion), to which Rastas hope to return.

**Marcus Garvey**
The Jamaican Black nationalist leader who founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association and promoted a return to Africa. Rastas regard him as a prophet, crediting him with foretelling the crowning of a Black king in Africa.

**Kebra Nagast**
The 14th-century Ethiopian national epic, an important text for Rastas. It tells how the Queen of Sheba visited Solomon, gave up sun worship, and bore Menelik I, founder of the Solomonic dynasty from which Haile Selassie claimed descent.

**First of the mahavratas**
In Jainism, ahimsa (non-violence, "non-injury") is the first and greatest of the five mahavratas, the "great vows" taken by monks and nuns, which help the soul reach moksha. Ascetics must avoid harming any jiva (living soul), even insects and the tiniest one-sensed beings such as plants. Laypeople take the milder anuvratas ("lesser vows"), which apply ahimsa less strictly, chiefly to animals.

**Ahimsa, anekantavada, and aparigraha**
The three core tenets of Jainism: ahimsa (non-violence), anekantavada (non-absolutism, the idea that truth has many sides), and aparigraha (non-acquisition or non-attachment to possessions).

**Mahatma Gandhi and satyagraha**
Gandhi, influenced by Jain thought, made ahimsa a cornerstone of satyagraha ("truth force"), his method of non-violent resistance used in the Indian independence movement.

**Muhpatti (mukhavastrika)**
A cloth worn over the mouth by some Svetambara Jain monks and nuns so that they do not accidentally inhale or harm tiny organisms in the air.

**Rajoharan**
A soft broom carried by Svetambara ascetics to gently sweep the ground or a seat before walking or sitting, so they do not crush insects. The Svetambara tradition traces itself to the monks who stayed in Magadha during a twelve-year famine, while those who went south became the Digambaras.

**Avoiding root vegetables and eating after dark**
To minimize harm, observant Jains of both the Digambara and Svetambara sects avoid root vegetables such as potatoes, onions, and garlic, since uprooting them kills the whole plant and the many tiny organisms living in it. Strict practitioners also never eat after sunset or in the dark, when insects could be accidentally swallowed.

**One of the five yamas**
In Hinduism, ahimsa is the first of the five yamas, the ethical restraints that form the first of the eight limbs in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras. The Yoga Sutras state that when one is firmly established in ahimsa, all hostilities cease in one's presence.

**Hand with a wheel on the palm**
The symbol of ahimsa in Jainism: an open, raised hand with a wheel (the dharmachakra) on the palm, often with the word "ahimsa" written in its center. The wheel represents the resolve to halt the cycle of rebirth through non-violence, and the hand forms part of the official Jain emblem.

**Acaranga Sutra**
The oldest Svetambara Jain scripture, which deals with monastic conduct. It declares that all the arhats (perfected beings) teach non-violence toward all living beings as the pure, eternal dharma.

**Parishahas**
The twenty-two hardships, such as hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and insect bites, that Jain ascetics must endure calmly rather than react against. Bearing them peacefully is part of a life of non-injury.

**Watching the path ahead (irya samiti)**
Jain monks must walk carefully, looking several feet ahead on the ground so they do not step on living creatures. This rule of careful movement is one of the samitis (rules of vigilance).

**Personified in the Puranas**
In the Hindu Puranas, Ahimsa is personified as a goddess and devoted wife. Ahimsa is also an important ethical principle in Buddhism.

**Sawm**
Fasting, the fourth of the Five Pillars of Islam, which is observed during Ramadan. Adult Muslims abstain from food, drink, and sexual relations from dawn until sunset each day. The sick, elderly, pregnant, and travelers are exempt, and those who cannot make up the missed days pay fidyah, a compensation such as feeding the poor.

**Iftar**
The meal eaten right after sunset to break each day's fast, often shared with family or the community. Following the example of Muhammad, it traditionally begins with eating dates (often an odd number, such as three) and drinking water.

**Suhoor (suhur)**
The meal eaten before dawn, ahead of the fajr (dawn) prayer that marks the start of each day's fast. Together with iftar, it bounds each day of fasting.

**Laylat al-Qadr (Night of Power)**
The night commemorating when the angel Gabriel (Jibril) first revealed the Quran to Muhammad. The first verses revealed were the opening of Surah 96 (al-Alaq), which says God created man from a clot. The Quran calls it "better than a thousand months," and it falls on one of the odd-numbered nights in the last ten nights of Ramadan, most often marked on the 27th.

**Eid al-Fitr**
The "Festival of Breaking the Fast," celebrated on the first day of the following month, Shawwal, once the new crescent moon is sighted. It begins with a special congregational prayer and is marked by feasting and sweets, and fasting is forbidden on that day.

**Tarawih**
Special optional (sunnah) prayers performed in congregation each night of Ramadan after the night (isha) prayer. One juz (one-thirtieth of the Quran) is often recited each night, so the whole Quran is completed over the month.

**White thread and black thread**
A verse in Surah al-Baqarah ("The Cow," Quran 2:187) says the fast begins at dawn, when "the white thread becomes distinct from the black thread." This defines when daybreak starts. In far-northern places such as Iqaluit, where dawn and dusk are hard to define, some Muslims follow the fasting times of cities further south, such as Ottawa.

**Hilal (crescent moon)**
Ramadan is the ninth month of the lunar Islamic calendar, between Sha'ban and Shawwal. It begins with the sighting of the hilal, the first thin crescent of the new moon, and ends with the sighting of the next crescent, which marks Eid al-Fitr.

**I'tikaf**
A voluntary spiritual retreat, often spent in a mosque during the last ten days of Ramadan. Worshippers seclude themselves for prayer and Quran recitation, partly so they do not miss Laylat al-Qadr.

**Gates of Heaven opened and Hell closed**
According to a hadith, when Ramadan begins, the gates of Paradise are opened, the gates of Hell are shut, and the devils (shayatin) are chained. This is why believers are said to be protected from Satan's influence during the month.

**Zakat al-Fitr**
A required charitable donation given at the end of Ramadan, before the Eid prayer, so that the poor can also celebrate Eid. It is traditionally measured as a set quantity of a staple food, about three kilograms of grain such as rice or wheat, or its price.

**Six days of Shawwal**
According to a hadith, a Muslim who fasts all of Ramadan and then fasts six more days in Shawwal earns the reward of fasting for an entire year.

**Niyyah**
The intention to fast, which must be made before each day's fast begins. Without it, the fast is not considered valid.

**Mesaharati, fanous, and bedug**
Regional Ramadan customs. In Egypt and other Arab countries, a mesaharati walks the streets beating a drum to wake people for suhoor, and colorful lanterns called fanous are hung. In Java, a large drum called the bedug announces prayer times and the end of the fast, and some Indonesians prepare for the month with a ritual bath called padusan.

**Origin of the name and the Battle of Badr**
The name Ramadan comes from an Arabic root meaning "scorching heat." Important historical events in the month include Muhammad's victory at the Battle of Badr in 624, and the death of Ali, the first Shia Imam, who was struck down in a mosque in Kufa and is buried at Najaf.

**The Beatitudes**
The series of blessings that opens the sermon, such as "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven," "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth," and blessings for those who mourn and for the peacemakers. Matthew has eight or nine of them, depending on how they are counted; Luke's shorter parallel, the Sermon on the Plain, has four, paired with four woes.

**The Lord's Prayer ("Our Father")**
The model prayer Jesus teaches in Matthew 6, beginning "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name" and including "Give us today our daily bread." Its Greek word for "daily," epiousios, appears nowhere else, and Jerome's Vulgate rendered it "supersubstantial" in Matthew. The closing doxology "for thine is the kingdom, the power, and the glory" is found in later Byzantine-type manuscripts and is generally considered a later addition.

**"Salt of the earth" and "light of the world"**
Jesus calls his listeners the salt of the earth, asking what can restore salt that has lost its savor, and the light of the world, like a city on a hill. He adds that no one lights a candle (lamp) and puts it under a bushel; it goes on a candlestick to give light to the whole house.

**Wise and foolish builders**
The parable that closes the sermon. Whoever hears and does Jesus's words is like a wise man who built his house on the rock, which stood through rain and floods; whoever ignores them is like a foolish man who built his house on the sand, which fell.

**"Consider the lilies of the field"**
Jesus tells his audience not to worry about food or clothing. The fowls (birds) of the air are fed without sowing or reaping and the lilies grow without toiling or spinning, and he asks whether worrying can add a cubit to one's height or an hour to one's life; "take no thought for the morrow."

**"Turn the other cheek"**
Jesus replaces "an eye for an eye" with "resist not evil": if someone strikes your right cheek, offer the other. He also says to give your cloak to someone who takes your coat, and if forced to go one mile, go two (the origin of "go the extra mile"), and to love your enemies.

**The Antitheses ("You have heard it said... but I say unto you")**
A section of Matthew 5 in which Jesus quotes a commandment of the Mosaic Law and then makes it stricter. Anger and calling a brother "Raca" (a term of contempt) put one in danger of the council, looking at a woman with lust is already adultery in the heart, and instead of swearing oaths (even by your own head, since you cannot make one hair white or black) you should "let your yes be yes." The chapter ends with "Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect."

**Matthew chapters 5–7**
The sermon is the first of Jesus's five major discourses in the Gospel of Matthew, given early in his ministry. He goes up a mountain in Galilee to deliver it, traditionally placed at the Mount of Beatitudes near the Sea of Galilee.

**The Cost of Discipleship by Dietrich Bonhoeffer**
A 1937 book by the German Lutheran pastor and anti-Nazi dissident, a large part of which is a commentary on the Sermon on the Mount. It contrasts "cheap grace," meaning forgiveness without repentance or obedience, with "costly grace," which demands that one follow Christ.

**False prophets: "figs from thistles"**
Jesus warns of false prophets who come in sheep's clothing but are inwardly ravenous wolves. He asks whether people gather grapes from thorns or figs from thistles, and says "by their fruits ye shall know them."

**"Judge not" and the speck and the beam**
Jesus says "Judge not, that ye be not judged," and asks why one sees the speck (mote) in a brother's eye while ignoring the beam (plank) in one's own. He tells hypocrites to first remove the beam from their own eye.

**"Pearls before swine"**
The sermon is the source of the saying not to give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine, lest they trample them and turn on you. It warns against offering precious teachings to those who will only scorn them.

**"No man can serve two masters"**
Jesus says no one can serve both God and mammon (wealth), and urges storing up treasure in heaven rather than on earth, "for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." The same chapter says the eye is the lamp of the body and that almsgiving, prayer, and fasting should be done in secret, not to be seen by others.

**"Ask, and it shall be given you," the Golden Rule, and the narrow gate**
In Matthew 7 Jesus promises "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you." The chapter also gives the Golden Rule (do to others what you would have them do to you) and contrasts the wide gate that leads to destruction with the narrow gate that leads to life.

**New Moses and Luther's interpretation**
Many interpreters see Jesus teaching the law from a mountain as a parallel to Moses receiving the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai, with Jesus as a "new Moses." Martin Luther rejected the Catholic reading that its hardest commands were "counsels of perfection" for monks and clergy, and argued that they govern the Christian's personal, spiritual life rather than the work of governments.

**Killing Laius at the crossroads**
Oedipus unknowingly kills his real father, King Laius of Thebes (son of Labdacus), at a place where three roads meet in Phocis, where the roads to Delphi, Daulis, and Thebes join. They quarrel over the right of way, Laius strikes him with a goad or scepter, and Oedipus kills him and all but one of his servants. The survivor later claims a band of robbers did it.

**Jocasta**
The queen of Thebes, Laius's widow, and Oedipus's mother, whom he marries without knowing who she is. They have four children: Eteocles, Polynices, Antigone, and Ismene. When the truth comes out in Oedipus Rex, she hangs herself.

**Blinding himself with Jocasta's pins**
After finding Jocasta's body, Oedipus pulls the gold pins (brooches) from her dress and stabs out his own eyes, so he will not have to look upon what he has done.

**The riddle of the Sphinx**
The Sphinx terrorizes Thebes by asking travelers what walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening. Oedipus answers "man" (a baby crawls, an adult walks, and an old man uses a cane), and the Sphinx kills herself. As a reward he becomes king of Thebes and marries the widowed queen.

**Mount Cithaeron and the pierced ankles**
Because an oracle warned that his son would kill him, Laius has the infant Oedipus's ankles pierced and bound together and orders him left to die on Mount Cithaeron. The servant gives him to a shepherd instead. The name Oedipus means "swollen foot," after this injury.

**Polybus and Merope**
The childless king and queen of Corinth (the queen is called Periboea in some sources) who raise Oedipus as their own son. When he hears an oracle that he will kill his father and marry his mother, he flees Corinth to avoid them, which leads him straight to Thebes.

**Oedipus Rex (Oedipus Tyrannus)**
Sophocles's tragedy, also called Oedipus the King.
