It opens with Thebans placing olive branches wrapped in wool on an altar, begging Oedipus to end a plague, and Creon returns from Delphi with word that Laius's killer must be found. Oedipus vows to find the murderer and slowly discovers it is himself.

**Tiresias**
The blind prophet of Thebes. Oedipus summons him for help finding Laius's killer, and when Tiresias reluctantly tells him "you yourself are the criminal you seek," Oedipus angrily accuses him and Creon of plotting against him and mocks his blindness. Tiresias laments that "wisdom is a dreadful thing when it brings no profit to its possessor."

**The messenger from Corinth and the shepherd**
A messenger arrives to report that Polybus has died and that Corinth wants Oedipus as king. Trying to ease Oedipus's fear, he reveals that Polybus and Merope were not his real parents, since he himself, as a shepherd on Cithaeron, received the baby from one of Laius's servants. Oedipus then threatens that old herdsman with torture until he confirms the truth.

**Oedipus at Colonus**
Sophocles's last play. The blind, exiled Oedipus, guided by Antigone, arrives at Colonus near Athens and takes refuge in a grove sacred to the Furies (Eumenides). Prophecy says the land where he is buried will be blessed, so Theseus protects him from Creon. After three peals of thunder, Oedipus goes off to die in a secret place that only Theseus may see.

**Cursing Eteocles and Polynices**
Oedipus curses his sons to kill each other, in Oedipus at Colonus because they did not help him in exile, and in the epic Thebaid because they served him at the silver table and with the golden cup of his ancestor Cadmus, against his wishes. The brothers agree to rule Thebes in alternate years, then kill each other in single combat during the war of the Seven Against Thebes (dramatized by Aeschylus).

**Antigone and Ismene**
Oedipus's daughters by Jocasta, so they are also his half-sisters. At the end of Oedipus Rex he asks Creon to care for them, and Antigone guides her blind father into exile. Her later decision to bury Polynices against Creon's decree, which gets her sealed in a tomb where she hangs herself, is the subject of Sophocles's Antigone.

**"Count no mortal happy"**
The closing lesson of Oedipus Rex: no one should be called happy until he has died free of suffering. E. R. Dodds's famous essay "On Misunderstanding the Oedipus Rex" argues against reading the play as simply about fate or a tragic flaw.

**Early epic versions: Hesiod and the Oedipodea**
In Works and Days Hesiod says some of the generation of heroes died fighting at seven-gated Thebes for the flocks of Oedipus. In the lost epic Oedipodea, attributed to Cinaethon of Sparta, Oedipus's children are born to a second wife, Euryganeia, rather than to Jocasta.

**Later adaptations: Dryden and Velikovsky**
John Dryden and Nathaniel Lee wrote an English Oedipus that adds a new character, Adrastus. The fringe writer Immanuel Velikovsky's book Oedipus and Akhnaton argues that the Oedipus myth was based on the Egyptian pharaoh Akhenaten.

**Slaying the Minotaur in the Labyrinth**
Theseus's most famous feat. Because Athens owed Crete a tribute of youths and maidens after the death of King Minos's son Androgeus, Theseus volunteered to sail to Crete as one of them. There he entered the Labyrinth built by Daedalus and killed the Minotaur, the bull-headed son of Minos's wife Pasiphae and the Cretan Bull.

**Ariadne's thread and abandonment on Naxos**
Minos's daughter Ariadne fell in love with Theseus and gave him a ball of thread (and in some versions a sword) so he could find his way back out of the Labyrinth. She fled Crete with him, but Theseus abandoned her on the island of Naxos, where the god Dionysus later found and married her.

**Black sails and the death of Aegeus**
Theseus had promised his father, King Aegeus of Athens, that his ship would return with white sails if he survived. He forgot to change the black sails, and Aegeus, seeing them from a cliff, threw himself into the sea, which became known as the Aegean Sea. Theseus then became king of Athens.

**Pirithous and the Chair of Forgetfulness**
Theseus and his friend Pirithous, king of the Lapiths, descended to the underworld to abduct Persephone as a bride for Pirithous. Hades tricked them into sitting on the Chair (or Throne) of Forgetfulness (Lethe), to which they became stuck. Heracles later freed Theseus, tearing part of his thighs or buttocks off the seat (so his Athenian descendants were said to have small buttocks), but Pirithous was left behind.

**Sword and sandals under a boulder**
Before leaving Troezen, Aegeus hid his sword and sandals beneath a heavy rock, telling Theseus's mother Aethra that their son should come to Athens once he could lift it. Theseus did so, and when the sorceress Medea, then Aegeus's wife, tried to poison him at a feast, Aegeus recognized the sword and knocked the cup away. Theseus's conception had followed a Delphic oracle telling Aegeus "do not loosen the bulging mouth of the wineskin" until he reached home; Aethra slept with both Aegeus and Poseidon on the same night.

**Procrustes**
A bandit who forced travelers to fit his bed, stretching those who were too short and cutting off the limbs of those who were too long. Theseus killed him in the same way, on his own bed.

**Sinis**
The "Pine-Bender," a bandit who tied travelers between two bent pine trees and let them spring back, tearing the victims apart. Theseus killed him by his own method. Theseus fathered Melanippus with Sinis's daughter Perigune, who had hidden in a patch of asparagus.

**Sciron**
A bandit who forced travelers to wash his feet on a cliff and then kicked them into the sea, where a giant turtle ate them. Theseus threw Sciron off the cliff to the turtle. Sciron was the grandfather of Peleus, and so the great-grandfather of Achilles.

**Periphetes, the Crommyonian Sow, and Cercyon**
Other foes on Theseus's land journey from Troezen to Athens, often called his "six labors." Periphetes was a club-wielding bandit; Theseus asked to inspect his bronze club and killed him with it, keeping it as his weapon. The Crommyonian Sow (sometimes named Phaea, or an old woman of that name who owned it) was a monstrous pig, and Cercyon was a wrestler at Eleusis whom Theseus defeated in a wrestling match.

**The Marathonian Bull**
Medea sent Theseus to capture or kill the rampaging bull at Marathon (the Cretan Bull that Heracles had brought to Greece, and the father of the Minotaur), hoping it would kill him. On the way he was sheltered by the old woman Hecale, who died before he returned, so he founded honors in her memory.

**Abduction of Helen**
With Pirithous, Theseus kidnapped the young Helen of Sparta. In retaliation, her brothers the Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux) rescued her and carried off Theseus's mother Aethra, who was later freed by Theseus's sons Demophon and Acamas at Troy.

**Phaedra and Hippolytus**
Theseus's second wife Phaedra, the sister of Ariadne, was cursed by Aphrodite to fall in love with her stepson Hippolytus, Theseus's son by the Amazon queen. When Hippolytus rejected her, she accused him of rape; Theseus cursed his son, who was dragged to death by his own horses when a bull from Poseidon frightened them. This is the subject of Euripides's Hippolytus.

**Ship of Theseus**
The Athenians preserved the ship Theseus sailed to Crete and sent it on an annual sacred voyage to Delos, during which executions were banned (delaying Socrates's death, as Plato's Phaedo notes). According to Plutarch, its decaying planks were replaced one by one, inspiring the philosophical paradox of whether an object whose parts have all been replaced is still the same object.

**Retrieving Minos's ring from the sea**
On the voyage to Crete, King Minos threw a ring into the sea and challenged Theseus to prove he was a son of Poseidon. Theseus dove down and returned with the ring, along with a golden crown given to him by the sea goddess Amphitrite (or Thetis).

**Death on Skyros and Athenian hero**
Theseus was credited with the synoikismos, the unification of the villages of Attica into the single city-state of Athens. Ousted by Menestheus, he fled to the island of Skyros, where King Lycomedes pushed him off a cliff. The Athenian general Cimon later brought back his supposed bones, and the Temple of Hephaestus in Athens was long misnamed the Theseion after him.

**Olive tree contest with Poseidon**
Athena and Poseidon competed to become patron of the city ruled by the half-snake king Cecrops. Poseidon struck the Acropolis with his trident to produce a salt spring, while Athena created an olive tree; her gift was judged superior, and the city was named Athens in her honor. Phidias later made a colossal gold-and-ivory statue of Athena Parthenos for the Parthenon there.

**Birth from Zeus's head**
Zeus swallowed his pregnant first wife Metis after she turned into a fly, fearing a prophecy that her son would overthrow him. He later suffered a tremendous headache, and when Hephaestus (or Prometheus) split his skull with an axe, Athena sprang out fully grown and in full armor.

**Arachne**
A mortal weaver who boasted that her skill surpassed Athena's. In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Arachne wove a flawless tapestry depicting the gods' misdeeds, and the enraged Athena tore it up; after Arachne hanged herself, Athena turned her into a spider.

**Erichthonius and the daughters of Cecrops**
Hephaestus tried to rape Athena, but his semen fell on the earth (Gaia), which gave birth to Erichthonius. Athena hid the baby, who was part snake or guarded by a snake, in a box and gave it to Cecrops's daughters Aglauros, Herse, and Pandrosos, forbidding them to open it; Aglauros and Herse looked inside, went mad, and threw themselves off the Acropolis. Erichthonius later became king of Athens.

**Medusa and the aegis**
When Poseidon slept with (or raped) Medusa in Athena's temple, Athena transformed Medusa's beautiful hair into snakes, making her a Gorgon. Athena then helped Perseus kill Medusa, giving him a polished shield to see her reflection, and placed the Gorgon's head on her own aegis.

**Pallas epithet**
Athena is often called Pallas Athena. In one version, she accidentally killed her childhood friend Pallas, daughter of Triton, while sparring, then took her name and carved a wooden statue of her; in another, she killed and flayed the giant Pallas during the Gigantomachy and used his skin for her aegis or cloak.

**Tiresias**
In one account, Tiresias accidentally saw Athena bathing naked and was struck blind. Because his mother was her companion, Athena could not undo the blindness but compensated him with the gift of prophecy.

**Mentor and Odysseus**
In the Odyssey, Athena disguises herself as Odysseus's old friend Mentor to guide his son Telemachus. She is Odysseus's divine protector throughout his journey home and disguises him as an old beggar on his return to Ithaca; Homer often calls her "gray-eyed" (glaukopis).

**Enceladus under Sicily**
During the Gigantomachy, the war between the gods and the giants, Athena crushed the fleeing giant Enceladus by hurling the island of Sicily on top of him. He is said to lie beneath Mount Etna.

**The Palladium and Ajax the Lesser**
The Palladium was a sacred wooden statue of Athena that protected Troy; Odysseus and Diomedes stole it, and in Roman tradition Aeneas brought it to Italy. During the sack of Troy, Ajax the Lesser dragged Cassandra away from Athena's statue and raped her, so Athena destroyed him on his voyage home.

**Trial of Orestes**
In Aeschylus's Eumenides, Orestes is tried before the Areopagus in Athens for killing his mother Clytemnestra. When the jury's votes are tied, Athena casts the deciding vote to acquit him, establishing that ties favor the defendant.

**Invention of the flute and Marsyas**
Inspired by the hissing of the Gorgons' snakes, Athena invented the aulos (flute), but threw it away when she saw how playing it puffed out her cheeks and distorted her face. The satyr Marsyas picked it up and later lost a fatal musical contest to Apollo.

**Helping heroes**
Athena aided many heroes: she gave Bellerophon the golden bridle used to tame Pegasus (earning the Corinthian epithet Chalinitis), gave Heracles a bronze rattle made by Hephaestus to scare off the Stymphalian Birds, and helped Diomedes wound both Aphrodite and Ares in the Iliad. She also tricked Hector into facing Achilles by disguising herself as his brother Deiphobus.

**Tydeus**
Athena favored the hero Tydeus, one of the Seven Against Thebes, and planned to make him immortal as he lay dying. When she saw him eating the brains of his enemy Melanippus, she was disgusted and withdrew the gift.

**Owl and Nyctimene**
The owl is Athena's sacred animal and a symbol of wisdom. In one myth, Nyctimene, who had been raped by her father, fled in shame and was turned by Athena into an owl.

**Affair with Aphrodite and Hephaestus's net**
Ares had an affair with Aphrodite, the wife of the smith god Hephaestus. Hephaestus pretended to leave for Lemnos, then caught the lovers in bed with an unbreakable golden net and called the other gods to look, and they laughed that the slow, lame god had caught the swift one. The bard Demodocus sings this story in Book 8 of the Odyssey, where Poseidon offers to guarantee the fine Ares owes.

**Phobos and Deimos**
The sons of Ares and Aphrodite, personifications of fear (Phobos) and terror or dread (Deimos). They accompany their father into battle, and today they are the names of the two moons of Mars.

**Alectryon turned into a rooster**
Ares posted the youth Alectryon to keep watch during his trysts with Aphrodite, but Alectryon fell asleep. The sun god Helios saw the lovers and told Hephaestus, so Ares turned Alectryon into a rooster, which ever since has crowed to announce the rising sun.

**Wounded by Diomedes in the Iliad**
In Book 5 of the Iliad, the Greek hero Diomedes, aided by Athena, drove his spear into Ares, who let out a scream as loud as ten thousand warriors and fled to Olympus. There Zeus told Ares that he was the most hateful to him of all the gods.

**Trial for killing Halirrhothius (the Areopagus)**
Ares killed Halirrhothius, a son of Poseidon, for raping (or attempting to rape) Ares's daughter Alcippe. He was tried by the gods in the first murder trial and acquitted, and the hill in Athens where the trial was held, the Areopagus ("Hill of Ares"), became the seat of the Athenian court that heard homicide cases.

**Cadmus and the dragon of Ares**
When Cadmus founded Thebes, he killed a dragon that guarded a spring sacred to Ares (in some accounts the dragon was Ares's son). On Athena's advice he sowed the dragon's teeth, which sprang up as armed warriors called the Spartoi. Cadmus had to serve Ares for eight years in penance, but then married Ares's daughter Harmonia.

**Imprisoned by the Aloadae in a bronze jar**
The giant twins Otus and Ephialtes (the Aloadae) bound Ares and imprisoned him in a bronze jar for thirteen months. According to the Iliad, Hermes rescued him; in other versions Artemis tricked the giants into killing each other.

**Cycnus and the fight with Heracles**
Cycnus, a son of Ares, robbed and killed travelers and planned to build a temple from their bones. Heracles killed him, and when Ares tried to avenge his son, Heracles wounded him in the thigh before Zeus separated them with a thunderbolt.

**Harmonia and her cursed necklace**
Harmonia was the daughter of Ares and Aphrodite and the wife of Cadmus. She received a cursed necklace (and in some versions a robe) as a wedding gift, which brought misfortune to her descendants, the royal house of Thebes.

**Killing Adonis as a boar**
In some versions of the myth, the jealous Ares took the form of a wild boar and killed Adonis, the mortal youth loved by Aphrodite.

**Enyo**
A war goddess who accompanied Ares on his chariot into battle. She is variously called his companion, lover, sister, or daughter, and in some accounts she bore him the war god Enyalius.

**Sisyphus and Thanatos**
When Sisyphus chained up Thanatos, the personification of death, no one could die, which frustrated Ares because the men in his battles would not die. Ares freed Thanatos and handed Sisyphus over to him.

**Amazons: Penthesilea and Hippolyta's girdle**
Ares was the father of the Amazons, including Penthesilea, who fought for Troy and was killed by Achilles. He also gave the queen Hippolyta her famous girdle (belt), which Heracles was sent to obtain as his ninth labor.

**Thrace and his sacred animals**
Ares was born in Thrace, a region the Greeks saw as warlike, and fathered Thrax, its namesake. His sacred animals include the vulture, which feeds on battlefield carrion, and the bronze-beaked Stymphalian Birds were also sacred to him; the Golden Fleece hung in a grove dedicated to him in Colchis.

**Mars, his Roman counterpart**
Ares was identified with the Roman war god Mars, who fathered Romulus and Remus with the Vestal Virgin Rhea Silvia. Mars was worshipped with distinctively Roman rites such as the suovetaurilia sacrifice, the leaping Salii priests with their sacred shields (ancilia), and Augustus's Temple of Mars Ultor ("the Avenger"); many questions require Ares rather than Mars, so listen for whether the clues are Greek or Roman.

**Eurydice**
Orpheus's wife, who died from a snakebite. Orpheus descended to the underworld to bring her back, and Hades and Persephone agreed on the condition that she walk behind him and that he not look back until they reached the upper world. He looked back just before leaving, and she vanished back into the underworld forever.

**Looking back**
The fatal act at the climax of the myth. Against Hades' command, Orpheus turned to check that Eurydice was following him on the way out of the underworld, causing her to fall away and be lost a second time.

**Sirens**
As a member of Jason's Argonauts, Orpheus saved the crew by playing his lyre and singing louder than the Sirens, drowning out their deadly, seductive song so the sailors did not steer toward them.

**Maenads**
The frenzied female followers of Dionysus, sometimes identified as Thracian or Ciconian women, who tore Orpheus limb from limb. Reasons given include his spurning of women (and of Dionysus) after Eurydice's death; in Ovid, the stones they threw at first fell harmlessly, charmed by his music.

**Singing severed head**
After the dismemberment, Orpheus's head kept singing as it floated down the Hebrus River in Thrace and across the sea. It came ashore on the island of Lesbos, where it was buried and was said to deliver oracles.

**Aristaeus**
A minor god of beekeeping and herding, son of Apollo, whose lustful pursuit of Eurydice caused her death: while fleeing him, she stepped on a snake and was bitten. Virgil's Georgics tells this story as part of the tale of Aristaeus losing his bees.

**Calliope**
The Muse of epic poetry, Orpheus's mother. His father is usually the Thracian king Oeagrus, though Apollo is sometimes named instead; Apollo is also said to have taught him music.

**Orphism (Orphic mysteries)**
A mystery religion attributed to Orpheus. Its myths include the god Zagreus, a child of Zeus who was killed and eaten by the Titans and then reborn as Dionysus, and a cosmogony in which the first god Phanes (also linked with Eros) hatches from a cosmic egg made by Chronos (Time).

**Charming the underworld**
Orpheus's music was so moving that it put the three-headed watchdog Cerberus to sleep, persuaded Charon to ferry him across without payment, made the Furies weep, and briefly relieved the torments of figures like Tantalus. It also softened the hearts of Hades and Persephone.

**Metamorphoses, Book X**
In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Orpheus sings a cycle of stories after losing Eurydice, including the tales of Ganymede, Hyacinthus, Pygmalion, Cyparissus, and Myrrha. Ovid also says he turned to loving young men and introduced pederasty to the Thracians.

**Helicon River**
According to Pausanias, when the women who murdered Orpheus tried to wash his blood off their hands in the river Helicon, the river sank underground to avoid being made an accomplice to the murder.

**Sonnets to Orpheus**
A cycle of 55 sonnets written by the German poet Rainer Maria Rilke in 1922, opening with the line "There rose a tree. Oh pure transcendence!" (also translated "There the tree rises. Oh pure surpassing!").

**Margaret Atwood's "Orpheus"**
Atwood wrote poems about the myth, including one told from Eurydice's point of view, in which she describes being pulled back "out to the green light that had once grown fangs and killed me," the snake that ended her first life.

**Musaeus and Linus**
Legendary musicians associated with Orpheus. Musaeus was often called his disciple or son, while Linus, who in another tradition tutored Heracles in music, is sometimes made his brother or teacher.

**Libethra**
A town in Macedonia near Mount Olympus where, according to Pausanias, Orpheus's tomb stood until it was destroyed when the river Sys flooded. Orpheus was also associated with Pimpleia, a nearby site linked to the Muses.

**Mistletoe**
The only thing in the world that did not swear never to harm Baldr, because his mother Frigg thought it too young or harmless to ask. Loki fashioned a dart or spear from mistletoe, and it is the most famous giveaway for Baldr's death.

**Hodr**
Baldr's blind brother. While the gods amused themselves by throwing objects at the seemingly invulnerable Baldr, Loki guided Hodr's hand to throw the mistletoe, killing Baldr. Hodr and Baldr are said to return reconciled after Ragnarok.

**Frigg's oath**
After Baldr suffered ominous dreams of his death, his mother Frigg extracted an oath from every object and creature in the world not to harm him, overlooking only the mistletoe.

**Thokk**
A giantess, usually understood to be Loki in disguise, who was the only being in the world that refused to weep for Baldr. Hel had promised to release Baldr if all things wept for him, so Thokk's refusal kept him in the underworld.

**Hyrrokkin**
A giantess who arrived at Baldr's funeral riding a wolf with vipers for reins. She pushed his ship out to sea so forcefully that fire flew from the rollers and the earth trembled, and Thor had to be restrained from striking her.

**Hringhorni**
Baldr's ship, called the greatest of all ships. It was used as his funeral pyre, and it was so heavy that the gods needed Hyrrokkin to launch it.

**Vafthrudnir's riddle**
Odin won a contest of wisdom against the giant Vafthrudnir in the Eddic poem Vafthrudnismal by asking what he had whispered into Baldr's ear on the funeral pyre, a question only Odin himself could answer.

**Draupnir**
Odin's magical gold ring, which drips eight new rings of equal weight every ninth night. Odin placed it on Baldr's funeral pyre, and Baldr later sent it back to Odin from Hel through Hermod.

**Nanna and Forseti**
Nanna is Baldr's wife, who died of grief at his funeral and was burned beside him. Their son Forseti is the Norse god of justice and reconciliation, who settles disputes in his hall Glitnir.

**Hermod's ride to Hel**
Baldr's brother Hermod rode Odin's eight-legged horse Sleipnir for nine nights to reach Hel and beg for Baldr's return. Hel agreed on the condition that everything in the world weep for Baldr.

**Baldrs draumar and Vegtam**
The Eddic poem "Baldr's Dreams," in which Odin, disguised as the wanderer Vegtam, rides to Hel and raises a dead seeress (volva) to learn the meaning of Baldr's nightmares. On the way he passes a bloodied hound, and the volva reveals his identity at the end.

**Litr**
A dwarf who wandered in front of Thor during Baldr's funeral. Thor, who was consecrating the pyre with his hammer, kicked him into the fire, where he burned alive.

**Vali**
A son of Odin and the giantess Rindr, born specifically to avenge Baldr. He grew to adulthood in a single day and killed Hodr.

**Breidablik**
Baldr's hall, the most beautiful in Asgard, a place where nothing unclean or evil can exist. It reflects Baldr's status as the radiant, beloved god of light.

**Saxo Grammaticus's Balderus**
In the Danish historian Saxo's Gesta Danorum, Baldr appears as a demigod who competes with the human Hotherus (Hodr) for Nanna, daughter of King Gewar. Hotherus kills him using a sword obtained from the forest satyr Miming.

**Kīlauea**
Pele is believed to live in the Kīlauea volcano on the Big Island of Hawai'i, specifically in the Halema'uma'u crater within its summit caldera. She is the Hawaiian goddess of volcanoes, fire, and lava, and eruptions are seen as her work.

**Hi'iaka carried as an egg in her armpit**
Pele's favorite younger sister, Hi'iaka, was born as an egg. Pele carried it under her armpit to keep it warm on her voyage to Hawai'i, which is why her sister's full name is Hi'iaka-i-ka-poli-o-Pele, "Hi'iaka in the bosom of Pele." Hi'iaka became a patron of hula and healing.

**Sled race with Poli'ahu**
Pele challenged the snow goddess Poli'ahu of Mauna Kea to a hōlua (sled) race and lost. In anger she cheated, sending streams of lava after her rival, and Poli'ahu nearly fell in before covering the lava with snow. The story explains the fire-versus-snow rivalry of Hawai'i's mountains.

**Nāmaka-o-Kaha'i**
Pele's older sister, a sea goddess, who drove Pele away from their homeland and chased her across the Hawaiian islands, flooding each fire pit Pele dug. Nāmaka eventually killed Pele in battle, after which Pele's spirit took up residence in Kīlauea.

**Haumea**
Pele's mother, an earth and fertility goddess. In some accounts Pele's father is Kāne Milohai, and she was born in a land called Honua-mea, the origin of her epithet Pele-honua-mea.

**Kamapua'a**
The hog-man demigod who was Pele's lover and enemy. When he tried to assault Pele and her sisters, the fertility goddess Kapo sent away her detachable vagina, which lured Kamapua'a after it and let them escape.

**Lohiau**
A handsome chief of Kaua'i whom Pele met in a dream and fell in love with. She sent Hi'iaka to bring him to her, and her jealousy over Hi'iaka's dealings with Lohiau is the core of the long Pele and Hi'iaka saga.

**Lono-makua**
A god associated with fire whom Pele stayed close to at home before her exile. In some versions he keeps the fire in her armpit or helps her carry it.

**Siblings Kapo and Kamohoali'i**
Among Pele's many siblings are Kapo, a goddess of fertility and sorcery, and Kamohoali'i, a shark god who in some versions guided her canoe to Hawai'i.

**Creator of the Hawaiian islands**
Pele is credited with building the Hawaiian islands as she dug fire pits along the chain while fleeing Nāmaka-o-Kaha'i. Their order of formation matches the islands' real geological age, from northwest to southeast.

**Laka and the Menehune**
Some quizbowl questions list Laka, a goddess of hula, and the Menehune, a legendary race of small people who built fishponds and other works overnight, among Pele's associates or children. Other traditions make Laka a sister.

**Perseus and the mirrored shield**
The hero Perseus, son of Zeus and Danae, cut off Medusa's head. Because looking directly at her turned people to stone, he watched her reflection in a polished shield given by Athena and struck while the Gorgons slept.

**Chrysaor and Pegasus**
When Perseus beheaded Medusa, two offspring fathered by Poseidon sprang from her neck: the winged horse Pegasus and the giant warrior Chrysaor, whose name means "golden sword." Chrysaor later became the father of the three-bodied giant Geryon.

**Athena's aegis**
After Perseus finished his quest, he gave Medusa's head to Athena, who placed it (the gorgoneion) on her aegis, a protective goatskin or shield, where its face terrifies her enemies.

**Polydectes of Seriphos**
The king of the island of Seriphos who wanted to marry Danae and so sent her son Perseus away to fetch Medusa's head. At a feast he claimed he would marry Hippodamia and asked guests for horses as gifts; Perseus, who had none, rashly promised the Gorgon's head instead. On his return Perseus turned Polydectes and his court to stone and made Polydectes's brother, the kind fisherman Dictys, king.

**Stheno and Euryale**
Medusa's two sisters, the other Gorgons, daughters of the sea deities Phorcys and Ceto. They were immortal, while Medusa was the only mortal Gorgon, which is why Perseus could kill her; after her death they chased him, but he escaped wearing a helmet of invisibility.

**Poseidon in Athena's temple**
In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Medusa was a beautiful maiden, proud of her hair, whom Poseidon raped in Athena's temple. Athena punished Medusa for defiling the temple by turning her hair into snakes and giving her a petrifying face.

**The Graiae (Grey Sisters)**
Three old women, sisters of the Gorgons, who shared one eye and one tooth among them. Perseus stole the eye as they passed it around and would not give it back until they told him the way to the nymphs who held the gear he needed to find Medusa.

**Winged sandals, helm of invisibility, and the kibisis**
The gear Perseus used on the quest. Hermes's winged sandals let him fly, the Cap of Hades made him invisible, and the kibisis was a magic bag or pouch that held the head safely. The bag was given to him by nymphs (sometimes called the Stygian nymphs, and in some versions linked to the Hesperides).

**Coral from her blood**
When Perseus laid the head down on seaweed or plants by the shore, its power hardened them to stone and created coral. Some accounts connect this to the coral of the Red Sea.

**Libyan snakes, the amphisbaena, and Mopsus**
As Perseus flew over the Libyan desert, drops of blood falling from Medusa's head turned into venomous snakes, including the amphisbaena, a serpent with a head at each end. This explained why Libya was full of snakes, and in the Argonautica the Argonaut seer Mopsus dies there from the bite of one of them.

**Atlas turned to stone**
When the Titan Atlas refused Perseus hospitality, Perseus showed him Medusa's head and turned him into stone, forming the Atlas Mountains in North Africa.

**Andromeda and the sea monster**
On his way home, Perseus used the head (or his sword) to kill the sea monster sent to devour the Ethiopian princess Andromeda, who had been chained to a rock to atone for her mother Cassiopeia's boast. He then married her.

**Petrifying the wedding attackers**
At Perseus's wedding to Andromeda, her former betrothed (Phineus, in some accounts Agenor) burst in with about two hundred armed men. Perseus held up Medusa's head and turned them all to stone.

**The mound in Argos**
According to the travel writer Pausanias, Medusa's head was buried under a mound in the marketplace of Argos, next to the tomb of Perseus's daughter Gorgophone, said to be the first widow to remarry.

**Changing depictions of Medusa**
In early Greek art Medusa was a grotesque monster, sometimes shown with a horse's body, linked to her union with Poseidon, god of horses. From the 5th century BCE she was increasingly portrayed as beautiful; the poet Pindar calls her "fair-cheeked."

**Weighing of the heart against the Feather of Ma'at**
Anubis's most famous role: in the Hall of Two Truths, he weighs the heart of a dead person on a scale against the feather of Ma'at, goddess of truth and order, earning him the title "Guardian of the Scales." This judgment, depicted in the Book of the Dead, decides whether the soul may pass on to the afterlife (the Field of Reeds).

**Ammit**
The monstrous "Devourer of the Dead," with a crocodile's head, a lion's forequarters, and a hippopotamus's hindquarters. Ammit waits beside the scales during the weighing of the heart, and Anubis lets her eat the hearts of those who fail, destroying their souls, while protecting the innocent from her.

**Branding Set as a leopard**
While Anubis guarded Osiris's body, Set disguised himself as a leopard to attack or steal it. Anubis branded him all over with a hot iron rod, which explains the leopard's spots, and in some versions flayed Set and wore his skin, explaining why Anubis's priests wore leopard skins.

**Kebechet**
Anubis's daughter, a goddess of purification whose name means "cooling water." She was depicted as a serpent (sometimes with a star-studded body) and gave cool water to the spirits of the dead during embalming and in the afterlife.

**Son of Nephthys and Osiris**
In the best-known account, Nephthys disguised herself as her sister Isis to sleep with Osiris, and Anubis was born from this union; Isis later raised him. Other traditions name Set or Ra as his father, or other goddesses such as Bastet or Hesat as his mother.

**Opening of the Mouth ceremony**
A funerary ritual in which a priest wearing an Anubis mask touched the mouth of the mummy or a statue with ritual tools. It restored the dead person's ability to eat, drink, speak, and breathe in the afterlife (the Duat).

**Embalming Osiris and inventing mummification**
After Set killed Osiris, Anubis helped Isis embalm his body and wrapped it in linen to prevent decay, inventing mummification. This made Anubis the patron god of embalmers and cemeteries, and in one story he was given Osiris's organs.

**Jackal head**
Anubis is depicted as a man with the head of a black jackal or as a reclining black jackal (canine), likely because jackals scavenged around cemeteries. His black color symbolized the fertile Nile soil and rebirth, not evil.

**Psychopomp and identification with Hermes**
Anubis guided the souls of the dead into the Duat (underworld) and to Osiris for judgment. Because of this role as a psychopomp, Greeks and Romans identified him with Hermes, producing the combined god Hermanubis.

**Cynopolis**
The Greek name ("City of the Dog") of the city in Upper Egypt's 17th nome that was the center of Anubis's cult. His consort Anput was the personification of that nome.

**Imiut fetish**
A cult object associated with Anubis: a headless animal skin (often described as a feline or bull hide) tied to a pole standing in a pot. It was carried in processions and placed in tombs.

**The Tale of Two Brothers**
An Egyptian New Kingdom story whose elder brother, Anpu, shares Anubis's name. Anpu's wife falsely accuses his younger brother Bata of seduction; Bata cuts off his own genitals, which a catfish eats, to prove his innocence, and Anpu kills his wife. Later Anpu searches for years to find Bata's heart and revives him.

**Epithets ("He who is upon his mountain," "Lord of the sacred land," "First of the Westerners")**
Titles describing Anubis as the guardian of necropolises, which lay in the desert hills to the west. He was called "First of the Westerners" (Khenti-Amentiu) before Osiris took over that title, and was also called "Subduer of the Nine Bows," the traditional enemies of Egypt.

**Maa kheru ("true of voice") and the negative confession**
Before the weighing of the heart, the dead person recited the "negative confession," denying sins before 42 divine assessors. Those who passed the judgment were declared "maa kheru," meaning "true of voice" or justified.

**Wepwawet**
A jackal god whose name means "Opener of the Ways," who was often confused with Anubis and is sometimes called his son. The epithet "Opener of the Ways" is sometimes also applied to Anubis himself.

**Cow goddess**
Hathor is usually depicted as a cow, a woman with a cow's head, or a woman with cow's ears. She often wears a headdress of cow horns enclosing a sun disk, and she is a goddess of love, music, dance, joy, and motherhood.

**Sekhmet and the destruction of humanity**
When humans plotted against Ra, he sent his Eye, Hathor, to punish them, and she became the raging lioness Sekhmet. To stop her from wiping out humanity, Ra flooded the fields with beer dyed red to look like blood; she drank it, became drunk, and returned peacefully as Hathor.

**Eye of Ra**
Hathor is one of the goddesses identified as the Eye of Ra, the violent, protective female force of the sun god. This role links her to Sekhmet and to the sun disk on her headdress.

**Dancing naked before Ra**
During the contest between Horus and Set, Ra was insulted and sulked alone. His daughter Hathor cheered him up by dancing and exposing herself to him, making him laugh and return to judge the dispute.

**"House of Horus"**
The meaning of Hathor's Egyptian name (Hwt-Hor). It refers to her role as a sky goddess who contains the falcon god Horus, and in some traditions she is his mother or wife.

**Dendera**
The site of Hathor's chief cult center and her great temple in Upper Egypt, which is one of the best-preserved temples in Egypt.

**The Distant Goddess and Thoth**
In one myth, the Eye of Ra left Egypt in anger and roamed as a wild cat or lioness, killing all who approached. Thoth persuaded her to return by telling her stories.

**Aphrodite**
The Greeks identified Hathor with their own goddess of love and beauty, Aphrodite, because of her associations with love, sexuality, and joy.

**Lady of the West**
Hathor also had a funerary role, welcoming the dead into the afterlife. As "Lady of the West" she is associated with the Theban necropolis, and she is sometimes shown with Osiris.

**Dream interpretation and her priesthood**
People visited Hathor's temples to have their dreams interpreted. Her cult was unusual in that both women and men served as her priests.

**Quetzalcoatl**
The "Feathered Serpent," one of the most important Aztec gods, associated with wind, learning, and creation, and sometimes described as a white god. Tricked by his rival Tezcatlipoca into getting drunk and sleeping with his sister, he leaves in shame (in some versions on a raft of serpents) or burns himself and becomes the morning star (Venus).

**Huitzilopochtli**
The Aztec god of war and the sun, whose name means "Hummingbird of the South" or "Left-Handed Hummingbird." He was the patron of the Mexica, and the Aztecs believed they had to offer him human sacrifices, especially hearts and blood, to keep the sun strong and moving across the sky.

**Coatlicue and the ball of feathers**
Huitzilopochtli's mother Coatlicue ("Serpent Skirt") becomes pregnant when a ball of feathers falls into her clothing while she sweeps on Coatepec (Snake Mountain). Her daughter Coyolxauhqui and her 400 sons, the Centzon Huitznahua, try to kill her for the shameful pregnancy, but Huitzilopochtli is born fully armed and kills them, dismembering his sister, whose head becomes the moon.

**Tezcatlipoca**
The "Smoking Mirror," a dark, powerful god of night, sorcery, and fate and the arch-rival of Quetzalcoatl. He is shown with an obsidian mirror in place of the foot he lost to the earth monster Cipactli.

**Cipactli and the creation of the earth**
A primordial crocodile-like monster of the waters. Tezcatlipoca uses his own foot as bait to catch it, losing the foot in the process, and he and Quetzalcoatl tear the monster apart to make the earth and the heavens. The Aztecs believed in thirteen heavens and nine underworld levels.

**The Five Suns**
Aztec cosmology holds that the world has been created and destroyed four times, with each age ruled by a different sun. The earlier ages were ended by jaguars, wind, a rain of fire, and a flood (whose people turned into fish), and the present age is the Fifth Sun, Nahui Ollin ("Four Movement"), which is destined to end in earthquakes. In the first age, the one-footed Tezcatlipoca was a dim, half-sized sun until Quetzalcoatl knocked him out of the sky with a club.

**Nanahuatzin and the rabbit in the moon**
To create the Fifth Sun the gods gather at Teotihuacan, where the humble, sore-covered god Nanahuatzin leaps into a bonfire and becomes the sun. The proud Tecciztecatl jumps in second and also becomes a sun, so the gods throw a rabbit at his face to dim him, making him the moon and leaving the image of a rabbit on it.

**Mictlan and the bones of humanity**
Mictlan is the Aztec underworld, ruled by Mictlantecuhtli. To create the humans of the Fifth Sun, Quetzalcoatl goes down to Mictlan to steal the bones of earlier humans. The goddess Cihuacoatl grinds the bones into powder, and Quetzalcoatl sheds his own blood on them to bring the new people to life.

**Xolotl**
A dog-headed god of death, lightning, and monsters, often called Quetzalcoatl's twin. He accompanies Quetzalcoatl to Mictlan, guides the dead to the underworld, and is linked to Venus as the evening star.

**Templo Mayor and Tenochtitlan**
The Templo Mayor was the great pyramid at the center of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan (modern Mexico City). It had twin temples on top, one dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and one to the rain god Tlaloc, and it was the sacred center of Aztec religion.

**Eagle on a cactus eating a snake**
Huitzilopochtli tells the wandering Mexica to settle where they see an eagle perched on a cactus devouring a snake. They see this sign on an island in Lake Texcoco and found Tenochtitlan there, and the image appears on the modern Mexican flag.

**Tlaloc**
The Aztec rain and fertility god, honored with child sacrifices since children's tears were thought to bring rain. He rules Tlalocan, a paradise of eternal springtime. When he was the third sun, Tezcatlipoca stole his wife Xochiquetzal, and in his grief he rained fire on the world and destroyed it.

**Xipe Totec**
"Our Lord the Flayed One," an Aztec god of agriculture, spring, and renewal. His priests wore the flayed skins of sacrificial victims, and he was said to have flayed himself to give food to humanity, symbolizing a seed shedding its husk.

**New Fire Ceremony**
A ritual held every 52 years when the Aztec calendar cycle ended. All fires were put out, and priests on a hill near Tenochtitlan watched for the stars to keep moving; then a new fire was kindled in the chest of a sacrificed victim and spread throughout the land, ensuring the world would go on.

**Teotihuacan and Hernan Cortes**
Teotihuacan is an older ruined city whose name, given by the Aztecs, means "city of the gods" in Nahuatl, the Aztec language. The Aztec Empire fell to the Spanish conquistador Hernan Cortes in 1521, and a famous (but disputed) story says the emperor Moctezuma II believed Cortes was the returning Quetzalcoatl.

**Amaterasu hiding in a cave**
The Shinto sun goddess Amaterasu, angered by her brother's violence, shut herself in the cave Ama-no-Iwato and plunged the world into darkness. The other kami lured her out with laughter (provoked by the goddess Ame-no-Uzume's bawdy dance) and a mirror that showed her own radiant reflection. Japan's emperors claim descent from her.

**Flayed horse thrown at a loom**
The outrage that drove Amaterasu into the cave: the storm god Susano'o flayed a piebald horse and hurled it into her weaving hall, killing one of her weaving maidens. It is one of the most repeated clues for Japanese myth.

**Yamata no Orochi**
The eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent slain by the exiled Susano'o. It had eaten seven of an elderly couple's eight daughters, so Susano'o set out eight vats of strong sake, got the serpent drunk, and cut it to pieces with his ten-span sword (Totsuka no Tsurugi), then married the surviving daughter, Kushinada-hime.

**Kusanagi (the Grass-Cutter Sword)**
The sword Susano'o found inside one of Orochi's tails, which chipped his own blade. He gave it to Amaterasu, and it later became one of the imperial regalia. Its name, "grass-cutter," comes from a later legend in which the hero Yamato Takeru used it to mow down a burning field.

**Izanagi and Izanami**
The primordial husband-and-wife creator kami. Standing on the Floating Bridge of Heaven (Ame-no-ukihashi), they stirred the ocean with the jeweled spear Ame-no-nuboko, and brine dripping from its tip formed Onogoro, the first island. They built a home there around a great central pillar and gave birth to the islands of Japan and many kami.

**Izanami's death and the underworld Yomi**
Izanami died after giving birth to the fire god Kagutsuchi. Izanagi followed her to the underworld Yomi but saw her rotting, maggot-ridden body and fled, throwing objects including peaches at his pursuers. After he sealed the entrance with a boulder, she vowed to kill 1,000 people a day, and he answered that he would cause 1,500 to be born.

**Birth of Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi, and Susano'o**
When Izanagi purified himself in water after leaving Yomi, gods were born from his washing: Amaterasu from his left eye, the moon god Tsukuyomi from his right eye, and Susano'o from his nose.

**Jimmu**
The legendary first emperor of Japan, a descendant of Amaterasu, according to the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. On his campaign eastward to conquer the Yamato region he was guided by Yatagarasu, a three-legged crow, and he fought peoples later called Emishi, whose name is written with characters meaning "shrimp barbarians."

**Three Sacred Treasures**
The imperial regalia of Japan: the sword Kusanagi, the mirror Yata no Kagami (the mirror used to lure Amaterasu from the cave), and the jewel Yasakani no Magatama. Amaterasu gave them to her grandson Ninigi when he descended to rule the earth, and they passed to his great-grandson Jimmu. They are presented at the emperor's enthronement.

**Akitsushima (Dragonfly Island)**
A classical poetic name for Japan. In one story, Jimmu looked out over the land and said it resembled two dragonflies mating, forming a ring. In another, a dragonfly protected Emperor Yūryaku by eating an insect that bit his arm.

**Jimmu's ancestry and marriage**
Jimmu was the grandson of Hoori (Yamasachihiko), who lost his brother's borrowed fishhook and went to the palace of the sea god to find it, and Toyotama-hime, the sea god's daughter. Jimmu's empress was said to be the child of a woman impregnated by the god Ōmononushi, who had taken the form of a red arrow.

**Momotarō**
"Peach Boy," the hero of a famous Japanese folktale. He was found inside a giant peach floating down a river by an elderly couple, and he traveled to Onigashima, the island of ogres (oni), with a dog, a monkey, and a pheasant to defeat them.

**Inari**
The Shinto kami of rice, fertility, and prosperity, whose messengers are foxes (kitsune). In folklore, foxes grow more tails as they gain age and wisdom, up to nine. Inari shrines are known for their rows of red torii gates.

**Urashima Tarō**
A fisherman who saved a turtle and was rewarded with a stay at Ryūgū-jō, the undersea palace of the dragon god Ryūjin. When he returned home, about 300 years had passed. Ryūjin is also said to own two jewels that control the tides.

**Raijin and other folk tales**
Japanese parents tell children to cover their belly buttons during thunderstorms or the thunder god Raijin will eat their navels. Other tales say the jellyfish lost its bones as punishment for failing to bring Ryūjin a monkey's liver, and that the sea cucumber had its mouth slit for staying silent when the other sea creatures vowed to serve the descendants of the heavenly kami.

**Murder of Osiris**
Set's most famous act. Jealous of his brother Osiris, king of Egypt, he tricked Osiris into lying down in a custom-made chest (coffin), sealed it, and threw it into the Nile. When Isis recovered the body, Set cut it into 14 pieces and scattered them across Egypt, then took the throne.

**Stone boat race**
One of the contests between Set and his nephew Horus. They agreed to race boats made of stone. Horus secretly built a wooden boat and plastered it to look like stone, while Set built a real stone boat that sank, so he lost.

**Defeating Apep (Apophis)**
Set rode on the prow of the sun god Ra's solar barge during its nightly journey through the underworld and speared the chaos serpent Apep, which tried to swallow the sun each night. This role made him a protector of Ra despite his villainy elsewhere.

**The Contendings of Horus and Seth**
A New Kingdom text describing the 80-year struggle between Set and Horus, Osiris's son, for the throne of Egypt before a tribunal of gods. Its episodes include the boat race, the lettuce trick, and Set gouging out Horus's eye.

**Lettuce and semen**
In the Contendings, Set tried to humiliate Horus by sexually dominating him, but Horus caught Set's semen. Isis then spread Horus's semen on lettuce, Set's favorite food (said to be the only thing he ate), and when the gods summoned the semen, it answered from inside Set, shaming him before the tribunal.

**Horus's eye and Set's testicles**
In their fights, Set tore out Horus's eye, which was later restored and became the Eye of Horus, a symbol of healing and protection. Horus in turn tore off Set's testicles, which was said to explain the barrenness of Set's desert domain.

**Nephthys and Anubis**
Set's wife and sister. She disguised herself as her sister Isis and slept with Osiris, conceiving Anubis, which angered Set.

**God of the "Red Land" and foreigners**
When Geb divided Egypt, he gave the fertile black land of the Nile valley to Horus and the barren desert, the "red land" (deshret), to Set. Set was also the god of storms, chaos, violence, and foreign lands.

**Hyksos worship at Avaris**
The Hyksos, foreign rulers of northern Egypt, made Set their chief god at their capital Avaris and identified him with the Canaanite storm god Baal. The Hyksos king Apepi was a devotee. The later 400 Year Stela commemorated the 400th anniversary of Set's cult there.

**Ombos (Nubt)**
Set's main cult center in Upper Egypt, near Naqada. He was called "the Ombite" ("he of Nubt"), and some of the earliest images of the Set animal date to the Naqada period.

**Isis's trick**
In the Contendings, Isis disguised herself as a widow and told Set that a stranger had stolen her son's inheritance. When Set said this was wrong, he condemned himself, since he had stolen Horus's inheritance.

**Anat and Astarte**
To settle the dispute, the goddess Neith advised that Horus receive the throne and that Set be compensated with two foreign goddesses, the Canaanite Anat and Astarte, as wives.

**Typhon**
Greek writers, especially Plutarch in On Isis and Osiris, identified Set with Typhon, the monstrous enemy of Zeus.

**The Set animal and was scepter**
Set is depicted with the head of an unidentified creature with a long curved snout and tall flat-topped ears, sometimes with a forked tail. He often holds the was scepter, a staff topped with the head of a similar animal. He was also associated with pigs, hippos, and donkeys.

**Slaying Medusa**
Perseus's most famous feat was beheading Medusa, the only mortal of the three Gorgons (her immortal sisters were Stheno and Euryale), whose gaze turned people to stone. He avoided her gaze by looking only at her reflection in a polished shield. He then escaped the pursuing sisters while invisible, and later gave the head to Athena, who placed it on her aegis.

**Killing Acrisius with a discus**
An oracle told King Acrisius of Argos that his daughter's son would kill him. Years later, while competing in funeral games held by King Teutamides of Larissa, Perseus threw a discus (or quoit) that the wind carried astray. It struck and killed Acrisius, fulfilling the prophecy by accident.

**Danae and the shower of gold**
To keep the prophecy from coming true, Acrisius locked his daughter Danae in a bronze chamber or tower. Zeus reached her in the form of a shower of golden rain and fathered Perseus.

**Cast out to sea in a chest and rescued by Dictys on Seriphos**
After Perseus was born, Acrisius locked Danae and the baby in a wooden chest and threw it into the sea. It washed up on the island of Seriphos, where the kindly fisherman Dictys took them in and raised Perseus. After returning, Perseus made Dictys king of Seriphos.

**Polydectes and the bride-gift**
Dictys's brother Polydectes, king of Seriphos, wanted to marry Danae and wanted Perseus out of the way. When each guest brought a horse as a gift (supposedly for the bride-price of Hippodamia), Perseus had no horse and rashly offered anything else, so Polydectes demanded Medusa's head. When Perseus returned, he turned Polydectes and his court to stone with the head.

**Gifts from the gods: winged sandals, cap of invisibility, shield, kibisis, and harpe**
Perseus was equipped by several gods and nymphs. Hermes gave him winged sandals and an adamantine sickle (harpe), and Athena gave him a polished bronze shield. Hades's helmet (cap) of invisibility and a magic bag (kibisis) that expanded to hold the head came from the nymphs (Hesperides) in some accounts, from the gods in others.

**The Graeae and their shared eye**
The Graeae (Gray Sisters) were three ancient sisters of the Gorgons who shared a single eye and a single tooth. Perseus grabbed the eye as they passed it between them and held it hostage until they told him the way to the nymphs who held the magic items and to the Gorgons' lair.

**Rescuing Andromeda from Cetus**
On his way home, Perseus came upon the Ethiopian princess Andromeda, daughter of King Cepheus and Queen Cassiopeia. She had been chained to a rock as a sacrifice to the sea monster Cetus because Cassiopeia boasted that she (or her daughter) was more beautiful than the Nereids. Perseus killed the monster and married Andromeda.

**Phineus and the wedding fight**
Andromeda had earlier been promised to Phineus, Cepheus's brother. Phineus (sometimes paired with Agenor) and his followers attacked Perseus at the wedding feast, and Perseus turned them to stone with Medusa's head. This Phineus is not the blind seer met by the Argonauts.

**Pegasus and Chrysaor**
When Perseus cut off Medusa's head, the winged horse Pegasus and the warrior Chrysaor, her children by Poseidon, sprang from her neck. Pegasus was later tamed by the hero Bellerophon.

**Turning Atlas to stone**
When the Titan Atlas refused Perseus hospitality, fearing that a son of Zeus would steal his golden apples, Perseus showed him Medusa's head and turned him into the Atlas Mountains of North Africa.

**Founding Mycenae and the Cyclopean walls**
Perseus founded Mycenae, by legend at a spot where the cap (mykes) of his scabbard fell off or where he found a mushroom (also mykes) that held water to quench his thirst. Its massive walls were said to have been built by the Cyclopes, which gave the name "Cyclopean masonry."

**Trading kingdoms with Megapenthes**
Ashamed of having killed his grandfather, Perseus did not take the throne of Argos. He traded it to his cousin Megapenthes, son of Proetus (Acrisius's brother, whom Perseus killed in some versions), for Tiryns. In one account Megapenthes later killed Perseus.

**Snakes of Libya**
As Perseus flew over Libya carrying Medusa's head, drops of her blood fell to the sand and became venomous snakes. One of them later killed the Argonaut seer Mopsus.

**Descendants: Electryon, Alcmene, and Heracles**
Perseus and Andromeda's sons included Electryon and Sthenelus. Electryon's daughter Alcmene was Heracles's mother, making Heracles Perseus's great-grandson, and Sthenelus was the father of Eurystheus, who assigned Heracles his labors.

**Abduction of Persephone**
Hades seized Persephone, the daughter of Demeter, while she was picking flowers (lilies, in Ovid near Henna in Sicily, or in the plain of Nysa), opening a chasm in the earth to carry her down in his chariot. The nymph Cyane tried to stop him and dissolved into a pool from grief, and Demeter's mourning during her search made the earth barren.

**Pomegranate seeds**
While in the underworld, Persephone ate pomegranate seeds (often six), and anyone who eats the food of the dead must remain there. As a compromise, she spends part of each year with Hades, causing winter, and returns to her mother each spring. Ascalaphus revealed that she had eaten the seeds and was punished by being pinned under a boulder.

**Minthe**
A nymph who tried to seduce Hades or was loved by him. Persephone, jealous, transformed her into the mint plant.

**Pirithous, Theseus, and the Chair of Forgetfulness**
Theseus and his friend Pirithous descended to the underworld to kidnap Persephone as Pirithous's bride. Hades tricked them into sitting on stone chairs that bound them (in some versions with snakes) and made them forget; Heracles later freed Theseus, who left part of his thighs stuck to the seat, but Pirithous remained trapped forever.

**Cerberus**
Hades' three-headed watchdog, who guards the gates of the underworld so the dead cannot leave. For his twelfth labor, Heracles captured Cerberus, with Hades permitting it only if Heracles used no weapons; Orpheus lulled the dog to sleep with music, and Psyche got past it with barley or honey cakes.

**Helm of Darkness**
A helmet of invisibility forged for Hades by the Cyclopes during the Titanomachy, the war against the Titans. Perseus borrowed it to escape Medusa's Gorgon sisters after beheading her.

**Leuce**
A nymph, daughter of Oceanus, who was loved by Hades. When she died, he turned her into a white poplar tree in the Elysian Fields.

**Rivers of the underworld and Charon**
The underworld, which shares Hades' name, has five rivers: the Styx, Acheron, Lethe (the river of forgetfulness), Phlegethon (a river of fire), and Cocytus. The ferryman Charon carries the souls of the dead across to Hades' realm.

**Elysium, Asphodel, and Tartarus**
The regions of Hades' realm. Elysium (the Elysian Fields) is a paradise for heroes and the virtuous, the Asphodel Meadows hold ordinary souls, and Tartarus is the deep pit where the wicked, such as Sisyphus, Tantalus, Tityos, and the Danaids, are punished.

**Plouton and other epithets**
Because the Greeks feared saying his name, Hades was called by euphemisms such as Plouton ("the wealthy one," "giver of wealth," since precious metals and fertile crops come from beneath the earth), Clymenus ("renowned"), Polydegmon ("receiver of many"), and Eubuleus. Plouton became the Roman Pluto.

**Judges of the dead**
Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Aeacus judged the souls of the dead in Hades' realm, deciding whether they went to Elysium, Asphodel, or Tartarus. Minos cast the deciding vote, and Aeacus is said to hold the keys of Hades' palace.

**Wounded at Pylos**
When Heracles attacked the city of Pylos, Hades fought on the side of its defenders, and Heracles wounded him in the shoulder with an arrow.

**Psyche's descent**
In Apuleius's tale of Cupid and Psyche, Venus's final task for Psyche was to travel to the underworld and bring back a box containing some of Persephone's (Proserpina's) beauty.

**Orpheus and Eurydice**
The musician Orpheus descended into the underworld and moved Hades and Persephone with his music to let his dead wife Eurydice return, on condition that he not look back. He looked back just before leaving, and she was lost forever.

**Asclepius**
The healer Asclepius, son of Apollo, began raising the dead, including Hippolytus. Hades complained that his realm was losing souls, and Zeus struck Asclepius down with a thunderbolt.

**Dashavatara (the ten avatars)**
Vishnu comes down to earth in different forms (avatars) whenever dharma (cosmic order) is threatened. The standard list of ten is Matsya (fish), Kurma (turtle), Varaha (boar, who lifted the earth goddess Bhumi out of the ocean on his tusks after killing the demon Hiranyaksha), Narasimha (man-lion), Vamana (dwarf), Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, the Buddha (added to the list around the Gupta period; some lists use Balarama instead), and Kalki. Helena Blavatsky claimed in Isis Unveiled that the sequence mirrors Darwinian evolution.

**Krishna and the Bhagavad Gita**
Krishna, the eighth avatar, is the blue-skinned king of Dvaraka. In the Mahabharata he gave his Narayani army to Duryodhana and joined the Pandava side himself as Arjuna's unarmed charioteer at the Kurukshetra War. The Bhagavad Gita, a 700-verse dialogue within the epic, records how he urged Arjuna to do his duty as a warrior, taught paths such as bhakti yoga, and revealed his cosmic, many-armed form, declaring "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds," a line J. Robert Oppenheimer famously quoted.

**Krishna's childhood: the butter thief, Kamsa, Putana, and Govardhan Hill**
Krishna was the eighth child of Devaki and Vasudeva. To save him from his tyrannical uncle Kamsa, king of Mathura, he was swapped at birth and raised by the cowherds Nanda and Yashoda in Gokul. As a child he was nicknamed Makhan Chor ("butter thief"), sucked the life out of the demoness Putana when she tried to feed him poisoned breast milk, and lifted Govardhan Hill on one finger to shelter the villagers from storms sent by an angry Indra. He later killed Kamsa, put Ugrasena back on the throne, and danced the rasa lila with the gopis (cowherd women) led by his beloved Radha while playing the flute.

**Rama and the Ramayana**
Rama, the seventh avatar, is the hero of Valmiki's epic Ramayana. His stepmother Kaikeyi had him exiled for fourteen years, and in the forest his wife Sita was kidnapped by the demon king Ravana. With his brother Lakshmana, the monkey king Sugriva, and the devoted Hanuman, he attacked Lanka, killed Ravana, and rescued Sita.

**Vamana and the three steps**
As the dwarf Brahmin Vamana, Vishnu asked the generous demon king Mahabali (Bali) for only as much land as he could cover in three steps. Once Bali agreed, Vamana grew to cosmic size (as Trivikrama), covered the earth and the heavens in two strides, and placed his third step on Bali's head, pushing him down to the underworld.

**Narasimha, Hiranyakashipu, and Prahlada**
The demon king Hiranyakashipu had a boon that he could not be killed by man or beast, indoors or outdoors, by day or by night, or by any weapon. To save the demon's son Prahlada, a devotee of Vishnu, Vishnu burst out of a pillar as Narasimha, half man and half lion. He killed Hiranyakashipu at twilight, on the threshold of the palace, holding him across his thighs and tearing him open with his claws. The festival of Holi is linked to this story.

**Kalki**
The tenth and final avatar, still to come, who will appear at the end of the current dark age, the Kali Yuga. He will ride a white horse (Devadatta) and carry a blazing sword to destroy evil, including the demon Kali, and begin a new Satya Yuga (golden age).

**Garuda**
Vishnu's vahana (mount) is Garuda, the eagle-like king of birds. Garuda was born from the second of two eggs laid by Vinata, who was the sister and rival of Kadru, mother of a thousand serpents, and he is the enemy of snakes.

**Reclining on Shesha, with Brahma born from his navel**
Vishnu is often shown sleeping on the cosmic ocean on the coils of the many-headed serpent Shesha (Ananta), a pose called Anantashayana or Ananthapadmanabha. A lotus grows from his navel, and from it the creator god Brahma is born.

**Lakshmi**
Vishnu's consort is Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth and fortune, who often sits at his feet or on a lotus. She rose from the Churning of the Ocean of Milk and chose Vishnu as her husband. Her avatars include Sita, the wife of Rama.

**Churning of the Ocean of Milk and Kurma**
The gods (devas) and demons (asuras) churned the cosmic ocean of milk to obtain amrita, the elixir of immortality, using Mount Mandara as the churning rod and the serpent Vasuki as the rope. When the mountain began to sink, Vishnu took the form of the turtle Kurma and held it up on his back.

**Mohini**
Mohini is Vishnu's only female form, a beautiful enchantress. After the churning, she distracted the demons and gave all the amrita to the gods. When the demon Rahu (Rahu-Ketu) slipped in to drink it, she cut off his head with Vishnu's discus. In another story, Mohini tricked the demon Bhasmasura, whose touch burned anyone to ash, into putting his hand on his own head.

**Preserver in the Trimurti**
Vishnu is the preserver (sustainer) of the universe in the Hindu Trimurti, along with Brahma the creator and Shiva the destroyer. He is known by a thousand names, including Narayana and Hari, the Bhagavata Purana is devoted to him and his avatars, and Vaishnavism, including the Hare Krishna movement, worships him as the supreme god.

**Four arms with conch, discus, mace, and lotus**
Vishnu is usually depicted as blue-skinned with four arms, holding the conch Panchajanya, the spinning discus Sudarshana Chakra, the mace Kaumodaki, and a lotus. He also has the sword Nandaka, and the Vishnupad Temple at Gaya holds a large footprint said to be his.

**Parashurama**
The sixth avatar, a warrior Brahmin who carries an axe given to him by Shiva. After a king killed his father, he swore to wipe out the Kshatriya (warrior) class and did so twenty-one times, filling five lakes with their blood. In one story, when Ganesha would not let him enter Mount Kailash, Parashurama threw the axe, which broke off one of Ganesha's tusks.

**Contendings with Set**
Horus, son of Isis and Osiris, fought his uncle Set (Seth), who had murdered and dismembered Osiris, for the throne of Egypt. The Contendings of Horus and Seth describe a dispute that dragged on for eighty years before the Ennead, the council of gods, ruled in Horus's favor and made him king. Set was sent off to rule the deserts and storms.

**The stone boat race**
In one of the contests, Horus and Set agreed to race in boats made of stone. Horus secretly built his boat out of wood (cedar) and plastered or painted it gray so that it looked like stone, while Set built a real stone boat, which sank. This is the most frequently mentioned contest.

**Wedjat (Eye of Horus)**
During their fighting, Set gouged out Horus's eye (or both eyes). The wedjat (also spelled wadjet or udjat) eye became a protective amulet representing healing and wholeness. Horus's right eye was associated with the sun and his left, damaged eye with the moon, which explains why the moon is dimmer than the sun. The parts of the eye symbol were also used to write fractions from one half to one sixty-fourth.

**Hathor heals his eyes with milk**
After Set tore out Horus's eyes and buried them on a mountainside, where they grew into lotus flowers, the goddess Hathor restored his sight by pouring gazelle milk into the empty sockets. Hathor is also usually named as Horus's wife, and in a yearly festival her statue traveled from her temple at Dendera to his at Edfu to reunite the couple.

**Four Sons of Horus and the canopic jars**
Horus's four sons, Imsety (human-headed), Hapi (baboon-headed), Duamutef (jackal-headed), and Qebehsenuef (falcon-headed), each guarded one cardinal direction and one of the organs removed during mummification. Their heads appear on the lids of the four canopic jars that held those organs.

**Falcon-headed sky god and the pharaohs**
Horus is usually shown as a falcon or a man with a falcon's head, often wearing the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt. Each living pharaoh was considered an earthly embodiment of Horus, while a dead king became identified with Osiris.

**Harpocrates and the finger to the lips**
Horus the Child (Har-pa-khered) was shown as a naked boy with the sidelock of youth and a finger to his lips. The Greeks and Romans misunderstood the gesture as a call for silence and worshipped him as Harpocrates, god of silence and secrets; he was linked to the phrase "sub rosa." Aleister Crowley's religion Thelema says the world is now in the "Aeon of Horus."

**Sobek retrieves his severed hands**
After Horus's semen was involved in a contest with Set, Isis cut off his hands, which she considered polluted, and threw them into the marshes or the Nile, then made him new ones. The crocodile god Sobek fished the original hands out of the water with a fish trap.

**The contaminated lettuce**
When Set tried to seduce or rape Horus to show his dominance over him, Horus caught Set's semen in his hand. Isis then had Horus put his own semen on the lettuce in Set's garden, which Set ate. When the gods called out to each spirit, Set's semen answered from the marshes, while Horus's answered from inside Set, proving to the Ennead that Horus had dominated him.

**The hippopotamus contest and Isis's beheading**
Horus and Set changed into hippopotamuses and competed to see who could stay underwater longer. Isis threw a copper harpoon to help her son, but she first struck Horus by mistake, and when she then hit Set, she released him out of pity because he was her brother. In a rage, Horus cut off his mother's head, which the gods later restored, sometimes as a cow's head.

**Set's lost testicles**
In the battle in which Horus lost his eye, he tore off one of Set's testicles (or both). This was said to explain why Set's domain, the desert, is infertile.

**Conception and birth on Chemmis**
Isis conceived Horus by reassembling and briefly reviving the dead Osiris, making a replacement for his missing phallus. She then hid the infant Horus from Set in the papyrus marshes on the island of Chemmis in the Nile Delta, where he was raised with the help of the cobra goddess Wadjet (called Buto by the Greeks).

**Nekhen (Hierakonpolis) and Edfu**
Nekhen in Upper Egypt was the oldest center of Horus worship; the Greeks called it Hierakonpolis, "City of the Hawk." The Ptolemaic Temple of Edfu, one of the best-preserved temples in Egypt, was also dedicated to him and held an annual Festival of Victory celebrating his defeat of Set.

**Forms: Horus the Elder, Behdety, and Ra-Horakhty**
Horus appears in many forms. Horus the Elder (Haroeris, Heru-ur) was an older form linked to Nekhen. Horus of Behdet (Behdety) was shown as the winged sun disk, and Horakhty ("Horus of the Two Horizons") was merged with Ra as Ra-Horakhty, the rising and setting sun. As Mekhenty-er-irty, a form of him without eyes, he was linked to the blind and to nights with no moon.

**Mjolnir, made by Brokkr and Eitri (Sindri)**
The dwarf brothers Brokkr and Eitri (also called Sindri) forged Thor's hammer Mjolnir. They also made the gold-bristled boar Gullinbursti for Freyr and Odin's self-multiplying ring Draupnir, which drips eight new rings every ninth night.

**Loki's bet and his mouth sewn shut**
Loki bet his head that Brokkr and Eitri could not make gifts better than those of the Sons of Ivaldi. He turned into a fly (or gadfly) and stung Brokkr to spoil the work, but still lost. Loki then argued the dwarves could take his head but not his neck, so Brokkr sewed his lips shut instead.

**Sons of Ivaldi: Sif's golden hair and Gungnir**
After Loki cut off the hair of Thor's wife Sif, the dwarf Sons of Ivaldi made her new hair of real gold. In the same batch they forged Odin's spear Gungnir and Freyr's folding ship Skidbladnir.

**Four dwarves holding up the sky**
According to the Prose Edda, the gods made the sky from the skull of the giant Ymir. Four dwarves named Nordri, Sudri, Austri and Vestri (North, South, East and West) hold it up at its four corners.

**Fjalar, Galar and the Mead of Poetry**
These two dwarves murdered the wise being Kvasir and mixed his blood with honey in the vessels Son, Bodn and the kettle Odrerir to make the Mead of Poetry. Anyone who drinks it becomes a poet or scholar.

**Killing Gilling and his wife**
Fjalar and Galar drowned the giant Gilling by overturning his boat, then killed his grieving wife by dropping a millstone on her head. Gilling's son Suttung took the Mead of Poetry from them as compensation for his parents' deaths.

**Gleipnir, the chain that binds Fenrir**
The dwarves made the magic fetter Gleipnir to bind the wolf Fenrir. It was made from six impossible things, including the sound of a cat's footsteps, the breath of a fish, the beard of a woman and the roots of a mountain.

**Born as maggots in Ymir's flesh**
In Snorri's Prose Edda (Gylfaginning), the dwarves first appeared as maggots in the flesh of the dead giant Ymir, and the gods then gave them human form and reason. The Voluspa instead says they were made from "Brimir's blood" and "Blain's limbs," usually read as names for Ymir.

**Alviss turned to stone**
In the Eddic poem Alvissmal, the dwarf Alviss ("All-Wise") comes to marry Thor's daughter Thrud. Thor stalls him with a long quiz about the names of things until the sun rises, and the sunlight turns Alviss to stone.

**Brisingamen**
The goddess Freyja got her famous necklace Brisingamen from four dwarves who forged it, in exchange for spending a night with each of them.

**Svartalfar (dark elves) and Nidavellir**
Snorri Sturluson describes "dark elves" (svartalfar) in a way that has led many scholars to treat them as the same as dwarves. The dwarves' home is often called Nidavellir or Svartalfheim, one of the nine worlds.

**Dvalinn and the runes**
Dvalinn is one of the most famous dwarves, said in the Havamal to have carved runes for the dwarves. The Fafnismal says some of the Norns are the daughters of Dvalinn.

**Lit kicked onto Baldr's pyre**
At the funeral of Baldr, who was killed by a mistletoe dart, the dwarf Lit ran in front of Thor while he was blessing the pyre with Mjolnir. Thor kicked Lit into the fire, and he burned up with Baldr.

**Hreidmar, Fafnir and the dwarf Andvari**
In the Volsung legend, Hreidmar and his sons Fafnir, Regin and Otr are sometimes described as dwarves. Fafnir later turned into a dragon to guard the cursed gold the gods took from the dwarf Andvari, and the hero Sigurd killed him. Andvari inspired the dwarf Alberich, who steals the Rhinegold in Wagner's Ring of the Nibelung.

**Tyrfing and Svafrlami**
King Svafrlami trapped the dwarves Dvalinn and Durin outside their rock and forced them to forge the sword Tyrfing. In revenge they cursed it to kill a man every time it was drawn and to bring about three great evils.

**Death of Baldr by mistletoe**
Loki engineered the death of Baldr, Odin and Frigg's beloved son. Frigg had made everything in creation swear not to harm Baldr except the mistletoe, a fact Loki learned by disguising himself as an old woman. He then gave a mistletoe dart, spear, or arrow to Baldr's blind brother Hodr and guided his aim, killing Baldr.

**Giving birth to Sleipnir**
When a giant mason was building the walls of Asgard with the help of his stallion Svadilfari, and was about to win the sun, the moon, and Freya as payment, Loki turned himself into a mare to lure the horse away so the walls would go unfinished. Loki later gave birth to the eight-legged horse Sleipnir, which became Odin's steed, so Loki is the "mother" of Sleipnir.

**Bound beneath a venom-dripping serpent**
As punishment for Baldr's death, the gods bound Loki to a rock using the entrails of his son Narfi (or Nari), who had been torn apart by Loki's other son Vali after Vali was turned into a wolf. The giantess Skadi fastened a serpent above him whose venom drips onto his face. His faithful wife Sigyn catches the venom in a bowl, but when she leaves to empty it, the poison hits him and his writhing causes earthquakes. He stays bound until Ragnarok.

**Fenrir, Jormungandr, and Hel**
Loki's three monstrous children with the giantess Angrboda of the Iron Wood. Fenrir is the great wolf who kills Odin at Ragnarok, Jormungandr is the Midgard Serpent that Odin threw into the ocean surrounding the world, and Hel, who is half blue and half flesh-colored, rules the underworld of the dishonorable dead, to which Odin sent her.

**Lokasenna**
"Loki's Quarrel" or "Loki's Flyting," a poem in the Poetic Edda (Codex Regius) set at a feast held by the sea giant Aegir. Loki kills Aegir's servant Fimafeng for being praised, is driven out, then returns and trades insults with every god and goddess (including accusations of incest and of effeminate sorcery) until Thor threatens to smite him.

**Escaping as a salmon**
After the Lokasenna, Loki fled and hid in a house with four doors, often transforming into a salmon at Franang's Falls. He invented the fishing net, then burned it when the gods approached, but the gods used its ashes to make their own net and caught him in salmon form.

**The bet with Brokkr and Sindri**
After cutting off the golden hair of Thor's wife Sif, Loki had the Sons of Ivaldi make her new hair along with other treasures such as the folding ship Skidbladnir. He then bet his head that the dwarves Brokkr and Sindri (Eitri) could not make better gifts, and turned into a fly to sting Brokkr, which caused Mjolnir's handle to come out short. Loki lost the bet but avoided beheading by arguing he had never wagered his neck, so Brokkr sewed his lips shut instead.

**Idunn and Thiazi**
When the giant Thiazi, in eagle form, seized Loki (who had struck him with a pole), Loki agreed to lure the goddess Idunn and her apples of immortality out of Asgard. When the gods began to age, Loki rescued her by borrowing a falcon-feather cloak and turning her into a nut; Thiazi chased him in eagle form and was burned to death by a fire at Asgard's walls. To compensate Thiazi's daughter Skadi, Loki made her laugh by tying his testicles to the beard of a goat.

**Eating contest against Logi**
While traveling with Thor to the hall of the giant Utgard-Loki, Loki competed in an eating contest against Logi, who devoured not only the meat but the bones and the trough. Logi was later revealed to be fire itself in disguise.

**Killed by Heimdall at Ragnarok**
At the end of the world, Loki breaks free and leads the giants against the gods, and he and the watchman god Heimdall kill each other. Earlier, Loki and Heimdall fought in the form of seals over Freya's necklace Brisingamen, which Loki had stolen and Heimdall recovered.

**Thokk**
A giantess, presumed to be Loki in disguise, who was the only being that refused to weep for Baldr. Hel had agreed to release Baldr if everything in the world mourned him, so Thokk's refusal ("Let Hel hold what she has") kept Baldr in the underworld.

**Otr and Andvari's gold**
While traveling with Odin and Hoenir, Loki killed an otter with a stone; it was actually Otr, son of the sorcerer Hreidmar. To pay the wergild (blood money) of filling and covering the otter's skin with red gold, Loki borrowed a net from the sea goddess Ran, caught the dwarf Andvari, and extorted his treasure and cursed ring. This story opens the Volsunga saga.

**Thor's journey to Thrym**
When the giant Thrym stole Mjolnir and demanded Freya as a bride, Loki accompanied Thor to Jotunheim with Thor disguised as Freya and Loki as her maid. Loki explained away Thor's huge appetite and fiery eyes until Thor recovered his hammer.

**Naglfar**
The ship made from the fingernails and toenails of the dead, which sails against the gods at Ragnarok. Loki stands at its helm in some accounts.

**Farbauti and Laufey**
Loki's parents, the giant Farbauti and Laufey (also called Nal), which makes Loki part giant despite living among the Aesir. His brothers are Helblindi and Byleistr, and he is also called Lopt.

**Io and the gadfly**
Io was a mortal lover of Zeus whom he turned into a white heifer to hide her from Hera. Hera claimed the cow, set the hundred-eyed (or thousand-eyed) giant Argus Panoptes to guard her, and later sent a gadfly to sting her and drive her across the world.

**Peacock and the eyes of Argus**
After Hermes killed Argus to free Io, Hera placed Argus's many eyes on the tail feathers of her sacred bird, the peacock. Peacocks also pull her chariot.

**Tiresias**
The Theban seer, whom Hera turned into a woman after he struck a pair of mating snakes with a stick. Years later, Zeus and Hera asked him whether men or women enjoy sex more; when he answered women, Hera blinded him, and Zeus compensated him with prophecy.

**Judgment of Paris**
When Eris's golden apple marked "to the fairest" sparked a contest among Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite, the Trojan prince Paris served as judge. Hera offered him kingship over all of Europe and Asia, but he chose Aphrodite, who offered him Helen.

**Ixion and Nephele**
