The Lapith king Ixion tried to seduce or rape Hera, so Zeus formed a cloud in her likeness, Nephele. Ixion slept with the cloud, fathering Centaurus (ancestor of the centaurs), and was punished by being bound to an eternally spinning fiery wheel in Tartarus.

**Serpents in Heracles's cradle**
Jealous of Zeus's son by Alcmene, Hera sent two snakes to kill the infant Heracles, who strangled them. She persecuted him all his life, sending monsters such as the Nemean Lion and the Hydra and driving him mad so that he killed his own children, until he became a god and she gave him her daughter Hebe as a wife.

**Lamia**
A Libyan queen loved by Zeus. Hera killed her children (or drove her to kill them) and cursed her with sleeplessness, turning her into a monster who devours other people's children.

**Cleobis and Biton**
Two sons of Cydippe, a priestess of Hera at Argos, who pulled their mother's cart to Hera's festival when no oxen were available. When Cydippe prayed for the best gift a mortal could receive, Hera let them die peacefully in their sleep, a story told by Herodotus.

**Galanthis and Eurystheus**
Hera delayed Heracles's birth by having Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth, sit with her limbs crossed outside Alcmene's room, and she hastened the birth of Eurystheus so he would rule over Heracles. Alcmene's servant Galanthis tricked Eileithyia into releasing the spell, and Hera turned Galanthis into a weasel.

**Milky Way**
Hera was tricked into nursing the infant Heracles, and when she pulled him away from her breast, the spilled milk sprayed across the sky to form the Milky Way.

**Cuckoo**
Zeus won Hera by disguising himself as a bedraggled cuckoo in a storm. Hera took pity and held the bird to her breast, and Zeus resumed his true form and ravished her; the story is set on Mount Thornax.

**Hephaestus and the golden throne**
Hera threw her son Hephaestus off Olympus because he was lame or ugly. In revenge he sent her a golden throne that trapped her, and he released her only after Dionysus got him drunk and brought him back to Olympus.

**Hung from the sky with golden chains**
In the Iliad, Zeus punished Hera for raising a storm against Heracles by hanging her from the sky with golden bonds and anvils tied to her feet. Hephaestus was thrown from Olympus by Zeus for trying to help her.

**Leto and Delos**
Out of jealousy, Hera forbade Leto, pregnant with Apollo and Artemis by Zeus, from giving birth on any land. Leto finally gave birth on the floating island of Delos.

**Boopis and the spring of Canathus**
Homer's epithet for Hera is boopis, "cow-eyed." She bathed every year in the spring of Canathus near Nauplia to renew her virginity.

**Enkidu**
Gilgamesh's wild-man companion and best friend. The gods had the goddess Aruru form him from clay to counter Gilgamesh's harsh rule over Uruk. After being civilized, Enkidu fought Gilgamesh (in the Standard Babylonian version, as Gilgamesh was about to sleep with a bride before her groom) and the two became inseparable. The gods decreed Enkidu's death for the killing of Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven, and his loss drives Gilgamesh's quest for immortality.

**Humbaba and the Cedar Forest**
Humbaba (Huwawa) is the monstrous guardian of the Cedar Forest, who can hear a deer stir from sixty leagues away and is protected by seven auras (terrors). Gilgamesh and Enkidu travel there and, with the help of thirteen winds sent by the sun god Shamash, defeat and kill him. In a Sumerian version, Gilgamesh tricks Humbaba into giving up his auras by offering gifts including his sisters. Afterward the heroes cut down cedars and make a great gate for a temple.

**Utnapishtim**
The survivor of the great flood (the Mesopotamian Noah), who was granted immortality by the gods and lives "far away" with his wife. He tells Gilgamesh the story of the flood in Tablet XI. To test whether Gilgamesh can conquer death, Utnapishtim challenges him to stay awake for six days and seven nights; Gilgamesh falls asleep at once, and his wife bakes a loaf of bread for each day he sleeps, the stale and moldy loaves proving his failure.

**The plant of immortality stolen by a snake**
Utnapishtim tells Gilgamesh of a prickly plant at the bottom of the sea that restores youth. Gilgamesh ties stones to his feet to sink down and pick it, but while he bathes in a pool on his way home, a snake steals and eats it, then sheds its skin. This explains why snakes shed their skin and seem to renew themselves.

**The Bull of Heaven**
After Gilgamesh rejected the seductive advances of the goddess Ishtar (Inanna), listing the fates of her past lovers, she had her father Anu send the Bull of Heaven (Gugalanna in Sumerian) to ravage Uruk. Gilgamesh and Enkidu killed it, and Enkidu insulted Ishtar by throwing the bull's thigh at her.

**Shamhat**
The temple prostitute (harlot) whom Gilgamesh, on a trapper's request, sends out to the wilderness to seduce Enkidu. After sleeping with her for six days and seven nights, Enkidu is shunned by the animals he lived with, and she civilizes him with bread, beer, and clothing before bringing him to Uruk.

**Scorpion-men at Mount Mashu**
On his quest for Utnapishtim, Gilgamesh reaches the twin peaks of Mount Mashu, guarded by a pair of scorpion monsters. They let him pass along the Road of the Sun, a pitch-dark tunnel through which he travels for twelve "double hours" before emerging into a garden of jewel-bearing trees.

**Siduri**
An alewife or tavern-keeper who lives by the sea at the edge of the world. She at first mistakes the ragged Gilgamesh for a criminal and bars her door, then advises him to enjoy life and directs him to the ferryman Urshanabi.

**Urshanabi and the Stone Things**
Urshanabi is Utnapishtim's ferryman, who crosses the Waters of Death with the help of the "Stone Things." Gilgamesh rashly smashes them, so he must cut hundreds of long punting poles (and finally use his clothes as a sail) to cross the deadly waters.

**Ninsun and the dreams of the meteor and axe**
Gilgamesh's mother is the wise goddess Ninsun, and his father is the hero-king Lugalbanda. Before Enkidu arrives, Gilgamesh dreams of a meteor (a rock from the sky) and an axe that he cannot lift but is drawn to as if to a wife. Ninsun interprets both as signs that a mighty companion is coming.

**Pukku and mikku**
In the Sumerian tale often called "Gilgamesh, Enkidu, and the Netherworld" (appended as Tablet XII of the Babylonian epic), Gilgamesh drives a snake, the Anzu bird, and the demon Lilith out of the goddess Inanna's huluppu tree. From its wood he makes a pukku and mikku (perhaps a drum and drumstick or a ball and mallet), which fall into the underworld. Enkidu goes down to retrieve them but is trapped, and his ghost later tells Gilgamesh about the fates of the dead, such as how a man with seven sons lives like a companion of the gods.

**Mourning until a maggot fell from Enkidu's nose**
After Enkidu's death, Gilgamesh refused to let him be buried, clinging to the corpse for seven days until a maggot fell from its nostril. The sight of decay drove him to wander the wilderness in animal skins in search of immortality.

**Two-thirds divine king of Uruk**
Gilgamesh is the legendary king of the Sumerian city of Uruk, two-thirds god and one-third man. At the start of the epic he oppresses his people, not leaving "a girl to her mother," and the epic ends with him admiring Uruk's great walls.

**"He who saw the deep"**
The incipit (opening words) and ancient title of the Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh, attributed to Sin-leqi-unninni, is Sha naqba imuru, "He who saw the deep (abyss)." The earlier Old Babylonian version begins Shutur eli sharri, "Surpassing all other kings." It is the oldest surviving epic poem.

**Gilgamesh and Aga**
A Sumerian poem in which Aga (Agga), king of Kish, besieges Uruk after Gilgamesh refuses to submit to Kish's demand for labor in digging wells. Gilgamesh's warrior Birhurturra goes out to face the besiegers, and Gilgamesh drives Aga back when he appears on the walls.

**Chang'e and Hou Yi**
The Chinese moon goddess. Her husband, the archer Hou Yi, shot down nine of the ten suns and received an elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West; Chang'e drank it (in some versions to keep it from the thief Feng Meng) and floated up to the moon, where she lives in the Guanghan Palace. She is honored at the Mid-Autumn Festival, when mooncakes are eaten, and in Journey to the West, Zhu Bajie is banished from heaven for flirting with her.

**Jade Rabbit**
The rabbit that lives on the moon as Chang'e's companion, pounding the elixir of immortality (or, in Japan and Korea, rice cakes) with a mortar and pestle. China's Yutu lunar rover was named after it.

**Selene and Endymion**
Selene, the Greek Titan goddess of the moon, is a daughter of Hyperion and sister of Helios and Eos, and she drives a chariot across the night sky. She fell in love with the shepherd Endymion, who was granted eternal sleep and youth, and in some accounts she bore him fifty daughters. Her Roman counterpart is Luna.

**Tsukuyomi**
The Shinto moon god, born when Izanagi washed his right eye after returning from the underworld, alongside his siblings Amaterasu and Susanoo. He killed the food goddess Ukemochi in disgust because she produced food from her mouth and body, and his angry sister Amaterasu refused to see him again, which is why the sun and moon are separated.

**Coyolxauhqui and Huitzilopochtli**
The Aztec moon goddess who led her four hundred brothers in an attack on their mother Coatlicue. The newly born war god Huitzilopochtli killed her, cutting off her head and throwing it into the sky, where it became the moon.

**Thoth and Khonsu's five extra days**
Ra had forbidden the sky goddess Nut to give birth on any day of the year. Thoth gambled with the moon god Khonsu and won enough of the moon's light to create five extra days, on which Nut bore Osiris, Horus the Elder, Set, Isis, and Nephthys. Thoth himself, depicted as an ibis or baboon, was also a lunar god.

**Tecciztecatl and the rabbit**
In the Aztec creation of the Fifth Sun at Teotihuacan, the proud god Tecciztecatl hesitated out of fear before leaping into the sacrificial fire after Nanahuatzin. Both became suns, so the gods threw a rabbit in Tecciztecatl's face to dim him, creating the moon and its rabbit-shaped markings. He is often identified with the moon god Metztli and depicted with a seashell on his back.

**Mani and Hati**
Mani is the Norse personification of the moon and brother of Sol, the sun. He took the children Hjuki and Bil up from the earth to follow him, and he is chased by the wolf Hati, who will devour him at Ragnarok.

**Nanna and Sin**
The Mesopotamian moon god, called Nanna by the Sumerians and Sin by the Akkadians and Babylonians. He is the son of Enlil and husband of Ningal, his sacred city was Ur, and he is described as having a beard of lapis lazuli.

**Mama Quilla**
The Inca moon goddess, wife (and sister) of the sun god Inti. She was said to weep tears of silver and was associated with the calendar and with women.

**Artemis**
The Greek goddess of the hunt, also identified with the moon. Her brother Apollo tricked her into shooting Orion, she had Actaeon torn apart after he saw her bathing, and in one account she helped her mother Leto deliver her twin Apollo.

**Self-sacrificing hare**
In a Buddhist Jataka tale, a hare with no food to offer a hungry beggar threw itself into a fire to feed him; the beggar (the god Sakra) placed its image on the moon. In an Aztec version, Quetzalcoatl imprints a rabbit on the moon after it offers itself as food.

**Wu Gang and the osmanthus tree**
A Chinese woodcutter banished to the moon as punishment and forced to chop down a self-healing osmanthus (cassia) tree forever, since every cut closes up again.

**Tale of the Bamboo Cutter**
A Japanese folktale in which an old bamboo cutter finds a tiny girl, Princess Kaguya, inside a bamboo stalk, after which he finds gold in other stalks. She is really from the Capital of the Moon and eventually returns there, and the grieving emperor orders her letter and the elixir she left him burned on the highest mountain, Mount Fuji.

**Ganesha and Chandra**
In Hindu myth, the moon god Chandra laughed at Ganesha when he fell after a feast. Ganesha broke off one of his tusks, threw it at the moon, and cursed him, explaining the moon's waxing and waning.

**Hanuman**
The monkey god of Hindu myth and the most loyal devotee of Rama in the Ramayana. He is the son of the wind god Vayu and Anjana, and he is the most common giveaway for monkeys.

**Vanaras**
The race of monkey-like (sometimes described as ape-like) forest beings in the Ramayana, said to have been created to help Rama. Hanuman, Sugriva, Vali, Nala and Nila are all vanaras.

**Carrying the mountain of herbs for Lakshmana**
When Rama's brother Lakshmana was gravely wounded in battle, Hanuman was sent to fetch a healing herb (sanjeevani) from the Himalayas. Unable to tell which plant it was, he lifted the whole mountain and carried it back to Lanka.

**Sugriva and the kingdom of Kishkindha**
Sugriva is the king of the vanaras, who live in the forest kingdom of Kishkindha. Rama helped him regain his throne, and in return Sugriva's monkey army helped rescue Sita from the demon king Ravana.

**Vali and the demon Mayavi**
Vali, Sugriva's older brother, chased the demon Mayavi into a cave, and Sugriva, thinking Vali was dead, sealed the cave and took the throne. Vali escaped and drove Sugriva out, until Rama killed Vali, after which Sugriva married Vali's widow Tara. Vali had a boon that gave him half the strength of anyone he fought.

**Rama Setu (Adam's Bridge) to Lanka**
The vanara army built a bridge across the sea to Lanka so Rama could reach Ravana's kingdom and rescue Sita. It was built by Nala and Nila, whose boon meant that any stone they put in the water would float.

**Burning Lanka with his tail**
When Hanuman leapt across the sea to find Sita, Ravana's men captured him and set his tail on fire. Hanuman escaped and used his burning tail to set the city of Lanka ablaze.

**Trying to swallow the sun**
As a child, Hanuman mistook the sun for a ripe fruit and leapt up to eat it. Indra struck him with his thunderbolt (vajra) on the jaw, which gave him his name ("hanu" means jaw), and Vayu withdrew the air from the world in anger until the gods revived Hanuman and gave him boons.

**Hanuman Chalisa**
A devotional hymn of forty verses (chalisa means forty) praising Hanuman, written by the poet Tulsidas. It is one of the most widely recited Hindu prayers.

**Sun Wukong in Journey to the West**
The Monkey King of Chinese myth, born from a stone, who wields a magic staff that can change size. In the novel Journey to the West, he protects the monk Xuanzang (Tripitaka) on his pilgrimage to India, along with Pigsy (Zhu Bajie) and Sandy (Sha Wujing). Some scholars think he was inspired by Hanuman.

**Hanuman tearing open his chest**
To prove his devotion, Hanuman ripped open his chest to reveal images of Rama and Sita in his heart. He also defeated the demon Kalanemi, who disguised himself as a sage to stop Hanuman's search for the healing herb.

**Three wise monkeys**
Mizaru, Kikazaru and Iwazaru, the monkeys who "see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil." A famous carving of them is at the Toshogu shrine in Nikko, Japan.

**Dream on Monkey Mountain**
A play by the Saint Lucian writer Derek Walcott. Its main character, the charcoal burner Makak (named for the macaque monkey), is jailed by Corporal Lestrade alongside the thieves Souris and Tigre and has visions of returning to Africa.

**"Interpreter of Maladies"**
In Jhumpa Lahiri's short story, Mrs. Das drops a trail of puffed rice that leads a group of monkeys to attack her son Bobby, whom she has confessed was fathered by another man.

**Monkeys in Asian folktales**
In Tibetan myth, the first Tibetans were born from the union of a monkey and a rock ogress (demoness). In the Japanese folktale of the crab and the monkey (Saru Kani Gassen), a monkey kills a crab and is later killed in revenge by the crab's children and their allies.

**Dismembered into fourteen pieces by Set**
Osiris's jealous brother Set (Seth) murdered him and cut his body into fourteen pieces, which he scattered across Egypt or threw into the Nile. His wife Isis, often helped by her sister Nephthys, searched for and recovered thirteen of the pieces, then bound them back together, making Osiris the first mummy.

**Isis and Horus**
Isis is Osiris's sister-wife, who restored his body and briefly revived him (in some versions with a spell taught by their father Geb) so she could conceive their son Horus. Horus later avenged his father by battling Set for the throne of Egypt, and "father of Horus" and "husband of Isis" are the standard giveaways.

**Atef crown and crook and flail**
Osiris's signature regalia. The atef is a tall white crown flanked by two ostrich feathers, said to represent truth and justice (the feathers of Ma'at), and the crook and flail he holds across his chest symbolize kingship and his claim to the throne of Egypt.

**The chest or coffin thrown into the Nile**
Set tricked Osiris into lying down in a beautiful chest built exactly to his measurements, then shut the lid, sealed it with molten lead, and threw it into the Nile, where Osiris drowned. Plutarch says Set (Typhon) was helped by seventy-two accomplices and by Aso, a queen of Ethiopia.

**The tamarisk tree and palace at Byblos**
The coffin floated to Byblos in Phoenicia, where a tamarisk (or erica) tree grew around it. King Malcander (also spelled Malacander) cut down the tree and used its trunk as a pillar in his palace. Isis came to Byblos, worked as a nursemaid for the queen (Astarte in Plutarch), and tried to make the royal baby immortal by holding him in fire, much like Demeter at Eleusis, before she recovered the coffin.

**Djed pillar**
A pillar-shaped symbol of stability and continuity that represents Osiris's backbone. It is linked to the pillar at Byblos that held his body, which Isis anointed after retrieving it.

**Green (or black) skin**
Osiris is usually shown as a mummified king with green or black skin. The color stands for vegetation, fertility, the black silt left by the Nile floods, and his death and rebirth. He was also an agricultural god, and the grain god Neper is sometimes shown as wheat sprouting from his body.

**Eldest son of Geb and Nut**
Osiris was the first child of the earth god Geb and the sky goddess Nut. His siblings are Isis, Set, and Nephthys (and in some accounts Horus the Elder). In the myth recorded by Plutarch, the five siblings were born on five extra (intercalary) days that Thoth won from the moon god Khonsu in a game, because Ra had forbidden Nut to give birth on any day of the year.

**The fish that ate his phallus**
The one piece of Osiris that Isis never found was his phallus, which was eaten by fish, most often named as the oxyrhynchus (in some accounts a catfish or other species). For this reason priests of Osiris refused to eat fish. Isis fashioned a replacement phallus, sometimes described as golden, before she conceived Horus.

**Nephthys and the birth of Anubis**
Osiris fathered the jackal god Anubis with his sister Nephthys, Set's wife, who in many versions disguised herself as Isis. This affair is sometimes given as Set's motive for killing him. Nephthys nonetheless helped Isis search for Osiris's body and helped raise Horus, earning the title "nurse-mother."

**Serapis**
Under the Ptolemaic pharaohs, Osiris was combined with the Apis bull of Memphis to form the Greco-Egyptian god Serapis (Osiris-Apis). The Serapeum of Alexandria, the main center of Serapis's cult, was destroyed in 391 CE by a Christian mob led by Patriarch Theophilus.

**Ruler of the Duat and judge of the dead**
Osiris rules the Duat, the Egyptian underworld, and presides over the judgment of the dead. There, in the Hall of Two Truths, a dead person's heart is weighed against the feather of Ma'at. The pure go on to the Field of Reeds, while Ammit devours the hearts of the wicked. In many accounts Osiris took over the role of lord of the dead from Anubis.

**"Foremost of the Westerners" (Khenti-Amentiu)**
An epithet Osiris took after being merged with Khenti-Amentiu, the jackal god of the necropolis at Abydos, by the Middle Kingdom. The "West" refers to the land of the dead, since the sun sets in the west. He was also associated with Wepwawet, the "Opener of the Ways."

**Abydos and its festival**
Abydos was Osiris's chief cult center and his supposed burial place. It held a great temple and an annual festival, the Osiris mysteries, recorded on the Ikhernofret Stela, in which his image was carried on the Neshmet bark in a procession led by Wepwawet. Worshippers also made "Osiris gardens," beds of sprouting grain shaped like the god.

**Banebdjedet, the ram of Mendes**
Osiris's ba (soul) was worshipped at the city of Mendes as a sacred living ram called Banebdjedet. The Book of the Heavenly Cow identifies this ram god as Osiris's soul.

**Retrieving bones from Mictlan to create humanity**
At the start of the Fifth Sun (the current world age), Quetzalcoatl traveled to Mictlan, the Aztec underworld, to retrieve the bones of the people of the previous age from the death god Mictlantecuhtli. After returning, the bones were ground into a flour by the goddess Cihuacoatl ("Snake Woman"), and Quetzalcoatl sprinkled them with his own blood, drawn from his penis, to create the humans of the fifth world.

**The conch shell with no holes**
To test Quetzalcoatl, Mictlantecuhtli demanded that he blow a conch shell trumpet that had no holes. Quetzalcoatl had worms bore holes in it and bees fly inside to make it sound. Mictlantecuhtli then had a pit dug for him; startled by quail, Quetzalcoatl fell in and the bones broke, explaining why people come in different sizes.

**Sleeping with his sister and self-immolation**
Tricked by his rival Tezcatlipoca, who showed him a distorted image of himself in a mirror and got him drunk on the alcoholic drink pulque, Quetzalcoatl broke his vow of celibacy by sleeping with his sister, a celibate priestess. In shame he lay in a stone chest or threw himself on a funeral pyre and burned himself, and his heart rose into the sky as the morning star, the planet Venus.

**Tezcatlipoca**
Quetzalcoatl's chief rival and sometimes brother, whose name means "Smoking Mirror." Tezcatlipoca lost a foot (replaced with an obsidian mirror) to the earth monster Cipactli, which the two gods helped kill to create the earth. In the cycle of world ages, the two repeatedly toppled each other's suns; Quetzalcoatl once struck Tezcatlipoca into the sea, where he became a jaguar. Quetzalcoatl is sometimes called the "White Tezcatlipoca."

**Xolotl**
Quetzalcoatl's dog-headed twin brother, a psychopomp god of fire, sickness, and the underworld, who accompanies him to Mictlan. Xolotl represents the evening star, complementing Quetzalcoatl as the morning star, so both are associated with Venus.

**Raft of snakes and Hernan Cortes**
In the legend of his exile from the city of Tollan, Quetzalcoatl sailed east on a raft of serpents, promising to return. Because he was sometimes described as light-skinned and bearded, a later legend claims that Moctezuma II mistook the Spanish conquistador Hernan Cortes for the returning god, easing the conquest of Tenochtitlan.

**Ehecatl**
Quetzalcoatl's aspect as the wind god, depicted wearing a conical hat and a mask with a duck-like beak through which he blows the wind. Ehecatl blew on the motionless sun and moon to set them moving, and was worshipped in round temples. He fell in love with the goddess Mayahuel, bringing love (and the maguey plant) into the world.

**Wind jewel**
A pendant cut from a cross-section of a conch shell, called the "spirally voluted wind jewel" (ehecailacacozcatl). Quetzalcoatl wears it as a symbol of the wind, and priests and rulers wore similar shell ornaments.

**Birth from Chimalman**
In one version of his birth, the virgin goddess Chimalman conceived Quetzalcoatl after swallowing an emerald (a precious green stone). In another, the hunting god Mixcoatl shot an arrow at Chimalman and fathered him. Other sources name Coatlicue or the dual creator Ometeotl as his parent.

**Humans turned into monkeys**
Quetzalcoatl ruled one of the earlier world ages, or Suns. That age ended when a great hurricane swept the world away and its people were turned into monkeys.

**Turning into an ant to find maize**
After a red ant revealed where it was getting maize, Quetzalcoatl turned himself into a black ant and followed it into the Mountain of Our Sustenance (Tonacatepetl). He carried the corn kernels back to give food to the newly created humans.

**One Reed**
Quetzalcoatl's calendar name, Ce Acatl ("One Reed"). The coincidence that Cortes arrived in a One Reed year (1519) fed the legend that he was the returning god.

**Tollan**
The legendary Toltec city (Tula) whose priest-king, Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl, is often conflated with the god. He ruled as a wise, celibate king who opposed human sacrifice, until Tezcatlipoca tricked him into abdicating and leaving.

**Patron of priests, learning, and the calendar**
Quetzalcoatl was the patron of Aztec priests and was credited with inventing books and the calendar. A temple dedicated to him at Teotihuacan (the Temple of the Feathered Serpent) may have been used to track the 260-day ritual calendar, and the Great Pyramid of Cholula, the largest pyramid in the world by volume, was dedicated to him.

**Kukulcan**
The Maya equivalent of Quetzalcoatl, whose name likewise means "feathered serpent." He is most famously associated with El Castillo, the pyramid at Chichen Itza.

**Arcturus and the juggled eyeballs**
In a widely told story, Coyote showed off by juggling his own eyeballs, sometimes to impress women. He tossed one too high, it stuck in the sky, and it became the star Arcturus, which is one of the most common clues for him.

**Kicking a ball of mud to create humans**
Several traditions credit Coyote with creating humanity by kicking or rolling a ball of mud or dirt. Related stories have him make plants or the land from a ball of mud brought up by ducks.

**Changing Bear**
In a Navajo story, Coyote marries Changing Bear Maiden and uses his magic to corrupt her, turning her evil. Pretending to comb her brothers' hair, she murders them, sometimes in revenge after they leave Coyote behind on a hunt or after his death; usually one brother survives.

**Creating the Milky Way**
In Navajo myth, the Black God was carefully placing the constellations in the sky. The impatient Coyote grabbed the rest of the stars (from a blanket or pouch) and flung or blew them all across the sky at once, creating the scattered Milky Way.

**Stealing the Water Monster's baby**
In the Navajo emergence story, Coyote stole the child or children of the Water Monster (sometimes called the Water Buffalo), sometimes at First Woman's urging. The furious monster caused a great flood that destroyed the Third World, forcing First Man, First Woman, and the other beings to climb up into the Fourth World.

**Becoming the Moon**
Coyote once took the job of being the Moon so he could see everything below. He lost the position because he spied on people and tattled on everything they did.

**Name-giving day**
The Great Spirit was going to give each animal a new name, with the first to arrive getting the best choice. Coyote propped his eyes open with small sticks to stay awake all night, but still overslept and arrived too late; the sticks gave him his slanted eyes.

**Breaking the giant's leg**
Coyote tricked a giant, who was chasing or holding children captive, by claiming he could make the giant run faster. He broke the giant's leg and spat on it, pretending to heal it, which left the giant crippled and slowed so the children could escape.

**Stealing fire from the Fire Beings**
Like Prometheus, Coyote stole fire from the Fire Beings on their mountain to give to humans. Animals helping him in the relay were marked by it: Chipmunk got his stripes, Squirrel's tail curled, and Frog lost his tail.

**The Shadow People**
In a Nez Perce story resembling the Orpheus myth, Coyote traveled to the land of the Shadow People to bring back his dead wife. He was told not to touch her until the journey was complete, but he embraced her too early, making it impossible for the dead to ever return.

**Making death permanent**
In some myths Coyote decided that death should be permanent, for example by throwing a stone into a lake (it sank rather than floated). Later his own son was fatally bitten by a rattlesnake, and when Coyote pleaded for his life he was reminded of his own decision, and he shed the first tears.

**Hiding his organs**
Coyote survives fatal wounds because he hides his vital organs elsewhere, often in his tail or up in the mountains. In one story this lets a maiden kill him four times without success.

**Old Man and Raven**
Coyote is sometimes called "Old Man" and is the main trickster of the American West and Southwest. He is often compared with Raven, the trickster of the Pacific Northwest, with whom he shares many traits.

**The Twins and the Horned Serpent**
In Navajo myth, the Hero Twins (Monster Slayer and Born for Water) are warned to stay away from Coyote, who is said to spy for the Horned Serpent and to have been following the Navajo since the beginning of time.

**Saynday's race**
In a Kiowa story, Coyote tricked the trickster Saynday into a race by pretending to be weak and feeble.

**Battle of Camlann**
Arthur's final battle, in which he and his son Mordred mortally wound each other after Mordred usurps the throne. In Malory the battle begins by accident when a knight draws his sword to kill an adder, and the night before, Arthur dreams of being tied to a wheel that plunges into black water full of serpents.

**Uther Pendragon, Igraine, and Gorlois**
Arthur's father, Uther Pendragon, lusted after Igraine, wife of the Duke of Cornwall, Gorlois. With Merlin's magic, Uther took on Gorlois's appearance and slept with Igraine at Tintagel Castle, conceiving Arthur.

**Avalon**
The mystical island to which the mortally wounded Arthur is carried after Camlann, in a black barge with fairy queens, often including Morgan le Fay. He is said to rest there to be healed, and legend holds he will one day return as the "once and future king."

**Mordred and Morgause**
Arthur unknowingly slept with his half-sister Morgause (in some versions Morgan le Fay), conceiving Mordred. In Malory, Arthur tries to have Mordred killed by setting adrift all children born on May Day, but Mordred survives to usurp the kingdom.

**Excalibur and the Lady of the Lake**
Arthur's sword, which in Malory he receives from the Lady of the Lake. As Arthur lies dying after Camlann, Sir Bedivere reluctantly throws Excalibur back into the lake, where an arm rises from the water to catch it.

**Guinevere and Lancelot**
Arthur's queen, daughter of King Leodegrance, had an adulterous affair with Lancelot, Arthur's greatest knight. The affair split the Round Table and led Arthur to besiege Lancelot's castle in France, giving Mordred the chance to seize power.

**Sword in the Stone**
The young Arthur proved his right to be king by pulling a sword from a stone (or an anvil on a stone), something no other man could do.

**Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur**
The 15th-century English prose compilation, the most influential retelling of the Arthurian legend, covering Arthur's birth, his knights, the Grail quest, and his death. Many quizbowl clues about Arthur, such as the Questing Beast and the May Day children, come from it.

**Geoffrey of Monmouth**
The 12th-century cleric whose History of the Kings of Britain (Historia Regum Britanniae) popularized Arthur across Europe. It tells of Arthur's conception at Tintagel, his war against Rome, and his final battle against Mordred.

**Questing Beast and King Pellinore**
In Malory, Arthur sees the Questing Beast, a creature with a serpent's head and a leopard's body that makes the noise of baying hounds, after sleeping with Morgause. King Pellinore, who hunts the beast, defeats Arthur in a joust, and Arthur survives only because Merlin casts a spell on Pellinore.

**Lucius Tiberius**
The Roman emperor who demands tribute from Arthur. Arthur leads a campaign on the continent, killing the giant of Mont Saint-Michel along the way, and defeats Lucius in Gaul, in some versions being crowned emperor at Rome.

**Nennius and Mount Badon**
The Historia Brittonum, attributed to the monk Nennius, lists twelve battles that Arthur won against the Saxons, culminating at Mount Badon (Mons Badonicus), where he is said to have killed 940 men single-handedly.

**Culhwch and Olwen**
A Welsh tale from the Mabinogion in which Arthur helps his kinsman Culhwch win the hand of the giant's daughter Olwen. The quest's tasks include hunting the enchanted boar Twrch Trwyth, and Arthur sends warriors including Kay and Bedwyr to help.

**Sir Ector, Sir Kay, and "Wart"**
Arthur was raised in secret by Sir Ector, whose son Kay became Arthur's seneschal. In T. H. White's The Once and Future King, the young Arthur is nicknamed "Wart" and is educated by Merlin.

**Merlin and the scabbard**
The wizard Merlin arranged Arthur's conception and served as his advisor. He told Arthur to value Excalibur's scabbard ten times more than the sword, since anyone wearing it would lose no blood however badly wounded.

**Hiding in the cave (Ama-no-Iwato)**
After her brother Susanoo's rampage, Amaterasu shut herself inside the Heavenly Rock Cave, plunging the world into darkness. The other gods had to devise a way to lure her back out to restore the sun.

**Susanoo throws a flayed horse into her weaving hall**
Susanoo, the storm god, flayed a heavenly piebald horse and threw it through the roof of Amaterasu's sacred weaving hall, causing a weaving maiden to die of fright. This outrage was what made Amaterasu hide in the cave.

**Sacred mirror (Yata no Kagami)**
The gods hung a mirror outside the cave. When Amaterasu peeked out, she saw her own bright reflection and was drawn further out, and the gods quickly blocked the cave behind her. The mirror is said to represent her and is kept at the Ise Shrine.

**Ame-no-Uzume's dance**
The goddess Ame-no-Uzume danced wildly on an overturned tub outside the cave, exposing herself and making the assembled gods roar with laughter. Amaterasu grew curious about the noise and looked out, falling for the trick with the mirror.

**Ninigi and the Three Sacred Treasures**
Amaterasu sent her grandson Ninigi down from heaven to rule Japan, giving him the three imperial regalia: the mirror Yata no Kagami, the jewel Yasakani no Magatama and the sword Kusanagi (the "grass-cutter"). These treasures remain symbols of the emperor's authority.

**Ancestor of the Japanese imperial family**
Through Ninigi, whose great-grandson Jimmu became the legendary first emperor of Japan, the imperial dynasty claims direct descent from Amaterasu.

**Ise Grand Shrine rebuilt every 20 years**
Amaterasu's chief shrine, the Inner Shrine (Naiku) at Ise, is torn down and rebuilt on an adjacent plot every twenty years in a ritual called Shikinen Sengu. It is the most sacred site in Shinto.

**Born from Izanagi's left eye**
When the creator god Izanagi purified himself after visiting the underworld, Amaterasu was born from the washing of his left eye. The moon god Tsukuyomi came from his right eye and Susanoo from his nose; these three are the most important children of Izanagi.

**Contest with Susanoo: sword and jewels**
To test Susanoo's intentions, Amaterasu and her brother held a contest of producing children. She broke his sword into three pieces, chewed them and spat out three goddesses, while he chewed her string of jewels and produced five male gods.

**Sun goddess of Shinto**
Amaterasu Omikami ("Great Divinity Illuminating Heaven") is the sun goddess and ruler of the heavenly realm Takamagahara. She is the most important deity of Shinto, and one of her other names is Ohirume-no-muchi.

**Silkworms and the start of agriculture**
In the Nihon Shoki, after the food goddess Ukemochi was killed, rice, grain and silkworms came from her body. Amaterasu planted the grains in her fields and put the silkworms in her mouth to draw out thread, starting rice farming and silk production.

**Golden apples and the footrace**
Atalanta, warned that marriage would ruin her, agreed to marry only a suitor who could beat her in a footrace, and those who lost were killed. Hippomenes (called Melanion in some versions) received three golden apples from Aphrodite and dropped them during the race; Atalanta stopped to pick them up, lost the race, and married him.

**Calydonian Boar Hunt**
A great hunt for a monstrous boar that Artemis sent to ravage Calydon after its king, Oeneus, forgot to sacrifice to her. Many heroes took part, and Atalanta drew first blood by wounding the boar with an arrow before Meleager killed it.

**Meleager and the boar's hide**
Meleager, son of Oeneus, killed the Calydonian Boar and, in love with Atalanta, awarded her its hide as the prize for drawing first blood. This angered the other hunters, since a woman had received the prize.

**Turned into lions**
Atalanta and her husband Hippomenes made love in a sacred temple, variously said to belong to Cybele (Rhea) or Zeus, in many versions because Aphrodite was angry that they had not thanked her for the apples. As punishment, they were turned into lions, which were believed not to mate with one another, and in some versions they were yoked to pull Cybele's chariot.

**Hylaeus and Rhoecus**
Two centaurs who tried to rape Atalanta, often placed during the time of the Calydonian Boar Hunt. She shot and killed both of them with her arrows.

**Plexippus and Toxeus and Althaea's log**
Meleager's uncles, the sons of Thestius, took the boar's hide from Atalanta, and Meleager killed them. His mother Althaea, their sister, avenged them by burning a log that the Fates had linked to Meleager's life, killing him.

**Parthenopaeus**
Atalanta's son, fathered by Melanion, Meleager, or Ares depending on the source, and one of the Seven Against Thebes. In Aeschylus's Seven Against Thebes, his shield shows the Sphinx devouring a Theban.

**Suckled by a she-bear**
Atalanta's father, who wanted a son, exposed her as an infant on Mount Parthenion. A she-bear, sent by Artemis in some versions, nursed her until hunters found and raised her; she became a virgin huntress devoted to Artemis.

**Wrestling Peleus**
At the funeral games held for King Pelias of Iolcus, Atalanta defeated Peleus, the future father of Achilles, in a wrestling match.

**Iasus and Schoeneus**
Atalanta's father is named differently in different traditions: Iasus (with Clymene) in the Arcadian version, or Schoeneus in the Boeotian version. She is therefore often called an Arcadian huntress.

**Only female Argonaut**
In some versions, Atalanta sailed with Jason's Argonauts, making her the only woman on the expedition. One tradition says Medea healed her when she was wounded in Colchis.

**Spring at Cyphanta**
According to Pausanias, when Atalanta was thirsty while hunting near Cyphanta in Laconia, she struck a rock with her spear and a spring of water flowed out.

**Sleipnir**
Odin's eight-legged horse in Norse myth and the most common giveaway for this answer. The Grimnismal calls it the best of all horses, runes are said to be carved on its teeth, and Hermod rides it down to Hel to try to bring back the dead god Baldr.

**Svadilfari and the building of Asgard's walls**
A giant (a hrimthurs, or frost giant) offered to build Asgard's walls by a deadline, helped only by his powerful stallion Svadilfari. To keep the gods from losing the wager, Loki turned himself into a mare and lured Svadilfari away; the wall went unfinished, and Loki later gave birth to Sleipnir.

**Mares of Diomedes**
Man-eating horses owned by Diomedes, king of the Bistones in Thrace. Capturing them was Heracles' eighth labor; he fed Diomedes to his own horses. Heracles' young companion and lover Abderus was eaten while guarding them, and Heracles founded the city of Abdera near his grave.

**Pegasus**
The winged horse of Greek myth, born from the neck of the beheaded Medusa. Its hoof struck Mount Helicon and opened the Hippocrene spring, which inspired the Muses. Bellerophon tamed it with a golden bridle and rode it against the Chimera, but when he tried to fly up to Olympus, Zeus sent a gadfly that stung Pegasus and threw Bellerophon to the ground.

**Xanthus and Balius**
Achilles' immortal horses, given to his father Peleus by Poseidon as a wedding gift. In Book 19 of the Iliad, Hera gives Xanthus the power of speech, and he warns Achilles that "a great god and powerful Destiny" will cause his death. The Furies (Erinyes) then take away his voice.

**Arion**
An immortal, extremely fast horse born after Poseidon, in the form of a stallion, raped Demeter, who had disguised herself as a mare. In the Arcadian version, the goddess Despoina was born from the same union. Arion carried King Adrastus of Argos to safety, making him the only one of the Seven Against Thebes to survive.

**Gullfaxi**
"Golden Mane," the horse of the giant Hrungnir. Hrungnir bet that Gullfaxi was better than Sleipnir, and Odin staked his head on a race. After Thor killed Hrungnir, he gave Gullfaxi to his young son Magni, who had freed him from under the dead giant's leg.

**Gulltopr**
"Golden Top," the golden-maned horse of Heimdall, the watchman of the Norse gods. Heimdall rides it to Baldr's funeral.

**Epona**
A Celtic and Gallo-Roman goddess of horses and fertility, often shown riding a horse or sitting between horses. Roman cavalry soldiers also worshipped her. The Welsh queen Rhiannon is often thought to be a later version of her.

**Rhiannon**
A heroine of the First Branch of the Welsh Mabinogion who first appears riding a white horse that none of Pwyll's men can catch. After her infant son vanishes, her maids smear a dog's blood on her face so that she is blamed for killing him. As punishment she must sit by the gate, tell visitors her story, and offer to carry them on her back like a horse.

**Arvakr and Alsvidr**
"Early Awake" and "All Swift," the two horses in Norse myth that pull the sun's chariot, driven by Sol. They are always chased across the sky by the wolf Skoll, who will finally swallow the sun at Ragnarok.

**Skinfaxi and Hrimfaxi**
"Shining Mane" and "Frost Mane," the Norse horses ridden by Dagr (Day) and Nott (Night). Skinfaxi's mane lights up the sky and earth, and the foam from Hrimfaxi's bit falls as morning dew.

**"Hector, tamer of horses"**
Hector's most frequent epithet in the Iliad, which also forms the poem's final line, about his funeral. Horses are closely tied to Troy: the city was conquered with the wooden Trojan Horse, and Poseidon, creator of the horse, was its god.

**Horses of Tros and Laomedon**
Zeus gave the Trojan king Tros a set of divine horses to make up for carrying off his son Ganymede. Tros's descendant Laomedon promised these horses to Heracles for saving his daughter Hesione from a sea monster. When Laomedon refused to pay, Heracles sacked Troy.

**Susanoo's flayed horse**
In Japanese Shinto myth, the storm god Susanoo rampages through the weaving hall of his sister, the sun goddess Amaterasu, and throws in a horse he has flayed through a hole in the roof. The horror drives Amaterasu to hide in a cave, which plunges the world into darkness.

**Vritra**
The serpent or dragon demon who hoarded all the world's waters, causing drought. Indra slew him and released the waters, the central heroic deed of the Rigveda and the most common clue for Indra.

**Vajra**
Indra's thunderbolt weapon, crafted for him by the divine artisan Tvashtri. He used it to slay Vritra, and it marks him as the Hindu god of storms, thunder, and rain.

**Airavata**
The white elephant, often described as having four tusks, that serves as Indra's mount. It is one of the most recognizable giveaways in his iconography.

**Soma**
The sacred ritual drink of the Vedas. Indra drank great quantities of it (in one account three bowls) to gain strength before battling Vritra and storming his ninety-nine fortresses.

**Ahalya and Gautama Maharishi**
Indra disguised himself as the sage Gautama to seduce Gautama's wife Ahalya. When the sage caught him, he cursed Indra so that his body was covered with a thousand vaginas (later sometimes changed into a thousand eyes).

**Arjuna**
The great archer hero of the Mahabharata, born when Kunti invoked Indra with her mantra. Indra is the second god Kunti calls upon, after Dharma (Yama), making him Arjuna's divine father.

**Agni**
The Vedic fire god, described as Indra's twin brother. Both were born from the mouth of the cosmic giant Purusha, and Indra once unsuccessfully tried to protect the Khandava forest from the hungry Agni.

**King of the devas**
Indra is the ruler of the gods (devas) and the head of the Vedic pantheon, and he is the most frequently invoked deity in the Rigveda. His importance declined in later Hinduism with the rise of the Trimurti of Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva.

**The Maruts**
The storm gods who serve as Indra's attendants and companions. They helped him rescue the cattle stolen by the demon Vala, who had hidden them in a cave.

**Mount Meru and Svarga**
Indra rules from a palace in his heaven, Svarga, on top of the cosmic mountain Meru. His capital city there is called Amaravati.

**Hanuman and the sun**
As an infant, the monkey god Hanuman mistook the sun for a fruit and leapt to eat it. Indra struck him with his thunderbolt to stop him, injuring Hanuman's jaw.

**Govardhan Hill**
Krishna persuaded his foster father Nanda and the people of Vrindavana to stop their worship (puja) of Indra. The angry Indra sent torrential rains, and Krishna held Govardhan Hill aloft like an umbrella to shelter everyone.

**Sachi**
Also called Indrani, she is Indra's wife. When the mortal king Nahusha usurped Indra's throne and tried to claim Sachi, Indra had hidden in the stalk of a lotus, and he later returned to rescue her and reclaim his position.

**Indra's net**
A metaphor, prominent in Mahayana Buddhism, of an infinite net with a jewel at each knot, each jewel reflecting all the others. It illustrates the emptiness and interconnectedness of all things.

**Sakra**
The name under which Indra appears in Buddhist and Jain texts. Comparative scholars link him with other Indo-European thunder gods such as Zeus, Thor, and Perun.

**Phoenix**
A mythical bird that bursts into flames when it dies and is reborn from its own ashes; some accounts say this happens every 500 years. Related birds include the Egyptian Bennu, linked to the creation of the world, and the Chinese fenghuang, which appears in times of peace and happiness.

**Stymphalian birds**
Man-eating birds with bronze beaks and sharp, metallic feathers that infested a marsh at Lake Stymphalus in Arcadia, where they had fled from wolves. For his sixth labor, Heracles frightened them into the air with bronze rattles (krotala) made by Hephaestus and given by Athena, then shot them down.

**Raven, the Pacific Northwest trickster**
The main trickster and culture hero of the Pacific Northwest peoples, playing the role Coyote plays elsewhere. He steals the sun, moon, and stars (often kept in a box) to bring light to the world, or makes another bird drop the box of light. Smoke from escaping through a smoke hole turned him from white to black, and in some stories he creates rivers by stealing water.

**Huginn and Muninn**
Odin's two ravens, whose names mean "Thought" and "Memory." Every day they fly over Midgard and return to sit on his shoulders and whisper the news of the world into his ears.

**Thunderbird**
A huge bird spirit of many Native American cultures, which makes thunder by beating its wings. In Algonquian myth it fights the Underwater Panther (or Great Horned Serpent) that rules the underworld and is often drawn as an X-shaped motif. In Pacific Northwest stories it battles a whale, and it often sits at the top of totem poles.

**Garuda**
The king of birds in Hindu myth, an eagle-like being who is Vishnu's mount. He stole the amrita (nectar of immortality) from the gods as a ransom to free his mother Vinata from slavery to the snakes (nagas), who became his enemies.

**Leda and the swan**
Zeus took the form of a swan to seduce Leda, queen of Sparta, who then bore children including Helen and the twins Castor and Pollux. The constellation Cygnus ("swan") is linked to this myth and to Cygnus, the friend of Phaethon who was turned into a swan while mourning him.

**Harpies and Sirens**
Hybrid creatures with birds' bodies and the heads of women. The Harpies ("snatchers") stole food and people, while the Sirens sang to lure sailors to their deaths.

**The Morrigan and Cu Chulainn's death**
The Irish war goddess Morrigan often takes the form of a crow or raven. At the end of his life, Cu Chulainn ties himself to a standing stone so he can die on his feet, and only when a raven lands on his shoulder do his enemies know he is dead. Bran the Blessed, the giant Welsh king, has a name meaning "raven."

**Magpie bridge (Qixi)**
In the Chinese tale of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl, the lovers are separated by the Milky Way. Once a year, on the seventh day of the seventh month (the Qixi festival), a flock of magpies forms a bridge across the sky so they can meet.

**Roc**
An enormous bird of Arabian and Persian legend, best known from the voyages of Sinbad the Sailor. It is said to be strong enough to carry off elephants.

**Simurgh**
A wise and ancient bird of Persian myth. In the Shahnameh, it raises the abandoned hero Zal and later teaches him how to deliver his son Rustam by an early form of Caesarean section.

**Coronis and Apollo's raven**
A white raven (or crow) told Apollo that his lover Coronis had been unfaithful. In his anger Apollo turned the bird's feathers black, which explains why ravens are black.

**Alcyone and Ceyx**
After King Ceyx drowned, his grieving wife Alcyone threw herself into the sea, and the gods turned both into kingfishers (halcyons). Calm "halcyon days" at sea are the days when Aeolus, Alcyone's father, stills the winds so she can nest.

**Eagle of Zeus**
The eagle is Zeus's emblem. It carried the boy Ganymede up to Olympus, and as Prometheus's punishment it ate his liver every day while he was chained to a rock. The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was founded where an eagle was seen on a cactus eating a snake.

**Pomegranate seeds**
The most common clue for Persephone. Because she ate pomegranate seeds in the Underworld (any food there binds a person to it), she had to spend part of every year with Hades, a third or a half depending on the source. Her mother Demeter mourns while she is gone, which explains winter and the barren seasons.

**Abduction by Hades**
While Persephone was picking flowers, Hades burst out of the earth in his chariot and carried her down to be his queen, with Zeus's approval. When the earth opened, the swineherd Eubuleus's pigs fell into the chasm. The Roman poet Claudian left the story unfinished in his epic De raptu Proserpinae (Proserpina is her Roman name).

**Eleusinian Mysteries**
The most famous secret rites of ancient Greece, held at Eleusis near Athens in honor of Demeter and Persephone, the "two goddesses," with Persephone as the younger. Initiates went through rituals in the great hall called the Telesterion, which likely reenacted her abduction and return.

**Pirithous and Theseus**
Theseus helped his friend Pirithous go down to the Underworld to kidnap Persephone as Pirithous's bride. Hades tricked them into sitting on stone seats (the Chairs of Forgetfulness), which held them fast, in some versions with coiling serpents. Heracles freed Theseus when he came to fetch Cerberus, but Pirithous stayed trapped forever.

**Ascalaphus**
The Underworld gardener (or a son of Acheron) who revealed that Persephone had eaten the pomegranate seeds, which bound her to Hades. As punishment, Demeter pinned him under a heavy rock. In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Persephone herself splashes him with water from the Phlegethon and turns him into a screech owl.

**Kore**
"The Maiden," Persephone's common title, especially in cult and in the Mysteries. Her symbols include the sheaf of wheat, the torch, and the pomegranate.

**Enna**
The place where she was most often said to have been abducted: the meadows of Enna (Henna) in Sicily, where she was gathering lilies and violets. The Homeric Hymn to Demeter places the event on the Nysian plain instead.

**Zagreus**
In Orphic religion, Zagreus is the son of Zeus and Persephone and an early form of Dionysus. The Titans tore him apart and ate him, but his heart was saved, and he was reborn as Dionysus. Humans were said to come from the Titans' ashes.

**Minthe**
A nymph loved by Hades. In jealousy, Persephone turned her into the mint plant, in some versions after trampling her underfoot.

**Cyane**
A Sicilian nymph who tried to stop Hades from carrying Persephone away. Hades struck the ground with his scepter and opened a path to the Underworld through her pool. Grieving, Cyane wept until she dissolved into the water of her own spring.

**Adonis**
Aphrodite hid the infant Adonis in a chest and gave it to Persephone to keep, but Persephone fell in love with him and refused to give him back. Zeus settled the quarrel by dividing Adonis's year between the two goddesses (in some versions with a third left for Adonis to choose).

**Sirens (daughters of Achelous)**
In Ovid's version, the Sirens were Persephone's companions, daughters of the river god Achelous. After she disappeared, they prayed for wings so they could search for her over the sea, and they became bird-women.

**Demeter's search (Hecate and Baubo)**
Demeter searched the earth for her daughter holding torches lit from Mount Etna, with the goddess Hecate and her torch helping her. At Eleusis, the bawdy old woman Baubo (in other versions Iambe) made the grieving Demeter laugh with crude jokes and gestures.

**Despoina**
"The Mistress," a goddess worshipped in Arcadian mystery cults alongside Demeter. She is closely identified with Persephone, though in Arcadian myth she is a daughter of Demeter and Poseidon. Persephone was also called "source of the Eumenides" (the Furies).

**Sisyphus and Merope**
Before he died, Sisyphus told his wife Merope not to give him proper funeral rites. In the Underworld, he complained to Persephone that his wife had disrespected him and persuaded her to let him go back to the living to punish her. Once there, he refused to return.

**Founder of Thebes**
Cadmus's defining role and the usual giveaway: he is the legendary founder of the city of Thebes in Boeotia. He first built its citadel, later called the Cadmea after him.

**Search for Europa**
Zeus, disguised as a white bull, carried off Cadmus's sister Europa from Phoenicia. Their father Agenor sent his sons to find her and forbade them to return without her, so Cadmus never went home and settled in Greece instead.

**Agenor and his brothers Phoenix, Cilix, and Thasus**
Cadmus was the son of Agenor, king of Tyre or Sidon in Phoenicia. His brothers also gave up the search for Europa and founded places named after themselves: Phoenix (Phoenicia), Cilix (Cilicia), and Thasus (the island of Thasos).

**Following the cow**
The Delphic oracle told Cadmus to stop searching for Europa, follow a cow, and found a city where it lay down from exhaustion. That spot became Thebes.

**Dragon of Ares**
When Cadmus sent his companions to fetch water for a sacrifice, a serpent sacred to Ares, which guarded the spring (called the Ismenian spring, Dirce, or in some sources Castalia), killed them. Cadmus then killed the dragon.

**Sowing the dragon's teeth / the Sparti**
On Athena's advice, Cadmus sowed the dragon's teeth in the ground, and armed warriors sprang up. He threw a stone among them, and they fought each other until only five were left. These "Sparti" ("sown men") helped him build Thebes and became the ancestors of its noble families.

**Harmonia**
Cadmus's wife, the daughter of Ares and Aphrodite. Before he could marry her, Cadmus had to serve Ares for a period (often given as eight years) to atone for killing the dragon. The gods attended the wedding.

**Necklace of Harmonia**
A wedding gift to Harmonia, often said to have been made by Hephaestus, that brought disaster to everyone who later owned it. It later played a central part in the war of the Seven Against Thebes.

**Transformation into serpents**
At the end of their lives, Cadmus and Harmonia were turned into serpents, which some link to his killing of the dragon of Ares. Afterward they were taken to the Elysian Fields (or the Isles of the Blessed).

**Semele and Agave**
Two of Cadmus's daughters. Semele was the mortal mother of Dionysus by Zeus, and Agave, in a Bacchic frenzy, tore apart her own son Pentheus, Cadmus's grandson and successor as king of Thebes. His other daughters were Ino and Autonoe.

**Bringing the alphabet**
Cadmus was credited with bringing the Phoenician alphabet to Greece, the origin of Greek writing. Greek letters were sometimes called "Cadmean letters."

**Illyria and the Encheleans**
Late in life, Cadmus and Harmonia left Thebes for Illyria. There Cadmus led the Enchelean people against their enemies and became a king. In some accounts his daughter Agave, who had fled there, killed the Illyrian king Lycotherses.

**Membliarus on Thera**
During his wanderings, Cadmus stopped on the island of Thera (Santorini) and left his kinsman Membliarus there to found a Phoenician settlement.

**Reassembling Osiris's body**
After Set murdered her husband and brother Osiris and cut his corpse into fourteen (sometimes forty-two) pieces scattered across Egypt, Isis searched for them with her sister Nephthys. She found every piece except the phallus, which had been eaten by a fish, so she made him a golden (or magical) phallus, reassembled him, and revived him as ruler of the dead. Isis is a daughter of Geb and Nut and a member of the Ennead of Heliopolis.

**Ra's secret name**
Isis fashioned a snake out of earth or clay mixed with the aging sun god Ra's saliva and placed it in his path. When it bit him, only she could cure the poison, and she refused until Ra revealed his secret true name to her, giving her great magical power.

**Tyet ("Knot of Isis")**
A knot-shaped amulet resembling an ankh with drooping arms, also called the Girdle, Buckle, or Blood of Isis. It is Isis's characteristic symbol and was often placed with the dead for protection.

**Byblos and the tamarisk tree**
In Plutarch's account, Set sealed Osiris in a chest that floated to Byblos in Phoenicia, where a tamarisk (or cedar) tree grew around it and was cut down to become a pillar in the king's palace. Isis traveled to Byblos, retrieved the coffin from the pillar, and brought it back to Egypt; the pillar is linked to Osiris's Djed pillar.

**Seven scorpions and the rich woman's son**
While hiding from Set, Isis was guarded by seven scorpions led by Tefen. When a rich woman refused Isis shelter (while a poor fisher-girl took her in), the scorpions stung the rich woman's son, and Isis, taking pity, healed the child by invoking the scorpions' names. The story is recorded on the Metternich Stela, a magical healing stela.

**Throne headdress**
Isis is usually depicted as a woman wearing a headdress shaped like a throne, which is also the hieroglyph of her name (Aset). It reflects her role as the symbolic mother and protector of the pharaoh and of the throne itself.

**Burning away a baby's mortality**
While at Byblos, Isis served as nurse to the infant son of the queen (named Astarte in Plutarch, with the king called Malcander; the child is sometimes named Dictys) and tried to make him immortal by placing him in a fire each night. The queen saw this and screamed, breaking the spell, a story closely paralleling Demeter's attempt to immortalize Demophon.

**Kite form and the conception of Horus**
Isis transformed into a kite (a bird of prey), which is her sacred bird, and hovered over Osiris's revived body, fanning breath into him with her wings and conceiving their son Horus. She and Nephthys were also depicted as kites mourning the dead on coffins.

**Birth of Horus in the papyrus marshes**
Isis gave birth to Horus in hiding in the papyrus marshes of the Nile Delta at Chemmis, protecting him from Set. In one version she entrusted him to the goddess Buto (Wadjet), whose island was made to float free so Set could not find it.

**Nephthys disguised as Isis (Anubis)**
Nephthys disguised herself as Isis to sleep with Osiris (or in other versions Set), and from this union the jackal-headed god Anubis was born. Isis later adopted or raised Anubis.

**The Golden Ass (Apuleius)**
In Apuleius's Roman novel The Golden Ass (Metamorphoses), the hero Lucius, transformed into a donkey, is restored to human form by Isis, who appears to him as Queen of Heaven and tells him to eat roses carried in her procession. Lucius then joins her mystery cult, making this the main literary source for the Isis mysteries in the Roman world.

**Contendings of Horus and Set**
In this myth of the struggle for Osiris's throne, Isis tricks the ferryman Nemty with a golden signet ring to reach an island, and helps Horus put his semen on lettuce that Set eats. She cuts off Horus's hands after Set's semen defiles them, and when she harpoons Set (in hippopotamus form) and then lets him go, the enraged Horus cuts off her head.

**Philae**
An island temple complex in southern Egypt that was the center of Isis's cult and among the last places where traditional Egyptian religion was practiced. Isis worship spread throughout the Mediterranean, with temples such as the Iseum Campense in Rome.

**Sirius (Sopdet)**
Isis was identified with Sopdet, the goddess of the star Sirius, whose rising heralded the Nile's annual flood. The Nile floods were also said to be the tears Isis shed for Osiris.

**Isis nursing Horus (Isis lactans)**
Images of Isis seated and nursing the infant Horus (Harpocrates) were widespread in the Greco-Roman world. They are widely thought to have influenced Christian images of the Virgin Mary holding or nursing the infant Jesus.

**Gambling with Khonsu for five extra days**
Ra had forbidden the sky goddess Nut from giving birth on any day of the year. Thoth played a game (often said to be senet) against the moon god Khonsu and won a portion (one seventy-second) of the moon's light, which he used to create five extra days outside the 360-day year. On these epagomenal days Nut gave birth to Osiris, Horus the Elder, Set, Isis, and Nephthys, completing the 365-day calendar.

**Ibis head and baboon form (A'an)**
Thoth is usually shown as a man with the head of an ibis, a long-beaked wading bird, whose curved beak was linked to the crescent moon. He was also depicted as a dog-faced baboon, notably in his form A'an, the god of equilibrium; both animals were sacred to him.

**Scribe at the weighing of the heart**
In the judgment of the dead in the Hall of Ma'at (Hall of Two Truths), Thoth stands beside the scales on which Anubis weighs the dead person's heart against the feather of Ma'at. He records the result on his scribe's palette and announces the verdict.

**Hermes Trismegistus and Hermopolis**
The Greeks identified Thoth with Hermes, and the fusion produced Hermes Trismegistus ("thrice-great Hermes"), the legendary author of the Hermetic writings. Thoth's cult center was Khmun in Middle Egypt, which the Greeks called Hermopolis ("city of Hermes").

**Ma'at and Seshat**
Ma'at, goddess of truth, justice, and cosmic order, is often called Thoth's consort or feminine counterpart, and the two stand together on the sun god's boat. Seshat, the goddess of writing and measurement who wears a leopard skin, is described as either his wife or his daughter and helped him create writing.

**Book of Thoth**
A legendary book of magic written by Thoth containing two powerful spells, one granting understanding of the speech of animals and power over heaven and earth, the other allowing one to see the gods. In the Egyptian tale of Setne Khamwas, Prince Neferkaptah retrieved it from the Nile near Coptos, where it lay in a gold box nested inside other boxes and guarded by serpents; it was later buried with him in his tomb.

**Helping Isis resurrect Osiris**
After Set murdered and dismembered Osiris, Thoth, as the master of magic, gave Isis the magic words needed to reassemble and revive her husband. He also gave her incantations to heal the infant Horus.

**Restoring the Eye of Horus**
During the struggle between Horus and Set, Set tore out or injured Horus's (left) eye. Thoth healed and restored it; the restored eye, the wedjat, became a symbol of protection and wholeness and was linked to the waxing and waning moon.

**Arbiter between Horus and Set**
As a god of mediation and law, Thoth judged disputes between gods, especially the contest between Horus and Set for Osiris's throne. When Set ate lettuce covered in Horus's semen, Thoth summoned the semen, which emerged from Set's head as a golden sun disk that Thoth took and wore on his own head.

**Seven scorpions and the healing of Horus**
In one myth, Thoth sent seven scorpions to protect Isis while she hid from Set in the marshes. In another, he helped heal the infant Horus after he was stung by a scorpion.

**Ra's solar barque and Apep**
Thoth stood with Ma'at on either side of Ra's solar boat as it traveled across the sky and through the underworld each night. He helped defend Ra against the chaos serpent Apep (Apophis).

**Bringing Tefnut back from Nubia**
In the myth of the "Distant Goddess," Tefnut (or the Eye of Ra) fled angrily to Nubia in the form of a lioness, leaving Egypt dry. Thoth, sometimes with Shu, was sent to calm her and persuade her to return.

**Inventor of writing and "Tongue of Ra"**
Thoth was credited with inventing hieroglyphic writing and was the patron of scribes, as well as a god of magic, mathematics, astronomy, and knowledge; he was also called the "Tongue of Ra." He was considered the author of spells in the Book of the Dead.

**Creator god of the Hermopolitan Ogdoad**
In the cosmology of Hermopolis, centered on the Ogdoad, a group of eight primordial deities, Thoth was sometimes regarded as a creator god. Originally a lunar deity, he was sometimes identified or conflated with the moon god Khonsu.

**Identification with Moses (Artapanus)**
The Hellenistic Jewish writer Artapanus of Alexandria claimed that Moses was the one the Egyptians honored as Thoth (Hermes), presenting Moses as the source of Egyptian learning and culture.

**Remus**
Romulus's twin brother and co-founder of Rome. After a dispute over where to build the city, Remus mockingly leapt over Romulus's newly built low wall to show how weak its defenses were, and he was killed for it, either by Romulus himself or, in some versions, by Romulus's foreman Celer. Romulus then named the city after himself.

**Rape of the Sabine Women**
Rome was short of women, so Romulus invited the neighboring Sabines to the Consualia, a festival of the god Consus (sometimes identified with Neptune), and his men seized the Sabine women as wives. Romulus himself married one of them, Hersilia.

**Rhea Silvia**
The twins' mother, a Vestal Virgin of Alba Longa and daughter of King Numitor, through whom they descended from Aeneas. She became pregnant by the war god Mars, so Romulus is often called a son of Mars.

**The she-wolf (Lupa) and the Tiber**
The newborn twins were ordered killed and were set adrift on the Tiber River. They washed ashore and were suckled by a she-wolf in a cave called the Lupercal, and they were fed by a woodpecker (associated with the god Picus). The shepherd Faustulus and his wife Acca Larentia then raised them.

**Augury contest on the Palatine and Aventine**
To settle where the city would be founded, the twins watched for omens from the gods. Remus, on the Aventine Hill, saw six vultures first, but Romulus, on the Palatine Hill, then saw twelve. Each claimed victory, and the quarrel led to Remus's death. Romulus founded the city on the Palatine.

**Quirinus**
Romulus vanished in a sudden storm or whirlwind while reviewing his troops and was said to have been taken up to heaven, where he was worshipped as the god Quirinus. A rival story says the senators murdered him. Tradition dates his disappearance to 716/715 BC.

**Titus Tatius**
The king of the Sabines, who attacked Rome to avenge the abduction. The Sabine women threw themselves between the armies to stop the fighting, after which the two peoples merged and Tatius ruled jointly with Romulus until Tatius's death.

**Amulius and Numitor**
Amulius usurped the throne of Alba Longa from his brother Numitor (the twins' grandfather), forced Rhea Silvia to become a Vestal, and ordered the twins killed. When grown, Romulus and Remus killed Amulius and restored Numitor to the throne. Romulus was later offered the kingship of Alba Longa.

**Celer and the Celeres**
Celer was Romulus's foreman, who oversaw the building of the walls and in some accounts killed Remus. Romulus's personal bodyguard of 300 horsemen, the Celeres ("swift ones"), was said to take its name from him.

**Lemuria**
A Roman festival for appeasing restless spirits of the dead (lemures). According to Ovid, Romulus instituted it to placate the angry ghost of Remus, and its name was originally "Remuria."

**Acron**
The king of the Sabine town of Caenina, who attacked Rome after the abduction of the Sabine women. Romulus killed him in single combat and dedicated his armor to Jupiter Feretrius as the first spolia opima.

**Numa Pompilius**
Romulus's successor and the second king of Rome, a peaceful, pious Sabine credited with founding many of Rome's religious institutions.

**Founding Roman institutions**
Romulus is credited with creating the Senate (originally 100 senators or "fathers"), dividing the people into three tribes (the Ramnes, Tities, and Luceres), and building Roma Quadrata, the "square Rome" settlement and wall on the Palatine.

**Aeneas and Alba Longa**
Through Rhea Silvia, Romulus descended from the Trojan hero Aeneas, whose son Ascanius founded Alba Longa, the city where the twins were born. Virgil's Aeneid foretells Romulus's founding of Rome.

**Matsya, the first avatar of Vishnu**
In the Hindu flood myth, Vishnu takes the form of the fish Matsya. Manu rescues a tiny fish that keeps growing larger every time he moves it to a bigger container, until he recognizes it as the god (Narayana). The fish warns him of a coming flood and tows his boat to safety.

**Manu's boat tied to the fish's horn**
During the flood, Manu ties his ship to a horn on Matsya's head, using the serpent Vasuki as a rope. The boat carries Manu, the seven sages and the seeds of all life, so the world can be repopulated afterwards.

**Salmon of Knowledge (bradan feasa)**
In Irish myth, a salmon gains all the world's knowledge by eating nine hazelnuts that fall into a well (or pool) of wisdom. The poet Finnegas catches it, but his young pupil Fionn mac Cumhaill (Finn McCool) burns his thumb while cooking it and sucks it, gaining the wisdom himself.

**Feeding of the five thousand**
In the Gospels, Jesus feeds a crowd of about five thousand people with only five loaves of bread and two fish, with leftovers to spare. It is one of his most famous miracles.

**Pisces**
The constellation and zodiac sign of two fish tied together. In Greek myth, Aphrodite and her son Eros turned into fish and jumped into a river to escape the monster Typhon.

**Namazu**
A giant catfish in Japanese folklore that lives under the earth and causes earthquakes when it thrashes. The god Kashima keeps it pinned down with a great stone (the kaname-ishi), and earthquakes happen when he lets his guard slip.

**Ichthys**
The early Christian fish symbol, drawn with two crossing arcs. The Greek word for fish, ichthys, works as an acronym for "Iesous Christos, Theou Yios, Soter," meaning "Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior."

**Jonah swallowed by a great fish**
In the Hebrew Bible, the prophet Jonah tries to avoid God's command to preach in Nineveh by sailing away. He is thrown overboard and swallowed by a great fish (often called a whale), and spends three days inside it before being spit out on land.

**Shakuntala's ring found in a fish**
King Dushyanta gives his wife Shakuntala a signet ring, but because of a curse he forgets her once she loses it. A fisherman later finds the ring inside a fish and brings it to the king, whose memory returns when he sees it. The tale is best known from Kalidasa's play Shakuntala.

**Loki as a salmon**
After causing the death of Baldr, Loki hides from the Aesir by turning into a salmon in a waterfall. The gods drag a net through the river to catch him, and Thor finally grabs him by the tail, which explains why salmon have narrow tails.

**Vainamoinen's kantele from a pike's jawbone**
In the Finnish epic Kalevala, the hero Vainamoinen kills a giant pike and makes the first kantele (a Finnish zither-like instrument) from its jawbones. He then plays music so beautiful that all creatures come to listen.

**Hero Twins' ashes become fish**
In the Maya Popol Vuh, the Hero Twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque let themselves be burned in an oven in Xibalba, and the lords of the underworld throw their ground bones into a river. Their remains turn into catfish (or fish-men) and then come back to life as the twins.

**Two golden fish in Buddhism**
A pair of golden fish is one of the Eight Auspicious Symbols of Buddhism. They stand for beings living without fear, swimming freely in the ocean of suffering (samsara) without drowning.

**Arjuna's fish-eye archery feat**
In the Mahabharata, at the contest to win Draupadi's hand, suitors must shoot the eye of a fish target while looking only at its reflection. Arjuna succeeds, famously saying he could see nothing but the fish's eye.

**Apkallu and other fish-bodied figures**
In Mesopotamian legend, the seven apkallu sages who brought civilization to humans are often depicted as part fish, wearing fish skins. Other fish-hybrid clues include Capricorn's sea-goat (a goat's head on a fish's body) and the ten Kara fish that guard the Gaokerena tree of life in Zoroastrian tradition.

**Jormungandr (the Midgard Serpent)**
The Norse "World Serpent," a child of Loki and the giantess Angrboda, which grew so large that it encircles the earth while biting its own tail. Thor once lifted it in disguise as a giant grey cat in Utgard-Loki's hall, and at Ragnarok Thor will kill it but walk only nine steps before dying from its venom.

**Thor's fishing trip with Hymir**
Thor went fishing with the giant Hymir, who refused to provide bait, so Thor tore the head off Hymir's largest ox and used it to hook Jormungandr. The frightened Hymir cut the line before Thor could kill the serpent; the scene is carved on stones such as the Hørdum Stone.

**Medusa's hair**
The Gorgon Medusa had living snakes in place of hair, and her gaze turned onlookers to stone. This is one of the most common giveaways for snakes in Greek myth.

**Nidhogg**
The Norse serpent or dragon that gnaws at the roots of the world tree Yggdrasil from the spring Hvergelmir in Niflheim. It is also said to chew on the corpses of the dead.

**Python at Delphi**
The serpent that guarded the site of Delphi, sent by Hera to hound the pregnant Leto so she could not give birth anywhere the sun shone. Leto's son Apollo later killed Python and took over Delphi as the site of his oracle.

**Tiresias and the mating snakes**
The Theban seer Tiresias came upon two mating snakes and struck one, which turned him into a woman for seven years. After striking a pair again he became a man, and he later angered Hera by telling her and Zeus that women enjoy sex more than men.

**The infant Heracles strangling snakes**
Hera sent two serpents into the cradle of the baby Heracles to kill him, but he strangled them with his bare hands. This was the first sign of his superhuman strength.

**Quetzalcoatl and Kukulkan (the feathered serpent)**
Quetzalcoatl is the feathered serpent god of the Aztecs, associated with wind and learning, whom Moctezuma II allegedly identified with Hernán Cortés; he departed on a raft of serpents. His Maya counterpart Kukulkan is honored at El Castillo in Chichen Itza, where shadows on the stairs form a serpent descending at the equinoxes.

**Laocoön and his sons**
The Trojan priest Laocoön warned the Trojans against accepting the Trojan Horse. Two sea serpents sent by a god (Poseidon or Athena in different versions) then came out of the sea and crushed him and his two sons.

**The ouroboros and the caduceus**
The ouroboros is the ancient symbol of a serpent eating its own tail, representing eternity and cyclic renewal. The caduceus is the herald's staff of Hermes, which has two snakes entwined around it.

**Nagas: Vasuki, Sesha, and Ananta**
Nagas are the divine serpent beings of Hindu mythology and the enemies of the eagle Garuda. The naga king Vasuki served as the churning rope wrapped around Mount Mandara during the churning of the Ocean of Milk, while the thousand-headed Sesha (also called Ananta) is the serpent on which Vishnu sleeps.

**Fafnir**
In Norse legend, Fafnir killed his father Hreidmar to take a cursed treasure including the ring Andvaranaut, then turned into a serpent or dragon to guard it. The hero Sigurd killed him at the instruction of Fafnir's brother Regin, and while roasting Fafnir's heart Sigurd tasted its blood and gained the ability to understand birds.

**Eurydice's death**
On her wedding day, Eurydice, the wife of Orpheus, was bitten by a snake while fleeing from Aristaeus and died. Orpheus then descended to the underworld to try to bring her back.

**Yamata no Orochi and Kusanagi**
In Japanese myth, the storm god Susanoo slew the eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent Yamata no Orochi after getting it drunk on sake, having turned the princess Kushinadahime into a comb to protect her. In one of its tails he found the sword Kusanagi ("Grass-Cutter"), which became one of Japan's imperial regalia.

**The Rainbow Serpent**
A creator figure in Australian Aboriginal mythology, associated with rain, water holes, fertility, and the cycle of life. It is said to have shaped the land and established laws during the Dreamtime.

**Jotunn and Jotunheim**
In Norse mythology, the giants are called jotunn (plural jotnar) and live in the realm of Jotunheim. They are the chief enemies of the Aesir gods, and the "frost giants" (hrimthursar) are their best-known variety.

**Ymir and Audhumla**
Ymir is the primordial frost giant, formed in the void Ginnungagap where the ice of Niflheim met the heat of Muspelheim, from venom of the rivers Elivagar. He was nourished by the milk of the primeval cow Audhumla, and Odin and his brothers killed him and built the world from his body. His blood drowned nearly all the giants except his grandson Bergelmir, who survived with his wife in a hollow tree trunk or boat and repopulated the race.

**Utgard-Loki and Skrymir**
The giant king of Utgard who, disguised as the huge giant Skrymir, asks whether a leaf or acorn has fallen on his head after Thor strikes him three times with his hammer.
