In his hall, Thor tries to drain a drinking horn connected to the sea and wrestles the old woman Elli (Old Age), Loki loses an eating contest to Fire, and Thor's servant Thjalfi races Hugi (Thought).

**Surtr and the fire giants**
Surtr is the fire giant who leads the sons of Muspell out of Muspelheim at Ragnarok. His forces break the rainbow bridge Bifrost, he kills the god Freyr, who had given away his sword, and he sets the world ablaze.

**Gigantomachy**
The Greek war between the Olympian gods and the Gigantes, children of Gaia born from the blood of the castrated Uranus. It took place on the plain of Phlegra, and the gods won only after recruiting the mortal Heracles, because a prophecy said they needed a mortal's help.

**Alcyoneus and Porphyrion**
The two leaders of the Greek Giants. Alcyoneus was immortal while standing on his native land of Pallene, so Heracles dragged him beyond its borders to kill him. Zeus filled Porphyrion with lust for Hera to provoke him, and he was then struck down by Zeus's thunderbolt and Heracles's arrows.

**Gaia's herb of invulnerability**
Before the Gigantomachy, Gaia sought a magic herb that would make the Giants invincible. Zeus forbade the sun, moon, and dawn (Helios, Selene, and Eos) to shine so she could not find it, and took the plant himself.

**Otus and Ephialtes (the Aloadae)**
Twin giants who piled Mount Ossa on Mount Olympus and Mount Pelion on Ossa to storm heaven, and imprisoned Ares in a bronze jar for thirteen months until Hermes freed him. Artemis tricked them by leaping between them as a deer, so that they killed each other with their spears.

**Thiazi, Idunn, and Skadi**
The giant Thiazi, in the form of an eagle, forces Loki to help him kidnap Idunn, keeper of the gods' apples of youth. Loki rescues her by turning her into a nut and flying her back, and Thiazi dies when his feathers catch fire. His daughter Skadi, a giantess associated with skiing, later receives compensation from the gods, and Odin turns Thiazi's eyes into stars.

**Thrym and the stolen Mjolnir**
The giant Thrym steals Thor's hammer Mjolnir, hides it deep underground, and demands the goddess Freyja as his bride in return. Thor disguises himself as Freyja in a bridal veil, reclaims the hammer at the wedding feast, and kills Thrym.

**Hrungnir and Gullfaxi**
Hrungnir bets that his horse Gullfaxi can outrun Odin's eight-legged Sleipnir, leading to a duel with Thor. Tricked into standing on his shield and paired with the clay giant Mokkurkalfi, he is killed by Thor, but a piece of his whetstone lodges permanently in Thor's forehead.

**Angrboda, Bestla, and other giantesses**
Many important Norse figures have giant blood. The giantess Angrboda bears Loki's children Fenrir, Jormungandr, and Hel (whose skin is half blue and half flesh-colored) in the Iron Wood. Odin's mother Bestla was a giantess, and Jarnsaxa bore Thor's son Magni.

**Jack and the Beanstalk**
In the English folktale, Jack climbs a beanstalk to a giant's castle and steals a hen that lays golden eggs, among other treasures. The giant chants "Fee-fi-fo-fum, I smell the blood of an Englishman," and Jack chops down the beanstalk to kill him. In related Cornish tales, Jack the Giant Killer slays giants such as Cormoran.

**Welsh and British giants**
In the Mabinogion, the giant Ysbaddaden sets Culhwch impossible tasks, including hunting the boar Twrch Trwyth, before he can marry Olwen. The giant king Bran the Blessed asked that his head be buried in London to protect Britain from invasion. Geoffrey of Monmouth tells of Corineus throwing the giant Gogmagog off a cliff.

**Paul Bunyan and American giants**
The giant lumberjack Paul Bunyan, with his blue ox Babe, is credited in American tall tales with creating features such as Minnesota's 10,000 lakes. The Cardiff Giant was a famous 1869 hoax, a stone figure buried by George Hull and "discovered" by well diggers, which P. T. Barnum then copied.

**Fishing up islands with a magic fishhook**
Maui's most famous feat. While fishing with his brothers, he used a magical hook (made from his grandmother's jawbone in Maori versions) to haul land up from the ocean floor. In Hawaiian tradition this is how the Hawaiian Islands were raised, and in Maori tradition the great fish he caught became New Zealand's North Island (Te Ika-a-Maui, "the fish of Maui").

**Slowing the sun**
Because the sun crossed the sky too quickly for people to finish their work or for crops to grow, Maui snared it with a lasso, often made from his sister's hair, and beat it with his jawbone weapon. The beaten sun agreed to move more slowly, giving longer days.

**Hine-nui-te-po and the obsidian teeth**
Maui's death in the Maori tradition. To win immortality for humanity, he tried to crawl through the body of the sleeping goddess of death and night, Hine-nui-te-po ("Great Woman of Night"), taking a small form such as a worm. A fantail bird burst out laughing, waking her, and she crushed him between the obsidian teeth of her vagina, so humans remain mortal.

**Mahuika and the burning fingernails**
To bring fire to humanity, Maui tricked the fire goddess Mahuika into giving him her burning fingernails (and toenails) one after another, putting each out until she had only one left. When she threw it at him in rage and set the world on fire, Maui escaped in the form of a hawk or eagle and called for rain to put out the blaze. The fire went into certain trees, which is why fire can be made by rubbing their wood together.

**Muri-ranga-whenua's jawbone**
Maui's grandmother, from whom he got the enchanted jawbone that is his most important possession. He used it as a weapon to beat the sun and as the hook to fish up land.

**Taranga and the journey to the underworld**
Maui's mother. Because he was born prematurely, she wrapped him in her topknot and threw him into the sea, which gives him the name Maui-tikitiki-a-Taranga. Later he secretly followed her as she entered the underworld by pulling up a tuft of reeds, followed her in the form of a pigeon, and met his father Makea-tutara there.

**Tuna (Kuna Loa), the eel**
A giant eel who harassed or attacked Maui's wife Hina. Maui killed him; in Hawaiian versions the eel is called Kuna Loa ("long eel") and Maui slays him with a stone axe.

**Hina**
The name of Maui's wife in some traditions and of his mother in others (especially Hawaiian versions). In one story Maui's mother asks him to slow the sun so her kapa cloth has time to dry.

**Learning fire from the mud hen**
In a Hawaiian version of the fire myth, the 'alae (mud hens) were the only ones who knew how to make fire. Maui caught one and forced it to teach him the secret of rubbing sticks together.

**Stealing bananas from his blind grandmother**
In a Hawaiian story, Maui's mother sent him to steal the bananas his blind grandmother was cooking, until she recognized him by his smell or touch. She then helped him in his plan to snare the sun.

**Making birds visible**
In one myth, only Maui could see birds until he made them reveal themselves to people, filling the forests with their songs.

**Mafui'e and the earthquake god**
In a Samoan version of the fire myth, Maui (called Ti'iti'i) goes to the underworld and wrestles the earthquake god Mafui'e for the secret of fire. He breaks off Mafui'e's right arm but spares the left one, so the god can still cause earthquakes.

**Namesake of the island of Maui**
Maui is a trickster hero and demigod across Polynesia, and the Hawaiian island of Maui bears his name. The island was badly damaged by the 2023 Lahaina wildfires.

**Golden Fleece**
The fleece of a golden ram, kept in Colchis by King Aeetes, hanging from a tree in a sacred grove and guarded by a sleepless dragon. Jason's quest to retrieve it is his defining story, and Medea put the dragon to sleep so he could take it.

**Medea**
The sorceress daughter of King Aeetes of Colchis, who fell in love with Jason and helped him complete his tasks and escape. Jason later abandoned her, and in revenge she killed his new bride and their own children, then fled in the chariot of her grandfather Helios.

**Fire-breathing oxen and dragon's teeth**
Aeetes demanded that Jason yoke a pair of bronze-hoofed, fire-breathing bulls (the Khalkotauroi), plow a field with them, and sow it with dragon's teeth. Medea gave him an ointment that made him invulnerable, and when armed warriors (the Spartoi) sprang up from the teeth, he threw a rock among them so they fought and killed each other, much like Cadmus at Thebes.

**One sandal and Pelias**
Jason's uncle Pelias had usurped the throne of Iolcus and received an oracle warning him to beware a man wearing one sandal. Jason lost a sandal while carrying an old woman (Hera in disguise) across the Anauros River, and when he arrived at Iolcus, Pelias sent him on the seemingly impossible quest for the Fleece.

**Hypsipyle and Lemnos**
Lemnos was an island whose women had killed all their men (and who had been cursed with a foul smell for neglecting Aphrodite). Jason stayed with their queen Hypsipyle and fathered twin sons, Euneus and Nebrophonus (or Thoas), until Heracles urged the Argonauts to leave.

**Creusa (Glauce)**
The princess of Corinth, daughter of King Creon, whom Jason agreed to marry after he and Medea fled to Corinth. Medea sent her a poisoned wedding dress (and crown) that burned her to death, the central event of Euripides's play Medea.

**Phineus and the Harpies**
A blind seer tormented by the Harpies, who snatched or fouled his food. The Argonauts (especially the winged Boreads, Zetes and Calais) drove the Harpies away, and in return Phineus told Jason how to reach Colchis and how to pass the Symplegades.

**Symplegades and the dove**
The Clashing Rocks at the entrance to the Black Sea, which smashed together on anything passing between them. On Phineus's advice, Jason released a dove first; when the rocks closed on it and lost only its tail feathers, the Argo rowed through as they reopened.

**Death under the Argo**
After losing Medea and the favor of the gods, Jason grew old and unhappy. He died while sleeping beneath the rotting hull of the Argo when a piece of it fell on him.

**Cyzicus**
The hospitable king of the Doliones, who welcomed the Argonauts. When a storm blew the Argo back to his land at night, the two sides mistook each other for enemies, and Jason accidentally killed Cyzicus, then gave him a grand funeral.

**Apsyrtus**
Medea's brother. Medea (in some versions with Jason) killed him and scattered his dismembered body in the sea to slow Aeetes's pursuit, and the pair were later purified of the murder by Medea's aunt Circe.

**Talos**
A bronze giant who guarded Crete by hurling rocks at approaching ships. Medea killed him on the voyage home by removing the bronze nail that sealed his single vein, letting his ichor drain out.

**Chiron**
The wise centaur who raised and trained Jason in secret after Pelias usurped the throne from Jason's father Aeson. Jason's mother is named Alcimede.

**Ljubljana dragon**
According to a later legend, Jason founded Ljubljana, the capital of Slovenia, after slaying a dragon there on his way home with the Argonauts. The dragon is still the city's symbol.

**Argonautica and the speaking prow**
Apollonius of Rhodes's epic Argonautica tells the story of the voyage and includes an ekphrasis describing Jason's embroidered cloak. The Argo itself contained a prophetic piece of oak from Zeus's sacred grove at Dodona that could speak and guide the crew.

**Persephone's abduction by Hades and the seasons**
Demeter's daughter Persephone (Kore) was kidnapped by Hades to be queen of the underworld. Demeter's grief as she wandered the earth searching for her caused a year-long famine, and because Persephone had eaten pomegranate seeds in the underworld, she must spend part of each year there; Demeter's mourning during those months explains winter.

**Demophon in the fire**
While searching for Persephone, Demeter, disguised as an old woman named Doso, became nurse to Demophon, the baby son of King Celeus and Queen Metanira of Eleusis. She anointed him with ambrosia and secretly held him in the hearth fire each night to burn away his mortality, but Metanira walked in and screamed, so the goddess revealed herself and the boy remained mortal.

**Pelops's shoulder**
When Tantalus cooked his son Pelops and served him to the gods, Demeter, distracted by grief over Persephone, was the only one who ate, consuming his shoulder. When the gods restored Pelops to life, he was given an ivory shoulder in its place, made by Hephaestus or by Demeter herself.

**Triptolemus**
A prince of Eleusis (in most versions the elder son of Celeus and Metanira) whom Demeter taught the secrets of agriculture in place of immortalizing Demophon. She gave him a winged chariot drawn by serpents (dragons), in which he flew around the world teaching people to plant grain.

**Eleusinian Mysteries**
The most famous secret religious rites of ancient Greece, held at Eleusis in honor of Demeter and Persephone. Initiates drank the barley drink kykeon and were shown sacred objects (the hiera); one ancient source says the climax was the display of "an ear of wheat reaped in silence."

**Thesmophoria**
A festival for Demeter Thesmophoros ("Law-Bringer") and Persephone that only married women citizens could attend. Piglets were thrown into underground pits, commemorating the swineherd Eubouleus, whose pigs were swallowed by the earth along with Persephone when Hades took her; their decayed remains were later mixed with the seed grain.

**Erysichthon and Mestra**
Erysichthon, a Thessalian king, cut down a sacred grove of Demeter's, including a giant oak. Demeter cursed him with insatiable hunger; he sold his daughter Mestra again and again to buy food (she escaped each time by shapeshifting) and eventually devoured himself.

**Iasion and Plutus**
At the wedding of Cadmus and Harmonia, Demeter lay with the mortal Iasion in a thrice-plowed field. Zeus killed Iasion with a thunderbolt, and Demeter bore Plutus, the god of wealth (and in some versions Philomelus, linked to the constellation Bootes).

**Poseidon, Arion, and Despoina**
While Demeter was searching for Persephone, Poseidon pursued her; she turned into a mare and hid among the horses of King Onkios, but Poseidon became a stallion and mated with her. She bore the swift, talking horse Arion and the goddess Despoina ("the Mistress").

**Lyncus turned into a lynx**
Lyncus, a king of Scythia, tried to murder Triptolemus while he was a guest, in order to take credit for the gift of agriculture. Demeter turned Lyncus into a lynx as punishment.

**Ascalabus turned into a lizard**
While searching for Persephone, the thirsty Demeter drank a vessel of water (or barley drink) eagerly, and a boy named Ascalabus (or Abas in another version) mocked her. She splashed him with the drink and turned him into a spotted lizard (gecko).

**Iambe and Baubo**
Women who made the grieving Demeter laugh at Eleusis, Iambe with crude jokes and Baubo with an obscene gesture (in one version revealing the infant Iacchus). Their jests were commemorated in the ritual joking and the drinking of kykeon in Demeter's rites.

**Homeric Hymn to Demeter**
The main ancient source for Persephone's abduction, Demeter's stay at Eleusis, and the founding of the Eleusinian Mysteries. A second Homeric hymn to Demeter is only three lines long, one of the shortest in the collection.

**Epithets: Deo, Sito, Thesmophoros**
Demeter was also called Deo, Sito ("of the grain"), and Thesmophoros ("Law-Bringer"). The Mycenaean Linear B title si-to-po-ti-ni-ja ("Lady of the Grain") is thought to refer to an early form of her.

**Eternal punishment of hunger and thirst**
Tantalus is punished in Tartarus by standing in a pool of water beneath fruit-laden branches. Whenever he bends to drink, the water recedes, and whenever he reaches for the fruit, the branches move out of reach. This punishment gives English the word "tantalize."

**Serving Pelops to the gods**
Tantalus killed his son Pelops, cooked him, and served him at a banquet to test whether the gods were truly all-knowing. The gods recognized the meal and refused it, and they restored Pelops to life.

**Pelops's ivory shoulder**
Demeter, distracted by grief over her lost daughter Persephone, absent-mindedly ate Pelops's shoulder at the banquet. When the gods brought Pelops back to life, they replaced the missing shoulder with one made of ivory.

**Stealing nectar and ambrosia**
Tantalus, a favorite of the gods, was invited to dine with them on Olympus. He stole their nectar and ambrosia to share with mortals, and in some versions he also revealed the gods' secrets to humans.

**Niobe**
The daughter of Tantalus, who boasted that her fourteen children made her superior to Leto, who had only two. Leto's children Apollo and Artemis killed all of Niobe's children, and the grieving Niobe was turned into a weeping rock on Mount Sipylus.

**Pelops's chariot race against Oenomaus**
Pelops, son of Tantalus, won the hand of Hippodamia by defeating her father, King Oenomaus, in a chariot race. He won by bribing Oenomaus's charioteer Myrtilus to sabotage his master's chariot, then killed Myrtilus, bringing a curse on his descendants, the house of Atreus.

**King of Mount Sipylus (Lydia)**
Tantalus ruled from Mount Sipylus in Lydia (or Phrygia) in Asia Minor. In some accounts he was killed when a boulder from Mount Sipylus fell on him.

**Pandareus and the golden dog**
Pandareus stole a golden dog, which had guarded the infant Zeus on Crete, and gave it to Tantalus to keep. When Tantalus swore falsely to Hermes that he did not have the dog, he was punished, in some versions by being buried under Mount Sipylus.

**Son of Zeus and Plouto**
Tantalus was the son of Zeus and the nymph Plouto, who in some accounts was the daughter of Himas. This divine parentage explains why he was invited to dine with the gods.

**Broteas**
Another son of Tantalus, a hunter and sculptor who was considered ugly. He was said to have carved the oldest image of the mother goddess on Mount Sipylus.

**Tantalus, first husband of Clytemnestra**
A grandson or descendant of the original Tantalus who shared his name. He was Clytemnestra's first husband until Agamemnon killed him and their infant child and took Clytemnestra as his own wife.

**Golden net of Hephaestus**
Aphrodite's husband, the lame smith god Hephaestus, learned of her affair with Ares and forged an unbreakable golden net to trap the lovers in bed, then summoned the other gods to laugh at them. In the Odyssey the bard Demodocus sings this tale, noting how Hephaestus pretended to leave for Lemnos and how the slow god caught the swift one.

**Ares**
The war god and Aphrodite's most famous lover. Their children include Phobos (Fear), Deimos (Terror), and Harmonia, and the affair is the single most common clue for Aphrodite.

**Birth from sea foam**
Aphrodite was born from the foam (aphros) that formed when Cronus castrated Uranus and the severed genitals fell into the sea. This origin underlies her "Urania" (heavenly) aspect, and she is often depicted arriving on land on a scallop shell.

**Adonis**
A beautiful youth loved by Aphrodite, who fought a custody battle over him with Persephone. When he was killed by a boar, his blood was turned into anemone flowers.

**Judgment of Paris**
At the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, Eris threw a golden apple inscribed "to the fairest" (te kalliste). The Trojan prince Paris awarded it to Aphrodite over Hera and Athena because she promised him Helen, which sparked the Trojan War.

**Hippomenes and Atalanta**
Aphrodite gave Hippomenes three golden apples to drop during his footrace against the swift Atalanta, letting him win her hand. When the couple failed to thank her, they were turned into lions.

**Anchises and Aeneas**
Aphrodite seduced the Trojan shepherd Anchises, as told in a Homeric Hymn, and bore him the hero Aeneas. When Anchises boasted of sleeping with her, Zeus struck him with a thunderbolt, laming him (blinding him in some versions).

**Cythera and Cyprus**
The two islands that both claimed to be Aphrodite's birthplace and were early centers of her cult. They give her the epithets Cytherea and Cypris.

**Eros**
The winged god of desire, armed with a bow and arrows, usually called Aphrodite's son. He is often shown accompanying her.

**Hermaphroditus and Salmacis**
Aphrodite's son by Hermes. The nymph Salmacis fell in love with him while he bathed in her pool, and the gods merged the two into a single intersex being.

**Dione and Diomedes**
In the Iliad, the Greek hero Diomedes wounds Aphrodite in the hand while she is protecting Aeneas on the battlefield. She flees to her mother, the Titaness Dione, who comforts and heals her.

**Pandemos and Urania**
Two aspects of Aphrodite: Urania, the "heavenly" goddess born from Uranus, and Pandemos, the goddess "of all the people." Theseus is said to have founded a temple to Aphrodite Pandemos in Athens, which was ritually purified with the blood of a dove.

**Psyche**
Aphrodite's daughter-in-law, the mortal wife of Eros, whose story is told in Apuleius's The Golden Ass. Aphrodite set her impossible tasks, including sorting grain (accomplished with the help of ants) and fetching a box of beauty from Persephone in the underworld.

**The Charites (Graces)**
Aglaea, Euphrosyne, and Thalia, goddesses of charm and beauty who serve as Aphrodite's attendants. They are often shown bathing and dressing her.

**Pygmalion**
A sculptor who fell in love with the ivory statue of a woman he had carved. Aphrodite answered his prayers and brought the statue to life (later named Galatea).

**Jason and the Golden Fleece**
Medea is a sorceress princess of Colchis, daughter of King Aeetes, granddaughter of the sun god Helios, and a priestess of Hecate. When Jason and the Argonauts come for the Golden Fleece, she falls in love with him and uses her magic to help him win it. In Pindar's Fourth Pythian Ode, Aphrodite gives Jason the iynx, a wryneck bird tied to a spinning wheel, as a love charm to win Medea.

**Poisoned robe for Glauce**
When Jason abandons Medea in Corinth to marry Glauce (also called Creusa), daughter of King Creon, Medea sends the bride a poisoned robe and golden crown. When Glauce puts them on, she bursts into flames, and Creon dies too when he embraces his daughter's body.

**Killing her own children**
Medea's ultimate revenge on Jason is murdering their sons, named Mermeros and Pheres in some sources. In other versions the Corinthians kill the children. Hera is sometimes said to have made the children immortal.

**Euripides's Medea**
The famous 431 BCE tragedy. Creon banishes Medea from Corinth because he fears her, she gives a celebrated speech on the miserable lot of women and of a foreign "barbarian" bride, and Jason sneers that women only care about whether "everything is fine in bed" and wishes there were no female sex. It ends with the murders of Glauce, Creon, and her children.

**Dragon chariot of Helios**
At the end of Euripides's play Medea escapes Corinth with her children's bodies in a flying chariot drawn by dragons (serpents), sent by her grandfather Helios, and flies toward Athens.

**Absyrtus (Apsyrtus)**
Medea's brother (or half-brother). To slow her father's pursuit of the fleeing Argo, she chops him to pieces and scatters the parts so Aeetes must stop to gather them; in Apollonius of Rhodes's Argonautica she lures him into an ambush where Jason kills him. Circe later purifies them of the murder, and the islands named for him, the Absyrtides, were said to be cleared of snakes that Medea confined in his tomb.

**Pelias's daughters and the ram**
To avenge Jason on his usurping uncle King Pelias of Iolcus, Medea chops up an old ram and boils it in a cauldron, and it jumps out as a young lamb. Convinced, Pelias's daughters cut up and boil their own father, but she gives them no magic and he stays dead. In one version she disguises herself as a priestess of Artemis to win access to the palace.

**Aegeus and the wineskin oracle**
In Euripides's play King Aegeus of Athens passes through Corinth on his way to King Pittheus of Troezen, puzzling over an oracle telling him not to "unstop the wineskin's neck" (or "foot") until he gets home. Medea promises to cure his childlessness with drugs in exchange for refuge in Athens, and she later marries him.

**Attempting to poison Theseus**
In Athens Medea recognizes Aegeus's long-lost son Theseus and tries to have him poisoned at a feast. Aegeus recognizes his son's sword just in time, knocks the cup away, and drives Medea out of Athens.

**Talos**
The bronze giant who guards Crete by throwing boulders at ships. His life depends on a single vein sealed at the ankle by a bronze nail. Medea bewitches him by summoning the Keres (death spirits) with her evil eye, and in Apollodorus she removes the nail so his ichor drains out and he dies.

**Fire-breathing bulls and the dragon's teeth**
Aeetes demands that Jason yoke a pair of bronze-footed, fire-breathing bulls and sow dragon's teeth, which sprout into armed warriors. Medea gives Jason a protective ointment and advises him to throw a stone into the crowd of warriors so they fight one another.

**The Promethean ointment**
The ointment she gives Jason comes from a crocus-like flower that grew from the ichor dripping from Prometheus's wounds in the Caucasus. She carries its juice in a shell, and it makes the wearer invulnerable to bronze and fire for one day.

**Rejuvenating Aeson**
In Ovid's Metamorphoses Medea restores youth to Jason's aged father Aeson by draining his blood and replacing it with a magic potion she brews from herbs. In the same work she draws the moon down from the sky for her witchcraft.

**Wedding in the cave of Macris**
While the Argonauts flee the Colchians, King Alcinous of the Phaeacians rules that he will hand Medea back only if she is still a virgin. Medea and Jason hurriedly marry in the sacred cave of Macris on the island of Drepane (Scheria) so that she can stay with him.

**Later life and adaptations**
In later myth Medea returns to Colchis and helps depose her uncle Perses, who had usurped Aeetes's throne, and some sources say she married Achilles in the Isles of the Blessed after her death. Her story was retold in Seneca's Latin tragedy Medea and in a 20th-century adaptation by the poet Robinson Jeffers.

**Creator god of the Trimurti**
Brahma is the creator in the Trimurti, the Hindu triad of supreme gods, alongside Vishnu the preserver and Shiva the destroyer. He should not be confused with Brahman, the abstract ultimate reality of the Upanishads, or with Brahmins, the priestly caste.

**Saraswati, his daughter and consort**
Brahma created the goddess Saraswati and became infatuated with her beauty. In the myth, he grew extra heads so he could keep looking at her as she moved around him, and she later became his consort; in some versions he chased her in various animal forms, including a bull and a horse.

**Fifth head cut off by Shiva**
As Saraswati moved upward to escape his gaze, Brahma grew a fifth head facing the heavens. Shiva cut off this fifth head as punishment for his lust (or, in other versions, his arrogance), leaving him with four.

**Four heads and the four Vedas**
Brahma is depicted with four heads facing the four directions, which are said to represent the four Vedas (and, in some interpretations, the four castes). In his four arms he holds items such as the Vedas, a water pot, a sacrificial ladle or spoon, and a rosary or scepter.

**Born from the lotus in Vishnu's navel**
In one creation account, Brahma sits on a lotus that grows out of the navel of Vishnu as Vishnu sleeps on the cosmic waters. From there Brahma creates the universe.

**Golden egg (Hiranyagarbha)**
In another account, Brahma is born from a golden cosmic egg or womb, the Hiranyagarbha, that floated on the primordial waters, sometimes said to have developed from a seed. He is thus described as self-born (Svayambhu).

**Temple at Pushkar**
Brahma is rarely worshipped, and the red-spired temple at Pushkar in Rajasthan is the most famous of his very few temples. The rarity of his worship is explained by curses laid on him, by Shiva or by Saraswati in different myths.

**Lie about the endless lingam**
Brahma and Vishnu argued over which of them was supreme, and Shiva appeared as an endless pillar of fire (the lingam). Vishnu searched for its base and Brahma for its top, and when Brahma falsely claimed he had found the top, Shiva cursed him never to be widely worshipped.

**The hamsa**
Brahma's vahana (mount) is the hamsa, a swan or goose. One of his epithets is "the One Swan."

**Prajapati and the mind-born sons**
Brahma absorbed the older Vedic creator god Prajapati and is often identified with him. "Prajapati" also became the title of the sages Brahma created from his mind (the manasaputras), and he also created the four Kumaras and is the father of Manu, the progenitor of humanity.

**A day of Brahma (kalpa)**
In Hindu cosmology, a single day of Brahma, called a kalpa, lasts 4.32 billion human years. The universe is created at the start of each of his days and dissolved at its end.

**Demons born from his thigh**
In one myth, Brahma created the asuras (demons) from his thigh. He is credited with creating all beings, gods and demons alike.

**Rajas guna**
Of the three gunas (qualities of nature), Brahma is associated with rajas, the quality of activity and passion, which suits his role as creator. Vishnu is associated with sattva (goodness) and Shiva with tamas (darkness or inertia).

**Brahmapura on Mount Meru**
Brahma's city, Brahmapura, sits atop Mount Meru, the sacred mountain at the center of the universe in Hindu cosmology.

**Cattle Raid of Cooley (Táin Bó Cúailnge)**
The central epic of Ireland's Ulster Cycle, in which Queen Medb (Maeve) of Connacht invades Ulster to steal the great brown bull Donn Cuailnge. Because the men of Ulster are disabled by a curse, the teenage Cu Chulainn defends the province almost single-handedly, fighting Medb's champions one at a time in single combat at fords.

**Gae Bulg (Gae Bolg)**
Cu Chulainn's deadly barbed spear, given to him by the warrior-woman Scathach. It was made from the bone of a sea monster (named Curruid or Coinchenn in different sources) that died fighting another sea monster; it is described as having many barbs (thirty, or forty-nine, or seven points) that open inside the victim's body and cannot be removed without killing him.

**Connla (son by Aife)**
Cu Chulainn's son by Aife, the warrior-woman he defeated while training in Scotland. Cu Chulainn told Aife to instruct the boy never to reveal his name; when Connla later came to Ireland and refused to identify himself, Cu Chulainn killed him with the Gae Bulg, recognizing him only by the gold thumb-ring he had left for him.

**Scathach**
The warrior-woman of Scotland (on the Isle of Skye in later tradition) who trained Cu Chulainn in the arts of war, including the use of the Gae Bulg. Her sister and rival was Aife, whom Cu Chulainn defeated and with whom he fathered Connla.

**Hound of Culann (Setanta)**
Cu Chulainn's birth name was Setanta. As a boy arriving late to a feast held by the smith Culann for King Conchobar, he killed Culann's fierce guard dog by driving a hurling ball down its throat; he then offered to serve as Culann's guard dog until a replacement could be raised, earning the name Cu Chulainn, "Hound of Culann."

**Eating dog meat (breaking his geis)**
Cu Chulainn was bound by two taboos (geasa): never to eat dog meat (because of his name) and never to refuse hospitality. When an old woman (or old crone/hag in disguise) offered him dog meat, he had to break one, and eating it weakened him just before his final battle.

**Tied to a standing stone / the Morrigan as a crow**
Mortally wounded by Lugaid's spear, Cu Chulainn tied himself upright to a standing stone (pillar) with his belt so he could die on his feet facing his enemies. His foes dared not approach until the war goddess Morrigan, in the form of a crow or raven, landed on his shoulder, showing he was dead.

**Sword cuts off Lugaid's hand**
After Cu Chulainn died, his killer Lugaid came to behead him and take his sword, but the sword fell from the dead hero's hand and cut off Lugaid's hand. Lugaid's three magic spears had earlier killed Cu Chulainn's charioteer Laeg, his horse Liath Macha, and finally Cu Chulainn himself.

**Rejecting the Morrigan**
The triune war goddess Morrigan appeared to Cu Chulainn in disguise (as a beautiful young woman) and offered him her love, which he rejected. She then attacked him in animal forms during his fights at the fords, and she later appears as the crow at his death.

**Ferdiad**
Cu Chulainn's foster-brother and best friend, who had trained with him under Scathach. Medb pressured Ferdiad into fighting him at a ford during the Cattle Raid, and after a three-day duel Cu Chulainn killed him with the Gae Bulg and mourned him bitterly.

**Emer and Forgall Monach**
Emer was Cu Chulainn's wife. Her father Forgall Monach opposed the match and sent Cu Chulainn off to train with Scathach in hopes he would die; on his return Cu Chulainn stormed Forgall's fortress to win her. Emer's jealousy over the fairy woman Fand was ended when the sea god Manannan mac Lir shook his magic cloak between Cu Chulainn and Fand so they would never meet again.

**Warp spasm (ríastrad) and salmon leap**
In battle Cu Chulainn underwent the "warp spasm," a monstrous battle frenzy in which his body twisted and distorted and he killed indiscriminately. After one such frenzy as a youth, the women of Ulster bared their breasts; he looked away in embarrassment and was plunged into three tubs of cold water to cool him down. The "salmon leap" was one of the feats he learned from Scathach.

**Beheading game at Bricriu's Feast**
At Bricriu's Feast, Cu Chulainn competed for the "champion's portion" against other Ulster heroes. Only he kept his bargain to let a giant (Cu Roi in disguise) take an axe to his neck after beheading him, and he was spared and named champion; this episode parallels Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.

**Son of Lugh**
Cu Chulainn was conceived through the god Lugh, the Irish god of light and skill, and is sometimes considered his incarnation; his mortal mother was Deichtine, sister of King Conchobar. His conception story involves a baby, born the same night as two foals (colts), who died before Deichtine conceived Setanta.

**Derbforgaill and the 150 women**
Derbforgaill came to Cu Chulainn in the form of a swan, and he wounded her with his sling; because he sucked the stone out of her wound and tasted her blood, he could not marry her. When she later won a urination contest, the jealous women of Ulster mutilated her and she died, so Cu Chulainn destroyed their house and killed all 150 of them.

**Penelope, Telemachus, and the suitors**
Odysseus's faithful wife Penelope and his son Telemachus wait for him in Ithaca while over a hundred suitors (108 in one count) occupy his palace. On his return he and Telemachus slaughter the suitors, and the twelve disloyal maids who slept with them are hanged. Penelope stalls the suitors by promising to remarry once she finishes weaving a burial shroud for Odysseus's father Laertes, secretly unraveling each day's work at night.

**Calypso**
The nymph who holds Odysseus captive on her island of Ogygia for about seven or eight years, offering him immortality if he stays. She lets him go only after Hermes brings Zeus's order to release him.

**Circe and moly**
On the island of Aeaea the witch Circe turns Odysseus's men into pigs. Hermes gives Odysseus the magic herb moly, which protects him from her spells, and Circe later advises him on his route, including the warning about Helios's cattle.

**Cattle of Helios**
Sacred cattle of the sun god on the island of Thrinacia. Both Tiresias and Circe warn Odysseus not to harm them, but his starving crew slaughters them, and Zeus destroys their ship in a storm, leaving Odysseus as the sole survivor.

**The bed built from a living olive tree**
Odysseus built his marriage bed around the trunk of an olive tree growing in his palace courtyard, so it cannot be moved. When Penelope tests him by asking a servant to move the bed, his angry explanation of this secret proves his identity to her.

**Shooting an arrow through twelve axes**
The contest Penelope sets for her suitors: string Odysseus's great bow and shoot an arrow through the holes of twelve axe heads lined up in a row. Only the disguised Odysseus succeeds, and he then turns the bow on the suitors.

**Polyphemus and "Nobody"**
The cyclops son of Poseidon who traps Odysseus and his men in his cave and eats several of them. Odysseus gets him drunk, tells him his name is "Nobody" (or "No man"), and blinds him with a sharpened stake, so when Polyphemus cries that "Nobody" is hurting him, the other cyclopes do not come to help. The blinding earns Odysseus Poseidon's lasting anger.

**Argos (Argus)**
Odysseus's old dog, neglected and lying on a dung heap. He recognizes his master through his beggar's disguise after twenty years, wags his tail, and dies.

**Eurycleia and the scar**
Odysseus's old nurse recognizes him while washing the disguised beggar's feet when she sees the scar on his thigh, which he got from a boar hunt as a young man while visiting his grandfather Autolycus.

**Nausicaa, Alcinous, and Arete**
After being shipwrecked on Scheria, the island of the Phaeacians, Odysseus is found by the princess Nausicaa while she washes clothes by the shore. He wins the help of her parents, King Alcinous and Queen Arete (he clasps Arete's knees as a suppliant), and tells them the story of his wanderings at their court.

**The Sirens, Scylla, and Charybdis**
Odysseus has his crew plug their ears with beeswax and tie him to the mast so he can hear the Sirens' song without wrecking the ship. He then sails between Scylla, a six-headed monster that snatches six of his men, and Charybdis, a ship-swallowing whirlpool.

**Laestrygonians, Lotus-Eaters, and Cicones**
Other stops on his voyage. At Ismarus his men sack the city of the Cicones (sparing Maron, a priest of Apollo, who gives them strong wine) but are routed by a counterattack; the Lotus-Eaters' fruit makes some crewmen forget home; and the cannibal Laestrygonians crush all of his ships except his own with boulders.

**Irus, Eurymachus, and Antinous**
Figures in the palace while Odysseus is disguised as a beggar. He beats the rival beggar Irus in a boxing match, and the suitors insult him: Antinous throws a footstool at him and Eurymachus later throws one too. Antinous is the first suitor Odysseus kills, and Eurymachus is soon after.

**Trojan War exploits: Skyros, the Palladium, and Ajax**
Odysseus is the cleverest Greek at Troy. He exposes Achilles, who is disguised as a girl on Skyros, steals the Palladium statue from Troy with Diomedes, and beats Ajax in a speech contest for Achilles's armor, which drives Ajax to suicide. He also thinks up the Trojan Horse.

**Tennyson's "Ulysses" and Kazantzakis's sequel**
In Tennyson's dramatic monologue "Ulysses," the aging king complains that he must "mete and dole / Unequal laws unto a savage race" and decides to sail out again, "to strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield." Nikos Kazantzakis's epic The Odyssey: A Modern Sequel follows him on new journeys that end with his death among the ice near the South Pole.

**Bhagavad Gita**
The section of the Mahabharata in which Krishna, serving as Arjuna's charioteer on the battlefield of Kurukshetra, counsels him when he despairs at having to fight his own relatives and teachers. Krishna teaches him about duty (dharma), selfless action, and devotion, and reveals his divine cosmic form.

**Winning Draupadi at the svayamvara**
Disguised as a Brahmin during the Pandavas' exile, Arjuna won the princess Draupadi at a svayamvara (a ceremony where a bride chooses among suitors) by stringing a massive bow and hitting a revolving target. When the brothers returned home, their mother Kunti, not seeing the prize, told them to share it, so Draupadi became the wife of all five Pandavas.

**Killing Karna**
Karna, the great archer fighting for the Kauravas, was Arjuna's chief rival and secretly his elder half-brother. During their duel at Kurukshetra, Karna's chariot wheel sank into the earth, and Arjuna killed him on Krishna's urging.

**The parrot's eye**
The teacher Drona tested his students by having them aim at a wooden bird in a tree and asking what they saw. The others described the tree, the branches, or the whole bird, but Arjuna replied that he saw only the bird's eye, showing his perfect concentration, and Drona let only him shoot.

**Defeating Bhishma**
During the Kurukshetra war, Arjuna brought down the Kaurava commander Bhishma, his great-uncle, by shooting from behind Shikhandi, whom Bhishma refused to fight. Bhishma fell onto a bed of arrows, where he lay immobile until he chose to die.

**Sitting at the foot of Krishna's bed**
Before the war, Arjuna and Duryodhana both went to ask the sleeping Krishna for help; Duryodhana sat at the head of the bed and Arjuna at its foot. Since Krishna saw Arjuna first when he woke, Arjuna got first choice, and he chose the unarmed Krishna himself over Krishna's army.

**Year in disguise at King Virata's court**
During the Pandavas' final year of exile, which they had to spend unrecognized, Arjuna lived at King Virata's court disguised as a eunuch dance teacher named Brihannala. When the Kauravas raided Virata's cattle, he revealed his identity to Prince Uttara, protected him, and defeated the Kaurava army.

**Abhimanyu**
Arjuna's son by Subhadra, Krishna's sister. After the Virata episode, Abhimanyu married Virata's daughter Uttara; he was later killed during the war after entering the chakravyuha formation, which he knew how to enter but not how to leave.

**Third of the Pandavas**
Arjuna is the third of the five Pandava brothers and the third son of Kunti, born after Yudhishthira and Bhima. He was fathered by the god Indra and is considered the greatest archer of his age.

**Gandiva**
Arjuna's divine bow, which he received from the fire god Agni. He used it throughout the Kurukshetra war, earning him the epithet Gandivadhari ("bearer of Gandiva").

**Hou Yi shoots down nine of the ten suns**
In Chinese myth, ten suns (sons of the sun goddess Xihe) once rose together and scorched the earth. The archer Yi (Hou Yi) shot down nine of them, leaving one sun, and was rewarded with an elixir or pill of immortality.

**Chang'e, the moon goddess**
Yi's wife, who swallowed his pill of immortality and floated up to the moon, where she lives with a Jade Rabbit as her companion. She is honored during the Mid-Autumn Festival, when people eat mooncakes and admire the full moon.

**The Jade Emperor and the Great Race (zodiac)**
The Jade Emperor, ruler of heaven and head of the celestial bureaucracy, held a race among the animals to set the order of the twelve-year zodiac. The clever Rat rode across the river on the Ox's back and jumped ahead to finish first, followed by the Ox; the Pig came last. The cycle includes the Rabbit (2023) and the Dragon.

**The Cowherd and the Weaver Girl**
One of the "Four Great Folktales." The cowherd Niulang hides the clothes of seven bathing fairies and marries the weaver Zhinü, but her mother, the Queen Mother of the West, separates them with the Milky Way. Niulang follows her into the sky wearing his ox's hide, and the lovers became the stars Altair and Vega. Each year on the seventh day of the seventh month (Qixi), a bridge of magpies lets them meet.

**Pangu and the cosmic egg**
In the Chinese creation myth, the hairy, horned giant Pangu grew inside a black cosmic egg for 18,000 years, then broke it open and separated heaven (yang) from earth (yin). He pushed them apart, growing ten feet taller each day for another 18,000 years, and when he died his body became the features of the world.

**Nüwa**
A goddess with a serpent's lower body who created humanity by shaping people from yellow clay. After the sky was damaged, she repaired it with five-colored stones and cut the legs off a giant turtle to replace the pillars holding up the heavens.

**Gonggong smashes Mount Buzhou**
The water god Gonggong, angry after losing a battle, rammed his head into Mount Buzhou, one of the pillars holding up the sky. This tilted the heavens and earth and caused floods and disaster, which Nüwa then repaired.

**The Four Great Folktales**
Besides the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl, these are: Lady Meng Jiang, whose weeping for her husband, who died building it, made part of the Great Wall collapse; the Butterfly Lovers, Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai, who turn into butterflies after death; and the Legend of the White Snake, about a snake spirit who gains magical powers and human form and falls in love with a man.

**Nian**
A beast that attacked villages at the start of the new year. It feared the color red, loud noises, and fire, which is said to explain the red decorations and firecrackers of Lunar New Year, a festival that also features dragon and lion dances.

**Sun Wukong, the Monkey King**
The mischievous monkey hero born from a stone, best known from the novel Journey to the West. He rebels against the Jade Emperor and wreaks havoc in heaven before being imprisoned under a mountain by the Buddha, and later escorts the monk Tang Sanzang to India.

**Gun and the swelling earth (xirang)**
When a great flood covered the land, the Four Mountains (the emperor Yao's advisers) chose Gun to stop it. He stole xirang, a self-expanding magical soil, from heaven to dam the waters, and was executed for it; his son Yu the Great later controlled the flood and founded the Xia dynasty.

**The Eight Immortals**
A group of Daoist immortals, each with a special emblem. One of them, Li Tieguai, is a lame, deformed beggar who walks with an iron crutch and carries a gourd (calabash) that releases vapor or holds medicine.

**Guardian lions**
Stone lion statues placed in pairs at the gates of palaces, temples, and homes to give protection. The male usually rests a paw on a ball (representing the world), and the female holds a cub.

**The Yellow Emperor and the Three Pure Ones**
The Yellow Emperor (Huangdi) is a legendary sage-ruler and culture hero regarded as the ancestor of the Chinese people. The Three Pure Ones are the highest deities of Daoism, the religion into which much of Chinese mythology was absorbed.

**Utgard-Loki's cat**
During Thor's visit to the giant king Utgard-Loki, Thor was challenged to lift a huge gray cat but could raise only one of its paws off the ground. Utgard-Loki later revealed that the cat was the Midgard Serpent in disguise, and that the gods had been terrified when Thor lifted it even that far.

**Thor's fishing trip with Hymir**
Thor went fishing with the giant Hymir and hooked the serpent from the ocean floor. Just as Thor was about to strike it with his hammer, the frightened Hymir cut the fishing line (and, in some versions, Thor's grip), letting the serpent sink back into the sea.

**Ox-head bait (Himinhrjóðr)**
For the fishing trip, Thor tore the head off Hymir's largest ox, Himinhrjóðr ("Heaven-bellower" or "Sky-bellower"), and used it as bait for the serpent. The Ardre VIII picture stone may show this ox being killed.

**Nine steps at Ragnarok**
At Ragnarok, Thor and the serpent will kill each other. Thor will slay it with his hammer Mjölnir, then stagger nine steps before dying from the venom it spat at him.

**Wrapping around Midgard**
Jormungandr, the "World Serpent" or "Midgard Serpent," lies in the ocean that surrounds the human world, Midgard. It is so long that it encircles the earth and grasps its own tail, like an ouroboros.

**Children of Loki and Angrboda**
Jormungandr is one of three monstrous children of the trickster Loki and the giantess Angrboda. Its siblings are the wolf Fenrir and Hel, ruler of the dead.

**Thrown into the sea by Odin**
According to the Prose Edda, the gods feared Loki's monstrous children, so Odin threw the serpent into the ocean. There it grew until it surrounded the whole world.

**Altuna Runestone**
An 11th-century Swedish runestone that depicts Thor's fishing trip. Thor holds his hammer, and the serpent is on the line. Thor's foot breaks through the bottom of the boat, a detail from the myth in which he braced himself so hard that his feet went through the planks.

**Gosforth Cross and Hørdum Stone**
Other carved stones that depict the fishing trip. The Gosforth Cross is a 10th-century stone cross in Cumbria, England, and the Hørdum Stone is in Denmark. Like the Altuna Stone, the Hørdum Stone shows the god's foot pushing through the boat's planks.

**Ragnarsdrápa kenning**
Bragi Boddason's skaldic poem Ragnarsdrápa, one of the earliest surviving pieces of skaldic verse, describes Thor's fishing trip. It contains an early kenning for the serpent that can be translated literally as "string of the side-rowed ship's road" (that is, the cord that lies around the sea).

**Hymiskvida**
The Poetic Edda poem that tells of Thor's visit to Hymir to get a giant brewing cauldron, including the fishing expedition in which Thor hooks the serpent. It is a major source for the story along with Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda (Gylfaginning).

**Naglfar**
A ship made from the untrimmed fingernails and toenails of the dead, which carries the forces of the giants and the dead to the battle. Its completion signals the arrival of Ragnarok, which is why the dead were supposed to be buried with trimmed nails, to delay its construction.

**Fimbulwinter**
"The great winter," three consecutive winters with no summer between them that precede Ragnarok. It is a time of bitter cold, strife, and moral collapse, and it is said to follow the death of the god Baldr.

**Surtr and the sons of Muspell**
Surtr is the fire giant who leads the forces of Muspelheim, the realm of fire, into battle, wielding a sword that shines "brighter than the sun." At the end of the battle he sets fire to the whole world, consuming the world tree Yggdrasil.

**Lif and Lifthrasir**
The two humans who survive Ragnarok by hiding in the wood of Hoddmimir's Holt, living on the morning dew. They go on to repopulate the renewed world, which scholars such as Rudolf Simek connect with a cyclical view of the end of the world.

**Fenrir, Odin, and Vidar's shoe**
The monstrous wolf Fenrir, Loki's son, breaks free and swallows Odin, which is Frigg's "second sorrow" after Baldr's death. Odin's son Vidar avenges him by stepping into Fenrir's jaw with a thick shoe made from all the leather scraps ever cut from shoes and tearing the wolf apart; the Gosforth Cross in England is thought to show this scene. Vidar and his half-brother Vali survive Ragnarok.

**Thor's nine steps**
Thor fights the world serpent Jormungandr, another of Loki's children, and kills it with his hammer Mjolnir. He then walks nine steps before falling dead from the serpent's venom.

**Golden game pieces**
After Ragnarok, the surviving gods meet on the plain of Idavoll in a reborn, green world and find in the grass the golden game pieces (chess-like playing pieces) that the gods had once owned. In the Voluspa, the seeress (volva) sees the earth rise again from the sea, with an eagle hunting fish over a waterfall.

**Vigrid**
The vast plain, said to be a hundred leagues wide in each direction, where the final battle between the gods and their enemies takes place.

**Gjallarhorn and Bifrost**
Heimdall, the watchman of the gods, blows the Gjallarhorn to announce the start of Ragnarok and summon the gods to battle. The rainbow bridge Bifrost, which he guards, breaks under the forces of Muspell riding across it.

**Three roosters and Eggther**
The Voluspa says three roosters crow before Ragnarok: Fjalar in the giants' realm, Gullinkambi among the gods, and a soot-red rooster in the underworld of Hel. Meanwhile the giants' herdsman Eggther sits on a mound and joyfully plays his harp.

**Loki's escape**
Loki, bound after causing Baldr's death, breaks free at Ragnarok and leads the forces of Hel and the giants against the gods. He and Heimdall kill each other in the battle.

**Skoll and Hati**
Two wolves that chase the sun and the moon across the sky. At Ragnarok they finally catch and devour them, plunging the world into darkness.

**Freyr without his sword**
The god Freyr had given away his magic sword to his servant Skirnir in exchange for winning the giantess Gerd. Without it, he fights Surtr with only an antler and is killed.

**Garm and Tyr**
The monstrous hound Garm, which guards the gates of Hel, breaks loose at Ragnarok. He and the one-handed war god Tyr kill each other.

**Gimli and Sindri**
Halls where the righteous will live after Ragnarok. Gimli is a hall roofed with gold, brighter than the sun, and Sindri is a hall of red gold in the mountains.

**Daphne and the laurel tree**
A nymph whom Apollo pursued after Eros struck him with a golden arrow and her with a lead one. To escape him, she prayed to her father, the river god Peneus, who turned her into a laurel tree; Apollo then made the laurel wreath his sacred symbol and an emblem of victory.

**Python and Delphi**
Apollo slew the giant serpent Python, which had pursued his mother Leto, at Delphi near the Castalian Spring, earning the epithet Pythius. He then took over the site as his oracle, where his priestess, the Pythia, delivered prophecies, possibly aided by intoxicating fumes.

**Niobe's children**
Niobe, queen of Thebes, boasted that her fourteen children made her superior to Leto, who had only two. In revenge, Apollo shot her seven sons and Artemis her seven daughters, and the grieving Niobe was turned to stone.

**Hyacinthus**
A Spartan youth beloved by Apollo. While the two were throwing the discus, the jealous west wind Zephyrus (also in love with the boy) blew Apollo's discus into Hyacinthus's head, killing him; Apollo turned his blood into the hyacinth flower.

**Coronis and Asclepius**
Coronis, pregnant with Apollo's son, had an affair with the mortal Ischys. A bird (a crow or raven), formerly white, reported the affair, and Apollo turned it black; Coronis was killed by Artemis or Apollo, but Apollo saved the unborn Asclepius, who became a great healer. When Zeus struck Asclepius down with a thunderbolt for raising the dead (such as Hippolytus), Apollo killed the Cyclopes who forged Zeus's thunderbolts.

**Admetus**
As punishment for killing the Cyclopes, Apollo had to serve the Thessalian king Admetus as a herdsman for a year. Apollo helped him win Alcestis by yoking a lion and a boar to a chariot, as her father Pelias demanded, and he got the Fates drunk so they would let someone else die in Admetus's place.

**Marsyas**
A satyr who challenged Apollo to a musical contest, playing the aulos (double flute) against Apollo's lyre. After Apollo won, he had Marsyas flayed alive for his presumption.

**Leto and Delos**
Apollo is the son of Zeus and the Titaness Leto and the twin brother of Artemis. Because the jealous Hera forbade any land to receive Leto, she gave birth on the floating island of Delos.

**Tityos**
A giant who tried to rape Leto, sent by Hera in some versions. Apollo and Artemis shot him down, and in the underworld he was punished by having vultures eat his liver.

**Cassandra**
A Trojan princess, daughter of Priam, to whom Apollo gave the gift of prophecy in an attempt to win her love. When she refused him, he cursed her so that no one would ever believe her prophecies.

**Midas and Pan**
In a musical contest between Apollo and Pan, the mountain god Tmolus judged Apollo the winner. When King Midas disagreed and favored Pan, Apollo gave him the ears of a donkey.

**Lyre from Hermes**
The infant Hermes stole Apollo's cattle and invented the lyre from a tortoise shell. To make peace, Hermes gave Apollo the lyre, which became Apollo's signature instrument, and Apollo let Hermes keep the cattle.

**Aristaeus and Cyrene**
Apollo fathered the minor god Aristaeus, patron of beekeeping and herding, with the huntress nymph Cyrene, whom he saw wrestling a lion and carried off to Libya.

**Cyparissus**
A youth beloved by Apollo who accidentally killed his beloved tame stag. He was so grief-stricken that he asked to mourn forever and was turned into the cypress tree, a symbol of mourning.

**Plague arrows in the Iliad**
In Book I of the Iliad, Apollo shoots plague arrows at the Greek camp because Agamemnon dishonored his priest Chryses by refusing to return his daughter Chryseis. Apollo also sides with the Trojans throughout the poem, for example rescuing Aeneas from Diomedes.

**Apep (Apophis), the serpent of chaos**
Ra's archenemy is Apep, a giant serpent of chaos and darkness who lives in the underworld. Every night Apep tries to stop or swallow Ra's boat, sometimes with a hypnotic gaze, and Ra must defeat him so the sun can rise again. Ra is defended by Set, who stands at the prow of the boat and spears the serpent, and by the coiled protector serpent Mehen. In one form, the "Great Cat" of Heliopolis, Ra himself cuts off Apep's head.

**The solar barque: Mandjet and Mesektet**
Ra sails across the sky by day in a boat called the Mandjet ("Boat of Millions of Years"). At sunset he moves into the night boat, the Mesektet, and travels through the Duat (underworld) during the twelve hours of night, rising again in the east each morning.

**Isis learns Ra's secret name**
Ra kept a secret true name that held his power. When he grew old and drooled, Isis mixed his saliva with earth (clay) to make a poisonous snake, which bit him. Only she could cure the poison, and she agreed to do it only if he told her his secret name. With that name she gained great magical power, which she used to benefit her son Horus.

**Sekhmet and the red beer (the Destruction of Mankind)**
In the Book of the Heavenly Cow, humans plotted against the aging Ra, and he sent his Eye, in the form of the goddess Hathor turned into the bloodthirsty lioness Sekhmet, to slaughter them. When he changed his mind, he had seven thousand jars of beer dyed red with ochre (in some versions pomegranate juice) and poured over the fields. Sekhmet drank it, thinking it was blood, became drunk, and stopped, and she became the gentle goddess Hathor again. Ra then withdrew into the sky on the back of the cow goddess Nut, who was held up by Shu and eight Heh gods (the "Infinite Ones").

**The Eye of Ra**
The Eye of Ra is an independent goddess, his violent, protective power, who can take the form of Hathor, Sekhmet, Bastet, Tefnut, or Wadjet. In the myth of the Distant Goddess she leaves Egypt in anger and is coaxed home, in one Demotic version by a baboon telling her fables, including the mouse and the lion. She also appears as the uraeus, the rearing cobra coiled around the sun disk on Ra's head.

**Khepri, Ra, and Atum (Khnum): forms through the day**
Ra appears in different forms during the day. Khepri, a scarab beetle rolling the sun disk the way a dung beetle rolls a ball of dung, is the morning sun. Ra is the sun at midday. Atum, or the ram-headed Khnum, is the sun in the evening as it sinks in the west. Ra is often merged with Atum as Atum-Ra.

**Heliopolis, the Mnevis bull, and the Bennu bird**
Ra's main cult center was Heliopolis (Iunu), home of the Ished tree, a sacred tree of life. The black Mnevis bull worshipped there was considered his living embodiment, and his soul (ba) was linked with the Bennu, a heron-like bird that inspired the Greek phoenix.

**Amun-Ra and Ra-Horakhty**
Ra was merged with many other gods. During the New Kingdom, the Theban god Amun was fused with him as Amun-Ra, king of the gods. Ra-Horakhty ("Ra-Horus of the Two Horizons") combined him with Horus, which is why Ra is usually shown as falcon-headed. The pharaoh Akhenaten pushed aside these cults in favor of the worship of the sun disk, the Aten.

**Nut forbidden to give birth and the five extra days**
Ra forbade the sky goddess Nut from giving birth on any day of the 360-day year. Thoth gambled with the moon god Khonsu (in some versions playing senet) and won enough moonlight to create five extra (epagomenal) days, on which Nut gave birth to Osiris, Isis, Set, Nephthys, and in some lists Horus the Elder.

**Shu and Tefnut, born from spit or a sneeze**
As creator, Ra (as Atum-Ra) produced his first children, Shu (god of air, whose name means "emptiness") and Tefnut (goddess of moisture), by spitting or sneezing them out. They gave birth to Geb (earth) and Nut (sky), making Ra the grandfather of Geb and Nut and the ancestor of the whole Ennead, the nine gods of Heliopolis. In one story he grieved when Shu and Tefnut went missing.

**Humans created from his tears**
Humans were said to have been created from the tears (and sometimes sweat) of Ra; Egyptian words for "tears" and "people" sound alike. Humans were called "the cattle of Ra."

**Rising from the primeval waters of Nun**
In Heliopolitan creation myths, Ra appeared from Nun (Nu), the dark primeval waters of chaos, either on the first mound of land (the benben) or blossoming out of a blue lotus flower. Nun also sometimes acts as his adviser.

**Hathor dances to cheer him up**
In the Contendings of Horus and Seth, Ra was insulted and lay down sulking. His daughter Hathor danced naked (or exposed herself) in front of him and made him laugh, which cheered him up so he returned to judging the case. Ra is also called the father of Ma'at, whose feather is weighed against the hearts of the dead.

**Falcon head, sun disk, and the "Son of Ra"**
Ra is usually shown as a falcon-headed man wearing a sun disk circled by a uraeus cobra. Egyptian pharaohs claimed to be his descendants, and "Son of Ra" became one of the standard royal titles.

**Amaterasu hiding in the cave**
Amaterasu, the Shinto sun goddess, retreated into the Heavenly Rock Cave (Ama-no-Iwato) after her storm-god brother Susanoo wrecked her rice fields and threw a flayed horse into her weaving hall, killing one of her weaving maidens. The world went dark until the goddess Ame-no-Uzume danced on an overturned tub, making the gods laugh, and Amaterasu peeked out and was drawn out by her own reflection in a mirror.

**Amaterasu's birth, regalia, and shrine**
Amaterasu was born from the left eye of Izanagi as he purified himself after visiting the underworld. She sent her grandson Ninigi to rule Japan with the three imperial regalia (a jewel, a sword, and a mirror), and she is worshipped at the Ise Grand Shrine; the red sun on the flag of Japan reflects her importance.

**Hou Yi shooting down nine suns**
In Chinese myth, the goddess Xihe bore ten suns, which lived in a mulberry tree and took turns crossing the sky. When all ten rose at once and scorched the earth, the archer Hou Yi shot down nine, leaving one, and was rewarded with an elixir of immortality.

**The three-legged crow**
In East Asian folklore, the sun is inhabited or represented by a three-legged crow, sometimes called Yangwu or Sanzuwu. The ten suns of Xihe are often depicted as such crows.

**The Aztec Five Suns**
The Aztecs believed the world had passed through four earlier ages, or "suns," each destroyed: the first when Tezcatlipoca's sun was struck down with a stone club and jaguars devoured humanity, the second when hurricanes blew humans away and turned them into monkeys, the third by Tlaloc's rain of fire, and the fourth by Chalchiuhtlicue's flood. The current world is the Fifth Sun, Nahui Ollin ("4 Movement"), destined to end in earthquakes.

**Nanahuatzin and Tecciztecatl**
When the gods gathered at Teotihuacan to create a new sun, the proud Tecciztecatl was too frightened to leap into the sacrificial bonfire. The humble, sore-covered Nanahuatzin jumped in first and became the sun, and Tecciztecatl followed and became the moon.

**The Aztec Sun Stone and Tonatiuh**
The Aztec Sun Stone, a giant carved basalt disc often called the Aztec calendar stone, has the face of the sun god Tonatiuh at its center with his tongue protruding, surrounded by the glyph for "Movement" and symbols of the previous suns. Warriors who died in battle were thought to accompany Tonatiuh across the sky, and women who died in childbirth (the cihuateteo) escorted him as he set in the west.

**Huitzilopochtli and human sacrifice**
Huitzilopochtli, the Aztec war god often represented as a hummingbird, was associated with the sun. The Aztecs offered human hearts and blood to nourish the sun so that it would keep moving and not go dark.

**Ra's solar barge and Apep**
The Egyptian sun god Ra crossed the sky by day in a boat and journeyed through the underworld (the Duat) by night in his night barge, a journey depicted hour by hour in the Amduat. Each night he and his defenders, including the serpent Mehen, fought the chaos serpent Apep (Apophis), and at dawn he was reborn in the east as Khepri, the scarab beetle shown pushing the sun disk.

**Ra's secret name**
The goddess Isis made a poisonous snake from Ra's spittle and had it bite him. She would only cure him when he revealed his secret name to her, which gave her great power.

**Surya, Kunti, and Karna**
Surya is the Hindu sun god, who drives a chariot driven by his charioteer Aruna and is celebrated at the Sun Temple of Konark. Kunti used a mantra given to her by the sage Durvasa to summon Surya, who fathered Karna, born with earrings and invulnerable armor, and then restored her virginity; Surya is also counted among the Adityas, sons of Aditi that include Mitra, cognate with the Iranian Mithra.

**Hanuman trying to eat the sun**
As a child, the monkey god Hanuman mistook the rising sun for a ripe fruit, such as a mango, and leapt into the sky to eat it. Indra struck him on the jaw with his thunderbolt (vajra), which gave Hanuman his name, meaning "having a damaged jaw."

**Helios and Phaethon**
The Greek sun god Helios drove a chariot pulled by horses across the sky each day. His son Phaethon begged to drive it, lost control, and scorched the earth (which was said to have turned the Ethiopians' skin dark), until Zeus struck him down with a thunderbolt and he fell into the river Eridanus; his grieving sisters, the Heliades, were turned into poplar trees. Helios also lent Heracles the golden cup in which he sailed back east each night, so Heracles could cross the ocean.

**Sol and the Norse sun**
In Norse myth, the sun goddess Sol (Sunna) is the daughter of Mundilfari, sister of the moon Mani, and wife of Glenr. She drives the sun's chariot pulled by the horses Arvakr and Alsvidr, shielded from the sun's heat by the shield Svalinn, while the wolf Skoll chases her. "Alfrodull" ("elf-disc") is a kenning for the sun, and the Danish Bronze Age Trundholm sun chariot depicts a horse pulling a gilded sun disk.

**Inti and the Inca**
Inti was the Inca sun god, son of the creator Viracocha, worshipped at the Coricancha temple in Cusco and in the Inti Raymi festival. Carved stones called intihuatanas ("hitching posts of the sun") were thought to tie the sun in place, as at Machu Picchu, where the Torreon is also thought to be a sun temple.

**Temple doors open in war, closed in peace**
The gates of the shrine of Janus in the Roman Forum (the Janus Geminus) were kept open whenever Rome was at war and closed only in times of peace. Because Rome was almost always fighting somewhere, the doors were rarely shut; the shrine was traditionally said to have been built by King Numa Pompilius.

**Two faces**
Janus is shown with two faces looking in opposite directions, one toward the past and one toward the future. This fits his role as the god of beginnings, endings, transitions, gates and doorways.

**Namesake of January**
The first month of the Roman year, Ianuarius (January), is named after Janus as the god of beginnings.

**Hot springs against the Sabines**
When the Sabines under Titus Tatius attacked Rome to avenge the abduction of the Sabine women, the traitor Tarpeia had let them into the citadel. Janus made a jet of boiling, sulfurous water burst from the ground at a gate, driving the invaders back, and one explanation for keeping his temple open in wartime was so he could come out to help Rome again.

**Carna and Cardea**
The nymph Carna (called Crane in Ovid) tricked her suitors by sending them into a cave and running away. Janus, who could see behind him, caught her; afterwards he made her Cardea, goddess of door hinges, and gave her a hawthorn branch to keep evil away from doorways.

**Sheltering Saturn in Latium**
When Saturn was driven out of the heavens by Jupiter, Janus, then king of Latium, welcomed him. The two ruled together during the Golden Age, and Saturn taught the people agriculture.

**Camese (Camasene) and Tiberinus**
In one tradition Janus came to Latium from Thessaly and married Camese (Camasene), ruling the land with her. Their son Tiberinus drowned in the river Albula, which was renamed the Tiber after him.

**Juturna and Fontus**
Janus was also called the husband of the water nymph Juturna, and their son was Fontus (Fons), the god of springs and wells. Juturna had earlier been one of Jupiter's lovers, an affair the nymph Lara revealed to Juno.

**Ovid's Fasti, Book 1**
Ovid's unfinished poem on the Roman calendar opens with an interview with Janus himself. He explains his two faces, why he receives the first offerings of incense and wine, why one side of the bronze as coin shows a ship, and the stories of Saturn and the Sabine attack.

**No Greek equivalent**
Unlike most major Roman gods, Janus has no counterpart in the Greek pantheon. The Etruscan god Culsans, a two-faced guardian of doorways, is often compared to him.

**First to be invoked in prayers**
In Roman ritual, Janus was called on first at the start of prayers and sacrifices, while Vesta was invoked last. He was also honored with the title "pater" (father), and the opening verses of the Carmen Saliare, the hymn of the Salian priests, were addressed to him.

**Key and staff**
Janus was often shown holding a key, as the god of doors, and a staff, the symbol of a doorkeeper or guide.

**Inventor of coins**
Janus was said to be the first to mint coins, and Roman bronze coins (the as) carried his two-faced head on one side and the prow of a ship on the other. He was also credited with teaching law and civilization.

**Epithets: Geminus, Matutinus, Consivius**
Janus had many surnames, including Geminus ("twin," for his double face), Matutinus (god of the morning) and Consivius ("the sower").

**Ianiculum and the Argiletum**
The Janiculum hill across the Tiber was said to be named after Janus, who ruled from a settlement there. His shrine in the Forum stood near the Argiletum, a street whose gate was linked to him.

**Stealing fire for humanity**
Prometheus's defining act. Against Zeus's wishes he steals fire from the gods and gives it to mortals, which is why he is seen as the great benefactor of humankind and why Zeus punishes him so harshly.

**Eagle eating his liver**
Zeus has Prometheus chained to a rock in the Caucasus Mountains, where an eagle (some sources say a vulture) comes every day to eat his liver, which grows back each night so the torment never ends.

**Heracles frees him**
Heracles (Hercules) eventually shoots the eagle and frees Prometheus from his chains. Some accounts place the rock on Mount Elbrus, the highest peak in the Caucasus.

**Trick at Mecone (the sacrifice trick)**
At Mecone Prometheus divides a slaughtered ox into two portions: the edible meat hidden inside the ox's unappetizing stomach (or hide), and the bare bones wrapped in shiny fat. Zeus chooses the fat-covered bones, which sets the precedent that humans burn the bones and fat for the gods and keep the meat for themselves. Hesiod tells the story in the Theogony.

**Deucalion, Pyrrha, and the flood**
Prometheus's son Deucalion and Deucalion's wife Pyrrha (daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora) survive the flood Zeus sends to end the Bronze Age, after Prometheus tells them to build a chest or ship. Afterward they repopulate the earth by throwing stones over their shoulders, which turn into people.

**Prometheus Bound**
A tragedy traditionally credited to Aeschylus. Hephaestus chains Prometheus to the rock while Kratos (Power) and Bia (Force) look on, and Kratos mocks him. A chorus of Oceanids visits him, he lists the arts and skills he gave humanity, and at the end Zeus blasts him into an abyss with a thunderbolt.

**Io**
The maiden whom Zeus turned into a heifer, chased across the world by a gadfly sent by Hera. In Prometheus Bound she visits the chained Titan, who prophesies that her suffering will end in Egypt, where she will regain her human form, and that Heracles will be one of her descendants.

**Epimetheus**
Prometheus's brother, whose name means "afterthought" or "hindsight" (Prometheus means "forethought"). Prometheus warns him not to accept gifts from Zeus, but Epimetheus marries Pandora anyway. In Plato's version, Epimetheus hands out all the good traits to the animals, leaving nothing for humans, so Prometheus has to steal fire to make up for it.

**Pandora**
The first woman, made by Hephaestus on Zeus's orders as punishment for Prometheus's theft of fire. She is given to Epimetheus and opens the jar (later called a box) that releases evils into the world.

**Thetis's son prophecy**
Prometheus knows the secret that the sea nymph Thetis will bear a son greater than his father. By revealing it, he warns Zeus not to father a child with her, and in some versions this earns him his release. Thetis instead marries the mortal Peleus and gives birth to Achilles.

**Creating humans from clay**
In many traditions Prometheus shapes the first humans out of clay or earth, which makes him the creator as well as the protector of humankind.

**Fennel stalk**
In Hesiod, Prometheus smuggles the stolen fire to humans inside a hollow stalk of giant fennel. Some later versions say he lit it from the sun.

**Chiron's immortality**
After Heracles accidentally wounds the centaur Chiron with a poisoned arrow, Chiron, in unending pain, gives up his immortality in exchange for Prometheus's release, according to Apollodorus.

**Medea's Promethean herb**
In Apollonius of Rhodes's Argonautica, Medea gathers a flower that sprang from the blood (ichor) dripping from Prometheus's wounds in the Caucasus. She makes it into an ointment that makes Jason invulnerable for the trials set by King Aeetes.

**Son of Iapetus, ally of Zeus in the Titanomachy**
Prometheus is a Titan, the son of Iapetus and brother of Atlas and Epimetheus. Despite being a Titan, he sided with Zeus against the other Titans in the Titanomachy. In Athens he was honored with a torch race and worshipped alongside Hephaestus by craftsmen such as potters.

**Cadmus**
The Phoenician prince who founded Thebes in Boeotia while searching for his sister Europa, who had been abducted by Zeus. The Delphic oracle told him to follow a cow and found a city where it lay down to rest. He married the goddess Harmonia, and after eight years of servitude to Ares for killing his dragon, he and Harmonia were eventually turned into snakes.

**Dragon's teeth and the Spartoi**
Cadmus killed a dragon (or water serpent) sacred to Ares and, on Athena's advice, sowed its teeth in the ground. Fully armed warriors sprang up and fought one another until only five survived; these "Spartoi" ("sown men") became the ancestors of the Theban nobility.

**Oedipus**
The most famous king of Thebes. Unknowingly fulfilling a prophecy, he killed his father Laius at a crossroads and married his mother Jocasta; when the truth came out, he blinded himself. Sophocles' Oedipus Rex, Oedipus at Colonus, and Antigone are known as the Theban plays.

**Sphinx's riddle**
A monster with a woman's head and a lion's body that terrorized Thebes and killed those who could not answer its riddle about what walks on four legs, then two, then three. Oedipus answered "man," freeing the city and winning the throne and the widowed queen Jocasta as his reward.

**Seven Against Thebes**
After Oedipus's sons Eteocles and Polynices agreed to alternate ruling and Eteocles refused to give up the throne, Polynices and his father-in-law Adrastus, king of Argos, led seven champions against the city's seven gates. The brothers killed each other in single combat. The expedition is the subject of Aeschylus's play Seven Against Thebes and of Statius's epic Thebaid.

**Amphion and Zethus**
Twin sons of Zeus and Antiope who built the walls of Thebes. Amphion played his lyre so beautifully that the stones moved into place by themselves, while his brother Zethus hauled stones by brute strength. To avenge their mother, they tied their cruel aunt Dirce to the horns of a bull.

**Laius and Jocasta**
The king and queen of Thebes and parents of Oedipus. Warned that his son would kill him, Laius had the infant exposed, but Oedipus survived and later killed him. Jocasta married her son unknowingly and hanged herself when she learned the truth.

**Chrysippus**
A son of Pelops whom Laius abducted and raped while teaching him to drive a chariot. Pelops's curse on Laius for this crime was said to be the source of the misfortunes of Laius's family and of Thebes.

**Necklace of Harmonia**
A cursed necklace given to Harmonia, the first queen of Thebes, at her wedding to Cadmus; it brought disaster to everyone who owned it. Polynices used it to bribe Eriphyle into persuading her husband, the seer Amphiaraus, to join the Seven; Amphiaraus was swallowed by the earth with his chariot and charioteer, and his sons later killed Eriphyle.

**Tydeus and Melanippus**
Tydeus, one of the Seven and the father of Diomedes, was mortally wounded by the Theban defender Melanippus and in turn killed him. When Tydeus ate Melanippus's brains, a disgusted Athena withheld the immortality she had planned to give him.

**Epigoni**
The sons of the Seven, including Alcmaeon, Diomedes, and Thersander, who succeeded where their fathers had failed and sacked Thebes ten years later. The blind Theban prophet Tiresias died while fleeing the city during this attack.

**Niobe**
Queen of Thebes, daughter of Tantalus, and wife of Amphion. She boasted that her fourteen children made her greater than Leto, who had only two, so Leto's children Apollo and Artemis killed them all, and the grieving Niobe was turned to stone.

**Semele**
A Theban princess, daughter of Cadmus, and mother of Dionysus by Zeus. Tricked by the jealous Hera, she asked Zeus to show himself in his full divine form and was burned to death; Zeus saved the unborn Dionysus and sewed him into his thigh.

**Capaneus**
One of the Seven, who boasted that not even Zeus could stop him from burning Thebes. While scaling the city's walls, he was struck down by Zeus's thunderbolt.

**Creon, Antigone, and Menoeceus**
Creon ruled Thebes after the deaths of Eteocles and Polynices and forbade the burial of Polynices and the Argive attackers; Antigone defied him and buried her brother. During the siege, a prophecy said the city would be saved if Creon's son Menoeceus sacrificed himself, and he leapt from the walls.

**Cattle of Apollo**
On the very day he was born, the infant Hermes stole a herd of Apollo's sacred cattle. He drove them backward (pulling them by their tails) and wore specially woven sandals so that the reversed tracks would confuse anyone following him. This theft, told in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, made him the patron god of thieves.

**Tortoise-shell lyre**
