Hermes invented the first lyre by stringing cow-gut sinews across the shell of a tortoise. When Apollo discovered the cattle theft, Hermes appeased him by giving him the lyre, and Apollo let him keep the cattle in exchange; the lyre became Apollo's signature instrument.

**Caduceus**
Hermes' herald's staff, entwined with two snakes and often topped with wings. It is frequently contrasted with the Rod of Asclepius, the medical symbol, which has only one snake.

**Winged sandals and winged cap**
Hermes' signature accessories as the swift messenger of the gods; the sandals are called talaria and the cap is the petasos. He lent the winged sandals to Perseus for his quest to slay Medusa, and also directed Perseus to the Graeae.

**Moly**
A magical herb with a black root and white flower that Hermes gave to Odysseus in the Odyssey. It protected Odysseus from the sorceress Circe's potion, which had turned his men into pigs.

**Argus Panoptes / Argeiphontes**
At Zeus's command, Hermes lulled the hundred-eyed giant Argus to sleep (with music and stories) and then killed him, freeing Io, Zeus's lover, whom Hera had turned into a cow and set Argus to guard. This deed gave Hermes the epithet Argeiphontes, "slayer of Argus."

**Maia and Mount Cyllene**
Hermes is the son of Zeus and Maia, the eldest of the Pleiades and a daughter of Atlas, which makes Hermes a grandson of Atlas. He was born in a cave on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia, where he was also worshipped as a fertility god.

**Battus**
An old man who witnessed Hermes stealing Apollo's cattle. He promised to keep the secret but then revealed it when the disguised Hermes tested him with a bribe, so Hermes turned him to stone. In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Hermes similarly turned Aglauros to stone for demanding gold to let him see her sister Herse.

**Hermaphroditus and Salmacis**
Hermaphroditus was the son of Hermes and Aphrodite. The nymph Salmacis fell in love with him and, when he rejected her, prayed never to be separated from him, so the gods merged their bodies into one being with both male and female features.

**Pan and Dryope**
Hermes fathered the goat-legged god Pan, in one version with the nymph Dryope. She ran away screaming in horror when she saw the hairy, goat-like baby, but Hermes brought the infant to Olympus, where the gods delighted in him.

**Herms**
Square stone pillars topped with a bust of Hermes' head and bearing male genitalia on the shaft. They were set up as boundary markers, at crossroads and roadsides, and outside houses and gymnasia, reflecting Hermes' role as god of boundaries, travelers, and luck.

**Psychopomp**
Hermes served as "conductor of souls" (Psychopompos), guiding the dead to the underworld. In this role he also crossed the boundary of death in other myths, such as bringing the slain Protesilaus back from the dead for a short time.

**Calypso**
In the Odyssey, Zeus sent Hermes to Calypso's island of Ogygia to order the nymph to release Odysseus, whom she had held for seven years, so he could return home.

**Autolycus**
A son of Hermes known as a master thief and trickster, inheriting his father's cunning. Autolycus was the maternal grandfather of Odysseus, making Hermes Odysseus's great-grandfather.

**Hermes Trismegistus**
"Thrice-great Hermes," a figure formed by syncretizing Hermes with the Egyptian god of writing and wisdom, Thoth. The esoteric Hermetic tradition is based on mystical, alchemical, and philosophical texts attributed to him.

**Brisingamen and the four dwarves**
Freyja's famous golden necklace (sometimes called a torc or collar). According to the Sörla þáttr, she saw four dwarves forging it and agreed to spend a night with each of them in exchange for it.

**Folkvangr and Sessrumnir**
Folkvangr is Freyja's field or meadow in Asgard. Half of all warriors slain in battle go to her there, and she gets first choice of them, while the other half go to Odin's Valhalla. Her great hall there is Sessrumnir ("seat-room"), which shares its name with a ship and may itself be imagined as one.

**Thor disguised as Freyja (Thrymskvida)**
In the Eddic poem Thrymskvida, the giant Thrym steals Thor's hammer Mjolnir and demands Freyja as his bride in exchange. Freyja angrily refuses, so Thor dresses as her in bridal clothes and wears Brisingamen, with Loki disguised as his bridesmaid. At the wedding feast Thor eats an entire ox and eight salmon, then grabs the hammer and kills the giants.

**Chariot pulled by two cats**
Freyja rides in a chariot drawn by two cats, often described as blue or gray; some sources name them Bygul and Trjegul. One story says her husband brought them to her.

**Hildisvini and Ottar**
Freyja's boar, whose name means "battle swine," and which she rides. In the poem Hyndluljod it is her mortal lover and servant Ottar in disguise.

**Tears of red gold for Odr**
Freyja's husband Odr (Od or Odur) often leaves on long journeys, and while he is gone she weeps tears of red gold (in some accounts amber). She wanders the world searching for him under different names.

**Falcon-feather cloak (Valshamr)**
Freyja owns a cloak of falcon feathers that lets the wearer turn into a falcon and fly. Loki borrows it to fly to the giant Thjazi's hall and rescue the goddess Idunn, and again in Thrymskvida to search Jotunheim for Thor's stolen hammer.

**Hyndluljod (Lay of Hyndla)**
An Eddic poem in which Freyja visits the giantess and seeress Hyndla in her cave, rides with her to Valhalla (Hyndla rides a wolf), and makes her recite the ancestry of Ottar so he can win a bet about his lineage. When Hyndla refuses to give Ottar a memory ale so he can remember the genealogy, Freyja threatens her with fire and forces her to hand it over.

**Heimdall and Loki fight as seals**
Loki steals Brisingamen by turning into a flea (or a fly) to get into Freyja's locked chamber. Heimdall recovers the necklace by fighting Loki at the rock Singasteinn, with both gods in the form of seals.

**Seidr and the Vanir**
Freyja is a Vanir goddess, the daughter of the sea god Njord and the twin sister of Freyr. After the war between the Aesir and Vanir ended in a truce, she came to live among the Aesir as a hostage and taught them seidr, a form of magic concerned with seeing and shaping fate that was regarded as a women's art. The Heimskringla calls her a priestess of the sacrifices.

**Lokasenna**
An Eddic poem set at the sea giant Aegir's feast, where Loki insults all the gods in a flyting (an exchange of insults). He calls Freyja a harlot and accuses her of sleeping with every god and elf present, including her twin brother Freyr.

**Hnoss and Gersemi**
Freyja's two daughters by Odr. Both names mean "treasure," and they are so named because of their beauty.

**The giant builder of Asgard's wall**
A giant (a frost giant, or hrimthurs) offered to build a wall around Asgard and asked for Freyja, the sun, and the moon as payment. Loki sabotaged him by turning into a mare and luring away his stallion Svadilfari, and Thor killed the builder.

**Pouring ale for Hrungnir**
When the giant Hrungnir came to Asgard as a guest, Freyja alone dared to keep filling his drinking horn. Drunk, he boasted that he would carry off Freyja and Sif and destroy Asgard, which led to his duel with Thor, who killed him.

**Sörla þáttr and the endless battle of the Hjadnings**
In the Sörla þáttr, Odin makes Freyja start a never-ending war as the price for returning Brisingamen. The kings Hedin and Hogni, each with twenty subordinate kings, fight over and over, with the slain rising again to keep fighting, for 143 years until a Christian man in the service of King Olaf Tryggvason ends it.

**Dipped in the River Styx by Thetis (the heel)**
Achilles's mother, the sea nymph Thetis, dipped him as a baby in the River Styx to make him invulnerable, but the heel she held him by stayed dry and remained his one weak spot. In another version she put him in a fire, sometimes after anointing him with ambrosia, to burn away his mortal parts, but Peleus interrupted her. The phrase "Achilles' heel" comes from this story.

**Killed by Paris's arrow**
Achilles was killed when the Trojan prince Paris shot him in the heel (or ankle) with an arrow, which Apollo guided and which some accounts say was poisoned. In some versions this happened at the temple of Thymbraean Apollo, where Achilles had gone to meet the Trojan princess Polyxena, with whom he had fallen in love.

**Patroclus**
Achilles's closest friend (in some later readings, his lover). While Achilles refused to fight, Patroclus went into battle wearing Achilles's armor to rally the Greeks and was killed by Hector with help from Apollo. His death brought Achilles back into the war. After Achilles died, their ashes were mixed in a single urn.

**Killing Hector and dragging his body around Troy**
To avenge Patroclus, Achilles killed the Trojan champion Hector, after Athena tricked Hector into standing and fighting by appearing as his brother Deiphobus. Achilles then dragged Hector's corpse behind his chariot around the walls of Troy (three times in many accounts) and around Patroclus's tomb. In Book 24 of the Iliad, Priam, Hecuba's husband, sneaked into the Greek camp, kissed Achilles's hands, and ransomed the body for burial.

**Briseis and the quarrel with Agamemnon**
At the start of the Iliad, Agamemnon was forced to give back his captive Chryseis, daughter of a priest of Apollo, and took Achilles's captive concubine Briseis to replace her. Achilles withdrew from the fighting in anger. Even an embassy led by his old tutor Phoenix, who told him the cautionary story of Meleager and offered many gifts, could not bring him back.

**"Sing, goddess, the rage of Achilles"**
The opening line of Homer's Iliad, which names its subject as the wrath (menis) of Achilles, "son of Peleus." The poem covers a few weeks near the end of the Trojan War, from his quarrel with Agamemnon to Hector's funeral.

**Penthesilea and Thersites**
Achilles killed Penthesilea, the Amazon queen who fought for Troy, and fell in love with her as she died, or as he took off her helmet. When the ugly, foul-mouthed soldier Thersites mocked his grief (in some versions gouging out the dead queen's eyes), Achilles killed him with a blow.

**Shield of Achilles**
After Patroclus lost Achilles's armor to Hector, Thetis asked Hephaestus to forge new armor. Book 18 of the Iliad describes the shield in detail: the earth, sky, sea, sun, moon, and constellations (Pleiades, Hyades, Orion, and the Bear); a city at peace with a wedding and a lawsuit, and a city at war; plowing, harvesting, a vineyard, herds, and a dance, all surrounded by the stream of Ocean.

**Disguised as a girl at the court of Lycomedes on Skyros**
Knowing Achilles would die if he went to Troy, Thetis hid him dressed as a girl (sometimes called Pyrrha or Aissa) among the daughters of King Lycomedes on Skyros. Odysseus exposed him by offering gifts of jewelry with weapons hidden among them, sometimes adding a trumpet alarm, and Achilles grabbed the weapons.

**Deidamia and Neoptolemus**
While hiding on Skyros, Achilles fathered Neoptolemus (also called Pyrrhus) with Lycomedes's daughter Deidamia. The seer Helenus prophesied that the Greeks needed Neoptolemus to take Troy, and after Achilles died, his ghost demanded that Polyxena be sacrificed on his tomb.

**Contest between Ajax and Odysseus for his armor**
After Achilles died, Telamonian Ajax (Ajax the Greater) and Odysseus each claimed his divine armor. When it was awarded to Odysseus, Ajax went mad and killed himself.

**Fighting the river god Scamander**
In Book 21 of the Iliad, Achilles killed so many Trojans that their bodies choked the river Scamander (Xanthus). The angry river god rose up to drown him, and Hephaestus saved Achilles by driving back the river with fire.

**Memnon**
After the events of the Iliad, Achilles killed Memnon, the Ethiopian king and son of Eos (Dawn) and Tithonus, who had killed Nestor's son Antilochus while Antilochus was saving his father. Memnon's mourning followers were turned into birds (the Memnonides).

**Marriage of Peleus and Thetis and the prophecy**
Zeus and Poseidon both wanted Thetis until a prophecy (from Themis or Prometheus) warned that her son would be greater than his father. She was married instead to the mortal Peleus, who had to wrestle her while she changed shapes. At their wedding, Eris threw in the golden apple that led to the Judgment of Paris. Chiron gave Peleus an ash spear and Poseidon gave the immortal horses Balius and Xanthus, which Achilles later used at Troy.

**Telephus healed by his spear**
On the way to Troy, Achilles wounded Telephus, king of Mysia, with his spear. An oracle said only the weapon that caused the wound could heal it, so Telephus, in one version by threatening the infant Orestes, made the Greeks help him, and Achilles cured him with rust scraped from the spear. Achilles was raised and taught by the centaur Chiron, who made him a great runner, and his speed is the basis of Zeno's paradox of Achilles and the tortoise.

**Chiron**
The wise and civilized centaur who lived on Mount Pelion in Thessaly and tutored many Greek heroes, including Achilles, Jason, Asclepius, and Heracles, in medicine, music, archery, and hunting. He is the most famous centaur and the most common giveaway.

**Centauromachy with the Lapiths**
At the wedding of the Lapith king Pirithous and Hippodamia, the drunken centaurs, led by Eurytion (also called Eurytus), tried to carry off the bride and other women. This sparked a battle between the centaurs and the Lapiths, aided by Theseus, which became a famous subject of Greek art, including the Parthenon metopes.

**Ixion and Nephele**
Most centaurs descend from Ixion, a Thessalian king and in some accounts the first murderer of a relative, who tried to seduce Hera. Zeus fashioned a cloud, Nephele, in Hera's likeness, and from Ixion's union with it came the centaurs (or their ancestor Centaurus). Ixion was punished by being bound to a fiery wheel.

**Nessus and Deianira**
The centaur Nessus tried to rape Heracles's wife Deianira while ferrying her across a river, and Heracles shot him with an arrow poisoned by the Hydra's blood. The dying Nessus told Deianira to keep his blood as a love charm; she later smeared it on a robe for Heracles, and the poison killed him.

**Pholus and the jar of wine**
During his labor to capture the Erymanthian Boar, Heracles was entertained by the hospitable centaur Pholus, who served him cooked meat while eating his own raw. When Pholus opened a jar of sacred wine, the smell maddened the other centaurs, who attacked. Heracles drove them off with poisoned arrows, and Pholus died after accidentally dropping one of the arrows on his foot.

**Chiron gives up his immortality**
Chiron was wounded by one of Heracles's Hydra-poisoned arrows during the fight that followed Pholus's feast, and because he was immortal, he suffered endlessly from a wound he could not heal. He gave up his immortality in exchange for the release of Prometheus and was placed in the sky as a constellation.

**Caeneus**
A Lapith warrior who was born a woman, Caenis, and was transformed by Poseidon into an invulnerable man. Since weapons could not wound him, the centaurs killed him in the battle with the Lapiths by burying or pounding him into the ground under rocks and uprooted fir trees.

**Cronus and Philyra**
Chiron's parentage differs from that of other centaurs: he is the son of the Titan Cronus, who took the form of a horse, and the Oceanid Philyra. This explains his immortality and wisdom. He married the nymph Chariclo.

**Peleus and Thetis**
Chiron rescued Peleus after the king Acastus abandoned him on Mount Pelion and hid his sword. Chiron also advised Peleus on how to win the sea nymph Thetis by holding on as she shapeshifted, and their wedding took place outside Chiron's cave.

**Rhoecus and Hylaeus**
Two centaurs who tried to rape the huntress Atalanta in the wilderness and were shot dead by her arrows.

**Hylonome and Cyllarus**
In Ovid's Metamorphoses, the female centaur Hylonome killed herself after her beloved husband Cyllarus died in the battle against the Lapiths.

**Sagittarius**
The zodiac constellation Sagittarius is depicted as a centaur archer. Chiron is also associated with the constellation Centaurus.

**Theseus cuts off Eurytion's ears**
In some versions, after Eurytion attempts to abduct Hippodamia at Pirithous's wedding, the Lapiths and Theseus mutilate him by cutting off his ears and nose before throwing him out.

**Cyprian centaurs and other analogues**
A separate tribe of horned centaurs on Cyprus was said to be born when Zeus's seed fell on the earth (Gaia). Comparable half-horse beings in other cultures include the Filipino tikbalang and the Hindu kinnaras.

**Bull of Heaven**
In the Epic of Gilgamesh, Ishtar propositions Gilgamesh, who rejects her by listing the terrible fates of her previous lovers. Furious, she demands that her father Anu give her the Bull of Heaven, which she sends to ravage Uruk; Gilgamesh and Enkidu kill it.

**Seven gates of the underworld**
In the Descent of Ishtar (or Inanna), she travels to the underworld and must remove one article of clothing or jewelry at each of seven gates. She arrives before the throne completely naked and powerless.

**Ereshkigal**
Ishtar's sister and the queen of the underworld (called Irkalla or Kur). Ishtar's descent into Ereshkigal's realm ends with Ishtar being killed or imprisoned there.

**Tammuz (Dumuzid)**
Ishtar's principal lover or husband, a shepherd god of fertility. Some versions say she descended to the underworld to rescue him; in the Sumerian version, when she returns and finds that he has not mourned her, she has him dragged down to the underworld to take her place.

**Namtar and the sixty diseases**
Namtar, Ereshkigal's vizier and minister of fate, imprisoned Ishtar in the underworld and struck her with sixty diseases. While she was gone, all sexual activity and reproduction ceased on Earth.

**Asushunamir and the water of life**
To rescue Ishtar, the god Ea (Enki) created Asushunamir, a sexless or eunuch being who charmed Ereshkigal into granting the water of life. Ishtar was sprinkled with it (by Namtar on Ereshkigal's orders) and revived.

**Gala-tura and kur-jara**
In the Sumerian version of the descent, Inanna's attendant Ninshubur seeks help, and Enki fashions these two genderless beings from the dirt under his fingernails. They sympathize with Ereshkigal's pains, earn her favor, and revive Inanna's corpse with the food and water of life.

**Enkidu and the thigh**
After the Bull of Heaven is killed, Ishtar curses Gilgamesh from the walls of Uruk, and Enkidu tears off the bull's thigh and hurls it at her face. Ishtar gathers prostitutes and courtesans to mourn the bull, and the gods then decree Enkidu's death.

**Huluppu tree**
In a Sumerian tale, Inanna plants a huluppu (willow) tree in her garden, intending to carve it into a throne and bed. A serpent, the Anzu bird, and the demoness Lilith move into it and Inanna weeps, until Gilgamesh drives them out; she gives him a drum and drumstick (the pukku and mikku) made from its wood.

**Eight-pointed star and Venus**
Ishtar's symbol is an eight-pointed star (along with the rosette), and she is identified with the planet Venus. With the moon god Sin and the sun god Shamash she forms an astral triad.

**Lions**
Ishtar's sacred animal is the lion. She is often depicted standing on lions or riding a chariot drawn by them, and lions decorated her monumental Ishtar Gate in Babylon.

**The me**
The me were the divine decrees governing civilization. Inanna got Enki drunk and made off with them in her Boat of Heaven to her city of Uruk, escaping the sea monsters and other creatures Enki sent after her.

**Ishtar Gate**
A blue glazed-brick gate built by Nebuchadnezzar II on the north side of Babylon, decorated with lions, bulls, and dragons (mushussu). It is now reconstructed in Berlin's Pergamon Museum.

**Shukaletuda**
A gardener who raped the sleeping Inanna under a tree. In her fury, she unleashed plagues upon the land, including turning all the waters to blood, and with Enki's help eventually tracked him down and killed him.

**Inanna, Astarte, and Uruk**
Ishtar is the Akkadian and Babylonian name of the Sumerian Inanna, and she is identified with the West Semitic Astarte. Her principal cult center was Uruk (biblical Erech), and in The Curse of Agade she abandons the city of Akkad during the reign of Naram-Sin.

**Dido and Carthage**
Aeneas's tragic love affair in Book 4 of Virgil's Aeneid. Dido, the queen of Carthage (who earlier fled from Tyre), falls in love with him, but Mercury reminds him of his duty to found a new home in Italy and he sails away. Dido has her sister Anna build a pyre, then stabs herself with Aeneas's sword on it and curses him, which Virgil presents as the origin of the enmity between Rome and Carthage.

**Anchises carried out of Troy**
Aeneas's father, a mortal whom Venus (Aphrodite) seduced while disguised as a princess near Mount Ida. Anchises is lamed by Zeus's thunderbolt for boasting of the affair, so Aeneas carries him on his back out of burning Troy, a famous image of Roman pietas (devotion to family, gods, and country).

**Turnus and the belt of Pallas**
Turnus, king of the Rutulians, is Aeneas's main enemy in Italy and his rival for Lavinia. Turnus kills Pallas, the young son of Aeneas's ally Evander, and takes his sword belt. At the very end of the Aeneid the defeated Turnus begs for mercy, but Aeneas sees Pallas's belt on him and kills him in rage.

**The Cumaean Sibyl and the golden bough**
The Sibyl of Cumae, named Deiphobe, is a prophetess of Apollo who guides Aeneas into the underworld near Lake Avernus in Book 6. To enter he must pluck a golden bough as a gift for Proserpina, and two doves sent by his mother lead him to it.

**Visiting Anchises in the underworld**
In Elysium the ghost of Anchises shows Aeneas the parade of future Roman heroes, ending with the young Marcellus, Augustus's nephew and heir, who died early. On the way Aeneas meets Dido's silent ghost and tells her "invitus, regina, tuo de litore cessi" ("unwillingly, queen, I left your shore"), a line Virgil adapted from Catullus 66, a poem about the lock of Berenice's hair.

**Gates of horn and ivory**
The two gates of Sleep at the exit of the underworld: true dreams pass through the gate of horn, and false dreams through the gate of ivory. Puzzlingly, Anchises sends Aeneas and the Sibyl out through the ivory gate.

**Lavinia, Latinus, and Amata**
Lavinia, daughter of King Latinus of Latium, is destined to marry Aeneas, which makes her his second wife after Creusa. Juno sends the Fury Allecto to madden Latinus's wife Amata and Turnus so they resist the marriage and start the war. Omens of Aeneas's arrival include a swarm of bees on a sacred laurel and Lavinia's hair seeming to catch fire.

**Creusa**
Aeneas's first wife, the mother of Ascanius. She is lost as the family flees burning Troy, and when Aeneas goes back to search for her, her ghost tells him to go on and that he will find a new kingdom and a new wife.

**Ascanius (Iulus)**
Aeneas's son, also called Iulus, from whom the Julian family (Julius Caesar and Augustus) claimed descent. He founds the city of Alba Longa, and by shooting the pet stag of Silvia, daughter of Latinus's herdsman, he sparks the war between the Trojans and the Latins.

**Celaeno and eating their tables**
Celaeno, queen of the Harpies, curses the Trojans by prophesying that they will be so hungry they will eat their own tables. The prophecy comes true harmlessly in Italy when they eat the flat loaves of bread they had used as plates, and Ascanius jokes that they are eating their tables.

**Palinurus**
Aeneas's helmsman. The god Somnus (Sleep) lulls him to sleep and he falls overboard, the single life Neptune demands as the price for the fleet's safe passage to Italy. Aeneas later meets his unburied ghost in the underworld.

**Fighting Diomedes in the Iliad**
In Homer's Iliad Aeneas is a Trojan prince and cousin of Hector. Diomedes crushes his hip with a huge boulder. Aphrodite tries to carry him off and is wounded, Apollo rescues him and leaves a phantom double on the battlefield, and Leto and Artemis heal him. Later Poseidon whisks him away from a fight with Achilles because he is fated to survive.

**Hector's ghost and the Penates**
On the night Troy falls, Hector's ghost appears to Aeneas in a dream and tells him to flee because the city is lost, entrusting him with Troy's sacred objects. Aeneas carries the Penates (household gods) with him to Italy, and his mother Venus also urges him to escape.

**Shield of Aeneas**
The shield Vulcan forges for Aeneas at Venus's request in Book 8. It shows the future history of Rome, with Augustus's victory over Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium at its center, including Egyptian gods like Anubis fighting against Neptune and Minerva.

**Jupiter Indiges and the Numicus River**
After his death Aeneas was worshipped as Jupiter Indiges. In Ovid's version, the river Numicus washes away his mortal parts and he becomes a god, while other accounts say he was buried on its banks.

**Bellerophon**
The Corinthian hero, said to be a son of Poseidon or of King Glaucus, who tamed and rode Pegasus. He is by far the most common clue associated with the winged horse.

**Gadfly and the flight to Olympus**
Grown arrogant after his victories, Bellerophon tried to ride Pegasus up to Mount Olympus. Zeus sent a gadfly to sting Pegasus, who threw Bellerophon back to earth, where he landed in a thornbush on the Aleian Plain and wandered lame and alone.

**Birth from Medusa**
Pegasus and his brother Chrysaor sprang from the neck of the Gorgon Medusa when Perseus beheaded her (in some versions from her blood falling into the sea). Poseidon was their father.

**Hippocrene and Mount Helicon**
Pegasus struck Mount Helicon with his hoof, creating the spring Hippocrene ("horse's fountain"), sacred to the Muses and a source of poetic inspiration. In one version, Helicon was swelling with delight at the Muses' singing contest against the Pierides, and Pegasus stamped on it to stop it from growing.

**Chimera**
The fire-breathing monster with a lion's head, a goat's body, and a serpent's tail. Riding Pegasus, Bellerophon killed it from the air, a task assigned by King Iobates of Lycia.

**Golden bridle from Athena**
Athena gave Bellerophon a golden bridle, which allowed him to tame Pegasus. He found the bridle beside him when he woke up in her temple.

**Polyeidos**
The Corinthian seer who advised Bellerophon to sleep in Athena's temple in order to learn how to catch Pegasus. This led to Athena's appearance in a dream and the gift of the golden bridle.

**Carrier of Zeus's thunderbolts**
After Bellerophon's fall, Pegasus continued to Olympus, where he served Zeus by carrying his thunder and lightning. Some sources pair him with horses named Bronte (Thunder) and Astrape (Lightning).

**Peirene spring at Corinth**
Bellerophon caught Pegasus while the horse was drinking at the spring of Peirene in Corinth, using Athena's bridle.

**Amazons**
After the Chimera, Iobates sent Bellerophon against the Solymi and the Amazons. Riding Pegasus, Bellerophon defeated them by dropping boulders on them from above.

**Anteia and Proetus**
Anteia (also called Stheneboea), wife of King Proetus of Tiryns, falsely accused Bellerophon of assault after he rejected her advances. Proetus sent him to Iobates with a sealed letter asking for his death, leading to the dangerous tasks Bellerophon completed with Pegasus.

**Lead-tipped spear**
Bellerophon killed the Chimera by thrusting a lump of lead on his spear into its mouth. The monster's fiery breath melted the lead, which then choked or burned it to death.

**Pegasus constellation**
Zeus placed Pegasus among the stars as the constellation Pegasus. A legend says a feather fell from him at the city of Tarsus, which took its name from it.

**Springs from his hoofprints**
Wherever Pegasus struck the earth with his hoof, a freshwater spring was said to burst forth, Hippocrene being the most famous.

**Beheaded by Shiva while guarding Parvati's bath**
Parvati made Ganesha from clay (or turmeric paste scraped from her body) and breathed life into him so he could guard the door while she bathed. When he refused to let Shiva enter, Shiva cut off his head; to console Parvati, Shiva replaced it with the head of an elephant, the first creature found, giving Ganesha his famous appearance.

**Race with Kartikeya (Skanda) for the mango of knowledge**
Ganesha and his brother Kartikeya (also called Skanda or Murugan), who rides a peacock, competed to go around the world three times, with a golden mango (fruit) of wisdom as the prize. While Kartikeya flew around the world, Ganesha simply walked around his parents Shiva and Parvati, explaining that they were his whole world, and won.

**Scribe of the Mahabharata**
The sage Vyasa asked Ganesha to write down the Mahabharata as he dictated it. Ganesha agreed on condition that Vyasa never pause, and when his pen broke (in a common version), he snapped off one of his own tusks to keep writing; this is why he is shown with a broken tusk and called Ekadanta ("one-tusked").

**Mouse (rat) mount**
Ganesha's vahana, or vehicle, is a mouse or rat (Mushika), usually shown at his feet. It symbolizes his ability to overcome even the smallest obstacles, or the control of desire.

**"Remover of Obstacles" and Lord of Beginnings**
Ganesha's main role is as Vighneshvara or Vighnaharta, the remover (and placer) of obstacles. He is the patron of letters and wisdom, and he is traditionally worshipped first at the start of any puja, ceremony, journey, or new venture.

**Cursing the moon (Chandra)**
After a big meal of sweets, Ganesha fell from his mouse and his belly burst open, spilling its contents. The moon god Chandra laughed at him, so Ganesha tied up his stomach with a snake and cursed the moon; the curse explains the moon's waxing and waning, and why it is bad luck to look at the moon on Ganesha's festival.

**Ganesh Chaturthi and modak**
Ganesha's birthday festival, celebrated for ten days in the month of Bhadrapada (August–September), especially in Maharashtra, with clay idols later immersed in water. Devotees offer him modak, sweet dumplings of rice flour filled with jaggery and coconut, which is his favorite food, so he is called Modakapriya ("lover of modak").

**Kubera's feast and the handful of rice**
The wealth god Kubera held a lavish feast to show off his riches and invited Ganesha, who ate all the food and then began to devour Kubera's palace and city of Alakapuri. Only a handful of roasted rice given in humility by Shiva finally satisfied him, teaching Kubera a lesson about pride.

**Consorts Buddhi and Siddhi (and Kala Bou)**
Ganesha's wives are often given as Buddhi (intellect, wisdom) and Siddhi (spiritual power, success), sometimes with Riddhi (prosperity). In Bengal, his consort is the Kala Bou ("banana bride"), a banana tree wrapped in a sari during Durga Puja.

**Mudgala Purana (eight incarnations)**
A Purana devoted to Ganesha that describes eight incarnations of him, each defeating a demon representing a vice; for example, Vighnaraja overcomes Mamasura, the demon of possessiveness. A separate text, the Sritattvanidhi, illustrates thirty-two forms of Ganesha.

**Ashtavinayaka and the Morgaon temple**
A pilgrimage to eight Ganesha temples in Maharashtra, which traditionally begins and ends at the Mayureshwar temple at Morgaon. There Ganesha, in a form riding a peacock, is said to have slain a demon.

**Parashurama's axe**
In one explanation of the broken tusk, the warrior sage Parashurama came to visit Shiva, and Ganesha, guarding the way, blocked him. Parashurama threw the axe Shiva had given him, and Ganesha, out of respect for his father's weapon, let it strike and break off his tusk.

**Shani's gaze**
In an alternative account of how Ganesha lost his head, the planet god Shani (Saturn), whose gaze was cursed to be destructive, looked at the newborn Ganesha, causing his head to burn up or fall off. It was then replaced with an elephant's head.

**Iconography: pot belly, noose, goad, and sweets**
Ganesha is typically shown with four or more arms, a large pot belly symbolizing the universe or his vast knowledge, and a snake belt. He often holds a noose (pasha), an elephant goad (ankusha), his broken tusk, and a bowl of sweets such as modak or laddoo.

**Vishnu's conch and discus**
In one story, Ganesha took Vishnu's conch, and Vishnu, hearing it sound from Mount Kailash, had to perform a puja to Ganesha to get it back. In another, Ganesha swallowed Vishnu's discus, and Vishnu made funny faces until Ganesha laughed and spat it out.

**Trojan Horse**
After a ten-year siege, the Greeks pretended to sail away, leaving behind a giant wooden horse devised by Odysseus and built by Epeius. Greek soldiers hidden inside emerged at night to open the gates and sack the city. This is the most famous giveaway for Troy.

**Walls built by Apollo and Poseidon for Laomedon**
Apollo and Poseidon, sentenced to serve the Trojan king Laomedon after rebelling against Zeus, built Troy's walls, with help in some versions from the mortal Aeacus. Laomedon refused to pay them, and Poseidon sent a sea monster to ravage the land.

**Hesione and Heracles's sack of Troy**
To appease the sea monster, Laomedon exposed his daughter Hesione to be devoured. Heracles rescued her in exchange for Laomedon's divine horses, given by Zeus as compensation for abducting Ganymede. When Laomedon again refused to pay, Heracles and Telamon sacked Troy, and Hesione became Telamon's wife and the mother of Teucer.

**Priam (Podarces)**
Troy's last king, Priam, was originally called Podarces. After Heracles's sack, Hesione ransomed her brother with her veil, and he was renamed Priam, from a Greek word for "to buy." He is killed by Achilles's son Neoptolemus at the city's fall.

**Hector and Achilles**
Hector, Priam's eldest son and Troy's greatest champion, kills Patroclus and is then killed by Achilles in a duel. Achilles drags his corpse behind his chariot around the city or Patroclus's tomb until Priam ransoms the body.

**Astyanax**
The infant son of Hector and Andromache, who in the Iliad is frightened by his father's plumed helmet. After the city falls, the Greeks throw him from Troy's walls, often at the hands of Neoptolemus.

**Laocoon and Sinon**
The Trojan priest Laocoon warned against accepting the wooden horse and threw a spear at it, and he and his sons were then killed by sea serpents. The Greek Sinon, left behind on purpose, convinced the Trojans that the horse was an offering and that he had escaped being made a human sacrifice.

**Helen and the Judgment of Paris**
The Trojan prince Paris, raised on Mount Ida, awarded the golden apple to Aphrodite in exchange for Helen, wife of Menelaus of Sparta. His abduction of Helen started the Trojan War, and her former suitors were bound by the Oath of Tyndareus to help recover her.

**Dardanus and the founding of Troy**
Dardanus, a son of Zeus and the Pleiad Electra, fled Samothrace after his brother Iasion was killed and founded the royal line of the region. His descendant Ilus founded the city of Ilium and received the Palladium, a sacred wooden statue of Pallas Athena that protected the city until Odysseus and Diomedes stole it.

**Scaean Gate and the Scamander River**
The Scaean Gate was Troy's main gate, the site of many scenes in the Iliad. The Scamander (Xanthus) River flows across the Trojan plain, and a prophecy said Troy would fall if the horses of Rhesus drank from it, so Diomedes and Odysseus killed them first.

**Protesilaus**
The first Greek to leap ashore at Troy, fulfilling a prophecy that the first to land would be the first to die; he was killed by Hector. Odysseus, to avoid being first, threw his shield down and jumped onto it.

**Hecuba and the Trojan Women**
Priam's wife Hecuba is the subject of Euripides's tragedies Hecuba, in which she avenges the deaths of her children Polyxena and Polydorus, and The Trojan Women. In some versions she is turned into a dog after the fall of the city.

**Cassandra**
Priam's daughter, a prophetess cursed by Apollo never to be believed, foretold Troy's fall. During the sack she was raped by Ajax the Lesser in Athena's temple, which angered Athena and brought disaster on the Greek fleet returning home.

**Aeneas and Brutus**
The Trojan prince Aeneas escaped the burning city and went to Italy, where he fought Turnus for the hand of Lavinia and became the ancestor of the Romans. His descendant Brutus is the legendary founder of Britain.

**Hissarlik and Schliemann**
The archaeological site of Troy lies at Hissarlik in northwestern Turkey. Heinrich Schliemann excavated it in the 1870s, revealing nine layers of settlement.

**Sewn into Zeus's thigh**
Dionysus's mortal mother Semele, a Theban princess, was tricked by a jealous Hera into asking her lover Zeus to appear in his full divine glory, and she was burned to death by the sight. Zeus rescued the unborn Dionysus and sewed him into his thigh until he was ready to be born, earning Dionysus the epithet "twice-born."

**Maenads and the death of Pentheus**
The Maenads (Bacchants or Bacchae) were Dionysus's frenzied female followers. In Euripides's The Bacchae, the Theban king Pentheus bans Dionysus's worship and mocks him as an effeminate foreigner; the god lures him to spy on the Maenads' rites on Mount Cithaeron, where they tear him apart, led by his own mother Agave. The Maenads also tore apart the singer Orpheus.

**Pirates turned into dolphins**
Tyrrhenian pirates kidnapped Dionysus, intending to sell him as a slave. The god made vines grow over the ship and wild beasts appear, and the terrified sailors leapt overboard and became dolphins. Only the helmsman Acoetes, who had recognized the god and tried to protect him, was spared.

**Zagreus**
In Orphic tradition, an earlier incarnation of Dionysus born to Zeus and Persephone. As an infant guarded by the Curetes, Zagreus was lured away, torn apart, and eaten by the Titans, except for his heart, which Athena saved; from it he was reborn as Dionysus. Because humans arose from the ashes of the Titans, Orphics held that people contain a divine Dionysian element, which later Neoplatonists like Olympiodorus used to argue against suicide.

**Ariadne on Naxos**
After the Cretan princess Ariadne helped Theseus kill the Minotaur, Theseus abandoned her on the island of Naxos. Dionysus found her there and made her his wife.

**Thyrsus**
The staff carried by Dionysus and his followers, made from a fennel stalk wrapped in ivy and tipped with a pine cone, sometimes said to drip honey. It is a symbol of fertility and of the god himself.

**Nonnus's Dionysiaca**
A 48-book Greek epic by the late-antique poet Nonnus of Panopolis, the longest surviving poem from antiquity. It narrates Dionysus's campaign against India, where he defeats the Indian king Deriades (son of the Hydaspes River), and his triumphant return.

**Ampelos**
A beautiful youth loved by Dionysus, who died after being thrown by a wild bull he was riding. Dionysus mourned him, and Ampelos was transformed into the first grapevine, giving the god his domain over wine.

**Midas and Silenus**
When the drunken satyr Silenus, Dionysus's elderly tutor and companion, wandered into the lands of King Midas of Phrygia, Midas hosted him kindly and returned him. As a reward, Dionysus granted Midas's wish that everything he touched would turn to gold, which became a curse when his food turned to gold too.

**Lycurgus**
A Thracian king who persecuted Dionysus and attacked his nurses, driving the young god to take refuge in the sea. Dionysus drove him mad, and in his madness Lycurgus killed his own son, mistaking him for a vine (ivy).

**City Dionysia and Athenian drama**
The great Athenian festival of Dionysus Eleuthereus, featuring a procession (pompe) carrying the god's statue and ritual phalluses. At it, playwrights such as Aeschylus and Sophocles competed with tetralogies of tragedies and a satyr play in the Theater of Dionysus, making him the patron god of theater. He was also honored at the Lenaia and the Anthesteria, at which the wife of the archon basileus was ritually married to the god, and with choral hymns called dithyrambs.

**Omophagia and sparagmos**
The ecstatic rites of Dionysus's cult, in which worshippers tore a live animal (often a bull) apart with their bare hands (sparagmos) and ate its raw flesh (omophagia). These rites echo the dismemberment of Zagreus and the deaths of Pentheus and Orpheus.

**Thiasus**
Dionysus's ecstatic retinue of Maenads and satyrs. His Maenads are also called Bassarids after the bassaris fox skin that Dionysus wore, and his other attributes include ivy, grapevines, leopards, and the two-handled wine cup called the kantharos.

**Ino and Athamas**
Semele's sister Ino and her husband Athamas raised the infant Dionysus. Hera punished them by driving them mad; Athamas killed one of their sons, and Ino leapt into the sea with the other. Dionysus was then raised by the nymphs of Mount Nysa.

**Rescuing Semele from the underworld**
After becoming a god, Dionysus descended to the underworld to retrieve his mother Semele, renamed her Thyone, and brought her to Mount Olympus. In some accounts he took Hestia's place as one of the twelve Olympians.

**Buying the stories from Nyame**
Anansi's most famous tale: he asked the Akan sky god Nyame (often called his father) for ownership of all the world's stories. Nyame set the price as capturing Onini the python, Osebo the leopard, the Mmoboro hornets, and Mmoatia the fairy (or dwarf); Anansi succeeded, and the stories became known as Anansesem, "spider stories."

**Calabash of wisdom and Ntikuma**
Anansi tried to hoard all the world's wisdom in a calabash gourd or pot and hide it at the top of a tree. He struggled to climb with the pot tied to his front until his son Ntikuma laughed and suggested tying it to his back; realizing he did not hold all wisdom, Anansi dropped the pot and wisdom spread throughout the world.

**Mmoboro hornets and the fake rain**
To capture the hornets, Anansi poured water over their nest and covered his own head with a wet banana leaf or calabash, claiming it was raining. He offered them shelter in an empty gourd, then plugged it shut once they flew in.

**Mmoatia and the gum doll**
To capture the fairy Mmoatia, Anansi carved a doll (an akua'ba) covered in sticky gum, set a bowl of mashed yams before it, and placed it where she played. When the doll ignored Mmoatia's thanks, she slapped it and became stuck, a tale that is the ancestor of the tar baby story.

**Onini the python**
Anansi staged a loud argument with his wife Aso about whether the python was longer than a palm branch. The proud Onini offered to be measured, lay down beside the branch, and Anansi tied him to it.

**Osebo the leopard**
Anansi dug a pit on the leopard's path to trap him. He then pretended to help Osebo out and either bound or struck him, capturing him for Nyame.

**One ear of corn to a hundred slaves**
In a famous series of trades, Anansi set out with a single ear of corn and kept trading up, at one point obtaining a dead body and tricking villagers into thinking their children had killed a chief's son. He ended with one hundred slaves (or servants), sometimes to present to Nyame.

**Tar baby and Br'er Rabbit**
In other tales Anansi himself is caught when he strikes and kicks a sticky tar baby and becomes stuck to it. Enslaved Africans brought his stories to the Americas, where they influenced Br'er Rabbit and survive as tales of "Anansi," "Nanzi," or "Aunt Nancy."

**Thin legs from the eight strings**
The greedy Anansi tied a string to each of his eight legs and gave the other ends to people cooking at different homes, so he would be called to each meal. When they all pulled at once, his legs were stretched long and thin.

**Tiger tied to the tree**
Anansi convinced Tiger that he would pick lice from his hair, then tied Tiger to a fruit tree by his hairs. A hunter later found Tiger stuck there and killed him.

**Killing the ram**
In one origin tale, Anansi killed the king's (or Nyame's) prized ram and lied about it. As punishment he was kicked or smashed into pieces, which is how he took on his spider form.

**Rise-up-and-make-love-to-Aso**
Aso's jealous husband, who could not father children, challenged anyone to try to seduce her. Anansi told him his name was "Rise-up-and-make-love-to-Aso," so the husband unknowingly invited him in by calling out his name, and Anansi married Aso.

**Cockroach's coconuts**
Anansi cut down coconuts from Cockroach's yard, which started a fight between the two.

**Kwaku Anansi and his family**
"Anansi" means spider in the Akan language, and "Kwaku" is the name for a male born on Wednesday, the day his soul first appeared. He is a trickster of the Ashanti (Akan) people of Ghana, son of Nyame and the earth goddess Asase Ya, and his wife is Aso.

**Anansi and Death**
In one tale Anansi is caught stealing food from Death, which leads Death to come to the town. In another he escapes Death by shoving Death's head into a barrel of flour and running away.

**Finn MacCool (Fionn mac Cumhaill) and the Salmon of Knowledge**
Finn is the leader of the Fianna, a band of warriors, and the central hero of the Fenian Cycle of Irish myth. As a boy he cooked the Salmon of Knowledge for the poet Finn Eces, who had spent seven years trying to catch it. When Finn burned his thumb on the fish and sucked it, he gained all the world's knowledge, and afterward he could call up wisdom by sucking his thumb. Legend says he sleeps beneath Ireland until the hour of its need.

**Cu Chulainn and the Gae Bulg**
Cu Chulainn is the great hero of the Ulster Cycle. He learned warfare, including the "salmon leap," from the warrior woman Scathach, who gave him the barbed spear Gae Bulg, which inflicts wounds that cannot be survived. He used it to kill his foster-brother Ferdiad and, without knowing who he was, his own son Connla.

**The Cattle Raid of Cooley (Tain Bo Cuailnge) and Queen Medb**
The central epic of the Ulster Cycle. Queen Medb (Maeve) of Connacht invaded Ulster to steal the prized Brown Bull of Cooley. While the men of Ulster lay weakened by a curse, the teenage Cu Chulainn held off her armies alone, fighting champions one by one at a river ford. In battle he went into the riastrad, a monstrous "warp spasm" or battle frenzy.

**Oisin and Tir na nOg**
Oisin (Ossian) is Finn's son, a poet who narrates much of the Fenian Cycle. He went with the fairy woman Niamh on the magical horse Enbarr, which could cross the sea, to Tir na nOg, the "Land of the Young." When he returned to Ireland, he touched the ground (dismounted or fell from the horse) and at once aged the 300 years that had passed. Irish myth also includes other otherworld paradises, such as Mag Mell, and the immram genre of voyages to magical islands.

**Diarmuid and Grainne**
Grainne, daughter of the High King Cormac mac Airt, was engaged to the aging Finn MacCool but eloped with the young warrior Diarmuid Ua Duibhne, whose "love spot" on his forehead made any woman who saw it fall in love with him. Finn chased them for years, and when Diarmuid was gored by a boar, Finn let him die by twice letting the healing water drain from his hands.

**Sadhbh, the deer woman**
Sadhbh was Finn's wife, who had been turned into a deer by a druid. Finn's hounds Bran and Sceolan recognized her and refused to kill her. She became a woman again on Finn's land and gave birth to Oisin, whose name means "little deer."

**The Morrigan**
The shape-shifting Irish goddess of war, fate, and death, often appearing as a crow. She is often described as a triple goddess made up of Badb, Macha, and Nemain. She clashed with Cu Chulainn during the Tain, partly over a cow, and her crow perched on his shoulder when he died. She is also linked to the festival of Samhain.

**Lebor Gabala Erenn (The Book of Invasions)**
A medieval pseudo-history describing successive waves of settlers in Ireland: Cessair (a granddaughter of Noah, with Ladra), then Partholon, Nemed, the Fir Bolg, the Tuatha De Danann, and finally the Milesians (Gaels). The early settlers fought the Fomorians, a monstrous race whose leader Cichol Gricenchos fought the first battle in Ireland. When the Milesians arrived, the goddess Eriu asked that the island be named after her, which gives the name Eire.

**Battles of Mag Tuired, Nuada's silver arm, and Lugh vs. Balor**
In the first Battle of Mag Tuired ("Plain of Pillars"), the Tuatha De Danann defeated the Fir Bolg, but their king Nuada lost his arm to Sreng. Because a king had to be physically whole, Nuada could not rule until he was given a silver arm (Airgetlam). In the second battle, against the Fomorians, Balor of the Evil Eye, whose eye destroyed whatever it looked at, killed Nuada. His own grandson Lugh of the Long Arm then shot a stone from his sling through that eye, so the eye's gaze turned on and destroyed the Fomorian army.

**Tuatha De Danann: the Dagda and the craft gods**
The Tuatha De Danann are the divine race of Irish myth, told in the Mythological Cycle. The Dagda, their father-figure god, owned a club that killed with one end and brought back to life with the other, and a cauldron that never emptied. The three craft gods are Goibniu the smith, Luchta the carpenter (wright), and Creidhne the metalworker (goldsmith), who made weapons together for the second Battle of Mag Tuired.

**The Lia Fail and the Hill of Tara**
The Lia Fail ("Stone of Destiny") stood on the Hill of Tara, the seat of the High Kings of Ireland. It was said to roar with joy when the rightful king touched it. It was one of the four treasures the Tuatha De Danann brought to Ireland.

**Geis and the death of Cu Chulainn**
A geis is a magical taboo or obligation laid on an Irish hero. Cu Chulainn ("Hound of Culann") had a geis against eating dog meat and another against refusing hospitality. Three hags offered him dog meat, which forced him to break one of them, and the weakened hero was killed by Lugaid. He tied himself to a standing stone so he could die on his feet.

**The Children of Lir**
The four children of Lir were turned into swans by their jealous stepmother Aoife and doomed to spend 900 years on Irish waters. The spell was broken when they heard the bell of a Christian church, after which they turned back into very old humans and died.

**Finn, Benandonner, and the Giant's Causeway**
Finn is said to have built the Giant's Causeway, a formation of basalt columns in Northern Ireland, to reach the Scottish giant Benandonner. When the bigger giant came, Finn's wife Oonagh disguised Finn as a baby and served Benandonner a griddle cake with the iron griddle baked inside, while the "baby" ate an ordinary one. Terrified of how big the father must be, Benandonner fled and tore up the causeway behind him.

**Banshees, leprechauns, puca, and Saint Patrick**
Irish folklore includes the banshee, a female spirit whose wailing foretells a death and which is linked to the custom of keening (mourning cries) at funerals. It also includes the leprechaun, a fairy shoemaker with a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow, and the puca, a shape-shifter. Saint Patrick, who Christianized Ireland, is said to have driven out its snakes and explained the Trinity with a shamrock.

**Coatlicue and the ball of feathers**
Huitzilopochtli's mother, the earth goddess Coatlicue ("Serpent Skirt"). While she was sweeping on the mountain Coatepec, a ball of feathers fell from the sky. She tucked it into her waistband and became pregnant with him, and this miraculous conception is clued in almost every question.

**Coyolxauhqui**
Huitzilopochtli's sister, who was outraged by their mother's pregnancy and led her brothers to kill Coatlicue. Huitzilopochtli beheaded and dismembered her and threw her body down the mountain; in one telling her head was thrown into the sky and became the moon. A huge carved stone showing her dismembered body was found at the foot of the Templo Mayor.

**Born fully armed**
Just as his siblings arrived to kill Coatlicue, Huitzilopochtli burst from her womb fully grown, dressed, and armed for war, ready to defend her.

**Four Hundred Southerners (Centzon Huitznahua)**
Huitzilopochtli's many brothers, also called the Four Hundred Stars, who joined Coyolxauhqui's attack on their mother. He killed or scattered them, and they became the stars of the southern sky. The myth represents the rising sun driving away the moon and stars.

**Xiuhcoatl**
The "turquoise (or fire) serpent," Huitzilopochtli's weapon, with which he pierced and killed Coyolxauhqui. He is sometimes called the "Turquoise Prince."

**"Left-handed hummingbird" (or "Hummingbird of the South")**
The meaning of Huitzilopochtli's name, from huitzilin ("hummingbird") and a word meaning "left" (to the Aztecs, also the south). He was often shown with hummingbird feathers, a blue-and-black striped face, and a hummingbird helmet.

**Templo Mayor**
The Great Temple at the center of Tenochtitlan, which had twin shrines on top: one to Huitzilopochtli and one to the rain god Tlaloc. It symbolized the mountain Coatepec. At its rededication in 1487, enormous numbers of captives were reportedly sacrificed, and their skulls were displayed on a skull rack (tzompantli).

**Eagle on a cactus / founding of Tenochtitlan**
As patron god of the Mexica (Aztecs), Huitzilopochtli led them on their migration from Aztlan. He told them to settle where they saw an eagle perched on a cactus eating a snake. They saw it on an island in Lake Texcoco and founded Tenochtitlan (modern Mexico City); the image is on the Mexican flag.

**Copil's heart**
Huitzilopochtli's nephew Copil, son of the sorceress Malinalxochitl, rebelled against him. After Copil was killed, his heart was thrown into Lake Texcoco, and the cactus where the eagle perched grew from that spot.

**Human sacrifice and the sun**
Huitzilopochtli was identified with the sun, which fought darkness every day. The Aztecs believed he needed human blood and still-beating hearts to keep up his strength, so these sacrifices kept the sun moving and delayed the end of the world (the end of the Fifth Sun).

**Amaranth dough effigy (Panquetzaliztli)**
At his festival, Panquetzaliztli, a life-sized image of Huitzilopochtli was made from amaranth dough. A priest ritually "killed" it with an arrow, and the body was broken up and eaten; the young men who ate it had to serve the god for a year.

**Paynal**
Huitzilopochtli's messenger or lieutenant. During Panquetzaliztli, a priest dressed as Paynal ran a long, fast procession around the Valley of Mexico.

**Brother of Quetzalcoatl / Blue Tezcatlipoca**
In Aztec creation accounts, Huitzilopochtli is one of the four sons of the creator pair, and is sometimes called the Blue Tezcatlipoca. He and his brother Quetzalcoatl were tasked with creating the world and humans.

**Paradise of warriors and the sun's companions**
The souls of warriors who died in battle or on the sacrificial stone went to the sun's eastern paradise and escorted Huitzilopochtli across the sky. Women who died in childbirth, who were honored like fallen warriors, escorted the sun from noon to sunset.

**Odin hanging for nine days and nights to learn the runes**
In the Rúnatal section of the Hávamál, Odin describes hanging himself from the windswept tree for nine days and nights, wounded by his own spear and sacrificed "myself to myself," without food or drink. At the end of this ordeal he peered down and seized the runes, gaining their wisdom and magic.

**Ratatoskr**
The squirrel that runs up and down the trunk of Yggdrasil, carrying insults and gossip between the eagle perched at the top of the tree and the dragon Nidhogg at its roots. He is one of the most common giveaway clues for the tree.

**Nidhogg (Nithogg)**
The dragon or serpent ("Malice Striker") that lies near the roots of Yggdrasil in Niflheim, next to the spring Hvergelmir, and gnaws at the tree's root. Many other serpents also gnaw at the roots below.

**Ash tree connecting the Nine Worlds**
Yggdrasil is an enormous ash tree at the center of the Norse cosmos whose branches and roots hold together the Nine Worlds, with Asgard near the top, Midgard in the middle, and Niflheim and Hel below. In the Prose Edda, its three roots reach to the Aesir, to the frost giants in Jotunheim, and to Niflheim.

**Four harts: Dáinn, Dvalinn, Duneyrr, and Duraþrór**
Four stags that live on Yggdrasil and nibble at its branches and leaves. They are sometimes interpreted as representing the four winds.

**The eagle and the hawk Vedrfolnir**
An unnamed eagle, said to possess much wisdom, sits at the top of Yggdrasil. Between its eyes sits the hawk Vedrfolnir, and this eagle is the creature that trades insults with Nidhogg through Ratatoskr.

**Well of Urd and the Norns**
The Well of Urd (Urdarbrunnr) lies beneath one of Yggdrasil's roots, and the three Norns, Urd, Verdandi, and Skuld, who shape fate, live there and water the tree with water and white clay to keep it from rotting. The Aesir hold their daily court at this well; Thor must wade the rivers Kormt, Ormt, and the two Kerlaugs to get there because he cannot cross the Bifrost bridge.

**Mimir's well**
A well of wisdom located under the root of Yggdrasil that reaches toward the frost giants, guarded by the wise being Mimir. Odin gave up one of his eyes to drink from it.

**Hvergelmir**
A spring or well (whose name is often translated "Roaring Kettle") under the root that reaches into Niflheim, filled with serpents and home to Nidhogg. It is the source of many rivers, fed by liquid that drips from the antlers of the stag Eikthyrnir.

**Name meaning "Ygg's horse" (gallows)**
The name Yggdrasil is usually interpreted as "horse of Ygg," Ygg ("the Terrible One") being one of Odin's names. "Horse" was a poetic term for gallows, so the name refers to Odin's hanging from the tree.

**Lif and Lifthrasir in Hoddmimis holt**
The two humans who will survive the Fimbulwinter and Ragnarok by hiding in Hoddmimis holt ("Hoddmimir's wood"), usually identified with Yggdrasil. They live on morning dew and repopulate the world afterward.

**Grímnismál ("noblest of trees")**
In this Eddic poem, Odin (disguised as Grimnir) lists the best things of each kind, naming Yggdrasil first as the noblest of trees, followed by the ship Skidbladnir and the horse Sleipnir. The poem also says the tree "suffers agony more than men know," as the harts bite it above, it rots at the side, and Nidhogg gnaws below.

**Shaking at Ragnarok**
According to the Völuspá, Yggdrasil trembles and groans when Ragnarok begins, one of the signs of the end of the world. Sources disagree on whether it is ultimately destroyed in the fire of Surt or survives.

**Laerad (Laeradr) and Mimameidr**
Laerad is a tree standing over Valhalla whose leaves are eaten by the goat Heidrun (whose udders produce the mead drunk by the einherjar) and the stag Eikthyrnir; it is often identified with Yggdrasil. Mimameidr ("Mimir's tree"), mentioned in the poem Fjölsvinnsmál, is also thought to be another name for the world tree.

**Rhea's stone**
Cronus swallowed each of his children at birth to prevent a prophecy that one would overthrow him. When Zeus was born, his mother Rhea hid him and gave Cronus a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes to swallow instead; Zeus later forced Cronus to vomit up his siblings Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, and Poseidon.

**Amalthea and the Kouretes on Mount Ida**
The infant Zeus was hidden in a cave on Mount Ida in Crete, where he was nursed by the goat (or nymph) Amalthea and fed honey by nymphs such as the daughters of Melisseus. The Kouretes (Curetes) clashed their shields and spears to drown out his crying, and the Dactyls, born when Rhea pressed her fingers into the earth, also watched over him. In one version he was hung from a tree so that Cronus, who ruled sky, earth, and sea, could not find him.

**Europa and the white bull**
Zeus transformed into a beautiful white bull to abduct the Phoenician princess Europa, carrying her on his back across the sea to Crete. There she bore him Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Sarpedon, and Zeus gave her gifts including the bronze giant Talos, the hound Laelaps, and a javelin that never missed.

**Ganymede and the eagle**
Zeus took the form of an eagle (or sent his eagle) to carry off the beautiful Trojan shepherd boy Ganymede, who became cupbearer of the gods on Olympus. Zeus compensated Ganymede's father Tros with divine horses and later placed Ganymede in the stars as Aquarius. He also abducted the nymph Aegina as an eagle.

**Leda and the swan**
Zeus seduced the Spartan queen Leda in the form of a swan. She bore eggs from which came Helen and Polydeuces (Pollux), and in many versions Castor and Clytemnestra.

**Danae and the golden shower**
King Acrisius of Argos locked his daughter Danae in an underground bronze chamber after an oracle said her son would kill him. Zeus came to her as a shower of gold, and she gave birth to the hero Perseus.

**Metis and the birth of Athena**
Zeus's first wife Metis was prophesied to bear a son who would overthrow him, so Zeus tricked her into turning into a fly and swallowed her. He later suffered a terrible headache, and when Hephaestus (or Prometheus) split his head open with an axe, Athena sprang out fully armed.

**Semele and Dionysus**
Hera tricked the Theban princess Semele into asking Zeus to reveal his true divine form, and she was incinerated by his radiance. Zeus rescued the unborn Dionysus and sewed him into his thigh until he was ready to be born.

**Titanomachy, Kampe, and the Hundred-Handers**
To win the ten-year war against Cronus and the Titans, Zeus killed the dragon-woman Kampe, the jailer of Tartarus, and freed the Cyclopes and the Hecatoncheires (Briareos, Cottus, and Gyges). After victory, he and his brothers divided the cosmos, with Zeus taking the sky.

**Thunderbolt**
Zeus's signature weapon, forged for him by the Cyclopes, who also made Poseidon's trident and Hades's helm of invisibility. He used it to strike down figures such as Phaethon (who lost control of Helios's chariot), the healer Asclepius, and Salmoneus, a king who impersonated Zeus by driving his chariot over a bronze bridge to mimic thunder.

**Typhon**
A monstrous serpentine giant who challenged Zeus and, in one version, cut out Zeus's sinews and hid them in a cave. Hermes and Aegipan recovered the sinews, and Zeus defeated Typhon with thunderbolts and buried him beneath Mount Etna.

**Lycaon**
An Arcadian king who tested Zeus's divinity by serving him human flesh. Zeus turned him into a wolf, and the cult of Zeus Lykaios on Mount Lykaion was associated with human sacrifice and werewolf legends; Zeus's anger at mankind's wickedness also led to the great flood that only Deucalion and Pyrrha survived.

**Statue of Zeus at Olympia**
A colossal gold-and-ivory (chryselephantine) statue of the seated Zeus made by Phidias for the temple at Olympia, holding a figure of Nike in his right hand. It was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World; the Zanes were bronze statues of Zeus near the Olympic stadium paid for by fines on cheating athletes.

**Baucis and Philemon**
An elderly Phrygian couple who hospitably fed Zeus and Hermes when they visited in disguise, after everyone else had turned them away. As Zeus Xenios, god of xenia (hospitality to guests), he spared them from a flood and turned them into an intertwined oak and linden tree at their deaths.

**Callisto and other disguises**
Zeus disguised himself as Artemis to seduce her follower Callisto, mother of Arcas. He also became a dove to seduce Phthia and turned Eurymedousa into an ant, and he punished the nymph Chelone, who refused to attend his wedding to Hera, by turning her into a tortoise.

**Amaterasu and the cave**
The Shinto sun goddess. Angered by her brother, the storm god Susanoo, who wrecks her rice fields and kills one of her weaving maidens, she hides in a cave (Ama-no-Iwato) and plunges the world into darkness. The other gods lure her out with a raucous dance and a mirror that dazzles her with her own reflection. She is worshipped at the Ise Grand Shrine, the Japanese emperors claimed descent from her, and she banished her brother, the moon god Tsukuyomi.

**Hou Yi shoots down nine suns**
In Chinese myth the ten suns, sons of the goddess Xihe, live in a giant mulberry tree in the east and normally take turns crossing the sky. When all ten rise at once and scorch the earth, the archer Hou Yi shoots down nine of them, leaving one. He is rewarded with an elixir of immortality, which his wife Chang'e drinks.

**Three-legged crow**
In Chinese and wider East Asian folklore the sun is home to, or represented by, a three-legged crow, sometimes called Yangwu or Jinwu. In some versions of the Hou Yi story, each sun he shoots falls to earth as a dead crow.

**Surya, Kunti, and Karna**
Surya is the Hindu sun god. In the Mahabharata the young princess Kunti tests a mantra given to her by the sage Durvasa and accidentally summons Surya, who fathers Karna with her and then restores her virginity. Karna is born wearing divine earrings and armor, and he later fights for the Kauravas against his own half-brothers, the Pandavas.

**Hanuman tries to eat the sun**
As a child, the monkey god Hanuman mistakes the rising sun for a ripe fruit (often a mango) and leaps into the sky to eat it. Indra strikes him on the jaw with his thunderbolt, which is said to be the origin of the name Hanuman ("one with a damaged jaw").

**Ra and the solar barque**
The Egyptian sun god Ra sails across the sky by day and through the underworld (Duat) by night in a boat called the solar barque. Every night the chaos serpent Apep (Apophis) tries to destroy it, and gods like Set and the serpent Mehen defend Ra. The Amduat describes this twelve-hour night journey.

**Khepri, Atum, Horakhty, and the Aten**
Egyptians saw the sun in several aspects: Khepri, the scarab beetle who rolls the sun disk up into the sky each morning, Ra or Ra-Horakhty (Ra merged with Horus) at midday, and Atum, the setting sun of evening. Nefertem was linked to the lotus from which the sun rose, and under the pharaoh Akhenaten the sun disk itself was worshipped as the Aten.

**Ra's secret name and the beer of Sekhmet**
Isis creates a snake that poisons the aged Ra and will cure him only once he tells her his secret name, which gives her power. In another myth Ra sends his Eye, as the lioness Sekhmet, to punish humanity, then stops her slaughter by flooding the fields with 7,000 jars of beer dyed red with ochre to look like blood, which she drinks until she falls asleep.

**Helios, Phaethon, and the sun chariot**
The Greek sun god Helios (Roman Sol) drives the sun across the sky in a chariot pulled by fiery horses. His son Phaethon begs to drive it for a day, loses control, and scorches the earth, which was said to turn the Ethiopians' skin dark, until Zeus strikes him down with a thunderbolt.

**Inti and the Coricancha**
Inti is the Inca sun god, son of the creator Viracocha and father of Manco Capac, the first Inca ruler. His main temple was the Coricancha in Cusco, he was celebrated in the Inti Raymi festival, and carved stones called intihuatanas ("hitching posts of the sun") were linked to him. The Torreon at Machu Picchu is also thought to be a sun temple.

**Nanahuatzin and the Fifth Sun**
In Aztec myth the world has gone through a series of suns. The humble, sore-covered god Nanahuatzin throws himself into a bonfire at Teotihuacan and rises as the Fifth Sun, the current one. The Aztecs also worshipped Huitzilopochtli, a war and sun god symbolized by the hummingbird, and offered human sacrifices to keep the sun moving. The Maya sun god (God G) was Kinich Ahau, and in the Popol Vuh the hero twin Hunahpu, who shot down the false sun Seven Macaw with his blowgun, becomes the sun.

**Sol and the wolf Skoll**
In Norse myth the sun goddess Sol, daughter of Mundilfari, sister of the moon god Mani, and wife of Glenr, drives the sun's chariot, pulled by the horses Arvakr and Alsvidr. The shield Svalinn protects the earth from her heat, and the wolf Skoll chases her and will swallow her at Ragnarok. Alfrodull ("elf-glory") is a poetic name for the sun.

**Surya's family and chariot**
Surya rides a chariot drawn by seven horses. His wife Saranyu, unable to bear his brightness, leaves a shadow double (Chhaya) in her place, and his children include Yama and Manu, the healer twins called the Ashvins, and the monkey king Sugriva. He has many names, such as Aditya, Ravi, and Bhaskar, and the most famous temple to him is the Sun Temple at Konark, said to have once held a floating idol held up by magnets.

**Maui snares the sun**
In Polynesian (Maori) myth the trickster hero Maui catches the sun, Tama-nui-te-ra, with ropes and beats it so it will move more slowly across the sky, giving people longer days.

**Dazhbog, the Trundholm Sun Chariot, and the Kalevala**
Dazhbog was a Slavic sun god. The Trundholm Sun Chariot is a Bronze Age Danish artifact of a horse pulling a gilded sun disk. In the Finnish Kalevala the sun is often described as silver, and it tells mothers such as Marjatta where to find their missing children.

**Polyphemus and the curse on Odysseus**
Poseidon's son Polyphemus, a Cyclops born to the nymph Thoosa, was blinded by Odysseus, who had told him his name was "Nobody." Polyphemus prayed to his father for revenge, and Poseidon became the main adversary of the Odyssey, delaying Odysseus's return home for years; he also turned the ship of the Phaeacians to stone after they carried Odysseus back to Ithaca.

**Contest with Athena for Athens (saltwater spring vs. olive tree)**
Poseidon and Athena competed to become patron of Athens. Poseidon struck the Acropolis with his trident to create a saltwater spring (sometimes called the Erechtheis), but Athena's gift of the olive tree was judged better; in anger Poseidon flooded the Attic plain. Poseidon was also worshipped at Athens alongside, and identified with, the king Erechtheus.

**Medusa in Athena's temple (Pegasus and Chrysaor)**
In Ovid's version, Poseidon raped (or seduced) Medusa in Athena's temple, and Athena punished Medusa by turning her into a snake-haired Gorgon. When Perseus later beheaded Medusa, Poseidon's children by her, the winged horse Pegasus and the warrior Chrysaor, sprang from her neck.

**Trident and earthquakes ("Earth-Shaker")**
Poseidon's signature weapon is the three-pronged trident, with which he strikes the ground to cause earthquakes and stirs up storms at sea. His common epithet is "Earth-Shaker" (Ennosigaios), and he is the Greek god of the sea, earthquakes, and horses, equivalent to the Roman Neptune.

**Walls of Troy and King Laomedon**
As punishment from Zeus, Poseidon and his nephew Apollo served the Trojan king Laomedon, and Poseidon built the walls of Troy. When Laomedon refused to pay them, Poseidon sent a sea monster to ravage Troy, which Heracles later killed; this grudge helps explain Poseidon's support of the Greeks in the Trojan War.

**Amphitrite and Triton**
Poseidon's wife was the Nereid Amphitrite, who at first fled from him until a dolphin found her and brought her back to be his bride. Their son Triton is a merman who blows a conch shell. In one story, Amphitrite turned Poseidon's lover Scylla into a horrible sea monster out of jealousy.

**Demeter, the stallion, and Arion**
While searching for Persephone, Demeter turned into a mare to escape Poseidon, but he changed into a stallion and mated with her. Their offspring were Arion, a swift immortal horse that could speak (later given to Adrastus), and the goddess Despoina.

**Creator and patron of horses**
Horses were sacred to Poseidon, who is said to have created the first horse (in one version, when Demeter asked him for the most beautiful animal). He rides a chariot pulled by hippocamps (sea-horses), and he gave the immortal horses Balius and Xanthus to Peleus as a wedding gift.

**Caenis transformed into Caeneus**
Poseidon raped the Lapith woman Caenis and then offered her any wish; she asked to become a man so she could never be violated again. Poseidon made her the man Caeneus with impenetrable skin, and Caeneus was later crushed into the earth with fir trees and stones by the centaurs.

**Pasiphae and the Cretan Bull**
Poseidon sent a magnificent white bull from the sea to King Minos of Crete, expecting it to be sacrificed to him. When Minos kept it instead, Poseidon made Minos's wife Pasiphae lust after the bull, and their union produced the Minotaur.

**Tyro and Enipeus (Pelias and Neleus)**
Poseidon disguised himself as the river god Enipeus, whom Tyro loved, in order to seduce her. Tyro bore him the twins Pelias (later the king who sent Jason after the Golden Fleece) and Neleus (father of Nestor of Pylos).

**The Aloadae (Otus and Ephialtes)**
Poseidon's giant twin sons by Iphimedia, who had longed for him to father her children. The Aloadae tried to storm Olympus by piling mountains on one another; Artemis, in the form of a deer, darted between them, and they killed each other with their spears trying to hit her.

**Theseus and Aethra**
Aethra slept with both the Athenian king Aegeus and Poseidon on the same night, so the hero Theseus is often called a son of Poseidon. Poseidon is also named as the father of other heroes and figures, including Bellerophon and the bandit Sinis, whom Theseus killed.

**Laocoon and the serpents**
When the Trojan priest Laocoon warned against bringing the Trojan Horse into the city, two huge sea serpents emerged from the sea and killed him and his sons. Some accounts attribute these serpents to Poseidon.

**Mestra's shapeshifting**
Poseidon, her lover, gave Mestra, the daughter of Erysichthon, the power to change her shape. Her father repeatedly sold her into marriage to pay for food for his insatiable hunger, and she escaped each time by transforming.

**Clytemnestra and Aegisthus**
Agamemnon's wife Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus murdered him when he returned home from the Trojan War. This is the most frequent clue for him, and it usually comes paired with his status as Clytemnestra's husband.

**Iphigenia sacrificed at Aulis**
To get a favorable wind for the Greek fleet stuck at Aulis, Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia to Artemis. He lured her there by falsely claiming she was going to marry Achilles, and this sacrifice became Clytemnestra's main motive for killing him.

**Leader of the Greeks in the Trojan War**
Agamemnon was the commander-in-chief of the Achaean (Greek) forces at Troy. His brother Menelaus was the husband of Helen, whose abduction by Paris started the war.

**Briseis and the quarrel with Achilles**
At the start of Homer's Iliad, Agamemnon takes Achilles' war prize, the captive woman Briseis, to make up for losing his own. The insult leads Achilles to withdraw from the fighting, and their quarrel drives the plot of the epic.

**Chryseis and Apollo's plague**
Agamemnon captured Chryseis, daughter of Apollo's priest Chryses, and humiliated Chryses when he came to ransom her. Apollo sent a plague on the Greek camp until Agamemnon gave her back, which is why he then seized Briseis.

**Angering Artemis by killing her stag**
The reason Artemis stopped the winds at Aulis: Agamemnon killed a deer sacred to her and boasted that he was a better hunter than the goddess. Artemis then demanded the sacrifice of his daughter.

**Cassandra**
The Trojan prophetess, daughter of Priam, whom Agamemnon took home as a war prize and concubine after Troy fell. In Aeschylus's play she foretells the murders and recounts the curse on the house of Atreus, and Clytemnestra kills her along with Agamemnon.

**Agamemnon (Aeschylus play)**
The first play of Aeschylus's Oresteia trilogy, followed by The Libation Bearers and The Eumenides. It shows Agamemnon's return from Troy and his murder by Clytemnestra, with a chorus of old men of Argos commenting on events.

**Murdered in the bath**
In the usual version, Clytemnestra trapped Agamemnon in a robe or net while he was in his bath and then struck him down with an axe or sword. In Aeschylus's play, she rejoices at being spattered with his blood, comparing it to spring rain on the crops.

**The purple carpet**
In Aeschylus's Agamemnon, Clytemnestra persuades her husband to walk into the palace on rich purple tapestries. This act of arrogance (hubris) foreshadows his death inside.

**Kingdom of Mycenae (or Argos)**
Agamemnon ruled Mycenae, though Aeschylus and some other sources place him in Argos. After his father Atreus was killed by Thyestes, he fled to Tyndareus of Sparta and later returned to take back the throne.

**Atreus and the house of Atreus**
Agamemnon and Menelaus are called the Atreidae, the sons of Atreus (some sources make them his grandsons through Pleisthenes). Their family was cursed by the feud between Atreus and his brother Thyestes, whose son was Aegisthus.

**Orestes and Electra**
Agamemnon's children Orestes and Electra avenged his death by killing Clytemnestra and Aegisthus. This revenge is the subject of Aeschylus's Libation Bearers and of the Electra plays by Sophocles and Euripides.

**Marriage to Clytemnestra via Tyndareus**
While in exile with King Tyndareus of Sparta, Agamemnon married Tyndareus's daughter Clytemnestra, while Menelaus married her sister Helen. In some versions he first killed Clytemnestra's previous husband, Tantalus, so her brothers the Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux) marched against him.

**"The face of a dog but the heart of a deer"**
Achilles' insult to Agamemnon in Book 1 of the Iliad, calling him a coward who never fights in the front lines. Later in the Iliad, Agamemnon is wounded and driven from battle by Coon, son of Antenor, who was trying to avenge his brother Iphidamas.

**Medea**
Euripides's most famous tragedy, set in Corinth, in which the Colchian sorceress Medea takes revenge on her husband Jason after he abandons her to marry Glauce, daughter of King Creon. She sends Glauce a poisoned robe and golden crown that burn her and Creon to death, kills her own children, and escapes in a dragon-drawn chariot sent by her grandfather Helios.

**The Bacchae**
A tragedy in which Dionysus returns to Thebes to punish his family for denying his divinity and slandering his mother Semele. When King Pentheus tries to chain him, Dionysus leaves him tying up a bull, then persuades him to dress as a woman to spy on the maenads from a pine tree; the maenads, led by Pentheus's mother Agave, mistake him for a mountain lion and tear him apart, and Agave carries home his head.

**The Trojan Women**
A tragedy about the captive women of Troy after its fall, including Hecuba, Cassandra, and Andromache. The Greek herald Talthybius announces their fates and that Andromache's infant son Astyanax will be thrown from the walls; the boy is buried on the bronze shield of his father Hector, and the play ends with Hecuba trying to leap into the burning city before being restrained.

**Iphigenia at Aulis**
Euripides's last play, in which Agamemnon is told he must sacrifice his daughter Iphigenia to Artemis so the Greek fleet can sail for Troy, which leads to a quarrel with Menelaus. Iphigenia is lured to Aulis with the promise of marriage to Achilles; the play won first prize at the City Dionysia after Euripides's death, together with The Bacchae.

**Iphigenia in Tauris**
