A play in which Iphigenia, rescued from the sacrifice at Aulis by Artemis, serves as a priestess in the land of the Taurians, where she must ritually sacrifice any strangers who land there. She recognizes two captured Greeks as her brother Orestes and his friend Pylades and escapes with them.

**Alcestis**
A play in which Alcestis agrees to die in place of her husband, King Admetus, a servant describing her as both alive and dead. Heracles, a guest who behaved drunkenly in the mourning household, repays Admetus's hospitality by wrestling Death (Thanatos) at her tomb and bringing her back.

**Hippolytus**
A tragedy in which Aphrodite makes Phaedra fall in love with her stepson Hippolytus, who has spurned the goddess in favor of the chaste Artemis. After Phaedra kills herself and falsely accuses him, his father Theseus curses him, and a bull sent from the sea by Poseidon frightens his horses, causing his fatal chariot crash.

**Hecuba**
A play about the Trojan queen Hecuba after the fall of Troy, in which her daughter Polyxena is sacrificed at the tomb of Achilles. The chorus of captive women curse the sea breeze that will carry them away, and Hecuba takes revenge on Polymestor for murdering her son Polydorus.

**Ion**
A play in which Ion, a temple servant at Delphi believed to be an orphan, is actually the son of Apollo and the Athenian queen Creusa. Creusa tries to poison Ion before mother and son recognize each other through the basket in which she had abandoned him as a baby.

**Electra**
Euripides's version of the Electra story, in which Electra has been married off to a poor peasant farmer. Its recognition scene with her brother Orestes mocks the tokens in Aeschylus's Libation Bearers, such as the matching footprints and lock of hair.

**The Phoenician Women**
A play about the war between Oedipus's sons Eteocles and Polynices over Thebes, unusual for having Jocasta still alive during the siege. Creon's son Menoeceus kills himself over the lair of the serpent killed by Cadmus to fulfill a prophecy of Tiresias that Thebes will be saved, despite his father's attempts to stop him.

**Cyclops**
The only complete satyr play that survives from ancient Greece, a comic retelling of Odysseus's encounter with the Cyclops Polyphemus. The drunken Polyphemus calls the satyr Silenus "Ganymede" and drags him into his cave.

**Children of Heracles and The Suppliants**
Two plays in which Athens protects suppliants. In Children of Heracles, Macaria offers herself as a sacrifice to fulfill an oracle given to King Demophon, and Iolaus captures their persecutor Eurystheus; in The Suppliants, Theseus helps Adrastus recover the bodies of the Argive champions who died attacking Thebes so they can be buried.

**Rhesus**
A play of disputed authorship, traditionally attributed to Euripides, set during the Trojan War. The Trojan spy Dolon disguises himself in a wolf skin and walks on all fours to sneak toward the Greek camp, and the Thracian king Rhesus is killed in his sleep by Odysseus and Diomedes.

**Reputation: Aristophanes, deus ex machina, and few victories**
Euripides was the youngest of the three great Athenian tragedians, after Aeschylus and Sophocles, and wrote around 90 plays but won only four victories in his lifetime, with another awarded after his death. In Aristophanes's comedy The Frogs, Aeschylus mocks his verse by showing that any of his prologues can be finished with the phrase "lost his little oil flask," and he was known for his heavy use of the deus ex machina. The German Romantic critics August Wilhelm and Friedrich Schlegel later attacked him as inferior to his predecessors.

**The Oresteia**
Aeschylus's trilogy, first staged in 458 BCE and the only complete Greek tragic trilogy to survive. It consists of Agamemnon, The Libation Bearers, and The Eumenides, and it follows the curse on the house of Atreus from Agamemnon's murder to Orestes's trial.

**Seven Against Thebes**
A tragedy in which Eteocles, king of Thebes, defends the city against an army led by his exiled brother Polynices and six other Argive champions, one stationed at each of Thebes's seven gates. The two brothers kill each other in single combat, fulfilling their father Oedipus's curse.

**The Eumenides and the "Kindly Ones"**
The final play of the Oresteia. The Furies (Erinyes) pursue Orestes for killing his mother Clytemnestra, and Athena sets up a trial at the Areopagus in Athens; after Orestes is acquitted, Athena persuades the Furies to accept a new home and they are renamed the Eumenides, or "Kindly Ones."

**Apollo's argument that only the father is the true parent**
During Orestes's trial in The Eumenides, Apollo argues that the mother is merely a nurse for the seed planted by the father, so killing a mother is not killing a blood relative. He cites Athena, born from Zeus's head without a mother, as proof.

**Agamemnon and the purple carpet**
In Agamemnon, the king returns victorious from Troy and Clytemnestra persuades him to walk into the palace on rich purple (crimson) tapestries, an act of arrogance that offends the gods. She then murders him in his bath, along with his captive concubine Cassandra.

**Cassandra**
The Trojan prophetess brought home by Agamemnon as a war prize. In Agamemnon she foresees both his death and her own before entering the palace, where Clytemnestra kills her.

**The Persians**
The oldest surviving Greek tragedy (472 BCE) and a rare play on a recent historical event: the Greek victory over Xerxes at the Battle of Salamis. It is set at the Persian court, where Queen Atossa summons the ghost of her husband Darius, who blames their son Xerxes's arrogance for the disaster.

**The Suppliants and the Danaids**
A play in which the fifty daughters of Danaus (the Danaids) flee to Argos to escape forced marriage to their cousins, the fifty sons of Aegyptus. King Pelasgus and the Argive people vote to give them refuge. It was part of a tetralogy with the lost plays The Egyptians, The Danaids, and the satyr play Amymone, and it predates Euripides's play of the same name.

**Prometheus Bound**
A tragedy (traditionally attributed to Aeschylus, though its authorship is debated) in which the Titan Prometheus is chained to a rock in the Caucasus as punishment from Zeus for giving fire to humanity.

**Death by a tortoise dropped by an eagle**
According to legend, Aeschylus died in Sicily when an eagle, mistaking his bald head for a rock, dropped a tortoise on it to crack the shell.

**Battle of Marathon**
Aeschylus fought for Athens against the Persians at Marathon in 490 BCE, where his brother Cynegeirus was killed, and probably also at Salamis. His epitaph reportedly mentions only his military service at Marathon, not his plays.

**The Great Dionysia**
The Athenian festival of Dionysus where tragedies were performed in competition. Aeschylus was a frequent participant and won first prize many times, and he is credited with adding a second actor to tragedy.

**Lock of hair from Orestes**
In The Libation Bearers, Electra finds a lock of hair and footprints at Agamemnon's tomb and recognizes that her brother Orestes has returned. The siblings reunite and Orestes kills Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus.

**Capaneus and Tydeus at the gates**
Two of the Seven attackers whose shields and boasts are described in Seven Against Thebes. The blasphemous Capaneus boasts that not even Zeus could stop him, and Zeus strikes him down with a thunderbolt. Tydeus attacks the Proetid gate; in the wider myth he is given the head of the Theban Melanippus and eats its brain, which disgusts Athena so much that she withholds the immortality she meant to give him.

**Bhagavad Gita and Arjuna's charioteer**
The Bhagavad Gita, a 700-verse section of the Mahabharata, is a dialogue between Krishna and the Pandava prince Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra. Serving as Arjuna's charioteer, Krishna convinces the despairing Arjuna to fulfill his dharma as a warrior and fight, even against his own cousins and elders, and teaches him paths such as karma yoga and bhakti yoga.

**"Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds"**
In the Gita, Krishna reveals his cosmic, multi-armed universal form (Vishvarupa) to Arjuna and declares himself to be Time or Death, the destroyer of worlds. J. Robert Oppenheimer famously quoted the line after the first atomic bomb test.

**Kamsa**
Krishna's tyrannical uncle, the king of Mathura, who was warned that the eighth child of his sister Devaki would kill him. He imprisoned Devaki and her husband Vasudeva, killed their first six sons, and sent many demons after the infant Krishna, who eventually returned to Mathura, killed Kamsa, and restored Kamsa's father Ugrasena to the throne.

**Switched at birth**
To protect the newborn Krishna from Kamsa, Vasudeva carried him out of Mathura across the Yamuna to Gokul, swapping him with the baby daughter of Nanda and Yashoda (the goddess Yogamaya). When Kamsa tried to kill the girl, she rose into the sky and told him his slayer had already been born. Krishna was then raised by Nanda and Yashoda among the cowherds.

**Govardhan Hill**
When Krishna persuaded the cowherds to stop worshipping Indra, the angry god sent torrential rains. Krishna lifted Mount Govardhana on one finger (often his little finger) and held it up as an umbrella for seven days to shelter the villagers of Vrindavan.

**Makhan Chor ("butter thief")**
As a mischievous child, Krishna was famous for stealing butter and curds from the milkmaids, sometimes with his friends forming a human pyramid to reach the pots hung from the ceiling. He is often depicted as a child eating butter.

**Radha, the gopis, and the flute**
In his youth in Vrindavan, Krishna played the flute and enchanted the gopis (cowherd girls), dancing with them in the Rasa Lila. His favorite was Radha, who is worshipped as his divine consort. He is usually shown with blue or dark skin, and his name means "black" or "dark."

**Death by Jara's arrow**
At the end of his life, while Krishna was resting or meditating in the forest, the hunter Jara mistook his foot for a deer and shot it with an arrow. The arrow's tip was made from a piece of the iron pestle (or bolt) that had doomed the Yadavas, fulfilling Gandhari's curse that Krishna and his clan would perish 36 years after the war.

**Duryodhana chooses the Narayani Sena**
Before the war, Duryodhana and Arjuna both came to Krishna in Dvaraka for help, standing at the head and the foot of his bed as he slept. Krishna offered either his army, the Narayani Sena, or himself as a non-combatant; Duryodhana chose the army and Arjuna chose Krishna, who became his charioteer.

**Putana**
A demoness sent by Kamsa who disguised herself as a beautiful woman and tried to kill the infant Krishna by breastfeeding him with poison. Krishna sucked the life out of her along with the milk.

**Kaliya**
A many-headed serpent who poisoned the Yamuna River. Krishna jumped into the water and danced on Kaliya's hoods until the serpent submitted and left, purifying the river.

**Balarama**
Krishna's older brother, often considered an incarnation of the serpent Shesha. He was transferred from Devaki's womb to that of Rohini, is fair-skinned, and wields a plow (hala) as a weapon.

**Narakasura and the 16,100 wives**
Krishna slew the demon Narakasura with his discus, the Sudarshana Chakra, and freed the 16,100 women Narakasura had held captive. To preserve their dignity, Krishna married all of them.

**Dvaraka and Jarasandha**
To protect the Yadavas from repeated attacks by Kamsa's father-in-law Jarasandha, Krishna moved the population of Mathura to Dvaraka, a city built by the divine architect Vishvakarma. Jarasandha was later killed in a wrestling duel by the Pandava Bhima, with Krishna's guidance.

**Eighth avatar of Vishnu and Hare Krishna**
Krishna is usually counted as the eighth of the ten avatars (Dashavatara) of Vishnu, followed by the Buddha and Kalki. He is the focus of the Bhagavata Purana and the Hare Krishna movement (ISKCON), whose mantra chants his name, and of the devotional poet Meerabai, said to have merged into his statue at the end of her life.

**Net trapping Ares and Aphrodite**
After Helios told Hephaestus that his wife Aphrodite was having an affair with Ares, Hephaestus forged a fine, nearly invisible golden net over his bed. It caught the lovers in the act, and he summoned the other gods, who roared with laughter; Poseidon pleaded for their release, guaranteeing that Ares would pay the adulterer's fine. The story is told in Book 8 of the Odyssey.

**Thrown from Olympus to Lemnos**
Hephaestus was cast down from Mount Olympus, either by his mother Hera, ashamed of his lameness, or by Zeus, for siding with Hera. In the Iliad he falls for a whole day and lands on the island of Lemnos, where the Sintian people cared for him; the fall is sometimes said to have caused his lameness, and Lemnos became sacred to him.

**Golden throne trapping Hera**
In revenge for being thrown from Olympus, Hephaestus sent his mother Hera a beautiful golden throne. When she sat in it, invisible chains bound her, and no other god could free her.

**Return of Hephaestus**
Ares failed to force Hephaestus back to Olympus, but Dionysus got him drunk on wine and brought him back slumped on the back of a mule, a scene often shown in Greek vase painting, such as on the François Vase. Hephaestus then freed Hera, and in some versions he was given Aphrodite as his wife in exchange.

**Erichthonius**
When Hephaestus tried to rape Athena, his semen fell on her leg; she wiped it off with wool and threw it to the ground, impregnating Gaia (the Earth). The child, Erichthonius (sometimes identified with Erechtheus), became a king of Athens; Athena hid the infant in a box and gave it to the three daughters of Cecrops, who were forbidden to open it.

**Husband of Aphrodite**
Hephaestus, considered the ugliest of the gods, was married to Aphrodite, the most beautiful, in some versions so that the other gods would not fight over her. In other sources (Homer's Iliad and Hesiod's Theogony), his wife is instead the Grace Charis or Aglaea.

**Fighting the Scamander**
In Book 21 of the Iliad, the river god Scamander (Xanthus) floods and nearly drowns Achilles, who has choked its waters with Trojan corpses. Hera sends Hephaestus, who attacks the river with fire, boiling and drying it up until it yields.

**Pandora**
At Zeus's command, Hephaestus fashioned Pandora, the first woman, out of clay or earth, as a punishment for mankind after Prometheus stole fire. The other gods then gave her gifts.

**Armor of Achilles**
In Book 18 of the Iliad, Achilles' mother Thetis asks Hephaestus to make new armor for her son after Patroclus loses his old armor to Hector. Hephaestus forges it, including an elaborately decorated shield showing scenes of the cosmos, cities, and everyday life.

**Automatons**
Hephaestus built many self-moving creations: golden mechanical maidens who served him, three-legged tripods on golden wheels that moved on their own, the fire-breathing bronze bulls of King Aeetes that Jason had to yoke, the gold and silver dogs guarding King Alcinous's palace, and the bronze giant Talos, who guarded Crete until Medea removed the nail that sealed his single vein.

**Splitting Zeus's head**
When Zeus suffered a terrible headache after swallowing the pregnant Metis, Hephaestus (or Prometheus in some versions) split his head open with an axe, and Athena sprang out fully armed.

**Born from Hera alone**
In Hesiod's Theogony, Hera conceived Hephaestus by herself, without a father, in anger at Zeus for producing Athena on his own. In other accounts, he is the son of Zeus and Hera.

**Forge beneath Mount Etna**
Later tradition placed Hephaestus's workshop under the volcano Mount Etna in Sicily (or on Lemnos), where the Cyclopes worked as his assistants. His Roman counterpart, Vulcan, gives us the word "volcano."

**Periphetes**
A club-wielding son of Hephaestus who robbed and murdered travelers on the road near Epidaurus. Theseus killed him and took his bronze club as his own weapon.

**Cabeiri**
Mysterious deities worshipped in mystery cults on Samothrace and Lemnos, often described as the sons of Hephaestus by the nymph Cabeiro, a daughter of Proteus.

**Lover of Aphrodite**
Adonis was a strikingly handsome mortal youth with whom Aphrodite fell in love. His name became a byword for male beauty.

**Killed by a boar**
Despite Aphrodite's warnings not to hunt wild beasts, Adonis went hunting and was gored to death by a wild boar. In some versions, the boar was the jealous Ares in disguise.

**Anemone flowers from his blood**
As Aphrodite mourned Adonis, she sprinkled nectar on his blood, and the anemone, a short-lived red flower, sprang up from it. The flower's brief bloom symbolizes his short life.

**Myrrha and Cinyras (birth from incest)**
Adonis's mother Myrrha (also called Smyrna) was cursed to desire her own father, King Cinyras, and tricked him into sleeping with her in the dark. When Cinyras discovered the truth he tried to kill her, and the gods turned her into a myrrh tree, from which Adonis was born.

**Cinyras's arrow and the myrrh tree**
In one account of Adonis's birth, Cinyras shot an arrow into (or struck) the myrrh tree that Myrrha had become, splitting it open and releasing the baby Adonis.

**The chest given to Persephone**
Aphrodite hid the infant Adonis in a chest and gave it to Persephone, queen of the underworld, for safekeeping. Persephone opened it, fell in love with the child, and refused to give him back.

**Dividing the year between Aphrodite and Persephone**
Zeus (or the Muse Calliope, in some versions) settled the dispute by dividing Adonis's year into thirds: one third with Persephone, one third with Aphrodite, and one third wherever he wished, which he also chose to spend with Aphrodite. This cycle links him to the yearly death and rebirth of vegetation.

**Tammuz (Dumuzid)**
Adonis's worship was linked and often syncretized with that of the Mesopotamian shepherd god Dumuzid (Tammuz), the lover of Inanna (Ishtar), who also dies and spends part of each year in the underworld. Adonis's name likely comes from the Semitic word "adon," meaning "lord."

**Gardens of Adonis**
During the festival of the Adonia, women planted fast-growing seeds in shallow pots or small plots called "gardens of Adonis." The plants sprouted quickly and withered in the sun within about eight days, symbolizing Adonis's early death, and the women then mourned him.

**Golgos and Beroe**
According to some accounts, Golgos and Beroe were the children of Adonis and Aphrodite. Golgos was the namesake founder of the city of Golgi on Cyprus, and Beroe was associated with the city of Beirut.

**Phaethon**
Helios's son, who begged to drive his father's sun chariot for one day. He lost control of the horses and scorched the earth, which in myth turned Africa into desert and darkened the skin of the Ethiopians. Zeus struck him down with a thunderbolt, and he fell into the river Eridanus.

**Cattle of Thrinacia**
Helios's sacred herds on the island of Thrinacia. In the Odyssey, both Tiresias and Circe warn Odysseus not to harm them, but while Odysseus sleeps, his starving crew, urged on by Eurylochus, slaughter and eat some. Helios demands revenge, and Zeus destroys their ship with a thunderbolt, killing everyone except Odysseus.

**Lampetia and Phaethusa**
Helios's daughters who tend his herds on Thrinacia; Phaethusa uses a copper staff. Lampetia brings Helios the news that Odysseus's men have slaughtered his cattle.

**Heliades (poplars and amber)**
Phaethon's sisters, the daughters of Helios, mourned him so long by the Eridanus that they turned into poplar trees. Their tears hardened into amber.

**Golden cup for Heracles**
On his way to steal the cattle of Geryon (his tenth labor), Heracles was so bothered by the heat that he aimed his bow at Helios. Admiring his boldness, Helios lent him the huge golden cup (or bowl) in which the sun sails back east across Oceanus each night, and Heracles used it to sail to the island of Erytheia.

**Rhodes**
The island most associated with Helios. When the gods divided up the earth, Helios was away and was left out, so he chose Rhodes, which was just rising from the sea. The Colossus of Rhodes was a statue of him, and in the Rhodian festival (the Halieia), worshippers threw a chariot and four horses into the sea in his honor.

**Circe, Aeetes, and Pasiphae**
Helios's children with the Oceanid Perse. They are the sorceress Circe of Aeaea, King Aeetes of Colchis (father of Medea), and Pasiphae, wife of King Minos of Crete and mother of the Minotaur.

**Revealing Ares and Aphrodite's affair**
Helios, who sees everything from the sky, told Hephaestus that his wife Aphrodite was sleeping with Ares. Hephaestus then caught them in a fine net. Ares had posted the youth Alectryon to warn of Helios's approach, and when Alectryon fell asleep, Ares turned him into a rooster, which now always crows at sunrise.

**Clytie**
An Oceanid nymph who loved Helios. He rejected her after she told Leucothoe's father about their affair. She wasted away staring at the sun as it crossed the sky and was turned into a flower that always faces the sun (the heliotrope, often called a sunflower).

**Leucothoe**
A Persian princess whom Helios seduced by disguising himself as her mother so he could enter her room. When her father found out, he buried her alive, and Helios turned her body into a frankincense plant. Ovid tells the story in the Metamorphoses.

**Hyperion and Theia**
Helios's parents, both Titans. His sisters are Eos (the dawn) and Selene (the moon), and he is often called a Titan himself.

**Pyrois, Aethon, and Phlegon**
Names of the fire-breathing horses that pull Helios's chariot across the sky every day (a fourth is usually named Eous). Their names refer to fire and burning.

**Medea's dragon chariot**
Helios gave his granddaughter Medea a chariot drawn by winged dragons (serpents). In Euripides's Medea, she escapes in it from Corinth after killing her two sons.

**Panoptes and conflation with Apollo**
Like Argus, Helios was called Panoptes ("all-seeing"), and he was often called on as a witness to oaths. In the Hellenistic period he was increasingly identified with Phoebus Apollo. The Roman emperor Julian the Apostate tried to revive worship of the sun god, and Plato's Republic compares the sun to the Form of the Good.

**Acrocorinth**
According to Pausanias, Helios and Poseidon competed for Corinth. The Hundred-Handed Briareus, who judged the dispute, gave the Isthmus to Poseidon and the Acrocorinth, the city's high citadel, to Helios.

**Gleipnir**
The magical fetter the dwarves make to finally bind Fenrir. It looks like a thin silken ribbon but is made of six impossible things: the sound of a cat's footfall, the beard of a woman, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish, and the spittle of a bird. Because these were used up, they no longer exist in the world.

**Tyr loses his hand**
Fenrir suspects a trick and agrees to be bound with Gleipnir only if one of the gods puts a hand in his mouth as a pledge of good faith. Only Tyr, the god of war and law who had also been the only god brave enough to feed the wolf, does so. When Fenrir cannot break free, he bites off Tyr's right hand.

**Killing Odin at Ragnarok**
At Ragnarok, the end of the world in Norse myth, Fenrir breaks free of Gleipnir and swallows Odin, the chief of the gods. He advances with his lower jaw on the earth and his upper jaw against the sky, and flames burn from his eyes and nostrils.

**Vidar and the thick shoe**
Odin's son Vidar avenges his father by killing Fenrir. In Snorri's Prose Edda he steps on the wolf's lower jaw with a thick shoe made from all the leather scraps people have ever cut away, then tears the jaws apart; in the poem Voluspa he stabs the wolf in the heart.

**Skoll and Hati**
Fenrir's sons, born to a giantess in the forest Ironwood (Jarnvid). Skoll chases the sun, whose chariot is pulled by the horses Arvakr and Alsvidr, and Hati chases the moon (Mani). At Ragnarok they catch and swallow the sun and moon.

**Son of Loki and Angrboda**
Fenrir is one of three monstrous children of the trickster god Loki and the giantess Angrboda. His siblings are the world serpent Jormungandr and Hel, ruler of the dead. Prophecies said these children would bring disaster, so the gods brought the wolf to Asgard to keep watch on him.

**Laeding and Dromi**
The first two iron fetters the gods use on Fenrir as he grows alarmingly large. They present the binding as a test of strength, and he easily breaks both, which gave rise to sayings about "getting loose from Laeding" and "striking out of Dromi."

**River Van**
After he is bound, the gods jam a sword into Fenrir's mouth, with the hilt against his lower jaw and the point against his upper jaw, to keep him from biting. Drool and blood flowing from his mouth form the river Van, which gives him the name Vanagandr ("monster of the Van").

**Lyngvi, Amsvartnir, Gelgja, Gjoll, and Thviti**
Fenrir is bound on the island of Lyngvi in the lake Amsvartnir. The gods attach a cord called Gelgja to Gleipnir, thread it through a boulder called Gjoll, and fix it deep in the earth with a stone called Thviti.

**Gylfaginning (Prose Edda)**
Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda tells the full binding story in its Gylfaginning section, where the figure High explains it to the disguised king Gangleri. High says the gods did not simply kill Fenrir because they did not want to defile their sacred places with his blood.

**Thorwald's Cross and the Gosforth Cross**
Viking Age stone crosses with Fenrir imagery. Thorwald's Cross on the Isle of Man shows Odin, with a raven on his shoulder, being devoured by Fenrir, and the Gosforth Cross in Cumbria is usually read as showing Vidar confronting the wolf, scenes that may parallel Christian images of Satan's defeat.

**Alternate names: Fenrisulfr, Hrodvitnir, Vanagandr**
Fenrir is also called the Fenris wolf (Fenrisulfr), Hrodvitnir ("famous wolf"), and Vanagandr ("monster of the river Van"). Any of these may appear as accepted answers.

**Sacrificing an eye at Mimir's well**
Odin gave up one of his eyes in exchange for a drink from the well of Mimir, which lies beneath a root of Yggdrasil and grants wisdom. This is why he is depicted as one-eyed. He also preserved the severed head of Mimir (killed by the Vanir) with herbs and magic so he could keep consulting it for advice and prophecy.

**Hanging from Yggdrasil for nine days and nights**
In the Havamal, Odin describes hanging himself from the World Tree, wounded by his own spear and "sacrificed to himself," for nine days and nights without food or drink. At the end of this ordeal he discovered and seized the runes, the magical alphabet (including letters like fehu, uruz, and ansuz).

**Huginn and Muninn**
Odin's two ravens, whose names mean "Thought" and "Memory." They fly across the world each day and return to perch on his shoulders and report the news they have gathered. Their presence is how scholars identify the earliest depictions of Odin.

**Mead of Poetry**
A drink brewed by the dwarves Fjalar and Galar from the blood of the wise being Kvasir, later held by the giant Suttung inside a mountain and guarded by his daughter Gunnlod. Disguised as the farmhand Bolverk, Odin worked for Suttung's brother Baugi (after tricking Baugi's nine servants into killing each other over a whetstone he tossed in the air), turned into a snake to slither through a hole Baugi drilled, and slept with Gunnlod for three nights to win three drinks. He escaped as an eagle, and the mead he spilled out of his rear end became the share of bad poets.

**Sleipnir**
Odin's eight-legged horse, the swiftest of all steeds. Sleipnir was born to Loki, who had turned into a mare to distract the stallion Svadilfari while a giant was building the walls of Asgard. Odin rides him to the underworld in some myths.

**Killing Ymir with Vili and Ve**
Odin and his brothers Vili and Ve, sons of Borr and the giantess Bestla, slew the primordial frost giant Ymir and built the world from his body. Borr's father Buri was licked out of a block of salty ice by the cow Audhumla.

**Killed by Fenrir at Ragnarok**
At the end of the world, Odin is swallowed and killed by the monstrous wolf Fenrir, Loki's son. His son Vidar then avenges him by stepping into the wolf's jaws with a special thick shoe (made from leather scraps) and tearing the jaws apart.

**Gungnir**
Odin's spear, which never misses its target. It was forged by the dwarven Sons of Ivaldi, and Odin wields it in battle at Ragnarok. He is also wounded by it while hanging on Yggdrasil.

**Geri and Freki**
Odin's two wolves, whose names both mean "greedy" or "ravenous." Odin lives on wine (or mead) alone and gives all the food set before him in Valhalla to these wolves.

**Draupnir**
A gold arm ring forged by dwarves, which drips eight new rings of equal weight every ninth night. Odin placed it on the funeral pyre of his son Baldr.

**Hlidskjalf**
Odin's high seat or throne, from which he can see across all the worlds. From here he watches events such as the reign of his foster son Geirroth.

**Ask and Embla**
The first man and woman, created from two tree trunks (ash and elm) found on the seashore. Odin gave them breath or spirit, while his companions (Vili and Ve, or Hoenir and Lodurr) gave them other gifts like sense and appearance.

**Geirroth and the Grimnismal**
In the Eddic poem Grimnismal, Odin visits his foster son King Geirroth in the guise of the wanderer Grimnir. Mistaken for a sorcerer, he is tortured between two fires until he reveals himself, and Geirroth dies by falling on his own sword.

**Vafthrudnir**
A wise giant whom Odin, disguised as Gagnrad, challenges to a contest of wisdom on pain of losing one's head in the Vafthrudnismal. Odin wins with an unanswerable question: what did he whisper into the ear of his son Baldr on Baldr's funeral pyre?

**High, Just-As-High, and Third**
The three mysterious figures who answer the questions of King Gylfi in the Gylfaginning section of Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda. They are often interpreted as guises or aspects of Odin himself.

**The Twelve Labors for King Eurystheus**
After Hera drove Heracles mad and he killed his first wife Megara and their children, he served his cousin Eurystheus, king of Tiryns, as penance by performing twelve labors. Eurystheus was so frightened of Heracles and the creatures he brought back that he hid in a bronze wine jar (pithos). He also refused to count two labors, the Hydra (because Iolaus helped) and the Augean stables (because Heracles asked Augeas for payment), so ten tasks grew to twelve.

**Nemean Lion**
The first labor. The lion's hide could not be pierced by arrows, so Heracles strangled it with his bare hands. He then wore its skin as his trademark cloak, and that lion pelt and his club are his standard attributes.

**Lernaean Hydra and Iolaus**
The second labor was to kill the many-headed serpent of Lerna, which grew back two heads for each one cut off. Heracles drove it from its lair at the spring of Amymone with flaming arrows, and his nephew and charioteer Iolaus burned (cauterized) each neck stump with a torch so the heads could not regrow. Hera sent a giant crab that pinched Heracles's foot during the fight. Heracles dipped his arrows in the Hydra's poisonous blood and buried its immortal head under a rock.

**Deianira, Nessus, and the poisoned shirt**
Heracles won his second wife Deianira by wrestling the river god Achelous and breaking off one of his horns. When the centaur Nessus tried to carry her off, Heracles shot him with a Hydra-poisoned arrow. The dying Nessus told Deianira that his blood was a love charm. Years later, jealous of Heracles's captive Iole, she soaked a shirt (tunic) in it and sent it to him with the herald Lichas. The poison burned Heracles's flesh, he hurled Lichas into the sea, and he had himself burned alive on a pyre on Mount Oeta. He then rose to Olympus as a god and married Hebe, goddess of youth.

**Augean stables**
For one labor Heracles had to clean the enormous, filthy cattle stables of King Augeas of Elis in a single day. He did it by diverting the rivers Alpheus and Peneus through them. When Augeas refused to pay the promised tenth of his cattle, Heracles later deposed him and put his son Phyleus on the throne.

**Birth from Alcmene, Amphitryon, and Iphicles**
Zeus took the form of Amphitryon to sleep with his wife Alcmene, so Heracles was born alongside his mortal twin half-brother Iphicles, Amphitryon's son. Hera had the birth goddess Eileithyia delay Heracles's birth so that Eurystheus would be born first and inherit power. Alcmene's servant Galanthis tricked Eileithyia into ending the delay and was turned into a weasel. Heracles's birth name was Alcaeus (or Alcides).

**Strangling the snakes in the cradle**
As an infant, Heracles strangled two serpents that Hera sent to kill him, while his twin Iphicles screamed in terror. This is the first proof of his superhuman strength.

**Serving Queen Omphale**
After throwing Iphitus, son of King Eurytus, from the walls of Tiryns, Heracles was told by an oracle (the priestess Xenoclea) that he could be purified only by being sold into slavery. He served Queen Omphale of Lydia, often described as wearing women's clothes and doing spinning while she wore his lion skin. During this period he also captured the Cercopes, mischievous thieves whom he hung upside down from a pole on his shoulder and then released because their jokes amused him.

**Stymphalian Birds and the krotala**
Another labor was to drive off the metal-feathered, man-eating birds of Lake Stymphalia. Athena gave Heracles bronze krotala (rattles or castanets made by Hephaestus), and their noise scared the birds into the air so he could shoot them.

**Bow and poisoned arrows, given to Philoctetes**
Heracles's arrows, dipped in the Hydra's blood, killed Nessus, the Stymphalian birds, and Geryon. Because Philoctetes lit Heracles's funeral pyre, he received the bow and arrows. The seer Helenus later prophesied that the Greeks needed these weapons to take Troy, so they fetched Philoctetes from Lemnos, where he had been left with a festering snake bite.

**Cattle of Geryon and the cup of Helios**
For the tenth labor Heracles fetched the cattle of the three-bodied giant Geryon from the far west, killing the two-headed dog Orthrus and the herdsman Eurytion. When the sun's heat bothered him, he aimed an arrow at Helios, who admired his boldness and lent him his golden cup (boat) to sail across the ocean.

**Capture of Cerberus**
The twelfth and final labor was to bring the three-headed hound of Hades up from the underworld. Heracles wrestled the dog into submission with his bare hands. While in the underworld he freed Theseus and lifted the boulder pinning Ascalaphus.

**Hylas and the Argonauts**
Heracles sailed with the Argonauts, accompanied by his beloved young companion Hylas, son of the Dryopian king Theiodamas, whom Heracles had killed. When Hylas was pulled into a spring by water nymphs in Mysia, Heracles stayed behind searching for him and the Argo left without him.

**Linus and Chiron**
As a youth Heracles killed his music teacher Linus (who also taught Orpheus) by striking him with a lyre after being scolded. He also accidentally wounded the wise centaur Chiron with a poisoned arrow while fighting centaurs, a related story to the one in which his poisoned arrows killed the centaur Pholus during the hunt for the Erymanthian Boar.

**Wrestling Antaeus and Thanatos**
Heracles defeated the Libyan giant Antaeus, a son of Poseidon and Gaia who drew strength from touching the earth, by lifting him off the ground and crushing him. He also wrestled Thanatos (Death) to bring Alcestis back to her husband Admetus. Other popular side adventures include killing the Egyptian king Busiris, who sacrificed strangers, and his first sack of Troy after King Laomedon refused him the promised horses, sparing only Priam (Podarces), who was ransomed by his sister Hesione.

**Anansi**
The trickster of Akan (Ashanti) folklore in West Africa, who usually takes the form of a spider. He is the owner of all stories, and his tales spread through the Caribbean and the American South, where some merged with the Br'er Rabbit stories.

**Buying the world's stories from Nyame**
The most famous Anansi tale. The sky god Nyame owned all stories and sold them to Anansi for a seemingly impossible price: Onini the python, Osebo the leopard, the Mmoboro hornets, and Mmoatia the fairy. Anansi captured each by trickery and delivered them, so stories became known as "spider stories" (Anansesem).

**Anansi measuring the python**
To capture Onini, Anansi and his wife Aso staged a loud argument over whether the python was longer than a palm branch. The offended python stretched out along the branch to prove it, and Anansi tied him to it.

**Arachne**
In Greek myth, especially Ovid's Metamorphoses, Arachne was a mortal weaver from Lydia who boasted she was better than Athena (Minerva). In their weaving contest, Arachne flawlessly depicted the gods' crimes, particularly Zeus's seductions. The jealous goddess tore up the tapestry, Arachne tried to hang herself, and Athena sprinkled her with the juice of aconite (Hecate's herb), turning her into a spider.

**Arachne's family**
Arachne was the daughter of Idmon of Colophon, a dyer of wool in Tyrian purple. Her son Closter was credited with inventing the spindle.

**Spider Grandmother (Hopi)**
In Hopi mythology, Spider Grandmother (Kokyangwuti) is a creator figure who helped make humanity and guided the people upward through the First, Second, and Third Worlds into the present Fourth World.

**Spider Woman (Navajo)**
In Navajo (Diné) myth, Spider Woman (Na'ashjé'ii Asdzáá) helps the Hero Twins, Monster Slayer (Naayéé' Neizghání) and Born for Water (Tó Bájísh Chíní), on their journey to their father, the Sun, giving them protective eagle feathers. She is also credited with teaching the Navajo to weave.

**Iktomi**
The spider trickster spirit of the Lakota. He is a shapeshifter who often breaks cultural taboos (in one story he marries his own daughter), and his tales serve as cautionary examples.

**Anansi and the pot of wisdom**
Anansi tried to hoard all the world's wisdom in a pot or calabash and hide it at the top of a tree. When he struggled to climb with it tied to his front, his son pointed out it would be easier on his back, and in frustration Anansi dropped it, scattering wisdom throughout the world.

**Teotihuacan Spider Woman**
Archaeologists' name for the "Great Goddess" of the ancient Mesoamerican city Teotihuacan, shown in murals with spider-related imagery such as a mouth-mask resembling spider fangs.

**Jorōgumo**
A Japanese yōkai, a spider that can transform into a beautiful woman to lure men to her lair, where she binds them in silk and eats them.

**Robert the Bruce's spider**
According to Scottish legend, the defeated king Robert the Bruce, hiding in a cave, watched a spider repeatedly fail and then succeed at spinning its web. This inspired him to keep fighting the English, leading to his victory at Bannockburn.

**Guardian of Bifrost**
Heimdallr is the watchman of the Norse gods, stationed at the rainbow bridge Bifrost that connects Asgard to the other worlds. Guarding against the approach of giants is his defining role and the most common giveaway.

**Gjallarhorn**
The horn that Heimdallr will sound to alert the gods and announce the beginning of Ragnarok, the final battle at the end of the world.

**Kills and is killed by Loki at Ragnarok**
Heimdallr and Loki are bitter enemies, and at Ragnarok they are destined to slay each other in combat.

**Brisingamen and the seal fight**
When Loki steals Freyja's necklace Brisingamen, Heimdallr takes the form of a seal and fights Loki, also in seal form, to recover it. The fight takes place at the rock Singasteinn, near the islet Vagasker.

**Nine mothers**
Heimdallr was born of nine mothers, often described as sisters or maidens. The Lay of Hyndla names some of them, including Gjalp and Greip, and they are sometimes identified with the nine wave daughters of the sea giant Aegir and Ran.

**Rig and the Rigsthula**
In the Eddic poem Rigsthula, Heimdallr, wandering under the name Rig, visits three couples, sleeps between each husband and wife, and fathers Thrall, Karl, and Jarl, the ancestors of the serfs, free farmers, and nobles. Jarl's son Kon the Young becomes a king who understands the speech of birds. The Voluspa likewise addresses humanity as Heimdallr's children.

**Gullintanni ("golden-toothed")**
An epithet of Heimdallr referring to his teeth of pure gold. He is also called Hallinskidi and Vindhler.

**Hears grass and wool grow**
Heimdallr's senses are extraordinarily keen: he needs less sleep than a bird, can see a hundred leagues by night as well as by day, and can hear grass growing in the ground and wool growing on sheep.

**Thrymskvida plan to disguise Thor**
In the Eddic poem Thrymskvida, after the giant Thrym steals Thor's hammer Mjolnir and demands Freyja as his bride, Heimdallr proposes that Thor dress as Freyja in a bridal veil to retrieve it.

**"Whitest of the gods"**
Heimdallr is called the whitest or brightest of the Aesir. In the Lokasenna, Loki mocks him for being doomed to stand watch with a wet or muddy back, after Heimdallr tells Loki he is drunk.

**Hofund**
Heimdallr's sword, whose name means "head." Heimdallr's head is a kenning for "sword" because, according to a lost poem cited in the Skaldskaparmal, Heimdallr was pierced or struck by a man's head.

**Himinbjorg**
Heimdallr's hall, whose name means "Heaven's Mountain" or "Cliffs of Heaven." It stands near Bifrost at the edge of heaven, and there he drinks fine mead.

**Gulltoppr**
Heimdallr's horse, whose name means "golden mane" or "golden forelock."

**Well of Mimir**
The Voluspa says that Heimdallr's hearing (or his horn) is hidden in Mimir's well beneath Yggdrasil, paralleling Odin's eye, which is also pledged there. He is sometimes said to drink from it to gain wisdom.

**Turning Odysseus's men into pigs**
Circe's most famous act and the usual giveaway. In Book 10 of the Odyssey, she welcomes Odysseus's scouts into her house, feeds them food mixed with a magic drug, and taps them with her wand, turning them into swine.

**Moly**
A magic herb with a black root and a milk-white flower that Hermes gives Odysseus to protect him from Circe's drugs. Protected by it, Odysseus resists her spell and frees his men.

**Aeaea**
Circe's island home, where she lives in a stone house in a clearing surrounded by tame wolves and lions (probably men she has enchanted). Some sources even call Circe herself "Aeaea."

**Telegonus and the stingray spear**
Circe's son by Odysseus, the hero of the lost epic Telegony. Searching for his father, he lands on Ithaca and accidentally kills Odysseus with a spear tipped with a poisonous stingray spine, which fulfills the prophecy that Odysseus's death would come "from the sea." Circe gave him the spear.

**Scylla**
Circe loved the sea god Glaucus, a former fisherman, but he loved the nymph Scylla instead. In jealousy, Circe poisoned the pool where Scylla bathed and turned her into the many-headed monster who lives in a strait opposite the whirlpool Charybdis. Ovid tells the story in the Metamorphoses.

**Purifying Jason and Medea of Apsyrtus's murder**
In Apollonius's Argonautica, Jason and Medea come to Aeaea after murdering Medea's brother Apsyrtus. Circe, who is Medea's aunt, purifies them with the blood of a piglet, but once she learns what they did, she sends them away.

**Advice on the Underworld and Tiresias**
Circe tells Odysseus he must journey to the Underworld (the Nekyia) to consult the dead seer Tiresias about how to get home to Ithaca. She explains how to pour libations and sacrifice a ram and a ewe so the shades will come to drink the blood. When he returns, she warns him about the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, and not to eat the cattle of her father Helios.

**Elpenor**
The youngest of Odysseus's crew, who drunkenly fell asleep on the roof of Circe's house and broke his neck falling off as the crew was leaving. His ghost meets Odysseus in the Underworld and asks for a proper burial, which they give him, marking his tomb with his oar.

**Picus**
A Latin king who loved the nymph Canens and rejected Circe. In Ovid's Metamorphoses, the angry Circe turned him into a woodpecker (picus in Latin).

**Helios and Perse**
Circe's parents: the sun god Helios and the Oceanid Perse. Her siblings include Aeetes, king of Colchis and father of Medea, and Pasiphae, wife of Minos.

**Sword and oath**
Protected by moly, Odysseus draws his sword on Circe as Hermes instructed. She then swears an oath by the gods not to harm him or "unman" him, and he becomes her lover for a year.

**Eurylochus**
Odysseus's second-in-command, who leads the scouting party to Circe's house. Suspecting a trap, he stays outside, so he is the only one not turned into a pig, and he escapes to warn Odysseus.

**Latinus and Agrius**
At the end of Hesiod's Theogony, Circe and Odysseus are named as parents of Agrius and Latinus, who rule over the Tyrsenians (Etruscans). This connects her to Italian legend.

**Madeline Miller's Circe**
A 2018 novel retelling her life. In it, Helios banishes her to Aeaea to avoid angering Zeus, and after Odysseus's death at Telegonus's hands she marries Telemachus.

**Bhagavad Gita**
The most famous section of the Mahabharata, a dialogue on the battlefield of Kurukshetra in which Krishna, serving as Arjuna's charioteer, persuades the hesitant warrior to fight his own relatives and teachers in fulfillment of his dharma as a kshatriya (warrior). It is the most common giveaway for the epic.

**Kurukshetra War, Pandavas vs. Kauravas**
The epic's central conflict is an eighteen-day war at Kurukshetra between two branches of the Kuru dynasty: the five Pandava brothers (Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula, and Sahadeva) and their hundred cousins, the Kauravas, led by Duryodhana.

**Draupadi's disrobing**
After Yudhishthira wagers and loses Draupadi in the dice game, the Kauravas attempt to strip her in the royal court. Her sari miraculously grows endlessly, often attributed to Krishna's intervention, so that she cannot be disrobed.

**Rigged game of dice**
Yudhishthira loses his kingdom, his brothers, himself, and Draupadi in a dice game rigged by Shakuni on behalf of Duryodhana. As a result, the Pandavas are sent into twelve years of forest exile, including time in the Kamyaka forest, followed by a thirteenth year in disguise.

**Draupadi marries five brothers**
Arjuna wins Draupadi at her svayamvara by shooting an arrow through the eye of a rotating mechanical fish while looking only at its reflection. When the brothers return home and tell their mother Kunti to see what they have brought, she tells them to share it equally without looking, so all five marry Draupadi.

**Vyasa and Ganesha**
The epic is attributed to the sage Vyasa, who dictated it to Ganesha. Ganesha agreed to write it only if Vyasa never paused, and Vyasa required that Ganesha write only what he understood; Ganesha broke off his tusk to use as a pen.

**Bhishma's bed of arrows**
Bhishma, the celibate grand-uncle of both sides, vowed never to fight a woman, so the Pandavas put Shikhandi, who was born female and later became a man, in front of him in battle. Pierced by Arjuna's arrows, he lies on a bed of arrows, delaying his death until the winter solstice and reciting teachings such as the Vishnu Sahasranama to Yudhishthira.

**Gandhari's blindfold and the hundred pots**
Gandhari, wife of the blind king Dhritarashtra, blindfolds herself for life to share her husband's suffering. She gives birth to a ball of flesh that is divided into 101 pots of ghee, producing the hundred Kaurava sons and one daughter, Duhshala.

**Kunti and Karna**
Kunti, the Pandavas' mother, received a boon to summon any god to father a child. As an unmarried girl she bore Karna to the sun god Surya and set him adrift on a river in a basket, where he was raised by a charioteer. Karna fights for the Kauravas and is killed by Arjuna.

**Illusory floor in the Pandava palace**
In the Pandavas' magnificent hall at Indraprastha, Duryodhana mistakes a polished floor for water and then falls into a real pool he takes for floor. Draupadi's mocking laughter deepens his humiliation and hatred of the Pandavas.

**House of lac**
Duryodhana tries to kill the Pandavas by having them stay in a palace made of lac (wax) and other flammable materials, which is then set on fire. The Pandavas escape through a secret underground tunnel.

**Death of Drona**
To kill the Kaurava general and archery teacher Drona (Dronacharya), Yudhishthira, who had never lied, announces that "Ashwatthama is dead," quietly adding that it was an elephant. Drona, believing his son is dead, lays down his arms and is killed; Yudhishthira's chariot, which had floated above the ground because of his truthfulness, sinks to earth.

**Ekalavya's thumb**
Ekalavya, a tribal youth of low birth, secretly masters archery by practicing before a clay image of Drona; he reveals his skill by shooting arrows into a barking dog's mouth to silence it. Drona demands his right thumb as a teacher's fee, and Ekalavya cuts it off.

**Yudhishthira and the dog**
At the end of the epic, the Pandavas and Draupadi climb the Himalayas toward heaven, and all except Yudhishthira fall along the way because of their faults. Yudhishthira refuses to enter heaven without the loyal dog accompanying him, which turns out to be the god Dharma in disguise.

**Bhima and Duryodhana's thighs**
The mighty Pandava Bhima kills the demon Bakasura and later fulfills a vow by killing Duryodhana with a mace blow to the thighs. After the war, the grieving Dhritarashtra crushes an iron statue of Bhima, believing it to be Bhima himself.

**Sita and Ravana**
Rama's wife Sita is abducted by Ravana, the ten-headed rakshasa (demon) king of Lanka, while Rama is lured away in the forest. Rama's campaign to rescue her and his eventual killing of Ravana, often with an arrow to the chest, form the core of the Ramayana and are the most common giveaway for him.

**Seventh avatar of Vishnu**
Rama is the seventh of the ten principal avatars (incarnations) of the preserver god Vishnu, coming after Parashurama and before Krishna. Questions about Vishnu frequently list Rama among his avatars.

**Ramayana**
The Sanskrit epic attributed to the sage Valmiki, whose title means "Rama's journey" or "Rama's way." It chronicles Rama's exile, the abduction of Sita, and the war against Ravana, and has many regional versions across South and Southeast Asia.

**Hanuman**
The monkey (vanara) devotee of Rama and son of the wind god Vayu. He leaps to Lanka, burns the city with his tail after it is set on fire, and carries an entire mountain to obtain a healing herb for Rama's wounded brother Lakshmana. In a famous devotional story, Hanuman tears open his own chest to reveal images of Rama and Sita in his heart.

**Fourteen-year exile in the Dandaka forest**
Rama is banished from the kingdom of Ayodhya for fourteen years and lives in the Dandaka forest with Sita and his brother Lakshmana. During this exile Sita is kidnapped.

**Kaikeyi and Manthara**
Kaikeyi, one of King Dasharatha's wives and Rama's stepmother, is persuaded by her scheming hunchbacked maidservant Manthara to demand that Rama be exiled and her own son Bharata be made heir. Dasharatha, bound by an earlier promise of two boons to her, is forced to agree.

**Bharata and the sandals**
Rama's half-brother Bharata refuses to usurp the throne and instead places Rama's sandals on the throne of Ayodhya, ruling as regent in Rama's name until his return.

**Lakshmana**
Rama's loyal younger half-brother, who accompanies him into exile and fights beside him at Lanka. Late in the story, Lakshmana allows the sage Durvasa to interrupt Rama's private meeting with the god of time, and in consequence he ends his life in the Sarayu River.

**Breaking Shiva's bow**
Rama wins Sita's hand at her svayamvara (bride-choosing contest) by stringing and breaking the great bow of Shiva (Rudra), called Pinaka, a feat no other suitor could manage.

**Golden deer (Maricha)**
The demon Maricha, whom Rama had earlier driven far away with an arrow, takes the form of a golden deer to lure Rama away from Sita, allowing Ravana to abduct her. The vulture Jatayu tries and fails to stop the kidnapping.

**Bridge to Lanka**
Rama's monkey army builds a bridge of floating stones across the sea to Lanka, allowing his forces to invade. Before this, Rama threatens to dry up or destroy the ocean when the sea god Varuna does not respond to his prayers.

**Sugriva and Vibhishana**
Rama allies with Sugriva, the exiled vanara (monkey) king, whose army aids the rescue. He is also joined by Vibhishana, Ravana's righteous brother, whom Rama crowns king of Lanka after Ravana's death.

**Sita's trial by fire and banishment**
After rescuing Sita, Rama doubts her purity and she undergoes an ordeal by fire (agni pariksha), emerging unharmed. Later, when his subjects murmur about her fidelity, Rama banishes the pregnant Sita to the forest.

**Lava and Kusha**
Rama's twin sons, born in exile in the hermitage of Valmiki, who teaches them their father's story. They later capture the horse from Rama's ashvamedha (horse sacrifice) and fight his forces before being recognized as his sons.

**Ahalya and Tataka**
Two early episodes from Rama's youth: he slays the demoness Tataka (Tadaka) after being told by the sage Vishvamitra that killing an evil woman is no sin, and the touch of his foot frees Ahalya, a woman cursed to become stone.

**Hiding in the Heavenly Rock Cave**
After her brother Susanoo's rampage through heaven, Amaterasu shuts herself inside the cave Ama-no-Iwato, plunging the world into darkness. This is the most famous story about the Shinto sun goddess and appears in nearly every question.

**Flayed horse thrown into her weaving hall**
Susanoo's worst offense is hurling a flayed (skinned) horse, often described as a dappled pony, through the roof of Amaterasu's sacred weaving hall. One of her weaving maidens is killed by a shuttle in the chaos, and Amaterasu retreats into the cave. He also defiles her rice fields and halls, including with feces.

**Uzume's dance**
To lure Amaterasu out, the goddess Ame-no-Uzume performs a wild, bawdy dance on an overturned tub, exposing herself and making the assembled gods roar with laughter. Curious about the noise, Amaterasu peeks out.

**Yata no Kagami (the sacred mirror)**
The gods hang a mirror and jewels on a sacred tree outside the cave. When Amaterasu sees her own dazzling reflection, she steps out, and the strong god Ame-no-Tajikarao pulls her the rest of the way so light returns. This mirror became one of the Imperial Regalia and is said to be kept at the Ise Shrine.

**Born from Izanagi's left eye**
After returning from the underworld Yomi, the creator god Izanagi purifies himself by washing. Amaterasu is born from his left eye, the moon god Tsukuyomi from his right eye, and the storm god Susanoo from his nose. Together they are called the Three Precious Children, and Amaterasu is given rule over the High Plain of Heaven (Takamagahara).

**Ninigi and the Three Sacred Treasures**
Amaterasu sends her grandson Ninigi down from heaven to rule the earth, giving him the mirror Yata no Kagami, the jewel Yasakani no Magatama, and the sword Kusanagi. These became the Imperial Regalia of Japan.

**Descent of the imperial family**
Japan's emperors, who sit on the Chrysanthemum Throne, traditionally claim descent from Amaterasu through Ninigi; Ninigi's great-grandson is the first emperor, Jimmu. Emperors continued to invoke this descent even after Emperor Hirohito's 1946 Humanity Declaration renounced imperial divinity.

**Sword-chewing contest with Susanoo**
To test whether Susanoo's intentions are pure, the siblings hold a contest of producing children. Amaterasu breaks Susanoo's sword into pieces, chews them, and spits out three goddesses, while Susanoo chews her jewels or necklace and produces five male gods.

**Ise Grand Shrine**
Amaterasu's chief shrine is the Inner Shrine (Naiku) at Ise, founded according to tradition by the princess Yamatohime. It is ritually torn down and rebuilt every twenty years, and an imperial princess called the saio once served there as priestess.

**Killing of the food goddess**
In one version, the moon god Tsukuyomi kills the food goddess Uke Mochi after she produces food from her mouth, nose, and rear. Disgusted, Amaterasu refuses ever to see him again, which explains why the sun and moon are never in the sky together and the separation of day and night. In the Kojiki, Susanoo kills a similar food goddess, Ogetsu-hime.

**Kusanagi**
The "grass-cutting" sword that Susanoo finds inside a tail of the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi. He presents it to Amaterasu to reconcile with her, and she later passes it to Ninigi.

**Ninigi's marriage**
Ninigi chooses to marry Konohanasakuya-hime, the princess of blossoms, and rejects her sister Iwanaga-hime, the princess of rocks. As a result, he and his descendants, the emperors, become short-lived like flowers instead of enduring like stone.

**Yatagarasu**
A three-legged crow that serves as Amaterasu's messenger and, in legend, guides Emperor Jimmu through the mountains during his conquest.

**Shinmei and Tensho Daijin**
Alternate names for Amaterasu. Shinmei shrines dedicated to her form a network modeled on Ise, and Tensho Daijin is the Sino-Japanese reading of her title.

**Origin of rice and silkworms**
From the body of the slain food goddess came rice, grains, and silkworms. Amaterasu planted the seeds in the fields of heaven and placed the silkworms in her mouth to draw silk thread, establishing agriculture and sericulture (silk farming).

**Mjolnir**
Thor's hammer, which can level mountains and always returns to his hand when thrown. It was forged by the dwarves Brokkr and Eitri (Sindri) in a contest Loki arranged against the Sons of Ivaldi. Loki, in the form of a fly or gadfly, bit Brokkr's eyelid during the forging, so the hammer's handle came out too short, which is why it is wielded with one hand.

**Disguised as Freya to recover his hammer from Thrym**
In the Eddic poem Thrymskvida, the giant Thrym steals Mjolnir and demands the goddess Freya as his bride in exchange. On Heimdall's advice, Thor dresses as the bride, with Loki as his maid; Loki explains away "Freya's" huge appetite and fierce red eyes by claiming she had not eaten or slept for eight nights out of excitement. When the hammer is laid in the bride's lap to bless the wedding, Thor seizes it and kills Thrym and his family.

**Killing Jormungandr at Ragnarok**
Thor's archenemy is the Midgard Serpent Jormungandr, Loki's monstrous son that encircles the world. At Ragnarok Thor kills the serpent but is poisoned by its venom, walks nine steps, and dies.

**Fishing with Hymir**
Thor went fishing with the giant Hymir, ripping the head off Hymir's best ox to use as bait, and hooked the Midgard Serpent. The terrified Hymir cut the line before Thor could kill it. The trip was part of a quest with Tyr to obtain a cauldron large enough for the sea god Aegir to brew ale for the gods, during which Thor smashed a goblet or chalice against Hymir's skull.

**Contests at Utgard-Loki's hall**
On a journey to Jotunheim, Thor slept with his companions inside what turned out to be the glove of the giant Skrymir and failed three times to kill him with his hammer. At Utgard-Loki's hall, Thor failed to empty a drinking horn (its end was in the sea), could lift only one paw of a gray cat (the Midgard Serpent in disguise), and lost a wrestling match to the old woman Elli (old age itself). Skrymir turned out to be Utgard-Loki in disguise.

**Alviss**
A dwarf who wanted to marry Thor's daughter Thrud. In the Alvissmal, Thor quizzed him about the names of things in different worlds until dawn, when the sunlight turned the dwarf to stone.

**Tanngnjostr and Tanngrisnir**
Thor's two goats, "Teeth-barer" and "Teeth-grinder," which pull his chariot. Thor can eat them and resurrect them by blessing their bones and skins with Mjolnir. When Thjalfi, son of the farmer Egil, broke a thigh bone to suck out the marrow, one goat came back lame, so Thjalfi and his sister Roskva became Thor's servants as compensation.

**Sif's golden hair**
Thor's wife Sif had her hair cut off by Loki as a prank. Thor forced Loki to replace it, so Loki had the Sons of Ivaldi make a new head of hair from real gold, which led to the creation of Mjolnir and other treasures.

**Harbard**
A ferryman (Odin in disguise) who refused to take Thor across a river. In the Harbardsljod, the two trade insults, with Harbard mocking Thor's poor clothes and suggesting that Sif has a lover, and Thor ends up walking around the water.

**Hrungnir**
A giant who drunkenly challenged Thor while feasting in Valhalla, after losing a horse race to Odin. In their duel Thor's hammer shattered Hrungnir's whetstone, a piece of which lodged in Thor's head. The seeress Groa tried to sing it out, but stopped when Thor distracted her with news of her husband Aurvandil, whose frostbitten toe Thor had broken off and thrown into the sky as a star.

**Geirrod and the giantess Grid**
On his way to the giant Geirrod, Thor received a magic belt, iron gloves, and a staff from the giantess Grid. He killed Geirrod by catching a red-hot iron bolt the giant threw and hurling it back through a pillar.

**Megingjord and Jarngreipr**
Thor's belt of strength, which doubles his power, and his iron gloves, which he needs to wield Mjolnir. Together with the hammer they make up his main possessions.

**Kicking Litr into Baldr's pyre**
During Baldr's funeral, Thor blessed the pyre with his hammer and, annoyed when the dwarf Litr ran in front of him, kicked Litr into the flames.

**Family and home**
Thor is the son of Odin and the earth giantess Jord, the husband of Sif, and the lover of the giantess Jarnsaxa. His sons Magni and Modi inherit Mjolnir after Ragnarok, and his daughter is Thrud. He lives in Thrudvangar (Thrudheim), in the hall Bilskirnir with 540 rooms.

**Svadilfari's master**
Thor killed the giant mason who was building the walls of Asgard, after the giant became enraged when Loki, disguised as a mare, lured away his stallion Svadilfari.

**Chimera**
The monster Bellerophon is most famous for killing, and the most common giveaway for him. It was a fire-breathing hybrid with a lion's head, a goat's body (often with a goat's head rising from its back), and a snake's tail, and it was ravaging Lycia.

**Pegasus**
The winged horse born from the neck of Medusa when Perseus beheaded her. Bellerophon tamed Pegasus and rode it to fight the Chimera from the air, out of reach of its fiery breath.

**Golden bridle from Athena**
On the advice of a seer, Bellerophon slept in Athena's temple. He dreamed that the goddess set a golden bridle beside him and woke to find it really there; with it he caught and tamed Pegasus.

**Polyeidus**
The Corinthian seer who told Bellerophon to sleep in Athena's temple to receive the bridle. Bellerophon then found Pegasus drinking at the spring of Pirene in Corinth.

**Stheneboea (Anteia)**
The wife of King Proetus of Tiryns (or Argos), called Anteia in the Iliad and Stheneboea in later sources. She fell in love with Bellerophon, and when he rejected her, she falsely accused him of trying to seduce or rape her. This is a version of the "Potiphar's wife" story pattern.

**Proetus**
The king who gave Bellerophon refuge after his exile and was married to Stheneboea. Unwilling to kill a guest himself, which would violate xenia (the sacred guest-host bond), he sent Bellerophon to his father-in-law in Lycia carrying a message that asked for his death. Questions sometimes misspell his name as "Proteus."

**Iobates and the "folded tablet"**
In Book 6 of the Iliad, Bellerophon carries a folded tablet with "murderous symbols" to King Iobates of Lycia, which is the only mention of writing in Homer. Iobates feasted him for nine days before reading it and, also bound by xenia, sent him on deadly tasks instead of killing him outright: the Chimera, then the Solymi, the Amazons, and an ambush.

**Gadfly and the flight to Olympus**
Grown proud after his successes, Bellerophon tried to ride Pegasus up to Mount Olympus. Zeus sent a gadfly to sting the horse, which threw Bellerophon back to earth. In many versions he landed in a thorn bush and was blinded or lamed, while Pegasus went on to Olympus.

**Plain of Aleion**
According to the Iliad, after becoming "hateful to the gods," Bellerophon wandered alone over the Aleian plain, avoiding other people. Later accounts describe him as a blind, crippled wanderer.

**Philonoe**
Iobates's daughter, whom Bellerophon married after the king saw that the gods protected him. Bellerophon received half of Lycia's kingdom and later inherited the throne.

**Glaucus and Diomedes in Iliad Book 6**
Bellerophon's grandson Glaucus, a Lycian ally of Troy, tells the story of his ancestor when he meets Diomedes in battle. Diomedes realizes that his grandfather Oeneus once hosted Bellerophon, and that the two exchanged gifts (a belt from Oeneus, a golden cup from Bellerophon). So the two men exchange armor instead of fighting.

**Hipponous**
Bellerophon's original name. According to one explanation, he was renamed "slayer of Belleros" after he killed a man of that name; other versions say he killed his own brother. The killing forced him into exile from Corinth.

**Sisyphus and Glaucus of Corinth**
Bellerophon's grandfather was Sisyphus, the king punished in the underworld by forever rolling a boulder uphill. His father Glaucus (whose wife was Eurynome) was torn apart by his own mares, which Aphrodite had driven mad. Some accounts make Poseidon Bellerophon's true father.

**Lead-tipped spear**
Bellerophon killed the Chimera by putting a lump of lead on his spear (or arrow) and thrusting it into the monster's mouth. Its fiery breath melted the lead, which ran down its throat and killed it.

**Laodamia and Sarpedon**
Bellerophon's daughter Laodamia had a son, Sarpedon, by Zeus; Sarpedon later led the Lycians at Troy. According to the Iliad, Artemis killed Laodamia in anger. Bellerophon's son Isander was killed fighting the Solymi.

**Twelfth and final labor of Heracles**
Heracles' last labor for King Eurystheus was to bring Cerberus up from the underworld. Hades allowed it only if Heracles subdued the dog without weapons, so he wrestled it into submission; in some versions Persephone simply gave him the dog.

**Three-headed guard dog of the underworld**
Cerberus guards the gates of Hades, letting the dead enter but stopping them from leaving. He is almost always shown with three dog heads, though Hesiod's Theogony gives him fifty and calls him "brazen-voiced."

**Drugged honey cake from the Cumaean Sibyl**
In Book 6 of Virgil's Aeneid, the Sibyl of Cumae leads Aeneas into the underworld. She throws Cerberus a honey cake laced with sleep-inducing drugs, and the dog gulps it down and falls asleep so they can pass.

**Orthrus (Orthus)**
Cerberus's brother, a two-headed dog who guarded the cattle of the monster Geryon. Heracles killed Orthrus during his tenth labor, when he stole Geryon's cattle.

**Typhon and Echidna**
Cerberus's parents. This monstrous pair also produced the Lernaean Hydra, the Chimera and Orthrus.

**Eurystheus hiding in a jar**
King Eurystheus of Tiryns, who assigned Heracles his labors, was so terrified when Heracles brought back Cerberus that he hid in a large storage jar (pithos). This was the last of several times he hid in the jar to avoid Heracles' monstrous catches.

**Snake tail and serpent mane**
Cerberus is often described or depicted with a serpent for a tail and snakes growing from his neck or back, like a mane.

**Aconite from Cerberus's saliva**
When Heracles dragged Cerberus into the daylight, foam or saliva dripped from the dog's mouths onto the ground. The poisonous plant aconite (wolfsbane) grew where it fell, which is why it was linked to Medea and other witches.

**Nemean Lion skin**
Heracles wore the impenetrable hide of the Nemean Lion, killed in his first labor, while fighting Cerberus. The dog's teeth and the snake-tail's bites could not pierce it.

**Rescuing Theseus from the Chair of Forgetfulness**
During the trip to the underworld, Heracles found Theseus and Pirithous stuck to magical chairs (the Chairs of Forgetfulness) as punishment for trying to kidnap Persephone. He freed Theseus but had to leave Pirithous behind.

**Orpheus and his lyre**
When Orpheus went to the underworld to bring back his wife Eurydice, he lulled Cerberus to sleep with his lyre music.

**Tainaron (Taenarum)**
The cape at the southern tip of the Peloponnese, where a cave was thought to be an entrance to the underworld. Heracles went down there to fetch Cerberus, and the historian Hecataeus of Miletus explained the myth away by saying "Cerberus" was really a deadly snake that lived at Tainaron.

**Menoetes and Ascalaphus**
Two side characters from the labor. Heracles wrestled Menoetes, the herdsman of Hades' cattle, and freed Ascalaphus, who had been pinned under a heavy rock for telling on Persephone for eating pomegranate seeds.

**Heracles' poplar wreath**
On his way back from the underworld, Heracles wore a wreath of poplar leaves. The sweat from his head bleached the inner side of the leaves white, which explains the two-toned leaves of the white poplar.

**Grove of Demeter at Hermione**
In Euripides' play Heracles, the hero says he left Cerberus for a time in the grove of Demeter (Chthonia) at the city of Hermione, in the Argolid, before bringing it to Eurystheus.

**Nidhogg (Nidhoggr)**
A Norse dragon or serpent that gnaws at the roots of the world tree Yggdrasil from its dwelling near the spring Hvergelmir. It is the single most frequent clue for dragons in Norse contexts.

**Ladon and the Apples of the Hesperides**
In Greek myth, Ladon is a serpent-like dragon, sometimes described as hundred-headed, that guards Hera's tree of golden apples in the garden of the Hesperides. Heracles kills or bypasses it during his eleventh labor to obtain the apples.

**Fafnir and Andvaranaut**
Fafnir is a dwarf (or giant) in Norse legend who kills his father Hreidmar to seize the cursed treasure of the dwarf Andvari, including the ring Andvaranaut, and transforms into a dragon to guard the hoard. The hero Sigurd kills him by hiding in a pit and stabbing him from below as he crawls over it to drink at a stream.

**Sigurd tastes the dragon's heart**
While roasting Fafnir's heart at the instruction of the smith Regin, Fafnir's brother, Sigurd burns his thumb, puts it in his mouth, and gains the ability to understand birds. The birds warn him that Regin plans to betray him.

**Jormungandr, the Midgard Serpent**
The child of Loki who grows so large that it encircles the world, biting its own tail. Thor nearly hooks it while fishing with the giant Hymir using an ox head as bait, is tricked into trying to lift it disguised as a cat by Utgard-Loki, and at Ragnarok kills it before dying from its venom after walking nine steps.

**Yamata no Orochi and Kusanagi**
An eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent-dragon of Japanese myth slain by the storm god Susanoo after he gets it drunk on sake. Susanoo discovers the sword Kusanagi ("Grasscutter") inside one of its tails; it later became one of Japan's imperial regalia.

**Chinese dragons (long)**
East Asian dragons are wingless, serpentine, generally benevolent beings that control water, rain, and wind. They are the only mythical animal in the Chinese zodiac, appear in Chinese New Year dances, and are paired with the fenghuang (phoenix) as the yang to its yin.

**Dragon Kings of the Four Seas**
Four Chinese dragon kings rule the seas of the north, south, east, and west. In the novel Fengshen Yanyi (Investiture of the Gods), the child hero Nezha feuds with Ao Guang, Dragon King of the East Sea, after killing his son.

**Imperial dragon symbolism**
The dragon was the symbol of the Chinese emperor; five-clawed dragons were reserved for the Son of Heaven. The Han founder Liu Bang was said to have been conceived after his mother dreamed of a dragon.

**Azure Dragon (Qinglong)**
One of the Four Symbols of Chinese astrology, the Azure Dragon represents the east and the season of spring. It is known as Seiryu in Japan.

**Imugi**
In Korean mythology, imugi are serpent-like creatures that seek to become full dragons, often by obtaining a magical wish-granting orb called the yeouiju or by surviving a thousand years.

**Cadmus and the dragon's teeth**
The Greek hero Cadmus kills a dragon sacred to Ares that guarded a spring at the site of Thebes. Sowing its teeth produces armed warriors called the Spartoi; Jason later performs the same task with dragon's teeth in Colchis.

**Saint George**
The Christian martyr who, in legend, slays a dragon that terrorized a town and demanded tribute, rescuing a princess offered to it as a sacrifice.

**Vritra and Tiamat**
Vritra is a Vedic serpent-dragon who hoards or imprisons the world's waters until the god Indra slays him with his thunderbolt (vajra). Tiamat is the Babylonian primordial sea goddess, often depicted as a dragon, whom Marduk kills to form heaven and earth from her body.

**Merlin's red and white dragons**
In Geoffrey of Monmouth's British legend, the young Merlin reveals two dragons fighting in a pool beneath Vortigern's collapsing tower. The red dragon represents the Britons and the white dragon the Saxons.

**Drinking the halahala poison**
During the Churning of the Ocean of Milk (Samudra Manthan), the gods and asuras released a deadly poison called halahala that threatened to destroy the world. Shiva drank it to save creation, and it stuck in his throat (in some versions Parvati grabbed his throat to stop it from reaching his stomach), turning his throat blue. This earned him the epithet Nilakantha, "the blue-throated one."

**Beheading Ganesha**
Parvati created a boy to guard her chamber while she bathed. When the boy refused to let Shiva in, Shiva cut off his head in anger; to console the grieving Parvati, he replaced it with the head of an elephant (in some versions with Brahma's help). The boy became Ganesha, the elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati.

**Nataraja**
Shiva's form as the "Lord of the Dance," famously depicted in medieval Chola bronzes. He dances within a ring of flames while trampling the dwarf Apasmara, who represents ignorance, and beats a small drum (damaru) whose rhythm creates and sustains the universe. His cosmic dance of destruction and renewal is the Tandava, whose gentler counterpart, performed by Parvati, is the Lasya.

**The Destroyer of the Trimurti**
Shiva forms the Hindu Trimurti, or triad of supreme gods, alongside Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver, with Shiva as the destroyer. He developed from the fierce Vedic storm god Rudra, who is honored in hymns such as the Shri Rudram.

**Third eye and the burning of Kama**
Shiva has a third eye on his forehead that can reduce things to ashes, which gives him the epithet Tryambaka. When the demon Taraka could only be killed by a son of Shiva, the love god Kama (Kamadeva) shot Shiva with an arrow to break his meditation and make him desire Parvati, and Shiva burned Kama to ashes with his third eye. The story is told in Kalidasa's Kumarasambhava, and Shiva's son Kartikeya was later born and defeated Taraka.

**Sati and Daksha's sacrifice**
Shiva's first wife Sati was the daughter of Daksha Prajapati, who despised Shiva and did not invite him to a great yajna (sacrifice). Insulted on her husband's behalf, Sati immolated herself in the sacrificial fire. The enraged Shiva and his attendants destroyed the sacrifice and beheaded Daksha, and Sati was reborn as Parvati.

**Pillar of fire**
In the Shiva Purana, Brahma and Vishnu argued over who was supreme, and Shiva appeared as an endless column of fire (the jyotirlinga) to settle the dispute. Vishnu, as a boar, dug down and admitted he could not find its base, while Brahma, as a swan, flew up and falsely claimed to have found its top. For this lie, Shiva (in his fierce form Bhairava) cut off one of Brahma's five heads.

**Nandi**
The white bull that serves as Shiva's mount (vahana) and as the gatekeeper of his home. Statues of Nandi typically face the main shrine in Shiva temples.

**Mount Kailash and Ravana**
Shiva lives with Parvati and their family atop Mount Kailash in the Himalayas. When the demon king Ravana tried to lift and uproot the mountain, Shiva pressed it down with his toe, pinning Ravana beneath it for a thousand years. Ravana sang Shiva's praises until he was released, and Shiva rewarded him with the sword Chandrahasa.

**The Ganges flowing from his hair**
When the river goddess Ganga descended from heaven, her torrent would have shattered the earth, so Shiva caught her in his matted locks and released her gently. He is therefore depicted with the Ganges flowing from his hair, which also holds a crescent moon.

**Lingam**
An aniconic, phallic stone pillar that is Shiva's most common object of worship. Devotees make offerings to it, and on Maha Shivaratri ("Great Night of Shiva") they recall the legend of a hunter who, hiding from tigers in a bilva (bael) tree, unknowingly dropped its leaves onto a lingam below and so won Shiva's favor.

**Race around the world between his sons**
Shiva and Parvati offered a prize (often a magic mango) to whichever of their sons, Kartikeya or Ganesha, could circle the world first. Kartikeya flew off on his peacock, but Ganesha simply walked around his parents, reasoning that they were his whole world, and won.

**Ardhanarishvara**
Shiva's androgynous form, in which he is fused with Parvati: the right half of the body is male (Shiva) and the left half is female (Parvati). It symbolizes the unity of the masculine and feminine principles.

**Trishula and vibhuti**
Shiva wields a trident called the trishula and is usually depicted covered in white ash, seated on an animal skin. His devotees mark their foreheads with three horizontal lines of sacred ash called vibhuti.

**Bhasmasura**
A demon who was granted the power to turn anyone to ash by placing his hand on their head, and then tried to use it on Shiva himself. Vishnu, taking the form of the enchantress Mohini, tricked Bhasmasura into imitating a dance move that placed his hand on his own head, reducing him to ash.

**Iphigenia at Aulis**
Agamemnon angered Artemis (often by killing a stag in her sacred grove or boasting he was a better hunter), so she stopped the winds and stranded the Greek fleet at Aulis before the Trojan War. The seer Calchas advised that Agamemnon sacrifice his daughter Iphigenia; in some versions Artemis whisked Iphigenia away at the last moment and replaced her with a deer.

**Actaeon**
A hunter who stumbled upon Artemis bathing naked. As punishment, she turned him into a stag, and he was chased down and torn apart by his own hunting dogs.

**Calydonian Boar**
A monstrous boar Artemis sent to ravage Calydon in Aetolia after King Oeneus forgot to include her when making sacrifices to the gods. It was killed in the famous Calydonian Boar Hunt led by Oeneus's son Meleager and featuring the huntress Atalanta.

**Niobe's children**
