Queen Niobe boasted that she was superior to Leto because she had fourteen children while Leto had only two. Artemis and Apollo killed all of them, with Artemis typically shooting the daughters and Apollo the sons, and the grieving Niobe turned to stone.

**Otus and Ephialtes (the Aloadae)**
Two giant sons of Poseidon who grew enormously each year and plotted to storm Olympus, wanting Artemis and Hera as brides. Artemis turned into a deer and darted between them, so that when they threw their javelins at her they killed each other.

**Leto and Delos**
Artemis and her twin Apollo were born to Leto and Zeus. Hera forbade Leto from giving birth on any land, so she delivered them on the floating island of Delos; Artemis was born first and immediately helped her mother deliver Apollo, which is why she was linked to childbirth.

**Tityos**
A giant who tried to assault Leto, who had earlier been pursued by the serpent Python at Hera's command. Artemis and Apollo shot him down, and he was punished in Tartarus by vultures eating his liver.

**Callisto**
A nymph in Artemis's band of virgin huntresses who was seduced by Zeus and bore a son, Arcas. She was turned into a bear (by Artemis, Hera, or Zeus depending on the version) and later placed in the sky as the constellation Ursa Major.

**Brauron and "playing the bear"**
Artemis's cult site in Attica, said to have been founded by Iphigenia. Young Athenian girls served Artemis there by "playing the bear" (the arkteia) before marriage, since the bear was her sacred animal, and girls dedicated their toys to her before marrying.

**Orion**
The giant hunter, sometimes called the only man Artemis loved. In one version Apollo tricked her into shooting at a distant dot in the sea, which turned out to be Orion swimming; in others she killed him with a scorpion or for attempting to assault her.

**Admetus and Alcestis**
Apollo helped King Admetus meet Pelias's challenge of yoking a lion and a boar to a chariot to win Alcestis's hand. At the wedding Admetus forgot to sacrifice to Artemis, who filled his bridal chamber with snakes until Apollo appeased her.

**Chione**
A woman who bore children to both Hermes and Apollo and then boasted that she was more beautiful than Artemis. Artemis shot her through the tongue with an arrow.

**Adonis and Hippolytus**
Hippolytus, a chaste devotee of Artemis, died because of Aphrodite's scheming. In some myths Artemis avenged him by sending the boar that killed Aphrodite's beloved Adonis.

**Artemis Orthia**
A sanctuary of Artemis at Sparta where, as a rite of passage, Spartan boys were ritually flogged at her altar (the diamastigosis) in an endurance contest.

**Lake Nemi and Ephesus**
Lake Nemi in Italy, called "Diana's Mirror," held a sacred grove of Diana ruled by a priest-king (the rex Nemorensis) who gained the post by killing his predecessor, the subject of the opening of Frazer's The Golden Bough. In the Book of Acts, Paul's preaching in Ephesus angered the silversmith Demetrius and others who made silver shrines of Artemis, whose temple there was a Wonder of the Ancient World.

**Apple of Discord, "To the Fairest"**
Eris, the goddess of discord, was not invited to the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, so she threw in a golden apple inscribed "To the Fairest." Hera, Athena and Aphrodite each claimed it, and the dispute set off the chain of events that led to the Trojan War.

**Judgment of Paris**
Zeus had the Trojan prince Paris decide which goddess deserved the apple. Paris gave it to Aphrodite, who had promised him the most beautiful woman in the world, Helen of Sparta, and his abduction of her started the Trojan War.

**Hippomenes (Melanion) and Atalanta's footrace**
The huntress Atalanta would only marry a man who could beat her in a footrace, and losers were killed. Aphrodite gave Hippomenes (called Melanion in some versions) three golden apples, which he dropped during the race; Atalanta stopped to pick them up, so he won and married her.

**Idunn and the apples of youth**
In Norse myth, the goddess Idunn keeps a box (eski) of apples that the gods eat to stay young. Without them, the Aesir begin to age and grow gray.

**Thiazi's kidnapping of Idunn**
The giant Thiazi, in the form of an eagle, captured Loki and forced him to lure Idunn and her apples out of Asgard. When the gods started aging, they made Loki get her back, so he borrowed Freyja's falcon form, turned Idunn into a nut and flew her home, and the gods killed Thiazi as he chased them.

**Heracles' eleventh labor**
King Eurystheus ordered Heracles to bring back golden apples from the Garden of the Hesperides. On the way he caught the sea god Nereus to make him reveal where the garden was, and survived King Busiris of Egypt, who tried to sacrifice him.

**Atlas fetches the apples**
In one version of the eleventh labor, Heracles held up the sky while Atlas, father of the Hesperides, collected the apples. When Atlas wanted to leave Heracles holding the sky forever, Heracles asked him to take it back for a moment to adjust his cloak, then walked off with the apples.

**Garden of the Hesperides**
The garden at the western edge of the world where the golden apples grew. It was tended by the Hesperides, nymphs of the evening often called the daughters of Atlas.

**Ladon**
The hundred-headed dragon that never slept and coiled around the golden apple tree in the Garden of the Hesperides. In some versions Heracles killed Ladon to take the apples, and Hera placed it in the sky as the constellation Draco.

**Gaia's wedding gift to Hera**
The golden apple tree first came from Gaia, who gave it to Hera (or to Zeus and Hera) as a wedding present. Hera planted it in the Garden of the Hesperides, and the tree was sacred to her.

**The Firebird and Prince Ivan**
In the Russian fairy tale, the Firebird keeps stealing golden apples from the tsar's orchard at night. Prince Ivan (Ivan Tsarevich) sets out to catch it, beginning his adventures with the gray wolf.

**Manannan mac Lir's Silver Bough**
In Irish myth, the sea god Manannan mac Lir gave King Cormac mac Airt a silver branch hung with three golden apples. When shaken, it played music so sweet that it put listeners, even the sick and wounded, to sleep.

**Volsung's conception**
In the Volsunga saga, King Rerir and his wife could not have a child. Frigg (through Odin) sent them an apple, carried by the giantess Hljod in the form of a crow, and after eating it the queen conceived the hero Volsung.

**Skirnir's wooing of Gerd**
In the Eddic poem Skirnismal, Freyr's servant Skirnir offers the giantess Gerd eleven golden apples and the ring Draupnir to persuade her to marry Freyr. When she refuses the gifts, he threatens her with curses until she agrees.

**Golden apples in Slavic and Balkan folklore**
Golden apples appear across Eastern European tales: thieving peahens steal them in a Bulgarian tale, zmeu dragons take them in Romanian legend, and in some Slavic myths the thunder god Perun throws golden apples as balls of lightning.

**Brisingamen and the four dwarves**
Freya's famous golden necklace (sometimes described as a torc or collar). According to the Sörla þáttr, she saw four dwarves forging it and agreed to spend a night with each of them in exchange for it.

**Thor disguised as Freya (Thrymskvida)**
In the Eddic poem Thrymskvida, the giant Thrym steals Thor's hammer Mjolnir and demands Freya as his bride in exchange. Freya angrily refuses, so Thor dresses as her in bridal clothes and wears Brisingamen, with Loki disguised as his bridesmaid. At the wedding feast Thor eats an entire ox and eight salmon, then grabs the hammer and kills the giants.

**Folkvangr**
Freya's field or meadow in Asgard. Half of all warriors slain in battle go to her there, and she gets first choice of them, while the other half go to Odin's Valhalla.

**Chariot pulled by two cats**
Freya rides in a chariot drawn by two cats, often described as blue or gray; some sources name them Bygul and Trjegul. One story says her husband brought them to her.

**Hildisvini**
Freya's boar, whose name means "battle swine," and which she rides. In the poem Hyndluljod it is her mortal lover and servant Ottar in disguise.

**Hyndluljod (Lay of Hyndla) and Ottar**
An Eddic poem in which Freya visits the giantess and seeress Hyndla in her cave, rides with her to Valhalla (Hyndla rides a wolf), and makes her recite the ancestry of Ottar so he can win a bet about his lineage. When Hyndla refuses to give Ottar a memory ale so he can remember the genealogy, Freya threatens her with fire and forces her to hand it over.

**Falcon-feather cloak (Valshamr)**
Freya owns a cloak of falcon feathers that lets the wearer turn into a falcon and fly. Loki borrows it to rescue the goddess Idunn from the giant Thjazi, and again in Thrymskvida to search for Thor's stolen hammer.

**Tears of red gold for Odr**
Freya's husband Odr (Od or Odur) often leaves on long journeys, and while he is gone she weeps tears of red gold (in some accounts amber). She wanders the world searching for him under different names.

**Seidr**
A form of Norse magic or sorcery concerned with seeing and shaping fate, regarded as a women's art. Freya, a Vanir goddess who came to live among the Aesir as a hostage after the Aesir-Vanir war, first taught it to the Aesir, including Odin.

**Lokasenna**
An Eddic poem set at the sea giant Aegir's feast, where Loki insults all the gods in a flyting (an exchange of insults). He calls Freya a harlot and accuses her of sleeping with every god and elf present, including her twin brother Freyr.

**Heimdall and Loki fight as seals**
Loki steals Brisingamen by turning into a flea (or a fly) to get into Freya's locked chamber. Heimdall recovers the necklace by fighting Loki at the rock Singasteinn, with both gods in the form of seals.

**Sessrumnir**
Freya's large and beautiful hall in Folkvangr, where she keeps the slain warriors. Its name means "seat-room," and it is also the name of a ship, so the hall may itself be imagined as a ship.

**Hnoss and Gersemi**
Freya's two daughters by Odr. Both names mean "treasure," and they are so named because of their beauty.

**The giant builder of Asgard's wall**
A giant (a frost giant, or hrimthurs) offered to build a wall around Asgard and asked for Freya, the sun, and the moon as payment. Loki sabotaged him by turning into a mare and luring away his stallion Svadilfari, and Thor killed the builder.

**Sörla þáttr and the endless battle of the Hjadnings**
In the Sörla þáttr, Odin makes Freya start a never-ending war as the price for returning Brisingamen. The kings Hedin and Hogni, each with twenty subordinate kings, fight over and over, with the slain rising again to keep fighting, for 143 years until a Christian man in the service of King Olaf Tryggvason ends it.

**Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex**
De Beauvoir's 1949 book, a founding text of second-wave feminism. It argues that throughout history men have defined themselves as the norm and woman as the "Other," a lesser being defined only in relation to man.

**"One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman"**
The most famous line of The Second Sex, which opens its second volume. It means that "woman" is not a natural given but a role produced by society, and it anticipates the later distinction between sex and gender.

**Woman as the "Other"**
De Beauvoir's key concept: man is the Subject, the "Absolute," while woman is made the Other, objectified and defined in relation to him. The idea is borrowed from Hegel's master-slave dialectic.

**"Facts and Myths" and "Lived Experience"**
The titles of the two volumes of The Second Sex. "Facts and Myths" covers biology, psychoanalysis, history, and myths about women, while "Lived Experience" traces women's lives from childhood through marriage and old age.

**Betty Friedan's "the problem that has no name"**
Friedan's phrase in The Feminine Mystique (1963) for the widespread dissatisfaction of American suburban housewives, who asked themselves "Is this all?" The book grew from her survey of her fellow Smith College graduates and helped launch second-wave feminism in the US.

**National Organization for Women (NOW)**
A US women's rights organization founded in 1966, with Betty Friedan as its first president. It campaigned for equal pay, the Equal Rights Amendment, and reproductive rights.

**Donna Haraway's "A Cyborg Manifesto"**
A 1985 essay by Donna Haraway that uses the cyborg, a hybrid of human and machine, as an image for a feminism that blurs boundaries between human and animal, organism and machine, and physical and non-physical. It challenges feminism based on fixed identities and urges people to learn from "our fusions with animals and machines."

**The waves of feminism**
The movement is often divided into waves. The first wave (19th to early 20th century) focused on legal rights such as suffrage. The second wave (1960s to 1980s) addressed work, family, sexuality, and reproductive rights. The third wave (1990s onward) stressed diversity and intersectionality.

**Kimberlé Crenshaw and intersectionality**
The legal scholar Crenshaw coined "intersectionality" in 1989 to describe how overlapping identities such as race, gender, and class combine to create added layers of discrimination, as Black women face. The idea is central to third-wave and Black feminism.

**Mary Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman**
A 1792 founding work of feminism, partly written in response to Charles Maurice de Talleyrand's report proposing that girls receive only a domestic education. Wollstonecraft argued women deserve the same education as men. After her death, her husband William Godwin published his Memoirs of her life.

**Germaine Greer**
An Australian radical feminist best known for The Female Eunuch (1970). It argues that women have been cut off from their own sexuality and energy by a consumer, male-dominated society.

**Shulamith Firestone's The Dialectic of Sex**
A 1970 radical feminist book by Firestone that applies Marxist ideas to the relationship between the sexes. It sees biological reproduction as the root of women's oppression and devotes a chapter to Freudianism, which it calls "misguided feminism."

**bell hooks's Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center**
A 1984 book by bell hooks (who wrote her name in lowercase). It criticizes mainstream feminism for centering on white, middle-class women and calls for including the experiences of Black and working-class women.

**Existentialism and de Beauvoir**
De Beauvoir was an existentialist philosopher and partner of Jean-Paul Sartre. Her The Ethics of Ambiguity discusses types of people such as the "sub-man," the "nihilist," and the "adventurer." Note: one question in this set had existentialism as its answer.

**The Social Contract**
Rousseau's 1762 treatise on political legitimacy, arguing that rightful authority comes only from an agreement in which individuals submit to the "general will" of the community. It is his most famous political work and a frequent giveaway.

**"Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains"**
The famous opening line of The Social Contract. It expresses Rousseau's view that existing societies have corrupted humanity's natural freedom, and it is often linked to the ideals that inspired the French Revolution.

**Emile, or On Education**
Rousseau's 1762 treatise on education, following a fictional boy named Emile through stages of development under a tutor. It argues that children should learn through experience and natural growth rather than rote instruction, and it delays religious instruction until adolescence (around age fifteen).

**The Savoyard Vicar (Savoyard Priest)**
A character in Book IV of Emile who delivers the "Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar," a statement of natural religion based on conscience and reason rather than church doctrine. Its unorthodox views helped get Emile banned and burned in Paris and Geneva.

**Discourse on Inequality**
Rousseau's 1755 essay (Discourse on the Origin and Basis of Inequality Among Men) that distinguishes natural (physical) inequality from moral or political inequality. It portrays humans in the state of nature as solitary and relatively content, corrupted later by property and society.

**The fence and "This is mine"**
A famous passage opening Part Two of the Discourse on Inequality: the first man who enclosed a piece of land, said "This is mine," and found people simple enough to believe him was the true founder of civil society. Rousseau presents private property as the origin of moral inequality.

**Amour de soi and amour propre**
Two forms of self-love in Rousseau's thought. Amour de soi is natural, healthy self-preservation, while amour propre is a socially derived self-love based on comparison and the opinions of others, which breeds vanity and inequality. In the state of nature, Rousseau pairs self-preservation with pity (compassion) as humanity's two pre-rational principles.

**Confessions**
Rousseau's autobiography, published posthumously in the 1780s, notable for its candid self-revelation. It recounts embarrassing episodes from his life, such as childhood mischief like urinating in a neighbor's cooking pot, and is considered a founding work of modern autobiography.

**Breastfeeding advocacy**
Emile urged mothers to nurse their own children rather than send them to wet nurses, part of Rousseau's broader call for a more natural upbringing. The idea became fashionable among upper-class French women after the book's publication.

**General will**
The central concept of The Social Contract: the collective will of the people aimed at the common good, as distinct from the "will of all," which is merely the sum of private interests. Rousseau held that citizens who obey the general will are obeying themselves and thus remain free.

**French Revolution**
Rousseau's ideas about popular sovereignty and natural freedom were a major inspiration for revolutionaries such as Robespierre, though Rousseau died in 1778, over a decade before the Revolution began.

**"A spectre is haunting Europe"**
The famous opening line of the Manifesto: "A spectre is haunting Europe – the spectre of communism." The preamble says all the powers of old Europe, including the Pope, the Tsar, Metternich, Guizot, French Radicals, and German police spies, have entered into a "holy alliance to exorcise" this spectre.

**"The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles"**
The opening sentence of Section I, "Bourgeois and Proletarians," which states the work's central thesis. It traces history through oppressor and oppressed classes, such as freeman and slave or lord and serf, down to the modern struggle between the bourgeoisie (owners of the means of production) and the proletariat (wage workers).

**Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, 1848**
The Manifesto was written by Marx and Engels for the Communist League and published in London in February 1848, just as revolutions broke out across Europe. It is a short pamphlet promoting communism as the outcome of a proletarian revolution against capitalism.

**Ten-point program**
The list of ten measures at the end of Section II, which the authors say will be applicable in most advanced countries. It includes a heavy progressive income tax, abolition of the right of inheritance, centralization of credit in a state bank, establishment of industrial armies (especially for agriculture), and free education for all children in public schools.

**"Workers of the world, unite!"**
The closing slogan of the Manifesto, more literally "Proletarians of all countries, unite!" It follows the line "The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win."

**Specters of Marx and "hauntology"**
Jacques Derrida's 1993 book Specters of Marx, whose title alludes to the Manifesto's opening "spectre." In it Derrida coined "hauntology," a pun on "ontology," for the way the ideas and themes of the past keep returning to haunt the present.

**"Abolition of private property"**
The Manifesto says the theory of the communists can be summed up in this single sentence. It specifies that it means the abolition of bourgeois property, used to exploit others' labor, rather than personal belongings.

**Abolition of the family and religion**
In Section II the authors answer objections that communists want to abolish the family, pleading guilty to wanting "to stop the exploitation of children by their parents." They also dismiss objections from religion and morality, which they see as reflecting ruling-class interests.

**The bourgeoisie as its own "grave-diggers"**
At the end of Section I, the Manifesto argues that by building modern industry and gathering workers together in factories, the bourgeoisie creates the proletariat that will overthrow it. "What the bourgeoisie therefore produces, above all, are its own grave-diggers."

**"All that is solid melts into air"**
A famous phrase from Section I describing how capitalism constantly revolutionizes production and dissolves traditional social relations, so that man is finally compelled to face "his real conditions of life, and his relations with his kind." Marshall Berman used it as the title of his 1982 book on modernity.

**"Idiocy of rural life"**
The Manifesto praises the bourgeoisie for rescuing much of the population from the "idiocy of rural life." Eric Hobsbawm, in his introduction to the Verso edition, noted that the original sense is closer to the "isolation" of rural life, from the Greek idiotes, a private person cut off from public affairs.

**Discovery of America and rounding of the Cape**
Section I explains that the discovery of America and the rounding of the Cape of Good Hope opened new markets and trade. This fueled the rise of the bourgeoisie and the decline of feudal society.

**Proudhon's Philosophy of Poverty**
In Section III, which critiques other socialist writings, the Manifesto names Pierre-Joseph Proudhon's Philosophy of Poverty as an example of "Conservative, or Bourgeois, Socialism." It says economists, philanthropists, and humanitarians belong to this camp, which seeks to fix social problems while keeping bourgeois society intact.

**Section IV and other opposition parties**
The short final section describes where communists stand in relation to various opposition parties. It mentions supporting the Social-Democrats in France and the Radicals in Switzerland, and it ends with the call for workers to unite.

**"The free development of each is the condition for the free development of all"**
The Manifesto's description, at the end of Section II, of the association that will replace class-divided bourgeois society once class distinctions disappear.

**Leviathan**
Hobbes's 1651 masterpiece of political philosophy and the universal giveaway. Named after a sea monster from the Book of Job, it argues that people should submit to an all-powerful sovereign to escape the chaos of the state of nature, and its famous frontispiece shows a giant crowned figure made up of many tiny people.

**"Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short"**
Hobbes's description of human life in the state of nature, from chapter 13 of Leviathan. In this condition there is "no culture of the earth," "no commodious building," no arts, no letters, and no industry, because no one can trust that they will enjoy the fruits of their labor.

**"War of all against all" (bellum omnium contra omnes)**
Hobbes's term for the state of nature, a condition of perpetual war in which every person is an enemy to every other. He names competition, diffidence (distrust), and glory as the three principal causes of quarrel among men.

**Social contract and absolute sovereign**
Hobbes argued that people escape the state of nature by agreeing, through a covenant, to transfer their rights to a sovereign with absolute and indivisible power, a theory influenced by Jean Bodin. Subjects owe obedience as long as the sovereign protects them, since the right to self-preservation can never be given up.

**Natural equality: the ability to kill**
Hobbes argued that humans are roughly equal in body and mind, because even the weakest person can kill the strongest through cunning or by joining with others. This equality creates mutual fear and drives the war of all against all.

**"Kingdom of Darkness" and the "Confederacy of Deceivers"**
The title of Part IV of Leviathan, which attacks those who misinterpret Scripture to gain power, especially the Catholic Church. Hobbes describes the Kingdom of Darkness as a "confederacy of deceivers" and compares the papacy to a "kingdom of fairies," with the Pope as the ghost of the dead Roman Empire.

**"Of Man" and the opening chapters of Leviathan**
Part I of Leviathan builds Hobbes's political theory from definitions about human nature. He defines imagination as "nothing but decaying sense," describes passions as the interior beginnings of voluntary motions, and rejects any summum bonum (greatest good) in favor of continual desire.

**Three types of commonwealth**
In Leviathan, Hobbes recognizes only three forms of commonwealth based on who holds sovereignty: monarchy (one), aristocracy (an assembly of some), and democracy (an assembly of all). He considered monarchy the best.

**Justice as keeping covenants**
Hobbes's third law of nature is that men perform their covenants. He defines injustice as nothing other than the failure to perform a covenant, so that whatever is not unjust is just; before covenants and a sovereign exist, there is no justice or injustice.

**De Cive (On the Citizen)**
Hobbes's 1642 Latin treatise that first set out the political arguments he later expanded in Leviathan. It forms the third part of his Elements of Philosophy trilogy.

**De Corpore and De Homine (Elements of Philosophy)**
Hobbes's philosophical trilogy consists of De Corpore (On the Body), on materialist metaphysics and natural philosophy, De Homine (On Man), and De Cive (On the Citizen), progressing from bodies to humans to political society.

**English Civil War and exile**
Hobbes fled to Paris around 1640 as conflict between king and Parliament grew, and he wrote Leviathan in exile there, shaped by the chaos of the English Civil War. While in Paris he served as mathematics tutor to the future Charles II.

**Translation of Thucydides**
Hobbes published the first English translation directly from the Greek of Thucydides's History of the Peloponnesian War in 1629. He presented it partly as a warning about the dangers of democracy.

**Third Objections to Descartes**
Hobbes wrote the third set of objections published with Descartes's Meditations, arguing from a materialist standpoint against Descartes's claim that the mind is an immaterial substance.

**Born of fear: the Spanish Armada**
Hobbes was born prematurely in 1588 in Malmesbury, supposedly because his mother went into labor on hearing of the approaching Spanish Armada. He later quipped that "fear and I were born twins," and Leo Strauss argued that Hobbes made the fear of violent death the foundation of his moral and political philosophy.

**Russell's teapot**
Bertrand Russell's analogy for the burden of proof. If he claimed a tiny china teapot orbits the sun between Earth and Mars, too small to be seen by telescopes, no one could disprove it, but it would be absurd to expect others to believe it. Likewise, he argued, the burden is on believers to prove God exists, not on atheists to disprove it.

**Why I Am Not a Christian**
Russell's 1927 lecture, given at Battersea Town Hall in London, arguing against belief in God and Christianity. He rejects the standard arguments for God and claims religion is based mainly on fear, including fear of death and of the unknown.

**The problem of evil**
The most common argument for atheism. It says the existence of suffering and evil is incompatible with, or makes unlikely, a God who is all-powerful (omnipotent), all-knowing (omniscient), and perfectly good (omnibenevolent).

**William Rowe's "friendly atheism"**
Rowe gave a well-known "evidential" version of the problem of evil, which says pointless suffering makes God's existence unlikely. He also described "friendly atheism," the view that an atheist can believe a theist is rationally justified in their belief even though the atheist thinks it is false.

**Pascal's wager**
An argument from Blaise Pascal's Pensées against atheism. Believing in God has an infinite possible reward and only a finite cost, while disbelief risks infinite loss, so a rational person should bet that God exists.

**William Paley's watchmaker analogy**
A design argument against atheism from Paley's Natural Theology (1802). Finding a watch on a heath, we would conclude it had a designer, and Paley argued the complexity of living things likewise implies a divine designer.

**Baron d'Holbach's The System of Nature**
A 1770 book by the French Enlightenment philosopher Baron d'Holbach that openly argues for atheism and materialism. It describes the universe as nothing but matter in motion governed by natural laws, and it was one of the first openly atheist works to become widely read.

**The Cult of Reason**
An atheistic movement during the French Revolution, organized by radicals including Antoine-François Momoro, Jacques Hébert, and Pierre-Gaspard Chaumette. Churches such as Notre-Dame were turned into "Temples of Reason," and at festivals a woman in red, white, and blue played Liberty or Reason. Robespierre replaced it with the deist Cult of the Supreme Being in 1794.

**William Lane Craig: the Kalam argument and fine-tuning**
Craig is a modern Christian philosopher known for debating atheists. He defends the Kalam cosmological argument (whatever begins to exist has a cause, the universe began to exist, so the universe has a cause) and the argument that the universe's physical constants are "fine-tuned" to allow life.

**Reformed epistemology and "properly basic" beliefs**
A response to atheism led by Alvin Plantinga. It argues that belief in God can be "properly basic," meaning it is rational to hold without being based on evidence or argument, just as belief in other minds or in the past is.

**Voltaire and the deists**
Deists such as Voltaire believed in a creator God known through reason, not revelation, and rejected atheism. Voltaire famously said that "if God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him."

**The ontological argument and Gaunilo's island**
St. Anselm's argument in the Proslogion holds that God, "that than which nothing greater can be conceived," must exist, since existing in reality is greater than existing only in the mind. The monk Gaunilo answered with a parody about a perfect island. Note: one question in this set had "the existence of God," the opposite of atheism, as its answer, so these clues point to theism.

**New Atheism**
A 21st-century movement of outspoken critics of religion, often linked to the "Four Horsemen": Richard Dawkins (The God Delusion), Christopher Hitchens (God Is Not Great), Sam Harris (The End of Faith), and Daniel Dennett (Breaking the Spell).

**Pierre-Joseph Proudhon**
The French thinker often called the "father of anarchism" and the first person to call himself an anarchist, in his 1840 book What Is Property?. He is famous for the slogan "property is theft."

**The Poverty of Philosophy (Karl Marx)**
Karl Marx's 1847 attack on Proudhon, written in response to Proudhon's The System of Economic Contradictions, or The Philosophy of Poverty. Its title reverses the title of Proudhon's book.

**Emma Goldman**
A Lithuanian-born anarchist writer and speaker active in the United States, nicknamed "Red Emma." She founded the anarchist magazine Mother Earth and was deported to Russia in 1919.

**Leon Czolgosz and William McKinley**
Leon Czolgosz, a self-described anarchist, assassinated President William McKinley in 1901. He said he had been inspired by Emma Goldman's speeches, and Goldman was briefly arrested afterward.

**Peter Kropotkin**
A Russian prince who gave up his title to become a leading anarchist thinker. He wrote The Conquest of Bread and Mutual Aid, which argues against social Darwinism that cooperation, not just competition, drives evolution.

**William Godwin's Political Justice**
William Godwin's 1793 Enquiry Concerning Political Justice argued that government corrupts people and should give way to rational individuals governing themselves, making it an early anarchist work. Thomas Malthus wrote his Essay on the Principle of Population partly to answer Godwin's optimism. Godwin was the husband of Mary Wollstonecraft and the father of Mary Shelley.

**Mikhail Bakunin**
A Russian revolutionary and founder of collectivist anarchism. He clashed with Karl Marx in the First International, warning that a Marxist workers' state would become a new tyranny.

**"Without a ruler"**
The word anarchism comes from the Greek anarchos, meaning "without a ruler." Anarchism holds that the state and government are unnecessary and harmful, and that society should be organized through voluntary cooperation.

**Anarchy, State, and Utopia (Robert Nozick)**
A 1974 libertarian book by Robert Nozick that begins with "Anarchy." It is not an anarchist work: it argues that a minimal state can be justified against anarchists, and it uses the Wilt Chamberlain example to argue that patterned theories of distributive justice are unjust.

**Anarcho-syndicalism**
A form of anarchism that sees labor unions and the general strike as the main tools for overthrowing capitalism and the state. In its vision, workers' unions would run society after the revolution.

**Propaganda of the deed**
The idea that violent acts, such as assassinations and bombings, can inspire revolution better than words. Anarchists using this tactic in the late 1800s and early 1900s killed several heads of state, including McKinley.

**Circle-A and the black and red flag**
Common anarchist symbols. The capital A inside a circle (often read as "anarchy is order") and the diagonally split black-and-red flag of anarcho-syndicalism are widely used by modern anarchists.

**Alexander Berkman**
A Russian-born anarchist and longtime partner of Emma Goldman. He tried to assassinate the industrialist Henry Clay Frick in 1892 and later edited anarchist publications such as Mother Earth.

**Paul Goodman**
An American social critic and author of Growing Up Absurd (1960), who combined anarchism with pacifism. His writings influenced the New Left and the youth movements of the 1960s.

**The Republic**
Plato's most famous dialogue, which seeks to define justice for both individuals and the city-state. Socrates, talking with Glaucon, Adeimantus, and Thrasymachus, describes an ideal city called Kallipolis ruled by philosopher-kings, and the work also explains how an excess of freedom causes democracy to decay into tyranny. It is the most common title clue for Plato.

**Allegory of the Cave**
A parable in Book VII of the Republic. Prisoners chained in a cave see only shadows cast on a wall and mistake them for reality. One prisoner escapes, ascends painfully into the sunlight, and sees the true world, but when he returns to free the others, they reject him and would kill him. It illustrates the philosopher's journey from appearances to knowledge of the Forms.

**Philosopher-kings**
The rulers of Plato's ideal city in the Republic, who are fit to govern because they have knowledge of the Forms and especially the Form of the Good. The "Ship of State" parable compares them to a true navigator, dismissed as a useless "stargazer" by self-flattering sailors.

**Theory of Forms**
Plato's doctrine that the physical objects we perceive are imperfect copies of eternal, unchanging, abstract Forms (Ideas), which are the most real kind of being. In the Parmenides, Plato himself raises an objection to this theory called the "Third Man" argument.

**Ring of Gyges**
A story told by Glaucon in Book II of the Republic about a shepherd who finds a ring that makes him invisible and uses it to seduce the queen, kill the king, and take the throne. It raises the question of whether anyone would act justly if they could never be caught.

**Socrates**
Plato's teacher and the main speaker in most of his dialogues. Plato chronicled his trial and death in the Apology, Crito, and Phaedo, and his works are the main source for what is known of Socrates' philosophy.

**Symposium**
A dialogue set at a drinking party at the house of the poet Agathon, where the guests give speeches about love (eros). Aristophanes tells the myth that humans were once double beings who were split in half by Zeus and now seek their other half. Socrates relays the teaching of the priestess Diotima, who describes love as the child of Resource and Poverty and as a ladder of ascent to absolute Beauty, and a drunken Alcibiades arrives at the end to praise Socrates.

**Meno**
A dialogue in which Socrates leads Meno's slave boy, using only questions, to work out how to double the area of a square. This is meant to show that learning is really recollection (anamnesis) of knowledge the soul already has. It also features Meno answering what virtue is by listing examples, which Socrates compares to giving a swarm of bees instead of defining what a bee is.

**Apology**
Plato's account of Socrates' defense speech at his trial for impiety and corrupting the youth of Athens, against accusers Meletus, Anytus, and Lycon. Socrates calls himself a gadfly stinging Athens, explains the Delphic oracle's claim that no one is wiser than he, declares that "the unexamined life is not worth living," and is sentenced to death.

**Euthyphro**
A dialogue in which Socrates questions Euthyphro, who is prosecuting his own father for murder, about the nature of piety. It poses the famous "Euthyphro dilemma": is something pious because the gods love it, or do the gods love it because it is pious?

**Tripartite soul and the chariot allegory**
Plato's division of the soul into reason, spirit, and appetite, which the Republic maps onto the rulers, guardians (auxiliaries), and producers of the ideal city. In the Phaedrus, the soul is compared to a charioteer (reason) driving two winged horses, one noble (spirit) and one unruly (appetite).

**Phaedo and Crito**
Two dialogues about Socrates' final days. In the Crito, Socrates refuses his friend Crito's offer to help him escape from prison, arguing that he is bound by an implied agreement with the laws of Athens. The Phaedo gives arguments for the immortality of the soul, including the cyclical and affinity arguments, and ends with Socrates' last words, that a rooster is owed to Asclepius.

**The Academy**
The school Plato founded in Athens around 387 BCE, often considered the first institution of higher learning in the Western world. Aristotle studied there for about twenty years.

**Timaeus and Critias**
Paired late dialogues. In the Timaeus, the title character describes how a divine craftsman (the Demiurge) created the cosmos, linking the elements to regular polyhedra now called Platonic solids. The Critias tells the story of the lost island of Atlantis.

**Neoplatonism and Plotinus**
A later revival of Plato's philosophy founded by Plotinus, whose Enneads describe reality as successive emanations from "The One," and continued by his student Porphyry. Later revivals of Plato include the Florentine Marsilio Ficino and the Cambridge Platonists led by Ralph Cudworth.

**The World as Will and Representation**
Schopenhauer's magnum opus (first published 1818/1819, also translated as The World as Will and Idea) and the near-universal giveaway. It argues that the world as we experience it is mere representation, while the underlying reality is a single blind, striving Will, and its four books cover epistemology, metaphysics of nature, aesthetics, and ethics.

**"Will to life" and its negation**
Schopenhauer's term (Wille zum Leben) for the blind, ceaseless striving that drives all living things and causes endless suffering. He argued that salvation lies in denying or negating the will to life through asceticism and resignation.

**Pessimism**
Schopenhauer is the archetypal "pessimistic" philosopher, holding that life is fundamentally suffering because desire can never be permanently satisfied. Nearly every question calls him a pessimist in its giveaway.

**Kant and the "thing-in-itself"**
Schopenhauer saw himself as Kant's true heir. He identified Kant's unknowable "thing-in-itself" (noumenon) with the Will, which we know directly through our own bodies, and our body is both will from the inside and representation from the outside. His magnum opus includes an appendix, "Critique of the Kantian Philosophy."

**Aesthetics as escape and the supremacy of music**
In the third book of his magnum opus, Schopenhauer argues that aesthetic contemplation gives a temporary escape from the suffering of willing. Music is the highest art because it is not a copy of the Ideas but a direct copy of the Will itself, a view that deeply inspired Richard Wagner.

**Upanishads, Vedas, and Buddhism**
Schopenhauer was one of the first Western philosophers to draw heavily on Indian thought, quoting the Upanishads and comparing his ideas to Buddhism. He based his ethics of compassion on the Sanskrit phrase "tat tvam asi" ("thou art that"), meaning that the self and others are ultimately one.

**On the Fourfold Root of the Principle of Sufficient Reason**
Schopenhauer's 1813 doctoral dissertation. It divides the principle of sufficient reason (adopted from Leibniz) into four forms governing becoming (fiendi), knowing (cognoscendi), being (essendi), and acting (agendi). In it he mocks the ontological argument for God as a "charming joke."

**"Schopenhauer as Educator"**
The third of Friedrich Nietzsche's Untimely Meditations. Nietzsche praises Schopenhauer's honesty, cheerfulness, and steadfastness as a model for renewing German culture, contrasting him with figures like David Strauss, and it contains the line "There is in the world one road whereon none may go, except thou."

**On the Basis of Morality and compassion (Mitleid)**
A prize essay arguing that compassion, not Kantian duty, is the foundation of morality. It names egoism, malice, and compassion as the three basic incentives of human action. The Royal Danish Society of Sciences declined to award it its prize even though it was the only entry.

**The Art of Being Right**
A satirical treatise (also called The Art of Controversy) listing 38 stratagems for winning arguments regardless of truth. The final stratagem is to "become personal, insulting, and rude" when your opponent is winning, that is, an ad hominem attack.

**"On Women"**
A notoriously misogynistic essay from Schopenhauer's collection Parerga and Paralipomena (Greek for "additions and omissions"). It claims women are not meant for much mental or physical work and cannot take a purely objective interest in anything.

**Animals and poodles**
Schopenhauer loved his pet poodles and argued strongly for compassion toward animals. He criticized thinkers like Spinoza and Kant for treating animals as mere means for human use, and held that cruelty to animals shows a lack of goodness.

**On Vision and Colors**
A treatise on color theory written after discussions with Goethe, whose own theory of colors Schopenhauer partly adopted and partly corrected. He later sent the work to Charles Locke Eastlake, the English translator of Goethe's Theory of Colours, explaining his views on how the retina produces color.

**Rivalry with Hegel**
As a lecturer at the University of Berlin, Schopenhauer deliberately scheduled his lectures at the same time as Hegel's. Almost no students came, and his academic career failed; he despised Hegel for the rest of his life.

**On the Freedom of the Will**
Another prize essay, in which Schopenhauer denies free will, arguing that every action follows necessarily from a sufficient motive acting on a person's fixed character. It was published together with On the Basis of Morality as The Two Fundamental Problems of Ethics.

**Das Kapital (Capital: A Critique of Political Economy)**
Marx's longest and most important work, whose first volume appeared in 1867 (Engels edited the later volumes after Marx's death). It analyzes capitalism through the commodity, the labor theory of value, and surplus value, and it is the most common giveaway for Marx.

**The Communist Manifesto**
An 1848 pamphlet Marx wrote with Friedrich Engels for the Communist League. It describes history as class struggle between the bourgeoisie (owners) and the proletariat (workers) and calls for a proletarian revolution. It is almost always mentioned near the end of a question.

**"A spectre is haunting Europe"**
The opening line of The Communist Manifesto, which continues "the spectre of communism." It is one of the most frequently quoted lines from Marx.

**"The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles"**
The first sentence of the first section of The Communist Manifesto. It sums up Marx's view that history is driven by conflict between economic classes, such as freeman and slave, lord and serf, and bourgeoisie and proletariat.

**"Workers of the world, unite!"**
The rallying cry that closes The Communist Manifesto, often rendered as "proletarians of all countries, unite!" The book ends by saying the workers "have nothing to lose but their chains."

**Commodity fetishism**
A concept from the first volume of Das Kapital. Under capitalism, social relations between people (the labor that made a product) appear as relations between things, so commodities seem to have value in themselves. Later thinkers like Georg Lukacs extended the idea into "reification."

**Theses on Feuerbach**
A short set of notes from 1845 criticizing the materialism of Ludwig Feuerbach, a fellow Young Hegelian. The famous eleventh thesis says "philosophers have only interpreted the world in various ways; the point is to change it." Another thesis calls the human essence "the ensemble of the social relations."

**Base and superstructure**
Marx's model of society. The economic "base" (the forces and relations of production) shapes the "superstructure" of law, politics, religion, and culture. Marx was said to have "stood Hegel on his head" by making material conditions, rather than ideas, the driving force of history.

**The Poverty of Philosophy**
Marx's 1847 attack on the anarchist Pierre-Joseph Proudhon. Its title reverses Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty, and in it Marx criticized Proudhon's economics, including how he took the division of labor for granted.

**Linen and the coat (the value-form)**
The opening chapter of Das Kapital explains the "value-form" of commodities by comparing amounts of goods, such as 20 yards of linen being worth one coat. Marx uses these examples to show how money emerges as the general form of value, and he separates a good's use-value from its exchange-value.

**Surplus value and the labor theory of value**
Marx argued that a commodity's exchange value comes from the labor needed to produce it. Capitalists pay workers less than the value their labor creates and keep the difference, called surplus value, which Marx saw as exploitation. He contrasted the simple circuit C-M-C (sell a commodity to buy another) with the capitalist circuit M-C-M' (invest money to get more money).

**Alienation and "species-being" (Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844)**
In his early Paris Manuscripts, Marx argued that under capitalism workers are alienated (estranged) from the products they make, from the act of working, from other people, and from their "species-being," meaning their essential human nature.

**"Religion is the opium of the people"**
A line from Marx's Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right. Just before it he calls religion "the sigh of the oppressed creature," meaning that religion gives comfort but also distracts people from changing their real conditions.

**The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Napoleon**
Marx's analysis of Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte's 1851 coup in France. It opens by saying that history repeats itself, "first as tragedy, then as farce," comparing the nephew's coup to that of his uncle Napoleon I.

**Critique of the Gotha Program**
An 1875 letter in which Marx attacked the program uniting the German socialist parties at Gotha, which he saw as too reformist. It contains the slogan "from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs" and discusses the "dictatorship of the proletariat," a temporary stage before full communism.

**Summa Theologica**
Aquinas's most famous work, a huge, unfinished summary of Catholic theology written for students. It is the most common giveaway for him, and it contains his Five Ways of proving that God exists.

**Quinque viae (Five Ways)**
Aquinas's five arguments for the existence of God, found in the Summa Theologica: the argument from motion, from efficient causation, from contingency, from degrees of perfection, and from design (final cause). They are the most frequently clued part of his thought.

**Unmoved mover / first cause**
The first two of the Five Ways. Everything that moves is moved by something else, and every effect has an efficient cause, so the chain must end in a first unmoved mover or first cause, which Aquinas identifies with God. He took the idea from Aristotle.

**Summa Contra Gentiles**
A four-book work of apologetics defending Christian faith against non-believers ("gentiles"), especially Muslims and Jews. Tradition says the Dominican Raymond of Penafort asked for it to help missionaries. It divides truths about God into those beyond human reason and those that natural reason can prove.

**On the Unity of the Intellect, Against the Averroists**
A treatise attacking the Averroist teaching, held by Siger of Brabant, that all humans share one intellect or soul. Aquinas argued that Averroes, called "The Commentator," had misread Aristotle.

**Arguments from contingency and from degree**
The third and fourth Ways. The argument from contingency says that things which could fail to exist depend on a necessary being. The argument from degree says that the varying degrees of goodness and truth in things point to a highest, perfect being.

**Objection-and-reply format ("I answer that")**
Each article of the Summa Theologica asks a question, lists objections, gives a counter-statement, and then begins Aquinas's own answer with "I answer that" (respondeo) before replying to each objection. In this way he asks and then answers his own questions.

**Four types of law**
In the Summa Theologica Aquinas divides law into eternal law (God's rational plan for the universe), divine law (revealed in Scripture), natural law (eternal law as human reason grasps it), and human law (laws made by people).

**Just war theory**
Aquinas said a war is just only if it has three things: proper authority (it is declared by a legitimate ruler), a just cause, and right intention (it aims at good and avoids evil). He built on ideas from Augustine.

**Doctrine of double effect**
Aquinas's principle, first stated in his discussion of killing in self-defense, that an act with both a good and a bad effect can be allowed if only the good effect is intended. It became a key rule in Catholic moral theology.

**Albertus Magnus and Aristotle**
Aquinas studied under the Dominican Albertus Magnus. He was a great admirer of Aristotle, whom he called "the Philosopher," and he worked to bring Aristotle's philosophy into harmony with Christian theology. He called Peter Lombard, author of the Sentences, "the Master."

**Essence and existence**
Aquinas taught that in created things essence (what a thing is) and existence (that it is) are distinct, and that only in God are they identical. Sartre's existentialist claim that "existence precedes essence" reverses the traditional view that essence comes first.

**On the Principles of Nature**
An early short work in which Aquinas, following Aristotle, links matter with potency and form with act, and explains the four causes and the principles of change.

**Death on the way to the Second Council of Lyon**
Aquinas died in 1274 while travelling to the Second Council of Lyon, leaving the Summa Theologica unfinished. His secretary, Reginald of Piperno, completed it as the "Supplement," using Aquinas's earlier writings.

**Dominican Order and titles**
Aquinas was an Italian Dominican friar and a leading Scholastic thinker. He is known as the "Angelic Doctor" (Doctor Angelicus) and the "Common Doctor" (Doctor Communis). Later thinkers such as the School of Salamanca developed his philosophy, which is known as Thomism.

**Democracy in America (Alexis de Tocqueville)**
A two-volume study (1835 and 1840) by the French aristocrat Alexis de Tocqueville, written after he traveled through the United States. It is the most common giveaway for democracy, and it examines how American representative democracy works and where it is headed.

**"Tyranny of the majority"**
Tocqueville's warning that in a democracy the majority can oppress minorities and crush dissenting opinion through law and social pressure. John Stuart Mill borrowed the phrase in On Liberty.

**Study of prisons with Gustave de Beaumont**
Tocqueville and his friend Gustave de Beaumont officially came to America in 1831 to study its prison system. Their travels led Tocqueville to write Democracy in America, which argues that the spread of democracy and equality is inevitable.

**Perpetual Peace and democratic peace theory**
In his 1795 essay Perpetual Peace, Immanuel Kant argued that republics with representative government would be unlikely to go to war with each other. This idea led to the modern democratic peace theory, which holds that mature democracies rarely fight one another. Kant himself criticized direct "democracy" as despotic, a "contradiction of the general will," because the many decide over the individual without his consent.

**Democracy and Education (John Dewey)**
A 1916 book by the American pragmatist John Dewey. It argues for progressive, experience-based education that prepares citizens to take part in a democratic society.

**Plato's ship of state**
In the Republic, Plato compares a democracy to a ship whose sailors fight over the helm, while the shipowner (the people) cannot steer and the true navigator (the philosopher), dismissed as a "stargazer," is ignored. The image argues that ruling well needs expert knowledge.

**Plato's Republic ranking of constitutions**
In Books 8 and 9 of the Republic, Socrates describes the decline of the ideal city through timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, and finally tyranny. Democracy is ranked just above tyranny, which it is said to produce, and the tyrant is called the most miserable person because he is a slave to his passions.

**Aristotle's perversion of polity**
In his Politics, Aristotle classifies governments by whether one, few, or many rule and whether they rule for the common good. Rule by the many for the common good is "polity," and its corrupt form, ruling only for the poor majority, is democracy.

**Athenian direct democracy**
Democracy began in ancient Athens, where adult male citizens voted directly on laws in the Assembly instead of electing representatives. The word comes from the Greek demos ("people") and kratos ("power" or "rule").

**The Crisis of Parliamentary Democracy (Carl Schmitt)**
A 1923 work by the German legal theorist Carl Schmitt, who later joined the Nazi Party. Schmitt argued that liberalism, with its endless parliamentary debate, is fundamentally incompatible with democracy, which depends on the identity of rulers and ruled.

**Democracy and Its Critics (Robert Dahl)**
A 1989 book by the American political scientist Robert Dahl. It sets out five criteria for a democratic process, including effective participation, voting equality, and enlightened understanding.

**"The Priority of Democracy to Philosophy" (Richard Rorty)**
An essay by the American pragmatist Richard Rorty. He argues that liberal democracy does not need a philosophical foundation and comes before any philosophical justification of it.

**"The Rise of Illiberal Democracy" (Fareed Zakaria)**
A 1997 essay in Foreign Affairs by Fareed Zakaria. He warns that many countries hold free elections while ignoring constitutional limits and basic liberties, producing "illiberal democracies."

**Soft despotism and literature in democratic ages**
In the second volume of Democracy in America, Tocqueville warns of "soft despotism," in which a powerful, caring government keeps citizens in a state of comfortable dependence. The same volume argues that democratic literature and language produce many "new ideas" and "new words."

**"Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it."**
Santayana's most famous aphorism and his near-universal giveaway, often misquoted with "history" in place of "the past." It comes from Reason in Common Sense, the first volume of The Life of Reason.

**Skepticism and Animal Faith**
Santayana's 1923 work of epistemology, which opens with the claim that philosophy must "plunge in medias res" ("into the middle of things"). Radical skepticism leaves only an empty, momentary intuition of "essences," so knowledge must instead rest on "animal faith," an instinctive, non-rational trust in the existence of the external world.

**The Realms of Being**
Santayana's multivolume magnum opus, which divides reality into four realms: essence, matter, truth, and spirit. In it he describes matter as "often untoward, and an occasion of imperfection or conflict in things."

**The Life of Reason**
Santayana's five-volume work (1905–1906), subtitled "The Phases of Human Progress." It traces how reason operates in common sense, society, religion, art, and science, and it is the source of his most quoted lines.

**The Last Puritan**
Santayana's only novel (1935), subtitled "A Memoir in the Form of a Novel." It traces the life of Oliver Alden, a New England heir crippled by his inherited puritanism, who is contrasted with his lively European cousin Mario.

**The Sense of Beauty**
Santayana's 1896 treatise on aesthetics, which defines beauty as "pleasure objectified," meaning pleasure that we experience as a quality of the object itself. It rejects Kant's idea that aesthetic judgment is disinterested.

**"The Genteel Tradition in American Philosophy"**
Santayana's 1911 lecture, later collected in Winds of Doctrine (1913). It criticizes the polite, inherited Calvinist and transcendentalist idealism of American intellectual life, and Winds of Doctrine also critiques contemporaries such as Henri Bergson and Bertrand Russell.

**Reason in Religion and "aesthetic Catholicism"**
A volume of The Life of Reason that treats religion as poetry and symbol rather than literal truth. Although Santayana did not believe in God, he admired the beauty and tradition of the Catholicism he was raised in and called himself an "aesthetic Catholic."

**Matter, essence, truth, and spirit**
The four "realms" of Santayana's ontology. Essences are timeless forms or qualities, matter is the blind physical flux that actually exists, truth is the complete record of what exists, and spirit is consciousness, which is produced by matter.

**The Idea of Christ in the Gospels**
A late work by Santayana (1946) that treats Jesus as a poetic and imaginative ideal rather than a historical or divine figure.

**Spanish-American naturalist**
Santayana was born in Madrid in 1863 as Jorge Agustín Nicolás Ruiz de Santayana y Borrás and was raised in Boston. He taught philosophy at Harvard, where his colleagues included William James, before he left for Europe and spent his last years in Rome, and he is classified as a materialist and naturalist.

**Ezra Pound's Canto 81**
One of Pound's Pisan Cantos, which describes Santayana arriving in the port of Boston and keeping a trace of his Spanish pronunciation throughout his life.

**John Lachs**
The American philosopher known as a leading scholar of Santayana's thought. He wrote and edited several books on him.

**Positivism**
The philosophy Comte founded, holding that real knowledge comes only from observation and experience organized by science, not from theology or metaphysical speculation. He believed society, like nature, follows laws that science can discover.

**Law of Three Stages**
Comte's theory that human thought and society pass through three stages: the theological stage, which explains the world through gods; the metaphysical stage, which explains it through abstract essences and causes; and the positive, or scientific, stage, which relies on observed laws.

**Coining "sociology"**
Comte invented the word "sociology" for the scientific study of society, and he is often called the father of sociology. He saw it as the final and most complex science.

**Coining "altruism"**
Comte also coined "altruism" (from the French altruisme, from the Latin alter, "other") as the opposite of selfishness. Living for others was the central moral principle of his Religion of Humanity.

**Henri de Saint-Simon**
The French social theorist who was Comte's mentor and employer. Comte borrowed ideas from him, such as dividing history into "critical" and "organic" periods and giving spiritual power to an enlightened elite, before the two had a bitter split in 1824.

**Hierarchy of the sciences**
Comte ranked the sciences by how general and how complex they are, with each depending on the ones before it: mathematics, astronomy, physics, chemistry, biology, and finally sociology. Astronomy was the first natural science to reach the positive stage.

**Fetishism, polytheism, and monotheism**
Comte divided the theological stage into three phases: fetishism (or animism), which gives life to objects; polytheism, belief in many gods; and monotheism, belief in one god.

**Religion of Humanity**
The secular religion Comte founded late in life, which worshipped humanity itself instead of God. It had priests, a calendar of saints, and nine sacraments, including "incorporation." T. H. Huxley mocked it as "Catholicism minus Christianity."

**Clotilde de Vaux**
A woman Comte loved intensely shortly before her early death in 1846. His mourning for her and his idealization of her inspired the Religion of Humanity.

**Harriet Martineau**
The English writer and early sociologist who translated and condensed Comte's Course of Positive Philosophy into English in 1853. Comte approved of her version so much that it was translated back into French.

**The Subjective Synthesis**
The last work Comte wrote before his death in 1857, a philosophical treatment of mathematics. It was meant to be the first part of a larger series that he did not finish.

**Course of Positive Philosophy**
Comte's major six-volume work (1830–1842), which sets out positivism, the Law of Three Stages, and the hierarchy of the sciences.

**Discipline and Punish**
Foucault's 1975 book, subtitled "The Birth of the Prison," and his most common giveaway. It traces the shift in Western punishment from public torture of the body to modern institutions that discipline and observe people, arguing that the prison model spreads throughout schools, factories, barracks, and hospitals.

**Bentham's Panopticon**
Jeremy Bentham's design for a circular prison in which a central watchtower lets a guard see every cell while prisoners cannot tell when they are being watched. In Discipline and Punish, Foucault uses this "unequal gaze" as the model for modern surveillance societies, where people internalize observation and police themselves.

**Execution of Robert-François Damiens**
Discipline and Punish opens with a graphic account of the 1757 public torture and execution of Damiens, who attempted to assassinate King Louis XV. Foucault contrasts this "spectacle of the scaffold" with the rigid timetable of a later juvenile prison, such as the rules of the Mettray Penal Colony.

**Las Meninas and The Order of Things**
The Order of Things (1966), subtitled "An Archaeology of the Human Sciences," opens with an analysis of Diego Velázquez's painting Las Meninas and the shifting relationships among painter, subjects, and viewer. The book examines how the fields that became biology, economics, and philology emerged, and ends with the image of man being erased "like a face drawn in sand at the edge of the sea."

**Episteme**
Foucault's term for the underlying, largely unconscious system of assumptions that determines what counts as knowledge in a given era. In The Order of Things he distinguishes the Renaissance, Classical, and Modern epistemes.

**Madness and Civilization (History of Madness)**
Foucault's first major book (1961), titled History of Madness in full and abridged in English as Madness and Civilization. It argues that the "Age of Reason" redefined madness as the excluded "Other" of reason, and that the mad were treated with more tolerance in earlier periods.

**The Great Confinement**
Foucault's term, from History of Madness, for the mass internment of the poor, idle, and insane in houses of confinement such as Paris's Hôpital Général beginning in the mid-17th century. He argues it marked a new way of separating "unreason" from society.

**Lepers and the Ship of Fools**
History of Madness opens by describing how the leprosaria of medieval Europe emptied as leprosy declined, and how the mad later inherited the role of excluded outcasts. He discusses the Renaissance image of the Ship of Fools, a boat carrying the insane from town to town.

**Pinel and Tuke**
In History of Madness, Foucault critiques the celebrated asylum reformers Philippe Pinel, who freed the insane from chains in Paris, and Samuel Tuke of the Quaker York Retreat. He argues their "humane" reforms replaced physical restraint with a subtler moral and psychological control over patients.

**The Birth of the Clinic and the "medical gaze"**
Foucault's 1963 book on the rise of modern clinical medicine. He coined the "medical gaze" (or "clinical gaze") to describe how doctors began to separate a patient's body and disease from the patient's identity as a person.

**The History of Sexuality and the "repressive hypothesis"**
Foucault's unfinished multivolume study. Its first volume, The Will to Knowledge (1976), rejects the "repressive hypothesis" that Victorian society simply silenced sex, arguing instead that it produced an explosion of discourse about sexuality, and that the structure of religious confession was carried over into medicine and psychotherapy.

**Biopower and biopolitics**
Foucault's concept for the modern state's power over the life of populations, through birth rates, health, and sexuality. He contrasted sovereign power to "make die and let live" with biopower's ability to "make live and let die," and developed the idea in The Will to Knowledge and lecture series such as Society Must Be Defended.

**Docile bodies**
In Discipline and Punish, Foucault describes how disciplinary techniques such as timetables, drills, and spatial arrangement produce "docile bodies" that can be used, transformed, and improved. He says discipline produces an individuality that is cellular, organic, genetic, and combinatory.

**The Archaeology of Knowledge and "archaeological method"**
Foucault's 1969 book explaining his "archaeological" method of uncovering the rules that govern discourse in a period. It treats language as a field of "statements" whose meaning depends on their context. He later supplemented archaeology with a "genealogical" method borrowed from Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morality.

**"What Is an Author?"**
Foucault's 1969 essay arguing that the author is not the source of a text's meaning but an "author function" that classifies and organizes discourse. Other shorter works sometimes clued include This Is Not a Pipe, on René Magritte, and Death and the Labyrinth, on Raymond Roussel.

**Aristophanes' myth of the split humans**
The comic playwright Aristophanes claims humans were once round, double creatures with four arms, four legs, and two faces, until Zeus cut them in half for their arrogance. Love is the longing of each half to find its "other half," and the myth also explains why some people love the same sex and others the opposite sex.

**Diotima of Mantinea**
A priestess, possibly fictional, whose teachings on love Socrates recounts as the centerpiece of the dialogue. She is the only female voice in the work, and Socrates presents her as the person who taught him about Eros.

**The ladder of love**
Diotima's account of how a lover climbs step by step from loving one beautiful body, to all beautiful bodies, to beautiful souls, laws and institutions, and knowledge, until finally seeing Beauty itself, the eternal Form of beauty. This ascent is the dialogue's most famous philosophical idea.

**Alcibiades' drunken speech about Socrates**
Near the end, the Athenian politician Alcibiades bursts in drunk and praises Socrates instead of love. He describes how he tried and failed to seduce Socrates, who was unmoved by physical pleasure, and he recalls Socrates' toughness on military campaign.

**Silenus statues and Marsyas**
Alcibiades compares Socrates to hollow statues of the ugly satyr Silenus that open to reveal little images of the gods inside: ugly on the outside, divine within. He also calls Socrates a more wonderful performer than the satyr Marsyas, because Socrates enchants people with words alone instead of the flute.

**Aristophanes' hiccups and Eryximachus**
Aristophanes gets hiccups when his turn comes, so the doctor Eryximachus speaks in his place and suggests cures such as holding his breath, gargling, or sneezing. Eryximachus says love operates throughout nature as a harmony or agreement of opposites, as in medicine and music. John Adams later joked that all he learned from Plato's Symposium was a cure for the hiccups.

**A drinking party at Agathon's house**
The title means "drinking party." The tragic poet Agathon hosts the gathering to celebrate his first victory in the tragedy competition, and the guests agree to drink moderately and each give a speech in praise of Eros, the god of love.

**Apollodorus and Aristodemus (the frame story)**
The dialogue is narrated by Apollodorus, who tells an unnamed friend about the party years afterward. He heard about it from Aristodemus, a follower of Socrates who was actually there.

**Pausanias' Heavenly and Common love**
Pausanias argues there are two Aphrodites and so two kinds of love. "Common" (Pandemian) love comes from the Aphrodite born of Zeus and Dione and seeks bodies. "Heavenly" (Uranian) love comes from the Aphrodite born of Uranus alone, with no mother, and seeks souls and virtue. He defends the lover's willing "slavery for the sake of virtue" and discusses how Athenian law and custom treat love.

**Phaedrus and Achilles and Patroclus**
Phaedrus gives the first speech, calling Eros the oldest of the gods. He argues love makes people brave and willing to die for one another, and says an army of lovers would be unbeatable, citing Achilles avenging Patroclus and Alcestis dying for her husband.

**Love as the child of Resource and Poverty**
Diotima says Eros is not a god but a spirit between gods and mortals, born to Poros (Resource) and Penia (Poverty). Love is therefore always needy but always resourceful, and it seeks the beauty and wisdom it lacks. This is why love is linked to philosophy, the love of wisdom.

**Agathon's speech**
The host praises Eros himself as the youngest, most beautiful, and most delicate of the gods, in a polished, poetic speech. Socrates then questions him and gets him to admit that love desires beauty and so must lack it.

**Socrates' sandals and trance on the porch**
At the start, Aristodemus meets Socrates freshly bathed and wearing fancy sandals, unusual for him, as he heads to the party. On the way Socrates falls into thought and stands still on a neighbor's porch for a long time, arriving late.

**Xenophon's Symposium**
Xenophon also wrote a Symposium starring Socrates. It is set at a party given by the wealthy Callias, who is in love with the young athlete Autolycus.

**Kierkegaard's "In Vino Veritas"**
The first section of Kierkegaard's Stages on Life's Way, "In Vino Veritas," imitates Plato's Symposium. In it several characters give speeches about love and women at a banquet.

**Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus**
Wittgenstein's only book published in his lifetime (1921), a short work organized as seven main numbered propositions with nested sub-propositions. It sets out a picture theory of language and a logical atomism that differs from Bertrand Russell's, and its title echoes Spinoza's Tractatus Theologico-Politicus. Russell wrote its introduction, which Wittgenstein felt misunderstood the book.

**"The world is everything that is the case"**
The famous opening proposition of the Tractatus, also translated "The world is all that is the case." It introduces the view that the world is made up of facts, not things.

**"Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent"**
The final proposition (7) of the Tractatus, also translated "What we cannot speak about we must pass over in silence." It expresses Wittgenstein's view that ethics, aesthetics, and metaphysics lie beyond what language can meaningfully say.

**Beetle in a box**
A thought experiment from the Philosophical Investigations. Everyone has a box containing something they call a "beetle," but no one can look into anyone else's box. Because the word's meaning cannot depend on the hidden contents, the example shows that private inner sensations cannot give words their meaning. It is the most common clue for Wittgenstein.

**Private language argument**
Wittgenstein's argument in the Philosophical Investigations that a language understandable only to a single speaker, referring to his private sensations, is incoherent. In one example, a man writes the letter "S" in a diary or calendar each time he has a certain sensation, but he has no criterion of correctness for using "S" properly.

**Philosophical Investigations**
Wittgenstein's major later work, published posthumously in 1953 and edited by G. E. M. Anscombe and Rush Rhees. It opens with a quotation from Augustine's Confessions about learning language, criticizes his own earlier Tractatus, and argues that meaning is found in use. It also includes the example of a shopkeeper handing over "five red apples."

**Language games and the builders**
Wittgenstein's idea that words get their meaning from their use in particular activities, or "language games." His first example in the Philosophical Investigations is a primitive language of builders who use only the words "block," "pillar," "slab," and "beam."

**Picture theory of language**
The central theory of the Tractatus: propositions are logical pictures of possible facts that share a logical form with reality. Wittgenstein was reportedly inspired by reading that a Paris court used toy cars and dolls to reconstruct a traffic accident.

**Family resemblance**
Wittgenstein's later idea that members of a category such as "games" do not share a single common essence but instead share a network of overlapping similarities, like resemblances among family members. It replaced his earlier view that meaning required strict definitions.

**Rule-following paradox and Kripke's "quus"**
Wittgenstein's puzzle about how any past use of a rule can determine its correct future application. In Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language, Saul Kripke illustrated it with "quus," a function identical to addition for small numbers but returning 5 for larger inputs, and proposed a "skeptical solution."

**On Certainty**
Wittgenstein's final notes, published posthumously and edited by Anscombe and G. H. von Wright, which respond to G. E. Moore's "Here is one hand" argument against skepticism. It argues that some propositions function as "hinges" that are exempt from doubt and uses the image of a "river-bed" of thoughts in which some propositions are hardened and others fluid.

**The Blue and Brown Books**
Notes from Wittgenstein's Cambridge lectures in the 1930s that anticipate the Philosophical Investigations. The Blue Book criticizes philosophers' "craving for generality" and compares grammatically similar sentences like "A has a gold tooth" and "A has a toothache."

**Duck-rabbit**
An ambiguous drawing discussed in the Philosophical Investigations that can be seen as either a duck or a rabbit. Wittgenstein uses it to explore "seeing-as" and how perception involves interpretation.

**"If a lion could talk, we could not understand him"**
A remark from the Philosophical Investigations suggesting that understanding language depends on sharing a "form of life," not just knowing the words.

**Popper's poker and the Haidbauer incident**
Two famous biographical anecdotes. In 1946 at Cambridge, Wittgenstein allegedly brandished a fireplace poker during an argument with Karl Popper, who then gave as an example of a moral rule "Not to threaten visiting lecturers with pokers." Earlier, while a schoolteacher in rural Austria, he struck a pupil named Josef Haidbauer, who collapsed, an incident that led to Wittgenstein leaving teaching.

**Utilitarianism**
The ethical theory that Bentham founded, later developed by John Stuart Mill. It holds that the right action is the one that produces the greatest overall happiness, measured as pleasure minus pain. Bentham's version, which judges each individual action by its consequences, is now often classed as act utilitarianism.

**Panopticon**
Bentham's design for a prison (also proposed for factories, schools, and hospitals) in which a central watchtower lets a single guard observe all the inmates, who cannot tell whether they are being watched at any moment. Michel Foucault made it a central image of modern surveillance and discipline in Discipline and Punish.

**Felicific calculus**
Bentham's method, also called the hedonic calculus, for measuring the amount of pleasure and pain an action will cause by adding and subtracting them. It weighs factors including intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity (nearness), fecundity, purity, and extent (the number of people affected).

**An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation**
Bentham's most famous work, printed in 1780 and published in 1789. It sets out the principle of utility and the felicific calculus and applies them to law and punishment. It opens by declaring that "Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure."

**"The greatest happiness of the greatest number"**
The slogan summarizing Bentham's "greatest happiness principle," which he described as the measure of right and wrong and the foundation of morals and legislation.

**Auto-icon**
After Bentham's death in 1832, his body was dissected for science as he had requested, and his skeleton was padded, dressed in his own clothes, and topped with a wax head to form what he called an "auto-icon." It is displayed at University College London, and it is said to be brought to some meetings of the college council.

**"Nonsense upon stilts"**
Bentham's mocking description of natural and inalienable rights, which he considered meaningless fictions. The phrase comes from his attack on the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, known as Anarchical Fallacies.

**William Blackstone and A Fragment on Government**
Bentham's 1776 A Fragment on Government attacked the English jurist William Blackstone, whose Commentaries on the Laws of England praised the existing common law. It grew out of Bentham's longer critique of Blackstone, A Comment on the Commentaries.

**"Offences Against One's Self"**
