Bentham's essay, written around 1785 but unpublished in his lifetime, arguing that homosexual acts cause no harm to others and should therefore not be punished. It is one of the earliest known arguments in English for decriminalizing homosexuality.

**Pannomion**
Bentham's term for his goal of a complete, codified body of law based on the principle of utility. He offered to draft such codes for several countries.

**Four sanctions**
Bentham identified four sources of the pleasures and pains that motivate behavior: the physical, political, moral, and religious sanctions. He later added the sanction of sympathy.

**Philip Beauchamp**
The pseudonym under which Bentham's controversial critique of religion, Analysis of the Influence of Natural Religion on the Temporal Happiness of Mankind (1822), was published. The work argued that religion does more harm than good to human happiness.

**"Emancipate Your Colonies!"**
Bentham's 1793 pamphlet addressed to the National Convention of revolutionary France, urging the French to give up their colonies.

**Defence of Usury**
Bentham's 1787 work arguing against legal limits on the interest rates that lenders may charge. It criticized Adam Smith's support for such limits.

**John Stuart Mill**
The English philosopher who wrote On Liberty, published in 1859. Mill is also the author of Utilitarianism and The Subjection of Women, and he dedicated On Liberty to his late wife, Harriet Taylor.

**Harm principle**
The work's central idea. The only legitimate reason for society or the state to use power over an individual against their will is to prevent harm to others; a person's own good, physical or moral, is not enough reason.

**"Tyranny of the majority"**
Mill warns in Chapter I that in popular governments the majority can oppress individuals, not only through laws but through the pressure of public opinion and custom. He borrowed the phrase from Alexis de Tocqueville's Democracy in America.

**"Of Individuality, as One of the Elements of Well-Being"**
The title of Chapter III. Mill argues that people should be free to develop their own characters and "experiments of living," and he praises "individuality of power and development."

**Assumption of infallibility**
In Chapter II, on liberty of thought and discussion, Mill argues that silencing any opinion assumes that we cannot be wrong. Since we can be wrong, a silenced opinion might be true, and even false opinions help keep true beliefs alive and understood.

**Truth does not always triumph over persecution**
Mill rejects the comforting idea that truth always wins out against persecution in the end. He argues that history shows persecution has often succeeded in stamping out true ideas, so free discussion must be actively protected.

**Ban on eating pork**
In Chapter IV, Mill imagines Muslims (he writes "Mahomedans") forming a majority in a country and banning pork. He uses the example to show that the majority's disgust or religious feelings do not justify interfering with people's private conduct.

**"An Akbar or a Charlemagne"**
Mill limits his principles to mature, "civilized" societies. He says that "barbarians" who are not yet capable of improving themselves through free discussion can only hope for obedience to a ruler like the Mughal emperor Akbar or the Frankish king Charlemagne.

**The unsafe bridge**
Mill's example of when interference is allowed. If a public official sees someone about to cross a bridge known to be unsafe, and there is no time to warn him, the official may seize him and turn him back, because no one truly wants to fall into the river.

**"A state which dwarfs its men"**
From the work's closing paragraph: "a State which dwarfs its men, in order that they may be more docile instruments in its hands even for beneficial purposes, will find that with small men no great thing can really be accomplished." Mill warns against government that stifles individual development.

**Wilhelm von Humboldt**
The Prussian thinker whose work The Limits of State Action influenced Mill. On Liberty opens with an epigraph from Humboldt about the importance of human development in its richest diversity, and helped introduce his ideas to English readers.

**Liberty and the social contract**
Questions on liberty in general also mention Jean-Jacques Rousseau, whose The Social Contract opens with "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains." In the same work, Rousseau quotes the Latin saying that he prefers dangerous liberty to peaceful slavery.

**The Prince**
Machiavelli's most famous work, a short treatise written around 1513 and published in 1532 after his death. It gives frank advice on how a ruler can gain and keep power, setting aside conventional morality when necessary, and it is the most common giveaway for him.

**"It is much safer to be feared than loved"**
The best-known line of The Prince, from Chapter 17. Machiavelli argues that a ruler would ideally be both loved and feared, but since that is hard, fear is more reliable because people break bonds of love when it suits them, while fear of punishment holds firm. He adds that the prince should still avoid being hated.

**The lion and the fox**
In Chapter 18 of The Prince, Machiavelli says a ruler must imitate both animals: the fox to recognize snares and the lion to frighten off wolves. Cunning and force are both needed, since neither alone is enough. He cites the Roman emperor Septimius Severus as a ruler who combined the two.

**Discourses on Livy**
Machiavelli's longer work on republics, a commentary on the first ten books of Livy's history of Rome, Ab urbe condita. It examines Roman political history to propose "new modes and orders," argues that conflict and debate between nobles and the people kept Rome free and healthy, and includes a long discussion of conspiracies.

**Mercenaries and auxiliaries**
Machiavelli repeatedly argues that hired mercenary troops are "useless and dangerous" and that auxiliaries (armies borrowed from another ruler) are even worse. He favored a citizen militia, which he actually organized for Florence. In The Prince he uses the parable of David, who refused Saul's armor and went to face Goliath with only his sling and his knife, to show that one should rely on one's own arms.

**Lorenzo de' Medici**
The dedicatee of The Prince. Machiavelli dedicated the work to Lorenzo di Piero de' Medici, ruler of Florence, hoping to win back favor after the Medici returned to power and he was dismissed, briefly imprisoned, and tortured.

**Fortune (Fortuna)**
In Chapter 25 of The Prince, Machiavelli compares fortune to a raging river that floods the land but whose damage can be limited with dikes and embankments built in calm times. He also calls fortune a woman whom it is "necessary to beat and ill-use" to hold her down, arguing that bold virtù can master chance.

**Numa Pompilius and civil religion**
In the Discourses, Machiavelli argues that Numa, Rome's second king, mattered even more than its founder Romulus, because Numa introduced religion, which made Romans obedient and united. Machiavelli treats religion as a useful tool for social cohesion, and he argues that Christianity would be a more effective civil religion if it were more like ancient Roman religion.

**Cesare Borgia**
The son of Pope Alexander VI, held up in The Prince as a model of a new prince who acquired a state through fortune and others' arms and then worked to secure it through his own skill. Machiavelli praises his decisive and sometimes cruel actions, such as his execution of his harsh deputy Remirro de Orco.

**The Art of War**
Machiavelli's treatise on military affairs, written as a dialogue. It praises the Roman military, attacks the use of mercenaries, and promotes citizen soldiers. It includes the saying that war makes thieves and peace hangs them.

**Call to unify Italy**
The final chapter (Chapter 26) of The Prince is an exhortation to free Italy from foreign "barbarians" and unify it under a strong leader, ideally from the house of Medici. It ends with lines from Petrarch.

**Learning "not to be good"**
In Chapter 15 of The Prince, Machiavelli writes that a prince who wants to keep his position must learn how "not to be good" and to use or not use that knowledge as needed. This passage is often cited as the origin of the "problem of dirty hands," the idea that political leaders may need to do morally wrong things for good ends.

**Appearing to have virtue**
In Chapter 18 of The Prince, Machiavelli says a ruler should appear to be merciful, faithful, humane, upright, and religious, while being ready to act otherwise when necessary. In Chapter 17 he contrasts Hannibal, whose "inhuman cruelty" kept his army united, with Scipio, whose excessive leniency led his soldiers to mutiny. The Prince breaks with the traditional "mirrors for princes" genre, which taught rulers to be truly virtuous.

**Secretary of the Second Chancery**
Machiavelli's post in the Florentine Republic, to which he was elected in 1498, shortly after the fall and execution of the preacher Girolamo Savonarola. He served as a diplomat and administrator until the Medici returned in 1512.

**The Mandrake (La Mandragola)**
Machiavelli's comedy, about a young man who tricks a jealous old husband into helping him sleep with the husband's wife, using a fake potion made from mandrake root. He also wrote The Life of Castruccio Castracani, a partly fictionalized biography of a Lucchese warlord that ends with a collection of sayings attributed to him.

**Summa Theologica**
Aquinas's unfinished masterpiece (also called Summa Theologiae), begun around 1266. It is a vast, systematic synthesis of Aristotelian philosophy and Catholic theology, and its title is the most common giveaway for him.

**Quinque viae (Five Ways)**
Aquinas's five arguments for the existence of God in the Summa Theologica. They argue from motion (the "unmoved mover" or "first mover," the Prima Via), efficient causation (the "first cause"), contingency (a necessary being), degrees of perfection, and design (the teleological argument). They are a posteriori arguments drawn from features of the world, not ontological arguments.

**"The Commentator"**
Aquinas's name for Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the Andalusian philosopher famous for his commentaries on Aristotle. Aquinas calls Aristotle simply "The Philosopher," and he gives similar titles to others: Peter Lombard is "The Master" and St. Paul is "The Apostle."

**Principle of double effect**
Aquinas's principle, first stated in his discussion of killing in self-defense. An act with a good intended effect can be permissible even if it also causes a foreseen bad effect, such as an attacker's death. Philippa Foot's article that introduced the trolley problem has "double effect" in its title, and Alasdair MacIntyre also discussed the principle.

**Summa contra Gentiles**
Aquinas's four-book apologetic work defending Christianity against non-believers ("gentiles"), including Muslims and Jews. According to legend, Raymond of Penafort commissioned it. It distinguishes truths demonstrable by natural reason from revealed truths that are beyond human reason.

**On the Unity of the Intellect against the Averroists**
Aquinas's treatise (De unitate intellectus) written against Siger of Brabant and the Latin Averroists. It rejects the Averroist claim that all humans share a single intellect, arguing that Averroes had misread Aristotle.

**Just war**
In the Summa Theologica, Aquinas built on Augustine's City of God to set three conditions for a just war: the authority of the sovereign (proper authority), a just cause (such as avenging a wrong), and right intention (advancing good, with the aim of peace).

**Sed contra / "I answer that" (Respondeo)**
The fixed format of each article in the Summa Theologica. It opens with objections introduced by "it seems that" (videtur quod), then a counterstatement beginning "sed contra" ("on the contrary"), then Aquinas's own answer beginning "Respondeo" ("I answer that"), and finally replies to each objection.

**Doctor Angelicus**
Aquinas's traditional title, "the Angelic Doctor." He is also called Doctor Communis ("Common Doctor"). He was a Dominican friar born near Aquino in Italy.

**Albertus Magnus**
The Dominican scholar, known as "Doctor Universalis," who taught Aquinas and shared his interest in Aristotle.

**Aeterni Patris**
The 1879 encyclical of Pope Leo XIII that promoted the revival of Scholastic philosophy and made Aquinas's thought central to Catholic teaching. The later Thomist Jacques Maritain claimed that Aquinas's distinction between essence and existence contained the seeds of an existentialism.

**On Being and Essence**
Aquinas's early treatise (De ente et essentia) on the distinction between a thing's essence and its existence. It discusses how essence is found in composite substances, in the soul and the intelligences, and in God, the first cause. Sartre's view that existence precedes essence is often presented as a reversal of Aquinas's position.

**Contra Errores Graecorum**
Aquinas's treatise "Against the Errors of the Greeks," written at the request of Pope Urban IV, which addresses the theology of the Eastern Church. In it he argues that the Greek term "hypostasis" and the Latin "persona" express the same meaning, showing the importance of careful translation.

**"Straw"**
Near the end of his life, Aquinas had a mystical experience in 1273 and stopped writing, saying that everything he had written seemed like straw compared to what he had seen. He died in 1274 on his way to the Second Council of Lyon, and his assistant Reginald of Piperno oversaw the completion of the Summa Theologica. Dante's Divine Comedy repeats a rumor that Charles of Anjou had him poisoned.

**Beatific vision**
Aquinas's view that the ultimate end and happiness of human existence is the direct vision of God's essence after death. He also divided law into four types: eternal, natural, human, and divine.

**Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous**
Berkeley's 1713 work, the most common giveaway for him, subtitled "In Opposition to Sceptics and Atheists." Hylas (from the Greek hyle, "matter") defends the existence of material substance in a roughly Lockean way, while Philonous ("lover of mind"), who speaks for Berkeley, gradually convinces him that only minds and their ideas exist. It opens with Philonous admiring the beauty of the morning.

**"Esse est percipi" ("To be is to be perceived")**
Berkeley's famous principle that for ordinary objects, existing just means being perceived. Things like tables and trees are collections of ideas, so they cannot exist apart from a mind that perceives them. Minds themselves exist by perceiving (esse est percipere).

**Immaterialism**
Berkeley's own name for his form of idealism, which denies that matter exists independently of minds. The world consists only of spirits (minds) and their ideas. Since our ideas of sense are not caused by us, Berkeley concludes they must be caused by another spirit, God.

**The "master argument"**
Berkeley's argument that we cannot conceive of a mind-independent object. If you try to imagine a tree in a park or books in a closet with no one perceiving them, you are still conceiving of them yourself, so the attempt defeats itself. It appears in both the Principles and the Three Dialogues.

**A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge**
Berkeley's 1710 work, the first systematic statement of his immaterialism and the source of "esse est percipi." It attacks Locke's doctrine of abstract ideas and argues that only spirits and ideas exist, with God maintaining the regularity of the ideas we perceive. The Three Dialogues present its arguments in a more popular form.

**Rejection of the primary-secondary quality distinction**
John Locke held that primary qualities (such as shape, size, and motion) truly belong to objects, while secondary qualities (such as color, taste, and heat) exist only in the mind. Berkeley argued that primary qualities cannot be abstracted from secondary ones and vary with the perceiver just as much, using examples like a mite that sees its own foot as large, so both kinds of qualities are mind-dependent.

**The Analyst**
Berkeley's 1734 critique of the calculus of Isaac Newton and Leibniz, subtitled "A Discourse Addressed to an Infidel Mathematician" (probably Edmond Halley). Berkeley mocked Newton's fluxions and infinitesimals as "ghosts of departed quantities," arguing that mathematicians accepted ideas as obscure as any religious mystery. James Jurin replied with Geometry No Friend to Infidelity.

**An Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision**
Berkeley's 1709 work on perception, which argues that distance, depth, and magnitude are not directly seen. The eye sees only light and color, and we learn to judge distance by experience, associating visual ideas with ideas of touch. Berkeley later described the regular ideas of nature as a divine language through which God speaks to us.

**Alciphron, or the Minute Philosopher**
Berkeley's 1732 work in seven dialogues defending Christianity against "free-thinkers," whom he calls "minute philosophers." It targets writers such as Bernard Mandeville and the Earl of Shaftesbury, and it contains an influential view of language, arguing that words can serve purposes such as arousing emotion rather than only naming ideas.

**Siris and tar-water**
Berkeley's last major work, Siris (1744), begins by praising tar-water (pine tar mixed with water) as a cure-all medicine and moves through a chain of reflections to philosophical and theological conclusions, including that physical effects require active, spiritual causes.

**Samuel Johnson's "I refute it thus"**
According to James Boswell, Samuel Johnson responded to Berkeley's immaterialism by forcefully kicking a large stone and declaring, "I refute it thus." The response is famous but is generally considered to miss Berkeley's point, since Berkeley never denied that we perceive stones.

**De Motu**
Berkeley's 1721 essay on motion, which criticizes Newton's ideas of absolute space and motion and argues that terms like "force" are mathematical hypotheses useful for calculation rather than descriptions of real things. Karl Popper saw this instrumentalist view, which rejects essentialist explanations, as "Berkeley's razor" and called Berkeley a precursor of Ernst Mach.

**Berkeley, California**
The city in California, home of the University of California, Berkeley, is named after him, inspired by his poem containing the line "Westward the course of empire takes its way." His name is pronounced "BARK-lee."

**Bermuda project and Bishop of Cloyne**
Berkeley planned to found a college in Bermuda to educate colonists and Native Americans, and he lived in Rhode Island while waiting for funding that never came. When the project failed, he gave his farm and books to Yale and books to Harvard. He later became the Anglican Bishop of Cloyne in Ireland.

**The limerick "no one about in the Quad"**
Ronald Knox's limerick about a tree that continues to exist when "there's no one about in the Quad." The reply verse explains that the tree continues to be because it is always observed by God, summarizing Berkeley's view that God's perception keeps things in existence.

**Plucked chicken: "Behold, a man!"**
When Plato defined man as a "featherless biped," Diogenes plucked a chicken, brought it to the Academy, and declared "Behold! I've brought you a man!" According to the story, Plato then added "with broad, flat nails" to his definition. This is the most common clue for Diogenes.

**Lamp in search of an "honest man"**
Diogenes famously wandered around in broad daylight carrying a lit lamp or lantern, claiming he was searching for an honest man. The stunt mocked the vice and deceit he saw in the society around him.

**Alexander the Great: "Stand out of my light"**
When Alexander the Great visited Diogenes and offered him anything he wished, Diogenes asked only that Alexander step aside because he was blocking the sunlight. Alexander supposedly replied, "If I were not Alexander, I would wish to be Diogenes."

**Founder of Cynicism ("the dog")**
Diogenes is regarded as the founder, or the most famous early figure, of the Cynic school. Critics called him a "dog" for his shameless public behavior, and the school's name comes from the Greek word kynikos, meaning "dog-like."

**Living in a pithos (tub or barrel)**
Diogenes lived in a large ceramic storage jar called a pithos, often described as a tub or barrel, in the marketplace (agora) of Athens. It is the best-known example of his deliberate poverty.

**Student of Antisthenes**
Diogenes was a follower of Antisthenes, a pupil of Socrates who is often seen as the forerunner of Cynicism. In one story, Antisthenes tried to drive Diogenes away by beating him with a staff, but Diogenes refused to leave and became his disciple.

**Diogenes Laertius, Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers**
A later writer who shares the name Diogenes, nicknamed Laertius, wrote this biographical compilation, probably in the 3rd century AD. It is a principal source for ancient Greek philosophy, and many of the anecdotes about Diogenes of Sinope come from it.

**"Deface the currency"**
According to one story, the Oracle of Delphi told Diogenes to "deface the currency." This was linked to an episode in Sinope in which Diogenes, or his father, a moneyer, debased the city's coinage, leading to his exile. Diogenes took the phrase as a motto for overturning conventional values.

**Sold into slavery: "ruling men"**
After being captured by pirates and put up for sale as a slave, Diogenes said that the only thing he was good at was "ruling men." He pointed to a buyer, traditionally the Corinthian Xeniades, and said that this man needed a master.

**Shamelessness, self-sufficiency, and asceticism**
Diogenes' philosophy rested on self-sufficiency (autarkeia), shamelessness, outspokenness (parrhesia), and a simple life lived "according to nature." He openly rejected social convention, for example by eating, urinating, and defecating in public.

**Spitting in a rich man's face**
While at a wealthy man's house, Diogenes was told not to spit because everything was so clean. He spat in the host's face, saying it was the only dirty place he could find.

**Refuting Eubulides' "horned" paradox**
Eubulides of Megara posed a sophism: "What you have not lost, you still have; you have not lost horns, so you have horns." Diogenes is said to have refuted it simply by touching his forehead.

**Diogenes of Apollonia**
A Presocratic philosopher with the same name who held that air is the fundamental substance. He is credited with suggesting that meteorites come from outer space, and Aristotle preserved his description of the blood vessels.

**Diogenes of Oenoanda**
An Epicurean of the 2nd century AD who had Epicurus's teachings carved into an enormous inscription on a portico wall in his hometown of Oenoanda in Lycia, in modern Turkey.

**Lucretius's On the Nature of Things (De Rerum Natura)**
A Latin epic poem from the 1st century BC by the Roman poet Lucretius. It sets out Epicurean physics and ethics, including atomism and the mortality of the soul, and is the most famous surviving account of the school.

**Ataraxia and aponia**
The twin goals of the Epicurean life. Ataraxia is tranquility, or freedom from mental disturbance and fear, and aponia is the absence of bodily pain. Together they make up the highest pleasure.

**Epicurus and the pursuit of pleasure**
The Greek philosopher who founded the school, which holds that pleasure is the highest good and pain the only evil. Epicurus meant a modest life of simple pleasures and friendship, not wild indulgence.

**The Garden**
Epicurus's school, founded in Athens around 307–306 BC and named after the garden where its members lived and studied. It was a community built on friendship that unusually admitted women and slaves.

**Tetrapharmakos ("fourfold cure")**
A four-part summary of Epicurean ethics: do not fear the gods, do not worry about death, what is good is easy to get, and what is terrible is easy to endure. Its name comes from a four-ingredient ancient medicine.

**Letter to Menoeceus and "death is nothing to us"**
Epicurus's letter on ethics, which opens by saying that no one is too young or too old to study philosophy. It argues that "death is nothing to us," because when death is present we no longer exist to experience it.

**Atomism of Democritus**
Epicurean physics adopted Democritus's theory that everything is made of indivisible atoms moving in a void. Epicureans added the "swerve" (clinamen), a random deviation of atoms that allows for free will.

**Kinetic vs. katastematic pleasure**
The Epicurean division of pleasure into "kinetic" pleasures, which are active and come from satisfying a desire, and "katastematic" pleasures, which are static states of being free from pain and disturbance. Epicureans valued the static kind most.

**Philodemus of Gadara and the Villa of the Papyri**
Philodemus was an Epicurean philosopher and poet of the 1st century BC. Many of his works survived as carbonized scrolls in the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum, which was buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD.

**Principal Doctrines and the Vatican Sayings**
The Principal Doctrines are forty short maxims summarizing Epicurus's teachings, preserved by Diogenes Laertius. The Vatican Sayings are a similar collection of Epicurean maxims found in a manuscript in the Vatican Library.

**Diogenes Laërtius, Book X**
The tenth book of Lives of Eminent Philosophers is devoted to Epicurus and preserves three of his letters and the Principal Doctrines. It reports that Epicurus advised Pythocles to flee from all forms of conventional education and that he called Plato's followers "flatterers of Dionysius."

**Hermarchus**
Epicurus's pupil and successor as head of the Garden. He wrote a polemic Against Empedocles.

**Dante's Sixth Circle**
In Dante's Inferno, Epicurus and his followers, who "make the soul die with the body," are punished among the heretics in flaming tombs in the Sixth Circle of Hell.

**Aristippus of Cyrene and Stoicism**
The Cyrenaic school of Aristippus, which also held pleasure to be the good but favored intense physical pleasures, is seen as a forerunner of Epicureanism. Epicureanism is usually contrasted with its Hellenistic rival, Stoicism.

**Nicomachean Ethics**
Aristotle's major ethical work, traditionally said to be named after his son (or father) Nicomachus. It argues that the highest human good, a complete and self-sufficient end toward which all actions aim, is eudaimonia, and it develops his virtue ethics and the doctrine of the mean.

**Lyceum, Plato, and Alexander the Great**
Aristotle studied at Plato's Academy for about twenty years, later tutored the young Alexander the Great, and founded his own school in Athens, the Lyceum, whose members were called Peripatetics. He fled Athens after Alexander's death; these biographical facts appear in nearly every giveaway.

**Doctrine of the mean (golden mean)**
Aristotle's view, set out in Book II of the Nicomachean Ethics, that each virtue is a mean between two vices, one of excess and one of deficiency. For example, courage lies between rashness and cowardice; he compares finding the mean to an archer aiming at a target.

**Eudaimonia**
Usually translated as "happiness" or "flourishing," eudaimonia is for Aristotle the ultimate goal of human life. He defines it as an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue over a complete life, not a passing feeling.

**Four causes**
In the Physics and Metaphysics Aristotle holds that to know a thing fully we must grasp its four aitia (causes or explanations): the material cause (what it is made of), the formal cause (its form or essence), the efficient cause (what brought it about), and the final cause or telos (its purpose).

**Organon and the syllogism**
The Organon ("tool" or "instrument") is the name later given to Aristotle's six works on logic, including the Categories, On Interpretation, Prior Analytics, Posterior Analytics, Topics, and On Sophistical Refutations. In the Prior Analytics he invented the syllogism, a deductive argument from a major and a minor premise, classically illustrated by "All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal." Francis Bacon titled his Novum Organum as a response.

**Unmoved (prime) mover**
In the Metaphysics (Book Lambda) Aristotle argues that to avoid an infinite regress of motions there must be an eternal, unmoved mover that moves things as a final cause, by being loved, and whose activity is "thought thinking itself." He speculated that there may be 47 or 55 unmoved movers for the heavenly spheres.

**Categories**
The first work of the Organon, listing ten categories of being, including substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, and time. It distinguishes primary substances (individual things) from secondary substances (species and genera) and properties "said of" a subject from those "in" a subject; Porphyry's Isagoge is an introduction to it, and Kant criticized the list as derived without a principle.

**Metaphysics**
Aristotle's study of "being qua being," compiled after the Physics. It includes the four causes, the law of non-contradiction, a philosophical lexicon in Book Delta, actuality and potentiality in Book Theta, and the unmoved mover. Avicenna said he read it forty times without understanding it until he found al-Farabi's commentary.

**Hylomorphism and substance**
Aristotle's theory that every natural substance (ousia) is a compound of matter (hyle) and form (morphe). He developed it in opposition to his teacher Plato's theory of separate Forms, locating form within individual things.

**Actuality and potentiality**
Aristotle's distinction between what something already is (actuality, energeia) and what it is capable of becoming (potentiality, dynamis), as an acorn is potentially an oak. It is central to his account of change and is developed in Book Theta of the Metaphysics.

**Politics and natural slavery**
In the Politics Aristotle calls man a "political animal," says the city is prior to the family and the individual, and argues that some people are slaves by nature. He classifies three correct constitutions (kingship, aristocracy, polity) and their three deviant forms (tyranny, oligarchy, democracy).

**Poetics and catharsis**
Aristotle's work on tragedy, which roots poetry in the human instinct for imitation (mimesis). It says tragedy achieves catharsis, a purging of pity and fear, lists six elements of tragedy (plot, character, thought, diction, song, and spectacle, or opsis), and discusses hamartia, the hero's error.

**Sea battle and future contingents**
In On Interpretation, chapter 9, Aristotle asks whether the statement "there will be a sea battle tomorrow" is already true or false. The problem of future contingents prompted Diodorus Cronus's "master argument" and G. E. M. Anscombe's essay "Aristotle and the Sea Battle."

**On the Soul and Rhetoric**
On the Soul (De Anima) describes three kinds of soul: nutritive (shared even with plants), perceptive, and intellectual, and it describes an active intellect that is "deathless and everlasting." The Rhetoric analyzes the modes of persuasion, ethos, pathos, and logos, and defines the enthymeme, an argument with an unstated premise.

**Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologica**
The most famous scholastic work, by the Dominican friar Thomas Aquinas. It opens with the "Five Ways," five proofs of God's existence, the first of which argues from motion that there must be an unmoved "prime mover."

**Ockham's Razor**
The principle of parsimony associated with the scholastic William of Ockham: entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity. In other words, the simplest explanation that works is usually the one to choose.

**Peter Abelard and Heloise**
Peter Abelard was a brilliant scholastic teacher in Paris who had a love affair with his student Heloise and was castrated by men sent by her uncle. He described these events in his letters with Heloise and in his History of My Calamities. He was also condemned after Bernard of Clairvaux denounced him to the Pope.

**Sic et Non**
Abelard's work ("Yes and No"), which sets out 158 theological questions alongside quotations from Church authorities that seem to contradict one another. It encouraged readers to resolve the conflicts through reason, a key method of scholasticism.

**Peter Lombard's Four Books of Sentences**
A collection of theological opinions from Scripture and the Church Fathers, arranged by topic. It became the standard theology textbook of medieval universities, earning Lombard the title "Master of the Sentences" (Magister Sententiarum), and many scholastics wrote commentaries on it.

**Duns Scotus and the univocity of being**
John Duns Scotus, the "Subtle Doctor," argued that "being" means the same thing (is univocal) when said of God and of creatures. His followers' school of thought is called Scotism.

**Anselm of Canterbury**
Often called the father of scholasticism. He is famous for the ontological argument for God's existence in his Proslogion and for describing theology as "faith seeking understanding."

**Dialectical reasoning**
Scholasticism emphasized dialectic: posing questions, setting out arguments on both sides, and resolving apparent contradictions through careful logical reasoning. It drew heavily on Aristotle's logic to make Christian theology systematic.

**Named for the schools**
The term scholasticism comes from the Latin scholasticus, meaning "belonging to a school." The movement developed in the cathedral schools and early universities of medieval Europe, such as the University of Paris.

**"Doctors" of the schools**
Leading scholastics were given honorary titles as "Doctors." For example, Aquinas was the "Angelic Doctor," Duns Scotus the "Subtle Doctor," and William of Ockham the "Invincible Doctor."

**Reconciling Aristotle with Christianity**
A major goal of scholasticism, especially after Aristotle's works were rediscovered in Western Europe in the 12th and 13th centuries, was to harmonize Greek philosophy with Christian teaching. Aquinas's work is the best-known example.

**Two Treatises of Government**
Locke's 1689 work of political philosophy. The First Treatise attacks the divine right of kings, and the Second Treatise (on the "true original, extent, and end of civil government") sets out the state of nature, natural rights, government by consent, and the right to overthrow a government that betrays its people. It is the most common title giveaway.

**"Life, liberty, and property (estate)"**
Locke's list of natural rights that every government exists to protect. In the Second Treatise he writes that "no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions," and Thomas Jefferson adapted the idea as "life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness" in the Declaration of Independence.

**Tabula rasa ("blank slate")**
Locke's empiricist claim that the mind at birth is like "white paper, void of all characters," and that all ideas come from experience through sensation and reflection. He gives the example that no one can have the idea of a pineapple's taste without having tasted one.

**An Essay Concerning Human Understanding**
Locke's major 1689 work of epistemology. It argues against innate ideas, defines knowledge as the perception of agreement or disagreement between ideas, discusses language (including the chapter "Of the Abuse of Words" and the coinage "sortal"), and contains his theory of personal identity.

**Rejection of innate ideas**
Book I of the Essay denies that people are born with any innate principles or ideas. Gottfried Leibniz rebutted the Essay chapter by chapter in his New Essays on Human Understanding, comparing the mind to a block of marble whose veins already mark out the shape of Hercules.

**Labor theory of property ("mixing" labor)**
Locke argued that a person gains ownership of something from nature by mixing his labor with it, for example by picking apples from a tree or gathering acorns. Karl Marx built on such ideas in his labor theory of value, and Robert Nozick objected by asking whether pouring a can of tomato juice into the sea would make the sea yours.

**Lockean proviso and the spoilage limit**
Locke limited the acquisition of property by requiring that "enough, and as good" be left for others and that a person take no more than he can use before it spoils. Robert Nozick named the first condition the "Lockean proviso" in Anarchy, State, and Utopia. Locke argued that the invention of money allowed accumulation and inequality, writing "in the beginning all the world was America."

**A Letter Concerning Toleration**
Locke's 1689 letter, addressed to an "Honoured Sir," arguing that the civil magistrate has no authority over "the care of souls" and that religious dissenters should be tolerated. It excludes atheists, since "promises, covenants, and oaths... can have no hold upon an atheist," and Catholics, whom he saw as loyal to a foreign power.

**Robert Filmer's Patriarcha**
Filmer's defense of absolute monarchy, which claimed that kings inherited their authority from Adam as the first father. Locke's First Treatise refutes it point by point, arguing for example that God, not the father, is the giver of life.

**Primary and secondary qualities**
In the Essay Locke distinguished primary qualities that belong to objects themselves, such as shape, size, solidity, and motion, from secondary qualities like color, taste, and sound, which are powers to produce sensations in us.

**Molyneux's problem**
A question posed to Locke by the Irish scientist William Molyneux: if a man born blind who could tell a cube from a sphere by touch were suddenly given sight, could he tell them apart by sight alone? Locke discussed it in the second edition of the Essay and answered no.

**Prince and cobbler (personal identity)**
Locke argued that personal identity consists in continuity of consciousness, carried by memory, not in sameness of body or soul. He imagines the soul of a prince, with its memories, entering the body of a cobbler, so that the cobbler's body would then be the same person as the prince.

**Slavery and the state of war**
In the Second Treatise Locke argues that no one can sell himself into slavery, because no one has absolute power over his own life, and that legitimate slavery is only a continuation of the state of war against an unjust aggressor. In practice, as secretary to the Earl of Shaftesbury, he helped write the Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina, which allowed slavery.

**Right of revolution and the separation of powers**
Locke held that when a government violates the trust of the people or loses their consent, it is dissolved and the people may resist and replace it, citing the royalist jurist William Barclay in his chapter on "the dissolution of government." He also distinguished the legislative, executive, and federative (foreign-affairs) powers.

**Some Thoughts Concerning Education and The Reasonableness of Christianity**
Some Thoughts Concerning Education (1693) gives Locke's advice on raising children and criticizes harsh schooling, shaped by his own years under Richard Busby at Westminster School. The Reasonableness of Christianity (1695) defends a simple, rational Christian faith, though Leo Strauss read Locke as a secret hedonist hiding his true views.

**Grue and bleen**
Nelson Goodman's invented, time-dependent predicates. Something is "grue" if it is observed before a certain future time and is green, or is not observed before then and is blue, and "bleen" is the reverse. Every emerald seen so far is both green and grue, so the same evidence seems to support two contradictory predictions.

**Goodman's "New Riddle of Induction"**
Nelson Goodman's puzzle, built on the grue example, about which generalizations past evidence actually supports. It shifts Hume's question of whether induction is justified to the question of which predicates can properly be used in inductive reasoning.

**David Hume's "problem of induction"**
Hume argued that inductive inferences, which assume the future will resemble the past, cannot be justified by reason, since denying them involves no contradiction, and cannot be justified by experience without arguing in a circle. He concluded that induction rests on custom or habit.

**The sun rising tomorrow**
Hume's classic example: even though the sun has risen every day that anyone has observed, it is not a contradiction to think "the sun will not rise tomorrow." No amount of past observation proves it will rise again.

**Contrast with deduction**
Induction moves from specific observations to general conclusions or predictions and gives only probable, not certain, conclusions. Deduction moves from premises to conclusions that must follow if the premises are true.

**Fact, Fiction, and Forecast**
Nelson Goodman's 1955 book that presents the grue thought experiment and the new riddle of induction.

**Projectible predicates**
Goodman's term for predicates like "green" that can legitimately be "projected" from observed cases to unobserved ones, unlike gerrymandered predicates like "grue." He argued that induction only works with projectible predicates, and that projectibility depends on how well a predicate has been used in past predictions ("entrenchment").

**Hempel's raven paradox**
Carl Hempel noted that "all ravens are black" is logically equivalent to its contrapositive, "all non-black things are non-ravens." So observing a green apple seems to confirm that all ravens are black, which is a paradox about how inductive evidence confirms a theory.

**"Relations of ideas" and "matters of fact"**
Hume's division of knowledge, known as "Hume's fork." Relations of ideas, such as math, can be known by reason alone, while matters of fact can only be reached through experience and inductive inference, which assumes the uniformity of nature.

**Uniformity principle**
The assumption that nature is uniform, meaning the future will resemble the past. Hume argued that this principle cannot be proven by demonstrative (deductive) reasoning or by moral (probable) reasoning, since probable reasoning itself depends on it.

**Karl Popper and falsifiability**
Karl Popper rejected induction as the method of science. He argued that theories can never be verified by piling up observations, only falsified, so bold, easily falsifiable theories are better. He also divided Hume's problem into a logical problem and a psychological problem.

**Max Black and counterinduction**
Max Black tried to justify induction with an inductive argument, saying that inductive reasoning has worked in the past, so it will work in the future. Critics, notably Wesley Salmon, answered that a "counterinductive" rule (expecting the future to differ from the past) could justify itself in exactly the same way, so the argument proves nothing.

**Hilary Kornblith's Inductive Inference and Its Natural Ground**
A 1993 book in which Hilary Kornblith defends a naturalist account of induction. He grounds its reliability in the real existence of natural kinds in the world, a notion drawn from W. V. O. Quine.

**Francis Bacon's "true induction"**
In the Novum Organum (1620), Francis Bacon proposed a new, careful method of "true induction" as the basis of science. He warned that four "idols" (of the tribe, cave, marketplace, and theater) distort human reasoning.

**David Hume**
The Scottish empiricist philosopher who wrote this work, first published in 1748. He wrote it as a shorter, more readable version of the ideas in Book 1 of his earlier A Treatise of Human Nature, which had sold poorly.

**"Relations of ideas" and "matters of fact" (Hume's fork)**
The work's central distinction. Relations of ideas, like the truths of math, can be known with certainty by reason alone, while matters of fact, like "the sun will rise tomorrow," can only be known through experience, and their denial is not a contradiction. This division is known as "Hume's fork."

**Missing shade of blue**
A possible counterexample that Hume raises against his own theory. A person who has seen every shade of blue except one could probably imagine the missing shade without ever having had an impression of it. Hume admits the case but dismisses it as too unusual to change his general principle.

**"Of Miracles"**
Section X of the work, which defines a miracle as a "violation of the laws of nature." Hume argues that the uniform experience behind a law of nature will always outweigh human testimony that a miracle happened, so a wise person should never believe such reports.

**Problem of induction**
Hume asks what justifies inductive inferences, such as expecting the future to resemble the past. He concludes that such reasoning cannot be justified by reason or experience without circularity, and that it rests on custom or habit. This casts doubt on how far scientific claims can be trusted.

**"Of the Origin of Ideas" (impressions and ideas)**
Section II, where Hume divides perceptions into impressions (vivid sensations and feelings) and ideas (faint copies of them). He argues that ideas lack the force and liveliness of impressions and that every simple idea ultimately comes from an impression.

**"Of Probability"**
Section VI, which argues that there is no real chance in the universe. What people call chance or luck is just ignorance of the real causes of events, and belief in an outcome grows stronger as more possible cases favor it.

**Custom and necessary connection**
In the sections on cause and effect and "Of the Idea of Necessary Connexion," Hume argues that we never observe a necessary link between a cause and its effect, only one event regularly following another. Our idea of necessity comes from the mind's habit of expecting the effect after seeing the cause.

**Billiard balls**
Hume's famous example of causation. When one billiard ball strikes another, we see only one motion followed by another and never the "power" that connects them, so the effect could not be predicted before experience.

**"Commit it then to the flames"**
The famous ending of Section XII. Hume says that if a book contains no abstract reasoning about quantity or number and no experimental reasoning about matters of fact, it should be burned, because it can contain "nothing but sophistry and illusion."

**John Locke and empiricism**
The Enquiry is a key text of British empiricism, the view that all knowledge comes from experience. It builds on the work of John Locke, whose An Essay Concerning Human Understanding has a similar title.

**"Of Liberty and Necessity"**
Section VIII, where Hume offers a compatibilist answer to the free will debate. He argues that human actions are caused like everything else, but that this necessity is consistent with liberty, meaning the power to act according to one's own will.

**Stealing pears (Confessions)**
In Book 2 of his Confessions, Augustine describes how, as a teenager, he and his friends stole pears from a neighbor's tree, not because they were hungry but for the thrill of doing wrong, and threw most of them to pigs. He uses the episode to study the nature of sin. It is the most frequent clue for him.

**City of God**
Augustine's longest work, written after the Visigoths sacked Rome in 410 AD. Pagans blamed Christianity for Rome's fall, and Augustine answers by contrasting the eternal City of God with the Earthly City, arguing that the City of God will triumph.

**Just war**
Augustine is credited with developing the Christian theory of "just war," the idea that a Christian may fight in war under certain conditions, such as a just cause and right intention. Thomas Aquinas later expanded the theory.

**Confessions**
Augustine's spiritual autobiography in thirteen books, often called the first major Western autobiography. It describes his sinful youth and his conversion to Christianity, and its final books turn to philosophical questions such as memory, time, and a commentary on the opening of Genesis.

**Conversion from Manichaeism**
Before becoming a Christian, Augustine was for about nine years a follower of Manichaeism, a dualist religion that taught a struggle between equal forces of good and evil. He later passed through Neoplatonism before converting to Christianity, and the Confessions describes his rejection of both.

**"Take up and read" (tolle lege)**
While weeping in a garden in Milan, Augustine heard a child's voice chanting "take up and read." He opened the Bible at random to a passage from Paul's Letter to the Romans about giving up indulgence, and this moment sealed his conversion.

**Monica**
Augustine's devout Christian mother, who prayed for years for his conversion and is now a saint. In the Confessions, Augustine describes a shared mystical vision with her at Ostia shortly before her death.

**Ambrose of Milan**
The bishop of Milan whose sermons and allegorical reading of Scripture deeply influenced Augustine and helped lead him to Christianity. Ambrose baptized Augustine in 387.

**Time as a "distension of the mind"**
In Book 11 of the Confessions, Augustine admits he knows what time is until someone asks him to explain it. He concludes that time is a distentio animi, a stretching of the mind through memory, attention, and expectation, while God exists outside of time.

**Evil as the absence of good**
Augustine argued that evil is not a substance in its own right but a privation, or lack, of good. This view let him reject the Manichaean belief that evil is a power equal to good.

**On Christian Doctrine (enjoying the Trinity)**
In this work, Augustine distinguishes things to be used from things to be enjoyed and says that the only proper object of enjoyment is the Holy Trinity. The work also discusses signs, including the ambiguous signs that make Scripture hard to understand.

**Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations**
Ludwig Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations opens by quoting the Confessions, where Augustine describes learning language as an infant by seeing adults point to objects and name them. Wittgenstein criticizes this "Augustinian picture" of language.

**De Magistro (On the Teacher)**
A dialogue between Augustine and his son Adeodatus about how words and signs teach. It uses the difference between "walking" and "hurrying" to show that pointing to an action cannot fix which meaning is intended, anticipating Quine's indeterminacy arguments.

**On Free Choice of the Will**
A dialogue between Augustine and his friend Evodius about where evil comes from. Augustine argues that evil comes from the free choice of the will turning away from God, not from God himself. In later controversies he strongly opposed Pelagius, who denied original sin.

**Lucretia and the pirate (City of God)**
In City of God, Augustine argues that the Roman heroine Lucretia was wrong to kill herself after being raped, because chastity is a virtue of the mind that rape cannot destroy. He also tells of a pirate who told Alexander the Great that the only difference between them was the size of their fleets, to argue that kingdoms without justice are just large robber bands.

**The Incoherence of the Incoherence (Tahafut al-Tahafut)**
Averroes's most famous work, a point-by-point defense of philosophy against al-Ghazali's attack in The Incoherence of the Philosophers. Its title answers Ghazali's directly, and it is the most common title clue and giveaway for him.

**Commentaries on Aristotle**
Averroes wrote short, middle, and long commentaries on nearly all of Aristotle's works, reviving the careful study of Aristotle. They were so influential in Latin Europe that medieval scholastics simply called him "The Commentator," just as Aristotle was "The Philosopher."

**Refuting Neoplatonist readings of Aristotle**
Averroes tried to recover the "pure" Aristotle by removing the Neoplatonic elements that earlier Muslim philosophers, especially Avicenna (Ibn Sina) and al-Farabi, had blended into Aristotelian thought.

**"Double truth"**
A doctrine linked to Averroes's Latin followers, the "Latin Averroists" such as Siger of Brabant, holding that something can be true in philosophy while its opposite is true in theology. Averroes himself argued that philosophy and religion agree, so the doctrine is usually credited to his heirs rather than to him.

**Rejection of the wahm (estimative faculty)**
In his theory of memory, Averroes describes a process of "spiritualization" in which perceptions are progressively stripped of their matter. The theory resembles Avicenna's account of the internal senses, but Averroes rejects Avicenna's distinct estimative faculty, the wahm, which was supposed to grasp non-sensory meanings such as a sheep sensing a wolf's hostility.

**God as simple, changeless, and the source of plurality**
Averroes held that God is perfectly simple and unchanging, yet can be the cause of a complex, plural world. He explained this by God's single, timeless act of knowing all of reality at once, rather than by a series of separate acts that would introduce change into God.

**Ibn Rushd of Córdoba**
Averroes is the Latinized name of Abu al-Walid Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a 12th-century philosopher born in Córdoba in Muslim Spain (al-Andalus). He also served as a qadi (Islamic judge) and as court physician to the Almohad caliphs.

**The Decisive Treatise (Fasl al-Maqal)**
A legal-philosophical work arguing that Islamic law actually commands the study of philosophy for those capable of it. It holds that true philosophy and true revelation cannot conflict, and that apparent conflicts should be resolved by interpreting scripture allegorically.

**Unity of the intellect (monopsychism)**
Averroes's reading of Aristotle's De Anima, holding that there is a single material (possible) intellect shared by all humans. Thomas Aquinas attacked this view in On the Unity of the Intellect against the Averroists, since it seemed to rule out personal immortality.

**Condemnations of 1270 and 1277**
The Bishop of Paris, Étienne Tempier, condemned lists of propositions associated with the Latin Averroists, including the eternity of the world and the unity of the intellect. These condemnations show how controversial Averroes's influence was at the University of Paris.

**Kitab al-Kulliyat (Colliget)**
Averroes's encyclopedia of medicine, known in Latin as the Colliget. It reflects his career as a physician alongside his philosophical and legal work.

**Appearances in Dante and Raphael**
In the Inferno, Dante places Averroes in Limbo among the virtuous non-Christians, describing him as the one "who made the great commentary." Averroes is also traditionally identified as a turbaned figure in Raphael's fresco The School of Athens.

**A Theory of Justice**
Rawls's landmark 1971 book, which revived social contract theory and dominated later Anglo-American political philosophy. It is the standard giveaway for Rawls.

**Veil of ignorance**
In Rawls's thought experiment, the parties choosing principles of justice do not know their own place in society: their class, talents, race, sex, or conception of the good. Since no one can tailor the rules to benefit themselves, the principles they choose are fair.

**Original position**
The hypothetical starting situation in A Theory of Justice, in which rational parties behind the veil of ignorance agree on the basic principles that will govern their society. It is Rawls's version of the "state of nature" in earlier contract theories.

**"Justice as fairness"**
Rawls's name for his overall conception of justice. Justice comes from principles that would be agreed to under fair conditions, namely the original position.

**Difference principle**
Part of Rawls's second principle of justice. It says social and economic inequalities are permissible only if they work to the greatest benefit of the least-advantaged members of society. It is often linked to "maximin" reasoning, which means choosing the option whose worst outcome is best.

**Liberty principle**
Rawls's first principle of justice, which gives each person an equal right to the most extensive scheme of basic liberties compatible with the same liberties for all. It has priority over the second principle. Rawls held that the basic liberties do not include laissez-faire economic rights such as unrestricted freedom of contract or ownership of the means of production.

**Fair equality of opportunity**
The other part of Rawls's second principle. Offices and positions must be open to all under conditions of genuinely fair, not merely formal, equality of opportunity.

**Overlapping consensus (Political Liberalism)**
In Political Liberalism (1993), Rawls argued that citizens holding different religious, moral, and philosophical doctrines can still endorse the same political conception of justice, each for their own reasons. This shared agreement is the "overlapping consensus."

**Reflective equilibrium**
Rawls's method of justification. One adjusts general principles and considered judgments about particular cases back and forth until they fit together coherently.

**The Law of Peoples and "realistic utopia"**
Rawls's 1999 book extends his theory to international relations. He describes a "realistic utopia" of liberal and "decent" peoples, each united by a common government, common sympathies, and a moral nature, and lists eight principles of justice that should govern relations among them.

**Ideal vs. non-ideal theory**
Rawls first works out what a perfectly just society would require, assuming everyone complies with just institutions (ideal theory). Only then does he address how to reform an unjust real world (non-ideal theory).

**Primary goods**
The all-purpose goods Rawls assumes any rational person wants, whatever else they want. They include rights and liberties, opportunities, income and wealth, and the social bases of self-respect. The parties in the original position choose principles by how they distribute these goods.

**Simone de Beauvoir**
The French existentialist philosopher and novelist who wrote The Second Sex, published in 1949. She was the lifelong partner of Jean-Paul Sartre, and the book is a founding text of second-wave feminism.

**"One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman"**
The most famous line of the book, which opens its second volume. It means that "woman" is a role built by society and upbringing rather than a fixed biological fact, and it is the most common giveaway for the work.

**Woman as the Other**
Beauvoir's central argument is that man has defined himself as the Subject, the Absolute, and has defined woman only in relation to himself, as the "Other." This makes woman the "second sex."

**Immanence versus transcendence**
Existentialist terms used throughout the book. Transcendence is free, creative action that projects a person into the future. Immanence is passive repetition and confinement, the condition Beauvoir says society has forced on women, while men claim transcendence.

**"Biology," "Psychoanalysis," and "Historical Materialism" ("Destiny")**
The opening part of Volume One, titled "Destiny." It examines and rejects biological, Freudian psychoanalytic, and Marxist historical-materialist explanations of why women are subordinate.

**"History" and "Myths"**
The next parts of Volume One. They trace women's position from early nomadic societies to modern times, then analyze myths of femininity, including how male writers such as Montherlant, D. H. Lawrence, Claudel, Breton, and Stendhal portray women.

**The angel in the introduction**
The introduction asks who is qualified to judge "the woman question." Men and women are both "judge and party" to the case. An angel, being neither man nor woman, would be impartial, but it would be "ignorant of all the basic facts" of the problem.

**Two volumes: "Facts and Myths" and "Lived Experience"**
The book is split into two volumes. The first examines the "facts and myths" about women, and the second describes women's "lived experience" from childhood to old age.

**"Formative Years" and "Situation"**
Sections of Volume Two. They follow women's lives from childhood, girlhood, and sexual initiation, then look at the married woman, the mother, and the prostitute, showing how society shapes each stage of life.

**"Justifications": the narcissist, the woman in love, and the mystic**
Chapters of Volume Two describing ways women try to justify their confined existence. They do so through self-love, through total devotion to a man, or through religious mysticism.

**"The Independent Woman" and liberation**
The closing part of the book. Beauvoir argues that economic independence, work, and freedom are the route to women's liberation, while noting the obstacles that even independent women still face.

**Hegel's master-slave dialectic and Sartrean existentialism**
Beauvoir draws on Hegel's account of self-consciousness meeting an "other," and on the existentialist ideas of freedom and bad faith that she shared with Sartre, to explain how men made women the Other.

**English translations and the Index of Forbidden Books**
The book was first translated into English by zoologist H. M. Parshley in 1953, in an abridged version that was heavily criticized. A complete translation by Constance Borde and Sheila Malovany-Chevallier followed in 2009. The Vatican placed the book on its Index of Forbidden Books.

**Diogenes of Sinope**
The most famous Cynic, a Greek from Sinope on the Black Sea who lived mostly in Athens and Corinth in the 4th century BCE. He lived in deliberate poverty, mocked social customs and famous people, and is the central figure in almost every Cynicism question.

**Searching with a lamp for an honest man**
Diogenes' best-known stunt: he walked around in broad daylight with a lit lamp or lantern, saying he was looking for an honest man (literally "a human being"). It mocked how few people he thought truly lived virtuously.

**Living in a jar (tub or barrel)**
Diogenes lived on the street in a large ceramic storage jar (a pithos), often called a tub or barrel, and begged for food. He used it to show that a person needs almost nothing to be happy.

**"Dog-like" (kynikos)**
The school's name comes from the Greek word for "dog." The Cynics were called dogs for their shameless public behavior, such as eating, urinating, and defecating in public, and they embraced the dog as their symbol. Antisthenes called himself the "absolute dog."

**The plucked chicken: "Behold, Plato's man!"**
When Plato defined man as a "featherless biped," Diogenes plucked a chicken, brought it to Plato's Academy, and declared, "Behold a man!" Plato then reportedly added "with broad, flat nails" to his definition.

**Antisthenes**
A student of Socrates, and earlier of the sophist Gorgias, traditionally named as the founder of Cynicism. He taught that virtue alone is enough for happiness and that pleasure and luxury should be rejected.

**Crates of Thebes and Hipparchia of Maroneia**
Crates, a student of Diogenes, gave away his fortune to live as a Cynic. He married Hipparchia, the sister of his student Metrocles, and the couple lived together in Cynic poverty in public. Crates wrote a poem describing an ideal island-city called Pera, named for the Cynic's beggar's bag, and a set of later letters on ascetic training was attributed to the Cynics.

**"Stand out of my sunlight" (Alexander the Great)**
In a famous story, Alexander the Great visited Diogenes and offered him anything he wanted. Diogenes, sunning himself, replied only that Alexander should stand out of his light. Alexander reportedly said that if he were not Alexander, he would wish to be Diogenes.

**"Citizen of the world" (cosmopolitanism)**
When asked where he came from, Diogenes said he was a kosmopolitēs, a "citizen of the world," rejecting loyalty to any one city-state. It is the origin of the word "cosmopolitan."

**Parrhesia and anaideia**
Two key Cynic practices. Parrhesia means frank, fearless free speech, speaking the truth to anyone, even the powerful. Anaideia means shamelessness, deliberately ignoring social customs to show they are artificial.

**Living according to nature: autarkeia and askesis**
The Cynics held that the goal of life is eudaimonia (flourishing), reached by virtue and living in agreement with nature rather than nomos (social convention). This required autarkeia, or self-sufficiency, and askesis, a strict training of the body and mind through hardship.

**"Defacing the currency"**
According to legend, Diogenes and his father, a banker, were exiled from Sinope for defacing coins, and an oracle told Diogenes to "deface the currency." The Cynics took this as a slogan for rejecting and remaking society's customs, playing on the Greek words nomisma (coin) and nomos (custom or law).

**Heracles**
The Cynics adopted the hero Heracles as their model and patron because of his endurance of hard labors and his self-sufficiency. His capture of the three-headed dog Cerberus from the underworld was a favorite story.

**Later Cynics: Bion, Peregrinus, and Demonax**
Bion of Borysthenes developed the "diatribe," a lively moral lecture that influenced the Christian sermon. In Roman times Peregrinus Proteus left Christianity for Cynicism and publicly burned himself to death at the Olympic Games, and Demonax of Cyprus led a gentler version of Cynicism. Both were written about by the satirist Lucian.

**Peter Sloterdijk's Critique of Cynical Reason**
A 1983 book by the German philosopher Sloterdijk. It argues that modern "cynicism," jaded and knowing despair, dominates contemporary culture, and urges a return to "kynicism," the ancient Cynics' cheeky, physical defiance of power.

**Spinoza's Ethics, Demonstrated in Geometrical Order**
Baruch Spinoza's masterpiece, published after his death in 1677. It is modeled on Euclid's Elements, building from definitions and axioms to numbered propositions and proofs, and its preface promises to treat human actions and desires as if they were "lines, planes, and bodies." It opens with Part I, "Of God."

**"God or Nature" (Deus sive Natura)**
Spinoza's Ethics argues that God is the only substance in the universe and is identical with nature, a position later labeled pantheism. Thought and extension are two attributes of this one substance, and individual things are its "modes." Views like these led to Spinoza's expulsion from Amsterdam's Jewish community in 1656.

**"Of Human Bondage"**
The title of Part IV of Spinoza's Ethics. It argues that people are in bondage to their emotions (affects) when they are passive and driven by them, and that reason offers the way to freedom.

**Conatus**
Spinoza's term for the striving of each thing to "persevere in its being." In the Ethics, the affects (emotions) are explained as increases or decreases in this striving.

**Adequate and inadequate ideas**
A distinction in Spinoza's Ethics. Inadequate ideas come from confused sense experience and imagination (such as a child's image of a winged horse), while adequate ideas come from reason and intuition. Spinoza ranks imagination, reason, and intuition as three kinds of knowledge, and he praises seeing things sub specie aeternitatis, "under the aspect of eternity."

**Nicomachean Ethics**
Aristotle's major work on ethics, named after his son (or, in some accounts, his father) Nicomachus. Aristotle also wrote the Eudemian Ethics, named for his student Eudemus of Rhodes. The Nicomachean Ethics' fifth book discusses justice, and its final book praises the contemplative life as the highest.

**Eudaimonia**
Greek for "happiness" or "flourishing," which Aristotle names as the ultimate goal of human life in the Nicomachean Ethics. He defines it as an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue (arete).

**Doctrine of the mean (golden mean)**
Aristotle's idea that each virtue is a midpoint between two vices, one of excess and one of deficiency. For example, courage lies between cowardice and rashness.

**Akrasia**
Greek for "weakness of will" or lack of self-control, meaning acting against one's better judgment. Aristotle discusses it in Book VII of the Nicomachean Ethics.

**G. E. M. Anscombe's "Modern Moral Philosophy"**
A 1958 essay by Elizabeth Anscombe that coined the term "consequentialism." It argued that modern moral theories should be set aside and helped revive virtue ethics, an Aristotelian approach focused on character and human flourishing (sometimes called the "aretaic turn").

**After Virtue**
A 1981 book by Alasdair MacIntyre that helped revive virtue ethics. It opens by comparing modern moral talk to an imagined world in which science has been destroyed and only fragments of it remain, and it favors an Aristotelian view of the virtues.

**Principia Ethica and the naturalistic fallacy**
G. E. Moore's 1903 book argued that "good" is a simple, indefinable property. He called the mistake of defining good in terms of natural properties, such as pleasure, the "naturalistic fallacy." The book is a founding text of metaethics, the branch that asks what moral claims mean (for example, the debate between cognitivism and non-cognitivism).

**Deontology and the categorical imperative**
Deontology judges actions by duties and intentions rather than by results. Its most famous form is Immanuel Kant's ethics, which rests on the categorical imperative and the "good will" and includes the ideal of a "Kingdom of Ends."

**Utilitarianism**
A consequentialist theory that the right action produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number. It was founded by Jeremy Bentham, who proposed a "hedonic calculus," and developed by John Stuart Mill in his book Utilitarianism. Henry Sidgwick compared egoism, intuitionism, and utilitarianism in The Methods of Ethics.

**The Ethics of Ambiguity**
A 1947 book by Simone de Beauvoir that develops an existentialist ethics. It describes ethics as "the triumph of freedom over facticity."

**Zeno of Citium**
The founder of Stoicism, who began teaching in Athens around 300 BCE. According to legend, he died after tripping and breaking his toe outside his school, taking the fall as a sign that it was his time.

**Meditations**
A set of twelve books of private reflections written in Greek by the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius, much of it composed while he was on military campaign near the Danube frontier. It opens with Marcus thanking those who raised him, beginning with his grandfather Verus for his kindly disposition. It urges a "cosmic perspective" on life and contains lines like "Soon you'll be ashes or bones. A mere name at most."

**Marcus Aurelius**
The Roman emperor (reigned 161–180 CE) and author of the Meditations, often called the last great Stoic and the most famous example of the "philosopher-king."

**Epictetus**
A former slave turned Stoic teacher, a student of Musonius Rufus, who wrote nothing himself. His student Arrian recorded his teachings in the Discourses and the Enchiridion. One anecdote describes how he calmly accepted the theft of his iron lamp, reasoning that the thief had only gained a lamp at the price of his own character.

**The Enchiridion and the Discourses**
Two works compiled by the historian Arrian from the lectures of Epictetus. The Enchiridion ("Handbook") opens by distinguishing things within our control from those outside it and compares life to good behavior at a banquet. The Discourses are longer, more detailed records of his teaching.

**Prohairesis**
Epictetus's term for the faculty of moral choice or volition. It is the only thing truly within a person's power and what separates humans from other animals. Through it we choose how to judge and respond to impressions, so external events and "things indifferent" need not disturb us.

**Stoa Poikile ("Painted Porch")**
The painted colonnade in the Athenian agora where Zeno taught. The school's name comes from the Greek word stoa, meaning "porch."

**Seneca the Younger**
A Roman Stoic statesman who tutored the emperor Nero. He wrote the Letters to Lucilius, the essay On Mercy (De Clementia), often called an early example of the "mirror for princes" genre, and bloody tragedies such as Hercules Furens. He held that the wise man does not love wealth but still prefers it to poverty.

**Chrysippus**
The third head of the Stoa and a pupil of Cleanthes, often called the school's "second founder" for systematizing its doctrines. He developed an influential system of propositional logic, argued that fate and free will are compatible using the analogy of a cylinder rolling down a slope, defended divination, and is said to have died of laughter after joking about giving wine to a donkey eating figs. The Academic Skeptic Carneades opposed his ideas.

**Ekpyrosis**
The Stoic doctrine that the universe is periodically consumed in a great conflagration and then reborn in an endless cycle. It built on Heraclitus's idea of a primordial fire, which the Stoics identified with God and the world.

**Pneuma**
The "breath of life" in Stoic physics: a sustaining force of fire and air that pervades all matter, holds objects together as unified wholes, and gives them their qualities. It acts as the vehicle of logos, the rational principle that structures the world.

**Virtue is the only good**
The core ethical claim of Stoicism: virtue alone is sufficient for happiness (eudaimonia), and things like health, wealth, and reputation are "indifferents." The Stoic ideal is the sage, a person of moral and intellectual perfection who is free from destructive passions (apatheia). The four cardinal virtues are wisdom, courage, justice, and temperance.

**Cleanthes**
Zeno's successor as head of the Stoic school and the teacher of Chrysippus. He is known for his Hymn to Zeus and for the saying "Fate guides the willing, but drags the unwilling."

**Logic, physics, and ethics**
The three divisions of Stoic philosophy. The Stoics compared philosophy to a fenced field in which logic is the fence, physics the soil and trees, and ethics the fruit.

**James Stockdale**
A U.S. Navy officer who credited the teachings of Epictetus with helping him endure more than seven years as a prisoner of war in Vietnam. His writings helped popularize Stoicism in the U.S. military.

**Anselm's ontological argument (Proslogion)**
St. Anselm of Canterbury's Proslogion (c. 1078) defines God as "that than which nothing greater can be conceived." It argues that a being existing in reality is greater than one existing only in the understanding, so God must exist in reality. It is the first and most famous ontological argument, meaning an argument for God's existence from the concept of God alone.

**Gaunilo's "lost island" (On Behalf of the Fool)**
The monk Gaunilo of Marmoutiers replied to Anselm with a parody, a reductio ad absurdum. By the same reasoning, he argued, one could prove that a perfect "lost island," more excellent than all others, must exist. His title refers to the fool of Psalms 14:1 and 53:1, who "hath said in his heart, There is no God."

**Aquinas's Five Ways (Summa Theologica)**
In the Summa Theologica, Thomas Aquinas rejected Anselm's ontological argument and gave five proofs of God's existence. They argue from motion (the "unmoved" or "first mover," borrowed from Aristotle's prime mover), from efficient causation (the "first cause"), from contingency, from degrees of perfection, and from the ordered design of the world (the teleological argument). In the same work he also answers the objection that the existence of evil disproves God.

**Russell's teapot**
Bertrand Russell imagined a china teapot orbiting the Sun between Earth and Mars, too small to be detected by telescopes. He argued that the burden of proof lies on the person making an unfalsifiable claim, not on the doubter. Russell also argued for atheism in his 1927 Battersea Town Hall lecture "Why I Am Not a Christian," where he said religion rests mainly on fear.

**Pascal's Wager (Pensées)**
In his posthumously published Pensées (1670), Blaise Pascal argued that believing in God is the rational bet. If God exists, the believer gains infinitely (eternal life) and the unbeliever risks infinite loss (damnation). If God does not exist, either party loses only a finite amount.

**"God is dead" (Nietzsche)**
Friedrich Nietzsche's famous declaration, most memorably spoken by the madman in The Gay Science. The madman says "we have killed him" and asks "What festivals of atonement, what sacred games shall we have to invent?", which expresses Nietzsche's worry about the loss of meaning that would follow the collapse of belief in God.

**"Existence is not a predicate" (Kant)**
Immanuel Kant's objection to the ontological argument in the Critique of Pure Reason. He argued that existence does not add anything to the concept of a thing, so it cannot be one of the perfections that a supremely perfect being must have.

**Modal ontological arguments (Plantinga, Hartshorne, Gödel)**
These 20th-century versions use modal logic. In The Nature of Necessity, Alvin Plantinga used the S5 system to give a "victorious" argument that if a maximally great being is possible, it exists in all possible worlds. Charles Hartshorne defended a modal version against Kant's objection. Kurt Gödel wrote a formal ontological proof, which Jordan Howard Sobel criticized for leading to "modal collapse," the conclusion that every truth is necessary.

**Watchmaker analogy (William Paley)**
William Paley's teleological argument, or argument from design. Just as finding a watch implies a watchmaker, the complex design of nature implies a divine designer. Richard Dawkins's "Ultimate Boeing 747 gambit" is a modern argument against design reasoning of this kind.

**Kalam cosmological argument (al-Ghazali, William Lane Craig)**
This argument holds that whatever begins to exist has a cause, the universe began to exist, and therefore the universe has a cause. It was developed in medieval Islamic theology by al-Ghazali, whose Incoherence of the Philosophers attacks the philosophers' inability to prove God's existence. William Lane Craig revived it, and he also argues from the "fine-tuning" of the universe.

**Problem of evil**
This is the classic argument against God's existence: how can an omnipotent, omniscient, and omnibenevolent God allow suffering? Hume asked "Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? Then is he impotent," and William Rowe pointed to a fawn dying slowly in a forest fire. Responses include Augustine's view of evil as a privation of good, Leibniz's Theodicy ("best of all possible worlds"), John Hick's "soul-making" theodicy, and Alvin Plantinga's Free Will Defense, which uses the idea of "transworld depravity."

**Descartes's Meditations (Third and Fifth)**
In the Third Meditation, René Descartes argues that his idea of an infinite, perfect God could only have been caused by God himself (the "trademark" argument). In the Fifth Meditation, he gives his own ontological argument, saying that God's existence is as inseparable from God's essence as three angles are from a triangle, and that God has a "true and immutable nature."

**Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion**
David Hume's posthumously published dialogue, in which three characters debate the existence and nature of God. Cleanthes defends the design argument, Demea defends an a priori cosmological argument and orthodox piety, and the skeptic Philo raises objections to both.

**Spinoza: "God or Nature" (Deus sive Natura)**
