In his Ethics, Baruch Spinoza argued that God is the single infinite substance, with infinitely many attributes including thought and extension. He identified God with nature itself. Other early modern clues include George Berkeley, for whom God's perception keeps unperceived objects in existence, and Christian Wolff, who made God one of the three objects of special metaphysics, along with the soul and the world.

**"If God does not exist, everything is permitted"**
This idea is associated with Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov, which holds that morality collapses without God. Simone de Beauvoir rejected it in The Ethics of Ambiguity, arguing that without God humans bear even more responsibility for their actions.

**Allegory of the Cave**
The most famous passage of the Republic, at the start of Book VII. Prisoners chained in a cave see only shadows cast on a wall by objects carried in front of a fire, and they take those shadows for reality. One prisoner is freed and makes a hard climb out into the sunlight. The story illustrates Plato's Theory of Forms and the role of philosophical education. It is the most common giveaway.

**Philosopher-kings**
Plato's ideal rulers. Socrates argues that cities will have no rest from trouble until philosophers rule or rulers become philosophers, because only philosophers know the Form of the Good. The work lays out a long education for them, including mathematics and geometry.

**Ring of Gyges**
A story Glaucon tells in Book II. A Lydian shepherd finds a ring that makes him invisible, then uses it to seduce the queen, kill the king, and take the throne. Glaucon uses the story to argue that people are just only out of fear of being caught, and he challenges Socrates to show that justice is worth having for its own sake.

**Noble Lie (Myth of Metals)**
A founding myth proposed in Book III. Citizens are told they were born from the earth and that the god mixed gold, silver, or bronze and iron into their souls, which fixes their places as rulers, auxiliaries, or farmers and craftsmen. Belief in the myth is meant to keep the classes content and the city stable.

**The Divided Line**
An analogy in Book VI that divides a line into the visible realm and the intelligible realm, and then subdivides each. The four segments run from images and shadows (illusion), to physical objects (belief), to mathematical reasoning, to understanding of the Forms (the highest, philosophical knowledge).

**Analogy of the Sun and the Form of the Good**
In Book VI, Socrates compares the Form of the Good to the sun. Just as the sun gives light that lets us see and also makes things grow, the Good makes the Forms knowable and is the source of their being.

**Myth of Er**
The story that ends the Republic in Book X. Er, a soldier who seems to have died in battle, revives on his funeral pyre and describes the afterlife. He sees the just rewarded and the unjust punished, the Spindle of Necessity that turns the heavenly bodies, and souls choosing their next lives by lottery.

**Thrasymachus: "Justice is the advantage of the stronger"**
In Book I, the sophist Thrasymachus argues that justice is simply whatever benefits those in power. Socrates spends much of the dialogue answering this challenge, along with Glaucon's.

**Cephalus, Polemarchus, and the opening definitions of justice**
The dialogue opens at the house of the old man Cephalus in the Piraeus, after his son Polemarchus urges Socrates to stay. Cephalus suggests justice is telling the truth and paying what you owe. Socrates refutes this with the case of returning weapons to a friend who has gone mad, and Polemarchus then defines justice as helping friends and harming enemies.

**Ship of State**
An analogy in Book VI. A strong but deaf and shortsighted shipowner is surrounded by quarreling sailors who seize the ship, while they dismiss the true navigator as a useless "stargazer." It shows how democracies ignore those with real knowledge.

**Guardians, auxiliaries, and producers (the tripartite city and soul)**
The ideal city, sometimes called Kallipolis, has three classes: guardian rulers, auxiliaries (soldiers), and producers. They match the three parts of the soul: reason, spirit, and appetite. Justice means each part does its own job without interfering with the others. Guardians give up private property and share wives and children in common.

**Banishing the poets (the three beds)**
In Book X, Socrates argues that poets and painters are imitators who know nothing of the truth. There are three beds: the Form of the bed made by god, the bed made by a carpenter, and a painting of a bed, which is an imitation of an imitation. Most poetry is therefore banished from the ideal city.

**Decline of regimes**
In Books VIII and IX, Socrates describes how the ideal aristocracy decays, starting when rulers fail to breed the right successors. It declines through timocracy, oligarchy, and democracy into tyranny. The tyrant is called the most miserable man because he is a slave to his own passions.

**Karl Popper's The Open Society and Its Enemies**
Popper's first volume, "The Spell of Plato," attacks the Republic as a blueprint for a totalitarian state. He criticizes its noble lie, its censorship of art, and its raising of children apart from their parents.

**The painted statue (purple eyes)**
An analogy in Book IV. One would not paint a statue's eyes purple, the most beautiful color, if that ruined the whole statue. In the same way, the city should make the whole community happy rather than giving any one class, even the guardians, the greatest happiness.

**On Liberty**
Mill's 1859 essay and his most famous work. It defends individual freedom of thought, speech, and action against both government and social pressure, and it is usually the final giveaway for Mill.

**Harm principle**
The central idea of On Liberty. Society may only use force against an individual to prevent harm to others, never just for that person's own good. People should be free to pursue their own desires as long as they do not harm anyone else.

**"Tyranny of the majority"**
A phrase Mill borrowed from Alexis de Tocqueville's Democracy in America and used in On Liberty. It describes how a democratic majority, through laws or social pressure, can oppress individuals and minorities as harshly as a despot.

**Utilitarianism**
Mill's 1861 book defending the moral theory founded by Jeremy Bentham. It upholds the "Greatest Happiness Principle," which says actions are right "in proportion as they tend to promote happiness" and wrong as they tend to produce the opposite.

**"Better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied"**
A famous line from Utilitarianism; Mill also says it is "better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied." Unlike Bentham, who treated all pleasures as equal in kind (he said push-pin, a children's game, was as good as poetry), Mill distinguished higher, intellectual pleasures from lower, bodily ones. He did this partly to answer critics who called utilitarianism a philosophy "worthy only of swine."

**The Subjection of Women**
Mill's 1869 essay arguing for "perfect equality" between the sexes. It compares the legal position of married women to slavery and calls women's subordination one of the chief hindrances to human improvement. It was shaped by his wife, Harriet Taylor Mill.

**Harriet Taylor**
Mill's close intellectual partner and, from 1851, his wife. He credited her with major influence on On Liberty and The Subjection of Women.

**A System of Logic**
Mill's 1843 treatise on logic and scientific method. It champions inductive reasoning, which draws general laws from particular observations, as the basis of the empirical sciences.

**Mill's methods**
Five methods of inductive inference from A System of Logic for finding causes: the method of agreement, the method of difference, the joint method of agreement and difference, the method of residues, and the method of concomitant variations.

**Denotation and connotation (Dartmouth example)**
In A System of Logic, Mill distinguished what a name refers to (its denotation) from the attributes it implies (its connotation), anticipating Gottlob Frege's sense-reference distinction. He argued that proper names have denotation but no connotation, noting that the town of Dartmouth would keep its name even if the river Dart changed course and it no longer sat at its mouth.

**Free speech argument (infallibility)**
In On Liberty, Mill argues that silencing any opinion assumes we cannot be wrong. Whether the silenced opinion is true, false, or partly true, expressing it moves society closer to the truth, because even false views keep true beliefs from becoming "dead dogma."

**Principles of Political Economy**
Mill's 1848 economics textbook, which built on the work of David Ricardo. It allows some government intervention in free markets, and it argues that a "stationary state" without endless economic growth could be preferable for quality of life and for nature.

**"A Few Words on Non-Intervention"**
An 1859 essay on foreign policy. It argues that going to war for an idea is as criminal as going to war for territory or revenue, but it also treats "civilized" and "barbarous" nations differently.

**James Mill and Mill's Autobiography**
Mill's father, James Mill, a follower of Jeremy Bentham, gave him an intense education, teaching him Greek at age three. Mill's Autobiography (1873) describes this upbringing and the mental crisis he went through in his early twenties.

**Member of Parliament for Westminster**
Mill served in the House of Commons from 1865 to 1868. In Parliament he argued for women's suffrage, and in an 1868 speech he defended capital punishment as more humane than life imprisonment and as a deterrent.

**Francis Fukuyama, The End of History and the Last Man**
Fukuyama's 1992 book, which grew out of a 1989 essay, argued that the triumph of liberal democracy after the Cold War marked the "end of history," meaning the endpoint of humanity's ideological evolution. The "last man" in the title is borrowed from Nietzsche.

**Thomas Carlyle's "Great Man" theory**
Carlyle argued, notably in On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1841), that history is largely shaped by the deeds of heroic individuals. Social historians oppose this view by stressing the role of ordinary people and broad social forces.

**Hegel's Lectures on the Philosophy of History**
G.W.F. Hegel saw history as the self-unfolding of the World Spirit (Weltgeist) and as progress in the consciousness of freedom. In the Oriental world "one is free," in the Greek and Roman world "some are free," and in the Germanic world "all are free." He notoriously claimed that Africa was "no historical part of the world." Hegel also wrote that the "owl of Minerva" spreads its wings only at dusk, meaning that philosophy understands an era only after it has passed.

**Herodotus, "the Father of History"**
The Greek author of the Histories, an account of the Greco-Persian Wars, whom Cicero called the father of history. Other famous historians mentioned in clues include Thucydides, Livy, Edward Gibbon (The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire), David McCullough, and Stephen Ambrose.

**Giambattista Vico, The New Science**
Vico's 1725 work presents a cyclical theory of history. Nations pass through an age of gods, an age of heroes, and an age of men, which he linked to the poetic tropes of metaphor, metonymy, synecdoche, and irony. A "barbarism of reflection" leads to collapse and a return (ricorso) to the start of the cycle.

**Historical materialism (Marx and Engels)**
In The German Ideology, Marx and Engels developed the materialist conception of history, which explains historical change by successive economic stages defined by their "modes of production." The Communist Manifesto opens by declaring that "the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles."

**Walter Benjamin, "Theses on the Philosophy of History"**
Benjamin's 1940 essay, also called "On the Concept of History," opens by comparing historical materialism to a chess-playing automaton like the Mechanical Turk, secretly operated by a hunchbacked dwarf representing theology. Its ninth thesis describes the "angel of history," based on Paul Klee's Angelus Novus, who sees the past as a single catastrophe piling wreckage upon wreckage.

**Hayden White, Metahistory**
White's 1973 book analyzes 19th-century historical writing with the tools of literary criticism. He argues that historians shape their narratives through modes of "emplotment" (romance, tragedy, comedy, satire), argument, and ideological implication, grounded in the four master tropes.

**Leopold von Ranke**
A 19th-century German historian who founded modern source-based historiography. He insisted that historians show the past "as it actually was" (wie es eigentlich gewesen) instead of passing moral judgment on it, an approach often called historical positivism.

**Michel Foucault, History of Madness and The Archaeology of Knowledge**
Foucault's History of Madness traces how Western society defined and confined the mad. In The Archaeology of Knowledge, he argued that the apparent continuities in the history of ideas break down into discontinuities on closer inspection.

**Alexandre Kojève**
A Russian-French philosopher whose 1930s Paris lectures on Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit popularized the idea of an "end of history." His reading strongly influenced Fukuyama.

**George Santayana: "doomed to repeat it"**
In The Life of Reason, Santayana wrote that "those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it." The line is often paraphrased in terms of being doomed to repeat history.

**E.H. Carr, What Is History?**
Carr's 1961 lectures argued that historical "facts" are selected and interpreted by the historian. He stressed the selectivity and subjectivity involved in writing history.

**Annales school and cliometrics**
The French Annales school, founded by Marc Bloch and Lucien Febvre and later led by Fernand Braudel, emphasized the longue durée, the long-term social, economic, and geographic structures of history. Cliometrics is the application of economic and statistical methods to history. The American Historical Review (AHR), a leading journal in the field, is based at Indiana University Bloomington.

**Bossuet, Discourse on Universal History**
Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, a 17th-century French bishop, wrote this 1681 work, which presents world history as unfolding under divine providence. It is an early example of the philosophy of history.

**William James**
The American philosopher and psychologist, called the "Father of American Psychology," who popularized pragmatism. His 1907 lecture series Pragmatism made the movement famous, and he also wrote "The Will to Believe," "The Dilemma of Determinism," and works on radical empiricism.

**Charles Sanders Peirce (pronounced "purse")**
The logician and scientist generally regarded as the founder of pragmatism, which he developed in discussions at the Metaphysical Club in Cambridge, Massachusetts. He later renamed his version "pragmaticism" to distinguish it from James's. He also proposed the categories of Firstness, Secondness, and Thirdness (quality, relation, and representation).

**Squirrel around a tree**
The famous example in James's Pragmatism. A man chases a squirrel that keeps moving around the trunk of a tree, always facing him, and the question is whether the man "goes around" the squirrel. James resolves the dispute by showing that the answer depends on what "going around" practically means, which illustrates the pragmatic method.

**Pragmatism: A New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking**
James's 1907 book of lectures, which gave the movement its widest audience. It opens with "The Present Dilemma in Philosophy," includes the lecture "The One and the Many" on monism and pluralism, borrows Giovanni Papini's image of pragmatism as a hotel corridor that opens onto many rooms, and discusses Walt Whitman's poem "To You" in its final lecture.

**Tough-minded vs. tender-minded**
James's contrast in Pragmatism between two philosophical temperaments: the tough-minded empiricist, who goes by facts and tends to be materialist and skeptical, and the tender-minded rationalist, who goes by principles and tends to be idealist and religious. James offers pragmatism as a way to reconcile them.

**"Cash value"**
James's phrase for the practical difference an idea makes in experience. Pragmatism holds that the meaning and truth of a belief lie in its "cash value," that is, its usefulness and practical consequences, rather than its correspondence to an abstract reality.

**Richard Rorty and neopragmatism**
The American philosopher who revived pragmatism in the late twentieth century. His Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature (1979) rejects the correspondence theory of truth and the idea of the mind as a mirror of reality, and includes a thought experiment about "Antipodeans" who speak of their pains as the stimulation of C-fibers. He also wrote Consequences of Pragmatism and Contingency, Irony, and Solidarity, in which he describes private "ironists."

**"How to Make Our Ideas Clear"**
Peirce's 1878 essay that introduced the pragmatic maxim and distinguished three grades of clearness of conception. It includes the example that an untested diamond may as well be called soft, compares thoughts to musical notes and rests, and criticizes the doctrine of transubstantiation of communion wine.

**"The Fixation of Belief"**
Peirce's 1877 essay arguing that inquiry is a struggle to move from the irritation of doubt to settled belief. It lists four methods of fixing belief: tenacity, authority, the a priori method, and the method of science, which Peirce favors.

**John Dewey**
A pragmatist philosopher and educational reformer who founded the University of Chicago Laboratory School. He wrote Democracy and Education, My Pedagogic Creed, and Art as Experience, promoted "learning by doing," and developed instrumentalism, the view that ideas are tools for solving problems.

**Pragmatic maxim**
Peirce's principle that our whole conception of an object consists of our conception of its practical effects. It is the core method of pragmatism and is meant to clear away meaningless metaphysical disputes.

**"The Will to Believe"**
James's 1896 lecture defending religious faith. It argues that when a person faces a "genuine option" that is living, forced, and momentous, and the evidence cannot settle it, it is legitimate to believe without sufficient evidence, contrary to strict evidentialism.

**Instrumentalism**
Dewey's version of pragmatism, which treats ideas and theories as tools whose worth depends on how well they solve problems. Dewey describes inquiry as turning an indeterminate situation into a determinate one.

**George Herbert Mead**
A pragmatist associated with Dewey at the University of Chicago, whose distinction between the "I" and the "Me" in Mind, Self, and Society helped found the sociological approach known as symbolic interactionism.

**The Phenomenology of Spirit**
Hegel's 1807 masterwork, which traces the development of consciousness through a series of "shapes," from "sense-certainty" and "perception" (Wahrnehmung) through self-consciousness and reason, up to Spirit (Geist) and finally "Absolute Knowing." It is often compared to a Bildungsroman and is the most common title giveaway.

**Master-slave (lord-bondsman) dialectic**
A famous passage in the Phenomenology's section on the "Independence and Dependence of Self-Consciousness." Two self-conscious beings, each seeking recognition from the other, engage in a "struggle to the death"; one submits and becomes the bondsman, but through labor the bondsman ultimately gains a truer self-consciousness than the lord. The idea influenced Marx, Sartre, and many others.

**Dialectic ("thesis, antithesis, synthesis")**
Hegel's method, in which a concept generates its own contradiction and the two are resolved into a higher concept that preserves both. The triad "thesis, antithesis, synthesis" is a popular oversimplification (Hegel's own terms are closer to abstract, negative, and concrete), but quizbowl questions use it constantly as a giveaway.

**Aufhebung (sublation)**
Hegel's term for how a contradiction is overcome, which means both "to cancel or abolish" and "to preserve or lift up." In the Science of Logic, pure Being and pure Nothing are sublated into Becoming, which then passes into Determinate Being.

**Alexandre Kojève**
The Russian-born French philosopher whose lectures on the Phenomenology in Paris in the 1930s, published as Introduction to the Reading of Hegel, emphasized the master-slave dialectic and the "end of history." They shaped a generation of French thinkers.

**Elements of the Philosophy of Right**
Hegel's 1820 political treatise, which divides "right" into three spheres: abstract right (property and contracts), morality, and ethical life (Sittlichkeit), which itself consists of the family, civil society, and the state. Its preface says that "philosophy is its own time comprehended in thoughts," declares "what is rational is actual and what is actual is rational," and attacks Jakob Fries for his part in the Wartburg Festival.

**Owl of Minerva**
From the preface to the Philosophy of Right: "the owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of dusk," after philosophy "paints its grey in grey." The image means that philosophy can only understand an era after it has already passed. Andrew Cutrofello titled a book The Owl at Dawn as a "sequel" to Hegel.

**Science of Logic**
Hegel's major work of logic and metaphysics (1812–16), divided into the doctrines of Being, Essence, and Concept (Notion), and into objective and subjective logic. It begins with pure Being, which is indistinguishable from pure Nothing, and treats quality (determinateness), quantity (magnitude), and measure; a shorter version forms the first part of his Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences.

**Geist (Spirit) and the world-spirit**
Hegel's central concept of Spirit, a collective, developing consciousness. History is the process by which the world-spirit (Weltgeist) comes to know itself, working through national spirits (Volksgeister) and "great men" in what he called the "cunning of reason." He is also associated with the term Zeitgeist ("spirit of the age").

**Lectures on the Philosophy of History**
Hegel's lectures arguing that "reason is the substance of the universe" and that world history is the progress of the consciousness of freedom. Oriental despotism knew only one person as free, the Greeks and Romans some, and the Germanic world all. He infamously said Africa "is no historical part of the World," calling it "Unhistorical, Undeveloped Spirit."

**Young (Left) Hegelians and Right Hegelians**
After Hegel's death his followers split. The Young or Left Hegelians, including Ludwig Feuerbach, Bruno Bauer, and David Strauss, gave his ideas a radical and secular turn, while Right Hegelians such as Karl Daub and Johann Philipp Gabler stressed religion and the state.

**Karl Marx "standing Hegel on his head"**
Marx said that in Hegel the dialectic was "standing on its head" and had to be turned right side up. Marx kept Hegel's dialectical view of history but replaced his idealism with materialism, producing what became known as dialectical materialism.

**Antigone**
Hegel used Sophocles's Antigone in the Phenomenology to illustrate the clash between divine law (family duty, the "unwritten and infallible law of the gods") and human law (the state). He saw tragedy as a collision between two legitimate ethical powers.

**Absolute idealism**
Hegel's philosophical system, developed in dialogue with Friedrich Schelling and built on Kant and Fichte. It holds that reality is ultimately the self-unfolding of rational Spirit, so that "the real is rational and the rational is real."

**The state and critics like Karl Popper**
Hegel called the state "the march of God on earth" and the "actually existing, realized moral life," and he was seen as glorifying the Prussian state. Karl Popper, in The Open Society and Its Enemies, attacked him as a forerunner of modern totalitarianism.

**"7 + 5 = 12"**
The work's famous example of a synthetic a priori judgment. Kant argues that the concept of 12 is not contained in the concepts of 7, 5, and addition, so the statement adds knowledge (synthetic), yet it is known independently of experience (a priori).

**Synthetic a priori judgments**
The central question of the work is how synthetic a priori knowledge is possible. Kant argues such judgments underlie mathematics and physics, and that metaphysics, too, must be judged by whether it can achieve them.

**Phenomena and noumena**
Kant's distinction between things as they appear to us (phenomena), which we can know, and things-in-themselves (noumena), which lie beyond any possible experience and remain unknowable.

**Table of categories**
Kant's twelve pure concepts of the understanding, such as causality, which the mind uses to impose order on experience. They are arranged in a diamond-shaped table under four headings (quantity, quality, relation, and modality), with three categories under each.

**Transcendental Aesthetic**
The opening part of the work's Doctrine of Elements. It argues that space and time are not concepts or features of things-in-themselves but pure forms of intuition that the mind brings to experience, a view set against both Newton's absolute space and Leibniz's relational space.

**Immanuel Kant**
The German philosopher from Königsberg who published this work in 1781 and a heavily revised second edition in 1787. It is the first of his three Critiques, followed by the Critique of Practical Reason (1788) and the Critique of Judgment (1790).

**"Refutation of Idealism"**
A section added in the second edition. It argues against idealists who call outer experience "doubtful and indemonstrable," holding that the existence of things in space outside us is a necessary condition for inner experience of ourselves in time.

**Antinomies of pure reason**
Pairs of contradictory but equally provable claims, such as that the world has a beginning in time and that it does not, presented in the Transcendental Dialectic. Along with the Paralogisms and the Ideal of Pure Reason, they undermine traditional rational psychology, rational cosmology, and natural theology.

**Transcendental Doctrine of Elements / Transcendental Doctrine of Method**
The work's two main divisions. The long Doctrine of Elements contains the Transcendental Aesthetic and the Transcendental Logic (the Analytic and the Dialectic). The much shorter Doctrine of Method covers the discipline, canon, architectonic, and history of pure reason, ending with the "architectonic" and "history."

**Transcendental Analytic**
The part of the Transcendental Logic that explains how the understanding uses the categories to make experience of phenomena possible. It includes the transcendental deduction of the categories.

**House and ship example**
An example from the Second Analogy of Experience, which defends causality. The parts of a house can be viewed in any order the observer chooses, but the positions of a ship sailing downstream must be perceived in a fixed sequence. This shows that the concept of cause is needed to experience objective succession in time.

**Two straight lines cannot enclose a space**
A geometric example Kant uses to show that geometry is synthetic. The proposition cannot be derived from the concepts of "straight line" and "two" alone, so it must rest on intuition of space.

**Prolegomena to Any Future Metaphysics**
Kant's shorter 1783 work that restates and clarifies the arguments of this work, written partly in response to readers who found the original obscure or misread it.

**Transcendental unity of apperception**
Kant's term for the unified "I think" that must be able to accompany all of one's representations. He distinguishes this transcendental self from the empirical self, which we know only as it appears to us through inner sense and never as it is in itself.

**Thus Spoke Zarathustra (Also sprach Zarathustra)**
Nietzsche's philosophical novel (1883–1885) about a prophet named after Zoroaster, the founder of Zoroastrianism. It opens with Zarathustra descending from his mountain cave after ten years of solitude, meeting an old saint in the forest, and preaching in a marketplace where a tightrope walker falls after being startled by a jester. Other episodes include the fable of the spirit's three metamorphoses (camel, lion, child) and Zarathustra's animals, an eagle with a serpent coiled around its neck.

**"God is dead"**
Nietzsche's most famous proclamation, which appears most prominently in the "Parable of the Madman" in The Gay Science. A madman with a lantern announces in a marketplace that "God is dead... and we have killed him." It describes the collapse of belief in God as a foundation for European values.

**Übermensch (Overman or Superman)**
The ideal figure introduced in Thus Spoke Zarathustra, who creates his own life-affirming values beyond conventional Christian morality. Zarathustra describes man as "a rope, tied between beast and Übermensch," a bridge rather than an end in itself.

**On the Genealogy of Morals (Morality)**
Nietzsche's 1887 work of three essays tracing the origins of moral values. It argues that a "slave revolt in morality," driven by ressentiment, reversed noble values, equating powerlessness and meekness with goodness. It includes the parable of lambs who call birds of prey "evil," the "blond beast," the "breeding of an animal with the right to make promises," and a critique of the ascetic ideal promoted by priests.

**Master morality and slave morality**
Nietzsche's contrast between two value systems. Master morality, held by the noble and strong (such as the Romans), sorts actions into "good" and "bad," while slave morality, which he associated with Judaism and Christianity, sorts them into "good" and "evil" and praises humility and weakness. He develops the idea in Beyond Good and Evil and the Genealogy.

**Eternal recurrence**
The thought experiment that one's life will repeat in exactly the same way infinitely. In The Gay Science a demon steals into your loneliest loneliness and announces that you will live this life again innumerable times. It is central to Thus Spoke Zarathustra, where Zarathustra is at first horrified by the thought that even mediocre man will recur.

**The Gay Science**
Nietzsche's 1882 work, whose title comes from a Provençal expression for the art of poetry. It contains the Parable of the Madman, the first statement of eternal recurrence, and the image of the Buddha's shadow still shown in a cave long after his death.

**Beyond Good and Evil**
Nietzsche's 1886 book, which opens with "Supposing truth is a woman, what then?" Its first section, "On the Prejudices of Philosophers," asks why we value truth rather than untruth. It also says that "every profound spirit needs a mask" and presents the "will to power" as the basic drive behind all life.

**The Birth of Tragedy**
Nietzsche's first major book (1872), which argues that Greek tragedy arose from the fusion of two artistic impulses: the Apollonian (order, form, clarity, dream) and the Dionysian (frenzy, intoxication, the dissolution of the self).

**Ecce Homo**
Nietzsche's autobiography, completed in 1888 just before his mental collapse, with grandiose chapter titles like "Why I Am So Wise," "Why I Am So Clever," "Why I Write Such Good Books," and "Why I Am a Destiny (Fatality)." It begins "Above all, do not mistake me for someone else" and ends with "Dionysus versus the Crucified."

**Will to power**
Nietzsche's idea that the basic drive behind all living things is a striving to grow, expand, and dominate, rather than mere survival. He wrote that "this world is the will to power—and nothing besides!" Nazi propagandists distorted the concept.

**Amor fati ("love of fate")**
The attitude of embracing everything that happens, including suffering, as necessary. In Ecce Homo, Nietzsche calls it his "formula for greatness in a human being." It is closely tied to saying "yes" to life and to eternal recurrence.

**The Antichrist**
Nietzsche's 1888 polemic against Christianity, which he accuses of promoting weakness and "otherworldly hopes" that devalue this life. It criticizes Ernest Renan's portrayal of Jesus as a "genius," discusses the "redeemer type," and calls for a "revaluation of all values."

**Twilight of the Idols**
An 1888 work subtitled "How to Philosophize with a Hammer," in which Nietzsche "sounds out" old idols. It contains the line "without music, life would be a mistake" and a section tracing how the "true world" (Plato's Forms, Kant's noumena) finally became a fable.

**Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche and the horse in Turin**
Nietzsche's sister, who controlled his literary estate after his 1889 breakdown and edited his unpublished notes (as The Will to Power) to suit her nationalist and antisemitic views. According to legend, his breakdown began in Turin when he threw his arms around a horse that was being whipped.

**The Wealth of Nations**
Smith's 1776 masterpiece, fully titled An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations. It is a founding text of modern economics, arguing for free markets, the division of labor, and capital accumulation as the sources of national wealth, and it is the standard giveaway for Smith.

**The "invisible hand"**
Smith's metaphor for how individuals pursuing their own self-interest unintentionally promote the good of society as a whole. Although it became the symbol of free-market thinking, the phrase appears only once in The Wealth of Nations, and also once in The Theory of Moral Sentiments.

**The pin factory**
The famous example that opens The Wealth of Nations to show the power of the division of labor. Smith describes how a pin-making workshop of ten men, each doing a few specialized steps, could make about 48,000 pins a day, while one untrained worker alone might hardly make one, or certainly not twenty.

**The Theory of Moral Sentiments**
Smith's first book, published in 1759, which lays out his ethics. It bases morality on sympathy and includes sections such as "Of Sympathy" and "Of the Propriety of Action," where he calls hatred and resentment "unsocial passions."

**The "impartial spectator"**
The central idea of The Theory of Moral Sentiments. We judge our own conduct by imagining how an impartial, well-informed observer would see it, and Smith also calls this inner judge "the man within the breast."

**Sympathy**
For Smith, the basis of moral judgment is our ability to imagine ourselves in others' situations and share their feelings. This view built on the "moral sense" ideas of his teacher Francis Hutcheson and his friend David Hume.

**The butcher, the brewer, and the baker**
Smith's famous line that "it is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest." It illustrates how self-interested exchange benefits everyone.

**Critique of mercantilism**
The Wealth of Nations attacks the mercantile system, which held that national wealth means accumulating gold and silver through trade surpluses, tariffs, and monopolies. Smith targeted policies such as those of the French minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert and argued that such commercial restrictions hurt the nation.

**The diamond-water paradox**
Smith's paradox of value: water is extremely useful but nearly free, while diamonds are nearly useless but very expensive. He used it to distinguish "value in use" from "value in exchange."

**Labor theory of value and "real and nominal price"**
Smith argued that labor is the real measure of the exchangeable value of goods, distinguishing a commodity's "real price" in labor from its "nominal price" in money. David Ricardo later critiqued and developed these ideas.

**Glasgow and Francis Hutcheson**
Smith studied at the University of Glasgow under Francis Hutcheson and later held its chairs of Logic and then Moral Philosophy. He was a leading figure of the Scottish Enlightenment and a close friend of David Hume.

**Lectures on Jurisprudence**
Lectures Smith gave at Glasgow, known today from students' notes published long after his death. They contain early versions of many ideas in The Wealth of Nations, such as his account of the stages of society.

**"Das Adam Smith Problem"**
The supposed contradiction between the sympathy-based ethics of The Theory of Moral Sentiments and the emphasis on self-interest in The Wealth of Nations. The name was coined by German scholars in the 19th century.

**Stages of society**
Smith described human societies developing through four stages: hunting, herding (pasturage), agriculture, and commerce. Each stage has its own kinds of property and government.

**Dog exchanging bones and the "naked savages"**
In The Wealth of Nations, Smith remarks that "nobody ever saw a dog make a fair and deliberate exchange of one bone for another with another dog," saying the tendency to "truck, barter, and exchange" is unique to humans. He also claims that, thanks to the division of labor, a frugal European peasant lives better than an African king who is master of "ten thousand naked savages."

**Twin Earth and XYZ**
Hilary Putnam's thought experiment imagines a Twin Earth where a liquid that looks, tastes, and behaves exactly like water has the chemical formula XYZ instead of H2O. Putnam argues that when an Earthling and their Twin say "water" they mean different things, even though their mental states are identical.

**Thales of Miletus**
The first pre-Socratic philosopher, from the Ionian city of Miletus, held that water was the arche, the single underlying principle or substance from which everything comes. This is one of the most common giveaways for water in philosophy questions.

**Icosahedron**
In Plato's Timaeus, each classical element is assigned a Platonic solid, and the particles of water are icosahedra, the twenty-faced solid. Fire is the tetrahedron, air the octahedron, and earth the cube.

**Phlegm (the phlegmatic humor)**
In the ancient medical theory of the four humors, phlegm corresponded to water, sharing its cold and moist qualities. An excess of phlegm was thought to make a person calm, sluggish, or "phlegmatic."

**Jadeite and nephrite**
Two different minerals that were both called "jade." Putnam uses them to raise the question of whether a natural kind term like "water" picks out a substance with a single hidden structure, or whether one word can cover two substances that merely look alike.

**Semantic externalism ("The Meaning of 'Meaning'")**
The view, defended in Putnam's 1975 paper "The Meaning of 'Meaning'" through the Twin Earth case, that the meanings of words depend partly on the external world and not only on what is in a speaker's head. Putnam's slogan is that "meanings just ain't in the head."

**Opposite of fire**
Among the four classical elements, water is treated as the opposite of fire. In Aristotle's scheme, fire is hot and dry while water is cold and moist.

**Atlantis sinking into the sea**
In Plato's dialogues Timaeus and Critias, the island of Atlantis is defeated and swallowed by the sea in a single day and night. Questions use this as a giveaway, describing water as the element into which Atlantis sank.

**The four classical elements**
Water is one of the four elements of Greek natural philosophy, along with earth, air, and fire. Questions on the elements as a group often mention water as one member.

**Empedocles' Love and Strife**
Empedocles held that the four "roots" (earth, air, fire, and water) are combined by the force of Love and separated by the force of Strife. He was the first to propose all four elements together.

**Aristotle's On Generation and Corruption**
In this work Aristotle says each element combines two of the four basic qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry), with water being cold and wet. He uses this to explain how elements can change into one another, and he distinguishes true "coming-to-be" from mere alteration.

**Thales versus Heraclitus**
The pre-Socratics disagreed about which element was the basic substance. Thales chose water, while Heraclitus of Ephesus chose fire, which he linked to constant change.

**Aether (the fifth element)**
Aristotle added aether, or quintessence, as a fifth element that makes up the heavens. Unlike water and the other earthly elements, which move up or down, aether moves naturally in circles.

**Gettier problem ("justified true belief")**
Edmund Gettier's three-page 1963 paper "Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?" gave counterexamples to the traditional definition of knowledge as justified true belief (JTB). In his most famous case, Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get the job and that Jones has ten coins in his pocket. Smith therefore believes "the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket," which turns out true only because Smith himself unknowingly gets the job and has ten coins.

**Plato's Theaetetus**
A Platonic dialogue in which Socrates and the young mathematician Theaetetus try to define knowledge. Theaetetus proposes in turn that knowledge is perception, true belief, and true belief with an account (logos), and the dialogue ends without settling on an answer. It, along with the Meno, is the traditional source of the "justified true belief" analysis.

**James Frederick Ferrier**
A Scottish philosopher credited with coining the English word "epistemology" in his 1854 Institutes of Metaphysic. The book divides philosophy into "Epistemology, or Theory of Knowing" and "Ontology, or Theory of Being."

**Virtue epistemology (Ernest Sosa)**
An approach that evaluates beliefs in terms of the intellectual virtues of the believer. Ernest Sosa's "AAA" model judges a belief by whether it is Accurate, Adroit (skillful), and Apt (accurate because of skill), and fake barn cases are a standard test for such theories. Sosa's essay "The Raft and the Pyramid" inspired Linda Zagzebski's neo-Aristotelian version of virtue epistemology.

**Foundationalism vs. coherentism (the regress problem)**
These are two classic responses to the regress problem, which asks what justifies the beliefs that justify other beliefs. Foundationalism says some basic beliefs need no further support. Coherentism, defended for example by Harold Henry Joachim in The Nature of Truth, says beliefs are justified by fitting together in a coherent system. Susan Haack combined the two into "foundherentism."

**Reformed epistemology (Alvin Plantinga)**
A position developed by Alvin Plantinga, William Alston, and Nicholas Wolterstorff. It holds that belief in God can be "properly basic," meaning rational without being inferred from arguments or evidence. Critics raised the "Great Pumpkin objection," which asks whether, on this view, belief in Linus's Great Pumpkin from Peanuts could be properly basic too.

**Skepticism and reliabilism**
Skepticism, associated in antiquity with Pyrrho of Elis, claims that knowledge is impossible or unattainable. Reliabilism, which holds that a belief is justified if it was produced by a reliable process, is one modern response to skeptical challenges.

**W.V.O. Quine, "Two Dogmas of Empiricism"**
Quine's 1951 paper attacked the analytic/synthetic distinction and reductionism, two central assumptions of logical positivism. Quine later proposed "naturalized epistemology," which treats the theory of knowledge as part of empirical psychology.

**John Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding**
Locke's 1689 founding text of British empiricism, which argues that the mind begins as a blank slate (tabula rasa) and that all ideas come from experience. It is often cited as a foundational work of modern epistemology.

**Hume's fork; a priori vs. a posteriori**
David Hume divided all knowledge into "relations of ideas," which are known a priori and are certain, and "matters of fact," which are known a posteriori, from experience. A posteriori knowledge is knowledge derived from experience, while a priori knowledge is independent of it.

**Knowledge by acquaintance vs. knowledge by description**
Bertrand Russell's distinction between knowledge of things we directly experience, such as sense-data, and knowledge of things known only through descriptions, such as "the tallest man in the world." He developed it in his 1910-11 paper of that name and in The Problems of Philosophy.

**Timothy Williamson, Knowledge and Its Limits**
Williamson's 2000 book argues for a "knowledge-first" epistemology. It holds that knowledge is a basic mental state that cannot be analyzed into components such as justified true belief.

**Bayesian epistemology**
A 20th-century school, named for Thomas Bayes, that treats belief as degrees of probability, or credences. It updates credences on new evidence by Bayes' rule, a process called conditionalization, and uses "Dutch Book" arguments to show that incoherent credences can be exploited by a series of bets.

**A.J. Ayer, Language, Truth and Logic**
Ayer's 1936 book popularized logical positivism in English. It promoted the verification principle, which holds that a statement is meaningful only if it is either analytic or empirically verifiable.

**Nyaya and Vaisheshika**
Two orthodox schools of Indian philosophy that are centrally concerned with the means of valid knowledge, called pramanas. Nyaya in particular is known for its detailed theory of perception, inference, comparison, and testimony.

**Nicomachean Ethics**
Aristotle's main ethical work, named after his son (or possibly his father) Nicomachus. It argues that the highest human good is eudaimonia, or happiness/flourishing, which comes from living virtuously according to reason.

**Virtue as the mean between extremes (the golden mean)**
In Book II of the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle defines each moral virtue as a mean between two vices, one of excess and one of deficiency. For example, courage lies between cowardice and recklessness.

**Lyceum, Plato, and Alexander the Great**
Aristotle studied at Plato's Academy for about twenty years, tutored the young Alexander the Great in Macedon, and later founded his own school in Athens, the Lyceum. His followers were called Peripatetics, and many of his surviving works are lecture notes from the Lyceum.

**Metaphysics**
Aristotle's study of "being qua being," the most general science. It includes the distinction between potentiality and actuality (Book Theta), a "philosophical lexicon" defining key terms (Book Delta), the law of non-contradiction, the prime mover, and the opening point that "all men by nature desire to know." It was so named because it came "after the Physics" in the ancient arrangement of his works.

**Four causes**
Aristotle's four kinds of explanation for why a thing is as it is: the material cause (what it is made of), the formal cause (its form or structure), the efficient cause (what produced it), and the final cause, or telos (its purpose or end).

**Organon and the syllogism**
The Organon ("instrument") is the six-book collection of Aristotle's logical works: Categories, On Interpretation, Prior Analytics, Posterior Analytics, Topics, and Sophistical Refutations. In the Prior Analytics he developed the syllogism, a deductive argument. The stock example is "All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal."

**Categories**
A work listing ten basic kinds of things that can be said about anything, such as substance, quantity, quality, and relation. It also separates what is "said of" a primary substance from what is "in" one. Porphyry's Isagoge introduced it, and Boethius's commentaries passed down the square of opposition drawn from Aristotle's logic.

**Potentiality and actuality**
Aristotle's distinction between what a thing could become (potentiality, dynamis) and what it actually is (actuality, energeia). It is discussed most fully in Book Theta of the Metaphysics. An acorn, for example, is potentially an oak tree.

**Unmoved (prime) mover**
Aristotle's idea of a first, eternal being that causes all motion in the cosmos without being moved itself. It moves things by being an object of desire. Thomas Aquinas later used the idea in his proofs of God.

**Poetics: catharsis and hamartia**
Aristotle's work on tragedy. It says tragedy produces catharsis, the purging of pity and fear in the audience, and that the tragic hero falls because of hamartia, an error or "tragic flaw."

**Politics: natural slavery and forms of government**
In the Politics Aristotle argued that some people are slaves by nature. He also sorted governments into three good forms (monarchy, aristocracy, and polity) and their three corrupt forms (tyranny, oligarchy, and democracy).

**On the Soul (De Anima)**
Aristotle's work on the soul, which he saw as the form of a living body. It describes three levels of soul: the nutritive soul, found even in plants; the perceptive soul of animals; and the intellectual or rational soul, found only in humans.

**Hylomorphism (form and matter)**
Aristotle's theory that every natural body is made of matter combined with form. Unlike his teacher Plato, he held that forms do not exist separately but only in the substances they shape.

**Future contingents and the sea battle**
In On Interpretation, Aristotle asks whether the statement "there will be a sea battle tomorrow" is already true or false. The puzzle is about fatalism. Diodorus Cronus's "Master Argument" was a reply to it.

**Averroes, Avicenna, and Bekker numbers**
Aristotle was hugely influential in medieval Islamic philosophy. Averroes, known as "The Commentator," wrote famous commentaries on his works. Avicenna said he only understood the Metaphysics after reading a commentary by al-Farabi. Today, passages in Aristotle are cited by Bekker numbers, which come from Immanuel Bekker's 19th-century edition.

**The Analects**
The collection of sayings and conversations of Confucius (Kongzi), compiled by his disciples after his death. It is the foundational text of Confucianism and the most common giveaway for the school.

**Mencius and the "four sprouts"**
Mencius (Mengzi), called the "Second Sage" of Confucianism, argued that human nature is naturally good. He held that everyone has four sprouts of virtue: compassion, shame, deference (humility), and a sense of right and wrong, which grow into benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom if cultivated.

**Child falling into a well**
Mencius's famous thought experiment for human goodness: anyone who suddenly sees a child about to fall into a well would feel alarm and compassion, not out of self-interest but because the heart of compassion is innate. He calls this feeling the sprout of benevolence.

**Ren (benevolence, humaneness)**
The highest Confucian virtue, sometimes called the "virtue of virtues," meaning humaneness or love for others. In the Analects, Confucius explains that practicing ren means not looking at, listening to, speaking, or doing anything contrary to ritual propriety.

**Filial piety (xiao)**
The central Confucian duty of respect, obedience, and care toward one's parents and ancestors. The Yuan-dynasty text The Twenty-Four Filial Exemplars, compiled by Guo Jujing, collects stories of model filial children.

**Five Relationships**
The five basic human bonds that Confucianism holds should be governed by proper duties: ruler and subject, father and son, husband and wife, elder brother and younger brother, and friend and friend. Social harmony depends on each person fulfilling their role.

**Li (ritual propriety)**
The Confucian concept of ritual, etiquette, and proper conduct governing behavior in society, from ceremonies to everyday manners. Its rules and the school's virtues are recorded in the Book of Rites, one of the Five Classics.

**Rectification of names (zhengming)**
Confucius's doctrine that names and titles must accurately match reality and proper function, so that a ruler acts as a ruler and a father as a father. He said that when names are not correct, language does not accord with the truth of things and affairs cannot succeed.

**The stable fire: "Was anyone hurt?"**
An Analects anecdote in which Confucius, learning that the stables had burned down, asked only whether any people were hurt and did not ask about the horses. It is cited as an example of his humanistic concern for people (ren).

**Xunzi: human nature is evil**
Xunzi (Xun Kuang), a later Confucian who opposed Mencius by arguing that human nature is bad and that goodness comes only from deliberate effort, education, and ritual. He argued that people seek goodness outside themselves precisely because they lack it by nature.

**Zhu Xi and Neo-Confucianism**
Zhu Xi, the great Song-dynasty philosopher, synthesized Neo-Confucianism, which incorporated metaphysical ideas influenced by Buddhism and Daoism. He emphasized the "investigation of things" to understand underlying principle (li) and grouped the Four Books as the core of the Confucian curriculum.

**The Great Learning and the "investigation of things"**
One of the Four Books, which teaches that "illustrious virtue" is manifested through a chain of self-cultivation that begins with the investigation of things and extends to ordering the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the world.

**Junzi (gentleman or superior man)**
The Confucian ideal of the morally cultivated person who possesses benevolence and acts with propriety, as opposed to the "petty man." Confucius taught that anyone could become a junzi through learning and self-cultivation.

**Shu (reciprocity) and the "Silver Rule"**
Confucius defined shu as "do not impose on others what you yourself do not desire." Because this is a negative version of the Golden Rule, it is sometimes called the Silver Rule.

**Ru, the Five Classics, and the Four Books**
Confucians are called ru ("scholars") in Chinese, a term scholars like Robert Eno use for the school. Its canon includes the Five Classics (such as the Book of Odes, Book of Documents, Book of Changes, Book of Rites, and Spring and Autumn Annals) and the Four Books (the Analects, Mencius, the Great Learning, and the Doctrine of the Mean). Confucius summarized the three hundred Odes in one phrase: "Have no depraved thoughts" (swerving not from the right path).

**Abraham's sacrifice of Isaac**
The central subject of the book. Kierkegaard examines the story in Genesis 22, where God commands Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac on Mount Moriah, and he asks how Abraham's willingness to obey can be seen as faith rather than murder.

**Teleological suspension of the ethical**
The subject of the first of the book's three "Problemata": can the ethical, meaning universal moral duty, be set aside for a higher purpose (telos)? Kierkegaard suggests that in faith, the individual's relationship to God can rise above the ethical, so the religious sphere lies beyond the ethical.

**Knight of faith**
Kierkegaard's ideal figure, represented by Abraham. Having given up everything, the knight of faith believes "by virtue of the absurd" that he will get it all back in this life. Kierkegaard says such a knight might outwardly look like an ordinary shopkeeper or tax collector.

**Knight of infinite resignation**
The figure one step below the knight of faith, who gives up a finite thing they love, such as a beloved, and finds peace in that eternal loss but does not expect to get it back. Kierkegaard says he himself can make this movement but cannot make the movement of faith.

**Johannes de Silentio**
The pseudonym under which Kierkegaard published Fear and Trembling in 1843. The narrator repeatedly says he cannot understand Abraham and that faith, which embraces the absurd, is beyond him.

**The three Problemata**
The book's three central questions: whether there is a teleological suspension of the ethical, whether there is an absolute duty to God, and whether Abraham was ethically justified in hiding his purpose from Sarah, Eliezer, and Isaac.

**Agamemnon at Aulis and the tragic hero**
Kierkegaard contrasts Abraham with Agamemnon, who sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia for the sake of the Greek army. Agamemnon is a "tragic hero" because he acts for a higher ethical good that others can understand and sympathize with, while Abraham acts alone and in silence, beyond the ethical.

**Agnes and the Merman**
A Danish legend that Kierkegaard retells in Problema III. A merman sets out to seduce the innocent Agnes but is moved by her trust in him, and Kierkegaard uses the story to explore concealment, the demonic, and repentance.

**Regine Olsen**
Kierkegaard's former fiancée, whom he broke off his engagement with in 1841. Many readers see his own sacrifice of her behind the book's themes of resignation and faith.

**Repetition**
Another Kierkegaard book, published on the same day as Fear and Trembling (October 16, 1843) under the pseudonym Constantin Constantius.

**Jacques Derrida's The Gift of Death**
A work in which Derrida reads Fear and Trembling and introduces the formula "every other is wholly other" (tout autre est tout autre). He argues that any responsibility to one person sacrifices our responsibility to all others.

**The "Exordium" and its variations**
The book opens with a section, sometimes translated "Tuning Up," that imagines several different versions of Abraham's journey to Moriah, followed by a "Eulogy on Abraham" praising him as the father of faith.

**The "absolute duty to God"**
The subject of Problema II. Kierkegaard asks whether a person can owe God a duty that outranks every ethical duty, and he connects it to the idea of the "single individual" who stands in a private relationship to God.

**Principia Mathematica**
Russell's three-volume work (1910–13), co-written with Alfred North Whitehead (later the author of Process and Reality), which tried to derive all of mathematics from axioms of symbolic logic. It famously takes hundreds of pages to reach a proof that 1 + 1 = 2, remarking that "the above proposition is occasionally useful," and Kurt Gödel's incompleteness theorems later showed that its goal could not be fully achieved. Collaboration with Whitehead is the universal giveaway.

**Russell's teapot**
An analogy from Russell's article "Is There a God?": if he claimed that a china teapot too small to be seen by telescopes orbits the Sun between Earth and Mars, no one could disprove it, but that would not oblige anyone to believe it. It argues that the burden of proof lies with those making unfalsifiable claims, such as believers in God, and was later popularized by Richard Dawkins.

**Russell's paradox**
The paradox Russell discovered in naive set theory: does the set of all sets that are not members of themselves contain itself? If it does, it doesn't, and if it doesn't, it does. It is often illustrated by the barber who shaves all and only those who do not shave themselves.

**Letter to Frege and Basic Law V**
In 1902 Russell wrote to Gottlob Frege showing that his paradox could be derived from Frege's Basic Law V, undermining Frege's attempt to ground arithmetic in logic. Responses included Russell's own theory of types and the Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms for set theory.

**"On Denoting" and "the present King of France is bald"**
Russell's 1905 paper setting out his theory of descriptions. It analyzes a definite description like "the present King of France" as a claim with existential quantification (there is exactly one present King of France, and he is bald), so the sentence is simply false rather than meaningless, which preserves the law of the excluded middle. It rejects Frege's distinction between sense and reference.

**Criticism of Alexius Meinong**
Russell argued against Meinong's theory of objects, which held that non-existent things like golden mountains or round squares still "subsist" in some way. Russell said such objects violate the law of contradiction, and his theory of descriptions removes the need for them.

**Why I Am Not a Christian**
Russell's 1927 lecture and essay explaining his rejection of Christianity. It attacks the first-cause and design arguments, questions the supposed superlative wisdom and goodness of Christ, says religion is "based primarily and mainly upon fear," and calls the Christian religion, as organized in its churches, "the principal enemy of moral progress in the world."

**Theory of types**
Russell's solution to his paradox, which arranges sets and propositions in a hierarchy of types so that a set can only contain items of a lower type. Principia Mathematica uses a "ramified" version that requires the controversial axiom of reducibility, and Russell also proposed a "no-class" theory of classes.

**Logical atomism**
The view, set out in Russell's 1918 lectures "The Philosophy of Logical Atomism," that the world consists of discrete atomic facts and that an ideal logical language would mirror it with atomic propositions. It was developed alongside his student Ludwig Wittgenstein, whose later work turned against such views.

**Marriage and Morals**
Russell's 1929 book challenging Victorian views on sex, marriage, and contraception. The controversy over it led to the 1940 cancellation of his appointment to teach at the City College of New York.

**Knowledge by acquaintance and knowledge by description**
Russell distinguished knowledge of things we are directly aware of, such as sense-data, from knowledge of things we know only through descriptions. The distinction appears in The Problems of Philosophy and his writings on denoting.

**Neutral monism (The Analysis of Mind and The Analysis of Matter)**
In these works Russell argued that ultimate reality is neither purely mental nor purely physical but made of a neutral stuff underlying both. The Analysis of Matter proposed combining physics and psychology to understand the "intrinsic character" of the world.

**Russell-Einstein Manifesto and pacifism**
The 1955 manifesto, issued by Russell and signed by Albert Einstein and other scientists, warning of the dangers of nuclear weapons and calling for peaceful solutions. Russell was a lifelong activist who was imprisoned for opposing World War I and later protested the Vietnam War.

**Nobel Prize in Literature and A History of Western Philosophy**
Russell won the 1950 Nobel Prize in Literature for his varied writings. His popular works include A History of Western Philosophy, The Problems of Philosophy, What I Believe (which says the good life is "inspired by love and guided by knowledge"), and Roads to Freedom, which compares socialism, anarchism, and syndicalism.

**Five-minute hypothesis**
In The Analysis of Mind Russell noted that it is logically possible that the world sprang into existence five minutes ago, complete with false memories of a nonexistent past. It shows that memories cannot logically prove that the past happened.

**Pragmatism: A New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking**
James's 1907 lecture series and his most famous work. It argues that ideas should be judged by their practical consequences. James built on ideas from Charles Sanders Peirce, who founded pragmatism, and the two are usually named together as its founders.

**The squirrel and the tree**
The anecdote that opens the second lecture of Pragmatism. A man circles a tree while a squirrel on the trunk keeps moving to stay opposite him, and James asks whether the man "goes round" the squirrel. He settles the argument by showing that the answer depends on what "going round" means in practice.

**"Cash value" of truth**
James's pragmatic theory of truth says that a belief's truth lies in its practical "cash value," meaning how useful and workable it proves in experience. He held that truth "happens to" an idea: it is made true by events.

**"Tender-minded" vs. "tough-minded"**
A contrast between two philosophical temperaments in the first lecture of Pragmatism. The tender-minded are rationalist, idealistic, optimistic, and religious, while the tough-minded are empiricist, materialistic, pessimistic, and skeptical. James presents pragmatism as a way to reconcile the two.

**The Varieties of Religious Experience**
James's 1902 book, based on his Gifford Lectures in Edinburgh. It studies religion through personal experience, with lectures such as "Religion and Neurology" and "The Reality of the Unseen." It also lists four marks of mystical states: ineffability, a noetic quality, transiency, and passivity.

**"Healthy-mindedness" vs. "the sick soul"**
Two religious temperaments contrasted in The Varieties of Religious Experience. Healthy-minded people (which can be voluntary or involuntary) focus on goodness and ignore evil, while "sick souls" are deeply aware of evil and suffering. James calls Walt Whitman an example of healthy-mindedness, with an "inability to feel evil" and a soul of "sky-blue tint."

**"The Will to Believe"**
An 1896 lecture defending the right to hold religious faith without sufficient evidence. It replies to W. K. Clifford's claim that it is always wrong to believe anything on insufficient evidence.

**Live, forced, and momentous options**
In "The Will to Believe," James says a "genuine option" between beliefs must be live (both choices seem possible) rather than dead, forced (one cannot avoid choosing), and momentous (unique and important) rather than trivial. As an example of a momentous option, he imagines being invited on an expedition to the North Pole.

**"Stream of consciousness"**
A phrase James popularized in his 1890 textbook The Principles of Psychology, in a chapter called "The Stream of Thought." He described the mind as a continuous flow rather than a chain of separate ideas. The book also has a chapter on "The Consciousness of Self" and relies on introspection.

**James-Lange theory of emotion**
A theory named for James and the Danish physician Carl Lange. It holds that emotions are our perception of bodily changes. In James's example, a person meeting a bear does not run because they are afraid; they feel afraid because they notice their racing heart and running.

**"The Moral Philosopher and the Moral Life"**
An essay collected in The Will to Believe and Other Essays. It describes a utopia whose happiness depends on one "lost soul" suffering "lonely torture," which inspired Ursula K. Le Guin's story "The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas."

**Charles Renouvier and free will**
During a long depression, James read Charles Renouvier's essays on free will and decided, "My first act of free will shall be to believe in free will." This helped him recover.

**Radical empiricism and "pure experience"**
In Essays in Radical Empiricism, James argued that reality is made of "pure experience," which is neither mind nor matter. Both mind and matter are different arrangements of it.

**A Pluralistic Universe**
A 1909 book in which James rejects monism, the idea that reality is one unified whole like the Absolute of the idealists. Instead he defends a pluralistic view of a varied, open-ended universe.

**Henry James**
William James's younger brother, the famous novelist of The Portrait of a Lady and The Turn of the Screw. He is often mentioned to identify William.

**Existentialism Is a Humanism**
Jean-Paul Sartre's 1945 lecture, given at the Club Maintenant in Paris and published in 1946. It defends existentialism against Christian and Marxist critics who said it was an invitation to "quietism of despair." It includes the dilemma of Sartre's student, who must choose between joining the Free French forces and staying to care for his mother, to show that no ethical system can make the choice for us. Sartre later distanced himself from the lecture.

**"Existence precedes essence"**
The central slogan of Sartre's existentialism, stated in Existentialism Is a Humanism. Humans have no fixed, predefined nature; they first exist and then define themselves through their choices. Sartre adds that "in fashioning myself, I fashion man," meaning each choice sets an example for all humanity.

**Bad faith (mauvaise foi)**
Sartre's term in Being and Nothingness for self-deception, in which people deny their own freedom. His examples include a café waiter who acts his role too mechanically, as if he were only a waiter, and a woman on a date who lets her hand rest in a man's as if it were just a thing, to avoid deciding. Both deny the tension between their "facticity" (the facts of their situation) and their "transcendence" (their freedom).

**Being and Nothingness**
Sartre's 1943 main philosophical work. It contrasts "being-in-itself" (the fixed being of things) with "being-for-itself" (free human consciousness). It also analyzes "the look," in which being seen by another person makes us aware of our "being-for-others."

**No Exit**
Sartre's 1944 play in which three dead people, Garcin, Inès, and Estelle, are locked together in a drawing room that turns out to be Hell. There is no torturer; they torment each other, which leads to the famous line "Hell is other people."

**Søren Kierkegaard and Fear and Trembling**
The 19th-century Danish thinker usually called the father of existentialism. Fear and Trembling, written under the pseudonym Johannes de Silentio, studies Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac as a "leap of faith" beyond ethics. It is organized around three "Problemata," and it retells the legend of Agnes and the merman.

**The Sickness Unto Death**
Kierkegaard's work on despair, which he treats as a form of sin, from a Christian existentialist standpoint. It defines the self as "a relation that relates itself to itself."

**The Concept of Anxiety and Kierkegaard's pseudonyms**
In The Concept of Anxiety, Kierkegaard calls anxiety "the dizziness of freedom." He wrote many works under pseudonyms, such as Judge William, who argues for the ethical life in the second part of Either/Or.

**Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex**
A founding text of feminist existentialism, published in 1949. It argues that "one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman," meaning that womanhood is a social construction rather than a fixed essence.

**The Ethics of Ambiguity**
De Beauvoir's 1947 attempt to build an existentialist ethics around radical freedom. It analyzes types of people who flee or misuse freedom, including the "sub-man," the "serious man," the "nihilist," the "adventurer," and the "passionate man."

**Albert Camus and The Myth of Sisyphus**
Camus's 1942 essay on the absurd, the clash between our need for meaning and a silent universe. It asks whether the absurd justifies suicide, rejects suicide as an escape, and ends with the line "one must imagine Sisyphus happy," referring to the mythical king condemned to push a boulder uphill forever. Camus, also the author of A Happy Death, denied being an existentialist.

**Critique of Dialectical Reason**
Sartre's later, massive work combining existentialism with Marxism. It argues that human activity, or "praxis," is limited by the "practico-inert," meaning material conditions shaped by past human action. It also describes "seriality," the passive grouping of people such as those waiting in line for a bus, which Iris Marion Young later used to describe gender.

**Martin Heidegger and Being and Time**
Heidegger's 1927 book, built around the concept of Dasein, strongly influenced existentialism, although Heidegger rejected the label. In his "Letter on Humanism," written to Jean Beaufret, he criticized Sartre's lecture for staying within metaphysics.

**Karl Jaspers and Martin Buber**
Two German-language thinkers often linked to existentialism. Jaspers, author of Way to Wisdom, wrote about modes of "the Encompassing," and Buber's I and Thou contrasts "I-It" relationships, which treat others as objects, with "I-Thou" relationships of genuine encounter.

**Christian and Russian existentialists**
Besides Kierkegaard, religious existentialists include the theologian Paul Tillich and the Russian thinkers Nikolai Berdyaev and Lev Shestov.

**Rectification of names (zhengming)**
A Confucian doctrine that words must match reality, so a ruler must truly act as a ruler, a father as a father, and so on. In the Analects, Confucius says that if he governed, his first task would be to rectify names, because if names are not correct, speech does not accord with things and nothing can be accomplished.

**"Let the ruler be a ruler, the subject a subject"**
Confucius's answer in the Analects (12.11) to Duke Jing of Qi, continuing "the father a father, the son a son." It expresses the idea that social order depends on people fulfilling the roles their names describe. Xunzi later developed the theory in his chapter "Rectifying Names."

**Five basic relationships**
The Confucian relationships of ruler and subject, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger brother, and friend and friend. Each role carries its own duties, and Confucians held these relationships are stable only when names are used correctly.

**School of Names (Mingjia)**
A school of ancient Chinese thinkers, also called the "Logicians" or the "School of Forms and Names," who studied paradoxes, language, and argument during the Warring States period. Its best-known members are Gongsun Long and Hui Shi.

**"White horses are not horses"**
The famous paradox in Gongsun Long's White Horse Dialogue, a key text of the School of Names. It argues that "white horse" names a color plus a shape, while "horse" names only a shape, so the two terms are not identical.

**Hui Shi**
A leading thinker of the School of Names, known for a list of ten paradoxes, such as "I set off for Yue today and arrived yesterday." In the Zhuangzi he appears as Zhuangzi's friend and debating partner, most famously in the "happiness of fish" exchange on a bridge over the Hao River.

**Nominalism and William of Ockham**
The medieval view that universals (like "redness" or "humanity") are not real things existing outside the mind but only names or mental concepts applying to many individuals. The term comes from the Latin nomen, "name," and William of Ockham is its most famous defender.

**Proper names**
Names that pick out a specific individual, such as "Mencius" and "Confucius," as opposed to general terms like "philosopher." How proper names refer is a central question in the philosophy of language.

**Mingjiao ("teaching of names")**
A term used in Wei-Jin period China for the Confucian system of social roles, rituals, and moral norms. Neo-Daoist thinkers such as Xi Kang contrasted mingjiao with ziran, "naturalness" or spontaneity.

**Mill on names: denotation without connotation**
In A System of Logic, John Stuart Mill argued that proper names denote individuals without connoting any attributes; a name like "Dartmouth" names a town even if it no longer lies at the mouth of the Dart.

**Frege and Russell: names as descriptions**
Gottlob Frege distinguished a name's sense from its reference, using the example that "the Morning Star" and "the Evening Star" both refer to Venus. Bertrand Russell argued that ordinary proper names are disguised definite descriptions.

**Kripke's Naming and Necessity**
Saul Kripke's lectures (1970, published 1980) attacked descriptivism, arguing that proper names are "rigid designators" that refer to the same individual in every possible world. He proposed a causal-historical picture in which a name's reference is fixed by an initial "baptism" and passed along from speaker to speaker.

**"I think, therefore I am" (Cogito, ergo sum)**
Descartes's foundational certainty: even if he doubts everything, the very act of doubting proves that he exists as a thinking thing. The Latin form appears in the Principles of Philosophy, the French "je pense, donc je suis" in the Discourse on the Method, and the Meditations gives it as "I am, I exist." It is the universal giveaway.

**Meditations on First Philosophy**
Descartes's 1641 masterpiece, divided into six meditations often imagined as six days of reflection. The first is titled "What Can Be Called Into Doubt," and the work moves from radical doubt to the cogito, proofs of God's existence, and the distinction between mind and body.

**Melting wax argument**
In the Second Meditation, Descartes observes that a piece of beeswax near the fire loses its smell, color, shape, and hardness, yet we still judge it to be the same wax. He concludes that what remains is only something extended, flexible, and changeable, and that it is grasped by the intellect alone, not by the senses or imagination.

**Evil demon**
A skeptical thought experiment from the First Meditation in which an all-powerful, malicious deceiver (the "evil genius" or "malicious demon") feeds Descartes illusions of an external world, his body, and even mathematics. It pushes his method of doubt to its extreme and inspired the modern "brain in a vat" scenario, which Hilary Putnam answered with an externalist argument.

**Mind-body (Cartesian) dualism / "ghost in the machine"**
Descartes held that mind (res cogitans, a thinking, unextended substance) and body (res extensa, an extended substance whose essence is extension) are distinct substances. Gilbert Ryle ridiculed this view in The Concept of Mind (1949) as "the ghost in the machine" and a "category mistake," illustrated by a visitor to Oxford who sees all the colleges and asks "But where is the University?"

**Elisabeth of Bohemia and the interaction problem**
Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia asked Descartes in letters how an unextended mind could move an extended body. In his replies he compared the union of mind and body to the Scholastic notion of "heaviness," and the correspondence fed into The Passions of the Soul.

**Pineal gland**
Descartes identified this small gland in the center of the brain as the "principal seat of the soul," the place where mind and body interact. In his account, the soul moves the gland, which directs the flow of "animal spirits" through the nerves.

**The Passions of the Soul**
Descartes's last published work (1649), dedicated to Queen Christina of Sweden and growing out of his correspondence with Elisabeth. It explains emotions such as wonder, love, hatred, and desire as caused by the movement of "animal spirits."

**Discourse on the Method**
Descartes's 1637 work, written as a preface to three scientific essays: Optics (Dioptrique), Meteorology (Les Météores), and Geometry. It describes his method of rejecting anything open to doubt and gives provisional moral maxims, including the second maxim that a traveler lost in a forest should keep walking firmly in one direction.

**Cartesian circle**
The charge, raised by Antoine Arnauld and Marin Mersenne in the Objections and Replies, that Descartes's reasoning is circular. He uses "clear and distinct" perceptions to prove that God exists, but relies on a non-deceiving God to guarantee that clear and distinct perceptions are true.

**Proofs of God's existence (trademark and ontological arguments)**
In the Third Meditation Descartes argues that his idea of an infinite, perfect God must have been caused by an actually infinite being, since he himself is finite and imperfect. In the Fifth Meditation he gives an ontological argument that existence belongs to God's essence. He also sorts ideas into innate, adventitious (coming from outside), and factitious (invented).

**Dream argument**
In the First Meditation Descartes notes that dreams of sitting by the fire in his dressing gown feel just like waking life, so the senses cannot prove he is awake.
