He also mentions madmen who believe their heads are pumpkins or made of glass, and observes that "whether I am awake or asleep, two and three add up to five."

**Objections and Replies**
The set of objections to the Meditations by figures including Johannes Caterus, Thomas Hobbes, Antoine Arnauld (the Fourth Objections, which used a right triangle and the Pythagorean theorem as a counterexample), Pierre Gassendi, and Marin Mersenne, published with Descartes's responses. In the Seventh Replies he compared sorting true beliefs from false ones to emptying a basket of apples to throw out the rotten ones.

**Cartesian coordinate plane**
Descartes's analytic geometry, set out in La Géométrie, located points with coordinates relative to perpendicular axes, linking algebra and geometry. The coordinate system and the adjective "Cartesian" (from his Latin name Renatus Cartesius) both come from him.

**Animals as machines and the tree of philosophy**
Descartes viewed animal and human bodies as mechanical automata, comparing them in the Treatise on Man to the hydraulic statues in royal gardens, such as a Neptune that threatens visitors with its trident when they step on hidden plates. In the preface to the Principles of Philosophy he pictured philosophy as a tree whose roots are metaphysics, trunk is physics, and branches are the other sciences, with morals as the highest and most perfect.

**"The greatest happiness for the greatest number"**
The slogan summarizing utilitarianism: the right action is the one that produces the most overall happiness or good for the largest number of people. Mill calls a version of it the "Greatest Happiness Principle," and it appears in nearly every giveaway.

**Jeremy Bentham**
The English founder of utilitarianism, whose An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789) opens by declaring that nature has placed mankind under "two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure." He also asked of animals, "The question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?"

**Felicific (hedonic) calculus**
Bentham's method for measuring the pleasure and pain an action will produce, using factors such as intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, and extent. It was meant to make moral and legislative decisions quantifiable.

**John Stuart Mill's Utilitarianism**
Mill's 1861 book defending the theory against objections that it is "a doctrine worthy only of swine" and "godless." It distinguishes higher (intellectual) from lower pleasures, declares "it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied," discusses the "ultimate sanction" of the principle of utility, and links justice to utility in its final chapter.

**Panopticon**
Bentham's design for a circular prison in which a single watchman in a central tower could observe all the inmates without their knowing whether they were being watched at that moment.

**On Liberty and the harm principle**
Mill's 1859 essay, influenced by his wife Harriet Taylor, warns against the "tyranny of the majority" and argues that the only legitimate reason to use power against someone's will is to prevent harm to others. Mill also argued for equality of the sexes in The Subjection of Women.

**Act vs. rule utilitarianism**
Act utilitarianism judges each individual action by its consequences, while rule utilitarianism judges actions by whether they follow rules that generally maximize utility. J. J. C. Smart objected that rule utilitarianism leads to irrational "rule worship" or collapses into act utilitarianism, and R. M. Hare's "two-level" theory tried to combine them through "intuitive" and "critical" levels of moral thinking.

**Henry Sidgwick's The Methods of Ethics**
Sidgwick's 1874 treatise compares egoism, intuitionism, and utilitarianism, which he called "universalistic hedonism." Sidgwick also helped found Newnham College, Cambridge.

**Peter Singer and the drowning child**
The Australian utilitarian Peter Singer argued in "Famine, Affluence, and Morality" that failing to donate to famine relief is like refusing to wade into a pond to save a drowning child because it would muddy your clothes. His Animal Liberation applies the "equal consideration of interests" to animals and attacks "speciesism," and his ideas inspired the effective altruism movement.

**Robert Nozick's utility monster and experience machine**
Nozick's objections in Anarchy, State, and Utopia: the "utility monster" gains so much pleasure from resources that utilitarianism would require sacrificing everyone else to it. The "experience machine" would give you any pleasurable experience you want, yet most people would refuse to plug in, which challenges the hedonism behind classical utilitarianism.

**Bernard Williams's "Jim and the Indians" and Utilitarianism: For and Against**
In Utilitarianism: For and Against, co-written with J. J. C. Smart, who defends the theory, Williams imagines a visitor named Jim told by a captain named Pedro that he can save nineteen of twenty prisoners by shooting one himself. Williams uses the case to argue that utilitarianism ignores personal integrity.

**McCloskey's sheriff objection**
H. J. McCloskey imagined a sheriff who could prevent deadly riots by framing and executing an innocent man. The case shows that summing up happiness can seem to justify grave injustice.

**Derek Parfit's repugnant conclusion**
Parfit's argument, connected to his "mere addition paradox," that total utilitarianism implies that a huge population of people whose lives are barely worth living would be better than a smaller, very happy population.

**John Rawls and the "separateness of persons"**
In A Theory of Justice (1971) Rawls criticized utilitarianism for treating society as one big person whose happiness is maximized, ignoring the distinctness of individuals. The related "demandingness objection" says the theory asks too much, leaving no room for supererogatory acts that go beyond duty.

**Negative utilitarianism and other variants**
Karl Popper proposed minimizing suffering rather than maximizing happiness, which Ninian Smart labeled "negative utilitarianism." Other versions include G. E. Moore's "ideal utilitarianism," John Harsanyi's preference utilitarianism, William Paley's theological utilitarianism, and the anarchist utilitarianism of William Godwin's Enquiry Concerning Political Justice.

**Eichmann in Jerusalem**
Arendt's 1963 book, based on her reports for The New Yorker on the 1961 trial in Jerusalem of Adolf Eichmann, a Nazi official who organized the deportation of Jews to death camps. It is subtitled "A Report on the Banality of Evil" and is the most common giveaway for her.

**"Banality of evil"**
Arendt's famous phrase for her thesis that Eichmann was not a monster driven by "insane hatred" or ideological indoctrination but a "terrifyingly normal" bureaucrat. She argued that ordinary people can commit terrible crimes through thoughtlessness and careerism rather than deep malice.

**The Origins of Totalitarianism**
Arendt's 1951 book tracing the roots of Nazism and Stalinism. It is divided into three parts, on antisemitism, imperialism, and totalitarianism, and argues that nineteenth-century imperialism and the decline of the nation-state paved the way for totalitarian movements.

**The Human Condition**
Arendt's 1958 work of political philosophy, which divides human activity into labor, work, and action. It contrasts the ancient Greek distinction between the public and private realms with modern society.

**Labor, work, and action**
The three activities that make up the vita activa (active life) in The Human Condition. Labor meets biological needs and leaves nothing lasting, work fabricates a durable world of objects, and action is political activity carried out among other people through speech and deeds. Arendt cites Achilles as a figure who embodies action and its pursuit of immortal fame.

**Vita activa and vita contemplativa**
The active life and the contemplative life, a traditional distinction that Arendt takes up in The Human Condition. She argues that philosophy traditionally ranked contemplation above action, and she traces how the different parts of the vita activa were ranked and changed over history.

**Eichmann's "inability to think" and the categorical imperative**
Arendt noted that Eichmann spoke in "stock phrases and self-invented clichés" and showed an inability to think from anyone else's point of view. At his trial, Eichmann claimed to have lived by Kant's categorical imperative, but Arendt argued he had distorted it into obeying the will of the Führer instead of acting as if he himself were the legislator of universal law.

**Martin Heidegger**
The German philosopher who was Arendt's teacher at the University of Marburg and her lover in the 1920s. Heidegger later joined the Nazi Party, while Arendt, who was Jewish, fled Germany in 1933.

**The "social" realm**
In The Human Condition, Arendt argues that modernity blurred the classical distinction between the public (political) realm and the private (household) realm by creating a new "social" realm, in which economic and household concerns became public matters.

**Animal laborans and homo faber**
Arendt's terms for humans as laborers and humans as makers. In The Human Condition she argues that a hallmark of modernity is the victory of animal laborans over homo faber, as society came to value consumption and the life process above lasting work and political action.

**"Right to have rights"**
Arendt's phrase from The Origins of Totalitarianism. She argued that so-called universal human rights failed to protect stateless people and refugees, who in practice had rights only as citizens of a state, so the most basic right is the right to belong to a political community.

**Dreyfus affair and antisemitism**
The first part of The Origins of Totalitarianism deals with modern antisemitism and ends with a history of the Dreyfus affair, the case in France in which the Jewish army officer Alfred Dreyfus was falsely convicted of treason. Arendt examines how Jews' ambiguous position in relation to the nation-state made them targets.

**Terror and "superfluous" people**
In The Origins of Totalitarianism, Arendt distinguishes regimes that use terror only against political opponents from totalitarian regimes that use it against the entire population. She applies Kant's concept of "radical evil" to the totalitarian effort to make human beings "superfluous," and describes totalitarianism as the "most radical denial of freedom."

**On Revolution**
Arendt's 1963 comparison of the American and French Revolutions. She praises the American Revolution for founding a lasting body politic of freedom, the constitutio libertatis, while the French Revolution was overwhelmed by the "social question" of poverty.

**Sputnik**
The Human Condition begins with the 1957 launch of Sputnik, which Arendt calls an event "second in importance to no other," and reflects on humanity's desire to escape the earthly conditions of its existence.

**Achilles and the tortoise**
Zeno's most famous paradox. The swift runner Achilles gives a tortoise a head start, and by the time he reaches where the tortoise was, it has moved a little further, so the argument concludes that he can never catch it. It appears in nearly every question on Zeno.

**Arrow paradox**
Zeno argued that a flying arrow is at rest at every single instant, occupying a space exactly equal to itself, so it is "frozen" in place and never actually moves. Like his other paradoxes, it was meant to show that motion is impossible.

**Paradoxes of motion**
Zeno is known for a set of paradoxes arguing that motion, change, and plurality are illusions. Besides Achilles and the arrow, they include the Dichotomy, which says that to cross any distance you must first cross half of it, then half of what is left, and so on without end, and the Stadium (or moving rows).

**Parmenides**
Zeno was the student and defender of Parmenides of Elea, who held that reality is one, unchanging Being and that the senses deceive us about change. Zeno's paradoxes were meant to support his teacher by showing that believing in motion and plurality leads to absurd results.

**Elea and the Eleatic school**
Zeno came from Elea, a Greek colony in southern Italy, and belonged to the Eleatic school along with Parmenides and Melissus. The "of Elea" in his name separates him from Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism.

**Aristotle's Physics, Book 6**
Aristotle discusses and tries to answer Zeno's paradoxes in Book 6 of his Physics. He responds by separating the actual infinite from the potential (possible) infinite, arguing that a distance can be divided without end in principle but is never actually divided into infinitely many parts.

**Founder of dialectic**
Aristotle called Zeno the inventor of dialectic. Zeno's method was to take his opponents' assumptions and draw contradictions out of them, an early form of reductio ad absurdum argument.

**Biting the tyrant's ear**
Ancient stories say that Zeno was arrested for plotting against the tyrant Nearchus of Elea and that, under torture, he bit off the tyrant's ear (or, in other versions, his own tongue). Boethius mentions Zeno's bravery under torture in The Consolation of Philosophy.

**Plato's Parmenides**
In this Plato dialogue, Zeno and Parmenides visit Athens and talk with a young Socrates. Zeno reads from his book of arguments against plurality, and Socrates then questions Parmenides about the theory of Forms.

**Method of exhaustion**
A Greek mathematical technique, used most famously by Archimedes, that finds areas and volumes by filling a shape with more and more smaller pieces. Questions present it as an early mathematical answer to the infinite divisions in Zeno's arguments.

**"Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short"**
Hobbes's famous description in Chapter 13 of the life of man in the state of nature, where there is no common power to keep people in awe. It is the most common giveaway for Leviathan.

**"War of every man against every man" (war of all against all)**
In the state of nature, without a sovereign, people are in constant war because of competition, diffidence (distrust), and glory. Hobbes argues that men are naturally equal, because despite differences in strength and craft, even the weakest can kill the strongest. The Latin phrase bellum omnium contra omnes is associated with this idea.

**"Of the Kingdom of Darkness"**
The fourth and final part of Leviathan. It attacks a "confederacy of deceivers," above all the Roman Catholic Church, who keep people in spiritual ignorance. It names four causes of this darkness: misinterpretation of Scripture, the demonology of the heathen poets, mixing Scripture with the vain philosophy of the Greeks (especially Aristotle), and false traditions. It calls the "main abuse" of Scripture the claim that the Kingdom of God is the present church.

**Abraham Bosse's frontispiece**
The famous title page, designed by Abraham Bosse, shows a giant crowned sovereign rising over a landscape and town. His body is made of many small people, and he holds a sword and a crozier, symbolizing civil and church power. Panels below show military and ecclesiastical emblems. The title refers to the sea monster in the Book of Job.

**"Artificial man" and the body politic**
The introduction calls the commonwealth, or state, an "artificial man," of greater stature and strength than the natural man, created by human art. It begins by saying that "life is but a motion of limbs," so automata may be said to have artificial life.

**Laws of nature**
In Chapters 14 and 15, Hobbes lists nineteen laws of nature, in contrast to the single "right of nature," which is the liberty to use any means to preserve oneself. The first law is "to seek peace, and follow it," the second is to give up one's right to all things if others do the same, and the third is that men keep the covenants they make. All are summed up in the dictum "Do not that to another, which thou wouldest not have done to thyselfe."

**Covenant and the twelve rights of the sovereign**
People escape the state of nature by a covenant in which each "authorizes" one person or assembly to act as the "author" of all their actions, creating the commonwealth. In Part II, "Of Commonwealth," Hobbes lists twelve principal rights of the sovereign, including judicial and law-making power. Subjects cannot change the form of government, since a later covenant cannot override the earlier one.

**No summum bonum; violent death as the greatest evil**
Hobbes denies that there is a summum bonum, a single greatest good or final end, that all people pursue. Instead, he treats violent death as the greatest evil (summum malum), and the fear of violent death drives people to seek peace and form a commonwealth.

**Four parts: "Of Man," "Of Commonwealth," "Of a Christian Commonwealth," "Of the Kingdom of Darkness"**
The structure of the book. Part III argues that religious authority must be subordinate to the civil sovereign. Its reasoning is that no one can know whether another person's claimed divine revelation is genuine, so Scripture is authoritative only as interpreted under the sovereign. It warns that dividing spiritual and temporal power makes people "see double."

**Three kinds of commonwealth**
Hobbes says there are only three forms of government: monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy. "Tyranny" and "oligarchy" are just names for monarchy and aristocracy that people dislike. He argues that monarchy is best at avoiding civil war.

**Vital and voluntary motion; appetite and aversion**
Chapter 6 divides animal motion into involuntary "vital" motions, such as breathing and circulation, and "voluntary" motions caused by the imagination. The passions are forms of appetite and aversion, and the will is defined as "the last appetite in deliberating."

**"Decaying sense" and the "train of thoughts"**
Hobbes defines imagination as "nothing but decaying sense." To illustrate the "train of thoughts," he describes a discussion of the civil war in which someone asked the value of a Roman penny. The question seemed random but was linked by association to the betrayal of Christ for thirty pence.

**Speech, reason, and the "four abuses" of speech**
In Part I, which is laid out almost like a geometric demonstration, Hobbes says speech exists to transfer mental discourse into verbal discourse. He lists four abuses of speech, defines reason as "reckoning" (adding and subtracting), and calls "incorporeal substance" a self-contradictory term. In a later appendix, he defended God's corporeality, partly in response to Bishop John Bramhall.

**The Fool: "there is no such thing as Justice"**
In Chapter 15, echoing Psalms 14:1, Hobbes answers "the fool" who "hath said in his heart, there is no such thing as justice" and that breaking covenants can be rational. Hobbes argues that keeping covenants is required by reason.

**Liberty as "absence of external impediments"**
Hobbes defines liberty as the absence of external impediments to motion. He says that the liberty of subjects in a commonwealth lies in the "silence of the law," meaning whatever the sovereign has not forbidden.

**A Theory of Justice (John Rawls)**
Rawls's 1971 masterwork of political philosophy and by far the most common giveaway for this concept. It revives social contract theory to argue for "justice as fairness," the title of a 1985 Rawls essay that elaborated the book's themes.

**"Veil of ignorance" and the "original position"**
Rawls's central thought experiment. People choosing the basic principles of society stand in the "original position," behind a veil that hides their own race, class, talents, and place in society, so the principles they pick will be impartial and fair.

**"Difference principle"**
Rawls's principle that social and economic inequalities are acceptable only if they benefit the least advantaged members of society. Rawls argued that rational parties in the original position would adopt a "maximin" strategy (maximizing the minimum outcome) and therefore choose this principle.

**"Liberty principle"**
Rawls's first principle of justice, sometimes called the "greatest equal liberty principle." It holds that each person should have the most extensive basic liberties compatible with equal liberties for everyone else, and it takes priority over the difference principle.

**Robert Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia**
Nozick's 1974 libertarian response to Rawls. It defends an "entitlement theory" of justice, built around just acquisition and transfer and including a "Lockean proviso," and rejects "end-result" and "patterned" principles of distribution.

**Wilt Chamberlain argument**
Nozick's thought experiment in Anarchy, State, and Utopia. If a million fans each freely pay 25 cents to watch the basketball star Wilt Chamberlain, he ends up very rich, and Nozick argues that keeping any "patterned" distribution in place would require constantly interfering with people's free choices.

**Distributive justice**
The kind of justice concerned with how society's benefits and burdens, such as wealth, rights, and opportunities, are divided among people. Aristotle analyzed it using geometric proportion, and it is the main subject of Rawls's theory.

**Thrasymachus and "the advantage of the stronger"**
In Book I of Plato's Republic, the sophist Thrasymachus claims that justice is simply whatever benefits the stronger party (the rulers). Socrates also refutes Cephalus's view that justice is telling the truth and paying one's debts, and Polemarchus's view that it is doing good to friends and harm to enemies.

**Plato's Republic, Book IV: "minding one's own business"**
After building an ideal city as an analogy for the soul, Socrates defines justice as each part doing its own work, "having and doing what is one's own." Earlier in the dialogue, Glaucon tells the story of the Ring of Gyges, a ring of invisibility, to suggest that people act justly only out of fear of being caught.

**Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, Book V**
Aristotle divides justice into "universal" justice, which he calls virtue as a whole, and particular justice. Particular justice is split into distributive justice (geometric proportion) and "rectificatory" or corrective justice, and Aristotle traces injustice to pleonexia, the greedy desire for more than one's share.

**Michael Sandel**
Harvard communitarian philosopher who critiqued Rawls in Liberalism and the Limits of Justice, stressing the role of community. His popular Harvard course became the 2009 book Justice: What's the Right Thing to Do?, which opens with price gouging after Hurricane Charley and includes the chapter "Arguing Affirmative Action."

**Michael Walzer's Spheres of Justice**
A 1983 book arguing that different social goods, such as education, healthcare, and money, belong to separate "spheres" with their own distributive rules. Walzer calls this "complex equality" and attacks Rawls's single list of primary goods.

**Lady Justice**
The traditional personification of justice, a blindfolded woman holding balancing scales and often a sword. The blindfold stands for impartiality and the scales for weighing evidence fairly.

**Hume's "artificial virtue"**
David Hume called justice an artificial virtue that arises from human conventions rather than natural instinct. He called it a "cautious, jealous virtue" that would be unnecessary in a utopia of abundance and does not apply within a family.

**Retributive and restorative justice**
Two frameworks of criminal justice. Retributive justice focuses on punishing offenders in proportion to their crimes, while restorative justice focuses on repairing harm to victims and the community.

**"Gadfly" of the state**
In Plato's Apology, Socrates compares himself to a gadfly sent by the god to sting the large, sluggish horse of Athens into wakefulness. It is the single most common clue for Socrates and his trial, explaining his habit of pestering citizens with questions.

**Trial for impiety and corrupting the youth**
In 399 BCE Socrates was charged with asebeia (impiety, including not believing in the city's gods and introducing new divinities) and with corrupting the young men of Athens. He was convicted by a jury of Athenian citizens and sentenced to death.

**Drinking hemlock and the Phaedo**
Socrates was executed by drinking a cup of poison hemlock. Plato's Phaedo depicts his last day, when he gives arguments for the immortality of the soul (including the affinity argument and recollection) before drinking the poison; as numbness spreads up from his feet, his last words are "Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius."

**The Apology**
Plato's account of the defense speech Socrates gave at his trial ("apologia" means defense, not an apology). Xenophon also wrote a work with the same title about the trial. It ends with Socrates arguing that death is either a dreamless sleep ("a state of nothingness") or a journey to another place, and that only God knows whether the living or the dead are better off.

**Chaerephon and the Oracle at Delphi**
Socrates's friend Chaerephon asked the Pythian oracle at Delphi whether anyone was wiser than Socrates, and was told no one was. Socrates tested this by questioning politicians, poets, and craftsmen, and concluded that he was wisest only because he knew that he knew nothing.

**Meletus, Anytus, and Lycon**
The three accusers at Socrates's trial. Meletus is the chief prosecutor whom Socrates cross-examines, asking him to name who "improves" the youth and claiming Meletus accuses him of atheism. Anytus was a prominent democratic politician, and Lycon represented the orators.

**Horses and flute-playing arguments**
In the Apology, Socrates refutes Meletus by asking whether anyone believes in horsemanship but not horses, or in flute-playing but not flute-players. He argues that one cannot believe in divine activities (like his daimonion) without believing in divine beings. He also argues that just as only a few trainers improve horses, few people, not everyone, improve the young.

**"The unexamined life is not worth living"**
Socrates's famous declaration at his trial in the Apology. He says he cannot stop practicing philosophy even to save his life, because questioning oneself and others is what gives life its value.

**Free meals in the Prytaneum**
When asked to propose his own penalty after conviction, Socrates ironically suggests he deserves free meals in the Prytaneum, the honor given to Olympic victors and public benefactors, because he serves the city more than any Olympian.

**Crito and the Laws of Athens**
In Plato's Crito, Socrates's wealthy friend Crito offers to help him escape from prison. Socrates refuses by imagining the personified Laws of Athens addressing him, arguing that he has an implicit agreement with the city to obey its laws, an early version of social contract theory. The dialogue opens with Socrates recounting a dream of a woman in white who tells him "on the third day you will go to fertile Phthia," a line adapted from the Iliad that predicts his death.

**Daimonion (divine sign)**
Socrates claimed that an inner divine voice or sign, his daimonion, warned him whenever he was about to do something wrong. It never told him what to do, only what not to do, and his opponents cited it as evidence that he introduced new gods.

**Meno and the slave boy (recollection)**
In Plato's Meno, Socrates questions an uneducated slave boy and leads him to discover that a square built on the diagonal of a given square has double its area. Socrates uses this to argue that learning is really anamnesis, or recollection of knowledge the soul already had.

**Socratic method, elenchus, and irony**
Socrates's method of cross-examination (elenchus) involves asking questions to expose contradictions in someone's beliefs. His habit of feigning ignorance in these debates is called Socratic irony (from the Greek eironeia). Many early dialogues are "aporetic," ending in puzzlement without a firm answer.

**Euthyphro dilemma**
In Plato's Euthyphro, Socrates questions a priest who is prosecuting his own father for murder. He asks whether something is pious because the gods love it, or whether the gods love it because it is pious, a question still central to debates about divine command ethics.

**Midwife and Diotima**
In the Theaetetus, Socrates compares himself to a midwife (his mother was one) who cannot produce ideas himself but helps others give birth to theirs. In the Symposium, he says he learned the philosophy of love from the priestess Diotima, who told him Love is the child of Poros (Resource) and Penia (Poverty).

**Pascal's Wager**
Pascal's argument that it is rational to bet on God's existence: "If you gain, you gain all; if you lose, you lose nothing." Weighing the infinite gain of heaven, and the risk of eternal damnation, against the finite loss of worldly pleasures, he concludes one should live as though God exists, for example by taking the sacraments even while still skeptical. It is the most common clue for him.

**Pensées**
French for "Thoughts," the collection of fragments Pascal wrote for an unfinished defense of Christianity, published after his death in 1662. It contains the Wager and most of his famous aphorisms about faith, reason, and the human condition.

**The Provincial Letters**
A series of eighteen letters (1656–1657) Pascal published anonymously under the pseudonym Louis de Montalte. Written to defend the theologian Antoine Arnauld against condemnation by the Sorbonne, they satirize the Jesuits' casuistry (case-based moral reasoning) and their doctrine of "probabilism," which let a person follow any "probable opinion" backed by an authority, even a less likely one.

**Jansenism and Port-Royal**
Pascal sided with the Jansenists, a strict Catholic movement stressing original sin and divine grace, centered on the abbey of Port-Royal near Paris. The Jesuits were the Jansenists' main opponents, and Pascal's sister Jacqueline became a nun at Port-Royal.

**The "Night of Fire" and the Memorial**
On the night of November 23, 1654, Pascal had an intense mystical experience, recorded on a parchment beginning with the word "FIRE." He sewed this "Memorial" into the lining of his coat and kept it there until his death; it ends with Psalm 119:16, "I will not forget thy word."

**"The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know"**
Pascal's most quoted line from the Pensées, expressing his view that faith and truth are grasped by the heart and intuition, not just by logic. Related is his remark that "All our reasoning reduces itself to yielding to feeling."

**"The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me"**
A famous line from the Pensées expressing the dread a person feels before the vast, silent universe revealed by the new science. It is typical of his religious writing after the Night of Fire.

**Man between nothingness and infinity**
In the Pensées, Pascal describes finite humans as a middle point between nothing and everything, too large compared with the infinitely small and too small compared with the infinitely large to fully grasp either extreme.

**Mathematical mind vs. intuitive mind**
In the Pensées, Pascal distinguishes the esprit de géométrie (the mathematical mind, which reasons from a few clear principles) from the esprit de finesse (the intuitive mind, which grasps many subtle principles at once).

**Pascal's triangle**
The triangular array of numbers in which each entry is the sum of the two above it, giving the binomial coefficients. Pascal wrote a treatise on it, and it is a common giveaway in philosophy tossups.

**Correspondence with Fermat on probability**
In 1654 Pascal exchanged letters with Pierre de Fermat about the "problem of points," how to divide stakes fairly in an unfinished game of chance. This correspondence laid the foundations of probability theory.

**Fluid pressure, the hydraulic press, and the syringe**
Pascal studied hydrostatics and atmospheric pressure. Pascal's law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions, the principle behind the hydraulic press, and the SI unit of pressure, the pascal, is named for him.

**The cycloid prize**
In 1658 Pascal, writing under the pseudonym Amos Dettonville, offered a prize for problems about the cycloid, the curve traced by a point on a rolling circle. He judged the entries he received inadequate and published his own solutions.

**Projective geometry and the Essay on Conics**
As a teenager Pascal wrote an essay on conic sections containing Pascal's theorem (the "mystic hexagram"): the three intersection points of the opposite sides of a hexagon inscribed in a conic lie on a straight line.

**"Writ on the Signing of the Formulary"**
One of Pascal's last writings, from the formulary controversy, when Jansenists were ordered under Louis XIV to sign a formulary condemning propositions attributed to Jansen. Pascal urged them not to give in by signing without reservation.

**Jean-Jacques Rousseau's The Social Contract (1762)**
Rousseau's treatise, full title The Social Contract, or Principles of Political Right (Du contrat social). It argues that the only legitimate political authority comes from an agreement in which each person joins a collective body. It is the most common giveaway for this answer.

**"Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains"**
The famous opening line of Rousseau's The Social Contract. It introduces his question of how political authority over naturally free people can be made legitimate.

**General will and the sovereign**
In Rousseau's theory, the whole body of citizens forms "the sovereign," which acts through the general will, meaning the common good of all rather than the sum of private interests. Laws that the people have not approved are null and void, and the sovereign cannot alienate (give away) the general will. Anyone who refuses to obey the general will may be "forced to be free."

**Veil of ignorance and the original position**
John Rawls's thought experiment in A Theory of Justice (1971). In the "original position," people choose the principles of justice from behind a "veil of ignorance" that hides their own race, class, talents, and other personal details, so they cannot choose rules that favor themselves. It is Rawls's modern version of the social contract.

**State of nature and the "war of all against all" (Leviathan)**
In Thomas Hobbes's Leviathan (1651), life in the state of nature, before government, is a "war of all against all" in which life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." People escape it by making a contract that gives power to an absolute sovereign.

**John Locke's Second Treatise of Government and the right of revolution**
Locke argued that people leave the state of nature by consent, explicit or tacit, to form a government that protects their natural rights to life, liberty, and property. If the government breaks this trust, the people may rebel and form a new government.

**Critique of Hugo Grotius and "force does not create right"**
Early chapters of Rousseau's Social Contract attack Grotius's defense of slavery. Rousseau defines "alienate" as "to give or sell" and argues that no one can give up all his liberty. He says that force does not create right, because slaves obey out of fear of harm, not out of moral obligation.

**Hot climates and population growth**
Book III of Rousseau's Social Contract says that hot climates suit despotism or monarchy. Because moral qualities cannot be measured, he says population growth is the "surest mark" of a good government. The same section discusses the Roman comitia (popular assemblies) and Caligula's claim to be a god.

**Death penalty as a "gift made conditionally"**
Rousseau defended capital punishment in The Social Contract. He argued that a citizen's life is no longer just a gift of nature but "a gift made conditionally by the State," so a criminal who breaks the contract can lose it.

**David Hume's critique ("Of the Original Contract")**
In his essay "Of the Original Contract," Hume argued that real governments were almost never founded on consent. Instead, they began through conquest or usurpation and draw their authority from habit and tradition.

**Plato's Crito**
An ancient forerunner of social contract thinking. In the Crito, Socrates refuses to escape from prison before his execution, because by living in Athens he had implicitly agreed to obey its laws.

**David Gauthier's Morals by Agreement (1986)**
A contractarian work in which Gauthier argues that morality arises from rational bargaining between self-interested agents. Agents do best by being "constrained maximizers," meaning they cooperate with others who are also willing to cooperate.

**Charles Mills's The Racial Contract (1997)**
Mills argues that the real social contract of modern Western political thought was a "racial contract" among white people. In his view, this contract excluded non-white people and upheld white supremacy.

**Kant and Perpetual Peace**
Immanuel Kant treated the original contract as an "idea of reason," a test of a law's legitimacy rather than a historical event. In Perpetual Peace he applied contract-style reasoning between states and proposed a federation of free states to end war.

**Critique of Judgment**
Immanuel Kant's 1790 "third critique," a foundational work of this field. It analyzes judgments of taste, which it says are disinterested yet claim universal and necessary agreement (a "subjective universality"), and it grounds the experience of beauty in the "free play" of the imagination and understanding.

**The sublime**
A key concept in this field. Kant described it as the feeling aroused by overwhelming things such as violent storms or vast mountains, which seem to exceed our powers yet ultimately make us aware of our reason. Edmund Burke's Philosophical Enquiry contrasted the sublime with the beautiful.

**"The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction"**
Walter Benjamin's 1935 essay. It argues that mass reproduction techniques like photography and film destroy an artwork's "aura," its unique presence and authenticity. It also describes how, with secularization, authenticity replaced the "cult value" of art used in ritual.

**Aestheticization of politics**
The argument in the epilogue of Benjamin's essay that fascism brings this field into political life by turning politics into spectacle, which leads to war. Benjamin says communism responds by politicizing art.

**The Birth of Tragedy**
Friedrich Nietzsche's 1872 work on Greek tragedy. It describes tragedy as a fusion of the Apollonian (order, form, dream) and the Dionysian (frenzy, intoxication), blames Socrates and Euripides for killing tragedy through excessive rationalism, and praises Richard Wagner. Its 1886 edition added the preface "An Attempt at Self-Criticism."

**Apollonian and Dionysian**
The two opposing artistic forces in The Birth of Tragedy, named after the Greek gods Apollo and Dionysus.

**Poetics**
Aristotle's treatise on tragedy and poetry, an early work of this field. It defines key terms such as mimesis (imitation), peripeteia (reversal of fortune), anagnorisis (recognition), and catharsis.

**Beauty**
The central subject of this field. The Pythagoreans defined it through perfect proportion, Platonists up through the Middle Ages identified it with the good, and Roger Scruton's BBC documentary Why Beauty Matters defended it.

**"Significant form"**
Clive Bell's "aesthetic hypothesis," set out in his 1914 book Art. It holds that all true works of visual art share "significant form," arrangements of lines and colors that produce a peculiar "aesthetic emotion" in the viewer.

**Institutional theory of art**
George Dickie's view that something is a work of art if members of the "artworld" (artists, critics, museums) confer that status on it. It builds on Arthur Danto's essay "The Artworld."

**Arthur Danto**
An American philosopher and art critic who coined the term "the artworld." He argued that art theory, rather than visible features, makes objects such as Andy Warhol's Brillo Boxes count as art.

**Kierkegaard's aesthetic stage**
Søren Kierkegaard used this term for the first of his three stages of existence (aesthetic, ethical, religious), a life devoted to pleasure and immediacy. Fear and Trembling discusses Abraham's near-sacrifice of Isaac against these aesthetic and ethical categories.

**Philistines**
Matthew Arnold's term, in Culture and Anarchy, for the middle class who despise or ignore beauty, art, and culture.

**Democritus**
The ancient Greek philosopher from Abdera most associated with atomism. Building on his teacher Leucippus, he held that the universe consists only of atoms and void, and that matter cannot be divided infinitely. He was known as the "laughing philosopher."

**Clinamen ("swerve")**
The tiny, random swerve that Epicurean atoms make as they fall through the void. Without it, atoms would fall in parallel and never collide, and the swerve also breaks the chain of strict determinism, which Epicureans used to explain free will.

**Lucretius's De Rerum Natura (On the Nature of Things)**
A six-book Latin poem in dactylic hexameter by the Roman Epicurean Lucretius. It explains that the world consists of atoms and void, discusses the swerve, and argues that the soul (anima and animus) is made of atoms and dies with the body, so death should not be feared.

**"Indivisible"**
The word "atom" comes from the Greek atomos, meaning "uncuttable" or "indivisible," reflecting the ancient idea that atoms are the smallest units that cannot be split further.

**The void**
The empty space in which atoms move, according to Leucippus and Democritus. The atomists insisted that void must exist for atoms to move and combine, against Parmenides, who denied that empty space ("what is not") could exist.

**Leucippus**
The Greek philosopher, Democritus's teacher, who is traditionally credited as the first to propose atomism. Tradition attributes to him a lost book called the Great World-System (Megas Diakosmos).

**Response to Parmenides**
Atomism was developed partly to answer Parmenides, who argued that change and motion are illusions because something cannot come from nothing. The atomists accepted that atoms themselves are unchanging and eternal, but explained change as the rearrangement of atoms in the void.

**Vaisheshika school and paramanu**
An ancient school of Indian philosophy, founded by Kanada, that proposed an atomic theory. Its atoms, called paramanu, came in four kinds, corresponding to the elements earth, water, fire, and air. Atoms combine in pairs called dvyanuka (dyads), and three dyads form a tryanuka (triad), the smallest visible particle.

**Stephen Greenblatt's The Swerve**
Greenblatt's 2011 book, subtitled "How the World Became Modern," which won the Pulitzer Prize. It tells how the Italian humanist Poggio Bracciolini rediscovered a manuscript of Lucretius's De Rerum Natura in 1417, and argues that its atomist ideas helped shape the modern world.

**"By convention sweet, by convention bitter"**
A fragment of Democritus stating that qualities like sweet, bitter, hot, cold, and color exist only "by convention," while "in reality" there are only atoms and void. It is an early version of the distinction between primary and secondary qualities.

**Hook-shaped atoms**
The atomists held that atoms differ in shape, size, and arrangement. Some were thought to have hooks, barbs, or eye-like sockets that let them catch onto each other and stick together to form solid bodies.

**Eidola**
In Democritus's theory of perception, eidola are thin films or images made of atoms that constantly flow off the surfaces of objects and enter the senses. A story, which Plutarch reports and doubts, says Democritus blinded himself so his mind would not be distracted by sight.

**John Dalton**
The English chemist who revived atomism as a scientific theory in the early 1800s. He proposed that each element consists of identical atoms with a characteristic weight and that compounds form when atoms combine in fixed ratios.

**Niels Bohr's model**
Bohr's 1913 model of the atom, in which electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels, much like planets orbiting the sun. Modern science shows that atoms are not actually indivisible but are composed of protons, neutrons, and electrons.

**Aruni**
Uddalaka Aruni, a sage of the Upanishads. The German Indologist Hermann Jacobi compared him to Thales of Miletus and credited him with an early theory of tiny invisible particles.

**Summa Theologica**
Aquinas's unfinished masterpiece, a huge systematic synthesis of Christian theology with Aristotelian philosophy, written as a guide for students of theology. He stopped writing it in 1273, shortly before his death. It is the standard giveaway for Aquinas.

**Five Ways (quinque viae)**
Aquinas's five arguments for the existence of God near the start of the Summa Theologica. They argue from motion (the "unmoved" or "first mover," the Prima Via), from efficient causation (the "first cause"), from contingency, from degrees of perfection, and from the governance and order of the world (the teleological argument).

**Summa Contra Gentiles**
An apologetic work aimed at non-Christians. It argues that truths reached by natural reason do not contradict the revealed truths of faith, and it separates truths that natural reason can reach from divine truths beyond it. It contrasts "the philosopher," who considers what belongs to creatures' proper natures, with "the believer," who considers creatures only as they relate to God.

**"The Philosopher" and "The Commentator"**
In his writings, Aquinas refers to Aristotle simply as "the Philosopher" and to the Muslim philosopher Averroes (Ibn Rushd), famous for his commentaries on Aristotle, as "the Commentator."

**Scholastic article format: "Sed contra" and "I answer that"**
Each article of the Summa Theologica poses a question, lists objections, and then gives a contrary authority introduced by "Sed contra" ("On the contrary"). Aquinas's own answer follows, introduced by "Respondeo dicendum" ("I answer that"), and he ends with replies to each objection.

**Just war theory**
In the Summa Theologica, Aquinas gives three conditions for a just war: the authority of the sovereign (proper authority), a just cause such as avenging a wrong, and right intention, meaning the aim of promoting good and securing peace.

**Principle of double effect**
Aquinas first formulated this principle in his discussion of killing in self-defense. An action with both a good and a bad effect can be permissible if the bad effect is not intended and is proportionate to the good. The Thomist philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre is among later moral thinkers who draw on this tradition.

**On the Unity of the Intellect Against the Averroists**
Aquinas's treatise attacking the Averroist doctrine, which held that all humans share a single intellect. He argued instead that each human has an individual intellect. He also wrote On the Eternity of the World, which argues that reason alone cannot prove that the world had a beginning in time.

**Student of Albertus Magnus; Dominican friar**
Aquinas joined the Dominican order and studied under Albertus Magnus, who reportedly defended his quiet pupil, nicknamed "the Dumb Ox." He is honored as the "Angelic Doctor" (Doctor Angelicus) and "Common Doctor" (Doctor Communis).

**Contra Errores Graecorum**
A treatise written at the request of Pope Urban IV. It examines alleged errors of the Greek (Orthodox) Church and argues that terms such as the Greek "hypostases" and the Latin "personae" must be translated carefully.

**On Being and Essence (De ente et essentia)**
An early metaphysical treatise. It explains how essence is found in composite substances, in separate substances (souls and intelligences), and in the First Cause, God, whose essence is identical with his existence.

**Beatific vision**
Aquinas held that the ultimate end of human existence and perfect happiness is the direct vision of God's essence, granted to the blessed after death.

**Aeviternity (aevum)**
A mode of duration between time and eternity that Aquinas assigned to beings such as angels. These beings are unchanging in their nature but are not eternal in the way God is, so they only partly transcend time.

**Convertibility of goodness and being**
Aquinas argued that "good" and "being" are the same in reality and differ only in concept. A thing is good insofar as it actually exists.

**Commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences**
Like other medieval theologians, Aquinas wrote a commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences, the standard theology textbook of the medieval universities, early in his career.

**Being and Nothingness**
Sartre's 1943 philosophical masterpiece, subtitled "An Essay on Phenomenological Ontology." It is the source of most of his key concepts, including bad faith, being-in-itself and being-for-itself, and "the look," and it is the most common giveaway for him.

**Bad faith and the waiter**
Bad faith (mauvaise foi) is Sartre's term for self-deception, in which a person denies their own freedom. His most famous example is a café waiter whose movements are too precise and "waiter-like," as if he were a machine playing a role instead of a free person choosing to be a waiter.

**The woman on a date and the gay man (facticity and transcendence)**
Two more examples of bad faith from Being and Nothingness. A woman lets a man hold her hand while acting as if her hand were just an object, to avoid deciding how to respond to his advances. A gay man refuses to admit his homosexuality. Each wrongly denies either their "facticity" (the facts of their situation and past) or their "transcendence" (their freedom to go beyond those facts).

**Being-in-itself vs. being-for-itself (en-soi and pour-soi)**
The basic contrast of Being and Nothingness. Being-in-itself is the solid, fixed being of things like rocks. Being-for-itself is human consciousness, which is free and never complete, and which Sartre says longs in vain to become a fixed in-itself.

**Existentialism Is a Humanism and "existence precedes essence"**
Sartre's 1945 lecture at the Club Maintenant in Paris, published in 1946 and later partly disowned by him. It states that "existence precedes essence": humans first exist and only afterward define themselves through their choices. It also says that "man is condemned to be free" and that "in fashioning myself, I fashion man," so anguish comes from knowing that one's choices legislate for all mankind.

**The student's dilemma**
An anecdote from Existentialism Is a Humanism. During World War II, a student asked Sartre whether he should leave his mother to join the Free French forces or stay to care for her. Sartre argues that neither Christian nor Kantian ethics can settle the question, so the student must simply choose.

**No Exit ("Hell is other people")**
Sartre's 1944 play in which three dead people, Garcin, Inès, and Estelle, are trapped together in a room in Hell. Their torture is each other's judging gaze, which leads to the famous line "Hell is other people."

**"The look" (the keyhole and the mannequin)**
In Being and Nothingness, Sartre describes how another person's gaze turns us into objects. In his example, a man peeping through a keyhole suddenly hears footsteps and feels shame at being seen. He also discusses the sense of being looked at by what turns out to be a mannequin. The idea anticipated Laura Mulvey's theory of the "gaze."

**Pierre in the café**
An example from Being and Nothingness of how nothingness enters the world. Sartre arrives late at a café expecting his friend Pierre, and Pierre's absence fills the whole café as a "nothingness" that results from negative judgment and expectation.

**Critique of Dialectical Reason**
Sartre's later, unfinished attempt to unite existentialism with Marxism, introduced by Search for a Method. It argues that free human activity, or "praxis," is limited by the "practico-inert," meaning the material results of past action. One example is Chinese peasants clearing forests, which later caused floods.

**Nausea and the refused Nobel Prize**
Nausea (1938) is Sartre's first novel, about Antoine Roquentin's disgust at the bare, meaningless existence of things. Sartre was awarded the 1964 Nobel Prize in Literature but refused it, saying a writer should not let himself be turned into an institution.

**Simone de Beauvoir**
Sartre's lifelong companion and lover and a fellow existentialist. She wrote The Second Sex and The Ethics of Ambiguity.

**Anti-Semite and Jew**
Sartre's 1946 essay analyzing antisemitism. It argues that being Jewish is defined largely by how others view and treat a person, and it describes the antisemite as someone acting in bad faith who plays with language rather than using it responsibly.

**The Family Idiot**
Sartre's huge, unfinished study of the novelist Gustave Flaubert, which applies existential psychoanalysis and Marxism to Flaubert's life.

**Political engagement (Fanon, Algeria, and Camus)**
Sartre wrote the preface to Frantz Fanon's anti-colonial The Wretched of the Earth, in which he defends anti-colonial violence. His opposition to the Algerian War led protesting French veterans to chant "Shoot Sartre!" His sympathy for Soviet communism caused a famous break with Albert Camus in the 1950s.

**"Best of all possible worlds" (Theodicy)**
In his Theodicy (1710), Leibniz answered the problem of evil by arguing that a perfectly good, wise, and powerful God must have created the best of all possible worlds. The evils in it are part of the best overall arrangement. This is the most common clue and a frequent giveaway.

**Invention of calculus and the dispute with Newton**
Leibniz developed differential and integral calculus independently of Isaac Newton and first published it in 1684. This led to a bitter priority dispute between their supporters. Leibniz's notation, including dy/dx for derivatives and the elongated-S integral sign, is the one still used today.

**Monads (Monadology)**
In the Monadology (1714), Leibniz argued that reality is ultimately made of monads: simple, indivisible, non-extended substances with perceptions and appetitions. Monads are "windowless," meaning that nothing can enter or leave them and they do not causally interact. The soul is a dominant monad that rules over a body.

**Pre-established harmony**
Leibniz's explanation of why monads, including mind and body, appear to interact even though they do not affect one another causally. God set them up at creation so that their states unfold in perfect coordination, like clocks synchronized in advance.

**New Essays on Human Understanding (Theophilus vs. Philalethes)**
Leibniz's chapter-by-chapter dialogue response to John Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding. Theophilus, who speaks for Leibniz, defends innate ideas against the empiricist Philalethes, who speaks for Locke, and rejects the "tabula rasa." He compares the mind to a block of veined marble whose veins already outline the shape of a statue.

**Dr. Pangloss in Voltaire's Candide**
Voltaire satirized Leibnizian optimism through the tutor Pangloss. Pangloss keeps insisting that everything is for the best "in this best of all possible worlds," even as he and Candide suffer one disaster after another.

**Principle of Sufficient Reason**
Leibniz's principle that nothing happens without a reason why it is so and not otherwise. Together with the principle of contradiction, it is one of the two great principles of his reasoning, and he used it to argue that God chose to create the best world.

**Mill argument**
In the Monadology, Leibniz imagined a thinking machine enlarged until one could walk inside it as if it were a mill. One would see only parts pushing one another and never find perception, so he concluded that perception cannot be explained mechanically.

**Identity of indiscernibles**
Leibniz's principle that no two distinct things can share all their properties, so objects with identical properties are the same object. It is often called "Leibniz's Law," along with its converse, the indiscernibility of identicals.

**Discourse on Metaphysics (1686)**
An early summary of Leibniz's metaphysics that he discussed in letters with the theologian Antoine Arnauld. It describes God as "an absolutely perfect being." In one thought experiment, he asks what good it would do you to become the King of China if you had to forget who you were, an illustration of the importance of memory to personal identity.

**Leibniz–Clarke correspondence**
An exchange of letters (1715-16) with Samuel Clarke, a defender of Newton. Leibniz argued for a relational theory of space and time, in which space is only the order of relations among things, against Newton's absolute space.

**Universal characteristic ("real characters")**
Leibniz dreamed of a characteristica universalis, a universal symbolic language whose "real" characters would represent ideas directly rather than words. Combined with a calculus of reasoning, it would let disputes be settled by calculation.

**Dynamics vs. Cartesian mechanics**
Leibniz criticized Descartes's physics, arguing that the quantity conserved in collisions is vis viva (mass times velocity squared), not quantity of motion. He called his science of force "dynamics."

**Pacidius Philalethi and visit to Spinoza (1676)**
In 1676, around the time he visited Baruch Spinoza at The Hague, Leibniz wrote the dialogue "Pacidius Philalethi." It analyzes the continuum and the problem of motion raised by Zeno's paradoxes.

**Aristotle's Organon**
The collection of Aristotle's six works on logic: Categories, On Interpretation, Prior Analytics, Posterior Analytics, Topics, and On Sophistical Refutations. It was the foundation of Western logic for about two thousand years. The Prior Analytics sets out the theory of the syllogism, and its rediscovery in the Middle Ages influenced Peter Abelard.

**Syllogism**
The central argument form of Aristotelian logic, which draws a conclusion from a major premise and a minor premise. A standard example takes the form "All A are B; C is an A; therefore C is B."

**Sea battle and future contingents**
In On Interpretation, Aristotle asks whether the statement "there will be a sea battle tomorrow" is already true or false today. This "problem of future contingents" led Diodorus Cronus to formulate his "master argument" and later inspired Jan Łukasiewicz's three-valued logic. On Interpretation is also the basis of the "square of opposition."

**Saul Kripke and modal logic**
Modal logic studies necessity and possibility. As a teenager, Saul Kripke developed a semantics for it in which a statement is necessary if it holds in all possible worlds and possible if it holds in some, with "accessibility relations" linking the worlds.

**Jan Łukasiewicz and many-valued logic**
The Polish logician Łukasiewicz created "deviant" finite-valued (polyvalent) systems with truth values beyond true and false, inspired by Aristotle's sea battle. Many-valued and fuzzy logics are also used to analyze vagueness.

**Law of the excluded middle and law of noncontradiction**
Two basic laws of classical logic. The excluded middle says every statement is either true or false (which follows from bivalence), and noncontradiction says no statement can be both true and false at once.

**First-order (predicate) logic and quantifiers**
A system in which predicates apply to variables and evaluate to true or false. It uses the existential quantifier, written as a backwards E (∃, "there exists"), and the universal quantifier, written as an upside-down A (∀, "for all").

**Propositional (zeroth-order) logic and George Boole**
The simplest form of logic, dealing with whole propositions joined by connectives like NOT, AND, OR, and "if p then q." George Boole developed an algebra of such true-or-false values, and truth tables are used to evaluate the statements.

**De Morgan's laws**
Rules relating the logical operators. They state that "not (A and B)" is equivalent to "(not A) or (not B)," and that "not (A or B)" is equivalent to "(not A) and (not B)."

**Porphyry's Isagoge and the Porphyrian tree**
Porphyry's introduction to Aristotle's Categories, which was the standard logic textbook for centuries. It is associated with the "Porphyrian tree," which classifies species by genus and differentia.

**Graham Priest and paraconsistent logic**
Priest wrote An Introduction to Non-Classical Logic and is known for dialetheism, the view that some contradictions are true. He discussed the "Logic of Paradox" (LP), a system tied to the Argentine philosopher Florencio Asenjo.

**C. S. Peirce and the Peirce arrow**
The American pragmatist approached logic through the "logic of relations." The "Peirce arrow" is the NOR operator, which is true only when both of its inputs are false.

**Chrysippus and Stoic logic**
The Stoic Chrysippus developed a logic based on whole propositions rather than Aristotle's "terms," making Stoic logic an early forerunner of propositional logic. Rules like modus ponens ("if p then q; p; therefore q") and modus tollens ("if p then q; not q; therefore not p") are central to it.

**William of Ockham's Summa Logicae**
The medieval nominalist William of Ockham laid out his philosophy in this "Summa of Logic." Ockham is also known for "Ockham's razor," the principle of not multiplying entities beyond necessity.

**Arthur Prior and temporal logic**
The New Zealand logician Arthur Prior founded temporal (tense) logic, which adds operators for statements about the past and future. Other major works titled for logic include Hegel's Science of Logic, which analyzes the doctrines of being, essence, and concept, and John Stuart Mill's A System of Logic, which sets out his five methods of induction, including the method of residues and the method of concomitant variations.

**"It is better to be feared than loved"**
The most famous claim in Niccolò Machiavelli's The Prince, from Chapter 17 on cruelty and mercy. Machiavelli says a ruler would ideally be both feared and loved, but if he must choose, fear is safer. He also warns that the ruler must avoid being hated.

**The fox and the lion**
Chapter 18 advises that a ruler must know how to act like a beast as well as a man. He should imitate the fox to recognize traps and the lion to frighten wolves, using both cunning and force. This openly rejects Cicero's De Officiis, which condemned both fraud and force.

**Cesare Borgia**
The ruthless son of Pope Alexander VI, held up in The Prince as a model of a new prince who rose to power through fortune and others' arms. Machiavelli says Borgia's downfall came when he allowed the election of his enemy, Pope Julius II.

**Lorenzo de' Medici, the dedicatee**
The Prince is dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici, Duke of Urbino. According to a famous story, Lorenzo cared more about a pair of hunting dogs he received at the same time than about the book.

**Fortune as a woman and a flooding river**
Chapter 25, the penultimate chapter, compares fortune (Fortuna) to a violent river that can be controlled with dikes and embankments if prepared for in advance. It also says fortune is a woman who must be beaten and subdued by the bold.

**Mercenaries and auxiliary troops are "useless and dangerous"**
Chapters 12–13 attack the use of hired mercenaries and borrowed auxiliary soldiers, which Machiavelli says are disloyal and motivated only by money. He urges princes to rely on their own armed citizens.

**Septimius Severus**
The Roman emperor praised in Chapter 19 as a ruler who knew well how to be both "the fox and the lion." He is used as an example of how a ruler can avoid contempt and hatred.

**Remirro de Orco**
Cesare Borgia's harsh lieutenant in the Romagna, who restored order with great cruelty. Borgia then had him cut in two and displayed in the piazza of Cesena, which satisfied and stunned the people and redirected their hatred away from Borgia.

**Virtù**
Machiavelli's key concept of a ruler's skill, energy, and capacity for decisive action, which is not the same as moral virtue. Virtù is set against fortune throughout the book.

**Agathocles of Syracuse and "criminal virtue"**
Chapter 8 discusses rulers who gain power through wickedness, such as Agathocles, who massacred the senators and rich citizens of Syracuse to seize control. Machiavelli says such methods can win power but not glory.

**Armed prophets: Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, and Theseus**
Chapter 6 praises these founders as men who rose through their own virtù and arms. Machiavelli concludes that armed prophets conquer while unarmed prophets fail, and he also frequently draws on Xenophon's biography of Cyrus the Great.

**Generosity vs. stinginess**
Chapter 16 argues that a reputation for generosity forces a prince to exhaust his resources and raise taxes, which makes him hated. It is better to be thought a miser.

**Flatterers and advisers**
Chapter 23 warns princes to avoid flatterers by choosing wise advisers and letting them speak the truth only when asked. Emperor Maximilian I is given as an example of an indecisive ruler who never took or refused advice clearly.

**Mirrors for princes and Gramsci's "Modern Prince"**
The Prince is the best-known example of the "mirrors for princes" genre of advice books for rulers, which also includes Erasmus's Education of a Christian Prince. Antonio Gramsci equated the prince with the revolutionary party in "The Modern Prince," and Max Weber and Roger Boesche compared the book to the Indian Arthashastra.

**Mary Dietz's "Trapping the Prince"**
A 1986 essay arguing that Machiavelli deliberately gave Lorenzo bad, paradoxical advice to bring about the Medici's downfall and restore the Florentine republic. It is related to the "republican" reading of the book held by Rousseau and Garrett Mattingly, which treats it as satire. The book was written in exile in 1513, which Machiavelli described in a letter to Francesco Vettori that tells how he put on courtly robes each evening to converse with the ancients.

**Sayings of Confucius ("The Master said")**
The Analects (Lunyu) is a collection of the sayings and conversations of Confucius, put together by his disciples and their followers after his death. Many passages begin "The Master said," and this is the most common giveaway for the text.

**Ruler compared to the North (Pole) Star**
An early passage (2.1) says that one who governs by virtue is like the North Star, which "dwells in its place" while all the other stars turn toward it and pay it reverence. It expresses the Confucian idea that a ruler leads by moral example, not by force.

**Ren (humaneness)**
The central Confucian virtue, translated as "humaneness," "benevolence," "goodness," or "compassion." The Analects says that filial piety and respect for elder brothers are the root of ren.

**Li (ritual propriety)**
The rituals, ceremonies, and rules of proper conduct that Confucius saw as essential to an orderly society. The Analects says that disorder follows when ritual decays and music collapses.

**Junzi (the gentleman) versus the "small man"**
The junzi, or "gentleman" or "exemplary person," is the morally cultivated ideal person of the Analects. He is often contrasted with the xiaoren, or "small man," who is concerned only with profit and self-interest.

**Filial piety (xiao)**
Devotion and respect toward one's parents and ancestors. It is a key Confucian virtue in the Analects, together with fraternal submission (respect for elder brothers).

**Five relationships**
The Confucian hierarchy of social bonds: ruler and subject, father and son, elder and younger brother, husband and wife, and friend and friend. Each one involves reciprocal duties, and the ruler-subject bond is modelled on the father-son bond. The list was later made standard in Confucian tradition.

**Rectification of names (zhengming)**
The idea in the Analects (13.3) that social disorder arises when things are not called by their proper names. Rulers, ministers, fathers, and sons must live up to what their titles mean.

**The "Silver Rule"**
Confucius's negative form of the Golden Rule: "Do not impose on others what you do not wish for yourself." It is linked to shu, or reciprocity.

**Loyalty and reciprocity (zhong and shu)**
In Analects 4.15, the disciple Zengzi explains that the "one thread" running through the Master's Way is just loyalty and reciprocity. The scholar Bryan Van Norden has questioned whether this passage is authentic.

**Twenty books, with titles like "In the Village"**
The Analects is traditionally divided into 20 books, each named after words in its opening line. Examples are "Eight Rows of Dancers" (Book 3, which opens by criticizing the Ji family for using a ritual dance reserved for the king), "In the Village" (Book 10), and "Men of Former Times" (Book 11).

**"When three walk together, there must be one who can be my teacher"**
A well-known saying from Book 7: in any group of people there is someone to learn from. You can copy their good qualities and correct in yourself the faults you see in them.

**Five excellent practices and four bad practices**
In the final book, Confucius lists five virtues a ruler should practise and four evils to avoid, including cruelty, oppression, and stinginess.

**Textual history: Lu and Qi versions, Zhang Yu, and the Brooks**
In the Han dynasty, Zhang Yu combined the Lu and Qi versions of the text into the basis of the standard version. Song-dynasty scholar Zhu Xi made it one of the Four Books of Confucianism. In modern times, E. Bruce and A. Taeko Brooks argued that the text was built up in layers over a long period.

**Family Sayings of Confucius (Kongzi Jiayu)**
A related collection of Confucius's sayings that was long dismissed as a forgery. More recent scholarship has reconsidered it as a possibly authentic early source that supplements the Analects.

**"Two Dogmas of Empiricism"**
W. V. O. Quine's 1951 essay, one of the most influential works of twentieth-century analytic philosophy and the most common clue for empiricism. It attacks two central assumptions of logical positivism and argues instead that our beliefs face the test of experience as a whole, as a connected "web."

**The analytic-synthetic distinction and reductionism**
The two "dogmas" Quine attacked. The first is the idea that there is a sharp line between analytic statements, true by meaning alone, and synthetic statements, true because of facts about the world. The second is the idea that each meaningful statement can be translated into statements about immediate experience.

**John Locke's An Essay Concerning Human Understanding**
Locke's 1689 work, a founding text of British empiricism. It argues against innate ideas and holds that all our ideas come from experience, either through sensation of the outside world or reflection on the workings of our own minds.

**Tabula rasa**
Latin for "blank slate," the image associated with Locke's view that the mind at birth contains no innate ideas and is "written on" by experience. Locke himself mostly used the metaphor of "white paper."

**British empiricists: Locke, Berkeley, and Hume**
The three classic British empiricists of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. John Locke founded the tradition, George Berkeley pushed it toward idealism by denying the existence of material substance, and David Hume took it toward skepticism about causation, induction, and the self.

**Rationalism**
The position traditionally contrasted with empiricism, which holds that significant knowledge can be gained through reason alone, independent of sense experience. Its classic proponents were the continental thinkers René Descartes, Baruch Spinoza, and Gottfried Leibniz.

**Wilfrid Sellars's "Empiricism and the Philosophy of Mind"**
Sellars's 1956 essay, which attacks what he called "the Myth of the Given," the idea that some knowledge, such as raw sense experience, is given directly and independently of any other beliefs and can serve as the foundation for all other knowledge.

**"The Myth of the Given"**
Sellars's name for the foundationalist assumption that certain basic experiences can justify beliefs without depending on any other knowledge. Sellars argued that knowing anything requires already having a network of concepts and beliefs, so nothing is simply "given."

**Constructive empiricism**
The view proposed by Bas van Fraassen in his 1980 book The Scientific Image. It holds that science aims only at theories that are "empirically adequate," meaning they correctly describe what is observable, and that accepting a theory does not require believing its claims about unobservable entities.

**Scientific realism**
The view, opposed by van Fraassen's constructive empiricism, that scientific theories should be understood literally and that well-confirmed theories are approximately true, including their claims about unobservable things like electrons.

**Common Sense**
Paine's 1776 pamphlet arguing for American independence from Britain, the best-selling publication of the Revolution. It is the most common giveaway for him and is usually paired with The Age of Reason at the end of a question.

**The absurdity of an island ruling a continent**
A key argument in Common Sense: it is unnatural for a small island like Britain to govern a whole continent across the ocean. Paine uses it to argue that America should break free.

**The Age of Reason**
Paine's work of religious criticism (1794–1807), subtitled "Being an Investigation of True and Fabulous Theology." It defends deism, attacks the Bible as divine revelation, and rejects organized churches; much of it was written in France under threat of arrest and while he was imprisoned.

**Deism**
The belief in a single creator God known through reason and nature rather than through revelation, miracles, or scripture. The Age of Reason revived interest in it; Paine stated his creed as "I believe in one God, and no more; and I hope for happiness beyond this life."

**The "Satan problem" and "Christian mythologists"**
In The Age of Reason, Paine mocks how "Christian mythologists" had to free Satan from the pit after his fall so that the Christian story could work. He sarcastically notes that Christianity in effect promises the devil "ALL the Jews, ALL the Turks" and everyone else who does not accept Christ.

**The American Crisis**
A series of pamphlets Paine wrote during the Revolutionary War to keep up morale. The first opens "These are the times that try men's souls," attacks "the summer soldier and the sunshine patriot," and notes that "Tyranny, like hell, is not easily conquered"; Washington had it read to his troops.

**Rights of Man**
Paine's 1791–1792 reply to Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, defending the French Revolution and natural rights. He rejects Burke's view that wisdom and authority pass down through inherited institutions and nobility, arguing that no generation can bind those that come after it.

**"Society in every state is a blessing, but government... is but a necessary evil"**
The opening argument of Common Sense, distinguishing society, which arises from human needs, from government, which exists only because of human wickedness. Paine also criticizes the English "mixed" constitution of king, lords, and commons as unable to restrain the king.

**Agrarian Justice**
Paine's 1797 pamphlet arguing that because the earth was originally common property, landowners owe society a "ground-rent." He proposed a national fund to give every person a lump sum at age 21 and a yearly pension after age 50, an early forerunner of guaranteed-income and social security proposals.

**Imprisonment in revolutionary France**
Paine was elected to the French National Convention but opposed the execution of Louis XVI and was imprisoned in the Luxembourg Prison during the Reign of Terror (1793–1794). He narrowly escaped execution, and he worked on The Age of Reason during this period.

**"Filthy little atheist"**
Theodore Roosevelt's notorious insult for Paine, reflecting how The Age of Reason's attacks on Christianity damaged his reputation in America. The label is inaccurate, since Paine was a deist who believed in God.

**Appendix to Common Sense and the Quakers**
Later editions of Common Sense in 1776 added an appendix and an "Epistle to Quakers" criticizing the Quakers' leaders for opposing the Revolution. Paine's father was a Quaker.

**Justified true belief**
The classical definition of knowledge, usually traced to Plato's dialogue Theaetetus: knowledge is a belief that is justified and also has this property. "True" is one of the three conditions in that definition.

**Gettier problems**
Counterexamples from Edmund Gettier's 1963 paper "Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?" In the most famous one, a job applicant named Smith justifiably believes that the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket. The belief turns out true only by luck, so justified true belief does not seem to be enough for knowledge.

**Semantic theory of truth ("Snow is white")**
Alfred Tarski's theory, laid out in "The Concept of Truth in Formalized Languages." It is captured by the T-schema: "'Snow is white' is true if and only if snow is white." Tarski required a definition to be materially adequate and formally correct, treated sentences as the bearers of this property, and held that it can be defined for an object language only in a separate metalanguage.

**Truth tables**
Diagrams, popularized by Ludwig Wittgenstein in the Tractatus, that list every combination of true and false values for a statement's components. A statement with N components needs 2 to the N rows, and the tables show how logical operators such as "not," "and," and "or" determine whether a compound statement is true.

**Correspondence theory**
The view that a statement is true when it corresponds to reality, meaning to facts or states of affairs in the world. It is the most traditional theory of truth.

**Coherence theory**
The rival view that a statement is true if it is consistent with a larger system of beliefs or propositions. Coherentists reject the correspondence theory.

**Deflationary theory**
The view that saying a proposition p "is true" adds nothing to simply asserting p, so the word "true" is redundant. The redundancy theory is one version of it.

**Pragmatist theory (William James)**
Pragmatists tie truth to usefulness and practice. William James called it "the expedient in our way of thinking," and Charles Sanders Peirce saw truth as the opinion inquiry is fated to reach in the end, its ultimate goal or "end of inquiry."

**"Will to truth"**
A phrase from the opening section of Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil, which questions why philosophers value truth at all. Nietzsche suggests that this "will to truth" is itself an expression of the will to power.

**Language, Truth and Logic**
A. J. Ayer's 1936 book, the key British statement of logical positivism (logical empiricism). It holds that meaningful statements must be either analytic or empirically verifiable, and "truth" is the second of the three nouns in its title.

**Donald Davidson**
An American philosopher who built a theory of meaning on Tarski's work, holding that knowing a sentence's meaning amounts to knowing the conditions under which it would be true (its truth conditions). The "slingshot argument," which he used, claims that all true sentences refer to the same thing.

**Richard Rorty**
