Mehmet Oz had lived for decades in Cliffside Park, New Jersey, and moved to Pennsylvania shortly before his campaign. Fetterman repeatedly mocked him as a carpetbagger, for example by flying a banner and enlisting New Jersey celebrities to "welcome" him.

**Pat Toomey**
A Republican U.S. senator from Pennsylvania from 2011 to 2023. His decision not to seek reelection in 2022 opened the seat that Fetterman won over Oz.

**Josh Shapiro and the I-95 collapse**
Pennsylvania's Democratic governor since 2023, governing from the capital, Harrisburg. In June 2023 a tanker truck fire caused part of Interstate 95 in Philadelphia to collapse. His administration reopened the highway in just 12 days, and his approval ratings rose afterward.

**Tom Wolf**
Pennsylvania's Democratic governor from 2015 to 2023, with John Fetterman as his lieutenant governor in his second term. Josh Shapiro succeeded him.

**Conor Lamb and Tim Murphy**
Republican congressman Tim Murphy resigned in October 2017 after it came out that he, an anti-abortion politician, had urged his mistress to have an abortion. Democrat Conor Lamb won his seat in a March 2018 special election and later lost the 2022 Democratic Senate primary to Fetterman, as did state representative Malcolm Kenyatta.

**Four Seasons Total Landscaping**
A landscaping company in northeast Philadelphia where Rudy Giuliani held a widely mocked press conference in November 2020 while challenging Joe Biden's victory in Pennsylvania.

**Kathy Barnette**
A conservative commentator who surged late in the 2022 Republican Senate primary but finished third behind Oz and McCormick. Some of her supporters blamed Fox News host Sean Hannity, who backed Oz, for her loss.

**Jeffrey Yass and Students First**
Jeffrey Yass, co-founder of the trading firm Susquehanna International Group, is Pennsylvania's richest man and a major Republican and school-choice donor. He has funded the Students First PAC, which backs school-choice candidates in the state.

**Dean Browning**
A white Republican politician from the Lehigh Valley who, in November 2020, tweeted a criticism of Barack Obama while claiming to be a "black gay guy." The tweet was apparently meant to be posted from another account, and it went viral.

**Philadelphia and Jim Kenney**
Philadelphia is Pennsylvania's largest city. Democrat Jim Kenney was its mayor from 2016 to 2024.

**Succeeded Liz Truss as prime minister**
Sunak became the Conservative British prime minister in October 2022, after Liz Truss resigned following only about 49 days in office. He was the first British prime minister of Indian descent and the first Hindu to hold the office, and he served until July 2024.

**First prime minister appointed by King Charles III**
Sunak was the first prime minister invited to form a government by King Charles III, who became king in September 2022. Truss had been appointed by Queen Elizabeth II two days before the queen's death.

**Chancellor of the Exchequer resignation**
Sunak served as Chancellor of the Exchequer (Britain's finance minister) under Boris Johnson from 2020 to 2022. He resigned in July 2022, the same evening as Health Secretary Sajid Javid, after the Chris Pincher scandal: Johnson had promoted Pincher despite knowing of misconduct allegations against him. A wave of resignations followed that forced Johnson out.

**2022 leadership contest and "fairytale economics"**
In the summer 2022 Conservative leadership election to replace Johnson, Sunak finished second to Liz Truss in the vote of party members. During the campaign he attacked her plans for unfunded tax cuts as "fairytale" economics that could cause an "inflationary spiral." After her mini-budget crashed the markets, his warnings seemed justified.

**Partygate fine**
In April 2022, police fined Sunak, along with Boris Johnson, for breaking COVID lockdown rules by attending a gathering held for Johnson's birthday in June 2020 at 10 Downing Street. Johnson is a former mayor of London.

**Infosys and Akshata Murty**
Sunak's wife, Akshata Murty, is the daughter of N. R. Narayana Murthy, a co-founder of the Indian IT giant Infosys. Her shares in the company make the family very wealthy, and her non-domiciled tax status caused controversy in 2022.

**Winter Economy Plan**
A package of measures Sunak announced as chancellor in September 2020 to support jobs and businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic. It replaced the furlough scheme with a new job-support scheme. Sunak was also known for the furlough program and the "Eat Out to Help Out" restaurant discount scheme.

**Forests and Climate Leaders' Partnership (FCLP)**
An international initiative that Sunak helped launch at the COP27 climate summit in Egypt in November 2022 to halt and reverse forest loss by 2030. At the launch he said that "for too long the world's forests have been undervalued and underestimated."

**"100% of women don't have penises"**
Comments Sunak made in a 2023 interview defending his view of biological sex in the debate over transgender rights. He added that people should show "tolerance for those who are thinking about changing their gender."

**2024 general election defeat**
Sunak called an early general election for July 2024, announcing it in the rain outside Downing Street. The Conservatives lost in a landslide to Keir Starmer's Labour Party, and Sunak stepped down as party leader. Kemi Badenoch succeeded him.

**Rwanda plan and "Stop the boats"**
Sunak's signature immigration policy aimed to deter migrants crossing the English Channel in small boats by deporting asylum seekers to Rwanda. "Stop the boats" was one of his five main pledges, but legal challenges kept the deportation flights from taking off.

**Windsor Framework**
A 2023 agreement Sunak negotiated with the European Union that revised the post-Brexit Northern Ireland Protocol and eased trade checks between Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

**Jair Bolsonaro**
The far-right former army captain who won Brazil's 2018 presidential election and served from 2019 to 2022. He became known for inflammatory remarks, including past homophobic comments and the slogan that "a police officer who does not kill is not a police officer," and for downplaying COVID-19, promoting chloroquine, catching the virus himself, and joking that a vaccine could turn people into alligators.

**Operation Car Wash (Lava Jato)**
A huge bribery and money-laundering investigation that began in 2014 and centered on the state oil company Petrobras, which awarded inflated contracts in exchange for kickbacks to politicians. It also led to enormous penalties for the construction firm Odebrecht and the meatpacking company JBS, and it implicated many leading politicians.

**Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva**
The Workers' Party leader who served as president from 2003 to 2010. He was convicted in a Car Wash case and barred from the 2018 election, so the party nominated Fernando Haddad instead; after his convictions were annulled, Lula defeated Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.

**Dilma Rousseff's impeachment**
Rousseff, Lula's Workers' Party successor, was impeached and removed from office in 2016 amid the Car Wash scandal, formally for manipulating the federal budget. Earlier, as energy minister, she led the Light for All rural electrification program, and her governments ran the housing program My House, My Life.

**Michel Temer**
Rousseff's vice president, who became president after her impeachment and was later also implicated in Car Wash. Before the impeachment, he wrote her a complaining letter that began with the Latin phrase "Verba volant, scripta manent" ("spoken words fly away, written words remain"), and a samba school mocked him as a vampire during the 2018 Carnival.

**Sergio Moro**
The federal judge who oversaw the Operation Car Wash trials and convicted Lula. He later became Bolsonaro's justice minister.

**Glenn Greenwald and The Intercept**
An American journalist living in Brazil whose outlet, The Intercept, published leaked private messages showing Moro and Car Wash prosecutors coordinating with each other. In January 2020, Brazilian prosecutors charged Greenwald in connection with the hacking of officials' phones, though the charges were later dropped.

**2019 Amazon rainforest fires**
A surge in fires in the Brazilian Amazon in 2019, mostly set to clear land, drew global criticism of Bolsonaro's environmental policies. Bolsonaro suggested without evidence that environmental organizations had started the fires.

**Brazil vs. Germany 7–1 (Mineirazo)**
In the 2014 World Cup semifinal in Belo Horizonte, host Brazil lost 7–1 to Germany, a humiliation nicknamed the "Agony of Mineirão" after the stadium. During that match, Miroslav Klose became the World Cup's all-time top scorer, and after Germany won the final, the team was criticized for letting the singer Rihanna kiss the trophy.

**2002 World Cup final**
Brazil beat Germany 2–0 in the 2002 final in Yokohama, Japan, with Ronaldo scoring both goals in the second half. They were the first goals that German goalkeeper Oliver Kahn had allowed since the tournament's opening round.

**Teori Zavascki**
A Supreme Federal Court justice in charge of Car Wash cases involving politicians. He died in a plane crash off the coast of Rio de Janeiro state in January 2017.

**Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (UCKG)**
A large Brazilian Pentecostal church that supported Bolsonaro. Its bishop Marcelo Crivella became mayor of Rio de Janeiro and cut city funding for the "samba schools" that compete in Carnival by half.

**PCC and Red Command prison riots**
In January 2017, a wave of deadly riots spread through Brazilian prisons, beginning in the city of Manaus. They came from a war between the country's two biggest criminal gangs, the São Paulo-based First Capital Command (PCC) and the Rio-based Red Command (CV).

**Carlos Ghosn**
A businessman born in Brazil who led the automakers Renault and Nissan. He was arrested in Japan in 2018 on financial misconduct charges and removed as Nissan's chairman, but in 2019 he escaped to Lebanon while out on bail.

**Belo Monte Dam and Itaipu**
The Belo Monte Dam on the Xingu River in the state of Pará is a controversial hydroelectric project that displaced thousands of people. Brazil's largest dam is Itaipu, which it shares with Paraguay on the Paraná River.

**Travis Kalanick**
Co-founder of Uber with Garrett Camp in 2009 and its aggressive, controversial CEO until 2017. He resigned in June 2017 after a string of scandals, especially the sexual harassment investigation, and Dara Khosrowshahi replaced him as CEO.

**Lyft**
Uber's main American ride-hailing competitor. Almost every question mentions it as a hint, and Uber employees were accused of ordering and then canceling rides from rivals such as Lyft and Gett to disrupt their service and recruit their drivers.

**Greyball**
A secret software tool, revealed by The New York Times in 2017. Uber used it to identify likely regulators and law enforcement officers and show them a fake version of the app, so they could not hail rides during sting operations in cities where Uber was banned or restricted.

**Susan Fowler and the Eric Holder investigation**
In a 2017 blog post, former Uber engineer Susan Fowler described sexual harassment and how the company's HR department ignored her complaints. Uber hired former U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder to investigate, with board member Arianna Huffington involved. The fallout pushed out executives, including Amit Singhal, who resigned after failing to disclose a harassment allegation from his time at Google, and eventually Kalanick himself.

**"God View"**
An internal tool that let Uber employees see the real-time locations of riders. After reports of misuse in 2014, Senator Al Franken wrote to the company raising privacy concerns.

**#DeleteUber**
A 2017 boycott campaign; writer Dan O'Sullivan's tweet helped start the hashtag. During a taxi strike at JFK Airport protesting Donald Trump's travel ban, Uber turned off surge pricing, which critics saw as strikebreaking. In the backlash, Kalanick quit Trump's business advisory council.

**Waymo lawsuit**
Waymo, Google's self-driving car company, sued Uber in 2017, accusing it of using trade secrets that engineer Anthony Levandowski took when he left Waymo and founded Otto, a self-driving truck startup Uber then bought. The case settled in 2018, with Uber giving Waymo equity.

**London license denial**
In 2017, Transport for London refused to renew Uber's license to operate in the city over safety and conduct concerns, a decision backed by Mayor Sadiq Khan. Uber kept running while it appealed and later regained its license.

**UberPop protests in France**
UberPop was a cheap service using unlicensed, non-professional drivers. In June 2015, French taxi drivers protested violently against it, and the musician Courtney Love said her car was attacked in Paris. Uber suspended UberPop in France soon afterward, and German courts had banned the service as well.

**Kalamazoo shooting**
In February 2016, Uber driver Jason Dalton killed six people in a shooting spree in the Kalamazoo, Michigan area, reportedly picking up passengers between the attacks. The case raised questions about Uber's driver screening.

**Emil Michael's plan to target journalists**
In 2014, Uber senior vice president Emil Michael suggested the company spend money hiring researchers to dig up dirt on journalists who criticized it, particularly the tech journalist Sarah Lacy. The remarks caused a public uproar.

**Bill de Blasio dispute**
In summer 2015, New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio proposed capping the number of for-hire vehicles, a plan aimed at Uber. Uber fought back with a large public campaign, including a "de Blasio" option in its app, and the mayor dropped the plan. Critics also attacked Uber for classifying its drivers as independent contractors rather than employees.

**Christopher Knittel's discrimination study**
A 2016 study co-authored by MIT economist Christopher Knittel found that ride-hailing customers with Black-sounding names faced longer waits and more frequent cancellations. Uber was the largest company in the study.

**David Plouffe**
Barack Obama's 2008 campaign manager, whom Uber hired in 2014 to lead its policy and political strategy as it battled regulators.

**"Puppies on demand"**
A promotional campaign in which Uber partnered with animal shelters to deliver puppies to customers for short playtime visits, with the option to adopt them.

**2018 Mexican presidential election**
López Obrador won the presidency of Mexico in 2018 in a landslide, taking about 53 percent of the vote on his third attempt. He served a single six-year term from December 2018 to September 2024, as Mexico's constitution forbids reelection.

**AMLO**
López Obrador's four-letter nickname, formed from the initials of Andrés Manuel López Obrador. It is used almost universally in Mexican and international media and often appears in questions as a giveaway.

**2006 election and the sit-in**
Running as the candidate of the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), López Obrador lost the 2006 presidential election to Felipe Calderón of the National Action Party by roughly half a percentage point. Alleging fraud, he led supporters in a weeks-long sit-in that blocked Mexico City's Zócalo and the Paseo de la Reforma, and he declared himself Mexico's "legitimate president."

**Mayor of Mexico City**
From 2000 to 2005 López Obrador served as Head of Government of the Federal District, the post equivalent to mayor of Mexico City. His popular social programs there, such as pensions for the elderly, made him a national figure and the front-runner for the 2006 election.

**The desafuero and the hospital access road**
In 2004–2005 the Mexican Congress voted to strip López Obrador of his immunity from prosecution, a process called the desafuero, over his alleged defiance of a court order to halt construction of an access road to a hospital on expropriated land. The move was widely seen as an attempt to keep him off the 2006 ballot; it backfired, and the charges were dropped after mass protests.

**Carlos Slim**
The Mexican telecommunications billionaire with whom López Obrador formed a public–private partnership as mayor to restore Mexico City's historic center. The project helped renovate the colonial downtown area around the Zócalo.

**1996 Pemex protest and the bloody shirt**
In 1996 López Obrador led protests in his home state of Tabasco in which demonstrators blockaded oil wells of Pemex, Mexico's state oil company, demanding compensation for pollution damage. He gained national prominence when he was photographed with blood on his shirt after clashing with police.

**Tepetitán, Tabasco**
López Obrador was born in 1953 in the village of Tepetitán in the municipality of Macuspana, in the southeastern state of Tabasco. His early political career, including a run for governor of Tabasco, was centered in that state.

**Death of his brother José Ramón**
As a teenager in 1969, López Obrador was present when his younger brother José Ramón was killed by a gunshot in their family's store in Tabasco. The incident has been the subject of conflicting accounts and occasional attacks by his political opponents.

**Rocío Beltrán Medina**
López Obrador's first wife, who died of lupus in 2003 while he was mayor of Mexico City. He later married the writer and academic Beatriz Gutiérrez Müller.

**Morena**
The National Regeneration Movement, the left-wing political party López Obrador founded after splitting from the PRD; it was registered as a party in 2014. Morena carried him to the presidency in 2018 and became Mexico's dominant party.

**Fourth Transformation**
López Obrador's name for his political project, presenting it as the fourth great transformation of Mexican history after independence, the 19th-century Reform, and the Mexican Revolution. He promised to end corruption and govern with austerity, refusing to live in the Los Pinos presidential residence and putting the presidential plane up for sale.

**Las mañaneras**
The daily early-morning press conferences López Obrador held throughout his presidency, often lasting hours. He used them to set the news agenda and attack critics in the press.

**"Hugs, not bullets"**
López Obrador's slogan ("abrazos, no balazos") for his security policy, which aimed to address the root causes of cartel violence instead of pursuing direct military confrontation. He also created the National Guard, a new militarized police force.

**Claudia Sheinbaum**
López Obrador's protégé and successor, a former mayor of Mexico City, who won the 2024 presidential election as Morena's candidate. She became Mexico's first woman president.

**Xi Jinping**
The leader of the People's Republic of China, who succeeded Hu Jintao as Communist Party General Secretary in 2012 and as President in 2013. He is a "princeling" (the son of revolutionary leader Xi Zhongxun), and as a young official he visited Muscatine, Iowa, in 1985 with an agricultural delegation; nearly every question ends with "led by Xi Jinping."

**Zero-COVID policy**
China's strict pandemic strategy, officially called "dynamic clearing," relied on mass lockdowns, quarantine camps, and frequent PCR testing (often every 72 hours) to stamp out every outbreak. China abruptly relaxed it in December 2022, and as cases surged while official counts denied a rise, the U.S. and EU countries began requiring negative COVID tests from travelers arriving from China.

**A4 Revolution (white paper protests)**
Nationwide protests in November 2022 against zero-COVID, set off by a deadly apartment fire in Urumqi, Xinjiang, that killed at least ten people and was blamed on lockdown measures. Protesters held up blank sheets of A4 paper to symbolize censorship. A month earlier, a lone protester hung banners on Beijing's Sitong Bridge denouncing Xi as a dictator and traitor and broadcast "we want to eat, we want freedom, we want to vote."

**Uyghurs and Xinjiang**
China has detained an estimated one million or more Uyghur Muslims and other minorities in "re-education camps" in the northwestern Xinjiang region, drawing accusations of crimes against humanity and genocide. In December 2020 the U.S. banned cotton imports from the XPCC (Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps), a paramilitary conglomerate linked to forced labor.

**Belt and Road Initiative**
Xi's global infrastructure program, under which China has spent hundreds of billions of dollars on ports, railways, and roads abroad. China has also been accused of secretly building a naval base for its own use at Cambodia's Ream Naval Base.

**Alibaba, Singles' Day, and Ant Group**
Alibaba is the Chinese e-commerce giant founded by Jack Ma, whose 2014 New York listing was the largest IPO in U.S. stock market history. It turned "Singles' Day" (November 11) into the world's biggest online shopping event, and its financial affiliate Ant Group had its record IPO suspended at the last minute in November 2020 as regulators cracked down on Ma's businesses.

**Tencent and WeChat**
Tencent is the Chinese tech giant that developed WeChat, the dominant messaging and payment app in China, and owns the web portal QQ. WeChat Pay and Alibaba's Alipay let users send each other digital "red envelopes" of money, a modern version of a Lunar New Year tradition.

**Huawei and Meng Wanzhou**
Huawei is China's largest telecom equipment maker, and its subsidiary HiSilicon designs its chips. Its CFO Meng Wanzhou, daughter of founder Ren Zhengfei, was arrested in Canada in 2018 at the request of the U.S. over charges related to violating sanctions on Iran, and she spent nearly three years under house arrest in Vancouver.

**ByteDance and TikTok**
ByteDance is the Beijing-based developer of TikTok. In 2020 the Trump administration tried to force the sale of TikTok's U.S. operations, with Oracle and Walmart nearly acquiring them, and India banned TikTok and over 200 other Chinese apps after a deadly border clash with China.

**Evergrande and the property crisis**
Evergrande was once China's largest real estate developer, but it collapsed under more than $300 billion in debt beginning in 2021, symbolizing a wider property crisis. In 2021, the city of Kunming demolished fifteen unfinished apartment towers of the stalled Sunshine City II project.

**Disputes with Japan**
China and Japan dispute the Senkaku Islands (called the Diaoyu Islands in China), with frequent incursions by Chinese coast guard ships. Other flashpoints include Japanese officials' visits to the Yasukuni Shrine, which honors war criminals, the portrayal of the Rape of Nanking in Japanese textbooks, and China's 2023 ban on Japanese seafood after Japan began releasing treated water from the Fukushima nuclear plant.

**Bo Xilai and Neil Heywood**
Bo Xilai was the powerful Communist Party chief of Chongqing and a rising princeling. His downfall began in 2012 when his wife, Gu Kailai, was convicted of murdering the British businessman Neil Heywood, and in 2013 Bo was sentenced to life in prison for bribery, embezzlement, and abuse of power.

**Chen Guangcheng**
A blind, self-taught legal activist who exposed forced abortions under China's one-child policy. In April 2012 he escaped house arrest and took refuge in the U.S. embassy in Beijing, causing a diplomatic crisis before he was allowed to leave for the United States.

**Princelings and the "Fifth Generation"**
"Princelings" are the children of senior Communist Party revolutionaries, and Xi's Fifth Generation of leadership (following Mao's First Generation, then Deng, Jiang Zemin, and Hu Jintao) was dominated by them. In 2013 the U.S. SEC began investigating J.P. Morgan's "Sons and Daughters" program for hiring princelings to win business in China.

**Deng Xiaoping's "cat theory" and Special Economic Zones**
Deng Xiaoping, China's leader after Mao, justified market reforms with the saying "it doesn't matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice." His reforms created Special Economic Zones and other development zones such as Hainan and Shanghai's Pudong, leading to the rapid growth that made China the world's second-largest economy after it passed Japan in 2010.

**Gretchen Whitmer**
The Democratic governor of Michigan since 2019, who governs from Lansing. She succeeded Rick Snyder after the 2018 election and became nationally known for her COVID-19 restrictions and her clashes with President Trump, who called her "that woman from Michigan."

**Wolverine Watchmen kidnapping plot**
A plot by members of a militia group to kidnap Governor Whitmer, uncovered by the FBI in October 2020. Whitmer said Trump's rhetoric had helped inspire it.

**Rick Snyder and the right-to-work law**
Snyder was the Republican governor of Michigan from 2011 to 2019 and appointed emergency financial managers for struggling cities, including Detroit. In December 2012, after earlier saying the issue was too divisive, he signed laws making Michigan the 24th "right-to-work" state, following Indiana's lead, so that workers could not be required to pay union fees. The bills were passed by a Republican-controlled legislature and signed in the George W. Romney Building in Lansing.

**Jennifer Granholm**
A former Democratic governor of Michigan, from 2003 to 2011. In December 2020 Joe Biden announced her as his nominee for Secretary of Energy.

**Detroit bankruptcy**
In July 2013 Detroit filed for Chapter 9 bankruptcy, the largest municipal bankruptcy in U.S. history.

**Kevyn Orr**
The bankruptcy lawyer whom Governor Snyder appointed in 2013 as Detroit's unelected emergency manager, with broad power over the city's finances.

**Kwame Kilpatrick**
A former mayor of Detroit who resigned in 2008 after a scandal over text messages showing an affair with his chief of staff, Christine Beatty, and his lies about it under oath. He faced felony charges and was later convicted on federal corruption charges.

**Dave Bing**
A former NBA star with the Detroit Pistons who became mayor of Detroit after Kwame Kilpatrick.

**Rashida Tlaib**
A Democrat elected to the U.S. House from Detroit in 2018. She became the first Palestinian-American woman in Congress.

**Abdul El-Sayed**
A public health official who finished second to Whitmer in the 2018 Democratic primary for governor. Self-funding Indian-American businessman Shri Thanedar finished third.

**Brian Calley**
Snyder's lieutenant governor, who lost the 2018 Republican primary for governor to Bill Schuette. Snyder notably declined to endorse Schuette.

**Debbie Stabenow**
A longtime Democratic senator from Michigan who won re-election in November 2018.

**Lee Chatfield and Mike Shirkey**
The Republican leaders of the Michigan House and Senate who challenged Whitmer's emergency powers during the pandemic. In October 2020 the Michigan Supreme Court ruled that she lacked the authority to keep extending her emergency orders.

**Detropia**
A 2012 documentary by Heidi Ewing and Rachel Grady about Detroit's economic decline, with a title combining "Detroit" and "utopia."

**Big Three automakers**
General Motors, Ford, and Chrysler, all headquartered in the Detroit area and known as the "Big Three." They were helped by federal programs like the 2009 "Cash for Clunkers" car rebate program.

**Kim Jong-un**
The current supreme leader of North Korea, who took power in 2011 after the death of his father, Kim Jong-il. He is the third generation of the Kim dynasty, which was founded by his grandfather Kim Il-sung.

**Juche**
North Korea's official state ideology, usually translated as "self-reliance." Developed under Kim Il-sung, it stresses political, economic, and military independence and is used to justify the country's isolation and the rule of the Kim family.

**"Hermit Kingdom"**
A nickname for North Korea, one of the most isolated countries in the world. The name was originally used for the Joseon dynasty of Korea, which tried to shut itself off from foreign influence in the 1800s.

**Assassination of Kim Jong-nam**
Kim Jong-un's estranged half-brother was killed with the VX nerve agent at Kuala Lumpur International Airport in Malaysia in February 2017. North Korean agents convinced two young women, Siti Aisyah of Indonesia and Doan Thi Huong of Vietnam, that they were taking part in a TV prank show when they smeared the poison on his face.

**Sony Pictures hack and The Interview**
In 2014, hackers linked to North Korea broke into Sony Pictures, leaking emails and unreleased films, in retaliation for the comedy The Interview, starring Seth Rogen and James Franco. The film depicts a plot to assassinate Kim Jong-un.

**Lazarus Group**
A state-backed North Korean hacking group blamed for the Sony hack, the 2017 WannaCry ransomware attack, and large thefts of cryptocurrency used to fund the regime.

**Bangladesh Bank heist and the "Shalika Foundation"**
In 2016, hackers tied to the Lazarus Group used the SWIFT banking network to try to steal nearly 1 billion dollars from Bangladesh's central bank account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. About 81 million dollars was stolen, but one transfer to a "Shalika Foundation" in Sri Lanka was stopped after a bank noticed that "Foundation" was misspelled.

**USS Pueblo**
A US Navy intelligence ship seized by North Korea in January 1968. Its crew of 82 was held for 11 months before being released, and the ship is still displayed in Pyongyang as a museum.

**Blue House raid**
In January 1968, commandos from North Korea's Unit 124 infiltrated Seoul in an attempt to assassinate South Korean President Park Chung-hee at the Blue House, the presidential residence. The raid failed, and two days later North Korea seized the USS Pueblo.

**"Balloon war"**
In 2024, North Korea sent hundreds of balloons carrying trash and manure across the border into South Korea, in response to South Korean activists who had sent balloons carrying anti-regime leaflets north.

**Nuclear weapons program**
North Korea carried out its first nuclear test in 2006 and has conducted six in total. It has also tested intercontinental ballistic missiles despite UN sanctions, which led to summits between Kim Jong-un and Donald Trump in 2018 and 2019 that failed to produce a disarmament deal.

**Diego Maradona lying in state**
Argentina's most famous footballer, who led the national team to the 1986 World Cup title, died in November 2020. His coffin lay in state at the Casa Rosada, the presidential palace in Buenos Aires, where huge crowds of mourners gathered and clashed with police.

**Legalization of abortion (2020)**
In December 2020, Argentina's Congress legalized elective abortion up to the 14th week of pregnancy, after a similar bill had failed in the Senate in 2018. It made Argentina the largest country in Latin America to legalize abortion at the time.

**Green handkerchiefs**
The green scarves (pañuelos verdes) worn by Argentine activists campaigning for legal, safe, and free abortion. The symbol, inspired by the white headscarves of the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo, spread across Latin America as the "green wave" of abortion-rights movements.

**Alberto Fernández**
The Peronist president of Argentina from 2019 to 2023, who championed the abortion legalization bill. Soon after taking office he traveled to the Vatican to meet Pope Francis, seeking support in Argentina's debt negotiations.

**Pope Francis**
Born Jorge Mario Bergoglio in Buenos Aires, he was Archbishop of Buenos Aires before becoming the first Latin American pope in 2013. He is Argentina's most famous native son in religious affairs and died in 2025.

**2020 wealth tax on the richest citizens**
In late 2020, Argentina passed a one-time "solidarity contribution" levied on roughly 12,000 people with fortunes above 200 million pesos to fund the country's COVID-19 response. Rates on domestic assets ranged up to about 3.5 percent.

**2001 debt default**
At the height of a severe economic crisis in late 2001, Argentina defaulted on about 100 billion dollars of sovereign debt, then the largest default in history. The crisis brought bank withdrawal limits (the corralito), riots, and a rapid succession of presidents.

**Paul Singer and NML Capital**
Singer's hedge fund, Elliott Management, through its subsidiary NML Capital, bought defaulted Argentine bonds cheaply and refused restructuring deals, suing for full repayment. These "holdout" or "vulture fund" creditors won a large settlement in 2016 under President Mauricio Macri.

**ARA Libertad**
An Argentine navy training frigate that was detained at the port of Tema in Ghana in 2012 at the request of NML Capital, which sought to seize it as payment for defaulted debt. It was released after an international tribunal on the law of the sea ordered Ghana to let it go.

**Buenos Aires**
The capital and largest city of Argentina, located on the Río de la Plata. It is home to the Casa Rosada and the Plaza de Mayo, the main site of Argentine political protest.

**Cristina Fernández de Kirchner**
Argentina's president from 2007 to 2015 and later vice president under Alberto Fernández. She survived an assassination attempt in 2022 when a gun aimed at her failed to fire, and that same year was convicted of fraud related to public works contracts.

**Javier Milei**
The libertarian economist elected president of Argentina in 2023, who campaigned while brandishing a chainsaw to symbolize slashing government spending. He pursued drastic austerity to fight the country's very high inflation.

**Lionel Messi and the 2022 World Cup**
Argentina's star forward, who captained the national team to victory over France in the 2022 World Cup final in Qatar. It was Argentina's third World Cup title and its first since Maradona's 1986 triumph.

**Chancellor of Germany**
Scholz, of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), served as Chancellor of Germany from December 2021 to May 2025. He succeeded Angela Merkel, under whom he had served as Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister.

**"Traffic light" coalition**
The governing coalition Scholz formed after the 2021 election, named for the parties' colors: the red SPD, the yellow Free Democratic Party (FDP), and the Greens. It collapsed in November 2024 when Scholz fired FDP Finance Minister Christian Lindner over budget disputes, leading to an early election that Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats won in 2025.

**Zeitenwende speech**
A speech Scholz gave to the Bundestag on February 27, 2022, days after Russia invaded Ukraine. Declaring a "Zeitenwende," or "turning point in history," he announced a 100 billion euro special fund for the German military and a commitment to raise defense spending, reversing decades of German caution about military power.

**Nord Stream 2**
The pipeline built to carry Russian natural gas under the Baltic Sea to Germany. Scholz halted its certification in February 2022 after Russia recognized two breakaway regions in eastern Ukraine, and it never went into operation.

**Global minimum corporate tax**
As German Finance Minister, Scholz was a leading supporter of a global minimum corporate tax rate of 15 percent, which G7 finance ministers backed in 2021 alongside the Biden administration. The plan was then adopted as part of a broader international agreement negotiated through the OECD.

**"Overcoming capitalism"**
As a young leader of the SPD's youth wing in the 1980s, Scholz wrote an article calling for capitalism to be overcome. Later, as a moderate politician, he distanced himself from it by saying he had "made almost all possible mistakes at some point."

**Mayor of Hamburg**
Before becoming Finance Minister, Scholz served as First Mayor of Hamburg from 2011 to 2018. During his tenure the city hosted the 2017 G20 summit, which was marred by violent riots.

**Cum-Ex scandal**
A huge German tax fraud scheme in which banks and investors claimed refunds for taxes that had never been paid. Scholz faced questions over meetings he held as Mayor of Hamburg with executives of the Warburg bank, which was involved in the scheme, and said he could not remember the details.

**"Scholzomat"**
A nickname given to Scholz for his dry, robot-like way of speaking and his habit of repeating the same phrases without revealing much.

**Taurus missiles and aid to Ukraine**
Germany under Scholz became one of Ukraine's largest military backers, but he was often criticized for hesitating, first over sending Leopard 2 tanks, which he approved in January 2023, and then by refusing to supply long-range Taurus cruise missiles out of fear of escalation with Russia.

**Yevgeny Prigozhin**
The Russian businessman who financed and led the Wagner Group, a private military company that served the Kremlin's interests abroad while giving it some deniability. He made his fortune through catering contracts with the Russian government, which earned him the nickname "Putin's chef." He is the most common giveaway for Wagner.

**June 2023 mutiny**
On June 23–24, 2023, Prigozhin led an armed rebellion against Russia's military leadership. Wagner forces seized the southern city of Rostov-on-Don and advanced to within about 200 km (125 miles) of Moscow before Prigozhin called off the march. In a deal brokered by Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, charges were dropped and Wagner fighters were offered relocation to Belarus.

**August 2023 plane crash**
Two months after the mutiny, on August 23, 2023, the private jet carrying Prigozhin exploded and crashed in Russia's Tver region, killing everyone on board. Wagner co-founder Dmitry Utkin was also on the plane. The crash was widely seen as revenge ordered by the Kremlin.

**Dmitry Utkin**
A former Russian military intelligence officer who co-founded and commanded Wagner in the field. The group's name is usually traced to his call sign, "Wagner," after the composer Richard Wagner. He died in the same plane crash as Prigozhin.

**New Island restaurant**
A floating restaurant on a boat in St. Petersburg that Prigozhin ran. It hosted Vladimir Putin and visiting dignitaries, including George W. Bush during a 2006 visit, and it helped Prigozhin win Putin's favor.

**Prigozhin's criminal past**
In 1981, as a young man in Leningrad, Prigozhin was convicted of crimes including a robbery in which he choked a woman and took her earrings. He spent about nine years in prison before going into business selling hot dogs and later running restaurants.

**Battle of Bakhmut**
Wagner fighters led Russia's long, bloody assault on the eastern Ukrainian city of Bakhmut, which Russia claimed to have captured in May 2023. Wagner recruited large numbers of Russian prison inmates for the battle by promising them pardons. Prigozhin publicly blamed Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu and Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov for heavy losses and ammunition shortages.

**Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 and the Donbas war**
Wagner first appeared in 2014, fighting alongside Russian-backed separatists in Crimea and eastern Ukraine. MH17 was shot down over separatist-held Donbas in July 2014 by a Russian Buk missile, killing all 298 people on board, and some reports have alleged that Wagner was involved.

**Operations in Africa**
Wagner deployed mercenaries to support governments and factions in countries including the Central African Republic, Mali, Libya, Sudan and Mozambique, often in exchange for access to gold, diamonds and other resources. Human rights groups accused its fighters of abuses against civilians. After Prigozhin's death, much of this network was brought under Russian Defense Ministry control as the "Africa Corps."

**Syria**
Wagner fighters helped defend Bashar al-Assad's government during the Syrian civil war. In February 2018, near Deir ez-Zor, U.S. forces killed many Wagner-linked fighters who attacked a position held by U.S.-backed forces.

**Internet Research Agency**
A St. Petersburg "troll farm" funded by Prigozhin that ran social media disinformation campaigns, including efforts to interfere in the 2016 U.S. presidential election. Prigozhin was indicted in the U.S. over it.

**Wagner emblem**
The group's emblem and insignia have featured military symbols such as crossed swords and a star on a red background. A skull in crosshairs was also widely used.

**Abenomics and its "three arrows"**
Abe's namesake economic program, launched after he returned to power in 2012, built on three "arrows": aggressive monetary easing (large-scale quantitative easing aimed at hitting a two percent inflation target), flexible fiscal stimulus, and structural reform. The "three arrows" and the two percent inflation target are the most common clues for him.

**Tetsuya Yamagami**
The man who shot and killed Abe on July 8, 2022, using a homemade gun. Yamagami blamed the Unification Church for bankrupting his family through his mother's huge donations, and he targeted Abe because of Abe's ties to the church.

**Unification Church**
The religious movement founded by Sun Myung Moon, known for its mass weddings called "Blessing ceremonies." Abe gave a video speech to a church-affiliated event in September 2021, and after his death the many ties between Liberal Democratic Party members and the church became a major scandal.

**Nara campaign speech**
Abe was shot while giving a street campaign speech in Nara City for Kei Sato, a Liberal Democratic Party candidate in the 2022 House of Councillors election. He was serving as a former prime minister at the time.

**Article 9**
The clause of Japan's postwar pacifist constitution, written during the American occupation, that renounces war and the maintenance of armed forces. Abe spent much of his career pushing to revise it, partly citing threats from North Korea, but he left office without achieving the change.

**Liberal Democratic Party (LDP)**
The conservative party that has dominated Japanese politics since 1955. Abe led it and became Japan's longest-serving prime minister, with terms in 2006–2007 and 2012–2020.

**State funeral**
About three months after the assassination, Abe received a state funeral in September 2022, the first for a former prime minister since Shigeru Yoshida's in 1967. It was heavily protested and hurt the approval ratings of Prime Minister and LDP leader Fumio Kishida.

**Ulcerative colitis resignations**
Abe resigned as prime minister twice because of this chronic bowel disease: first in 2007, when he was replaced by Yasuo Fukuda, and again in September 2020, when Yoshihide Suga succeeded him.

**Moritomo Gakuen and Kake Gakuen scandals**
Two favoritism scandals of Abe's second term. His wife, Akie Abe, was named honorary principal of a nationalist elementary school run by Moritomo Gakuen, which bought government land at a vastly reduced price. Abe also faced accusations that he helped a friend's group, Kake Gakuen, win approval for a new veterinary school.

**Party of Hope and the 2017 snap election**
Tokyo governor Yuriko Koike formed the Party of Hope just before Abe called a 2017 snap election, which he justified by redirecting consumption tax revenue toward education. The new party ran on a "12 zeros" platform and, like Koike's Tomin First party, opposed his consumption tax increase.

**Shukyo nisei**
Japanese for "second-generation believers," the children raised inside religious groups such as the Unification Church. Yamagami's story of abuse and neglect as one of them drew wide public sympathy after the shooting.

**Hak Ja Han**
The widow of Sun Myung Moon and leader of the Unification Church. Yamagami said he had originally wanted to attack her, but he targeted Abe instead as a prominent supporter of the church.

**Pearl Harbor visit**
In December 2016 Abe and Barack Obama visited Pearl Harbor together. In his speech there Abe vowed "we must never repeat the horrors of war again" and quoted Ambrose Bierce's line "the brave respect the brave."

**Partnership for Quality Infrastructure**
An Abe-era program to fund high-quality infrastructure in Asia and beyond, launched as Japan's answer to China's Belt and Road Initiative.

**First meeting with President-elect Trump**
In November 2016 Abe became the first foreign leader to meet Donald Trump after his election victory. He went on to build one of the closest personal relationships with Trump of any world leader.

**SNC-Lavalin affair**
A 2019 scandal in which Trudeau and his staff were accused of improperly pressuring the attorney general to let the Quebec-based engineering and construction company SNC-Lavalin avoid criminal prosecution for bribery in Libya through a deferred prosecution agreement. Ethics Commissioner Mario Dion concluded that Trudeau had "directly and through his senior officials used various means to exert influence," and Trudeau's close adviser Gerald Butts resigned during the scandal.

**Jody Wilson-Raybould**
The attorney general and justice minister at the center of the SNC-Lavalin affair. She refused to intervene in the prosecution, was moved to the post of Veterans Affairs minister, resigned from cabinet, and was expelled from the Liberal caucus in 2019 along with her ally Jane Philpott, a former cabinet minister.

**Blackface and brownface photos**
During the 2019 campaign, photos emerged of Trudeau in blackface and brownface, including one of him dressed as Aladdin in brownface at a 2001 "Arabian Nights" party at the school where he taught. Trudeau apologized and admitted he had been too enthusiastic about costumes.

**WE Charity scandal**
In 2020, Trudeau's government awarded the youth organization WE Charity a contract to run a student volunteer grant program. It came out that WE had paid Trudeau's mother and brother to speak at its events, and the charity withdrew from the contract amid an ethics investigation.

**2021 snap election and Erin O'Toole**
Trudeau called an early election for September 2021, hoping to win back a majority, but his Liberals ended up with almost the same number of seats and remained in a minority government. Erin O'Toole's Conservative Party actually won more of the popular vote.

**2019 election and Andrew Scheer**
In the October 2019 election, Trudeau's Liberals lost their parliamentary majority after the SNC-Lavalin and blackface scandals but stayed in power with a minority government. Andrew Scheer's Conservatives gained seats, winning 121.

**Aga Khan vacation**
In 2017, Canada's ethics commissioner found that Trudeau had broken the Conflict of Interest Act by vacationing on the private Bahamas island of the Aga Khan, the spiritual leader of Ismaili Muslims, whose foundation lobbied the Canadian government.

**Freedom Convoy and the Emergencies Act**
In early 2022, truckers protesting COVID-19 vaccine mandates occupied Ottawa and blockaded border crossings. Trudeau invoked the Emergencies Act for the first time in Canadian history to end the protests.

**"Two Michaels" and Meng Wanzhou**
After Canada arrested Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou in 2018 on a U.S. extradition request, China detained two Canadians, Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor. All three were released in September 2021 after Meng reached a deal with U.S. prosecutors.

**Hardeep Singh Nijjar**
A Sikh separatist leader and Canadian citizen who was shot dead in British Columbia in 2023. Trudeau told Parliament there were credible allegations linking agents of the Indian government to the killing, setting off a major diplomatic dispute with India.

**Jagmeet Singh**
The leader of the left-leaning New Democratic Party (NDP). He criticized Trudeau over the blackface photos and the expulsion of Jody Wilson-Raybould, and he unsuccessfully challenged Trudeau in the 2019 and 2021 elections.

**Residential school graves**
In 2021, possible unmarked graves of Indigenous children were found at former residential schools, the church-run boarding schools Indigenous children were forced to attend. Trudeau ordered flags on federal buildings lowered to half-mast in response.

**Pierre Trudeau and the 2025 resignation**
Justin Trudeau is the son of Pierre Trudeau, who served as prime minister for most of the period from 1968 to 1984. Justin became Liberal prime minister in 2015 and announced in January 2025 that he would resign.

**Boxing match against Patrick Brazeau**
In 2012, before becoming prime minister, Trudeau beat Conservative senator Patrick Brazeau in a charity boxing match that raised money for cancer research.

**Jaspal Atwal**
A Sikh extremist who had been convicted of attempting to murder an Indian cabinet minister. He was invited to a dinner reception during Trudeau's 2018 trip to India, causing an embarrassing controversy, and the invitation was withdrawn.

**September 2024 federal indictment over Turkish bribes**
In September 2024 Adams became the first sitting New York City mayor to be indicted on federal charges. Prosecutors accused him of bribery, wire fraud, and soliciting illegal foreign campaign contributions, saying he accepted luxury travel and other benefits from Turkish officials and businesspeople. The case was later dismissed in 2025 after the Justice Department moved to drop it.

**The Turkish House (Turkevi Center) and the Fire Department**
A central allegation in the indictment. Adams allegedly pressured the New York City Fire Department (FDNY) to let the new Turkish consulate tower in Manhattan open in 2021, even though it had not passed fire-safety inspections, so that it would be ready for a visit by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

**Straw donor probe and Turkish Airlines upgrades**
The federal investigation began around 2023 and looked into whether foreign money, especially from Turkey, was routed to Adams's campaign through "straw donors" (people who give in their own names using someone else's money). Investigators also examined free or discounted upgrades on Turkish Airlines that Adams received.

**Kathy Hochul**
The Governor of New York. After Adams was indicted she refused to use her power to remove him from office. She had also criticized him for how slowly his administration responded to the arrival of large numbers of migrants in New York City.

**Brianna Suggs**
Adams's chief campaign fundraiser. In November 2023 the FBI raided her Brooklyn home, and agents soon afterward seized two of Adams's phones (and an iPad) as part of the investigation into his campaign financing.

**KSK Construction**
A Brooklyn construction company with ties to Turkey that was linked to the straw donor investigation. Investigators looked into whether donations to Adams's campaign connected to the company were illegal contributions tied to the Turkish government.

**Mohamed Bahi**
Adams's liaison to the city's Muslim community. He was arrested in October 2024 and charged with crimes connected to the investigation of straw donations to Adams's campaign, including tampering with witnesses and destroying evidence.

**Sheena Wright**
Adams's First Deputy Mayor, the second-highest official in his administration. She resigned in October 2024 amid the wave of federal investigations and resignations that hit his inner circle.

**Kathleen Corradi, the "rat czar"**
In 2023 Adams appointed Kathleen Corradi, a former schoolteacher, as the city's first Director of Rodent Mitigation, nicknamed the "rat czar." Her job was to fight New York's well-known rat problem.

**"Trash revolution"**
Adams's phrase for his plan to make New Yorkers put garbage in sealed, rolling containers (wheelie bins) instead of piling plastic trash bags on the sidewalk. Keeping bags off the street was meant to cut off a major food source for rats.

**"Popular knapsack with many different locations"**
A line from a 2011 public service announcement Adams made as a New York State Senator. In it he warned parents that children can hide drugs, weapons, and other contraband in their bedrooms and backpacks, and he showed hidden compartments to make his point.

**Jeanie Dubnau and the "plantation" remark**
At a 2023 community meeting, Adams told 84-year-old Holocaust survivor Jeanie Dubnau, who had interrupted him, not to treat him like "someone that's on the plantation that you own." He was criticized for the remark but refused to apologize.

**2021 mayoral election: Curtis Sliwa, Maya Wiley, and Andrew Yang**
Adams won the 2021 Democratic primary, the city's first ranked-choice mayoral primary, over rivals including Maya Wiley, Andrew Yang, and Kathryn Garcia. In the general election he defeated Republican Curtis Sliwa, the founder of the Guardian Angels crime-patrol group.

**2021 residency controversy**
During the 2021 campaign, critics claimed that Adams, who was then Brooklyn Borough President, actually lived in Fort Lee, New Jersey. To answer the rumors he invited reporters to tour the apartment in his Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn building that he said was his home.

**Former transit police officer**
Before entering politics Adams worked for the New York City Transit Police and then the NYPD, retiring as a captain. He made public safety a major theme of his campaign and co-founded the group 100 Blacks in Law Enforcement Who Care.

**Ron DeSantis**
The Republican governor of Florida since 2019, governing from the capital Tallahassee. He became a national conservative figure by banning school mask mandates during COVID-19, rejecting the College Board's AP African American Studies pilot course, and fighting "woke" policies; critics also mocked him for allegedly wearing height-boosting boots.

**Champlain Towers South collapse**
The partial collapse of a beachfront condominium in Surfside, in Miami-Dade County, in June 2021, which killed 98 people. A 2018 report by Morabito Consultants had warned of major structural damage, possibly made worse by saltwater corrosion. Surfside mayor Charles Burkett and Miami-Dade mayor Daniella Levine Cava were prominent in the response, and Levine Cava ordered an audit of older high-rises.

**Andrew Gillum**
The Democratic former mayor of Tallahassee who narrowly lost the 2018 governor's race to DeSantis. Donald Trump called him a "thief" during the campaign.

**Charlie Crist and Nikki Fried**
Crist, a former Republican governor who became a Democrat, criticized long voting lines under Governor Rick Scott in 2012. As a congressman, he beat Agriculture Commissioner Nikki Fried in the 2022 Democratic gubernatorial primary and then lost to DeSantis in a landslide.

**"Don't Say Gay" law and the Disney feud**
The 2022 Parental Rights in Education Act, called "Don't Say Gay" by opponents, restricted classroom instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity. After Disney CEO Bob Chapek pledged to help repeal it, DeSantis retaliated by moving to strip the special self-governing tax status of Disney's Reedy Creek Improvement District.

**Martha's Vineyard migrant flights**
In September 2022, DeSantis's administration chartered flights that took about 50 mostly Venezuelan migrants from Texas to the wealthy Massachusetts island of Martha's Vineyard. The stunt protested federal immigration policy and drew lawsuits and accusations that the migrants were deceived.

**15-week abortion ban**
A law DeSantis signed in April 2022 that banned most abortions after 15 weeks of pregnancy, months before the Supreme Court's Dobbs decision. Florida later adopted a stricter six-week ban.

**Marco Rubio and Rick Scott**
Florida's two Republican U.S. senators for most of the late 2010s and early 2020s. Rubio served in the Senate from 2011 until he became Donald Trump's Secretary of State in 2025, and Scott was Florida's governor from 2011 to 2019 before joining the Senate.

**Social media deplatforming law (SB 7072)**
A 2021 Florida law that would have penalized social media companies for banning political candidates. The tech industry groups NetChoice and CCIA sued to block it, arguing that it violated the First Amendment and Section 230. Around the same time, Florida also passed a ban on transgender girls in girls' school sports.

**Parkland aftermath (Scott Israel and Kyle Kashuv)**
After the 2018 Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School shooting in Parkland, DeSantis suspended Broward County Sheriff Scott Israel days into his term over the department's response. Kyle Kashuv, a conservative gun-rights activist who survived the shooting, had his Harvard admission rescinded after racist messages he wrote earlier surfaced.

**Palm Beach: Mar-a-Lago and the Jeffrey Epstein plea deal**
Donald Trump's Palm Beach resort Mar-a-Lago was called the "Winter White House," and he hosted Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe there in April 2018. In 2008, Alex Acosta, then U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida, approved a lenient plea deal for Palm Beach financier Jeffrey Epstein, which forced Acosta to resign as Trump's Labor Secretary in 2019.

**2012 election and PolitiFact**
Florida was the closest state in the 2012 presidential election, and the Republican National Convention was held in Tampa. PolitiFact, founded by the St. Petersburg (now Tampa Bay) Times, rates false claims as "Pants on Fire" and named a Romney ad about Jeep moving production to China its 2012 "Lie of the Year." Florida politicians in clues from that era include DNC chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz and Tea Party congressman Allen West, who claimed 78 to 81 House Democrats were communists.

**Maxwell Frost and Byron Donalds**
Frost, a Democrat from the Orlando area elected in 2022, became the first member of Gen Z in Congress. Donalds is a Black Republican congressman from southwest Florida and a member of the House Freedom Caucus.

**The Perfect Neighbor**
An Oscar-nominated documentary built largely from police body-camera footage about the 2023 killing of Ajike "AJ" Owens, a Black mother in Ocala. Her white neighbor Susan Lorincz shot her through a closed door after a dispute over children playing, and Lorincz was later convicted of manslaughter.

**Citrus greening (HLB)**
Huanglongbing, a bacterial disease spread by the Asian citrus psyllid insect, which makes fruit green, bitter, and misshapen. It has devastated Florida's once-dominant orange industry and caused a steep fall in production.

**Narendra Modi and the BJP**
Narendra Modi has been India's Prime Minister since 2014, leading the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Nearly every current-events question on India ends with "led by Narendra Modi," and many clues concern BJP policies criticized as hostile to India's roughly 200 million Muslims.

**Revocation of Article 370**
In August 2019, a presidential order revoked Article 370 of the Indian constitution, which had given Jammu and Kashmir, India's only Muslim-majority state, special autonomous status. The state was reorganized into two union territories, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, and the region was placed under a long internet blackout and mass detentions, including of former Chief Minister Omar Abdullah.

**Citizenship Amendment Act (2019)**
A 2019 law (introduced as the Citizenship Amendment Bill) that offered a fast track to citizenship for persecuted Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian refugees from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan, but excluded Muslims. It sparked nationwide protests and accusations of religious discrimination.

**National Register of Citizens (NRC)**
A citizenship registry carried out in the northeastern state of Assam, where about two million people were left off the final list in 2019 because they could not prove their legal status. Critics feared that, combined with the Citizenship Amendment Act, it would be used to strip Muslims of citizenship, and some of those excluded were sent to detention centers.

**Farm laws and the farmers' protests**
In September 2020, India passed three farm acts deregulating the sale, pricing, and storage of agricultural produce. Farmers, especially from Punjab and Haryana, blockaded the highways into New Delhi with tractors and camps for over a year, and the government repealed the laws in late 2021.

**Kashmir dispute**
Kashmir is a Himalayan region claimed by India, Pakistan, and China. India controls Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, and the territory has been the cause of several wars and ongoing tension with Pakistan.

**Line of Actual Control, Galwan, and Pangong Lake**
The Line of Actual Control is the de facto border between India and China. In 2020 the two sides clashed near Pangong Lake and in the Galwan Valley in Ladakh, leaving soldiers dead on both sides; afterward India banned TikTok and dozens of other Chinese apps.

**Demonetisation (2016)**
In November 2016, Modi's government suddenly invalidated all 500 and 1000 rupee banknotes to fight "black money," causing cash shortages and strict limits on ATM withdrawals. Former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh called it "organised loot and legalised plunder," opposition parties held a "Day of Outrage," and the plan involved Reserve Bank Governor Urjit Patel.

**Indian National Congress**
India's historic main party, long associated with the Nehru–Gandhi family. A Congress-led alliance lost heavily to the BJP in the 2014 and 2019 general elections; other opposition parties include the CPI(M), Shiv Sena, Trinamool Congress, and Samajwadi Party, and a Communist-led government rules the southwestern state of Kerala.

**Amit Shah**
Modi's closest ally and India's Home Minister since 2019. He pushed through both the abrogation of Article 370 and the Citizenship Amendment Act.

**Bangalore, Flipkart, and the IT industry**
Bangalore (Bengaluru) is known as India's "Silicon Valley." It is home to the e-commerce giant Flipkart, which Walmart acquired in 2018 and which runs the "Big Billion Days" sales, while Tata Consultancy Services is another giant of the Indian IT industry.

**Reliance Jio**
The mobile network of Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries. Its heavily subsidized launch in 2016 drove India's mobile data prices down to among the cheapest in the world.

**Adani Group and Hindenburg Research**
The Adani Group is a massive conglomerate run by billionaire Gautam Adani, who is seen as close to Modi. In January 2023 the short-seller Hindenburg Research accused the group of widespread stock manipulation and accounting fraud, wiping out tens of billions of dollars in market value.

**Serum Institute of India**
The world's largest vaccine manufacturer by volume, based in Pune. During the COVID-19 pandemic it produced Covishield, the local version of the Oxford–AstraZeneca vaccine; Covaxin was India's homegrown vaccine, made by Bharat Biotech.

**Persecution of Muslims and critics**
Clues about religious tension under the BJP include lynchings by Hindu "cow protection" vigilantes, right-wing TV stories about so-called "love jihad," and fake "auction apps" that put Muslim women up for sale. The government also jailed critics such as the climate activist Disha Ravi, for sharing a farmers' protest "toolkit" linked to Greta Thunberg, and the Muslim comedian Munawar Faruqui, for a joke he never actually told.

**Evo Morales**
Bolivia's first indigenous president, an Aymara former leader of coca growers' unions, who governed from 2006 to 2019. He resigned in November 2019 amid protests and pressure from the military, which his supporters call a coup, and went into exile in Mexico and then Argentina.

**2019 Bolivian general election**
The October 2019 election in which Morales sought a fourth term. A suspicious pause in the preliminary vote count, followed by a jump in Morales's lead that gave him a first-round victory, set off mass protests, and an audit by the Organization of American States reported serious irregularities.

**Jeanine Áñez**
An opposition senator who declared herself interim president in November 2019 after Morales and his constitutional successors resigned. Her government was marked by deadly crackdowns on pro-Morales protesters at Sacaba and Senkata, and she was later convicted and sentenced to prison for her role in taking power.

**MAS (Movement for Socialism)**
The left-wing party founded by Morales's coca-grower movement, which dominated Bolivian politics from 2006 onward. It returned to power when Luis Arce won the 2020 election, but it later split between supporters of Arce and Morales and collapsed in the 2025 election.

**Term limits ruled a human rights violation**
In 2016 Bolivian voters narrowly rejected a referendum that would have let Morales run for a fourth term. In 2017 the Plurinational Constitutional Tribunal overrode that result, ruling that term limits violated candidates' human rights under the American Convention on Human Rights.

**Plurinational Legislative Assembly**
Bolivia's two-chamber national legislature, consisting of a Chamber of Deputies and a Chamber of Senators. Its name reflects the country's 2009 constitution, which renamed it the "Plurinational State of Bolivia" to recognize its many indigenous nations.

**Truth Commission**
A commission created by Bolivia's legislature to investigate human rights abuses, such as killings, torture, and forced disappearances, committed under the military dictatorships of 1964 to 1982. In 2019 the Assembly extended its deadline to produce a final report.

**Luis Arce**
Morales's former economy minister, who won the 2020 presidential election for MAS after a year of interim government. He later broke with Morales, and their feud split the party.

**2024 coup attempt**
In June 2024, General Juan José Zúñiga led troops and an armored vehicle into La Paz's Plaza Murillo and rammed the doors of the presidential palace. The attempt collapsed within hours, and Zúñiga was arrested.

**La Paz and Sucre**
Bolivia has two capitals: La Paz, the seat of government and one of the world's highest capital cities, and Sucre, the constitutional capital and seat of the judiciary.

**Lithium and the Salar de Uyuni**
Bolivia holds some of the world's largest lithium reserves, much of it under the Salar de Uyuni, the world's largest salt flat. Control and development of lithium, a key battery material, is a major political and economic issue in the country.

**Wiphala**
A multicolored checkered flag representing the Andean indigenous peoples, recognized as a national symbol under the 2009 constitution. During the 2019 crisis, some anti-Morales police and protesters burned or cut it from their uniforms, provoking outrage among indigenous Bolivians.

**Muhammadu Buhari**
A former military ruler from northern Nigeria who was elected president in 2015 and served until 2023. He was criticized for spending long periods in the United Kingdom for medical treatment, reportedly including for the inner-ear disorder Ménière's disease, and for failing to defeat Boko Haram.

**Bola Tinubu and the 2023 election**
A former governor of Lagos State and longtime "kingmaker" in the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), who won the February 2023 presidential election using the Yoruba slogan "Emi lokan" ("It's my turn"). As a southerner succeeding the northern Buhari, he fit Nigeria's informal practice of rotating the presidency between north and south.

**Boko Haram and the Chibok kidnapping**
An Islamist militant group based in northeastern Nigeria, founded by Mohammed Yusuf and later led by Abubakar Shekau, whose name is usually translated as "Western education is forbidden." In 2014 it kidnapped 276 schoolgirls from Chibok, sparking the "Bring Back Our Girls" campaign.

**Goodluck Jonathan**
A southerner from the People's Democratic Party (PDP) who became president in 2010 after President Umaru Musa Yar'Adua died in office, and served until losing to Buhari in 2015. In 2012, he tried to rename the University of Lagos after the politician Moshood Abiola, but backed down after protests.

**#EndSARS and the Lekki Toll Gate shooting**
In 2020, mass protests erupted against SARS, a police unit (the Special Anti-Robbery Squad) accused of brutality, extortion, and killings. On October 20, 2020, soldiers opened fire on peaceful protesters at the Lekki Toll Gate in Lagos.

**Niger Delta and Ken Saro-Wiwa**
The oil-rich Niger River delta in the south produces most of Nigeria's oil, and oil spills there have caused severe environmental damage. The writer and activist Ken Saro-Wiwa led protests by the Ogoni people against the damage and against oil companies like Shell, and he was executed by the military government in 1995.

**Peter Obi and Atiku Abubakar**
Tinubu's main rivals in the 2023 presidential election. Atiku Abubakar of the PDP finished second, while Peter Obi of the Labour Party, who drew strong support from young voters, narrowly beat Tinubu in Tinubu's home state of Lagos.

**Biafra and the Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB)**
Biafra was the breakaway state in southeastern Nigeria whose secession attempt led to the Nigerian Civil War from 1967 to 1970. IPOB is a modern separatist movement seeking Biafran independence, and its leader, Nnamdi Kanu, has been on trial on terrorism charges.

**Twitter ban**
In June 2021, Nigeria suspended Twitter after the company deleted a tweet by Buhari that threatened secessionists and referred to the Biafran Civil War. The ban was lifted in January 2022.

**Herder–farmer conflict and bandits**
In Nigeria's Middle Belt, deadly clashes over land and water between mostly Muslim Fulani herders and mostly Christian farmers have killed many people over decades. In the northwest, armed gangs called bandits, many of them Fulani, have carried out massacres and mass kidnappings.

**Jangebe and Kagara school kidnappings**
In February 2021, gunmen kidnapped schoolboys from a school in Kagara in Niger State and hundreds of schoolgirls from a school in Jangebe in Zamfara State. They were part of a wave of mass kidnappings for ransom at schools in northern Nigeria.

**Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala**
A Nigerian economist and former finance minister who became director-general of the World Trade Organization in 2021, the first woman and the first African to hold the job.

**Lagos and Abuja**
Lagos is Nigeria's largest city and commercial center, while Abuja, in the center of the country, is the capital. Nigeria is Africa's most populous country and has the largest economy and population in ECOWAS, the Economic Community of West African States.

**Hausa-Fulani, Yoruba, and Igbo**
Nigeria's three largest ethnic groups. The mostly Muslim Hausa-Fulani dominate the north, the Yoruba the southwest, and the Igbo the southeast.

**Prebendalism**
A term coined by political scientist Richard Joseph for Nigeria's system of patronage, in which government offices are treated as personal sources of wealth to be shared among the officeholder's ethnic, religious, or political supporters.

**Anthony Albanese and the Labor Party**
Albanese led the center-left Australian Labor Party to victory over the Liberal-National Coalition in the 2022 election and became prime minister, governing from the capital, Canberra. He was re-elected in a landslide in 2025.

**Liberal-National Coalition**
The long-standing alliance of Australia's center-right Liberal Party and the rural-based National Party, which is the main rival to Labor. It governed under prime ministers such as John Howard, Malcolm Turnbull, and Scott Morrison.

**Scott Morrison and the "quiet Australians"**
The Liberal prime minister from 2018 to 2022. After his surprise 2019 election win, he declared that "the quiet Australians" had won a great victory, and he lost power to Albanese in 2022.

**2019–2020 bushfires and the Hawaii vacation**
The catastrophic "Black Summer" wildfires burned huge areas of Australia and killed vast numbers of animals, including kangaroos and koalas. Morrison was heavily criticized for vacationing in Hawaii during the crisis, and lingering smoke disrupted the Australian Open tennis tournament in Melbourne.

**Offshore detention on Nauru and Manus Island**
Australia sent asylum seekers who arrived by boat to detention centers on the island nation of Nauru and on Manus Island in Papua New Guinea. The Guardian published a database of leaked reports of abuse at the Nauru center, and the Manus arrangement was wound down by 2019.

**One Nation and Pauline Hanson**
One Nation is a far-right, anti-immigration party led by Pauline Hanson. When Hanson returned to the Senate in 2016, Labor senator Sam Dastyari sarcastically invited her to share a "halal snack pack," a popular kebab-shop dish.

**Malcolm Turnbull and the Trump phone call**
The Liberal prime minister from 2015 to 2018. In a tense February 2017 phone call, he pushed Donald Trump to honor an Obama-era deal for the U.S. to resettle refugees held in Australia's offshore centers, and his government also tried to change the words "insult" and "offend" in Section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act.

**John Howard and the AWB scandal**
Howard was the Liberal prime minister from 1996 to 2007. In 2006 his government faced a scandal after the Australian Wheat Board (AWB), Iraq's largest food supplier under the UN oil-for-food program, was found to have paid illegal kickbacks to Saddam Hussein's regime; his Labor opponent at the 2004 election was Mark Latham.

**2025 election and teal independents**
In the 2025 election, Labor greatly increased its majority while the Coalition suffered heavy losses, partly after reversing a policy to end work from home for public servants. "Teal" independents, socially liberal candidates focused on climate action, kept their seats, Clive Palmer's right-wing Trumpet of Patriots party flopped, and veteran election analyst Antony Green retired from broadcasting afterward.

**Novak Djokovic's deportation**
In January 2022, the Serbian tennis star was deported before the Australian Open because he was not vaccinated against COVID-19, after a legal battle over his visa.

**Penny Wong**
Albanese's foreign minister. At a Pacific Islands Forum meeting in Fiji in 2022, she promised that Australia would "end the climate wars" and help make the "Pacific family" even stronger.

**Harold Holt and "All the way with LBJ"**
The Liberal prime minister who expanded Australia's role in the Vietnam War, pledging in 1966 to go "all the way with LBJ" in support of U.S. President Lyndon B. Johnson. In December 1967, he disappeared while swimming at Cheviot Beach in Victoria, and his body was never found.

**Kevin Rudd and the Stolen Generations apology**
In 2008, Labor prime minister Kevin Rudd formally apologized to the Stolen Generations, the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children who had been removed from their families under government policies.

**Edmund Barton and the Hopetoun Blunder**
Barton was Australia's first prime minister when the federation formed in 1901. He took office after the "Hopetoun Blunder," in which the first Governor-General, Lord Hopetoun, first invited William Lyne instead of Barton to form a government, but Lyne could not get enough support.

**Robert Menzies and "The Forgotten People"**
Menzies founded the modern Liberal Party and is Australia's longest-serving prime minister. In a 1942 radio speech called "The Forgotten People," he praised the middle class as the backbone of the nation.

**Governor of California**
Newsom, a Democrat, has been governor of California since 2019 and governs from Sacramento. This is the main giveaway.

**September 2021 recall election**
A special election in which California voters were asked whether to remove Newsom from office early. Newsom easily survived it, defeating all of the replacement candidates.

**Larry Elder**
A conservative talk radio host who was the leading Republican replacement candidate in the 2021 recall and won the most votes among the replacement candidates.

**Kevin Paffrath**
A YouTuber who makes videos about real estate and finance, and the best-known Democrat running as a replacement candidate in the 2021 recall.

**The French Laundry**
A famous restaurant in Yountville in Napa Valley. In November 2020, Newsom attended a lobbyist's birthday dinner there that broke his own COVID-19 rules on gatherings, causing a scandal that helped fuel the recall effort.

**John Cox**
A Republican businessman whom Newsom defeated in the 2018 governor's race. Cox ran again in the 2021 recall and brought a live bear to campaign events to contrast himself, the "beast," with Newsom, whom he called a "pretty boy."

**Project Roomkey**
A program Newsom launched early in the COVID-19 pandemic that used state and federal money to put homeless people at high risk from the virus into hotel and motel rooms.

**SB 9**
A housing law Newsom signed in September 2021 that lets owners build duplexes on, or split, lots that had been zoned only for single-family homes. It was meant to ease California's housing shortage.

**Statewide stay-at-home order**
In March 2020, Newsom issued the first statewide COVID-19 stay-at-home order in the United States, making him a national figure in the pandemic response.

**Mayor of San Francisco**
Before becoming governor, Newsom was mayor of San Francisco. In 2004 he drew national attention by directing the city to issue marriage licenses to same-sex couples.

**"Special military operation" in Ukraine**
Putin's official euphemism for Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which he announced in a televised speech on February 24, 2022. He claimed the goals were to "demilitarize" and "denazify" Ukraine.

**Dmitry Medvedev and the "tandemocracy"**
Because Russia's constitution barred more than two consecutive presidential terms, Putin stepped aside in 2008 for his ally Medvedev and served as his Prime Minister. They swapped back in 2012, and observers called the power-sharing arrangement a "tandemocracy."

**Yevgeny Prigozhin and the Wagner Group mutiny**
Prigozhin, nicknamed "Putin's chef" because his catering company won Kremlin contracts, led the Wagner Group private military company. In June 2023 Wagner forces seized Rostov-on-Don and marched toward Moscow before calling off the revolt, and Prigozhin died in a plane crash two months later.

**ICC arrest warrant**
In March 2023, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin over the unlawful deportation of children from occupied Ukraine. Because South Africa was an ICC member that would have been obliged to arrest him, he attended the August 2023 BRICS summit in Johannesburg only by video.

**"Z" symbol**
A letter painted on Russian military vehicles invading Ukraine that became a pro-war and pro-Putin propaganda symbol inside Russia. It does not exist in the Cyrillic alphabet.

**Macron and the long table**
In February 2022, French President Emmanuel Macron met Putin at the Kremlin across an extremely long white table after reportedly refusing a Russian PCR test, which raised fears that Russia could take his DNA. Images of the meeting became a symbol of Putin's isolation.

**2020 constitutional amendments**
A package of constitutional changes approved in a 2020 national vote that reset the count of Putin's presidential terms to zero. It allows him to potentially stay in office until 2036.

**Nord-Ost theater hostage crisis**
In October 2002, Chechen militants took about 850 people hostage at a Moscow theater during a performance of the musical Nord-Ost. Russian special forces pumped an aerosolized chemical agent into the building before storming it, killing all the attackers and well over 100 hostages, mostly from the gas, and Putin defended the operation.

**Second Chechen War and Grozny**
The war Putin oversaw as Prime Minister and then President, beginning in 1999, which reconquered the breakaway republic of Chechnya. Russian forces besieged and largely destroyed the Chechen capital Grozny, and the war cemented Putin's tough-leader image.

**KGB career and succeeding Boris Yeltsin**
