Putin spent about 16 years as a KGB foreign intelligence officer, including a posting in Dresden, East Germany. He later headed the FSB, became Prime Minister in 1999, and became acting president when Boris Yeltsin resigned on New Year's Eve 1999.

**Evan Gershkovich**
A Wall Street Journal reporter arrested by Russian authorities in Yekaterinburg in March 2023 on espionage charges that he and the U.S. denied. He was convicted and sentenced to 16 years, then freed in an August 2024 prisoner exchange.

**Tucker Carlson interview**
In February 2024, the American commentator Tucker Carlson conducted a long one-on-one interview with Putin in Moscow, Putin's first with a Western media figure since the invasion. Putin opened it with a lengthy history lecture on Russia and Ukraine.

**Marina Ovsyannikova**
A Channel One editor who interrupted a live state news broadcast in March 2022 by holding up a sign reading "No war" and warning viewers that they were being lied to. She was fined, later placed under house arrest, and fled Russia.

**"A Plea for Caution From Russia"**
Putin's September 2013 op-ed in The New York Times, which argued against U.S. military strikes on Syria over chemical weapons. It also criticized the idea of American exceptionalism.

**"Gay propaganda" law**
A 2013 law signed by Putin that banned promoting "non-traditional sexual relations" to minors. Russia also restricted adoptions of Russian children by foreign same-sex couples, and later laws extended these limits.

**Cassette Scandal (Georgiy Gongadze)**
A political crisis that began in 2000 after investigative journalist Georgiy Gongadze, founder of the news site Ukrainska Pravda, was kidnapped and murdered. Secret audio recordings made in President Leonid Kuchma's office appeared to show Kuchma ordering action against Gongadze, sparking mass "Ukraine without Kuchma" protests.

**Orange Revolution**
A largely nonviolent 2004 protest movement centered in Kyiv's Independence Square against a fraudulent presidential runoff that had declared Viktor Yanukovych the winner. Ukraine's Supreme Court annulled the result, and opposition candidate Viktor Yushchenko won the rerun election.

**Euromaidan**
Mass protests that began in November 2013 after President Viktor Yanukovych backed out of an association and trade agreement with the European Union in favor of closer ties with Russia. Violent clashes, including on Hrushevskoho Street in Kyiv, led to Yanukovych fleeing the country in February 2014 in what is also called the Revolution of Dignity.

**Heavenly Hundred**
The name given to the roughly one hundred protesters killed during Euromaidan, most of them shot in and around Kyiv's Independence Square (Maidan Nezalezhnosti) in February 2014. The riot police unit Berkut, blamed for much of the violence, was disbanded afterward.

**Viktor Yanukovych**
Pro-Russian politician whose fraudulent 2004 victory was overturned by the Orange Revolution. He won the presidency in 2010, jailed his rival Yulia Tymoshenko, and was ousted in February 2014 after the Euromaidan protests, after which he fled to Russia.

**Yulia Tymoshenko**
A leader of the Orange Revolution, known for her braided hairstyle, who served as prime minister. She finished second to Yanukovych in the 2010 presidential election, was then jailed on charges widely seen as politically motivated, and was released in 2014 after Yanukovych's fall.

**Volodymyr Zelenskyy**
Former comedian and actor who starred in the TV show "Servant of the People," then won the 2019 presidential election and named his party after the show. He called a snap parliamentary election during his inauguration speech and has led Ukraine's resistance to the 2022 Russian invasion.

**Siege of Mariupol**
A months-long 2022 Russian siege of this port city on the Sea of Azov, documented in the Oscar-winning film "20 Days in Mariupol." Defenders, including members of the Azov Regiment (formerly Azov Battalion), made a last stand in the Azovstal steel plant before surrendering in May 2022.

**Crimea annexation**
In February and March 2014, shortly after Yanukovych's ouster, Russian troops in unmarked uniforms, nicknamed "little green men," seized the Crimean Peninsula on the Black Sea. Russia then annexed Crimea, including the naval city of Sevastopol, after a disputed referendum.

**Viktor Yushchenko's dioxin poisoning**
During the 2004 campaign, opposition candidate Viktor Yushchenko was poisoned with TCDD, a highly toxic dioxin, which left his face severely disfigured. He became president after the Orange Revolution forced a rerun of the election.

**Donbas, MH17, and the Minsk agreements**
The Donbas is the eastern region of Ukraine (Donetsk and Luhansk) where Russian-backed separatists began fighting Ukrainian forces in 2014. Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 was shot down over the region in July 2014, and the Minsk agreements of 2014–2015 tried unsuccessfully to end the conflict.

**Filtration camps and deported children**
During the 2022 invasion, Russia was accused of screening Ukrainian civilians in "filtration camps" and forcibly relocating Ukrainian children to Russia. The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin in 2023 over the unlawful deportation of children.

**Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant**
The largest nuclear power plant in Europe, located in southeastern Ukraine. Russian forces seized it in March 2022, its reactors were later put into shutdown, and its safety has been a major international concern during the war.

**Petro Poroshenko**
A confectionery tycoon nicknamed the "Chocolate King" for his Roshen candy company, who was elected president in 2014 after Euromaidan and led Ukraine during the early Donbas war. He lost the 2019 election in a landslide to Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

**Budapest Memorandum**
A 1994 agreement in which Ukraine gave up the nuclear weapons it inherited from the Soviet Union in exchange for security assurances from Russia, the United States, and the United Kingdom. Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea is widely viewed as a violation of it.

**Green New Deal**
A 2019 congressional resolution Ocasio-Cortez cosponsored with Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey, calling for a ten-year national mobilization to eliminate U.S. greenhouse gas emissions while guaranteeing jobs and economic justice. The 14-page resolution is her signature policy and the most common clue for her.

**Defeat of Joe Crowley (2018 primary)**
In June 2018, Ocasio-Cortez, then a 28-year-old former bartender and activist, upset Joe Crowley, the fourth-ranking House Democrat, in the Democratic primary for New York's 14th district. It was one of the biggest upsets of the 2018 election cycle.

**The Squad**
The nickname for four progressive women of color elected to the House in 2018: Ocasio-Cortez, Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts, and Rashida Tlaib of Michigan. The group is known for championing policies like Medicare for All and the Green New Deal and for clashing with both Republicans and Democratic leadership.

**Youngest woman ever elected to Congress**
Ocasio-Cortez was 29 when she won the general election in November 2018, making her the youngest woman ever elected to the U.S. Congress at the time.

**Queens and the Bronx (New York's 14th district)**
Her congressional district covers parts of Queens and the Bronx in New York City. Questions often end by calling her a progressive representative from New York City.

**Democratic socialist**
Ocasio-Cortez is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America and is one of the most prominent left-wing figures in American politics. She has advocated policies such as abolishing ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) and Medicare for All.

**Marjorie Taylor Greene**
The far-right Republican congresswoman from Georgia who taunted Ocasio-Cortez, calling her a "little girl," and challenged her to a debate over the Green New Deal, boasting that she had read "all 14 pages" of it.

**Paul Gosar's anime video**
In 2021, Arizona Republican Paul Gosar posted an edited video based on the anime Attack on Titan that showed his character killing Ocasio-Cortez and attacking Joe Biden. The House censured Gosar and removed him from his committees over it.

**Among Us Twitch stream**
In October 2020, Ocasio-Cortez livestreamed herself playing the game Among Us on Twitch to encourage voting, joined by streamers such as Pokimane and fellow Squad member Ilhan Omar. It drew hundreds of thousands of viewers and became one of the most-watched streams on the platform.

**"Born to Run" and the Working Families Party line**
After his primary loss, Joe Crowley played a guitar rendition of Bruce Springsteen's "Born to Run" and dedicated it to Ocasio-Cortez. She later accused him of running a third-party campaign against her because he remained on the November ballot as the Working Families Party nominee.

**Annabel Palma**
A former New York City councilwoman whom Joe Crowley sent to take his place at a 2018 primary debate against Ocasio-Cortez. His absence was widely criticized and helped her portray him as out of touch with the district.

**Means of Production campaign ad**
Her viral 2018 campaign video, "The Courage to Change," was produced by the progressive film collective Means of Production. It showed her taking the subway and talking about the struggles of working people in her district, and it helped launch her campaign into national prominence.

**hbomberguy's Donkey Kong 64 stream**
In January 2019, Ocasio-Cortez made a surprise appearance on YouTuber hbomberguy's marathon Donkey Kong 64 charity stream, which raised money for the transgender youth charity Mermaids.

**Tucker Carlson and the "War on Cauliflower"**
Fox News host Tucker Carlson devoted a segment to what he called Ocasio-Cortez's "War on Cauliflower," part of his frequent mockery of her views on food, climate, and the economy.

**Sunscreen TikTok with Charlotte Palermino**
In 2023, Ocasio-Cortez was criticized for appearing in a TikTok video with skincare influencer Charlotte Palermino in which they discussed sunscreen and her skincare routine.

**George Floyd and Derek Chauvin**
George Floyd was a Black man killed by Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin on May 25, 2020, after being detained for allegedly using a counterfeit $20 bill at the Cup Foods store. Chauvin knelt on Floyd's neck for about nine minutes (originally reported as 8 minutes and 46 seconds) while Floyd repeatedly said "I can't breathe," sparking nationwide protests; Chauvin was convicted of murder in 2021.

**Ilhan Omar**
A Somali-American Democratic congresswoman representing Minneapolis and a member of "The Squad," reflecting Minnesota's status as home to the largest Somali-American community in the U.S. She drew controversy for a 2019 tweet saying support for Israel was "all about the Benjamins," which was criticized as an antisemitic trope about AIPAC, and for describing 9/11 as "some people did something." House Republicans removed her from the Foreign Affairs Committee in 2023, and she defeated Don Samuels in a 2024 primary.

**Tim Walz**
Democratic governor of Minnesota since 2019, governing from the capital of St. Paul, who responded to the George Floyd protests and ordered 8 minutes and 46 seconds of silence in Floyd's memory. In 2024 he became Kamala Harris's vice-presidential running mate after popularizing calling Republicans like J.D. Vance "weird," and in the vice-presidential debate he admitted misstating that he had been in Hong Kong during the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre.

**Derek Chauvin's trial**
Chauvin's 2021 murder trial in Minneapolis was presided over by Judge Peter Cahill and prosecuted by attorneys including Matthew Frank, working under Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, the first Muslim elected to Congress. Witnesses included off-duty firefighter Genevieve Hansen and use-of-force expert Barry Brodd, who testified for the defense; fellow officers Tou Thao and J. Alexander Kueng were tried separately.

**Darnella Frazier**
The teenager who filmed the bystander video of George Floyd's murder at age 17, which spread worldwide and was key evidence at Chauvin's trial. She received an honorary courage award from PEN America and a special citation from the Pulitzer Prize board.

**Amy Klobuchar**
Minnesota's senior U.S. senator, who ran for president in 2020 and faced reports that she mistreated her Senate staff. In 2022 she pulled her Journalism Competition and Preservation Act from a committee vote after Ted Cruz added an amendment she opposed.

**Daunte Wright**
A 20-year-old Black man shot and killed during a traffic stop in Brooklyn Center, a suburb of Minneapolis, in April 2021, while Chauvin's trial was underway nearby. Officer Kim Potter said she meant to draw her Taser but fired her handgun instead, and she was convicted of manslaughter.

**Philando Castile**
A Black school cafeteria supervisor shot and killed by officer Jeronimo Yanez during a 2016 traffic stop in Falcon Heights, near St. Paul, after he told the officer he was carrying a licensed firearm. His girlfriend, Diamond Reynolds, livestreamed the aftermath on Facebook.

**Justine Damond and Mohamed Noor**
Justine Damond, an Australian-American woman, was shot and killed in 2017 by Minneapolis police officer Mohamed Noor after she called 911 to report a possible assault behind her home. Noor was convicted, though his murder conviction was later overturned on appeal, leaving a manslaughter conviction.

**Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party (DFL)**
Minnesota's affiliate of the Democratic Party, formed in 1944 when the state's Democrats merged with the Farmer-Labor Party. Politicians like Walz, Klobuchar, and Omar belong to it; DFL Representative Collin Peterson lost his long-held seat to Republican Michelle Fischbach in 2020.

**Al Franken and Tina Smith**
Former comedian Al Franken won a Senate seat in 2008 after a months-long recount, finally beating incumbent Norm Coleman by a few hundred votes. When Franken resigned amid sexual misconduct allegations, Governor Mark Dayton appointed his own lieutenant governor, Tina Smith, who then won the 2018 special election over Karin Housley.

**Tim Pawlenty**
Republican governor of Minnesota from 2003 to 2011 and a 2012 presidential hopeful, alongside fellow Minnesotan Michele Bachmann, who gave the Tea Party response to Obama's 2011 State of the Union. Pawlenty tried to return as governor in 2018 but lost the Republican primary.

**Jesse Ventura**
A former professional wrestler who was elected governor in 1998 on the Reform Party ticket and served until 2003. He appointed Dean Barkley to briefly fill the U.S. Senate seat left open when Paul Wellstone died in a 2002 plane crash.

**Raised-fist sculpture at George Floyd Square**
A large metal sculpture of a raised fist, made by artist Jordan Powell-Karis, installed at the intersection of 38th Street and Chicago Avenue in Minneapolis, where Floyd was killed. The site became a memorial known as George Floyd Square.

**Line 3 pipeline protests**
Protests against Enbridge's Line 3 oil pipeline replacement, which crosses northern Minnesota through treaty lands of the Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) people. Water protectors argued it threatened wild rice lakes and the climate, and more than a thousand people were arrested in 2021.

**Justin Jones and Justin Pearson ("Tennessee Three")**
Two young Black Democratic state representatives whom the Republican-controlled Tennessee House expelled in April 2023. They had led a gun control protest from the chamber floor with a bullhorn after the Covenant School shooting. Their local governments quickly reappointed them, and both later won back their seats in special elections. A third protester, Gloria Johnson, a white woman, survived her expulsion vote by one vote, which led to accusations of racism.

**Covenant School shooting**
On March 27, 2023, a shooter killed three nine-year-old children and three adults at the Covenant School, a private Christian elementary school in Nashville, before being killed by police. Commentator Steven Crowder later leaked pages from the shooter's writings, and the motive remained unclear.

**Tyre Nichols**
A 29-year-old Black man who was beaten by Memphis police officers after a traffic stop for alleged reckless driving in January 2023 and died three days later. The five officers charged were themselves Black. After the killing, Memphis disbanded the officers' SCORPION unit (Street Crimes Operation to Restore Peace in Our Neighborhoods).

**Adult Entertainment Act (drag ban)**
A 2023 Tennessee law restricting "adult cabaret" performances in public or where children might see them, widely seen as targeting drag shows. A federal judge blocked it as unconstitutional, though an appeals court later reversed that ruling. Tennessee also passed a ban on gender-affirming care for minors.

**Bill Lee**
The Republican governor of Tennessee since 2019, who signed the drag and gender-affirming care bans. Soon afterward, a high school yearbook photo surfaced showing Lee dressed in a women's cheerleader uniform.

**Nashville Christmas bombing**
On December 25, 2020, Anthony Quinn Warner set off a bomb inside his recreational vehicle in downtown Nashville and was killed in the blast. The explosion damaged an AT&T building and disrupted telecommunications across the region, and no clear motive was found.

**Nashville**
The capital of Tennessee, where the state legislature meets, and the center of the country music industry. In 2023 Taylor Swift set attendance records during three Eras Tour concerts at the city's Nissan Stadium.

**Cameron Sexton and Bill Lafferty**
Sexton is the Republican Speaker of the Tennessee House, who led the push to expel Jones and Pearson. During a tense 2023 session, as Sexton was clearing the chamber, Republican Rep. Bill Lafferty shoved Justin Jones.

**Rick Tillis's seat**
Rick Tillis, a Tennessee state representative and brother of U.S. Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, was at the center of a strange allegation that another Republican House leader had urinated on his seat in the chamber. Justin Jones brought up the accusation.

**Tucker Carlson's "sharecropper" remark**
In April 2023, the Fox News host Tucker Carlson said Justin Pearson "talked like a sharecropper," a remark that was widely condemned as racist.

**Scott Cepicky's "at war for the Republic"**
A Republican Tennessee state representative who, in leaked audio, defended his vote to expel the Democratic lawmakers by saying he was "at war for the Republic."

**Spotless giraffe**
In 2023, Brights Zoo near Limestone, Tennessee, announced the birth of a rare giraffe with no spots, believed to be the only one of its kind in the world. She was named Kipekee, Swahili for "unique."

**Memphis**
Tennessee's second-largest city, on the Mississippi River, where Tyre Nichols was killed. It is also known for Graceland, Elvis Presley's home, and as the site of Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination.

**2002 Gujarat riots**
Deadly anti-Muslim violence in the state of Gujarat, which Modi governed as Chief Minister, triggered when a train fire at Godhra killed 58 Hindu pilgrims. More than a thousand people, mostly Muslims, were killed, including in a massacre at the Gulbarg Society housing complex in Ahmedabad; critics accused Modi of failing to stop or even encouraging the violence, though a Supreme Court-appointed investigation cleared him in 2012.

**Ram Mandir and the Babri Masjid site in Ayodhya**
The Babri Masjid, a 16th-century mosque in Ayodhya, was demolished by Hindu nationalists in 1992, who believe the site is the birthplace of the god Rama. A 2019 Supreme Court ruling awarded the land for a Hindu temple, which Modi praised and compared to the fall of the Berlin Wall (both happened on November 9); he consecrated the Ram Mandir temple in January 2024, shortly before national elections.

**Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)**
India's Hindu nationalist party, which Modi leads. It won a landslide over the long-dominant Indian National Congress party in 2014, making Modi prime minister, and won a majority again in 2019.

**2024 election and the National Democratic Alliance**
During the 2024 general election, Modi used the slogan "Abki baar, 400 paar" ("This time, more than 400"), meaning seats for his alliance. Instead, the BJP lost its majority in the Lok Sabha, the lower house of Parliament, even losing the Faizabad seat that includes Ayodhya, and Modi formed a coalition government through the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance.

**Rahul Gandhi and the "Modi surname" case**
Rahul Gandhi, leader of the opposition Indian National Congress, asked in a 2019 campaign speech why all thieves share the surname Modi. He was convicted of criminal defamation in 2023 and disqualified from Parliament until the Supreme Court suspended his conviction.

**BBC documentary and tax raids**
In 2023, the BBC aired "India: The Modi Question," a documentary examining Modi's role in the 2002 Gujarat riots, which the government blocked from being shared in India. Weeks later, Indian tax officials searched the BBC's offices in New Delhi and Mumbai in what they called an income tax "survey."

**Killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar**
Nijjar, a Canadian Sikh activist for Khalistan, a proposed independent Sikh state, was shot dead outside a gurdwara in British Columbia in June 2023. Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were credible allegations linking Indian government agents to the killing, triggering a diplomatic crisis.

**Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA)**
A 2019 law passed by Modi's government that offers a fast track to Indian citizenship for persecuted religious minorities from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan, including Hindus, Sikhs, and Christians, but not Muslims. Critics called it discriminatory, and it sparked mass protests.

**2016 demonetization**
In November 2016, Modi suddenly announced that all 500- and 1,000-rupee banknotes were no longer legal tender, aiming to fight corruption and "black money." The move caused cash shortages, long bank lines, and daily limits on ATM withdrawals.

**"The age of expansionism is over"**
A line from Modi's July 2020 speech to troops in Ladakh, after a deadly clash with Chinese soldiers in the Galwan Valley along the disputed India–China border. It was read as an implicit rebuke of China.

**Chief Minister of Gujarat**
Before becoming prime minister in 2014, Modi served as Chief Minister of the western Indian state of Gujarat from 2001 to 2014. His supporters promoted the state's economic growth as the "Gujarat model."

**U.S. visa ban and Madison Square Garden speech**
The United States denied Modi a visa in 2005 over his role in the Gujarat riots, a ban that ended when he became prime minister. In September 2014, he gave a speech to a cheering crowd of about 19,000 Indian Americans at New York's Madison Square Garden.

**India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement**
A 2015 agreement under Modi that settled the border with Bangladesh by exchanging 162 enclaves, small pockets of territory belonging to one country but surrounded by the other. Residents were allowed to choose their citizenship.

**"56-inch chest"**
A boast Modi made during his 2014 campaign, claiming he had a 56-inch chest to signal toughness and strength in standing up to rivals like Pakistan. The phrase became a widely mocked catchphrase associated with him.

**Crackdown on Greenpeace and the Ford Foundation**
In 2015, Modi's government restricted foreign funding to nonprofits such as Greenpeace India and the Ford Foundation, accusing them of harming national interests. U.S. Ambassador Richard Verma warned that such actions could have a "chilling effect" on civil society.

**2012 Benghazi attack**
On September 11, 2012, militants attacked the US diplomatic compound and a nearby CIA annex in Benghazi, Libya's second-largest city. Four Americans were killed, and the attack became a long-running political controversy in the United States, including over Hillary Clinton's handling of it as Secretary of State.

**J. Christopher Stevens**
The US Ambassador to Libya who died in the Benghazi attack, the first US ambassador killed in the line of duty since 1979. Information officer Sean Smith and two CIA security contractors were also killed.

**Ansar al-Sharia**
The Islamist militia blamed for the 2012 Benghazi attack. It was led in Benghazi by Muhammad al-Zahawi, and it later fought against Khalifa Haftar's forces before being weakened and dissolving in 2017.

**Muammar Gaddafi**
The longtime dictator who ruled Libya from his 1969 coup until he was overthrown and killed during the 2011 civil war, which was backed by NATO airstrikes. His fall left Libya divided among rival governments and militias.

**Gaddafi's tent in Westchester County**
During his 2009 visit to the UN General Assembly in New York, Gaddafi, who liked to stay in a Bedouin tent while traveling, had a tent set up on Donald Trump's Seven Springs estate in Westchester County. Local officials objected, and it was taken down.

**Government of National Accord**
A UN-backed unity government formed in 2015–2016 and based in Tripoli. It was meant to unite the rival General National Congress in Tripoli and the House of Representatives based in eastern Libya, but it failed to end the country's split.

**Khalifa Haftar**
A Libyan general who commands the Libyan National Army in eastern Libya. In 2014 he launched "Operation Dignity" against Islamist militias in Benghazi, and he later backed the eastern House of Representatives against the Tripoli-based government.

**Ahmed Abu Khattala**
A Libyan militant captured by US special forces in 2014 for his role in the Benghazi attack. He was tried in the United States and convicted on terrorism-related charges in 2017.

**Libyan Investment Authority and Goldman Sachs**
After international sanctions on Libya were lifted in the 2000s, Goldman Sachs arranged derivative trades for Libya's sovereign wealth fund, the Libyan Investment Authority, which lost about 1.2 billion dollars. The fund sued in London, claiming it had been taken advantage of, but lost the case in 2016.

**Benina Airport and the 2014 no-fly zone**
Benghazi's international airport, which was closed during the 2014 fighting between Haftar's forces and Islamist militias. The government also declared a no-fly zone over Benghazi in May 2014.

**Yussef al-Mangoush**
Libya's army chief of staff, who left office in June 2013 after deadly clashes in Benghazi between protesters and an Islamist-leaning militia.

**Huda Ben Amer**
A Gaddafi loyalist who served as mayor of Benghazi and fled the city during the 2011 uprising. She was notorious for her role in a televised public hanging of a dissident in 1984.

**737 MAX**
Boeing's best-selling narrow-body airliner and the most common giveaway for the company. The plane was grounded worldwide from 2019 to 2020 after two fatal crashes, and it came under scrutiny again in 2024 after an in-flight door plug blowout.

**Alaska Airlines Flight 1282**
A January 2024 flight departing Portland, Oregon, on which a door plug covering an unused (optional) emergency exit blew out of a 737 MAX 9, causing uncontrolled decompression. The NTSB investigated and found that the four bolts meant to hold the plug in place were missing.

**MCAS (Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System)**
Flight-control software on the 737 MAX that automatically pushed the plane's nose down based on a single sensor reading. It was blamed for two fatal crashes, and Boeing was criticized for not telling pilots enough about it.

**Jakarta and Addis Ababa crashes**
The two fatal 737 MAX crashes linked to MCAS: Lion Air Flight 610, which crashed shortly after leaving Jakarta in October 2018, and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302, which crashed shortly after leaving Addis Ababa in March 2019. Together they killed 346 people.

**Starliner**
Boeing's crew capsule built for NASA's Commercial Crew Program, a rival to SpaceX's Crew Dragon. Its first crewed test flight launched in June 2024, but thruster failures and helium leaks led NASA to send it back to Earth without its crew.

**Sunita Williams and Barry "Butch" Wilmore**
The two NASA astronauts who flew Starliner's June 2024 crewed test flight to the International Space Station. Their planned roughly week-long mission stretched to about nine months, and they eventually returned aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon.

**John Barnett and Joshua Dean**
Two whistleblowers who raised quality and safety concerns about Boeing aircraft production and died in 2024. Barnett was a former Boeing quality manager, and Dean had worked at the fuselage supplier Spirit AeroSystems.

**Dave Calhoun**
Boeing's CEO from 2020 to 2024, who took over after the 737 MAX crashes and announced his departure amid the fallout from the Alaska Airlines door plug incident. He oversaw the company's 2022 headquarters move.

**Move from Chicago to Arlington, Virginia**
In 2022 Boeing announced it would move its corporate headquarters from Chicago to Arlington, Virginia, putting it closer to federal regulators and its Pentagon customers.

**iPad training course**
A 2019 revelation that pilots switching to the 737 MAX from earlier 737 models got only a short iPad-based course on the differences, which said little about MCAS, instead of simulator training.

**Lockheed Martin documents scandal**
In the early 2000s Boeing was investigated for improperly getting proprietary documents from rival bidder Lockheed Martin during a U.S. Air Force rocket-launch contract competition. That competition pitted Boeing's Delta IV against Lockheed's Atlas V.

**Air Force tanker contract**
An early-2000s deal worth roughly twenty billion dollars for about one hundred refueling tanker aircraft based on the Boeing 767, which Boeing would build at its Puget Sound facilities in Washington State. The deal later fell apart amid an ethics scandal.

**Puget Sound**
The region around Seattle, Washington, home to Boeing's major commercial airplane factories in Everett and Renton. It is where Boeing historically built most of its jetliners.

**Brazilian airline merger stake**
Boeing once considered buying a stake in a proposed merger between two Brazilian airlines, which worried antitrust regulators.

**1991 Nobel Peace Prize**
Suu Kyi won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991 for her nonviolent struggle for democracy in Myanmar (Burma). She was under house arrest at the time, so her sons accepted it for her, and she gave her acceptance lecture only in 2012.

**House arrest**
The military junta first placed her under house arrest in 1989 and held her at her family's lakeside home on Inya Lake in Yangon for about 15 of the next 21 years. She was finally released in November 2010.

**National League for Democracy (NLD)**
The pro-democracy party she co-founded in 1988 and led. It won the 1990 election, which the junta ignored, and later swept the 2015 and 2020 elections.

**State Counsellor**
A post created in 2016, after the NLD's 2015 victory, so that Suu Kyi could lead the government even though she could not be president. She held it until the 2021 coup and was Myanmar's de facto leader.

**2008 constitution's presidential bar**
The military-drafted 2008 constitution bars anyone whose spouse or children are foreign nationals from becoming president. The clause was widely seen as aimed at Suu Kyi, whose late husband, the Oxford scholar Michael Aris, was British, as are their two sons.

**Rohingya crisis**
Suu Kyi was sharply criticized internationally for refusing to condemn, or even discuss, the military's violent campaign against the Rohingya Muslim minority in Rakhine State. In 2019 she personally defended Myanmar against genocide charges at the International Court of Justice, and several honors given to her were revoked.

**8888 Uprising**
The 1988 mass pro-democracy uprising, named for its peak on August 8, 1988. Suu Kyi had returned to Burma that year to care for her dying mother, and she emerged as the movement's leader.

**Shwedagon Pagoda speech**
On August 26, 1988, Suu Kyi made her first major political speech, to a crowd of about half a million people at the Shwedagon Pagoda, Yangon's great gilded Buddhist stupa. The speech launched her as a national figure.

**"Daw"**
A Burmese honorific for an older or respected woman, roughly "Madam" or "Aunt." She is commonly called "Daw Aung San Suu Kyi," or simply "The Lady."

**Aung San**
Her father, the general who led Burma's independence movement and is considered the founder of the modern nation. He was assassinated in 1947, when she was two, and his legacy gave her enormous popular appeal.

**2021 coup and imprisonment**
On February 1, 2021, the Tatmadaw (military) under Min Aung Hlaing overthrew her government and detained her. The junta then charged her with a long list of offenses, beginning with illegally importing walkie-talkies, and sentenced her to decades in prison.

**Freedom from Fear**
Her best-known essay and the title of a 1991 collection of her writings. It argues that "it is not power that corrupts but fear," the fear of losing power for those who hold it and the fear of punishment for those subject to it.

**Keir Starmer**
The leader of the Labour Party since 2020, succeeding Jeremy Corbyn. He led the party to a landslide victory in the July 2024 general election and became Prime Minister, succeeding the Conservative Rishi Sunak.

**Opposition to the Conservatives**
Labour is the main center-left party in the United Kingdom and the traditional rival of the Conservative (Tory) Party. It served as the official opposition from 2010 until its 2024 election win, and this rivalry is the usual giveaway.

**Jeremy Corbyn and antisemitism**
Corbyn, Labour's left-wing leader from 2015 to 2020, was suspended in 2020 and then denied the party whip after downplaying a report from the Equality and Human Rights Commission that found the party had failed to deal with antisemitism. He was expelled in 2024 after announcing he would run as an independent in his Islington North seat, which he went on to win.

**2019 general election**
Under Corbyn, Labour suffered a landslide defeat to Boris Johnson's Conservatives in 2019, winning only 202 seats, its fewest since 1935. Many traditionally Labour seats in northern England, the so-called "Red Wall," flipped to the Conservatives.

**Shami Chakrabarti**
A human rights lawyer and former director of the group Liberty who led a 2016 inquiry into antisemitism and other forms of racism within Labour. Corbyn then nominated her for a peerage in the House of Lords, which critics saw as a reward and which undermined trust in the inquiry.

**Beergate**
A 2022 controversy over Keir Starmer and his deputy Angela Rayner being filmed with beer and a takeaway meal at a gathering in Durham during COVID-19 lockdown restrictions in 2021. Durham police investigated and found no rule had been broken. It was the Labour counterpart to the Conservatives' "Partygate" scandal.

**Sadiq Khan**
The Labour Mayor of London since 2016 and the first Muslim mayor of a major Western capital. During a 2019 feud on Twitter, Donald Trump called him a "stone cold loser."

**Rachel Reeves and the "non-dom" loophole**
Reeves, Labour's Shadow Chancellor who became Chancellor of the Exchequer in 2024, promoted a pledge to abolish "non-domicile" tax status, which let wealthy UK residents avoid UK tax on income earned abroad.

**Fatboy Slim violin lessons**
Keir Starmer has said in interviews that as a child he took violin lessons alongside Norman Cook, the musician later known as the DJ Fatboy Slim.

**October 2022 polling lead**
During the turmoil of Liz Truss's short premiership and the fallout from her mini-budget, polls in October 2022 showed Labour leading the Conservatives by around 30 points, a level not seen in decades.

**Defeating Marine Le Pen (2017 and 2022)**
Macron beat far-right leader Marine Le Pen in the runoffs of two French presidential elections. In May 2017 he won about 66 percent of the vote against her as the National Front candidate, and in the 2022 rematch he defeated her again, by then leading the renamed National Rally, to win a second term.

**En Marche! and Renaissance**
The centrist political movement Macron founded in April 2016, whose initials match his own. It was renamed La République En Marche! after his 2017 victory and Renaissance in 2022, and it leads the centrist Ensemble coalition in Parliament.

**2023 pension reform, Article 49.3, and Élisabeth Borne**
In March 2023, Macron's government raised the retirement age from 62 to 64 by using Article 49.3 of the French Constitution, which lets the government pass a bill without a vote in the National Assembly. The move sparked mass strikes and protests, and the government of Prime Minister Élisabeth Borne, only the second woman to hold the post, narrowly survived the resulting no-confidence votes.

**Yellow Vest protests (gilets jaunes)**
A protest movement that began in November 2018 against a planned fuel tax increase and broadened into anger over the cost of living and Macron's perceived elitism. Protesters wearing the yellow high-visibility vests French drivers must carry occupied traffic roundabouts across France, and some protests in Paris turned violent.

**2019–2020 pension strikes**
Macron's first-term plan to merge France's 42 separate pension systems into a single points-based system triggered one of the longest transportation strikes in modern French history, organized by unions including the CGT. The plan was suspended in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic.

**"Jupiterian" president**
Macron said he wanted to be a "Jupiterian" president, comparing himself to Jupiter, the king of the Roman gods, who stays above the everyday fray. Critics used the label to attack him as aloof and arrogant; his 2017 official portrait notably included two smartphones on his desk.

**Rothschild banker and the Nestlé–Pfizer deal**
After graduating from the elite ENA school and working as a civil servant, Macron became an investment banker at Rothschild & Co. He made his fortune by leading Nestlé's 2012 purchase of Pfizer's baby-food business, a deal worth about $12 billion.

**Minister of Economy under François Hollande**
Macron served as Minister of the Economy, Industry and Digital Affairs from 2014 in the Socialist government of Prime Minister Manuel Valls under President François Hollande. He resigned in 2016 to launch his own presidential campaign.

**Benalla affair**
A 2018 scandal involving Alexandre Benalla, a security aide to Macron who was filmed beating protesters while wearing a police helmet at a May Day demonstration in Paris. The revelation that he had been only lightly punished caused Macron's approval ratings to drop.

**Great National Debate and closing the ENA**
In response to the Yellow Vest protests, Macron launched the "great national debate" in 2019, a series of town halls and public consultations across France. He later announced the closure of the École nationale d'administration (ENA), the elite civil service school he had attended, replacing it with a new institute.

**Samuel Paty and French secularism**
Samuel Paty was a schoolteacher beheaded near Paris in October 2020 after showing his students caricatures of the Prophet Muhammad during a class on free speech. Macron defended secularism (laïcité) and the right to publish the cartoons, prompting protests and boycotts in some Muslim-majority countries.

**AUKUS submarine dispute**
In September 2021, Australia canceled a multibillion-dollar deal to buy French submarines in favor of nuclear-powered submarines under the new AUKUS pact with the United States and United Kingdom. France responded by recalling its ambassadors to the U.S. and Australia.

**"We must not humiliate Russia"**
A 2022 remark by Macron arguing that Russia should not be humiliated so that a diplomatic exit from the war in Ukraine would remain possible. Ukrainian officials and other critics condemned the statement.

**Hoodie war-room photos**
In March 2022, early in the Russian invasion of Ukraine, official photos showed an unshaven Macron in jeans and a hoodie in the Élysée Palace. Critics mocked them as an attempt to imitate Volodymyr Zelenskyy's wartime look.

**Brigitte Macron's official status**
In 2017, Macron faced backlash, including a petition, over plans to create an official "first lady" role for his wife Brigitte, his former high school teacher. The plan came while he was pushing a law to "moralize" politics, including banning lawmakers from employing family members, and he settled for a transparency charter instead.

**April 6 Youth Movement**
An Egyptian activist group founded in 2008 to support a planned April 6 strike by textile workers in the industrial city of Mahalla al-Kubra. It modeled its nonviolent tactics and clenched-fist logo on Otpor!, the Serbian student movement that helped topple Slobodan Milošević, and it played a leading role in the 2011 revolution.

**Abdel Fattah el-Sisi**
The army chief who led the military's overthrow of President Mohamed Morsi in 2013 and became Egypt's president in 2014. His rule has been marked by harsh repression of dissent and a struggling economy.

**Mohamed Morsi and the Muslim Brotherhood**
Morsi, a leader of the Islamist Muslim Brotherhood, won the 2012 presidential runoff to become Egypt's first democratically elected president. After mass protests against his rule, the military removed him in July 2013, and he died in court in 2019 while on trial.

**Hosni Mubarak**
Egypt's president from 1981 until he was forced to resign during the 2011 revolution. In June 2012 he was sentenced to life in prison for complicity in the killing of protesters, though the conviction was later overturned.

**2012 presidential election**
Egypt's first free presidential election after Mubarak's fall. Its runoff pitted Morsi, the Muslim Brotherhood's candidate, against Ahmed Shafik, a former air force commander who had served as Mubarak's last prime minister, and Morsi narrowly won.

**Freedom and Justice Party**
The political party founded by the Muslim Brotherhood in 2011. It won the largest share of seats in the 2011–2012 parliamentary elections and was later dissolved by court order after Morsi's ouster.

**Amr Moussa**
A former Egyptian foreign minister and secretary-general of the Arab League, who was an early front-runner in the 2012 presidential race. He lost support during the campaign and failed to make the runoff.

**Tamarod**
Arabic for "rebellion," a grassroots campaign launched in 2013 that claimed to have gathered over 20 million signatures demanding Morsi's resignation. Its mass protests on June 30, 2013 preceded the military coup that removed him.

**Metrojet Flight 9268**
A Russian charter flight from the Red Sea resort of Sharm el-Sheikh to St. Petersburg that broke apart over the Sinai Peninsula in October 2015, killing all 224 people on board. The Sinai branch of the Islamic State claimed responsibility for planting a bomb on the plane.

**EgyptAir hijacking and the iPhone-case bomb**
In March 2016, Seif Eldin Mustafa hijacked an EgyptAir domestic flight from Alexandria to Cairo and forced it to land in Larnaca, Cyprus. His "suicide belt" turned out to be fake, made of iPhone cases, and all passengers were released unharmed.

**Sisi's "sell myself" speech and the eBay listing**
In a 2016 speech about Egypt's economic troubles, Sisi declared that he would sell himself if it would help the country. Mocking Egyptians then listed him for sale on eBay before the listing was removed.

**Sisi's red carpet**
In 2016 Sisi was criticized for having a red carpet several kilometers long unrolled along a road for his motorcade at a time of economic austerity. His government defended it as a reusable carpet used for official ceremonies.

**Anwar al-Balkimy's nose job**
A member of parliament from the Salafist Nour Party who claimed in 2012 that he had been beaten and robbed by gunmen. It emerged that his bandaged face was actually the result of a nose job, and he resigned from the party in disgrace.

**Hazem Salah Abu Ismail**
A popular Salafist preacher disqualified from the 2012 presidential race because his mother had held United States citizenship, which Egyptian election rules prohibited for a candidate's parents.

**2011 attack on the Israeli embassy**
In September 2011, protesters in Cairo broke into the building housing Israel's embassy, forcing the evacuation of the ambassador and most staff. The attack followed anger over the killing of Egyptian border guards during an Israeli pursuit of militants.

**Justin Trudeau**
The Liberal Party leader who became Canada's prime minister in 2015, governing from the capital, Ottawa. He is the son of former prime minister Pierre Trudeau and is the most common giveaway for this country in current events questions.

**"Freedom Convoy" and the Emergencies Act**
In early 2022, truckers and supporters protesting COVID-19 vaccine mandates occupied downtown Ottawa and blockaded border crossings. Trudeau responded by declaring a national public order emergency under the Emergencies Act, the first time that law had ever been used.

**James Smith Cree Nation stabbings**
In September 2022, the worst mass stabbing in Canadian history took place on the James Smith Cree Nation and in the nearby village of Weldon in Saskatchewan, killing 11 people. Brothers Myles and Damien Sanderson were the suspects, and the attacks took place at 13 separate locations; Damien was found dead and Myles died in police custody soon after his arrest.

**Jagmeet Singh and the New Democratic Party (NDP)**
Jagmeet Singh is the leader of the left-leaning New Democratic Party, one of Canada's major national parties. When photos of Trudeau in blackface and brownface surfaced in 2019, including one from a school yearbook, Singh said they showed a "pattern of behavior."

**Bloc Québécois**
A federal political party that runs candidates only in Quebec and supports Quebec sovereignty. It is a frequent clue for Canada's party system alongside the Liberals, Conservatives, and NDP.

**Pierre Trudeau and the October Crisis**
Pierre Trudeau was prime minister for most of the period from 1968 to 1984. In the 1970 October Crisis, the Quebec separatist group FLQ kidnapped British diplomat James Cross and Quebec minister Pierre Laporte, and Trudeau used the War Measures Act during peacetime, famously saying "just watch me" when asked how far he would go.

**"Fuddle duddle" and the "walk in the snow"**
Two famous Pierre Trudeau episodes. In 1971 he was accused of swearing in the House of Commons and claimed he had only said "fuddle duddle," and in 1984 he said he decided to retire after a long walk in the snow.

**Residential schools and Pope Francis's visit**
In 2021, possible unmarked graves were found with ground-penetrating radar at former residential schools, church-run boarding schools that Indigenous children had been forced to attend. In July 2022, Pope Francis visited Canada on what he called a "penitential pilgrimage" to apologize for the Catholic Church's role in the schools.

**Whisky War and Hans Island**
A long and mostly friendly dispute with Denmark over tiny Hans Island between Greenland and Canada's Ellesmere Island, in which the two sides took turns leaving bottles of liquor on the island. In June 2022, the countries agreed to split the island, giving Canada a land border with Denmark.

**Meng Wanzhou**
The chief financial officer of the Chinese tech company Huawei, nicknamed the "Princess of Huawei." She was arrested in Vancouver in 2018 on a U.S. extradition request and released in 2021 after reaching a deal with U.S. prosecutors.

**September 2021 snap election and the gravel incident**
Trudeau called an early federal election for September 2021, and the Liberals won another minority government. During a campaign stop in London, Ontario, a protester threw gravel at him.

**Pierre Poilievre**
A politician elected leader of Canada's Conservative Party in 2022. He was criticized for promoting Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies as a way to "opt out of inflation."

**Julie Payette**
A former astronaut who served as Governor General, the representative of the British monarch in Canada. She resigned in January 2021 after a review found she had created a toxic workplace and mistreated her staff.

**William Amos**
A Liberal member of Parliament from Quebec who in 2021 was accidentally seen naked on camera during a virtual session of the House of Commons. Weeks later, he was caught on camera urinating during another virtual session.

**Fairy Creek protests**
Protests and blockades on Vancouver Island in British Columbia against a logging company cutting old-growth forest in the Fairy Creek watershed. They led to more than a thousand arrests, among the largest acts of civil disobedience in Canadian history.

**1MDB scandal**
1Malaysia Development Berhad was a state investment fund set up in 2009 under Prime Minister Najib Razak. Billions of dollars were stolen from it and spent on luxury real estate, art, a yacht, and Hollywood films, making it one of the largest financial scandals in history.

**Jho Low**
The Malaysian financier accused of masterminding the 1MDB theft, including moving money without approval from Malaysia's central bank, Bank Negara. He became known for extravagant parties, including a birthday party where Britney Spears popped out of a cake, and for giving Leonardo DiCaprio a Picasso painting. He remains a fugitive.

**Najib Razak**
Malaysia's prime minister from 2009 to 2018 and leader of the UMNO party. About 700 million dollars from 1MDB-linked sources ended up in his personal accounts. He was arrested in July 2018 after his coalition lost power, and he was later convicted and imprisoned.

**Goldman Sachs**
The investment bank that raised billions in bonds for 1MDB, much of which was stolen. In 2020 Goldman agreed to pay a 2.9 billion dollar penalty to US authorities, and it reached a separate settlement with Malaysia. Its bankers Tim Leissner and Roger Ng faced US charges; Leissner pleaded guilty and Ng was convicted in 2022.

**Malaysia Airlines Flight 370**
A flight from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing that vanished in March 2014 with 239 people aboard. Investigators believe it turned south and crashed in the southern Indian Ocean, but the main wreckage has never been found.

**Malaysia Airlines Flight 17**
A flight from Amsterdam to Kuala Lumpur that was shot down over eastern Ukraine in July 2014, four months after MH370 disappeared, killing all 298 people aboard. An international investigation found it was hit by a Russian Buk missile fired from territory held by Russian-backed separatists.

**Assassination of Kim Jong-nam**
The estranged half-brother of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un was killed with the VX nerve agent at Kuala Lumpur International Airport in February 2017. Two women, Siti Aisyah of Indonesia and Doan Thi Huong of Vietnam, said they believed they were taking part in a TV prank. The murder charge against Siti Aisyah was dropped, and Doan Thi Huong pleaded guilty to a lesser charge.

**Mahathir Mohamad and the 2018 election**
Mahathir, who had already been prime minister from 1981 to 2003, returned at age 92 to lead the opposition Pakatan Harapan coalition to victory in 2018. It was the first time the Barisan Nasional coalition, dominated by UMNO, had lost power since independence.

**Anwar Ibrahim and Reformasi**
Anwar was Mahathir's deputy until he was fired and expelled from UMNO in 1998 and jailed on sodomy and corruption charges widely seen as politically motivated. His supporters launched the Reformasi reform movement. He was pardoned in 2018 and became prime minister in 2022.

**Yang di-Pertuan Agong**
The title of Malaysia's king, who is chosen in rotation from the hereditary rulers of nine Malay states and serves five-year terms. In January 2019, Sultan Muhammad V of Kelantan became the first king to abdicate, after reports that he had married a former Russian beauty queen.

**Petronas Towers**
Twin skyscrapers in Kuala Lumpur that were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004. They are named for the state oil company Petronas.

**Bumiputera**
The term, meaning "sons of the soil," for ethnic Malays and other Indigenous peoples of Malaysia. Affirmative action policies favoring Bumiputera over the wealthier ethnic Chinese and Indian minorities are a long-running source of racial tension.

**Fahmi Reza**
A Malaysian graphic artist arrested and convicted for posting a caricature of Najib Razak as a clown in 2016. The image spread widely as a symbol of protest against Najib's government.

**Batu Caves and Kek Lok Si Temple**
The Batu Caves, near Kuala Lumpur, are limestone caves containing a major Hindu temple complex and a giant golden statue of the god Murugan. Kek Lok Si is a large Buddhist temple near George Town on the island of Penang.

**Borneo, Sarawak, and Mount Kinabalu**
Malaysia is split between the Malay Peninsula, east of the Strait of Malacca, and the northern part of the island of Borneo. Its Bornean state of Sarawak borders Brunei and Indonesian Kalimantan, and Mount Kinabalu in the state of Sabah is its highest peak.

**Justice and Development Party (AKP)**
The conservative, Islamist-rooted party Erdoğan co-founded in 2001 and has led ever since. The AKP won the 2002 elections and has governed Turkey continuously, first with Erdoğan as Prime Minister (2003–2014) and then as President.

**President of Turkey / Prime Minister of Turkey**
Erdoğan served as Turkey's Prime Minister from 2003 to 2014 and has been President since 2014, making him the dominant Turkish politician of the 21st century. This is the usual giveaway for him.

**July 2016 coup attempt**
A failed military coup against Erdoğan in July 2016. The plotters called themselves the "Peace at Home Council" (after Atatürk's motto "Peace at home, peace in the world"), seized the state broadcaster TRT, and occupied key sites in Istanbul and Ankara before the attempt collapsed. It was followed by mass purges of the military, judiciary, schools, and press.

**Fethullah Gülen and the Hizmet movement**
Gülen was a Muslim cleric living in Pennsylvania whose Hizmet ("Service") movement was once allied with the AKP. The two broke after 2013 corruption investigations targeted Erdoğan's government, and Erdoğan blamed Gülen for the 2016 coup, purging tens of thousands of suspected Hizmet members.

**2017 constitutional referendum**
A referendum held after the 2016 coup attempt that narrowly approved changing Turkey from a parliamentary to a presidential system. It gave Erdoğan sweeping executive powers, abolished the post of Prime Minister, and reset the term count so he could keep running.

**2023 election and Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu**
Erdoğan won a runoff in May 2023 against Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu, leader of the secularist CHP (Republican People's Party) and candidate of the opposition Nation Alliance. Kılıçdaroğlu's supporters often made a heart gesture with their hands, and Erdoğan's campaign was accused of showing a doctored video linking his opponent to the Kurdish militant PKK.

**Table of Six**
The nickname for the six-party opposition bloc (the Nation Alliance) that united against Erdoğan in 2023. It included the DEVA party of Ali Babacan and the Future Party of Ahmet Davutoğlu, both founded by former senior AKP figures who broke with Erdoğan.

**Operation Sledgehammer (Balyoz)**
An alleged secularist military coup plan from 2003 aimed at toppling the AKP government. Hundreds of officers were convicted in the resulting trials, which were later overturned amid claims that the evidence was forged, and the case is tied to struggles with Turkey's secular "deep state."

**Mayor of Istanbul and the 1997 Siirt poem**
Erdoğan first gained prominence as the Islamist Welfare Party mayor of Istanbul (1994–1998). After reciting a poem attributed to Ziya Gökalp at a 1997 rally in Siirt, with lines comparing mosques to barracks and minarets to bayonets, he was convicted of inciting religious hatred, jailed, and banned from politics. A 2002 constitutional amendment let him enter parliament and become Prime Minister.

**Jailing of journalists and the seizure of Zaman**
Erdoğan's government has imprisoned hundreds of journalists. In March 2016 authorities seized the Gülen-linked newspaper Zaman, prompting Morton Abramowitz and Eric Edelman to write in the Washington Post that "democracy cannot flourish under" him.

**"White Palace" (Ak Saray)**
The enormous presidential palace complex Erdoğan built in Ankara, opened in 2014 at a cost of about $615 million. It was controversial because it was built on the protected Atatürk Forest Farm land, in defiance of court orders.

**Shimon Peres and the 2009 Davos panel**
At the 2009 World Economic Forum in Davos, Erdoğan confronted Israeli President Shimon Peres over the Gaza war, telling him "when it comes to killing, you know well how to kill," and then walked off the stage.

**Sweden joining NATO**
Erdoğan long blocked Sweden's NATO membership, accusing it of harboring Kurdish militants. He reversed course in 2023, sending the accession protocol to the Turkish parliament, which ratified it in early 2024.

**Lifting the headscarf ban**
Erdoğan's government lifted Turkey's long-standing ban on Islamic headscarves in universities and public institutions. This caused tension with the secular establishment and military, which saw itself as the guardian of Atatürk's secularism.

**Joseph Votel and U.S. tensions**
Erdoğan lashed out at General Joseph Votel, head of U.S. Central Command, after Votel said the post-coup purges had jailed many of the Pentagon's Turkish military contacts. The exchange reflected strained U.S.–Turkey relations after the coup.

**Viktor Orbán**
Hungary's long-serving prime minister, in office from 1998 to 2002 and again from 2010. He is known for nationalist, anti-immigration policies and for clashing with the European Union over the rule of law and democracy.

**Fidesz**
Orbán's party. It began in 1988 as a liberal youth movement opposing communism but became a right-wing nationalist party, and it has used large parliamentary majorities to rewrite Hungary's constitution and election rules.

**Illiberal democracy**
A term Orbán openly embraced in a 2014 speech, saying Hungary would build an "illiberal state." It describes a system that holds elections but weakens checks on power such as independent courts, a free press, and civil society.

**"Make Europe Great Again"**
The slogan of Hungary's rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union from July to December 2024, borrowed from Donald Trump's "Make America Great Again." It reflected Orbán's close ties to Trump and his goal of pushing the EU in a more nationalist direction.

**George Soros and the "Soros Empire"**
Soros is a Hungarian-born American billionaire who funds liberal causes. Orbán's government has made him a constant target, blaming his so-called "Soros Empire" for encouraging migration to Europe, passing "Stop Soros" laws, and driving the Soros-founded Central European University out of Budapest.

**David Pressman**
The openly gay U.S. ambassador to Hungary under President Joe Biden. He marched in Budapest Pride, which was seen as a rebuke to the Orbán government's laws restricting LGBTQ content.

**Budapest Pride and LGBTQ laws**
Orbán's government passed a 2021 law banning depictions of homosexuality for minors and, in 2025, a law banning Pride events. Budapest's mayor helped organize the 2025 march anyway, and it drew a very large crowd.

**Budapest**
Hungary's capital and largest city, formed by joining Buda and Pest on either side of the Danube River. It is home to the Hungarian Parliament Building.

**Migration and the border fence**
During the 2015 European migrant crisis, Orbán's government built a razor-wire fence along Hungary's southern border with Serbia and Croatia. Opposing migration has been a core part of his politics ever since.

**Katalin Novák pardon scandal**
Novák, a Fidesz ally, was Hungary's first female president. She resigned in February 2024 after it emerged that she had pardoned a man convicted of helping cover up child sexual abuse at a children's home, a rare major scandal for Orbán's camp.

**"Party of God"**
The literal meaning of the Arabic name Hezbollah. It is a Shia Islamist political party and militant group based in Lebanon, and it is one of the most powerful non-state armed groups in the Middle East.

**Iranian Revolutionary Guards**
Hezbollah was formed in the early 1980s, during the Lebanese Civil War and after Israel's 1982 invasion of Lebanon, with help from Iranian Revolutionary Guard troops sent to Lebanon's Bekaa Valley. Iran has remained its main sponsor, supplying money, training, and weapons.

**Revolutionary Justice Organization and Organization of the Oppressed on Earth**
Names used by groups linked to Hezbollah to claim responsibility for kidnappings and attacks in the 1980s, including the taking of Western hostages in Beirut. They are generally seen as cover names or fronts for Hezbollah.

**Muhammad Hussein Fadlallah**
An influential Lebanese Shia cleric often described as Hezbollah's spiritual mentor, although he denied holding any formal role in the group. The group's political and military leader during that period was its secretary-general, Hassan Nasrallah.

**Hassan Nasrallah**
Hezbollah's secretary-general from 1992 until Israel killed him in an airstrike on Beirut in September 2024. He led the group through the 2000 Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon and the 2006 war with Israel, and he was succeeded by Naim Qassem.

**Alliance with Amal**
Amal is Lebanon's other major Shia party. In the 2005 parliamentary elections, Hezbollah and Amal ran a joint list that swept the seats in southern Lebanon, making Hezbollah a powerful force in Lebanon's parliament as well as on the battlefield.

**Southern Lebanon and conflict with Israel**
Southern Lebanon, which borders Israel, is Hezbollah's main base. From there the group fought Israel's occupation until 2000, fought the 2006 Lebanon War, and has repeatedly fired rockets into northern Israel, including after the October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel.

**2024 pager and walkie-talkie attacks**
In September 2024, thousands of pagers and walkie-talkies used by Hezbollah members exploded at almost the same time across Lebanon, killing and wounding many people. The attacks, widely attributed to Israel, came just before Israel's major escalation against the group that fall.

**Assassination of Rafic Hariri**
Former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafic Hariri was killed by a massive truck bomb in Beirut in February 2005. A UN-backed Special Tribunal for Lebanon later convicted Hezbollah members of the killing, though the group denied involvement.

**1983 Beirut barracks bombing**
In October 1983, suicide truck bombs destroyed the barracks of U.S. Marines and French paratroopers in Beirut, killing 241 American and 58 French service members. The attack was claimed by a group calling itself Islamic Jihad and is widely attributed to the militants who formed Hezbollah, with Iranian backing.

**Jacinda Ardern**
The Labour Party leader who was prime minister of New Zealand from 2017 to 2023. She was internationally praised for her response to the Christchurch shootings and to COVID-19, and she resigned unexpectedly in January 2023. She is the most common giveaway for the country.

**Christchurch mosque shootings**
On March 15, 2019, a white supremacist gunman killed 51 people at the Al Noor Mosque and the Linwood Islamic Centre in Christchurch, livestreaming the first attack on Facebook. Ardern's government quickly banned most semi-automatic weapons in response.

**Chris Hipkins**
A Labour politician who succeeded Ardern as prime minister in January 2023. He served for less than a year, until Labour lost the October 2023 election and Christopher Luxon of the National Party became prime minister.

**Judith Collins and the National Party**
Collins led the center-right National Party, the main opposition to Labour, into the 2020 election. She resigned as leader in November 2021 after a scandal in which she abruptly demoted rival Simon Bridges over an old allegation of inappropriate comments.

**2020 election landslide**
In the October 2020 general election, Ardern's Labour Party won a landslide over Collins's National Party. It became the first party to win an outright majority under New Zealand's mixed-member proportional (MMP) system.

**Winston Peters and New Zealand First**
Peters leads the populist New Zealand First party. He served as deputy prime minister in Ardern's first government from 2017 to 2020 and left the office after his party failed to win any seats in the 2020 election.

**2023 FIFA Women's World Cup**
New Zealand co-hosted the tournament with Australia, and the opening match was played at Auckland's Eden Park. Hours before it began, a gunman shot and killed two people at a construction site in central Auckland, New Zealand's largest city.

**Hei-tiki and the necktie dispute**
In 2021, Te Pāti Māori co-leader Rawiri Waititi was ejected from Parliament for refusing to wear a necktie, which he called a "colonial noose." He wore a hei-tiki, a traditional Māori greenstone pendant, instead. Parliament later dropped the requirement for male members to wear ties.

**Auckland Anniversary Weekend floods and "media drongos"**
Record rainfall caused deadly flooding in Auckland in late January 2023, during the Auckland Anniversary holiday weekend. Auckland mayor Wayne Brown was criticized for his slow response and for a leaked text calling reporters "media drongos," Australian and New Zealand slang for fools.

**Tooth Fairy as an essential worker**
During the strict COVID-19 lockdown in April 2020, Ardern reassured children that the Tooth Fairy and the Easter Bunny counted as essential workers. New Zealand's strict elimination strategy kept COVID cases very low early in the pandemic.

**"Sorry sunshine, wrong place"**
The response a New Zealand official gave at an October 2020 press conference to an American questioner who denied COVID-19. It is often cited as an example of the country's blunt dismissal of pandemic misinformation.

**Climate emergency declaration**
In December 2020, Ardern's government declared a climate emergency and pledged that the public sector would become carbon-neutral by 2025. Judith Collins opposed the declaration, calling it a gesture rather than real action.

**Wellington and Aotearoa**
Wellington is New Zealand's capital, while Auckland is its largest city. Aotearoa, the Māori name for the country, is an accepted answer.

**"I need ammunition, not a ride"**
Zelenskyy's reported reply to an American offer to evacuate him from Kyiv at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. The line became a symbol of Ukrainian defiance.

**President of Ukraine**
Zelenskyy was elected president of Ukraine in 2019 and has led the country through Russia's full-scale invasion. Russia calls the invasion a "special military operation."

**Celebrity background and Servant of the People**
Before entering politics, Zelenskyy was a comedian and actor. He starred in the TV series Servant of the People, in which he played a teacher who unexpectedly becomes president, and his real party took its name from the show.

**December 2022 address to Congress**
Zelenskyy's first trip abroad after the invasion began was to Washington. In his speech to a joint session of Congress, he presented a Ukrainian flag signed by soldiers on the front line in Bakhmut and received a U.S. flag that had flown over the Capitol.

**March 2022 virtual address to Congress**
In a video speech to the U.S. Congress, Zelenskyy asked for a no-fly zone over Ukraine, invoking Pearl Harbor and 9/11.

**"Tear down this wall"**
In a March 2022 speech to the German Bundestag, Zelenskyy echoed Ronald Reagan's famous challenge to Mikhail Gorbachev and addressed it to Chancellor Olaf Scholz. He also criticized Germany for backing the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline with Russia.

**Nord Stream 2**
A natural gas pipeline from Russia to Germany under the Baltic Sea. Zelenskyy condemned it as a tool that made Europe dependent on Russia and funded its war.

**"Never again" proving "worthless"**
In a speech, Zelenskyy argued that the world's post–World War II promise of "never again" was being shown to be worthless by Russia's atrocities in Ukraine.

**United24**
A fundraising platform Zelenskyy launched in May 2022 to collect donations from around the world for Ukraine's defense, medical aid, and reconstruction.

**Vilnius NATO summit and cluster munitions**
At the July 2023 NATO summit in Vilnius, Lithuania, Zelenskyy thanked Joe Biden for the U.S. decision to send Ukraine cluster munitions. The decision was controversial because these weapons can leave unexploded bomblets that endanger civilians.

**Wagner Group mutiny**
After the failed June 2023 rebellion against Moscow by Yevgeny Prigozhin's Wagner Group mercenaries, Zelenskyy said the mutiny showed that Vladimir Putin was "weak."

**Snake Island**
A small Ukrainian island in the Black Sea that became famous at the start of the war when its defenders defied a Russian warship. In a video marking 500 days of the full-scale invasion, Zelenskyy laid flowers at a memorial there.

**Ali Khamenei and Tehran**
Ayatollah Ali Khamenei has been Iran's Supreme Leader, the country's highest political and religious authority, since 1989. Tehran is Iran's capital. Iran is the largest Shiite Muslim country, and its government is a theocracy set up after the 1979 Islamic Revolution. Khamenei and Tehran are the most common giveaways.

**Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA)**
The 2015 nuclear deal between Iran and the P5+1 (the U.S., UK, France, Russia, China and Germany). Iran agreed to limit uranium enrichment, cut its enriched-uranium stockpile, and allow international inspections in exchange for relief from sanctions. Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif negotiated it for Iran. Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from the deal in 2018, which Khamenei sharply condemned.

**Uranium enrichment and the IAEA**
Western concern about Iran's nuclear program centers on its enrichment of uranium, which could be used to build nuclear weapons. Nuclear agreements limited Iran to low enrichment levels, restricted enrichment to a single facility, banned new heavy-water facilities, and expanded monitoring by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

**Ebrahim Raisi's helicopter crash**
Raisi, a hardline cleric and former judiciary chief, won Iran's 2021 presidential election. He had been a member of the conservative Combatant Clergy Association. He died in a helicopter crash in northwestern Iran in May 2024, and First Vice President Mohammad Mokhber served as acting president until a new election was held.

**Masoud Pezeshkian**
A reformist politician and cardiac surgeon who won the 2024 snap presidential election held after Raisi's death. He defeated the hardline former nuclear negotiator Saeed Jalili in a runoff.

**Qasem Soleimani and the Quds Force**
Soleimani commanded the Quds Force, the branch of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that runs operations abroad. A U.S. drone strike killed him near Baghdad's airport in January 2020. In April 2019 the U.S. had designated the IRGC a terrorist organization. In March 2022 the IRGC fired missiles at Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan, drawing widespread condemnation.

**"Axis of Resistance" (Hezbollah, Hamas, Houthis)**
The name for Iran's network of allied militant groups opposed to Israel and the United States. Iran is the main sponsor of Lebanon's Hezbollah (led for decades by Hassan Nasrallah), the Palestinian group Hamas, and the Houthi rebels in Yemen.

**Hassan Rouhani**
A relatively moderate cleric who won Iran's 2013 presidential election, succeeding Mahmoud Ahmadinejad (a former mayor of Tehran). Rouhani's government negotiated both the 2013 interim nuclear deal and the 2015 JCPOA.

**Geneva interim agreement (Joint Plan of Action)**
A six-month interim nuclear deal reached in Geneva in November 2013. Iran agreed to dilute or convert its uranium enriched above 5% and accept more IAEA oversight in return for limited sanctions relief. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called it a "historic mistake." At the UN in 2012, Netanyahu had drawn a red line on a cartoon bomb diagram to warn against Iran's nuclear progress.

**Assassination of Ismail Haniyeh**
In July 2024, Hamas political leader Ismail Haniyeh was killed in Tehran, where he had come for Pezeshkian's inauguration. According to reports, the explosive had been hidden in advance in the guesthouse where he was staying. Israel was widely blamed and later acknowledged responsibility.

**Kerman bombing**
In January 2024, two suicide bombings struck crowds in the city of Kerman at a memorial marking the anniversary of Qasem Soleimani's death, killing nearly 100 people. The Islamic State (ISIS-K) claimed responsibility.

**Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752**
In January 2020, days after Soleimani's killing, Iranian air defenses accidentally shot down this passenger jet shortly after it took off from Tehran for Kyiv, killing all 176 people on board. Iran at first denied responsibility before admitting the mistake.

**Guardian Council and Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani**
The Guardian Council is the body of clerics and jurists that vets candidates for Iranian elections. Before the 2013 election it cut hundreds of registered candidates down to eight and disqualified Rafsanjani, a former president who led Iran from 1989 to 1997.

**Tanker incidents of 2019**
In June 2019 Iran was accused of attacking tankers near the Strait of Hormuz, including the Japanese-owned Kokuka Courageous. That July, British forces seized the Iranian tanker Grace 1 off Gibraltar. In May 2020, an Iranian navy ship accidentally hit the Iranian support vessel Konarak with a missile during exercises, killing 19 sailors.

**Evin Prison**
A notorious Tehran prison used to hold political prisoners and detained foreign and dual nationals. One of them was the British-American-Iranian conservationist Morad Tahbaz, who went on a hunger strike there.

**Aung San Suu Kyi**
Myanmar's leading pro-democracy figure and the daughter of independence hero Aung San. She won the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize while under house arrest, which lasted for about 15 of the years between 1989 and 2010, and she later became the country's de facto leader. The military deposed and imprisoned her in the 2021 coup. She is the most common giveaway for Myanmar.

**Rohingya**
A mostly Muslim ethnic minority from western Myanmar. The Buddhist-majority state denies them citizenship and treats them as illegal immigrants from Bangladesh. Military "clearance operations," especially in 2017, killed thousands and drove hundreds of thousands across the border, and the UN and other bodies have described the campaign as genocide.

**Rakhine State**
The western coastal state, formerly called Arakan, where most Rohingya lived. It was the site of anti-Rohingya riots in 2012, of killings in Maungdaw township and elsewhere in 2014, and of the 2017 military crackdown. Aung San Suu Kyi's government was widely criticized for doing little to stop the atrocities there and for defending the army.

**National League for Democracy (NLD)**
The pro-democracy party led by Aung San Suu Kyi. It won the 1990 election, but the junta refused to hand over power. It later won 43 of the 44 seats it contested in the 2012 by-elections and swept the 2015 general election, defeating Thein Sein's military-backed USDP. Its 2020 landslide was the pretext for the 2021 coup.

**Naypyidaw**
Myanmar's purpose-built capital. The junta began moving the government there from Yangon (Rangoon), still the largest city, in 2005, and it was officially named the capital in 2006. Soldiers occupied Naypyidaw during the coup of February 1, 2021.

**Tatmadaw and the 2021 coup**
The Tatmadaw is Myanmar's armed forces. On February 1, 2021, it overthrew the elected NLD government. The coup's opening moments were famously caught in the background of a fitness instructor's aerobics video, and protesters adopted the three-finger salute from The Hunger Games, which led to arrests.

**Min Aung Hlaing**
The commander-in-chief of the Tatmadaw who led the 2021 coup and became Myanmar's military ruler. He also oversaw the 2017 campaign against the Rohingya and has been targeted by international sanctions and prosecutors.

**Walkie-talkie charges**
After the coup, the junta's first charge against Aung San Suu Kyi was illegally importing walkie-talkie radios found at her home without permission. This was followed by many other charges that together brought sentences of decades in prison.

**Bangladesh and Cox's Bazar**
Myanmar's western neighbor, to which most Rohingya refugees have fled. The refugee camps near the city of Cox's Bazar, such as Kutupalong, hold around a million Rohingya and are among the largest refugee settlements in the world.

**Thein Sein and Than Shwe**
Than Shwe was the junta leader who dissolved the ruling State Peace and Development Council in 2011 and handed power to a nominally civilian government. Thein Sein, a former general from the USDP party, was president from 2011 to 2016 and oversaw a period of reforms.

**Kachin, Karen, and Kokang conflicts**
Myanmar has fought ethnic insurgencies for decades. They include the Kachin independence movement in the far north, the Karen National Liberation Army in the southeast, and clashes with ethnic Chinese militias in the Kokang region near China. A 2015 Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement failed to end the fighting.

**8888 Uprising and SLORC**
A mass pro-democracy uprising named for its peak on August 8, 1988 (8/8/88). The military crushed it and took power as the State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC). SLORC then held the 1990 election, which the NLD won, and ignored the result.

**Saffron Revolution**
The 2007 protests, led largely by Buddhist monks named for the color of their robes, that broke out after the junta sharply raised fuel prices. The military violently put them down.

**Inn Din massacre and the Reuters journalists**
In 2017, soldiers and villagers killed ten Rohingya men in the Rakhine village of Inn Din during operations aimed at ARSA (the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army) militants. Reuters reporters Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo, who investigated the killings, were jailed in 2018 under the colonial-era Official Secrets Act. UN special rapporteur Yanghee Lee was barred from entering the country to investigate such abuses.

**State Counsellor and Htin Kyaw**
The 2008 constitution bars anyone whose children are foreign citizens from the presidency, which kept Aung San Suu Kyi from the office because her sons are British. After the 2015 election, her close ally Htin Kyaw succeeded Thein Sein as president, and the NLD created the post of State Counsellor in 2016 so she could lead the government.

**July 2023 coup**
On July 26, 2023, members of Niger's presidential guard detained President Mohamed Bazoum and seized power. The coup was the latest in a wave of military takeovers in the Sahel, and pro-junta crowds in the capital waved Russian flags and denounced France.

**Mohamed Bazoum**
