Cape Morris Jesup, in Peary Land, is Greenland's northernmost point and one of the northernmost land points on Earth. Peary Land is too dry to support an ice sheet. Cape Farewell is the island's southernmost point.

**Constituent country of Denmark: home rule and leaving the EEC**
Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark and is not independent. It gained home rule in 1979 and left the European Economic Community in 1985, mainly over fishing rules, but it still uses the Danish krone. Its official language is Greenlandic (Kalaallisut), and Danish is also widely used. In Greenlandic the island is called Kalaallit Nunaat.

**Erik the Red and the Norse settlements**
Erik the Red founded the first Norse colonies around 985 CE. He gave the mostly icy island the appealing name "Greenland" to attract settlers from Iceland. The Norse founded the Eastern and Western Settlements, which had died out by the 1400s. The ruins of Hvalsey Church, the best-preserved Norse building there, stand in the old Eastern Settlement. Gunnbjörn Ulfsson, a Norwegian blown off course, is credited with first sighting the island.

**U.S. purchase attempt and the WWII occupation**
After World War II the United States tried to buy Greenland from Denmark, and in 1946 the Truman administration offered $100 million, but Denmark refused. During the war, after Germany occupied Denmark, the U.S. took over Greenland's defense and built bases with code names beginning "Bluie." It also obtained cryolite, a mineral needed to refine aluminum, from the mine at Ivittuut.

**Gunnbjørn Fjeld**
The highest mountain in Greenland and in the entire Arctic, rising about 3,700 meters in the Watkins Range on the east coast. It is named for Gunnbjörn Ulfsson.

**Isua Greenstone Belt**
A belt of rocks in southwest Greenland, about 3.7–3.8 billion years old, among the oldest on Earth. Structures found there in 2016 were proposed as stromatolites, which would make them one of the oldest possible signs of life, though this claim is disputed.

**Alfred Wegener and Eismitte**
Wegener, the German scientist who proposed continental drift, died in Greenland in late 1930. He was returning from a supply trip to Eismitte ("mid-ice"), his expedition's research station in the center of the ice sheet.

**Camp Century and Dansgaard–Oeschger events**
Camp Century was a U.S. military base built inside tunnels in the ice sheet during the Cold War. Ice cores drilled there and later at other Greenland sites revealed Dansgaard–Oeschger events: sudden, intense warming spikes during the last glacial period.

**Kvanefjeld mining project**
A proposed rare-earth and uranium mine in southern Greenland. Opposition to it was the central issue of the 2021 election, which the Inuit Ataqatigiit party won, and the project was then halted.

**Disko Bay, Godhavn, and Sisimiut**
Disko Bay is a large bay on the west coast where several of Greenland's few towns are located. Godhavn (Qeqertarsuaq) on Disko Island was founded under the Royal Greenland Trade Department (KNI), the Danish colonial trading monopoly. Sisimiut, the second-largest town after Nuuk, is the northernmost port that stays ice-free all year.

**Thule and Dorset cultures**
The Dorset culture was an early Paleo-Eskimo people of the Arctic who lived in Greenland until the Thule people replaced them. The Thule spread east from Alaska around 1000–1300 CE and were the ancestors of the modern Inuit, who make up most of Greenland's population today.

**Big Bend National Park and the Rio Grande**
The Rio Grande forms Texas's border with Mexico. Big Bend National Park, in remote Brewster County, is named for a sharp bend the river makes, and it is the only U.S. nesting site of the Colima warbler. Brewster County is so large that it could hold the state of Connecticut.

**Austin**
The state capital, in central Texas. Lady Bird Lake, a reservoir on the Colorado River, runs through downtown, and nearby Bracken Cave holds the world's largest bat colony, millions of Mexican free-tailed bats.

**Houston and Buffalo Bayou**
Texas's largest city, the seat of Harris County, built along Buffalo Bayou near Galveston Bay. It is the largest U.S. city with no formal zoning laws, it was home to Enron, and its sprawl and pavement worsened the flooding from Hurricane Harvey in 2017.

**Brazos River**
A major river that flows southeast across central Texas into the Gulf of Mexico. It passes through Waco, where the historic Waco Suspension Bridge, finished in 1870, crosses it.

**Edwards Plateau and the Hill Country**
The Edwards Plateau is a limestone upland in south-central Texas whose eastern edge forms the scenic Hill Country, near Austin. German immigrants settled towns there such as New Braunfels and Fredericksburg in the 1840s.

**Permian Basin (Midland and Odessa)**
A huge oil- and gas-producing region in West Texas and southeastern New Mexico, centered on the cities of Midland and Odessa. It is the most productive oil field in the United States.

**Galveston hurricanes**
Galveston, an island city on the Gulf Coast, was struck in 1900 by the deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history, a hurricane that killed around 8,000 people. A seawall was then built to protect the city, but Hurricane Ike still caused heavy damage in 2008.

**Red River and the Panhandle**
The Red River forms most of the border between Texas and Oklahoma before flowing on to join the Atchafalaya and Mississippi in Louisiana. North of it, the Texas Panhandle, which contains Amarillo and Lubbock, borders Oklahoma's panhandle and covers much of the flat Llano Estacado (Staked Plain).

**Spindletop**
A salt dome oil field near Beaumont, close to Port Arthur, where a giant gusher in 1901 started the Texas oil boom. The discovery turned Texas into a center of the petroleum industry.

**Dallas-Fort Worth and the Barnett Shale**
The Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex, which includes Plano and Arlington, is the largest metropolitan area in Texas. It sits on top of the Barnett Shale, a formation with huge natural gas reserves that is hard to study and drill because of the city above it.

**Katy Freeway**
The section of Interstate 10 west of Houston, which has up to 26 lanes in places and is often called the widest highway in the United States.

**Guadalupe Peak**
The highest point in Texas, in the Guadalupe Mountains of West Texas near the New Mexico border.

**El Paso**
The westernmost major city in Texas, on the Rio Grande directly across the border from Ciudad Juárez, Mexico.

**Corpus Christi and the Coastal Bend**
Corpus Christi is a Gulf Coast port city in the Coastal Bend region, which, like Galveston, is often hit by hurricanes.

**Caddo Lake**
A cypress-swamp lake on Texas's eastern border with Louisiana. It is often described as the only large natural lake in Texas.

**Shared by Malaysia, Indonesia, and Brunei**
Borneo is the third-largest island in the world, after Greenland and New Guinea. It is the only island divided among three countries: Indonesia in the south, the Malaysian states in the north, and the small sultanate of Brunei on the northwest coast.

**Kalimantan**
The Indonesian name for Borneo, and the name for the Indonesian part of the island, which covers about three-quarters of it. It contains the Kapuas River, the longest river in Indonesia, and the city of Banjarmasin.

**Sabah and Sarawak**
The two Malaysian states on northern Borneo, often called East Malaysia. Sarawak lies to the west, with its capital at Kuching, and Sabah lies to the northeast. Malaysia also governs the small federal territory of Labuan off the coast.

**Mount Kinabalu and the Crocker Range**
Mount Kinabalu in Sabah is the highest mountain on Borneo and lies in the Crocker Range, protected by Kinabalu National Park. Low's Gully, a deep chasm on its summit plateau, shows signs of past glacial activity.

**Gunung Mulu National Park and its caves**
A park in Sarawak famous for its karst limestone landscape and huge caves. It holds the Sarawak Chamber, the largest underground chamber in the world, along with Clearwater Cave, one of the longest cave systems in the world, and Deer Cave, which has one of the largest cave passages known.

**Dayak people**
The collective name for the many indigenous peoples of Borneo's interior, especially in Sarawak and Kalimantan. Many have opposed the logging and deforestation of their lands.

**Nusantara, Indonesia's new capital**
Because Jakarta on the island of Java is sinking and overcrowded, President Joko Widodo announced in 2019 that Indonesia would build a new capital, Nusantara, in East Kalimantan on Borneo.

**Brunei and Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah**
The small, oil-rich sultanate on Borneo's north coast, ruled by Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah, one of the world's richest people. Its state ideology is Melayu Islam Beraja (MIB, "Malay Islamic Monarchy"), and its oil revenues, largely through Brunei Shell Petroleum (BSP), fund generous subsidies for its citizens.

**Makassar Strait, Wallace's Line, and Sulawesi**
The Makassar Strait separates Borneo from the island of Sulawesi to the east. Wallace's Line, the boundary between Asian and Australasian animal life, runs through this strait. Borneo also borders the Java Sea to the south and the Sulu Sea and Palawan to the northeast.

**Orangutans and deforestation**
Borneo is one of only two islands (with Sumatra) where orangutans live in the wild, and its population has fallen by about half because of logging and palm-oil plantations. The 2007 "Heart of Borneo" declaration by the three countries aimed to protect the island's ancient rainforest, which is often said to be about 140 million years old.

**Peat swamp forests and the Mega Rice Project**
Borneo has huge tropical peat swamp forests. Indonesia's Mega Rice Project in the 1990s drained large areas of them in Central Kalimantan to grow rice and failed. The draining and burning of peatlands releases huge amounts of carbon dioxide and has made Indonesia one of the world's largest emitters.

**The White Rajas and the Brooke family**
The British adventurer James Brooke was made Raja of Sarawak by the Sultan of Brunei in 1841, and his family ruled Sarawak as the "White Rajas" for about a century. Separately, northern Borneo (today's Sabah) was leased by local sultans to British interests and became British North Borneo.

**Bruno Manser and the Penan**
Bruno Manser was a Swiss environmentalist who lived with the nomadic Penan people of Sarawak and campaigned against logging on their land. He disappeared in 2000 and is presumed dead. His activism targeted the government of Sarawak's longtime chief minister Abdul Taib Mahmud, which oversaw massive deforestation.

**Danum Valley, dipterocarps, and kerangas**
Danum Valley in Sabah is a protected area of lowland rainforest. Borneo has the world's greatest diversity of dipterocarps, tall tropical hardwood trees that dominate its forests. Kerangas is a type of tropical heath forest that grows on poor, sandy soils on the island.

**Bre-X and the Busang mine**
In the 1990s, the Canadian company Bre-X claimed it had found a huge gold deposit at Busang in Kalimantan. The samples turned out to be faked, the mine was worthless, and the company collapsed in one of the biggest mining frauds in history.

**Grand Canyon and the Colorado River**
The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon in northern Arizona over millions of years, and the state's nickname is the "Grand Canyon State." John Wesley Powell led the first known expedition down the river through the canyon in 1869. This is the most common giveaway for Arizona.

**Grand Canyon trails and rocks (Bright Angel, Kaibab, Vishnu Schist)**
The Bright Angel Trail, which follows the Bright Angel Fault, and the Kaibab trails are the main hiking routes from the rim down into the Grand Canyon. At the bottom of the canyon lie very old metamorphic rocks such as the Vishnu Schist and the Brahma Schist, which are among the oldest rocks exposed there.

**Grand Canyon Skywalk**
A horseshoe-shaped glass walkway that sticks out over the edge of the Grand Canyon at Eagle Point, on the Hualapai Reservation. Visitors can look straight down through its glass floor.

**Phoenix, Maricopa County and the "Valley of the Sun"**
Phoenix is Arizona's capital and largest city, in Maricopa County, the state's most populous county. Its metropolitan area, called the "Valley of the Sun," includes cities such as Chandler, Glendale, Mesa and Scottsdale.

**Humphreys Peak**
Arizona's highest point, one of the San Francisco Peaks, a volcanic group near Flagstaff in northern Arizona.

**Painted Desert and Petrified Forest National Park**
The Painted Desert is a region of colorful, banded badlands in northeastern Arizona. Part of it lies in Petrified Forest National Park, which is known for its fossilized logs, turned to stone over millions of years.

**Tucson and Pima County**
Tucson is Arizona's second-largest city and the seat of Pima County, the state's second most populous county, in the Sonoran Desert of southern Arizona. Maricopa and Pima together hold most of the seats in the state legislature.

**Navajo Nation (Window Rock) and the Hopi Reservation**
The Navajo Nation, the largest Native American reservation in the U.S., covers much of northeastern Arizona and has its capital at Window Rock. It completely surrounds the much smaller Hopi Reservation.

**London Bridge in Lake Havasu City**
In the late 1960s, the businessman Robert McCulloch bought London's old London Bridge, shipped it to Arizona stone by stone, and rebuilt it in Lake Havasu City, which he had founded.

**Joe Arpaio**
The longtime sheriff of Maricopa County, who called himself "America's Toughest Sheriff" and was known for his harsh jails and immigration crackdowns. He lost his 2016 reelection race to Paul Penzone.

**Sedona and its red rocks**
A town in central Arizona famous for its red sandstone buttes and formations, such as Cathedral Rock, which is among the most photographed sites in the state. It is a popular area for hiking and mountain biking.

**Horseshoe Bend**
A tight, horseshoe-shaped bend in the Colorado River near the city of Page, in northern Arizona. It is a well-known viewpoint reached by a short trail.

**Gila River and the Sonoran Desert**
The Gila is Arizona's longest river, flowing west across the southern part of the state to join the Colorado near Yuma. Much of southern Arizona lies in the Sonoran Desert, known for its saguaro cacti.

**Barringer Crater (Meteor Crater)**
A meteorite impact crater about 1.2 kilometers wide near Flagstaff and Winslow. It is named for Daniel Barringer, who argued that it was created by an impact rather than a volcano.

**No daylight saving time**
Arizona and Hawaii are the only U.S. states that do not observe daylight saving time, although the Navajo Nation within Arizona does observe it.

**"China's Sorrow"**
The river's nickname, earned by its frequent and catastrophic floods, which have killed millions of people over Chinese history. The Yellow River (Huang He) is China's second-longest river after the Yangtze.

**Loess Plateau and silt**
The river takes its name and color from loess, a fine, wind-blown yellow silt largely carried from the Gobi Desert, which it picks up crossing the Loess Plateau. This load makes it the world's muddiest major river and makes the soil of its basin very fertile.

**Grand Canal (Sui dynasty)**
The huge canal system finished under the Sui dynasty in the early 7th century. It linked the Yellow River with the Yangtze to the south, carrying grain from the south to the northern capitals.

**Bayan Har Mountains (source)**
The river rises in the Bayan Har Mountains on the Tibetan Plateau in Qinghai. Near its source it flows through the twin lakes Gyaring and Ngoring.

**Bohai Sea and the Yellow Sea**
The river empties into the Bohai Sea, the innermost gulf of the Yellow Sea, north of the Shandong Peninsula. The Yellow Sea, named for the river's silt, lies between China and Korea and includes the Liaodong Peninsula and Bohai; the Hai River also drains into it.

**Changes of course and levees**
As silt raised the riverbed, people built ever-higher levees, until the river flowed above the surrounding plain. When the levees failed, the river shifted its mouth dramatically, sometimes north and sometimes south of the Shandong Peninsula.

**Wei River**
The Yellow River's largest tributary, flowing east through the Guanzhong basin past Xi'an. During the Qin dynasty, the Zhengguo (Chengkuo) Canal drew water from a Wei tributary to irrigate the region.

**Ordos Loop**
The great northward bend the river makes around the Ordos Plateau in Inner Mongolia and Ningxia. Paleolithic human remains have been found in the area.

**1938 Yellow River flood**
To slow the advancing Japanese army during the Second Sino-Japanese War, Nationalist forces broke the river's dikes at Huayuankou. The flood shifted the river's course and killed hundreds of thousands of civilians.

**Siege of Kaifeng (1642)**
During the rebellion at the end of the Ming dynasty, the river's dikes were broken during the siege of Kaifeng. The flood destroyed the city and killed most of its inhabitants.

**Shang dynasty oracle bones**
The Shang dynasty, which followed the semi-legendary Xia, flourished in the Yellow River basin. Its rulers practiced divination by carving questions on turtle shells and ox shoulder blades and reading the cracks made by heat. These are the earliest known Chinese writing.

**Erlitou culture and ding cauldrons**
A Bronze Age culture in the middle Yellow River valley, often linked to the Xia dynasty. It produced some of the earliest Chinese ritual bronzes, including early ding (three- or four-legged cauldrons).

**Longshan culture and millet**
The Neolithic Longshan culture of the lower Yellow River is known for thin, polished black pottery and rammed-earth walls. Millet was first domesticated in the Yellow River basin, which made it a cradle of Chinese agriculture.

**I Ching and the Records of the Grand Historian**
The I Ching (Book of Changes) is an ancient divination text based on combinations of three broken or solid lines (trigrams), from the Yellow River civilization. Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian describes the early dynasties based along the river.

**Sanmenxia Dam**
The first major dam built on the Yellow River, finished around 1960 in Henan. It quickly filled with silt and had to be rebuilt. Downstream, the river passes cities such as Luoyang, Kaifeng, and Jinan.

**Atlanta**
The capital and largest city of the U.S. state of Georgia. Its landmarks include the High Museum of Art, Piedmont Park, and the National Center for Civil and Human Rights, which opened in 2014.

**Savannah**
Georgia's oldest city, on the Atlantic coast near the South Carolina border. It is known for its historic squares, Forsyth Park, and Bonaventure Cemetery.

**Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport**
Atlanta's airport, the busiest in the world by passenger traffic. It is often used as a clue for both the city and the state.

**1996 Summer Olympics and Centennial Olympic Park**
Atlanta hosted the 1996 Summer Olympics. Centennial Olympic Park was built for the Games, and it was the site of a pipe bombing during them.

**Tbilisi**
The capital of the country of Georgia, in the Caucasus between Russia and Turkey. A question that asks for the shared name usually pairs Tbilisi with Atlanta.

**Abkhazia and South Ossetia**
Two breakaway regions that Georgia claims as its territory. Both are backed by Russia, which recognized their independence after the 2008 Russo-Georgian War.

**Juliette Gordon Low**
The founder of the Girl Scouts of the USA, which she started in Savannah in 1912. Her birthplace in Savannah is a historic site.

**Savannah Bananas**
A Savannah baseball team famous for "Banana Ball," an entertainment version of baseball with its own unusual rules.

**Vidalia onions**
Sweet onions grown around the city of Vidalia in southeast Georgia, which holds an annual onion festival.

**Stone Mountain**
A huge granite dome near Atlanta, carved with a large relief of Confederate leaders Jefferson Davis, Robert E. Lee and Stonewall Jackson.

**Ebenezer Baptist Church**
The Atlanta church where Martin Luther King Jr. and his father were pastors. It is part of the historic district that includes King's birthplace and his tomb.

**Spelman, Morehouse and Emory**
Universities in Atlanta. Spelman (for women) and Morehouse (for men) are historically Black colleges, and Emory is a major private research university.

**South Georgia**
A remote island in the South Atlantic that, together with the South Sandwich Islands, forms a British Overseas Territory. Its economy relies on licensed fishing for the Patagonian toothfish, which it celebrates with a holiday.

**Caucasian Iberia**
An ancient kingdom in what is now eastern Georgia. It shares the name Iberia with the much larger Iberian Peninsula of Spain and Portugal.

**Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline**
An oil pipeline opened in 2005 that carries crude oil from the Caspian Sea at Baku, Azerbaijan, through Tbilisi, Georgia, to the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan, Turkey. It lets Caspian oil reach world markets without passing through Russia.

**Aconcagua**
The highest peak in the Andes and in the Americas, at about 22,840 feet, in Argentina's Mendoza Province. It is the second-highest of the Seven Summits, and its name may come from Mapudungun, the language of the Mapuche. Matthias Zurbriggen made the first ascent in 1897 by way of the Valle de las Vacas ("Valley of the Cows"), and the peak's Polish Glacier is a well-known climbing route.

**Chimborazo**
An inactive volcano in Ecuador. Because Earth bulges at the equator, its summit is the farthest point on Earth's surface from the planet's center, though it is far from the highest peak above sea level.

**Salar de Uyuni**
The world's largest salt flat, on the Bolivian Altiplano near the town of Uyuni. It holds a large share of the world's lithium reserves, and flamingos breed in the area.

**Lake Titicaca**
A large lake on the Altiplano on the border of Peru and Bolivia, often called the highest navigable lake in the world. The ancient city of Tiwanaku developed near its southern shore.

**Subduction of the Nazca Plate**
The Andes formed, and are still rising, as the oceanic Nazca Plate dives beneath the South American Plate along the Pacific coast. This subduction also causes the range's many volcanoes and earthquakes.

**Inca Empire, Machu Picchu, and the Sacred Valley**
The Inca Empire was centered in the Andes, with its capital at Cusco. Machu Picchu sits above the Urubamba Valley, also called the Sacred Valley of the Incas. Andean peoples organized themselves in kinship groups called ayllu, farmed on terraces, and preserved potatoes as freeze-dried chuño.

**Altiplano**
The high plateau of the central Andes, mostly in Bolivia and Peru, home to Lake Titicaca and many Aymara people. Llamas and vicuñas live there. La Paz, Bolivia's seat of government, is on its edge and is the highest capital city in the world.

**Andean condor**
A huge vulture with a white feather collar around its neck, named after the range. It is often called the largest bird of prey in the world and is a national symbol of several Andean countries.

**Andean cock-of-the-rock**
A bright orange-red bird with black wings that lives in the cloud forests of the eastern Andes. It is the national bird of Peru. The spectacled (Andean) bear and the Andean flicker, a ground-dwelling woodpecker found in places like Bolivia's Sajama National Park, also live in the range.

**Tierra del Fuego (southern end)**
The Andes run for about 7,000 km along western South America and end in the Tierra del Fuego archipelago at the continent's southern tip. This makes them the longest continental mountain range in the world.

**Christ the Redeemer of the Andes**
A statue of Christ placed in 1904 at the high pass between Mendoza, Argentina, and Chile (the Uspallata or La Cumbre Pass), south of Aconcagua. It celebrates the peaceful settlement of a border dispute between the two countries.

**Potosí silver mines**
Cerro Rico ("Rich Hill") at Potosí, in the Bolivian Andes, was the Spanish Empire's greatest source of silver in the colonial era. The Andes are still a major mining region, with mines such as Yanacocha, a huge gold mine in Peru.

**Atacama Desert rain shadow**
The Andes block moist air from the east, which helps make the Atacama Desert of northern Chile, to the west of the range, the driest non-polar desert in the world. The Atacama region also has large lithium deposits.

**Ojos del Salado**
The highest active volcano in the world, on the Chile–Argentina border. Its name means "eyes of the salty one," after the salt lagoons on its slopes.

**Puya raimondii**
The "Queen of the Andes," the largest bromeliad in the world. It grows at high altitude in Peru and Bolivia and sends up a giant flower spike once before dying. The Andean cloud forests are also home to the cinchona tree, whose bark gave the antimalarial drug quinine.

**Sahel**
The semi-arid transitional belt of grassland and savanna that borders the desert to the south, stretching across Africa from Senegal and Mali to Sudan. It is threatened by desertification as the desert expands southward.

**Tibesti Mountains and Emi Koussi**
A volcanic mountain range mostly in northern Chad, home to the Toubou people. It contains the desert's highest point, Emi Koussi, a huge shield volcano, along with other high peaks such as Bikku Bitti in Libya.

**Tuareg**
A Berber (Amazigh) nomadic people of the central desert, inhabiting areas such as the Aïr Massif in Niger. They historically led camel caravans carrying salt and other goods, for example from the Taoudenni salt mines to Timbuktu, and founded trading towns such as Agadez.

**Richat Structure ("Eye of the Sahara")**
A roughly 30-mile-wide eroded geological dome of concentric rock rings on the Adrar Plateau in Mauritania, easily visible from space. The French naturalist Théodore Monod studied it and sought to explain its origin.

**Great Green Wall**
A pan-African project to plant a belt of trees and vegetation across the Sahel to slow the southward spread of the desert.

**Ergs and the Great Sand Sea**
Ergs are vast sand seas of shifting dunes. Major ones include the Grand Erg Occidental and Grand Erg Oriental in Algeria, which lie south of the Atlas Mountains, and the Great Sand Sea on the Egypt–Libya border near the oasis town of Siwa.

**Sirocco**
A hot, dry, dusty wind that originates in the desert and blows north across the Mediterranean toward southern Europe.

**Saharan pump theory**
The hypothesis that periods of heavy rainfall, such as the Neolithic Subpluvial ("Green Sahara"), periodically turned the desert into grassland, letting humans and animals migrate across it before the land dried out again.

**Tassili n'Ajjer and prehistoric rock art**
A sandstone plateau in southeastern Algeria known for thousands of prehistoric rock paintings and engravings from periods such as the "Round Head" and Bubaline periods, often painted over by later art. The "Cave of the Swimmers" at Gilf Kebir in Egypt is another famous rock art site.

**Trans-Saharan trade and Timbuktu**
Camels made long-distance caravan trade across the desert possible, mainly in gold and salt. Timbuktu, on the desert's southern edge, was a key trading and scholarly center of the Mali Empire, home to Sankore University. Ibn Battuta described the Taghaza salt mine, and empires like Kanem-Bornu traded across the region.

**Qattara Depression**
A large depression in northwestern Egypt that is the lowest point in the desert, about 133 meters below sea level.

**Fennec fox**
A tiny nocturnal fox with enormous ears that radiate heat, native to the desert. The deathstalker scorpion is another characteristic animal.

**Aouzou Strip and the Toyota War**
A strip of land in northern Chad, said to be rich in uranium, claimed and occupied by Libya. In the 1987 "Toyota War," Chadian forces in Toyota pickup trucks drove out the Libyan army.

**French nuclear tests**
France conducted its first nuclear bomb test, Gerboise Bleue, in 1960 near Reggane in the Algerian desert.

**Bodélé Depression**
A dried lakebed in Chad that is the world's largest single source of airborne dust. Dust storms from it carry mineral nutrients across the Atlantic that fertilize the Amazon Rainforest. Nearby Lake Chad, on the desert's southern edge, has shrunk dramatically.

**White Nile and Blue Nile meet at Khartoum**
The Nile's two main branches, the White Nile and the Blue Nile, join at Khartoum, the capital of Sudan. From there the river flows north through Sudan and Egypt to the Mediterranean. At about 6,650 km, it is traditionally called the longest river in the world, and its basin spans eleven countries.

**Aswan High Dam and Lake Nasser**
Completed in 1970 near the First Cataract in southern Egypt, the Aswan High Dam ended the river's annual flooding downstream. It created Lake Nasser, one of the world's largest artificial lakes. An earlier, smaller Aswan Low Dam had been built at the cataract in 1902.

**Lake Victoria and Ripon Falls**
The White Nile leaves Lake Victoria at Jinja, Uganda, where Ripon Falls once marked its outlet. The falls, along with Owen Falls, were submerged by the Owen Falls Dam, now called the Nalubaale Dam (from the Luganda name for the lake).

**Lake Tana and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam**
The Blue Nile flows out of Lake Tana in the Ethiopian Highlands and supplies most of the Nile's water and silt. Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) on the Blue Nile has caused disputes with Egypt and Sudan. In Sudan, the Gezira Scheme irrigates farmland between the Blue and White Niles.

**Rosetta and Damietta branches (Nile Delta)**
North of Cairo the Nile fans into a large delta and reaches the Mediterranean through two main distributaries, the Rosetta branch in the west and the Damietta branch in the east. The delta stretches roughly from Alexandria to Port Said and includes coastal lagoons such as Lake Burullus.

**Six cataracts and the Great Bend**
Between Khartoum and Aswan the Nile crosses six cataracts (shallow rapids), numbered from the First Cataract at Aswan upstream to the Sixth. In Sudan it loops through a huge S-shaped "Great Bend." The Merowe Dam near the Fourth Cataract has flooded lands of the Manasir people.

**Kagera River (farthest source)**
The main river flowing into Lake Victoria and the Nile's most distant headstream. It forms part of the border between Rwanda and Tanzania and passes Rusumo Falls. Its headwaters, such as the Ruvyironza in Burundi and the Rukarara in Rwanda, are contenders for the Nile's ultimate source.

**Sudd wetlands and the Jonglei Canal**
A vast swamp on the White Nile in South Sudan, downstream of Juba, where much of the river's water evaporates. Invasive South American water hyacinth has clogged it further. The unfinished Jonglei Canal was planned to carry water around the Sudd. Tributaries near the swamp include the Bahr el Ghazal ("River of Gazelles") from the west and the Sobat from the east.

**Abu Simbel and Philae relocation**
When Lake Nasser rose behind the Aswan High Dam, UNESCO led a campaign in the 1960s to save Nubian monuments. Ramesses II's rock-cut temples at Abu Simbel were cut into blocks and moved to higher ground, and the Temple of Isis on Philae Island was moved to the nearby island of Agilkia.

**Annual flood and the seasons Akhet, Peret, Shemu**
Ancient Egypt depended on the Nile's yearly flood, which left fertile black silt. The Egyptians called their land Kemet ("black land") after that soil. Their calendar had three seasons tied to the river: Akhet (inundation), Peret (growing) and Shemu (harvest).

**Nubia: Kerma, Napata and Meroë**
Upstream of the First Cataract lay Nubia, home of the Kingdom of Kush. Its successive centers were Kerma, Napata and Meroë, and the culture of Meroë wrote in the Meroitic script.

**Giza pyramids, Memphis and Saqqara**
The Great Pyramid of Giza, the only surviving Wonder of the Ancient World, stands on the Nile's west bank near Cairo. Fine white limestone for its casing was quarried at Tura and ferried across the river. Saqqara was the necropolis of the ancient capital Memphis. To the southwest, the ancient Bahr Yussef canal carried Nile water into the Faiyum basin and Lake Moeris.

**Cairo and its expansion**
Egypt's capital sits at the head of the delta and is crossed by bridges such as the 6th October Bridge. To handle growth, Egypt built satellite cities such as 6th of October City and 15th of May City, and more recently a New Administrative Capital east of Cairo.

**Murchison Falls and Lake Kyoga**
In Uganda, the Victoria Nile flows through Lake Kyoga and then forces through a narrow gorge at Murchison Falls before entering Lake Albert.

**Nile crocodile**
The Nile crocodile is the largest crocodile species in Africa and lives throughout the river system. It was sacred to the ancient Egyptian god Sobek.

**Bosporus and the Sea of Marmara**
The Bosporus (Bosphorus) is the narrow strait at Istanbul that links the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara. Together with the Dardanelles, these form the Turkish Straits, the Black Sea's only outlet to the Aegean and Mediterranean.

**Strait of Kerch and the Sea of Azov**
The Kerch Strait, known in antiquity as the Cimmerian Bosporus, separates the Crimean Peninsula from Russia's Taman Peninsula and connects the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov to the north. The Sea of Azov, fed by the Don and Kuban Rivers, is the shallowest sea in the world.

**Crimean Peninsula**
A large peninsula jutting into the northern Black Sea, with coastline on both the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. Russia annexed it from Ukraine in 2014, and it is home to the cities of Sevastopol and Yalta.

**Sevastopol and Yalta**
Two Crimean cities on the Black Sea. Sevastopol is the historic base of the Russian Black Sea Fleet, and Yalta is a resort city famous as the site of the 1945 Yalta Conference.

**Danube, Dnieper, and Dniester Rivers**
The major rivers draining into the western and northern Black Sea. The Danube, which passes through the Iron Gate gorge, ends in a large delta near Sulina in Romania. The Dnieper and Dniester flow through Ukraine, as does the Southern Bug.

**Odessa**
A major Ukrainian port city on the northwestern shore of the Black Sea. It is a common city clue along with Varna in Bulgaria and Novorossiysk in Russia.

**Sochi**
A Russian resort city on the eastern shore of the Black Sea, near the Caucasus Mountains. It hosted the 2014 Winter Olympics.

**Black Sea deluge hypothesis (Noah's Flood)**
Geologists William Ryan and Walter Pitman proposed in their book Noah's Flood that around 7,600 years ago the Mediterranean broke through the Bosporus and rapidly flooded a freshwater lake. They argued that this catastrophic rise in water level may have inspired the Biblical flood story.

**Meromictic sea with an anoxic bottom layer**
The Black Sea is the world's largest meromictic basin, meaning its upper and lower layers do not mix. More than 90% of its volume lacks oxygen, which preserves ancient shipwrecks such as those found near Sinop. A saline undersea river flowing along its floor from the Bosporus was the first such river discovered.

**Montreux Convention (1936)**
An international agreement that gives Turkey control over the Bosporus and Dardanelles. It guarantees free passage for civilian ships in peacetime but restricts the entry of warships into the Black Sea.

**Abkhazia and Sukhumi**
Abkhazia is a breakaway region of Georgia on the eastern shore of the Black Sea, and Sukhumi is its capital. It was involved, along with South Ossetia, in the 2008 Russo-Georgian War.

**Varna and Burgas**
Bulgarian port and resort cities on the western shore of the Black Sea. Nearby Sozopol, once the Greek colony Apollonia, hosts the Apollonia arts festival.

**Ancient Greek colonies and kingdoms (Pontus Euxinus)**
The Greeks called the sea Pontus Euxinus and founded colonies on it such as Tomis (modern Constanța) and Histria in Romania, shipping grain from its shores back to Greece. The Pontic Steppe and the ancient Scythians lay to the north, and the kingdoms of Pontus, Paphlagonia, and Bithynia lay along its southern shore.

**Trabzon (Trebizond)**
A Turkish port on the southeastern coast of the Black Sea. As Trebizond, it was the capital of the Empire of Trebizond, a Byzantine successor state that lasted until 1461.

**Named for its dark color**
The sea's name is often explained by the dark storms and shadows over its waters, or by an old system in which colors stood for compass directions, with black meaning north. Questions often end by calling it the "colorful" sea north of Turkey and south of Ukraine.

**Denali (Mount McKinley)**
The highest peak in North America (about 20,310 feet), located in Denali National Park. Its Koyukon Athabaskan name means "the tall one" or "the high one"; it was officially called Mount McKinley after President William McKinley until a 2015 renaming restored Denali (the federal name was changed back to McKinley in 2025). A popular climbing route up it is the West Buttress, and nearby Mount Foraker is in the same park.

**Prudhoe Bay and the Trans-Alaska Pipeline**
Prudhoe Bay on the North Slope is the largest oil field in the United States. An 800-mile, largely above-ground pipeline carries its oil south to the ice-free port of Valdez on Prince William Sound. Oil revenue funds the Alaska Permanent Fund, which pays an annual dividend to every resident.

**Exxon Valdez oil spill**
In 1989 the oil tanker Exxon Valdez ran aground on Bligh Reef near Valdez in Prince William Sound, spilling roughly 11 million gallons of crude oil. It was one of the worst environmental disasters in U.S. history.

**Juneau**
The state capital, located in the southeastern Panhandle on the Gastineau Channel. It cannot be reached by road from the rest of North America and is accessed mainly by air or by the Alaska Marine Highway ferry system.

**Anchorage**
The state's largest city, on Cook Inlet near the Chugach Mountains. Its Ted Stevens International Airport is among the busiest cargo airports in the world, its Lake Hood is the world's busiest seaplane base, and it has a coastal trail named for governor Tony Knowles.

**Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes**
An ash-filled valley in Katmai National Park created by the 1912 eruption of Novarupta, the largest volcanic eruption of the 20th century. It was named for the thousands of fumaroles (steam vents) that rose from the ash flow after the eruption.

**Katmai National Park and Kodiak Island**
Katmai, centered on Mount Katmai, is famous for brown bears catching salmon. Kodiak Island, the second-largest island in the U.S., lies off the Alaska Peninsula, is home to the huge Kodiak bear, and was home to the Alutiiq people. Three Saints Bay on Kodiak was the site of the first Russian settlement in the region.

**Aleutian Islands**
A volcanic island chain stretching west toward Asia, including Unimak, Attu, Kiska, and the Islands of the Four Mountains. Japan occupied Attu and Kiska in World War II, and Dutch Harbor on Amaknak Island, once a military base, is now a major fishing port.

**Mount Shishaldin**
A volcano on Unimak Island in the Aleutians, often called the most symmetrical volcanic cone on Earth.

**Utqiagvik (Barrow) and the North Slope Borough**
Utqiagvik, formerly called Barrow, is the northernmost city in the U.S., on the Beaufort Sea near Point Barrow, the state's northernmost point. It is the seat of the North Slope Borough. Alaska is divided into boroughs instead of counties, and the vast Unorganized Borough covers more than half of the state.

**Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race**
An annual long-distance dog sled race that starts in the Anchorage area and ends in Nome on Norton Sound by the Bering Sea, passing checkpoints such as Kaltag along the way.

**Yukon River**
One of the longest rivers in North America (often listed as the third longest). It flows west across the state and empties into the Bering Sea. The Kuskokwim River, which rises west of Mount Gerdine, is another major river.

**Wrangell-St. Elias National Park**
The largest national park in the United States by area. Alaska as a whole contains 17 of the 20 highest peaks in the U.S. Other national parks include Gates of the Arctic, Glacier Bay (a humpback whale habitat), Lake Clark (with the Chigmit Mountains and Dall sheep), and Kobuk Valley, whose sand dunes are the northernmost dune field in the U.S. and were studied by NASA as an analog for Mars.

**1964 Good Friday earthquake**
A magnitude 9.2 earthquake, the most powerful in North American recorded history. It caused tsunamis that hit Whittier, Kodiak, and Seward, and it destroyed much of the town of Valdez.

**Seward's Purchase and Russian America**
Alaska was explored by Vitus Bering's expedition, colonized by the Russian-American Company, and bought from Russia in 1867 by Secretary of State William Seward (critics called it "Seward's Folly"). The Tlingit fought the Russians at the Battle of Sitka in 1804, and a legacy of Russian rule is that Alaska has the highest share of Orthodox Christians of any U.S. state.

**Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, and Shikoku**
Japan's four main islands. Honshu is the largest and holds Tokyo, Osaka, Kyoto, and Mount Fuji; Hokkaido is the northernmost; Kyushu (home to the volcano Mount Aso) and Shikoku lie to the southwest.

**Kuril Islands dispute (Northern Territories)**
The Soviet Union seized the southern Kurils, including Iturup and Kunashir, at the end of World War II, and Japan still claims four of them as its "Northern Territories." Russia controls them, and the dispute has kept the two countries from signing a formal peace treaty.

**Sakhalin (Karafuto)**
A large island north of Hokkaido, separated from it by the La Pérouse Strait. Japan controlled its southern half as Karafuto from 1905 to 1945 but no longer disputes Russian ownership.

**Seikan Tunnel**
A rail tunnel under the Tsugaru Strait linking Honshu to Hokkaido, long the world's longest undersea tunnel. Shinkansen service now runs through it toward Hakodate, with an extension to Sapporo under construction.

**Shinkansen (bullet trains)**
The world's first high-speed rail network, opened in 1964 between Tokyo and Osaka and operated by the Japan Railways (JR) companies. Spotting "Doctor Yellow," a yellow track-inspection train, is said to bring good luck.

**Hokkaido, the Ainu, and Sapporo**
Hokkaido, formerly called Ezo (Yezo), is home to the Indigenous Ainu people, who traditionally held the Iomante bear-sending ritual. Its capital Sapporo hosted the 1972 Winter Olympics.

**Tokyo (formerly Edo)**
Japan's capital, whose metropolitan area, including Yokohama, is the world's most populous. Landmarks include the Tokyo Skytree, the Rainbow Bridge over Tokyo Bay, the Shibuya and Ginza districts, and the National Diet, Japan's legislature.

**Mount Fuji**
Japan's tallest mountain, an active volcano on Honshu. The Aokigahara forest, infamously nicknamed the "suicide forest," lies at its base.

**Akashi Kaikyō Bridge and the Inland Sea**
The world's longest suspension bridge until Turkey's 1915 Çanakkale Bridge surpassed it in 2022. It links Honshu to Awaji Island and is part of the project connecting Honshu and Shikoku across the Seto Inland Sea.

**Okinawa and the Ryukyu Islands**
Okinawa, Japan's southernmost prefecture, consists of the Ryukyu archipelago, which was once an independent kingdom.

**Fukushima disaster (2011)**
The Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami of March 2011 caused meltdowns at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant, run by TEPCO, leading Japan to shut down its nuclear reactors for a time.

**Japanese food: sushi, okonomiyaki, and Ramune**
Sushi combines vinegared rice with fish, often wrapped in nori seaweed, and conveyor-belt sushi restaurants charge by colored plate. Okonomiyaki is a savory pancake of cabbage, flour, eggs, yam, and stock; Ramune is a soda in a bottle sealed with a marble.

**Lake Biwa**
Japan's largest lake, on Honshu near Kyoto. It drains via the Yodo River into Osaka Bay and the Inland Sea.

**Hiroshima Peace Memorial (Genbaku Dome)**
The ruined domed building preserved as a memorial to the victims of the August 1945 atomic bombing of Hiroshima.

**Senkaku (Diaoyu) Islands dispute**
Uninhabited islands in the East China Sea controlled by Japan and claimed by China. Japan's government purchase of several of them in September 2012 set off anti-Japanese protests in China, around the time Shinzo Abe's LDP returned to power.

**Appalachian Trail: Springer Mountain to Mount Katahdin**
The roughly 2,200-mile hiking trail that runs the length of the range, from its southern end at Springer Mountain, Georgia, to its northern end at Mount Katahdin in Maine's Baxter State Park. The fugitive accountant James "Bismarck" Hammes famously hid from authorities for years by hiking it.

**Mount Mitchell and the Black Mountains**
Mount Mitchell in North Carolina is the highest peak in the Appalachians and the highest point in the United States east of the Mississippi River. It is in the Black Mountains, a subrange of the Blue Ridge.

**Blue Ridge Mountains**
A major subrange (or province) of the southern Appalachians, running from Pennsylvania through Virginia and North Carolina into Georgia. It includes the Great Smoky Mountains and the Black Mountains.

**Great Smoky Mountains, Clingmans Dome, and Newfound Gap**
A subrange on the North Carolina–Tennessee border, protected by Great Smoky Mountains National Park. Its signature haze comes from volatile organic compounds released by trees. Its highest point is Clingmans Dome (officially renamed Kuwohi), Newfound Gap is its main mountain pass, and Cades Cove was a settlement in the area before the park was created. The resort towns of Gatlinburg and Pigeon Forge, home of Dollywood, sit at its edge.

**Catskill, Pocono, Allegheny, Tuscarora, and White Mountains**
Other subranges of the Appalachian system that clues name. The Catskills are in New York, the Poconos and Tuscarora Mountains are in Pennsylvania, the Alleghenies run through Pennsylvania, Maryland, and West Virginia, and the White Mountains are in New Hampshire.

**Shickshocks (Chic-Chocs) and Notre Dame Mountains**
The northernmost parts of the Appalachian chain, in Quebec's Gaspé Peninsula and southern Quebec. They show that the range extends from Georgia well into Canada.

**Coal mining and mountaintop removal**
The Appalachians hold major coal deposits, including the anthracite fields of northeastern Pennsylvania, the largest source of anthracite in the Americas. In states such as West Virginia and Kentucky, mountaintop removal mining, which blasts away summits to reach coal seams, has caused severe environmental damage.

**Formation from the collision of Laurentia and Gondwana**
The Appalachians formed through several mountain-building episodes, ending when the continents Laurentia (ancestral North America) and Gondwana collided to form the supercontinent Pangaea. Morocco's Atlas Mountains formed in the same collision and were once part of the same chain.

**Appalachian dulcimer**
A fretted string instrument from the region, usually played on the lap. It is plucked or strummed, even though the name "dulcimer" usually refers to the hammered dulcimer.

**Hillbilly Elegy**
J. D. Vance's 2016 memoir about his family's roots in Appalachian Kentucky and the struggles of working-class Appalachian culture.

**Appalachian English and a-prefixing**
The dialect of the region is known for "a-prefixing" of progressive verbs (as in "a-huntin'"), a usage that linguists have shown follows consistent grammatical rules.

**Melungeons**
A mixed-race group of people traditionally living in the southern Appalachians, especially in eastern Tennessee and southwestern Virginia.

**Foxfire**
A magazine started by high school students in Rabun County, Georgia, in 1966. It recorded oral histories, crafts, and folk traditions of Appalachian people and was later collected into a popular series of books.

**Project Greek Island and the Greenbrier**
A secret Cold War program that built an emergency bunker for the U.S. Congress beneath the Greenbrier resort in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia, in the Allegheny Mountains.

**New River Gorge**
A deep gorge in West Virginia carved by the New River through the Appalachians, now a national park. The river cuts across the range and serves as a corridor for plants and animals.

**Toronto and Ottawa**
Toronto is Ontario's capital and Canada's largest city. Ottawa, the national capital, is also in Ontario, which makes Ontario the province with both the country's largest city and its capital. Ontario is Canada's most populous province.

**CN Tower**
The communications tower in downtown Toronto. It held the record as the world's tallest freestanding structure for over 30 years until the Burj Khalifa in Dubai passed it. Toronto also has the PATH underground pedestrian and shopping network and the Casa Loma mansion.

**Thunder Bay and Isle Royale**
Thunder Bay is a port city on the northwest shore of Lake Superior. Ferries run from the area to Isle Royale, a U.S. national park island in the lake. The town of Nipigon, at the mouth of the Nipigon River, is nearby.

**Golden Horseshoe**
The densely populated, horseshoe-shaped urban region wrapping around the western end of Lake Ontario, from Oshawa through Toronto, Mississauga, and Hamilton to the Niagara area. GO Transit runs its regional trains and buses.

**Four of the five Great Lakes and Niagara Falls**
Ontario borders Lakes Superior, Huron, Erie, and Ontario, but not Lake Michigan. It shares Niagara Falls with New York State. Point Pelee National Park, on a peninsula in Lake Erie, is the southernmost point of mainland Canada.

**Lake Nipigon and Lake Simcoe**
Lake Nipigon, north of Lake Superior, is the largest lake entirely within Ontario. Lake Simcoe, north of Toronto, was named by John Graves Simcoe, the first lieutenant governor of Upper Canada, after his father. The name "Toronto" is often traced to an Indigenous term for the fishing area at the Narrows near the lake.

**Georgian Bay and Manitoulin Island**
Georgian Bay is a large arm of Lake Huron, and its southern end borders the Golden Horseshoe region. Manitoulin Island in Lake Huron is the largest freshwater lake island in the world. Ferries reach it from Tobermory at the tip of the Bruce Peninsula.

**Upper Canada**
Ontario's name before Confederation. It was the English-speaking province upstream on the St. Lawrence, as opposed to French-speaking Lower Canada (Quebec). In 1867 it joined Quebec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick as one of the four founding provinces of Canada.

**Family Compact and the Rebellion of 1837**
The Family Compact was a small, closed group of officials who controlled the government of Upper Canada; the political system John Graves Simcoe set up helped it form. Anger at the group led William Lyon Mackenzie to lead the failed Upper Canada Rebellion of 1837.

**Windsor and the Ambassador Bridge**
Windsor, near Lake St. Clair, sits directly across the Detroit River from Detroit, Michigan. The two are linked by the Ambassador Bridge, one of North America's busiest border crossings.

**James Bay and the Albany River**
Ontario's northern coast lies on Hudson Bay and the western half of James Bay. The Albany River flows into James Bay and separates the Kenora and Cochrane districts. The Cree community of Attawapiskat, near James Bay, became known for its poor living conditions and the campaign for a school led by the young activist Shannen Koostachin.

**Rideau Canal**
The canal linking Ottawa to Kingston on Lake Ontario, opened in 1832. It is the oldest continuously operated canal system in North America and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Kingston lies near the Thousand Islands, where the St. Lawrence River begins.

**Lake of the Woods**
A lake that Ontario shares with Manitoba and Minnesota, at Ontario's western edge. Rainy Lake, on the Ontario–Minnesota border, is in the same area.

**Highway of Heroes**
The stretch of Highway 401 between CFB Trenton and Toronto. Funeral processions carrying the bodies of fallen Canadian soldiers travel it, and crowds gather on its overpasses to pay respects.

**London on the Thames and Kitchener-Waterloo**
Southwestern Ontario has a city named London on its own Thames River. The "Tri-Cities" of Kitchener, Waterloo, and Cambridge form another major urban area. Sarnia, on the Michigan border, was the western terminus of the Grand Trunk Railway.

**Sydney**
The largest city and capital of New South Wales, on the state's Pacific coast. As Australia's most populous city, it is the most common giveaway for the state.

**Jervis Bay Territory**
A small federal territory on the south coast that is entirely surrounded by New South Wales. It was separated from the state in 1915 to give the Australian Capital Territory (Canberra) access to the sea.

**Borders: Queensland, Victoria and South Australia**
New South Wales lies south of Queensland, north of Victoria, and east of South Australia, on Australia's eastern coast. These neighbors are standard locator clues near the end of questions.

**Blue Mountains**
A rugged range west of Sydney that blocked inland settlement for decades. In 1813, Gregory Blaxland, together with William Lawson and William Wentworth, found the first route across them, opening the interior to farming.

**Albury and Wodonga**
Albury, on the Hume Highway (the main road between Sydney and Melbourne), sits on the Murray River, which forms most of the border with Victoria. It is twinned with Wodonga directly across the river in Victoria.

**New England Tableland**
An elevated plateau in the state's northeast that includes the city of Armidale and Round Mountain, and which rises near Tamworth. It is part of the Great Dividing Range.

**Riverina, Murrumbidgee River and Wagga Wagga**
The Riverina is an agricultural district in the southern part of the state. The Murrumbidgee River, a major tributary of the Murray, flows through it past Wagga Wagga, the region's largest inland city.

**Cape Byron**
The easternmost point of mainland Australia, on the northeast coast of New South Wales near the town of Byron Bay.

**Newcastle and Gosford**
Coastal cities north of Sydney. Newcastle, at the mouth of the Hunter River, is the state's second-largest city and a major coal-exporting port. Gosford is the main city of the Central Coast, between Sydney and Newcastle.

**Port Macquarie**
A coastal city on the state's mid-north Pacific coast, at the mouth of the Hastings River. It was founded in 1821 as a penal settlement.

**One third of Australia's population**
New South Wales is Australia's most populous state, home to about a third of the country's people, most of them in the Sydney area.

**Named after Wales**
The name comes from Wales, a country of the United Kingdom. James Cook claimed the coast for Britain in 1770 and gave it the name.

**Kata Tjuta (the Olgas)**
A group of 36 domed rock formations about 25 km west of Uluru, formerly called the Olgas. The two landmarks share Uluru–Kata Tjuta National Park, and they are thought to connect beneath the surrounding sand.

**Anangu people**
The Aboriginal traditional owners of Uluru, many of whom speak the Pitjantjatjara language. They ask visitors not to photograph certain sacred parts of the rock, such as sections of its northeast face.

**Alice Springs**
The town in the center of the Northern Territory that is the usual gateway for visitors, about 450 km by road northeast of Uluru. Many tourists also fly into Ayers Rock Airport near the resort town of Yulara.

**Northern Territory**
The Australian territory where Uluru lies, in its southwest corner. The territory also contains the MacDonnell Ranges.

**Red sandstone monolith**
Uluru is a huge red rock formation made of arkose, a coarse sandstone rich in feldspar, which has a grain similar to granite. It rises about 348 m above the surrounding desert, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

**1985 handback**
In 1985 the Australian government under Prime Minister Bob Hawke returned ownership of Uluru and the park to the Anangu, who leased it back to the national parks service. The campaign for the handback was led by the Central Land Council.

**William Gosse and the name Ayers Rock**
In 1873 the surveyor William Gosse became the first European to see the rock. He named it Ayers Rock after Sir Henry Ayers, then Chief Secretary of South Australia.

**Ernest Giles**
An explorer who traveled through the area in 1872 and saw Kata Tjuta, and who also found the nearby Finke River and Lake Amadeus. He was overshadowed by Gosse, who reached Uluru itself the next year.

**Dual naming in 1993**
In 1993 the landmark was officially given the dual name "Ayers Rock / Uluru," which was reversed to "Uluru / Ayers Rock" in 2002.

**Tjukurpa (the Dreamtime)**
The Anangu belief system and law, which describes how ancestral beings created the land, including Uluru. Songlines and stories such as that of Kalaya the emu are tied to the rock.

**Mutitjulu Waterhole**
A permanent waterhole at the base of Uluru, sacred to the Anangu. The nearby Aboriginal community of Mutitjulu is named after it.

**Azaria Chamberlain**
A nine-week-old baby who disappeared from a campsite near Uluru in 1980. Her mother Lindy claimed a dingo took her, and was wrongly convicted of murder before being exonerated. The phrase "a dingo ate my baby" was later parodied on Seinfeld.

**Climbing ban and Pauline Hanson**
Climbing Uluru, long discouraged by the Anangu, was banned in October 2019. In 2019, before the ban took effect, the right-wing politician Pauline Hanson attempted the climb for a TV segment in protest and got stuck partway up.

**Petermann Orogeny**
A mountain-building event in central Australia over 500 million years ago that formed the ancient mountains whose eroded sediments became the rock of Uluru and Kata Tjuta.

**Mount Conner**
A flat-topped mesa east of Uluru, often mistaken for it by travelers. Along with Uluru and Kata Tjuta, it is one of the three great rock formations of the region.

**Lemurs**
A group of primates found naturally only on this island, the most common giveaway. Species include the ring-tailed lemur, the golden-crowned sifaka, the Alaotra gentle lemur (locally called the bandro), and the aye-aye, the largest nocturnal primate, which uses an extremely long, thin middle finger to pull grubs out of wood. Like most of the island's wildlife, lemurs evolved in isolation after the island split from India roughly 90 million years ago.

**Mozambique Channel**
The arm of the Indian Ocean that separates the island, the fourth-largest in the world, from mainland southeast Africa. Nearby are Comoros and the French department of Mayotte to the northwest and Réunion and Mauritius to the east. The country was a French colony and was called the Malagasy Republic from 1958 to 1975.

**Antananarivo**
The capital and largest city, located in the Central Highlands. Many of its 19th-century buildings were designed by the French adventurer Jean Laborde under Queen Ranavalona I of the Merina Kingdom.

**Avenue of the Baobabs**
A dirt road in the western Menabe region near Morondava lined with giant baobab trees; it was the country's first protected natural monument. Nearby are the "Baobabs Amoureux," two intertwined trees. Most of the world's baobab species are native only to this island.

**Tsingy de Bemaraha**
A national park of jagged limestone pinnacles formed by karst erosion, located north of the Avenue of the Baobabs. "Tsingy" is said to mean "the place where one cannot walk barefoot." Similar formations occur at the Ankarana Reserve in the northern Diana region.

**Lake Alaotra**
The country's largest lake, in the northeast near Toamasina. It is the center of the nation's rice production and the habitat of the endangered Meller's duck and the Alaotra gentle lemur, which is threatened by the destruction of reed beds.

**Malagasy language and Austronesian settlement**
The main language, Malagasy, is the westernmost Austronesian language and is closely related to languages of Borneo, reflecting settlement by seafarers from Southeast Asia who crossed the Indian Ocean. It also contains Bantu and Swahili loanwords from later African contact.

**Fossa**
The island's largest native carnivore, a cat-like predator related to mongooses that hunts lemurs. Other endemic mammals include tenrecs and the fanaloka (Malagasy civet), and the island once had dwarf hippopotamuses and the giant, now-extinct elephant bird.

**Merina people**
The island's largest ethnic group, living in the Central Highlands. Their Merina Kingdom unified much of the island in the 19th century before French colonization. Other groups include the Betsileo and the northern Tsimihety.

**Madagascar periwinkle**
A flowering plant native to the island that is the source of the vinca alkaloids vinblastine and vincristine, chemotherapy drugs used against Hodgkin's lymphoma and childhood leukemia.

**Canal des Pangalanes**
A chain of natural lakes, rivers, and artificial canals running for hundreds of kilometers along the east coast, built in large part during the French colonial era as an inland waterway.

**Famadihana ("turning of the bones")**
A funerary tradition in which families exhume the remains of their ancestors, rewrap them in fresh cloth, and dance with them during a celebration, typically every several years.

**Vanilla**
The country is the world's largest producer of vanilla, supplying roughly 80 percent of the global crop, and it is also a major producer of cloves.

**"The Red Island" and laterite soils**
A nickname for the country due to its red lateritic soils. Erosion of the deforested Central Highlands washes this red soil into rivers, discoloring them.

**Maromokotro and the Tsaratanana Massif**
Maromokotro, in the Tsaratanana Massif in the north, is the country's highest point. The northern tip of the island is Cap d'Ambre, near the city of Antsiranana (formerly Diego-Suarez).

**Amazon rainforest and Amazon River**
Brazil contains the majority of the Amazon rainforest, the world's largest tropical rainforest, and most of the Amazon River's course. Spanish explorers named the river after the Amazons of Greek myth when they met fierce women warriors there. It is the most common giveaway, and the river also names the Amazon river dolphin, or boto, a pink dolphin that eats piranhas among other fish.

**Manaus and the Rio Negro**
Manaus is the capital of Amazonas, Brazil's largest state, located where the dark Rio Negro meets the main Amazon. It boomed during the late 19th-century rubber boom, which paid for its famous opera house, the Teatro Amazonas; the rubber boom also built up Belém.

**Uncontacted tribes and Bolsonaro-era deforestation**
Brazil has more uncontacted Indigenous peoples than any other country. Many are threatened by logging, mining and ranching in the Amazon, and deforestation rose sharply under President Jair Bolsonaro (2019–2022).

**Yanomami**
An Indigenous people living in the Amazon along the Brazil-Venezuela border. The anthropologist Napoleon Chagnon made them famous, and controversial, with his book "Yanomamö: The Fierce People."

**Pantanal**
The world's largest tropical wetland, lying mostly in the Brazilian states of Mato Grosso do Sul and Mato Grosso. It is known for its wildlife, including large populations of capybaras, caimans and jaguars.

**Christ the Redeemer and Rio de Janeiro**
A giant statue of Jesus with outstretched arms that stands on Corcovado mountain above Rio de Janeiro, Brazil's second-largest city. Rio lies on Guanabara Bay, contains the large urban Tijuca Forest, and is known for its annual Carnival and its hillside slums called favelas. It was Brazil's capital until 1960.

**Brasília (Lúcio Costa and Oscar Niemeyer)**
Brazil's capital since 1960, a planned city laid out by the urban planner Lúcio Costa in a shape often compared to an airplane or bird, with major buildings by the architect Oscar Niemeyer. Niemeyer's Cathedral of Brasília is a hyperboloid structure made of 16 curved concrete columns.

**São Paulo**
Brazil's largest city and the largest city in the Southern Hemisphere, as well as the country's main economic center.

**Iguaçu (Iguazu) Falls**
A huge system of waterfalls on the Iguaçu River, on the border between Brazil's state of Paraná (capital Curitiba) and Argentina, Brazil's southwestern neighbor.

**Marajó Island and Marajoara culture**
Marajó is a large island at the mouth of the Amazon in the state of Pará. It was home to the Marajoara culture, a pre-Columbian society known for its elaborate painted pottery and earthen mounds.

**Percy Fawcett and the "Lost City of Z"**
A British explorer who disappeared in the Brazilian Amazon in 1925 while searching for a lost city he called "Z." Archaeologists have since found large ancient settlements in the upper Xingu region, such as Kuhikugu, that some link to his search.

**Pirahã language (Daniel Everett)**
An isolate language spoken by a small Amazonian tribe. The linguist Daniel Everett argued that it lacks recursion, making it a counterexample to Noam Chomsky's theory of Universal Grammar.

**Last of the Tanaru ("Man of the Hole")**
The last surviving member of an uncontacted tribe in the state of Rondônia, who lived alone for decades in a protected territory and was known for digging deep holes. He died in August 2022.

**Getúlio Vargas**
Brazil's dictator (1930–1945) and later elected president. His "March to the West" pushed settlement into the interior, and his nationalization policies banned the use of minority languages, such as the German dialects East Pomeranian and Hunsrückisch and the Italian-based Talian spoken in the south.

**Ouro Preto and the gold rush**
A colonial mining town in Minas Gerais founded during the gold rush of the late 17th and 18th centuries. It is famous for its Baroque churches and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

**Lemurs**
Primates found natively only on Madagascar. They are the most common giveaway, appearing at the end of almost every question.

**Antananarivo**
The capital and largest city of Madagascar, in the Central Highlands. It is the usual capital giveaway.

**Mozambique Channel**
The arm of the Indian Ocean that separates Madagascar from the southeastern African mainland (Mozambique).

**Lake Alaotra**
Madagascar's largest lake, in the northeast of the country, inland from Toamasina. It is the center of the island's rice production, and it is home to endangered waterbirds such as Meller's duck.

**Avenue of the Baobabs**
A dirt road in the western Menabe region, near Morondava, lined with tall native baobab trees. Nearby are the "Baobab Amoureux," two baobabs whose trunks are twisted together. Most of the world's baobab species are found only on Madagascar.

**Fossa and aye-aye**
Two animals found only on Madagascar. The fossa is a cat-like carnivore related to mongooses, and the aye-aye is the world's largest nocturnal primate, a lemur with a very long, thin middle finger it uses to dig out grubs.

**Tsingy de Bemaraha**
A national park in western Madagascar known for its "forest" of sharp limestone needles called tsingy. The name is said to mean "the place where one cannot walk barefoot."

**Merina people**
Madagascar's largest ethnic group, centered in the Central Highlands. The Merina kingdom unified most of the island in the 19th century under rulers such as Queen Ranavalona I.

**Malagasy**
The name of Madagascar's people and their Austronesian language. Under French rule the country was called the Malagasy Republic.

**Austronesian settlement from Borneo**
Madagascar was first settled by Austronesian seafarers from the Borneo region who crossed the Indian Ocean. It is the westernmost point of the Austronesian expansion, which is why Malagasy is related to languages of Indonesia.

**Vanilla**
Madagascar produces about 80 percent of the world's vanilla, and it is also a leading producer of cloves.

**Madagascar periwinkle**
A flowering plant native to Madagascar that is the source of the chemotherapy drugs vinblastine and vincristine, used against Hodgkin's lymphoma and leukemia.

**Traveller's tree (ravenala)**
A plant native to Madagascar with a large fan of leaves. It appears on the national emblem.

**Canal des Pangalanes**
A chain of natural rivers and lagoons on Madagascar's east coast, joined by artificial canals, that stretches for hundreds of kilometers. Work on it began under French rule in the late 19th century.

**Neighbors: Mayotte, Comoros, Réunion and Mauritius**
The French department of Mayotte and the nation of Comoros lie northwest of Madagascar, while Réunion and Mauritius lie to the east. Madagascar is also the world's fourth-largest island.

**Acadia National Park and Mount Desert Island**
Acadia, the most frequent giveaway for Maine, is a national park on the rocky Atlantic coast. Most of it lies on Mount Desert Island, and it also includes parts of the Schoodic Peninsula and Isle au Haut. Features include Eagle Lake and the glacial erratic boulder called Bubble Rock.

**Augusta**
The capital of Maine, located on the Kennebec River. It appears in nearly every final line, often alongside the state's largest cities, Portland, Bangor, and Lewiston.

**Mount Katahdin and Baxter State Park**
Mount Katahdin is Maine's highest peak and the northern end of the Appalachian Trail. It sits inside Baxter State Park, a large wilderness park in the north-central part of the state. In 1939, twelve-year-old Donn Fendler survived nine days lost on Katahdin, a story later told in the book "Lost on a Mountain in Maine."

**Cadillac Mountain**
The highest point on Mount Desert Island, inside Acadia National Park. It is the tallest mountain along the U.S. Atlantic coast, and at certain times of year it is one of the first places in the country to see the sunrise.

**Moosehead Lake and the Kennebec River**
Moosehead Lake is the largest lake in Maine and the source of the Kennebec River, which flows south through Augusta into the Gulf of Maine. The lake also hosts an annual International Seaplane Fly-In each September.

**Portland and Casco Bay**
Portland is Maine's largest city and main seaport, on Casco Bay, and shares its name with Portland, Oregon. Its Munjoy Hill is home to the Portland Observatory, the last remaining maritime signal tower in the United States.

**Penobscot River, Penobscot Bay, and Bangor**
The Penobscot River flows past the city of Bangor into Penobscot Bay, a center of the state's lobster fishing. Bangor is home to a 31-foot statue of the folk-hero lumberjack Paul Bunyan, and Isle au Haut sits at the entrance to the bay.

**Hundred-Mile Wilderness**
A stretch of the Appalachian Trail in Maine leading toward Katahdin. It is known as the longest and most remote section of the trail without roads or towns, so hikers must carry all their supplies.

**Aroostook County and the Aroostook War**
Aroostook is Maine's large, northernmost county, which includes the cities of Presque Isle and Caribou. It gives its name to the "bloodless" Aroostook War (1838–1839), a border dispute with British Canada that was settled by the Webster–Ashburton Treaty of 1842.

**Quoddy Head and Eastport**
West Quoddy Head, a state park near Lubec, is the easternmost point of the contiguous United States, so it is often called the closest U.S. point to Africa. The nearby city of Eastport claims to be the first in the nation to see the sunrise. The Old Sow whirlpool, the largest tidal whirlpool in the Western Hemisphere, lies off Eastport.

**Campobello Island**
A Canadian island in New Brunswick whose only road link is a bridge from Lubec, Maine. It is famous as the site of Franklin D. Roosevelt's summer home.

**New Hampshire as its only neighbor**
Maine is the only U.S. state that borders exactly one other state, New Hampshire, to its west. Its other land borders are with the Canadian provinces of Quebec and New Brunswick.

**Down East, the Schoodic Peninsula, and Bar Harbor**
"Down East" is the name for Maine's eastern coastal region, which includes towns such as Ellsworth and Calais. The Schoodic Peninsula, the only mainland part of Acadia, lies across Frenchman Bay from the tourist town of Bar Harbor on Mount Desert Island.

**Saint John River and the Republic of Madawaska**
The Saint John River forms part of Maine's northern border with New Brunswick before flowing into the Bay of Fundy. The Republic of Madawaska was an unrecognized "republic" in the disputed borderland along this river.

**Kennebunkport and Walker's Point**
Kennebunkport, a coastal town in southern Maine, is home to Walker's Point, the summer estate of the Bush family, including President George H. W. Bush.

**Davos and the World Economic Forum**
Davos is a resort town in the eastern canton of Graubünden (Grisons) that hosts the World Economic Forum's annual meeting of world leaders every January. Davos was also famous for its tuberculosis sanatoriums in the late 1800s and early 1900s.

**Bern, Zurich, and Geneva**
Bern is Switzerland's capital, Zurich is its largest city, and Geneva, at the western end of Lake Geneva, is its second largest. Geneva hosts the headquarters of the International Red Cross and many other international organizations.

**Romansh**
A Romance language spoken mostly in Graubünden in the east, for example in the Surselva valley. It is one of Switzerland's four national languages, along with German, French, and Italian.

**Cantons**
Switzerland is a federation (the Swiss Confederation) made up of 26 states called cantons, such as Zurich, Geneva, Lucerne, Uri, and Ticino.

**Matterhorn and Zermatt**
The Matterhorn is a pyramid-shaped Alpine peak on the border between Switzerland and Italy. The car-free resort town of Zermatt lies at its foot, and the Gornergrat ridge above Zermatt has an observatory and a famous railway.

**Gotthard Base Tunnel**
A 57-kilometer railway tunnel through the Alps that opened in 2016 as the world's longest and deepest rail tunnel. It links the canton of Uri in the north to Italian-speaking Ticino in the south.

**Lake Lucerne**
A lake in central Switzerland whose German name, Vierwaldstättersee, means "lake of the four forest cantons." A critic compared Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 14 to moonlight on this lake, which gave it the nickname "Moonlight Sonata"; the city of Lucerne on its shore has the covered wooden Chapel Bridge.

**Lausanne and the IOC**
Lausanne, on the north shore of Lake Geneva, is the headquarters of the International Olympic Committee. The Jura Mountains rise to its northwest.

**Neutrality**
Switzerland is famous for its long-standing policy of armed neutrality, which kept it out of both World Wars. Infrastructure such as the Sonnenberg Tunnel near Lucerne was built to double as a huge nuclear fallout shelter.

**Glacier Express and the Rhaetian Railway**
The Glacier Express is a scenic train running between St. Moritz and Zermatt. The Rhaetian Railway runs the Albula and Bernina lines in Graubünden, including the circular Brusio spiral viaduct.

**Bern landmarks**
Bern's Old Town on the Aare River includes the Bear Pit (BärenGraben), where the city's symbolic bears are kept, the Nydegg Church, and the Marzilibahn, a short funicular railway.

**Montreux and Chillon Castle**
Montreux is a town on Lake Geneva famous for its annual jazz festival. Nearby Chillon Castle sits on a rock in the lake and is one of Switzerland's best-known castles.

**Castles of Bellinzona**
Three medieval castles in Bellinzona, the capital of Ticino, that guarded the Alpine routes into Italy. They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

**Basel**
A city on the Rhine River in the northwest, where Switzerland borders France and Germany. It is one of the country's largest cities and a center of the pharmaceutical industry.

**Flims Rockslide**
A huge prehistoric landslide near Flims in Graubünden, the largest visible one in the world. It blocked the valley of the Rhine about 10,000 years ago.

**Ushuaia**
The largest city of Tierra del Fuego and capital of Argentina's Tierra del Fuego Province. Lying on the Beagle Channel, it is generally considered the southernmost city in the world, and many tourist cruises to Antarctica depart from it. Its name comes from the Yaghan language.

**Strait of Magellan**
The sea passage that separates Tierra del Fuego from the South American mainland and the rest of Patagonia. Ferdinand Magellan sailed through it in 1520 and is credited with naming the islands "Land of Fire" after the many native campfires he saw along the shore.

**"Land of Fire"**
The English translation of Tierra del Fuego, an archipelago at the southern tip of South America that is divided between Argentina (eastern part) and Chile (western part). Its main island is called Isla Grande de Tierra del Fuego.

**Mount Darwin (Monte Darwin)**
One of the highest peaks of the archipelago, in the Cordillera Darwin of the Chilean section. It was named for Charles Darwin, who visited the region during the survey voyage of the HMS Beagle. Monte Sarmiento is another major peak of the range.

**Yaghan (Yagan) people and language**
An indigenous seafaring people of the region's southern islands. Their language is famous as the source of "mamihlapinatapai," often called the most untranslatable word (a look shared by two people who each wish the other would act first). Its last native speaker, Cristina Calderón, died in 2022.

**Navarino Island and Puerto Williams**
A Chilean island south of the Beagle Channel. It holds the town of Puerto Williams, one of the world's southernmost settlements, as well as Yaghan middens and a museum of Yaghan culture.

**Selk'nam (Ona) genocide**
The Selk'nam, also called the Ona, were the main indigenous people of the large island. They were massacred in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by gold prospectors and sheep ranchers, and many survivors were relocated to a Salesian mission on Dawson Island. Other native groups include the Haush and the Alacaluf (Kawésqar).

**Julius Popper and the gold rush**
A Romanian-born engineer and adventurer who led a gold rush in Tierra del Fuego that began in the 1880s. He is notorious for his role in killing the Selk'nam, and the rush brought many Croatian immigrants who settled towns such as Porvenir in the Chilean section.

**Beagle Channel**
A strait along the southern coast of the main island, named after HMS Beagle. Ushuaia lies on it. Argentina and Chile disputed the Picton, Lennox, and Nueva Islands at its eastern end in the Beagle conflict, which nearly led to war in 1978 and was settled through papal mediation in 1984.

**Invasive beavers**
North American beavers were introduced in 1946 to start a fur trade. With no natural predators, they spread widely and destroyed forests, prompting a huge eradication effort described as one of the largest ever planned.

**Cape Horn**
The southernmost headland of the archipelago, on Chilean Hornos Island. It marks the northern edge of the Drake Passage, which separates South America from Antarctica.

**Robert FitzRoy and the Beagle voyages**
Captain of HMS Beagle, who surveyed the region and brought four Fuegian natives back to England on his first voyage. He returned three of them home on the second voyage, which also carried Charles Darwin.

**Isla de los Estados (Staten Island)**
