The Great Escarpment is the steep edge of the high interior plateau of southern Africa, and its highest eastern section is the Drakensberg, shared with Lesotho. Tugela Falls in the Drakensberg is often called one of the tallest waterfalls in the world.

**Table Mountain and Cape Town**
Table Mountain is the flat-topped mountain overlooking Cape Town, reachable by cable car. Cape Town's harbor area, the Victoria and Albert Waterfront, is a popular tourist destination.

**Cape Agulhas and the Cape of Good Hope**
Cape Agulhas is the true southernmost point of Africa and is used as the dividing point between the Atlantic and Indian Oceans. The more famous Cape of Good Hope, at the tip of the Cape Peninsula, is often wrongly thought to be the southernmost point.

**Kimberley and the Big Hole**
Kimberley, in Northern Cape province, was the center of the diamond rush of the 1870s. The Big Hole is a giant, mostly hand-dug former diamond mine there, and the city was besieged by Boer forces during the Second Boer War.

**Kruger National Park**
South Africa's largest and most visited game reserve, in the northeast along the border with Mozambique. Its northern tip reaches the Limpopo River, which forms part of South Africa's northern border with Zimbabwe and Botswana.

**Blyde River Canyon and the Three Rondavels**
A large canyon in Mpumalanga province often called the world's largest "green canyon" because of its lush plant cover. The Three Rondavels are rock peaks there shaped like traditional round huts.

**False Bay and Simon's Town**
False Bay is a large bay on the east side of the Cape Peninsula near Cape Town. The town of Simon's Town on its shore is the main base of the South African Navy.

**Gauteng, Johannesburg, and the Highveld**
Gauteng is South Africa's smallest but most populous province, located on the high interior grassland plateau called the Highveld. It contains Johannesburg, the largest city, and Pretoria, the administrative capital.

**Fynbos and rooibos**
Fynbos is a shrubland with a Mediterranean-type climate found in the Western Cape, part of the Cape Floral Region, one of the most plant-rich places on Earth. One of its plants is rooibos, used to make a red herbal tea.

**Great Karoo and the Kalahari**
The Great Karoo is a dry semi-desert plateau in the interior, lying below the Great Escarpment to its north. The Kalahari Desert extends into the north of the country, where the Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park is shared with Botswana; to the south, the Cango Caves lie in the Swartberg Mountains.

**Zulu and Sotho languages**
Two of South Africa's official languages, both Bantu languages. Zulu is especially known for its click consonants, borrowed from the Khoisan languages of the region.

**Pikes Peak**
The most famous summit of the Rockies' Front Range in Colorado, near Colorado Springs. It is the classic giveaway for the range, and the view from its top inspired the song "America the Beautiful."

**Mount Elbert and Mount Massive**
Mount Elbert in Colorado's Sawatch Range is the highest peak in the Rocky Mountains, at about 14,440 feet. Nearby Mount Massive is, despite its name, only the second highest.

**Grand Teton and the Teton Range**
The Teton Range in northwestern Wyoming is a dramatic subrange of the Rockies, protected in Grand Teton National Park. Climbers commonly reach the top of Grand Teton by the Owen-Spalding route.

**Continental Divide**
The line separating rivers that drain to the Pacific from those that drain to the Atlantic and Arctic. Through most of North America it follows the crest of the Rockies.

**Yoho, Jasper, Banff, and Kootenay National Parks**
Neighboring national parks in the Canadian Rockies of Alberta and British Columbia. In Yoho, the Canadian Pacific Railway crosses the Divide at Kicking Horse Pass, and the Kicking Horse River starts there. Jasper contains the source of the Athabasca River.

**Glacier National Park**
A park in the Rockies of northwestern Montana, bordering Canada's Waterton Lakes. Its shrinking glaciers include Jackson and Blackfoot Glaciers. The Flathead River valley runs through the range nearby.

**Liard River (northern terminus)**
The Liard River in northern British Columbia is usually considered the northern end of the Rockies. The Muskwa Ranges of the northern Canadian Rockies hold Muncho Lake and the Battle of Britain Range, whose peaks have World War II names such as Mount Roosevelt and Churchill Peak.

**Rocky Mountain National Park and the Front Range**
The Front Range is the easternmost range of the Rockies in Colorado, rising west of Denver. Rocky Mountain National Park, named for the range, protects part of it.

**Subranges: Wind River, Uinta, Bitterroot, San Juan, Sawtooth**
Major subranges include the Wind River Range in Wyoming, the Uinta Mountains in Utah (which unusually run east–west), the Bitterroot Range on the Idaho–Montana border, and the San Juan Mountains in southwestern Colorado. Idaho's Sawtooth National Recreation Area is also in the range. Canadian subranges include the Clark and Salish ranges.

**South Pass**
A broad, low pass in Wyoming's Wind River area that became the main route of the Oregon Trail across the Rockies. Benjamin Bonneville led the first wagon train over the Divide through it in 1832.

**Lewis and Clark crossing the Bitterroots**
The Lewis and Clark Expedition struggled across the Bitterroot Range on the Lolo Trail in 1805 on its way to the Pacific.

**Sources of the Peace, Fraser, and Athabasca Rivers**
Several major Canadian rivers begin in the Canadian Rockies. The Fraser flows to the Pacific at Vancouver, while the Peace and Athabasca drain toward the Arctic through the Mackenzie system. The Blaeberry River also begins there.

**Uravan Mineral Belt**
A mining district on the Colorado Plateau in western Colorado and eastern Utah. Its name comes from the uranium and vanadium it produced.

**Canada lynx in the San Juan Mountains**
Colorado reintroduced the threatened Canada lynx to the San Juan Mountains of the southern Rockies, where most of the state's population now lives.

**Rocky Mountain oysters**
A Western novelty dish of breaded, deep-fried bull (or other animal) testicles, also called prairie oysters.

**Vancouver and the 2010 Winter Olympics**
Vancouver is British Columbia's most populous city, and it hosted the 2010 Winter Olympics. Many of the events were held at the Whistler Blackcomb ski resort to the north.

**Victoria and Vancouver Island**
Victoria, the provincial capital, is on the southern tip of Vancouver Island, which also contains the city of Nanaimo. The island and the city are both named for the British naval captain George Vancouver, who mapped the coast in the 1790s, and Victoria is famous for the Butchart Gardens.

**Fraser River and the Fraser Canyon Gold Rush**
The Fraser is British Columbia's longest river. It reaches the sea near Vancouver, separating the city from its suburbs of Richmond and Surrey. The 1858 Fraser Canyon Gold Rush brought thousands of prospectors and led Britain to create the Colony of British Columbia that year.

**Gastown and its steam clock**
Vancouver's oldest neighborhood grew around a saloon opened in 1867 by "Gassy Jack" Deighton. It is known for a steam-powered clock built by Raymond Saunders in 1977.

**Stanley Park**
A large urban park on a peninsula in Vancouver between English Bay and the Burrard Inlet. It is named for Governor General Lord Stanley (Frederick Stanley) and is famous for its totem poles.

**Strait of Georgia and the Strait of Juan de Fuca**
The Strait of Georgia separates Vancouver Island from the mainland, and the Strait of Juan de Fuca to the south separates the island from Washington State. Both are part of the Salish Sea.

**Kelowna and Okanagan Lake**
Kelowna is the main city of the Okanagan Valley, a fruit- and wine-growing region in the province's interior. It lies on Okanagan Lake, a long, narrow lake carved by glaciers.

**Kwakiutl (Kwakwaka'wakw) and Tsimshian peoples**
Indigenous First Nations of the British Columbia coast. The Haida of the Haida Gwaii archipelago and the Nuu-chah-nulth of Vancouver Island are other major coastal peoples.

**Western terminus of the Canadian Pacific Railway**
Vancouver became the western end of Canada's first transcontinental railway in 1887. Port facilities on the Burrard Inlet and the Fraser River delta still make the area Canada's busiest gateway to the Pacific.

**Expo 86**
A world's fair held in Vancouver in 1986. Before it opened, many low-income residents were evicted from the Downtown Eastside, a neighborhood that later opened North America's first legal supervised drug injection site, Insite, in 2003.

**Nootka Crisis**
A 1789 dispute that began when Spaniard Esteban José Martínez seized British ships belonging to the trader John Meares at Nootka Sound, on the west coast of Vancouver Island. Spain and Britain nearly went to war before signing the Nootka Conventions, which opened the coast to British trade. Juan Pérez had been the first European to reach the area in 1774, and the region's trade in sea otter pelts made it valuable.

**On-to-Ottawa Trek (1935)**
A Depression-era protest in which unemployed relief-camp workers, led by Arthur "Slim" Evans, set out from Vancouver to travel by freight train to Ottawa. The march was stopped at Regina, where it ended in the Regina Riot.

**Mount Robson and Mount Fairweather**
Mount Robson is the highest peak in the Canadian Rockies. Mount Fairweather, on the border with Alaska, is the highest point in British Columbia.

**Kamloops and Nanaimo**
Both cities grew from early fur-trading or Hudson's Bay Company posts. Kamloops is in the interior at the meeting of the North and South Thompson Rivers, and Nanaimo is on the east coast of Vancouver Island.

**Joined Confederation in 1871 as the sixth province**
British Columbia joined Canada in 1871 after Ottawa promised to build a transcontinental railway to it. Its flag shows a Union Jack with a crown at its center, above a setting sun over wavy blue and white lines.

**Jebel Toubkal**
The highest peak of the Atlas Mountains and of North Africa, at about 4,167 meters, located in the High Atlas roughly 60 kilometers south of Marrakesh. It is the most frequently mentioned peak in questions on the range.

**Aurès Mountains**
The easternmost subrange of the Atlas system, in northeastern Algeria and extending toward Tunisia. Its highest peak is Djebel Chélia, and it is home to the Chaoui Berber people.

**Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia**
The Atlas Mountains stretch about 2,500 kilometers across the Maghreb of northwest Africa through these three countries, running roughly parallel to the Mediterranean coast and separating it from the Sahara.

**Subranges: High, Middle, Anti, Tell, and Saharan Atlas**
The system is divided into several subranges. The High Atlas, Middle Atlas, and Anti-Atlas are in Morocco, while the Tell Atlas runs along the Mediterranean coast and the Saharan Atlas (including the Ksour, Amour, and Ouled Naïl ranges) runs farther inland.

**Berbers (Amazigh)**
The Indigenous people who primarily inhabit the Atlas, speaking Berber languages alongside Arabic. Groups include the Shleuh (Chleuh) of Morocco, the Chaoui of the Aurès, and the Kabyle of Algeria, whose mountain villages were studied by sociologist Pierre Bourdieu.

**Titan Atlas**
The range is named after Atlas, the Titan of Greek mythology condemned to hold up the sky (heavens). Greek legend placed him in northwest Africa.

**Rif Mountains**
A mountain range along Morocco's Mediterranean coast, to the north of the Atlas. It is geologically separate, belonging to the Betic-Rif system tied to Spain, and is separated from the Atlas by the Sebou River valley.

**Marrakesh and Fes**
Moroccan cities in the foothills of the Atlas. Marrakesh, founded by the Berber Almoravid dynasty, lies on the plain north of the High Atlas, within sight of Toubkal.

**Draa River**
A river formed by the joining of the Dadès and Imini rivers, which rise in the High Atlas, flowing south toward the Sahara. The Dadès Gorge is a famous canyon in the range.

**Ouarzazate and the Noor Solar Power Station**
Ouarzazate is a city south of the High Atlas near the Anti-Atlas. Outside it lies the Noor Ouarzazate solar complex, one of the largest concentrated solar power plants in the world.

**Barbary lion and Atlas bear**
The Barbary (Atlas) lion was a lion subspecies of the region, hunted heavily, including by the Romans for gladiatorial games, and now extinct in the wild. The Atlas bear, Africa's only native bear, is extinct.

**Cuvier's gazelle**
A gazelle native to the Atlas Mountains, named for the French naturalist Georges Cuvier. The range is also home to the Atlas cedar and a dwarf viper among the shortest of all vipers.

**Hautes Plaines and chotts**
The High Plateaus (Hautes Plaines) between the Tell Atlas and Saharan Atlas in Algeria contain shallow salt lakes called chotts, such as Chott ech Chergui and Chott el Hodna.

**Grand Erg Occidental**
The "Great Western Erg," a vast sea of sand dunes in the Algerian Sahara just south of the Atlas Mountains.

**Orogeny**
The Atlas were first formed during the Alleghenian (Variscan) orogeny hundreds of millions of years ago. They were later uplifted again during the Alpine orogeny, as Africa collided with Europe and Iberia.

**Largest lake in Africa, named for Queen Victoria**
Lake Victoria is Africa's largest lake by area and the largest tropical lake in the world. Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania share it. It sits in a shallow basin between the two arms of the East African Rift, east of the Albertine (Western) Rift, and it is named after the British monarch Queen Victoria.

**Source of the White Nile**
The lake's outflow at Jinja, Uganda, is the traditional source of the White Nile. The river crosses Uganda through Lake Kyoga and continues into South Sudan. The original outlet was Ripon Falls, which was submerged when a dam was built. The lake also has a smaller outlet, the Katonga River.

**John Hanning Speke and Richard Burton**
In 1858 Speke became the first European to see the lake. He named it after Queen Victoria and claimed it was the source of the Nile. The claim led to a bitter public feud with Richard Burton, his former expedition partner. In 1875 Henry Morton Stanley sailed around the lake and confirmed Speke's claim.

**Owen Falls Dam (Nalubaale Dam)**
A hydroelectric dam near Jinja, completed in 1954 and later renamed the Nalubaale Power Station. It flooded Ripon Falls and now regulates how much water leaves the lake into the Nile. Nalubaale is also the lake's Luganda name.

**Kagera River**
The largest river flowing into the lake. It enters on the west side in Tanzania. Its headwaters include the Ruvuvu River, and it passes over Rusumo Falls on the Rwanda–Tanzania border.

**Ukerewe Island**
The largest island in the lake, in Tanzania. It is known for a large community of people with albinism, many of whom moved there to escape persecution. The Kerewe people who live there carve wooden sculptures.

**Nile perch and cichlids**
The Nile perch, a large predatory fish brought into the lake in the 1950s, wiped out hundreds of the lake's native cichlid species. The case is a classic example of the damage invasive species can do. Hubert Sauper's 2004 documentary Darwin's Nightmare examines the Nile perch fishing industry and its effects on local people.

**Ssese Islands**
An archipelago of more than 80 islands in the northwest part of the lake, in Uganda. Bugala, the largest, has oil-palm plantations whose palm oil is shipped across the lake to refineries in Jinja.

**Kampala and Entebbe**
Uganda's capital, Kampala, lies on the lake's northern shore. Nearby Entebbe, Uganda's main international airport city, is also on the shore and is home to the Entebbe Zoo (the Uganda Wildlife Education Centre).

**Kisumu and Winam Gulf**
Kisumu is Kenya's main port on the lake. It lies on Winam Gulf (formerly Kavirondo Gulf), the lake's northeastern arm. Rusinga Island, in the gulf, is famous for early ape fossils such as Proconsul.

**Mwanza and Bismarck Rock**
Mwanza is Tanzania's main port on the southern shore. Bismarck Rock, a famous balancing rock formation, stands in the water there. Speke Gulf and Emin Pasha Gulf are inlets along the southern shore.

**Water hyacinth**
An invasive floating plant from South America that has formed huge mats on the lake. The mats choke harbors, block boats, and reduce the oxygen in the water.

**Migingo Island dispute**
In the late 2000s Kenya and Uganda disputed control of Migingo, a tiny, densely crowded rock island valued for its rich Nile perch fishing grounds.

**Rubondo Island National Park**
A national park in Tanzania covering Rubondo Island and nearby islets in the southwest part of the lake.

**Nam Lolwe and Nalubaale**
Native names for the lake. Nam Lolwe is the Luo name used in Kenya, and Nalubaale is the Luganda name used in Uganda.

**New Madrid earthquakes**
A series of powerful earthquakes in 1811–1812 centered near New Madrid, Missouri, in the New Madrid Seismic Zone. They were so violent that parts of the Mississippi briefly flowed backward. They also created Reelfoot Lake in northwest Tennessee.

**Lake Itasca**
The traditional source of the Mississippi, a small glacial lake in Itasca State Park in Clearwater County, northern Minnesota. From there the river flows about 2,300 miles south to the Gulf of Mexico.

**New Orleans and the Gulf of Mexico**
The river flows past New Orleans before emptying into the Gulf of Mexico through its delta in Louisiana. Algiers Point, across from the French Quarter, is the deepest spot on the river, and the New Orleans neighborhood of Algiers is named for it.

**Atchafalaya River and the Old River Control Structure**
The Atchafalaya is a distributary that branches off the lower Mississippi in Louisiana. It offers a much shorter, steeper route to the Gulf, so the Mississippi tends to shift its main channel into it (a process called avulsion). The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built the Old River Control Structure to limit how much water the Atchafalaya takes and to keep the main river flowing past Baton Rouge and New Orleans.

**Cairo, Illinois and the Ohio River**
The Ohio River joins the Mississippi at Cairo (pronounced "CAY-ro"), at the southern tip of Illinois. This confluence is often used as the dividing point between the Upper and Lower Mississippi.

**Great Mississippi Flood of 1927**
The most destructive river flood in U.S. history. It covered huge areas of the lower Mississippi valley and displaced hundreds of thousands of people, many of them Black sharecroppers. It led to the Flood Control Act of 1928, which gave the federal government responsibility for levees and flood control. Another major flood struck the upper Mississippi in 1993.

**Kentucky Bend**
A loop of the river creates an exclave of Fulton County, Kentucky. The land is surrounded by Missouri and Tennessee and cut off from the rest of Kentucky. River course changes after the New Madrid earthquakes played a part in creating it.

**St. Anthony Falls and the I-35W bridge collapse**
St. Anthony Falls in Minneapolis is the only natural major waterfall on the Mississippi. The I-35W bridge, which crossed the river just downstream, collapsed during rush hour in August 2007 and killed 13 people.

**St. Louis, the Gateway Arch, and the Eads Bridge**
The Gateway Arch in St. Louis stands on the river's west bank. The nearby Eads Bridge, completed in 1874, was the first major steel-truss bridge across the Mississippi. To prove to the public that it was safe, an elephant was led across it.

**Missouri River ("Big Muddy")**
The Mississippi's longest tributary, nicknamed "the Big Muddy" for its heavy load of sediment. It joins the Mississippi just north of St. Louis. Measured together, the Missouri–Mississippi system is one of the longest river systems in the world.

**Memphis and other river cities**
Memphis, Tennessee is the largest city directly on the river. Other river cities include Minneapolis–St. Paul, Vicksburg, Natchez, and Baton Rouge. The Great River Road, a National Scenic Byway, follows the river for its full length.

**Bonnet Carré Spillway and Lake Pontchartrain**
A flood-control structure upstream of New Orleans. During high water it diverts some of the Mississippi's flow into Lake Pontchartrain to protect the city.

**Marquette and Joliet**
In 1673 the Jesuit missionary Jacques Marquette and the explorer Louis Jolliet became the first Europeans to explore and map much of the Mississippi. They traveled down it from Wisconsin to near the mouth of the Arkansas River.

**Asian carp**
Invasive carp species, such as silver and bighead carp, escaped into the Mississippi basin and spread quickly from the 1990s on. In some stretches they now make up the large majority of the fish biomass and crowd out native species.

**Huey P. Long Bridges**
Two Louisiana bridges across the lower Mississippi named for Governor Huey P. Long. One is near New Orleans (in Jefferson Parish) and the other is in Baton Rouge.

**Mohenjo-daro and Harappa**
The two greatest cities of the Bronze Age Indus Valley (Harappan) Civilization, which flourished in the Indus basin of modern Pakistan and northwest India from roughly 3300 to 1300 BCE. They are the most common giveaway clue for the river.

**Great Bath**
A large, waterproofed brick pool at Mohenjo-daro, probably used for ritual bathing. It was excavated in the 1920s, and Mortimer Wheeler later conducted major excavations at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa.

**Indus Waters Treaty (1960)**
A water-sharing agreement between India and Pakistan brokered by the World Bank. It divides the Indus system's rivers, giving the eastern tributaries mainly to India and the western ones mainly to Pakistan; the Indus flows through Ladakh in India before entering Pakistan.

**Tarbela Dam**
A huge earth-filled dam on the Indus in Pakistan, among the largest in the world. It was built as part of the works that compensated Pakistan for water allocated to India under the Indus Waters Treaty.

**Indus seals and undeciphered script**
Thousands of small square seals, often carved with animals such as a unicorn-like bull, bear a writing system that has never been deciphered, one of the biggest mysteries of the civilization.

**Punjab ("five rivers")**
The Punjab region is named for the five rivers (Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej) that flow into the Indus. The Indus flows through Pakistan's Punjab and Sindh provinces before emptying into the Arabian Sea.

**"Dancing Girl"**
A small bronze statuette of a nude young woman found at Mohenjo-daro, one of the most famous artworks of the Indus Valley Civilization.

**Lothal**
An Indus Valley site in Gujarat, India, known for its dockyard and as a port. Remains of domesticated chickens were found there.

**Rakhigarhi**
One of the largest Indus Valley sites, in Haryana, India. It was the source of the first ancient DNA genome sequenced from the Harappan civilization.

**Indus River dolphin (bhulan)**
A freshwater dolphin species found in the Indus system that is functionally blind, navigating by echolocation in the river's muddy water.

**Flush toilets and urban planning**
Indus cities had grid layouts, standardized bricks, covered drains, and some of the oldest known toilet and sewage systems in the world.

**Earliest cotton and dentistry**
The Indus Valley yields the earliest known evidence of cotton cultivation, and at Mehrgarh archaeologists found the earliest evidence of dentistry, teeth drilled with bow drills.

**Shyok, Gilgit, Hunza, and Kabul rivers**
Major tributaries of the upper Indus. The Shyok rises from the Rimo Glacier in the Karakoram; the Hunza flows into the Gilgit, which joins the Indus; and the Kabul River enters from Afghanistan.

**Thar Desert**
The desert straddling India and Pakistan to the east of the lower Indus. Reduced river flow has been linked to increased desertification in the region.

**Oldest, deepest, and most voluminous freshwater lake**
Lake Baikal in southern Siberia is the deepest lake in the world, at about 1,620 meters (over 5,300 feet), and the oldest, at about 25 million years. It holds about 20 percent of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water, making it the largest freshwater lake by volume and second only to the saltwater Caspian Sea among all lakes. It has a long, crescent shape.

**Angara River and Irkutsk**
The Angara is the only river that flows out of Baikal. It runs past the city of Irkutsk and joins the Yenisei River. Its tributaries include the Biryusa and Chuna, which join to form the Taseyeva.

**Selenga River**
The largest of the hundreds of rivers that flow into Baikal, entering from Mongolia through a large delta on the eastern shore. Other inflowing rivers include the Barguzin and the Sarma.

**Olkhon Island and the Small Sea Strait**
Olkhon is Baikal's largest island, about 45 miles long, and is inhabited mostly by Buryats. The Small Sea (Maloye More) Strait separates it from the western shore.

**Nerpa (Baikal seal)**
A small seal found only in Lake Baikal, one of the few seal species that lives entirely in fresh water. It feeds largely on golomyanka fish.

**Buryats, Buryatia, and Ulan-Ude**
The Buryats are a Mongolic people native to the lands around Baikal, who call the lake the "blue eye." The eastern shore lies in the Republic of Buryatia, whose capital is Ulan-Ude, while the western shore lies in Irkutsk Oblast.

**Golomyanka**
Translucent, oily fish found only in Lake Baikal. Unusually, they give birth to live young, and they are a main food source for the nerpa.

**Baikal Rift Zone**
Baikal sits in a continental rift valley where the Earth's crust is slowly pulling apart. The rift is still widening, and the deep basin beneath the lake is filled with thick layers of sediment.

**"North Sea" and other names**
In historical Chinese texts, Baikal was called the "North Sea" (Beihai). It is also nicknamed the older sister of Mongolia's Lake Khövsgöl, which lies to its southwest.

**Environmental threats: the Baikalsk mill, Transneft pipeline, and Angarsk**
The Baikalsk pulp and paper mill polluted the lake for decades before closing in 2013. In the 2000s, protests forced the oil company Transneft to reroute a planned pipeline away from the shore. A proposed uranium enrichment center in nearby Angarsk also raised fears for the lake.

**Ushkany Islands, Barguzin Bay, and Proval Bay**
Features of the lake. The Ushkany Islands are a breeding ground for nerpa, Barguzin Bay on the eastern shore is the largest bay, and Proval Bay formed when an 1862 earthquake caused land in the Selenga delta to sink.

**Dark ice rings**
Satellite images have shown giant dark rings, several kilometers wide, forming in Baikal's winter ice. They are thought to be caused by warmer water rising and swirling beneath the ice.

**Mir-1 and Mir-2 submersibles**
In 2008–2010, the Russian deep-sea submersibles Mir-1 and Mir-2 made a series of dives to explore the bottom of Lake Baikal.

**Severobaykalsk and the Baikal–Amur Mainline**
Severobaykalsk, on the northern tip of the lake, is a station on the Baikal–Amur Mainline (BAM), a railway running east from Baikal to the Amur River region.

**Kurbat Ivanov**
A Russian Cossack explorer who in 1643 became the first European known to reach Lake Baikal.

**River Thames and Tower Bridge**
London lies on the River Thames. Tower Bridge, a Victorian bascule bridge whose roadway lifts to let ships pass, is the city's most famous crossing, and it was decorated with Olympic rings for the 2012 Games.

**Buckingham Palace**
The London residence of the British monarch, in the City of Westminster. It is a common giveaway for the city.

**Big Ben and the Houses of Parliament**
Big Ben is the nickname of the great bell in the clock tower of the Palace of Westminster, possibly named after Sir Benjamin Hall, who oversaw its installation. Claude Monet painted a famous series of the Houses of Parliament, and Westminster Abbey stands nearby.

**Tower of London and its ravens**
A historic fortress on the Thames. At least six ravens are kept there because of a legend that if they ever leave, the Tower and the kingdom will fall.

**Trafalgar Square and Nelson's Column**
A large public square in central London commemorating the 1805 Battle of Trafalgar. At its center, a statue of Admiral Horatio Nelson stands on top of a tall column.

**St. Paul's Cathedral**
A domed Anglican cathedral on Ludgate Hill, designed by Christopher Wren and rebuilt after the Great Fire of 1666. Its dome contains the Whispering Gallery, where a whisper against the wall can be heard on the opposite side.

**The Shard**
A glass, pyramid-shaped skyscraper designed by Renzo Piano and owned largely by Qatari investors. When completed in 2012 it became the UK's tallest building, surpassing One Canada Square at Canary Wharf.

**The Gherkin**
The nickname of 30 St Mary Axe, a rounded, pickle-shaped glass skyscraper by Norman Foster, originally built for the insurance company Swiss Re.

**London Underground ("the Tube")**
London's subway system, the oldest in the world. It is known for Harry Beck's diagram-style map, the phrase "mind the gap," and its red roundel logo crossed by a blue bar, and three of the four bombs in the 7 July 2005 attacks exploded on it. A form of mosquito called Culex molestus lives in its tunnels.

**London Eye**
A giant Ferris wheel on the south bank of the Thames that opened in 2000, a common modern giveaway for the city.

**British Museum**
A major museum of world history and culture in Bloomsbury, holding objects such as the Rosetta Stone and the Elgin Marbles.

**Walkie-Talkie**
The nickname of 20 Fenchurch Street, a skyscraper that widens toward the top. Its curved glass face reflected concentrated sunlight onto the street when it was built, melting parts of parked cars.

**Millennium Bridge**
A steel footbridge across the Thames linking St. Paul's Cathedral with Tate Modern. It swayed noticeably when it opened in 2000 and was closed for about two years for modifications that stopped the wobble.

**London Bridge in Lake Havasu City**
The 1830s London Bridge was sold in the 1960s, taken apart, and rebuilt in Lake Havasu City, Arizona.

**Kew Gardens**
The Royal Botanic Gardens in the borough of Richmond upon Thames, home to one of the world's largest herbariums. Hampton Court Palace is in the same borough.

**Buenos Aires and the Río de la Plata**
Argentina's capital, Buenos Aires, sits on the Río de la Plata (River Plate), a wide estuary formed where the Paraná and Uruguay Rivers meet. Uruguay's capital, Montevideo, lies across the estuary from it.

**Aconcagua**
The tallest mountain in the Western and Southern Hemispheres, at about 6,961 meters, located in the Andes of Mendoza Province. Its name is often said to mean "Sentinel of Stone." It was first climbed in 1897 by Matthias Zurbriggen via the Horcones Valley, and its Polish Glacier names a well-known climbing route.

**Pampas**
Vast, fertile, low-lying grasslands in central and eastern Argentina that also reach into Uruguay and southern Brazil. They are the center of Argentina's cattle ranching, gaucho culture, and grain farming.

**Patagonia**
The sparsely populated region of dry plateaus and scrubland in southern Argentina, which it shares with Chile. Argentina took control of it through military campaigns in the 1870s and 1880s.

**Paraná River, Rosario, and Corrientes**
The Paraná is Argentina's main river and forms part of its border with Paraguay. Rosario, a major port settled heavily by Italian immigrants, and Corrientes both lie on it, and the Yacyretá Dam is on the stretch shared with Paraguay.

**Chubut Province and Y Wladfa**
Welsh settlers founded the Y Wladfa colony in Chubut Province in Patagonia in 1865, and Welsh is still spoken in towns there. Rawson is the provincial capital, and Comodoro Rivadavia, an oil port on the Gulf of San Jorge, is also in Chubut.

**Ushuaia and Tierra del Fuego**
Argentina holds the eastern half of the Tierra del Fuego archipelago, which it shares with Chile. Its capital there is Ushuaia, on the Beagle Channel, which claims to be the southernmost city in the world. Another city in the province, Río Grande, is known for assembling electronics.

**Perito Moreno Glacier and Los Glaciares National Park**
Perito Moreno is a huge glacier in Santa Cruz Province, one of the few in the world that is not shrinking. It lies in Los Glaciares National Park, which also contains Mount Fitz Roy, a peak on the poorly defined border with Chile in the Southern Patagonian Ice Field.

**Iguazú Falls**
A vast system of waterfalls on the Iguazú River, on Argentina's border with Brazil. The river flows into the Paraná soon after the falls.

**Falkland Islands dispute**
Argentina claims the British-held Falkland Islands, which it calls the Malvinas, as well as South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands. The dispute led to the 1982 Falklands War, which Britain won.

**Mapuche people**
An Indigenous people of southern Chile and Argentina who live in the Pampas and Patagonia.

**Mar Chiquita**
A large salt lake in Córdoba Province, northeast of the city of Córdoba, which is Argentina's second-largest city.

**Laguna del Carbón**
Argentina's lowest point, about 105 meters below sea level, in Santa Cruz Province in Patagonia. It is also the lowest point in the Western and Southern Hemispheres.

**Avenida 9 de Julio**
A very wide avenue in Buenos Aires named for July 9, 1816, the date Argentina declared independence. Other Buenos Aires clues include the Galileo Galilei Planetarium and the villas miserias, or squatter slums.

**Nahuel Huapi National Park**
Argentina's oldest national park, in the Andean lake district of northern Patagonia, near the resort city of San Carlos de Bariloche.

**Kibo, Mawenzi, and Shira**
The three volcanic cones that make up Kilimanjaro. Kibo is the tallest and is dormant, while Mawenzi, with its jagged peaks, and Shira, now a worn-down plateau, are extinct.

**Uhuru Peak**
Kilimanjaro's summit on the rim of Kibo, about 5,895 meters (19,341 feet) high. Its Swahili name means "Freedom Peak," and it was renamed when Tanganyika became independent in 1961.

**Hans Meyer and Ludwig Purtscheller (1889)**
German geographer Hans Meyer and Austrian climber Ludwig Purtscheller made the first recorded ascent of Kilimanjaro in 1889. Meyer named the summit Kaiser-Wilhelm-Spitze after the German emperor Wilhelm II.

**Highest freestanding mountain in the world and the tallest in Africa**
Kilimanjaro is the highest point in Africa and the tallest mountain in the world that is not part of a range. It is a dormant stratovolcano in northeastern Tanzania, near the border with Kenya.

**Barranco Wall**
A steep rock cliff, often called the Great Barranco Wall, that climbers scramble up on the Machame and Lemosho routes. Like the Western Breach, it was formed by ancient lava flows and landslides.

**Moshi**
The Tanzanian town on Kilimanjaro's southern slopes that serves as the main starting point for climbs. It is also the gateway to Kilimanjaro National Park.

**Chagga people**
A Bantu-speaking people who have long farmed the mountain's southern and eastern slopes. In Chagga belief, their chief god lives on the mountain.

**Furtwängler and Rebmann Glaciers**
Glaciers on Kibo's shrinking ice cap. The Rebmann Glacier is named for missionary Johannes Rebmann, while the Furtwängler Glacier sits near the summit. Kilimanjaro's ice fields have lost much of their area and could disappear within decades.

**Saddle Plateau**
A high, wide plain about 4,400 meters up that lies between the Kibo and Mawenzi cones.

**Western Breach and Lava Tower**
The Western Breach is a large gap in the wall of Kibo's crater, created by a landslide, and it offers a steep route to the summit. The Lava Tower is a volcanic rock formation that climbers pass on the western routes.

**Johannes Rebmann**
A German missionary who in 1848 became the first European to report seeing Kilimanjaro. He described the "dazzling whiteness" of its snow, and European geographers at first refused to believe there could be snow near the equator.

**Garden of Senecios (giant groundsels)**
An area of giant groundsels, plants that grow only in East Africa's high mountains, which is passed on several climbing routes. These plants belong to the genus Dendrosenecio, and one species is named for Kilimanjaro.

**Reusch Crater and Gilman's Point**
The Reusch Crater is the inner crater at the top of Kibo, named after the missionary and climber Richard Reusch. Gilman's Point and Stella Point are spots on the crater rim where climbers on different routes reach the top before walking to Uhuru Peak.

**Machame and Lemosho Routes**
Two of the most popular climbing routes. Machame, nicknamed the "Whiskey Route," is the most popular, and Lemosho crosses the Shira Plateau. Both pass the Barranco Wall, while the Mweka trail is often used for the descent.

**German East Africa border and the Queen Victoria myth**
During the colonial era, Kilimanjaro was placed in German East Africa, while Kenya to the north became British. A popular myth says that Queen Victoria gave the mountain to her grandson Wilhelm II as a birthday present, which explains the kink in the border, but historians have debunked it.

**Old Faithful**
The park's most famous geyser and the near-universal giveaway. It erupts quite predictably, usually every 60 to 110 minutes, though not "every hour on the hour" as popular lore says. Members of the 1870 Washburn Expedition gave it its name.

**Yellowstone Caldera (supervolcano)**
The park sits on North America's largest active supervolcano, whose caldera formed in huge eruptions. Heat from the magma beneath powers the park's geysers, hot springs, mud pots and fumaroles. The park lies mostly in northwestern Wyoming, with slivers in Montana and Idaho, just north of Grand Teton National Park.

**Grand Prismatic Spring and Morning Glory Pool**
Grand Prismatic Spring is the largest hot spring in the United States. Its rainbow colors come from mats of heat-loving (thermophilic) bacteria that grow in rings by water temperature. Morning Glory Pool is a hot spring tinted blue and yellow by bacteria. Visitors throwing in debris have cooled it and changed its colors.

**First national park (1872)**
President Ulysses S. Grant signed the Yellowstone National Park Protection Act in 1872, making it the first national park in the US and widely considered the first in the world. It is also a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

**Wolf reintroduction (1995)**
Gray wolves, wiped out in the park by the 1920s, were reintroduced in 1995–96, a landmark case of restoring an apex predator and its effects across the ecosystem. Packs such as the Druid Peak pack in the Lamar Valley, near Druid Peak in the Absaroka Range, became famous with wildlife watchers.

**Thomas Moran and William Henry Jackson**
The painter Thomas Moran and the photographer William Henry Jackson went with Ferdinand Hayden's 1871 geological survey of the region. Their images helped persuade Congress to protect the area as a park.

**Washburn Expedition and Truman Everts**
The 1870 Washburn–Langford–Doane Expedition, which included Nathaniel Pitt Langford, explored the area and named Old Faithful. Expedition member Truman Everts was separated from the group and survived alone in the wilderness, later telling the story in "Thirty-Seven Days of Peril."

**Steamboat Geyser and Norris Geyser Basin**
Steamboat Geyser, in the Norris Geyser Basin, is the world's tallest active geyser, though its eruptions are irregular. The colorful mud pots and hot springs of Artist Paintpots lie just south of Norris.

**Obsidian Cliff**
A cliff of volcanic glass about 200 feet tall, beside the Grand Loop road between Mammoth Hot Springs and Norris. For thousands of years Native Americans quarried its obsidian to make tools, and they traded it across North America.

**Northern Pacific Railway "Wonderland"**
The Northern Pacific Railway promoted the park to tourists as "Wonderland," including in a pamphlet called "Alice's Adventures in the New Wonderland." It brought visitors to a station at Livingston, Montana, from which they toured sites such as West Thumb.

**Robert Reamer and the Old Faithful Inn**
The architect Robert C. Reamer designed the Old Faithful Inn, a rustic log lodge with a steep shingled roof that was finished in 1904. He also designed the Canyon Hotel and the Roosevelt Arch at the park's north entrance.

**"Zone of Death"**
The roughly 50-square-mile strip of the park that lies in Idaho. In his paper "The Perfect Crime," law professor Brian Kalt argued that the constitutional rules on jury districts could make it impossible to prosecute a crime committed there.

**Nez Perce flight (1877)**
While fleeing the US Army in 1877, Chief Joseph's Nez Perce passed through the newly created park in about two weeks, encountering tourists along the way.

**Yellowstone River and its Grand Canyon**
The Yellowstone River is the longest undammed river in the contiguous United States. Inside the park it cuts the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone, with its Upper and Lower Falls. The 1869 Cook–Folsom–Peterson Expedition was among the first to explore and describe it.

**Yellowstone bison**
Yellowstone is the only place in the US where wild bison have lived continuously since prehistoric times. Its herd survived the near-extinction of the species in the 19th century.

**Mungo Park**
A Scottish explorer who was the first modern European to reach the interior Niger, in 1796. He mapped much of its course and died on the river at the Bussa rapids in 1806 during his second expedition.

**Inner (Inland) Niger Delta**
A huge wetland in central Mali, roughly the size of Belgium, where the river spreads into lakes, channels and floodplains. The river loses about two-thirds of its potential flow here to evaporation and seepage, starting near the city of Ségou.

**Bani River**
The Niger's main tributary in Mali. It joins the Niger at the city of Mopti, at the edge of the Inner Delta, but does not make up for the water lost there.

**Namesake of Niger and Nigeria**
The river gives its name to two countries: Niger, with capital Niamey, and Nigeria, with capital Abuja. This is the usual giveaway.

**Timbuktu, Djenné and Bamako**
Major cities along the river's course in Mali. Timbuktu and Djenné were great centers of trade and Islamic learning (both famous for mud-brick architecture), and Bamako is Mali's capital.

**Fouta Djallon highlands**
The highlands of Guinea where the Niger rises, at Tembakounda, only about 240 km from the Atlantic. The river first flows inland, northeast toward the Sahara, before turning back toward the sea.

**Boomerang shape**
The river's strange arc, flowing northeast toward the desert and then southeast to the Gulf of Guinea, puzzled European geographers for centuries. Some, including the traveler Ibn Battuta, thought it was connected to the Nile.

**Oil Rivers**
The name for the Niger Delta region of Nigeria, originally because of the palm oil trade and now home to Nigeria's petroleum industry. Over thirty million people live in the delta, which opens onto the Gulf of Guinea near the Bight of Bonny.

**Joliba**
The Niger's name in the language of the Mandinka people, meaning roughly "great river."

**Lake Debo**
A wide, lake-like section of the river in the Inner Delta in central Mali, the same country as Djenné. Settlements with mud houses sit on islands in the lake.

**Benue River**
The Niger's largest tributary, which joins it at the Nigerian city of Lokoja. It is a common tributary clue along with the Bani.

**Massina Empire and Hamdullahi**
A 19th-century Fulani Islamic state founded by Seku Amadu in the Inner Delta. Its capital was Hamdullahi, near Mopti.

**Mali and Songhai Empires**
Medieval West African empires centered on the Niger, which carried trade and linked cities like Timbuktu and Gao.

**Pinasses**
Long wooden boats, now often motorized, that carry people and cargo between river ports in Mali such as Koriomé, the port of Timbuktu.

**The Cruelest Journey**
A 2004 account by Kira Salak of her solo kayak trip down the Niger to Timbuktu, retracing part of Mungo Park's route.

**Santa Fe and Albuquerque**
Santa Fe is New Mexico's capital and the oldest state capital in the United States, founded by the Spanish around 1610; it was also the western end of the 19th-century Santa Fe Trail. Albuquerque is the state's largest city, and the pair appears in nearly every giveaway.

**Trinity test and White Sands**
The Trinity test of July 16, 1945, the first detonation of a nuclear weapon, took place in what is now the White Sands Missile Range near Alamogordo. The Army took over the nearby McDonald Ranch House, where the bomb's plutonium core was assembled. White Sands National Park, a field of white gypsum dunes, lies within the area.

**Los Alamos National Laboratory**
The lab in northern New Mexico where the Manhattan Project designed the first atomic bombs under J. Robert Oppenheimer. The nearby Bandelier National Monument preserves Ancestral Pueblo cliff dwellings, and the town has been threatened by major wildfires. Albuquerque's minor-league baseball team, the Isotopes, is named for this nuclear history.

**Taos art colony**
An artists' colony that grew up in the early 20th century at Taos, whose painters depicted Native American pueblo life. Taos Pueblo, the northernmost of New Mexico's pueblos and home to the Tiwa-speaking people, is a centuries-old multistory adobe complex. Mary Austin and photographer Ansel Adams published the 1930 photobook Taos Pueblo.

**Carlsbad Caverns National Park**
A national park in the Guadalupe Mountains of southeastern New Mexico, famous for its limestone caves. Its "Big Room" is one of the largest cave chambers in North America. The park also contains Lechuguilla Cave, which has sections with names like "Chocolate High."

**Roswell**
A city on the Pecos River in southeastern New Mexico, known for the 1947 "Roswell incident," a crash that UFO conspiracy theorists claim involved an alien spacecraft.

**Zia sun symbol flag**
New Mexico's flag shows a red sun symbol of the Zia Pueblo people on a field of yellow (gold). The symbol is a circle with four groups of rays pointing in the four directions.

**Wheeler Peak and the Sangre de Cristo Mountains**
Wheeler Peak is New Mexico's highest point. It sits in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, the southernmost range of the Rocky Mountains, which end at Glorieta Pass near Santa Fe. Raton Pass on the Colorado border crosses the same region.

**Chaco Canyon and El Morro**
Chaco Culture National Historical Park preserves the large "great houses" of the Ancestral Puebloans in northwestern New Mexico. El Morro National Monument in the Zuni Mountains is a sandstone bluff covered in inscriptions left by travelers. Both are on the Trail of the Ancients Scenic Byway, and the nearby Aztec Ruins National Monument is misnamed, since it was built by Puebloans, not Aztecs.

**Pecos River and Rio Grande**
The Pecos River starts in northern New Mexico and flows south through Roswell into Texas. The Rio Grande flows south through the state, cutting the Rio Grande Gorge near Taos and passing Albuquerque, and then forms the border with Texas and Mexico at El Paso.

**Zuni, Acoma, and the Seven Cities of Cibola**
The Zuni have their reservation mainly in New Mexico. Their settlement of Hawikuh was mistaken by Coronado's 1540 expedition for one of the legendary golden Seven Cities of Cibola. Hernando de Alvarado, one of Coronado's officers, was likely the first European to reach the Acoma Pueblo ("Sky City").

**Llano Estacado**
The "Staked Plains," a huge, flat mesa that New Mexico shares with the Texas Panhandle; New Mexico holds its western part. The Mescalero Ridge (Caprock) is its western escarpment.

**Death Comes for the Archbishop and Saint Francis Cathedral**
Willa Cather's 1927 novel is a fictional version of Archbishop Jean-Baptiste Lamy, who built the Cathedral Basilica of St. Francis of Assisi in Santa Fe. Also in northern New Mexico is El Santuario de Chimayó, a pilgrimage church whose soil is believed to heal.

**Georgia O'Keeffe and Ghost Ranch**
The modernist painter moved permanently to New Mexico after her husband, photographer Alfred Stieglitz, died in 1946. She lived at Ghost Ranch and Abiquiú and painted the region's desert landscapes and bones.

**Albuquerque International Balloon Fiesta and Sandia Peak Tramway**
Albuquerque hosts the world's largest hot-air balloon festival each October. The Sandia Peak Tramway carries visitors from the city to the top of the Sandia Mountains and is one of the longest aerial trams in the Americas.

**Everglades ("River of Grass")**
A vast, slow-moving sawgrass wetland in southern Florida, protected in part by Everglades National Park, the largest national park in the state. It is home to crocodiles, alligators, manatees, and mangroves, and it is threatened by invasive species such as the Burmese python and the melaleuca tree. Marjory Stoneman Douglas made the phrase "River of Grass" famous in her 1947 book on the region.

**Lake Okeechobee**
Florida's largest lake and the largest freshwater lake entirely within the state. It is fed mainly by the Kissimmee River and Taylor Creek, and its water historically spilled south into the Everglades.

**Kissimmee River**
A river in central Florida that flows south from near Orlando into Lake Okeechobee. It forms the northern headwaters of the Everglades system.

**Britton Hill**
Florida's highest natural point, at only 345 feet, in the Panhandle near the Alabama border. It is the lowest state high point in the United States.

**Big Cypress National Preserve and the Ten Thousand Islands**
Big Cypress is a swampy preserve in Collier County just north of Everglades National Park, crossed by the Tamiami Trail. The Ten Thousand Islands are a maze of mangrove islets off Florida's southwestern coast.

**St. Johns River**
Florida's longest river, which unusually flows north through northeastern Florida before reaching the Atlantic at Jacksonville. Blount Island lies on it and has the southernmost American shad run.

**Dry Tortugas National Park and Fort Jefferson**
A remote group of islands about 70 miles west of Key West. It contains Fort Jefferson, a 19th-century fort that is the largest masonry structure in the Western Hemisphere.

**Cape Canaveral and Kennedy Space Center**
Located on Florida's Atlantic coast, these are the main launch sites of the American space program. Kennedy Space Center is on Merritt Island, just northwest of Cape Canaveral.

**St. Augustine**
Founded by the Spanish in 1565, it is the oldest continuously inhabited European settlement in the continental United States. Nearby Fort Caroline National Memorial marks a French Huguenot colony led by Jean Ribault that the Spanish destroyed in 1565.

**Florida Keys (Key Largo, Key West, Seven Mile Bridge)**
A chain of coral islands curving southwest from Florida's southern tip, connected by the Overseas Highway and its Seven Mile Bridge. They are home to the endangered Key deer and the American crocodile, and Ernest Hemingway's former home in Key West is known for its six-toed (polydactyl) cats.

**Biscayne Bay**
A shallow lagoon on Florida's southeastern coast, between Miami and the barrier islands. The southern part of the bay is protected as Biscayne National Park, and Miami lies on a plain between the bay and the Everglades.

**Jacksonville**
Florida's most populous city and, by land area, the largest city in the contiguous United States at about 875 square miles. It lies on the St. Johns River, and its Riverplace Tower was once the tallest concrete building in the world.

**Miami and Orlando**
Miami, in Miami-Dade County, is famous for its Little Havana Cuban-American neighborhood and its Calle Ocho festival. Orlando in central Florida is home to Walt Disney World and Epcot, and Disney also developed the nearby planned town of Celebration in Osceola County.

**Tallahassee**
The capital of Florida, located in the northern Panhandle.

**Pensacola, the "City of Five Flags"**
A Panhandle city on the Gulf Coast nicknamed for the five governments that have ruled it: Spain, France, Britain, the Confederacy, and the United States.

**Border between Texas and Mexico**
The Rio Grande forms the international boundary between Texas and Mexico for about 1,900 km, from El Paso to the Gulf of Mexico. This is the standard giveaway.

**El Paso and Ciudad Juárez**
Twin cities facing each other across the river, one of the busiest border crossing points between the United States and Mexico.

**Laredo and Nuevo Laredo**
Twin border cities on the river in south Texas and Tamaulipas, connected by major international trade bridges.

**Matamoros and Brownsville**
Twin cities near the river's mouth on the Gulf of Mexico. Matamoros is on the Mexican side and Brownsville on the Texas side. South Padre Island lies just north of the mouth.

**Big Bend National Park**
A Texas national park named for the large bend the river makes along the border. It contains the Chisos Mountains.

**Río Bravo**
The river's name in Mexico, in full Río Bravo del Norte ("wild river of the north"). "Rio Grande" is Spanish for "big river."

**San Juan Mountains**
The range in southwestern Colorado where the river rises. From there it flows south through New Mexico, passing Albuquerque.

**Elephant Butte Reservoir and Truth or Consequences**
A large reservoir on the river in New Mexico, just north of the town of Truth or Consequences. The town renamed itself in 1950 after the radio quiz show Truth or Consequences.

**Chamizal dispute**
A border dispute between the U.S. and Mexico caused by the river shifting its course near El Paso, which moved a tract of land called El Chamizal. It was settled by the Chamizal Convention of 1963, which returned most of the land to Mexico.

**Pecos and Conchos Rivers**
Major tributaries of the Rio Grande. The Pecos joins from Texas, and the Río Conchos joins from the Mexican state of Chihuahua, providing much of the lower river's water.

**Falcon International Reservoir**
A reservoir on the border between Texas and Tamaulipas, formed by Falcon Dam. The Rio Grande is its main inflow.

**Bagdad, Tamaulipas**
A now-vanished port at the river's mouth on the Mexican side. It boomed during the American Civil War as an outlet for Confederate cotton that got around the Union blockade, and it was later destroyed by hurricanes.

**Rio Grande do Norte and Rio Grande do Sul**
Two Brazilian states whose names begin with "Rio Grande." They are named for different rivers, not this one, but they appear as wordplay lead-ins.

**Jakarta and the planned capital in East Kalimantan**
Jakarta, on the northwest coast of Java, is Indonesia's capital and largest city, and it is the giveaway in nearly every question. Because Jakarta is sinking and badly overcrowded, President Joko Widodo (Jokowi) began moving the capital to a new planned city, Nusantara, in the province of East Kalimantan on Borneo.

**Java and the Sunda Strait**
Java is the most populous island on Earth and Indonesia's political and economic heart. Besides Jakarta, it contains the major cities of Surabaya and Bandung. The Sunda Strait separates Java from Sumatra, and the two are the country's most populous islands.

**Sumatra and the Strait of Malacca**
The large western island where the cities of Medan and Palembang and the Barisan Mountains are located. The Strait of Malacca, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, separates it from the Malay Peninsula and Malaysia. Sumatra's northern tip is Aceh province, where a long separatist insurgency ended with a peace deal in 2005, after the 2004 tsunami.

**Lake Toba**
A huge crater lake in northern Sumatra, in the homeland of the Batak people. It formed from the Toba supereruption about 74,000–75,000 years ago, one of the largest known volcanic eruptions. Some scientists think the eruption caused a years-long volcanic winter.

**Kalimantan (Borneo)**
Kalimantan is the Indonesian part of Borneo, an island Indonesia shares with Malaysia and Brunei. It holds Indonesia's largest rivers, the Kapuas, Mahakam, and Barito. The Kapuas rises in the Müller Mountains and flows to the South China Sea near the city of Pontianak in West Kalimantan.

**Sulawesi and the Makassar Strait**
Sulawesi (formerly Celebes) is an oddly shaped island made up mostly of four long peninsulas. The Makassar Strait separates it from Borneo to the west.

**Wallace Line**
A boundary between Asian and Australasian animal life, drawn by the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace. It runs through Indonesia between Borneo and Sulawesi and between Bali and Lombok, so species to the west are mostly Asian and those to the east are more Australian.

**Puncak Jaya and Papua (New Guinea)**
Puncak Jaya (Carstensz Pyramid), about 4,884 m, is Indonesia's highest mountain and the tallest island peak in the world. It is in the Papua region on the western half of New Guinea, which Indonesia shares with Papua New Guinea. The Doberai (Bird's Head) Peninsula is at New Guinea's western end.

**Krakatoa and Tambora**
Two famous Indonesian volcanoes. Tambora, on the island of Sumbawa, erupted in 1815 in the largest eruption in recorded history, which caused the "Year Without a Summer" (1816). Krakatoa, in the Sunda Strait, erupted catastrophically in 1883.

**Babirusa and anoa**
Animals found only in parts of Indonesia, especially Sulawesi. The babirusa is a "pig-deer" whose upper tusks grow up through the top of its snout and curve back toward its face. The anoa is a small forest buffalo.

**Java Man (Homo erectus)**
In 1891 the Dutch anatomist Eugène Dubois found a skullcap at Trinil on Java's Solo River. He named it Pithecanthropus erectus, and the fossil, called "Java Man," is now the type specimen of Homo erectus.

**Homo floresiensis ("the Hobbit")**
A small hominin species, under four feet tall as an adult, discovered in 2003 in Liang Bua cave on the island of Flores. The Indonesian anthropologist Teuku Jacob controversially took the bones and damaged them while arguing that they belonged to small modern humans, not a new species.

**Gamelan and wayang**
Gamelan is Indonesia's traditional percussion ensemble of gongs and metallophones, tuned to the slendro and pelog scale systems. It accompanies wayang, the shadow-puppet theater, in which a puppeteer called the dalang moves the puppets with rods.

**Batik and the Saman dance**
Batik is a wax-resist method of dyeing cloth in which hot wax is applied with a small spouted tool called a canting. The Saman is a dance of the Gayo people of Aceh, in which performers sit in a line and clap and move in rapid unison.

**Maluku Islands and the Banda Sea**
The Maluku Islands (Moluccas), the historic "Spice Islands" east of Sulawesi, were once the world's only source of cloves and nutmeg. The Banda Sea lies among them.

**Uluru (Ayers Rock) and Kata Tjuta (the Olgas)**
Uluru is a huge sandstone monolith in the Outback of the Northern Territory that glows red at sunset and is sacred to the local Aboriginal Anangu people. Kata Tjuta, a group of dome-shaped rock formations also called the Olgas, rises just to its west in the same national park, and Alice Springs is the nearest large town.

**Tasmania and the Bass Strait**
Tasmania is the island state south of the mainland, separated from Victoria by the Bass Strait and formerly called Van Diemen's Land. It is home to the Tasmanian devil, a carnivorous marsupial endangered by Devil Facial Tumor Disease (DFTD), and was the last stronghold of the thylacine, or "Tasmanian tiger," which went extinct in the 20th century.

**Great Barrier Reef**
The world's largest coral reef system, lying in the Coral Sea off the coast of Queensland near the city of Cairns. It is threatened by coral bleaching and other damage.

**Great Dividing Range and Mount Kosciuszko**
The long mountain chain running down Australia's east coast. It contains Mount Kosciuszko, the country's highest peak, the Blue Mountains, named for the blue haze given off by eucalyptus trees, and the Grampians at its southern end in Victoria.

**Sydney Opera House and Sydney Harbour Bridge**
Sydney, the capital of New South Wales and Australia's largest city, is known for its Opera House, whose white shell-shaped roofs look like sails. The nearby steel arch Harbour Bridge is nicknamed "the Coathanger," and Circular Quay is the harbor's ferry hub.

**Platypus and monotremes**
The duck-billed platypus is one of the few egg-laying mammals, or monotremes; it hunts using electroreception in its bill, and males deliver venom through spurs on their hind legs. Australia is also home to most of the world's marsupials, including kangaroos and koalas.

**Coober Pedy and Lake Eyre**
Coober Pedy is a South Australian town known as the opal capital of the world, where many residents live in underground homes called dugouts to escape the heat. Nearby Lake Eyre (Kati Thanda) is Australia's largest lake and lowest point, and is usually a dry salt flat.

**Rabbit-proof fence and dingo fence**
In the early 1900s, Western Australia built a series of very long fences, one ending near Broome, to stop the spread of invasive rabbits. A separate dingo fence, one of the longest structures in the world, was built in the east to keep wild dingoes away from sheep.

**Emu War**
In 1932, soldiers armed with machine guns were sent to the Campion district of Western Australia to kill emus that were damaging crops. The large flightless birds largely outlasted the campaign.

**Murray-Darling Basin and Great Artesian Basin**
The Murray and Darling Rivers of the southeast form Australia's largest river system, whose basin covers about one-seventh of the country. The Great Artesian Basin, covering about one-fifth of the country, is one of the largest underground freshwater reservoirs in the world and a key water source for the dry interior.

**Canberra and Walter Burley Griffin**
Australia's capital is a planned city designed by American architect Walter Burley Griffin, built around an artificial lake and a Parliamentary Triangle of government buildings. Questions often contrast it with the larger cities of Sydney, Melbourne, Perth, and Adelaide.

**Torres Strait Islanders and Aboriginal peoples**
Australia's two groups of Indigenous peoples. The Torres Strait separates the Cape York Peninsula of Queensland from Papua New Guinea to the north, and its islanders have their own distinct culture.

**Nullarbor Plain**
A huge, flat, almost treeless limestone plain along the south coast, often called the world's largest single piece of limestone. Its name comes from Latin for "no tree."

**Christmas Island and Norfolk Island**
External territories of Australia. Christmas Island in the Indian Ocean is famous for the yearly migration of millions of red crabs and as a destination for asylum seekers arriving by boat, while many people on Norfolk Island in the Pacific descend from the mutineers of HMS Bounty.

**Kimberley region and the Hamersley Range**
The Kimberley is a rugged region in northern Western Australia whose largest town is Broome, bordered by the Tanami and Great Sandy Deserts. The Hamersley Range in the Pilbara to the south is the center of Australia's huge iron ore mining industry.

**Arches National Park (Delicate Arch)**
A park near the town of Moab with over 2,000 natural sandstone arches. The famous Delicate Arch is a freestanding arch that appears on Utah license plates. The Devils Garden area holds the long, thin Landscape Arch, and other features include the maze-like Fiery Furnace and rock towers such as the Three Gossips and The Organ.

**Bryce Canyon National Park (hoodoos)**
A park in southern Utah with the world's largest concentration of hoodoos, the tall, thin spires of eroded rock. The Queens Garden Trail and the Navajo Loop pass formations such as Thor's Hammer.

**Zion National Park**
Utah's oldest and most-visited national park, near the Arizona border. Hikers wade up the Virgin River through the slot canyon called the Narrows and climb the steep fin of Angels Landing. The park also includes the Kolob Canyons section, and the Zion–Mount Carmel Tunnel leads into its main canyon.

**Great Salt Lake**
The largest saltwater lake in the Western Hemisphere, a remnant of the prehistoric Lake Bonneville, fed by the Bear, Weber and Jordan Rivers. It contains Antelope Island and Gunnison Island, and arms such as Willard Bay. The Lucin Cutoff railroad causeway splits it, leaving the saltier north arm pinkish from salt-loving microbes. Lake-effect snow from it is credited for the state's "Greatest Snow on Earth" slogan.

**Bonneville Salt Flats**
A vast, flat crust of salt west of the Great Salt Lake, left on the dried bed of Lake Bonneville. Its hard, level surface has hosted many world land-speed records.

**Salt Lake City and Temple Square**
The capital, founded in 1847 by Mormon pioneers led by Brigham Young, who proposed a state called "Deseret." Called Great Salt Lake City until 1868, it is home to Temple Square, the headquarters of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, where a statue of the angel Moroni tops the Salt Lake Temple. The Seagull Monument honors the gulls said to have saved settlers' crops from a cricket swarm in 1848. The beehive is Utah's emblem, and since 2024 it has appeared on the state flag. The first KFC franchise also opened in the Salt Lake area in 1952.

**Canyonlands National Park**
A park of canyons and mesas near Moab, divided into districts including Island in the Sky, the Needles, the Maze, and the rivers themselves. The Colorado River, Utah's largest, flows past Moab and meets the Green River inside the park. Utah is the northwestern state of the Four Corners region.

**Capitol Reef National Park (Waterpocket Fold)**
A park built around the Waterpocket Fold, a nearly 100-mile monocline (a "wrinkle in the Earth") in south-central Utah. Its features include the Golden Throne and white sandstone domes that early settlers compared to capitol buildings.

**Pando**
A clonal colony of quaking aspen in Fishlake National Forest. All its trunks share one root system, making it one of the heaviest known organisms on Earth.

**Wasatch Range and Wasatch Front**
The mountain range east of Salt Lake City. The Wasatch Front is the narrow urban corridor below it, running roughly from Ogden in the north to Provo in the south. Its ski resorts, such as Snowbasin and Solitude, inspired license plates reading "Greatest Snow on Earth" and later "Life Elevated."

**Park City and the Sundance Film Festival**
A ski town in the Wasatch Mountains that hosted the Sundance Film Festival, founded with Robert Redford's backing, for decades. It is also home to the US Ski Team.

**2002 Winter Olympics**
Salt Lake City hosted the 2002 Winter Olympics, with the opening and closing ceremonies at the University of Utah's Rice-Eccles Stadium.

**Spiral Jetty and Promontory Summit**
Robert Smithson's 1970 earthwork Spiral Jetty is a huge coil of basalt rock, often crusted white and pink with salt, jutting into the north arm of the Great Salt Lake. North of the lake at Promontory Summit, the Golden Spike was driven in 1869 to complete the first Transcontinental Railroad.

**Dixie and Grand Staircase–Escalante**
Southwestern Utah around St. George in Washington County is called "Dixie" because early Mormon settlers tried to grow cotton there. The region includes the Hurricane Cliffs and Dixie National Forest. Next to it is the vast Grand Staircase–Escalante National Monument, a series of cliff terraces stepping up toward Bryce Canyon.

**Kings Peak and the Uinta Mountains**
Utah's highest point, Kings Peak, is in the east–west Uinta Mountains in the northeast. The region also includes the southern part of Flaming Gorge Reservoir, the western part of Dinosaur National Monument, and the Uintah and Ouray Indian Reservation of the Ute people.

**Three Gorges Dam**
The world's largest dam and largest hydroelectric power station, built across the Yangtze in Hubei province. Its reservoir displaced well over a million people. Because the dam holds back so much water, scientists have calculated that it very slightly slows Earth's rotation and lengthens the day.

**Baiji (Lipotes vexillifer)**
The Yangtze River dolphin, a freshwater dolphin found only in the Yangtze. It was declared functionally extinct after a 2006 survey, making it the first dolphin species driven to extinction by humans. Qiqi, a captive male who died in 2002, is the best-known individual.

**Shanghai and the East China Sea**
The Yangtze empties into the East China Sea near Shanghai. The Huangpu River, which flows through central Shanghai, joins the Yangtze just before its mouth.

**Chang Jiang, the longest river in China and Asia**
The Chinese name for the Yangtze is Chang Jiang ("Long River"). At about 6,300 km it is the longest river in Asia and the third longest in the world, and it flows south of China's other great river, the Yellow River (Huang He).

**Geladaindong Peak and the Tanggula Mountains**
The Yangtze's traditional source is a glacier on Geladaindong in the Tanggula (Dangla) Mountains of Qinghai province, on the Tibetan Plateau. Later surveys proposed sources farther away, such as Jari Hill.

**Grand Canal**
The ancient artificial waterway linking Beijing and Hangzhou. It crosses and connects the Yangtze with the Yellow River to the north and was a key route for carrying grain north.

**Jinsha River, Tiger Leaping Gorge, and the Three Parallel Rivers**
The Jinsha ("Golden Sands") River is the name for the Yangtze's upper course. In Yunnan it is the easternmost of the Three Parallel Rivers (with the Mekong and Salween), makes a sharp hairpin turn at Shigu, and cuts through the deep Tiger Leaping Gorge. It is joined by the Min River at Yibin, after which it is called the Yangtze.

**Dongting Lake and Poyang Lake**
Two large lakes connected to the middle Yangtze. Dongting Lake in Hunan absorbs floodwaters and helps moderate the river's floods, and Poyang Lake in Jiangxi, China's largest freshwater lake, drains into the Yangtze through an outflow channel.

**Wuhan, Chongqing, and Nanjing**
Major cities on the Yangtze. Chongqing sits where the Jialing River joins it, Wuhan sits where its largest tributary, the Han River, joins it, and Nanjing lies downstream in the delta region.

**1931 China floods**
Catastrophic floods along the Yangtze and other rivers in 1931, often called the deadliest natural disaster in recorded history. The river also had several other deadly floods in the early 20th century.

**Ash Dykes**
A Welsh explorer who in 2019 became the first person to walk the full length of the Yangtze, a trek of about a year.

**Chinese alligator and Dabry's sturgeon**
Endangered animals of the Yangtze basin. The Chinese alligator survives in the wild only in the river's lower reaches, and Dabry's sturgeon (the Yangtze sturgeon) has been declared extinct in the wild.

**Amethyst Incident**
In 1949, during the Chinese Civil War, the British warship HMS Amethyst was shelled by Communist forces and trapped on the Yangtze for about three months before escaping downriver.

**Battle of Red Cliffs**
A famous battle fought on the Yangtze in 208–209 CE, in which the allied forces of Liu Bei and Sun Quan defeated the much larger army of Cao Cao. It is a central episode in the novel "Romance of the Three Kingdoms."

**Gezhouba Dam**
An earlier dam on the Yangtze at Yichang in Hubei, downstream of the Three Gorges Dam. The river is also dammed on its upper course by projects such as the Xiluodu Dam.

**Strait of Gibraltar**
The narrow strait between Spain and Morocco that connects the Mediterranean to the Atlantic Ocean. It is the most common giveaway clue for the sea.

**Separates Europe and Africa**
The Mediterranean lies between southern Europe and North Africa, with the Levant to its east and Asia Minor (Anatolia) to its northeast. Its African port cities include Alexandria, Benghazi, Tripoli, and Tunis, and its coast forms the northern shores of Libya and Algeria.

**Zanclean flood and the Messinian salinity crisis**
About 6 to 5.3 million years ago, the closure of Atlantic connections such as the Betic Corridor cut the Mediterranean off, and it largely evaporated, leaving thick salt deposits (the Messinian salinity crisis). The Zanclean flood, when Atlantic water poured in through the Strait of Gibraltar, refilled it about 5.33 million years ago.

**Calypso Deep**
The deepest point of the Mediterranean, roughly 5,100 meters deep, in the Hellenic Trench of the Ionian Sea southwest of Pylos, Greece.

**Dardanelles, Sea of Marmara, and Bosporus**
The Turkish straits connecting the Mediterranean (via the Aegean) to the Black Sea. The Dardanelles leads into the Sea of Marmara, and the Bosporus links Marmara to the Black Sea; Cape Helles and Kum Kale mark the Dardanelles' entrance.

**Adriatic and Aegean Seas**
Major arms of the Mediterranean. The Adriatic lies between Italy and the Balkans and receives the Po River near Venice, while the Aegean lies between Greece and Turkey and contains the Cyclades and Santorini.

**Major islands: Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica, Cyprus, and Crete**
The Mediterranean's largest islands. Sicily is the biggest; the Strait of Bonifacio separates Corsica from Sardinia; and Cyprus, with its capital at Nicosia, is an island nation in the eastern part of the sea.

**Balearic Islands**
A Spanish autonomous archipelago in the western Mediterranean, including Majorca, Minorca, and Ibiza, with its capital at Palma.

**Ebro and Rhône rivers**
Major rivers flowing into the western Mediterranean from Spain and France. Dams on the Ebro and other rivers have reduced freshwater inflow, contributing to rising salinity.

**Mistral and sirocco**
Characteristic Mediterranean winds. The mistral is a cold, dry northerly wind blowing down the Rhône valley, while the sirocco is a hot wind from the Sahara; together with summer heat they drive high evaporation.

**Lighthouse of Alexandria (Pharos)**
One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, a lighthouse that stood on the island of Pharos off Alexandria, Egypt. Its ruins lie on the seafloor of the harbor.

**Alboran and Tyrrhenian Seas**
Sub-seas of the Mediterranean. The Alboran Sea is its westernmost part, just east of the Strait of Gibraltar, and the Tyrrhenian Sea west of Italy contains the volcanic Aeolian Islands.

**"Great Sea" and "Mare Nostrum"**
Ancient names for the Mediterranean. The Romans called it Mare Nostrum ("Our Sea"), and the Hebrew Bible calls it the "Great Sea."

**Barbary Coast and Rif Mountains**
The Barbary Coast was the North African coastline of Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Libya, notorious for corsairs, and the Rif Mountains of northern Morocco rise along the sea's southwestern shore.

**Barcelona Convention and Bouri oil field**
The Barcelona Convention (1976) is the treaty among Mediterranean states for protecting the sea from pollution. The Bouri field, offshore from Libya, is the largest producing oil field in the Mediterranean.

**Minneapolis and St. Paul (the Twin Cities)**
St. Paul is Minnesota's capital, and Minneapolis is its largest city; together they form the Twin Cities metropolitan area on the Mississippi River, where most of the state's population lives. This is the standard giveaway.

**Lake Itasca**
A lake in north-central Minnesota recognized as the source of the Mississippi River. Visitors at Itasca State Park can wade across the river's tiny headwaters.

**Duluth**
A port city at the western tip of Lake Superior, near the Wisconsin border. It is a major shipping point for iron ore from the nearby iron ranges.

**Mesabi Range**
The largest iron ore range in the state, in the northeastern Arrowhead region. Its high-grade ore has run out, but low-grade taconite is still mined here, around towns such as Hibbing; the older Vermilion and Cuyuna Ranges are no longer active.

**Northwest Angle**
A piece of Minnesota north of the 49th parallel, cut off from the rest of the state by the Lake of the Woods, resulting from an error in early border treaties. It is the only part of the contiguous United States north of the 49th parallel and contains the site of the French Fort Saint Charles.

**"Land of 10,000 Lakes"**
Minnesota's nickname, referring to its many glacial lakes (it actually has more than 11,000 lakes of at least 10 acres).

**St. Anthony Falls**
The only major natural waterfall on the Mississippi River, located in Minneapolis. It powered the flour mills that made Minneapolis a major milling city.

**Voyageurs National Park**
Minnesota's only national park, centered on the Kabetogama Peninsula near the Canadian border. It is named after the French-Canadian fur traders (voyageurs) who traveled its waterways by canoe, and it lies west of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness.

**Mall of America**
One of the largest shopping malls in the United States, located in the Minneapolis suburb of Bloomington. Bloomington also submitted a bid to host the 2027 World's Fair.

**Fort Snelling**
A historic fort at the confluence of the Mississippi and Minnesota Rivers. During World War II it housed the Military Intelligence Service Language School, which trained soldiers in Japanese.

**Bde Maka Ska**
A lake in Minneapolis formerly named Lake Calhoun, after pro-slavery politician John C. Calhoun. It was renamed with its Dakota name, a change confirmed in 2020 after a court challenge.

**Eagle Mountain**
Minnesota's highest point, located in Cook County in the Arrowhead region. Minnesota's Cook County is not to be confused with Cook County, Illinois, home of Chicago.

**Somali community**
Minnesota, especially the Twin Cities, has the largest Somali population in the United States and one of the largest concentrations outside East Africa.

**Pipestone and Jeffers Petroglyphs**
Pipestone National Monument in southwest Minnesota preserves quarries of red pipestone (catlinite) used by Native Americans to carve sacred pipes. The nearby Jeffers Petroglyphs are ancient rock carvings on the same Red Rock Ridge.

**Minnehaha Falls and St. Urho's Day**
Minnehaha Falls is a waterfall in Minneapolis on Minnehaha Creek near its junction with the Mississippi. St. Urho's Day is a mock holiday honoring a fictional saint, invented in Minnesota and celebrated by Finnish Americans.

**Helena**
The capital of Montana, in the west-central part of the state. It began as a gold-rush town in the 1860s and is the giveaway at the end of almost every question.

**Glacier National Park and Going-to-the-Sun Road**
Montana's most famous national park, in the northern Rockies along the Canadian border. Going-to-the-Sun Road crosses the park over Logan Pass, passing Lake McDonald, Heavens Peak, and Saint Mary Lake. Stanley Kubrick filmed the opening shots of The Shining along Saint Mary Lake. With Canada's Waterton Lakes National Park, Glacier forms the Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park.

**Triple Divide Peak**
A mountain in Glacier National Park where the Continental (Great) Divide meets the Northern (Laurentian) Divide. Rain falling on it can drain to the Pacific Ocean, the Atlantic (through the Gulf of Mexico), or Hudson Bay and the Arctic.

**Butte, the Berkeley Pit, and Anaconda Copper**
Butte, in Silver Bow County, was a booming copper-mining city run by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was the home of the "Copper King" William A. Clark, whose mansion still stands there.
